The Detailed Exposition of the Vinaya (Vinayavibhaṅga)

Toh 3 in the Kangyur is the Vinaya Vibhaṅga, known in Tibetan as Dulwa Rnampar Jepa (འདུལ་བ་རྣམ་པར་འབྱེད་པ), meaning "The Detailed Exposition of the Vinaya." It is a foundational Vinaya text — one of the great disciplinary scriptures of the Buddhist canon — that provides a systematic, rule-by-rule analysis and explanation of monastic conduct, elaborating on the precepts governing the behavior of ordained monks and nuns. As its opening verse suggests, the text reveres the Buddha as the supreme lord of the Vinaya and situates the monastic code as the very root and cause of all Buddhist practice. Belonging to the Vinaya section of the Kangyur, it represents one of the most extensive and authoritative texts on monastic discipline preserved in the Tibetan canonical tradition.

In the language of India: Vinaya Vibhaṅga. In the Tibetan language: The Detailed Exposition of the Vinaya (Skt. vinaya-vibhaṅga). First fascicle.

Homage to the Three Jewels.

I pay homage to the Victor, born of noble royal lineage,
who tamed his disciples and thoroughly subdued all faults,
the buddha, foremost lord of the Vinaya.
Now I shall speak briefly in praise of the Vinaya.

The far shore unseen, the depths unfathomed,
the ocean of the Vinaya divided by the distinctions
drawn by the assemblies of masters wrapped in the dense darkness of ignorance —
I have not the strength or the wit to praise all its qualities.

Just as in this world there is a great root-tree,
which is the ground for both spreading and sustaining,
so too has it been said that the Vinaya
is the cause and root of all the assemblies of the sacred Dharma.

Just as the earth is the foundation of all living beings,
from which all grains grow and arise,
so too the Vinaya is the foundation of those who strive in the vows,
and from it likewise does all merit arise.

Moral discipline has been understood as the dwelling-place of all virtuous qualities,
and it has been said that the dwelling of moral discipline is the Vinaya.
If one abides in this, one will reach the final end;
if one does not abide in this, how could one ever reach it?

Just as a dam of solid stone that cannot be eroded
will turn back even a great river,
so too this noble dam of the Vinaya
will turn back the river of broken moral discipline.

The buddhas and the pratyekabuddhas,
the awakening they attained — the pure disciples of the Sage,
and sentient beings who are arhats endowed with qualities:
even for all of these, it has been said, the Vinaya was the cause.

As long as in this world the supreme treasury of all Victors,
this complete Vinaya, endures,
so long shall this lamp of the Dharma remain,
and if it is turned back, peace will be attained.

When a buddha no longer dwells, one resorts
to the worldly ślokas (metrical verses) and to such and such branches of the sūtras.
Without guidance into training, the Vinaya too would be no more.
Therefore the Victors have declared this to be most rare.

This is the iron hook for the unrestrained mind, like an elephant;
this is the bridle for those disciples who are yet untamed.
Like the embankment that marks the field's boundary,
the Vinaya is the dam that holds back every defilement.

The treatises of the Victor, the Teacher,
are said to be the sūtras and the Abhidharma; but the Vinaya
is both the Teacher himself and the treatise directly —
for this reason it becomes worthy of double veneration: as the Buddha and as the Dharma, both in one.

The buddhas who dwell in dependence upon it
regard it with reverence and honor it as their guru.
It is that which protects, serving as protector and as refuge.
Therefore strive earnestly and pay homage to the Vinaya.

Whoever grows careless toward the compassionate teaching of the Teacher
and allows even a little to pass by —
that one, through other forces of suffering, attains a state of misery,
as when a mango grove is ruined by the intrusion of a bamboo thicket.

Here there are those who recite even the great royal words,
yet if recited only a few times without continuity, no cessation of faults is attained.
If the scriptural teachings of the Sage are recited improperly,
one will go to the animal realm, like an eel's fin shaken by a nāga.

That by which individual liberation is to be attained,
the great ocean of the Vinaya of the buddhas —
bottomless and boundless —
is the very heart and essence of all that abides.

This is the supreme guide of all the phenomena
of the holy Dharma, the king of Dharma.
This is the great warehouse of training and the great marketplace
for the merchant-community of monks.

This is the medicine that clears the poison from those seized by broken moral discipline.
This is the iron hook for two-footed youth
who are confused and bewildered by their prime of life.

This is the means of crossing to liberation
from saṃsāra, which is deeper than the ocean.
This is the certain dam and bridge
for those who journey on to better realms.

This is the path that defeats the afflictions,
the supreme guide for the noble ones.
This is what stands like the first step of the stairway
by which one enters the city of liberation.

"When I have passed into nirvāṇa, this will be your Teacher" — with reverence, the Self-Arisen One himself solemnly praised it before the assembly of monks.

Since it is understood that this Vinaya is the very analysis of individual liberation, those who long for liberation should attend to it with reverence and diligence.

Here ends the Praise of the Vinaya.

Even across ten million eons, the chance to hear the Vinaya, to receive and hold it, is hard to find — and harder still to put it into practice.

The arising of buddhas is a blessing.
The teaching of the Dharma is a blessing.
The harmony of the Saṅgha is a blessing,
and the austerity of those in harmony is a blessing.

To see the noble ones is a blessing.
To keep company with the holy is a blessing.
If the childish are not encountered,
one dwells in perpetual ease.

To see one of moral discipline is a blessing.
To see one of great learning is a blessing.
To see an arhat who is fully freed
from renewed existence is a blessing.

A river easy to enter, with pleasant banks, is a blessing.
A person accustomed to the Dharma is a blessing.
One who has attained wisdom is a blessing.
One in whom pride and conceit are exhausted is a blessing.

Those who are resolute, with senses tamed,
who have grown old in tranquil hermitages,
and those of great learning who dwell in forest groves
once the flush of youth has passed — their dwelling is a blessing.

To the Lion of the Śākyas, pressing palms together with ten fingers,
I have set forth the Vinaya with full emphasis:
listen to me for the sake of those to be tamed.

Having heard it, practice exactly as the great sage has declared,
and toward even the subtler faults, be careful and conscientious.

The mind-horse, which even with constant effort is hard to rein in,
is broken by this Vinaya — the sharp hundred-pointed goad of harmony.

Those great ones who turn back and do not cross the boundary at a mere word of rebuke: they are fine human horses, and they will pass surely through the battle with the afflictions.

Those who lack this goad and never come to desire it will be roiled by the battle of the afflictions and will wander without rest, scattered and lost.

For twelve years the śrāvaka Saṅgha of the Blessed One was without fault and without blemish. Then the Blessed One summarized the sūtra of individual liberation for the śrāvakas in brief:

Do not commit any evil.
Accomplish virtue in full abundance.
Tame your own mind completely.
This is the teaching of the buddhas.

Restraint of body is good.
Restraint of speech is good.
Restraint of mind is good.
Restraint in all things is good.
The monk who is restrained in all things
is fully freed from every suffering.

Guarding speech, and with the mind fully restrained,
not committing any non-virtue of body,
having purified these three paths of action,
one attains the path proclaimed by the great sage.

Thus he taught.

When the thirteenth year arrived, the Blessed One, the buddha, was residing in the Kalandaka village in the land of the Śroṇas. At that time in Kalandaka village there lived a certain son of Kalandaka named Supriya, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and extensive property, and whose holdings were broad and vast, with wealth rivaling that of Vaiśravaṇa and comparable to Vaiśravaṇa in riches. He had taken a wife from his own social rank and delighted in sporting with her, enjoying her company and living in pleasure with her.

Then at another time he came to have full confidence in the buddha, full confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He went for refuge to the buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He abandoned the taking of life and turned back from taking life. He abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the heedless states induced by fermented grain-liquor and prepared intoxicants, and turned back from those heedless states induced by fermented grain-liquor and prepared intoxicants.

He continued to foster that same faith as before, and then, having shaved off his hair and beard, he put on ochre-colored robes and, in genuine faith, went forth from home into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, he still lived mixing and staying together with relatives, just as he had done when he was a householder.

Then the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, thought to himself: "Having gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and discipline, I am still living and mixing together with relatives just as I did when I was a householder. I have not found what is to be found, and what I have found is not good — rather, I have found fault and not found the good. Let me part from my relatives, take up my bowl and robes, and go wandering from region to region."

And so the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, parted from his relatives, took up his bowl and robes, and went wandering from region to region. At that time there was a harsh and grievous famine, such that wandering mendicants found it difficult to obtain food, and even parents found it hard to give food to their own children and to do what was needed for them — let alone for wandering mendicants, of whom nothing need be said.

Then the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, thought to himself: "Right now there is this harsh and grievous famine, wandering mendicants find it difficult to obtain food, and even parents find it hard to give food to their own children and to do what is needed for them — let alone for wandering mendicants, of whom nothing need be said. And yet I have wealthy relatives with great resources. Let me go to the village of Kalandaka, visit my relatives there, arrange for the Saṅgha to be provided with food, and have the Saṅgha supplied with porridge, soup for drinking, regular meals by turns, invited meals, the eighth-day feast, the fourteenth-day feast, fish feasts, and various small special offerings."

So the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, stayed in whatever regions he pleased for as long as he liked, then took up his bowl and robes and set off for the village of Kalandaka. Wandering along in stages, in time he arrived at the village of Kalandaka and took up residence in a forest hermitage at the edge of that village.

The venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, then went to visit his relatives, and upon arriving before them he recited praises of the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and had food arranged for the Saṅgha. He had the Saṅgha provided with porridge, soup for drinking, regular meals by turns, invited meals, the eighth-day feast, the fourteenth-day feast, fish feasts, and various small special offerings.

At that time the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was one who dwelt in the forest, wore the three robes, collected rags from charnel grounds, and went on alms-round in strict order from house to house.

Then, on another occasion, having first satisfied the community of monks with a meal of porridge, he put on his lower robe in the morning, took up his bowl and robes, and entered the village of Kalandaka for alms. Going through the village of Kalandaka on his alms-round in order, he came to his own former home. At that home he received no gift and was not sent away — but left quickly.

At that moment, something improper concerning the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, had come to pass outside. An old female servant, seeing that the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, had received no gift at his own former home and had not been sent away but had departed swiftly, observed this.

Having seen this, she went to where the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was, and when she arrived she said to the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka: "My lady, please know this. The reverend Bhadradatta came home late, late indeed, to his own former home, and received no gift there and was not sent away, but departed swiftly."

Then the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, thought to herself: "Alas — can it be that my son Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, is feeling desire, or disenchantment, or a wish to wander, and is no longer seeking the life of a renunciant? Or that he has grown weary of the renunciant's way, or that depression has arisen in him, or that he is troubled by doubt, or that he is reviling it, or that he wishes to abandon the renunciant's way entirely? I wonder whether something of that sort has come to pass." Thinking and knowing this, she came out from the village of Kalandaka, went to where the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was, and when she arrived said to him:

"My son Bhadradatta, if you are feeling desire, or disenchantment, or a wish to wander, and are no longer seeking the renunciant's way, or have grown weary of the renunciant's way, or depression has arisen in you, or you are troubled by doubt, or you are reviling it, or you wish to abandon the renunciant's way — then, my son Bhadradatta, know this: the wealth of women that belongs to women, called women's treasure, or women's dowry, or the substance that is women's domain — that which was your mother's silver and great heap of gold is such that a person standing at one end cannot see a person sitting at the other end, and a person sitting at one end cannot see a person standing at the other end. That belongs to your mother. And beyond that, there is your father's silver and unstamped gold amounting to many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands — and what need is there even to speak of your father and others? My son Bhadradatta, come back. Remain here, enjoy pleasures, give gifts, and make merit."

When she had spoken thus, the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, said to his mother: "Mother, I am not feeling desire, or disenchantment, or a wish to wander while failing to seek the renunciant's way, nor am I weary of the renunciant's way, nor has depression arisen in me, nor am I troubled by doubt, nor do I revile it. I will not abandon the renunciant's way."

Then the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, thought: "Even though I have said all this, I have not been able to turn my son Bhadradatta back. Let me go home and keep his former wife hidden away." So the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, went home and said to her daughter-in-law: "Dear daughter, whenever the time comes and the lunar signs are favorable for you, let her be informed." The former wife of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, listened respectfully and replied: "As my lady commands."

Then, at another time, when the former wife of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, found that the time had come and the lunar signs were favorable, she went to where the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was and said to her: "Dear mother-in-law, now that the time has come and the lunar signs are favorable, please tell me what I should do. For his sake, with what sort of massage should I massage him, with what sort of bath should I bathe him, and with what fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, garments, and ornaments should I adorn myself, so that Bhadradatta, when he was still a householder, would delight in—"

"massage him with such a massage as he would delight in and find pleasing, bathe him with such a bath, and adorn yourself with such fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, garments, and ornaments."

Then the former wife of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, received instruction from her mother-in-law as to what kind of massage to give, what kind of bath to prepare, and with what fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, garments, and ornaments to adorn herself so that the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, when he was still a householder, would rejoice and find pleasing. She gave him just such a massage, bathed him with just such a bath, and adorned herself with just such fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, garments, and ornaments. She then went to where the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was, and said to his mother: "Dear mother-in-law, in a situation like this, what should I do?"

Then the mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, mounted a single carriage together with her daughter-in-law, set out from the village of Kalandaka, and traveled to where the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was. She rode by carriage as far as the road permitted, then dismounted and went on foot alone to where the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was.

At that time the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, was pacing back and forth in an open, unenclosed walking place outside his dwelling. The mother of the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, caught sight of her son from a great distance. When she saw him, she went to where he was and said to him:

"My son, Bhadradatta, if you have no disaffection, no disenchantment, no wish to wander away, if you are not one who fails to seek the purpose of the ascetic's way of life, not one who is weary of the ascetic's way of life, not one who is despondent, not one who wavers in doubt, not one who is disparaging, and not one who wishes to abandon the ascetic's way of life — then, my son, your wife is now in her season, the lunar signs are favorable. Bestow upon her a little of the seed. Since you have no son, it would not be fitting that all the property over which you hold authority should, by whatever means, come to be controlled by the king."

Now the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, had not yet established a foundation in the training, and had not perceived any fault in it. Seeing a young woman of fair complexion and lovely appearance such as would arouse attachment, he was overcome by desire in his mind. Overwhelmed by desire, he found himself with a body utterly tormented and a mind utterly tormented, and with that tormented body and tormented mind he said to his mother:

"Mother, may I do as you ask? My son Bhadradatta — yes, regarding the matter of the seed, it is entirely fitting."

Then the venerable Bhadradatta, son of Kalandaka, heeded his mother, took his former wife by both hands, went to one side, set aside his monastic robes, and engaged in sexual intercourse with her two or three times. He was a being in his last existence, one who seeks conduct, one who had grasped the essence of liberation, one oriented toward nirvāṇa.

Turned away from cyclic existence, one who did not seek death and rebirth in any of the existences of saṃsāra, one who held a final body — this being passed away from a wholesome divine realm and entered the womb of that woman who was the mother of living beings.

Now a woman skilled in the ways of women possesses five qualities unmixed with others. What are those five? She knows when a man has become aroused and knows when the arousal has passed. She knows the time and knows the lunar signs. She knows when a being has entered and is dwelling in the womb. She knows from whom the being dwelling in the womb has entered. And she knows whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, it rests leaning against the right hip, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning against the left hip.

She, delighted and gladdened, said to Śyāmā: "Dear mother, please be informed. A being has entered into me, and since it rests leaning against my right hip, it will certainly be a boy."

She too, delighted and gladdened, spoke thus: she would cause to be announced by name the offering of gifts — saying that this nephew, seen to be devout toward her for such a long time, had been born in accordance with her and not contrary to her, that he performs her tasks, that he tends to her in return for her having tended to him, that he partakes of his share, that her lineage and family line would continue for a long time, that when they had died and the proper time had come, whether a little or a great deal of giving had been done and merit had been made, let him go and follow wherever these two had been reborn — she would have this proclaimed, announced by name.

Knowing that a being had entered, and in order to bring the one dwelling in the womb to full maturity, she arranged for the chambers of an upper storey to be made available, and had her waited upon without any hindrance: in the cold season with implements for warmth, and in the warm season with implements for coolness; with food prescribed by physicians that was not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too hot, not too pungent, and that was free from bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, heat, and pungency; with garlands and ornaments adorning her body, moving about as though in the pleasure grove of divine maidens; so that she would not descend from couch to couch, from seat to seat, to the ground below, and that she would not hear even the slightest disagreeable sound.

After eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and a boy appeared — handsome of form, pleasing to behold, beautiful, radiant, with a complexion like gold, bearing a head like a parasol, with long arms, a broad forehead, arching eyebrows, and a high bridge of the nose.

The relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day, the third set of seven days from the birth, a great birth-feast was held, and they proceeded to give the boy a name. They thought: "Since this boy was found through the matter of the seed, let the boy's name be Sāvana," and so his name was given as Sāvana.

The boy Sāvana was entrusted to eight nurses — two nurses to hold him on their laps and keep him alive, two nurses to give him suck, two nurses to bathe and cleanse him of impurity, and two nurses to play with him as companions. Those eight nurses nourished and raised him with milk, yogurt, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other principal provisions of every kind, and swiftly grew him like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

When he had grown up, he took up the study of letters, numbers, calculation, reckoning on the fingers, drawing out, inserting, and setting down, and reached the end of learning in letters, as well as the ability to open, to read, and —

mastery, clear conduct, and these eight forms of examination: examination of precious stones, examination of land, examination of cloth, examination of wood, examination of elephants, examination of horses, examination of women, and examination of men — in all of these he became proficient.

Then at another time he came to have manifest faith in the Buddha, manifest faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He abandoned the taking of life and turned back from taking life. He abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct in the pursuit of desires, false speech, and the heedless indulgence in fermented grain-liquor and brewed liquor, and turned back from the heedless indulgence in fermented grain-liquor and brewed liquor.

Continuing in that very faith which had come down from his father, and nurturing it further, he shaved off his hair and beard, dressed himself in saffron-colored robes, and with perfectly pure faith went forth from home into homelessness in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, he dwelt alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, persistence, and self-abandonment. Dwelling alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, persistence, and self-abandonment, he realized through his own direct knowledge, and in that very lifetime accomplished and witnessed, that supreme culmination of the holy life for the sake of which noble sons shave off their hair and beard, dress in saffron-colored robes, and with perfectly pure faith go forth from home into homelessness. He came to know directly: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. I know no further becoming beyond this." He became an arhat, free of attachment toward the three realms, with a mind equally disposed toward a clod of earth and gold, equal to the sky and the palm of the hand, his awareness like sandalwood placed at rest, having cleaved through the mouth of the den of birth. He attained the knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the individual discriminating awarenesses. He turned his back on becoming, on the gains that come from desire, and on honors. He became one to be venerated, celebrated, and addressed directly by the gods of the sense faculties and those with faculties close by.

Then the venerable Śāṇavāsa, upon attaining arhatship and fully realizing with individual knowledge the joy and happiness of complete liberation, at that moment spoke this verse:

I have obtained my share from among the Dharmas.
I do not enrich myself with my father's wealth.
I learned only after much procrastination —
and yet I was greatly delayed in youth.

At that time the Blessed One was seated before a retinue of many hundreds of monks and was teaching the śrāvakas the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom in order to free attachment from attachment, teaching the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom in order to free aversion from attachment, and in order to free delusion from attachment.

At that time the venerable Śāṇavāsa, the son of Kalandaka, was present in that very assembly and was in harmony with it. Yet just as the Blessed One taught, step by step, the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom in order to free attachment from attachment, and the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom in order to free aversion from attachment and delusion from attachment — even so, the venerable Śāṇavāsa, the son of Kalandaka, began to feel a measure of remorse, grew deeply remorseful, became utterly remorseful, and sat there filled with regret, having obtained remorse, silent, with loosened shoulders, downcast face, and no confidence.

Then at another time, while a great many monks were wandering about in their travels, they went to the place where the venerable Śāṇavāsa, son of Kalandaka, was staying. Having arrived, they exchanged various pleasantries with the venerable Śāṇavāsa, son of Kalandaka, delighting and rejoicing together with him, and then sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, those many monks said this to the venerable Śāṇavāsa, son of Kalandaka:

"Venerable Śāṇavāsa, in the past, whenever you saw monks who had just arrived unexpectedly, you would greet them with friendly words and accept their alms-bowls, their robes, their staffs, their strainers, their round water vessels, their oil containers, their hats, their sandals with straps, and their slippers. But now, when you see monks who have just arrived unexpectedly, you have grown somewhat remorseful, deeply remorseful, utterly remorseful, and you sit there filled with remorse. You have obtained remorse, you are silent, your shoulders are loose, your face is downcast, you have no confidence, and you remain sunk within yourself. Venerable Śāṇavāsa, surely there is no physical affliction or mental distress troubling you now?"

"Venerable ones, there is no physical affliction of any kind troubling me now. Yet I do have a mental distress. Venerable ones, what is the mental distress that afflicts you?" At that point he explained the matter in full to the monks, yet those monks neither praised nor dissuaded him from it — they neither praised nor dissuaded him — and rising from their seats, they went to the place where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, those many monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.

When this was reported, the Blessed One addressed those many monks thus:

"Monks, among the many phenomena that resemble the bases of defilement, Śāṇavāsa, son of Kalandaka, has been the first to commit this one — namely, what was done through the condition of unchaste conduct."

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis, and this occasion, convened the community of monks. The Tathāgata convened the community of monks, seeing it to be necessary for two purposes: so that all my hearers might come to know of it fully, and so that a proper foundation for training in the Vinaya might be well established.

The blessed buddhas inquire knowingly. They inquire knowingly but do not inquire unknowingly. They inquire at the right time and do not inquire at the wrong time. They inquire about what is meaningful and do not inquire about what is without meaning. Therefore, when blessed buddhas inquire about something without meaning, they check and turn it aside with a word. And when blessed buddhas inquire about something meaningful, they know the right time to do so.

Thus the Blessed One inquired of the venerable Śāṇavāsa, son of Kalandaka: "Śāṇavāsa, is it true that you have done something so unseemly?"

"Blessed one, it is true."

The Blessed One declared: "What is not proper conduct for a monk, what is not in accordance with it, what is not fitting, what does not accord with proper conduct — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth into renunciation. Śāṇavāsa, I have taught the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom in order to free attachment from attachment, and to free aversion from attachment —"

"— and in order to free delusion from attachment, I have taught the Dharma of liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom. Why have you done something so unseemly? You, deluded man — it would be better to place one's own limb into the mouth of a black snake whose venom spreads swiftly, whose poison is fierce, whose poison is sharp, than to do as you have done with a woman." Thus he rebuked him.

Then the Blessed One, having rebuked him many times over, addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits fully, one should establish rules of training in the Vinaya for the hearers. They are as follows: for the sake of gathering the Saṅgha together; for the sake of benefiting the Saṅgha; for the sake of the Saṅgha dwelling at ease; for the sake of subduing those individuals who are shameless and disrespectful; for the sake of those who have a sense of shame dwelling at ease; for the sake of causing those who have no faith to generate faith; for the sake of those who have faith continuing to grow further; for the sake of restraining the defilements of this very life; for the sake of warding off those of future lives; and for the sake of the pure conduct I teach, which is of widespread benefit to many beings, being correctly demonstrated for a long time among gods and humans alike. Thus should my hearers proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya: Whatever monk, having taken up the same training together with the monks, without having relinquished that training and without having made clear that his training has deteriorated, engages in the act of unchastity — the way of sexual intercourse — that monk has incurred a defeat and may not remain."

Thus did the Blessed One establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The awakened Blessed One was residing in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the Kalandaka birds.

At that time, a certain monk was dwelling in a forest thicket near Rājagṛha. Then that monk, having tempted a female forest monkey repeatedly with food, engaged in the act of unchastity — the way of sexual intercourse — with her.

Thereafter, a great number of monks, wandering on their alms rounds, happened to come to the place where that monk's thicket was, and went there. They engaged in various conversations that brought open delight and full satisfaction to that monk, and they sat down to one side. Then that female monkey, remembering that same former evil and improper act, went to the place where that monk was and gazed directly into his face, and bared her rump, and attempted to entice that monk in such a manner — yet he repelled her out of shame before those other monks. The monkey gazed into his face a second time and a third time, and bared her rump, and attempted to entice that monk in such a manner — and he repelled her a second time and a third time, out of shame before those monks.

Then that monkey, having become angry, agitated, and fierce, and being displeased in mind, used her claws on his face, nose, robe, and feet, and went off to one side, and sat crouching like a dog, whimpering.

Then those monks said to that monk: "Venerable one, why does this forest monkey gaze into your face and bare her rump, and try to entice you in such a manner — while you repel her out of shame before us? Why does this forest monkey gaze into your face a second and third time and bare her rump, and try to entice you in such a manner —"

while we repel him out of shame before us. And yet this forest monkey, angered, agitated, and fierce, displeased in mind, scratched his face, nose, robe, and feet with her claws, went off to one side, and sat crouching like a dog, whimpering."

And at that point those monks related the whole matter in full to that monk. When they had spoken thus, those monks said to that monk: "Venerable one, has the Blessed One not prohibited unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse? Venerable ones, it has indeed been prohibited — but that prohibition applies to human beings, not to one born in the animal realm." Those monks neither praised nor reproved him, and without either praising or reproving they rose from their seats, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived they bowed with their heads to the Blessed One's two feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, a great many monks then related that matter in full to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, since I have already prohibited it even for human beings, what need is there to speak of one born in the animal realm? Monks, that deluded man has incurred defeat."

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this case, convened a gathering of the community of monks. From the words "The blessed buddhas, while knowing full well, make inquiry" down to "the Blessed One rebuked that monk," everything proceeds as before. "Monk, is it true that you did such an ugly thing as this?" "Venerable one, I did." The blessed Buddha then, from the words "this is not the conduct of a renunciant" down to "you deluded man — it would be better for you to have thrust a limb of your own body into the mouth of a black serpent whose venom spreads swiftly, whose venom is fierce, whose venom is sharp, rather than to do what you have done; but what has been done cannot apply to one born in the animal realm" — the Blessed One delivered a rebuke in full.

Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, for that reason the former rule is the primary ruling, and this is the supplementary ruling. My hearers are to recite this training rule of the Vinaya in this way:

Furthermore, whatever monk, while sharing the same training equally with the monks and without having relinquished the training, without having declared the training to be impaired, engages in unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse — even if it be with one born in the animal realm — that monk has incurred defeat and is not to remain in the community.

Now as to the phrase 'whatever monk': a monk is of four kinds — a monk in name, a monk by self-proclamation, a monk for the sake of alms, and a monk through having overcome the afflictions. Among these, who is a monk in name? Whoever bears the name, is addressed by that name, is referred to by the second term, by an honorific term, by a designation, by a calling, by an appellation, by a conventional expression — 'a monk,' or 'one of the monk's kind,' or 'one who has become like a monk' — such a one is called a monk in name. Who is a monk by self-proclamation? Whoever, while not being a monk, declares himself to be one, and who dwells in deception and claims to be a monk — such a one is called a monk by self-proclamation. Who is a monk for the sake of alms? Whoever sustains his life by wandering for alms in the proper manner — such a one is called a monk for the sake of alms. Who is a monk through having overcome the afflictions?

Whoever abandons, fully understands, cuts off at the root, renders without remainder like a palm tree cut down at its base, and brings to the nature of non-arising in future lives — those very things which are defilements (āsravas) that utterly afflict through the outflows, that produce renewed existence, that are accompanied by the fever of sickness, whose karmic maturation is suffering, and which will lead to birth, aging, and death in future lives — such a one is called a monk by reason of having overcome the afflictions.

In this context, because it is not appropriate to establish here a petition and an unshakeable act of four motions, what is meant by full ordination is understood to mean a monk. Therefore the phrase "and what monk" is stated.

The phrase "together with monks" refers to others besides that one — those who practise the holy life in conformity with the Dharma, those who lead a pure life of equal conduct.

The phrase "having become equal in training" means this: whatever is to be trained in by a monk who has been fully ordained for a hundred years, that same training is also to be trained in by one newly fully ordained today; and whatever is to be trained in by one newly fully ordained today, that same training is also to be trained in by one who has been fully ordained for a hundred years. What is equal here is equality in moral discipline itself, equality in training itself, and equality in the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra — that is what is meant by "having become equal in training." Therefore the phrase "having become equal in training" is stated.

Regarding the phrase "without having surrendered the training," the question arises: in what circumstances is the training considered not surrendered? It is as follows. If a monk, in anger, overwhelmed by the force of rage, surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who is out of his mind, whose thoughts are disordered, or who is oppressed by painful sensations surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who is insane surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one whose thoughts are disordered and who is oppressed by painful sensations surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who is dull-witted, mute, or deaf surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who perceives solitude as solitude surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who perceives what is solitary as not being solitary surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who perceives what is not solitary as solitary surrenders the training, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If a central-country person intends to surrender the training to another central-country person using a borderland dialect, and that central-country person does not understand the borderland words that were spoken, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If a borderlands person intends to surrender the training to another borderlands person using the speech of the central country, and that borderlands person does not understand the central-country words that were spoken, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If a borderlands person intends to surrender the training to a central-country person using a borderland dialect, and that central-country person does not understand the borderland words that were spoken, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If a central-country person intends to surrender the training to a borderlands person using central-country speech, and that borderlands person does not understand the central-country words that were spoken, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one surrenders the training to someone who is asleep, to someone in meditative absorption, to a god, to an emanation, to an animal, or to a reflection, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one who does not possess a tongue surrenders the training to another who does not possess a tongue, it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. If one has no intention to give it up, wishes to remain in the renunciant's way of life, has no wish to remain in household life, and does not make this known clearly to even a single person who understands the natural state of things — it is to be said that the training has not been surrendered. Therefore the phrase "without having surrendered the training" is stated.

Regarding the phrase "without having caused a deterioration of the training," there is also the case of one who has surrendered the training and yet has not caused a deterioration of the training.

There is also the case of one who has caused a deterioration of the training without having surrendered it. And there is the case of one who has both caused a deterioration of the training and surrendered it. And there is the case of one who has neither surrendered the training nor caused a deterioration of it.

Of these, first: the case of one who has surrendered the training without having caused a deterioration of it is as follows. A monk who is experiencing desire, or who is experiencing discontentment, or who wishes to wander about, and who either does not seek the state of an ascetic, or who is weary of the ascetic's way of life, or who is dejected, or who is in doubt, or who is speaking disparagingly, or who wishes to relinquish the ascetic's state entirely — such a one goes before a monk and says these words: "Venerable one, please hear me. I, who am called such-and-such, surrender the training." If he says this, it is to be declared that the training has been surrendered. If he says, "I surrender the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha," it is to be declared that the training has been surrendered. If he says, "I surrender the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā," it is to be declared that the training has been surrendered. If he says, "I surrender to the abbot and the preceptor," it is to be declared that the training has been surrendered. If he says, "I am a layman," or "I am a novice," or "I am an eater," or "I am a paṇḍaka," or "I have expelled a nun," or "I have killed my mother," or "I have killed my father," or "I have killed an arhat," or "I have created a schism in the Saṅgha," or "With malicious intent I have drawn blood from a Tathāgata," or "I am a tīrthika," or "I have entered among the tīrthikas," or "I am dwelling as a thief," or "I am dwelling separately," or "Please accept me as one who should not be allowed to remain" — or even if he says, "I, one such as I, am content with those who share the same view and who walk in the holy life as companions" — if he says this, it is to be declared that the training has been surrendered. Thus it is that one has surrendered the training without having caused a deterioration of it.

As for how one may cause a deterioration of the training without having surrendered it: a monk who is experiencing desire, or who is experiencing discontentment, or who wishes to wander about and does not desire the state of an ascetic, or who is weary of the ascetic's way of life, or who is dejected, or who is in doubt, or who is speaking disparagingly, or who wishes to relinquish the ascetic's state entirely — such a one goes before a monk and says these words: "Venerable one, please know this: the holy life is difficult to lead; solitude is difficult to maintain; delight in being alone is difficult; dwelling in remote places — in forests, at the foot of mountains, at the edges of charnel grounds — is difficult to bear; dwelling alone in isolation is suffering. I remember my father and mother, my brothers and sisters. Let me be taught crafts; let all of my livelihood be sought out; let me be established in a good household." When he speaks in this way, expressing desire, or discontentment, or a wish to wander and a lack of desire for the ascetic's state, or weariness of the ascetic's way of life, or dejection, or doubt, or disparagement, or a wish to relinquish the ascetic's state entirely — whatever speech, words, expressions, sounds, utterances, definite statements, forms of expression, vocal sounds, verbal actions, and vocal communications he produces — if by these he says, "Venerable one, please hear me: I, who am called such-and-such, surrender the training," or "I surrender the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha," or "I surrender the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā," or "I surrender to the abbot and the preceptor," or "I am a layman," or "I am a novice," or "I am an eater," or "I am a paṇḍaka," or "I have expelled a nun," or "I have killed my mother," or "I have killed my father," or "I have killed an arhat," or "I have created a schism in the Saṅgha," or "With malicious intent I have drawn blood from a Tathāgata," or "I am a tīrthika," or "I have entered among the tīrthikas," or "I am dwelling as a thief," or "I am dwelling separately," or "Please accept me as one who should not be allowed to remain" —

But he does not say, "I am content to remain with those who share compatible Dharma practices and who live the holy life alongside me, such as you." In that case, the training has been transgressed and yet the training has not been surrendered.

How then does one both transgress the training and surrender the training? It is as follows. When a monk is filled with desire, or with discontent, or with the wish to wander about and has no wish to continue the way of the ascetic, or is wearied of the way of the ascetic, or is overcome with exhaustion, or is filled with doubt, or is filled with disgust, or wishes to abandon the way of the ascetic entirely, he goes before a monk and says: "Venerable one, please know this: the holy life is difficult to live. Strict seclusion is difficult to maintain. Finding delight in solitude is difficult. It is difficult to bear deeply within oneself dwelling in remote lodgings, forests, groves, the foot of mountains, and the farthest reaches of the open air. Dwelling alone in a wilderness is painful. I think of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters. Let me be apprenticed to a craft. Let me seek out the limits of my livelihood. Let me be entrusted to good households." And so, whether he is filled with desire, or discontent, or the wish to wander about and has no wish for the way of the ascetic, or is wearied of the way of the ascetic, or is overcome with exhaustion, or is filled with doubt, or is filled with disgust, or wishes to abandon the way of the ascetic entirely — whatever speech, words, common expressions, utterances, statements, definitive words, verbal pathways, verbal sounds, verbal actions, and verbal communications there may be that express such desire, discontent, wish to wander, unwillingness to continue the way of the ascetic, weariness with the way of the ascetic, exhaustion, doubt, disgust, or wish to abandon the way of the ascetic entirely — and he speaks them, saying: "Venerable ones, please hear me. I, known by the name such-and-such, surrender the training," or "I surrender the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha," or "I surrender the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā," or "I surrender the abbot and the preceptor," or "I am a layman," or "I am a novice," or "I am an eater," or "I am a paṇḍaka," or "I have expelled a nun," or "I have killed my mother," or "I have killed my father," or "I have killed an arhat," or "I have created a schism in the Saṅgha," or "With malicious intent I have drawn blood from a Tathāgata," or "I am a tīrthika," or "I have entered among the tīrthikas," or "I am dwelling as a thief," or "I am dwelling separately," or "Please accept me as one who should not be allowed to remain" — or even if he says, "I am content to remain with those who share compatible Dharma practices and who live the holy life alongside me, such as you" — in any such case, it should be declared that the training has been surrendered. And so the training has been both transgressed and surrendered.

How then does one neither surrender the training nor transgress it? It is by none of those modes described above. Therefore, it is said, the training has not been transgressed.

Unchaste conduct refers to two parties giving themselves to each other. The act of sexual intercourse is precisely that unchaste conduct. Dharma — here the term "Dharma" is used to name what is not Dharma at all. "If he engages in it" means if he practises it excessively. "Even with a female born in an animal realm, or with one like unto such" refers to a female monkey, or to one who resembles or is included among the like of a female monkey. "A monk" refers to whoever possesses the essential properties of a monk. What are the essential properties of a monk? Full ordination. What is full ordination? It is the carrying out of the formal act consisting of the motion and the three proclamations, together with the deliberation itself, the proper deliberation, the bringing to completion, the proper bringing to completion — and that individual's consent, explicit consent, non-retraction, and non-reversal — together with whatever speech, words, common expressions, utterances, statements, definitive words, verbal pathways, verbal sounds,

verbal actions, and verbal intimations there may be. The word "that" is a term of immediate indication and of comprehensive indication. The phrase "has incurred defeat" means: it has come to its end, it is a transgression, it is a diminishment, it stands at the conclusion, it is a cutting off, it is contrary to the mind.

Moreover, whoever commits that transgression becomes, immediately upon committing it, unfit to be a monk, unfit to be a contemplative, unfit to be a son of the Śākyas. He falls away from the substance of monkhood. His mode of the contemplative life is shattered — degraded, broken, fallen, defeated — and his mode of the contemplative life can never be restored. It is as follows: just as when the crown of a palm tree is cut off it can no longer turn green, nor can it grow and spread and become expansive, so too when a monk has done such a deed, he becomes immediately upon doing it unfit to be a monk, unfit to be a contemplative, unfit to be a son of the Śākyas. He falls away from the substance of monkhood. His mode of the contemplative life is shattered — degraded, broken, fallen, defeated — and his mode of the contemplative life can never be restored. It is for this reason that it is said, "has incurred defeat."

The phrase "should not dwell" means that monks should not dwell together with such a person in the restoration ceremony, in the invitation ceremony, in the formal act requiring one motion, in the formal act requiring a motion and two proclamations, or in the formal act requiring a motion and four proclamations. He should not be appointed to any of the twelve roles to which persons are appointed. It is for this reason that it is said, "should not dwell."

Now, in what circumstances does one incur the transgression?

In verse summary: alone and in three locations, with woman, man, and neuter, inclining toward contact and striving, causing intoxication and taking by force.

If a monk engages in the practice of unchastity — the act of sexual intercourse — he incurs defeat. If a monk engages in the practice of unchastity in any of three locations, he incurs defeat. If he causes the organ to enter, whether into the urinary passage or the anal passage, he incurs defeat immediately upon insertion. If a monk engages in the practice of unchastity with any of the three — a woman, a man, or a neuter — he incurs defeat.

If a monk's mind inclines toward contact, falls toward contact, and has fallen toward contact, and with a mind so inclining, so falling, and so fallen, he causes his organ — with an interval and together with an interval, or with an interval and without an interval, or without an interval and together with an interval, or without an interval and without an interval — to enter into the urinary passage or the anal passage of a living human woman who is undamaged, he incurs defeat immediately upon insertion.

If a monk's mind inclines toward contact, falls toward contact, and has fallen toward contact, and with a mind so inclining, so falling, and so fallen, he causes his organ — with an interval and together with an interval, or with an interval and without an interval, or without an interval and together with an interval, or without an interval and without an interval — to enter into the urinary passage or the anal passage of a living human woman who is damaged, he incurs a gross offense immediately upon insertion.

If a monk's mind inclines toward contact, falls toward contact, and has fallen toward contact, and with a mind so inclining, so falling, and so fallen, he causes his organ — with an interval and together with an interval, or with an interval and without an interval, or without an interval and together with an interval, or without an interval and without an interval — to enter into the urinary passage or the anal passage of a dead human woman who is undamaged, he incurs defeat immediately upon insertion.

If a monk's mind inclines toward contact, falls toward contact, and has fallen toward contact, and with a mind so inclining, so falling, and so fallen —

fallen toward contact, and with a mind so inclining, so falling, and so fallen, he causes his organ — with an interval and together with an interval, or with an interval and without an interval, or without an interval and together with an interval, or without an interval and without an interval — to enter into the urinary passage or the anal passage of a dead human woman who is undamaged, he incurs defeat immediately upon insertion.

Just as with a living and a dead human woman, so too it is the same with a living non-human woman, a dead non-human woman, a living female born in an animal womb, and a dead female born in an animal womb. And with a living man and a dead man, it is likewise through both openings of the wound. Just as with a living man and a dead man through both openings of the wound, so too with a living non-human male and a dead non-human male through both openings of the wound, and with a living male born in an animal womb and a dead male born in an animal womb through both openings of the wound. Just as with a man, so too it is the same with a living human pandaka and a dead human pandaka through both openings of the wound, with a living non-human pandaka and a dead non-human pandaka through both openings of the wound, and with a living pandaka born in an animal womb and a dead pandaka born in an animal womb through both openings of the wound.

When a monk makes an attempt upon a sleeping monk, if the monk who is being acted upon does not know it at the beginning, does not know it in the middle, and does not know it at the end, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk makes an attempt upon a sleeping monk, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning but does not know it in the middle and does not know it at the end, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk makes an attempt upon a sleeping monk, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning and knows it in the middle but does not know it at the end, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk makes an attempt upon a sleeping monk, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning, knows it in the middle, and knows it at the end, but knowing it does not consent, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk makes an attempt upon a sleeping monk, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning, knows it in the middle, and knows it at the end, and knowing it does consent, then both are to be expelled.

Just as with a monk acting upon a monk, so too it is the same with a monk acting upon a nun, a female probationer, a male novice, a female novice; with a nun acting upon a monk or a male novice; with a female novice acting upon a monk or a male novice; and with a male novice acting upon a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice.

When a monk causes a monk to become intoxicated with grain liquor and then makes an attempt upon him, if the monk who is being acted upon does not know it at the beginning, does not know it in the middle, and does not know it at the end, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk causes a monk to become intoxicated with grain liquor and then makes an attempt upon him, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning but does not know it in the middle and does not know it at the end, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk causes a monk to become intoxicated with grain liquor and then makes an attempt upon him, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning, knows it in the middle, and knows it at the end, but knowing it does not consent, then the one who makes the attempt is to be expelled. When a monk causes a monk to become intoxicated with grain liquor and then makes an attempt upon him, if the monk who is being acted upon knows it at the beginning, knows it in the middle, and knows it at the end, and knowing it does consent, then both are to be expelled.

Just as it is with a monk acting upon a monk, so too it is the same when a monk acts upon a nun, a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice monk, or a novice nun; when a nun acts upon a monk or a novice monk; when a female trainee acts upon a monk or a novice monk; when a novice nun acts upon a monk or a novice monk; and likewise with all such combinations involving novice nuns.

Just as it is with grain liquor, so too it is the same with prepared liquor, compounded liquor, and intoxicating drinks made from roots, from stalks, from leaves, from flowers, or from fruits; and likewise with spells, incantations, or medicines used to disturb the mind or induce sleep.

When a monk seizes another monk by force, holding him in suspense, and makes an attempt upon him: if, at the moment of entry, the monk who is acted upon makes it his own, both are to be expelled. If he does not do so at the moment of entry but does so at the moment of full insertion, both are to be expelled. If he does not do so at the moment of entry nor at the moment of full insertion, but does so at the moment of withdrawal, both are to be expelled. If he does not do so at the moment of entry, nor at the moment of full insertion, nor at the moment of withdrawal, then the one who made the attempt is to be expelled.

Just as it is with a monk acting upon a monk, so too it is the same in all combinations: a monk with a nun, a female trainee, a novice monk, or a novice nun; a nun with a monk or a novice monk; a female trainee with a monk or a novice monk; a novice nun with a monk or a novice monk; and a novice monk with a monk, a female trainee, a novice monk, or a novice nun.

The Vinaya, its Distinctions. The Second Fascicle.

In summary verse:

One with a cushion at the back and one hanging down,
one who delights in adornment and belongs to a company, an old woman,
and a monk who lies asleep —
seeking these involves no offense.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was a householder living in Śrāvastī who took a wife from among his equals in station. He sported with her, rejoiced in her, and passed his time in happiness with her. At a certain later time, as he was thus sporting, rejoicing, and living in happiness with her, a being entered into his wife's womb. After eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and the child that was born had a back that was soft and exceedingly soft, like that of a rabbit or a cat. His kinsmen gathered and came together, and on the twenty-first day after the birth they held a great birth-feast and proceeded to give the child a name, deliberating as to what it should be. They thought to themselves: because this child's back is soft and exceedingly soft, like that of a rabbit or a cat, let the child's name be Soft-Back. And so they gave him the name Soft-Back.

He was raised and nurtured with milk, yogurt, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and many other excellent provisions, and he grew quickly, like a lotus growing in a pond. When he had grown up, he went forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, one morning he put on his lower robe, took up his outer robe and his alms bowl, and went out for alms into the very village or township near which he was staying — but he did not guard his body, did not restrain his faculties, did not establish mindfulness, and entered upon his alms round without care. Having made his way through that village or township on his alms round and finished his meal,

he returned from the alms round for the after-meal food, set down his alms bowl and outer robe, washed both feet, and entered his dwelling in order to settle properly within. At that time, when his mind became thoroughly ensnared by attachment toward sensual objects, he made use of his own limbs in an appropriate way, inserted himself, and applied effort. Then at another time, a great many wandering monks who were traveling about came to where that monk was dwelling, and those monks saw him doing as he did. Seeing this, they were displeased and deeply dissatisfied, and they said these words to that monk: "Venerable one, what are you doing?" He replied, "I am making contact with something of my own." The monks said, "Venerable one, did the Blessed One not prohibit the unchaste practice, the act of sexual intercourse?" He replied, "Venerable ones, he prohibited it, but that pertains to what belongs to another — not to what is one's own." Those monks neither praised nor reproached him, neither commended nor turned him back, but departed and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, they bowed their heads to the Blessed One's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those many monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "O monks, if I have prohibited what belongs to another, what need is there even to mention what belongs to oneself? That deluded one has incurred defeat." When a monk's mind inclines toward, falls upon, and has fallen upon a support — and with a mind that inclines toward, falls upon, and has fallen upon that support, he makes use of his limbs in an appropriate way and inserts himself, whether by himself or into another — the moment of insertion is the moment of defeat.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There in Śrāvastī a certain householder took a wife of equal birth and made merry with her, rejoiced with her, and passed his time with her in delight. Then at another time, while they were making merry, rejoicing, and taking delight together, a being entered into his wife's womb, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth, and a boy was born with limbs of surpassingly excellent measure. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — the third set of seven days after the birth — they held a great birth celebration and proceeded to give the boy a name. "What shall the boy's name be?" They thought to themselves: "Because this boy's limbs are of surpassingly excellent measure, this boy shall be called 'Pendent' " — and they gave him the name Pendent. He was nourished and raised on milk, curds, butter, the essence of clarified butter, and many other excellent provisions, and he grew swiftly, like a lotus growing in a pond.

When he had grown up, he went forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, one morning he put on his lower robe, took up his outer robe and his alms bowl, and went out for alms into the very village or township near which he was staying — but he did not guard his body, did not restrain his faculties, did not establish mindfulness, and entered upon his alms round without care. Having made his way through that village or township on his alms round and finished his meal, he returned from the alms round for the after-meal food, set down his alms bowl and outer robe, washed both feet, and entered his dwelling in order to settle properly within.

At that time, his mind became entirely ensnared by attachment to sensual objects. He then made his own limb serviceable for that purpose, introduced it into his own urinary passage, and exerted himself. Then at another time, a great many wandering monks came to the place where that monk was staying, and those monks saw him doing this. Seeing it, they were displeased and deeply dissatisfied, and said to that monk: "Venerable one, what are you doing?" "I am gratifying myself by touch." "Venerable one, has not the Blessed One forbidden the unchaste practice, the act of sexual intercourse?" The other monks replied: "Venerable ones, it has been forbidden — but that pertains to another's passage, not to one's own." Those monks neither praised him for it nor turned him back from it. Having neither praised him nor turned him back, they departed, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they prostrated themselves at the Blessed One's feet with their heads and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the many monks reported this matter to the Blessed One in full detail. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, when I have already forbidden even another's passage, what need is there even to speak of one's own? That deluded man has incurred defeat. Monks, when a monk's mind is inclined toward filth, falls toward filth, and has fallen into filth — when his mind is inclined toward filth, falls toward filth, and has fallen into filth — if he makes his own limb serviceable for that purpose and introduces it into his own or another's urinary passage and exerts himself, he incurs defeat the moment it is introduced."

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in the noble land there was a merchant caravan leader named Joyful — wealthy, possessed of abundant riches, of great resources, holdings extensive and wide-ranging, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, a rival to Vaiśravaṇa himself in wealth. He had taken a wife from among his own social equals, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and took his pleasure. He sported, rejoiced, and took his pleasure with her, yet they had no son and no daughter. Having no son and earnestly desiring one, he offered prayers to the gods of peace, to the water deity, to the malevolent spirits, to Śakra, to Brahmā, and to other such divine beings — and also to the following further categories of deity: the gods of the pleasure grove, the gods of the forest, the gods of the crossroads, the gods of the three-way junctures, the gods who receive torma offerings, the co-natal gods, the gods of the same Dharma nature, and the gods who ever follow as attendants. Now, in the world there exists a saying of the following kind: "From the causes of such prayers, sons and daughters are born." But it is not so. If it were so, then from those prayers alone each person would have a thousand sons, just like a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Sons and daughters are born rather from the coming together of three conditions made fully present. What are those three? First, the father and mother come together in desire and union; second, the mother is in her season and her fertile time has arrived; and third, a gandharva is nearby and wishing to enter. When those three conditions are fully present, sons and daughters are born. Now, while he was thus engaged, earnestly occupied with his prayers, a being died and passed away from among the divine realms and entered the womb of that man's household mistress.

There are certain women who are skilled in reading the nature of things, and they possess five unmixed qualities. What are those five? They know when a man has become attached and when he is free from attachment; they know the time and recognize the days of the month; they know when a being has entered and is dwelling in the womb; they know from whom that being entered and is dwelling in the womb; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, it rests leaning to the right side, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning to the left side.

Now the household mistress was filled with joy, and, delighted, she spoke to her husband: "O son of my lord, a sentient being has entered within me — I know this because it rests leaning to the right flank, so it is certainly a boy. Please be glad." And he, too, was filled with joy, and, delighted, he straightened his upper body, extended his right hand, and made this solemn declaration: "May I behold the face of this son whom I have long desired; may he be born in harmony with me and not in discord; may he perform my deeds; may he care for me in return for the care I give him; may he enjoy his inheritance; may he cause my lineage and family to endure for a long time; and when we have died and our time has come, may he, having given gifts large or small and having made merit in our name, go forth to wherever the two of us are reborn and follow after us." Thus he made this solemn declaration.

Then, knowing that a sentient being had entered, in order to bring the one dwelling in the womb to full maturity, in the chamber of the fine upper-story apartment, he arranged for her comfortable care: when cold, things that relieve cold; when warm, things that relieve warmth; food prepared on the physician's advice that was not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too hot, and not too pungent — food from which bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, heat, and pungency had been removed entirely. He had her attended to, without harm and without the least unpleasant sound reaching her, wandering as if she were the body of a goddess's daughter adorned with necklaces, earrings, and ornaments moving through a pleasure grove — going from couch to couch, from seat to seat, never descending to the bare floor.

After eight or nine months had passed, a boy was born from her delivery: handsome of form, lovely to behold, beautiful, radiant, resembling the color of gold, furnished with a head like a parasol, long-armed, with a large fontanelle, with gracefully arched brows and a well-bridged nose.

Then his kinsmen and relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — that is, three groups of seven days — after the birth, they held a great birth-feast and set about giving the boy a name, deliberating on what name he should receive. Now the general custom in the central region was that whoever was handsome, lovely to behold, and beautiful should be called "Beautiful." Thinking of this, they considered: "Because this boy is handsome, lovely to behold, and beautiful, and because he is the son of the caravan leader Joyous, let his name be Śobhānanda — Beautiful-Joy." And so he was given the name Śobhānanda.

The boy Śobhānanda was then entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to carry him and keep him alive, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to bathe him and clean him, and two nurses to play with him. Those eight nurses nourished and raised him with milk, curd, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and many other finest provisions, causing him to grow quickly, like a lotus dwelling in a pond. When he had grown up, he was taught writing, numbers, and

arithmetic, accounting — addition, subtraction, and setting down figures. He became fully accomplished in writing: composing, reading, mastering a subject, making its application clear, and examining. He also became skilled in the eight kinds of examination, which are as follows: examining precious gems, examining land, examining cloth, examining wood, examining elephants, examining horses, examining women, and examining men.

His father arranged the three grades of his wife's retinue — the highest, the middle, and the lowest. He had the three residential quarters prepared for his use in each of the three seasons: winter, spring, and summer. He had the three pleasure gardens likewise prepared for the winter season, the spring season, and the summer season. There, within the grounds belonging to the fine upper chambers, women — with no men present — would play, take delight, and amuse themselves with music.

Now the caravan leader Joyous was perpetually absorbed in accounts and ledgers, and was also practicing their arrangement and presentation. Śobhānanda said to him: "Father, why do you remain so constantly absorbed in your accounts?" He replied: "My son, can wealth truly be won merely by playing in the fine upper chambers? I must think about the work of the household too."

Śobhānanda, understanding that his father was urging him on for his own benefit, touched his father's two feet and said: "Father, if you would grant me permission to do so, I will go to another land and earn wealth." His father replied: "My son, since we have wealth in abundance, why go to another land? Stay here." He said: "Father, I will not leave a bad son behind." The caravan leader Joyous, thinking that this was indeed what the boy desired, took the keys and the crooked keys and the like, opened the seven treasury storehouses full of worked gold, of unworked gold, and of silver, displayed them, and said: "My son Śobhānanda, we have wealth in this measure. You stay right here, enjoy whatever you wish, give generously, and accumulate merit. There is no need to go to another land."

He replied: "Father, if you set a bad example before a bad son, what will that bad son then set before his own sons?" The caravan leader Joyous thought: "What he says is good. After I am gone, he will need to learn to manage the affairs of the household. Therefore, for as long as I live, let him go on a trading expedition to another land; there too he will come to know his father's friends and contacts. In that way, when I am gone, the path this one travels will have no darkness."

Knowing and understanding this, he spoke to his wife: "My good woman, after I am gone, Śobhānanda will need to manage the affairs of the household. Therefore, for as long as I live, let him go on a trading expedition to another land; there too he will come to know his father's friends and contacts. In that way, when I am gone, the path this one travels will have no darkness." She replied: "My lord's son has done no wrong — let it be as you say; I agree."

Then the caravan leader Joyous spoke to Śobhānanda: "My son, I am glad that you have set your mind on undertaking a trading expedition to another land. After I am gone, you will need to manage the affairs of the household. Therefore, for as long as I live, go on a trading expedition to another land; there too you will come to know your father's friends and contacts. In that way, when I am gone, the path you travel will have no darkness." Śobhānanda said: "Father, I shall do as you command."

Then the caravan leader Joyous had a proclamation made throughout Rājagṛha: "Hear this, all you wise ones — merchants dwelling in Rājagṛha and merchants who have come from various directions! The caravan leader Śobhānanda is setting out on a trading expedition to another land."

"All of you who wish to travel to another land together with the caravan leader Śobhānanda, without hazard of passes, without mountain crossings, and without river crossings — let those who are willing to journey to another land on such terms assemble their goods accordingly." Five hundred merchants who wished to travel to another land on such terms assembled their goods accordingly.

The caravan leader Joyous invited those merchants as guests, fed them, and then said: "Wise ones, just as Śobhānanda is my son, so too is he yours. There are three obstacles for merchants who travel to foreign lands: gambling, unsuitable women, and intoxicants. You must certainly turn away from these harmful things and devote yourselves fully to what is beneficial. If, by turning away from harm and devoting yourselves to benefit, you are able to remain firmly established, that is well and good. But if you are unable to remain firm, you must abandon your goods, recoup whatever price you can, and go on your way." He spoke also to Śobhānanda: "Son Śobhānanda, just as you are my son, so too are you the son of all these merchants. Listen to their words and counsel, and bear their instructions in mind."

The caravan leader Śobhānanda said: "Father, I will act as you command." Having heard this from the caravan leader Joyous, he performed auspicious rites, propitious ceremonies, and rites for good fortune. Then, loading abundant goods onto carts, pack-carriers, mules, horses, mares, oxen, and donkeys, he set out for another land together with five hundred merchants. Traveling gradually through towns, villages, districts, and royal residences, he arrived at Śrāvastī, and there he deposited his goods in a great warehouse and settled in.

At that time in Śrāvastī there lived a beautiful courtesan (a seller of her form) named Bhadramukhī — lovely in appearance, delightful to behold, beautiful, and pleasing to men. She would enjoy herself in the company of men for the price of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. She heard tell that there had arrived in the city a young man named Śobhānanda, son of the caravan leader Joyous — a man of great wealth and fine appearance, lovely to behold and beautiful — and that he had come with five hundred merchants and deposited his goods in a very large warehouse.

Hearing this, she thought to herself: "If I do not rob him of all his goods, I shall not deserve the name 'the Beautiful One.'" She said to her serving-maid: "Girl, the caravan leader Śobhānanda is a man of great wealth. He has brought his goods here and stored them in a large warehouse.
