Take incense and garlands and go to him. Bow at his feet and say these words: 'My lady Bhadramukhī prostrates herself at your feet. Noble son, why have you forsaken your own palace and taken up lodging in a warehouse like an ordinary man? This is your palace — please come hither.' Say that to him."

The maid said: "As my lady commands." She took incense and garlands, went to where the caravan leader Śobhānanda was, and said to him: "My lady Bhadramukhī prostrates herself at your feet, and sends you this incense and these garlands. She says: 'Noble son, why have you forsaken your palace and taken up lodging in a warehouse like an ordinary man? This is your palace — please come hither.'"

Śobhānanda said: "Girl, you may go. I shall put on these garlands and incense and come." Then the serving-maid went back to where the courtesan Bhadramukhī was, and reported to Bhadramukhī everything that had been said in the conversation she had had with the caravan leader Śobhānanda.

Then the courtesan Bhadramukhī, having heard from the serving-maid messenger what had been said, felt joy and gladness arise within her. She had the house washed and swept clean, strewed it with flowers of every variety, and perfumed it with sweet-smelling incense. She spread out a bed furnished with a canopy and bolsters, and sat there waiting, intent above all else on the caravan leader Śobhānanda.

The caravan leader Śobhānanda, for his part, adorned himself with perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, mounted his riding animal, and set off surrounded by a retinue of young servant boys. Gloriously beautiful in the full radiance of his youth, he made his way to the place where the courtesan Bhadramukhī resided.

Bhadramukhī saw the caravan leader Śobhānanda approaching in all the splendor of his youthful beauty. Upon seeing him she asked the serving-maid messenger: "Girl, is that the caravan leader Śobhānanda?" She replied: "My lady, that is none other than the caravan leader Śobhānanda himself."

Then the courtesan Bhadramukhī, feeling joy and gladness arise within her, spoke these verses:

Whether born of noble lineage or not,
whether a man who has lost his wealth or one endowed with riches —
the sight of one rich in beauty
steals away the hearts of women.

He rode his mount for as long as the road permitted, then dismounted and began to enter the courtesan Bhadramukhī's house on foot. She came down quickly, quickly from the upper floor, went out to receive him, embraced him with all her limbs, led him inside the house, and seated him on the women's seat. She asked: "What is the name of this noble son?" He replied: "Śobhānanda." She said: "How wonderful! Your name matches your beauty, and your beauty matches your name. If your mother and father have not yet requested that you be given the name Śobhānanda, then I myself shall make the request for that name today." He then asked her: "And what is your name?" She replied: "Bhadramukhī." He said: "How wonderful! Your name matches your beauty, and your beauty matches your name. If your mother and father have not yet requested that you be given the name Bhadramukhī, then I myself shall make the request for that name today."

Śobhānanda said: "Bhadramukhī, what is the fee for one night?" She replied: "The noble son speaks not like a common man." Her serving-maid messenger then said: "One night is five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." Śobhānanda instructed his man: "Send her five hundred kārṣāpaṇas every day." And so he stayed and sported with her, enjoyed himself, and indulged in pleasures with her. Since desires, when pursued, know no turning back, no satiation, and no end, many days passed and still he was not sated, and his man continued bringing five hundred kārṣāpaṇas day after day.

Now the merchants said: "Good friends, since the caravan leader Śobhānanda is nowhere to be seen, as he was entrusted to us by a companion, let us search everywhere for him." The merchants asked his servants: "Where has the caravan leader gone?" They replied: "The very day the caravan leader departed for Śrāvastī, he entered the house of a courtesan and has been staying there — have you only now remembered?" The merchants said: "Good friends, it was wrong of us to have left the caravan leader Śobhānanda and let him be forgotten like this. His father will have a grievance against us for it." The merchants then sent a large message to Śobhānanda conveying the words of his fellow merchants: "Please come back." That messenger delivered the message to Śobhānanda, and Śobhānanda was about to set out —

Bāṇamālikā seized him by the hem of his robe and said: "Noble son, those who wish to enjoy pleasures are maintained by two things: a handsome appearance and youth. Since you are endowed with good looks and the bloom of youth, spend this time of youth in play, joy, and pleasure — and in old age apply yourself to acquiring wealth." Śobhānanda said to that messenger: "Go now, and come back." The messenger went and said to the merchants: "The caravan leader says: 'Go now, and come back.'" The merchants gathered together, and while they were staying there, Śobhānanda took hold of them all. All the merchants gathered and went to the courtesan's house. The merchants waited at the door and said to a servant: "Good man, go and tell the caravan leader that the company of merchants is waiting at the door and wishes to see the caravan leader." The servant went and reported this to Śobhānanda, and Śobhānanda was about to come out — but again the courtesan Bāṇamālikā seized him by the hem of his robe and said: "Noble son, let those merchants too enjoy pleasure here together with me — stay and take your pleasure along with them." Since the pursuit of pleasures only increases entanglement, Śobhānanda said: "I will come out when I am free of all that binds me." The servant went and told the company of merchants: "The caravan leader says: 'I will come out when I am free of all that binds me.'" The merchants said: "Alas! Śobhānanda has fallen into what is wrong and is heading into ruin!" And so they abandoned all their goods, took their payment, and departed. From that time on, the man who had been paying Bāṇamālikā five hundred kārṣāpaṇas each day ceased to bring payment any longer.

Then at another time Bāṇamālikā questioned that man and said: "Good man, why do you no longer bring the kārṣāpaṇas?" He replied: "The associates have left — from where should I bring them? Or did the associates perhaps take away Śobhānanda's goods as well?" "They did." Bāṇamālikā spent two or three days taking her pleasure together with Śobhānanda and then said: "Noble son, I have no fields, no workers to manage my affairs, and no townspeople who have pledged goods and are going to other districts. I can only live on whatever I obtain from someone like you — so either give me kārṣāpaṇas, or let another man take your place." Śobhānanda said: "Bāṇamālikā, have you no affection for me at all?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble son, have you not heard the saying:

There is no affection for those with a crowd of companions —
they by nature do not stay long.
Like birds on a fruitless tree,
they abandon the old and move on.

Śobhānanda said: "Bāṇamālikā, as long as a man gives you wealth, so long you are under his power?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble son, have you not heard the saying:

As long as Śakra (Indra) sends down rain,
so long do rivers and streams flow down the mountains.
As long as a man gives wealth,
so long does a courtesan's man hold sway.

Śobhānanda said: "Bāṇamālikā, do you lead any man you like astray?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble son, have you not heard the saying:

A courtesan makes a man glad with embrace and sweet words
as though he were her own body,
dwelling with him through the evening and the middle of the night —
then from dawn onward casts him off like old grass.

Śobhānanda said: "Bāṇamālikā, do you behave in this way toward men of wealth?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble son, have you not heard the saying:

We use men with wealth,
and even those who have spent it all,
as cattle graze on fresh green grass.

Have you not heard this saying?"

Now Śobhānanda had begun to feel desire arise, and Bāṇamālikā thought to herself: "This Śobhānanda is handsome, pleasant to look upon, and beautiful. Even though he has come from very far away, he is just the sort of man with whom one should sport, rejoice, and take pleasure. Therefore, so long as no other man comes bearing five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, I shall sport with this one, rejoice with him, and take pleasure with him." Having understood this and recognized it clearly, Bāṇamālikā took hold of Śobhānanda by the edge of his garment and said: "Noble son, will you not laugh with me here in the house?" "You may laugh at me if you wish — but stop. Let him not leave."

Now Śobhānanda was greatly overcome with desire, and just then another man arrived bearing five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and entered the house. He said: "Let Bāṇamālikā enjoy herself with me — and let the other one go." Bāṇamālikā drew a curtain directly in front of Śobhānanda, shutting him off, and began to take pleasure with the newcomer. Śobhānanda, perceiving and understanding clearly that Bāṇamālikā was taking pleasure with that man right there before him, went away.

Not knowing his way along the main road, Śobhānanda did not know where to go. Just then he saw a monk who had gone through Śrāvastī on his alms round and was coming back out. Śobhānanda followed directly behind that monk. The monk went to the monastery, set his bowl and water pot together to one side, shook out his outer robe, washed his two feet, dried his two hands, drew water, picked off the leaves that had clung to him, sat down, and began to prepare his food. Śobhānanda stood before him.

The monk said to Śobhānanda: "Fair one, do you want what remains in the bowl?" Śobhānanda, perceiving and understanding clearly that if he did not eat he would die of hunger, said: "Noble one, yes, I do."

The monk gave Śobhānanda what remained in the bowl, and Śobhānanda ate it. When he had eaten, the monk asked: "Fair one, where do you come from?" Śobhānanda answered: "Noble one, I am from a region of border guardsmen, in a city called Āryarāja. There was a caravan leader named Priya, and his son am I, Śobhānanda. I came seeking many debts owed to me, but a certain improper woman did me harm."

The monk said: "Fair one, why do you not go forth into the renunciant life?" Śobhānanda thought to himself: "If I return to Āryarāja, who will be there to spit on the ground? It will fall only upon me alone." Perceiving and understanding this clearly, he said: "Noble one, I will go forth."

The monk gave Śobhānanda the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him. Then, for two or three days thereafter, he had him learn the rules of proper conduct, and said: "Fair one, a wild animal is not healed by another wild animal. Śrāvastī is vast; it is both your own domain and your father's territory — gather alms and sustain yourself."

Śobhānanda put on his lower robe in the morning, took his bowl and his Dharma robe, and entered Śrāvastī to go on the alms round.

Now the courtesan Bāṇamālikā felt remorse. She thought: "Because I desired kārṣāpaṇas I drove away the caravan leader's son Śobhānanda, who was so handsome and in the full bloom of youth — that was wrong of me. I should have known that even if such a man comes from very far away, he is exactly the sort with whom one should take pleasure and rejoice." She instructed a young female servant: "Girl, if you happen to see the caravan leader's son Śobhānanda, let him come in."

Not knowing his way around the neighborhood, Śobhānanda arrived on his alms round at none other than the very house of the improper woman.

The young female servant who had been posted as lookout saw him and, overjoyed, went to Bāṇamālikā and whispered: "My lady, the handsome Śobhānanda is at the door." Bāṇamālikā said, "Let him come in." The girl said, "He has gone forth into the religious life." Bāṇamālikā said, "Even so, let him come in."

The servant let Śobhānanda enter, and when the courtesan Bāṇamālikā saw him, she beat her breast and said: "Śobhānanda, why did you abandon a fine young man's life and go forth?" Śobhānanda replied: "Unfortunate woman — while you disport yourself in pleasure with other men right before my very eyes, how could I not go forth?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble one, a woman's domain is one of constant transgression where a man is concerned, and so I beg you to forgive me my transgression. Now please take your belongings back from me, and let us enjoy pleasure together." Śobhānanda replied: "At that time you utterly ruined me over money and material concerns — do you now wish to ruin me utterly in my moral discipline as well?" Bāṇamālikā said: "Noble one, pull the robe from outside and push it inside — pull it from inside and push it outside! What violation of moral discipline is there in that?" For Śobhānanda realized and understood: "She knows that all the elder monks who come here on their alms round do exactly this without missing a beat — and so she speaks in this way." Śobhānanda set down his alms bowl and his monastic robe in one corner, and then pulled them from outside and pushed them inside, pulled them from inside and pushed them outside — and thus found himself entirely bereft of wonder. Then Bāṇamālikā filled his alms bowl with pure and choice food and drink, gave it to him, and said: "Noble one, if you should wish to come again, please do so." Śobhānanda took his alms and departed.

Now, to whatever degree the Blessed One taught the Dharma of mental liberation and liberation through wisdom in order to free attachment from attachment, in order to free aversion from attachment, in order to free delusion from attachment — to just that degree the venerable Śobhānanda, as he sat there, became a little remorseful, became more remorseful, became deeply remorseful, and was filled with regret, overcome by regret, and said nothing at all. He became vacant, his gaze wandered, his shoulders drooped, his face fell, he had no confidence, his mind turned inward, and he sat there like a clump of blue grass that has been trodden down and left to wither and dry up.

The monks said to him: "Venerable Śobhānanda, do you not have some physical affliction, or some inner torment of mind?" And he, out of shame, neither spoke nor said anything at all.

A physician who happened to come that way was addressed by the monks: "Good young man, examine this one — what sickness does he have?" The physician began to examine him, and seeing that his senses were clear, said: "Noble ones, since his senses are clear, there is no physical illness whatsoever. However, there is an inner torment of mind that has not at all been suppressed." The monks said: "Good man, what kind of inner torment of mind does he have?" The physician said: "Noble ones, we physicians heal the body, but it is not for us to heal the mind.

"It is the noble ones themselves who heal the mind — the noble ones will understand." So saying, he departed.

The monks then addressed Mañjudeva: "Friend, here you have neither father nor mother nor any other relative. We alone are your companions in the holy life, and so we have been attending to you. Tell us what has happened."

Mañjudeva then related to those monks the whole affair in full detail.

The monks said: "The venerable one has been burned by his fruit alone. By the mere act of going forth, the venerable one has cast a blot upon the teaching." Yet even as Mañjudeva said this, those monks neither praised nor refuted him, and without having praised or refuted him they rose and went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those monks reported the whole affair in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that one too has incurred a defeat. When a monk inclines the mind toward intercourse, falls toward intercourse, and has fallen into intercourse — and because the mind inclines toward intercourse, falls toward intercourse, and has fallen into intercourse — he causes what produces outflow to draw outward and discharge inward, or to draw inward and discharge outward: he thereby incurs a defeat."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. There was a certain householder in Śrāvastī who had taken a wife from an equal family, and that wife came to her end through her own karma. He took a second, and she too came to her end. In the same way he took wife after wife up to a seventh, and she too came to her end. That householder, through the karma of having accumulated slander, came to bear the name "wife-killer."

That householder then looked for a girl, but found none to give him, and the families said: "Why should we give our daughter to you?" He sought for matchmakers, but even they said: "Why should we go about seeking a bride only to have her come into your household?" The householder, utterly discouraged by everything, began to attend to his own household chores himself. Then on another occasion a young friend of the householder came and, seeing him, asked: "What are you doing?" "I am attending to the household chores." He asked: "Why are you doing the household chores yourself?" The householder said: "I took one wife and she came to her end through her own karma. I took a second and she too came to her end. In the same way I took wives up to a seventh and she too came to her end." He said: "Why not seek others?" The householder said: "When I have sought them, no one will give them — the families say, 'Why should we give our daughter to you?'" He said: "Then why not seek matchmakers?" The householder said: "I sought them too, but they said, 'Why should we go about seeking a bride for you only to have her come into your household?'"

Not far from that householder's house there lived an old woman of a guild family, and that young friend said to the householder: "Why not bring that old guild woman in?" The householder said: "Do you want me to make a wife of her?" He said: "Let that woman — who is wicked and of evil ways — come in after turning away from those unwholesome ways."

When the young friend pressed that householder again and again, he went to the old guild woman's house and said, "Greetings, greetings." The old woman replied: "Welcome! What do you wish?" The householder said: "If I were to seek you, whose would you be?" The old woman replied: "I belong to whoever gives me food and clothing." The householder said: "Would you not everywhere practise your former afflictions?" The old woman replied: "Do I not see that I am old? I have turned back from those sinful, unvirtuous ways." The householder said: "Come in then, and I will provide you with food and clothing. You shall keep the doors and doorposts of my household." So that householder brought the old guild woman into his home, handed her the keys and the crooked keys, and said: "This is your house — I shall act according to what you give me." The old guild woman set to work keeping the doors and doorposts of that householder's home, and in not a long while, with good clothing and good food, her skin, flesh, and blood grew full and lustrous.

Then, from near the gateway of that house, the old guild woman saw a great many young women going off toward the Jeta Grove and asked them where they were going. The young women said: "We are going to the Jeta Grove." The old woman said: "Wait just until that one has put on her clothes and ornaments." So while she dressed herself in clothes and ornaments, the young women went on ahead and left. The old woman too put on her clothes and ornaments and quickly, quickly slipped out after them.

By the time those young women had entered the monastery, there was a monk inside who, with his cell door left unlocked, had fallen asleep, and whose robe had become dishevelled while his limbs had fallen into an exposed and unseemly state. Seeing him thus, those young women laughed and came back out of the monastery. The old guild woman was also going in, and when she saw those young women coming out she said: "What are you laughing at? Have you not heard the saying, 'One who laughs at a dwelling place becomes a stumbling block for oneself'?" The young women fell completely silent and went on their way.

The old guild woman, thinking to herself "I wonder whether those girls might have seen a crow or a monkey here — let it not go to waste," entered with her mind intent and making a careful inspection. And when she had gone in, she saw the monk lying there just as he was. Having seen him, desire arose in her, and the old guild woman lay herself down upon that monk and began to make advances. But the monk, overcome by deep sleep, did not wake up. The old guild woman thought to herself: "We guild women know sixty-four arts — and this ordained one knows sixty-five, inasmuch as he accepts the touch and takes possession of it while giving not a word." Having recognized and understood this, when the time came that the old guild woman had untangled herself and disengaged, she woke the monk up and said: "Noble one, my shawl — where on earth might it be? If you would be so kind, please return it."

The monk said: "You, miserable ruiner of dwellings — so long as you do not take possession of me, perhaps I might come to your house some time." The monk then thought with remorse: "Has a defeat (pārājika) not come upon me?" and he told the whole matter in detail to the other monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One then addressed that monk: "Monk, did you take possession of the touch?" He replied: "Venerable One, I did not take possession of the touch —"

"I was from the very beginning overcome by deep sleep, so how could I have taken possession of the touch?" The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, for this monk who did not take possession of the touch there is indeed no transgression. Nevertheless, I shall establish rules of conduct for monks who dwell near villages. A monk who dwells near a village, when he lies down to sleep in the daytime with his robe loosened, must either firmly bolt every door, or station a monk as a guard, or bind up his robe. If he does not firmly bolt every door, does not station a monk as a guard, and does not bind up his robe, and yet in that same way loosens his robe and lies down to sleep, he will incur a serious offense."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At Śrāvastī there was a certain monk who dwelt in a forest hermitage and had attained the fourth meditative concentration. He would go again and again to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and of the senior monks, the elders, and so the younger monks came to know him well. Then on another occasion he fell ill with a skin disease, and those younger monks said to him: "Elder, have you fallen ill with a skin disease?" He replied: "Yes, friends, it is so." They said: "Elder, why do you not go to a physician for treatment?" He replied: "Friends, this is the way of things — unwanted by many people, unpleasant to many people, disagreeable to many people, unwelcome to many people — shared by all the world: the thing called death will come, and it will lead both this disease and me myself from this world to the next. What is there, then, to be done?" They said: "Elder, has not the Blessed One declared that a virtuous person of good ethical conduct, so long as he lives, continually accumulates great merit, and for as long as great merit accumulates, for that long he shall rejoice in the higher realms? Come, please attend to the matter." When he had been pressed by them with urgency, he went to the physician. The physician, seeing him, said: "Noble one, have you fallen ill with a skin disease?" He replied: "Yes, friend, it is so. It is for that very purpose that I have come. Please prescribe medicine for me." "Noble one, take warm broth, anoint your body with mustard oil, and sit in the shade, and you will recover." "Friend, please give me some mustard oil." "Noble one, we physicians prescribe medicine; we do not supply it. If we were to supply it to each and every person, we would have neither shelter nor provisions." "As it happens, a certain great householder has come down with a disease of this kind. I have prepared mustard oil that will thoroughly cure his skin disease. Go to him and ask him for it." "Friend, he will not give it." "Noble one, go — he is a person of faith and he will give it." "Friend, then by your saying so it will be as though you yourself have given it." So he went and arrived at the house of that householder, and when the householder saw him coming from afar he said: "Noble one, have you fallen ill with a skin disease?" "Yes, friend, it is so." "Noble one, anoint your body with mustard oil and sit in the shade, and you will recover." "Friend, it is for that very purpose that I have come. I know that you have mustard oil that will thoroughly cure my skin disease — please give it to me, and it will be merit for you." "Noble one, I shall make an offering with all due solemnity —"

"— if you come to beg alms from me." "Very well, please eat." The householder satisfied him with good food, then filled a small bowl with mustard oil that would thoroughly cure the skin disease and gave it to him. The monk said "Thank you" and left, going to a forest dwelling. He put on rags, anointed his body with that mustard oil, and sat in the sun. A feeling of comfort arose in him, and he fell asleep. While he slept, the limbs of his body were seized by insects called uddzating, and having been worked upon by them his clothing fell away. Just then a great young woman who was heavy with child came along that way, and she saw the monk in that altered state. Seeing him, desire arose in her, fully enveloped in attachment to sensual objects, and she began to act upon the monk. When the monk awoke, he was too feeble to resist. When she had become free of that envelopment, she said: "Noble one, my husband is somewhere in such-and-such a direction — if you should wish, do come." The monk said: "I, a wretch who defiles the resting place, will not make even that my own — would I then come to your house?" The monk grew remorseful, thinking: "Has a defeat, a root downfall, come upon me?" He reported the full circumstances to the other monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then said to that monk: "Monk, did you not take hold of the contact?" He replied: "Venerable One, I did not take hold of the contact. Since from the very beginning I have been free from attachment to sensual objects, how could I take hold of the contact?" The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, for a monk who does not take hold of contact there is no downfall. Nevertheless, I shall establish rules of conduct for monks who dwell in forest hermitages. A forest-dwelling monk who, in the daytime, lets down his upper robe and falls asleep must either have that area enclosed with branches, fence posts, or railings, or have a guardian monk posted, or have his robes tied. If he lets down his upper robe and falls asleep without enclosing that area with branches, fence posts, or railings, without posting a guardian monk, and without tying his robes, he incurs a wrong."

The monks were uncertain, and they put all their uncertainty to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, if this monk was already free from attachment to sensual objects, why did the limbs of his body become workable?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, in one who has not been freed from attachment, the limbs of the body become workable through five causes; in one who has been freed from attachment, through four. What are the five causes for one not freed from attachment? Being overcome by defecation, being overcome by urination, being overcome by wind, being seized by insects called uddzating, and being fully enveloped by attachment to sensual objects — that is the fifth. Those are the five causes for one not freed from attachment. What are the four causes for one freed from attachment? Being overcome by defecation, being overcome by urination, being overcome by wind, and being seized by insects called uddzating. Those are the four causes for one freed from attachment. At that time this monk's limbs became workable because they were seized by insects called uddzating — and that is why his body became workable."

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga. The third bundle.

The monks, having developed doubt, asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to resolve all their doubts. "Venerable one, the elder Śubhakara, son of Kalanda, saw the Saṅgha of monks — which was without fault and without blemish — create a blemish from the very beginning in this way: through the condition of unchaste conduct a blemish was produced."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now but also in times past did he create a blemish from the very beginning in a world that was without fault and without blemish — by producing a blemish through the condition of unchaste conduct. Listen to this.

"Monks, there is a time when this world disintegrates. When the world disintegrates, most sentient beings are reborn in the class of the gods of Luminosity (the Ābhāsvara gods of the form realm). There they are form-born from mind, lacking nothing, with faculties unimpaired, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, possessed of good color, self-luminous, traversing the sky, feeding on joy, sustained by joy as their nourishment, long-lived and dwelling there for a great span of time.

"At that time this great earth becomes nothing but water and nothing but ocean. Upon that great earth turned to nothing but water and nothing but ocean, the wind causes foam to gather all over, to consolidate all over, and to spread all over — just as when boiled milk cools, the wind causes foam to gather all over it, to consolidate all over it, and to spread all over it. In the same way, upon the great earth turned to nothing but water and nothing but ocean, the wind causes foam to gather all over, to consolidate all over, and to spread all over. That becomes an earth-essence of excellent color, excellent fragrance, and excellent taste. In color it is like this: like ghee. In taste it is like this: like uncooked wild honey.

"Monks, there is also a time when this world reforms. When the world reforms, some sentient beings from that class of the gods of Luminosity, their lifespan exhausted, their merit exhausted, their store of merit depleted, die and transmigrate — and they come to be in the very same condition as human beings, arriving here. Here too they are form-born from mind, lacking nothing, with faculties unimpaired, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, possessed of good color, self-luminous, traversing the sky, feeding on joy, sustained by joy as their nourishment, long-lived and dwelling there for a great span of time.

"At that time there is no arising of the sun or moon in the world. There is no arising of stars in the world. There is no night and no day. There is no moment, no interval, no instant. There is no month, no fortnight, no season, no year. There is no female, no male — beings go simply by the count of 'sentient being, sentient being.'

"Then a certain sentient being of a covetous nature tastes the earth-essence with the tip of a finger. The more it tastes, the more it craves; the more it craves, the more it comes to eat of it, resorting to the eating of solid food. Other sentient beings then see that sentient being tasting the earth-essence with the tip of a finger — and the more it tastes, the more it craves, and the more it craves, the more it comes to eat of it, resorting to the eating of solid food. Seeing this, those sentient beings too begin to taste the earth-essence with the tip of a finger. The more they taste, the more they crave; the more they crave, the more they come to eat of it, resorting to the eating of solid food."

Because those sentient beings had begun eating the earth-essence as their food and had consumed it, hardness and heaviness arose in their bodies, and whatever fine, bright complexion they had possessed disappeared. Darkness arose in the world. Monks, it is in the nature of reality that when darkness arises in the world, the sun and moon too appear in the world. Stars appear in the world, and night and day appear, and moments, instants, and brief intervals appear, and months and fortnights and seasons and years appear. Those beings ate that food and, sustained by it, lived long and endured for a great while. Among them, whoever ate very little became endowed with fine complexion, while whoever ate a great deal became ugly in complexion. Thus, because there were two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion became manifest. And when two kinds of complexion had come to be, one sentient being would belittle another, saying: "Ha! I am endowed with fine complexion, whereas you are ugly in complexion." Because they had become proud on account of their complexion, and because they had fully taken up those sinful, unwholesome qualities, the earth-essence disappeared.

Monks, when the earth-essence had disappeared for those sentient beings, they gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them, lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" Just as today, when people find some good and delicious food, they use the old words that have been preserved in letters, giving voice to them and saying: "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" — in the very same way, those sentient beings too, when the earth-essence was gone, gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them, lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" — yet what those words mean they do not know.

Monks, when the earth-essence had disappeared for those sentient beings, there arose earth-cream splendid in color, splendid in fragrance, and splendid in taste. In color it was like the kuṅkuma flower. In taste it was like fresh honey of young bees, unboiled. Those beings ate that and, sustained by it, lived long and endured for a great while. Among them, whoever ate very little became endowed with fine complexion, while whoever ate a great deal became ugly in complexion. Thus, because there were two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion became manifest. And when two kinds of complexion had come to be, one sentient being would belittle another, saying: "Ha! I am endowed with fine complexion, whereas you are ugly in complexion." Because they had become proud on account of their complexion, and because they had fully taken up those sinful, unwholesome qualities, the earth-cream disappeared.

Monks, when the earth-cream had disappeared for those sentient beings, they gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them, lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Alas! Alas!" Just as today, when people are struck by some suffering or mental distress, they use the old words that have been preserved in letters, giving voice to them and saying: "Alas! Alas!" — in the very same way, those sentient beings too, when the earth-cream was gone, gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them,

lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Alas! Alas!" — yet even as they said "Alas! Alas!," they did not know the meaning of what was said; they did not know the meaning of what was said.

Monks, when the earth-cream had disappeared for those sentient beings, a grove of bamboo-shoots appeared — its color magnificent, its fragrance magnificent, its taste magnificent. Its color was like this: like the flower of the kadam tree. Its taste was like this: like unboiled honey of wild bees. Those beings ate of it and, sustained by that food, lived long and endured for a great time. Of those who ate but little, their complexion became beautiful; of those who ate much, their complexion became poor. And so it was that, on account of two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion appeared. When two kinds of complexion appeared, one sentient being would look down upon another sentient being, saying: "Hey, sentient being! I have a beautiful complexion, while you have a poor complexion!" — and so they would despise one another. Because they had become arrogant on account of their complexion, through taking up those very sinful, unwholesome qualities, the grove of bamboo-shoots disappeared.

Monks, when the grove of bamboo-shoots had disappeared for those sentient beings, they gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them, lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Begone! Begone!" — just as today, when people are reviled with some sharp abuse, they use those very same old words that have been preserved in letters, giving voice to them and saying: "Begone! Begone!" — in the very same way, those sentient beings too, when the grove of bamboo-shoots was gone, gathered together, and grief arose in them, despondency arose in them, lamentation arose in them, and they cried out: "Begone! Begone!" — yet even as they said "Begone! Begone!," they did not know the meaning of what was said; they did not know the meaning of what was said.

Monks, when the grove of bamboo-shoots had disappeared for those sentient beings, rice appeared — unsown, uncultivated, without husk, without chaff, pure and clean, ripening in one day, so that when threshed in the evening it was restored by morning, and when threshed in the morning it was restored by evening; indeed, however much was threshed, it kept replenishing itself and showed no sign of diminishing. Those beings ate of it and, sustained by that food, lived long and endured for a great time.

Because those sentient beings ate the uncooked grain of that unsown, uncultivated rice as their beginning of food, differentiated faculties arose among them: some were endowed with male faculties, and some were endowed with female faculties. And then those who were endowed with male faculties and those who were endowed with female faculties looked upon one another eye to eye. The more they looked upon one another eye to eye, the more attachment arose in them. The more attachment arose in them, the more they came together. The more they came together, the more they engaged in wrong conduct. Other sentient beings, seeing sentient beings engage in wrong conduct, threw clods of earth, threw ashes, threw sand and gravel, saying aloud: "Perish, wicked being! Perish, wicked being! Do your wicked deed elsewhere! Why, O sentient being, do you harm another sentient being?" — just as today —

just as today, when sentient beings take a bride or a groom, flour is scattered, and fragrant substances, flowers, fruits, and grains are scattered as well, and the words are spoken, "May you be at ease together" — so too, in that ancient time, when those sentient beings saw sentient beings engage in wrong conduct with other sentient beings, they threw clods of earth and threw ashes, sand, and gravel, saying aloud: "Perish, wicked being! Perish, wicked being! Why, O sentient being, do you harm another sentient being?"

Monks, thus what was formerly known as contrary to Dharma is now known as Dharma; what was formerly known as contrary to discipline is now known as discipline; and what was formerly deserving of reproach is now deserving of praise. They would abstain from it for a single day, or for two or three or even seven days. Because those sinful sentient beings felt deep revulsion toward that ignoble and unworthy conduct, they entered upon a vow of restraint. Then they began to build enclosures, saying to one another, "Let us do what should not be done here somewhere else; let us do what should not be done here somewhere else" — and from this saying arose the name "house" (khyim khyim, meaning "home"). Monks, this was the very first arising in the world of all the affairs of the household; and that came about through Dharma, not through what is contrary to Dharma. The Dharma here is this: it is the supreme Dharma of the victorious lords of kings.

Monks, at that time and at that moment, the very first sentient being who rebuked another sentient being for that conduct — that was none other than Kalandaka's son Svāgata. Just as at that time he introduced the very first blemish into a world that was flawless and free of turbulence, namely by making unchaste conduct the occasion for turbulence, so now too he has introduced the very first blemish into the flawless and untarnished Saṅgha of monks, making unchaste conduct the occasion for turbulence.

Monks, therefore train yourselves thus: strive to abandon attachment, strive to abandon aversion, strive to abandon delusion. Train yourselves thus, O monks. For one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by acute sensation, there is no transgression. The first defeat is hereby complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at Veṇuvana. At that time the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, was staying in a secluded forest dwelling at Rājagṛha. Then, when the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, entered Rājagṛha on alms round, the cow-herders, cattle-herders, grass-cutters, wood-cutters, travelers, and road-side vendors of Rājagṛha broke up and ransacked the secluded grove, carrying off all the grass and wood. Afterward, when the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, returned, he saw that the grove had been broken up and ransacked and that all the grass and wood had been carried off. Seeing this, he gathered grass and wood and made another shelter. When the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, went on alms round into Rājagṛha a second and a third time, the cow-herders, cattle-herders, grass-cutters, wood-cutters, travelers, and road-side vendors of Rājagṛha

broke up and ransacked the secluded grove, carrying off all the grass and wood. Afterward, when the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, returned, he saw that the grove had been broken up and ransacked and that all the grass and wood had been carried off.

Then the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, thought to himself: "How painful it is, how unbearable, that from the moment I entered upon my alms-round in Rājagṛha, the cow-herders, cattle-herders, grass-cutters, wood-cutters, travelers, and road-side vendors of Rājagṛha have now broken up and ransacked the grove and carried off all the grass and wood — not once, not twice, but three times. I am skilled in my father's craft and trade. Let me build all the dwelling places out of clay."

And so the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, trod the clay with his body again and again, rinsed it with water free of living creatures, and set about building the foundation, the roof, the pillars, and the upper courses of walls for the dwelling. He also made niches for robes, robe-hooks, platforms, seats, stools, low stools, and door-panels. When he saw that the clay had dried, he coated it with pigment and painted it, then pressed in wood, dung, and dry grass, firing it in a kiln. That dwelling, so perfectly fired and so supremely finished, turned red — a deep red color, radiant with a crimson glow — like the bandhujīvaka flower.

Then the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, thought to himself: "My dwelling is perfectly fired and supremely finished, red, deep red in color, radiant with a crimson glow, like the bandhujīvaka flower. Let me now hold a housewarming festival for the dwelling."

And so the monk Dhanavatī, formerly a potter, had the neighboring monks look after the dwelling, and taking his bowl and robe he went off on a walking tour through the countryside.

Now, by the very nature of things, the Buddha, the Blessed One, while living and dwelling, vital and well, would from time to time — in accordance with those who were to be tamed — travel down to the hells, travel through the realms of animals, travel through the realms of hungry ghosts, travel through the realms of gods, travel through the countryside, travel along river banks, travel through forests, travel through charnel grounds, travel through mountains, and travel to monastic halls.

On this occasion, since the Blessed One intended to travel to monastic halls, he said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and inform the monks: 'The Tathāgata is now setting out to tour the monastic halls. Whichever of you wishes to accompany the Tathāgata on a tour of the monastic halls — let him take his robes.'"

The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One and replied "As the Blessed One commands," took up a bunch of keys, and walking from one courtyard to another, from one monastic hall to another, from one dwelling to another — going directly and without deviation through the walking paths — he saw the monks and said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is setting out to tour the monastic halls. Whichever of you wishes to accompany the Blessed One on a tour of the monastic halls — let him take his robes."

Those monks, having heard the venerable Ānanda and replied "As the elder commands," took their robes and went to where the Blessed One was.

Then the Blessed One, together with a great many monks, set out on a tour of the monastic halls.

Gradually touring the monastic halls and proceeding onward, the Blessed One arrived at the place where the former potter, the monk Nandaka, had his monastic hall. The Blessed One saw that the dwelling of the former potter, the monk Nandaka, was deeply dyed, most excellently dyed, red, of a red hue, of a red glow — just like the bandhujiīvaka flower. Having seen this, he addressed the monks: "Monks, whose dwelling is this?" "Venerable sir, it belongs to the former potter, the monk Nandaka." "Monks, on account of this, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) will slander us, saying: 'While the ascetic Gautama is still alive, among his hearers there have appeared certain teachings resembling the defilement-prone views of outsiders.' Therefore, tear down and dismantle that dwelling."

And so those monks, by the command and instruction of the Teacher, tore down and dismantled the dwelling. The Blessed One, having had the dwelling torn down and dismantled, departed.

When the former potter, the monk Nandaka, arrived, he saw his dwelling torn down and dismantled. Upon seeing this he said to the monks nearby: "Venerable ones, who has torn down and dismantled my dwelling?" "Venerable sir, it was the monks, by the command and instruction of the Teacher." "If the Blessed One, the lord of Dharma, the Sugata, the lord of Dharma, tore it down, then the tearing down was good."

At that time in the city of Rājagṛha, a report of the former potter, the monk Nandaka, mixed with the talk of the great retinue of foresters, went about, and people said: "There is a companion worth speaking of and spending time with."

Then the former potter, the monk Nandaka, thought to himself: "In the city of Rājagṛha, among the great retinue of foresters, there is someone spreading a report about me, saying I am a companion worth speaking of and spending time with. For this reason I should make all my dwelling furnishings from wood." Knowing and understanding this, he went to where the great retinue of foresters was, and going there, he said to the great retinue of foresters: "Dear friend, know this: King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, who arose from Māgadhā, granted me certain timbers — I wish to have them brought. Please give them to me. Noble one, if the deity requests timber from you as a petition, it is a fine petition — take whatever you like." Then the former potter, the monk Nandaka, from among those timbers belonging to King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady — timbers that had been set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to give to just anyone — he drew out some of the timber, had it cut and split, and had it carried away.

Now one of the great retinue of city guards, while patrolling the outer road of the fortress of Rājagṛha, saw someone drawing out timber — from those timbers of King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, that had been set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to give to just anyone — cutting and splitting it and hauling it away.

Upon seeing this, he saw that from the timbers of King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady — set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to give to just anyone — some timber had been drawn out, cut, split, and hauled away, and so —

he became afraid, alarmed, and his hair stood on end, thinking: might a spy, a thief, or some enemy have entered the city of Rājagṛha belonging to King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage?

He then went to where the chief of the great timber-guard was, and having gone there, he said this to the chief of the great timber-guard: "Friend, know this. While I was making my rounds along the outer roads of the fortress of the city of Rājagṛha, I saw that from the timbers of King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage — set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to give to just anyone — some timber had been drawn out, cut, split, and hauled away. Having seen this, I became afraid, alarmed, and my hair stood on end, thinking: might a spy, a thief, or some enemy have entered the city of Rājagṛha belonging to King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage — because some timber had been drawn out, cut, split, and hauled away from those timbers set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to give to just anyone? Friend, did you give the timber to anyone?"

"Friend, I did not give it to anyone. However, previously the monk Norchen, a potter by trade, came and said this: 'Friend, know this. King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage, gave me some timber, and I wish to haul it away — please give it to me.' And I said to him: 'Noble one, if the king has authorized the timber for you, then by all means, take as much as you wish.' And he hauled it away — or did he not?"

Then the chief of the great city-guard went to where King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage, was, and having gone there, spoke these words to King Ajātaśatru, son of the Vaidehi lady, born of the Māgadhā lineage: "May your majesty know this. While I was making my rounds along the outer roads of the fortress of the city of Rājagṛha, I saw that from the royal timbers — set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve out of your majesty's concern for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy for your majesty to bestow upon just anyone — some timber had been drawn out, cut, split, and hauled away. Having seen this, I became afraid, alarmed, and my hair stood on end, thinking: might a spy, a thief, or some enemy have entered your majesty's city of Rājagṛha — because some timber had been drawn out, cut, split, and hauled away from those timbers kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve out of your majesty's concern for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to bestow upon just anyone? And so I went to where the chief of the great timber-guard was, and having gone there, I said to the chief of the great timber-guard: 'Friend, know this. While I was making my rounds along the outer roads of the fortress of the city of Rājagṛha, I saw that from the timbers of your majesty — set aside, kept with great secrecy, guarded with great care, placed in reserve for the purpose of repairing what was broken and crumbled in the city of Rājagṛha, and not easy to bestow upon just anyone — some timber had been drawn out, cut,

and hauled away. If I were to say, "Friend, have you given the timber to someone?" and he were to reply, "Friend, I have given it to no one — however, previously the monk Norchen, a former potter, came and said this: 'Friend, know this. King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, has given me those timbers. I wish to have them transported, so give them to me.' And I said to him, 'Noble one, if His Majesty has authorized you to receive the reserved timbers, then the authorization is good — take whatever you please.' Did he then haul them away, or did that not happen?" — and if I were to ask, "Did His Majesty bestow the reserved timbers upon someone?" — "Respected friend, he gave them to no one." — this is what the chief of the great timber-guard said.

Then King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, said to a man: "Respected friend, come here. Go to where the chief of the great timber-guard is, and when you have gone there, say to him: 'Respected friend, King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, speaks to you thus.'" The man replied, "As His Majesty commands," and having received the order from King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, he went to where the chief of the great timber-guard was, and when he had arrived he said to him: "Friend, know this. King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, speaks to you."

The chief of the great timber-guard replied, "As His Majesty commands," and having received this from the man, he hastened to the presence of King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch.

Now at that moment the monk Norchen, the former potter, had for some reason gone up into Rājagṛha, and the chief of the great timber-guard caught sight of the monk Norchen, the former potter, from some distance away. Having seen him, he said to the monk Norchen, the former potter: "Noble one, please be informed — I summoned you on account of those reserved timbers. Friend, you should go ahead, and I too shall come."

Then the chief of the great timber-guard, the monk Norchen the former potter, and that man all went to where King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, was staying, and they waited at the gate of the palace.

Then that man went to where King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, was, and having arrived he said to King Ajātaśatru: "Your Majesty, the chief of the great timber-guard is waiting at the gate. That monk, too, has come along without being summoned. Your Majesty, please set aside the chief of the great timber-guard for the moment and first allow that monk to enter." The man replied, "As His Majesty commands," and having received this from King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, he went to where the monk Norchen, the former potter, was, and said to him: "Noble one, please be informed — King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, speaks to you."

The monk Norchen, the former potter, replied, "As His Majesty commands," and having received this from the man, he went to where King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, was. Having arrived, he greeted King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, with the word "Ārogya," and sat to one side.

As the monk Norchen, the former potter, sat to one side, King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, spoke to him thus: "Noble one, is it permissible to take timber that has not been given? It is not permissible, Your Majesty." "Then why did you take it?" "Because Your Majesty had granted it." "The noble one does not remember. I will recall what His Majesty intended. Not long after His Majesty assumed lordship and sovereign power over his father's kingdom, I issued a great royal proclamation of this kind to those ascetics and brahmins throughout my realm who are reputed to be of good character — that from that day forth they might freely make use of grass, timber, and water that had not been given — and I had it publicly declared with a lion's roar throughout the assembly with full acceptance. Noble one, it is on the basis of what I, for my part, had not seized that I spoke thus; what is involved here is something that had indeed been seized." "Your Majesty, whatever has not been seized — what has Your Majesty to do with that?"

When this was said, King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, grew furious and agitated and wrathful, and his displeasure showed: he furrowed his brow and raised three forehead-veins, creased his brow in anger, distorted his face, widened his eyes, and rubbed both his palms together, and said: "You of the class of slain ascetics — go! And do not act like that again!"

Then the wise ones of the retinue, knowing that King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, was so fierce, so rough, so formidable, and so utterly without hesitation, cried out in a great outcry, raising their voices high with a great clamor: "It is astonishing that he has been dismissed with the empty phrase 'You of the class of slain ascetics'!"

Then the monk Norchen, the former potter, went to the assembly hall and said to the monks: "Venerable ones, King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, has accused me and threatened me with the loss of my life." The monks asked, "Why?" He related to the monks what had occurred, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, put on your patched robe, go together with a wandering ascetic who accompanies monks from behind, enter Rājagṛha, and take up a position on the main road of the city of Rājagṛha, and on the lanes, the crossroads, the intersections, and at the places where proclamations are made. Then question the faithful and the unfaithful, the brahmins and householders, the villagers and townspeople, the wealthy and the merchants and the caravan leaders — ask them: 'Has King Ajātaśatru, born of the Vṛji lineage through the Māgadhā branch, accused someone and threatened him with the loss of his life for taking what had not been given?'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having received this from the Blessed One, he entered Rājagṛha and took up a position on the main road of the city of Rājagṛha, and on the lanes, the crossroads, the intersections, and at the places where proclamations are made, and he spoke to the faithful and the unfaithful, the brahmins and householders, the villagers and townspeople, the wealthy and the merchants and the caravan leaders:

"O wise ones, by how much has King Ajātaśatru of the Māgadhā branch, born of the Vṛji lineage, accused someone and threatened him with the loss of his life for taking what had not been given?" They replied: "Venerable Ānanda, by five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas."

Then the venerable Ānanda departed from Rājagṛha, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable One, I have just now seen fit to undertake this matter. Following a monk who was going along in the manner of a monk, I entered Rājagṛha and went to the main road of the city of Rājagṛha, and to the lanes, the crossroads, the intersections, and the places where proclamations are made, and I asked the faithful and the unfaithful, the brahmins and householders, the villagers and townspeople, the wealthy and the merchants and the caravan leaders: 'O wise ones, by how much has King Ajātaśatru of the Māgadhā branch accused someone and threatened him with the loss of his life for taking what had not been given?' And from their mouths came the reply: 'Venerable Ānanda, by five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas.'"

Then, on account of this occurrence and this basis and this occasion, the Blessed One convened an assembly of the community of monks. Now, a Tathāgata, when he beholds the two aspects of purpose, convenes the community of monks — as follows: so that it may be universally known to my hearers, and so that I may properly establish a rule of training in the Vinaya. The blessed buddhas act upon occasion with full knowing: they act with full knowing, and they do not act without knowing; they act at the right time, and they do not act at the wrong time; they act when there is purpose, and they do not act when there is no purpose. Thus the blessed buddhas, by the rule of propriety, refrain from acting when there is no purpose. And in this regard, since the blessed buddhas know the right time for acting when there is purpose, the Blessed One had previously asked the monk Nandaka the Potter: "Nandaka, is it true that you have done something as unseemly as that?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One then rebuked him: "That conduct is unworthy of a renunciant, is not fitting, is not proper, and is not in accord with the discipline — it is not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Nandaka, I have taught the Dharma of mental liberation and wisdom liberation in order to free attachment from attachment, and taught the Dharma of mental liberation and wisdom liberation in order to free aversion from attachment and delusion from attachment. Why have you done something so unseemly?" And thus he rebuked him.

Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, having seen ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers is to be established in the Vinaya — as follows: for the sake of uniting the Saṅgha; for the sake of the well-being of the Saṅgha; for the sake of the comfort of the Saṅgha; for the sake of restraining those individuals who are shameless and difficult to admonish; for the sake of the ease of those who are conscientious; for the sake of bringing those who are not yet truly faithful to faith; for the sake of increasing the faith of those who are already faithful; for the sake of restraining the defilements of this present life; for the sake of warding off those of future lives; and

for the sake of my pure conduct being widely beneficial to the many, and for the sake of its being correctly taught and lasting long among gods and humans alike.

My hearers are to be trained in the following rule, which is to be proclaimed as a basis of training in the Vinaya: Furthermore, whatever monk takes what has not been given that belongs to others residing in a village or residing in the wilderness — taking it in the category of theft — however much he takes without it being given, if he is then seized by a king or a great minister and told, "You, person, are a thief, a fool, a dullard, a robber," and is killed, or bound, or expelled — if a monk takes in such a manner what has not been given, that monk too has incurred defeat and is not to remain.

Now, as for the phrase "whatever monk": monks are of four kinds — the monk in name only, the monk by self-declaration, the monk for the sake of begging, and the monk who is such by reason of having destroyed the afflictions. In the present context, since one who cannot properly be settled by a formal motion or by a fourfold act of the Saṅgha is not qualified for full ordination, the one who has received full ordination is to be understood as the monk intended. Therefore the phrase "whatever monk" is used.

The phrase "belonging to others" refers to what belongs to men, women, or people of indeterminate sex.

"Residing in a village" means residing within an enclosure.

"Residing in the wilderness" means residing outside an enclosure.

"Not given" means not given by any man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex in connection with that property.

"In the category of theft" means that whatever is not given falls into the category of theft.

"Takes" means if one takes it.

"However much he takes without it being given" means to the value of five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas.

"A king" — this is as follows: if a woman has been anointed with sovereignty over a kingdom, she too is a king anointed at the crown in the royal warrior caste; and if one of the warrior caste, brahmin caste, merchant caste, or common caste has been anointed with sovereignty over a kingdom, that person too is a king anointed at the crown in the royal warrior caste.

"A great minister" refers to other than that — ministers, accountants, and those of high standing who govern the kingdom, who live by sharing a common password and whose livelihood depends upon that office.

"Seized" means apprehended.

The words "You, person, are a thief, a fool, a dullard, a robber" — these are words of insult.

"Saying" means declaring and proclaiming.

"Killed" means deprived of life.

"Bound" means bound with any of the three kinds of restraints — those made of iron, those made of wood, and those made of grass.

"Or expelled" means rendered without a place of resort, whatever form that may take.

"Monk" means whoever possesses the qualities of a monk. What are the qualities of a monk? Full ordination. What is full ordination? It is: the performance of the act of a formal motion and fourfold procedure; the scrutiny; the complete scrutiny; the bringing to completion; the full bringing to completion; and that individual's acceptance, explicit acceptance, non-reversal, and the state of non-reversal — as expressed in speech, in words, in conventional designation, in utterance, in statement, in definitive words, in the course of words, in the sound of words, in verbal action, and in verbal expression.

"That too" is a particle of specification and comprehensiveness.

"Has incurred defeat" means: it has come to its end; it is a transgression; it is a fall; it is a downfall; it is a severance; and it is what is contrary to one's aspiration.

Furthermore, whoever commits that transgression incurs, the very moment it is committed, the state of being unfit to serve as a monk, unfit to serve as a contemplative (śramaṇa), and unfit to be called a son of the Śākyas. He falls away from the substance of being a monk; his conduct as a contemplative is shattered; he is degraded, broken, fallen, and defeated. His conduct as a contemplative cannot be restored. It is just like this: when the top of a palm tree is cut off, it cannot turn green again, it cannot grow and spread and flourish. In the same way, when a monk has committed such an act, the very moment it is committed he becomes unfit to serve as a monk, unfit to serve as a contemplative, and unfit to be called a son of the Śākyas. He falls away from the substance of being a monk; his conduct as a contemplative is shattered; he is degraded, broken, fallen, and defeated. His conduct as a contemplative cannot be restored. It is for this reason that it was declared: "He has incurred defeat."

"He shall not dwell" means: monks shall not dwell together with such a person in the restoration ceremony, in the invitation ceremony, in a single motion, in a motion with one proclamation, or in a motion with three proclamations. Nor shall such a person be appointed to any of the twelve categories of persons. It is for this reason that it was declared: "He shall not dwell."

Now, how does a transgression come about?

Summary verse:

By oneself, by one not given,
by mind, by complete appropriation,
by perception, with four as the fourth —
the fifth is made twofold.

Summary verse:

By oneself, by what is not given,
by mind, by complete appropriation,
by perception, with four as the fourth —
the fifth is rendered twofold.

If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others — by any of three causes — he incurs defeat. What are the three? By oneself, by arrangement, or by commission.

How is it "by oneself"? By stealing oneself, by entering upon theft oneself, or by moving an object from place to place oneself. That is how it is "by oneself."

How is it "by arrangement"? By stealing through arrangement, by entering upon theft through arrangement, or by moving an object from place to place through arrangement. That is how it is "by arrangement."

How is it "by commission"? By stealing through commission of another, by entering upon theft through commission, or by moving an object from place to place through commission. That is how it is "by commission."

If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those three causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by three causes, he incurs defeat. What are the three? It is not given, it is heavy in value, and it is moved from place to place. How is it "not given"? When it has not been given by any man, woman, or person of the third gender. That is how it is "not given." How is it "heavy in value"? When it is five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas. That is how it is "heavy in value." How is it "moved from place to place"? When an object is taken from the location where it had been placed and moved to another location. That is how it is "moved from place to place."

If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those three causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by three causes, he incurs defeat. What are the three? Forming the intention, exerting effort, and moving it from place to place. How is it "forming the intention"? When a mind of theft has arisen and is present. That is how it is "forming the intention." How is it "exerting effort"? By exerting effort with the hands and feet.

That is how it is "exerting effort." How is it "moving from place to place"? One lifts it from the place where it had been set down and puts it in another place. That is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those three causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by three causes, he incurs defeat. What are the three? Being held by another, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "being held by another"? It is this: what is heavy in value is held by another man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. That is how it is "being held by another." How is it "being heavy in value"? Five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas. That is how it is "being heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? One lifts it from the place where it had been set down and puts it in another place. That is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those three causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by three causes, he incurs defeat. What are the three? Perceiving it as held by another, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "perceiving it as held by another"? It is this: the monk perceives these things of heavy value as being held by another man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. That is how it is "perceiving it as held by another." How is it "being heavy in value"? Five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas. That is how it is "being heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? One lifts it from the place where it had been set down and puts it in another place. That is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those three causes, he incurs defeat.

If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by four causes, he incurs defeat. What are the four? Being held by another, perceiving it as held by another, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "being held by another"? It is this: what is heavy in value is held by another man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. That is how it is "being held by another." How is it "perceiving it as held by another"? It is this: the monk perceives these things of heavy value as being held by another man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex. That is how it is "perceiving it as held by another." How is it "being heavy in value"? Five māṣakas, or more than five māṣakas. That is how it is "being heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? One lifts it from the place where it had been set down and puts it in another place. That is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those four causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by four causes, he incurs defeat. What are the four? Forming the intention, exerting effort, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "forming the intention"? A mind of theft has arisen and is present. That is how it is "forming the intention." How is it "exerting effort"? By exerting effort with the hands and feet.

That is how it is "exerting effort." How is it "heavy in value"? Five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas — that is how it is "heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? It is lifted from the place where it had been set down and placed in another place — that is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those four causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by four causes, he incurs defeat. What are the four? Being guarded, being claimed as one's own, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "being guarded"? People's valuable belongings have been placed in containers such as large bronze vessels, copper vessels, earthenware vessels, boxes, and leather bags, and moreover guards of the following kinds have been stationed there — troops of elephants, troops of cavalry, troops of charioteers, and troops of foot soldiers — and they are standing guard there. That is how it is "being guarded." How is it "being claimed as one's own"? People's valuable belongings have previously been placed in containers such as large bronze vessels, copper vessels, earthenware vessels, boxes, and leather bags, and those people claim those things as their own, saying, "These belong to us." That is how it is "being claimed as one's own." How is it "heavy in value"? Five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas — that is how it is "heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? It is lifted from the place where it had been set down and placed in another place — that is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those four causes, he incurs defeat.

Furthermore, if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by four causes, he incurs defeat. What are the four? Being guarded without being claimed as one's own, being claimed as one's own without being guarded, being heavy in value, and moving from place to place. How is it "being guarded without being claimed as one's own"? Bandits have sacked villages, towns, and districts, gathering everything into the wilderness, and there, when the people who owned those things have fled, robbers seize those stolen goods from them, pile them up, and keep watch over them without claiming them as their own. That is how it is "being guarded without being claimed as one's own." How is it "being claimed as one's own without being guarded"? People's valuable belongings have previously been placed in containers such as large bronze vessels, copper vessels, earthenware vessels, boxes, and leather bags, and those people claim those things as their own, saying, "These belong to us," but guards of the following kinds — troops of elephants, troops of cavalry, troops of charioteers, and troops of foot soldiers — have not been stationed there. That is how it is "being claimed as one's own without being guarded." How is it "heavy in value"? Five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas — that is how it is "heavy in value." How is it "moving from place to place"? It is lifted from the place where it had been set down and placed in another place — that is how it is "moving from place to place." If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those four causes, he incurs defeat.

If a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by five causes, he incurs defeat. What are the five? Not taking it with the perception that it is one's own, not taking it with the perception of entrusting it, not taking it with the perception that it is temporary, not making it known to another while taking it, and

with a stealing mind present in him — if a monk takes, without it being given, what is heavy in value belonging to others by those five causes, he incurs defeat. By five causes there is no transgression. What are the five? Taking it with the perception that it is one's own, taking it with the perception of entrusting it, taking it with the perception that it is temporary, making it known to another while taking it, and with no stealing mind present in him — by those five causes there is no transgression.

The Vinaya Analysis, the Fourth Fascicle. The summary verse:

Resting on the ground, resting in a vessel,
resting in a sack, resting in a pit —
the fifth is the root remedies;
these are the properly collected sections.

Now, what is heavy in value belonging to others — namely, neck ornaments, bracelets with decorations, arm ornaments, necklaces, finger rings, and strings of pearls — that is resting on the ground: if a monk, applying himself to them, lifts them from their resting place, puts on his lower robe, and sets off, then for as long as he has not grasped them firmly and not tucked them away, that constitutes a wrongdoing. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense. If that ground is smooth and of a single expanse, it is to be declared as a single case. If it is uneven, or cracked, or marked with writing, or variegated with many colors, it is to be declared as separate cases.
