Now, what is heavy in value belonging to others — namely, neck ornaments, bracelets with decorations, arm ornaments, necklaces, finger rings, and strings of pearls — that is resting in a vessel: if a monk, applying himself to them, lifts them from their resting place, puts on his lower robe, and sets off, then for as long as he has not grasped them firmly and not tucked them away, that constitutes a wrongdoing. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense. If that vessel is smooth and of a single piece, it is to be declared as a single case. If it is uneven, or cracked, or has a seam, or is marked with writing, or variegated with many colors, it is to be declared as separate cases.

Now, what is heavy in value belonging to others — namely, neck ornaments, bracelets with decorations, arm ornaments, necklaces, finger rings, and strings of pearls — that is resting in a sack: if a monk, applying himself to them, lifts them from their resting place, puts on his lower robe, and sets off, then for as long as he has not grasped them firmly and not tucked them away, that constitutes a wrongdoing. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense. If that sack is filled with grain of a single color, it is to be declared as a single case. If it is filled with grain of many different colors, it is to be declared as separate cases.

Now, what is heavy in value belonging to others — namely,

necklaces, bracelets with ornaments, armlets, pendants, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls lying in a basket — when a monk applies himself to them, causing them to rise from their seat, putting on his lower robe, and setting out, for as long as he does not grasp them firmly and does not tuck them away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, and brings them out and hoists them onto his shoulder, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense.

If that basket is filled with grain of a single color, it is to be declared as a single case. If it is filled with grain of many different colors, it is to be declared as separate cases. If that basket is full and the rim and mouth are intact, it is to be declared as a single case. If it is not full, then whatever divisions are made within it — whether separated by wooden partitions, by clay partitions, or by reed partitions — each of those is to be declared as a separate case.

Now, what is the boundary of the root action of persons in such matters — namely, a pack-saddle, fleeces, a mortar, a window-frame, a white donkey, and the like, standing nearby — when a monk applies himself to them, causing them to rise from their seat, putting on his lower robe, and setting out, for as long as he does not grasp them firmly and does not tuck them away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, brings them out, and hoists them onto his shoulder, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense.

Summary verse:
In the sky, three are to be counted;
birds, with three ornaments,
drawn by secret mantras —
this gathers the correct groupings.

Now, when cloths of many different colors have been laid out on the rooftops of people's houses, and a monk applies himself to them, causing them to rise from their seat, putting on his lower robe, setting out, erecting a ladder, adjusting the rungs and ropes of the ladder, casting off the hanging rope, and climbing up, yet for as long as he does not grasp them firmly and does not tuck them away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps them firmly, tucks them away, gathers up the cloths, and ties them into a bundle, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense.

Now, when cloths that have been laid out by a dyer are carried off by the wind and fall upon the walking paths, gardens, or gatehouses of monks, and a monk applies himself to them, causing them to rise from their seat, putting on his lower robe, and setting out, yet for as long as he does not grasp them firmly and does not tuck them away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps them firmly, tucks them away, gathers up the cloths, and ties them into a bundle, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense.

Now, on multi-storied buildings or atop multi-storied buildings, heavy valuables belonging to people — namely, necklaces,

anklets with ornaments, armlets, necklaces, finger-rings, and strings of pearls that have been set down — when a monk, applying himself to these, rises from his seat, puts on his lower robe, sets out, picks up the objects, adjusts a ladder or a rope-and-rung device, lets go of a supporting rope, and climbs up, yet for as long as he does not grasp them firmly and does not tuck them away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps them firmly and tucks them away, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a grave offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

Now, in people's homes or at waterside locations, decorative trees that have been grown and adorned with various ornaments — namely, necklaces, anklets with ornaments, armlets, necklaces, finger-rings, strings of pearls — and from which any food-lure ornament whatsoever is suspended: when a monk, applying himself to these, rises from his seat, puts on his lower robe, sets out, and takes hold of a bird, yet for as long as he does not grasp the ornament firmly and does not tuck it away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps it firmly and tucks it away, yet for as long as he has not moved it from place to place, and if he thinks, "I will steal this from the bird, not from a person," that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a grave offense; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense. But if he thinks, "I will steal from a person — where indeed is the ornament on the bird?" then for as long as he has not moved it from place to place, that constitutes a grave offense. If he moves it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

Now, in people's multi-storied buildings or on terraces, various ornaments have been set down — namely, necklaces, anklets with ornaments, armlets, necklaces, finger-rings, and strings of pearls — and from these any food-lure ornament whatsoever is suspended: when a monk, applying himself to these, rises from his seat, puts on his lower robe, sets out, and takes hold of a bird, yet for as long as he does not grasp the ornament firmly and does not tuck it away, that constitutes a serious offense. When he grasps it firmly and tucks it away, yet for as long as he has not moved it from place to place, and if he thinks, "I will steal this from the bird, not from a person," that constitutes a serious offense. If he moves it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a grave offense; if the object is not complete, he incurs a serious offense. But if he thinks, "I will steal from a person — where indeed is the ornament on the bird?" then for as long as he has not moved it from place to place, that constitutes a grave offense. If he moves it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

Now, in people's homes or at waterside locations, the following pet birds have been kept — namely, parrots, or mynah birds, or cuckoos, or kalavinka birds, or peacocks — and these have been adorned with various ornaments, namely necklaces, anklets with ornaments,

arm ornaments, necklaces, finger rings, and clusters of pearls. If a monk, with the intention of stealing from a person, causes the bird to rise from its perch, puts on a lower robe, starts to walk, and takes hold of the bird, then for as long as he has not yet touched the ornaments or made them slip off, that constitutes a grave offense. If he touches them and makes them slip off, yet for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, and he thinks to himself, "I shall steal from the bird, not from a person" — that too constitutes a grave offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense. If, however, he thinks to himself, "I shall steal from the person — where indeed is any ornament on the bird?" then for as long as he has not moved them from place to place, that constitutes a grave offense. If he moves them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

Regarding the two kinds of treasure — treasure that has an owner and treasure that has no owner — if a monk, for the sake of a treasure that has an owner, rises from his seat, puts on a lower robe, draws a ritual circle, plants khadira-wood pegs at the four directions, surrounds them with five-colored threads, kindles a fire, inserts fuel for the fire offering, recites secret mantras, and does all this thinking, "May there come to me a treasure that has an owner, and may there not come one that has no owner," then if indeed a treasure that has an owner comes to him and one without an owner does not come, for as long as it has not yet appeared before his eyes, that constitutes a grave offense. If it does appear before his eyes, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk makes preparations for a treasure that has an owner, yet thinks to himself, "May there come to me a treasure that has no owner, and may one that has an owner not come," then if indeed a treasure without an owner comes to him and one with an owner does not come, for as long as it has not yet appeared before his eyes, that constitutes a grave offense. If it does appear before his eyes, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a grave offense; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, for the sake of a treasure that has no owner, rises from his seat, puts on a lower robe, draws a ritual circle, plants khadira-wood pegs at the four directions, surrounds them with five-colored threads, kindles a fire, inserts fuel for the fire offering, recites secret mantras, and does all this thinking, "May there come to me a treasure that has no owner, and may there not come one that has an owner," then if indeed a treasure without an owner comes to him and one with an owner does not come, for as long as it has not yet appeared before his eyes, that constitutes a grave offense. If it does appear before his eyes, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a grave offense; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk makes preparations for a treasure that has no owner, yet thinks to himself, "May there come to me a treasure that has an owner, and may one without an owner not come" —

If indeed a treasure with an owner comes to him and one without an owner does not come, then for as long as it has not yet appeared before his eyes, that constitutes a grave offense. If it does appear before his eyes, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

A summary verse:

Earth cuttings, stone,
flat slabs, foundations,
wall-tops, coverings,
successive layers, robe-rack niches,
robe-racks, pairs,
iron pegs, seats and small seats,
armchair seats and door-lintels,
and three kinds of tree — these are the eight.

Now as follows: concerning those heavy goods of people, namely necklaces, ornamental anklets, armlets, garlands, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls, placed upon an earth cutting — when a monk, applying himself to them, causes one to rise from a seat, puts on a lower robe, walks away, yet for as long as he has not taken hold of them nor gathered them up, that constitutes a misdeed. If he does take hold of them and gather them up, yet for as long as he has not conveyed them from place to place, that constitutes a grave offense. If he does convey them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense.

If that earth cutting is spread with grasses of a single color, it is to be spoken of as a single portion. If it is spread with grasses of various colors, it is to be spoken of as separate portions.

Now as follows: concerning those heavy goods of people, namely necklaces, ornamental anklets, armlets, garlands, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls, placed upon a stone — when a monk applies himself to them, causing one to rise from a seat, and so forth, the sequence is the same as before, from "causing one to rise from a seat" down to "if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense." If that stone is smooth and of a single piece, it is to be spoken of as a single portion. If it is hollow, cracked, has divisions, has writing on it, or is marked with various colors, it is to be spoken of as separate portions.

Just as with stone, the same applies likewise to flat slabs, foundations, walls, wall-tops, coverings, successive layers, robe-rack niches, robe-racks, pairs, iron pegs, seats, small seats, armchair seats, door-lintels, and the three kinds of tree — namely flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and incense trees. The same principle applies to all of them. If a monk removes and steals a flowering tree, the value of the flowering tree is to be assessed, and if the object is complete, he incurs a defeat; if the object is not complete, he incurs a grave offense. Just as with a flowering tree, the same applies likewise to a fruit-bearing tree and an incense tree.

A summary verse:

Mounts and the house of scales,
riding an elephant, riding a horse,
riding a chariot, traveling on foot,
riding a litter, a cart,
a sedan-chair, and a child's conveyance.

Now as follows: concerning those heavy goods of people, namely necklaces, ornamental anklets, armlets, garlands, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls, placed upon a mount — when a monk, applying himself to them, causes one to rise from a seat, puts on a lower robe, walks away, and mounts the mount, yet for as long as he has not taken hold of them nor gathered them up, that constitutes a misdeed. If he does take hold of them

and gathers them up, then for as long as he does not convey them from place to place, a grave offense results. If he does convey them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results, while if the full threshold is not met, a grave offense results. If that mount is draped with cloths of a single color, it is to be declared as one category. If it is draped with cloths of various colors, it is to be declared as separate categories. Just as it is with the mount, so too is it with the house of scales.

Now as follows: concerning those heavy goods of people, namely necklaces, ornamental anklets, armlets, garlands, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls, placed upon the back of an elephant — when a monk, applying himself to them, causes one to rise from a seat, puts on a lower robe, walks away, and mounts the elephant, yet for as long as he has not taken hold of them nor gathered them up, that constitutes a misdeed. If he does take hold of them and gather them up, then for as long as he does not convey them from place to place, a grave offense results. If he does convey them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results, while if the full threshold is not met, a grave offense results. If those elephants are plump, with full hide, flesh, and blood, it is to be declared as one category. If they are lean, feeble, thin, dried up, or have not yet reached full body, then whichever of the following divisions applies — cut off at the jaw, cut off at the nose, cut off at the ears, cut off at the ribs, cut off at the waist, or cut off at the haunches — those are to be declared as separate categories.

Now, if on the back of the elephant there is erected a multi-storied pavilion, and within that multi-storied pavilion various ornaments have been placed — namely necklaces, ornamental anklets, armlets, garlands, finger-rings, and bundles of pearls — and a monk, applying himself to them, causes one to rise from a seat, puts on a lower robe, walks away, mounts the elephant, and enters the multi-storied pavilion, yet for as long as he has not taken hold of them nor gathered them up, that constitutes a misdeed. If he does take hold of them and gather them up, then for as long as he does not convey them from place to place, a grave offense results. If he does convey them from place to place, it is to be declared theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results, while if the full threshold is not met, a grave offense results. If that multi-storied pavilion is draped with cloths of a single color, it is to be declared as one category. If it is draped with cloths of various colors, it is to be declared as separate categories. Just as it is with the multi-storied pavilion, so too is it with a half-pavilion. Just as it is with riding an elephant, so too is it with riding a horse, riding a chariot, traveling on foot, riding a litter, a cart, a sedan-chair, and a child's conveyance.

Summary verse:

A boat set in motion, downstream, against the current, and with the current,
this shore, the far shore, dry land,
conveying through the shallows,
and consumption causing loss without ease.

If a monk with intent to steal causes a moored boat to move, a misdeed results. If he directs it downstream, then for as long as it remains visible before one's eyes, a grave offense results.

When it passes from sight, the theft is considered complete. The value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If he directs the boat against the current, then for as long as it has not passed beyond its mooring-place, a grave offense results. Once it has passed beyond its mooring-place, the theft is considered complete. The value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If he conveys it from this shore to the far shore, or draws it from the far shore to this shore, then for as long as it remains visible before one's eyes, a grave offense results. When it passes from sight, the theft is considered complete. The value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If he draws it up onto dry land and steals it, then for as long as it remains visible before one's eyes, a grave offense results. When it passes from sight, the theft is considered complete. The value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If, thinking "I will take it later," he hides it in the shallows, the theft is considered complete. The value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If, with the intention of causing loss without ease, thinking "Let it neither become someone else's nor become my own," he hides it in the shallows, or burns it, or breaks it, or tramples it, a grave offense results.

Summary verse:

Autumn crops arising, the three kinds of boat,
the goose and the utpala,
born from water and born from dry land,
the hunter's use, and the hateful fish.

Now, the boundaries of action regarding the autumn crops of people are as follows. The boundary of action for rice crops, for sugarcane crops, and for salt crops are all similar; they are in proximity to one another. Sometimes water is extremely abundant and sometimes water becomes extremely scarce. When water is extremely scarce, if a monk, thinking "Let my own crop flourish and let another's be ruined," diverts the irrigation channel to his own rice field and cuts off another's, and if his crop does indeed flourish while the other's is ruined, the value of that flourishing is to be assessed. If the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

When water is extremely abundant, if a monk, thinking "Let my own crop flourish and let another's be ruined," cuts off his own channel and diverts water to another's, and if his crop does indeed flourish while the other's is ruined, the value of that flourishing is to be assessed. If the full threshold is met, a defeat results; if the threshold is not met, a grave offense results.

If, with the intention of causing loss without ease, thinking "Let it neither become someone else's nor become my own," he diverts both his own channel and another's, a grave offense results.

What applies to the boundary of action for rice crops applies equally to the boundary of action for sugarcane crops and for salt crops.

There are three kinds of boat: a pot-shaped boat, a clay boat, and a raft.

There are four kinds of bundle: a bundle that is heavy and of great value, a bundle that is light but of great value, a bundle that is heavy but of little value, and a bundle that is light and of little value.

What is a bundle that is heavy and of great value? It is as follows: jewels, pearls, beryl (vaiḍūrya), white crystal, coral, silver, refined gold ore, the essence of stone, red coral, and right-spiraling shell —

— these constitute a bundle that is heavy and of great value. What is a bundle that is light but of great value? It is as follows: silks, wool from the silkworm (serin), saffron, and cardamom. These constitute a bundle that is light but of great value. What is a bundle that is heavy but of little value? It is as follows: iron, stone, and saltpeter. These constitute a bundle that is heavy but of little value. What is a bundle that is light and of little value? It is as follows: wool, hemp, cotton wadding, and nameru. These constitute a bundle that is light and of little value.

Now, when a bundle that is heavy and of great value and a bundle that is light and of little value are loaded together onto one boat, and that boat founders and does not make it across, and the bundles begin to float away — when the crew call out triumphantly, "Wise ones, whatever has sunk belongs to us, and whatever floats we will each pull out as we please" — then, for as long as a monk rises from his seat in order to retrieve the sunken bundle, puts on his lower robe, sets out, ties up his robe, enters the water, wades in deep, and comes up out of the water, yet does not grasp it or hold it fast, he incurs a wrong deed. If he grasps it and holds it fast, yet for as long as he does not carry it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. If he carries it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; its value is to be assessed; and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met, it incurs a grave offense. If he submerges it in the mud thinking "I will pick it up later," it is to be declared theft; its value is to be assessed; and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met, it incurs a grave offense. If he submerges it in the mud with the intention of causing harm, thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine," he incurs a grave offense.

Now, when a bundle that is light but of great value and a bundle that is heavy but of little value are loaded together onto one boat, and that boat founders and does not make it across, and the bundles sink — when the crew call out triumphantly, "Wise ones, whatever floats belongs to us, and whatever has sunk we will each pull out as we please" — then, for as long as a monk rises from his seat in order to retrieve the floating bundle, puts on his lower robe, sets out, ties up his robe, enters the water, wades in deep, and comes up out of the water, yet does not grasp it or hold it fast, he incurs a wrong deed. If he grasps it and holds it fast, yet for as long as he does not carry it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. If he carries it from place to place, it is to be declared theft; its value is to be assessed; and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met, it incurs a grave offense. If he submerges it in the mud thinking "I will pick it up later," it is to be declared theft; its value is to be assessed; and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met, it incurs a grave offense. If he submerges it in the mud with the intention of causing harm, thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine," he incurs a grave offense.

In the following case: in people's homes or at bodies of water, various ponds have been made, and in those ponds various birds kept for sport — namely geese, kāraṇḍava ducks, and cranes — adorned with various ornaments such as necklaces, ankle-rings with bells, armlets, garlands, chains, and strings of pearls —

If a monk, by way of preparation, causes it to rise from its seat, causes it to put on a lower garment, causes it to move, causes it to tie its cloth, causes it to enter the water, causes it to go into the depths, and takes hold of the bird — so long as he has not yet grasped at the ornament, not yet plucked it, he incurs a grave offense. When he grasps at it and plucks it, and so long as he has not yet conveyed it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. If he thinks to himself, "I shall steal from the bird, not from a person," he incurs a grave offense. When he conveys it from place to place, it is to be declared as theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a grave offense, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If he thinks, "I shall steal from a person — but where are the ornaments on the bird?" then so long as he does not convey it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. If he conveys it from place to place, it is to be declared as theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense.

In those same ponds, various garland-material grows from the water — namely blue lotuses (utpala), white water-lilies (kumuda), white lotuses (padma), supreme-fragrance flowers, soft-fragrance flowers, those that bloom in every season, those that bloom at all times, and those protected from all people — and in connection with these: if a monk, by way of preparation, causes it to rise from its seat, causes it to put on a lower garment, causes it to move, causes it to tie its cloth, causes it to enter the water, causes it to go into the depths — so long as he has not yet grasped at it, not yet plucked it, he incurs a grave offense. When he grasps at it and plucks it, and so long as he has not yet harvested it, not yet lifted it as a load, not yet conveyed it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. When he conveys it from place to place, it is to be declared as theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense.

On both banks of those same ponds, various garland-material grows from dry land — namely atimuktaka, campaka, yellow jasmine, varsika, mallikā, nava-mallikā, priyangu, yūthikā, and dhānuskari flowers, those that bloom in every season, those that bloom at all times, and those protected from all people — and in connection with these: if a monk, by way of preparation, causes it to rise from its seat, causes it to put on a lower garment, and causes it to move — so long as he has not yet grasped at it, not yet plucked it, he incurs a grave offense. When he grasps at it and plucks it, climbs the flowering tree, harvests the flowers, and fills a basket — so long as he has not yet conveyed it from place to place, he incurs a grave offense. When he harvests the flowers, fills a basket, and conveys it from place to place, it is to be declared as theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense.

In the following case: a skilled hunter of wild animals, or a student of such a hunter, has set out hunting equipment in a forest wilderness in order to drive many wild animals away, to harm them, and to torment them in an improper manner. If a monk, with the intention of stealing, steals that hunting equipment, the value of the hunting equipment is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If with the intention of causing no benefit — thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine" — he burns it, breaks it, or destroys it, he incurs a grave offense.

If, however, with a mind of compassion he thinks, "It would be wrong if these sentient beings were to be deprived of their lives on account of this; it would be wrong if this device were to generate a great deal of demerit for those sentient beings," and with that thought he burns it, breaks it, or destroys it, he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, with the intention of stealing, steals a wild animal that has been caught in a hunter's snare, the value of the wild animal is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If with the intention of causing no benefit — thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine" — he releases it, he incurs a grave offense. If with a mind of compassion he thinks, "It would be wrong if these sentient beings were to be deprived of their lives on account of this; it would be wrong if this device were to generate a great deal of demerit for those sentient beings," and with that thought he releases it, he incurs a grave offense.

Now, in this way, a fisherman, or a skilled student of a fisherman, has set fish traps at the bank of a river or at the mouth of a large pond in order to drive many fish away, to harm them, and to torment them in an improper manner. If a monk, with the intention of stealing, steals the fish traps, the value of the fish traps is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If with the intention of causing no benefit — thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine" — he burns, breaks, or destroys them, he incurs a grave offense. If with a mind of compassion he thinks, "It would be wrong if these sentient beings were to be deprived of their lives on account of this; it would be wrong if this device were to generate a great deal of demerit for those sentient beings," and with that thought he burns, cuts, or destroys them, he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, with the intention of stealing, steals fish that have been caught in a fish trap, the value of the fish is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If with the intention of causing no benefit — thinking "Let it become neither theirs nor mine" — he releases them, he incurs a grave offense. If with a mind of compassion he thinks, "It would be wrong if these sentient beings were to be deprived of their lives on account of this; it would be wrong if this device were to generate a great deal of demerit for those sentient beings," and with that thought he releases them, he incurs a grave offense.

A summary verse:

Water for humans on dry land,
and likewise water for animals there;
water for humans on the ocean,
and water for animals likewise.

Now, a very great number of merchants, taking provisions, have set out on a path through a wilderness. There, where water is scarce and precious, they have pooled their water supply in various containers — clay jars, leather bags, round vessels, and wooden troughs — and they dispense it in measured portions, saying, "This much is the share for a human being, and this much is the share for an animal." If a monk, with the intention of stealing, appropriates for himself the water that is the humans' portion, the value of that water is to be assessed at that time, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If he appropriates the water that is the animals' portion, the value of the animals' portion of water is to be assessed at that time, and if the full threshold is met it incurs a grave offense, while if the full threshold is not met he incurs a wrongdoing.

Now, a very great number of merchants from Jambudvīpa, seeking wealth, have boarded a ship and are venturing out onto the great ocean. Since the great ocean contains nothing but the taste of salt, they have there various containers —

rafts to collect the water, and there they distribute it, saying: this much water is the portion for the humans, and this much is the portion for the animals. If a monk, with intent to steal, appropriates for himself the water that is the humans' portion, the value of the humans' portion of water is to be assessed at that time, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If he appropriates for himself the water that is the animals' portion, the value of the animals' portion of water is to be assessed at that time, and if the full threshold is met it incurs a grave offense, while if the full threshold is not met he incurs a wrongdoing.

Summary verse: Taking theft step by step to completion, likewise generating each step, going from the dwelling to the corridor and so forth — these are the fully collected categories.

Now, when a preceptor and a teacher have set out to travel on a road, and they have entrusted their robes to the keeping of their attendants, if those attendants harbor a thieving intent and walk along taking steps to carry off the robes, each step incurs a wrongdoing. For as long as the object remains visible before their eyes, each such moment incurs a grave offense. Once it passes from sight, it is declared to have been stolen: the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense. If instead they take steps and move forward with the intent of stealing, each step incurs a wrongdoing. For as long as the object remains visible before their eyes, each such moment incurs a grave offense. Once it passes from sight, it is declared to have been stolen: the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense.

Now, when monks who share a dwelling with a preceptor and a teacher, and their attendants, steal those preceptors' and teachers' robes with thieving intent, and carry them off — going from the dwelling cell into the corridor, from the corridor into the dwelling cell, emerging again from the dwelling cell into the corridor, climbing up to an upper floor, then descending from there and coming down to a lower floor, entering a gatehouse, going out from the gatehouse onto the outer steps, descending from the outer steps into a stairwell, climbing from the stairwell up to a terrace, descending again from the terrace into the stairwell, going from the stairwell into a dense enclosure, and then emerging from that enclosure into the open — in all these movements, each single step incurs a wrongdoing. For as long as the object remains visible before their eyes, each such moment incurs a grave offense. Once it passes from sight, it is declared to have been stolen: the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met it constitutes a defeat, while if the full threshold is not met it incurs a grave offense.

Summary verse: Receiving a tip-off about the loot, repenting and turning back, and guiding the thieves to the house — these are the fully collected categories.

Now, a monk dwelling in a hermitage is approached by bandits who raid villages, and they ask him: "Noble one, do you know of any large village nearby?" He says: "Yes, I do." They say: "Noble one, then tell us — that village has many women and few men, the guard is lax, it is far from other settlements, there are no guard dogs, it is easy to enter and easy to leave. Are you able to tell us in which direction it lies, so that we may do our work there without harming or injuring anyone? If we return safely, we will give a share to you as well, noble one." If in response to this the monk says: "Knowledgeable ones, that village lies in such and such a direction — it has many women and few men, the guard is lax, it is far from other settlements, there are no guard dogs, it is easy to enter and easy to leave; you are indeed able to do your work there without harming or injuring anyone" — and having said this,

the thieves carry out their work there and return safely, then present the monk with a share of the stolen goods, and the monk accepts it for himself — the value of the stolen share is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat; if the threshold is not fully met, it is a grave offense.

If, however, that monk, having spoken those words, comes to regret them and goes to those thieves and says: "Knowledgeable ones, hear me well. Knowledgeable ones, take heed. I spoke those words like a child, a fool, someone confused and unskilled — I spoke carelessly and rashly, without having carefully assessed the situation. That village has few women and many men, its guard is tight, it lies close to other settlements, there are guard dogs, it is difficult to enter, and difficult to leave; you are not able to do your work there without harming or injuring anyone" — then regardless of whether the thieves carry out their work there or not, that same prior act of engagement incurs a grave offense for that monk.

If that monk searches for those thieves but does not find them, and then goes to that household and says: "Knowledgeable ones, be on your guard! Knowledgeable ones, be vigilant! Thieves who plunder villages are coming here today. They may rob you of your possessions, and it would be dreadful if you were to lose your lives entirely" — then regardless of whether the thieves carry out their work there or not, that same prior act of engagement incurs a grave offense for that monk.

Summary verse:

Field ground and undercroft below,
and likewise the upper cells above;
household ground has likewise two divisions,
and market ground is also twofold.

There are three kinds of ground: field ground, household ground, and market ground. Field ground is stolen in two ways: by means of a sickle-share, and by means of encirclement.

How is it done by means of a sickle-share? If a monk enters into a sickle-share arrangement together with a layperson for the sake of a plot of field ground — if the layperson causes the monk to suffer defeat, the monk incurs a grave offense. If the monk causes the layperson to suffer defeat, for as long as the layperson has not abandoned the undertaking, the monk incurs a grave offense. Once the layperson abandons the undertaking, it is to be declared a theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat; if the threshold is not fully met, it is a grave offense.

If a monk enters into a sickle-share arrangement together with a layperson for upper cells — if the layperson causes the monk to suffer defeat, the monk incurs a grave offense. If the monk causes the layperson to suffer defeat — since the king is the lord of all disputes for monks — it is to be declared a theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat; if the threshold is not fully met, it is a grave offense. Such is the way by sickle-share.

How is it done by encirclement? If a monk encircles a plot of field ground with walls, palings, stakes, a thorn fence, a ditch, or thorn-bushes — for as long as the boundary-tip does not meet another boundary-tip, the monk incurs a grave offense. When boundary-tip meets boundary-tip, it is to be declared a theft; the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it constitutes a defeat; if the threshold is not fully met, it is a grave offense.

Just as described for field ground, so too it is for household ground and market ground.

Summary verse:

Stray animals, taking, guarding,
reading out, parents, soliciting from those who come forward,
the great load, young and old alike,
what to ask, the small window, and reviling.

At the time when the Blessed One had realized unsurpassed primordial wisdom but the Teaching had not yet spread widely — at that time, when monks found it easy to beg and householders found it difficult to beg, there came an occasion when a great many monks, traveling through the provinces together with a company of merchants on a shared errand, arrived at the place of a weighing station. There the monks said to the merchants: "Good friends, we have certain goods that need to be weighed. Rather than having the weighers put them on the scales, please first retrieve them back from the weighing station." The merchants replied: "As you command, noble ones; it shall be done." And those merchants retrieved the monks' goods that needed weighing from the weighing station and returned them.

As the monks continued on their way, they returned to the monastery. The other monks greeted them, saying: "Welcome, welcome, venerable ones! How was your journey? Were you not harassed by the weighers, the bandits, or the ferryman who cuts the boat-rope?" They replied: "Venerable ones, the journey was comfortable; no one harassed us at all." The monks then asked: "Did you not have goods that needed to be weighed?" They replied: "We did have goods that needed to be weighed, but our merchant friends retrieved them from the weighing station and returned them to us." The monks then asked: "Was it permissible for you to have goods already entered for weighing recalled?" They replied: "It may have been permissible, or it may not have been — for we ourselves did the recalling." Then, fearing that a defeat-level transgression might have arisen for those monks, remorse arose in them, and they recounted the matter in full to the assembled monks. The monks then reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, no transgression arose for those monks. However, a monk should not have goods that have already been entered for weighing recalled. If a monk causes goods already entered for weighing to be recalled, he commits an offense requiring expiation."

At the time when the Blessed One was staying in the grove of the mango trees, he tamed Bimbisāra, King of Magadha — a king whose body was refined and beautiful — together with eighty thousand gods of Magadha and many hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders of Magadha, and then traveled to Śrāvastī. There he tamed Prasenajit, King of Kośala, by means of the discourse of the parable of the youth. The two kings then gave to the monks a grant of dismissal from the obligations of youth, and to the nuns a grant of dismissal from the obligations pertaining to a queen's retinue, releasing the monks free from weighers, free from bandits, and free from the ferryman who cuts the boat-rope.

At that time the Blessed One's Teaching had spread widely. Then, at another time when householders found it easy to beg and monks found it difficult to beg, a great many monks, traveling through the provinces together with a company of merchants on a shared errand, arrived at the place of a weighing station. Those merchants, touching the monks' feet with their own two feet, said: "Noble ones, while we are afflicted by cold when it is cold, and tormented by heat when it is hot, and harmed by hunger and thirst, and endangered by the touch of horseflies, insects, wind, sun, and venomous snakes — all that we do with enthusiasm, with effort, and with exertion is for the sake of acquiring possessions. All of this — the buddhas, the Dharma, and...

the Saṅgha — we wish to make offerings. Therefore it is fitting that the goods we have here for weighing be retrieved from the weighing station and given to us." The monks said: "Good friends, go ahead and retrieve them by measurement." And those monks retrieved the goods the merchants needed weighed, took them from the weighing station, and gave them over.

Later, as the monks continued traveling through the provinces, they returned to Śrāvastī. There the monks said to them: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How was the journey? Were you not troubled by toll-collectors, highway robbers, and those who cut ferry ropes?" They replied: "Venerable ones, we brought joy to others along the way — how much more so ourselves — and no one troubled us at all." The monks then said: "How did things go?" And those travelers gave a full account to the monks of what had occurred. The monks then asked: "Is it permitted for monks to retrieve goods that have been passed through customs?" They replied: "It may be permitted or it may not — but this is what we did." The monks then felt remorse, thinking: "Has there arisen for us a transgression that would constitute a defeat?" And they gave the monks a full account of the whole matter. The monks then reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, those monks have incurred no transgression — yet a monk should not retrieve goods that have already passed through customs. If a monk does retrieve goods that have already passed through customs, it becomes an offense of wrongdoing." Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training.

Now some time later, a great many monks, traveling through the provinces together with a company of merchants on a shared errand, arrived at the place of a weighing station. Those merchants, touching the monks' feet with their own two feet, said: "Noble ones, while we are afflicted by cold when it is cold, and tormented by heat when it is hot, and harmed by hunger and thirst, and endangered by the touch of horseflies, insects, wind, sun, and venomous snakes — all that we do with enthusiasm, with effort, and with exertion is for the sake of acquiring possessions. All of this — the buddhas, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha — we wish to make offerings to. Therefore it is fitting that the goods we have here for weighing be retrieved from the weighing station and given to us." Those monks said: "Good friends, the Blessed One has established a rule of training that a monk should not retrieve goods that have already passed through customs. Therefore we cannot do so."

The merchants, perceiving that these noble ones were refusing and thinking to themselves that they must find some other means, conferred with one another and said: "Noble ones, today we are busy. Without waiting for us to bring alms to you, please go into the village to collect alms." When those monks had entered the village for alms, the merchants placed the goods needing to be weighed into the monks' carrying bags, their alms bowls, and their containers for small items. The monks collected alms and came back out of the village. After they had eaten their meal, when they passed by the weighing station, the merchants began rifling through the vessels of those monks. The monks said: "Good friends, why are you going through our vessels?" The merchants replied:

"Noble ones, we are retrieving the goods we placed in your vessels here for weighing." The monks said: "Good friends, you have deliberately caused us to incur a transgression." The merchants replied: "Noble ones, in this matter there was neither a bodily action nor a verbal action on your part — how then could you have incurred a transgression?" The monks, thinking, "Has a defeat-level transgression not arisen for us?" arose with remorse, and they eventually departed back to Śrāvastī. When the other monks there said to them, "Welcome, welcome, venerable ones! Was the journey comfortable? Were you not harassed by gamblers, highwaymen, and river-crossing brigands?" they replied: "Venerable ones, we were not harassed by those, yet remorse has arisen in us, for the merchants placed goods needing to be weighed into the carrying bags, the alms bowls, and the containers for small items of those of us who had entered upon alms-round, and without our knowing it, we passed through the weighing station — and so we wondered whether a defeat-level transgression has not arisen for us." The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no transgression for those monks. However, monks are not to leave their vessels unattended and go off carelessly — a guard monk is to be appointed."

They appointed a guard monk and went on alms-round, and on one occasion, when that guard monk went to relieve himself, to urinate, or to fetch water, the merchants at that very moment placed the goods requiring weighing into the carrying bags, the alms bowls, and the containers for small items — and they passed through the weighing station in just that way. At that point the merchants rifled through the vessels of those monks, and the monks arose with remorse and reported it to the other monks. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no transgression for those monks. However, two guard monks are to be appointed."

When a large number of monks were travelling together with merchants who had business in common, they appointed two guard monks and entered upon alms-round. Whenever one of those two went to relieve himself, to urinate, or to fetch water, the merchants would seize that one by the hands, seize him by the feet, and meanwhile the others would load goods into the vessels. That monk, knowing that he should call back those who were nearby keeping pure conduct, called them back from their rounds — and the merchants then contrived such tricks that those two guard monks would in no way be able to report the matter to the other monks. When the group passed through the weighing station, the merchants rifled through the vessels, and the monks said to them: "Good friends, why are you rifling through the vessels?" They replied: "Noble ones, we are retrieving our goods for weighing that we placed in there." The monks then said to the two guard monks: "By your being appointed here you have caused us to incur a transgression," and challenged them angrily. The two recounted the full sequence of what had occurred. Remorse arose in those monks, thinking, "Has a defeat-level transgression not arisen for us?" and they reported the matter to the other monks at that time. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, there is no transgression for those monks. However, the goods requiring weighing on the scales should be taken out by a layman or a novice and returned to those merchants. If there is no layman or novice available, one should take them out oneself, place them in front of the merchants, and say: 'These are your goods — please take note of them.'"

The Vinaya Analysis, the Fifth Fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was a householder in Śrāvastī who took a wife from among his equals in station, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and took his pleasure. As they sported, rejoiced, and took their pleasure together, a son was born to him from that wife, who nursed and nurtured him, and raised him swiftly, like a lotus growing in a pond — and so forth as before up to that point.

When he had grown up, he went forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya. He went wandering through the countryside and found two large bolts of cloth. Knowing that the Blessed One had said that even one who has gone forth should provide for the needs of one's parents, he thought: "I will offer one to my father and the other to my mother." He remained in the countryside as long as he pleased, then, taking up his alms bowl and robes, set out traveling toward Śrāvastī. As he traveled along, step by step, he came to the place of the weighing scales, and the weighmaster said to him: "Noble one, do you not have some goods for weighing on the scales?" The monk replied: "Good sir, I have none." The weighmaster said: "Please let me look — do set them down." As the monk began to be examined, the weighmaster caught sight of the two large bolts of cloth and said: "Noble one, would one who has gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya tell a lie for the sake of a mere two bolts of cloth?" The monk replied: "Good sir, these two are not mine to dispose of." "Noble one, then whose are they?" "Good sir, one belongs to my father and the other to my mother." "Noble one, since you have sought neither your father nor your mother, hand over the toll and be on your way."

The monk was detained by that weighmaster for quite some time before being released, and he eventually made his way back to Śrāvastī. Remorse arose in him, and he reported the matter at that time to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, there is no transgression for that monk. Nevertheless, a monk should not proceed in that same way. Instead, one should speak a praise of one's parents before the weighmaster, saying: 'Good sir, the Blessed One has said that a father and mother who carry their children, sustain them, raise them, suckle them at the breast, and show them the variety of Jambudvīpa — these two do what is difficult to do. Were a son to carry one parent on one shoulder and the other on the other shoulder for a full hundred years, or were he to establish himself as a lord of wealth on this great earth with all its jewels, pearls, beryl, white quartz, coral, silver, rice, the essence of stones, crystal, rubies, right-spiraling conches, and all such riches — even that would not be adequate repayment for what a son owes his father and mother, nor would it come close. But if he leads parents who have no faith into complete and perfect faith, establishes them, disciplines them, and installs them in it; if he leads those who lack moral discipline into perfect moral discipline; if he leads those who are miserly into perfect generosity;"

"if he leads those two who lack wisdom into perfect wisdom, disciplines them, and installs them in it — by that much alone does a son render what he has done and what he has done in service for his father and mother." This is what should be said.

If, when one recites such a praise of one's father and mother, they let it go, then well and good. If they do not let it go, one should go before the adjudicator. If one does not go in like manner, there will be an offense.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who took a wife from among those of equal caste. With her he sported, rejoiced, and made merry. As he sported, rejoiced, and made merry with her, a son was born to him from that wife. He nurtured him, raised him, and caused him to grow swiftly, like a lotus growing in a pond. All that preceded is as before, up to the passage that reads "he raised him swiftly, like a lotus dwelling in a pond." When that son came of age, he went forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya.

The Blessed One declared:

Merit is something to be done.
Where merit is not made, suffering follows.
In this world and in the world beyond,
one who has made merit will rejoice.

Hearing this, the monks made a heartfelt request and began performing acts of offering to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and the teaching of the Blessed One flourished. Then a certain monk, knowing that begging from heartfelt motivation had become widespread and that these resources had been exhausted throughout Śrāvastī, thought: "I will go to the provinces and have them properly engaged there." He went to the provinces, and in those regions he had three chests filled with robes of various colors properly gathered as offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Having stayed in those provinces as long as he wished, he took up his bowl and robes and set out, journeying back toward Śrāvastī. As he travelled along the road, he came to the place of the adjudicator. The adjudicator said: "Noble one, do you not have even a small sum for the adjudicator's weighing?" The monk replied: "Good sir, I do not." The adjudicator said: "Please wait while I inspect." As he began to examine, he saw three chests filled with robes of various colors. He said: "Noble one, these three chests filled with robes of many colors — if even a small amount of them were to come to a mare's load, then you would need to pay the adjudicator's toll." The monk said: "Good sir, I have no authority over these. Noble one, then who does have authority?" "Good sir, one belongs to the Buddha, one to the Dharma, and one to the Saṅgha. Noble one, I have not obtained them from the Buddha, nor from the Dharma, nor from the Saṅgha. Grant the toll and let me pass." The adjudicator detained that monk for a long while and then released him, and the monk eventually returned to Śrāvastī. Remorse arose in him, and he reported the matter to the monks. The monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no transgression for that monk; however, a monk should not travel in that manner. Rather, in the presence of an adjudicator one should recite the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as follows: 'The Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and good conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,

the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans — the Blessed One, the Buddha.' The Dharma of the Blessed One is well proclaimed, visible to the eye, without sickness, not limited to a particular time, an invitation to come and see, bearing fruit for those who see it here and now, to be known individually by the wise, each for themselves. The Saṅgha of the śrāvakas of the Blessed One has entered well, has entered rightly, has entered directly, has entered harmoniously, has entered into the practice that accords with the Dharma, and acts in accordance with the Dharma. Within that Saṅgha there are those who have entered in order to realize directly the fruit of stream-entry, and those who have attained stream-entry; those who have entered in order to realize directly the fruit of once-returning, and those who have attained once-returning; those who have entered in order to realize directly the fruit of non-returning, and those who have attained non-returning; those who have entered in order to realize directly the fruit of arhatship, and those who have attained arhatship. Thus they are the four pairs of persons and the eight individual persons. This Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Blessed One is endowed with perfect moral discipline, endowed with perfect meditative absorption, endowed with perfect wisdom, endowed with perfect liberation, endowed with perfect knowledge and vision of liberation. It is worthy of offerings from afar, worthy of lavish offerings, worthy of joined palms in homage, worthy of reverence — the unsurpassed field of merit, the place where the world may earn merit.' If, upon reciting the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in this way, the captor releases one, that is good. If he does not release one, then one should determine the matter by casting lots, and to go otherwise would constitute a serious offense."

Some monks had begun sending items for the purpose of casting lots for the sake of the Three Jewels, and when they were at the place of lot-casting and had recited the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha yet were still not released, the monks gave from the share of one among them. The Blessed One declared: "One should give equally from all three shares." When the monks were giving equally from all three shares, they became separated from their traveling companions and were set upon by lions, tigers, and bandits. The Blessed One then declared: "Give from one person's share, and afterward make up the remaining shares."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there resided a monk who was versed in the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), a speaker of Dharma, endowed with the confidence that comes from reasoning and liberation. When he went travelling through the regions and eventually reached Rājagṛha, he spent the rains retreat there. When the three months had passed and he set out for Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, a noble one who sought a companion for the journey had just been engaged, and a caravan leader who had set out from Rājagṛha happened to arrive at Śrāvastī around the same time. That caravan leader went to the monk, recited the praises of the three bases of merit-making, organized offerings to them, and explained things this way and that in order to arouse in the monk's mind a clear and heartfelt faith. When faith arose in that man, he gave food to the monk, covered him with a fine and costly large length of cloth, prostrated at his feet from below, and said, "Noble one, please give me whatever instruction you command." The monk replied:

"Good man, I wish to go and pay homage at the feet of the Teacher in Śrāvastī. For that reason, please care for me with loving-kindness."

The householder replied, "Noble one, I shall do exactly as you command. Please proceed without hesitation."

That monk then set out together with that noble one and the caravan leader. The caravan leader said, "Noble one, you seek alms, while I seek merit. From Rājagṛha all the way to Śrāvastī, please allow me to attend to you with the least of trouble in regard to your robe, alms-food, lodging, provisions for illness, and medicinal requisites."

The monk accepted this offer. After some time, they arrived at the place of a customs post. The caravan leader's goods were assessed at the customs post, and when that caravan leader saw that his own goods had been assessed but the monk's large length of cloth had not been assessed, he realized that a situation had arisen where he alone would have to measure it through the customs post. Thinking to himself that he should put it into his own container, the caravan leader said to the monk, "Noble one, please return the large length of cloth."

The monk replied, "Good man, why do you say this? Have you come to regret your gift?"

The caravan leader replied, "Noble one, I have no regret at all. The matter is this: my own goods have been assessed at customs, but your large length of cloth has not. If the customs officers were to demand assessment of the large length of cloth, I alone would in effect have to declare it. So I shall take it back from the customs post and hand it over to you."

The monk said, "Good man, the Blessed One has set down a training rule that a monk must not remove from a customs post goods that are subject to customs assessment. If I were to incur a transgression, that would be improper, so I will not give it."

The caravan leader understood that the noble one was creating a difficulty and thought, "I shall find a moment for this." He said to the monk, "Noble one, I am busy today and cannot manage to procure even a small amount of alms for you. Please go ahead and enter the village for alms."

When the monk entered the village for alms, in the time during which he was thus occupied, the caravan leader placed that large length of cloth in his own container.

After some time, the customs officers asked the monk, "Noble one, do you have any goods subject to customs assessment?"

The monk replied, "Good man, there is one large length of cloth."

The customs officer said, "Noble one, please present it for inspection."

When the monk looked into his carrying bundle, the large length of cloth was nowhere to be found, and he turned this way and that, rubbing his two hands together.

The customs officer asked, "Noble one, why do you act like this?"

The monk replied, "Good man, the large length of cloth of mine has been stolen by those who take what is not given."

The customs officer replied, "Noble one, it was not stolen by those who take what is not given. Rather, I myself stole it. Therefore I have not obtained the customs payment."

When the monk had passed through the customs post, the caravan leader said to him, "Noble one, why are you troubled at heart? Good man, from your act of complete giving, merit has indeed arisen for you, but from the act of complete enjoyment, merit has not arisen."

"Noble one, why was my large length of cloth stolen by those who take what is not given?"

The caravan leader replied, "Noble one, it was not stolen by those who take what is not given. The matter is this: I myself, out of fear of the customs post, placed it into my own container and handed it over. In that case, what should I do? Should I declare it?" The monk replied:

"Good sir, it is indeed good that it was stolen by those who take what is not given, but it is not good that I have thereby incurred a transgression."

The caravan leader said, "Noble one, you had performed no bodily action and no verbal action in this matter — so why would you have incurred a transgression?"

That monk, having given rise to remorse, eventually departed and returned to Śrāvastī. The monks said to him, "Welcome, venerable one! Welcome! How was the journey?" That monk then recounted the matter to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, that monk has indeed incurred no transgression. Nevertheless, I shall now establish rules of proper conduct for monks who are traveling the road. A monk traveling the road who is going into a village for alms shall mark his container with a sign and proceed, and upon returning shall examine it carefully. If a monk traveling the road does not, having properly received the rules of conduct thus established, conduct himself in accordance with them, he commits a serious offense."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time two monks — one old and one young — set out to travel through a region. The old one was learned, had many goods, and many possessions. The young one was little-learned and lax regarding the three robes. Since the old monk had goods that needed to pass through a customs post, they eventually arrived at the place of the customs post. The old monk thought: "I have goods that need to pass through customs. If the customs officer asks me, 'Noble one, do you have any goods at all subject to customs duty?' and I say 'I do not,' that would be speaking a lie; but if I say 'I do,' I shall certainly be required to pay customs duty. Therefore I must find a way neither to pay customs duty nor to speak a lie." He then thought: "I will give these things to the young monk and retrieve them after passing through the customs post." So he said to the young monk, "Venerable one, hold my bowl and robe for a moment." The young monk understood that the elder would be slowed down and thought, "This way the gift to me will not be lost," and so he accepted them and carried them on ahead.

The customs officer saw him and said, "Noble one, do you have any goods at all subject to customs duty?" The monk replied, "Good sir, I do not." The customs officer paid no further attention to that monk and let him pass the customs post.

The old monk then followed behind, traveling light and unencumbered, and the customs officer did not question him at all. When the old monk had passed the customs post, he said, "Venerable one, bring the goods." The young monk replied, "Elder, what do you mean? Have you recovered from your fatigue?" The old monk said, "Venerable one, I did not give them to you out of fatigue. The matter was this: I had goods that needed to pass through customs, and I thought: if the customs officer were to ask me, 'Noble one, do you have any goods subject to customs duty?' and I were to say 'I do not,' that would be speaking a lie, but if I were to say 'I do,' I would certainly be required to pay customs duty. It was with that thought in mind that I gave you the bowl and robe. Now I have passed the customs post, so I take them back."

The young monk said, "In that case, the elder has saved himself and made this wretched one incur a transgression!"

The old monk said, "Venerable one, since you did not know, what transgression could you possibly have in this?"

That young monk, filled with remorse, eventually made his way back to Śrāvastī. The monks there said, "Welcome, venerable one, welcome! How was your journey — did you travel comfortably?" The monk replied, "What comfort was there on that journey?" The monks said, "Venerable one, why do you say that?" He then related to the monks what had happened. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk has no transgression. However, a monk who is traveling should not take goods subject to customs duty without first asking. When taking such goods, one should inquire: 'Householder, is there not even a small amount of goods here that are subject to customs duty?' If one takes them without asking, it becomes a serious offence. Furthermore, a monk must not carry goods subject to customs duty along the road. If one does so, it becomes a serious offence."

When the Blessed One had thus prohibited monks from carrying goods subject to customs duty along the road, sixty monks who were traveling through the countryside arrived at a certain mountain cliff. At that cliff there lived a householder who was wealthy, rich in possessions, and of great means, and who was also a man of faith. He invited those monks as his guests, gave them food, and draped a piece of cloth over each of them. The monks said to him, "Householder, the Blessed One has prohibited monks from carrying goods subject to customs duty along the road, and therefore we do not know how we are to accept these." The householder said nothing. The monks expressed their thanks, departed, and eventually made their way back to Śrāvastī. The other monks there asked them, "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How was your journey — did you travel comfortably?" They replied, "We traveled comfortably enough, but a certain householder gave us food and draped a piece of cloth over each of us. We said to him that the Blessed One had prohibited monks from carrying goods subject to customs duty along the road, and therefore we could not accept them — and so we did not take them."

The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They should be accepted. Having accepted them and made proper use of them, one may carry them along the road."

"Monks, when searching for dyes, wood, copper, and pots, some monks became weary and exhausted on the road, lost their purpose, and were set upon by lions, tigers, and bandits." The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Travel in a group at the border or go as you choose." When that very problem continued, the Blessed One declared: "It is permissible to anoint oneself with pressed cow-dung or to wash with it." When that very problem still persisted, the Blessed One declared: "One may even cut the hair of the face — the beard or the moustache. What I have permitted out of necessity must not be made into habitual ordinary practice. If one makes it into habitual practice, it becomes a serious offence."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. At that time a certain monk had committed to spending the rains retreat at Rājagṛha. The three months of the rains had passed and he had not obtained so much as his robe. He came to Śrāvastī solely to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and the monks there said to him:

"Venerable one, do not go until you have obtained your robe allowance." But he was unhappy at this and did not stay. Then a certain monk gave him a large piece of cloth, thinking: "If he makes this up into a robe here, he will not be seen by the celibate practitioners, so I will have a monk who is a friend of mine make it up for him." Knowing this, he said to the monk who was his friend: "Please make up this large piece of cloth into a robe before I have had a chance to visit the celibate practitioners, and have it stitched." But that monk was a lazy fellow, and he did not make it up. He had it stitched just as it was. As soon as the monk had picked up the bundle of cloth and set off, he eventually came to a place where dice players were gathered. One of the dice players said: "Noble one, do you have a little something suitable for wagering at dice?" "No, I do not." "Let me take a look." He began to examine it, and seeing the large piece of cloth he said: "Noble one, when you have gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, how can you speak a falsehood over a large piece of cloth?" The monk replied: "Good sir, I truly did not know. Noble one, when I had obtained this large piece of cloth, I said to my friend: 'While I go to visit the celibate practitioners, please make up this large piece of cloth into a robe and have it stitched.' But he was a lazy fellow and did not make it up, and I had it stitched just as it was." The dice player said: "Noble one, that is not your friend. Now this, you see, is my friend, and so give me the dice-stake you have received and go on your way." The monk was filled with remorse, and eventually he went to Śrāvastī. The monks said to him: "Venerable one, welcome, welcome. Did you travel comfortably?" He replied: "Venerable ones, I traveled comfortably." They said: "Venerable one, why do you say that?" And he then recounted the whole matter to the monks in full. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no offence for that monk, yet one must not take something without having first asked whether the other has made it up or not. If one takes it without asking, it becomes a serious offence."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. The group of six monks said: "Friends, Nanda and Upananda with their black begging bowls smear their feet with monkey grease. When they go out, they go prepared to acquire gains by their going; when they come back, they acquire gains by their unexpected return, and they please and attract many people. We are like frogs in a well, going nowhere and coming from nowhere, so how could we ever acquire gains or please and attract many people? We too shall set out. Where shall we go? Wherever our common purpose is accomplished." And so they began to search for their common purpose, and seeing on the north road some travelers whose purpose was the same, they went up to them and said: "Good sirs, where are you going, noble ones?" "Noble ones, we are going north." "Good sirs, we too will travel with you." "Noble ones, the northern road is rough and uneven, frequented by dogs, and the villages along it are places where women behave lewdly at every turn, so you will not enjoy it there." "Good sirs, even so, since we will get to see that country, let us go."

"Noble ones, if that is the case, then come, let us go in." And so the group of six, sharing a common purpose, set out together along the northern road and traveled on until at last they arrived there. Yet on the very same day that they arrived on the northern road, they became displeased with it. The next morning they rose early and set out along the road, and the merchants, seeing the group of six, bowed at their feet and said: "Noble ones, how is the northern road? You have not become displeased with it, have you?" "Good sirs, on the very same day we arrived on the northern road, we became displeased with it." "Noble ones, did we not tell you from the very beginning that the northern road is rough and uneven, frequented by dogs, and a place where women behave lewdly at every turn, so that you would not enjoy it there?" "Good sirs, is it indeed so then, shall we go on?" "Noble ones, we ourselves have not changed our route. Even so, there are other merchant friends of ours who have changed their route. Entrust yourselves to them and go with them." The group of six replied: "By all means, let it be so." And so the group of six, sharing a common purpose, set out together with those to whom they had been entrusted.

Now the group of six, in going about, would sometimes walk ahead of their companions out of fear of the dust, and sometimes behind them.
