When they began walking behind, some companions who were returning from the central region arrived, and the merchants welcomed those returning companions warmly, greeting them with joy one by one, and asked: "Where have you come from?" "From the central region." "Wise ones, were many profits obtained in the central region? Were you not ruined entirely by gamblers, thieves, or boatmen?" They replied: "Wise ones, indeed many profits were obtained in the central region. However, there were dishonest people there who, like white-robed robbers, were settled in the region, living by the patronage of gamblers, thieves, and boatmen, displeasing folk with falsehoods and stripping everyone of all their goods, so that ruin by gamblers, thieves, and boatmen did indeed occur."

Upon hearing this, the merchants were stricken with anguish, and going off to one side, they rested there with their arms folded, lost in troubled thought. The group of six arrived and said to them: "Wise ones, why are you sitting there with your arms folded, lost in troubled thought?" The merchants replied: "Noble ones, we set out eagerly, making every effort and exertion in order to acquire goods, enduring cold when it was cold, scorched by heat when it was hot, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and imperiled by the touch of horseflies, insects, wind, sun, and venomous snakes. We have indeed traveled to the central region, noble ones, and many profits have indeed been obtained there. Yet from our companions who are returning, we have heard that there are dishonest people settled there, like white-robed robbers, who live by the patronage of gamblers, thieves, and boatmen and who, displeasing folk with falsehoods, strip everyone of all their goods — and so we shall be ruined by gamblers, thieves, and boatmen."

The group of six said: "Good sirs, do those you regard as your friends also sit thus, lost in troubled thought?" "Noble ones, what of it? Will you petition the king on our behalf?" "Good sirs, we will not petition the king. But Śrāvastī has a gaming supervisor, and its gates are forty-eight —"

"There are thirty-six windows, so have your people enter through the windows and enjoy themselves — off you go."

The merchants were thoroughly pleased, and they went with the noble ones to a rocky outcrop not far from Śrāvastī. The group of six said: "Good friends, rest here for a while, and enter Śrāvastī by night. Release the mares, the oxen, and the donkeys." The merchants let them go, and rested a while, waiting for the time when the sun would set. They heard word that from the northern road a well-matched and splendid caravan was coming. They therefore made an offering cake to the yakṣas, pressed shut the gates, and remained where they were. The group of six said: "Wise ones, take your fill with your eyes open and go — we shall see to it that you enter comfortably through the windows without anyone knowing." They set off, and presently loaded up the donkeys, the mares, and the oxen, entered Śrāvastī through the windows, and by dawn had gone to the market street, spread out the northern traders' wares, and begun to sell them.

A certain man who had been separated from that same well-matched caravan entered through the gate, and the gamblers saw him and said: "Hey, friend, where have you come from?" The man said: "From a great rocky outcrop." They said: "Hey, friend, we have heard there is a northern traders' caravan at that rocky outcrop — did you not see it?" The man said: "Wise ones, I myself was with that caravan but then parted from it and came on; it had already gone ahead." When the gamblers heard this they became uneasy and said: "Hey, friend, we were holding the gates shut — how did it get in?" The man said: "Wise ones, if you do not believe me, come along to the market street and you will see for yourselves." They went to the market street together with him, and seeing the associates of the caravan spreading out the northern traders' wares and selling them, the gamblers asked: "Wise ones, how did you enter?" The associates said: "On foot." The gamblers said: "We know well enough how you entered on foot. Tell us exactly how you were let in and through which gate you entered, and we shall be friends with you." They said: "The noble ones of the group of six had us enter through the windows."

The gamblers then thought: "These group of six are unworthy monastics — we should feel contempt for them." And so they began to revile them, to mock them, and to speak ill of them, saying: "The conduct of the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan is scorched away, the conduct of brahmins is scorched away — and now they even harm the livelihoods of others."

At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not harm the livelihoods of others. If he does so, he shall be guilty of a serious offence."

The gamblers, thinking "These group of six are unworthy monastics and should be put to shame," waited for an opportunity; and in time it happened that the venerable Upananda, having dressed in his inner robe in the morning and taken up his bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms. A gambler saw him and said: "Noble one, I pay homage to you. Is there anything in your bowl? Please look." Upananda said: "Good sir, why do you ask? There is nothing in the bowl for gambling." The gambler said: "Noble one, may the wrong be appeased. I do not think that — but if there were a little cooked food and solid provisions in the bowl, I would take it from you and request it for myself." Upananda said: "Good sir, does a river run backwards against its current?"

"It is you who should give to me; it is not I who should give to you." The gambler said: "Noble one, I am amused." He called Upananda into his home, and filled the bowl with cooked food and solid provisions that had been prepared, and gave it to him. He said: "Noble one, please instruct me, and I will act according to your instruction and carry out everything the noble one commands." Upananda said with a pleasant expression: "May you be free from illness," and departed.

Now, the customary practice of the Group of Six was this: "Here we shall teach Dharma to the brahmins and householders who come and gather, refute opponents, proclaim our own fame, and also acquire gain." So they would take up their position either at a doorway or beside a road near a temple. And Upananda, having taken up his position beside the road near the temple, remained there engaged in the practice of not sleeping during the first and last watches of the night.

Then at another time some gambling merchants were passing not far from the temple, and Upananda, who was skilled in sounds, heard the sound of their footsteps approaching and stirred, and said: "Who are these people passing by?" The merchants remained silent. Upananda swiftly descended from the top of the temple, went to those merchants, and said: "Good sirs, who would be travelling at night with all their goods?" Those merchants replied: "Noble one, we are merchants who are gamblers." Upananda said: "Poor fellows! The king resides with us, provided with all his requisites. Even the elder Kauṇḍinya praises him, saying: 'May what has not come to this king come to be; may what has come grow, increase, and become abundant.' If you are going while rolling dice under his authority, why should we let it simply slip away? Today I shall have harm brought upon you." They were frightened and said: "Noble one, you are compassionate — please be forbearing, and we will provide whatever the noble one needs." Upananda said: "What will you do? Offer the price of the lodging." "Shall we offer it? We will offer it right now." They then departed from Upananda's presence, and went about saying: "Even King Prasenajit, who has arisen in the land of Kosala, does not get dice played against him — so what need is there to speak of the monk Upananda being paid off with a touch of the head?" Upananda also quickly finished his meal, and from the doorway began to wash his bowl and looked about in all four directions. A young man saw Upananda looking in all four directions and said: "Elder, why do you look about in all directions?" Upananda said: "Venerable sir, I am looking for those merchant friends of mine who entered Śrāvastī carrying their packs." The young man said: "Elder, they left just as long as it took you to finish your meal." Upananda grew indignant and thought: "I too have been deceived by them — I shall strike a knife with my fist and pound grass into the stone of my own loom, for I know what to do to them." When those merchants arrived again as before, Upananda caught them in that very same way a second time and said: "You have deceived me again," and the merchants replied —

"Venerable sir, some business came up for us, and that is why we left without taking our leave. Now we will offer you everything — that and more besides."

"You will offer it?"

"Yes, we will offer it."

That very day they departed from there and left the presence of Upananda, and they spread the saying everywhere: "If one would not even pay dice debts to King Prasenajit (Skt. prasenajit), who rules over Kosala, why say anything at all about paying a shaven-headed śramaṇa — a companion of Upananda?"

Upananda thought: "Those merchants have made me many promises, yet they have gone again without so much as a glance in my direction. That is not fitting. I shall rise still in the night and go to them." So he arranged his patched robe and went out into the street. The merchants had spread out their wares and were selling them, and when Upananda began to show them the mark, they said: "Venerable sir, please wait while we finish a transaction, and then we will come and pay you." Upananda said: "Very well, if you mean it." They replied: "Venerable sir, you need have no quarrel with us — please go." Upananda left and went quickly, very quickly, to the monastery, took his meal, washed his bowl, and began to look about in all directions. A young man said to him: "Elder, why do you keep looking all around?" Upananda replied: "Friend, I am looking for those merchant friends of mine who entered Śrāvastī carrying their packs." The young man said: "Elder, they left just as long as it took you to finish your meal." Upananda became greatly enraged, and scratching his head he thought: "I have now been deceived by them a second time. If I meet them again, I will introduce a rule of such a kind that they will never again be able to trade as merchants." However long it was, those merchants came again just as before, and Upananda said: "Wise ones, you have deceived me again and again. Now see what is to come." They replied: "Venerable sir, please be patient. We merchants are always distracted by the business of weighing and trading. We ask your forgiveness for what we promised before, and we will now offer all of that, whatever we promised before and whatever we promised since — every bit of it." Upananda, knowing that if he tried to press them into a corner they would understand and he should speak in a conciliatory way, said having understood and recognized this: "Good friends, will you truly offer it?"

"Venerable sir, we will truly offer it."

"If that is so, has any harm come to you? And as for us — would it not be bad if we were established near the monastery as merchants who are not considered merchants? So for now, stay here watching the road for as long as it takes." While they were staying there, Upananda went to where the dice players were.

At that time the dice players were saying among themselves: "Friends, the dice-cheating merchants are cheating at dice and slipping through the window, so that the tax revenues are not being collected, and the time has come. The king is fierce, and there is a situation such that he will have us — our sons, wives, and relatives — thrown into prison and put to death," and they sat there with deep anguish in their hearts.

Seeing them sitting thus in deep anguish, Upananda asked: "Why are you sitting there like that, with such anguish in your hearts?"

"Venerable sir, how could we not be in anguish? Those dice-cheating merchants are cheating at dice and slipping through the window, so that the tax revenues are not being collected, and the time has come. The king is fierce, and there is a situation such that he will have us — our sons, wives, and relatives — thrown into prison and put to death. Such is our situation."

"You wretches, who put you in charge of the dice hall? You deserve to be given many lashes or sent to be broken on the rack."

"Why do you not strip every last coin from even a single one of these dice-cheating merchants?"

"Venerable sir, Śrāvastī possesses the dice of omniscience, not the dice of wrongdoing. How then can we strip them of all their wealth?"

"You wretches! Śrāvastī has the dice of wrongdoing, not the dice of omniscience." Then he said: "Venerable sir, for as long as we have been working at dice, there was never a time when we had the dice of wrongdoing — how then would we have them now? You stay here, wretches, and I will go and have the dice-cheating merchants sent over. You seize them and strip them of all their wealth."

"If it is said that Śrāvastī has the dice of omniscience but not the dice of wrongdoing, then reply: 'Śrāvastī has the dice of wrongdoing, not the dice of omniscience.' If they say, 'For as long as we merchants have been in business, there was never a time when Śrāvastī had the dice of wrongdoing — how then would it have them now? Come, let us go before the merchants' assembly,' then drag them off to the royal palace. And if the king says, 'O wise ones, for as long as you have let Śrāvastī operate under my royal governance, there was never a time that I heard of Śrāvastī having the dice of wrongdoing — how then would it have them now?' then reply: 'Your Majesty, King Arada Brahmadatta, together with the merchants' assembly — whoever enters Śrāvastī from a pleasure grove, an assembly hall, or a great divine dwelling: that person has the dice of omniscience; and whoever enters Śrāvastī from a pleasure grove, an assembly hall, or a great divine dwelling: that person has the dice of wrongdoing. Ask the king whether this ordinance that has been established stands firm.' If he says it does stand firm, then say: 'Your Majesty, in a great treasury there is a box, and in that box is a copper tablet with writing on it — please examine it, Your Majesty.'"

When the dice-keepers had seized the dice-cheating merchants and stripped them of all their wealth, those merchants said: "Wise ones, why do you strip us of all our wealth? Śrāvastī has the dice of omniscience, not the dice of wrongdoing."

The dice-keepers replied: "Śrāvastī has the dice of wrongdoing, not the dice of omniscience."

The merchants said: "For as long as we merchants have been in business, there was never a time when Śrāvastī had the dice of wrongdoing — how then would it have them now? Come, let us go before the merchants' assembly."

The dice-keepers said: "Do not go to the merchants' assembly — come this way. We are going to the royal palace." And with that they dragged them off to the royal palace by force, despite their resistance. The merchants raised a cry to the merchants' assembly: "Wise ones, the dice-keepers have stripped us of all our wealth — come to our aid!" The merchants' assembly also went together with them before the king's presence and said: "Your Majesty, in your kingdom the dice-keepers have stripped merchants who have newly arrived of all their wealth — we beg you to grant them full protection."

The king commanded his ministers: "Wise ones, summon the dice-keepers." The ministers summoned the dice-keepers, and the king said:

"Wise ones, why have you stripped these merchants of all their wealth?" The dice-keepers replied: "Your Majesty, these merchants are cheats at dice, and Śrāvastī is known as a city where dishonest dice-players operate — for that reason we stripped them of all their wealth." The king said: "Wise ones, for as long as I have ruled my kingdom, I have never once heard that Śrāvastī harbors dishonest dice-players. Has it now become a city of dishonest dice-players? Acquire proper dice, and let them go." The dice-keepers replied: "Your Majesty, in the great treasury there is a chest, and in that chest there is a copper plate with an inscription upon it — may Your Majesty be pleased to examine it." The king commanded his attendants: "Bring that copper plate," and when it was brought and read aloud, the king heard his father's praises and spoke with a voice full of tears: "Wise ones, what my father did was done by Śakra (Indra), done by Brahmā — it is supremely authoritative. If they have been stripped of all their wealth, that is well."

The merchants, having lost all hope, went away with voices full of tears, and they said to the dice-keepers: "Wise ones, tell us — who reported on us?" The dice-keepers replied: "Who would report on you? We knew it ourselves — but out of compassion we let it pass. It is because you yourselves began to behave in a most outrageous manner that we lost our patience." The merchants said: "How can you claim to have had compassion? Tell us, and we will become friends with you." The dice-keepers replied: "It was the group of six noble ones." The merchants then began to abuse the renunciants who were sons of the Śākyan, saying: "The conduct of these renunciants, sons of the Śākyans, is burned away. The conduct of brahmins is burned away. One such as this even harms the livelihoods of others" — reviling them, spreading slander, and gossiping about them. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not harm the livelihood of others. If he does so, he is guilty of a serious offence."

Summary verse:

Those without feet, those with two feet,
those with four feet, and those with many feet —
all these classes are here collected.

"Those without feet" refers to snakes, leeches, and vermicular creatures. These are made use of for subsistence by three kinds of people: snake-charmers, royal physicians, and those who practice cupping. How do snake-charmers do so? Snake-charmers make their living in dependence on snakes — that is how snake-charmers do so. How do royal physicians do so? Royal physicians make their living in dependence on leeches — that is how royal physicians do so. How do those who practice cupping do so?

Those who practice cupping do so in the following way: they cause the worm-creatures to emerge, drawing them out and applying them to the surface of swollen flesh, and the worm-creatures become intoxicated and inebriate, drinking various kinds of intoxicating liquids. That is how those who practice cupping do so.

If a monk steals footless creatures, the value of the footless creatures is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression.

"Those with two feet" refers to humans and certain birds. Humans steal by three means: by location, by signal, and by sign. How is it done by location? When someone says: "When I am seen in the park, or in the assembly hall, or at such-and-such a divine shrine, know at that moment that you have done the deed" — that is how it is done by location. How is it done by signal? When someone says: "When I am seen in the morning, or at midday, or in the late afternoon, know at that moment that you have done the deed" — that is how it is done by signal. How is it done by sign? When someone says: "When you see me having had my hair and beard newly trimmed, or wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe, or carrying a bowl covered with a beeswax-leaf wrapping, or a hollow-handled bowl, or a bowl of melted butter, or a bowl of oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl with a lid of molasses — know at that moment that you have done the deed" — that is how it is done by sign.

If a monk steals a human being, the value of the human is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression.

Birds steal by two means: by entrapment and by coming into the open. How is it by entrapment? If a monk steals a bird by trapping it, the value of the bird is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression. That is how it is by entrapment.

How is it by coming into the open? When a trainer of birds, or a skilled student of such a trainer, sets fire to a forest in order to flush the birds out, to spoil their feeding grounds, or to cause them distress by improper means, and some birds, overcome and bewildered by the smoke, come to roost on the walking grounds of the monks, or in the courtyards, or in the gatehouse — if a monk then steals birds that have come in this way, the value of the birds is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression. That is how it is by coming into the open.

This is the Vinaya Analysis (Skt. Vibhaṅga), the sixth section.

"Those with four feet" refers to elephants, horses, mules, cattle, donkeys, goats, deer, buffalo, and pigs. These are stolen by two means: by luring from the herd and by prodding. How is it by luring from the herd? If a monk steals an elephant by luring it from the herd, for as long as it remains visible a serious transgression accrues; when it passes out of sight, it is declared stolen — the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression. That is how it is by luring from the herd.

How is it by prodding? If a monk prods an elephant, driving it against various trees, shrubs, walls, or other objects, for as long as it remains visible a serious transgression accrues; when it passes out of sight, it is declared stolen — the value is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression. That is how it is by prodding.

Just as it is with elephants, so too it is the same with horses and other remaining four-footed animals.

Now, "many-legged creatures" refers to ants, flat insects, sesame worms, caterpillars, carrion-eaters, scorpions, beetles, and crawling insects. These are used in three ways: by brigands, by those belonging to the great frontier-guard of cities, and by sea-merchants.

How do brigands use them? Brigands fill jars with many-legged creatures, leaving the lids off, and set them down. When they cut and sever whoever they wish to harm, they insert that person's foot or hand into those jars. When the creatures seize hold of the limb, they quickly pull it away, causing numerous deep wounds. That is how brigands do it.

How do those belonging to the great frontier-guard of cities use them? Those belonging to the great frontier-guard of cities fill jars with many-legged creatures, leaving the lids off, and set them down. When an enemy army approaches, they engage them in battle. If they are able to defeat the enemy, well and good. If they are not able, they hurl jars filled with many-legged creatures, with the lids left off, at the fence line; and when the creatures seize hold of the enemy troops, they scatter and flee. That is how those belonging to the great frontier-guard of cities do it.

How do sea-merchants use them? Sea-merchants fill jars with many-legged creatures, leaving the lids off. When they outfit sea-vessels and set out across the great ocean to seek wealth, and pirates bearing blue or black insignia come and attack their ships, the merchants engage those pirates in battle. If they are able to defeat them, well and good. If they are not able, they hurl the jars filled with many-legged creatures, with the lids left off; and when the creatures seize hold of the pirates, those pirates scatter and flee. That is how sea-merchants do it.

If a monk steals many-legged creatures, the value of the many-legged creatures is to be assessed, and if the full threshold is met, it is a defeat; if the full threshold is not met, it is a serious transgression.

A summary verse:

An outcast and one with mange,
a patched robe, for a while a time,
given by fine features and by wealth,
knowing it to be one's own, one takes the bowl.
Undefeated, concealed by a companion —
one who is self-shaming is indeed a thief.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two monks who were friends, companions, associates, and frequent companions — one known as the outcast and one known as the mangy one. The outcast was renowned and of great merit, but small of body. He had extra alms-bowls, robes, a net, a cup, and a belt. The mangy one was large of body, but of little renown and little merit. He made do with the three robes, yet those three robes of his were shabby, and the patched robe in particular was thoroughly worn out.

The monks said to the mangy one: "Venerable sir, if you have come to have few desires, why do you display yourself naked? Is it because you have obtained something, or because you have not obtained something?" The mangy one replied: "It is because I have not obtained something."

"Why do you not make use of them? You have abandoned the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Who then will give to you?" The mangy monk said: "You are his intimate companion, his constant visitor, his close friend, one who exchanges courtesies with him. He has extra alms-bowls, robes, a net, a cup, and a belt — why do you not ask him for them?" The mangy one replied: "He will not give them." "Have you ever asked him even once before?" "I have never asked him even once." "Are you going to remove your sandals merely at the sound of water? Go and ask — he will give them."

Encouraged by the monks, the mangy one went to the renowned monk's dwelling. Finding him absent, the mangy one thought: "The renowned monk is small of body, so I should measure this patched robe of his. If it fits my body, I will ask for it; if it does not fit, why should I put him in a position of owing me a debt of gratitude?" Thinking thus, the mangy one entered the renowned monk's cell and began to examine the patched robe. He saw that on the collar of the robe there was a red-and-yellow patched piece, and he took it, put it on, and stood adjusting it, checking side after side. At that moment the renowned monk arrived, and the instant he saw him he said: "Venerable sir, you have taken that patched piece with a mind to steal." The mangy one replied: "Venerable sir, I did not take it with a mind to steal. It was like this: since the renowned monk is small of body, I wished to measure his robe — thinking that if it fit my body I would ask for it, and if it did not fit, I thought: what use is this article to me?" The renowned monk said: "Venerable sir, why do you shift from one thing to another? You took it with a mind to steal, and so a defeat has occurred for you." The mangy one then felt remorse, thinking: "Has a defeat perhaps occurred for me?" And he reported the matter to the monks of that occasion. The monks informed the Blessed One, and the Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned that monk: "Monk, with what intention did you take that patched robe?" The mangy one reported to the Blessed One what had happened, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, for this monk whose intention was to examine and assess, there is no transgression. Nevertheless, a monk should not generate trust toward one in whom trust is not warranted. Friends, you see, are of three kinds: lesser, middling, and great. Toward a lesser friend one may place a small degree of trust, but not middling trust and not great trust. Toward a middling friend one may place small and middling trust, but not great trust. Toward a great friend one may place small, middling, and great trust. If a monk generates trust toward one in whom trust is not warranted, he incurs an offense."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two monks — intimate companions, constant visitors, close friends, who exchanged courtesies equally — named Sudarśana and Dhanadata. The alms-bowl of Sudarśana was beautiful, clear, round, and serviceable, and the alms-bowl of Dhanadata, though small, was also beautiful, clear, round, and serviceable. On a certain other occasion the two of them had finished the business of eating and

When they had finished washing their bowls, Sudarśana placed Dhanadata's small bowl inside his own bowl and said, "Venerable Dhanadata, one who possesses bowls like this — a bowl and a small bowl — practises the wholesome with a heart that is content with little." Dhanadata replied, "If you want it, take it." After some time had passed, a small piece of work came up for Dhanadata at a rocky cliff, and he said, "Venerable Sudarśana, a small piece of work has come up for me at a rocky cliff. For whoever does that work for me, I will give the small bowl." Sudarśana asked, "Will you give it?" "I will give it." "That is a bargain." But then, having said "That is a bargain," Sudarśana thought to himself, "On account of this, those who lead the holy life will say that Sudarśana works for wages," and so remorse arose in him and he did not go.

After some further time had passed, some work of his own came up for Sudarśana at that same rocky cliff. He thought, "I will go and do both tasks and come back," so Sudarśana went, did both tasks, and returned. He then said, "Venerable Dhanadata, I have accomplished your work; now give me the small bowl." Dhanadata replied, "You went for your own work, not for mine, so I will not give it." Sudarśana said, "If you will not give it, I will take it myself. See if you can stop me." Then, while Dhanadata had gone out, Sudarśana took the small bowl, placed it inside his own bowl, and set it down. When Dhanadata returned and the small bowl was not to be seen, he said, "Venerable Sudarśana, who has taken my small bowl?" Sudarśana replied, "Who had the power? I had the power — I took it." Dhanadata was displeased and said, "You have taken it with a thieving intention, and so a defeat-level offense has arisen for you." Sudarśana became remorseful, thinking, "Has a defeat-level offense truly arisen for me?" He then reported the matter to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned Sudarśana: "Monk, with what intention did you take that small bowl?" Sudarśana reported to the Blessed One exactly what had occurred, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, when a monk takes a small bowl understanding it as his own, in this case there is no offense. Furthermore, a monk should not work for wages; rather, let him work with open-handedness or with the wish to gain merit. If a monk works for wages, it becomes a serious matter."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two monks — constant companions who spoke freely together — named Ajita and Candragarbha (Śaśigarbha). Candragarbha was of great renown and great merit; he had extra bowls, robes, a net, a bowl-bag, and a waist-cloth. Ajita was of little renown and little merit; he made do with just the three robes, and those three robes were poor and his patched outer robe was entirely worn out. The monks said to Ajita, "Venerable, if you wish to have few desires, why do you expose yourself in this way? Is it because you have received something, or because you have not received anything?" Ajita replied, "It is because I have not received anything." "Then why do you not put yourself forward? Having abandoned the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, who will give to you?" "Monk Candragarbha — he is your companion who speaks freely with you.

goes freely." "He is your companion, your close friend, and there is a bond of mutual speech. If he has a spare alms bowl, a robe, a sitting cloth, a small bowl, or a belt, why do you not ask him for them?" Ajita said, "He will not give." "Have you ever asked him even once before?" "I have not asked even once." "Then why do you take off your sandals when you hear the sound of water? Go and ask him, and he will give."

The monks thus encouraged Ajita, and he went to Candragarbha's dwelling and said, "Venerable Candragarbha, give me an alms bowl." Candragarbha replied, "I will not give." Ajita said, "If you will not give an alms bowl, then give me a robe." Candragarbha replied, "Do you think I see you as a worthy lay donor to whom I should bow my head? If I will not even give you a word of greeting, how much less need there be any question of a robe." Ajita became annoyed and thought to himself, "If I am always the first to attend to all his immediate needs, yet he says, 'I will not even give you a word of greeting, so how much less a robe,' then if today I do not steal all his robes, I shall not be worthy of the name Ajita." And so Ajita stayed there watching for an opportunity, always keeping this plan in mind, intent on stealing Candragarbha's robes at some moment.

Then at a certain time, Candragarbha came to be engaged in the tasks of cooking and attending to the fire, and Ajita went to Candragarbha's side and said, "Venerable Candragarbha, I too will help." Candragarbha said, "Very well, do so then." Ajita began to turn over, dust off, shake out, and inspect Candragarbha's robes one after another. Candragarbha thought, "Watching him in this way, turning over and carefully inspecting my robes again and again, he will surely steal my robes." With this suspicion, Candragarbha turned his robes inside out, stuffed them into a bundle, placed them in his own sleeping place, and lay down on them.

The monks, not sleeping during the first or last watches of the night, were engaged in the practice of diligent striving, and Ajita called out, "Venerable Candragarbha, come here. Go and do your wholesome practice." Candragarbha said, "You go; I am tired and will come later." Ajita said, "Venerable, please come," and left the room. Candragarbha thought, "If I go, my robes will be ruined. But if I do not go, my wholesome practice will be entirely lost. What is the means by which my robes will not be ruined and my wholesome practice will not be lost either?" Thinking and reasoning this through, he placed his own bundle in Ajita's sleeping place, and placed the bundle that Ajita had control of in his own sleeping place, and lay down.

When the monks began reciting in the latter watch of the night, Candragarbha said to Ajita, "Venerable Ajita, get up and do your wholesome practice." Ajita said, "I have already done my wholesome practice. Now you go and do your wholesome practice. I am tired, tired, and I am resting," and so Candragarbha went off for the sake of his wholesome practice. Ajita waited a while and thought to himself whether it was yet the right time or not, and seeing that the moment was good, he took his own bundle from Candragarbha's sleeping place and left.

When dawn broke and night had become day, Ajita thought, "Let me look and see what kind of robes have made me guilty, and what transgression has arisen."

When he saw his own worn and tattered robes, he became distressed and thought: "It is only my own robe that has made me guilty of a defeat. What use is there in taking on an iron ball to swallow? I should return to lay life." And so he went before the Blessed One, thinking: "If I have the fortune, I will practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One. But if I have no such fortune, I will return to lay life." With that thought, he went to where the Blessed One was. At that time, the Blessed One was seated before a retinue of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One caught sight of the venerable Ajita while he was still far in the distance. Having seen him, the Blessed One said to the monks: "Monks, do you see that monk coming from far away?" "Venerable one, we see him." "Monks, this Ajita, free of delusion, has incurred a serious transgression on account of his own worn and tattered robe. Monks, since there are these and other faults of a theft-motivated mind, a monk must not take even his own alms-bowl or robe with a theft-motivated mind. If a monk takes his own alms-bowl or robe with a theft-motivated mind, it becomes a serious transgression."

Summary verse: A patchwork robe left hanging, begging grain and butter for a wager, a householder's son and grandson, a child of the divine servant Pilinda.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two nuns: one born in the east and one born in the south. The one born in the east was a nun who walked ahead; the one born in the south was a nun who followed behind. The two of them paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, approached his presence, bowed their heads to the Blessed One's two feet, and stood to one side. The Blessed One taught them the Dharma. They paid homage at the Blessed One's feet and departed. As they walked, the patchwork robe worn over the shoulder of the one born in the east, who was walking ahead, slipped and fell loose. The one born in the south, who was coming behind, called out: "Noble one! Avasaṭha! Avasaṭha!" But the one born in the east, carried away by the momentum of the Dharma teaching, did not notice, and the patchwork robe fell to the ground. The one born in the south picked it up, and thinking: "If I give it to her right now, the noble one will lose the merit of her wholesome state," she went to the assembly hall to give it to her there. When the two of them arrived at the assembly hall, the one born in the east, quickly and without delay, washed her two feet outside the assembly hall, entered, and sat down in a half-crossed posture. The one born in the south thought: "If I give it to her now, that very fault will be incurred," and so she resolved to give it to her a little later when she rose. She carried the patchwork robe to her own cell and placed it on the robe-rack.

On another day when night had turned to dawn, the one born in the east said: "Young woman, bring the patchwork robe — let us go for alms." The young attendant entered the cell, looked at the robe-rack, and not seeing the patchwork robe, said: "Noble one, the patchwork robe is not here." The one born in the east said: "Look in the cell of the one born in the south." When the attendant entered the cell of the one born in the south, she saw the patchwork robe placed on the robe-rack. Seeing it, she thought: "Who has brought the noble one's patchwork robe here?" The one born in the south, hearing this, said: "I brought it here." For the one born in the south had come to understand how things had come to pass.

That nun scolded her with hostility and said: "You placed it in your own cell with the intention to steal it, and by keeping it there a defeat has come upon you." The nun born in the south then felt remorse, thinking: "Has a defeat truly come upon me as well?" She reported the matter at that time to the nuns, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned that nun: "Nun, what did you mean when you said 'avasatha'?" She replied: "Venerable one, in the central land, a storehouse — and whatever fallen article there is — we call 'avasatha.'" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, this nun incurs no transgression by virtue of a term specific to language, a term specific to region, and a term specific to locality. However, every fault that has arisen came about through keeping another's fallen article for a long time. Therefore, neither a monk nor a nun should keep another's fallen article for a long time; if kept, it becomes a serious offence." After the Blessed One had declared that a monk or nun should not keep another's fallen article for a long time, there was a monk who saw a fallen article belonging to someone else, recognized it as belonging to a certain senior monk, went to that monk's cell, and knocked gently at the door, knock after knock. That monk, rising from meditative absorption, said: "Who is there?" The other said: "Venerable one, I have found this fallen article of yours — please take it." The monk replied: "It would be preferable for me to have been robbed of that article by those who take without being given. But disturbing me from such a fine sign of meditative absorption — that is not acceptable." That monk then felt remorse, thinking: "Have I incurred a transgression by disturbing a monk from meditative absorption?" He reported the matter to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk incurs no transgression. Furthermore, when a monk wishes to return an article on that account, he should hang it in plain sight before him on a peg and leave it there." There was then a monk who saw a fallen article belonging to someone else, recognized it as belonging to a certain senior monk, took it, went to that monk, and said: "Venerable one, I have found this fallen article of yours — please take it." That monk, being hostile toward him, said: "Venerable one, it is not that you found a fallen article — rather, you stole it with the intention to steal." That monk then felt remorse, thinking: "Have I incurred a transgression?" He reported the matter to the monks at that time, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk incurs no transgression. However, when a monk sees a fallen article belonging to a fellow monk, he should entrust it to the rector (Sanskrit: karma-kāraka), and the rector should make it known within the Saṅgha for two or three days. If the owner is identified, it should be given to him. If not, the Saṅgha may do with it as seems fit."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At Śrāvastī there was a nun named Rimā, an arhat who had conquered — she had conquered all that is to be conquered. A young spice-merchant's son conceived deep faith in her, prostrated at her feet, and said: "Noble Lady, whatever you might need, please command me and I shall accomplish it all." He offered her every requisite, and she accepted, saying: "Young man, very well, so be it."

Now at some later time the nun Rimā fell ill and was unable to go on alms-round, while the other nuns set out on their rounds. The young spice-merchant bowed to those nuns and asked: "Noble Ladies, the noble Rimā is not to be seen just now — where has she gone?" They replied: "Young man, she is unwell." He said: "Noble Ladies, I have supplied her with every requisite, and yet she has not sent me a single word in return. Should there be anything at all she needs, please let her know she should send word." They said: "Young man, very well, so be it," and departed.

He made that same offer three times over. Meanwhile a certain young woman noticed that this spice-merchant's son kept offering and offering again, and she thought: "Is he doing this out of pure faith, or is he doing it with ulterior motives — trying to seduce her? I should find out." She therefore brought him a small bowl and said to him: "Noble Rimā needs sesame oil." He at once pressed fresh sesame oil on the spot, filled the small bowl, gave it to her, and said: "Noble Lady, should she need anything more, please let her know she should send word." The young woman replied: "Young man, very well, so be it," and went away.

Then she used that sesame oil to massage the nun Rimā's hands, to massage her feet, and to massage her head and body, and she also used it as lamp oil.

Now at some later time the nun Rimā recovered from her illness and set out on alms-round. The young spice-merchant saw her, prostrated, and said: "Noble Lady, it is such a long time since I have seen you." She replied: "Son, I was ill." He continued: "Noble Lady, I supplied you with every requisite, and yet you did not send me so much as a single word in return. But then a certain noble lady came and said, 'The noble Rimā needs sesame oil,' and I immediately pressed fresh sesame oil on the spot, filled a small bowl, and gave it to her. She also told me that should you need anything more, please send word." The nun Rimā said: "Ārya, you have done no wrong," and she went on her way, completed her alms-round, returned to her dwelling, and said to the young woman: "Young woman, did you accept sesame oil just once from that great spice-merchant's son, doing so in my name?" The young woman replied: "Noble Lady, when I went on alms-round, he said to me three times: 'I have supplied the noble Rimā with every requisite, and she has not sent me a single word in return — should the noble Lady need anything, please let her know to send word.' When he kept offering again and again, the thought arose in me: is he doing this out of genuine faith, or is he doing it with ulterior motives — trying to seduce her? I want to find out. So I told him, 'The noble Rimā needs sesame oil,' and gave him a small bowl. He took the bowl, filled it with sesame oil, and gave it to me, and I used it to massage the noble Lady's hands, feet, head, and body, and as lamp oil." The nun Rimā asked: "Did she say that I had sent you to fetch sesame oil from him as repayment for some occasion? Did she instruct you to bring it back in exchange for something?" "She gave no such instruction whatsoever." Then another nun, one who had companions, said: "Noble Lady, do you suppose this amounts to something?"

This had spread the word about the noble Rimā throughout all of Śrāvastī, and those guilty of a defeat were living off her. The nun in question then felt remorse, thinking, "Has a transgression entailing defeat arisen for me?" She thereupon reported the matter to the nuns, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks brought it before the Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked that nun: "With what intention did you take the sesame oil?" "With the intention of nursing someone who was ill, Blessed One." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no transgression for this nun, since she acted with the intention of nursing the sick. Furthermore, monks and nuns should not administer medicine to a sick person without first asking that person. Rather, they should either obtain it from the Saṅgha's infirmary, or else ask the sick person what medicine they wish to be given — whether it be from a devoted donor, from a relative, or even from many relatives — and then obtain it from whatever source the person names. If a monk or nun administers medicine to a sick person without first asking, it becomes an offense involving a misdeed."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in the morning, dressed himself, took up his bowl and robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Going along from house to house, he came to the place where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's house stood. At that time the sons of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada were reading texts of the non-Buddhists. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw the sons of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada reading these non-Buddhist texts. Having seen this, he said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Householder, what are the boys reading?" "Noble one, they are reading non-Buddhist texts." "Householder, non-Buddhist texts are like iron thorns — they are difficult to understand, and even if understood they do not lead to certainty, nor do they bring about the exhaustion of defilements. The word of the Buddha, however, is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end — it leads to higher knowledge, to complete awakening, and to passing beyond sorrow. Why do they not read that instead?" "Noble one, who would permit them to read it?" "I will have them read it." "Noble one, please do graciously allow them to read it." The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the boys: "Boys, go today to the noble one at the Jeta Grove and read the word of the Buddha." Each day the boys adorned themselves with ornaments and, surrounded by a retinue of attendants, went to the Jeta Grove and began to read the word of the Buddha with the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Now in Śrāvastī there were thieves known as those of "the last month of autumn" whose customary practice was this: immediately after the invitation ceremony, they would deliberate among themselves, saying, "By doing what shall we obtain means of comfortable living for a whole year without having to work?" When those boys — adorned each day with all their ornaments and surrounded by their retinue of attendants — were going to the Jeta Grove to read the word of the Buddha with the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, these thieves waited for them along the road, intending to seize them. But the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana perceived that the boys had remained at home,

The householder, for his part, knew that the boys were in the presence of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and so the thought arose in the thieves' minds: "If we can strip the boys of their persons, we shall have enough to live on for the rest of our lives; and if we cannot, then by stripping them of their ornaments we shall be able to live in comfort for a whole year without having to work." They gave one another the signal and positioned themselves along the road. The boys then came along adorned with all their ornaments, and the thieves seized them.

The escort boys who had been sent along behind them saw that the boys had been seized by thieves, and they ran at once to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to report to him: "Householder, your sons have been taken by the thieves of the last month of autumn — please think of some means to help!" The householder Anāthapiṇḍada ran to the presence of Prasenajit, the king who had arisen in Kośala, and said: "Sire, my sons have been seized by the thieves of the last month of autumn — please bestow upon me the gift of my sons' return!" King Prasenajit gave orders to the young prince Ajātaśatru: "Go and quickly bring back the householder's sons along with the thieves." But Ajātaśatru had long been a close companion of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and so he did not set out at that very moment.

Then the gods who had faith in the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as follows: "Noble one, please take notice! Your attendants have been seized by the thieves of the last month of autumn — please exert yourself on their behalf!" The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reflected: "If I give no thought to the boys, for the time being the boys will experience the suffering that comes from being separated from their parents, and the parents too will experience the suffering that comes from being separated from their sons. Those who lack faith will find an opening to disparage the teaching, and even those who have faith will think, 'Look — even those going to the Jeta Grove are robbed by the thieves of the last month of autumn; who then will go there in future?' and they will turn away entirely. Therefore I shall display my miraculous power." With this thought and this understanding, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana miraculously conjured up the army of Ajātaśatru by his supernatural power, and drums were beaten with a resounding roll in all four directions. The thieves of the last month of autumn, realizing this, thought: "We are surrounded on all four sides by the troops of the commander Ajātaśatru — it is wrong to be caught; let us flee!" And so they abandoned the boys and dispersed.

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then dissolved the miraculous display he had conjured up and sat down near a tree by the roadside. When the boys arrived, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to them: "Boys, where have you been?" They replied: "Noble one, we were robbed by the thieves of the last month of autumn." "And who has freed you?" "The commander Ajātaśatru." "Boys, today your parents have been sitting in distress — go home now and comfort them." The boys returned home. The commander Ajātaśatru, meanwhile, equipped with a fourfold army — a corps of elephants, a corps of cavalry, a corps of chariots, and a corps of infantry — marched out from Śrāvastī.

When Ajātaśatru saw the boys he said: "Boys, where have you been?" And they replied:

"While we were going to the Jeta Grove, we were robbed by the thieves of the last month of autumn." "And who freed you?" "The commander Ajātaśatru." Ajātaśatru thought to himself: "I am marching on campaign right now — how could I have freed them? Surely it was some noble one of great supernatural power and great might who freed them." Having reflected and understood this, he asked: "Boys, whom did you see in that place?" "The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana." Ajātaśatru thought: "It was he who freed them — who else could have done it?" And understanding this, he rejoiced and rejoiced again, and uttered this solemn declaration: "In our land there dwells such a noble one, so great in supernatural power, so great in might, who is a protector for the welfare of this life, the welfare of the next life, and the welfare of both this life and the next — truly we have found what is most excellent to find." Uttering this praise, he marched on and entered Śrāvastī.

As he was pronouncing this praise and entering Śrāvastī, the group of six monks also came out. The group of six said: "Whose praises are you singing?" Ajātaśatru replied: "Yours." "What have we done?" "The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana freed the sons of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, who had been seized by the thieves of the last month of autumn." The group of six monks said: "We beggars — that may be so, yet there are some here who have great faith in naked wanderers. If only the naked ones had seen them, they too would have pointed out the way." The boys stood there in silence. Then the group of six said: "Nanda and Upananda, they have been made to hear this. A minor transgression has arisen — make them perform the act of expulsion from the dwelling."

The group of six went to the monastery and, after performing the meal duties, paid homage in order of seniority and went to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was. Having approached, they said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable one, we pay homage to you. Reverend ones, please open the matter of the Ārokya dwelling. We open the matter regarding the five classes of transgression. Did the elder free the sons of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada who had been seized by the thieves of the last month of autumn?" "It is so — I freed them." "Reverend one, we understand that the elder has understood. We wish that the elder remain, experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment. We do not wish that the elder, while showing compassion to one side and showing compassion to those nearby, should show no compassion to the thieves of the last month of autumn. As for the transgression of freeing the goods that others had made their own, please reverse it in accordance with the Dharma." "I see no transgression." "Reverend ones, since the Blessed One has said that when a transgression is not seen, the act of suspension from residence should be performed — therefore, let whoever is watching over the dwelling strike the gong. This act of suspension from residence is to be performed." Having gone to the dwelling-keeper, he said: "Venerable one, strike the gong. Since the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana will not reverse the transgression that has arisen in accordance with the Dharma, the act of suspension from residence is to be performed."

At that time the venerable Śāriputra, as the elder of the Saṅgha, overseeing the teaching and carefully attending to whether any discordant element might arise in the teaching through deceitful means, examined this proceeding and said to the dwelling-keeper: "Venerable one, who performs the act of full residence, or the act of basic full residence, or the act of satisfaction, or the act of basic satisfaction, or the act of expulsion?"

"No elder does so. For the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, not reversing in accordance with the Dharma the transgression that has arisen, an act of suspension from residence is performed on account of his not seeing the transgression."

The venerable monk said to the dwelling-keeper in a fitting manner: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, all-seeing, and has attained unsurpassed mastery over knowledge and all objects of knowledge; he cuts through every doubt. Go before him and ask. Whatever the Blessed One teaches you, hold to that accordingly."

The monks then presented the matter before the Blessed One. Since the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, act with full knowledge, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, what was the intention with which you displayed the miraculous powers? I thought to myself: if I give no thought to the boys, the boys will experience the suffering that arises from separation from their parents, and the parents will experience the suffering that arises from separation from their children. Those without faith will find their opportunity, and those who have faith, thinking that such displays are carried on here by those of base conduct in the last month of autumn, will be turned away — and then who will come to the Jeta Grove hereafter? I thought that it would change matters, and so I chose to display the miraculous powers."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, in Maudgalyāyana's displaying of miraculous powers with such an intention, there is no transgression."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the place of the Kalandakas.

Then the venerable Pilindavatsa, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robes, entered Rājagṛha for alms. Going from house to house for alms in due order, he came to the house of a certain soldier.

At that time the nephews of the venerable Pilindavatsa were reading the treatises of outsiders (tīrthikas). The venerable Pilindavatsa saw the nephews reading the treatises of outsiders. Having seen this, he said to the soldier: "Nephew-boys, what are you reading?" "Noble one, these are the treatises of outsiders." "Nephews, the treatises of outsiders are like iron grass — difficult to understand, and even when understood they do not lead one to certainty, nor do they bring the defilements to exhaustion. The word of the Buddha is wholesome in the beginning, wholesome in the middle, and wholesome at the end; it leads to direct knowledge, to complete awakening, and to passing beyond sorrow. Why do you not read that instead?" "Noble one, who will give us leave to read it?" "I will have you read it." "Noble one, please do give us leave to read it."

The soldier said to those boys: "Boys, go to the Bamboo Grove today, to the noble one's presence, and take up the word of the Buddha." Each day those boys, adorned with all their ornaments and surrounded by attendant youths sent with them, went to the Bamboo Grove and began to read the word of the Buddha under the venerable Pilindavatsa's guidance.

Now in Rājagṛha there were thieves known as the miscreants of the last month of autumn, who roamed about. Immediately after the invitation ceremony had been performed, these men conferred among themselves: "Friends, what act might we perform so that without exertion we could enjoy ourselves and live at ease throughout the year?" Those boys — the nephews of the noble Pilindavatsa — came each day adorned with all their ornaments, surrounded by attendant youths, going to the Bamboo Grove and reading the word of the Buddha under the noble Pilindavatsa. The thieves waited along the road,

Knowing that if they seized those boys, the noble Pilindavatsa's nephews, the boys would be confined at home, and knowing also that the brahmin attendants would remain at the noble Pilindavatsa's side, the thieves reasoned: "If we can abduct the boys, we shall have our livelihood secured for the rest of our lives; and if we cannot, we will steal their ornaments — either way, we will be able to enjoy ourselves throughout the year without any effort and live at ease." With this thought in mind, they gave the signal, went and stationed themselves along the road, and when the boys came adorned with all their ornaments, the thieves bundled them into a boat and carried them away.

The attendant youths who had been sent along behind the boys saw them being taken by the thieves, ran immediately to the soldiers of the venerable Pilindavatsa, and reported: "Master, your lord's sons have been abducted by the miscreants of the last month of autumn — please take heed!" The brahmin too ran off to Bimbisāra, the king of Magadha (whose epithet means "one of handsome form, essence of the splendid"), entered his inner chambers, and said: "O king, my sons have been carried off by the miscreants of the last month of autumn — please grant them your rescue!" King Bimbisāra then commanded the young prince Ajātaśatru (whose name means "he whose enemy is yet unborn"): "Go quickly, round up the brahmin's sons and the thieves!" But Ajātaśatru had for a long time been intimate with that brahmin and his household, and so he did not go at once.

Then those gods who had devotion toward the venerable Pilindavatsa spoke to him thus: "O noble one, please be aware — your nephews have been seized by the miscreants of the last month of autumn. Please exert yourself!" The venerable Pilindavatsa reflected: "If I give no thought to these boys, for the moment the boys will experience the suffering that comes from being separated from their parents, and the parents will experience the suffering that comes from being separated from their sons. The faithless will find occasion to slander, and even the faithful will think: 'So, all these boys can be abducted by the miscreants of the last month of autumn — who then will go to the Bamboo Grove from now on?' This would change everything. Therefore I shall display my supernatural powers." Having thought and understood this, the venerable Pilindavatsa went by supernatural power and sat down beside the boat — and the boat would not move.

The thieves wondered: "Why does this boat not move?" And they saw the venerable Pilindavatsa sitting nearby. Seeing him, they addressed him thus: "O noble one, why do you block us? Are things subject to aging — are we the only ones you would obstruct? If you had not attained such a collection of qualities as this, would you not today be robbed of your nephews? O noble one, please release us now!"

The venerable Pilindavatsa withdrew those supernatural exertions he had set in motion, and then said to the boys: "Boys, your parents are sitting in distress today — go home tomorrow morning." The boys went home with the noble one, and young Ajātaśatru too came out of Rājagṛha with the four divisions of his army — the host of elephants, the host of cavalry, the host of chariots, and the host of infantry — in full armor. When Ajātaśatru saw the boys, he said: "Boys, where were you going?" And they replied:

"As we were going to the Amra Grove, we were abducted by disciples of the last month of autumn who possess the left hand." "Then who freed you?" "It was the son of the noble Pilindavatsa." Ajātaśatru was pleased, most pleased, and gave voice to this solemn declaration: "We have gained a great gain, in that in our land there dwells such a noble one of such great supernatural power, of such great might, who provides refuge for the aims of this life and the aims of the next life and the aims of both this life and the next." And so he continued to give utterance to that praise.

As he was giving utterance to that praise and was entering Rājagṛha, the Group of Six came out as well, and the Group of Six said: "Whose praise are you uttering?" Ajātaśatru said: "Yours." "What have we done?" "The son of the noble Pilindavatsa freed the brahmin boys who had been seized by disciples of the last month of autumn." The Group of Six said: "We who are poor — and yet here some people have confident faith in naked ascetics. If only the naked ones could see, they would even point out the road. But these stand in silence." And the Group of Six said: "Agreed — let an understanding be reached concerning the Venerable Priya-Upananda. A downfall has arisen over a minor matter; send them into a hollow."

The Group of Six then went to the monastery, performed the meal duties, and paid homage in order of seniority. They went to where the venerable Pilindavatsa was staying and said to him: "Venerable one, we pay homage. Venerable ones, be so kind as to open the procedure for the monk Ārogy. Open the procedure with respect to the five categories of downfalls." "Did the elder rescue the brahmin boys who had been seized by disciples of the last month of autumn?" "Yes, I freed them." "Then we wish the elder to abide experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and the ease of entering meditative equipoise. Yet we hope that, while possessing one-pointed compassion, you will show compassion toward the brahmin boys but will not refrain from showing compassion toward the disciples of the last month of autumn. As for the downfall that arose from freeing property that others had claimed as their own, please restore it in accordance with Dharma." "I see no downfall." "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared: because a downfall is not acknowledged, the act of suspension from one's dwelling is to be performed. Strike the wooden gong for the attendant." Going to the attendant's quarters, they said: "Venerable one, strike the wooden gong. Because the venerable Pilindavatsa refuses to restore in accordance with Dharma the downfall that has arisen, the act of suspension from his dwelling is to be performed." At that time, the venerable Śāriputra was serving as the Saṅgha's elder, and seeing that in the practice of the teaching some slight irregularity through doctrinal cunning might arise, he said to the attendant: "Venerable one, who is it that is in complete residence, or initially in complete residence, or to be satisfied, or initially to be satisfied, that you would expel? There is no elder at all — it is this: because the venerable Pilindavatsa does not restore the downfall that has arisen in accordance with Dharma, the act of suspension from dwelling is being performed for him on account of not acknowledging a downfall." "Venerable monk, it is not appropriate to act thus toward an elder. This Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, all-seeing, having attained supreme sovereignty over knowledge and the knowable, and dispels all doubt. Go before him and inquire."

"Whatever the Blessed One has foretold for you, accept it just as it was spoken." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Because the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, perceive while knowing, the Buddha, the Blessed One, then addressed the venerable Pilindavatsa: "Pilindavatsa, with what intention did you display the miraculous power?"

"Blessed One, my thought was this: if I gave no thought to the children, they would for a time experience the suffering arising from separation from their parents, and their parents too would experience the suffering arising from separation from their children; those without faith would find an opening, and those with faith, thinking, 'Look — all these were seized by the demons of the last month of autumn,' would turn away, saying, 'Who would ever go to the Bamboo Grove again?' It was with this in mind that I thought to display the miraculous power."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, in Pilindavatsa's display of miraculous power with such an intention, there is no downfall."

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the seventh fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of Kalandaka. King Bimbisāra's regular practice was to go each day to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and of the elder monks, one by one. On a certain occasion, King Bimbisāra paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat before him in order to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One then perfectly instructed King Bimbisāra of Magadha, that skilled craftsman of form, as he sat there attentively, with discourse endowed with Dharma; he led him to take it up rightly; he gave him proper praise; he caused him to rejoice fully. In many ways he perfectly taught him with discourse endowed with Dharma, led him to take it up rightly, praised him properly, caused him to rejoice fully — and then said nothing further.

Thereupon King Bimbisāra of Magadha paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed, going to the shrine of the venerable Pilindavatsa. At that time the venerable Pilindavatsa was in that shrine repairing his matted hair and beard himself. The venerable Pilindavatsa saw King Bimbisāra of Magadha from a great distance. Seeing him, he washed his hands and feet and remained seated on a prepared seat. Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha prostrated at the feet of the venerable Pilindavatsa with his head and sat attentively to one side. Seated thus to one side, King Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the venerable Pilindavatsa: "Noble one, are you yourself repairing your matted hair and beard?"

"Great King, the one who goes forth does it himself — we have gone forth, so who else would do it?"

"Noble one, if that is so, then I offer my services to the noble one."

The Great King said the same thing a second, a third, and a fourth time. On the fifth occasion as well, when he said exactly those words — "I offer my services to the noble one" — one of the companions of the venerable Pilindavatsa who was truthful, harmonious, and bold enough to speak in rebuke said:

From that point on, the Great King had servants assigned to the preceptor, and the preceptor thought: "If I were simply to abandon this temple now, that would itself be an affront." The king said, "Noble one, have we not pledged this again and again?" "Great King, you pledged it not just once — this is in fact the fifth time." The king was forgetful, and it was his habit to have any small pledge he had made to anyone whatsoever written down in a record by a scribe who sat outside. So the king said to that man, "Hey, steward — is it true that I pledged this again and again?" "Sire, this is the fifth time." "In that case I have incurred a punishable offense; I shall offer the noble one five hundred servants." He then instructed his ministers: "Present five hundred servants to the noble one."

The venerable Pilindavatsa said, "Great King, I myself renounced having servants when I went forth — what use are servants to one who has gone forth? Accept them on behalf of the Saṅgha." "Noble one, if that is so, then I shall submit the matter to the Blessed One." "Noble one, please submit it without delay."

At that time the venerable Pilindavatsa reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Servants may be accepted on behalf of the Saṅgha." The venerable Pilindavatsa accepted those servants, and those servants were repeatedly sent to do work at the royal palace. They then said this to the venerable Pilindavatsa: "Noble one, we have been offered as servants to the noble ones. If we are content, why should we be repeatedly sent to do menial labor at the royal palace? Honorable ones, do not make trouble — I shall petition the king about this."

Some time later, Seniya, the son of the King of Magadha, a prince of fine appearance and handsome form, came to the venerable Pilindavatsa, paid homage at his feet, and sat before him. The venerable Pilindavatsa said, "Great King, do you not regret having offered servants for the sake of the Saṅgha?" "Noble one, I have not the slightest regret." "Then why were those servants again sent to do work at the royal palace?" Right there, seated on his throne, the king instructed his ministers: "Wise ones, do not send the servants of the noble ones to do work at the royal palace from now on." When the ministers told any of the workers to do work at the palace, those workers said, "We belong to the noble ones," and so the ministers reported to the king: "Sire, we are embarrassed to give orders to anyone, for when we told the workers to do menial labor at the royal palace, they said they belonged to the noble ones." The king said, "Go and let them all continue working." They were all again put to work at the royal palace, and once more they said to the venerable Pilindavatsa: "Noble one, in exactly the same way we are again being sent to do menial labor at the royal palace — did the noble one not petition?" "Good friends, I did petition, and I shall petition again."

The venerable Pilindavatsa spoke to Seniya, son of the King of Magadha, who had likewise come again: "Great King, what has happened? Have you had a change of heart and become regretful?"

"Noble one, what fault is there? The servants were again put to work in exactly the same way." "I had not yet been able to petition anyone; but when I did petition at the appropriate time, they replied that they belonged to us noble ones." "How wonderful — if the noble ones' boundary wall for their servants were built as a separate enclosure, these would be the king's, and those would be the noble ones'." The venerable Pilindavatsa said, "I shall present this to the Blessed One."

The venerable Pilindavatsa then reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I permit the building of a boundary wall for the servants." The monks, not knowing where to have the servants' boundary wall built, the Blessed One declared: "Have the boundary wall built in the area between the outside of the royal palace and the outside of the Bamboo Grove — wherever, upon hearing a call, one could accomplish the business of the Saṅgha."

The monks instructed the ministers: "The Blessed One has declared that a boundary wall is to be built on this side; let this be made known to you." The ministers had a drum beaten throughout Rājagṛha, and announced: "Those who are servants of the noble ones are henceforth to reside in the area between the outside of Rājagṛha and the outside of the Bamboo Grove; let them go there today and build the boundary wall." They went there and built the boundary wall.

Having built the servants' boundary wall, they went to the monastery and continued their work. The monks then showed them which work was allowable, saying, "This is allowable — do this," and "This is not allowable — do not do that." Because they performed the allowable work, they came to be called "servants" — lha-bong — by name. Because they maintained the pleasant grounds of the Saṅgha, they came to be called "groundskeepers" — tse-göd — by name.

As they all entered the monastery, the noise and clamor prevented the monks from achieving one-pointed concentration, and the Blessed One declared: "Admit only as many as are needed to accomplish the work, and not all of them." When the monks gave food and clothing to all of them, the Blessed One declared: "Give food and clothing to those who do the work, but not to all." When the monks abandoned the sick among them, the Blessed One declared: "Those who are sick are to be given food and clothing, and are also to be waited upon."

Then at some later time, the attendant who served as disciplinarian spoke to those servants: "Good people, since I am acting as disciplinarian, you must come inside early in the morning." Now in Rājagṛha there was a band of thieves who went about under the name "The Left Hand of the Last Month of Autumn," and no sooner had the invitation ceremony concluded than they deliberated among themselves: "Friends, what could we do so that we need not go searching year after year but could enjoy ourselves and live comfortably?" Then someone there who knew the ways of monks said, "Friends, the servants of the noble ones who are stationed outside the city — let us raid them." Others said, "Wait — even their masters, the monks themselves, get no more than a full belly despite soliciting a hundred doorways; so if even they have next to nothing, what need is there even to speak of their servants?" That person who knew the ways of monks then said:

"Friends, you do not understand. These servants eat food supplied by others and devote themselves to carrying out their own duties. By many means they accumulate wealth, and what they possess is nowhere to be found elsewhere in this city — so let us attack them a little."

Having signaled to one another, the thieves set out from their lair and began to attack the servants.

Now the gods who had faith in the venerable Pilindavatsa spoke to him thus: "Noble one, please take note: your servants are about to be set upon by those who sided with the last month of autumn — please make haste." The venerable Pilindavatsa reflected: if he gave no thought to his servants, the servants would for a time suffer the distress that arises from loss of property, the faithless would find an opportunity, and the faithful who had given gifts in accordance with the Dharma of giving would no longer be protected — and in the future, who would think of making offerings and rendering service to the monks who are sons of the Śākyan? He decided: "I shall display a manifestation of supernatural power." Having thus reflected and understood the situation, the venerable Pilindavatsa surrounded the settlement of the divine servants with an iron fence.

The thieves took up their stolen goods, and when they saw the noble one and the iron fence, they began to move about in every direction but could find no way out. They dropped the stolen goods, and both the noble one and the iron fence became invisible. They picked up the stolen goods again, and the iron fence reappeared. This happened seven times in succession. Then they said among themselves: "Friends, some noble one of great supernatural power, of great might, has his eyes upon us — let us drop the goods and flee." They threw the stolen goods to one side and ran away.

When the divine servants awoke, they cried out: "Friends, we are ruined! We are ruined!" And full of mental distress born of the loss of their property, they all assembled and began searching throughout the settlement of divine servants. In one spot they found all their goods heaped up and set down together. Then joy and gladness arose in them, and each took up their own belongings and went home to their respective houses. They posted guards at their individual homes.

As they slept, that god entered their dreams and said: "Friends, all this — your not being destroyed by those who sided with the last month of autumn — is due to the power of the noble Pilindavatsa."

Then, when night had turned to dawn, they all assembled and said: "Friends, a god appeared to us in our dreams and declared: 'All this — your not being destroyed by those who sided with the last month of autumn — is due to the power of the noble Pilindavatsa.' This is indeed exactly as he said, for apart from the noble Pilindavatsa, who else would have compassion on us?" At that, they cleaned and tidied themselves, and said they would go to the temple afterwards. They bathed, adorned themselves with white robes, perfume, and garlands, tidied themselves up, and went to the temple.
