Now Ānanda had risen early before dawn, taken the key and the hooked key, opened the gate of the temple, cleared away the lamp-stands, swept and wiped the temple, spread out the seats, scattered incense around the area of the stūpa, climbed to the upper story, struck the gaṇḍī bell, and looked out in all four directions. He saw the people in their white robes with perfume and

garlands, and thought: "Who are these people coming toward the temple — wealthy men, or merchants, or sea-captains?" But when they entered the precinct around the stūpa, he recognized them, and Ānanda reproached them angrily, saying: "Did I not tell you to come early this morning? Where have you been?" They replied: "Noble one, if venerable Pilindavatsa has not taken thought for us, we shall suffer distress this very day at the hands of the wicked ones of the last autumn month."

Ānanda reproached them angrily and said: "You should know that I will also lay a rule upon the one by whose power you are so proud." So knowing, he assembled the group of six monks, went to where the venerable Pilindavatsa was staying, and spoke to him thus: "Homage to the elder. Venerable ones, be at ease. Elder, please open the matter of the five classes of transgressions. Elder, did you obtain release for the servants' goods that the wicked ones of the last autumn month stole? That is correct — he did obtain release for them." "Elder, we understand. Please remain dwelling in the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment. But do not, we beg, show compassion only to one side — showing compassion to the servants while showing none to the wicked ones of the last autumn month. The transgression that has arisen from freeing goods claimed as one's own — please restore it properly in accordance with the Dharma." "No transgression is seen." "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has said that for one who does not see a transgression, the act of suspension from residence is to be performed. Steward, strike the gaṇḍī bell. The act of suspension from residence is to be performed." They went to the steward and said: "Venerable one, strike the gaṇḍī bell. Because he refuses to properly restore a transgression over a trifling matter, the act of suspension from residence is to be performed."

Now at that time the venerable Śāriputra was acting as elder of the Saṅgha and observing: might there not arise some discord in the teaching through dishonest conduct in Dharma? And because he was investigating conduct related to the community's affairs, he asked the steward: "Who is to be suspended, or fundamentally suspended, or to be pleased, or to be fundamentally pleased? Who is performing the expulsion? Nobody else is doing it. It is being done like this: because the venerable Pilindavatsa refuses to properly restore a transgression that has arisen, the act of suspension from residence is being performed on account of not seeing a transgression."

The venerable monk elder said, in a gentle and fitting manner: "Venerable ones, the awakened Blessed One is omniscient, all-seeing, supreme in knowledge and objects of knowledge, the one who cuts through all doubt. So go before him today and inquire about this matter, and hold precisely to whatever the Blessed One declares to you."

Then the monks petitioned the Blessed One: "Awakened Blessed Ones act even while knowing." The awakened Blessed One then asked the venerable Pilindavatsa: "With what intention did you display miraculous powers?" "Blessed one, I thought this: if I gave no thought to the servants, the servants would for a time experience the suffering born of separation from their wealth, and those without faith would also find an opportunity —

those with faith would likewise cease to cherish and protect the gift of Dharma that ought to be given as a gift, and from that point forward whoever thought of giving to and associating with the monks who are sons of the Śākyan would be turned away entirely. For this reason I displayed miraculous powers." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, for the monk Pilindavatsa there is no transgression in displaying miraculous powers with such an intention."

The monks grew doubtful, and in their doubt they petitioned the awakened Blessed One, the cutter of all doubt: "Venerable one, the elder Norchen saw the Saṅgha of monks as blameless and unblemished, yet at the very outset he caused a blemish to arise in it — look at how a blemish appeared through the condition of taking what was not given." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now — in times past as well, this one caused a blemish to arise in a world that was blameless and unblemished, and at the very outset it was through the condition of taking what was not given that the blemish appeared.

Listen to this, monks. There is a time when this world is destroyed. When the world is being destroyed, most sentient beings are reborn in the class of the gods of luminosity. There they are beings of form, mind-born, complete in all respects, with faculties unimpaired, possessed of all major and minor limbs, beautiful, endowed with fine complexion, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy, sustained by the food of joy, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration. At that time this great earth becomes nothing but water, nothing but ocean. Upon the surface of what the great earth has become — nothing but water, nothing but ocean — wind causes a film to gather, to thicken, and to spread over it entirely. Just as when boiled milk cools and wind causes a film to gather, to thicken, and to spread over it, so too upon the surface of what the great earth has become — nothing but water, nothing but ocean — wind causes a film to gather, to thicken, and to spread over it entirely. That is the earth-essence, perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, perfect in taste. In color it is like this: like butter, for example. In taste it is like this: like unboiled wild honey, for example.

Monks, there is also a time when this world is being formed. As the world is forming, some sentient beings pass away from that class of gods of luminosity, their lifespan exhausted, their karma exhausted, their merit exhausted, and they come here to be of the same fortune as human beings. Here too they are beings of form, mind-born, complete in all respects, with faculties unimpaired, possessed of all major and minor limbs, beautiful, endowed with fine complexion, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy, sustained by the food of joy, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration. At that time in the world the sun and moon had not yet appeared. In the world the stars had not yet appeared. Night and day had not yet appeared. Moments, instants, and brief intervals had not yet appeared. Months, fortnights, seasons, and years had not yet appeared. There was no woman and no man; beings were counted simply as beings, nothing more.

Then a certain sentient being of greedy nature tasted the earth-essence with the tip of a finger. As it tasted it again and again, so did its craving grow."

The more it craved, the more it ate of the earth-essence, consuming it in mouthful after mouthful. Other sentient beings, seeing that first being taste the earth-essence with the tip of a finger, and seeing how the more it tasted the more it craved, and how the more it craved the more it ate of the earth-essence in mouthful after mouthful, thought to themselves: "Ah, how fine that is! Ah, how good that is! Let us too taste the earth-essence with the tip of a finger." And so they too began to taste the earth-essence with the tip of a finger. The more they tasted, the more they craved. The more they craved, the more they ate of the earth-essence in mouthful after mouthful.

Because those sentient beings had eaten of the earth-essence in mouthful after mouthful, solidity and heaviness arose in their bodies, and whatever fair complexion they had possessed disappeared. Darkness arose in the world. Monks, it is the nature of reality that when darkness arises in the world, the sun and moon then appear in the world. And in the world, stars appear, and night and day appear, and moments, instants, and brief intervals appear, and months, fortnights, seasons, and years appear. They ate of that food and were sustained by it, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration.

Among them, those who ate but little became fair in complexion, while those who ate a great deal became poor in complexion. And so, two kinds of food giving rise to two kinds of complexion, one being would reproach another, saying: "Ha! I have a fine complexion, while you have a poor complexion." Because they became proud on account of their complexions, and because they thus took up those wicked, unwholesome qualities, the earth-essence disappeared.

Monks, when the earth-essence had disappeared, those beings gathered together in one place and lamented, grew despondent, and cried out again and again: "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" Just as nowadays, when people come upon some fine and savory food, they employ letters and old words to speak of it, saying "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" — in exactly the same way, those beings too, when the earth-essence had disappeared, gathered together and lamented, grew despondent, and cried out: "Alas, the essence! Alas, the essence!" — though when they said it they did not know the meaning of what they were saying. Such was the meaning of those words.

Monks, after the earth-essence had disappeared for those sentient beings, a growth appeared that was perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste. In color it was like the flower of the trumpet-vine. In taste it was like unboiled wild honey. They ate of that growth and were sustained by it, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration. Among them, those who ate but little became fair in complexion, while those who ate a great deal became poor in complexion. And so, owing to two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion became manifest, and when two kinds of complexion had come about, one being would reproach another,

"Hey there, sentient being! I have fine complexion, while you have poor complexion!" — and so one being would reproach another. As they grew arrogant on account of complexion, it was by reason of having fully taken up those very sinful, non-virtuous qualities that the growth disappeared for them.

Monks, when those sentient beings found that the growth had disappeared, they gathered together, assembled, and fell into sorrow, into despondency, into lamentation, crying out in this way: "Alas! Alas!" — just as today, when people are touched by nothing but pain and mental discomfort, they use written and verbal expressions, those same ancient words, to describe it, crying out: "Alas! Alas!" — so too those sentient beings, when the growth had vanished, gathered together, assembled, fell into sorrow, into despondency, into lamentation, crying out: "Alas! Alas!" — though they uttered those words, the meaning of what was said was this, and the meaning of the words "the meaning of what was said was this" they did not understand.

Monks, when those sentient beings found that the growth had disappeared, a grove of shoots appeared that was perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste. In color it was like the flower of the trumpet-vine. In taste it was like unboiled wild honey. They ate of that and were sustained by it, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration. Among them, those who ate but little became fair in complexion, while those who ate a great deal became poor in complexion. And so, owing to two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion became manifest, and when two kinds of complexion had come about, one being would reproach another: "Hey there, sentient being! I have fine complexion, while you have poor complexion!" As they grew arrogant on account of complexion, it was by reason of having fully taken up those very sinful, non-virtuous qualities that the grove of shoots disappeared for them.

Monks, when those sentient beings found that the grove of shoots had disappeared, they gathered together, assembled, and fell into sorrow, into despondency, into lamentation, crying out in this way: "It is gone! It is gone!" — just as today, when people are rebuked with some sharp reproach, they use written and verbal expressions, those same ancient words, to describe it, crying out: "It is gone! It is gone!" — so too those sentient beings, when the grove of shoots had vanished, gathered together, assembled, fell into sorrow, into despondency, into lamentation, crying out: "It is gone! It is gone!" — though they uttered those words, the meaning of what was said was this, and the meaning of the words "the meaning of what was said was this" they did not understand.

Monks, when those sentient beings found that the grove of shoots had disappeared, there arose uncultivated, unsown rice — grains of sāli rice without any husk, without any bran, pure and clean, ready to measure out in fistfuls, not covered over all around; when pressed on the western side, it would win out and spring back on the eastern side; when pressed on the eastern side, it would win out and spring back on the western side; when pressed on every side, it would spring back on every side; and it appeared so as not to be diminished by pressing. They ate of that and were sustained by it, long-lived and abiding for a vast duration. And because those sentient beings began to subsist on uncultivated, unsown sāli rice grain taken raw as their food, distinct sense faculties appeared among them — some came to possess male faculties, and some came to possess female faculties. Then those who possessed male faculties and

those who possessed female faculties gazed at one another, eye meeting eye. The more they gazed at one another, eye meeting eye, the more attachment arose in them all. The more attachment arose in them all, the more they pressed close together. The more they pressed close together, the more they engaged in sexual intercourse. Other sentient beings, seeing sentient beings engage in sexual intercourse with one another, threw dirt and threw clods of earth and threw ashes and threw sticks, crying out: "Vile creature! Doing what should not be done! Vile creature! Doing what should not be done! Hey, creature — why do you shame a sentient being?" — just as today, when sentient beings take a bride and groom, they scatter flour and scatter perfumes and flowers and fruits, saying, "May they be prosperous." In the same way, those beings, seeing sentient beings engage in sexual intercourse with one another, threw dirt, threw clods of earth, threw ashes and sticks, crying out: "Vile creature! Doing what should not be done! Vile creature! Doing what should not be done! Hey, creature — why do you shame a sentient being?"

Thus it is, monks, that what was formerly known as improper conduct is now known as proper conduct; what was formerly known as contrary to the Vinaya is now known as Vinaya; and what was formerly to be censured is now to be praised. And so they would conceal themselves for a day, or for two or three or seven days. Because those sinful beings fell so deeply into that ignoble and impure practice, they entered upon the ascetic observance of building houses, saying, "We shall do here what should not be done, we shall do here what should not be done" — and from that saying arose the very word and name "house." Monks, this was the first beginning of all the activities of the household arising in the world, and it arose rightly, not wrongly. The right way in this is as follows: the most excellent of laws belongs to the victorious sovereigns.

Then those beings, wishing to eat their morning meal, would go out for sāli rice in the morning; wishing to eat their evening meal, would go out for sāli rice in the evening. Then a certain sentient being of lazy character gathered at one stroke the sāli rice for both morning and evening. Another sentient being said to that one: "Hey, creature, come — let us go for sāli rice." That being replied: "Hey, creature, see to your own sāli rice yourself. I have already gathered the sāli rice for both morning and evening at one time." Then that second sentient being thought: "Ah, how excellent! Ah, how fine! I too shall gather sāli rice enough for two days, three days, seven days." And so that being gathered the sāli rice sufficient for two days, three days, and up to seven days. Then another sentient being said to that being: "Hey, creature, come — let us go for sāli rice." That being replied: "Hey, creature, see to your own sāli rice yourself. I have already gathered the sāli rice for two days, three days, and seven days." Then that sentient being thought: "Ah, how excellent! Ah, how fine!"

"I too shall gather sāli rice enough for half a month and a full month." And so that being gathered the sāli rice sufficient for half a month and a full month. Because those sentient beings had been consuming and eating up the sāli rice grain that grew without plowing or planting, simply by taking it and using it, the sāli rice came to have husks and bran, with the grain entirely wrapped around, and what had been cut did not grow back; it was clear that it had been cut, and the sāli rice stood in separate clumps, distinct from one another.

Then those sentient beings gathered together and, coming to assembly, lamented, became downcast, and cried out in distress: "Alas, O wise ones — once we were mind-born, made of form, complete in every way, with faculties unimpaired, endowed with all our limbs and secondary limbs, beautiful, with fine complexion, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy, sustained by joy as our food, long-lived and enduring for a great span. Then there came to us an earth-essence of excellent color, excellent fragrance, and excellent taste. Because we began eating and consuming that earth-essence as our food, our bodies became solid and heavy, and that fine and radiant complexion of ours disappeared. Darkness arose in the world. When we were eating that food, sustained by it, and living long for a great span, among us whoever ate the least food became fair in complexion, and whoever ate the most food became ugly in complexion. Thus, depending on just these two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion manifested; and when two kinds of complexion had appeared, one sentient being would disparage another, saying: 'Hey, creature — I am fine in complexion, while you are ugly in complexion!' Because we became proud on account of our complexion, it was precisely through taking up those evil, non-virtuous qualities that the earth-essence disappeared.

"When the earth-essence had disappeared, there arose an earth-film of excellent color, excellent fragrance, and excellent taste. We ate that, sustained by it, and lived long for a great span. Among us whoever ate the least became fine in complexion, and whoever ate the most became ugly in complexion. Thus, depending on just these two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion manifested; and when two kinds of complexion had appeared, one sentient being would disparage another, saying: 'Hey, creature — I am fine in complexion, while you are ugly in complexion!' Because we became proud on account of our complexion, it was precisely through taking up those evil, non-virtuous qualities that the earth-film too disappeared.

"When the earth-film had disappeared, there arose thickets of sprouts of excellent color, excellent fragrance, and excellent taste. We ate that, sustained by it, and lived long for a great span. Among us whoever ate the least became fine in complexion, and whoever ate the most became ugly in complexion. Thus, depending on just these two kinds of food, two kinds of complexion manifested; and when two kinds of complexion had appeared, one sentient being would disparage another, saying: 'Hey, creature — I am fine in complexion, while you are ugly in complexion!' Because we became proud on account of our complexion, it was precisely through taking up those evil, non-virtuous qualities that the thickets of sprouts disappeared.

"When the thickets of sprouts had disappeared, there arose sāli rice grain that grew without plowing or planting — with no husk, no bran, pure and clean, four-fingered in size, unwrapped all around, and when harvested in the evening it would grow back again by morning,

when harvested in the morning it would grow back again by evening. When it had been harvested, the stalks too grew back. When every stalk had been harvested, it came to pass that the harvested stalks no longer grew back. We ate of it and, sustained by that food, we lived long and endured for a very long time.

"Now, because we had consumed the sāli rice grain that grew without plowing or planting by simply going to gather and use it, there came a time when that sāli rice developed a husk, a bran, and a wrapping all around the grain, and when harvested the stalks no longer grew back, and the marks of harvesting became visible. And the sāli rice became established in separate stands — harvested ground here, unharvested ground there. Then the thought arose among us: 'Let us come together and assemble, divide the fields with boundaries, and establish which is yours and which is mine.' And so they came together and assembled, divided with boundaries, and established: 'This is yours, this is mine.'

"Monks, this was the very first arising in the world of the boundary of property — the first beginning of what pertains to property. And this took place through Dharma, not through what is contrary to Dharma. The Dharma here is this: it is the supreme Dharma of victorious lords and sovereigns.

"Then a certain sentient being, while having his own sāli rice, took the sāli rice of another without it having been given. Another sentient being saw this — saw that being taking the sāli rice of another without it being given, even while having his own. Having seen it, that sentient being said to the other: 'Hey, creature! Why do you take the sāli rice of another without it being given, when you have your own? Hey, creature — go, and do not act like that again!' Yet that sentient being, a second time and a third time, again took the sāli rice of another without it being given, even while having his own. The other sentient being, again seeing him take the sāli rice of another a second time and a third time without it being given, even while having his own, again said: 'Hey, creature! Why do you take the sāli rice of another without it being given, when you have your own?' — and that sentient being dragged him along, led him away, and denounced him before the assembly of the wise, saying: 'This sentient being takes the sāli rice of another without it being given, even while having his own!'

"Thereupon the other sentient beings said to that being: 'Hey, creature! Why do you take the sāli rice of another without it being given, when you have your own? Hey, creature — go, and do not act like that again!'

"Then the being who had taken without giving said to those sentient beings: 'O wise ones, this being here, on account of rice, has spoken against me, dragged me along, led me away, and denounced me before the assembly!'

"Thereupon those sentient beings said to the one who had spoken on account of the rice: 'Hey, creature! Why, on account of rice, did you speak against a sentient being, drag him along, lead him away, and denounce him before the assembly? Hey, creature — go, and do not act like that again!'

"Then those sentient beings thought: 'O wise ones, we see here one dragging along and leading away on account of rice, and denouncing before the assembly. Let us come together and assemble, and from among us appoint as lord of the fields whichever sentient being is most handsome, most pleasing to behold, most beautiful, and most physically imposing. Then whatever judgment he pronounces upon us shall be the judgment, and whatever benefit he bestows shall be the benefit.

'We shall give a rightful portion of whatever comes forth from our fields.' Having thus resolved, those sentient beings came together and assembled, and from among them they appointed as lord of the fields whichever one was most handsome, most pleasing to behold, most beautiful, and most physically imposing. They addressed him thus: 'Come here, O sentient being! Whatever judgment among us is to be judged, let it be judged. Whatever benefit is to be bestowed, let it be bestowed. And from whatever comes forth from our fields, we shall give you a rightful portion in accordance with Dharma.' And so it was that by reason of being honored by the many people, of being honored by the many people, he came to bear the name 'honored by the many, honored by the many.' And by reason of being lord of the fields, and of being one who protects them as was said, he came to bear the name 'Warrior-clan, Warrior-clan.' And by reason of conducting himself everywhere in the conduct of ethical discipline, and conducting himself everywhere in the conduct of wisdom, and by delighting the populace through Dharma, he came to bear the name 'King, King.'

Monks, this is the very first arising of the circle of the warrior nobility in the world, and it arose through Dharma, not through anything contrary to Dharma. And as for that Dharma — it is the supreme Dharma of the victorious lords.

Monks, what then is the first arising of the circle of the brahmins in the world? Monks, at that time some sentient beings, having understood that grasping is sickness, grasping is its fruit, grasping is pain, and grasping is the root of suffering, went forth from the village to a secluded place in the wilderness. There they made shelters of branches and leaves and took up their dwelling. Morning and evening, desiring morning food and evening food, they entered the village for alms. Then other sentient beings thought: 'These wise ones have understood that grasping is sickness, grasping is its fruit, grasping is pain, and grasping is the root of suffering, and have gone forth from the village to a secluded place in the wilderness, where they have made shelters of branches and leaves and taken up their dwelling. Morning and evening, desiring morning and evening food, they enter the village for alms — this is indeed a hard practice!' Thinking thus, those others resolved to give to them and to act in their service.

Then some among those sentient beings, not having fully comprehended that meditation and that deep solitude, went instead to the outskirts, made shelters of branches and leaves, and settled there, saying: 'Here let us compose texts of secret mantra and engage in the recitation of the Vedas.' And there they composed texts of secret mantra and engaged in recitation of the Vedas.

Then some among those sentient beings, not having fully comprehended that meditation, that deep solitude, those texts of secret mantra, and that recitation of the Vedas, came back from the wilderness to the edge of the village, built four-doored houses, and said: 'Here let us give gifts, accumulate merit, and satisfy to the best of our ability all the traveling people who come and arrive, with food and drink.' And there they gave gifts, accumulated merit, and satisfied to the best of their ability all the traveling people who came and arrived with food and drink. Because these ones dwelt in dependence on what was outside the village, and contemplated what was outside the village, they came to bear the name 'brahmin, brahmin.'

Furthermore, from the phrase 'these ones do not practice meditative concentration,' the act of taking up recitation came to bear the name 'taking up recitation, taking up recitation.' And because some returned from the wilderness back to the edge of the village, they came to bear the name 'villager, villager.'

Monks, this is the beginning of the arising of the circle of brahmins in the world, and it arose through the Dharma, not through what is contrary to the Dharma. In this regard, the Dharma is this: it is the supreme Dharma of the victorious lords.

Monks, what then is the beginning of the arising of the circle of the merchant class in the world? Monks, from that time some sentient beings applied themselves to separate household crafts and occupational activities, and because of the phrase 'these sentient beings carry out separate crafts and occupational activities,' they came to bear the name 'merchant class, merchant class.' Monks, this is the beginning of the arising of the circle of the merchant class in the world, and it arose through the Dharma, not through what is contrary to the Dharma. In this regard, the Dharma is this: it is the supreme Dharma of the victorious lords.

Monks, since by the very nature of reality the three circles arose in the world, a fourth circle — the circle of ascetics — will likewise arise in the world. How so? Monks, noble sons from warrior-caste households, shaving off hair and beard, donning saffron robes, and going forth from home to homelessness with perfect faith — the warrior caste ought to address them respectfully, pay homage to them, rise before them, fold their hands, and render them the act of bowing; and brahmins and the merchant class too ought to address them respectfully, pay homage to them, rise before them, fold their hands, and render them the act of bowing. Noble sons from brahmin households and from merchant-class households, shaving off hair and beard, donning saffron robes, and going forth from home to homelessness with perfect faith — the warrior caste ought to address them respectfully, pay homage to them, rise before them, fold their hands, and render them the act of bowing; and brahmins and the merchant class too ought to address them respectfully, pay homage to them, rise before them, fold their hands, and render them the act of bowing.

Monks, in that time and at that period, whichever sentient being first took without giving what was another's grain while his own grain still remained — that sentient being is a monk who possesses wealth. And just as at that time a world that was without fault and free of bubbles was, on that very first occasion, caused to bubble up by the condition of taking what was not given, so too today has that sentient being first caused the Saṅgha of monks — which is without fault and free of bubbles — to bubble up by the condition of taking what was not given.

Monks, therefore train in this way: strive to abandon attachment, strive to abandon aversion, and strive to abandon delusion. Thus, monks, should you train. For one who acts for the first time, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, and for one who is afflicted by feelings, there is no transgression.

The second defeat is complete.

Vinaya-vibhaṅga, the eighth section.

The general summary of the third defeat:

Rubbing, oneself, poison, a reanimated corpse, and warming — these are the topics of the summary.

The summary: rubbing, nursing, one with a mouth, Śirikā, the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, dwelling in a womb, and the caravan leader.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two monks, one called Rubbing and one called Nursing, who were on familiar terms with each other, were in the habit of visiting one another, and spoke of each other as companions and dear friends. Then at a certain later time Nursing fell ill, and while Rubbing was serving as his nurse, Nursing began crying out in the night. Rubbing asked him, "Venerable Nursing, why do you cry out?" Nursing replied, "I am hungry. I am thirsty." Rubbing said, "Venerable Nursing, settle your mind on the intention to go forth into the monastic life. Even if medicine were available right now, if there is no strength to receive and take it, what need is there to speak of medicine — there is none. Since Nursing has no faculty of discernment, he goes on crying out, 'I am thirsty, I am hungry,' until dawn comes." Then Rubbing said, "Venerable Nursing, I will go and ask the physician. In the meantime, please chew on a tooth-stick." Rubbing went to the physician and said, "A young man of good complexion is ill; please show what medicine is appropriate for him." The physician replied, "Noble monk, the medicine for that monk is such-and-such." While Rubbing was still at the physician's, Venerable Nursing rose from his bed, put on his lower robe, took his washing things, his pills, his head-pouring preparation, and his tooth-stick, came out to the porch, and began to discard his tooth-stick. The monks said to him, "Venerable Nursing, why do you cry out alone in the night?" Nursing said, "Venerable ones, I was alone, thirsty and hungry." Then one monk said, "Venerable Nursing, if I have some water-porridge, why would you not drink it?" Nursing said, "Please, pour it out," and he drank it. Other monks said, "We have milk-porridge, yoghurt-porridge, broth, meat, and sweet treats — why would you not eat?" Nursing, while guarding his practice of celibacy in relation to those monks and being somewhat drawn by craving, partook of a little of each. Having eaten too much, he lay down feeling ill. Rubbing also questioned the physician and came back quickly. Then the physician prepared the medicine as he had described and said, "Venerable Nursing, please rise and chew the tooth-stick." Nursing replied, "I have already discarded it." Rubbing said, "No harm done," and he anointed the maṇḍala, cleaned the vessel and the spoon, and said, "Please rise and eat." Nursing, being looked after by him, got up. Rubbing had him take the medicine, prepared it, and offered it, and Nursing filled the spoon two or three times, ate, and then lay back down feeling ill. Rubbing said, "Venerable Nursing, why do you not eat?" Nursing said, "I have no desire for it." Rubbing said, "You roused me in the night crying, 'I am hungry, I am thirsty,' and now you say you have no desire — now you are behaving badly." The monks said to Rubbing, "Venerable Rubbing, be careful with this one. He has drunk our water-porridge and milk-porridge, and eaten our broth, meat, and sweet treats." Rubbing said, "Venerable Nursing, is it true that you have done this?" Nursing, filled with remorse, lowered his gaze and said, "It is so." Rubbing said, "My alms bowl is empty, empty; my Dharma robe is worn thin; the side of virtue is fading away — and you are behaving this contrary way while I nurse you. It would be better that you had eaten poison."

"I have not been behaving in this contrary way. It is good that Nursing, out of shame, speaks of practicing pure conduct equal to mine. And yet, while my alms bowl is empty, empty, my Dharma robe is worn thin, and the side of virtue is fading away, he nurses me in my sickness — and because I am behaving in this contrary way, it would be better that I had eaten poison. Since I have not been behaving in this contrary way, I shall eat poison." With that thought arising in his mind, he rose and began to search among the vessels. He found a lump of poison in one of the bowls, and he ate it. The poison spread through him and, his mind overwhelmed, he began to die — saliva dripping from his mouth, his eyes rolling — and he cried out: "Servant, I am dying! I am dying!"

When the servant heard this, he looked up and, hurrying over quickly, said, "Venerable Rubbing, why do you cry out like that?" Rubbing said, "You — you told me, 'Venerable Rubbing, your alms bowl is empty, empty, your Dharma robe is worn thin, and the side of virtue is fading away, while I nurse you in your sickness, yet you behave in this contrary way — it would be better that you ate poison than that you behave in this contrary way.' Because you said that to me, the thought arose in my mind: 'It is good that Nursing speaks of practicing pure conduct equal to mine. And yet, while my alms bowl is empty, empty, my Dharma robe is worn thin, and the side of virtue is fading away, he nurses me in my sickness, and because I am behaving in this contrary way, it would be better that I ate poison than to go on behaving so contrarily.' That thought arose in my mind. I began searching among the vessels, I found a lump of poison in one of the bowls, and I ate it."

The servant, his face fallen with dismay, said, "Venerable one, you have done something terrible." Then they went to a physician. But the poison was of a sharp kind and could not be stopped — his time had come. The servant brought the physician and, upon arriving, saw that his time had come. Remorse arose in the servant's mind: "Have I caused him to die?" He then told the monks what had happened. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "O monks, that monk has no transgression. Moreover, a monk must not speak words of such a kind to a sick person — words that, upon hearing them, the sick person will strive to bring about their own death. If a monk speaks such words to a sick person — words that, upon hearing them, the sick person will strive to bring about their own death — this constitutes a serious offense. This, however, is merely an event that has occurred; the buddha, the Blessed One, does not yet lay down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya."

The buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there were two monks who were close companions — one named Lips and one named Śirikā — who walked together, spoke together, and addressed one another with the same warm familiarity. Lips had gone forth from the household of a hunter, and Śirikā had gone forth from a householder's family. At a certain time, two nephews of Lips, having lost their parents, were wandering here and there, and they came to the Jeta Grove and stood at the gate. Lips came out and recognized the two boys by their faces, and he said to them, "Where have your parents gone?" The two said, "Their time has come." When the kinsman heard this, he wept with tears in his voice and sat weeping, and the monks said to him,

The venerable Lips was asked about the two boys, and Lips said, "They are my two nephews." The monks then said, "Why do you not take them in?" Lips said, "I myself am barely managing to go about seeking alms — how am I to take these two in?" The monks said, "If they are willing, let them bring leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks to the monks, and the monks in turn will give the two of them the leavings from their alms bowls." Lips took the two of them in, and the two proved to be diligent, not lazy, and capable of effort, so they would bring leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks to the monks, and the monks in turn would give the two of them the leavings from their alms bowls. In no long time, the two had good clothing and good food, and their skin, flesh, and blood filled out, and they became sturdy and proud.

Then on another occasion the two were playing at the gate of the Jeta Grove when some of their kinsmen came by carrying bows and arrows in their hands, passing through the gate of the Jeta Grove to go in pursuit of wild game. These kinsmen saw the two boys and said to them, "You two, where have you come from to be here?" The two boys said, "Here, within this community of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyas, we dwell with our maternal uncle who has gone forth." The kinsmen said, "Your maternal uncle too has gone forth among ascetics who are sons of the Śākyas — those who follow a livelihood of doing nothing. Are you two also going to follow a way of doing nothing? Come here and follow the occupation of your father." The two said, "Our uncle has done us good, and we should ask him about it," and the two went off to where the venerable Lips was, and they said to the venerable Lips: "Uncle, we wish to follow the occupation of our father." Lips said, "I have been raising you two through gifts given in faith — why then do you wish to pursue such a wrongful livelihood as this?" The two said, "Uncle, to be adorned on the head with a golden garland is honorable; to follow the occupation of one's father is not otherwise — that is how it is." And making nothing of his words, the two went off and began to live by hunting wild game.

After some time had passed, Śirikā fell ill, and while Lips was nursing her through her sickness, Śirikā was beset by feelings of suffering and thought to herself: "I have discipline and moral conduct; if I were to go to another land, the higher realms would be as close as the width of a silk cloth, and liberation would be as close as the thickness of a veil. Should this body die, I will be reborn among the gods — so in every way I should bring about my own death." Then she thought again: "But bringing about my own death would be painful. I should find someone to kill me," and she fell to considering who there might be who could cut off her life. She then reflected that Lips's two nephews were fierce and red-handed, habituated to striking and to striking hard, who took the lives of others, who were ready to cut the lives of others, who lived by cutting the lives of others — and so the thought arose in her that they would be capable of killing her, whereas no one else could do it. She realized this and said to the venerable Lips:

"Venerable Lips, your two nephews are nowhere to be seen — where have they gone?"
Lips said,

"Do not take those two by name. The two of them are just the sort who commit such wrongdoing. I raised them by giving with faith, and now they have entered into a life of wrongdoing, following their father's trade — they take the lives of others; they live by cutting the lives of others."

Śirikā said, "Do not harbor malice toward those two on all sides. That is the discipline of the assembly. When the two of them were dwelling in the Jeta Grove, they did not so much as cut the life of a tiny worm. If, by living in that kind of company, they commit such wrongdoing, they should be kept well apart from those people. And consider this: when you go anywhere, I have no one to guard me — so if those two happen to appear, send them to me and let them be my guards."

Now, when Lips set out for alms, those two nephews of his were sitting in the marketplace selling meat. They saw him, rose, went to him, and touched his two feet. He said to them, "Boys, why have you come to Lips? We have come to our uncle. Why have you come to me? We have come to our uncle. All this time while I was ill, did the two of you not visit me even once? Uncle, we did not know. We have only just heard, and so we have come on that account."

"Nephews, do the two of you wish to be reborn among the gods?"

"Uncle, if even we of all people wish to be reborn among the gods, what need is there to speak of it? Of course we do."

"Nephews, if that is so, when I go to another region, the good years are only as much as a silk curtain drawn across them, and liberation is only as much as a veil drawn over it — yet if this body were to be reborn among the gods, then those who would harass me are a torment to me. So you two must kill me."

"Uncle, even if someone else were to kill you, we would still kill that person — let alone that we ourselves would kill uncle. Whatever Lips commands the two of you, do exactly as uncle says."

"Nephews, if that is so, let me say this: I am afflicted by painful feeling — kill me." The two of them then thought: surely this and the earlier conversation with uncle cannot have gone differently from this, and so uncle has sent us here for this purpose. Then the fiercer of the two drew a sharp blade, cut off her head, and covered it under her with a cloth.

Lips returned from her alms round. Seeing the figure covered with the cloth, she said, "The two of you are right here, yet is this one sleeping?" "Uncle, she lies there in a way that she will never rise again." When Lips then spoke words of astonishment, thinking she should inquire, she questioned the two of them, and they told her the whole account in full.

Lips was stricken with distress. She pulled back the cloth and, seeing what lay there, the thought arose in her — could I not have sought a sharp weapon myself? — and remorse arose in her too. Bereft of her companion, tormented by remorse, her mind filled with anguish, she was overcome with misery.

She then related everything in full to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk has incurred no transgression. Furthermore, a monk must not leave behind an unskilled attendant and go away from a sick person. If circumstances are such that he must go, he should instruct the unskilled attendant, saying, 'Do not let this person jump into fire, take poison, bring out a weapon, throw themselves into a ravine, tie themselves with a rope, or eat anything else that is harmful,' and only then depart. If a monk goes away without giving such instructions, he commits a serious offense."

This too was an occurrence, but the Blessed One, the Buddha, did not yet establish a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now there was a monk in Śrāvastī whose alms bowl had become cracked. The monks said to him, "Venerable one, since your alms bowl is cracked, why do you not fire it?" He replied, "For that one needs a kiln, fuel, sesame stalks, and many other implements." The monks said, "Venerable one, will it really not get done without an alms bowl?" He replied, "It will not get done without an alms bowl. There is a great household where a monk has fallen gravely ill and is suffering, and the illness is so severe that he will pass away before long. His alms bowl is clean and round and fit for use — I should take that one." The monks said, "Venerable one, is it right for you to harbor such a fierce, outcast-like attitude over an alms bowl?" The monk fell silent with embarrassment.

The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk has incurred no transgression. Furthermore, a monk must not harbor such a fierce, outcast-like attitude over an alms bowl. If a monk harbors such a fierce, outcast-like attitude over an alms bowl, he commits a serious offense. Moreover, a monk should look after his alms bowl as he would his own eye: what needs repair should be repaired; what needs to be fired should be fired. If a monk fails to repair what needs repairing or to fire what needs firing, he commits a serious offense."

This too was an occurrence, but the Blessed One, the Buddha, did not yet establish a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now there was a monk in Śrāvastī whose outer robe had become old, soiled with filth, and torn. The monks said to him, "Venerable one, your outer robe is old, soiled with filth, and torn — why do you not wash it, mend it, or turn it?" He replied, "For that one needs copper, water, wood, thread, dye, and many other things." The monks said, "Venerable one, will it really not get done without an outer robe?" He replied, "It will not get done without an outer robe. There is a great household where a monk has fallen gravely ill and is suffering, and the illness is so severe that he will pass away before long. His outer robe has been turned with dye of reddish-yellow colour —

— it should be taken for use." The monks said to him, "Venerable one, is it really fitting that you, for the sake of an outer robe, should arouse such a forceful and violent state of mind, as though you were a butcher?" He fell silent with shame, saying nothing. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, that monk has committed no transgression. Nevertheless, a monk should not arouse such a forceful and violent state of mind as though he were a butcher, for the sake of an outer robe. If a monk arouses such a forceful and violent state of mind as though he were a butcher, for the sake of an outer robe, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing. Furthermore, a monk should care for his outer robe as though it were his own skin — what needs washing should be washed, what needs mending should be mended, what needs to be turned should be turned. If a monk, when his outer robe needs washing, does not wash it, or when it needs mending does not mend it, or when it needs to be turned does not turn it, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing."

Now, this has come about — but for the time being the buddha, the Blessed One, has not yet laid down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a householder named Balasena — wealthy, of great means, and of great possessions — who had taken a wife from among an equal family. He sported with her, rejoiced with her, and lived in happiness and delight together with her. While they were thus sporting, rejoicing, and living in happiness and delight, his wife in due course became pregnant. After eight or nine months had passed she gave birth, and a handsome, pleasant-looking, and beautiful boy was born. On the twenty-first day, when the birth celebration was held on a great scale and the question arose of what name to give the child, the relatives said, "Because this boy is the son of householder Balasena, let him be called Senapa." And so he was given the name Senapa. Householder Balasena, continuing to sport, to rejoice, and to live in happiness and delight, had another son born, who was given the name Nyesena. Then, in due course, the wife of householder Balasena passed away, and she was adorned and wrapped in blue, yellow, red, and white cloth, carried to the charnel ground, cremated, and the mourning rites were performed, and he withdrew. Householder Balasena thought, "If I take another wife, my two boys will suffer. I shall manage the household of Senapa." And so he did manage that household. Then, in due course, householder Balasena became ill. Although he was tended with medicines made from roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, the illness did not subside but worsened, and he took leave of Senapa and Nyesena with a grieving heart, and said:

All that is accumulated reaches its end;
all that is lofty comes to fall.
All meetings end in parting;
all that lives ends in death.

And so he met with what is the nature of time. The two boys adorned him, wrapping him in blue, yellow, red, and white cloth, carried him to the charnel ground, and cremated him. After that, the mourning rites were performed, the funeral observances were completed, and they withdrew. Senapa then thought:

"When our father was still alive, others provided for our livelihood. Now that the time has come, we must attend to the affairs of the household. If we neglect and abandon the household duties, we will bring shame upon our kinsmen. I shall take my provisions and travel to another land." Recognizing this, Senapa said to his younger brother Nyesena: "Brother, when our father was still alive, others provided for our livelihood. Now that the time has come, we must attend to the affairs of the household. If we neglect and abandon the household duties, we will bring shame upon our kinsmen. You shall remain here and manage the affairs of the household, while I shall take my provisions and go to another land." Nyesena replied: "So be it."

Senapa took many provisions and departed for another land, and there he made great profits. He then sent a message to his younger brother Nyesena saying: "Brother, I have made great profits here and will return before long. Be steadfast, and be of great cheer and joy." Senapa traveled back and again made great profits, and afterward he sent the same kind of message again. Once more Senapa went back and forth and again made great profits, and again he sent the same kind of message. Thus Senapa continued to send messages at appropriate times and regular intervals.

Now it is the nature of things that:

Because one gains, attachment arises for the gain;
from that gain, clinging comes to be born.
A person overpowered by clinging
will fail to discern what should and should not be done.

And so it was that Senapa traveled to very distant places and thereafter sent no more messages. Then Senapa's wife, overcome by afflictions on account of fine clothes and good food, began to make advances to his younger brother Nyesena, but Nyesena withdrew his senses and sat apart. Since knowledge of the domain of women is learned only by those who have studied it well, Senapa's wife went to the house of a kinsman, put on soiled garments, sat and remained on a broken couch. His mother and the people of the household said to her: "Why are you sitting like this?" Senapa's wife replied: "Does one not know what brings harm in the domain of women? She has been grievously afflicted by the afflictions." They said: "Your brother-in-law Nyesena is handsome, lovely to look upon, and beautiful — why do you not make advances to him?" Senapa's wife said: "I tried to approach him but it did not succeed." They said: "Other women whose husbands have been away for a very long time and do not return at the right season — those women have the hardest time of it." Senapa's wife said: "When those women's husbands were away, at least their husbands sent messages at appropriate times and regular intervals. As for her, when her husband was still alive he too used to send messages at appropriate times and regular intervals, but now he sends none at all, so the right season has passed and is lost." Although they tried by many means to coax Senapa's wife up from the couch, she would not rise, and she said: "If she does not give herself to another, she will certainly bring disgrace upon both families." Then the father and mother of Senapa's wife and the assembled kinsmen and relatives began to take counsel.

Since she could not be turned away from this course and would certainly bring disgrace upon both families, they decided to invite the kinsmen as guests, give them a meal, and take counsel together, saying: "It is now the right moment to give her to him." Having deliberated thus, they invited the kinsmen as guests, gave them a meal, and said: "Kinsman, this wife of your elder brother has become utterly distracted through her constant indulgence in affliction, and will certainly bring disgrace upon both families. If you will live together with her, that would be well. If you will not, then we must give her to another." The kinsman thought to himself: "We raised her from childhood, and if she were to go to another and bring disgrace upon both families, that would not be good. I should make her my own." Recognizing this, he accepted and agreed. Then the kinsman brought Senapa's wife to his own home and made merry with her, took joy in her, and lived with her in happiness and delight.

When signs of pregnancy appeared in her, the other wives said: "Where has this come from?" Senapa's wife replied: "She is a woman of pure virtue only — do not slander her with lies." Her closest friend said: "Why keep it secret? This will certainly become known — speak up." Senapa's wife said: "It is from the kinsman." "Well then — whether from a husband or from a relation by marriage, there is no fault in this whatsoever."

When Senapa's wife had conceived, Senapa sent a message to the kinsman saying: "Tend to my younger brother carefully, with attentiveness and great cheer, and give him full provision and support. I myself will come in person exactly as the letter says." When the kinsman heard this, he was overcome with shame and thought: "When I longed to see my elder brother clearly, as one longs to see a cloud in the sky, he did not come — and now, having acted so wrongfully, he is coming. Among the grudges people hold, there are situations of this kind: a woman's grudge is bitter and final, and she will harm me. There is such a danger here — I must flee and go away." He thought again: "To abandon one's own district entirely is a painful thing. These śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas — having obtained from King Prasenajit of Kosala the renunciation that belongs to the young, they have gone forth into their ranks. What might I do among them?" And so the kinsman went to the Jeta Grove, approached a monk, and said: "Noble one, I wish to go forth." The monk replied: "Good sir, excellent — worldly possessions are subject to change; go forth." The monk received the kinsman into the going forth, conferred full ordination upon him, and then for the next two or three days had him study the rules of conduct, saying: "Good sir, a deer is not cured by a deer. Śrāvastī is vast — it is your own familiar domain and your father's district. Live by going on alms rounds." The kinsman, now a junior monk under his preceptor, replied: "So be it — I shall do as the preceptor commands," and in the morning, having put on his robe and taken up his bowl and outer garment, he entered Śrāvastī for alms.

Not knowing his way around the district, he went house by house and entered his own home. Senapa's wife saw the kinsman and struck her breast, saying: "Kinsman, why did you abandon her and go forth?" The kinsman replied: "And why do you say such a thing? Why do you say that I abandoned her and went forth? At the time when I longed to see my elder brother clearly, as one longs to see a cloud in the sky, he did not come —"

"Now, if I do such a wrong, he will come. Among all quarrels, there is this kind: a wife's final break of estrangement will harm me — that kind of situation exists."

Senapa's wife said: "If you first rescued yourself, how is she supposed to manage?" The kinsman replied: "It is you yourself who have thought it through under the power of affliction. I was made to act against my will — you know that yourself," and so saying, he left.

Now the kinsman's younger friend, a boy who had formerly been an incense seller, went to Senapa's wife's house and asked where the kinsman was. Senapa's wife said: "The kinsman made a clean break and went forth. He went among the śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), the sons of the Śākyas. If you don't believe it, go to the Jeta Grove and see for yourself."

He went to the Jeta Grove, but since all who had gone forth wore the same robes, he could not tell which one was the kinsman. He asked a monk: "Noble one, there is one here called Kinsman, the son of a householder of Śrāvastī — where has he gone forth?" That monk showed him, and the incense seller's boy went before the kinsman and said: "Kinsman, without consulting me, pursuing what goal did you go forth?" The kinsman replied: "And do you say the same thing — without consulting me, pursuing what goal did you go forth? At the time when I longed to see my elder brother clearly, as one longs to see a cloud in the sky, he did not come. Now, having done such a wrong as this, he will come. Among all quarrels, there is this kind: a wife's final break of estrangement will harm me — that kind of situation exists."

The incense seller's boy said: "We incense sellers are physicians by trade. If I were to give such a thing as an abortifacient that is administered to one who is bearing a child in the womb, it would cause the child in the womb to be torn apart piece by piece — so why did you not tell me? I can still give it even now." The kinsman consented.

Then the incense seller's boy ground sharp-cutting substances into a powder, gave it to a girl, and said: "Go to Senapa's house and say to Senapa's wife: 'The kinsman says — mix this powder with warm water and drink it, and you will recover.'" The girl obeyed her master's instruction, and heeding the incense seller's boy she went directly to Senapa's house. When she arrived, she said to Senapa's wife: "The kinsman's words are: 'Mix this powder with warm water and drink it, and you will recover.'" Senapa's wife mixed that powder with warm water and drank it, and thereupon the child she was bearing in the womb was torn apart piece by piece, and every sign of the child in the womb disappeared entirely.

Some time later, when her companions saw her, they said: "Where has the child you were carrying gone?" Senapa's wife said: "Did she not say from the very beginning that she herself was a woman of virtue and ask you not to slander her and treat her badly in every way? Go to her." Her dearest companion went to her and said: "You previously told her that what she carried was indeed from the kinsman — where has that child in the womb gone now?" Senapa's wife said: "It has gone exactly where it came from." "How so?" "The kinsman gave such a sharp powder, and on account of that, the child in the womb was torn apart piece by piece."

"The conduct of the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan is merely words. The conduct of the brahmins is merely words. For look — they destroy even what dwells in the womb." So they reviled them, mocked them, and spoke slander against them. The report that the kinsman had committed such and such an evil deed spread throughout Śrāvastī, and the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Kinsman: "Kinsman, is it true that you committed such an evil deed?" "Venerable One, I did not do it. Rather, I consented to it afterward." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the monk Kinsman has incurred no downfall. Nevertheless, a monk should not give consent to such a matter. If a monk does give consent to such a matter, he commits an offense of conflict."

In the meantime, the householder Doṇakṛta completed his affairs and approached Śrāvastī. Now the world desires prosperity and is at odds with decline and adversity, so some people ran quickly ahead and said to the householder's wife: "Your husband Doṇakṛta has come back to Śrāvastī — be glad!" Women are naturally clever without needing to be taught, and so the householder's wife, with a mind filled with spite, put on soiled and dirty clothes and sat slumped on a broken chair. Presently Doṇakṛta entered Śrāvastī, deposited his goods in the treasury, and came to his own home. He saw that the house had not been whitewashed, had not been swept, and had no brightness about it. He asked the maidservant: "Where has the mistress of the house gone?" The girl said: "My lord's wife has broken off her usual conduct and is sitting there on a broken chair."

Thereupon Doṇakṛta felt uneasy and went to his wife's side and said: "My dear, are you not glad that I have come?" She said: "My lord, I am not displeased that you have come. But these very guardians of yours, my lord — those men are thieves." "What did they do?" "Even while I was refusing, the kinsman forced himself on me and made me his own." "My dear, it is not that he has humiliated you — it is that he has humiliated me. Very well, I shall repudiate that one and have done with him entirely." "My dear, where is Kinsman?" "My lord, upon hearing of your return he took ordination." "Where?" "In the Jeta Grove, among the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan." "My dear, is that city without fear? I shall go there and utterly cut off all ties with him."

Now the world has friends, enemies, and those in between, and so some people went to the monk Kinsman and said: "Kinsman, your elder brother has come." Kinsman said: "What does he say?" They told him: "He is saying, 'Is that city without fear? I shall go there too and utterly cut off all ties with him.'" When Kinsman heard this he became distressed and thought: "Might not the very fear from which I took ordination pursue me even here? For our king did give a pardon for my youthful transgressions, yet I am still a guilty man. If there is a chance that harm could come to me here as well, I should flee and go." And so he told his preceptor in full detail of everything that had come about, saying: "Preceptor, the very fear from which I took ordination has now followed me here as well." The preceptor said:

"My child, where will you go?" "To Rājagṛha, Preceptor." "My child, there is a monk who is a friend of mine staying there. Carry a letter to him, stay in his company, and he will look after you with loving-kindness." "Excellent, Preceptor."

So Kinsman wrote that monk a letter in advance, saying: "This companion of mine I am sending to you in my stead. For his sake, please look after him with loving-kindness, just as you would delight in my presence here." Having written the letter, he entrusted it to his kinsman. The young man, full of anxiety and unease, glancing in all directions, set out and eventually made his way to Rājagṛha. There, following directions he had received, he went to that monk's dwelling, prostrated himself with his head at the monk's feet, presented the letter, and sat quietly to one side.

The monk took up the letter and said: "Welcome, venerable one, welcome! Just as you are his kinsman, so too shall you be mine. Be diligent in your training, and I shall provide you with an alms-bowl, robes, a straining cloth, a bowl stand, and a belt — you shall have no lack of these. Now, as for the practice of a monk, there are two: meditative concentration and recitation. Which do you prefer?" "I wish for meditative concentration." "Excellent, my child."

He gave him instructions, and his kinsman went to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove and, through diligence, effort, and exertion, abandoned all mental afflictions and directly realized the state of an arhat — an arhat freed from attachment, belonging to no higher of the three realms, his mind equal toward mud and gold, equal toward sky and the palm of a hand, like sandalwood placed in offering, his doors of sense burst open by knowledge, possessed of knowledge, supernormal cognition, and individual analytical understanding, turned away from the gains and esteem that come with existence and desire, fit to be honored, revered, and praised by gods together with Indra and their attendants.

In the meantime, the elder Sena went to the Jeta Grove and asked the monks there: "Noble ones, is there among you one who has gone forth from the household of a householder of Śrāvastī?" "There is." "Where has he gone?" "To Rājagṛha." "And what is he to you?" "He is my younger brother." Sena paid homage at the monks' feet and departed, thinking to himself: "Rājagṛha is not a city free of fear either, so I shall go there as well and utterly cut off all ties with him." And so he took provisions for the road, many in number, and coins, and set out for Rājagṛha.

He went to the Bamboo Grove and asked the monks there: "Noble ones, is there among you one who has gone forth from the household of a householder of Śrāvastī?" "He has come here." "And what is he to you?" "He is my younger brother." "Where is he now?" "In the charnel ground of the Cool Grove."

Sena went to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove. When he saw his kinsman, who had been a small child when he last knew him, now grown great, though he could not recognize him for his skill and the authority of his bearing, he looked carefully, and —

— by his face he recognized him. Sena thought: "If he recognizes me, he will certainly kill me, so I must devise a plan." He moved off to one side and sat looking around in all directions.

Just then, a hunter came along that road carrying a bow and arrows, having come in pursuit of a deer that had slipped away. Sena went up to that man and said: "Friend, where are you going with that bow and arrows?" The man replied: "Friend, a deer has escaped me." "And how much do you usually get from it?" "Friend, sometimes it works out, sometimes it does not." "And when it does, how much, more or less?" "Friend, something in the range of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." Sena said: "Friend, if that is so, kill this monk here and I will give you five hundred kārṣāpaṇas."

The hunter, his mind drawn on by desire, accepted five hundred kārṣāpaṇas from Sena. But then he reflected: "These monks have been entrusted to the care of King Bimbisāra, surrendered from his youth. I myself pass through this area all the time, and if I were to kill this monk, I too — along with my children, my relations, and my livestock — would certainly be imprisoned and put to death. Moreover, this householder is like the appearance of a white mushroom: no one knows where he has come from. In any case, I must kill him."

So the hunter loaded a poisoned arrow, drawing it back to his ear in the shape of a bow, and shot it into Sena's vital spot. Sena, overwhelmed by feelings of acute suffering, thought as he was dying: "Whatever is happening — my being slain — it is surely because this monk conspired with this hunter." And with that wrong aspiration he died, and was reborn as a snake, one that spreads its venom swiftly, under the threshold of the neighboring dwelling.

Now, arhats do not employ knowledge and vision without deliberate reflection, and so when a neighbor opened the door, the snake that spreads its venom swiftly killed him. Then, reborn on top of the threshold, it died there as well. Then, reborn beneath one of the legs of a chair, it died there too. In the same way, being reborn below things a second, third, and fourth time, it died each time. With each successive death, the poison grew keener and the body grew finer, so that it would take on the next existence through the moment of conception. After some time it was reborn on the flat board above that place, and it fell upon the body of the venerable Neyade as he had gone alone into seclusion and entered into proper composure.

Then the venerable Neyade said to the monks: "Venerable ones, a snake — one that spreads its venom swiftly — burning, sharp, of fierce poison, has fallen upon my body, fine as a needle used for applying eye-medicine. Venerable ones, take hold of my body from the extremities and carry it outside the assembly hall without letting it be shattered, as though it were a bundle of chaff."

At that time the venerable Śāriputra was sitting at the base of a tree not far from the venerable Neyade, having taken up his daytime abode there. The venerable Śāriputra heard those very words spoken by the venerable Neyade. Having heard them, he went to where the venerable Neyade was, approached him, and spoke to the venerable Neyade in these words:

"I myself do not see that the venerable Neyade's appearance has changed or that his faculties have become disordered. And yet the venerable Neyade has said these words: 'Venerable ones, the snake-venom spreading swiftly through my body, blazing, sharp, and virulent — fine as a needle used for applying eye-medicine — has fallen upon it heavily. Venerable ones, take hold of my body from the extremities and carry it outside the assembly hall without letting it be shattered, as though it were a bundle of chaff.' Now, venerable Śāriputra, for one who holds such views as these — 'The eye is the self; the eye belongs to the self. The ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are the self; the mind belongs to the self. Form is the self; form belongs to the self. Sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena are the self; phenomena belong to the self. The earth element is the self; the earth element belongs to the self. The water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are the self; the consciousness element belongs to the self. The aggregate of form is the self; the aggregate of form belongs to the self. The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are the self; the aggregate of consciousness belongs to the self' — for one who holds such views, it would indeed be the case that the appearance changes and the faculties become disordered. But as for me, venerable Śāriputra, since I do not hold such views as these — that the eye is the self or belongs to the self, that the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are the self or belong to the self, that form is the self or belongs to the self, that sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena are the self or belong to the self, that the earth element is the self or belongs to the self, that the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are the self or belong to the self, that the aggregate of form is the self or belongs to the self, that the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are the self or belong to the self — how could my appearance change or my faculties become disordered? The venerable Neyade, having long since abandoned and fully understood the grasping at self, the grasping at what is mine, the conceit of thinking 'I am,' clinging, and underlying tendencies — having, like a palm tree cut off at the root, been severed at the base, made without foundation, and rendered incapable of arising again — how could his appearance change or his faculties become disordered?"

Then the venerable Śāriputra, together with a great many monks, took hold of the venerable Neyade's body from the extremities and carried it outside the assembly hall. And the venerable Neyade's body shattered in a hundred pieces, like a bundle of chaff.

Then the venerable Śāriputra at that time spoke these verses:

One who has practiced the holy life well
and cultivated the path itself well —
at the end of life, finds joy,
just as one freed from illness.

One who has practiced the holy life well
and cultivated the path itself well —
at the end of life, finds joy,
just as one who has cast aside a poisoned vessel.

One who has practiced the holy life well
and cultivated the path itself well —
at death's end there is no sorrow,
like one who escapes a burning house.

One who has practiced the holy life well
and cultivated the path itself well —

when one perceives the world with wisdom
as no different from grass and wood,
then one longs for nothing else
beyond the joining that leaves no further becoming.

Then the venerable Śāriputra paid bodily homage to the body of the venerable Nanda, and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One with these words:

Venerable One, the snake's venom that has spread swiftly through the body of the venerable Nanda — burning, sharp, and fierce — is like this: it fell as fine as the tip of an eye-salve needle, and that body of his has crumbled like a stalk of hollow cane. Śāriputra, if at that time these verses and these mantra syllables had become manifest for the venerable Nanda, then the swift-spreading, burning, fierce snake's venom would not have taken hold in his body, and his body would not have crumbled like a stalk of hollow cane — not even in a hundred ways. Venerable One, what are those verses and those mantra syllables?

Then the Blessed One at that time spoke these verses:

I have loving-kindness for Āṅkura's realm,
and loving-kindness for the son of the earth-guardian.
I have loving-kindness for Lābu and for the swiftest,
and loving-kindness for the son born with a crest.

Gautama is black,
and toward the ill-eyed I have loving-kindness;
toward the nāga named Nandaka and Upanandaka,
toward those two I always have loving-kindness.

I have loving-kindness toward the footless ones,
and toward the two-footed I have loving-kindness.
I have loving-kindness toward the four-footed,
and toward the many-footed I have loving-kindness.

Toward all the nāgas that dwell supported by the ocean,
toward all of them I have loving-kindness.
Toward all sentient beings that dwell in the throat,
toward all such sentient beings I have loving-kindness.

May all sentient beings and all living creatures
and all spirits be without harm.
May all be endowed with happiness,
may all be free from illness.
May all see what is good,
and may no evil come to any.

Though I dwell always in the shelter
of a bird with snakes filling it,
may the swift-spreading venom and fierce poison
bring no harm to my life.

By the truth of my words
— that the Teacher is supreme in the world —
by that truth of my words,
may poison not enter my body.

Attachment, aversion, and delusion:
these are the three poisons of the world.
The awakened Blessed One is without poison;
by the truth of the Buddha, the poison is defeated.

Attachment, aversion, and delusion:
these are the three poisons of the world.
The Dharma of the Buddha is without poison;
by the truth of the Dharma, the poison is defeated.

Attachment, aversion, and delusion:
these are the three poisons of the world.
The Saṅgha of the Blessed One is without poison;
by the truth of the Saṅgha, the poison is defeated.

Venom and fierce poison are overcome,
thoroughly guarded by this protection.
All the buddhas have overcome poison —
O crawler, your poison too is overcome.

Now these are the mantra syllables:

Tadyathā: oṃ tumbile tumbile tumabe pratumabe naṭaṭe sunaṭaṭa kevaṭaṭe munaye samaye dante dantile nīle nīlakeśe bāle bālakobe ole nyaṅgole svāhā.

Śāriputra, if at that time these verses and these mantra syllables had become manifest for the young man of good family, Nanda, then the swift-spreading venom would not have taken hold in his body, and that body of his would not have crumbled in a hundred ways like a stalk of hollow cane. Then at that time the venerable Nanda, with those verses and

those mantra syllables not having been heard before, how could things now appear to him as they truly are in the presence of the Blessed One?

Then the venerable Śāriputra, delighting in and rejoicing at what the Blessed One had declared, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga. The ninth fascicle. The monks, having arisen in doubt, requested the buddha, the Blessed One, to resolve all their doubts.

Revered one, what action did the venerable Nanda perform such that, by the karmic maturation of that action, he was born into a household of wealth, great possessions, and abundant resources? What action did he perform such that he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One and, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhathood? And what action did he perform such that, even having attained arhathood, he passed into nirvāṇa through an illness tormented by poison?

The Blessed One declared: Monks, it was Nanda himself who found the collection of karma, who fully transformed the conditions, who abided like a flame, who performed and accumulated those actions that were bound to arise without fail. And those actions performed and accumulated by Nanda himself — by whom else could they be individually experienced? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous actions performed and accumulated ripen in just those appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said:

Even if a hundred aeons pass,
actions do not perish but are stored,
and when conditions and the time are met
they bear their fruits for embodied beings.

Monks, in a former time long past, in an age when no buddhas had appeared, there arose in the world solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas) of inferior rank — those compassionate toward the poor, fond of remote dwelling places, wandering alone like rhinoceroses, who had become fields of offering for the world.
