Now at a certain time, a hunter was sitting at a cliff face. Not far from that cliff there was a lake that served as a haven for many wild beasts and birds. Day after day that hunter would go there to drive away the many wild beasts and birds, to injure them, and to set many snares, traps, and nets in order to cause them suffering by improper means. And those snares, traps, and nets of his did catch game.

Now at another time, a solitary buddha who was wandering and traveling through the region went to that cliff and agreed to spend the night in what appeared to be a divine abode. Early the next morning he dressed himself, took up his almsbowl and Dharma robes, and entered the cliff face for alms. Having collected alms there, he thought to himself, "This divine abode is well-traveled by people during the day, so I shall eat my alms-food in a peaceful place outside the cliff." Leaving the cliff, thinking "This is peaceful, this is peaceful," he went toward that lake. Arriving there, he placed his almsbowl and water-vessel side by side at the edge. He washed both feet, wiped both hands, drew water, took up some leaves that had fallen, sat down, and performed the act of eating. Then he wiped both hands, rinsed his mouth, replaced the almsbowl and water-vessel just as they were, washed both feet, and leaning against the base of a tree, sat in cross-legged posture like a serpent king coiled at rest, abiding with peaceful comportment. That day, on account of the human scent, not a single wild beast was caught.

Then the hunter rose early the next morning and went to that very lake, where he began searching with his hunting dogs, his traps, and his snares. Not a single wild animal did he see. He thought to himself: if my dogs, traps, and snares are of any use, then what is the reason that today not a single animal has been caught? He began to make a circuit around the edge of the lake, and when he saw human footprints he followed them. He then saw the pratyekabuddha sitting in peaceful composure, and he thought: these gone-forth ones of peaceful mind take delight in dwelling in such places as this. If I do not kill him, he will certainly cut off my livelihood. I must kill him by any means. With a mind devoid of compassion, that one who had cast aside concern for the next world drew his poisoned arrow full to the ear, bent like the curve of a bow, and shot it into a vital point of that pratyekabuddha.

The great being, that pratyekabuddha, thought: it would not be right for this hunter, overcome by afflictions, to become so deeply fallen and ruined — I should extend a helping hand to him. And so, like a great king of geese spreading wide its wings, he rose up into the sky above and began to perform miracles: blazing with fire, shining with radiance, raining down water, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary beings quickly fix their minds upon miraculous displays, and so the hunter collapsed like a tree cut off at the root and prostrated himself at the feet of that pratyekabuddha, saying: "O worthy one who has become a true field of merit, please descend, please descend. Please extend your hand to pull me, who am sinking in the mire of afflictions, up from the depths."

Out of compassion for that hunter, the pratyekabuddha descended from the sky above. Then the hunter removed the arrow, closed the wound cleanly, and said: "Noble one, please draw near. If it would please you to heal this with a golden salve, I will provide that as well." The pratyekabuddha thought: whatever was to be obtained through this body of filth and pus, I have already obtained. Therefore, now I shall enter into the peaceful realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates. And so, right before that very hunter, he rose again into the midst of the sky, displayed various miracles, and passed into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates — the utterly peaceful passing beyond sorrow.

As the hunter was a man of wealth, he gathered all fragrant woods, built up the body into a pyre, and burned it. He then quenched the pyre with milk, placed the bones in a golden urn, and had a bodily reliquary stupa erected at a crossroads of a great thoroughfare. He raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and made offerings of fragrant substances, garlands and perfumes, incense, powders, and cymbals. He bowed at the feet of the stupa and made this aspiration prayer: "By whatever root of virtue there is in having made these offerings — and may it not be commensurate with the deed of having harmed such a truly worthy one, a true field of merit — may I be born handsome, pleasing to behold, and beautiful in a wealthy household of great resources and possessions, and may I attain such qualities of character that I please even a Teacher far more exalted than this one, without causing him any displeasure."

Now monks, whoever was the hunter at that time and on that occasion is none other than this very intimate disciple here.

As for the karma of having struck a pratyekabuddha (solitary buddha) with a poisoned arrow, the karmic maturation of that deed caused him to be tormented in the great hell of Unceasing Torment for an entire aeon. Then, through the remaining force of that same karma, he was struck by poison at the appointed hour across five hundred lifetimes. And even now, though he has attained the state of an arhat, he has passed into final nirvāṇa through that poison.

As for the one who made offerings and set forth that aspiration prayer, he has now been born handsome, pleasing to behold, and beautiful in a wealthy household of great resources and possessions. Having gone forth into my teaching and abandoned all afflictions, he has directly realized arhatship. And he has pleased me, the Teacher who surpasses even a hundred thousand billion pratyekabuddhas, without causing me any displeasure.

Therefore, monks, the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark. The karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright. And the karmic maturation of mixed actions is itself mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and actions that are mixed, and strive for actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train in this way.

Now, this account is incidental. The Buddha, the Blessed One, does not yet lay down rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There in Śrāvastī there lived a merchant. He had taken a wife from his own social class, and together with her he played, rejoiced, and enjoyed himself in pleasure. While they were playing, rejoicing, and enjoying themselves, a son was born to her. As the child was born, they gave him a name appropriate to his family line, raised him, cared for him, and he grew up.

In the course of time, the merchant's wife passed away, and he took another wife. The merchant said to this new wife: "My good woman, a child born of another woman can be of service, but one born of a rival cannot. This boy here is your own son, so you should attend to his needs."

Then after some time had passed, the second wife also conceived a child. She thought to herself: "Now that I too have a child of my own, this boy will become a rival to mine, so I shall not treat him well." From that moment on she gave the boy bad food, dressed him in poor clothing, and beat him again and again with her fists and with a switch.

The boy went to his father and said: "Father, this stepmother of mine gives me bad food and poor clothing, and beats me again and again with her fists and a switch."

The merchant said: "Son, whatever the case, put a stop to this — she must not continue to behave that way."

The merchant then said to his wife: "My good woman, did I not tell you from the very beginning that a child born of another woman can be of service, but one born of a rival cannot, and that this boy is your own son, and that you should attend to his needs? Why then do you give him bad food and poor clothing, and beat him again and again with your fists and a switch?"

The wife replied: "My lord's son, I will discipline him. Since he is the merchant's son, if he is not disciplined, the whole world will certainly reproach my lord's son himself."

The merchant said: "I have not appointed you to discipline him. Henceforth do not give him bad food and poor clothing, and do not beat him again and again with your fists and a switch."

Because that wife was greatly indulged by the merchant, she continued once more to give the boy bad food and poor clothing, and to beat him again and again with her fists and a switch. The boy thought to himself: "Since my father has not firmly restrained this stepmother of mine, she goes on giving me bad food and poor clothing, and beating me again and again with her fists and a switch. I will go forth into homelessness." And so he implored his father in every way he could, saying: "Father, even though you have restrained this stepmother of mine, she continues to give me bad food and poor clothing, and to beat me again and again with her fists and a switch. I will go forth into homelessness."

The merchant, being deeply in love with that wife and guarding her feelings, was unable to restrain her firmly, and so he said: "My son, this wife of your householder father is fierce and stubborn, and of a violent temper. Go, then, and take ordination. I will be able to see you living, and yet there is also the possibility that she might come to do you harm."

With his father's permission, the boy went to the Jeta Grove and approached a monk, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Noble one, I wish to go forth into homelessness."

The monk said: "Good-looking one, it is excellent that you have generated this intention. Pleasures and possessions are impermanent — go forth and take ordination."

The monk gave the boy the going forth and conferred upon him full ordination, and then said: "Good-looking one, the tasks of a monk are two: meditative concentration and study. I myself am one who practices meditative concentration. As for you — will you practice meditation or study?"

The boy replied: "Preceptor, I will study."

"Good, my son. You should read all three scriptural collections."

The boy thought: "There is much text, and one needs a preceptor to guide one through it. Here there is no one to instruct me in study, so I shall go to another region." And he went to another region. There he read all three scriptural collections, and became one who possessed all three collections, who proclaimed the Dharma, and who had the eloquence of reasoning and liberation.

He then reflected: "The Blessed One has declared to the monks that those who give birth to a child, nourish a child, raise a child, suckle a child, and show the child the manifold diversity of Jambudvīpa — these two perform a difficult deed. Even if a son were to carry his father on one shoulder and his mother on the other for a hundred full years, or even if he were to arrange for them to be the lords and owners of all the wealth of this great earth — its jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, the essence of the earth, burnished metal, red gold, and the swastika and all such riches — even that would not constitute a son having done something for his parents and having benefited them. But if his parents, who lack faith, he leads to take hold of perfect faith, tames them, introduces them to it, and establishes them firmly in it; if his parents, who lack moral discipline, he leads to take hold of perfect moral discipline; if his parents, who are miserly, he leads to take hold of perfect generosity; and if his parents, who lack wisdom, he leads to take hold of perfect wisdom, tames them, introduces them to it, and establishes them firmly in it — then, by that much, a son will have done something for his parents and will have truly benefited them."

When this was said, he thought: "My own father lacks faith; let me go to him and teach him the Dharma." And so, taking up his alms bowl and robes, he made his way toward Śrāvastī, and in due course arrived there. Upon entering Śrāvastī itself, he went to the Jeta Grove. Throughout Śrāvastī the word had spread: "A son of a certain great merchant has come from the provinces, having studied the three scriptural collections (Tripiṭaka), and has arrived at the Jeta Grove." When the merchant heard this, he thought: "My son has studied the three scriptural collections and come from the provinces to the Jeta Grove — I shall go and make him truly glad." The merchant went to the Jeta Grove, and upon seeing his son he said: "My son, though you renounced me and went forth, it is excellent that you have become a monk and have come to be deeply learned. I too rejoice entirely." Having said this, he sat down before him. The monk then taught the merchant the Dharma in such a way as to give rise in him to faith, so that he would take refuge and take hold of the bases of training. The merchant prostrated to his son's two feet and invited him for a meal the following day, and the son accepted in silence without saying anything. The merchant then prostrated to his son's two feet and departed. But on the way home a thought arose in him: "I have invited my son for a meal without first consulting anyone — yet my wife is fierce, quarrelsome, and domineering, and she will not treat my son with respect. How am I to manage this?" Then he thought again: "Well, the invitation has already been given, so there is nothing to be done about that. I must arrange things on all sides with pleasing and agreeable words, so that my wife will not be upset." And so he went home and said to his wife: "Good lady, do wandering, dying, and going forth amount to the same thing — or is there some slight difference?" The wife replied: "My lord's heir, there is not the slightest difference." The merchant said: "Good lady, others are saying that your fine son has become an excellent monk and, having studied the three scriptural collections in the provinces, has arrived at the Jeta Grove — and that he is not only fully equipped with the three scriptural collections, but also preaches the Dharma and is endowed with eloquence in reasoning and liberation." The wife replied: "My lord's heir, if that is so, why have you not brought him home as a guest? Good lady, he has been invited — go now and prepare food." That wife, freed from the grip of aversion toward him, prepared on that very day the foods that were of the cool variety, and prepared on the following morning the foods that were of the warm variety. Then she sent a messenger with the invitation: "Venerable one, you were invited for midday — please know that the time has now come." The monk, in the early morning, tied on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and robes, and went to his father's house, arriving and sitting down just as the seat was being spread. Then the merchant together with his wife, with their own hands, offered food to the monk until he was fully satisfied, and with their own hands they removed the bowl. Knowing that he was satisfied and that the meal was finished, and seeing him wipe his hands and set down the bowl, they prostrated to his feet and sat down before him to hear the Dharma. He then taught the Dharma to that mother as well, in such a way that upon hearing it she too would take refuge and take hold of the bases of training.

That household had become, as it were, a well for monks and nuns to draw from, and having been disciplined in this way, whatever the household members intended to give or do, all of it was directed toward the monks and the nuns.

Then some time later, the merchant fell gravely ill. His son, upon hearing that his father was ill, thought: "I will go and teach my father the Dharma in such a way that it will bring him the highest joy." The monk then went to him at an appropriate time and spoke thus: "Father, I will not cause you displeasure. Consider: relying on me as your spiritual friend, you have gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, taken up the bases of training, given gifts, and made merit. If you pass on to another realm, you have had a good year, and the higher realms are as close as a silk curtain — liberation is as near as a veil that merely covers it. Even when this body perishes, you will be born among the gods." He taught the Dharma in this way.

The merchant replied: "Son, it is just so. It is exactly so. Relying on you as my spiritual friend, I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, taken up the bases of training, given gifts, and made merit. If I pass on to another realm, I have had a good year, and the higher realms are as close as a silk curtain — liberation is as near as a veil that merely covers it. Even when this body perishes, I will be born among the gods."

Having taught his father the Dharma in this way, the monk's son departed.

A thought then arose in the merchant's mind: "My son, who possesses all three scriptural collections, who proclaims the Dharma, who has the eloquence of reasoning and of liberation — he will speak this to no one else. My affliction of suffering is without equal, and so I should put an end to myself." Then he thought again: "But to lay hands on oneself is painful. So who is there who could take my life from me?" He had a maidservant named Skyong-ma, who was fat, foolish, and of low intelligence. The merchant thought: "This maidservant Skyong-ma, being fat, foolish, and of low intelligence, she would be capable of taking my life — others could not do it."

Now not far from the merchant's house, a householder's son had taken a wife, and the merchant's wife was invited as a guest along with the maidservant Skyong-ma. When the bride had been received and the wedding feast was underway, the merchant's wife said to Skyong-ma: "Skyong-ma, go back and make sure the merchant does not fall asleep; I will follow shortly."

Skyong-ma heeded her mistress's words and went home. She went to the merchant's side, and the merchant said: "Skyong-ma, where have you come from to be here?" Skyong-ma replied: "My lord's son, the householder's great son, has taken a bride, and I went to look and pay respects before coming back." The merchant said: "Skyong-ma, is the bride fine? Is the son of my lord fine?" "Yes, the son of my lord is fine." "Well then, if I were to give you to him as a bride, would you be pleased?" "My lord's son would be pleased." "If that is so, and you do whatever I say, I will make you happy — know that." Skyong-ma replied: "My lord's son, I will do just so." "Skyong-ma, if that is so, then let something non-human enter my belly and tear it open." "My lord's son, what is the procedure?" "Skyong-ma, first squeeze my two feet. After that, the two calves. After that, the two knees. After that, the two thighs. After that, the hips. After that, the belly. After that, the chest. After that, squeeze the throat —"

"If I move, do not release." The foolish Skyong-ma did exactly as instructed and squeezed him firmly. The merchant thought to himself, "Oh dear — if Skyong-ma releases, what could be wrong with that?" — but at that, Skyong-ma squeezed even more tightly. A god spoke these verses:

Grasped by a dull-witted mind,
as a turtle grips and holds,
seized now in Skyong-ma's clutch —
I see no life left for you.

The merchant's time had come. Skyong-ma wrapped him in cloth and laid him out. Then the merchant's wife came in from outside and said, "Skyong-ma, have you been sitting here all this while letting the merchant sleep?" and she began to rouse the merchant. Skyong-ma said, "A wicked child drew out the enemy that was in this man's belly, and because of that he has fallen into this sleep — do not rouse him." The merchant's wife thought, "What sort of enemy is this? I must examine," and she began to investigate and saw that his time had come.

Then a thought arose in the merchant's wife: "This is not Skyong-ma's own wit. This is the wit of the monk who is the son of Bū-zan-mo and who possesses the three collections of scripture. When he has read through the three collections, teaching nothing of any other doctrine, he will not cause your father distress. If you go to another land, the harvest will be fine, and the higher realms will be fully covered with silk; liberation will be fully covered with a curtain — yet even when the body perishes, one will be reborn among the gods." She spoke these words in her grief and sorrow. "Now this body too has perished, and he has already been born among the gods. Come back — enjoy happiness together with me, carry on the household affairs as well."

Thus, overcome with grief, she spoke those words aloud. After that, having adorned the body with blue, yellow, red, and white robes, she had it cremated in the charnel ground outside Śrāvastī, and then performed the mourning rites.

From time to time the wife would repeat these very words. The monk who possessed the three collections of scripture heard that his father's time had come and thought, "This is indeed the nature of conditioned things, yet I will go and perform the mourning rites for that dear mother." He went, and while still at a great distance that dear mother caught sight of the monk. When she saw him, she again began to say, "The son of Bū-zan-mo, possessed of the three collections — when he has read through the three collections, teaching nothing of any other doctrine, he will not cause your father distress. If you go to another land, the harvest will be fine, and the higher realms will be fully covered with silk; liberation will be fully covered with a curtain — yet even when the body perishes, one will be reborn among the gods. Now this body too has perished, and he has already been born among the gods. Come back — enjoy happiness together with me, carry on the household affairs as well."

At this the monk was stricken with anguish and turned back from that very spot. A feeling of remorse arose in him, thinking, "Did I not cause him to die?" He then reported the matter to the other monks. The monks laid it before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, that monk has incurred no transgression. Nevertheless, a monk must not teach to a sick person any Dharma of that kind — having heard it, he thinks the sick person will die. If a monk teaches to a sick person Dharma of that kind — having heard it, he thinks the sick person will die — it becomes a serious offense. This, moreover, occurred before the time: the Blessed Buddha does not, in the Vinaya, lay down a rule of training for the hearers."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling in a grove of torch-trees on the bank of the pleasant river at Varaṇā. There the Blessed One taught the community of monks, saying: "Monks, cultivate the meditation on the unattractive. If you dwell on the unattractive, grow accustomed to it, and practice it repeatedly, it will yield great fruit and great benefit." And he praised the meditation on the unattractive and extolled its virtues. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, cultivate the meditation on the unattractive. If you dwell on it, grow accustomed to it, and practice it repeatedly, it will yield great fruit and great benefit." At that time the monks undertook the meditation on the unattractive. As they did so, they became weary and disgusted with their pus-filled bodies, grew troubled and full of doubt, condemned those bodies, and began drawing weapons on themselves, swallowing poison, hanging themselves with ropes, leaping into ravines — and in this way monks were also urging other monks to do the same. Then another monk who had become weary and disgusted with his pus-filled body, troubled, full of doubt, and condemning it, went to where the wandering ascetic Migalandika was staying, and arriving there, said to Migalandika: "Come here, dear friend. Take my life, and my bowl and robes shall be yours." Then Migalandika killed that monk, and carrying the blood-stained sword, made his way to the pleasant river and sat down on the bank of that river, squatting there, washing the sword stained with blood. A god of Māra's host who was sitting across the current of the pleasant river, undivided, then said to Migalandika: "Excellent, excellent, dear friend! In this way you cause monks who are endowed with moral discipline and virtue to cross over what they have not yet crossed, to be freed from what they have not yet been freed from, to breathe out where they have not yet breathed out, to pass fully into nirvāṇa who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — and in doing so great merit arises for you, and their bowls and robes become yours, which is moreover a gain beyond measure for you." When the god had spoken thus to him, Migalandika formed the view, extensively and with a most sinful character: "It is true that I cause monks who are endowed with moral discipline and virtue to cross over what they have not yet crossed, to be freed from what they have not yet been freed from, to breathe out where they have not yet breathed out, to pass fully into nirvāṇa who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — and great merit thereby arises for me, and their bowls and robes become mine, which is moreover a gain beyond measure for me." From that time onward Migalandika carried a sharp sword under his arm and wandered from park to park, from monastery to monastery, from house to house, from walkway to walkway, and along side-paths. Seeing various monks, he spoke to them thus: "You, ascetic — endowed with moral discipline, endowed with virtue — you who are to be helped across what you have not yet crossed, to be freed from what you have not yet been freed from, to breathe out where you have not yet breathed out, to pass fully into nirvāṇa who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — come now." Then a certain monk who was staying in a state of weariness and disgust with his pus-filled body, troubled and full of doubt and condemning it, came out, and said to Migalandika: "Dear friend, I have not yet crossed over — liberate me. I have not yet been freed — release me."

"I have not yet breathed out — cause me to breathe out. I have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — help me pass fully into nirvāṇa." Then Migalandika killed that monk. And in the same way he killed two, then three, until he had killed sixty monks.

At that time the monks became few, diminished, and hushed, and the monastic Saṅgha of monks grew thin. Then, on that very fifteenth day, the Blessed One took his seat on the cushion spread before the monastic Saṅgha of monks for the restoration ceremony (poṣadha). Having taken his seat, the Blessed One surveyed the entire assembly and then said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the condition, that the monks have now become few, diminished, and hushed, and the monastic Saṅgha of monks has grown thin?"

"Venerable One, at one time the Blessed One instructed the monastic Saṅgha of monks: 'Monks, cultivate the meditation on foulness. If you cultivate, habituate, and repeatedly practice the meditation on foulness, it will yield great fruit and great benefit.' And he both taught the meditation on foulness and spoke its praises. At that time the monks set about cultivating the meditation on foulness. But as they cultivated it, being wearied, troubled, full of doubt, and condemning this pus-filled body, some drew out weapons, some sought poison, some hanged themselves with rope, some leapt from precipices, and some monks incited other monks."

"Then a certain other monk, wearied, troubled, full of doubt, and condemning this pus-filled body, went to where the ascetic Migalandika was, and arriving there, said to him: 'Good friend, come — kill me. My alms bowl and robes, whatever they are, shall be yours.' Then Migalandika killed that monk, and with his sword stained with blood he went to where the pleasant river was, and arriving at the bank of the pleasant river, crouched down and began to wash the blood-stained sword."

"Then a god of the māra class (Skt. māra) came to the bank of the pleasant river without breaking its flow, and said to the ascetic Migalandika: 'Good friend — excellent, excellent! Thus you are one who helps monks endowed with moral discipline, endowed with virtue, to cross what they have not yet crossed, to be freed from what they have not yet been freed from, to breathe out where they have not yet breathed out, to pass fully into nirvāṇa who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — and great merit will be generated for you; and whatever alms bowls and robes are theirs shall become yours — this too is excellent gain for you.' Speaking thus, he caused Migalandika to form a very broad and sinful view, namely the thought: 'It is true that I help monks endowed with moral discipline, endowed with virtue, to cross what they have not yet crossed, to be freed from what they have not yet been freed from, to breathe out where they have not yet breathed out, to pass fully into nirvāṇa who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — and great merit is indeed generated for me; and whatever alms bowls and robes are theirs, those becoming mine — this too is excellent gain for me.' Having attained this broadly sinful view, Migalandika then took up a sharp sword under his arm and went from park to park, from monastery to monastery, from house to house,

from cloister to cloister, roaming through the passages and walkways, and whenever he caught sight of such and such a monk he would approach and say: "Reverend one, you who are endowed with moral discipline, endowed with virtue — you who have not crossed over, I will help you cross; you who have not been freed, I will free you; you who have not yet breathed out, I will let you breathe out; you who have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa, I will bring you to pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Then one monk, wearied by this body of pus and filth, overcome with torpor, afflicted with doubt and remorse, came forward from where he had been staying and addressed the ascetic Migalandika in these words: "Good sir, I have not yet crossed over — free me. I have not yet been freed — release me. I have not yet breathed out — let me breathe out. I have not yet passed fully into nirvāṇa — bring me to nirvāṇa."

Thereupon the ascetic Migalandika deprived that monk of his life. And in the same way, from a second and third up to sixty monks he deprived of their lives. This, reverend ones, was the cause and condition by which the number of monks had now become few, had diminished, had dwindled, and the Saṅgha of monks had grown thin.

"Ānanda, do the monks then stir up action against a monk?" "Reverend one, they do stir it up." The Blessed One, the Buddha, censured what was improper conduct for a renunciant, conduct not in conformity, not befitting, not in accord with the rule — that this was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. And having censured it in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks:

"Monks, therefore, seeing ten genuine benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be laid down — namely: for the cohesion of the Saṅgha; for the well-being of the Saṅgha; for the comfortable abiding of the Saṅgha; for the restraint of shameless persons; for the comfortable abiding of those who are conscientious; for the conversion of the faithless to faith; for the increase and growth of those who are already faithful; for the restraint of the defilements of this present life; for the prevention of defilements in future lives; and so that my holy life, being of great benefit to the many, widely proclaimed and fully expounded among gods and humans, may long endure.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Should any monk, with deliberate intention, deprive a human being — or one of human form — of life with his own hand, or procure a weapon for that person's death, or seek out a weapon for him, or cause him to be killed, or praise death to him, speaking thus: 'O person, what use is this wretched, impure, evil life to you? O person, death is better than living' — and with such intent of mind and such deliberation of mind, in various ways causes him to be killed or praises death to him, and that being at whose instigation this is done then dies — that monk too is one who has incurred defeat and is not to remain."

"Furthermore, 'any monk' — there are four kinds of monk: the monk in name only, the monk by self-proclamation, the monk who begs, and the monk by reason of having subdued the afflictions. What is the monk in name only? One whose name is given and spoken as 'monk,' or a secondary term, or a polite term, a concept, a designation, an appellation, a conventional expression — whether it be 'monk' or 'of the class of monks' —

"one who has become like a monk" — that is called the monk in name only.

What is the monk by self-proclamation? One who, while not actually being a monk, proclaims himself to be a monk, and who, while acting by stealth, pledges himself as a monk — that is called the monk by self-proclamation.

What is the monk who begs? One who sustains himself by living as a mendicant in conformity with the Dharma — that is called the monk who begs.

What is the monk by reason of having subdued the afflictions? One who has abandoned, thoroughly understood, cut off at the root, and rendered without remainder — like a palm tree felled at the base — and brought to the nature of non-arising in future lives those things which are the defilements, which cause renewed existence, which are accompanied by affliction, which ripen as suffering, and which lead to future birth, aging, and death — that is called the monk by reason of having subdued the afflictions.

In the present context, since one who has received full ordination through the act of the fourfold formal procedure with a motion is to be regarded as the monk who is intended, and since it is not fitting to leave aside an unshakable formal act established by a motion and three proclamations, therefore it is said again "any monk."

"A human being" means one who has obtained, within the mother's womb, these six faculties — the faculty of the eye, the faculty of the ear, the faculty of the nose, the faculty of the tongue, the faculty of the body, and the faculty of the mind.

"In the category of a human being" means one who has obtained, within the mother's womb, these three faculties — the faculty of the body, the faculty of feeling, and the faculty of the mind.

"Intentionally" means having deliberated.

"With his own hand" means with the hand, by hand.

"Takes life" means that the life of that being has been severed.

"Or provides him with a weapon" means a sword, a knife, or a water-blade.

"Or seeks to obtain a weapon-bearer for him" means a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex.

"Or causes him to die" — causing to die is of three kinds: one who has broken his moral discipline, one who possesses moral discipline, and one who is sick.

How is it in the case of one who has broken moral discipline? In this way: when a monk who has broken his moral discipline has obtained some leftover item — be it an alms bowl, a monastic robe, a strainer, a small cup, a belt, or any article whatsoever that belongs to the life of a renunciant — he thinks to himself: "For as long as this venerable one remains alive, I will not be able to obtain it; I will go to him and cause him to die." And he goes to that one and speaks thus: "Venerable one, you have broken your moral discipline, you are one of unwholesome qualities, you have engaged in misconduct in body, and you have engaged in misconduct in speech and mind. For as long as you continue to live, demerit will grow ever more abundant; and if demerit grows ever more abundant, you will be reborn for a long time in the hell realms." When he has spoken thus, that one who has broken moral discipline says to that monk: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" The monk replies: "Come here, venerable one. Abandon yourself! Kill yourself! Allow yourself to be deprived of life!" If that one who has broken moral discipline then abandons himself, kills himself, or proceeds to deprive himself of life, that monk incurs defeat.

If that one who has broken moral discipline thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will not abandon myself. I will not kill myself. I will not proceed to deprive myself of life" — and if he does not abandon himself,

does not kill himself, and does not proceed to deprive himself of life — then that monk incurs a grave offense by reason of that very prior act of engagement.

If that monk, having spoken those words, comes to feel remorse and goes before the one who has broken moral discipline, saying: "Venerable one, be informed of this. It was I who, being childish, dull, unclear, and unskilled, spoke words of doubt and uncertainty — words spoken without careful discernment — to the effect that if the venerable one were to please some virtuous friend, then that one could be lifted from this impure conduct of body and established in pure conduct of body, and lifted from impure conduct of speech and mind and established in pure conduct of speech and mind. In that case, venerable one, since your conduct of body, speech, and mind would be perfectly pure, even when this body perishes you would be reborn in a happy destiny, in a high realm, among the gods" — and if, when that monk has spoken thus, the one who has broken moral discipline says to him: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" and the monk replies: "Venerable one, do not abandon yourself. Do not kill yourself. Do not proceed to deprive yourself of life" — then even though the one who has broken moral discipline does not abandon himself, does not kill himself, and does not proceed to deprive himself of life, that monk still incurs a grave offense by reason of that very prior act of engagement.

If the one who has broken moral discipline thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will abandon myself. I will kill myself. I will proceed to deprive myself of life" — and if he does abandon himself, does kill himself, and does proceed to deprive himself of life, that monk incurs a grave offense by reason of that very prior act of engagement. So much, then, for the case of the one who has broken moral discipline.

Now, how does this apply to one who maintains moral discipline? Suppose a monk who maintains moral discipline, having some small remainder of a begging bowl, a robe, a net, a cup, a sash, or any article of a contemplative's livelihood left to him, thinks: "As long as this venerable one is alive, I will not come to obtain it. I shall go before him and have him killed." He then goes before that person and says: "Venerable one maintains moral discipline, has virtuous qualities, is generous to a fault, delights in giving away possessions, is one who continually offers gifts, is magnificent in giving, and delights in making the gift of generosity. If the venerable one were to go to another region, harvests are good there and the high realms are as close as the span of a silk cloth, while liberation is obscured only by a veil — and even when this body perishes, one would be reborn among the gods." When the monk has spoken thus, and the one who maintains moral discipline asks: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" the monk replies: "Come here, venerable one. Abandon yourself! Kill yourself! Allow yourself to be deprived of life!" If the one who maintains moral discipline then abandons himself, kills himself, or proceeds to deprive himself of life, that monk incurs defeat.

If the one who maintains moral discipline thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will not abandon myself. I will not kill myself.

I will not proceed to deprive myself of life." If that one who maintains moral discipline does not abandon himself, does not kill himself, and does not proceed to deprive himself of life, then for that monk, by that very prior effort, a grave offense is incurred.

If that monk, having spoken thus, comes to feel remorse, and goes to the one who maintains moral discipline and speaks as follows: "Venerable one, know this: it was I who was childish, foolish, unclear, and unskilled — acting in haste and confusion, speaking without having examined the matter properly, saying this: 'Venerable one, you who maintain moral discipline are one of virtuous qualities, generous in giving freely, delighting in extending a helping hand, one who makes offerings regularly, excelling in generosity, and rejoicing in the act of giving — therefore, as long as the venerable one lives for a long time, merit will increase greatly, and when merit increases greatly, one will long rejoice in the higher realms.' " When the monk has spoken thus, and the one who maintains moral discipline asks him: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" and the monk says: "Venerable one, do not abandon yourself! Do not kill yourself! Do not proceed to deprive yourself of life!" — then, even if that one who maintains moral discipline does not abandon himself, does not kill himself, and does not proceed to deprive himself of life, for that monk, by that very prior effort, a grave offense is incurred.

If the one who maintains moral discipline thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will abandon myself. I will kill myself. I will proceed to deprive myself of life" — and if that one then does abandon himself, does kill himself, or does proceed to deprive himself of life, then for that monk, by that very prior effort, a grave offense is incurred. Such is the case with regard to the one who maintains moral discipline.

As for the case of a sick person: a monk, when a sick person lacks a begging bowl, or a robe, or a net, or a cup, or a belt, or any remaining requisite for the livelihood of a contemplative, thinks to himself: "This venerable one who is ill, suffering, and gravely sick — for as long as he lives, he will not give these to me. Let me go to him and have him die." Having thought this, he goes to that person and says: "Venerable one, you are ill, suffering, and gravely sick. As long as the venerable one lives for a long time, feelings of pain — unbearable, harsh, burning, and disagreeable — will be experienced." When the monk has said this and the sick person asks: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" the monk replies: "Come here, venerable one. Abandon yourself! Kill yourself! Allow yourself to be deprived of life!" If that sick person then abandons himself, kills himself, or proceeds to deprive himself of life, that monk incurs defeat.

If that sick person thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will not abandon myself. I will not kill myself. I will not proceed to deprive myself of life." If that one does not abandon himself, does not kill himself,

does not proceed to deprive himself of life — that monk, through that very prior effort, incurs a grave offence.

If that monk, having spoken as described, then feels remorse and goes to that sick person, saying: "Venerable one, know this: it was I who was childish, foolish, unclear in mind, unskilled — I who spoke words without examination, following a confused tangle of thoughts and hasty conclusions. In this way, if the venerable one would please some good spiritual friend, he could attend upon you with medicines that are suitable and beneficial, with appropriate foods and diets, and with nursing care befitting your illness; and thus, before long, the venerable one will come to be at ease, free of illness, possessed of strength, and able to go wherever he pleases." When the monk has said this, and if that sick person then says to the monk: "Venerable one, then what am I to do?" — and the monk replies: "Venerable one, do not abandon yourself! Do not kill yourself! Do not proceed to deprive yourself of life!" — then even if that sick person does not abandon himself, does not kill himself, and does not proceed to deprive himself of life, that monk, through that very prior effort, incurs a grave offence.

If that sick person thinks: "That is indeed so" — yet nevertheless says: "I will abandon myself. I will kill myself. I will proceed to deprive myself of life" — and if he does abandon himself, does kill himself, and does proceed to deprive himself of life — that monk, through that very prior effort, incurs a grave offence. As for the sick person, that is simply how it is with him. It is for this reason that the phrase "caused him to die" is spoken.

Now regarding the phrase "or spoke praise of death in his presence": this means that praise of death is spoken before one who delights in dying. As for the phrase "O man" — this is an address, a respectful vocative. The words "What use is this wretched, defiled, miserable life? O man, it is better for you dead than alive" — these are words of disparagement, the commentary says, meaning they are uttered as reproach. The phrase "with the intention of the mind and the deliberate thought of the mind" means with the mind's manifest desire and the mind's conceptual determination. The phrase "in many ways" means in numerous modes. The mention of "caused him to die, or spoke praise of death before him" is stated in order to reverse the speaking of praise of death — in multiple modes — before one who delights in dying. The phrase "if that one then dies" means that it is through that monk himself alone, and not through another. The phrase "a monk" means whoever possesses the substance of a monk. What is the substance of a monk? It is full ordination. What is full ordination? It is the petition, the performance of the fourfold act of the community, the initial examination, the thorough examination, the completion, and the thorough completion; and that person's acceptance, explicit acceptance, non-reversal, the state of non-reversal, together with the speech, the words, the conventional expression, the utterance, the declaration, the definitive statement, the path of speech, the sound of speech, the act of voice, and the communicative expression of voice. The phrase "that" is an expression of direct and comprehensive indication. The phrase "has incurred defeat" means that one has reached the end, has fallen, has descended, stands at the last, is cut off, and is at variance with the mind.

Furthermore, whoever commits that transgression, immediately upon doing so they become unfit to be a monk, unfit to be a contemplative, unfit to be a son of the Śākyas. They fall away from the substance of monkhood; their manner of being a contemplative is destroyed — diminished, broken, fallen, and defeated — and that manner of being a contemplative cannot be recovered. It is just as when the crown of a palm tree is cut off: it cannot turn green again, cannot grow, flourish, or spread. Likewise, when a monk does such a thing, immediately upon doing so they become unfit to be a monk, unfit to be a contemplative, unfit to be a son of the Śākyas. They fall away from the substance of monkhood; their manner of being a contemplative is destroyed — diminished, broken, fallen, and defeated — and that manner of being a contemplative cannot be recovered. And for this reason it has been declared: "he has incurred defeat; he is not to remain."

The phrase "is not to remain" means that monks are not to carry out with such a person the restoration ceremony (poṣadha), the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā), a formal act with one motion, a formal act with two motions, or a formal act with four motions. He is not to be appointed to any of the twelve categories of persons. Therefore it has been declared: "is not to remain."

Here ends the Vinaya Analysis, the tenth fascicle.

Now, how does one incur a transgression in this matter? In summary:

By one's own taking hold,
by being cast outward,
and by what bears both together —
these constitute the complete set of categories.

How is it by one's own taking hold? When a monk, with murderous intent toward a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time," and then presses with a single finger, and that agent does indeed bring about the death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. Even if it does not happen at that time but does happen afterward as a result of what was done, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone.

Just as with a single finger — when one thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" — so too if one presses with two fingers, three, four, or five, with a fist, with an elbow, with a shoulder, with the head, with the chest, with the hip, with the thigh, with the knee, with the heel, with the ankle bone, with the sole of the foot, or even pressing with the big toe of the foot, and that agent does indeed bring about the death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. Even if it does not happen at that time but does happen afterward as a result, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone. Thus it is by one's own taking hold.

How is it by being cast outward? When a monk, with murderous intent toward a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time," and then hurls an arrow, and that agent does indeed bring about the death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. Even if it does not happen at that time but does happen afterward as a result, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone.

Just as with an arrow — when one thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" — so too if one uses an iron arrow, a half-arrow made of iron, a javelin tip, something like a saw-tooth blade, a four-cornered blade, a blade like a karavīra leaf, a blade like a bird's beak, a discus, a single-pointed vajra, a great arrow, or a single-pointed weapon,

even if one pierces with a seed of the Chinese juniper — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward as a result, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone — and so it is in the case of what is thrown outward.

How is it that both apply together? If a monk, with intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" and pierces with a sword — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone.

Just as with a sword, so too if one thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" and pierces with a lance, or a single-edged sword, or a double-edged sword, or a spear, or a short spear, or a throwing spear, or a notched blade, or a fire-iron, or even a grass arrow — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone. And so it is in the case where both apply together.

Summary verse: Preparation by poison and by powder; binding to the earth and to a tree; causing intoxication and causing fright; mechanical devices and hunting methods.

If a monk, with intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" — namely, by preparing a poison compound to be placed in food, to be eaten, to be licked, to be chewed, or to be drunk — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone.

If a monk, with intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" and prepares a poison-powder compound to be used in rinsing the mouth, or for bathing, or for rubbing, or in a garland, or a scent, or an unguent, or as incense smoke — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, then the monk incurs a grave offense by virtue of that prior act of engagement alone.

Binding is of two kinds: binding to the earth, and binding to a tree.

If a monk, with intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "May this agent, by this means, bring about that one's death at this time" — whether so that they may be devoured by lions, or tigers, or leopards, or wolves, or jackals; or so that they may be utterly dried out, utterly consumed, or utterly crushed by wind and sun; or so that, oppressed by the feebleness of hunger and thirst, they may die — and with that thought binds them to the earth and then inserts a stake up to its cross-piece — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat.

If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement. And just as with binding up to the cross-piece, so too: with the thought "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — whether so that they may be devoured by lions, or tigers, or leopards, or wolves, or jackals; or so that they may be utterly dried out, utterly consumed, or utterly crushed by wind and sun; or so that, oppressed by the feebleness of hunger and thirst, they may die — and with that thought inserts a stake up to the shoulder, or up to the thigh, or up to the waist, or up to the chest, or up to the throat — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement.

If a monk, with the intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — whether so that they may be devoured by lions, or tigers, or leopards, or wolves, or jackals; or so that they may be utterly dried out, utterly consumed, or utterly crushed by wind and sun; or so that, oppressed by the feebleness of hunger and thirst, they may die — and with that thought binds them to a tree, sets them there, and then binds them with wet rope to a pillar or a firm stake up to the cross-piece — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement.

And just as with binding up to the cross-piece, so too: with the thought "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — whether so that they may be devoured by lions, or tigers, or leopards, or wolves, or jackals; or so that they may be utterly dried out, utterly consumed, or utterly crushed by wind and sun; or so that, oppressed by the feebleness of hunger and thirst, they may die — and with that thought inserts a stake up to the shoulder, or up to the thigh, or up to the waist, or up to the chest, or up to the throat — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement.

If a monk, with the intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinks "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — whether so that they may be devoured by lions, or tigers, or leopards, or wolves, or jackals; or so that they may be utterly dried out, utterly consumed, or utterly crushed by wind and sun; or so that, oppressed by the feebleness of hunger and thirst, they may die — and with that thought causes them to be made intoxicated with liquor — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement.

And just as with liquor, so too: with the thought "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — whether by a king, or a minister, or thieves, or deceitful persons, or ransom-seekers, or enemies —

— or with the thought "may the enemies on the opposing side bring about death at this time" — whether through prepared liquor or grain-based liquor, whether prepared liquor or a drink made from roots, a drink made from stems, a drink made from leaves, a drink made from flowers, or a drink made from fruit, causing that person to become intoxicated; or through secret mantras, or medicines, or incantations, causing mental disturbance or inducing sleep — and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement.

If a monk, with the intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, engages in an undertaking with the thought "by this agent thus commencing, may this one's death be brought about at this time" — striking the chest — and with the thought "may whatever hand, or foot, or face, or limb, or secondary limb of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex who comes there be cut off," or "may that person in every respect be deprived of life" — and accordingly provides that person with a sword, or a knife, or a razor: if that agent then cuts off whatever hand, or foot, or face, or limb, or secondary limb, or in every respect deprives that person of life, and if that very agent, having so commenced, brings about death at that time, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time but happens afterward, the monk incurs defeat. If it does not happen at that time and does not happen afterward either, the monk incurs a grave offense through that very prior engagement. The same is to be said regarding mechanical devices and hunting implements.

Summary verse:

A zombie, and half a zombie,
pressing the side, and cutting off life,
a precipice, water, and fire,
an emissary, and cold and heat.

A monk, with the intent to kill a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, goes to a charnel ground on the fourteenth day of the waning fortnight of the month, and there seeks out a fresh corpse not yet damaged or decomposed — one not so much as disturbed by tiny insects — and having found one, rolls it up with white clay and works it over, and having done so, washes it with fragrant water, and having washed it with fragrant water, puts on it a garment of white cloth, and binds its two feet together with thread, and recites secret mantras — and it rises up and begins to stagger about. At that point, the monk places it on a chariot with two wheels, and hangs two bells at its neck, and gives into its hands a double-edged sword, and it rises up, lurching and clattering, and says: "Whom shall I let go? Whom shall I kill? Whom shall I deprive of life?" At that point, if the monk says to the zombie: "Do you know of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex?" and when it says "I know," the monk then says: "Release that one. Slay that one. Deprive that one of life." And if the zombie then releases, or slays, or deprives that person of life, the monk incurs defeat.

If, however, something acts as a protection at that moment — such as a garland of black wood hung at the door, or a full vase set in place, or a tethered cow and calf, or a tethered sheep, or a scattering of mustard seed set out, or a wheel inscribed at the threshold, or a fire lit there, or a Victor (a buddha image) placed there, or a Victor's teaching proclaimed there, or a wheel-turning king,

or a wheel-turning king present in the womb of a wheel-turning king's mother, or a bodhisattva present in the womb of a bodhisattva's mother, or someone reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra who has not yet recited it before, or someone chanting it at length with melodious voice when it has already been recited, or someone reciting any one of the four divisions of the sūtra collections when it has not previously been recited, or someone chanting it at length with melodious voice when it has already been recited, or one of these great and mighty great sūtras being recited or chanted — namely: the Lesser Emptiness, the Greater Emptiness, the Fifty-Three, the Net of Illusion, the Reception by the Embodied Essence, the Sacred Victory Banner, the All-Pervading, the Non-Pervading, the Harmonious Sūtra, and the Sūtra of the Great Assembly — then, because it amounts to releasing the zombie, the zombie will form the intention to kill the monk himself. If the zombie then kills the monk, the monk incurs a grave offence. If the monk kills the zombie, the monk incurs two grave offences: one arising from having killed the zombie, and the second from that very prior act of preparation.

What applies to a full zombie applies equally to a half-zombie, and yet there is this distinction between a full zombie and a half-zombie: placing it on a cart that has a single wheel, hanging a single bell around its neck, or giving it into its hand a sword with a single edge — this is called a half-zombie. The analysis of the transgressions is to be stated in every respect as before.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a woman, strikes a pregnant woman's belly thinking "I will kill the woman but not the one dwelling in the womb," and if the woman dies but the one dwelling in the womb does not die, the monk incurs defeat. If the one dwelling in the womb dies but the woman does not die, the monk incurs a grave offence arising from that very prior act of preparation. If both die, the monk incurs defeat. If neither dies, the monk incurs a grave offence arising from that very prior act of preparation.

If a monk, with the intention of killing the one dwelling in the womb, strikes a pregnant woman's belly thinking "I will kill the one in the womb but not the woman," and if the one dwelling in the womb dies but the woman does not die, the monk incurs defeat. If the woman dies but the one dwelling in the womb does not die, the monk incurs a grave offence arising from that very prior act of preparation. If both die, the monk incurs defeat. If neither dies, the monk incurs a grave offence arising from that very prior act of preparation.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, causes someone to rise from a seat, has them don a lower robe, has them walk, draws a maṇḍala, lights a fire, inserts fuel-sticks for burning, recites secret mantras, and thinks "May these fuel-sticks for burning be consumed, and may the life of some man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex be extinguished" — then, if those fuel-sticks burn yet the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is not extinguished, the monk incurs a grave offence. If those fuel-sticks burn and the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is thereby extinguished, the monk incurs defeat.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, causes someone to rise from a seat, has them don a lower robe, has them walk, pours a small measure of sesame or a small measure of white mustard into a mortar and strikes it with the tip of the pestle,

recites a secret mantra, thinking, "May these grains also become mixed, and may the life of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex be thereby extinguished" — then, if those grains become mixed but the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is not thereby extinguished, the monk incurs a grave offence. If those grains become mixed and the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is thereby extinguished, the monk incurs defeat.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, causes someone to rise from a seat, has them don a lower robe, has them walk, pours a small measure of milk or a small measure of yoghurt into a vessel and stirs it with a finger, recites a secret mantra, thinking, "May this too become blood, and may the life of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex be thereby extinguished" — then, if that liquid becomes blood but the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is not thereby extinguished, the monk incurs a grave offence. If that liquid becomes blood and the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is thereby extinguished, the monk incurs defeat.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, threads a needle with a five-coloured thread and sews a patch, recites a secret mantra, thinking, "May this patch also be sewn through, and may the life of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex be thereby extinguished" — then, if that patch is sewn through but the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is not thereby extinguished, the monk incurs a grave offence. If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, draws seven lines on the ground, recites a secret mantra, thinking, "May these lines also be crossed, and may the life of some man, or woman, or person of indeterminate sex be thereby extinguished" — then, if those lines are crossed but the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is not thereby extinguished, the monk incurs a grave offence. If those lines are crossed and the life of that man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex is thereby extinguished, the monk incurs defeat.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinking, "May this one, by means of such-and-such an action, meet their end at such-and-such a time," causes them to be thrown from a precipice — and if that person does indeed meet their end through that action, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

Similarly with regard to a precipice: if a monk, thinking, "May this one, by means of such-and-such an action, meet their end at such-and-such a time," causes them to fall to the ground from a mansion, or from a wall, or from the back of an elephant, or from the back of a horse, or from a coiled rope, or from a throne, or from a small seat, or from the shoulder, or from the chest, or from the hip, or from the thigh, or from the knee, or from the shin, or even from the ankle — and if that person does indeed meet their end through that action, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex,

a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, causes that person to be submerged in water, thinking, "By this act of engagement may this one meet their end," and if that person does indeed meet their end through that act of engagement, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, causes that person to be cast into fire, thinking, "By this act of engagement may this one meet their end," and if that person does indeed meet their end through that act of engagement, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

Just as it is with fire, so too, thinking, "By this act of engagement may this one meet their end," if a monk sets fire to a city, or sets fire to a village, or sets fire to a district, or to a royal palace, or causes that person to be driven into such a conflagration — or even causes only a spark to be introduced — and if that person does indeed meet their end through that act of engagement, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinking, "By this act of engagement may this one meet their end — whether devoured by lions, or by tigers, or by leopards, or by bears, or by wolves, or wasted away, utterly consumed, or utterly destroyed by sun and wind, or brought to their end through the debilitation of hunger and thirst" — sends that person off toward a place of danger, and if that person does indeed meet their end through that act of engagement, the monk incurs defeat. If that person does not meet their end at that time but dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs defeat. If that person neither meets their end at that time nor dies thereafter from that same cause, the monk incurs a grave offence by reason of that prior act of engagement alone.

If a monk, with the intention of killing a man, or a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex, thinking, "By this act of engagement may this one meet their end" — during those cold seasons and times of extreme cold, on the eighth-day intervals of those months when piercing winds arise that let no light through, causes that person to be held in the open above during the day and kept without shelter or covering through the night, and upon them repeatedly inflicts blows with a bundle of grass — and if that person does indeed meet their end through that act of engagement, the monk incurs defeat. Summary verse:

The warming house and the fire house,
the sunlit place and the second,
the protective enclosure — seventeen categories.
The cliff-dwellers and the aged are included.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in a pastoral region, in the finest forest of that pastoral place. There a certain monk who was an almsman used to go at regular, fitting times to the home of a certain householder, and would also give Dharma teachings there. In due course that monk established the householder in taking refuge and set him firmly in the bases of the training. Thereafter the monk again approached that householder and gave an extensive account in praise of the seven bases for the performance of merit arising from material goods. The householder said, "Noble one, I too would be pleased to perform some basis for merit arising from material goods for the Saṅgha." The almsman said, "Householder, do it well indeed! Noble one, what do you wish to do?" "Householder, the Saṅgha has no warming house — please let that be done." "Noble one, I do have kārṣāpaṇa coins, yet I have no assistant for merit." "Householder, I myself will be your assistant for merit." "Noble one, excellent!" That householder presented the almsman with kārṣāpaṇa coins, and the almsman set about having a warming house built for the Saṅgha.

Then, on a certain other occasion, a seasonal festival arose in that pastoral region, and the hired workers did not come. The almsman called to them and said, "Good friends, why have you not come today?" They said, "Noble one, today is a festival of the world, and for that reason we have not come." The almsman said, "Good friends — those who live by the fruit of merit, they have a festival; what sort of festival do you who live by the fruit of hired labor have? Come here and do your work, and for that reason I will give you double wages." They said, "Noble one, those who live by the fruit of merit always have their festival; but we live by the fruit of hired labor, and for that very reason a festival comes to us once in a hundred times — even if you were to give us triple wages, today we will not work." They refused and went away, and the almsman sat there feeling quite disheartened.

The householder thought, "How much of the virtuous giving that I intended to undertake has been accomplished, and how much has not?" and thinking thus, the next morning he rose early and went, and seeing that no work at all was being done he went to the almsman, prostrated at his feet, and said, "Noble one, are the hired workers not working today?" "Householder, they are not working."

"Why?" Because they said, "Today is a worldly festival, and so we will not work." The householder said, "Noble one, those workers live by the fruit of wage-labor, so if you do not pay them wages, noble one, it is no wonder that it did not succeed and nothing was accomplished." The almsman said, "Householder, even when I offered to double their wages it was not enough. They said, 'Those noble ones who live by the fruit of merit — for them every single day is a festival. But we live by the fruit of wage-labor, and for that very reason a festival comes to us once in a hundred times — even if you were to give us triple wages, today we will not work.'" The householder said, "Noble one, I do not do this for my own sake, nor for the sake of my relatives; I do it for the sake of the noble ones. Ah, would that the noble ones too might once in every hundred times keep an empty alms-bowl day!" The almsman then spoke to the monks about this matter, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "So long as no rule has been established, monks may keep an empty alms-bowl day."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks might keep an empty alms-bowl day so long as no rule had been established, the monks began to keep the empty alms-bowl day and proceeded to fling pot-scraping tools at one another. In the course of this, one monk flung a pot-scraper at another monk, it slipped from his hand and struck the other monk on the head, and the monk died on the spot. Those monks were stricken with remorse, and being ill at ease they said, "Venerable ones, because the almsman had nothing to do, and work has been abandoned, we have come to dislike our celibate practice, and we have fallen into remorse wondering whether a defeat downfall may not have occurred for us." At this the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "There is no downfall for you. Furthermore, monks should not fling pot-scrapers; rather they should pass them hand to hand. If something is sharp-edged or broken, one should give warning and then pass it. If one passes it without giving warning, it becomes a serious offense."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks should keep an empty alms-bowl day, the monks did their work in the early dawn, and brahmins and householders reproached them, mocked them, and criticized them, saying, "Why do these monks do their work in the early dawn like hired workers?" At this the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Do not work in the early dawn; do it once in this way instead." The monks then did their work in the afternoon in summer and in the morning in winter, whereupon the Blessed One declared, "Do it in the morning in summer and in the afternoon in winter."

When they reached the end of their allotted time and then went out on alms-rounds with bodies smeared with mud and filth, the non-believers would jeer at them saying, "Noble ones, you have even surpassed the hired workers — those workers abandon the meal-time altogether, yet you do not even abandon the meal-time!" At this the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Those who are on alms-rounds should, having prepared in advance, enter the village for alms at a suitable time, and

those who manage the Saṅgha's requisites should, having prepared in advance, send the monks off into the midst of the Saṅgha at a suitable time, knowing the right moment to do so."

Having declared that one should enter the village for alms after preparing in advance, and should likewise enter into the midst of the Saṅgha, the monks did not know how much preparation was to be considered sufficient. The Blessed One then declared, "The amount of preparation that is sufficient is just this: having washed both hands, both feet, and the alms bowl."

"Furthermore, I shall set out the rules of conduct for monks who do carrying work. A monk who does carrying work should, at the appropriate time of day, have boys employed for the morning shift. In the afternoon, those employed should be for carrying water and for massaging the hands and feet.
