If a monk who does carrying work does not properly take up and perform the rules of conduct as they have been prescribed, he shall incur an offense. As for the case of alms-gatherers in a pastoral area being made to build a warming hut, that full account is to be given in exactly the same way as the case of the fire house. There is, however, this distinction: after the Blessed One had declared that a monk should carry the empty frame before the ground has been leveled, the monks were doing the work on the fire house while moving the planks back and forth, and a carpenter was underneath them. While the planks were being moved, a plank slipped from a monk's hands and struck the carpenter on the head, killing him on the spot. Thereupon those monks, thinking with remorse that since they had dismissed the monk-workers from the alms-round, a defeat transgression might have come upon them, reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, 'Monks, you have incurred no transgression. Yet monks should not lift a load that is beyond their strength. If such a circumstance arises, lay people should in brief be engaged to help with lifting, and what is to be lifted and what is to be set down should be stated, so that lifting and setting down are done together. If monks lift a load beyond their strength, they incur an offense.'"

After the Blessed One had declared that monks should not lift loads beyond their strength, the monks did not know how much was within their strength and how much was beyond it. The Blessed One then declared, "Whatever is the load of one layman, that load should be carried by two monks."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Śārika subdued a wild woman and she took refuge and undertook the bases of training, she prostrated at the feet of the venerable Śārika and offered him all her possessions, and the venerable Śārika accepted them and said, "Sister, the teaching of the Blessed One has entered into taking care of others with benefit; therefore I too must bring benefit to others." The wild woman said, "Noble one, if that is indeed so and you are not unwilling, I have arranged a sage's seat for the noble one; it would be fitting for you to enjoy the sage's seat after going on alms-rounds and then depart." The venerable Śārika said, "Sister, let it be so." And so each day the venerable Śārika would go on alms-rounds, then enjoy the sage's seat at the wild woman's home, and depart.

Some time later an occasion arose for the venerable Śārika to go on a tour of the region, and the venerable Śārika thought, "I shall go and visit my sister." So the venerable Śārika went to the wild woman's home and said, "Sister, I am going on a regional tour. Please take care of your Dharma-body." The wild woman said, "Noble one, it would be fitting to return quickly. Please do not stay there long or take delight in it." The venerable Śārika looked after the wild woman and departed on his regional tour. Then the venerable Ānanda said to the monks, "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is going on a regional tour; whoever among you wishes to go on tour together with the Blessed One should prepare your robes and bowl."

When the venerable Śārika heard this, he thought, "Travelling as a buddha has eighteen benefits: freedom from the fear of kings, freedom from the fear of thieves, freedom from the fear of fire, freedom from the fear of humans, freedom from the fear of non-human beings, freedom from the fear of nāgas, freedom from the fear of the vicious, freedom from the fear of lions, freedom from the fear of tigers, freedom from the fear of bears, freedom from the fear of enemy armies, freedom from the fear of wolves, freedom from the fear of scorpions, freedom from the fear of foxes, freedom from the fear of crocodiles; from time to time one sees divine forms and hears divine sounds, one hears the speech of omniscient ones, and one partakes of Dharma-enjoyment and material enjoyment, and harm is rare when travelling as a buddha. Therefore I too shall turn back in order to go on tour together with the Blessed One." And so the venerable Śārika turned back.

In the meantime, a young woman in the wild woman's household had given birth to a baby boy, and the wild woman said to the boy's mother, "Daughter, wash this baby, wrap him in white cloth, and lay him on this sage's seat; he will live long and grow up with a long life." The young woman washed the baby, wrapped him in white cloth, and regularly laid him on that sage's seat.

Then on another day the venerable Śārika went on alms-rounds and came to the place of the wild woman's home. Now, arhats do not apply knowledge or perception without prior reflection; so the venerable Śārika sat down on that sage's seat in the usual way. As he was examining the scene around him, there came cries of "Noble one! Noble one! The baby!" — and the venerable Śārika quickly rose and looked, and saw that the baby had passed his time. The household members began to wail, and the venerable Śārika said, "Sister, do not weep. This sentient being has performed the karma that leads to a short life; and the Blessed One himself has declared, 'All formations are impermanent.' Nevertheless, it falls to me to wail here, for although I myself have attained arhathood, because of me the Blessed One will establish a training rule in the Vinaya by which the hearers shall abide."

He then reported the occasion to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, the monk Śārika has committed no transgression. Nevertheless, a monk must not sit down on a seat in another's home without examining it first. If he does so, it will constitute an offense of wrong conduct."

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a wealthy householder of great possessions and large estate — a companion in conversation, one spoken of with welcome, a friend and associate — and they were a pair joined in close mutual affection.

In time it came to pass that the two of them lost their wealth and their possessions were exhausted. They began to take counsel together: "We two have fallen into poverty and ruin right here. What is the use of living on and enjoying life in such a condition as this? Let us go forth into renunciation." And so the two of them went forth into renunciation in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya.

Then at a certain point one of them fell ill, and the other took to nursing him. The sick monk's condition was grave and he did not recover. The nurse-monk said to the sick monk, "Venerable one, when you were a householder in former times, did an illness such as this occur on more than one occasion?" "It occurred before as well." "Then what brought it to remission?" "A salt-medicine preparation." "Then why are you not drinking a salt-medicine preparation?" The nurse-monk prepared a salt-medicine preparation and administered it to the sick monk. The sick monk then met with the phenomenon of his time — that is, he died — and the monk who had nursed him was stricken with remorse, thinking, "Might it be that I gave him something that was not medicine?" He reported the matter to the other monks at that time, the monks brought it before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that monk has committed no transgression. Nevertheless, a monk must not administer medicine to a sick person on his own judgment without first consulting a physician. If no physician is available, he should consult an ordained physician. If there is no ordained physician, he should consult one trained by a physician. If there is no one trained by a physician, he should consult those who have themselves been afflicted by illness. If there is no one who has been afflicted by illness, he should consult the senior monks, the elders. If a monk administers medicine to a sick person on his own judgment, without consulting a physician or following the prescribed order of inquiry as taught, it will constitute a serious offense."

The monks were troubled by doubt, and in order to resolve all their doubts they addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, what was the cause, what was the condition, by which what was medicine for that monk became non-medicine?" The Blessed One declared: "In former times when he was a householder, his disorder was one of wind and phlegm; but now it has become one of wind and bile. Therefore what was medicine for him then has now become non-medicine for him."

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the Blessed One had set out the Truths before the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, together with eighty thousand gods and many hundreds and thousands of the brahmaṇas and householders of Magadha, at that time the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, had a proclamation sounded by drum throughout Rājagṛha, declaring: "Let the wise assemblies of merchants dwelling in Rājagṛha, those who circulate within the palace precincts, and those who have come from various regions, hear this: no one shall commit robbery in my territory. Whoever commits robbery in my territory, I shall expel him from the territory. As for whatever stolen goods belong to those who have been robbed, I will give restitution from my treasury and storerooms."

Then at the time when the Blessed One had tamed the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, by means of the sūtra of the simile of the youth, the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, likewise had a proclamation sounded by drum throughout Śrāvastī, declaring: "Let the wise assemblies of merchants dwelling in Śrāvastī, those who circulate within the palace precincts, and those who have come from various regions, hear this: no one shall commit robbery in my territory. Whoever commits robbery in my territory, I shall have him bound over to the capital case of death. As for whatever stolen goods belong to those who have been robbed, I will give restitution from my treasury and storerooms."

Now at that time, those robbers who dwelt in the territory of Magadha and

those robbers who dwelt in the territory of Kosala went as far as the border and encamped there. And the rumor spread everywhere that the robbers dwelling in the territory of Magadha and the robbers dwelling in the territory of Kosala had gone as far as the border, encamped there, and were about to join forces and make common cause.

Hearing this, those from Magadha, with their confederates dispersed, set out toward the territory of Kosala, while those from Kosala, with their confederates dispersed, set out toward the territory of Magadha. Then at a later time, the confederates from Magadha advanced into Kosala, and when they crossed the border and entered the territory of Kosala, the caravan leader spoke: "Friends, this King Prasenajit of Kosala is known to be fierce, ruthless, greatly savage, brave, and powerful. Even if our confederate robbers are defeated, he would still be able to give us the stolen goods. So release the confederates." The confederates replied, "Leader, if that is so, then we will do as you say," and they released the confederates.

Now the robbers had set out their decoy horses and encamped, and when the decoy horses saw the confederates being released, the robbers said: "Friends, the confederates have turned back. Let us go and break the alliance and destroy them." So they attacked the alliance as it entered the Śāla grove.

There some of the merchants were slain, and some fled. Those who fled came with dust-covered heads to King Prasenajit of Kosala and said: "Sire, we merchants have been declared unfit to trade in your territory. What happened? Sire, we were attacked by robbers."

The king commanded his military officer Āryajanman: "Young man, go at once and bring back those robbers and the stolen goods quickly." The military officer Āryajanman, obeying the command of King Prasenajit of Kosala, saying "As the king commands," armored the fourfold military force — the host of elephants, the host of cavalry, the host of chariots, and the host of infantry — and went swiftly and quickly to the Śāla grove. Meanwhile, the robbers had entered into the very dense heart of the Śāla grove, relaxed their guard, and were dividing the stolen goods. Āryajanman fell upon them, and there some of the robbers were slain, some fled, and sixty robbers were taken alive.

Then, victorious in battle, he took the robbers and the stolen goods and went to King Prasenajit of Kosala, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Sire, here are the robbers; here are the stolen goods."

The king said to the robbers: "Friends, did you not hear me have this proclamation sounded by drum: that no one shall commit robbery in my territory; that whoever commits robbery in my territory I shall bind over to the capital case of death; and that the stolen goods belonging to those who have been robbed I will give restitution from my treasury and storerooms?"

"Sire, we heard."

"Then why did you attack these merchants?"

"Sire, we had no livelihood."

"But even so, why did you slay others?"

"Sire, it was to inspire fear."

"I too will now inspire in you such fear as no one has ever inspired in you before."

The king, in his fury, commanded his ministers: "Friends, take these criminals to their place of execution today and cut off their hands and feet."

"Give back whatever was stolen from these merchants out of my treasury and storerooms." The ministers led those robbers to the charnel ground, cut off their hands and feet, and gave the merchants their stolen goods from the royal treasury and storerooms.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, again and again examine carefully your own ruin and the ruin of others. Again and again examine carefully your own prosperity and the prosperity of others. And why? Because both one's own ruin and the ruin of others are grounds for disenchantment, and because both one's own prosperity and the prosperity of others are likewise grounds for disenchantment."

Having so declared, the monks rose up again and again and set out to wander through the charnel ground. The nuns too rose up again and again and set out to wander through the charnel ground. At that time a great many people went wandering through the charnel ground, and they began to examine the robbers one by one. And then a certain other person who had been sitting there watching them said: "If someone who wished to do good were to pour a salt-water medicinal decoction into these people, when they die and pass from this place they would go on to drink the milk of young mothers."

Among those nuns there was one nun named Skyongma — a stout, foolish, dim-witted creature — who heard this and thought to herself: "If I am going to be wholly spent from a stock of merit such as this, then what do I gain by having gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya? Let me go and fetch salt-water medicinal decoction and pour it into these people." So nun Skyongma stepped out from among the nuns, went to her lodgings, gathered up a bag of salt-water medicinal decoction and sixty bowls, and went to where the robbers were. The robbers, tormented by painful sensations and heedless of their lives, were burning with thirst, and they thought: "Oh! If this noble woman were to pour water from that vessel to quench our thirst, how fitting that would be!" Skyongma, with a perception of merit, gave each one a bowl and let them drink the salt-water medicinal decoction; and whoever drank it died at that very moment, and thus all of them died at the right time. While Skyongma was administering the salt-water medicinal decoction to the robbers it became night, and when she arrived at the bolted door of the nuns' summer residence, Skyongma came and knocked at the door gently, tap by tap. The nuns asked: "Who is it knocking at the door?" Skyongma said: "It is I, Skyongma." "You — where have you come from at this hour of the night?" "Sisters, rejoice! Rejoice! Have you yourself realized arhatship, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of stream-entry? Or have you had a Dharma hall built for the Saṅgha?" "No, sisters, none of those." "Then have you provided cooked rice, or congee, or porridge, or a full bolt of cloth?" Skyongma said: "Sisters, is there really no work other than providing cooked rice, congee, porridge, and bolts of cloth? What else have you done?" "Have you seen those sixty robbers whose hands and feet were cut off?" "Yes, we have." "I fetched salt-water medicinal decoction, made them drink it, and when they drank it they died at the right time, and so they went on to drink the milk of young mothers." "You wretch! You, whose belly is destined to be filled by those who have lost their share — do you expect us to rejoice in that?"

Then she thought, "Has there perhaps come upon me a transgression amounting to a full defeat?" Remorse arose in her, and she immediately reported the matter to the monks. The monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "O monks, since that nun had both the perception and the intention, a defeat has occurred. Therefore, a monk or a nun must not administer medicine to a sick person with the intention that the sick person should die at the right time; one must administer medicine only with the intention that the sick person recover from illness. If a monk administers medicine to a sick person with the intention that the sick person should die at the right time, that constitutes a serious offence."

The awakened one, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At a certain time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had fully ordained and brought to complete ordination the group of seventeen young men born near Sārpaskṛta, beginners and youths. From that time onward, whenever any one member of the group of seventeen was assigned a duty, all of them would gather together and do it. So it was that one evening the same thing happened in that temple: a Dharma teaching was being given in the night, and all of them gathered together and made noise. The following day a warming house for the Saṅgha was arranged, and again all of them gathered together and made noise. The day after that, the duty of disciplinarian fell to one member of the group of seventeen, and on that day too all of them decorated the temple and stood assembled. Then when it came time for the disciplinarian to make the announcement, one thought arose in that member of the group of seventeen: "I alone will stay behind on account of exhaustion — why should the sixteen others be unable to make the announcement?" And in exactly the same way, the same thought arose in each of the others, so all sixteen went off separately to sleep. The disciplinarian alone, working from the night onward, at the break of dawn gathered up the lamp-vessels, opened the doors, swept the temple clean, applied plaster, arranged the time signal, spread out the seats, wafted incense around the area of the stūpa, then went up onto the roof of the temple and began to strike the gong. At the sound of the gong the sixteen awoke in their respective quarters, took their bowls, and came out. When they saw the disciplinarian running back and forth alone, they said to one another: "Venerable friends, while this one is running back and forth alone, did none of us among you help him?" One of them said: "The thought came to me: I will stay behind on account of exhaustion — why should the sixteen others be unable to make the announcement?" And in the same way the others said the same thing, and still others said the same thing, until all of them had said the very same words. Then the sixteen said: "Venerable friends, since this one is the first to go to all our immediate duties, our not having helped him was something we did badly, and he will reproach us for it. Let us eat our meal at once and then beg his pardon." So they ate, and then began to beg his pardon. The junior ones touched both his feet; the senior ones embraced him around the neck, saying "Venerable one, please grant forgiveness," but he sat there without saying a word. One of them who was his closest friend tickled him, and then he began to laugh and said "Forgiven!" The others thought, "That is a good method," and another also tickled him, and so on until all of them in turn had tickled him. At that, wind stirred upward in him and he died at the right time. They began to mourn for him with lamentation and grief,

The monks said, "Hey, you of the Group of Seventeen — why are you sitting there grieving and lamenting?" They replied, "We who were formerly the Group of Seventeen are now the Group of Sixteen. A beloved companion in the holy life has departed from us, and a defeat downfall has come about." The monks said "That is not good!" and left. Those sixteen then all departed together, and when other monks saw them sitting there absorbed in grief, those monks began to taunt them, saying, "These venerable ones of the Group of Seventeen flare up and die out in an instant, like a grass fire — one moment they are raucous and the next they are sitting there sunk in silence." But those sixteen, their hearts burned by the fire of grief, said nothing, and sat there even as the others mocked them. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no transgression for those monks. Yet a monk should not tickle. If he does, it is an offense entailing a penalty."

The Vinaya, Section Eleven.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. Not far from Śrāvastī there was a rocky cliff, and dwelling there was a householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and abundant means. He was a man of faith, of good character, and of wholesome intentions, and so he had a magnificent temple built for the Saṅgha — with lofty gabled roofs, with windows, with latticed windows, adorned with balustrades, a structure that could steal the heart and captivate the eyes, like a stairway to the heavens. Sixty monks spent the rains retreat in that temple, and when they had departed, the householder stationed a guard there, saying, "Let no one steal the seats or benches."

Now at another time sixty other monks were traveling on a journey through the region and came to that rocky cliff to seek lodging for the night. A man said to them, "Venerable ones, why do you not stay in the temple? There is a fine temple here." "Noble friend, where is it?" "Venerable ones, it is in this hermitage." So those monks went there, and when the guard saw them arrive he welcomed them with words of greeting, assigned them their quarters, and provided them with seats, small seats, cushions with inner padding, and similar furnishings. He swept and cleaned the place, and said to them, "Venerable ones, please wait a little while — I will go and inform the householder." He went to the householder and said, "Householder, rejoice! Sixty monks have arrived unexpectedly at your temple." The householder roused himself with zeal and said to his household people, "Good people, satisfy the Saṅgha of monks who have come to my temple with a well-prepared drink — with sugar, molasses, licorice, ginger, and the drink of Nepalese oranges." The householder prepared the well-prepared drink and went to the temple, and the monks, having washed, were seated each in their customary manner. The householder saw those monks from a great distance, and seeing the temple as though it were filled with lotus blossoms on a lake, moved by a surge of broad and deep faith, he spoke these verses:

Whether village or forest hermitage,
Whether valley or open plain,
Wherever noble ones abide and practice —
That ground itself becomes a place of joy.

Then, having prepared the well-prepared drink beforehand, he satisfied the community of monks with it from his own hands. He himself took up a small round vessel and, together with the community of monks, paid homage at the stūpa, then entered the temple and sat down to one side of the elders. The senior elder of the community gave the thanks-offering, and the householder prostrated at his feet and said, "Venerable ones, I request that tomorrow the noble Saṅgha accept noon refreshments at my home — whatever it pleases you to take." The monks accepted, and the householder prostrated at their feet and departed.

The next day, the householder satisfied the monks with an abundant meal, and at an off-hour also poured out drink for them; and the monks, in turn, taught the Dharma. Later, as before, the senior elder of the community again gave the thanks-offering. The householder sat to one side of the elders and spoke: "Noble ones, this temple was not built by me for my own sake, nor was it built for the sake of my relatives — it was built entirely for the sake of the noble ones. Therefore, please consent to observe the rains retreat here, and I shall ensure that the noble ones lack for none of their requisites."

The monks replied, "Householder, in Śrāvastī the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dharma, is himself present, and from time to time one hears news that a certain eminent monk has actualized arhatship, and a certain eminent monk has understood the interval up to the end of this unpleasant life. The king, too, has the very deepest faith in the teaching. There are also the garland-wearing queen, the royal-clan woman Varṣakula, the chaplain sage Jina, the elder Nyingpa, the laywoman Sāgā, the mother Mṛgadhāra, and many others who have faith — and through them great material provision and great Dharma provision alike will be obtained. We intend to go there."

The householder said, "Noble ones, Dharma provision depends on the noble ones themselves, while material provision depends on me. Therefore be pleased to stay, and not the slightest thing will be lacking." The senior elder of the community spoke: "Friends, the Blessed One has instructed that the faith of the faithful is to be increased and that the sponsor is to be treated with affectionate care. Therefore let us remain here." And so they resolved to remain there.

Then, with settled minds, they began to inspect that temple, both inside and outside, and they found it exceedingly delightful, adorned with abundant flowers and abundant fruit. The senior elder of the community spoke: "Friends, this temple is adorned with abundant flowers and abundant fruit and is exceedingly delightful. If we were to accept observing the earlier rains retreat here, we would not be able to enjoy all the flowers and fruits in full. Let us therefore definitely accept observing the later rains retreat." And so they accepted to observe the later rains retreat there.

The householder had only that single temple, and so everything he wished to give and to do he gave and did in that temple alone. As for that cliff face, since there was no other temple there either, whatever the cliff-dwellers wished to give and to do, they too gave and did in that very temple.

Since there was no other temple in the vicinity of that cliff face either, all those who lived near the cliff likewise gave and did in that very temple whatever they wished to give and to do. And so the monks who had accepted to observe the rains retreat there received abundant offerings.

When the invitation ceremony had just concluded at the end of the last month of autumn, those with sinister intentions gathered together and began to deliberate among themselves, saying: "What shall we do so that we may live in ease and plenty throughout the year without having to search for our needs?" And they conceived this thought: "We must destroy these renunciants, the sons of the Śākyas."

But others among them said: "Even if they were to recite a hundred times at a door without getting a full meal, it would be hard for them to fill their bellies. If they have nothing at all, why should we stay here this long?" Then one among them who knew something of monks' affairs said: "What do you know? Those monks have a great deal. For how could it be otherwise? The householder who owns this temple is a man of faith, good and virtuous in his intentions, and since this temple is his only one, everything he wishes to give and to do he gives and does in this temple alone. And since there is no other temple in this cliff area either, those who live on the cliff likewise give and do in this very temple whatever they wish to give and to do. And since there is no other temple in the vicinity of this cliff either, those who live near the cliff also give and do in this very temple whatever they wish to give and to do. That is why the monks who accepted to observe the rains retreat here have received abundant offerings. If you do not believe it, go and see for yourself — it will be evident to you with your own eyes."

"If that is so, you yourself go first and see with your own eyes, and we will come after." The other replied: "Excellent! Very well — I will go," and adjusting his robe, he paid homage to the stūpa with melodious verses from a noble tree, and entered that temple.

Just as he was entering the gatehouse, he found an elder monk sitting there. The man with sinister intentions bowed at the elder's feet and began to ask: "Noble one, this temple that steals the heart and dazzles the eyes, this stairway to the heavenly realms — who does it belong to?"

"Fair-faced one, it belongs to a great householder."

"Noble one, is this a proper temple, or is it a poor one?"

"Fair-faced one, what is a proper temple, and what is a poor one?"

"Noble one, where the furnishings are complete and well-appointed, that is a proper temple. Where the furnishings are absent, that is a poor one."

"Fair-faced one, then this is indeed a proper temple and not a poor one, for it has complete furnishings, and furnishings are not lacking here."

"Noble one, those who eat food never eat bare earth, and those who wear robes never wear tree-bark — so do you all happen to have any robes?"

Now the elder was of an upright and honest nature. He took the man with sinister intentions by the hand, led him inside a storeroom, and said: "Fair-faced one, look at these stacks of cloth and robes piled high."

"Noble one, are these yours, or do they belong to the Saṅgha?"

"Fair-faced one, these belong to me personally."

"Noble one, then you yourself are surely a senior elder of the Saṅgha, or perhaps a Dharma-teacher?"

"Fair-faced one, I am neither a senior elder of the Saṅgha nor a Dharma-teacher. Rather, I am a newly admitted member of the Saṅgha — a novice."

"Noble one, is there perhaps a little bedding here belonging to the Saṅgha?" "Fair-faced one, there is plenty. And for the time being, from my own painted storeroom you may also obtain those seven goods." "Noble one, please go then, and make this request: in this temple, is there anyone who does not do temple service? Now, are they cooking in earthenware vessels or in copper vessels?" "Fair-faced one, do you see these dwelling rooms?" "Noble one, I do." "Fair-faced one, these dwelling rooms are filled with copper vessels."

The man with sinister intentions thought: "I have now gathered good information — it is time to go." So the man with sinister intentions said: "Noble one, your side of virtue is entirely lost, and my own purpose has entirely miscarried, so I shall be going now." "Fair-faced one, be on your way then."

The man with sinister intentions paid homage at the feet of that elder and departed. He then went to those thieves and said: "Lotus-eyed ones, there is a great boat laden with all manner of goods moored on the bank — seize it! Seize it!" Then one among them said: "The sixty renunciants (pravrajyā) staying there are said to be masters of the throwing arts alone, so it will not be possible to overpower them in that way. When they gather at night to hear the Dharma, attack them then." Others said: "On what day does their Dharma hearing take place?" He replied: "On the eighth and the fourteenth, and since the eighth has already passed, it will take place on the fourteenth." They then counted the days on their fingers, and in due course the fourteenth arrived.

The elder of the Saṅgha recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra, the Saṅgha performed the restoration ceremony (poṣadha), and the Dharma-preacher ascended the lion throne and began to speak these words:

"The Tathāgata, foremost of men, steers the helm of discipline,
cuts the bonds of all entanglement — thus-gone.
Skilled in the pacification of the senses, in thorough calm,
residing in Śrāvastī, he acts in accordance with his word."

Just as he began to speak, the men with sinister intentions knocked at the gate. The monks, hearing this, said: "Wise ones, who are you?" "Noble ones, we are sons of good family." The monks thought: "Surely groups of people have come down from the rocky hills to hear the Dharma — it would not be right to break off. Open the gate." They opened the gate and those men entered. No sooner had they begun to attack than the monks said: "Wise ones! Did you not say you were sons of good family? And now you are attacking us?" They replied: "Noble ones, we have two names: outwardly we are called sons of good family; inwardly we are called thieves. You who name us thus are mistaken."

Those men with sinister intentions beat the monks and were done with it. The beaten monks then deliberated: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has said that the remainder should be donated — but what good does it do to have this householder give to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions? And what good has it done that he gave to us? If we go to Śrāvastī itself, those there who live the Brahma-like life will ensure that each of us is not wanting for Dharma robes." And so they resolved. As for how they would travel: they would travel by night under cover of darkness, and by day they would go in dense hiding. Without so much as a glance back at the householder, they departed. And in due course they arrived at last in Śrāvastī.

The monks who were keeping up their practice without sleeping at the first and last watches of the night — those monks saw these others wandering about, shivering, at the monastery gate in the dark, and said to them: "You naked wretches, what do you want here? This is not your monastery, and this is not your lodging." Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, we are not naked wretches." "Then who are you?" "We are monks." "Are the likes of you monks? What sort are those who have been stripped by robbers? What are your names?" "Buddharakṣita." "Dharmarakṣita." "Saṅgharakṣita." "Venerable ones, welcome! Welcome!" And with that, they opened the gate and let those monks in. To some of them they gave Dharma robes, to some they gave lower robes, to some they gave dust-cloaks, to some they gave alms bowls, and to some they gave water-strainers, and they made a full and proper distribution of everything. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not open the gate of the monastery at random to someone unknown. If someone wishes to enter at night, one should ask their name and which group they belong to, and if they are recognized, the gate should be opened, and if they are not recognized, the gate should not be opened. Furthermore, when the time comes for a Dharma-teaching, a monk on duty should be appointed as watchman. If robbers come, one should sound the gaṇḍī, sound the small gaṇḍī striker, sound the time-wheel, and raise a cry with the outer robe, the seven-cubit cloth, the five-cubit cloth, the coarse mat, the large gong, the small gong, the stick-bundle, and the small gong-clapper. Moreover, I shall set down rules for the elder of the community of monks to carry out universally. When the time for a Dharma-teaching has come, the monk on duty should ask the elder: 'Venerable one, have you had the monastery gate shut? Have you made a thorough inspection? Have you made a request of the Dharma-teacher? Have you had the toilet and urinal shelters cleared away?' If the elder of the community of monks, having thus received the rules I have set down for universal practice, does not properly take them up and apply them, he will be guilty of a serious offense."

Then the monks said to those monks who had been stripped by robbers: "Venerable ones, we have made a proper distribution to you, and yet you are still in want of Dharma robes. Now, the householder at whose monastery you were stripped — he is a man of faith, of good character, of wholesome intention. So today, if you go to his very monastery, he himself will see to it that you are not without Dharma robes." Those monks withdrew to one side and began to deliberate together among themselves: "Venerable ones, those who live the Brahma-like life here are indeed generous. Yet since we departed without so much as a glance back at that householder, if we now return to that very place, there is every chance he will make a proper distribution of Dharma robes to us." And so they turned back and went there again.

When the householder saw them, he said: "Noble ones, why did you depart without looking back at me?" The monks replied: "Householder, because the Blessed One said that the remainder should be donated, it occurred to us for a moment: what good is it that you gave to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and what good has it done that you gave to us? If we go to Śrāvastī, those there who live the Brahma-like life will see to it that we are not wanting for Dharma robes."

And so it was that they set off for Śrāvastī. The householder said: "Noble ones, if my temple has been broken into, do you think the goods belonging to me in the house have been destroyed as well? Noble ones, it is good that you have come — good indeed, for whatever reason you have come." And so that householder again, with great reverence and respect, made full provision for them and offered each and every monk a complete set of the thirteen requisites.

The thieves then returned and began beating on the door of the temple. When the monks heard this, they said: "Venerable ones, those wicked fellows have come back — sound the ghaṇṭā (the wooden sounding-board) to chase them off!" And so they began sounding an alarm with the ghaṇṭā's mallet, the time-wheel, the saṃghāṭī, the seven-cubit robe, the five-cubit robe, the carrying bag, the waistband, the under-robe, the bundle-strips, and the small under-sash. When the wicked ones were startled and began to flee, a deity spoke in verse:

Well has the Mighty One, foremost of bipeds, spoken —
the confession ceremony he set forth for the śrāvakas:
those who apply themselves to the confession with zeal are supreme.
The wicked ones who put on armor to go to battle beforehand —
these five hundred are not of that kind.

A monk who was knowledgeable about them said to the thieves: "Intelligent ones, why do you flee?" They replied: "You yourself say that the sixty who have gone forth and are staying here are masters of the throwing-spear alone — how could one not flee? Moreover, the names of such weapons as the ghaṇṭā and the rest — we had never heard them even once before." He said: "Those are not weapons." "Then what are they?" "First of all: what is called the ghaṇṭā — that is their drum. What is called the ghaṇṭā's mallet — that is what one strikes it with. What is called the time-wheel — that is what marks off the periods of time. The saṃghāṭī, the seven-cubit robe, and the five-cubit robe — these are the names of Dharma robes. What is called the carrying bag — that is what they are folded and placed in. The waistband, the under-robe, the bundle-strips, and the small under-sash — these are the names of girdles. So do not flee; go back and plunder it!" And having said that, they turned back.

When the thieves' commander set up a ladder and began to climb, there was an elderly monk who had been placed there as a night-watchman. He saw the thieves' commander climbing and thought: "These are the very wicked ones who robbed us of our bowls and Dharma robes and left us stranded. If I show equanimity toward them, they will rob us of our bowls and Dharma robes and strand us again — so I must frighten them." And so the elderly monk crept forward slowly and stealthily and hurled the ghaṇṭā at the head of the thieves' commander, crushing his skull. He was struck with a powerful blow and, beset by feelings of intense suffering, he fell with great difficulty and went off a little way — and the time of his death arrived. The elderly monk then raised the alarm, crying out "Thieves! Thieves!" and the monks, interrupting their Dharma listening, climbed up to the roof and said: "Where did those thieves go?" The elderly monk said: "They set up a ladder on this side and climbed, but I frightened them and they fled." The monks said: "If they have fled, that is good." They came down, and as the night was now turning to dawn, they began to do separate inspections of the rounds of the temple's perimeter.

When they separately inspected the place from which the thieves had climbed, they found blood. Following the trail of blood, they came upon the dead body of the captain of the thieves. Upon seeing this, they were seized with fear lest their training be broken, and they began to speak: "Venerable ones, we have already incurred a defeat — a root downfall has arisen for us through which we are defeated — and now that defeat stands." Remorse arose in them at that point, and they brought the matter before the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no downfall for you. However, a monk must not throw something at another person with such an intent as 'Let me strike this one at all costs' — rather, one should throw it to the side or behind, and should do a clapping-sound to cause alarm. If a monk throws with such a mind as 'Let me strike this one at all costs' and does strike, it becomes a serious offense."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had taken a wife from a family of equal standing, and he sported with her, delighted in her, and reveled with her. As he sported with her, delighted in her, and reveled with her, in the course of time his wife became pregnant with a sentient being. Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth a boy appeared. They raised him and nurtured him, and he grew to adulthood.

In the course of time the householder's relatives were exhausted and gone, and his wealth and possessions too were exhausted. His wife also reached her time and died. He spoke to his son: "My son, in the circumstances of my old age I am unable to go out to seek wealth, so I shall go forth into renunciation." The son said: "Father, if that is so, I too shall go forth." "Excellent, my son." So saying, he took the boy and went to the Jeta Grove, approached a monk, paid homage at his two feet, and said: "Noble one, I wish to go forth into renunciation." The monk asked: "Is this boy also going forth?" "Noble one, he is going forth." That monk, out of his fondness for the boy, ordained him along with the boy, receiving both into the going-forth.

By the nature of things, those in the senior class receive material offerings, and those in the junior class are assigned to duties. Since the boy was in the junior class he was constantly being assigned to duties, and he spoke to his father: "Father, whatever slight frustration has afflicted the two of us has come about from our lack of learning. Rise up, and let the two of us go to another region and acquire learning." The elder monk said: "Son, it is good — let us go." And the two of them set out for another region. However, since those of the junior class are precisely the ones assigned to duties, as soon as those two departed they were assigned to duties again. The son then said to the elder monk: "Father, though there are duties assigned to us in Śrāvastī, the Blessed One, the sovereign of the Dharma, dwells there in person, and from time to time one may hear of great monks who have directly actualized arhatship, and of others who have been told they have completed the path to the unlovely — one hears such proclamations given. The king too has very great faith in the teaching, and there are the queen Mṛgāramatā, the queen Kṣemā, the minister Prasenadeva-datta, and also Priyā and the laywoman Sāgā and the mother of Mṛgāra, and many others full of faith, so that there are great material enjoyments and great Dharma enjoyments to be had there. Let us go there," he said.

The two of them wandered at will through the countryside, and traveling in the direction of Śrāvastī they journeyed on and on until at last, making their way step by step, they arrived outside Śrāvastī. Just as they drew near to the Jeta Grove, a wooden signal board was struck, and the son said, "Father, they are striking the signal board at the temple — let us go quickly!" The elder was old and worn out, very weary and unable to walk, so he was moving along slowly when his son took him by the nape of the neck and pushed him forward, and the elder began to move quickly. The son thought to himself, "This is a good method — I should do it again." So the son pushed the elder in the same way once more, but this time the elder pitched forward and fell headlong to the ground, and his neck was broken by a wheel-rut in the road, and his time came. The son wept and cast the old man's body to one side of the road. He then took up the alms bowl and the robe and went to the Jeta Grove, and when the monks saw him they said, "Welcome, son of the elder! Welcome! Where is your elder?" At that the young novice began to weep. The monks asked, "Child, why do you weep?" The young novice said, "My elder has passed away." The monks said, "Child, such is the nature of all formations — be not sorrowful, for you have gone forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya." But the young novice said, "I killed him." The monks said, "Child, then you have committed an act without interval and a defeat downfall has arisen, and for a very long time you will dwell in the great Avīci hell — now indeed it is fitting to weep." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is no downfall for that monk. Moreover, monks, one who has entered the path must not be pushed when weary from the road. I shall establish rules of conduct for one who has entered the path: one who has entered the path and is weary from traveling should be allowed to rest. One may take the three robes, the alms bowl, the water strainer, the bowl vessel, and the articles of the needle case. One must be mindful of time: if one is able to go, then that is well; if one is not able to go, one should set out earlier — the alms bowl should be washed, the robe laid out, and the vessels given over for receiving and then inspected one by one. If, however, one is unable to come, food should be prepared and sent to meet one. If it is not the proper time, one should be received with drink. If one who has entered the path does not properly take up and act according to the rules of conduct as established, it becomes an offense." The monks, having doubts, put all their doubts to the Blessed One who cuts through all doubt: "Venerable One, this son of the elder, though he separated his father from his life, did not touch even the gross wrongdoing of an act without interval, and no defeat downfall has arisen — please look upon this." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only is it so at present — in the past as well this one did not touch even the gross wrongdoing of an act without interval even when separating his father from his life. Listen to this. Monks, in a former time long past there was a cook who lived on a certain cliff, and he took a wife from his own social class. With her he played, delighted, and made merry; he played, delighted, and made merry with her, and from his wife a son was born, and he raised and nurtured him until he grew up.

Now at another time a festival arose there on that cliff, and many garments that needed washing came to him. He said to his son: "Son, many garments need to be washed. I cannot go home to eat, so come here, bring the garments, and set out. Go back, bring food, and come." The son went along with him, carrying the garments. The son returned home, brought food, and came back. The cook ate the food and said: "Son, I am exhausted and will sleep. You go ahead and wash the garments." The son said: "So I will do." The cook lay down on one side and fell asleep. Now he was bald, and a fly settled on his head. When the cook's son had finished washing the garments and came to his father's side, he saw a fly on his father's head. He began to shoo it away, but the fly, drunk on blood, would not fly off, and the son became unable to bear it. He thought: "This fly is drinking my father's blood while he yet lives — I must kill it." The son struck at it with a flat stone, but the fly fled and he shattered his father's skull, and his father died then and there. A deity then spoke in verse:

The finest enemy is one possessed of wisdom;
not so a friend who lacks discernment.
Thinking to kill a fly with little wit,
he struck and broke his father's skull.

Monks, what do you think? He who was the cook at that time is this elder himself. He who was the cook's son at that time is this very son of the elder. And just as at that time, even in separating his father from his life, he did not touch even the gross wrongdoing of an act without interval — so too at present, even in separating his father from his life, he has not touched the gross wrongdoing of an act without interval, and no defeat downfall has arisen. For one who is a beginner, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who acts under the duress of painful sensation — for such a one there is no downfall. The third case of defeat is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall by the Monkey Pond. At that time five hundred fishermen were established along the Lovely River. Among them were two nets called Broad-Movement and Great-Movement. Sometimes they would put in the Broad-Movement net and sometimes the Great-Movement net: whenever fish were not being bought, they put in the Broad-Movement net, and whenever fish were being bought, they put in the Great-Movement net. At another time a festival arose in Vaiśālī, and they put in both nets: two hundred and fifty put in the Broad-Movement net, and two hundred and fifty put in the Great-Movement net. Those who had put in the Broad-Movement net arranged great heaps of fish, turtles, frogs, young crocodiles, and catfish and the like — heaps like piles of sesame, thick rice gruel, juniper, and broad beans. Those who had put in the Great-Movement net caught a crocodile-fish of great size, like a rabbit, that had come from the great ocean into the Lovely River and was lying there asleep, and they began to haul it in. As they hauled it, it awoke, and seized those two hundred and fifty fishermen together with the Great-Movement net, and moved off upstream. Those fishermen called out to the other two hundred and fifty fishermen: "Knowledgeable ones — the Great-Movement net has seized us; turn it back!"

When they heard this, the other two hundred and fifty fishermen also rushed in and joined them, yet the creature carried off all five hundred fishermen together with the Great-Movement net, moved upstream, and could not be restrained. Those helpless ones cried out on every side: "Knowledgeable ones — carry us away with the Great-Movement net and help us!" — and turning back those who had scattered like arrows, there were cowherds and ox-herders who had not yet perceived what was happening, and shepherds, and those who gather firewood, and those who gather grass, and those who live by traveling the roads, and those who live by guiding travelers along the roads, and yet others — many hundreds of thousands of living creatures — who turned back and, with their bodies and limbs hacking and tearing at it, with the net rent and utterly torn apart, they pulled that crocodile-fish from the water onto dry land. It had eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes. Some of its heads resembled the head of an elephant, some the head of a horse, and some resembled the heads of a she-camel, a donkey, an ox, a monkey, a lion, a tiger, a bear, a female bear, a mongoose, a cat, a goat, a sheep, a deer, a buffalo, a pig, and a dog. The word spread abroad that the five hundred fishermen of the Lovely River, using the Great-Movement net, had caught a crocodile-fish of the species that is as large as a rabbit, one that had come from the great ocean into the Lovely River, and had pulled it from the water onto dry land, and that it had eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes. Hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living creatures gathered on the banks of the Lovely River. Some of them were filled with wonder at the sight. Others were stirred by the roots of virtue they had planted in former lives. The six teachers dwelling and residing in Vaiśālī, Pūraṇa and the rest, were likewise struck with curiosity and came to the place. A great multitude of people arose in amazement, and standing there gazing with fixed eyes they said: "Knowledgeable ones — some of its heads resemble the head of an elephant; reckon from that. Some of its heads resemble those ranging up to the head of a dog; reckon from that as well."

Now, for the blessed buddhas (Skt. buddha) there is not the slightest trace of unknowing, of not-seeing, of ignorance, or of non-discernment. Therefore the blessed Buddha, endowed with great compassion, entered upon benefiting the world, the sole protector, the uniquely courageous one, without a second, who speaks nothing of a second, abiding in calm abiding and insight, making the three knowledges radiant, perfectly trained in the three trainings, skilled in the ground of the three fields of taming, who has crossed beyond the four rivers, well-established in the ground of practice of the four bases of miraculous power, long purified in the four means of attraction, not intimidated by the four fearlessnesses, who has abandoned the five limbs, who has truly transcended the five destinies, endowed with the six limbs, fully perfected in the six perfections, abiding in the six constant abidings, enriched with the flowers of the seven branches of awakening, who teaches the eight branches of the path, skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, endowed with the powers of the ten powers, whose fame has spread perfectly in the ten directions, who is supremely distinguished above those who exercise sovereignty over a hundredfold — it is the very nature of such ones to survey the world with the eye of a buddha three times by day and three times by night, observing who has declined and who has increased, who has been harmed, who has become wretched, who has become unhappy, and who has come to harm, wretchedness, and misery.

who is inclined toward the lower realms, who has fallen toward the lower realms, who is falling toward the lower realms — those I shall raise up from the path of the lower realms and establish in higher states, in liberation, and in the fruit. Those sunk in the mire of desire I shall draw out by the hand. Those bereft of the wealth of the noble ones I shall establish in lordship over the wealth of the noble ones. The world adorned by the arising of buddhas I shall make fruitful. Those whose roots of virtue have not yet been produced I shall cause to produce them. Those whose roots of virtue have already been produced I shall cause to ripen fully. Those that have fully ripened I shall cause to be completely liberated." With such knowing and seeing, the Blessed One's awareness engages.

Then it was said in verse:

One who dwells among sea-monsters, filled with poison,
may perhaps pass beyond their appointed time —
but the loving-kindness of a buddha for those to be tamed
shall never pass beyond its appointed time.

Just as a mother, toward her only beloved child,
thinks and acts to guard that child's very life,
so too the Tathāgata, toward those persons to be tamed,
thinks and acts to guard their very life.

The compassion that dwells in the stream of the omniscient one
is a young mother never wearying in seeking the calf to be tamed.
That loving-kindness for those fallen in existence and the lower realms
is like the love of a vast herd's mother-cow for her calf.

The Blessed One reflected: "These beings of the fish-species of the sea-monster have met with harm, distress, and misery. This is because they rendered special service to the buddhas of the past. Therefore, relying upon these fish of the sea-monster species, I have drawn forth a great host of those who have become tamed. For that reason I shall go to the bank of the pleasant river." And the Blessed One smiled.

Now it is the very nature of reality that whenever the Blessed Buddhas smile, rays of light of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, crystal, and silver in hue issue forth from their mouths. Some descend downward, and some ascend upward. Those that descend downward go into the hell realms — Reviving, Black Thread, Crushing Together, Crying Out, Great Crying Out, Hot, Very Hot, Unrelenting, Blister-Forming, Burst Blisters, Chattering Teeth, One Who Cries "Kyihu," One Who Cries "Achu," Split Like an Utpala Flower, Split Like a Lotus, and Split Wide Open Like a Great Lotus — and into whatever hot hells there are, those rays fall as coolness, and into whatever cold hells there are, they fall as warmth. In this way they sever the specific torments of those sentient beings, and those beings think to themselves: "Wise ones, have we died and transmigrated from here, or have we been born elsewhere?" In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sent forth an emanation. Upon seeing the emanation, they thought: "Wise ones, we have not died and transmigrated from here, nor have we been born elsewhere. Rather, by the power of this being we had not previously seen, our specific torments have been cut off." Their minds became filled with manifest faith toward the emanation, and

having exhausted the karma by which those sentient beings would have experienced the hells, they are made to take rebirth among those gods and humans who are vessels for the truths, wherever such a rebirth may occur.

Those who proceed upward are born among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Heaven Free from Strife, the Joyful Heaven, the Heaven of Delight in Emanation, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, the Heaven of Brahmā's Retinue, the Heaven of Brahmā's Ministers, the Great Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Minor Light, the Heaven of Boundless Light, the Heaven of Radiant Light, the Heaven of Minor Virtue, the Heaven of Boundless Virtue, the Heaven of Vast Virtue, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born Ones, the Heaven of Great Fruit, the Heaven of Non-Greatness, the Heaven of Non-Affliction, the Heaven of Sublime Appearance, the Heaven of Clear Vision, and the Heaven of Akaniṣṭha. Having arrived among those gods, they proclaim the words: "impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness," and they set forth and deliver the following two verses:

Undertake and bring forth what is to be done.
Enter into the teaching of the buddhas.
Like a great elephant against a house of mud,
crush the armies of the lord of death.

Whoever practices with utmost diligence
in this taming Dharma
shall, having utterly abandoned the cycle of rebirth,
make an end of suffering at last.

Then those rays of light, having traversed the great trichiliocosm, follow after the Blessed One himself, step by step. If the Blessed One intends to prophesy karma of the past, the rays sink into his back. If he intends to prophesy karma of the future, they sink into his front. If he intends to prophesy birth in the hells, they sink into the soles of his feet. If he intends to prophesy birth as an animal, they sink into his heels. If he intends to prophesy birth as a hungry ghost, they sink into his big toes. If he intends to prophesy birth as a human, they sink into his knees. If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king of power, they sink into his left palm. If he intends to prophesy the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king, they sink into his right palm. If he intends to prophesy birth as a god, they sink into his navel. If he intends to prophesy the awakening of a śrāvaka, they sink into his mouth. If he intends to prophesy the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they sink into his eyebrow hair. If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they sink into his uṣṇīṣa.

Then those rays of light, having circled the Blessed One three times, sank into the Blessed One's navel.

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and addressed the Blessed One with this question: "Venerable One, Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. Venerable One, what then is the cause of this smile? What is the condition?" And he also addressed him in verse:

They emerged from the gateway of the face,
blazing with a thousand varied hues,
illuminating all directions on every side,
like an outstretched parasol of sunlight.

Free from agitation and timidity, utterly beyond conceit,
the buddhas are the supreme cause for beings' journey onward.
Yet the Victor who subdues all foes does not without cause
display a smile white as a conch-flower's root and branch.

Therefore, O Steadfast One, knowing the time by your own mind,
O Sage, foremost of the herd, lord of ascetics and of birth,
dispel with words of certainty and with noble virtue
the doubt that has arisen in those listening beings filled with apprehension.

Steady as the king of salt-water mountains,
the protector buddhas do not show a sudden smile.
For what purpose does the Steadfast One display a smile?

The assembled multitude of people wished to hear it. The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, it is so. It is indeed so. Ānanda, the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas never display a smile without cause and condition. Ānanda, go and tell the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata wishes to proceed to the bank of the river. Among you, whoever wishes to go together with the Tathāgata to the bank of the river — let him take his robes and set out.'" The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he spoke to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One wishes to proceed to the bank of the river. Among you, whoever wishes to go together with the Blessed One to the bank of the river — let him take his robes and set out."

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the twelfth fascicle.

Then the Blessed One, himself tamed, surrounded by a retinue that was tamed; himself at peace, surrounded by a retinue at peace; himself liberated, surrounded by a retinue that was liberated; himself at ease, surrounded by a retinue at ease; himself subdued, surrounded by a retinue that was subdued; himself an arhat, surrounded by a retinue of arhats; himself free from attachment, surrounded by a retinue free from attachment; himself resplendent, surrounded by a retinue that was resplendent — encircled by a herd of bulls like the finest bull of the herd, encircled by a host of elephant calves like a great elephant, encircled by a host of fanged beasts like a lion, encircled by a flock of swans like the king of swans, encircled by a host of birds like the king of birds (Garuḍa), encircled by a host of disciples like a brahmin, encircled by a host of patients like a skilled physician, encircled by a host of troops like a hero, encircled by a host of those who have entered the path like a caravan guide, encircled by a host of merchants like a caravan leader, encircled by a host of merchants like a master merchant, encircled by a host of ministers like the king of a fortress, encircled by a host of a thousand sons like a wheel-turning monarch, encircled by a host of constellations like the moon, encircled by a host of a thousand rays like the sun, encircled by a host of gandharvas like the guardian of the directions (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), encircled by a host of flying vessels like the noble-born, encircled by a host of nāgas like Mignyi Zang (Varuṇa, king of nāgas), encircled by a host of yakṣas like the wealth-giver (Jambhala), encircled by a host of asuras like Thakzangri (Vemacitrin), encircled by a host of the gods of the Thirty-Three like Śakra (Indra, king of the gods), encircled by a host of Brahmā's realm like Brahmā himself — with his senses perfectly restrained, his conduct and comportment undisturbed, steady as an ocean of water, laden with virtue as a cloud is laden with rain, free from arrogance like the great king of elephants — his body beautifully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being, his form gloriously adorned with the eighty minor marks, ornamented with a bodily radiance of one fathom, possessed of a light exceeding a thousand suns, altogether glorious like a moving mountain of jewels — endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion — accompanied by the great śrāvakas: omniscient Kauṇḍinya, Udāyin, Mahānāman, Avikampita, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Nandaka (Nanda), and others, and further surrounded by a great Saṅgha of monks — he proceeded and walked toward that delightful bank of the river.

From a great distance, that retinue caught sight of the Blessed One accompanied by the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. When some among them who lacked faith saw this, they said, "The ascetic Gautama is known to be one who has no interest in spectacles — yet even he has come near, drawn by curiosity, to see the species of fish and sea-monsters." But those who were possessed of faith said to those lacking faith, "O wise ones, awakened buddhas, Blessed Ones, are precisely those who are free of all desire for spectacles. The Blessed One, taking the fish and sea-monsters as his occasion, intends to teach something wondrous and extraordinary to this great assembly of people — do not be mistaken about this." And they spoke these words in verse:

The Sage, possessing an intent free of all spectacle,
speaks purposelessly to the wretched where no spectacle exists.
This Victor, who is wholly devoted to benefiting others,
has surely come here for the welfare of embodied beings.

Then, upon seeing the Blessed One, that retinue immediately rose to their feet — for it had been the Blessed One's custom, even when he was still a bodhisattva, to rise in the presence of his father, his mother, his preceptors, his teachers, his gurus, and those who held the place of a guru. Thereupon the Blessed One proceeded into the midst of that retinue and took his seat upon a prepared throne placed at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Having seated himself, the Blessed One addressed those five hundred fishermen: "Good men, you are engaged in a livelihood that involves wrongful actions. Therefore you are now born into the lowly birth-station of fishermen, and at present you are violent, your hands are stained with blood, you are attached to the most depraved of depraved practices, you steal the lives of others, and you sustain yourselves by cutting the lives of others. When you die and pass on from here, what will your destiny be? What will your birth be? What will your future life be?"

They replied, "Blessed One, please declare to us what we should do."

The Blessed One declared, "Release these beings — the fish, the turtles, the frogs, the young of the sea-monster species that you are slaughtering, and the otters and so forth that you have pulled from the water."

"As the Blessed One has declared, so shall we release them," they said — and at the very moment the Blessed One finished speaking, they let them all go.

Then the Blessed One thought to himself: "I shall bring about by supernormal power a miracle of such a kind that all these living creatures — the fish, the turtles, the frogs, the young of the sea-monsters being slaughtered, the otters and the rest, all of them except for the species of adult fish-eating sea-monsters — will enter the pleasant river just as they naturally should in water; and that the sea-monster species too will recall their former births, will speak in human speech, and will converse together with me."

Then the Blessed One actually brought about that supernormal power, so that all those living creatures — the fish, the turtles, the frogs, the young of the sea-monsters being slaughtered, the otters and the rest, all except for the species of adult fish-eating sea-monsters — entered the pleasant river just as they naturally should in water; and the sea-monster species too recalled their former births, spoke in human speech, and conversed together with the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then addressed the sea-monster species: "Child, are you a novice?"

"Blessed One, I am a novice."

"Child, are you a novice?"

"Sugata, I am a novice."

"Child, have you engaged in misconduct of body?"

"Blessed One, I have."

"Child, have you engaged in misconduct of speech and mind?"

"Sugata, I have."

"Then who is your companion in non-virtue?"

"It is my mother, Blessed One."

"And where was she born?"

"Among the hell-beings."

"And where were you born?"

"As an animal."

"What do you think? When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?"

"Blessed One, among the hell-beings." "Sugata, among the hell-beings," the sea-monster said, and then broke into weeping.

The Blessed One then at that moment spoke these verses:

You were born in the realm of animals,
fallen into a state of no leisure.
Even now there is nothing I can do.
What use is there in weeping without purpose?

Have faith in me, the compassionate Victor,
think well of me with trusting devotion,
and being free of attachment to this animal birth,
from here you shall pass on to the higher realms.

With that, the sea-monster directed its mind toward the Blessed One with faith. The Blessed One then taught it the Dharma with these three phrases, in the gentlest way: "All formations (saṃskāra) are impermanent. All phenomena (dharma) are without self. Nirvāṇa is peace."

Then the assembly was filled with supreme wonder, and those among the wise said among themselves: "By the Blessed One's word, this one recalls its former births, speaks in human speech, and converses together with the Blessed One — who can this be? Blessed Buddhas are difficult to approach and difficult to bear, so we are unable to ask the Blessed One about this matter. Let us go to where the noble Ānanda is, approach the noble Ānanda, ask him this matter, and whatever the noble Ānanda teaches us in reply, that very thing we shall take to heart."

The assembly then went to where the venerable Ānanda was and said to him: "Noble Ānanda, by the Blessed One's word, this one recalls its former births, speaks in human speech, and converses together with the Blessed One — who is this?"

Ānanda replied: "O wise ones, ask the Blessed One himself about this matter."

"Noble Ānanda, Blessed Buddhas are difficult to approach and difficult to bear, so we dare not ask the Blessed One about this matter."

"O wise ones, I too find that Blessed Buddhas are difficult to approach and difficult to bear, so I myself am not able to ask the Blessed One about this matter. Nevertheless, I will ask for your sake."

So saying, Ānanda went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus:

"Reverend Blessed One, by your word, this one recalls its former births, speaks in human speech, and converses together with the Blessed One — who is this?"

"Ānanda, this is of the species of fish-eating sea-monsters. Ānanda, do you wish to hear an account of the former karmic activities of the species of fish-eating sea-monsters? If the Blessed One, drawing on the former karmic activities of the species of fish-eating sea-monsters, were to speak a Dharma-laden discourse to the monks and to the assembly of people —"

— would be retained by the monks and the assembly of people upon hearing it from the Blessed One, now is the time, O Blessed One; now is the time, O Sugata." "Ānanda, therefore listen, and attend most carefully; I shall speak." "So be it, Ānanda. Listen then."

Long ago, in this very Good Great Aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher — a Tathāgata, a foe-destroyer, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans — a Blessed One, a buddha, by name Kāśyapa. He dwelt attended by twenty thousand monks, near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the deer forest called Ṛṣivadana.

At that time, a king named Kṛkī ruled the city of Vārāṇasī. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and happy; the harvests were good; it was filled with many people and with a great populace; strife, conflict, foreign enemies, and internal discord had been completely pacified; it was free from bandits, famine, and disease; and rice, rows of sugar-cane, cattle, and buffalo were made to abound. He was a righteous king, a dharma-king, and he governed his realm by the Dharma.

Now at that time, a brahmin student who desired secret teachings and was seeking those secret teachings set out southward from the central land. He found a brahmin sitting there — one who had mastered the Vedas and their ancillary sciences and who had become a teacher to brahmins dwelling in various regions. The brahmin student went to that brahmin, and having approached with calm bearing and a tranquil manner of conduct, he bowed his head at his feet and sat down to one side.

The brahmin then welcomed him with words of greeting and said, "Ho there, student! From where have you come? What do you desire?" The student replied, "I have come from the central land and wish to place myself at my teacher's feet in attendance. For what purpose? In order to study the Vedas." "Excellent, student — so be it. You are a brahmin."

And so that student began to study the Vedas under that brahmin.

Now the customary practice among students was this: during times when they were not reading they would sometimes go to draw water at the riverbank, sometimes go toward the city, and sometimes go to fetch kindling wood. And it came to pass that at another such time, when they had not been reading and had gone to fetch firewood, an impromptu exchange of words arose among them along the way, something of this sort:

"Ho, you of the Kutsā lineage! You of the Bātsā lineage! You of the Śāṇḍilya lineage! You of the Bhāradvāja lineage! You of the lineage of the fifth! You of the lineage of the fifth-adjacent! Come now — let us ask one another from which region each has come."

One student said, "I have come from the eastern region." Another said, "I have come from the southern road." Yet another said, "I have come from the western land." And yet another said, "I have come from the northern road." That student said, "I have come from the central land."

The others said, "Wise ones, though we have seen and heard of all the regions, the central land we have not seen nor heard of."

And they also recited this verse:

In the east dwell those of keen intelligence.
In the south direction there are those who give.
In the western land there are the slanderous.
In the north direction speech is rough and coarse.

Then they asked, "Student, what is the central land like?"

"Wise ones, the central land is the finest of all regions. It has rice,

sugarcane plantations, cattle, and buffaloes in abundance, teeming with hundreds of wandering beggars, filled with people of the central land, shunned by the people of the borderlands, frequented by the learned. There flows the river Gaṅgā, renowned as a place of merit, auspiciousness, purity, and purity itself, its two banks moist and cool, called the dwelling place of sages, into which one hundred and eight tributaries flow. When sages practice austerities there, by the power of their very bodies they ascend to the higher realms. Oh wise ones, visit it, and ask about this further."

The student said, "Wise ones, are there, in the central land, those who are reckoned as learned?" The wise ones replied, "We have known from the very beginning, wise ones, that the central land is filled with people of the central land, shunned by those who are quarrelsome, and frequented by the learned — did you not say so?" "Student, you yourself said those words."

"Wise ones, in the central land it is like this: are there, for instance, those who are like our own preceptor — supreme orators of that kind?" The wise ones replied, "In the central land there are supreme orators of that kind, men so gifted in eloquent speech that even our own preceptor cannot look them in the face."

When that student had spoken in praise of the central land in this way, all of them became filled with the desire to go to the central land.

Then those students went and gathered kindling wood. Taking up their loads of kindling, they went to where the brahmin was. They arrived, set down their bundles of kindling to one side, went to where that brahmin was, and said to him, "Preceptor, please know this: this student has spoken such praises of the central land that all of us without exception now wish to go to the central land."

The brahmin said, "Children, must one travel as far as one has heard? Regions are pleasant to hear about, so you may listen, but you should not travel there."

"Preceptor, it is from the words of this student that we report: in the central land there are supreme orators, men of such eloquent speech that even our own preceptor cannot look them in the face."

"Children, do I say that I alone on this earth am the only speaker and there is no other speaker whatsoever? The earth holds many precious things, and therefore the surface of the earth is filled with wonders upon wonders."

"Preceptor, let us see that land as well, and we shall also draw close to the river's bank. We shall pay homage to those supreme orators. We shall also vanquish opponents. We shall also spread our own renown. We shall also secure material gain. We shall go to the central land."

Now the brahmin was affectionate toward his students and his retinue was small, and so he said to those students, "Children, if that is so, then take up the bark strips, the peeled sticks, the wands, the ladles for pouring, the ladles for filling, the balls, and go to the central land."

They took these things up, and the brahmin went forth together with those students to the central land. There he defeated some opponents and yoked them to the chariot of defeat. Some he struck with earthen pots shattered over their heads. Some he abandoned from afar, like a crow fleeing from a catapult's fulcrum. Some he received with parasols, victory banners, and flags. Some acknowledged him as their own preceptor, and in this way, gradually, defeating opponents in villages, cities, towns, market settlements, and trading posts, he arrived at Vārāṇasī.
