That brahmin thought, "Why should I abandon the root and cling to the branches, the leaves, and the foliage?"

All the opponents and all who were counted as learned were close to the king, and so that brahmin thought, "I too shall go before the king." So the brahmin went to where King Kṛkī was, and having arrived, he offered the king praises of victory and prayers for long life, then sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, he addressed King Kṛkī with these words: "O divine one, I have received a few letters from my teacher, and on that account I wish to settle a decisive debate together with opponents in the presence of the divine one."

The king spoke to his ministers: "O wise ones, is there in my land any opponent who can engage this brahmin in a decisive verbal contest?"

The ministers said: "O divine one, on a certain great rocky crag there lives a brahmin by the name of Śerśkya Śiwa, who has gone beyond the Vedas and the Vedic branches and who has the understanding of one who has entered deeply. He is skilled at making his own doctrine clear and sharp in cutting down the doctrines of others. Let that master be summoned." The king replied, "I will have him summoned." So they summoned him, and he came to where King Kṛkī was, and having arrived, he offered the king praises of victory and prayers for long life, and sat down to one side. The ministers said, "O divine one, this is that master."

The king greeted him with words of welcome and said: "Master, can you conduct a decisive debate together with this brahmin before me?"

Śerśkya Śiwa replied: "I shall cut him down to whatever degree, and in so doing shall please the king."

The king instructed the ministers: "O wise ones, prepare the arena of debate. Set out the positions of both sides." The ministers prepared the arena of debate and set out the positions of both sides.

Then the ministers prostrated at the two feet of the king and said, "O divine one, which side shall be granted the first position?" The king said, "This brahmin is a guest; let him take the first position."

The brahmin was given the first position and recited five hundred arguments drawn from the tantras. Śerśkya Śiwa rebutted them in turn: "This is without reasoning. This is inconsistent. This is untenable," heaping fault upon fault, until that brahmin sat there without a word to say. Among the grounds for refutation, the greatest is this: being unable to reply — that is defeat.

Then the king, greatly pleased, asked, "Master, where do you reside?" Śerśkya Śiwa replied, "O divine one, on a great rocky crag." The king said, "Go, and make use of that crag as the estate of your debate-victory." Śerśkya Śiwa was overjoyed, elated, and supremely delighted, and surrounded by wise people he went to that rocky crag.

Now, since the world desires prosperity, Śerśkya Śiwa took a wife of equal birth, and together with her he made merry, delighted, and took his pleasure. While they were making merry, delighting, and taking their pleasure, his wife gave birth to a shaggy-haired, yellowish-clad child, and seven times three — twenty-one days — after the birth, they held a great birth-celebration, and they set about giving the boy a name.

The relatives said: "This boy is the son of the brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa, and since his hair is also yellowish, let this boy's name be Śerśkya." And so they named him Śerśkya.

He was nourished with milk, yogurt, butter, clarified butter, and the essential cream of butter,

and raised up and developed swiftly by the choicest and finest of nourishments, like a lotus growing in a pond.

When he came of age, he became accomplished in letters, arithmetic, calculation, finger-reckoning, drawing out, entering, placing, dividing, and reading. At that time he mastered brahminical conduct and practice: purity, general deportment, the taking of ashes, the taking of the water-jar and the fire-vessel, the taking of earth, the arm-staff, the topknot, recitations of praise, the invocation known as "Kye," the Veda of grammatical expression, the Veda of sacrifice, the Veda of poetic composition, the Veda of statecraft and protection; and he became learned in the six duties of the brahmin: performing sacrifice, causing others to perform sacrifice, reciting, causing others to recite, giving, and receiving. He mastered the Vedas and their ancillary branches, and with a brilliance of mind like fire he could clearly expound his own position and refute the positions of others.

At that time the brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa set some five hundred brahmin youths to reciting the brahminical sacred formulas. Then one day, as the youth Śerśkya was reciting, he asked his father: "Father, what is the meaning of 'ritsa'?" The brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa replied: "My son, these are letters that have long fallen out of use; the words of the teachers are hard to know, and so those sages composed this treatise without understanding the meaning — I do not know what it signifies." Śerśkya said: "Father, I wish to find the meaning of that word 'ritsa.'" The brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa reflected: "A father's wish is for a son who equals or surpasses him; therefore, since this boy surpasses me, I should entrust these five hundred brahmin youths to him." Thinking thus, he recognized this to be so, and said to the brahmin youth Śerśkya: "My son, it is a father's wish to have a son who equals or surpasses him; therefore, since you surpass me, you should now set these five hundred brahmin youths to reciting the brahminical sacred formulas." Śerśkya replied: "As you command — I shall do so," and he began to lead those five hundred brahmin youths in the recitation of the brahminical sacred formulas. And the brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa, now free from duties, began to spend his time going wherever he pleased and enjoying himself in pleasurable activities.

Then on another occasion, a sage went out to discourse, and approaching a certain monk he asked: "Teacher, what is the meaning of this word?" The monk said: "Venerable one, that is not the proper way to ask that question; if you ask it that way, you will not get a complete answer. You should ask the question in this way: if you ask it thus, you will get the complete meaning of the word." The brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa thought: "If I cannot even ask a question of these people properly, how shall I ever be able to discourse together with them?" And with that he developed very deep faith in the monks, and at intervals he invited the monks as guests and served them food in his home.

Then on another occasion, having fallen ill, he said to the youth Śerśkya: "My son, from sunrise to sunset there is no one who can speak the way you can; therefore, after I am gone, you should speak together with all who debate and do so without fear and without hesitation."

"Excepting only the renunciants of the Kāśyapa lineage — for they possess a vast stream of learning, a profound stream of learning, a noble stream of learning; they cannot be defeated by worldly people, and they are unfathomable to those who have transcended the world; and they are many, harmonious, and do not seek material gain."

The youth Śerśkya said: "Father, I shall do so."

But the brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa did not rise from his sickbed. Though he was tended with medicines of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, he only grew worse, and in accordance with the way things are:

All that is accumulated must be exhausted to the end,
All that has risen high must fall.
All that has met must in the end be parted.
All that lives must in the end die.

He passed on in accordance with the law of his time. The youth Śerśkya and his household wrapped him in blue, yellow, red, and white cloth, carried him to the charnel ground, cremated him, and afterwards performed the mourning purification rites and settled there for a time.

The debaters who had come from the south heard that the brahmin Śerśkya Śiwa had passed on in his time. Hearing this, they began speaking among themselves: "Wise ones, the brahmin debater has passed on in his time — now let us go forth." And so they all gathered and went to the presence of King Kṛkī. They paid homage to the king with words of victory and long life and said: "O king, we have received a few letters from our teacher, and we wish to resolve a dispute in the matter of teaching before your royal presence."

The king said to his ministers: "Wise ones, summon that learned master." The ministers said: "O king, that brahmin debater has passed on in his time." The king said: "Then let these people gather here before me like warriors assembled for battle. Does that brahmin have a son or a younger brother?" A minister said: "O king, he has a son called the youth Śerśkya." The king said: "Summon the son of the learned master."

They summoned him, and he came before the king. He paid homage to the king with words of victory and long life and sat off to one side. The ministers said: "O king, this is the one called the youth Śerśkya, the son of the learned master." The king greeted him with words of welcome and then said: "Son of the learned master, these people who dwell in different regions have come to my presence wishing to debate with the brahmin. Are you able to debate with them? Whatever remuneration you desire, we shall gladly provide it to please you."

Then the arena of debate was arranged, the sides and the opposing sides were set out, and those debaters were made to state their positions first. And then, on whatever point any one of those debaters engaged the brahmin Śerśkya in debate, he left them without the power to respond, and they sat there without being able to say a word. For among the grounds of defeat, the chief is this: being without the power to reply is itself a defeat.

The king was amazed. "How wonderful," he thought, "that one so young in years possesses such eloquence and wisdom as this!" And filled with profound faith at that, he installed him on an elephant's back and anointed him sovereign of the realm of debate.

As for Śerśkya's mother, she harbored resentment within herself and fell into unwholesome thoughts, thinking: "That Śerśkya has swiftly seized the wealth and resources of the debaters — will he not meet with trouble on account of this?" Thus she sat there harboring that resentment and dwelling in unwholesome thoughts.

But the youth Śerśkya, having been anointed sovereign of the realm of debate, came surrounded by wise and learned people to his own home.

Then his mother, with respectful and earnest composure, said to him: "My son, have you defeated all the debaters?" Śerśkya said: "Mother, I have defeated them all — with the exception of the śramaṇas (wandering ascetics) of Kāśyapa." At that, Śerśkya's mother did as follows: she rubbed her two palms together.

The youth Śerśkya said: "Mother, why do you rub your two palms together?" The mother said: "My son, you still have rivals, and there exists a situation in which those śramaṇas of Kāśyapa could seize the wealth and resources of the debaters. So go and defeat them."

Śerśkya said: "Mother, my father has spoken to me thus: 'As long as the sun rises and sets each day, there is no other debater equal to you — therefore, once I am gone, you should speak with all debaters together, without fear and without hesitation — with the exception of the śramaṇas of Kāśyapa. For they possess a vast stream of learning, a profound stream of learning, a wholesome stream of learning; they cannot be defeated by worldly people, and what lies beyond the world is for them unfathomable in its depth. They are many, they are harmonious, and they do not seek after wealth and resources.' So he told me." The mother said: "My son, if your father has become a servant to the śramaṇas, will you too become a servant to the śramaṇas? Go and defeat them."

Since Śerśkya was respectful toward his mother, he took his mother's words to heart and set out. A noble debating sage and a certain monk had come from Vārāṇasī. Śerśkya saw that monk along the way and said: "Ho, monk, where have you come from?" "From the settlement of the debating sages." "In that settlement of debating sages, how many monks are there?" "Slightly more than twenty thousand monks." "Well then, if the monks are so numerous, how extensive is their treatise canon?" "Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka)." "What is the measure of the Baskets?" "One hundred thousand verses." "Is it fitting for a householder to take them up?" "The Sūtra Basket and the Abhidharma (the higher teachings) are fitting. But the Vinaya is the text of the ceremonial rule, so it is not fitting."

Śerśkya reflected: "The treatise that is the subject of their debate — they do not expound it to householders." Understanding this, he said: "Ho, monk, recite something from the word of the Buddha." That monk thought: "This brahmin is a debater — is he asking because he wants to gauge its measure, or is he asking because he wants to know everything?" Thinking he should see, the monk spoke a verse:

Where do the lakes turn back?
Where does the road turn back?
Where do all the world's pleasures and pains,
without remainder, cease?

Having recited it, he said: "Brahmin, tell me the meaning of this verse." The brahmin, having begun to analyze it through all the fields of knowledge, found that he knew neither the lake, nor the road, nor the turning back, and thought: "Has this not defeated me in my own eyes?" He looked in all four directions and reflected: "If there were some wise person here today, I would now be thoroughly defeated — so I must avoid this by every means." Understanding this, he said: "Ho, monk, that verse is endowed with a vast stream of meaning and is possessed of profound meaning. You too have come from Vārāṇasī, and I too have come from the settlement of the debating sages — so I cannot explain the meaning of this on the spot. Go now, and later it will not be difficult to explain its meaning." Having said this, he went to the settlement of the debating sages. There he saw monks engaged in the diligent practice of reading, recitation, and mental application. As soon as he saw them, his mind became filled with bright faith, and he thought:

Realizing that this was someone without compassion, one who had abandoned any thought of the next world, and that such a person would give rise to a mind of intense hatred toward the monks and would stir up conflict with them, he went to his own home. There his mother said to him: "My son, have you defeated the renunciants of Kāśyapa?" The young brahmin replied: "Mother, are you not pleased with the wealth I have won in debate? It seems you would prefer to have that wealth of victory seized away." "Son, what do you mean?" "Mother, today I went to the settlement of sages who are noble in speech, and just as I had gone a little way further I caught sight of a monk, and I said to him: 'Ho, monk, speak something of the Buddha's teaching.' He then recited the verse:

Where do the rivers turn?
Where does the road turn back?
Where do all the joys and sorrows of the world
Come to a complete and total cessation?

After he spoke this, I began to examine all fields of knowledge I possessed, yet I could not find the rivers, could not find the road, and could not find the turning point. Had there been anyone capable there at the time, I would have been utterly defeated on the spot." "Son, if that is so, go and learn the Buddha's teaching." "Mother, what am I to read? The treatises that these monks teach through their speech are not shown to householders." "Son, then go forth and learn." "Mother, having been born into the highest caste, how could I go forth into renunciation among those of different castes?" "Son, what — do you want bamboo and grass to sprout on your head? Then get out!" And when his mother pressed him insistently with deference, he went forth, going to the settlement of the sages of speech, and approaching a monk, he said: "Ho, monk, I wish to go forth." The monk thought to himself: "If I ordain this brahmin debater, he will become a treasure bestowed upon the teaching," and understanding this, said: "Brahmin, well and good, let it be so. Possessions are impermanent — go forth!" The young brahmin said: "Ho, monk, I am a brahmin of great learning, and so I shall proceed to the region to take my going forth here without delay." The monk then led that brahmin to the region and gave him the going forth and the full ordination, and set him firmly to reading and recitation. When that young monk read and recited, he read all three scriptural collections and became one endowed with the three collections of scripture, a proclaimer of Dharma, gifted with eloquence for reasoning and liberation. Whenever he wished to bestow the gift of hearing Dharma, he would have a lion throne adorned with many precious things prepared, would have conch shells wound and sounded, would have great drums beaten, and would gather an assembly including kings, and even the multitudes of common people would be filled with manifest faith.

The Dharma-proclaiming young monk thought: "Let me attain what is to be attained through what I have heard. I shall go to Vārāṇasī and pay homage to the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa." And so, delighting in traveling through the region, he set out wandering toward Vārāṇasī, and journeying on by stages, he at last arrived at Vārāṇasī.

Then his mother, having heard of this, went in search of her son to the settlement of the sages of speech, and seeing her son, said: "My son, have you defeated the renunciants of Kāśyapa?" "Mother, I possess only scripture, while they possess both scripture and realization — so how could I possibly defeat them?" "Son, you must certainly defeat them — defeat them!" The young monk, pressing his mother respectfully yet insistently, accepted her words and said: "Mother, when the lion throne has been prepared, the conch shells wound and about to be blown —"

"when the great drum has been beaten and the retinue together with the king has assembled — then, mother, you must come. Very well, son; you shall come." Then, at some later time, having been invited to teach the Dharma to the monks, the lion throne was prepared, the conch shells wound and blown, the great drum was beaten, and the retinue together with the king assembled. When the monk's mother heard the sound of the conch and the great drum, she went straightaway, without delay, to the settlement of the sages of speech, entered the assembly hall, and sat behind the lion throne. The monk who was to teach the Dharma ascended the lion throne and began to expound the teaching. Having taught as much Dharma as he taught, he then began to teach what was not Dharma. At that point the monks said to him: "Venerable one, do not harm the limits of the sūtras. Do not disturb the guidance of the Dharma. Do not tear open the womb of the Dharma. Do not lower the victory banner of the Dharma. Do not raise the victory banner of Māra. Do not cause sentient beings to incline toward the hells." The monk, humiliated, descended from the throne and said to his mother below: "Mother, did you see?" "Son, I saw. Did I not say to you from the very beginning: 'Mother, I possess only scripture, while they possess both scripture and realization — so how can I possibly defeat them'? Son, when you teach the Dharma, teach as much Dharma as there is to teach, and then teach what is not Dharma. If they then say to you: 'Venerable one, do not harm the limits of the sūtras; do not disturb the guidance of the Dharma; do not tear open the womb of the Dharma; do not lower the victory banner of the Dharma; do not raise the victory banner of Māra; do not cause sentient beings to incline toward the hells' — at that moment, strike them with the sword of words. Since they do wrong and are in dread of it, they will sit in silence; and thereby, in the eyes of the world, it will be understood that they have been defeated." "Mother, that method is good. But at that time you too must come." "Son, do as I say — I shall come." Then, at some point, a lion throne for hearing the Dharma was prepared, the monk was invited to teach the Dharma, the conch shells were wound and blown, the great drum was beaten, the retinue together with the king assembled, and the monk's mother came as before and sat behind the lion throne. The monk who was to teach the Dharma ascended the lion throne and began to expound the teaching. Having taught as much Dharma as there was to teach, he then began to teach what was not Dharma. The monks said to him: "Venerable one, do not harm the limits of the sūtras. Do not disturb the guidance of the Dharma. Do not tear open the womb of the Dharma. Do not lower the victory banner of the Dharma. Do not raise the victory banner of Māra. Do not cause sentient beings to incline toward the hells." The monk, goaded by his mother and unable to restrain himself, began to strike them with the sword of words: "You with the elephant's head — what do you know of Dharma or non-Dharma, of Vinaya or non-Vinaya? You with the horse's head! You with the tail-head! You with the donkey's head! You with the ox's head! You with the monkey's head! You with the lion's head! You with the tiger's head! You with the bear's head! You with the hyena's head! You with the owl's head! You with the cat's head! You with the goat's head! You with the sheep's head! You with the deer's head! You with the buffalo's head! You with the pig's head! You with the dog's head! — what do you know of Dharma or non-Dharma, of Vinaya or non-Vinaya?" At those words, the monks said:

"This man has begun to strike us with the sword of words — let us leave!" So said the monks. Those among them who had little discernment departed. Those who were patient-natured remained right there, thinking: if he teaches Dharma, let us listen; if he teaches non-Dharma, let it simply be what it is.

Then the yellow-clad Dharma-proclaimer, having verbally abused the monk-trainees (those in training and those beyond training) with eighteen verbal offenses, descended from the lion throne and said to his mother: "Mother, are you pleased? Is your son's mother happy? Come, let us go home."

The yellow-clad one replied: "Mother, I will not come, out of delight in the scriptural word of the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha Kāśyapa."

"Son, have you not heard that one must not make one's mother's words mere empty words? Come, let us go."

The yellow-clad one replied: "As I wander through saṃsāra, may I never be without a mother like you. But today, having relied on you as a harmful spiritual companion, I have uttered coarse verbal karma toward persons in training and beyond training, and I shall experience the unwanted ripening of that action individually."

Then that mother of the yellow-clad one began to cry out along the great roads, the markets, the crossroads, and the intersections of Vārāṇasī to those dwelling in Vārāṇasī, those going about the palace, and the townspeople: "Hear me! The monks of Kāśyapa have abducted my son — help me!" Those who were faithful among the crowd were truly relieved. Those who lacked faith jeered. When that mother of the yellow-clad one was being jeered, such an affliction came upon her that she vomited hot blood, and when her time came, she was born among the hell-beings.

As for the yellow-clad Dharma-proclaimer himself, because he had committed the eighteen verbal offenses toward monk-trainees and those beyond training, when his time came he was born here among the animals — in the form of a terrifying species of water-monster fish.

Then the assembly reflected with concern: "Wise ones, if the yellow-clad Dharma-proclaimer, who was endowed with the three baskets of scripture, possessed of reasoning and liberated eloquence, who filled the ear-canals of many hundreds of thousands of living beings — if he was born in the wretched realm of animals simply through verbal offenses, then for those of us who pass from this world, where will we go? What will our birth be? What will our next life be?"

Then the Blessed One, having understood with his mind the intentions, latent dispositions, constitutions, and natures of that assembly, taught the Dharma in such a way that, upon hearing it: some attained heat, some attained the summit, some attained acceptance, some attained the supreme mundane Dharma; some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some the fruit of once-returning; some the fruit of non-returning; some, having gone forth and abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship; some generated the mind set on the awakening of a śrāvaka; some on the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; and some generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. And of that assembly, the great majority were established as having turned toward the Buddha, as having arrived at the Dharma, and as having come to rest in the Saṅgha — such was the Dharma he taught.

Then the Blessed One, having accomplished the great purpose of taming beings, departed.

Then the makara of the fish clan thought to itself: "Since I have heard the Dharma of the three statements in the presence of the Blessed One and then proceeded to eat, this is not in keeping with my proper conduct." And so it entered upon a fast and abstained from food. Now, the hunger of those born in the animal destiny burns fierce and sharp, and when it had grown weak and faint with hunger, it turned its mind to the Blessed One with sincere faith — and when the right moment came, it was born among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. It is the natural condition of divine sons and daughters that, not long after birth, three thoughts arise: from where did I pass away, where have I been born, and by what karma was I born here? And so that being saw that it had passed away from among the animals and been born among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and that it had been born there because it had turned its mind to the Blessed One with sincere faith.

Then the former makara, now a divine son, thought to itself: "To approach the Blessed One by first arranging my dwelling and attending to my comforts and then going to see him and pay him homage — that is not in keeping with my proper conduct. Instead I will go to see the Blessed One and pay him homage without first arranging any dwelling at all."

And so the former makara, now a divine son, taking up shining, unstained pendant earrings and adorning his body with necklaces and bracelets, filled his cupped palms with divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white night-blooming lotuses, and white lotuses — and, radiant with colour of surpassing brilliance, he set out at nightfall, went to where the Blessed One was, scattered the flowers upon the Blessed One as an offering, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. And such was the power of the divine son's radiance that the entire palace building, every chamber of that many-storied mansion, was filled with a great blaze of light.

Then the Blessed One, having perceived the intention, latent disposition, constitution, and temperament of the former makara divine son, and having known what teaching would be heard by him so as to enable him — even as he sat on that very seat — to shatter with the vajra of wisdom the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, and directly to realize the fruit of stream-entry, taught him the Dharma in such a way as to lead him to a full and individual understanding of the Four Noble Truths.

And having seen the Truths, that divine son spoke aloud three times with deliberate intent these words:

"What the venerable Blessed One has done for me now, this no father has done, no mother has done, no king has done, no gods have done, no ancestors of former generations have done, no ascetics or brahmins have done, and no assembly of kin, friends, or relatives has done — for he has drained the ocean of blood and tears, freed me from the mountains of bones, closed the doors to the lower destinies, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, lifted me out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed me among gods and humans."

And he spoke again in verse:

By your power, O supremely mighty one,
with abundant faults, I have blocked the trail to lower birth,
become richly endowed with merit.
The path to higher realms was opened, and I myself
have come to gain even the track of nirvāṇa.

Relying on you, O utterly pure one,
today I have gained the eye that is free from fault and stainless,
and reached the peaceful, noble station — sublime joy —
and have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

One worshipped in all destinies by asuras, humans, and gods,
free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
seeing existence as empty — a rare and wondrous sight —
the Sage: today there is the fruit of beholding you.

Then, with gathered robes and long-hanging necklaces trailing —

he bowed at the feet with joy arising in his heart, circumambulated the Subduer of Foes (the Buddha) from the right, and departed into the sky in the direction of the divine world.

Then those who had formerly been like that nāga-spirit's son — like a merchant who finds profit, like a farmer who obtains a harvest, like a hero who triumphs in battle, like a sick person fully freed from all illness — departed in the very same manner in which they had come before the Blessed One, and returned to their own abodes.

Now the monks who dwelt in diligent practice, not sleeping in the first watch of the night or the last watch of the night, saw a great and vast radiance flood the presence of the Blessed One. Seeing this, their minds filled with wonder and doubt, and when dawn came they asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, last night who was it that came to behold you — the Lord of the Pure Abode (Brahmā), sovereign of the immaculate world? Or Śakra, lord of the gods? Or the Four World-Guardians? Or some other mighty and powerful son of the gods?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was not Brahmā, lord of the immaculate world, who came to behold me. It was not Śakra, lord of the gods. It was not the Four World-Guardians. It was not some other mighty and powerful son of the gods. Monks, do you see, then, that being of the nāga-fish lineage to whom I earlier taught the Dharma in three words? The Blessed One confirmed: 'Yes, we see.' Monks, that one passed away from there and was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and came to my presence last night. I taught him the Dharma, and he saw the truth, then returned to his own abode."

Again the monks asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, what karma did the former son of the nāga-spirit perform that he was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings? And what karma did he perform that he came to see the truth in the presence of the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the former son of the nāga-spirit had accumulated a store of karma, thoroughly transformed its conditions, dwelt close to it as to a lamp, and fashioned and gathered deeds certain to arise without fail. Monks, by whom else could the karma fashioned and gathered by that son of the nāga-spirit be experienced? Monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done and accumulated ripens solely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources."

Actions, even for a hundred aeons,
do not perish, but when the moment
and conditions come together,
they bear their fruit for embodied beings.

"Monks, there is karma to be experienced in the very life in which it is born, and there is karma to be experienced in another turn of lives. What is the karma to be experienced in the life in which it is born? When that being was still a nāga-fish, the pure and manifest faith in me that it generated — that is called karma to be experienced in the life in which it is born, and through its ripening it was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. What is the karma to be experienced in another turn of lives? It went forth into renunciation under the teaching of the completely and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa of the golden complexion; it received scriptural transmission, read, recited, became learned in the aggregates, learned in the elements, learned in the sense sources, learned in dependent origination,

learned in what is possible and what is impossible — that is called karma to be experienced in another turn of lives, and through the accumulated substance of that karma, having now been reborn as a son of the gods, it was caused to see the truth in my presence.

Monks, that being so: the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is itself mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and actions that are mixed, and strive for actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train in precisely this way.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga. The thirteenth fascicle.

Then those five hundred young men of good family thought to themselves: Friends, consider this — a preacher of Dharma, a śramaṇa, who possesses all three scriptural collections, who has become endowed with the eloquence of reason and liberation, who has filled the ear-cavities of many hundreds of thousands of living beings — if, through no more than a verbal misdeed, he came to be reborn in a wretched animal existence, then what of us, who are right now violent, red-handed, engaged in beating and extreme beating, who snatch away the lives of others, who incite the killing of others' lives, who make their livelihood by taking the lives of others? When those of us who pass away from here die and transmigrate, what will become of our destiny? What will our rebirth be? What will our future life be? If we were not born in lowly circumstances, we too should rejoice, strive, and make effort in going forth into renunciation under the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, so that we might cross over the rivers and truly pass beyond the conditionings. It is the very nature of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while alive, living, present, and dwelling, to survey the world with the buddha-eye, out of loving care for beings who are ripe for training, three times by day and three times by night. And the great śrāvakas likewise do so — so the elder Śāriputra, surveying the world with the śrāvaka-eye, saw those five hundred young men of good family sitting lost in thought, propping their chins on their hands, absorbed and settled in their own minds.

Having seen them, Śāriputra went to where those five hundred young men of good family were and said to them: Good friends, why do you sit propping your chins on your hands, absorbed and settled in thought?

They replied: Noble one, it is like this — a preacher of Dharma, a śramaṇa, who possessed all three scriptural collections and became endowed with the eloquence of reason and liberation, who filled the ear-cavities of many hundreds of thousands of living beings — if, through no more than a verbal misdeed, he came to be reborn in a wretched animal existence, then what of us, who are right now violent, red-handed, engaged in beating and extreme beating, who snatch away the lives of others, who incite the killing of others' lives, who make their livelihood by taking the lives of others? When those of us who pass away from here die and transmigrate, what will become of our destiny? What will our rebirth be? What will our future life be? If we were not born in lowly circumstances, we too should rejoice, strive, and make effort in going forth into renunciation under the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, so that we might cross over the rivers and truly pass beyond the conditionings. That is why it is altogether fitting that we sit absorbed in thought.

"Fair-featured ones, in this sacred teaching of the Lord of Sages what is held dear is not lineage, not household, not clan. In this sacred teaching of the Lord of Sages, what is held dear is practice." And further it was said in verse:

The Tathāgatas take no account of lineage,
of household, or of clan.
Though deeds have been performed across a long span of time,
it is the deeds themselves they fully examine.

"If you wish for the going forth into renunciation and full ordination as monks under the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, come here. You should go to where the Blessed One is, and the Blessed One will grant you the going forth."

"Excellent, noble one. If that is so, we will come to go forth in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the venerable Śāriputra led those five hundred young men of good family to where the Blessed One was and, arriving there, bowed with his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend One, these five hundred young men of good family wish for the going forth into renunciation and full ordination as monks under the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. May the Blessed One, out of compassion, please grant them the going forth and confer full ordination upon them."

The Blessed One, saying to them "Come, monks," gave them the going forth, and then declared, "Come, monks — live the holy life." At the very conclusion of the Blessed One's words, their bodies became shaved and robed in patched ochre cloth. It was as though seven days' growth of hair and beard had appeared, their hands were occupied with begging bowl and water vessel, and they abided as if they were monks who had been fully ordained for a hundred years.

And further it was said in verse:

The Tathāgata spoke the word "Come" —
and those who bore bodies shaved and robed in ochre cloth
instantly became utterly tranquil in their faculties,
their bodily forms covered by the intention of the Buddha.

Then the Blessed One, having given those five hundred young men of good family the going forth and full ordination, stayed at ease in Vaiśālī and set out wandering toward the village of Āmra-kāra. Going along, gradually wandering, he arrived at the village of Āmra-kāra and dwelt there in a grove of mango trees to the north of the village.

At that time there was a severe famine. The countryside was desolate. Mendicants found food hard to obtain, and parents themselves found it difficult even to think of feeding their own children — so what need to say anything about what happened to the mendicants?

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, right now there is a severe famine, the countryside is desolate, mendicants find food hard to obtain, and parents themselves find it difficult even to think of feeding their own children — so what need to say anything about what has befallen the mendicants? Therefore, monks, come here and according to whatever invitations have been given, whatever speech of arrival has been made, and whatever companionship of friends has been arranged, accept the rains retreat in the villages surrounding Vaiśālī. I too will accept the rains retreat right here in this village of Āmra-kāra, being served by the monk Ānanda. It is not fitting that all of you should be worn down by begging for alms."

Those monks, having heard this from the Blessed One, responded "Reverend One, as you command," and according to whatever invitations had been given, whatever speech of arrival had been made, and whatever companionship of friends had been arranged, they accepted the rains retreat in the villages surrounding Vaiśālī.

The Blessed One too accepted the rains retreat right there in that same village of Āmra-kāra, being served by the venerable Ānanda.

Then those five hundred monks thought to themselves: "Reverend ones, take note of this. The Blessed One has declared: 'Monks, at present the famine is severe and wretched; it is hard for wandering mendicants to find food, and even parents find it difficult to give food to their own children — how much more so for wandering mendicants. Monks, come here. According to whatever invitations had been given, whatever speech of arrival had been made, and whatever companionship of friends had been arranged, accept the rains retreat in the villages surrounding Vaiśālī. I too will accept the rains retreat right here in this village of Āmra-kāra, being served by the monk Ānanda. It is not fitting that all of you should be worn down by begging for alms.' Since we have no relatives here, and our relatives are settled in the fishing village, we should go to the fishing village, visit our relatives, make shelters of leaves and foliage in the surroundings of the fishing village, and accept the rains retreat there — that would be fitting." And so those five hundred monks went to the fishing village, visited their relatives, made shelters of leaves and foliage in the surroundings of the fishing village, and accepted the rains retreat there.

Then they thought to themselves: "Reverend ones, take note of this. We are ones of little learning, and should our relatives come to visit us, we would not be able to teach them the Dharma. We could say to our visiting relatives: 'Relatives, those of you in whose village this community of monks has accepted the rains retreat — those relatives of theirs have obtained a fine and excellent gain. For this monk has attained the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of selflessness in what is suffering, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of faultiness, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of the bloated, the perception of the putrefied, the perception of the festering, the perception of the gnawed-apart, the perception of the devoured, the perception of the blood-red, the perception of the scattered, the perception of bones, and the perception that analytically discerns emptiness. This monk has attained the first meditative concentration, the second, the third, and the fourth; loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sense base of infinite space, the sense base of infinite consciousness, the sense base of nothingness, the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning; the sphere of miraculous powers, the divine ear, the thorough knowledge of minds, the recollection of former abodes, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of defilements. This monk meditates upon the eight liberations (vimokṣas) of an arhat. This monk is liberated in both respects' — we should proclaim each other's qualities in this way. That would be fitting." And so, when their relatives came to visit, those monks began to proclaim each other's qualities to those visiting relatives.

"Relatives, those of you in whose village a community of monks accepted the rains retreat at such a lodging supplied by patrons — those relatives have obtained a fine acquisition indeed. This monk has attained the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of selflessness in what is suffering, the perception of repulsion toward food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of faultiness, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of the bloated, the perception of the festering, the perception of the worm-infested, the perception of the gnawed, the perception of the devoured, the perception of the blood-red, the perception of the scattered, the perception of bones, and the perception that analytically discerns emptiness. This monk has attained the first, second, third, and fourth meditative concentrations; loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning; the sphere of miraculous powers, the divine ear, the thorough knowledge of minds, the recollection of former abodes, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of defilements. This monk meditates upon the eight liberations of an arhat. This monk is liberated in both respects."

Those relatives then said, "Noble ones, have you yourselves attained such an accumulation of qualities?" "We have." The world is fond of qualities, so they at once took the matter away even from their own children and conceived the wish to offer alms to those monks.

Now, while the Blessed One, the Buddha, was living and dwelling, alive and present, it was natural that there were two great assemblies of hearers. The first was during the rains retreat, on the day of the middle month of the summer season. The second was on the full-moon day of the middle month of autumn. At that time, those who during the rains retreat, on the day of the middle month of the summer season, had taken up an instruction and accepted the rains retreat in villages, market towns, districts, and royal palaces — when the full-moon day of the middle month of autumn came around, they would report what they had attained, and would inquire below about what they had not yet attained, in order to attain it.

Then, after the three months of the rains retreat had passed, those monks who had accepted the rains retreat in the village of Pūrvavideha near Vaiśālī, wearing their robes and holding their robes, thin and emaciated, haggard, gaunt, and dried out, their bodies worn down, took up their begging bowls and robes and set off walking toward the village of Vaiśālī. As they were making their way and eventually arrived at the village of Vaiśālī, the Venerable Ānanda saw those very many monks from a great distance. Seeing them, delighted and gladdened at their conduct in the holy life, he greeted them with words of friendship, and took their begging bowls, robes, shoulder bags, water strainers, round vessels for pouring over the head, containers of oil, hats, worn sandals, and leather shoes, saying these words: "Welcome, venerable ones! You have come well! Venerable ones, where have you come from just now? Where did you accept the rains retreat?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we have come here from the village of Spongbyed. We accepted the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed."

"Venerable ones, did you accept the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed comfortably, in ease? Were you not wearied by going on alms round?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we did indeed accept the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed in ease and comfort at first, but we were wearied by going on alms round. So it appeared to us, venerable ones — wearied and troubled by the alms round, we became thin, feeble, gaunt, and thirsty; our complexions faded, and our skin, flesh, and blood diminished."

Those monks who had accepted the rains retreat in the vicinity of the fishermen's village — they too, once the three months of the rains retreat had passed, took up their robes and, possessing their robes, with their complexions, skin, flesh, and blood flourishing, they took up their begging bowls and robes and made their way, going and travelling toward the village of Vaiśālī. As they were making their way and eventually arrived at the village of Vaiśālī, the Venerable Ānanda saw those very many monks from a great distance. Seeing them, delighted and gladdened at their conduct in the holy life, he greeted them with words of friendship, and took their begging bowls, robes, shoulder bags, water strainers, round vessels for pouring over the head, containers of oil, hats, worn sandals, and leather shoes, saying these words: "Welcome, venerable ones! You have come well! Venerable ones, where have you come from just now? Where did you accept the rains retreat?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we have come here from the fishermen's village. We accepted the rains retreat in the fishermen's village."

"Venerable ones, did you accept the rains retreat in the fishermen's village comfortably, in ease? Were you not wearied by going on alms round?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we did indeed accept the rains retreat in the fishermen's village in ease and comfort, and we were not wearied by going on alms round. So it appeared to us, venerable ones — since we were not troubled by the alms round, our complexions, skin, flesh, and blood flourished."

"Venerable ones, at present there is a severe famine, the wilderness is hard to forage in, food is difficult to find, and even parents find it hard to give food to their own children or even to think of doing so — to say nothing of what happens when mendicants come looking for alms. So here, what was the cause and what was the condition for your not being wearied by the alms round?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we praised one another's virtuous qualities in the presence of our lay relatives, saying: 'This monk has attained the perception of impermanence; the perception of suffering in what is impermanent; the perception of no-self in what is suffering; the perception of disenchantment with food; the perception of non-delight in the entire world; the perception of faults; the perception of abandonment; the perception of freedom from attachment; the perception of cessation; the perception of death; the perception of the unattractive; the perception of the bluish-discoloured; the perception of the festering; the perception of the bloated; the perception of the worm-eaten; the perception of the devoured; the perception of the reddish; the perception of the scattered; the perception of bones; and the perception that individually discerns emptiness. This monk has also attained the first meditative concentration and the second —

the third and the fourth; loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sphere of boundless space, the sphere of boundless consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning; the domain of supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of previous lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of defilements. This monk is one who meditates upon the eight liberations of an arhat. This monk is one who is liberated from both sides." In this way they proclaimed one another's qualities to each other — whether accurately or inaccurately; inaccurately.

"Is it right for you, for the sake of a trifling gain, to claim for yourselves a supreme human quality that you do not possess? It may be permissible, or it may not be permissible — and yet you have spoken in this way." Monks of little worth — why do monks, for the sake of a trifling gain, claim a supreme human quality they do not possess? They reproach, rebuke, and condemn one another. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in reference to this occasion and this matter, convened the community of monks. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though they know, they inquire — and so forth, as before.

The Blessed One addressed the monks who were dwelling on the bank of the beautiful river: "Monks, is it true that you claimed, for the sake of a trifling gain, a supreme human quality that you did not possess?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One then condemned this thoroughly, saying that it is not in keeping with the conduct of a renunciant, not appropriate, not suitable, not in harmony with the rules — it is not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

"Monks, these three are thieves and great thieves found in the world and in existence. What are the three? Monks, here a thief attended by a retinue of a hundred, or attended by a retinue of a thousand, marches before those hundred or thousand, breaks into houses, cuts through fastenings, carries off plunder outright, lies in ambush on the road, sets fires, kills travelers on the way, steals from the royal treasury, sacks villages, sacks towns, and sacks provinces. That, monks, is the first thief and great thief found in the world and in existence.

"Monks, there is also another thief and great thief who is attended neither by a retinue of a hundred nor by a retinue of a thousand, and who marches before no such hundred or thousand, who does not break into houses, does not cut through fastenings, does not carry off plunder outright, does not lie in ambush on the road, does not set fires, does not kill travelers on the way, does not steal from the royal treasury, does not sack villages, does not sack towns, and does not sack provinces — and yet he makes his living by repeatedly selling grass, wood, flowers, fruit, leaves, or whatever belongings of the Saṅgha there may be, without supporting a household. That, monks, is the second thief and great thief found in the world and in existence.

"Monks, there is also another thief and great thief who is attended neither by a retinue of a hundred nor by a retinue of a thousand, and who marches before no such hundred or thousand —

does not sack households, does not cut bonds, does not seize by violent assault, does not lie in ambush on the road, does not set fires, does not kill travelers on the way, does not steal from the royal treasury, does not sack villages, does not sack towns, and does not sack provinces — and yet he does not make his living by repeatedly selling grass, wood, flowers, fruit, leaves, or whatever belongings of the Saṅgha there may be, and he does not support a household — and yet he speaks of the supreme human quality as being present when it is absent. That, monks, is the third thief and great thief found in the world and in existence.

"Monks, among thieves, any thief who is attended by a retinue of a hundred or a retinue of a thousand, who marches before such a hundred or thousand, who sacks households, cuts bonds, seizes by violent assault, lies in ambush on the road, sets fires, kills travelers on the way, steals from the royal treasury, sacks villages, sacks towns, and sacks provinces — that is but a small thing. Among thieves, any thief who makes his living by repeatedly selling grass, wood, flowers, fruit, leaves, or whatever belongings of the Saṅgha there may be, and does not support a household — that too is but a small thing. Monks, among all thieves, the one who speaks of the supreme human quality as being present when it is absent — that one is the greatest thief and great thief in the world together with its gods, its māras, its Brahmā, its ascetics and brahmins, its beings, its gods and humans.

The Blessed One having declared this, the Sugata having spoken thus, the Teacher then further declared these words in verse:

Whoever, not having become an arhat,
proclaims himself to be an arhat —
he is a thief among the world together with Brahmā,
and is to be declared one of corrupt moral discipline.

Thereupon the Blessed One, having censured this in many ways, addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — beginning with the words 'for the sake of sustaining the Saṅgha,' and ending with the words 'so that this holy life of mine, which is of benefit to many people, may be broadly and thoroughly demonstrated to gods and humans and may long endure' — just as before. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk who does not know, who does not fully know, who has not the supreme human quality, the utter and noble distinction of attainment, the knowledge, the seeing, and the abiding in direct experience — and who, being without it, falsely claims 'I know this, I see this' — then if a downfall arises from that, and wishing to purify it, he says at another time, whether asked or not asked: 'Venerable ones, I who did not know claimed to know, I who had not seen said that I saw — I spoke an empty, false lie' — then that monk, too, has incurred defeat and is not to remain in the community." Thus the Blessed One established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

Now, the many monks who were dwelling in lodgings in forest hermitages, at the foot of trees, and at the edges of cave retreats, striving in pursuit of the practice of yoga — relying on some slight grasping at the distinguishing characteristic that is the basis of calm abiding, and through worldly mental engagement suppressing the afflictions — on account of this they would experience, regarding objects of desire, attachment,

aversion and malice did not arise continually in their mental streams. After that, they would declare to one another: "Venerable ones, know this! Whatever is to be attained by those who dwell in forest hermitages, we have attained. Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done; we know nothing further beyond this existence." And having said that, they abandoned their forest dwelling places and entered lodgings at the edges of villages. There, they would repeatedly encounter objects of the feminine kind, and they would mix and dwell together with novices who frequented pleasure groves. Afflictions arose in them as well — attachment regarding objects of desire, and aversion and malice arose continually in their mental streams. And then they thought: "Venerable ones, know this! Whatever is to be attained by those who dwell in forest hermitages, we have attained. Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done; we know nothing further beyond this existence. Come, let us abandon our forest dwelling places and enter lodgings at the edges of villages." And having said this, they abandoned their forest dwelling places and entered lodgings at the edges of villages. There, they too repeatedly encountered objects of the feminine kind and mixed and dwelt together with novices who frequented pleasure groves. In them too afflictions arose — attachment regarding objects of desire, and aversion and malice arose continually in their mental streams. Then the Blessed One established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: "Furthermore, if a monk, without knowing or fully knowing, claims 'I know this, I see this' — claiming to possess a supreme human quality, a noble distinction, an attainment, knowledge, vision, and direct experience that do not exist in him — and if, arising from that transgression, wishing to purify himself, he then at another time, whether asked or not asked, says: 'Venerable ones, I spoke without knowing, claiming to know; I spoke claiming to see what I had not seen; I spoke what was empty and false' — that monk too has incurred defeat and is not to remain in the community."

When this rule of training had been established, those of us who were dwelling in forest hermitages, at the foot of trees, and at the edges of cave retreats — relying on some slight grasping at the distinguishing characteristic that is the basis of calm abiding, and through worldly mental engagement suppressing the afflictions — would find that attachment regarding objects of desire, and aversion and malice, did not arise continually in our mental streams. And we would declare to one another: "Venerable ones, know this! Whatever is to be attained by those who dwell in forest hermitages, we have attained. Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done; we know nothing further beyond this existence. Come, let us abandon our forest dwelling places and enter lodgings at the edges of villages." And having said this, we abandoned our forest dwelling places and entered lodgings at the edges of villages. There, we too repeatedly encountered objects of the feminine kind and mixed and dwelt together with novices who frequented pleasure groves, and in us too afflictions arose — attachment regarding objects of desire, and aversion and malice arose continually in our mental streams. Has there not now arisen in us a defeat transgression? Come, let us go to where the Venerable Ānanda is, and having gone, let us put this matter fully to him. Whatever the Venerable Ānanda instructs us, exactly that we shall take to heart.

Then they went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, they said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, please know this. The Blessed One established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: 'Furthermore, if a monk, without knowing or fully knowing, claims "I know this, I see this" —

— and that having given rise to that downfall, wishing to purify it, at another time whether asked or not asked, he says: 'Venerable ones, I spoke of knowing what I do not know, and spoke of seeing what I have not seen — I spoke emptily and falsely.' In that case, that monk too has incurred a defeat and is not to remain in the community." — the Blessed One having established this as a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: we who were dwelling in forest lodgings in secluded groves, at the foot of mountains, and on the edges of hayricks, relying upon a certain slight grasping at the defining characteristics that are the basis for calm abiding, and suppressing the afflictions by means of worldly mental application, such that attachment to sense objects and ill will did not arise continuously in our mental streams — we said to one another: "Venerable ones, know this! We have attained what forest-dwellers are supposed to attain. Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and we shall know no further existence beyond this." Having said so, we abandoned our forest lodgings and entered lodgings near villages. And there, repeatedly seeing women as objects of attention and dwelling together and mixing with novices of the pleasure gardens, afflictions arose in us as well — attachment to sense objects and ill will arose continuously in our mental streams. Has there not now arisen in us a defeat transgression? Come, let us go to where the Venerable Ānanda is, and having gone there, let us put this matter fully to him. Whatever the Venerable Ānanda instructs us, exactly that we shall take to heart." And so thinking, we went to put this very matter fully to the Venerable Ānanda.

Then the Venerable Ānanda led those many monks to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable Blessed One, the Blessed One established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: 'Furthermore, if a monk, without knowing or fully knowing, claims — when there is no supreme human Dharma, no attainment of something noble and distinguished, no knowing, no seeing, no touching or entering into it — "I know this, I see this" — and that having given rise to that downfall, wishing to purify it, at another time whether asked or not asked, he says: "Venerable ones, I spoke of knowing what I do not know, and spoke of seeing what I have not seen — I spoke emptily and falsely" — in that case that monk too has incurred a defeat and is not to remain in the community.' — the Blessed One having established this as a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: these venerable ones dwelling in forest lodgings in secluded groves, at the foot of mountains, and on the edges of hayricks, relying upon a certain slight grasping at the defining characteristics that are the basis for calm abiding, and suppressing the afflictions by means of worldly mental application, such that attachment to sense objects and ill will did not arise continuously in their mental streams — they said to one another: 'Venerable ones, know this! We have attained what forest-dwellers are supposed to attain. Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and we shall know no further existence beyond this.'

'Come, let us leave our forest dwellings and take up lodgings on the outskirts of towns.' Having said this, they abandoned their forest dwellings and moved into lodgings near villages. There, encountering women again and again, and living in association with novices who dwelt in pleasure groves, afflictions arose in them — attachment to sense pleasures and ill will arose continuously in their mental streams. And then remorse arose in them, with the thought: 'Has there not occurred in us a defeat, a root downfall?' For that reason I shall fully present this matter to the Blessed One, asking: 'Has there not occurred in them a defeat, a root downfall?'

The Blessed One declared: 'Ānanda, with the exception of conceited presumption, it has not.'

Then the Blessed One, having spoken praise in many categories of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who are equipped with the provisions for training, and having addressed the monks with words consonant with this, weighted toward this, and endowed with qualities appropriate to this, declared to the monks: 'Monks, the former was a rule, and this is a permission. My hearers shall recite the foundational rule of training in the Vinaya in the following way.'

Furthermore, any monk who, without directly knowing or fully knowing, without having the supreme human quality (uttaramanuṣyadharma), its culmination, that which is noble, that which is distinctly attained, the knowledge, the vision, and the direct experience — who, lacking these, claims "I know this" or "I see this," and who, wishing to purify a defeat-level downfall that has arisen, whether questioned at another time or not questioned, says: "Venerable ones, I, for my part, said I knew what I did not know" — who said "I see" what was not seen — if it is said that he spoke a specious lie, then with the exception of conceited presumption, that monk too has incurred defeat and is not to be allowed to remain.

Now the phrase "whatever monk" refers to the four classes of monks, as stated from there onward. In the present context, since it is not appropriate to establish the action of the fourfold assembly with a petition, one should understand "monk" to mean one who has received full ordination, and so on as before. Thus it is that "whatever monk" is taught.

As for the phrase "without directly knowing," what is it that is not directly known? Not directly knowing form, not directly knowing feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

As for "without fully knowing," what is it that is not fully known? Not fully knowing form itself, not fully knowing feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

As for "human quality," this refers to nirvāṇa, the quality belonging to human beings — attained by human beings, yet not attained by eunuchs, hermaphrodites, or those of indeterminate sex, let alone by hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, which goes without saying.

As for "supreme," the form realm is supreme relative to the desire realm, and the formless realm is supreme relative to the form realm.

Alternatively, "human quality" refers to the five hindrances, and "supreme" refers to the abandonment of those same hindrances.

As for "culmination," culmination here means nirvāṇa.

As for "noble," the noble ones are the buddhas and the śrāvakas of the buddhas.

As for "distinctly attained," the distinct attainments are the four fruits of the contemplative life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship.

As for "knowing," the knowings are fourfold: knowing suffering, knowing the origin, knowing cessation, and knowing the path. As for "seeing," the seeings are fourfold: seeing suffering, seeing the origin, seeing cessation, and seeing the path. As for "dwelling in contact," dwelling in contact refers to the four meditative concentrations (dhyānas), and it arises from meditative absorption, not from birth. As for "in the absence of," this means in the absence of that thing's substantiality. As for "while absent," this means with respect to oneself.

As for the phrase "one knows this" — what does one know? One knows suffering, the origin, cessation, and the path.

As for the phrase "one sees this" — what does one see? One sees gods (devas), nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas (Skt. garuḍa), gandharvas (Skt. gandharva), kinnaras (Skt. kinnara), great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas (Skt. kumbhāṇḍa), putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds. And gods in turn see oneself. Nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds in turn see oneself.

One hears the sounds of gods, and the sounds of nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds. And gods in turn hear one's own sound. Nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds in turn hear one's own sound.

One goes to behold gods, and one goes to behold nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds. And gods come to behold oneself. Nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds come to behold oneself.

One converses together with gods, speaks graciously with them, pleases each of them, and always dwells together with them. One converses together with nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds, speaks graciously with them, pleases each of them, and always dwells together with them. Gods in turn converse together with oneself, speak graciously with oneself, are each pleased with oneself, and always dwell together with oneself. Nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras,

great serpents, hungry ghosts, flesh-eaters, kumbhāṇḍas, putrescent ones, body-putrescent ones, and the flesh-eaters of charnel grounds in turn converse together with oneself, speak graciously with oneself, are each pleased with oneself, and always dwell together with oneself.

Without yet having attained them, I have attained the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of selflessness in what is suffering, the perception of repulsion toward food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of faults, the perception of abandonment, the perception of freedom from attachment, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of the bloated, the perception of the festering, the perception of the putrefied, the perception of the worm-eaten, the perception of the devoured, the perception of the blood-red, the perception of the scattered, the perception of a heap of bones, and the perception that individually examines emptiness.

Without yet having attained them, I have attained the first meditative concentration, the second, the third, and the fourth; loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; the sphere of supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of defilements. I am an arhat who meditates on the eight liberations and who is liberated from both sides.

The phrase "from a claim" means: from something one has taken upon oneself. "A transgression arose from that" refers to that very basis. "Wishing to be purified" means wishing to arise and clear oneself. "On some other occasion" means at another time. "Whether asked" means by others. "Whether not asked" means that in oneself remorse, slight remorse, manifest remorse, and deep remorse have arisen. The phrase "having spoken thus, venerable ones, I who did not know have declared that I knew" refers to mental consciousness. "Having declared, I saw what I had not seen" refers to visual consciousness. The phrases "having spoken empty falsehood" and so on are synonymous words for the act of having spoken. "If one says" means if one states it. "Except for overweening pride" means having set aside overweening pride. "Monk" means one who possesses the attributes of a monk, as before. "And that" is a phrase of concise and comprehensive indication. "Has incurred defeat" is as before. "Is not to be maintained" — up to the point of "is not to be appointed by the twelve persons" — is as before, and therefore it is said "is not to be maintained."

Now, how does a transgression arise in regard to this?

Summary verse:
Altering perception, and in forest hermitages
and in households displaying seats,
grasping one's own distinguishing marks,
and presenting oneself — these are the cases.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "I have seen gods," he incurs defeat. With nāgas,

with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "I have seen them," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "I have seen the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "I have heard the sound of the gods," he incurs defeat. With nāgas, with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "I have heard their sound," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "I have heard the sound of the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "I am going in order to see the gods," he incurs defeat. With nāgas, with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "I am going in order to see them," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "I am going in order to see the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "The gods are coming in order to see me," he incurs defeat. With nāgas, with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "They are coming in order to see me," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "Even the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground are coming in order to see me," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "I converse together with the gods, I speak of their comings and goings, I delight each of them individually, and I always dwell together with them," he incurs defeat. With nāgas, with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "I converse together with them, I speak of their comings and goings, I delight each of them individually, and I always dwell together with them," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "I converse together with the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground, I speak of their comings and goings, I delight each of them individually, and I always dwell together with them," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "The gods converse together with me, speak of coming to me, delight me individually, and always dwell together with me," he incurs defeat. With nāgas, with yakṣas, and so on as before, down to decomposing corpses — if he says "They also converse together with me, speak of coming to me, delight me individually, and always dwell together with me," he incurs defeat. Even if he says only this: "Even the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground converse together with me, speak of coming to me, delight me individually, and always dwell together with me," he incurs a grave offense.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, or his view — says "Though I have not attained it, I have attained the perception of impermanence," he incurs defeat. If he says he has attained, beginning with the perception of suffering in impermanence and continuing as before down to the perception that analytically discerns emptiness, he incurs defeat.

If a monk, having altered his perception — having altered his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought,

or his view — says "Though I have not attained it, I have attained the first meditative concentration," he incurs defeat. Likewise, if he says he has attained the second, the third, and the fourth, and, continuing as before, says "I am an arhat accomplished in the eight liberations (vimokṣa), and I am liberated in both respects," he incurs defeat.

Fourteenth fascicle of the Vinaya Analysis.

Now, when a great many monks are dwelling in a wilderness hermitage without a village nearby, and non-human beings are harming them there, and there is among them a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and the non-human beings do not harm that monk — then if another monk, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "I too am dwelling in that wilderness hermitage, and the non-humans do not harm me there," he incurs defeat.

When a great many monks are invited as guests to houses and given food to eat, and striped seats are spread out for them there, and there is among them a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and the striped seats are spread out for that monk — then if another monk, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "I too was invited as a guest to that house and ate there, and striped seats were spread out for me as well," he incurs defeat.
