When a great many monks dwelling in a hermitage, relying upon a slight grasping at the defining characteristic of calm abiding as their basis, suppress their afflictions through a worldly path, so that attachment toward sensual objects and malice do not arise pervasively in their mental continuum — then if a monk, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "I too am dwelling in that wilderness hermitage, and while dwelling there, relying upon a slight grasping at the defining characteristic of calm abiding, I have suppressed my afflictions through a worldly path, so that attachment toward sensual objects and malice do not arise pervasively in my mental continuum," he incurs a grave offense.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk who sees the gods" — and yet does not add "and that monk is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one who sees nāgas, yakṣas," and, continuing as before down to "one who sees decomposing bodies" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Even if he says "There exists a monk who sees the flesh-eaters of the charnel grounds" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk who hears the voices of gods" — and yet does not add "and that monk is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one who hears the voices of nāgas, yakṣas," and, continuing as before down to "one who hears the voices of decomposing bodies" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Even going so far as to say "There exists a monk who goes to see the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk who goes to see the gods" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one who goes to see the nāgas, the yakṣas," and, continuing as before down to "one who goes to see decomposing bodies" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. Even going so far as to say "There exists a monk who goes to see the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk to whom the gods come to see" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one to whom the nāgas, the yakṣas come," and, continuing as before down to "one to whom decomposing bodies come to see" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. Even going so far as to say "There exists a monk to whom the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground come to see" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk who converses together with the gods, who speaks of their comings and goings, who rejoices with each of them individually, and who dwells together with them constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one who converses together with the nāgas, the yakṣas," and, continuing as before down to "one who converses with decomposing bodies, speaks of their comings and goings, rejoices with each of them individually, and dwells together with them constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. Even going so far as to say "There exists a monk who converses together with the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground, who speaks of their comings and goings, who rejoices with each of them individually, and who dwells together with them constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk makes a self-referential disclosure and, having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, says "There exists a monk together with whom the gods converse, speak of their comings and goings, rejoice with him individually, and dwell together with him constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. If he says "There exists one together with whom nāgas, yakṣas," and, continuing as before down to "decomposing bodies converse, speak of their comings and goings, rejoice with him individually, and dwell together with him constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Even if he says "There exists a monk together with whom the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground converse, speak of their comings and goings, rejoice with him individually, and dwell together with him constantly" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

When a monk misrepresents himself, shifting his perception and altering his patience, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, and says "There exists a monk who has attained the perception of impermanence" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. Just as with the perception of impermanence, so too if he says, continuing as before down through the perception of individually discerning emptiness, "There exists one who has attained such" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

When a monk misrepresents himself, shifting his perception and altering his patience, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, and says "There exists a monk who has attained the first meditative concentration (dhyāna)" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense. Just as with the first meditative concentration, so too continuing as before through the second, the third, and the fourth, down to the monk who is an arhat accomplished in the eight liberations and who is liberated through both aspects — if he says "There exists such a one" and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Now, suppose a large number of monks are dwelling in a certain isolated forest hermitage, and non-human beings are afflicting them there. Among those monks there is one who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and the non-human beings do not afflict that one. Then a monk, misrepresenting himself and shifting his perception, alters his patience, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, and says "There exists a monk who dwells in that isolated forest hermitage and whom the non-human beings there do not afflict" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Now, suppose a large number of monks have been invited as guests into households to eat, and there, for them, striped seats have been spread and arranged. Among those monks there is one who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and striped seats are arranged for that one there. Then a monk, misrepresenting himself and shifting his perception, alters his patience, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and his view, and says "There exists a monk who was invited as a guest to that household and dined there, and for whom striped seats are likewise arranged" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Now, suppose a large number of monks dwelling in a forest hermitage, relying upon some small characteristic sign belonging to the defining mark of calm abiding, suppress their afflictions by means of a worldly path, so that attachment to sensual objects and malicious thoughts do not arise continuously in their mental stream. Then a monk, misrepresenting himself and shifting his perception, alters his patience, his desire, his intention, his conceptual thought, and

his view, and says: "Whatever monk dwells in that forest hermitage devoid of a village, and relying upon some small characteristic sign belonging to the defining mark of calm abiding, suppresses afflictions by means of a worldly path, so that attachment to sensual objects and malicious thoughts do not arise continuously in his mental stream — that exists" — and yet does not add "and that is I" — he incurs a grave offense.

Summary verse:

Mutual quarreling,
falling of rain, and the coming of night,
the hot springs of Rājagṛha,
and the sounds of the great elephants.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Pavilion with the Gabled Hall by the shore of the Monkey Pond. At that time, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, and the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī fell into mutual quarreling. Then King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, equipped his fourfold army with its divisions of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, and set about destroying and crushing the outlying territories. The people of the outlying territories who dwelt there sent word to the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, saying: "Wise ones, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, has equipped his fourfold army with its divisions of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, and is crushing and destroying the outlying territories." The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, upon hearing this, likewise equipped their own fourfold army with its divisions of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, and set out from Vaiśālī. As they were setting out, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, early in the morning, having arranged his robes and taken his almsbowl and outer cloak, entered Vaiśālī for alms. The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī caught sight of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana from a great distance. Seeing him, they thought to themselves: "Wise ones, this one is the third highest — it is said that there is nothing whatsoever that he does not know, has not seen, does not understand, or does not cognize. Let us ask him which side we will be victorious on." And so they asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Noble one, since King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, is crushing and destroying the outlying territories, and we are now going forth to do battle, which side will be victorious?" Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied: "People of the Vāsiṣṭha clan, you will be victorious." At those words, they rejoiced, thinking "The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana has prophesied our victory," and gladness, joy, exultation, delight, and happiness arose in them. Without even reckoning with King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, they advanced against him with utter confidence and without hesitation. Then King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, was defeated, terrified, broken, vanquished, and put to flight, and he fled to the bank of the river Gaṅgā. The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī followed right behind him, their minds filled with immense and exuberant joy. And King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, born of Magadha, thought to himself:

"These Licchavīs of Vaiśālī are vicious and crushing in their might. Should I enter the river Gaṅgā, there is every chance that they will drag me out with nets or fish me out with ladles, and torment me in ways utterly unseemly. It is better for me to die by rushing forward to meet them openly." Knowing this, he charged forward with the force of one resolved on death. Then his entire army turned back, and the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were defeated, terrified, broken, vanquished, and put to flight. Without making any detour whatsoever, King Ajātaśatru entered Vaiśālī, shut the gates, raised the drawbridge at the rampart's edge, and remained within. The forces of Ajātaśatru, king of Magadha, son of Vaidehī, having won the battle and overcome and expelled the inhabitants of that land, departed for Rājagṛha. Then the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, on the great roads, the lanes, the crossroads, and the junctions, began to mock, scoff, and jeer, saying: "If the noble great Maudgalyāyana has prophesied our victory, then what sort of victory is this — when Vaiśālī has been taken from us?"

While they were mocking thus, the six monks (the Group of Six) were also out on their alms round, and when they heard the Licchavīs heaping these reproaches on them, the Group of Six said: "Good sirs, whom are you mocking?" The Licchavīs replied: "We are mocking you. The noble great Maudgalyāyana prophesied our victory — so if Vaiśālī has been taken from us, how is that victory?" The Group of Six then said: "Good sirs, who won the very first engagement in battle? We did. If you yourselves were victorious, why then did you turn back afterward? Do you wish to conquer Magadha and seize Rājagṛha? Have you not heard the saying: when pressed too hard, even a fox becomes like a lion?" The Licchavīs had nothing to say and fell silent, at a loss for words. Then the Group of Six said: "Dear friends, that much has been settled for them — but a minor fault has now arisen here. Come back, go before him, and make him acknowledge it." Having performed the duties of the meal, they paid homage and went to where the venerable great Maudgalyāyana was staying. When they arrived, they spoke to the venerable great Maudgalyāyana as follows:

"Homage to the elder. Good health to you, venerable ones. Elder, please open the floor. Venerable ones, we open the floor regarding a downfall in one of the five categories. Elder, did you or did you not prophesy victory to the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī? You did prophesy it. Now if Vaiśālī has been taken from them, how is that a victory? Your black bowl does not feed you — that is why you tell everyone what to do, and yet it comes to nothing. Because you have burned up your alms territory, we cannot even get alms. The transgression that has fallen to you — redress it properly in accordance with the Dharma."

The venerable great Maudgalyāyana replied: "Venerable ones, I see no transgression."

The Group of Six said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that for one who does not see a transgression, the act of suspension must be carried out. Therefore why should we overlook this? Who is the monastery warden? He is someone of importance. Call for him. He has been called. Venerable one, strike the gaṇḍī." "Because the great Maudgalyāyana, for a trifling reason, does not redress a transgression that has occurred, the act of suspension for not seeing a transgression must be carried out." The monastery warden went to the senior elder of the Saṅgha's residence, and the Group of Six went with him. At that time the venerable Śāriputra was serving as the senior elder of the Saṅgha. It was always he who struck the gaṇḍī, and when the venerable one did so, which among the venerable ones would not fully remain?

remained fully, or be fully appeased, or be appeased from the ground, or be expelled" — these options were then examined according to the Dharma, and a resolution was sought. The Group of Six said: "No elder will fully remain, nor remain from the ground, nor be appeased, nor be appeased from the ground, nor be expelled. For the venerable great Maudgalyāyana, by covering up a transgression, causes the teaching of the Blessed One to be torn apart. He does not earn his living by means of a black alms-bowl. Therefore he makes a pledge to a superior person's code, announces it to all, and yet it comes to nothing, and because he has scorched his sphere of conduct, we ourselves cannot obtain alms either. Since a transgression has arisen with regard to him and he does not redress it properly according to the Dharma — because he does not see that transgression — the act of suspension must now be carried out."

The venerable monks struck the gaṇḍī for the elder monk, and said: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, sees all things, and has attained supreme sovereignty over knowledge and all that is to be known; he cuts through every doubt. Go before him and present this matter. Receive precisely what the Blessed One pronounces as his ruling, and hold to it as it truly is."

At that time the monks made their appeal to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, in battle, non-humans engage in combat first, and afterward humans engage in combat. Wherever the non-humans emerge victorious, humans too emerge victorious. Therefore, monks, when the great Maudgalyāyana made that prophecy to the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, it was at that very moment that the non-humans of Vaiśālī defeated the non-humans of Rājagṛha. And when those armies went to the bank of the Ganges, the non-humans of Rājagṛha defeated the non-humans of Vaiśālī. Now if the great Maudgalyāyana were to be asked about that as well, the great Maudgalyāyana would give prophecy about that too. Monks, there is no transgression in the great Maudgalyāyana having given prophecy with such an understanding. Just as the people of Vaiśālī won first, and later King Ajātaśatru defeated them on the bank of the Ganges by the force of death, so too in like manner it was King Ajātaśatru who won first, and afterward those people of Vaiśālī defeated him on the bank of the Ganges by the force of death — and this account should be set out in full."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Peaked House in the great forest near the Monkey Pond. At that time the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) announced that in twelve years a drought would come.

The venerable great Maudgalyāyana dressed in his robe in the morning, took up his alms-bowl and his monastic robe, and entered Vaiśālī to seek alms. The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī asked him: "Noble one, how long before the gods will send rain?" He said: "Friends of wisdom, after seven days have passed." Those people then announced: "The noble great Maudgalyāyana has prophesied that after seven days the gods will send rain." And so they took whatever grain was stored in their houses and storerooms and carried it outside and discarded it.

When precisely seven days had passed, the gods sounded thunder and the sky rumbled, and having split the earth open they sent forth rain. And those people were standing in the great avenues, the market streets, the crossroads, and the three-way junctions, saying: "Friends of wisdom, the non-Buddhists are truly holy —

"The śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), the sons of the Śākyan, are not like that — they simply wander about like moving trees, their bodies wrapped in saffron robes, and they know nothing whatsoever." And so they mocked, ridiculed, and reviled them.

While those people were mocking them in this way, the Group of Six had also gone out for alms, and hearing those people mock them, the Group of Six said: "Friends of wisdom, whom are you mocking?" "We are mocking you." "What have we done? The non-Buddhists proclaimed that in twelve years a famine would come, and the noble great Maudgalyāyana prophesied that after seven days had passed the gods would send rain. We took whatever grain was stored in our houses and storerooms and carried it outside and discarded it, and then the gods did not send rain." The Group of Six said: "Friends of wisdom, as for the conduct of non-Buddhists — even if there were clouds, even if thunder were to rumble from those clouds, even if lightning were to flash, even if a cool wind were to rise from the four directions, and even if the gods were to send just a slight drizzle of rain drop by drop, that is when they and the world would indeed say the gods without fail will send rain. So when heavy rain fell and split open the earth, what need is there even to speak of it? In this way, just as the noble great Maudgalyāyana prophesied, all the crops shall come to fruition." At these words, those people were rendered speechless and stood there in silence.

Then the Group of Six said: "Dear friends, we have made it clear enough to those people; nevertheless, a minor transgression has arisen in this matter, so come here. Go in their stead and make them feel at ease." Having done them the service of food and having paid homage, they went to where the venerable great Maudgalyāyana was and, having gone there, they said this to the venerable great Maudgalyāyana: "Venerable one, we pay homage. Venerables, be well. Venerable one, please open the matter when the time is right. Venerables, please open the matter regarding the five classes of transgression. The non-Buddhists proclaimed that in twelve years a famine would come, and you prophesied that rain would fall. If the hem of a monastic robe has been made improper by being soiled by mud, then since that is improper, take it off. Since you do not live by a black alms bowl, on that account everyone who knows is giving signs — and that too has come to nothing. Since you have burned up your domain of alms, we cannot even find alms. A transgression has arisen in you; please rectify it in accordance with the Dharma." The venerable one said: "Venerables, I see no transgression." The Group of Six said: "Venerables, the Blessed One has said that because one who does not see a transgression must be suspended from the community, therefore why should one be especially indifferent in this matter? Who is the guardian of the residence? Something quite important is happening. Summon him! He has been summoned." "Venerables, strike the wooden signal-board." "Since the great Maudgalyāyana, having committed a minor transgression, will not rectify it in accordance with the Dharma, let the act of suspension from the community be performed because he does not see the transgression."

The guardian of the residence went to where the Saṅgha's elder was, and the Group of Six went along with him. At that time the venerable Śāriputra was serving as elder of the Saṅgha. Whenever the wooden signal-board was struck, he would investigate in accordance with the Dharma which venerable one was fully present, or fully present from the beginning, or to be satisfied, or to be satisfied from the beginning, or to be expelled. The Group of Six said: "Venerable elder, no one is fully present, fully present from the beginning, to be satisfied, to be satisfied from the beginning, or to be expelled —

"For it is in this way that the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, through a transgression involving a physical fall, tears apart the teaching of the Blessed One. Because he does not live off a black alms-bowl, he claims mastery of the Dharma of men and proclaims to all that he knows — yet that too has come to nothing. He has burnt up his domain of activity, so that we cannot even find alms. When a transgression arises, he does not restore it in accordance with the Dharma, and so, since he dwells in non-acknowledgment of that transgression, we shall carry out the act of suspension."

The venerable ones said to the elder of the Saṅgha at the striking of the wooden signal-board: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, all-seeing, sovereign over knowledge and over all objects of knowledge without peer, and he cuts through all doubt. Therefore go before him today and present this matter. Whatever authoritative instruction the Blessed One gives you, accept it exactly as it is."

At that point the monks petitioned the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, even when rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they may proclaim — it is a great, overwhelming torrent that does not comprehend, and has five causes and five conditions. What are those five? It is like this: there are clouds, lightning flashes, thunder rolls from the clouds, cool winds arise from the four directions, and rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim. Yet because the fire element rises up exceedingly from within this great earth, it dries up that very rain before it has fallen halfway. This is how rain-callers may cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim — yet it is not understood: this is the first cause and the first condition for a great overwhelming torrent.

Furthermore, there are clouds, lightning flashes, thunder rolls from the clouds, cool winds arise from the four directions, and rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim. Yet because unequal winds arise in the sky, they carry that rain off to the forests of Daṇḍaka, and to the forests of Kaliṅga, and to the forests of Mataṅga. This is how rain-callers may cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim — yet it is not understood: this is the second cause and the second condition for a great overwhelming torrent.

Furthermore, there are clouds, lightning flashes, thunder rolls from the clouds, cool winds arise from the four directions, and rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim. Yet because the rain-bearing divine sons abide in utter intoxication and heedlessness, and abiding in utter intoxication and heedlessness, the gods do not cause the stream of water to flow down well at the proper times. This is how rain-callers may cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim — yet it is not understood: this is the third cause and the third condition for a great overwhelming torrent.

Furthermore, there are clouds, lightning flashes, thunder rolls from the clouds, cool winds arise from the four directions, and rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim. Yet because people are attached with unlawful desire, overwhelmed by the delight of craving, and bound by wrong conduct — those who are so attached with unlawful desire, overwhelmed by the delight of craving, and bound by wrong conduct — the gods do not cause the stream of water to flow down well for them at the proper times. This is how rain-callers may cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim — yet it is not understood: this is the fourth cause and the fourth condition for a great overwhelming torrent.

Furthermore, there are clouds, lightning flashes, thunder rolls from the clouds, cool winds arise from the four directions, and rain-callers cause the gods to bring down rain — this they proclaim. Yet —"

Yet the lord of the asuras (demigods) named Thunderous rises up from the great ocean and catches that rain in both hands, pouring it back into the great ocean. This is what rain-callers proclaim as the gods bringing down rain — yet it is not understood: this is the fifth cause and the fifth condition for a great overwhelming torrent.

Monks, thus, even when the gods have brought down rain at that time, the lord of the asuras named Thunderous rises up from the great ocean and catches that rain in both hands and pours it into the great ocean. Will all crops nonetheless come to completion?" — so one might ask. And if, monks, that question were put to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he would prophesy accordingly. Monks, there is no transgression for the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in making a prophecy with such a perception.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Monkey Pond pavilion, in the multi-storied hall. At that time there was living at Vaiśālī a śrāvaka of the naked ascetics, and his wife had become pregnant. On another occasion, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana dressed in the morning, took up his bowl and robe, and entered Vaiśālī for alms. As he was going on his alms round in sequence, he entered that man's house. The man thought to himself: "The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is said to be supreme among three — one in whom there is not even a trace of unknowing, unseeing, ignorance, or lack of discernment. I should ask him to declare whether this pregnant wife of mine will give birth to a boy or a girl." So, realizing this, he spoke these words to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Noble one, this attendant of mine is pregnant — is there a boy in her womb, or is there a girl?" He replied: "Good sir, it is a boy."

The householder, wishing for prosperity as worldly people do, was satisfied, joyful, and greatly delighted. He filled the bowl of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana with clean and pure food and drink, gave it to him, and said: "Noble one, please proceed." The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said "Thank you" and departed.

Not far from that house, a naked ascetic who was sitting there saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana go off with a full bowl. He thought to himself: "The only house that gives alms to me alone — it is not good that the monks, the sons of the Śākyan, should now frequent it. I will therefore go quickly to that householder and ask what conversation he had with him." He went swiftly to the householder and said: "Householder, did the ascetic Mahāmaudgalyāyana come?" "He came." "Did he ask you something?" "He did." "What did he ask?" "He asked whether, this attendant of mine being pregnant, there was a boy in the womb or a girl." "And what was said?" "He said it was a boy."

The naked ascetic was skilled in reckoning by inferential reasoning, and began to calculate. After a moment, seeing it as a girl, he changed his account accordingly and twisted his hands together. The householder asked the naked ascetic: "Why do you change your expression and twist your hands together?" The naked ascetic said: "I see a girl — I do not see a boy." The householder immediately flew into a rage, rose up, drew his three topknots erect and furrowed his brow in anger, saying: "You wretched naked ascetic, what do you know? Do you dare to impugn the knowledge of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana as defiled? The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana has prophesied that it is a boy —

"Do you dare say it is a girl?" And with that rebuke he began to calculate again, and seeing it was indeed a girl, he was completely flustered and said: "Even if the ascetic, the son of the Śākyas, has given a prophecy to that effect, still this is a girl and not a boy." When the nine months had passed and the birth occurred, a girl was indeed born. The householder, together with his household, declared that the naked ascetics were the true ones, and that the ascetics who were sons of the Śākyas were not so: "When the great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana prophesied that it was a boy, it has turned out to be a girl." And so they began to slander them, to mock them publicly, and to speak ill of them. The word spread from one person to the next, and the crowds of people dwelling in Vaiśālī, on the main roads, in the markets, at crossroads and at intersections, all fell to slandering. While they were slandering them, the Group of Six, in the morning, having put on their lower robes, took up their bowls and outer robes and went out to beg alms in Vaiśālī. They heard those people slandering them, and upon hearing it they said: "Good people, whom are you slandering?" "We are slandering you." "What have we done?" "The great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana prophesied that there was a boy in the womb of the naked ascetic's wife, and yet from it a girl was born." The Group of Six said: "Good people, in an ocean of knowledge spanning the whole world there can be mistakes. Only the Blessed One alone is the protector of phenomena; there is no other protector. Furthermore, when humans give birth, they give birth to either a boy or a girl — what other distinguishing mark could there be? Do you suppose it might be a dog, or perhaps a monkey?" Those people were left speechless and stood there unable to say a thing. Then the Group of Six said: "Friends, we have already made it clear enough to them; but a minor downfall has arisen over this small matter, so come back. Go before him and make your confession." And having eaten their meal, they paid homage and went directly to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, and addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thus: "Venerable one, we pay homage. May the venerable ones be well and free from illness. Venerable elder, please open a session. Venerable ones, we open a session regarding the five categories of downfalls. Venerable elder, did you or did you not prophesy that there was a boy in the womb of the naked ascetic's wife?" "I did prophesy it. Depart now, and may you experience joy and increase, and may you obtain grain, butter, and sugar. Since you do not sustain yourselves from a black bowl, the omniscient one gives signs of it — yet even that has come to nothing. Because you have scorched our alms-round territory, we cannot even obtain alms; and a downfall has arisen for you over this, so restore it properly in accordance with the Dharma." "Venerable ones, we do not see a downfall." The Group of Six said: "Venerable ones, since the Blessed One has declared that when a downfall is not seen, the act of formal suspension from residence should be performed, why then should we be indifferent to this? Who is the guardian of the house? It must be someone of importance. Summon him!" "He has been summoned." "Venerable one, sound the gong. Mahāmaudgalyāyana has incurred a downfall over a trifling matter and does not restore it properly; therefore, since he does not see the downfall, the act of formal suspension from residence is to be performed." The house-guardian went before the Saṅgha's elder, and the Group of Six went along with him. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra was serving as the Saṅgha's elder.

Whenever the gong was sounded, the venerable monks would ask, in the proper form of a Dharma matter, who was in residence, who had taken up residence from the beginning, who was to be made content, who was to be made content from the beginning, and who was being expelled. The Group of Six said: "No elder whatsoever is in residence, has taken up residence from the beginning, is to be made content, is to be made content from the beginning, or is being expelled. For the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana incurs a downfall through a fault of dissimulation and thereby tears apart the teaching of the Blessed One; he does not sustain himself by the black bowl, so he claims for himself the highest human Dharma and makes known to all that he is one who knows — yet this too has come to nothing, for he has consumed the alms-field and we cannot even obtain alms. Since a downfall has arisen and he does not restore it properly in accordance with the Dharma, and since he does not see the downfall, we will perform the act of formal suspension from residence." The venerable monks replied to the elder monk with words not befitting a monk: "The Blessed One, the buddha, is omniscient, sees all, has attained unsurpassed sovereignty over knowledge and objects of knowledge, and dispels all doubt. Go before him today and request this matter from him. Whatever the Blessed One proclaims to you, accept that as it truly is."

At that time the monks made their request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, these four domains are not to be speculated about. Those who engage in speculation about them will become intoxicated, bewildered, and will come to distraction of mind. What are the four? They are: speculation about the self, speculation about the world, speculation about the karmic maturation of sentient beings, and the buddha-domain of buddhas. Now, when the monk Maudgalyāyana made the prophecy at that time, that person was still a child; later, through the maturation of his karma, he became marked in that way. If the monk Maudgalyāyana had been asked further about that matter, the monk Maudgalyāyana would have prophesied further. Monks, there is no downfall for the monk Maudgalyāyana in having made a prophecy with such a perception."

The Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. In Rājagṛha there was a householder who heard it said that whoever gave food to the monastic Saṅgha of monks without making individual distinctions among them would in that very moment experience a great flourishing of wealth. Having heard this, he thought to himself: "That is an excellent method for acquiring wealth; I too shall give food to the monastic Saṅgha of monks without making individual distinctions." So he went to the market, bought a great deal of meat, and beneath it boiled a broth mixed with a great quantity of clarified butter in a copper vessel. He then sent word to the gatekeeper at the city gate: "Ho there, gatekeeper! If any monk enters for alms, send him to my house." The gatekeeper replied: "Householder, it shall be done." Whenever he saw a monk entering for alms, he said: "Noble one, a certain great householder today is offering alms to the monks; please go inside to him." And that monk went to his house. In this way the gatekeeper conveyed the message to all those on alms-round, and all those on alms-round went to the householder's house. The householder then filled each of their bowls with a very rich meat-broth and gave it to them.

That day the sky became overcast and the weather turned foul. The monks, having eaten, found they could not scrub those greasy bowls clean on the spot, and so they said: "There is hot water here; let us go to where the hot water is and wash them." So they went to where the hot water was and began to wash them.

Now, a young monk happened to wonder, with genuine curiosity, where this hot water was coming from. Not far away, the venerable Ānanda was washing his bowl. The young monk went over to him and asked: "Venerable Ānanda, where does this hot water come from?" Not far from there, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also washing his bowl. Ānanda said: "Go to him and ask about this small matter." So the young monk was sent to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The young monk approached him with a calm and dignified bearing, and asked with reverence: "Elder, where does this hot water come from?" He replied: "Venerable one, it comes from the great lake Anavatapta." When Ānanda heard this, he said: "Venerable one, do not harm the intent of the sūtras. Do not disturb the guidance of the Dharma. Do not break open the womb of the Dharma. Even if we ourselves have no direct realization of this, is there not scripture? The Blessed One has declared that the water of the great lake Anavatapta is endowed with eight qualities: it is cool, it is sweet, it is light, it is soft, it is clear, it is free from foul smell, it does not harm the throat when drunk, and it does not harm the stomach when drunk. Therefore, you have been deceived by the very first quality alone. You do not sustain yourself by a black alms-bowl, and so you make a display of knowing everything to no effect — and that too has come to nothing. Because you have scorched your own domain, we cannot even obtain alms. The transgression that has arisen for you — please restore it in accordance with the Dharma." "Venerable one, I see no transgression." The group of six monks then said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that for one who does not see a transgression, the act of formal suspension should be carried out. Therefore, why should we simply remain indifferent in this matter? Who is the monastery warden? He is quite something! Call him! Call him!" "Venerable one, strike the board." "Since the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has committed a transgression in this minor matter and will not restore it in accordance with the Dharma, the act of formal suspension for not seeing a transgression should be carried out against him." The monastery warden went to the elder of the Saṅgha, and the group of six went along with him. At that time the venerable Śāriputra was serving as the elder of the Saṅgha. Whenever the board was regularly struck, the venerable ones would be asked, as a matter of Dharma, who should be upheld, who should be upheld from the beginning, who should be satisfied, who should be satisfied from the beginning, and who should be removed. The group of six monks said: "Elder, no one is to be upheld, upheld from the beginning, satisfied, satisfied from the beginning, or removed. For the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana tears apart the teaching of the Blessed One with contaminating transgressions. He does not sustain himself by a black alms-bowl, and so he makes a display to humans of claiming a supreme teacher and knowing everything — and that too has come to nothing. Because he has scorched his own domain, we cannot obtain alms. Since he does not restore the transgression that has arisen in accordance with the Dharma, the act of formal suspension for not seeing a transgression should be carried out against him." "Venerable ones, it is not right to treat a senior monk of the Saṅgha in this way. The buddha Blessed One is omniscient, all-seeing, and has attained unsurpassed sovereignty over knowledge and its objects, and he cuts through all doubt. Go to him today and ask about this matter. Whatever the Blessed One declares to you, take it as it truly is." At that time the monks made their petition to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is indeed so. It is indeed so. That warm water comes from none other than the great unheated lake." The monks asked: "Blessed One, if that water comes from the great unheated lake, why is it warm?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is because that water passes over five hundred hells of short-lived beings as it flows down. If the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana were also asked about this, he too would give the same answer by scripture. Monks, there is no transgression in the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana having given a scriptural answer with a perception of that kind." The buddha Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the monks: "Venerable ones, while I had entered into meditative absorption on the sense base of nothingness, I heard on the bank of a slowly flowing pool the sounds of a great many chief elephants." At that time the venerable Ānanda was present right there in that company, and being in agreement he said: "Venerable one, do not harm the boundaries of the sūtra collections. Do not disturb the guide of the Dharma. Do not split open the womb of the Dharma. Although we have no such realization, is there also no scriptural authority for it? The Blessed One has declared that one who has entered into the meditative absorption on the sense base of nothingness has dismantled the perception of form and is separated from the perception of sound — therefore it is impossible that one who has dismantled the perception of form and is separated from the perception of sound should see forms and hear sounds. You do not sustain yourself by means of a black begging bowl, so you present yourself as all-knowing, and that too has come to nothing. You have scorched your alms-round domain, so we too cannot find alms. A transgression has arisen in you — restore it in accordance with the Dharma." The venerable one replied: "I do not see a transgression."

The group of six said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One should carry out the act of formal suspension for not seeing a transgression against him." They said this, and therefore: "Why in this matter should one be further treated with equanimity? Who is the room-guardian? Something has happened. Call someone. He has been called." "Venerable one, strike the wooden signal board. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has not restored in accordance with the Dharma a transgression that arose in a minor matter — carry out against him the act of formal suspension for not seeing a transgression." The room-guardian went to the place where the Saṅgha's senior monks were staying, and the group of six went along with him. At that time the venerable Śāriputra was presiding as senior monk of the Saṅgha. When the wooden board was continually struck, the venerable ones would ask, as a matter of Dharma, which monk among them was to be fully sustained, or completely sustained from the ground up, or satisfied, or satisfied from the ground up, or expelled. The group of six said: "No senior monk here is to be fully sustained, or completely sustained from the ground up, or satisfied, or satisfied from the ground up, or expelled — for the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana the Great, through a transgression he has fallen into, is tearing apart the teaching of the Blessed One. He does not sustain himself by a black begging bowl, and so he claims to know all things and presents himself as omniscient, and that too has come to nothing. He has scorched his alms-round domain, so we too find no alms. Since he does not restore in accordance with the Dharma the transgression that has arisen in him, and since he does not see a transgression, we shall carry out the act of formal suspension for not seeing a transgression. Venerable ones, the wooden signal board was struck against the senior monk of the Saṅgha without proper cause, in this manner: 'The buddha Blessed One is omniscient —

all-seeing, who has attained supreme mastery over what is to be known and over knowledge, who cuts through all doubt — go and present this matter to him today. Whatever the Blessed One declares to you, receive it as exactly so.'

At that point the monks appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, it is exactly so. It is exactly so. One who has entered meditative absorption into the sense base of nothingness, having dissolved the perception of form and being dissociated from the perception of sound — such a one, having dissolved the perception of form and being dissociated from the perception of sound, will not come to see forms nor come to hear sounds. That is not a possibility. Now, the monk Maudgalyāyana has attained the dhyānas, liberations, meditative absorptions, and meditative attainments. He enters and rises from these absorptions swiftly, and by this swiftness he is aware of the mind in meditative absorption yet unaware of the mind as it is arising. Monks, it was upon emerging that the monk Maudgalyāyana heard that sound. Monks, for the monk Maudgalyāyana there is no transgression in having made such a declaration with a perception of that kind. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, or who is mad, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by feeling. The fourth defeat is complete. The defeats are complete.'

The Vinaya, the Vibhaṅga, the fifteenth fascicle. Summary verse: emission of semen, lewd speech, flattery, a hut, a large dwelling, groundlessness, a slight thing, schism in the Saṅgha and siding with it, defaming a household, and a declaration causing discomfort of mind.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Charka's daily practice was this: whichever village or town he was residing near, he would rise early in the morning, go to the shrine hall, sweep it carefully, wash it well, and daub it with a paste of fresh cow dung. Then, outside the shrine hall, he would wash both feet, extend both hands, discard his tooth-stick, and in the early morning put on his lower robe. Taking his bowl and monastic robe, he would go into that very village or town to collect alms without guarding his body, without restraining his faculties, without establishing mindfulness. Having completed his alms round through that village or town and finished the meal, returning from the subsequent alms round for food he would set down his bowl and monastic robe, wash both feet, and enter the shrine hall in order to settle properly inside.

If at that time his mind became thoroughly bound by attachment to desire, he would make the form of his own limbs serviceable, grasp with both hands, exert himself, and emit semen.

Then, as a great many monks were wandering and walking through the shrine hall, they went over to where the venerable Charka was in the shrine hall. Coming there, they engaged in various conversations with the venerable Charka that were pleasing and gratifying, and then sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the many monks said to the venerable Charka: 'Venerable one, how do you endure? How do you fare? Do you dwell in the touch of ease? Have you not grown weary from the alms round?' The venerable Charka replied: 'Venerable ones, I endure well. I fare well. I dwell in the touch of ease. I have not grown weary from the alms round.' 'Venerable Charka, how you endure, how you fare,

dwelling in the touch of ease, and not growing weary from the alms round — venerable ones, the village or township upon which I depend and where I dwell: in the early morning I rise and go to the shrine hall, where I sweep and clean it thoroughly, smear it with a plaster of fresh cow dung, wash both feet outside the shrine hall, rinse my hands, set aside my tooth-stick, dress in my lower robe in the morning, take up my bowl and outer robe, and enter that very village or township for alms. Having collected alms in that same village or township, I perform the meal, and upon returning from the later alms collection I set aside my bowl and outer robe, wash both feet, and enter the shrine hall to settle properly within. If desire with its attachment should come to envelop my mind, I bring the limbs of my body into a serviceable condition, take them in both hands, work at it, and draw off the seminal fluid, so that I am free of fever, free of the burning that afflicts the whole body, and thus dwell in the touch of ease without weariness from the alms round. That, venerable ones, is how I endure, how I fare, how I dwell in the touch of ease, and how I am not wearied from the alms round.'

The monks neither praised nor contradicted what he had said; they neither applauded nor refuted it. Rising from their seats, they went to where the Blessed One was. Having gone there, they bowed their heads to the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, those many monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this circumstance, assembled the community of monks. The Tathāgata, perceiving both aspects of purpose, assembled the community of monks — that is, so that his hearers might come to know it fully, and so that a rule of training properly grounded in the Vinaya might be established. The blessed buddhas take action knowingly: they act knowingly, they do not act unknowingly; they act at the right time, they do not act at the wrong time; they act when there is purpose, they do not act when there is no purpose. Because the blessed buddhas do not act when there is no purpose, they repel pointless action with a water-strainer. And because the blessed buddhas know the right moment for purposeful action, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Charka: 'Charka, is it true that you did something as unseemly as this?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' The Blessed One said: 'That which is contrary to a monk's rule of conduct, not in harmony with it, not permissible, not in accord with the discipline — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Charka, I have taught the Dharma — the liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom — precisely in order to abandon attachment, to become free of attachment; I have taught the liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom in order to abandon aversion, to become free of attachment to it; and in order to abandon delusion, to become free of attachment to it. Why then did you do something as unseemly as this? You who are not deluded — why, with the very hands by which you receive what is given in faith by brahmin and householder faithful donors, did you do something as unseemly as this? You who are not deluded — you who are like a black snake spreading venom swiftly, a virulent poison —

it would be better to grasp it with both hands in that venomous state. For one who has fallen into that condition to take hold of the limbs of one's own body is not acceptable." Thus he rebuked him in every way.

"Cāraka, what do you think? Has your own body not been treated with due respect and care?" "Venerable one, it has indeed."

Then the Blessed One, having rebuked him with many expressions of censure, spoke to the monks: "Monks, seeing clearly ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — namely: for the sake of uniting the Saṅgha; for the sake of making the Saṅgha excellent; for the sake of the Saṅgha's comfortable dwelling; for the sake of restraining those individuals who are brazen and disrespectful; for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of those who are conscientious; for the sake of those who have not yet developed faith developing faith; for the sake of those who already have faith increasing and growing; for the sake of restraining the defilements of this present life; for the sake of turning back the defilements of future lives; and so that the holy life I have taught, which is of broad benefit to many beings, may long endure and be genuinely revealed to gods and humans alike. My hearers are to proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya in the following manner: 'If one intentionally emits semen, this is a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.'" The Blessed One thus established that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, a great many monks, while sleeping, had nocturnal emissions during their dreams, and semen was released. In those monks there was both perception and intention, and so remorse arose in them. They thought: "The Blessed One has established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers, declaring, 'If one intentionally emits semen, this is a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.' Now we, a great many monks lying asleep, have had nocturnal emissions during our dreams, and semen has been released. Since there was both perception and intention in us, has a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense occurred for us or not? Let us go to the venerable Ānanda and, having gone, tell him what has happened. Whatever instruction the venerable Ānanda gives us, we shall take that as authoritative."

Then those many monks went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, they said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, please hear this. The Blessed One has established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: 'If one intentionally emits semen, this is a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.' Now we, a great many monks lying asleep, had nocturnal emissions during our dreams and semen was released. Since there was both perception and intention in us, has a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense occurred for us or not?"

Then the venerable Ānanda led those many monks to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable Blessed One, you have established this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers: 'If one intentionally emits semen, this is a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.' Now here are these many venerable monks who, while lying asleep and during their dreams, had nocturnal emissions and semen was released.

"For these monks there was both perception and intention — has a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense therefore not arisen for them?"

The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, I do not say that these monks had neither perception nor intention — they did have both. But their perception and intention in this matter are not to be reckoned in the conventional way. Therefore, Ānanda, this is the exception for dreams."

Then the Blessed One uttered words of praise for those who desire the training, who revere the training, and who are furnished with the requisites for the training, and having done so, he delivered to the monks a discourse in accordance with this matter, extensive in its treatment and harmonious in character. He then addressed the monks thus:

"Monks, what was stated before was a rule, and what is now given is a permission. My hearers should recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: 'If one intentionally emits semen, save in a dream, this is a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.'"

The word "intentionally" means after deliberate consideration. The word "semen" refers to semen of five kinds: blue, yellow, red, thick, and thin. Of these, blue semen belongs to a wheel-turning king. Also blue is the semen of whichever eldest son of a wheel-turning king has reached the appropriate stage — eligible for enthronement but not yet enthroned. Yellow belongs to the other sons of a wheel-turning king. Red belongs to those on the periphery of the great wheel-domain, that is, those at the rim of the realm. Thick belongs to those whose faculties are fully matured. Thin belongs to those whose faculties are not yet fully matured. Also thin is the semen of one exhausted by a woman, exhausted by a burden, exhausted by the road, one who is old, or one who is in a state of decline.

The phrase "emits" means discharged immediately, that is, at once. The phrase "save in a dream" means setting aside the case of dreaming. The phrase "saṅghāvaśeṣa offense" means that this transgression depends upon the Saṅgha, is connected with the Saṅgha, and relies upon the Saṅgha — that is, one is lifted from this transgression by the Saṅgha, not by an individual. Moreover, the other four offenses entailing defeat have no remainder, whereas this one has a remainder; that is why it is called a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

As to how a transgression comes about in this case: it does so through five factors — desiring pleasure, desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

How does it come about through desiring pleasure? If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, holds it tightly, holds it firmly, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, holds it tightly, holds it firmly, and thereby also experiences and undergoes the pleasure of particular definite sensation, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, holds it tightly, holds it firmly, and thereby also experiences and undergoes the pleasure of arising contact, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, holds it tightly, holds it firmly, and thereby also experiences and undergoes the pleasure of emanating fragrance, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

If a monk, desiring pleasure, takes up and dwells upon an internal physical object, makes an effort, holds it tightly, holds it firmly, and thereby also experiences and undergoes the pleasure of particular definite sensation, the pleasure of arising contact, and the pleasure of rising fragrance, and emits semen, this becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a grave offense. And just as in the case of desiring pleasure, so too with desiring seed, desiring the power of a spell, desiring medicine, and desiring examination.

And just as with an internal physical object, so too the same exposition applies in full to taking up an external physical object.

The intermediate summary verse:

Moving and moving greatly,
space, force, and entering into a hollow,
rubbing all over and particular sensation,
measuring and looking,
turning back from a flowing stream and turning back from urine —
these are the collected categories.

If a monk emits semen through moving, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk emits semen through moving greatly, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk emits semen by gyrating the hips in the air, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk emits semen by applying force, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk emits semen that has entered into a hollow, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk experiences the pleasure of rubbing all over and emits semen, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk experiences the pleasure of particular definite sensation and emits semen, it becomes a grave offense. If no semen is emitted, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk, with a mind of complete attachment, measures the appearance of his own limbs, it becomes a grave offense. If a monk, with a mind of attachment, looks upon the appearance of his own limbs, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk, with a mind of attachment, directs the appearance of his own limbs against the current of a flowing stream, it becomes a grave offense. If he directs it with the current of the stream, it becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk, with a mind of attachment, directs the appearance of his own limbs in a direction other than toward urine, it becomes a grave offense. If he directs it in the direction of urine, it becomes a wrongdoing.

Wounds, swellings, scabies, leprosy, pustules, dropsy,

mange, swelling, pimples, discharges jumping outward, discharges jumping into a pool, contact with the thigh, contact with clothing, seeing forms that would produce attachment, recalling a previously enjoyed place, and emission that occurs as a result of undergoing a sweat-house treatment — in none of these cases is there a transgression. There is no transgression either for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is overcome by sensations. This concludes the first part of the chapter on the Saṅgha's rule against causing emission.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The conduct of the group of six was this: "We shall teach the Dharma to the brahmins and householders who come and arrive here; we shall defeat our opponents; and we shall proclaim our own renown." And so, not leaving the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended, some member of the group of six would rise at dawn before everyone else, discard the tooth-stick, put on a dyed reddish-yellow robe, and stand or sit at the gate of the Jeta Grove.

Now the conduct of the wives of the brahmins and householders living in Śrāvastī was to go to the park, enter the Jeta Grove, visit the temple, and go to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, the monks, and the elders. And so a great many wives of brahmins and householders had come out to the park, wishing to visit the temple, and made their way toward the Jeta Grove.

The group of six knew that among the people dwelling in those six great cities, there was not a single person whom they did not know by clan, by family line, by lineage, by name, by physical appearance, by craft, or by livelihood — none who was unseen, unheard of, unknown, or unrecognized. And so when Venerable Cāraka saw that great multitude of wives of brahmins and householders from quite some distance away, he said: "Welcome, mothers of the elder! Welcome, wives of the elder! Welcome, daughters-in-law of the elder! Welcome, daughters of the elder! Welcome, sisters of the elder! You are very welcome, you are very welcome! Why do you wander about for so long, like the moon?"

They replied: "Venerable Cāraka, since the Blessed One has well declared that the eight inopportune times are not the time for a person to practice the holy life, we — being burdened with the busyness of household life — are in the ninth inopportune condition."

Cāraka said: "Sisters, have you not heard someone say:

The deeds of kings such as those tainted with poison
and so on, left undone —
those very beings and their deeds alike
have come to ruin.
And even those very deeds,
before they could be fully accomplished,
death, the enemy of the world,
will come."

They replied: "Venerable Cāraka, it is precisely for that reason that we have come to the park — to enter the Jeta Grove, to visit the temple, and to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, the monks, and the elders."

Cāraka said: "Sisters, if that is why you have come, then the Blessed One has also declared, 'One should extract what is essential from a body that has nothing essential.' Excellent, excellent! Sisters, go in and look about just as one watches a spectacle and ask whatever you wish. Sisters, where do you intend to enter?"

"Venerable Cāraka, we wish to enter the monastery and visit the temple."

"Sisters, the Blessed One has said:

A wise person who directs the mind with care —"

"When one circumambulates the buddha stūpas, even a hundred thousand measures of gold from the Jambu River cannot equal the merit of a single step."

Having spoken thus, Cāraka said: "Excellent! Sisters, have you found any monk who will show you the temple?" The women replied: "Noble one, should we enter carrying our lamps on their stands and then go looking elsewhere? Venerable Cāraka, why leave here to seek another monk? Who among others is more distinguished than you? Please, show it to us yourself."

Then the venerable Cāraka thought to himself: "If I show them the temple, it may cause my own wholesome side to decline entirely. But if I do not show them, I will not receive so much as a scorched morsel of alms — and moreover, the Blessed One has declared that one should cause those who lack faith to take on a full and genuine faith, that one should tame them, hold them, and establish them well. Therefore I must engage these women in virtue and show them everything completely." Recognizing this, he took up various offerings — flowers, incense, and the like — held an alms bowl in his hand, and began to show them the temple in proper order.

"Sisters, this is the Blessed One's bathhouse. Here, three times by day and three times by night, the Blessed One surveys the world with the eye of a buddha and knows: who is declining, who is progressing, who has come to harm, who has fallen into distress, who has become unhappy, who has come to harm, distress, and misery, who is heading toward the lower destinies, who is about to fall into the lower destinies, who has fallen into the lower destinies — and those who have fallen into the path of the lower destinies I shall raise up and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruit. Those sinking in the mire of desire I shall draw out by the hand. Those who lack the wealth of the noble ones I shall establish in possession of the noble ones' wealth. The world adorned by the arising of a buddha I shall cause to bear its fruit. Those whose roots of virtue have not yet been planted, I shall cause them to be planted. Those whose roots of virtue have been planted, I shall cause them to fully ripen. Those whose roots of virtue have fully ripened, I shall cause them to be completely liberated."

With such knowledge and vision fully engaged, it was as follows:

A poisonous creature dwelling in a crocodile's lair
may well pass beyond its appointed time —
but the loving-kindness of a buddha toward those to be tamed
never passes beyond its appointed time.

Just as a mother who has only one beloved child
watches over and guards that child's life,
so too the Tathāgata watches over those to be tamed
and guards their life.

The mount of compassion dwelling in the stream of omniscience
seeks tirelessly for the foal that is to be tamed.
The loving-kindness toward those declining in existence and the lower destinies
is like a cow's love for a gravely weakened calf.

Thus it proceeds.

"Seek here to bow at the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, who possesses the ten powers, who is untroubled by the four kinds of fearlessness, who is pledged to the abode of the great waves as supreme leader of the herd, and who roars the lion's roar fully in the midst of the assembly.

This is the temple of the venerable Kauṇḍinya of universal knowledge. When the world was in the darkness of ignorance, without guide and without one to lead it fully, the Blessed One was the first to open someone's eye of Dharma with the probe of the ointment of the eye of wisdom. The Blessed One, the elders, those who are like regents, those who have long since gone forth, those who have visibly cultivated the pure life —"

— who among those who bear the victory banner of the patched robe was foremost in prophecy, and it is on account of him that the Blessed One first turned the wheel of Dharma, possessed of the Dharma, which is of benefit to the many, which brings happiness to the many, which arises out of compassion for the world, which is for the good and benefit and happiness of gods and humans — that wheel which no ascetic (śramaṇa), brahmin, god, māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world is able to turn in conformity with the Dharma — turning it three times in twelve aspects. It is on his account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Mahākāśyapa. He is like a great sal tree among brahmins, who abandoned one supreme household and went forth, endowed with sixty million in property. He possessed eighty small granaries of gold. He owned eighteen servant villages. He owned sixteen villages of laborers. He was endowed with an excellent brahmin woman whose body surpassed gold, and he abandoned her like the ash of a ripened fruit. In the final watch of the night he took up a patched robe of sewn cloth worth a hundred thousand, and went forth for the sake of whatever arhats there were dwelling in the world, in order to cultivate meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment, and he dwells in the forest. At the mere sight of him even intoxicated bull elephants are pacified and freed from their pride. He undertook to show the Blessed One at the Bamboo Grove Stūpa, and received the vow of a monk. The Blessed One also declared: "O monks, among my monk-disciples who are śrāvakas, who are of few wishes and know contentment, and who speak of the virtues of ascetic practice, the foremost is none other than the monk Mahākāśyapa." It is on account of him — whom the Blessed One thus praised — that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Śāriputra. He is the son who obtained the supreme attainment, who in two periods of eight years mastered the grammatical analysis of the sense faculties, who defeated all opponents. He went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared him the foremost among those of great wisdom and great eloquence. The Blessed One placed all the world at one-sixteenth of him, and the Blessed One proclaimed in verse:

All the wisdom of the entire world,
apart from that of the Tathāgata,
does not equal even a sixteenth part
of the wisdom of Śāriputra.

Even if this world with its gods
were to become equal to Śāriputra,
it still would not equal a sixteenth part
of the gnosis of the Tathāgata.

It is on his account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. He is the son born from the womb of a foremost one, who abandoned a kingdom without a crown and went forth. With the big toe of his right foot he shook, completely shook, and utterly shook the palace of Vijaya belonging to Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, three times. By his miraculous powers he traveled to the world-realm of the Blessed One endowed with rays of light in seven days and nights. He is the one whom the Blessed One declared foremost among those of great miraculous powers and great might. It is on his account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Aniruddha. He went forth from among humans of excellent fortune. He is the son of the paternal uncle of the Blessed One's father. When merchants who are at sea properly hear his name correctly proclaimed, their vessels will be well completed and will arrive safely.

It is on account of the one whom the Blessed One declared foremost among those endowed with the divine eye that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Ānanda. He is the one who for a long time attended upon the Blessed One, who served close at the Blessed One's feet, who was properly praised by the Teacher, who practiced a life equal to that of Brahmā, and who was properly venerated by the wise. He went forth from among the sons of the Blessed One's father's younger kinsmen. He is the one whom the Blessed One declared foremost among those of great learning, those who retain what they have heard, and those who have amassed learning. It is on his account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Nandā. She went forth as the child of the younger sister of the Blessed One. Had she not gone forth, she would have become a wheel-turning king endowed with power. She is the one whom the Blessed One declared foremost among those who desire the training, those who are devoted to the training, and those who have attained the requisites for the training. It is on her account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Rāhula. He went forth as the son of the Blessed One. Had he not gone forth, he would have become a king endowed with might, one reverenced by many kings, his royal lineage passing unbroken from one generation to the next. He is the one whom the Blessed One declared foremost among those who desire the training, those who are devoted to the training, and those who have attained the requisites for the training. It is on his account that reverence is sought here too at his feet.

This is the temple of the venerable Nanda. This is that of Upananda. This is that of Chanda. This is that of Svāgata. This is that of Nābhasa. This is my own temple. Shall we look at this one too? Noble one, shall we not look at the temple of the noble Śāriputra after having seen all the other temples? We now most earnestly wish to see this temple of the noble Śāriputra. Sisters, let it be so.

The venerable Śāriputra was a person of desire, and so in his temple there are floors swept with ground red kidney-bean flour, the walls somewhat freshly whitewashed, beds with hearts of calf set out, and ten drinking vessels filled with drink along with their accessories arranged there, and within the shrine various provisions in abundance.

The venerable Śāriputra addressed a great many wives of brahmins and householders who had come to his temple, saying: Sisters, shall the little child do it, or will you drink the drink? Noble one, can a river flow backward? Whatever it is that we would ask of the noble one, may the noble one grant us that very thing. Grant us what is rare for us.

Sisters, what is rare for you? Noble one, it is hearing the Dharma.

Sisters, the Blessed One has taught well that six things arising in the world are wondrous and marvelous. What are those six? A Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully awakened buddha; the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata; being human; being born in a central land; having all one's faculties intact; and having aspiration toward wholesome phenomena. Therefore, that you have now generated aspiration toward wholesome phenomena is like a buddha arising in the world. Excellent, excellent! Sisters, be seated, and I shall teach you the Dharma.

They paid homage at his two feet and sat before him in order to hear the Dharma.

He began to teach them the Dharma. The more he taught the Dharma, the more attached they became. The more attached they became, the more shameless they grew. The more shameless they grew, the more they began to stroke his limbs and extremities. It was just like a spirit that recites secret mantras aloud, or like one who has been pierced with a skewer of flesh and ash — in just the same way, the more he taught them the Dharma, the more attached they became, the more attached they became the more shameless they grew, and the more shameless they grew the more they began to stroke his limbs and extremities.

Now those among them who took possession of him sat together with him on raised seats, swinging, making noise, playing, shouting, laughing, acting with pride, and writhing their bodies. Those who did not take possession of him came out from there and gathered at the entrances, corridors, and doorways, where they spoke these words of blame:

From that which gives water, fire blazes forth.
From that which protects, terror is born.
Fear has arisen from what holds no fear.
Danger has sprung up from the very refuge.

"From that which was peace and happiness on our side, that which spoke of well-being and that which was to become well-being — from that, fear, plague, harm, contagious disease, and trouble have now arisen." They spoke in blame; they raised a clamor; they spoke reproachfully.

While they were blaming and complaining in this way, it came about that the monks became directly aware of it, and having heard these women blaming him, the monks said to them: "Sisters, whom do you blame? Noble ones, it is you we blame." The monks asked: "What have we done?" The women replied: "Noble ones, those limbs and extremities of ours that even our own husbands have never anointed — those the venerable Śārka has anointed." And they said: "If our parents or our brothers were to hear of this, they would not even send someone to the Jetavana, let alone come there themselves. Sisters, be quiet! This monk is one who went forth from a reciter's family, and though he possesses moral discipline, he is nevertheless one in whom attachment is predominant, and by his striving he removes afflictions." The women replied: "Noble ones, would a young bull with two sharp horns gore its own flanks? That would be improper. Sisters, be quiet and stop him." The women said: "Noble ones, if he is stopped, well and good. But if he is not stopped, we shall never again come to the Jetavana." The monks replied: "Sisters, be quiet — he shall be restrained, so that from now on he shall no longer act in this way."
