The monks instructed him and he departed, and the remaining monks also came out of the temple and left. Then the venerable Śārka, still laughing, came out of the temple, and the monks seeing him said: "Venerable Śārka, having done such an unseemly thing, why do you now laugh?" Śārka replied: "Have I drunk liquor? Have I eaten leavings? What is it that I have done, venerable ones? What else did I do? I went about reviling the many wives of brahmins and householders." Śārka said further: "Venerable ones, the nature of those who carry black begging-bowls is that out of stinginess they will not teach even a single four-line verse to anyone, yet they blame anyone else who teaches those very things." They said: "Have you really set those women in the truths?" He replied: "If one begins to bring their faculties to full maturity, in due course they too will come to see the truths."

The monks who were of few wants criticized, disparaged, spread rumors about, and rebuked him, saying: "Why do monks fill themselves with that very conduct that ought to be a cause of shame?" Then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this opportunity, convened a gathering of the monk Saṅgha — and so forth, as before.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Śārka: "Śārka, is it true that you did something so unseemly?" He replied: "Venerable one, I did."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, censured him, saying that such conduct was unbecoming of a monk, not in conformity with the rule, not appropriate, not in accord with proper discipline — it is not what one who has gone forth should do.

After censuring him in many ways, the Blessed One then spoke to the monks: "Therefore, monks, having fully seen the ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, makes bodily contact with a woman, or grasps her by the hand, or grasps her by the upper arm, or grasps her by the hair or garments connected with it, or touches or handles any other limb or secondary limb — if he does so for the sake of pleasure, it is a matter for the Saṅgha's decision."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to Śārka or any other who is similar to him.

As for "with a mind inflamed and disordered": there is a mind that is inflamed but not disordered; a mind that is disordered but not inflamed; a mind that is both inflamed and disordered; and a mind that is neither inflamed nor disordered. Of these, "inflamed but not disordered" refers to a mind that is attached, fully attached, and bound up. "Disordered but not inflamed" refers to a mind that is expectant and connected. "Both inflamed and disordered" refers to a mind that is attached, fully attached, and bound up, and also expectant and connected. "Neither inflamed nor disordered" is the mind that falls outside those three modes.

"With a woman" refers to a woman or a girl who is capable of engaging in unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse.

"Makes bodily contact" means body leaning against body.

"Does so" means having done it.

"Grasps her by the hand" means from the wrist downward.

"Grasps her by the upper arm" means from the elbow upward.

As for "grasps her by the hair," hair refers to the hair itself and to garments connected with it.

"Any other limb or secondary limb" refers to any other form of bodily member apart from grasping the hand and grasping the upper arm.

"For the sake of pleasure" means if he does so to savor the sensation.

"A matter for the Saṅgha's decision" means that the transgression depends upon the Saṅgha; it is therefore said to be "a matter for the Saṅgha's decision" — and so forth, as before.

How does this become a transgression? Through nine bases: touching, handling, pushing, grasping, pulling, drawing fully toward oneself, embracing from below, embracing from above, and pressing close.

As to how it becomes a transgression through touching — if a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, toward a woman or

a young woman capable of sexual intercourse — touching her on the crown of the head, if he touches her without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he touches her with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense.

Just as it is for the crown of the head, so too for the forehead, the cheek, the lips, the chin, the neck, the ear, the nose, the jaw, the shoulder, the armpit, the back of the hand, the chest, the back, the breast, the waist, the knee, the thigh, the ankle, the tip of the foot, and even the big toe — if he touches her without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he touches her with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense.

Just as with touching, so too with handling, delivering, and grasping — it is the same in each case.

How does it become a transgression through pulling? If a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, pulls a woman or a young woman capable of sexual intercourse from far away close to him, or from close by pulls her far away — if he pulls her without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he pulls her with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Thus it is through pulling.

How does it become a transgression through drawing fully toward oneself? If a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, draws a woman or a young woman capable of sexual intercourse fully from the feet upward to the crown, or from the crown downward to the feet, or from the left side across to the right, or from the right side across to the left — if he does so without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he does so with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Thus it is through drawing fully toward oneself.

How does it become a transgression through embracing from below? If a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, embraces a woman or a young woman capable of sexual intercourse from below, from the ground up to the tips of the feet — if he embraces from below without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he embraces from below with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense.

Just as it is from the ground to the tips of the feet, so too from the tips of the feet to the ankle, from the ankle to the thigh, from the thigh to the waist, from the waist to the breast, from the breast to the chest, from the chest to the back, from the back to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the neck, from the neck to the chin, from the chin to the jaw, from the jaw to the cheek, from the cheek to the forehead, from the forehead to the crown, from the crown to a low seat, from a low seat to a seat, from a seat to a cushioned seat, from a cushioned seat to the back of a horse, from the back of a horse to the back of an elephant, from the back of an elephant to an upper chamber — if he embraces from below in any of these without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he embraces from below with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Thus it is through embracing from below.

How does it become a transgression through embracing from above? If a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, a woman or

If he embraces from above, without clothing intervening, a young woman or girl capable of bearing the practice of sexual intercourse — going from the upper chamber to the back of an elephant — it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he embraces from above with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Just as it is from the upper chamber to the back of the elephant, so too from the back of the elephant to the back of a horse, from the back of a horse to a cushioned seat, from a cushioned seat to a seat, from a seat to a low seat, from a low seat to the crown, from the crown to the forehead, from the forehead to the cheek, from the cheek to the jaw, from the jaw to the collar, from the collar to the throat, from the throat to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the back, from the back to the lung, from the lung to the chest, from the chest to the waist, from the waist to the thigh, from the thigh to the knee, from the knee to the tip of the foot, from the tip of the foot to the ground — if he embraces from above without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he embraces from above with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Thus it is through embracing from above.

How does it become a transgression through pressing against? If a monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, presses against the crown of a woman or girl capable of bearing the practice of sexual intercourse without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he presses against with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Just as it is at the crown, so too at the forehead, the cheek, the lips, the collar, the throat, the ear, the nose, the jaw, the shoulder, the armpit, the palm, the lung, the back, the chest, the waist, the knee, the thigh, the knee-joint, the tip of the foot, and even the big toe — if he presses against without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision. If he presses against with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. Thus it is through pressing against.

Furthermore, how does it become a transgression through stroking? When a woman or girl capable of bearing the practice of sexual intercourse strokes the crown of a monk's head, if that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk. Just as it is at the crown, so too when she strokes the forehead, the cheek, the lips, the collar, the throat, the ear, the nose, the jaw, the shoulder, the armpit, the palm, the lung, the back, the chest, the waist, the knee, the thigh, the knee-joint, the tip of the foot, and even the big toe — if, with a mind inflamed and disordered, he savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense.

Just as it is with savoring, so too is it with pressing, offering, and grasping — they are the same in every respect.

How is it with drawing close? If a woman or girl who is capable of supporting unchaste conduct and the act of sexual intercourse draws a monk toward her from a distance, or draws him away from nearby to a distance, and if that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense. That is how it is with drawing close.

How is it with drawing all the way? If a woman or girl who is capable of supporting unchaste conduct and the act of sexual intercourse draws a monk all the way from the tips of the feet to the top of the head, or from the top of the head to the tips of the feet — or from the left lung to the right lung, or from the right lung to the left lung — and if that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk. That is how it is with drawing all the way.

How is it with embracing from below? If a woman or girl who is capable of supporting unchaste conduct and the act of sexual intercourse embraces a monk from below, from the ground up to the tips of the toes, and if that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk.

Just as it is from the ground to the tips of the toes, so too is it from the tips of the toes up to the ankle, from the ankle to the calf, from the calf to the knee, from the knee to the chest, from the chest to the lungs, from the lungs to the back, from the back to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the throat, from the throat to the ear, from the ear to the cheek, from the cheek to the jaw, from the jaw to the temple, from the temple to the forehead, from the forehead to a stool, from a stool to a chair, from a chair to a couch, from a couch to a horse's back, from a horse's back to an elephant's back, and from an elephant's back to an upper story — embracing from below in all of these cases. If that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk. That is how it is with embracing from below.

How is it with embracing from above? If a woman or girl —

a woman or girl who is capable of supporting sexual intercourse — if she embraces a monk from above, from an upper story onto the back of an elephant, and that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk.

Just as it is from an upper story onto an elephant's back, so too it is the same in turn from an elephant's back to a horse's back, from a horse's back to a palanquin, from a palanquin to a throne, from a throne to a low seat, from a low seat to the crown of the head, from the crown of the head to the forehead, from the forehead to the cheek, from the cheek to the chin, from the chin to the collar, from the collar to the throat, from the throat to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the back, from the back to the ribs, from the ribs to the chest, from the chest to the waist, from the waist to the hip, from the hip to the knee, from the knee to the shin, from the shin to the tip of the foot, and from the tip of the foot down to the ground — embracing from above in all of these cases. If that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk. That is how it is with embracing from above.

How is it with pressing close? If a woman or girl who is capable of supporting sexual intercourse presses close against the crown of a monk's head, and that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk.

Just as it is with the crown of the head, so too it is the same with the forehead, the cheek, the lips, the collar, the throat, the ear, the nose, the chin, the shoulder, the armpit, the elbow, the ribs, the back, the chest, the waist, the knee, the hip, the shin, the tip of the foot, and even the big toe — if she presses close against any of these. If that monk, with a mind inflamed and disordered, savors the sensation, fully comprehends it, becomes further attached, remains sitting in further attachment, and in that way draws his body close — then if he draws close without clothing intervening, it becomes a matter for the Saṅgha's decision for that monk. If he draws close with clothing intervening, it becomes a grave offense for that monk. That is how it is with pressing close.

Where the offense for one who is capable is a matter for the Saṅgha's decision, for one who is incapable it is a grave offense. With a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or a person of ambiguous sex, it is likewise a grave offense. Where the offense for one who is capable is a grave offense, for one who is incapable it is a misdeed. With a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or a person of ambiguous sex, it is likewise a misdeed. And with one born in an animal realm, it is also a misdeed.

Where the offense for one who is capable is a misdeed, for one who is incapable it is likewise a misdeed. With a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a person of ambiguous sex, or one born in an animal realm, it is likewise a misdeed. Where the woman is also one's mother and is perceived as one's mother, where she is also one's sister and is perceived as one's sister, where she is also one's daughter and is perceived as one's daughter, there is no transgression. Where one leaps into fire, is carried away by water, takes poison, draws a weapon, leaps from a precipice, is bound with a rope, or rescues from death one who is on the verge of dying, there is no transgression. For one who is a first offender, who is mad, who is mentally disturbed, or who is afflicted with acute pain, there is no transgression.

This completes the second Saṅgha Remainder concerning physical contact. End of the second Saṅgha Remainder.

The Analysis of the Vinaya, the sixteenth bundle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The conduct of the Group of Six was as follows: thinking, "We too shall teach the Dharma to the brahmins and householders who come and arrive here; we shall refute opponents; and we shall spread our own reputation," one or another of the Group of Six would not leave the gateway of the Jeta Grove empty, but would rise before dawn, discard the tooth-stick, put on a reddish-yellow patched robe, and walk about and sit at the gateway of the Jeta Grove.

The usual conduct of the wives of the brahmins and householders living at Śrāvastī was to go to the pleasure grove, to enter the Jeta Grove, to visit the temple, and to go to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and of the senior monks. So many wives of brahmins and householders would come out to the pleasure grove, and wishing to visit the temple, they would go toward the Jeta Grove. From that point, up to and including where it is said that he began to teach them the Dharma — all of this is to be understood exactly as was set forth in the context of the second Saṅgha Remainder.

The more he taught them the Dharma, the more they became attached to him. The more they became attached, the more they revealed themselves. The more they revealed themselves, the more those who were involved in affairs, who had collected foul words of base reproach that ought not to be uttered, began to speak to him in front of their husbands with utter frankness — just as, for example, a spirit that recites secret spells aloud, or one who has been stung by a meat-fly with a stinging tail: in the same way, the more he taught them the Dharma, the more they became attached. The more they became attached, the more they revealed themselves. The more they revealed themselves, the more those who were involved in affairs, who had collected foul words of base reproach that ought not to be uttered, began to speak to him in front of their husbands with utter frankness.

Then those among the husbands who were partial to him would sit with him on reclining seats, swinging back and forth, tapping along, playing about, chattering away, laughing, swaggering, and posturing with their bodies. But those who were not partial to him would depart from there and, in the walkways, in the clean areas, and at the gateways, would say and recite:

From that which brings water there arises fire;
from that which gives protection there arises fear.
From the fearless one fear has been born;
from the refuge fear has arisen.

In our direction there was happiness, peace,
words of well-being and blessing —
from that very source from which well-being was to come,
fear, plague, harm, contagious disease, and strife have appeared.

So they would heap abuse, they would mock and jeer, and they would spread malicious talk. And while they were heaping abuse —

— the monks became directly visible to those women as they were passing by. The women heard the monks heaping abuse on them, and those women said: "Sisters, whom are you mocking?" "Noble ones, we are mocking you." "What have we done?" "Noble ones, we heard from the venerable Cāraka words that we had never before heard from anyone — not from barbers, not from garland-makers, not even from the children of fishermen. If our parents and siblings were to hear this, they would not even give us so much as the Jeta Grove — to say nothing of anything more. Sisters, be quiet! That monk did indeed go forth from a family of precentors and he does possess moral discipline, yet because his attachment is excessive, this composition of his is meant to dispel afflictions." "Noble ones, what of it — would a bull with two sharp horns gore its own flank? That would be improper." "Sisters, be quiet — and put a stop to it!" "Noble ones, if he is stopped, then well and good. But if you will not stop him, we will never again come to the Jeta Grove." "Sisters, be quiet! Whatever happens, see to it that he does not continue to behave in this way — put a stop to it."

The monks instructed those women, and the women departed. The remaining ones too came out of the monastery and left. Then the venerable Cāraka came out of the monastery still laughing, and when the monks saw him they said: "Venerable Cāraka, why are you laughing after doing something so unseemly?" Cāraka said: "Did I drink liquor? Did I eat a meal in common? Venerable ones, did I even do that? What else have I done? Those many wives of brahmins and householders went away while heaping abuse." Cāraka said: "Venerable ones, the nature of those who hold the black bowl is that, out of miserliness, they do not show so much as a single four-line verse to anyone at all, and yet they heap abuse on whoever else teaches others." Those women said: "Did you then arrange those teachings on the truths for their sake?" He replied: "If they begin to ripen the faculties of those women, in the end they will come to see the truths as well." While the monks of few desires were saying — why do monks use the very limb by which they should be ashamed to puff themselves up? — while they were heaping abuse, speaking disparagingly, and spreading malicious talk, the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, in connection with this occurrence, this genesis, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and the rest follows as before. The buddha, the Blessed One, then questioned the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you did something so unseemly?" "Blessed holy one, it is so." The buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him: "That which is not the manner of an ascetic, not in accord, not fitting, not in keeping with proper conduct — that is not something one who has gone forth ought to do." Having rebuked him in this way, the Blessed One then rebuked him again through many synonymous expressions, and declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing the ten benefits clearly, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and the rest follows as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, with a mind that is agitated and disturbed, directs at a woman base and vulgar words of sensual import — of the kind that a young man speaks to a young woman — that is an offense entailing expiation (pācittika) requiring communal confession."

"Whatever monk" refers to Cāraka, or to anyone else of that kind.

Regarding the phrase "with a mind that is agitated and disturbed": there are minds that are agitated but not disturbed, minds that are disturbed but not agitated, minds that are both agitated and disturbed, and minds that are neither agitated nor disturbed. Of these, a mind that is agitated but not disturbed is a mind that has attachment, complete attachment, and entanglement. A mind that is disturbed but not agitated is a mind that is accompanied by longing and connected to its object. A mind that is both agitated and disturbed is a mind that has attachment, complete attachment, and entanglement, and is also accompanied by longing and connected to its object. A mind that is neither agitated nor disturbed is any mind that does not fall into those categories.

Regarding the phrase "directed at a woman": it refers to any woman or girl who is capable of understanding the full import of words spoken to her, whether those words were spoken well or badly.

Regarding the term "base and vulgar words": there are two kinds. The first is that which instigates a defeat, and the second is that which instigates expiation by the Saṅgha as a remainder. Why are these called base and vulgar? Because of what they are by their own nature and because of what they instigate.

The word "words" means utterances. Regarding the phrase "of sensual import": "sensual" means blameworthy, that is, what is reprehensible. "Communal confession" means going beyond the bounds of what is middling, which is contrary to proper conduct. "Of the kind that a young man speaks" — "man" here means a male, and "young" here means a woman. "Speaks" means saying something that has not been said before, or responding to something that has already been said. "Requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha" is as before.

As for how transgression arises in this case, it does so through nine bases: by making praise, by making disparagement, by making a request, by making an entreaty, by asking, by thoroughly asking, by announcing, by expressing a wish, and by rebuking.

How does transgression arise through making praise? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, your three bodily orifices are perfectly suited, perfectly placed, and perfectly formed," and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through making praise.

How does transgression arise through making disparagement? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, your three bodily orifices are not perfectly suited, not perfectly placed, and not perfectly formed," and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through making disparagement.

How does transgression arise through making a request? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, come here and let us do such-and-such," and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense.

That is how transgression arises through making a request.

How does transgression arise through making an offering? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, what such-and-such a man does with such-and-such a woman — that is her joy and delight. So if we too were to do such-and-such, that would become my joy and delight as well," and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through making an offering.

How does transgression arise through asking? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, if a man were to do such-and-such with a woman, that would become her joy and delight — so if I too were to do such-and-such with you, would that not become your joy and delight?" and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through asking.

How does transgression arise through fully asking? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, if a man were to do such-and-such with a woman, that would become her joy and delight — and if I were to do such-and-such with you, it would likewise become your joy and delight. Is that not so, or is it not? What do you think, Lady?" and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through fully asking.

How does transgression arise through describing? A monk, with a mind that is both agitated and disturbed, approaches a woman or girl capable of understanding the full import of well-spoken and badly-spoken words, and says to her: "Lady, the day before yesterday, in my dwelling, in a garden, or in a divine abode, or in some great and spacious chamber, a woman just like you came there for that very purpose. I spread a bed strewn with flowers, set up a lamp of sesame oil throughout the night, prepared such-and-such food for us to eat together and ate just such things, drank just such drinks, and together with her did such-and-such. If you, Lady, were to come there for that very purpose, I would spread a bed strewn with flowers, set up a lamp of sesame oil throughout the night, prepare just such food for us to eat together and eat just such things, drink just such drinks, and together with you I would do such-and-such as well," and then utters with sensual import the name "ears of grain" — this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he utters the words without using the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through describing.

How does transgression arise through expressing longing?

How does transgression arise through expressing longing? A monk, with a mind seized by lust, goes before a woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, and says the following: "Those who do such-and-such things together with a wife are happy and attain the higher realms. Therefore if I too were to do such-and-such together with a wife, I would become happy and would attain the higher realms." If, while saying this with sensual import, he utters the name "ears of grain," this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through expressing longing.

How does transgression arise through reviling? A monk, with a mind seized by lust, goes before a woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, and reviles her with terms of abuse such as "you are like a corpse" and the like. If, while reviling her in this way with sensual import, he utters the name "ears of grain," this incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through reviling.

Furthermore, how does transgression arise through praising? A woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, your three bodily doors are well formed, well positioned, and fine." When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through praising.

How does transgression arise through disparaging? A woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, your three bodily doors are ill formed, ill positioned, and unbecoming." When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how transgression arises through disparaging.

How does transgression arise through soliciting? A woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, come here; let us do such-and-such." When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense.

That is how it occurs by means of requesting. And how does it occur by means of beseeching? A woman or a girl capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, such-and-such that a woman and a man do together — that brings joy and delight to such-and-such a person. Noble one, if we too were to do such-and-such, it would bring joy and delight to me as well." When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how it occurs by means of beseeching.

And how does it occur by means of questioning? A woman or a girl capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, a man who does such-and-such to a woman — does that bring joy and delight to that woman? If she were to do such-and-such to the noble one, would it bring joy and delight to the noble one?" When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how it occurs by means of questioning.

And how does it occur by means of thorough questioning? A woman or a girl capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, a man who does such-and-such to a woman — that brings joy and delight to her; and if she were to do such-and-such to the noble one, it would bring joy and delight to the noble one as well. Is that so, or is it not so? Noble one, what does the noble one think of this?" When she says this, the monk, with a mind seized by lust, savors the taste of her words, attends to them with certainty, becomes greatly attached, remains sitting in great attachment, and then speaks back to her accordingly with sensual import, uttering the name "ears of grain." This incurs expiation requiring communal confession by the Saṅgha. If he does not utter the name "ears of grain," it becomes a grave offense. That is how it occurs by means of thorough questioning.

And how does it occur by means of declaration? A woman or a girl capable of understanding the full meaning of what is spoken, whether the words be proper or improper, comes before a monk and says: "Noble one, last night in her presence, in a grove or in a divine abode or in some great and spacious bed-chamber, there appeared a man of such-and-such a kind, come for that very purpose. She had spread and prepared a bed strewn with flowers, and set a butter-lamp burning in the middle of the night, and together with him she had prepared such-and-such arrangements and sought such-and-such food and sought such-and-such drink, and together with him she had done such-and-such. Noble one, if you too were to come for that very purpose —"

She had spread and prepared a bed strewn with flowers, and set a butter-lamp burning in the middle of the night, and together with the noble one she had prepared such-and-such arrangements and sought such-and-such food and sought such-and-such drink, and together with the noble one she had done such-and-such as well." When this is said, if the monk, with a mind aroused and inflamed, savors the taste of it, comes to a definite apprehension of it, becomes further attached to it, and, being further attached, remains in that state — and if, speaking accordingly in reply while in a state of sexual arousal, he utters the name called "ear of grain" — he incurs a Saṅgha Remainder offense. If he does not utter the name called "ear of grain," it becomes a serious transgression — and this is so because he speaks in reply.

Now, how does one speak in reply by way of entreaty? A woman or a girl who is able to understand the meaning of both well-spoken words and ill-spoken words comes before the monk and says: "Noble one, those noble ones who do such-and-such together with a noble one — they are happy and have attained a higher rebirth. She too, if she were to do such-and-such together with the noble one, would become happy and would attain a higher rebirth." When this is said, if the monk, with a mind aroused and inflamed, savors the taste of it, comes to a definite apprehension of it, becomes further attached to it, and, being further attached, remains in that state — and if, speaking accordingly in reply while in a state of sexual arousal, he utters the name called "ear of grain" — he incurs a Saṅgha Remainder offense. If he does not utter the name called "ear of grain," it becomes a serious transgression — and this is so because he speaks in reply by way of entreaty.

Now, how does one speak in reply by way of reviling? A woman or a girl who is able to understand the meaning of all the teachings, whether well-spoken or ill-spoken, comes before the monk and reviles him with revilings such as "he is like a corpse" and the like. If the monk, with a mind aroused and inflamed, savors the taste of it, comes to a definite apprehension of it, becomes further attached to it, and, being further attached, remains in that state — and if, speaking accordingly in reply while in a state of sexual arousal, he utters the name called "ear of grain" — he incurs a Saṅgha Remainder offense. If he does not utter the name called "ear of grain," it becomes a serious transgression — and this is so because he speaks in reply by way of reviling.

Where there is a Saṅgha Remainder offense with respect to one who is capable, there is a serious transgression with respect to one who is incapable. With respect to a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or one who has both characteristics, there is a serious transgression. Where there is a serious transgression with respect to one who is capable, there is a minor transgression with respect to one who is incapable. With respect to a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or one who has both characteristics, it is likewise a minor transgression. With respect to one born in an animal realm, it is likewise a minor transgression. Where there is a minor transgression with respect to one who is capable, there is likewise a minor transgression with respect to one who is incapable. With respect to a man, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or one who has both characteristics, it is likewise a minor transgression. With respect to one born in an animal realm, it is likewise a minor transgression.

When the words used are ambiguous with regard to language, ambiguous with regard to locality, or ambiguous with regard to region, there is no transgression. When one utters the name of a grain, the name of a grass, or the name of a winnowing basket, there is no transgression. For one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by feelings, there is no transgression.

This concludes the third Saṅgha Remainder, speaking in a state of sexual arousal.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The conduct of the Group of Six was as follows: "Here, we too shall teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who have come and arrived."

They also thought: "We shall silence our opponents and spread our own reputation." And so one or another of the Group of Six, unwilling to leave the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended, had the venerable Cāraka rise early, discard his tooth-stick, put on a reddish-yellow patched robe, and walk about and sit at the gate of the Jeta Grove.

Now the customary practice of the brahmin wives and householders' wives who lived in Śrāvastī was to go to the park, to enter the Jeta Grove, to visit the temple, and to go to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and of the elder monks. And so a great many brahmin wives and householders' wives came to the park, and wishing to see the temple, they went toward the Jeta Grove.

From the point where he began teaching them the Dharma — as was set forth in the context of the second Saṅgha Remainder — up to the point where he began teaching them the Dharma, the account runs as follows:

The more he taught the Dharma, the more they became attached. The more they became attached, the more they became aroused. The more they became aroused, he then began, in order to obtain bodily service from them in person, to utter this praise before them: "For a monk like me — one possessed of moral discipline, endowed with virtuous qualities, living the holy life — to be honored with this quality of sensual union: this honor is the highest of all forms of honor."

It was just as when a spirit recites a love spell aloud, or as when one is pressed upon by the poultice of meat and a whipping rod — in exactly the same way, the more he taught them the Dharma, the more they became attached. The more they became attached, the more they became aroused. The more they became aroused, he then began, before them, in order to obtain bodily service in person, to utter this praise: "For a monk like me — one possessed of moral discipline, endowed with virtuous qualities, living the holy life — to be honored with this quality of sensual union: this honor is the highest of all forms of honor."

Those among them who became his own then stayed with him, reclining on side-couches, fanning themselves, pressing close to him, playing with him, chattering noisily, laughing, showing pride, and moving their bodies about. Those who did not become his own departed from there. And in the walkways, courtyards, and gatehouse they recited these words:

From what gives water, fire blazes forth.
From what gives shelter, terror arises.
From the fearless one, fear has been born.
From the refuge, terror has come to be.

"In our quarter there was happiness, peace, the declaration of good fortune, the arising of good fortune — and from that very thing fear, plague, harm, epidemic disease, and conflict have arisen." Thus they spoke in reproach, flung words back, and gossiped.

As they were speaking in reproach and leaving, they came directly before the monks. The monks heard them speaking in reproach and said to them: "Sisters, whom do you reproach? Noble ones, it is you we reproach. What have we done? Noble ones, words that we have never heard even in our own homes — those we have heard from the noble Cāraka. If our fathers or brothers or sisters were to hear of this, they would not even give so much as food to the Jeta Grove, let alone what else might be expected. Sisters, be quiet. That monk has indeed gone forth from a chanter's family, he is possessed of moral discipline, and yet he is greatly overcome by attachment, so that this undertaking removes the afflictions." Noble ones, what is this?

Would a bull with two sharp horns gore its own flank? That would be unseemly. Sisters, be quiet and turn back." "Noble ones, if you turn back, then well and good. But if you do not turn back, we will no longer come to the Jeta Grove." "Sisters, be quiet. Turn back, and make sure that he never does such a thing again."

The monks then instructed them and sent them on their way, and the rest of the assembly also departed from the monastery. Then the venerable Cāraka came out of the monastery laughing, and when the monks saw this they said, "Venerable Cāraka, why do you laugh, having done something so unseemly?" Cāraka replied, "Have I been drinking ale, or eating garlic, or what? Venerable ones, have I even done that much? What else have I done? I departed having reviled a great many wives of brahmins and householders."

Cāraka then said, "Venerable ones, the nature of those with black begging bowls is that out of miserliness they will not show even a single verse of four lines to anyone, and yet they condemn the one who does show such things to others." They said to him, "Are you saying that what you did to them was truthful?" He replied, "If they were to begin ripening their faculties, they would in the end come to see the truth as well."

The monks scolded him, saying, "Why do monks of little benefit — why do monks use the very faculty by which one ought to feel shame to fill themselves with pride?" — and they censured him, spoke harshly, and reproached him. Thereupon the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this circumstance, convened the community of monks, and so forth as before. The buddha, the Blessed One, questioned the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you did something so unseemly?" "Blessed one, it is true." The buddha, the Blessed One, censured him, saying that what is unbecoming a monk, discordant with the Dharma, unsuitable, and contrary to proper conduct is not something that one who has gone forth should do. Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers," and so forth as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Furthermore, if any monk, with a mind that is both impassioned and altered, in the presence of a woman, for the sake of his own bodily service, were to speak praise in such terms as these — 'A monk like me, endowed with moral discipline, possessing virtuous qualities, who, practicing the holy life, is served in such an amorous manner by this virtue — that service is the highest of all services' — then there is a remainder for the Saṅgha."

Now the phrase "if any monk" refers to Cāraka or anyone else similar to him. "With a mind both impassioned and altered" — there are four possibilities: the mind may be impassioned but not altered; altered but not impassioned; both impassioned and altered; and neither impassioned nor altered. Of these, "impassioned but not altered" refers to a mind of attachment, total attachment, and entanglement. "Altered but not impassioned" refers to a mind possessed of longing and bound by longing. "Both impassioned and altered" refers to a mind of attachment, total attachment, and entanglement, which is also possessed of longing and bound by longing. "Neither impassioned nor altered" refers to a mind not belonging to any of those categories. "In the presence of a woman" refers to a woman, or —

a maiden — one capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings, whether well spoken or badly spoken. "In the presence of" means in front of, directly before. "For the sake of serving one's own body" means for the sake of making use of one's own body. "Such as one like me" — this is an expression of pointing out and indicating. "A monk" means one who possesses the qualities of a monk as described. "Possessed of moral discipline" means one who possesses the aggregate of moral discipline as described. "One who has virtuous qualities" means one who possesses the aggregate of meditative absorption as described. "In the holy life" means one who possesses the aggregate of wisdom as described. "Engaged in such intercourse as this" means one who is engaged in unchaste conduct. "By this Dharma" means: by this thing that is not the Dharma but is expressed by the word "Dharma" — and not by anything else. "If served" means if made use of. "Dear one" is an expression of affection. As for "this is the supreme among all services" — "supreme" means foremost. "If one speaks praise" means if one praises. As for "the Saṅgha remains," meaning that the transgression rests with the Saṅgha — and therefore, it is said, "the Saṅgha remains" — and so on up to that point, it is as before. Now, one may ask: how does a transgression arise in this case? It arises through eighteen bases: supreme, surpassing, supremely distinguished, excellent, beautiful, virtuous, worthy of veneration, worthy of praise, extensive — and the intensified forms of each: most supreme, most surpassing, most supremely distinguished, most excellent, most beautiful, most virtuous, most worthy of veneration, most worthy of praise, and most extensive.

Now, one may ask: how does the case of "supreme" apply? If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk possessed of moral discipline, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all acts of service" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk who has virtuous qualities, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk in the holy life, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one such as I, a monk endowed with moral discipline and wholesome qualities, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk endowed with moral discipline, in the holy life, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk with wholesome qualities and endowed with moral discipline, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk with wholesome qualities, in the holy life, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk in the holy life and endowed with moral discipline, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk in the holy life and with wholesome qualities, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following: "If one such as I, a monk endowed with moral discipline, with wholesome qualities, and in the holy life, is served by this Dharma that involves such intercourse as this, dear one, this is the supreme among all services" — then he incurs a transgression remaining with the Saṅgha.

And just as it is the supreme, so too it is the foremost, the distinguished, the excellent, the beautiful, the virtuous, the worthy of honor, the worthy of praise, the extensive, the most supreme, the most foremost, the most distinguished, the most excellent, the most beautiful, the most virtuous, the most worthy of honor, the most worthy of praise, and the most extensive.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses moral discipline, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses virtue, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses moral discipline and who possesses virtue, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses moral discipline and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses virtue and who possesses moral discipline, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "arising from an offering" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses virtue and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who follows the celibate life and possesses virtue, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who follows the celibate life and possesses virtuous qualities, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching a monk such as myself who possesses virtue, possesses virtuous qualities, and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "endowed with passion" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

The same applies equally to that which is foremost, supremely excellent, distinguished, fine, beautiful, wholesome, worthy of veneration, worthy of praise, vast, most supreme, most foremost, most distinguished, most fine, most beautiful, most wholesome, most worthy of veneration, most worthy of praise, and most vast.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who possesses virtue, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who possesses virtuous qualities and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who possesses virtue and is of wholesome character, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who follows the celibate life and possesses moral discipline, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who is of wholesome character and possesses moral discipline, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who is of wholesome character and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who follows the celibate life and possesses moral discipline, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who follows the celibate life and is of wholesome character, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind of desire and passion, goes to a woman or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of all teachings whether well spoken or badly spoken, and says to her the following:

"If one honours with this teaching of passion a monk who possesses moral discipline, is of wholesome character, and follows the celibate life, this service of honour is the foremost of all acts of honour" — yet if he does not say the words "such as myself" when he says this, a grave transgression is incurred.

And just as with "foremost," so too with each of the following synonyms in turn: supreme, excellent, surpassing, good, beautiful, virtuous, worthy of veneration, worthy of praise, vast — and likewise with the intensified forms: the most supreme, the most excellent, the most surpassing, the most good, the most beautiful, the most virtuous, the most worthy of veneration, the most worthy of praise, and the most vast.

This concludes the Vinaya-vibhaṅga.

The Seventeenth Fascicle.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of moral discipline were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of virtuous qualities were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of moral discipline and living the holy life were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of moral discipline and of virtuous qualities were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of moral discipline and living the holy life were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of virtuous qualities and of moral discipline were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of virtuous qualities and living the holy life were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk living the holy life and possessed of moral discipline were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk living the holy life and possessed of virtuous qualities were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

If a monk, with a mind aroused by lust, goes to a woman or a girl who is able to understand the full meaning of words spoken well and words spoken improperly, and speaks to her as follows: "If a monk possessed of moral discipline and virtuous qualities, living the holy life, were to be honoured in this way, through this act of honour, this act of service would be the foremost of all acts of honour" — and yet does not say the words "possessed of sexual union" nor the words "such as myself" — a grave transgression is incurred.

Likewise for "the best, the finest, the most excellent, the most superior, the most beautiful, the most wholesome, the most worthy of veneration, the most praiseworthy, the most extensive, and the most supremely best, the most supremely fine, the most supremely excellent, the most supremely superior, the most supremely beautiful, the most supremely wholesome, the most supremely worthy of veneration, the most supremely praiseworthy, and the most supremely extensive."

With respect to one capable of understanding: whatever remainder of the Saṅgha there is, for one incapable of understanding a grave transgression is incurred. With respect to a man, a woman, a eunuch, and a hermaphrodite also, a grave transgression is incurred. With respect to one capable of understanding, where a grave transgression applies, for one incapable of understanding a minor transgression applies. With respect to a man, a woman, a eunuch, and a hermaphrodite also, a minor transgression applies. With respect to one born in the realm of animals also, a minor transgression applies. With respect to one capable of understanding, where a minor transgression applies, for one incapable of understanding it is likewise a minor transgression. With respect to a man, a woman, a eunuch, and a hermaphrodite also, it is likewise a minor transgression. With respect to one born in the realm of animals also, it is likewise a minor transgression. For one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is assailed by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

The fourth section of the Saṅgha's surplus rules concerning honouring and praising is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was in Śrāvastī a man named Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, who was skilled at going among the brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī and conversing with them, accompanying them, befriending them, winning their affection, and gaining entry into their homes. And so those who had daughters to give in marriage went to Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and asked him: "Kṛṣṇa, do you know of any great household?" When he replied that he did, they would ask him: "What is that household like, Kṛṣṇa? Is the boy clever and free from laziness and capable of accomplishing things? Is the boy able to give the girl abundant food and clothing? And is his workload light?"

But if Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, were to report that the boy was not clever, was lazy, was not capable of accomplishing things, that the boy could not give the girl abundant food and clothing, and that his workload was heavy, then those people would not give their daughter to that boy. And if Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, were to report that the boy was clever, was free from laziness, was capable of accomplishing things, that the boy could give the girl abundant food and clothing, and that his workload was light, then those people would give their daughter to that boy.

Now those who had daughters to seek in marriage would likewise go to Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and ask him: "Kṛṣṇa, do you know of any great household?" When he replied that he did, they would ask him: "Kṛṣṇa, what is the girl of that household like? Is she clever and free from laziness and capable of accomplishing things? And is she able to dwell in the home with care and diligence?" If Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, were to report that the girl was not clever, was lazy, was not capable of accomplishing things, and that she was not able to dwell in the home with care and diligence, then those people would not seek that girl. But if Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, were to report that the girl was clever, was free from laziness, was capable of accomplishing things, and was able to dwell in the home with care and diligence, then those people would seek that girl.

Now when Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had reported in this way and any of those who had daughters to give in marriage came to give their daughter badly — that is, when a daughter was given and the boy turned out to be not clever, lazy, not capable of accomplishing things, unable to give the girl abundant food and clothing, and with a heavy workload — those people would speak ill of Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, saying: "Those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, has conversed, spoken pleasantly, chatted, befriended, won affection, and gained entry into their homes — it has turned out like this for them too." But when any of those who had daughters to give in marriage came to give their daughter well — that is, when a daughter was given and the boy turned out to be clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, able to give the girl abundant food and clothing, and with a light workload — those people would speak praise of Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, saying: "Those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, has conversed, spoken pleasantly, chatted, befriended, won affection, and gained entry into their homes — it has turned out like this for them too."

Likewise, when any of those who had daughters to seek in marriage came to seek a daughter badly — that is, when a daughter was taken and the girl turned out to be not clever, lazy, not capable of accomplishing things, and unable to dwell in the home with care and diligence — those people would speak ill of Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, saying: "Those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, has conversed, spoken pleasantly, chatted, befriended, won affection, and gained entry into their homes — it has turned out like this for them too." But when any of those who had daughters to seek in marriage came to seek a daughter well — that is, when a daughter was taken and the girl turned out to be clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, and able to dwell in the home with care and diligence — those people would speak praise of Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, saying: "Those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, has conversed, spoken pleasantly, chatted, befriended, won affection, and gained entry into their homes —

— conversed, spoken pleasantly, chatted, befriended, won affection, and gained entry into their homes — it has turned out like this for them too." In this way, both praise and blame arose simultaneously for Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, in Śrāvastī.

Then at another time he became filled with faith in the Buddha, filled with faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He abandoned the taking of life and turned back from the taking of life.
