He abandoned the taking of what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the state of heedlessness that is intoxication by grain-spirits or distilled liquors, and he turned back from that state of heedlessness.

After dwelling for a time as a householder in the household life, he extended and deepened that very same former faith, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and with genuine faith went forth from home into homelessness into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.

Having gone forth in this way, he continued, by virtue of his former friendships, to converse, speak pleasantly, chat, befriend, win affection, and gain entry into the homes of the brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī. Those among them who had sons to offer in marriage came to Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and asked: "Noble one, do you know of a suitable household?" He said he did, and they asked him: "Noble one, is that boy clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things? Is he in a position to give the girl abundant food and clothing, and is the burden of work light?" If Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, indicated, "Good people, that boy is in truth not clever, is lazy, incapable of accomplishing things, unable to provide the girl with abundant food and clothing, and the burden of work is heavy," then they would not give their daughter to that boy. But if Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, indicated, "Good people, that boy is in truth clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, able to provide the girl with abundant food and clothing, and the burden of work is light," then they would give their daughter to that boy.

Those among them who had daughters to offer in marriage also came to Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and asked: "Noble one, do you know of a suitable household?" He said he did, and they asked him: "Noble one, is that girl clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things? Is she able to dwell in the home with care and diligence?" If Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, indicated, "Good people, that girl is in truth not clever, is lazy, incapable of accomplishing things, and unable to dwell in the home with care and diligence," then they would not offer their daughter in marriage. But if Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, indicated, "Good people, that girl is in truth clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, and able to dwell in the home with care and diligence," then they would offer their daughter in marriage.

After Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had indicated in this way, if those who had given their daughter in marriage fared badly, they would say: "We asked Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and then gave our daughter in marriage, and that boy is not clever, is lazy, incapable of accomplishing things, and the boy is unable to provide the girl with abundant food and clothing — his burden is heavy." And so they would speak ill of those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had mingled in conversation, spoken of as a welcome visitor, befriended as a companion, held in esteem, and brought into their homes, saying, "It will turn out thus for them as well." But if those who had given their daughter in marriage fared well, they would say: "We asked Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and then gave our daughter in marriage, and that boy is clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, and the boy is able to provide the girl with abundant food and clothing — his burden is light." And so they would speak in praise of those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had mingled in conversation, spoken of as a welcome visitor, befriended as a companion, held in esteem, and brought into their homes, saying, "It will turn out thus for them as well."

Likewise, if those who had taken a daughter in marriage fared badly, they would say: "We asked Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and then took that girl in marriage, and that girl is not clever, is lazy, incapable of accomplishing things, and that girl is unable to dwell in the home with care and diligence." And so they would speak ill of those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had mingled in conversation, spoken of as a welcome visitor, befriended as a companion, held in esteem, and brought into their homes, saying, "It will turn out thus for them as well." But if those who had taken a daughter in marriage fared well, they would say: "We asked Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, and then took that girl in marriage, and that girl is clever, free from laziness, capable of accomplishing things, and that girl is able to dwell in the home with care and diligence." And so they would speak in praise of those with whom Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, had mingled in conversation, spoken of as a welcome visitor, befriended as a companion, held in esteem, and brought into their homes, saying, "It will turn out thus for them as well."

And so it came about that praise and blame arose for Kṛṣṇa, son of Mṛgādhāra, at one and the same time in Śrāvastī. Now, this had occurred for the time being, but the awakened Blessed One had not yet for his part established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

At that time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks (Skt. ṣaḍvargika), using with women the language one uses with a man, and using with men the language one uses with a woman, were acting as though they were wives or intimate female companions to one another. The non-Buddhist adherents who were learned said: "These monks, sons of the Śākyan, use with women the language one uses with a man, and use with men the language one uses with a woman, acting as wives or intimate female companions to one another. And others as well — brahmins and householders who have not properly taken up the rule of training — also use with women the language one uses with a man, and use with men the language one uses with a woman, acting as wives or intimate female companions. What distinction then, O learned ones, is there between the monks who are sons of the Śākyan and those brahmins and householders who have not properly taken up the rule of training? What difference in intention is there? What difference in conduct is there?" They mocked and taunted and gossiped, saying, "Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed wanderers?" Upon this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and

on account of this occasion, the Blessed One convened a gathering of the community of monks. Now, the Tathāgata, perceiving the twofold purpose of the matter, convened the community of monks, thinking: "This is so that my hearers may come to know everything fully, and so that I may properly establish the foundations of training in the Vinaya." The blessed buddhas deliberate knowingly — they deliberate knowingly, yet do not deliberate unknowingly; they deliberate at the right time, not at the wrong time; they deliberate when there is purpose, not when there is no purpose. Therefore, when the blessed buddhas encounter something purposeless, they turn it away like a bucket of water. In this regard, since the blessed buddhas know the right time when something purposeful presents itself, the Blessed One questioned the group of six, saying: "Monks, is it true that you behaved in such an unseemly manner?" "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed One then censured them, saying that such conduct was unworthy of one who has gone forth, did not accord with the ascetic life, was not proper, was not in conformity with the rule, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth — and so on in this fashion. After censuring them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, therefore, having perceived the ten benefits, one should establish the foundations of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so on as before. "My hearers shall recite this foundation of training in the Vinaya as follows: Should any monk address a woman using the language one uses with a man, or address a man using the language one uses with a woman, acting as wives or as intimate female companions — even if only a brief meeting occurs — he incurs a Saṅgha transgression."

"Should any monk" refers to those of the group of six or any other who behaves similarly. "Address a woman using the language one uses with a man" means: language expressing the intention of conduct proper to a man, spoken toward a woman. "Address a man using the language one uses with a woman" means: language expressing the intention of conduct proper to a woman, spoken toward a man. "Acting as wives or as intimate female companions" means: as one of seven kinds of wives or as one of ten kinds of intimate female companions.

What are the seven kinds of wives? A wife given in exchange for a water-libation, a wife purchased for a price, a wife obtained by force, a wife who has gathered together of her own accord, a wife who is sustained with food and clothing, a wife who has been broken and tamed, and a wife encountered briefly — that is the seventh. Of these, what is a wife given in exchange for a water-libation? It is a woman or girl whom her parents have given to a man, pouring a water-libation and saying, "Let her be your wife and mistress of your household," and who, having become that man's wife and mistress of his household, is guarded most carefully and kept most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife given in exchange for a water-libation. What is a wife purchased for a price? It is a woman or girl whom a man has purchased from her parents, saying, "Let her be my wife and mistress of my household," and who, having become that man's wife and mistress of his household, is guarded most carefully and kept most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife purchased for a price. What is a wife obtained by force? When a king who has been consecrated with the royal anointment of a kṣatriya marshals a fourfold army with all its divisions, goes to a foreign territory and province, and brings back those who had not come —

— and who, having arrived there, proclaims the victory: when a man seizes a woman or girl in that moment of triumph, saying, "Let her be my wife and mistress of my household," and she becomes his wife and mistress of his household, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife obtained by force.

Furthermore, what is another kind of wife obtained by force? It is as follows: when brigands have sacked a village, or sacked a town, or sacked a province, and a man, making his own head the banner of victory, seizes a woman or girl, saying, "Let this one be my wife and mistress of my household," and she becomes his wife and mistress of his household, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such too is a wife obtained by force.

What is a wife who comes of her own accord? When a woman or girl comes to a man of her own faith, her own inclination, and her own joy, and says, "O prince, come here. Make me your mistress of the household, and I will be your noble wife and lady of the household," and she becomes his wife and mistress of his household, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife who comes of her own accord.

What is a wife sustained by clothing and food? When a woman or girl comes to a man and says, "O prince, come here. Give me clothing and food, and I will be your noble wife and lady of the household," and she becomes his wife and mistress of his household, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife sustained by clothing and food.

What is a wife united by mutual agreement? When a woman or girl comes to a man and says, "O prince, come here. Whatever wealth you have and whatever wealth I have, let us pool it together and live on it jointly; and whatever sons or daughters may come from the two of us — when we two have died and our time has come, let us make offerings, whether small or great, perform acts of merit, and go together to whatever world we are reborn in, and may we follow each other there. I will name you in that dedication by name," and she becomes his wife and mistress of his household, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife united by mutual agreement.

What is a wife met for a time? When a man thinks, "Today I will enjoy pleasure with this one," and at that time he has occasion to meet with a woman or girl for just a moment, and he guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a wife met for a time.

What are the ten kinds of women who are under protection? They are: one guarded by her mother, one guarded by her father, one guarded by her brother, one guarded by her sister, one guarded by her husband's female relatives, one guarded by her clan, one guarded by her kinsmen, one guarded by her lineage, one guarded by those of shared blood, and the tenth is one who is not in dispute.

Of these, what is a woman under the protection of her mother?

A woman or girl whose husband has died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — and who dwells under her mother's care, while her mother guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her mother.

What is a woman under the protection of her father? A woman or girl whose husband has died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — and who dwells under her father's care, while her father guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her father.

What is a woman under the protection of her brother? A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — and who dwells under her brother's care, while her brother guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her brother.

What is a woman under the protection of her sister? A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — and who dwells under her sister's care, while her sister guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her sister.

What is a woman under the protection of her husband's female relatives? A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — and who dwells under the care of her husband's female relatives, while those relatives speak to her thus: "Whoever is seen by our son is also seen by you, and whoever is seen by you is also seen by our son; therefore maintain yourself as a daughter-in-law on our food and clothing, and make yourself pleasing as a daughter-in-law" — and having said so, those relatives guard her most carefully and keep her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her husband's female relatives.

What is a woman under the protection of her clan? A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings —

she dwells under the protection of a relative, and the relative says to her, "Whomsoever I see as my son, that same one is someone you may see; and whomsoever you see, that same one is someone I see as my son — so remain content with my food and clothing, and let yourself be pleased as a daughter-in-law" — and having said so, the relative guards her most carefully and keeps her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her relatives.

What is a woman under the protection of her clan? By "clan" is meant the brahmin caste, the warrior caste, the merchant caste, and the commoner caste. A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — she dwells under the protection of members of her own clan, and those clanspeople guard her most carefully and keep her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her clan.

What is a woman under the protection of her lineage? By "lineage" is meant the lineage of Kuśa, the lineage of Vātsya, the lineage of Śāṇḍilya, the lineage of Bharadvāja, the lineage of the fifth, the lineage of the near-fifth, and the lineage of Gautama. A woman or girl whose parents and husband have died and the time has come upon her, or who has been imprisoned or executed by the king, or who has fled out of fear of the king to another district or another land, or who has become mad, or mentally disturbed, or endangered by her feelings — she dwells under the protection of her lineage, and the members of that lineage guard her most carefully and keep her most hidden so that she may not go about with others out of desire — such is a woman under the protection of her lineage.

What is a woman who is without dispute? A fully ordained nun (bhikṣuṇī), a woman who lives by the rule, a wandering woman, one who follows in accord with a husband's marital bed, and one who conducts herself according to the Dharma — such is a woman who is without dispute.

Now, householders are of two kinds: the guardian and the non-guardian. A guardian is one who has become the master of a girl through giving or through taking by force, whether she has entered an upper chamber or a lower room, and whose word — even if it is not true — should be accepted. Such a person is called a guardian. A non-guardian is one who has not become the master of a girl through giving or through taking by force, whether she has entered an upper chamber or a lower room, and whose word — even if it is true — need not be accepted. Such a person is called a non-guardian.

There are three circumstances by which a message is conveyed in the inward direction but not in the outward direction. What are the three? By location, by sign, and by mark.

How is it by location? When someone says, "When you see me in a pleasure grove, an assembly place, or somewhere in a divine residence, know that the matter has been done." That is how it is by location.

How is it by sign? When someone says, "When I am in the morning, at midday, or —"

"—in the evening, when you see me snap my fingers, know that the matter has been done." That is how it is by sign.

How is it by mark? When someone says, "When you see me shortly after having had my head and beard shaved, or wearing a red-and-yellow patched robe, or carrying a bowl with a lotus-leaf cover, or a wooden-handled iron-staff bowl, or a bowl of clarified butter, or a bowl of oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl of molasses with a stopper — when you see me carrying any of these, know that the matter has been done." That is how it is by mark.

There are three circumstances by which a message is conveyed both in the outward direction and in the inward direction. What are the three? By word, by written message, and by hand-delivered letter.

The Vinaya Analysis, the eighteenth fascicle.

When a monk brings together and reconciles any combination of the first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is still in the midst of a quarrel and not yet after the quarrel has ended, and the division has not been made, the three lots have not been cast, the proper procedure has not been performed, it has not been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs a single offense of wrongdoing.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is both one that is still in the midst of a quarrel and one that is after the quarrel has ended, and the division has not been made, the three lots have not been cast, the proper procedure has not been performed,

it has not been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs two offenses of wrongdoing.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, but the three lots have not been cast, the proper procedure has not been performed, it has not been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs three offenses of wrongdoing.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, and the three lots have been cast, but the proper procedure has not been performed, it has not been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs three offenses of wrongdoing and one grave offense.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, and the three lots have been cast, and the proper procedure has been performed, but it has not been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs three offenses of wrongdoing and two grave offenses.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, and the three lots have been cast, and the proper procedure has been performed, and it has been announced that she is not a wife, but the bell has not been proclaimed, he incurs three offenses of wrongdoing, three grave offenses, and one saṅghāvaśeṣa.

When a monk brings together any combination of those same first three types of wife — one given through a water-rite, one purchased with a price, and one obtained by seizure — and the situation is one that is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, and the three lots have been cast, and the proper procedure has been performed, and it has been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has been proclaimed, he incurs three offenses of wrongdoing, four grave offenses, and two saṅghāvaśeṣas.

When a monk brings together wives other than the foregoing — in a situation where it is in the midst of a quarrel, and after the quarrel has ended, and the division has been made, and the three lots have been cast, and the proper procedure has been performed, and it has been announced that she is not a wife, and the bell has been proclaimed — he incurs a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk going to a household arrives there and says, "Why is the household of this great young man not being maintained?" he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. If he says, "Why is this great young woman not being escorted?" he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. If he says, "Why is this young man and this young woman not being joined together?" he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. If he says, "Why does this young man not go to the house of his wife?" he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. If he says, "Why is this young woman not being taken to her husband's house?" he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. In short, if a monk going to a household utters any words that are in accord with such matters, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing in every case. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations.

The fifth chapter, concerning the saṅghāvaśeṣa of acting as a matchmaker, is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, dwelling places of the following kinds had become numerous among the monks. Some said, "This dwelling place is far too long," and having abandoned it, had it rebuilt differently. Some said, "This dwelling place is far too short. This one is far too wide. This one is far too narrow. This one is far too old."

"This one is far too weak in structure," and "This one is built quite badly," and having abandoned it, had it rebuilt differently. By their building dwelling places and having them built, their duties and building works had become manifold, and they were abandoning the recitation of scriptural transmissions, reading, chanting, the practice of yoga, and contemplation, and were repeatedly calling up laborers — for timber, for hired men, and for cart work — so that brahmins and householders began to censure them.

At that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the eastern Kubjārāma, in the pleasant hall of Mṛgāramātṛ. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa heard that dwelling places of such a kind had become numerous among the many monks. Having heard this, he rose from his afternoon meditation, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Reverend One, at the present time dwelling places of this kind have become numerous among the monks. Some said, 'This dwelling place is far too long,' and having abandoned it, had it rebuilt. Some said, 'This one is far too short. This one is far too wide. This one is far too narrow. This one is far too old. This one is far too weak in structure. This one is built quite badly,' and having abandoned it, had it rebuilt. By their building dwelling places and having them built, their duties and building works became manifold, and they abandoned the recitation of scriptural transmissions, reading, chanting, the practice of yoga, and contemplation, and repeatedly called up laborers for timber posts, for hired men, and for cart work, so that brahmins and householders censured them. May the Blessed One, out of compassion, instruct the monks well regarding dwelling places and the foundations of dwelling places."

The Blessed One, by remaining silent, granted permission to the venerable Mahākāśyapa. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, understanding that the Blessed One's silence was his permission, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and withdrew from the presence of the Blessed One. Then that very night the venerable Mahākāśyapa, in order to guard the minds of those who live the holy life (brahmacarya), took up his bowl and monastic robe and went walking through the countryside.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident and this occasion and this context, convened the community of monks — and so on, as before. The buddha, the Blessed One, then asked the many monks: "Monks, is it true that dwelling places of this kind have become numerous among you, that some said, 'This dwelling place is far too long,' and had it rebuilt, that some said, 'This one is far too short, this one is far too wide, this one is far too narrow, this one is far too old, this one is far too weak in structure, this one is built quite badly,' and had it rebuilt?"

"Reverend One, it is so."

The buddha, the Blessed One, criticized those of great desire, who know no contentment, who are difficult to care for and difficult to satisfy. Then the Blessed One praised the qualities of having few desires, of knowing contentment, of being easy to care for, of being easy to satisfy, of being retiring, of using few requisites, of being disciplined, of being accomplished, and of knowing moderation. Having so praised them, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing these ten benefits fully, the training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be established" — and so on, as before. "My hearers in the Vinaya shall recite this training rule as follows:

"If a monk, having solicited materials himself, with no owner present, were to have a dwelling built for his own sake, he should have it built according to the prescribed measure. The prescribed measure for a dwelling is as follows: twelve Sugata-cubits in height on the inside and seven Sugata-cubits in width. That monk should bring along other monks to inspect the site. The monks who are brought should examine whether the site is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. If a monk, having solicited materials himself with no owner present, were to have a dwelling built for his own sake, yet fails to bring monks to inspect the site, or the monks who are brought are not shown the site, or the site is unsuitable, involves a dispute, or is unfit to build upon — if it exceeds the measure, it is an offence requiring forfeiture to the Saṅgha."

Now the word-by-word commentary:

"A monk" refers to the monk of this Dharma, that is, one who belongs to this teaching. "Having solicited himself" means begging that arises from one's own desire — from some people one solicits timber, from others grass, from others labour, from others the work of carpenters. "With no owner" means there is no owner who has appeared — neither a man, a woman, nor a person of indeterminate sex. "For his own sake" means dedicated to himself. "A dwelling" means any structure that can accommodate the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. "Were to have built" means by himself or by another.

"He should have it built according to the prescribed measure. The prescribed measure for a dwelling is as follows: twelve Sugata-cubits in height on the inside and seven Sugata-cubits in width." Here, "Sugata" means the Teacher. His twelve cubits — those twelve Sugata-heights — each correspond to twenty-eight standard hand-spans of a standard cubit, so the inner height amounts to twenty-eight standard cubits. The seven Sugata-widths — those seven Sugata-widths — each correspond to eleven and a half standard hand-spans of a standard cubit, so the inner width amounts to eleven and a half standard cubits.

"That monk should bring along other monks to inspect the site." As for "to inspect the site," this means for the purpose of examining whether the ground is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. "That monk" means whichever monk it is. "Should bring along monks" means not that he need bring as many monks as could lay eyes on the site, but rather the monks who are present there. If there happen to be snakes, harmful animals, insects, or ants at that site, then since it is unsuitable it should not be indicated. If it appears suitable, one should then examine what lies nearby: if the site belongs to the king, or is a stūpa ground, or belongs to a householder, or belongs to non-Buddhist adherents, or is a rains-retreat dwelling of nuns, or has trees that would need to be cut down, then since it involves dispute it should not be indicated. If the site is suitable and free from dispute, one should then examine the surrounding area within a circumference of a fathom all around: if the site rests upon a riverbank, upon a well, upon a road, or upon a cliff or ravine, then since it is unfit to build upon it should not be indicated. If the site is suitable and perfect in every respect, then that monk should go to the assembly hall, prepare the seats, strike the gong, and summon the monks with the words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in concord, he should remove his sandals, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage in order of seniority, and then sitting cross-legged to the side of the most senior monk, joining his palms, should speak these words:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the monk known as so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, have sought out a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon.

"I, the monk known as so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, having sought from the Saṅgha a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon, respectfully present this request. May the venerable, compassionate Saṅgha, out of compassion, please show me, the monk known as so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, a site that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon." This is to be repeated a second and a third time.

The other monks, however, should not simply follow that monk out of personal trust or confidence in him. Rather, either the entire Saṅgha should go to the site together, or monks appointed by the Saṅgha should be sent. These appointed monks should inspect the site with their own eyes. If the site harbors snakes, is a place of ill omen, frequented by beetles, or infested with ants, it is unsuitable and must not be indicated. If it is suitable, they must then examine the area immediately surrounding it. If the site rests upon land belonging to the king, upon land of a stūpa, upon land of a householder, upon land of non-Buddhists, upon the site of a nuns' rains-retreat dwelling, or upon land where trees that would need to be felled are standing, then it is a site in dispute and must not be indicated. If the site is suitable and free from dispute, they must then examine the perimeter, measuring approximately one armspan around its circumference. If the site rests upon a river or stream, upon a well, upon a road, or upon a ravine or gully, it may not be built upon and must not be indicated.

If the site is suitable and complete in every respect, the monks should then sit respectfully to one side, facing the elder, and speak these words: "Venerable elders, this site is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. Please now be aware that the time has come." After that, one monk should make the formal request and carry out the legal act.

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk, so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, has sought out a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. This monk, so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, requests of the Saṅgha that the site for a dwelling — suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon — be shown to him. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it pleases them, may the Saṅgha grant this. The Saṅgha shall show the monk so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon." This is the motion. The legal act is to be performed as follows:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk, so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, has sought out a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. This monk, so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, requests of the Saṅgha that the site — suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon — be shown to him. On his behalf, the Saṅgha shall show the monk so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, the site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. Those venerable ones who consent to the Saṅgha's showing the monk so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon should remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak."

The Saṅgha has consented and approved: the Saṅgha has shown the monk so-and-so, apprentice of the elder, a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. Since no one has spoken, it is so held.

The Saṅgha has shown the monk so-and-so, apprentice of the elder — whatever his name — a site for a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, and fit to build upon. He may proceed to have the dwelling constructed and should have no regrets in this matter.

The phrase "and also by the escorting monks" means: also by whichever monks escorted him there.

The word "site" means: whatever site is intended for the construction of a dwelling.

The word "suitable" means: free from snake-haunted places, inauspicious places, and the like.

The phrase "free from dispute" means: free from hearths, places used for tanning, and the like.

The phrase "fit to build upon" means: that there are no faults anywhere within the surrounding area of one standard measure around that site.

The phrase "should be inspected" means: should be individually examined.

The phrase "if a monk considers the site unsuitable" means: that snake-haunted places, inauspicious places, and the like predominate there.

The phrase "or subject to dispute" means: that it contains a hearth, or a place for tanning, or that it is subject to dispute or contention.

The phrase "not fit to build upon" means: that there is no surrounding area of one standard measure around that site.

"I myself initiated this; it has no owner; may I have the dwelling built for my own sake — or else may I not bring monks along to inspect the site, or may I not show the site to the escorting monks."

The phrase "if it exceeds the measure" means: if one has the dwelling built so as to exceed the measure as prescribed.

The phrase "a saṅghāvaśeṣa (Skt. saṅghāvaśeṣa) offense" — this is as before; therefore it is said to be a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

Now, as to how transgressions come about: if a monk has a dwelling built and has it built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred. If he has it built on a site subject to dispute, a grave offense is incurred. If he has it built on a site not fit to build upon, a grave offense is incurred. If he has it built without having shown the site, a grave offense is incurred. If he has it built so as to exceed the measure, a grave offense is incurred. If he has it built in violation of all these conditions, it becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a monk goes to another monk and says: "Please allow me to have built for my own sake a dwelling that is suitable, free from dispute, fit to build upon, properly shown, and within the proper measure" — and that other monk, acting on his behalf, has it built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If he has it built on a site subject to dispute, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If he has it built on a site not fit to build upon, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If he has it built without having shown the site, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If he has it built so as to exceed the measure, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If he has it built in violation of all these conditions, a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work.

If that monk then goes to the other and says: "Well done! Excellently done! I instructed you in exactly this way" — and then that monk also offers him timber, grass, clay, or mud — and if that monk then has it built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred by both. If he has it built on a site subject to dispute, a grave offense is incurred by both. If he has it built on a site not fit to build upon, a grave offense is incurred by both. If he has it built without having shown the site, a grave offense is incurred by both. If he has it built so as to exceed the measure, a grave offense is incurred by both. If he has it built in violation of all these conditions, a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense is incurred by both.

If that monk then goes to the other and says: "It was not well done. It was very poorly done. I gave you no such instruction" — and that monk does not offer him timber, grass, clay, or mud — and if that monk then has it built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work.

If one causes it to be built so as to occasion dispute, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If one causes it to be built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If one causes it to be built without having shown the site, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If one causes it to be built so as to exceed the measure, a grave offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. If one causes it to be built in violation of all these conditions, a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense is incurred by the one who carries out the work. For those who obtain what has been built and make use of what has been built, there is no transgression. For one who repairs what is old, there is likewise no transgression. For a first offender, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for those afflicted by painful sensation, there is no transgression. This is the sixth saṅghāvaśeṣa concerning dwelling places, and it is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the garden of Kubjā. The group of six were residing in temple buildings that others had caused to be built, and while they were staying in those places, they began to taunt Nandā and Upanandā, saying: "Look at these temple buildings — they are dilapidated ruins. They are cracked. Their boundaries are ruined. Their facades are ruined. They are like a widow's house." The monks then said to them: "Venerable ones, you are staying in temple buildings that others had built, for you are not even able to set one stone upon another, yet you taunt." When this was said, the group of six became swollen with pride and began to speak among themselves: "These black-bowled ones — Nandā and Upanandā — have said to us: 'You are staying in temple buildings that others had built, for you cannot even set one stone upon another, yet you taunt.' How utterly humiliating. Come away. Previously we caused no temple buildings whatsoever to be built — not one of any kind by these black-bowled ones. What sort of temple buildings shall we now cause to be built? If all of us devote ourselves to the work of our own hands, these black-bowled ones will constantly seek occasion against us, and they will find the occasion to say that all the group of six have taken to working with their own hands, and they will also go to the households where we beg alms and, pointing out our faults and failings, turn those households against us. We must not fail to go to whichever one among us is skilled, whose conduct is clear, and who is able to thread a needle through its eye, and encourage him. For that reason, whichever one among us is skilled, whose conduct is clear, and who is able to thread a needle through its eye — the venerable Dundupa among us, who is skilled, whose conduct is clear, and who is able to thread a needle through its eye — let us go to him and encourage him." And so they went to Dundupa and said to him: "Venerable Dundupa, these black-bowled ones have so utterly humiliated us, saying: 'You are staying in temple buildings that others had built, for you cannot even set one stone upon another, yet you taunt.' And so we thought: these black-bowled ones have humiliated us by saying, 'You are staying in temple buildings that others had built, for you cannot even set one stone upon another, yet you taunt.' Come away. Previously we caused no temple buildings at all to be built — not one of any kind by these black-bowled ones. Now let us cause temple buildings of just such a kind to be built."

"If all of us were to devote ourselves to manual work, the black-bowled ones would constantly be looking for an occasion against us, and they would find occasion to say that all the members of the six groups have taken up manual work. And they would go to the houses from which we beg alms, fault us for being busy, and bring those householders to turn against us. But if we can manage to rouse enthusiasm in the one among us who is skilled, whose conduct is exemplary, and who is capable of threading a needle, then it need not fall apart. Therefore, the one among us who is skilled, whose conduct is exemplary, and who is capable of threading a needle — venerable Dundupa is skilled, his conduct is exemplary, he is capable of threading a needle — and so let us rouse enthusiasm in him, let us go to him. We shall rouse enthusiasm in the venerable one for the sake of the temple building, and we petition you: overwhelm the black-bowled ones with this very point."

Dundupa said: "It is a good plan. Do so, then." They were glad at heart and departed.

The venerable Dundupa then washed both feet outside the temple building, entered it, sat down, and turned his mind to this thought: by whatever means the Saṅgha's temple building might be accomplished. He began to reflect on who among people had true devotion. And he thought to himself: "For the time being, in this world together with its gods, it is the Blessed One who commands devotion. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Kauṇḍinya. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Mahākāśyapa. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Śāriputra. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Aniruddha. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Aśvajit. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Bhadrika. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Vāṣpa. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Mahānāman. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Gavāṃpati. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Vimala. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Gavampati. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Ānanda. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Sundarananda, the nephew of the Blessed One by his younger sister. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Rāhula, the son of the Blessed One. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Vīranandana. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Nandika. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Upānanda. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Śīghragāmin. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Carka. One great house has devotion toward the venerable Nābhasa. Since it is not possible to have any of these engaged in the work, there is in Kauśāmbī a brahmin who is wealthy, of great possessions, with extensive property, expansive and broad — yet he is miserly and narrow-eyed, one who will not even give a scrap of food to a crow, and who holds tightly to all his goods. Yet he has much wealth and gold, and if one could get him to participate, the Saṅgha's temple building would be accomplished." Having entered upon that thought, he spent the night in great effort, and in the early morning he put on his lower robe, took his bowl and outer robe, and went into Kauśāmbī for alms. He passed through two or three houses collecting alms, took a small amount of flour, and started to enter that brahmin's house, when the doorman stopped him, saying: "Noble one, wait. Do not enter."

He then said:

"Good sir, the Blessed One taught five kinds of places that are not proper domains for us. They are: the dwelling of musicians, the dwelling of a woman of loose conduct, the dwelling of a liquor-seller, the dwelling of an outcaste, and a royal palace. Now, is this house the dwelling of a musician? Or is it the dwelling of a woman of loose conduct? Or a liquor-seller's dwelling? Or an outcaste's dwelling? Or a royal palace? Why then do you stop me?" The doorman replied: "Noble one, you may well take offense at many things, but this is not the dwelling of a musician, nor the dwelling of a woman of loose conduct, nor a liquor-seller's dwelling, nor an outcaste's dwelling, nor a royal palace. Rather, this is the house of a certain great brahmin." The venerable Udāyin thought: "Where there is not even a chance of a brief encounter, what else can there be?" He remained thus, stopped at the gate, his mind turned inward in reflection.

While he was sitting there, the son of the householder was born, and to mark the occasion, twelve assembled companies entered in festivity, with dance, song, and instrumental music. The doorman, occupied with attending to them and not looking toward the gate, gave the venerable Udāyin the opportunity to enter. He went in, and began to purify the ground of those free from attachment by conducting himself according to his way of practice. The brahmin, seeing him, said: "Venerable Udāyin, welcome! Please be seated on this cushion." Udāyin sat, but found no opening for meaningful conversation. So the venerable Udāyin said: "Brahmin, I have obtained a small amount of alms-flour. Please have it sieved and give it here." The brahmin instructed his daughter: "Daughter, gather the noble one's alms-flour and present it." When the daughter began to sieve it, the venerable Udāyin started to examine the flour. The brahmin said: "Noble one, what are you looking at?" "Living creatures." "If there are any, what should be done?" "Do not eat them." "If they were consumed, what fault would there be?" "Brahmin, the Blessed One has taught that one who thoroughly takes up, practices, and repeatedly commits the killing of living beings will, when this body breaks up and death comes, be reborn in a state of woe, an evil destiny, a fallen state, in the hells. And even if one were to come back among human beings in such a form, one's life would be short." And so forth — he went on to teach at length the paths of karma of the ten non-virtues and the ten virtues. The brahmin became filled with confident faith, and himself prepared food and pure drink, filled a vessel with what was wholesome, and said: "Noble one, out of kindness, please accept this." The venerable Udāyin thought: "If I accept it, it will be like cooking in a wooden vessel — what began as my first visit will end up as my last." He then said: "Brahmin, I have obtained just this small amount of alms-flour — I shall enjoy it entirely myself. As for accepting a gift given with faith, how could one rightly throw that away?" The brahmin said: "Noble one, the custom among us brahmins is this: if one obtains something inferior and then obtains something superior, one sets aside the inferior and thoroughly enjoys the superior. What fault is there in that for you all?" "Brahmin, we have properly undertaken the rules of training. You brahmins have not properly undertaken the rules of training, and so you brahmins do as you please. As for us, the Blessed One has proclaimed four noble lineages for us. What are the four? The noble lineage of being content with whatever robe one has; the noble lineage of being content with whatever alms-food one obtains; the noble lineage of being content with whatever dwelling and bedding one has; and the noble lineage of delight in relinquishment and delight in cultivation." The brahmin became greatly filled with confident faith, and said:

"Noble one, please come to this household at any time. Brahmin, this gatekeeper of yours is like the rod of Yama, the Lord of Death — do not let anyone in. Give him proper instructions, and then he will not obstruct me."

The brahmin called the gatekeeper and gave him proper instructions: "Head of household, this house belongs to the noble Dundupa. Do not obstruct him." He also gave instructions to the household members: "You must not be disrespectful toward the noble Dundupa."

The venerable Dundupa thought to himself: "This brahmin has indeed become filled with confident faith, yet if those with black begging bowls should enter here, that would inevitably cause disturbance. I should devise a skillful means." So Dundupa said to the gatekeeper: "Head of household, did you see how that brahmin came to have confident faith in me? You have seen it, noble one. Let only me enter here, and do not allow anyone with a black begging bowl to come in. If you allow anyone with a black begging bowl to enter, I will see to it that a great punishment befalls you. Noble one, please come and go with complete ease. As for yourself, even if you were to forget this for a time and another with a black begging bowl were to enter, what would that matter?"

The venerable Dundupa departed with a glad mind, and from then on he went to that brahmin's house regularly. When the brahmin likewise kept offering again and again, the venerable Dundupa would not accept his offerings but merely taught and retaught the Dharma of generosity and then departed.

Some time later, the venerable Dundupa spoke in praise of the seven bases of meritorious action arising from material gifts to that brahmin, and explained them extensively and well. The brahmin said: "Noble one, I too would perform some of the bases of meritorious action arising from material gifts." "Brahmin, do so." "Noble one, what should I do?" "Let a hall be built for the Saṅgha." The brahmin thought: "I have offered the noble Dundupa gifts in many forms, and he has accepted them but few times. Yet even that which he has accepted has been for the sake of the Saṅgha." Marveling at this, he said: "Noble one, I do have kārṣāpaṇas, yet the land is under the king's control, and there is no vacant plot where a hall for the Saṅgha could be built." "Brahmin, take heart in this small matter — I will obtain land from the king." "Noble one, if that is so, excellent!"

The venerable Dundupa thought: "How should I proceed — should I approach the king directly, or rather approach the ministers?" Then he reflected: "Some say that one should rely not on those on whom one merely relies but on those on whom one truly ought to rely." And so he began to approach the ministers, and after cultivating them for some time, the ministers asked: "Noble one, what is your wish?" Dundupa replied: "Good sirs, a brahmin has undertaken to build a hall for the Saṅgha, yet since the land is under the king's control and there is no site where the hall may be constructed, I wish to have this matter of the land brought before the king's ear — would you assist with this?" "Noble one, when the king is seated with a small retinue in a quiet place, we will inform you — watch for that time."

When, some time later, the king was seated with a small retinue in a quiet place, those ministers sent a great messenger to the venerable Dundupa, saying: "Noble one, the king is seated with a small retinue in a quiet place — come now!"

Dundupa arrived, greeted the king with "Arogyā," and sat to one side. The ministers then addressed the king: "Sire, this is the noble Dundupa — one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the three scriptural collections, who teaches the Dharma, and who is endowed with the eloquence of reasoning and liberation." The king said: "It is good that the noble one has come. For what purpose have you come?" Dundupa replied: "Sire, a brahmin has been given leave to build a hall for the Saṅgha, yet since the land is under the king's authority and there is no suitable site, it is fitting that Your Majesty grant a site. Noble one, save for the royal palace alone, wherever you please, grant leave to build the hall there." The venerable Dundupa said "Arogyā" to the king, and, his heart at ease, he departed from the royal palace and went to the dwelling of the six monks. There he said to them: "Friends, a certain distinguished brahmin benefactor has been commissioned to build a hall for the Saṅgha, and when I petitioned the king for a site, the king said: 'Noble one, save for the royal palace alone, wherever you wish, build the hall there.' So measure out the land."

They all assembled and went before that brahmin and said: "Brahmin, the king has authorized us, saying: 'Save for the royal palace alone, wherever you wish, build the hall there.' So bring the kārṣāpaṇas and proceed with the construction of the hall." The brahmin gave the six monks the kārṣāpaṇas, and they, having received the coins, began to deliberate among themselves, discussing in which direction the hall should be built.

Between Kauśāmbī and the pleasure grove of Ghāṃśakā there stood a beautiful shade tree. Beside that tree there was a brahmin accompanied by a very large retinue, having five hundred brahmin boys recite brahminic sacred texts. Those five hundred brahmin boys, whenever the six monks set out or returned from their alms round, would repeatedly call out: "Ho, six monks — did you get excellent alms food? Did you get alms food at all from the first house? Were your bowls full?" Because of this, the six monks thought to themselves: "Those five hundred brahmin students of that brahmin are always harassing us with their cries of 'Ho, six monks — did you get excellent alms food? Did you get alms food at all from the first house? Were your bowls full?' We must make them unhappy. If we have that beautiful shade tree cut down and build the hall in that spot, then they will never again pester us repeatedly in this way." Having thus resolved, they took the kārṣāpaṇas, went to the carpenters' market, and said to the skilled workers: "Work on the hall for these wages." And those workers were engaged.

The six monks gave those hired workers oil for their bodies and oil for their heads. Pleased, the workers said: "Noble ones, proceed — let the work orders reach us." The six monks said: "The work will indeed get done — stay for now." Having held them back for a while, when the sun had set those workers said: "Noble ones, we will return tomorrow — please give us today's wages." The six monks said: "You have done a great deal of work, so shall we give those wages then?" The workers replied: "Noble ones, of what you instructed us to do, we have not done it yet — skilled workers take up axes, adzes, and chisels, and set out to do the work." The hired workers, together with the six monks, took up axes, adzes, and chisels, and when they were out of sight they went to that beautiful shade tree. And the six monks said:

"Friends, cut down this monastery shade tree!" But those workers said: "Noble ones, this is the monastery shade tree — do we have two heads, that we would cut it down? We will not cut it down." The poor men said: "The land is under the king's authority, and he has given his solemn word to us that, excepting only the royal palace, wherever we wish we may build a temple. So who would cut off your head? Cut it down without fear or worry." They cut down that monastery shade tree, pulled out all the wood from the roots, and leveled that plot of ground in such a way that no one could tell where the monastery shade tree had stood. The six monks then began to survey the site with their eyes, saying: "Dear Nanda, Upananda — on this side let us build the Blessed One's bathroom; on this side let us build a gatehouse; on this side let us build a kitchen; on this side let us build a storeroom; on this side let us build a dwelling for the attendants." Having marked it all out, they left.

Now the practice of those brahmin boys was to take turns going each day to the foot of that monastery shade tree to make offerings: they would bow down, walk around it, and smear it with an ointment of cow dung mixed with ghee. One time it was a particular brahmin boy's turn, and he rose early in the morning and went there. Not finding the monastery shade tree, he came to the preceptor and said: "Preceptor, that monastery shade tree is gone." The brahmin said: "Alas, brahmin boy, did you not go the wrong way? In the night, where did that tree go?" Another brahmin boy who was with him broke into laughter and said: "Preceptor, this brahmin boy was out last night searching for fallen fruit, and that is why he did not see it." The brahmin then sent another more senior brahmin boy, and he likewise did not find it, and coming back he said: "Preceptor, it is so — that monastery shade tree is simply gone." Then they all gathered and went there, and finding that it was indeed so, one mindful brahmin boy among them said: "In this direction the preceptor used to recite his sacred formulas. In this direction I used to perform my own practice — how has this fault come about and what has happened? I do not understand." While they were standing there turning this over in their minds, a man came and said: "Brahmin, why do you and your retinue stand there, lost in thought? My friend, I do not know where in the night that shade tree that stood in this place has gone." The brahmin replied: "My friend, last night when my eyes stopped working in the dark, I saw the six monks right here, busy with axes, adzes, and chisels, together with some hired workers — could it not be that they cut it down?" The brahmin said: "My friend, yes, indeed that must be it." While they were standing there, having come to this understanding, the six monks arrived, and those monks said: "Brahmins, why do you stand there lost in thought? Noble ones, I do not know where in the night that monastery shade tree that stood in this place has gone." The six monks began to laugh, and the brahmin said: "Noble ones, did you not cut it down? You poor ones — you were always stationed near it, and you used to call out to us: 'Hey, six monks! Have you received the finest alms? Have you received alms at all? Is your bowl full?' That is why you should not be glad about this." And they derided them, saying: "That is the conduct of the monks, the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyans — it is mere talk; the conduct of brahmins — that too is mere talk; yet see, even the monastery shade tree has ended up being cut down."

They mocked them and spoke ill of them. The news passed from one to another, and the assembled people living in Kauśāmbī, as well as those who had come there from other regions, also heard of it; and they too, in the main roads, the market streets, the crossroads, and the three-way junctions, denounced, mocked, and spoke ill of them. Those among them who had no faith would not give alms even to those who had gone out on alms rounds. It was then that the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, given this occurrence, this occasion, and these circumstances, convened the community of monks — and so forth as before. He then declared: "My hearers are to train in the Vinaya, and the rule is to be recited as follows.

If a monk, in order to have a great monastery built for the Saṅgha by a donor who has a proprietor — whether male, female, or of indeterminate sex — wishes to inspect a site, then that monk is to invite other monks along. The monks who are brought along are to examine whether the site is suitable, free from dispute, and fit for construction.

If the monk either intends to have a great monastery built for the Saṅgha by such a donor without the site being suitable, or while it is disputed, or while it is unfit for construction — or if he does not bring monks along to inspect the site, or does not show the site to the monks who have been brought — that is an offense involving the remainder of the Saṅgha.

'A monk' means one of the six monks or, further, any follower of this Dharma. 'A donor who has a proprietor' means someone for whom a proprietor has arisen — whether male, female, or of indeterminate sex. 'For the Saṅgha' means for the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. 'A monastery' is a place in which the four modes of deportment — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down — can be accommodated. 'Great' has two meanings: greatness in terms of what is to be given, and greatness in terms of measure. Here it is the greatness of what is to be given that is intended, not greatness of measure. 'To have it built' means by oneself or by another. As for the clause 'in order to inspect the site, that monk is to bring monks along,' the phrase 'in order to inspect the site' means in order to examine whether the ground itself is suitable, free from dispute, and fit for construction. 'That monk' means whichever monk it may be. 'Is to invite monks along' means the monks who are present at that place; it does not mean that however many monks it would take for the site to be fully seen by all of their eyes are to be brought along.

If in that place there is a serpent's den, a den of vicious creatures, a scorpion's nest, or an anthill, then it is not to be pointed out, because it would be unsuitable. If it is suitable, one should then examine the vicinity more closely. If the site borders on royal ground, a stūpa site, a householder's property, a non-Buddhist's property, nuns' rain-retreat quarters, or if there are trees that would need to be felled, then it is not to be pointed out, because it would be disputed.

If the site is suitable and free from dispute, one should then examine the surrounding space — an area of how many fathoms encompassing it on all sides. If the ground of the site rests against a river, a well, a road, or a ravine, then it is not to be pointed out, because it would be unfit for construction.

If the site is suitable and complete in every respect, then that monk should go to the monastery, arrange the seats, strike the wooden gong, and summon the monks with words of inquiry. Once the entire Saṅgha is gathered and in harmony, he should remove his sandals, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, bow in order of seniority, then sit in a squatting posture off to the side near the most senior monk, join his palms together, and speak as follows.

May the venerable Saṅgha please give ear. I, the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, have sought a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. I, the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, request that the Saṅgha indicate to me a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. May the venerable and compassionate members of the Saṅgha, out of compassion, please grant to me, the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, the indication of a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction.

This is to be repeated a second and third time.

Those monks, however, should not go to the site out of personal faith in or partiality toward that monk. Rather, the entire Saṅgha should go there together, or the Saṅgha should send monks appointed by it. Those monks are to inspect the site with their own eyes. If there is found at that place a haunt of snakes, a haunt of malignant spirits, a haunt of crickets, or a haunt of ants, it is not to be pointed out, because it would be unfit. If it is suitable, then the immediate surroundings are to be carefully examined. If the site belongs to the king, to a stūpa, to a householder, or to a non-Buddhist adherent, or if it is a rains-retreat dwelling of nuns, or if there are trees that would need to be felled, it is not to be pointed out, because it would be a matter of dispute. If the site is suitable and free of dispute, then the surrounding perimeter of one bow-length on all sides is to be carefully examined. If the site there rests against a river, a well, a road, or a ravine, then it is not to be pointed out, because it would be unfit for construction.

If the site is suitable and complete in every respect, then those monks should sit respectfully off to the side near the most senior elder and speak as follows: "Venerables, this site is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. Please be aware that the time for it has now come."

After that, one monk is to make the motion and perform the formal act. May the venerable Saṅgha please give ear. The monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, has sought a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. The monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, requests that the Saṅgha indicate a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it consents, may the Saṅgha please grant permission, and may the Saṅgha indicate to the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. This is the motion.

The formal act is to be performed as follows. May the venerable Saṅgha please give ear. The monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, has sought a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. The monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, requests that the Saṅgha indicate a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. Therefore, the Saṅgha is to indicate to the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. Those venerable ones who consent to the Saṅgha's indication to the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, of a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction should remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and granted it. The Saṅgha has indicated to the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute,

and fit for construction has been granted. Since no one has spoken, it is held to be so.

The Saṅgha has given the indication to the monk so-and-so, son of so-and-so, of a site for a monastery that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction. He should proceed to build the monastery and should have no regret about this. As for the phrase "the monks who were brought along" — this refers to whatever monks were brought along to that place. The word "site" refers to whatever site is designated for the monastery. The word "suitable" means free from places inhabited by snakes, inauspicious places, and the like. The phrase "free of dispute" means free from hearths, uncovered latrines, and the like. The phrase "fit for construction" means that the perimeter of one bow-length surrounding it is free of faults. The phrase "should be inspected" means it should be examined individually.

The phrase "if the monk considers the site unsuitable" means that places infested with snakes, inauspicious places, and the like are predominant there. The phrase "or with dispute" means that there is a hearth, or an uncovered latrine, or dispute, or refuse. The phrase "unfit for construction" means that the surrounding perimeter of one bow-length is absent. If an owner causes a great monastery to be built for the Saṅgha, or if monks are not brought to inspect the site, or if the site is not shown to the monks who were brought along, that constitutes a Saṅgha-remainder offense — the earlier rule applies — and for this reason it was said to be a Saṅgha-remainder offense.

As for how a transgression arises in this matter: if a monk, in causing a monastery to be built for the Saṅgha, causes it to be built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense is incurred. If he causes it to be built on a site with dispute, a grave offense is incurred. If he causes it to be built on a site unfit for construction, a grave offense is incurred. If he causes it to be built without the indication having been given, a grave offense is incurred. If he causes it to be built in violation of all these conditions, it becomes a Saṅgha-remainder offense.

If a monk goes to another monk and says, "Let the indication be given of a site for a monastery for the Saṅgha that is suitable, free of dispute, and fit for construction," and if that monk then causes it to be built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense accrues to the one who actually does it. If he causes it to be built on a site with dispute, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built on a site unfit for construction, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built without the indication having been given, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built in violation of all these conditions, it becomes a Saṅgha-remainder offense for the one who does it.

Now if the one who was approached goes to the other and says, "Well done! Excellent! I give you this instruction," and that one then offers him wood, or grass, or dung, or clay, and then causes it to be built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense accrues to both of them. If he causes it to be built on a site with dispute, a grave offense accrues to both. If he causes it to be built on a site unfit for construction, a grave offense accrues to both. If he causes it to be built without the indication having been given, a grave offense accrues to both. If he causes it to be built in violation of all these conditions, it becomes a Saṅgha-remainder offense for both.

Now if the one who was approached goes to the other and says, "Not well done! Not at all well done! I gave you no such instruction," and that one does not offer him wood, or grass, or dung, or clay, yet still causes it to be built on an unsuitable site, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built on a site with dispute, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built on a site unfit for construction, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it.

If he causes it to be built without instruction, a grave offense accrues to the one who does it. If he causes it to be built in violation of all these conditions, it becomes a Saṅgha-remainder offense for the one who does it. If the cell was already built and he obtains it, or if he makes use of one already built, there is no transgression. There is also no transgression for repairing an old one. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations. The seventh Saṅgha-remainder rule concerning a dwelling-hall is thus complete.

The Vinaya-vibhaṅga, the nineteenth fascicle.

The blessed buddha Śākyamuni was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove of the Veṇuvana. At that time a wrongdoing arose. There was a man of the warrior class (kṣatriya), a man of great name, belonging to the warrior lineage, wealthy and possessed of many riches and great resources, whose domain of possession was vast and wide, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in riches, who was engaged in ruling a kingdom without a crown among the warriors. He had taken a wife of equal birth and lived with her in play, in joy, and in delightful enjoyment. Though they played together and rejoiced and lived in delight, they had no son and no daughter. Lacking a son and longing ardently for one, he made supplications to Śiva, to water deities, to spirits of ill form, to Śakra, to Brahmā, and to others of that kind; and also to various other classes of deity, such as the deities of pleasure parks, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, the deities who receive torma offerings, the deities born together with one, the deities of concordant disposition, and the deities who follow as attendants.

There is in the world a saying of this kind: "Sons and daughters are born from the cause of making supplications." But that is not so. If it were so, then each person who made such supplications would have a thousand sons, just like a wheel-turning king. Rather, sons and daughters are born when three conditions are simultaneously present. What are those three? The father and mother come together with desire; the mother's time has arrived and she is in her fertile season; and a gandharva (Skt. gandharva) is present nearby and ready to enter. When these three conditions are simultaneously present, sons and daughters are born.

Now while he was thus persisting in making his supplications, a being in its final existence, one who had lived the conduct of a final-existence being, who had grasped the essence of liberation, who was turned toward nirvāṇa, who was turned away from saṃsāra, who had no wish for death and transmigration or for rebirth in any of the destinies of existence, who held his last body — that being passed away from a fine divine realm and entered the womb of that householder's wife.

Some women who are skilled in the ways of women possess five qualities that are unmixed. What are those five? They know when a man has become attached and know when his attachment has passed; they know the right time and know their fertile season; they know when a being has entered the womb; they know from where the being that has entered the womb has come; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, it rests leaning to the right side of the flank, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning to the left side of the flank.

She, delighted and glad, spoke to the householder: "My lord's son, a being has entered into me — and since it rests here leaning to the right side of my flank, it will certainly be a boy. Please rejoice." He too, delighted and glad, straightened his upper body, stretched out his right hand, and spoke these words: "I shall now see the face of the son I have longed for these many years; one who is born in accord with me and not discordant with me; who performs my duties; who nurtures me in return for my having nurtured him; who enjoys his rightful share; and

who causes my lineage to continue for a long time, and who, when we have died and our time has come, will give gifts great or small and make merit on our behalf, and who will follow after us wherever those two have been reborn" — thus he deliberately uttered that earnest declaration.
