When they knew that a sentient being had entered her, they arranged for her care in the following manner, in order to bring to full maturation what was dwelling in the womb: in the upper chambers of the mansion, when it was cold, they provided cooling things, and when it was warm, they provided warming things; and they provided food prepared by a physician — not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too hot, not too sharp, and free from bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, heat, and sharpness. And her body, adorned with necklaces and ornaments, was like that of a divine maiden moving at ease in a pleasure grove. She was carried from couch to couch, and from seat to seat, and was not set down on the bare ground, lest she hear even the slightest unpleasant sound. Thus they attended to her without any harm.

When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and there came forth a boy handsome in form, lovely to behold, beautiful, radiant, of a color resembling gold, with a head like a canopy, long arms, broad shoulders at the collarbone, curved eyebrows, and a high-bridged nose.

His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — three groups of seven — they celebrated the birth feast on a grand scale, and they proceeded to give the boy a name, asking what name he should be given. Since his deportment — so long as he had not been taken down from the great bed he would not defecate or urinate — and since in the central lands, deportment in which the practice of the wise is manifest is called "like a jewel," the relatives said: "Friends, this boy belongs to the great warrior clan and is also the son of a noble family. Since he does not defecate or urinate so long as he has not been taken down from the great bed, and since, with the practice of the wise being manifest, he is also like a jewel — let the boy's name therefore be Warrior-Son Jewel." And so his name was fixed as Warrior-Son Jewel.

On the very same day that Warrior-Son Jewel was born, five hundred ministers also had sons born to them, and those sons too were given names suited to their households, and they were made into the companions of Warrior-Son Jewel.

The boy Warrior-Son Jewel was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses who would carry him at the hip and sustain him, two nurses who would suckle him, two nurses who would wipe away his impurities, and two nurses who would play with him. These eight nurses nourished and raised him with milk, curd, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other principal provisions of various kinds, and they caused him to grow swiftly, like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

While he was sitting in the lap of his nurse, a brahmin physiognomist saw him and examined him very carefully. The physiognomist thought to himself: "This boy is a field of merit for two-footed beings. For those who make offerings to him, those very acts of offering will bring exceedingly great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great breadth." The brahmin physiognomist then said to the nurse: "Give this boy to me for just a moment, so that I may make offerings to him." The nurse replied:

"Brahmin, it is not within my power to give this boy away. If you want the boy, go and make your request to the military commander."

The brahmin then went before the great warrior's encampment, and after first offering words of good omen, he spoke: "Military commander, this boy of yours is a field of merit for two-footed beings. For those who make offerings to him, those very acts of offering will bring exceedingly great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great breadth. Therefore, give this boy to me for just a moment, so that I may make offerings to him."

The military commander said: "Brahmin, if that is so, then take him and welcome."

The brahmin, filled with delight of mind, took the boy to his own home. He went to his wife and spoke of the boy's qualities: "Good woman, know this: this boy is a field of merit for two-footed beings. For those who make offerings to him, those very acts of offering will bring exceedingly great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great breadth. Therefore make offerings to him."

She heard him praise the boy's qualities, and a sense of joy arose in her. She said: "Brahmin, if that is so, wait a moment while I make the house ready and put everything in proper order." She had the house plastered and swept, then invited those dear and close to her heart from among her kinfolk and connections, and after that she bathed the boy with great honor, adorned him with incense and flowers, and anointed him well with honey and milk. Thus adorned and surrounded by his relatives, she brought him back to her own home.

When he had grown to maturity, he entered into the study of letters, numbers, arithmetic, finger-reckoning, casting up, entering, and setting down accounts. He brought his learning in letters to its completion, together with eight forms of expertise — skill in reading, in decipherment, in fluency of application, and in clarity of usage — as well as the eight sciences of assessment: the assessment of precious gems, of land, of cloth, of timber, of elephants, of horses, of women, and of men.

He was consecrated from the crown of the head in the manner of royal warriors, a lord of the realm who had attained power and diligence, who had prevailed over and established dominion over the maṇḍala of the great earth. And among the various crafts and occupational stations belonging to those who dwell in such a position, he became thoroughly trained in these: riding on the neck of an elephant, riding a horse, the methods of the chariot, the methods of the sword, the spear, pushing back and pushing forward, the technique of guiding with a hook, the casting of a lasso, the methods of firing a great bow, the posture of holding, the posture of training, the topknot strike, cutting, cleaving, striking to pierce — and also in these five modes of hitting a mark: hitting from a distance, hitting so as to make a sound, hitting a vital point, hitting without missing, and hitting with great force. He became trained and expert in all of these.

Those five hundred sons of ministers likewise became fully trained in the crafts and occupational stations.

His father established the three retinues of his wives — superior, middling, and lesser — in their proper order. He set them to occupy three residences: winter quarters, spring quarters, and summer quarters. He placed them in three pleasure gardens: those for winter, those for spring, and those for summer. There, within the enclosure of the fine upper palace chambers, in the absence of men, they played with musical instruments, took delight, and passed their time in pleasure and enjoyment.

Those five hundred companions likewise came to him at all three times of day, and together with him they played all manner of games, sharing in the joy of close companionship.

Then it came to pass that on a certain occasion the five hundred young men rose early in the morning and set out to drive wild game. But that day they did not find so much as a single animal. They thought to themselves: "Today we have not found even one animal — how then can we return home empty-handed? Let us stay here this very night, drive the game tomorrow, and then go home." And so they camped there that evening, and the following morning drove the animals, and then departed for their own homes as night fell and their eyes could no longer see the way.

Among themselves they thought: "Tonight I shall sleep, and tomorrow we go again like the young man." So when night brightened into dawn, and it came to the third day, the young man's attendant went to look after his master. The young man said to him: "Wise ones, you are born as my companions and playmates on the same ground — why have you not come to me all this while, arriving only today, the third day?" The young man replied: "We went off to drive wild game, and for that reason we did not come." "And what did you do there?" "Young man, we killed animals." "And what do those animals eat and drink?" "Young man, they feed on what they find, and drink whatever water they find."

"Wise ones, if that is how it is — what harm have those animals done to you, that you kill them?" "Young man, that brings us sheer delight." "Wise ones, that is not good delight. Delight obtained by harming others — abandon that."

The five hundred young men stood silent and said nothing. They left the royal palace and spoke among themselves: "Wise ones, this young man has no wish to abandon his wives' retinue and go away, and so he rebukes us for this. Therefore we must by some means make it known to the military commander, and by such a stratagem bring it about that he too will go to drive wild game — for then he will come along with us." Having made this plan, they went before the military commander, bowed at his feet, and said: "Commander, those young men who are born in the shade are surely ones who will be overpowered by the kings under the sun. Why then does the young man keep us in the shade and not send us to drive wild game with him? If we accompany him, we will be fierce and skilled, and the kings under the sun will not be able to overpower us." "Wise ones, if that is so, let the young man go now."

The commander summoned the young man and said: "Young man, your companions are going to drive wild game — go with them." "Father, if we do not harm the lives of others, why should I go with them?" "Young man, we of the warrior caste live by the sword. This is the way of the warrior caste and does not conflict with it — go." Since the young man was respectful and obedient to his father, he agreed, and the following day he went with them to drive wild game.

And the five hundred young men then began to deliberate among themselves: "Wise ones, this young man will pass the present commander and himself become commander. If we cultivate his friendship at this time, it will bear fruit. Let us now cultivate his friendship." And so with one mind they addressed him thus.

"Young man, you stay right here, and we shall arrange things so that the wild game comes to you alone, no matter what. Then you will be able to take your fill of the game."

They stationed the young man in a fixed position, then drove a great multitude of wild animals from every direction, pressing them in so tightly that the creatures, overcome by the terror of death, came crashing and tumbling toward the young man, panting and lolling out their tongues. The young man, watching from a distance as the animals were brought to this state, reflected: "Who among men could harden his heart to cast away all compassion and set his mind in fierce hatred against these creatures — to the point of taking their lives? What need is there even to speak of it?" Understanding this, he began to look out in all four directions, and not far off he saw a man sitting there. To protect the man's safety he shot two or three arrows, sending them between the animals' ribs and between their legs, and then drove them away from below, sitting still where he was. At that the wild animals scattered and fled.

The sons of the ministers thought to themselves: "The young man is trained in the five arts, so he will certainly have slain many game. Let us go quickly." They hurried over — and saw that not a single animal had been killed. They thought: "The young man has surely scattered them ahead with chariots and elephants, just as was done before." So they said: "Young man, where have the animals gone?"

"Wise friends, where are the animals? What animals? Whose animals are they? They are wild animals — they cannot be recalled. Running as they do, with such behavior and such speed, in the process they nearly killed even me."

The man who had been sitting there spoke up. "Wise friends, by placing your love of Dharma to one side you are nowhere near killing any animals. If this man had been willing, not a single animal would have escaped." At this the others grew indignant and spoke in one voice: "Wise friends, it was through our own broken-bodied and exhausted efforts that we drove those animals right here, so that he could kill them — and he has let them all slip away. Let us leave this one behind and go, and kill him ourselves."

But then they reconsidered: "If he were killed, word would travel from one person to the next until the commander heard, and that would bring harm to us. We should not kill him. Let us simply abandon him right here and leave." And so they went without a backward glance at him.

The young man thought: "These men and I were born as childhood companions together in the same land, playing on the ground side by side — and for the sake of nothing more than some wild game they have deserted me, abandoned me alone in the wilderness, and gone. Moreover, when my father has passed and I become commander, I will inevitably have to commit many wrongs in my dealings with sentient beings." His heart felt hollow and aching, as though pierced by a thorn. He went home and sat with his cheek resting in his hand, lost in his own thoughts.

Just then the retinue of his wife came and he saw them, but he turned his senses away. They passed word from one to the next until it reached the commander: the young man was deep in thought, paying no attention even to his own wife's retinue, and had turned his senses away. This was reported to him.

When the commander heard this he too became uneasy. He went to the young man and said: "My son, young man — why are you sitting there with your cheek in your hand, lost in thought? Your father has appointed me over you differently, and now that you are a powerful hunter, with red hands — one who has taken up the chase and excelled at it —

"— those who seize the life of others, who lead others to the cutting of life, who make their living by the cutting of the life of others: if I were to commit myself firmly to that karma, how could I bear it in my heart and not be overcome? My son, young man, if that is how it is for you, then sit comfortably, let go of your brooding, and do not go on as before."

Thereupon the young man, arising with certainty from the disquiet of mind that had been born from causing harm to sentient beings, became joyful, and thinking, "What is virtue?" he began to seek the joy of renunciation.

At that time, Pūraṇa and the other six teachers — all of them without omniscience, yet publicly claiming omniscience with arrogant pride — were nearby, and whenever wrongdoing arose they would resort to it and abide in it.

Then the young warrior Dhanaśreṣṭhi, without looking back at his father's retinue or his wife's retinue, went to where Kāśyapa Pūraṇa was and, having arrived, spoke these words to him:

"Learned one, what is your way of Dharma? What is the instruction you give to your disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life, and what are its benefits?"

Pūraṇa replied:

"Young man, my view is this, and this is what I teach: There is no giving. There is no sacrificial offering. There is no fire-oblation. There is no good conduct and no bad conduct. There is no fruit, no karmic maturation of deeds done well or done ill. There is no this world and no world beyond. There is no mother and no father. There are no beings born by spontaneous generation. In the world there exist no arhats who have rightly understood, who have rightly accomplished, who in this very life have directly known both this world and the world beyond through their own direct knowledge and proclaimed: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, the task is done, and we know of no further existence' — none who make that declaration exist. The life principle lives here and then is afterwards cut off, it is destroyed, and after death it does not appear again. The body of a person arises from the four great elements, and when the moment of death comes, the earth part of the body dissolves back into earth, the water part into water, the fire part into fire, and the wind part into wind. The sense faculties pass away following space. The corpse of the person is carried by four or five men to the charnel ground, where it is cremated and thereafter becomes invisible. What is burned becomes ash. The bones remain, the colour of a dove. Thus what is taught by a fool, give away; what is taught by the wise, take in. All those who assert the existence of anything whatsoever are speakers of empty, hollow falsehood. In this way both the fool and the wise man are afterwards cut off, destroyed, and do not appear again after death."

Then the warrior Dhanaśreṣṭhi thought to himself: "This teacher Pūraṇa has entered a wrong path. He is one who accomplishes an evil path well — a path filled with danger, one that the wise should abandon just as it is." Having understood this, he spoke in verse:

One who teaches the wrongly-minded wrong,
who is renowned as teacher of the low —
one whose Dharma is of such a kind,
what could that one's Dharma be at all?

Having said this, he left, as though striking an empty vessel.

Then the warrior Dhanaśreṣṭhi went to where Gosāla Maskarin was and, having arrived, spoke these words to him:

"Learned one, what is your way of Dharma? What is the instruction you give to your disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life,

what is the benefit?" Gosāla Maskarin replied: "Young man, I hold this view and speak thus: there is no cause, no condition for the defilement of sentient beings. Sentient beings become defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of sentient beings. Sentient beings become purified without cause, without condition. There is no cause, no condition for sentient beings coming to lack knowledge and vision. Sentient beings come to lack knowledge and vision without cause, without condition. There is no cause, no condition for sentient beings coming to have knowledge and vision. Sentient beings come to have knowledge and vision without cause, without condition. There is no strength, no diligence, no strength and diligence combined. There is no personal power, no overcoming of what lies beyond, no personal power and overcoming of what lies beyond combined. There is no power of self, no power of others, no power of self and others combined. All sentient beings, all living creatures, all beings have no might, no strength, no agency, no diligence, no overcoming of what lies beyond. The existences that connect to the various destinies are fixed and certain. Thus, among the six destinies, pleasure and suffering are experienced severally."

Then the warrior Dhanaśreṣṭhi thought to himself: "This teacher too, though learned, has entered a wrong path — one who perfects a bad path, a path filled with danger, which is precisely the kind that the wise should abandon." Having understood this, he spoke in verse:

One who teaches the wrongly-minded wrong,
who is renowned as teacher of the low —
one whose Dharma is of such a kind,
what could that one's Dharma be at all?

Having said this, he left, as though striking an empty vessel.

Then the warrior Dhanaśreṣṭhi went to where Saṃjaya Vairāṭīputra was, and having arrived, spoke these words to Saṃjaya Vairāṭīputra: "Learned one, what is your way of Dharma? What is the instruction you give to your disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life, and what is the benefit?"

Saṃjaya Vairāṭīputra replied: "Young man, I hold this view and speak thus: one who acts and one who causes others to act; one who cuts and one who causes others to cut; one who burns and one who causes others to burn; one who strikes and one who causes others to strike; one who harms living creatures; one who takes what is not given; one who engages in sexual misconduct; one who knowingly speaks falsehood; one who drinks intoxicating beverages; one who breaks into houses; one who unties knots; one who seizes by force; one who stands in the road and blocks it; one who destroys villages; one who destroys towns; one who destroys whole districts — even if one were to take all the sentient beings on this great earth and cut them, hack them, beat them, and tear them apart with a wheel whose rim is fitted with razor blades, making every one of those sentient beings cut up, sliced through, beaten, and torn, reducing them into one great plain of flesh, one great thicket of flesh, one great heap of flesh, one great mound of flesh — having made them into one great plain of flesh, one great thicket of flesh, one great heap of flesh, one great mound of flesh — in doing all this, there would be no evil arising from that basis, no evil that could arise from that basis. Were one to go about the south bank of the river Gaṅgā cutting, hacking, beating, and tearing apart, and were one then to go to the north bank of the Gaṅgā and give generously

and perform offerings and sacrifices — from that basis too there would be no evil and no merit, no evil or merit arising from that basis whatsoever. Through generosity, through restraint, through perfect moral discipline, through acting for the benefit of others, through harmonious conduct — even doing all these things produces no merit whatsoever.

Then the youth Nor thought to himself: This Teacher, learned though he claims to be, has entered upon a wrong path, a bad path, and is perfectly pursuing it — a path filled with danger, the kind that the wise must abandon, just as it truly is. Having understood this, he spoke these verses:

One who teaches with a corrupt and inverted mind,
who is known as a teacher of what is inferior —
if this is the nature of someone's Dharma,
what could be unlike Dharma, if not this?

Having said this, he struck his hand against his palm as if striking an empty vessel, and departed.

Then the youth Nor went to where the one with braided hair called Ajita was, and having arrived, he said this to the one with braided hair called Ajita: Learned one, what is the manner of your Dharma? What is the instruction you give to your disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life? What are its benefits?

Ajita replied: Young man, I hold the following view and speak as follows. These seven bodies are unmade, not made by what is made, uncreated, not created by what is created, incapable of being harmed, permanent, abiding like pillars. What seven? These: the body of earth, the body of water, the body of fire, the body of wind, pleasure, pain, and the living vital force — that is the seventh. These seven bodies are unmade, not made by what is made, uncreated, not created by what is created, incapable of being harmed, permanent, abiding like pillars. They do not move, do not undergo transformation, do not harm one another — whether for the sake of becoming merit, or becoming demerit, or becoming both merit and demerit, or becoming happiness, or becoming suffering, or becoming both happiness and suffering. When a person cuts off another person's head, he causes not even the slightest disturbance or harm to anything standing or abiding in the world, for the sword passes through the gaps between the seven bodies without impediment, and there is no harm done to the life therein. In that act there is no one who kills or causes killing, no one who urges or causes urging, no one who intends harm or causes another to intend harm, no one who makes known or causes another to make known anything whatsoever.

Whether foolish or wise, those beings who exist pass through eighty-four principal states of birth, sixty-six thousand and six hundred great conceptual states, five actions, three actions, two actions, one action, half an action, sixty-two actions, sixty-two intermediate conceptual states, one hundred and twenty hell realms, one hundred and twenty sense faculties, sixty-two elemental dust-particles, forty-nine thousand classes of nāgas, forty-nine thousand classes of garuḍas, forty-nine thousand classes of wanderers, forty-nine thousand classes of sustaining forces, forty-nine thousand classes of the naked ones, seven abodes of conscious beings, seven abodes of non-conscious beings, seven abodes of the naked ones, seven asuras, seven flesh-eaters, seven gods, seven humans, seven great oceans, seven hundred oceans, seven great dreams, seven hundred dreams, seven great decreases, seven hundred decreases, seven great increases, seven hundred increases, seven great awakenings, seven hundred awakenings —

seven great precipices, seven hundred precipices, seven noble lineages, ten states of clear distinction, and those eight grounds of a great being — through all of these one wanders in cyclic existence, bound by eighty-four thousand great eons, and thereby brings suffering to an end. It is just as when a ball of thread thrown from the sky above a haystack unravels and falls to the ground: even so, whether one is foolish or wise, one wanders through these for eighty-four thousand great eons and thereby brings suffering to an end.

In all of this, there is no monk or brahmin who can rightly say: "By my moral discipline, my vows, my austerities, or my life of celibacy, I shall ripen karma that is not yet ripe, and having brought already-ripened karma to fruition through direct contact, I shall thereby purify it." Pleasure and pain are fixed. There is no rising higher or falling lower — such a thing is impossible. The measure of cyclic existence is reckoned by this very nature alone, and by nothing other than it.

Then the youth Nor thought to himself: This teacher Śeṣalin has also entered upon a wrong path. He is one who skillfully pursues a bad path — a fearful path — of the kind that the wise must abandon, exactly as it truly is. And having understood this, he spoke a verse:

One who teaches with a corrupt and perverted mind,
who is renowned for teaching what is base —
if his Dharma is of such a kind,
what could his non-Dharma possibly resemble?

Having said this, he struck him as one would strike an empty vessel, and departed.

Then the youth Nor went to where Kātyāyana Nogcanga was, and when he arrived he spoke to Kātyāyana Nogcanga as follows: "Venerable one, what is your manner of Dharma? What is the instruction you give to disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life? What are its benefits?"

Nogcanga replied: "Young man, I hold this view and speak as follows. If anyone should come to me and ask: 'Does the other world exist?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world exists.' If anyone should ask: 'Does the other world not exist?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world does not exist.' If anyone should ask: 'Does the other world both exist and not exist?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world both exists and does not exist.' If anyone should ask: 'Does the other world neither exist nor not exist?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world neither exists nor does not exist.'

"Likewise, if anyone should come to me and ask: 'Is the other world of this very nature, or not of this very nature?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world is of this nature and not of this nature.' If anyone should ask: 'Is the other world otherwise, or not otherwise?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world is otherwise and not otherwise.' If anyone should ask: 'Is the other world not-otherwise, or not not-otherwise?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world is not-otherwise and not not-otherwise.' If anyone should ask: 'Is the other world of that very nature, or not of that very nature?' — to that I give a categorical answer: 'The other world is of that very nature and not of that very nature.'"

Then the youth Nor thought to himself: This teacher Nogcanga has also entered upon a wrong path. He is one who skillfully pursues a bad path —

a path that is dangerous and fearsome, just as it should be abandoned by the wise. Knowing this, the youth Nor spoke these verses:

One who teaches with inferior understanding, teaching wrongly,
renowned for teaching what is base —
if one's Dharma is of such a kind,
what could count as not-Dharma?

Having spoken thus, he struck the ground like an empty vessel and departed.

Then the youth Nor went to where the naked ascetic Genyikyi Bu Gerbu (Ājīvika) was, and arriving there, spoke to the naked ascetic Genyikyi Bu Gerbu as follows: "Wise one, what is your way of Dharma? What instruction do you give your disciples? What is the fruit of the holy life? What is its benefit?"

The naked ascetic replied: "Young man, I hold this view and speak thus: whatever feeling a person or individual experiences, any of it whatsoever — all of it arises from causes previously made. Old karma is purified through ascetic practice, and new karma is to be turned back by abstaining from action. Thus, henceforth there will be no more outflows. When there are no more outflows, karma is exhausted. When karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted. When suffering is exhausted, one arrives at the end of suffering."

Then the youth Nor thought to himself: This teacher, the so-called Wise One, has also entered upon a wrong path. He is one who skillfully pursues a bad path — a path that is dangerous and fearsome, just as it should be abandoned by the wise. Knowing this, he spoke these verses:

One who teaches with inferior understanding, teaching wrongly,
renowned for teaching what is base —
if one's Dharma is of such a kind,
what could count as not-Dharma?

Having spoken thus, he struck the ground like an empty vessel and departed.

Then the youth Nor went toward his own home, and arriving there, he leaned his arm against the base of the upper mansion, and stood absorbed in thought. He thought to himself: In all this world with its gods, its māras, and its Brahmā, among all the beings that include ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins, gods and humans — is there any ascetic or brahmin who could declare, in one word or two words or four words, a medicine, a mantra, or a knowledge-spell by which I might be perfectly freed from this desolate wilderness of saṃsāra?

Now at that very time, the buddha Blessed Ones possess not even the slightest degree of unknowing, unseeing, ignorance, or lack of discernment. Therefore the buddha Blessed Ones, endowed with great compassion, devoted to the welfare of the world, sole protectors, uniquely heroic, without a second, speaking no duality, entered into calm abiding and insight, who illuminate the three knowledges, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the ground of the three bases of Vinaya, who have crossed the four rivers, well established in the ground of the practice of the four bases of miraculous power, who have for a long time thoroughly purified themselves in the four means of attraction, who are without the fear of being intimidated by the four fearlessnesses, who have abandoned the five limbs, who have thoroughly transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with the six limbs, who have perfectly completed the six perfections, who abide in the six constant abidings, who are rich with the flowers of the seven branches of awakening, who teach the eight branches of the path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, who are endowed with the power of the ten powers, whose fame has spread throughout the ten directions, who are supremely exalted above those who hold sway over hundreds of thousands — the very nature of such beings is to survey the world three times by day and three times by night with the eye of a buddha, seeing who has declined, who has advanced, who has been harmed, who has become afflicted, who has become unhappy —

who has been harmed, who has declined, who has become unhappy — who is inclining toward the lower realms, who is falling toward the lower realms, who has already fallen into the lower realms — these I shall lift from the path of the lower realms and establish in the higher states, in liberation, and in the fruit. Those who have sunk into the mire of desire I shall draw out by the hand. Those who are without the wealth of the noble ones I shall establish in the lordship of noble wealth. The worlds adorned by the arising of buddhas I shall cause to bear fruit. Those in whom the roots of virtue have not yet arisen I shall cause to arise. Those in whom the roots of virtue have arisen I shall cause to fully ripen. Those that are fully ripened I shall cause to be completely liberated. Thus did that knowledge and vision engage.

Then it was said in verse:

The venomous creature dwelling in the crocodile's lair
may perhaps pass beyond its time —
but the loving-kindness of the buddhas toward those they tame
shall never pass beyond its time.

Just as a mother thinks only of her single beloved child
and guards that child's very life,
so too the Tathāgata thinks of those who are to be tamed
and guards their very lives.

The compassion that dwells in the mindstream of the omniscient one
is a mother who tirelessly seeks her calf among those to be tamed —
toward those to be tamed who have fallen into ruin through saṃsāra and the lower realms,
it is like the love of a mother cow for a calf utterly weakened and lost.

Thus when the Blessed One surveys the world with the eye of a buddha, he sees that the young man Norgye (the one called Gyad Bu Nor) — his mindstream now fully ripened, his former service to the previous buddhas made excellent — is, at this moment of ripening for taming, like fully ripened fruit that stands ready to be cut by a blade. Seeing this, the Blessed One reflects: "Is this one to be tamed by the Teacher himself, or by a śrāvaka?" He sees that it is to be by a śrāvaka. "Through which door will the taming proceed — through miraculous powers, or through conduct?" He sees that it is through conduct. For the Blessed One, in taming through conduct, sends the venerable Rataṭhula (the monk known as Ratathul) on his way, since it is through that conduct that the minds of gods and humans are to be drawn in.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ratathul: "Ratathul, you should be mindful in the presence of Gyad Bu Nor." The venerable Ratathul, without a word, accepted the instruction of the Blessed One. Then the venerable Ratathul, wishing to go beyond what was asked in response to the Blessed One's command, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet in prostration, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

That same night having passed, in the early morning the venerable Ratathul put on his robe, took up his bowl and Dharma robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having gone through Rājagṛha on alms-round and completed the business of the meal, he returned from the alms-round for the midday meal. Having set out his dwelling things for use in whatever way was fitting, he took up his bowl and Dharma robe, and set out walking in the direction of Gyad Bu Nor. Walking along gradually, he came to Gyad Bu Nor and found Gyad Bu Nor in a lotus grove.

Then the venerable Ratathul, in the early morning, having put on his robe and taken up his bowl and Dharma robe, walking forward and back, glancing slightly, looking carefully, drawing in and extending his limbs, his robe-cloth, his Dharma robe, and his bowl all held beautifully — entered Gyad Bu Nor for alms. At that time Gyad Bu Nor, being on the upper floor of his mansion, was looking out over the city in search of whatever virtue there might be to find; and Gyad Bu Nor saw the venerable Ratathul walking —

— walking forward and back, glancing slightly, looking carefully, drawing in and extending his limbs, his robe-cloth, his Dharma robe, and his bowl all held beautifully — as he walked for alms through the city, Gyad Bu Nor saw him from a great distance.

Having seen him, Gyad Bu Nor thought to himself: "Among all the renunciants who have come to dwell in this city, I have never before seen a single one whose conduct resembles that of this renunciant." And then he thought further: "There are renunciants who comport themselves properly in the city yet do as they please in the hermitage. I should therefore go and examine this one's conduct in the hermitage." Having thus resolved, he said to a man: "Good sir, come here. Follow behind this renunciant, step for step, and find out whether his conduct in the hermitage is as peaceful as it is in the city, or whether it is otherwise. Understand this and report back." That man replied, "As the young master commands," and having heard these words from Gyad Bu Nor, he followed behind the venerable Ratathul, step for step.

Then the venerable Ratathul, having completed his alms round through the city, went to the place of the lotus grove. Having arrived, he set his bowl and his water vessel down together to one side, shook out his robe-cloth, washed both feet, dried both hands, drew water, gathered up some fallen leaves, sat down, took his meal, discarded the fallen leaves, dried both hands again, set his bowl and water vessel together to one side, washed both feet, and, resting against the trunk of a great tree, sat in cross-legged posture with his body composed in the manner of the resting posture of the king of serpents, and remained there with peaceful comportment.

Then that man, his mind captivated — for the venerable Ratathul's peaceful conduct was such as to draw together the minds of gods and human beings — went to the place where Gyad Bu Nor was and, having arrived, said to Gyad Bu Nor: "Young master, please know this: the conduct with which that renunciant goes for alms in the city is surpassed a hundredfold, a thousandfold, by the conduct with which he dwells in the hermitage."

Then Gyad Bu Nor, his mind captivated upon hearing of the venerable Ratathul's conduct, so utterly splendid and complete, said to that man with respectful urgency: "Good sir, quickly prepare a comfortable mount, and I will ride it and go at once to see that renunciant." That man replied, "As the young master commands," and having heard these words from Gyad Bu Nor, he quickly prepared a comfortable mount. Gyad Bu Nor came to the place where the venerable Ratathul was, and said to him: "Young master Gorbu Drön, please know that the right moment has now come."

Then Gyad Bu Nor mounted the comfortable conveyance and set out from the city, directing his carriage toward the lotus grove; he rode as far as the road permitted, then descended from the mount and entered the lotus grove on foot. Gyad Bu Nor saw the venerable Ratathul sitting there, his faculties perfectly composed, in peaceful comportment.

Having seen him, he thought to himself: "To rouse this renunciant from his meditative absorption would not accord with my way of doing things. I shall wait until he rises from absorption, and only then go to him." Having thus resolved, he sat quietly to one side, remaining there, waiting for him to rise.

Then the venerable Ratathul, in the late afternoon, emerged from perfect inner settling, and sat quietly to one side. Then Gyad Bu Nor went to the place where the venerable Ratathul was, and having arrived, exchanged with the venerable Ratathul various words of mutual delight and satisfaction, and sat to one side.

Seated to one side, Gyad Bu Nor then said this to the venerable Ratathul: "Learned one, are you yourself a Teacher, or a śrāvaka?"

"Good friend, I am one who has entered the path of a śrāvaka teacher."

"Learned one, what is the difference between a Teacher and a śrāvaka?"

"Good friend, the difference is exceedingly great. It is like this: like the difference between Mount Meru, the king of mountains, and a mustard seed; like the difference between the great ocean and a cow's footprint; like the difference between the sun and a firefly; and like the difference between the sky and the hole at the root of a lotus."

"In this regard, just as is Mount Meru, the king of mountains, so should the Teacher be regarded; and just as is the mustard seed, so should the śrāvaka be regarded. Just as is the great ocean, so should the Teacher be regarded; and just as is the cow's footprint, so should the śrāvaka be regarded. Just as is the sun, so should the Teacher be regarded; and just as is the firefly, so should the śrāvaka be regarded. Just as is the sky, so should the Teacher be regarded; and just as is the hole at the root of a lotus, so should the śrāvaka be regarded."

Having said this, he then spoke in verse:

Whatever difference lies between the king of mountains and a mustard seed,
Whatever difference lies between the great ocean and a poisonous bull's footprint,
Whatever difference lies between the sun and a firefly,
Whatever difference lies between the sky and a lotus's root-hole —
Such is the difference between a buddha, a śrāvaka, and awakening.

Then Gyad Bu Nor thought to himself: "Given that this renunciant praises his Teacher so and yet speaks disparagingly of himself, it cannot be that the buddha is not excellent, nor can it be that the Dharma he has taught is not excellent." Recognizing this, he said the following to the venerable Ratathul: "Noble one, may you grant me the going forth and full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and may I live the holy life in the presence of the noble one."

"Good friend, have your parents consented?"

"Noble one, they have not consented."

"Good friend, the Tathāgata and the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata do not grant the going forth to a son of good family whose parents have not consented; they do not grant full ordination to such a one. Noble one, let me do just this much for you: grant me the going forth alone, and I shall myself act in such a way that my parents will come to give their consent."

The venerable Ratathul said to him, "Good friend, very well then — do as you have said."

Thereupon Gyad Bu Nor expressed open delight and rejoicing at the words of the venerable Ratathul, and then went to the place where his own home was. Having arrived, he spoke as follows to his father and mother: "Father and mother, please take note. With genuine and wholehearted faith in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."

"Dear boy, understand this: you are our only son, beloved and pleasing to behold. So long as we see you, nothing is amiss. If you were to die, we would be parted from you against our will — that is simply what must be. But to let you go while you are still alive — what need is there even to speak of it? Father and mother: if you consent, that is well and good. But if you do not consent, then from this day forward I shall seek neither food nor water from your hands."

"Dear boy, do not withhold consent from us. For as long as we live, remain before our eyes and think of nothing else."

Thereupon Gyad Bu Nor fasted for a single day. On the second through the sixth days he fasted as well. Then his father and mother said this to Gyad Bu Nor: "Dear boy, understand this. You are very young and given to pleasure; you do not know what suffering is. The holy life is difficult to live."

"It is hard to live in true seclusion. It is hard to find delight in solitude. It is hard to truly embrace dwelling in remote lodgings — in forest groves, at the foot of mountains, and at the edges of ravines. To dwell alone in the wilderness is suffering. For as long as you live you will have to dwell together with savage wild beasts. For as long as you live you will have to subsist on what others give you. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human pleasures. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human joys and amusements. Dear boy, come back. Stay here and enjoy pleasures to the full; give gifts and accumulate merit."

Even when they spoke thus, Gyad Bu Nor said nothing at all.

Then Gyad Bu Nor's father and mother instructed his relatives: "Come, kinsmen. Go and rouse the boy Gyad Bu Nor."

So Gyad Bu Nor's relatives went to where he was, approached him, and spoke to him thus: "Young master, please understand. You are very young and given to pleasure; you do not know what suffering is. The holy life is difficult to live. It is hard to live in true seclusion. It is hard to find delight in solitude. It is hard to truly embrace dwelling in remote lodgings — in forest groves, at the foot of mountains, and at the edges of ravines. To dwell alone in the wilderness is suffering. For as long as you live you will have to dwell together with savage wild beasts. For as long as you live you will have to subsist on what others give you. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human pleasures. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human joys and amusements. Young master, come back and stay here; enjoy pleasures to the full, bestow gifts, and accumulate merit."

Even when they spoke thus, Gyad Bu Nor said nothing at all.

Then Gyad Bu Nor's father and mother instructed his young male companions: "Come, young friends. Go and rouse the boy Gyad Bu Nor."

So Gyad Bu Nor's young companions went to where he was, approached him, and spoke to him thus: "Young master, please understand. You are very young and given to pleasure; you do not know what suffering is. The holy life is difficult to live. It is hard to live in true seclusion. It is hard to find delight in solitude. It is hard to truly embrace dwelling in remote lodgings — in forest groves, at the foot of mountains, and at the edges of ravines. To dwell alone in the wilderness is suffering. For as long as you live you will have to dwell together with savage wild beasts. For as long as you live you will have to subsist on what others give you. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human pleasures. For as long as you live you will have to keep apart from human joys and amusements. Young master, come back and stay here; enjoy pleasures to the full, bestow gifts, and accumulate merit."

Even when they spoke thus, Gyad Bu Nor said nothing at all.

Then Gyad Bu Nor's young companions went to where his father and mother were, approached them, and spoke to them thus: "Father and mother, please understand. Since the young man is calm, what is to be done by force? Going forth is praised by the wise; and if, having gone forth, he becomes joyful and content, then you will see him alive and well.

But even if he does not become joyful and content, sages do turn back, and apart from his father and mother there is no one else who can be his refuge. Therefore, going forth is good."

Then Gyad Bu Nor's father and mother spoke to Gyad Bu Nor thus: "Young son, is it not the case that going forth is good for you, and that staying at home is not good? Father and mother: going forth is indeed good for us, and staying at home is not good. Young son, know now that the time for it has come."

Then Gyad Bu Nor, with his parents' permission, gradually roused through nourishment the bodily vitality, strength, and diligence that had waned, and having emerged from his seclusion, he went to where the venerable Aśvajit was. Arriving there, he touched his head to the feet of the venerable Aśvajit and sat to one side. Seated to one side, Gyad Bu Nor spoke to the venerable Aśvajit thus: "Noble one, please know this. With my parents' permission, I wish to go forth and receive full ordination in the well-taught Dharma-Vinaya and obtain the status of a monk. I wish to live the holy life in the presence of the noble one."

The venerable Aśvajit said: "Well-favored one, excellent! Possessions are impermanent; going forth is good. Do it so. The Blessed One too, seeing rightly the five benefits, has taught that a wise person should aspire to going forth alone. What are the five? First, seeing rightly that one will attain one's own unsullied aim, a wise person should aspire to going forth alone. Second, seeing rightly that one will become an object of veneration and praise for those over whom one is a servant, an assignee, one under orders, one without independence, and one unable to go where one wishes, a wise person should aspire to going forth alone. Third, seeing rightly that one will attain accomplishment and the unsurpassed bliss of nirvāṇa, a wise person should aspire to going forth alone. Fourth, seeing rightly that even if one falls short of attaining the unsurpassed blissful nirvāṇa, one will be reborn among the gods, a wise person should aspire to going forth alone. Fifth, seeing rightly that going forth is praised in many ways by buddhas, by the holy śrāvakas of buddhas who have rightly understood and rightly accomplished, and by holy persons, a wise person should aspire to going forth alone."

Having said this, he gave him the going forth.

Then the venerable Aśvajit gave the son of good family Gyad Bu Nor the going forth and full ordination, and said: "Son, a monk's work is twofold: meditative concentration and recitation. Which do you wish — meditative concentration or recitation?"

Gyad Bu Nor said: "Preceptor, I will do both. By day I will do recitation; by night I will do meditative concentration."

The venerable Aśvajit said: "Son, do it so."

Then the venerable Gyad Bu Nor, reciting and chanting by day, mastered all three collections of scriptures. Practicing meditative concentration by night, he progressively attained ever higher distinctions of mental application, came to know this very wheel of saṃsāra in its five parts — moving and unmoving — and recognized the decline and downfall of all conditioning formations and

their dispersal and dissolution. Overpowered by the very nature of reality — the nature of dispersion and disintegration — and having abandoned all afflictions, he, noble sons, realized in that very lifetime, through his own direct knowledge, the supreme culmination of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family shave their hair and beard, don the ochre robes, and go forth from home into homelessness with genuine and wholehearted faith. He came to understand: "My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. I know no further existence beyond this." Thus he became an arhat, free from attachment to all three realms — one to whom a clod of earth and gold are equal, whose mind is like the sky and like the palm of the hand, like sandalwood set down without preference, who has torn open the shell of ignorance with wisdom, who has attained the three higher knowledges, the five superknowledges, and the four analytical discriminations — one who has turned his back on continued existence, on gain, and on honors born of desire, worthy of veneration, of reverence, and of being openly praised by gods together with Indra and those gods with their attendants.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the twentieth fascicle.

Just as, during the lifetime of the Buddha, the Blessed One — while he lived, dwelt, and was present — there were by the nature of things two great assemblies of śrāvakas: one at the time of the invitation ceremony at the full moon of the middle month of the rains, and the second at the full moon of the middle month of autumn; so too, for the great śrāvakas there were two great assemblies of śrāvakas: one at the full moon of the middle month of the rains, at the time of the invitation ceremony, and the second at the full moon of the middle month of autumn.

Now, those who, having taken on a commitment at the full moon of the middle month of the rains — having received counsel and accepted a rains retreat in towns, villages, districts, and royal palaces — would arrive at the full moon of the middle month of autumn and then report what they had attained, and, in order to attain what they had not yet attained, would seek below recitations from the collections of sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and would seek thorough questioning.

Then the venerable Aśvajit's fellow residents, and those attendants who had accepted a rains retreat in the region, once the three months of the rains had passed, took up their robe-cloth, received their robe-cloth, and taking up their bowls and robes, went to where the venerable Aśvajit was and arrived there. They prostrated with their heads at the venerable Aśvajit's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, some of them reported what they had attained, while others sought recitations from sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and sought thorough questioning.

The venerable Aśvajit resolved their doubts and uncertainties regarding the three collections and the path of meditative concentration, and they, having begun to speak among themselves — "Venerable ones, we have seen our preceptor and paid him our respects; now let us go to Rājagṛha to pay respects to the Blessed One" — departed.

Then the venerable Gyad Bu Nor, hearing them speak thus, thought to himself: "Alas, I too wish to behold the Blessed One!" and, knowing this wish had arisen in him, he went to where the venerable Aśvajit was. Arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the venerable Aśvajit's feet and spoke these words to him: "Preceptor, please hear me. I have seen the Blessed One through the dharmakāya — through the body of truth — but have not seen him through the form body. Therefore, if I may be permitted to go and behold the Blessed One's form body, please grant me this." The venerable Aśvajit said:

"My son, look with a careful and discerning eye. My son, Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and fully awakened buddhas — and their arising — are like this: they are as rare as the udumbara flower. Bear that in mind."

Then the venerable Gyad Bu Nor, having received his preceptor's permission, arose with a mind full of joy and gladness at the prospect of beholding the Blessed One. That very night passed, and in the early morning he girded his lower robe, took up his begging bowl and his Dharma robes, and went into the village of Sdigbyung to collect alms. Having completed his alms round in Sdigbyung and finished his meal, he returned from the later alms round, set out the bedding and provisions for comfortable use, took up his begging bowl and Dharma robes, and, accompanied by one preceptor and one teacher, set off walking toward Rājagṛha, journeying steadily onward until at last he arrived in Rājagṛha.

Then the venerable Gyad Bu Nor set down his begging bowl and Dharma robes, washed his two feet, and went to where the Blessed One was.

At that time the Blessed One was sitting before a great assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One caught sight of the venerable Gyad Bu Nor from a great distance. Having seen him, the Blessed One called out to the venerable Gyad Bu Nor: "Gyad Bu Nor, come here. Welcome. You have come at the right time. Gyad Bu Nor, sit down in whatever seat suits you."

Then the venerable Gyad Bu Nor prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

Now at that time in Rājagṛha there was a practice of assigning lodgings without regard to compatibility — lodgings of those who hold the sūtras and those who hold the Vinaya were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the sūtras and those who hold the mātṛkā were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the sūtras and those who preach the Dharma were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the sūtras and those who are practitioners of renunciation were assigned together. Lodgings of those who hold the Vinaya and those who hold the sūtras were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the Vinaya and those who hold the mātṛkā were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the Vinaya and those who preach the Dharma were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the Vinaya and those who are practitioners of renunciation were assigned together. Lodgings of those who hold the mātṛkā and those who hold the sūtras were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the mātṛkā and those who hold the Vinaya were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the mātṛkā and those who preach the Dharma were assigned together; lodgings of those who hold the mātṛkā and those who are practitioners of renunciation were assigned together. Lodgings of those who preach the Dharma and those who hold the sūtras were assigned together; lodgings of those who preach the Dharma and those who hold the Vinaya were assigned together; lodgings of those who preach the Dharma and those who hold the mātṛkā were assigned together; lodgings of those who preach the Dharma and those who are practitioners of renunciation were assigned together. Lodgings of practitioners of renunciation and those who hold the sūtras were assigned together; lodgings of practitioners of renunciation and those who hold the Vinaya were assigned together; lodgings of practitioners of renunciation and those who hold the mātṛkā were assigned together; and lodgings of practitioners of renunciation and those who preach the Dharma were assigned together.

When lodgings were assigned in this incompatible manner, the monks, out of mutual guardedness toward one another, did not cultivate the aspects of virtue, and they did not increase in virtuous qualities — like a blue lotus in a place without water.

The Blessed One reflected: "This Gyad Bu Nor, in the presence of former buddhas, and in the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, in a lifetime of one hundred years —

having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha Śākyamuni, may I become the foremost among those who assign lodgings" — it was with that aspiration that he had made this prayer. Reflecting thus, the Blessed One thought: "I should have this monk go around assigning lodgings to the monks."

The Blessed One then spoke to the monks: "Monks, you should appoint the monk Gyad Bu Nor, or any other monk of similar qualities, as assigner of lodgings. An assigner of lodgings who possesses five qualities should not be appointed if not yet appointed, and should be removed if already appointed. What are the five? He proceeds by desire, he proceeds by aversion, he proceeds by delusion, he proceeds by fear, and he does not know what lodgings have been received and what lodgings have not been received.

An assigner of lodgings who possesses five qualities should be appointed if not yet appointed, and should not be removed if already appointed. What are the five? He does not proceed by desire, he does not proceed by aversion, he does not proceed by delusion, he does not proceed by fear, and he knows what lodgings have been received and what have not been received.

The appointment should be made in this manner. Having prepared the lodgings and struck the wooden signal board, one summons the monks with words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is gathered and in harmony, one first asks the candidate with enthusiasm, saying: 'You, whose name is such-and-such — are you willing to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha? If you are willing, say that you are willing.' After that, a single monk makes a motion and the formal act is performed.

May the venerable Saṅgha hear. If the monk named such-and-such is willing to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha, and if the time is right for the Saṅgha and it consents, may the Saṅgha please grant approval. The Saṅgha hereby appoints the monk named such-and-such to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha. The monk named such-and-such will assign lodgings to the Saṅgha. This is the motion.

The formal act is to be performed as follows. May the venerable Saṅgha hear. The monk named such-and-such is willing to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha. Therefore, the Saṅgha hereby appoints the monk named such-and-such to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha. Those venerable ones who consent to the appointment of the monk named such-and-such as assigner of lodgings to the Saṅgha should remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved. The Saṅgha has appointed the monk named such-and-such to assign lodgings to the Saṅgha. Because no one has spoken, it is held to be so."

When the venerable Gyad Bu Nor was appointed as assigner of lodgings, he arranged those lodgings in a compatible manner: those who hold the sūtras were placed together with those who hold the sūtras; those who hold the Vinaya were placed with those who hold the Vinaya; those who hold the Mātṛkā were placed with those who hold the Mātṛkā; those who preach the Dharma were placed with those who preach the Dharma; and those who practice renunciation were placed with those who practice renunciation.

Because they received their lodgings compatibly, they refined one another through conversation and meaningful discourse, and they flourished in virtuous qualities — like a blue lotus in water.

For those who came in the early part of the night, the venerable Gyad Bu Nor would by his miraculous power kindle light from one finger and assign them their lodgings. For those who came even later in the night, the venerable Gyad Bu Nor would by his miraculous power kindle light from two fingers and assign them their lodgings.

Then those monks who wished to witness the venerable Gyad Bu Nor's superhuman qualities and his miraculous display made a deliberate plan and came at night. For those monks, the venerable Gyad Bu Nor would by his miraculous power kindle light from all five fingers and assign them their lodgings.

Those monks then thought to themselves: "For us to receive our lodging assignment from such a great śrāvaka as this, one who is like the Teacher himself, and then simply to lay our heads down and sleep — that is not in keeping with our proper conduct. Rather, we should devote ourselves to practice, not sleeping in the first part of the night nor in the last part of the night." And so they devoted themselves to practice, not sleeping in the first part of the night nor in the last part of the night. Because of this, what had not yet been attained came to be attained, and what had already been attained was not lost.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Among my monk disciples who assign lodgings, this one — my Gyad Bu Nor — is supreme."

Now, at a time when the Blessed One's teaching had flourished, faithful brahmins and householders would prepare food for the Saṅgha in their homes. The group of six monks would go to wherever food was being given out and enjoy it fully. The faithful brahmins and householders said to them: "Noble ones, you have come all together like a single canopy. Why did the senior elder monks not come?"

The group of six monks said: "They do not enjoy food of this sort."

"Well then, what kind of food do they enjoy?"

"They enjoy alms food."

"Noble ones, if the Blessed One has taught that those who give alms food are supreme, why then do you say that the elders do not enjoy food of this sort? Go. Do not come here again."

The group of six monks fell silent and left without a word.

The news passed from one person to another until the monks heard of it, and the monks at that time reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should appoint monk Gyad Bu Nor, or another of the same caliber, as food-server. One who possesses five qualities should not be appointed as food-server even if not yet appointed, and if already appointed should be removed. What are the five? One who goes by desire, one who goes by aversion, one who goes by delusion, one who goes by fear, and one who does not know who has or has not been appointed as food-server.

"One who possesses five qualities should be appointed as food-server even if not yet appointed, and if already appointed should not be removed. What are the five? One who does not go by desire, one who does not go by aversion, one who does not go by delusion, one who does not go by fear, and one who knows who has or has not been appointed as food-server.

"The appointment should be made as follows: After the lodgings have been laid out, the wooden signal-board is struck, and with the words of inquiry the monks are summoned. When the entire Saṅgha is seated and in concord, one first asks the willing candidate: 'You whose name is such-and-such, are you willing to serve as food-server for the monks?' If he is willing, he is to say: 'I am willing.'"

After that, a single monk is to make the formal motion and the act is to be performed. "Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear me. The monk named such-and-such is willing to serve as food-server for the monks. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha please grant its approval, and the Saṅgha shall appoint the monk named such-and-such as food-server for the monks. The monk named such-and-such is hereby appointed as food-server for the monks." This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows. "Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear me. The monk named such-and-such is willing to serve as food-server for the monks. The Saṅgha is appointing the monk named such-and-such as food-server for the monks. Those venerable ones who consent to the appointment of the monk named such-and-such as food-server for the monks are to remain silent; those who do not consent are to speak." The Saṅgha having consented and approved, the Saṅgha has appointed the monk named such-and-such as food-server for the monks. Since no one has spoken, it is so held.

Now, when the Venerable Jāyasena was appointed as food-server, he set out three grades of food for the Saṅgha: the excellent, the middling, and the poor. For monks who arrived unexpectedly, on the first day he would assign them excellent food, on the second day middling food, and on the third day poor food. On the fourth day, knowing their own circumstances, they were to go out on alms-round themselves.

At that time, the Venerable Jāyasena was residing in Rājagṛha, carrying out his regular residence, making the formal motion, receiving those newly arrived, assigning lodgings, and serving as food-server, and so he assigned food to the Saṅgha in proper accordance with custom, seniority, and rank, without skipping anyone in order.

Now the Venerable Jāyasena and a friendly monk — the two of them, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, having been enemies across many lifetimes — were wandering and traveling through the southern mountains. When they arrived at Rājagṛha, the two of them asked a monk: "Who is the venerable one appointed to assign lodgings for the Saṅgha?" He replied: "It is the Venerable Jāyasena." The two then went to where the Venerable Jāyasena was, and when they arrived they said to him: "Assign us our two lodgings."

At that time, whatever fine bedding there was had already been allocated to the elders among elders, and only the inferior pieces remained. Likewise, whatever temple quarters were in the central precinct had already been assigned to the elders among elders, and only the outlying temple quarters remained, so the Venerable Jāyasena assigned those two inferior bedding pieces and lodged them in the outlying quarters.

The two then asked: "Who is the food-server for the Saṅgha?" The Venerable Jāyasena replied: "It is I, Jāyasena." They said: "Then assign us our two food portions." The Venerable Jāyasena assigned those two excellent food on the first day. Then some faithful brahmins (brāhmaṇas) and householders asked: "Who will be coming here as guests tomorrow?" Others replied: "It will be the two friends, Jāyasena and the earth-born one." Those people then thought:

"Those two are of thoroughly depraved conduct — who would show them respect? Let them eat whatever is available and be gone." With that thought, those people showed no respect to the two and gave them inferior food.

On the second day, the Venerable Jāyasena assigned those two to the middling food portions. Likewise, when the faithful brahmins and householders asked, "Who will be coming here as guests tomorrow?" others replied, "It will be the two friends, Jāyasena and the earth-born one." Those people thought: "Those two are of thoroughly depraved conduct — who would show them respect? Let them eat whatever is available and be gone." And with that thought, those people showed no respect to the two and gave them inferior food.

On the third day, the Venerable Jāyasena assigned those two to the inferior food portions by natural consequence. Then the two, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, reflected: "Alas, this is suffering! Alas, this is unbearable!" The Venerable Jāyasena thought: "He has quite deliberately — three times in a row — set upon us with the most disagreeable and revolting food, food that would make anyone who ate it fall ill. What harm should we now do to him in this matter?"

At that time, the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, had a sister, a nun named Jāyā, who was residing in Rājagṛha during the nuns' rains retreat, in the royal pleasure garden. Then the nun Jāyā made her way to where the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, were staying, and having arrived, she bowed her head to the feet of the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, and sat down to one side.

When she had sat down to one side, the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, did not exchange words with the nun Jāyā, did not speak of her arrival, did not glance at her, and did not look at her at all. Then the nun Jāyā spoke to the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, saying: "Noble ones, why do you two not exchange words with me, not speak of my arrival, not glance at me, not look at me at all?"

"Sister, the Venerable Jāyasena has quite deliberately — three times in a row — set upon us with the most disagreeable and revolting food, food that would make anyone who ate it fall ill. Have you let that pass?"

"Noble ones, what then should I do?"

"Sister, come. Go to where the Blessed One is, and having arrived, say to the Blessed One: 'Venerable One, it is unseemly and improper that the noble Jāyasena should slander, with the charge of a defeat (pārājika), without basis and without grounds, a monk who is pure and without transgression and who has engaged in unchaste conduct together with me.' And we two shall likewise say to the Blessed One: 'So it is, O Blessed One; just so, O Sugata — we two also acknowledge exactly what our sister has reported.'"

"Noble ones, how could I falsely accuse a pure monk who has no transgression, charging him with an offense entailing defeat without any basis? Sister, for as long as you do not say that, for so long we two will not exchange words with you, will not speak of your arrival, will not glance at you, will not look at you at all."

Then the nun Jāyā sat for a short while in silence, and then spoke to the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, as follows:

"Noble ones, if that is so, then I shall say exactly that. Sister, until such time as we two have arrived at the place where the Blessed One is, please remain here for a while. When we two have come into the presence of the Blessed One, then you may follow after."

Then the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, went to the place where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. The nun Jāyā, realizing that the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, had left and that no great time had passed, went to the place where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, she prostrated with her head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the nun Jāyā addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend One, this is unseemly and improper — that the noble Śvetaketu (Jayabala) engaged in unchaste conduct with me and has thereby incurred a defeat."

The two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, likewise said: "O Blessed One, it is so. O Sugata, it is just so — we two also acknowledge exactly what our sister has reported."

At that very moment, the venerable Śvetaketu (Jayabala) was present there, right in that same assembly.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śvetaketu (Jayabala): "Śvetaketu (Jayabala), did you hear that?" "Blessed One, I heard it." "Śvetaketu (Jayabala), did you hear that?" "O Sugata, I heard it." "Śvetaketu (Jayabala), what do you think of this matter?" "Blessed One, I defer to whatever you know. O Sugata, I defer to whatever you know." "Śvetaketu (Jayabala), that response — 'I defer to whatever the Blessed One knows, I defer to whatever the Sugata knows' — is untimely; it is not the appropriate occasion. If you remember, say 'I remember.' If you do not remember, say 'I do not remember.'" "O Blessed One, I do not remember. O Sugata, I do not remember."

At that very moment, the venerable Śāriputra was sitting at the Blessed One's side, holding a fan, fanning the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend One, the nun Jāyā came to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with her head to the Blessed One's two feet, sat to one side, and then, seated to one side, addressed the Blessed One with these words: 'Reverend One, this is unseemly and improper — that the noble Śvetaketu (Jayabala) engaged in unchaste conduct with me and has thereby incurred a defeat.' And the two monks, Jāyasena and the earth-born one, likewise said to the Blessed One: 'It is so, O Blessed One; it is just so, O Sugata — we two also acknowledge exactly what our sister has reported.' Reverend One, for the sake of this matter, what fault has the venerable Śvetaketu (Jayabala) incurred? Śāriputra, that is for you yourself to inquire into — answer him in whatever way you are able to bear, exactly as it is. Śāriputra, if the nun Jāyā had come to that place, prostrated with her head to my two feet, sat to one side, and then, seated to one side, addressed me with these words: 'Reverend One, this is unseemly and improper — that the noble Śāriputra engaged in unchaste conduct with me and has thereby incurred a defeat,' and then—"

The monk Priya and the earth-born one likewise spoke thus to the Blessed One: "So it is, O Blessed One. So it is, O Sugata. We two, just as our sister has reported, we two acknowledge exactly the same." Then I said to you: "You have heard the charge — what do you think of it? How will you reply?" The Reverend One replied: "Reverend Sir, if I remember it, I will say I remember; if I do not remember it, I will say I do not remember." The Blessed One then said: "You are not deluded. In that case, if the venerable Jayabala, a monk pure and free of transgression, has attained that understanding, why would he fail to attain it?"

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you shall hold the venerable Jayabala to be one possessed of mindfulness. The nun Priyā shall be censured by her own admission. As for the monk Priya and the earth-born one — what did you see? How did you see it? Where did you see it? Since you two appeared there for some purpose, state clearly what you saw there and investigate the matter."

Having thus spoken, the Blessed One rose from his seat and went to the assembly hall in order to enter into inner meditative composure. Then a great many monks, knowing that the Blessed One had entered into inner meditative composure and that no long time had passed, held the venerable Jayabala to be one possessed of mindfulness, censured the nun Priyā by her own admission, and thoroughly questioned and examined the monk Priya and the earth-born one thus: "Venerable ones, what did you see? How did you see it? Where did you see it? Why, having gone there for some purpose, did you see it there?"

When the great many monks had thoroughly questioned and examined them, those two said: "Venerable ones, the venerable Jayabala has not incurred a defeat through unchaste conduct. For the venerable Jayabala struck us both three times with vile and utterly repugnant food — the sort that causes one's bowels to run loose if eaten — and because of that, we two spoke against the venerable Jayabala out of desire, out of aversion, out of delusion, and out of fear. The venerable Jayabala has not incurred a defeat through unchaste conduct. He is a monk who is pure and without transgression."

Then, the following morning, the Blessed One arose from inner meditative composure and took his seat on the throne arranged before the assembly of monks. A great many monks then reported to the Blessed One as follows: "Reverend Sir, we, a great many monks, knowing that the Blessed One had entered into inner meditative composure and that no long time had passed, held the venerable Jayabala to be one possessed of mindfulness, censured the nun Priyā by her own words and admission, and thoroughly questioned and examined the monk Priya and the earth-born one thus: 'Venerable ones, what did you see? How did you see it? Where did you see it? Why, having gone there for some purpose, did you see it there?' When we, the great many monks, had thoroughly questioned and examined them, from the mouths of those two came this: 'Venerable ones, the venerable Jayabala has not incurred a defeat through unchaste conduct. For the venerable Jayabala struck us both three times with vile and utterly repugnant food — the sort that causes one's bowels to run loose if eaten — and because of that, we two, speaking against the venerable Jayabala, spoke out of desire, out of aversion, out of delusion, and out of—'"

"— it was said out of fear alone. The venerable Gyabu Nor has not incurred a defeat through unchaste conduct. Thus, venerable ones, the monks are pure and without transgression," they said.

"Monks, why did those two, devoid of wisdom, knowingly speak false words for the sake of a mere trifle of material goods?"

Then the Blessed One, on that occasion, declared two verses:

One who is embodied and speaks falsehood
has transgressed the single Dharma,
and one who has renounced the world beyond —
there is no evil they will not commit.

Better that one should eat iron balls
blazing like tongues of flame
than that one who is morally corrupt and truly without restraint
should eat alms gathered throughout the land.

At that moment, the gods dwelling in the midst of the sky cried out, "Splendid! Splendid! Intolerable! Supremely intolerable! That monks who have spoken thus, for the sake of a mere trifle of material goods, should falsely accuse a pure monk without transgression, by means of a groundless charge of a defeating offense!" And they spoke again: "Who among the wise would delight in wandering through saṃsāra in this world? For even the wealth that liberates from the three realms of existence is now met with slander."

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this as the basis and in this context, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. "The Blessed One, the buddhas, though fully knowing, feigned not to know" — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One, the buddha, questioned the venerable Dzawo and Sala Lé Kyé, the two of them, saying: "You two, devoid of wisdom — is it true that you falsely accused a pure monk without transgression, by means of a groundless charge of a defeating offense?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One, the buddha, rebuked them with words such as these: "That is not the way of the ascetic, it is not appropriate, it is not fitting — it is not something that one who has gone forth ought to do." And so on, in the form of a rebuke.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, these three types of persons, if they do not abandon those ways, will go to the lower realms, will go to the hells. What are the three? First, there is the person who frequents sensual pleasures and also commits evil deeds — this is the first type of person who, if that is not abandoned, will go to the lower realms, will go to the hells.
