Furthermore, there is the person who is themselves morally degenerate yet speaks of others under the power of ethics — this is the second type of person who, if that is not abandoned, will go to the lower realms, will go to the hells. Furthermore, there is the person who themselves engage in unchaste conduct and yet falsely accuse another of the groundless charge of unchaste conduct, a defeating offense — this is the third type of person who, if that is not abandoned, will go to the lower realms, will go to the hells."

The Blessed One declared this, and having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, declared further:

In the mouth of a man, when he speaks
slandering words of blame,
an axe is born — and by it
he cuts himself down.

One who praises what should be blamed
and blames what should be praised —
from his mouth he breeds strife,
and one who brings strife finds no happiness.

This strife that loses one's own wealth at dice
is but a small and trifling thing;
but one who arouses fierce anger in the mind of the Sugata —
that strife here is exceedingly great.

One who slanders a noble one, relying on evil,
will go to the hells
for a hundred thousands, a hundred million,
thirty-six, and five more —
as many as those [aeons] may be.

Then the Blessed One, having censured this in many ways, addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, whatever monk, having become enraged and filled with aversion, thinking, 'By whatever means I will separate this one from the holy life,' should, on the basis of a groundless defeat, accuse a pure monk — one free of any transgression — with a matter involving a pārājika (root downfall), whether he is questioned about it at another time or not questioned, that dispute too is groundless; and if the monk, abiding in aversion and speaking from aversion, should say that he acted out of aversion — the remainder is for the Saṅgha to decide."

Now, "whatever monk" means: a friend, one born of the same soil, or another of that kind. "Having become enraged" means: having become agitated and disturbed. "Filled with aversion" means: having become displeased, and that agitation not having been cleared away. "Thinking, 'By whatever means I will separate this one from the holy life'" means: thinking, "By whatever means I will separate this one from the conduct of a renunciant." "A pure monk" means: a warrior's son, or another of that kind. "Free of any transgression" means: free of a transgression in that particular matter. "Groundless" means: without the three grounds — the ground of having seen, the ground of having heard, and the ground of having suspected. "With a matter involving a pārājika" means: by any one of the four matters — for that is something that is not Dharma expressed in the name of Dharma. "Should accuse" means: having leveled an accusation. "At another time" means: at a different time from that. "Whether questioned" means: questioned by others. "Or not questioned" means: he himself having become remorseful — somewhat remorseful, fully remorseful, or deeply remorseful. "That dispute too" refers to the four disputes: a dispute for the sake of quarreling, a dispute for the sake of not giving advice, a dispute concerning a transgression, and a dispute concerning an obligation. "Is groundless" means: those three grounds being absent. "The monk abiding in aversion" means: one who intends to make an accusation. "Should say that he acted out of aversion" means: one who says, "He has made a false accusation." "The remainder is for the Saṅgha to decide" — this is as before; thus it is said, "the remainder is for the Saṅgha to decide."

Now, how does a transgression occur in this matter? Accusing a pure person with ten grounds constitutes a transgression; with five grounds it does not constitute a transgression.

How does it constitute a transgression with ten grounds? When one, having altered one's perception and patience regarding something not seen, not heard, and not suspected, and having altered one's wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I have seen this," "I have heard this," "I suspect this" — all of these statements become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide. If one heard something and forgot it, or suspected something and forgot it, yet having altered one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I heard it and have not forgotten it," or "I suspected it and have not forgotten it" — all of those statements too become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide. Whether one trusted what one heard and says "I have seen it," or did not trust what one heard and says "I have seen it," or suspected what one heard and says "I have seen it," or did not suspect what one heard and says "I have seen it" —

or suspected what one heard and says "I have seen it" — all of those statements become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide, and one incurs a transgression through ten grounds. How is it that one does not incur a transgression through five grounds? If one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected something, and without having altered one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I have seen it," "I have heard it," or "I have suspected it" — one does not incur a transgression. If one heard something and forgot it, or suspected something and forgot it, and without having altered one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I heard it and have not forgotten it," or "I suspected it and have not forgotten it" — one does not incur a transgression. In this way, one does not incur a transgression through five grounds.

Just as one incurs a transgression through ten grounds and does not incur a transgression through five grounds when making a false accusation against a pure person, so too when making a false accusation against a pure person by representing them as impure, one likewise incurs a transgression through ten grounds and does not incur a transgression through five grounds.

For making a false accusation against an impure person, one incurs a transgression through eleven grounds and does not incur a transgression through six grounds. How is it that one incurs a transgression through eleven grounds? If, having not seen, not heard, and not suspected something, one alters one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, and then declares: "I have seen it," "I have heard it," or "I have suspected it" — all of those statements become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide. If one saw something and forgot it, or heard something and forgot it, or suspected something and forgot it, and having altered one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I saw it and have not forgotten it," "I heard it and have not forgotten it," or "I suspected it and have not forgotten it" — all of those statements too become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide. Whether one trusted what one heard and says "I have seen it," or did not trust what one heard and says "I have seen it," or suspected what one heard and says "I have seen it," or did not suspect what one heard and says "I have seen it," or suspected what one heard and says "I have seen it" — all of those statements become a matter for the Saṅgha to decide, and in this way one incurs a transgression through eleven grounds.

How is it that one does not incur a transgression through six grounds? If one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected something, and without altering one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I have seen it," "I have heard it," or "I have suspected it" — one does not incur a transgression. If one saw something and has not forgotten it, or heard something and has not forgotten it, or suspected something and has not forgotten it, and without altering one's perception, patience, wish, understanding, conceptual thought, and view, declares: "I saw it and have not forgotten it," "I heard it and have not forgotten it," or "I suspected it and have not forgotten it" — one does not incur a transgression. In this way, one does not incur a transgression through six grounds.

Just as one incurs a transgression through eleven grounds and does not incur a transgression through six grounds when making a false accusation against an impure person, so too when making a false accusation against an impure person by representing them as pure, one likewise incurs a transgression through eleven grounds and does not incur a transgression through six grounds.

When a public announcement has been made, there is no transgression. From the time something is inscribed on a surface onward, there is likewise no transgression.

thinking, "Just as I myself know it, so too does the whole world know it." There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The monks, having given rise to doubt, asked the Blessed One, the Buddha, to resolve all their doubts: "Venerable one, what action did the noble Gyabu Nor perform such that through the karmic maturation of that action he was born into a household that was wealthy, with abundant riches and great prosperity? What action did he perform such that he went forth into the Blessed One's teaching and, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhathood? What action did he perform such that even though he had attained arhathood, he was falsely accused of what was not true? And what action did he perform such that he was declared supreme among those who dwell in forest retreats?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, this noble son Gyabu Nor himself performed and accumulated karma that was gathered, that thoroughly transformed its conditions, that remained close like a lamp's flame, that would arise without fail. And those actions performed and accumulated by Gyabu Nor himself — could anyone else experience their maturation separately? Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, wholesome and unwholesome actions that have been performed and accumulated ripen in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases that have been appropriated, as it is said:

Even were it a hundred aeons,
actions do not perish or waste away.
When the conditions and the time are met
they come to bear their fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in a former time, long past, there was at a rocky cliff a merchant of great renown called Gyalchenchen. He set out with a vessel heading for the great ocean, and together with his company of like-minded companions he sailed out upon the great ocean. At a time when no buddhas had arisen, there appeared in the world pratyekabuddhas — humble and destitute — who cherished those who were lowly and poor, who delighted in remote and isolated dwellings, who lived alone like a rhinoceros's horn, and who had become worthy fields of merit for the world. Then a pratyekabuddha set out voyaging together with that very merchant, and that night he entered into meditative absorption in the fire element. Now the custom among the chief men of the crew was to take turns night by night keeping the fire-watch. On a certain night it was the turn of one man to keep the fire-watch. He, seeing that the pratyekabuddha was blazing like a mass of fire, was seized with amazement, and when dawn broke he said to the merchant Gyalchenchen: 'Merchant, this renunciant who set sail together with the merchant is a great being perfected in ascetic discipline. I saw him blazing through the night like a mass of fire.' The merchant replied: 'Good fellow, in which direction is he dwelling?' The man said: 'Right over there, merchant.' The merchant, filled with joy, went to him, prostrated at his two feet, and said: 'Noble one, it is your wish to go for alms, and I too am one who seeks merit. Please accept my alms offering and go forth.' The pratyekabuddha consented, and by and by, as the merchant Gyalchenchen traveled in succession through villages, hamlets, districts, royal palaces, and market towns, he arrived at the shore of the great ocean. There, having dispelled the weariness of the journey, he outfitted five hundred old boats with provisions of sour milk, and taking with him those who bailed the boats, the sailors, the helmsmen, the boat hands, and those who managed the sails, he went to where the pratyekabuddha was and arrived, and

prostrated with his whole body to his two feet and spoke these words to the pratyekabuddha: "Noble one, when I venture out upon the great ocean, will you, the noble one, also venture forth?" He replied: "Good sir, you are setting out upon the great ocean for the sake of your father and mother, your children, your wife, your male and female servants, your workers, those who live on wages, ascetics and brahmins, the poor and destitute — whereas I have left behind the affairs of household life, I have no inclination toward continued existence or worldly possessions, and I live without companion or associate. For whose sake, then, should I venture upon the great ocean?"

The merchant Gyalchenchen thought to himself: "I have offered alms to this noble one, and yet he has put on no robe. Let me now give him food, and then clothe him in a great bolt of cloth befitting one of high standing." And so the merchant satisfied him with food as alms, and then clothed him in a great bolt of cloth befitting one of high standing.

Thereupon the pratyekabuddha, having received the alms of food, and out of affectionate regard for him, rose up into the sky above like a king of geese spreading wide his wings, and began to perform miracles: blazing with fire, shining with radiance, letting fall rain, and sending forth lightning.

Now, ordinary persons are quick to fix their minds upon miraculous powers, and so the merchant fell to the ground at the feet of that pratyekabuddha as though a great tree had been cut down at its root, and began to make this aspiration: "By the root of virtue that I have created through making offerings to such a perfectly true field of merit as this, may I be reborn in a household that is wealthy, of great riches, and of great prosperity. And may I also attain qualities such as these — qualities by which one pleases a Teacher superior even to this, a Teacher most supremely excellent, without causing him displeasure." Thus he made his aspiration prayer.

Monks, the merchant Gyalchenchen of that time and that occasion is this very Gaurava, the son of a warrior. He made offerings to the pratyekabuddha and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, through making offerings to such a perfectly true field of merit, may I be reborn in a household that is wealthy, of great riches, and of great prosperity." By that aspiration, he was indeed reborn in a household that was wealthy, of great riches, and of great prosperity. And he also made this aspiration: "May I attain qualities such as these — qualities by which one pleases a Teacher most supremely excellent above this, without causing him displeasure." Through that aspiration, he went forth in my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and directly actualized the state of an arhat. And through this he pleased me, the Teacher most supremely excellent above ten trillion pratyekabuddhas, without causing me displeasure.

But hear now how, although he attained the state of an arhat, he came to be disparaged for something that was not right.

Monks, once upon a time in the past, on a certain rocky cliff, there lived a householder who was wealthy, of great riches, and of great prosperity, possessed of vast and extensive estates, endowed with wealth like the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa (the divine lord of riches), rivaling Vaiśravaṇa in his treasure. He took a wife from among his own equals in station, and together with her he sported, took delight, and enjoyed pleasures. Yet although he sported, took delight, and enjoyed pleasures with her, he had no son and no daughter. And he thought: "My household is endowed with great wealth, yet I have no son and no daughter. When I am gone, because I have no son, all my wealth will come under the king's control." And so he sat resting his chin upon his hand, absorbed in his own thoughts.

His wife saw this and said:

"O son of the lord, why do you sit resting your chin upon your hand, absorbed in your own thoughts?"

He replied: "Good woman, my household is endowed with great wealth, yet I have no son and no daughter. When I am gone, because I have no son, all my wealth will come under the king's control. How could I not sit absorbed in thought?"

The wife thought to herself: "Is it that he has no fortune, so that he has neither son nor daughter? Or is it that I too have no fortune, so that there is neither son nor daughter? If the latter is the case and there is no way to know whose fault it is, then he will certainly blame me and wish to take another wife. That is why he says these words: 'My household is endowed with great wealth, yet I have no son and no daughter; when I am gone, because I have no son, all my wealth will come under the king's control' — and sits there before me resting his chin upon his hand, feigning absorption in thought. Therefore, I had better first secure my own position."

And so she spoke: "Son of the lord, if indeed it is because I have no fortune that you have neither son nor daughter, then take another queen. After that you may well have both son and daughter."

He replied: "Good woman, have you not heard it said that a man who has two wives never once drinks warm water, never drinks cool water in peace, but his household is perpetually filled with quarreling, tale-bearing, dispute, and strife among all the household members, and he is never free to attend to his own affairs?"

The wife said: "Son of the lord, please do take another. If she should be like an elder or younger sister to me, I will care for her with the thought of a sister. If she should be like a daughter to me, I will care for her with the thought of a daughter."

The householder, moved by his wife's guileful and persuasive words, began to search for a girl. Now at a certain cliff-side dwelling there lived a householder who had taken a wife from among his own equals in station, and together with her he sported, took delight, and enjoyed pleasures. From their sporting, delight, and pleasures she bore two sons and a daughter, and having raised and brought up those children, that householder passed away in due time.

Then the first-mentioned householder, who was searching for a girl, approached that couple's daughter, took her as his bride with great and splendid ceremony, and brought her home. It is in the very nature of things that whatever is new overshadows and surpasses the old, and so the householder became greatly attentive to his new bride, his mind drawn to her.

Thereupon his first wife, driven by jealousy, purified her own womb and caused a sentient being to enter it. Filled with the greatest joy, she spoke to her husband: "Son of the lord, a being has entered me — rejoice!"

The householder said: "Good woman, excellent! If it is born as a boy, he shall become the master of the household after I am gone."

The first wife then said: "Son of the lord, if you do not cause the child dwelling in the womb of your new bride to be aborted in the manner of aborting, then this boy will become master of the household."

The householder replied: "Good woman, did I not make this very matter clear to you from the very beginning? And you have now begun it when nothing has yet changed."

That wife fell silent, without a word, having lost her nerve.

Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth a boy was born. A birth-celebration was held, a name fitting to the household was given, and the child was raised and nourished with milk, yoghurt, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other such finest and most excellent provisions.

nourishing him swiftly, like a lotus growing in a pond.

When he came to be able to speak, whatever he said he spoke truly and never told a lie. The name that had been given to fit the household now faded away, and the name Truth-Speaker came to be attached to him, and from his very mouth there arose the fragrance of blue lotus flowers.

His mother thought to herself: "Although I have a son, this householder still pays attention to that first wife, just as if fate had not changed, and keeps his heart bound to her. I must find some way to deal with this." And so, her mind overcome by jealousy and miserliness, she went to where the householder was and said: "My lord's son, as for this new wife of yours — do not be so very attached to her and so bound up with her in your heart."

The householder said: "Good woman, you have started again."

And she fell silent, without a word, having lost her nerve.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga (the Analysis of the Discipline), the twenty-first section.

Because there is nothing wicked that those who consort with men or women consumed by desire will not do, the mother said to her son: "Son, do you know what the greatest harm that women do is?"

The son replied: "Honored mother, it is jealousy and miserliness."

"Son, you are not wrong. You understand with wisdom, and that is indeed so. But she is defaming your stepmother to me, your mother. You must clarify the four great matters. Has she done so rightly or wrongly?"

"Mother, not rightly."

"Son, if I am known throughout the entire world as Truth-Speaker, how then could I now speak falsely? Son, when she carried you in her womb for nine months she would groan and writhe in pain and could not even utter a word. Therefore, do not say a word now, and when your father questions you, simply nod your head."

The son thought: "It would not be right to dismiss my mother's words as worthless," and so he said: "Mother, if that is so, then I will not refuse. I will nod."

She then bound the boy by an oath and went to the householder and said: "My lord's son, I have seen a fault in your new wife. What did she do? She was taking pleasure and sporting with another man."

The householder, seized by passion, said: "You wicked woman — you have done it again. My lord's son, do you not trust Truth-Speaker? I believe her — for if she speaks truth to the whole world, how could she speak falsely to me? My lord's son, if that is so, call her here while she is at play."

The householder called the boy and set him on his lap and said: "Son, is it true that this stepmother of yours was taking pleasure and sporting with another man?"

Now, women are skilled in these matters without having been taught, and so she covered the boy's mouth with her hand and said: "Son, this is like your own mother — do not say a word. If it is true, nod your head."

The boy nodded.

For karma that is exceedingly fierce and fully complete regards not the destruction of the body. And so from that very boy's mouth, in that very life, a foul stench arose.

Moreover, the report spread everywhere that Truth-Speaker had falsely slandered his stepmother with what was not true, and so he was not Truth-Speaker but a liar. The name Truth-Speaker, which had been his, faded away, and the name Liar came to be attached to him.

Then the householder said to that wife: "You have behaved badly. Do not remain in my house."

The wife protested that she had done no wrong, but fearing the blame and harsh words of the world, she was driven out of the house.

Discontented, she went to the house of her two brothers. The two brothers said to her: "Sister, why have you come here?" She replied: "My husband has driven me from his own house, saying that I behaved badly." They said: "If that is so, do not stay here either." She replied: "I did not behave badly. It is rather this: Truth-Speaker deceived me, and with what was not true he slandered me, saying that I am not Truth-Speaker but a liar. How is that known?" She continued: "If the two of you do not believe me, the neighbors will speak on your behalf, and they are persons of standing." Fearing the blame and harsh words of the world, the two of them went and questioned the householder's neighbors, and those neighbors said: "She did not behave badly. Rather, Truth-Speaker deceived her, and with what was not true he slandered her — he is not Truth-Speaker but a liar." Then the two brothers, seized by the anger that arose in them toward Truth-Speaker, made sure that their beloved kinsmen and close ones came to understand what had happened. They kept their sister in their own home and devoted themselves fully to seeking to expose him further.

Now, in a time when no buddhas had appeared in the world, there arose in the world solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas) of the lesser kind — those who had compassion for the poor and destitute, who delighted in dwelling in remote and lonely forest hermitages, who, like rhinoceroses, lived alone, and who had become worthy objects of offering for the world.

At a certain time, as one such solitary buddha was wandering through the region, he came to that rocky cliff. Early in the morning he had tied on his lower robe, taken up his bowl and his dharma robe, and was going from house to house in order on his alms round — his conduct being so serene that it drew the minds of gods and humans alike — when he entered that house. The stepmother who had been falsely slandered with what was not true saw him, and she thought: "From the very conduct of this one who has gone forth, it is clear that he is a great being of accomplished discipline. Whoever makes offerings to him and places aspirations before him — all that they think and all that they wish will be accomplished for them." Knowing this, she prostrated at his two feet and said: "Noble one, you seek alms, and I seek merit, so please take your midday meal right here." As that great being was one who had entered into the welfare of others, he accepted.

Then, having satisfied the solitary buddha with food accompanied by the proper offering, she prostrated at his two feet and made this wrongful aspiration, saying: "By the root of virtue of making such offerings to one who is a truly worthy field of merit — just as Truth-Speaker falsely slandered me without cause, though I had done nothing blameworthy and no harm had been done — so too, may I likewise, in whatever life and wherever that one is reborn, falsely slander him in that very place, until he attains the state of an arhat."

Her two brothers asked her: "Sister, what aspiration have you made?" She told them: "Brothers, it was this: such and such." The two of them said: "If that is so, we two are also your brothers, so the four witnesses should be called to hear it."

Now, monks, you should know this: the householder's son, Truth-Speaker, of that time and that age — he is Jātila Nanda of the present. The stepmother of that time and that age — she is the nun Mṛgī of the present. The two brothers of that time and that age — they are the monks Mitra and Jātilaka. The karmic maturation of the act of falsely slandering the stepmother with what was not true — through that ripening, for many hundreds of years...

...for many thousands of years he was tormented in the hell realms, and through the residual force of that very same karma, for five hundred lifetimes this one falsely slandered her with what was not true, and the two of them called the four witnesses against him. Thus it is that even now, having attained arhatship itself, the nun who is his friend falsely slandered him with what was not true, and his friend and the two born of the earth called the four witnesses against him.

As for the fact that he was declared supreme among those who dwell in forest lodgings — that came about through the power of aspiration. And where was that aspiration made? Monks, long ago in a time that has passed, in this very fortunate eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher — the Tathāgata, the arhat, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One — the buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world. He dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park forest called Ṛṣivadana near Vārāṇasī.

In that Teacher's dispensation this one went forth, and the monk who ordained him was declared supreme among those who dwell in forest lodgings by the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa. Now this one, practicing the holy life for as long as he lived, attained not even a single accumulation of good qualities, and at the time of his death he made an aspiration in these words: "Throughout the Blessed One's — the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened, the unsurpassed field of offering, Kāśyapa's — dispensation, I have practiced the holy life for as long as I lived and attained not a single accumulation of good qualities. By this root of virtue of practicing the holy life for as long as I lived, may I, in the future — when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, in the time when the Tathāgata, the arhat, the fully and perfectly awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the buddha and Blessed One to be called Śākyamuni, has been prophesied by the Blessed One Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, who said to the brahmin youth who was his teacher: 'Brahmin youth, in the future, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha and Blessed One named Śākyamuni' — in that dispensation may I go forth, and by abandoning all afflictions may I realize arhatship, and just as this preceptor was declared supreme among those who dwell in forest lodgings by the Blessed One Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, so too may I be declared supreme among those who dwell in forest lodgings by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the chief king of the Śākyas." Having begun to set down that aspiration, through the power of that aspiration, he has now been declared by the Tathāgata supreme among those who dwell in forest lodgings.

Monks, that being so: the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is also mixed.

Monks, therefore, having abandoned actions that are wholly dark and mixed, you should strive for actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train yourselves in just this way.

The eighth section on the Saṅgha's remainder, concerning baseless slander, is complete.


The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove of the Cool Forest. At that time the venerable Śreṇika Bimbisāra was sitting on Vulture Peak Hill at Rājagṛha...

Not far from there was a pond called the Stone-walled Pond. Beside it the venerable Nandaka used to spend his days.

Now, at the time when the blue-lotus-hued spiritual friend, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, had gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya in reliance on him, and had conquered what was to be conquered — fully achieved the arhat's liberation — at that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra, having learned of this and filled with faith, would go again and again to see the Blessed One and the elder monks, the elders. And in particular, thinking that it must be a hardship for the venerable Nandaka — though he had attained meditative absorption in the eight liberations of the arhat's liberation — to have set aside the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, and entering into meditative absorption and to apply himself instead to the administrative duties belonging to the Saṅgha, Bimbisāra would go again and again to look upon him.

Then on another occasion, having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and the elder monks, the elders, Bimbisāra went to where the venerable Nandaka was, arrived there, touched his head to the venerable Nandaka's two feet in homage, and sat down before him in order to hear the Dharma.

At that time, two monks — one called Friend and one called Earth-born — found a heap of dirty rags. These two had harbored enmity against the venerable Nandaka from life to life across many lifetimes, and were always striving to find some fault with him. So Friend said to Earth-born: "Earth-born, where shall we take these dirty rags to wash them?" Earth-born replied: "The Stone-walled Pond has little traffic and clean surroundings, so let us go there." The two of them carried the dirty rags, went to the Stone-walled Pond, rinsed the rags there, spread them out in the sun, and laid them down to dry.

At that time, herds of deer came to the Stone-walled Pond, drank the water, and then departed. Now it is the nature of deer to mount one another's backs, and so it happened that one stag mounted the back of a doe and began engaging in unchaste conduct, the act of mating.

Friend saw this and said: "Earth-born! Go and tell the monks that Nandaka has engaged in unchaste conduct, the act of mating, with the nun Utpalavarṇā." Earth-born replied: "Venerable Friend, even then it would have been better for the two of us to stay and do the work of washing right there. Do you really still want to take up that work of staying and washing?" Friend said: "Venerable Earth-born, at that time it was indeed not proper — but now I have a plan in mind. Did you not see Nandaka engaging in unchaste conduct, the act of mating, with the nun Utpalavarṇā? Venerable one, how could there be any lying about this? Come, let us go and report it to the monks."

Earth-born, deceived by Friend, was persuaded, and the two of them went to the monastery hall and said to the monks: "Venerable ones, we ourselves have seen the venerable Nandaka engaging in unchaste conduct, the act of mating, with the nun Utpalavarṇā. On whose faith or trust should we go?" The monks replied: "Venerable two — could you really be reviling, by a charge consistent with the portion belonging to others that is contrary to their part, one who has gods and humans within his purview, who does not abide among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals — a monk who is an arhat, who has attained meditative absorption in the eight liberations, who demonstrates the supreme superhuman miracle of the higher faculties of a noble one — accusing him in a manner that would bring about a defeat?"

The two of them said: "Venerable ones, we have not wronged him — rather, it is as follows: we should pluck out our own eyes that saw what they saw. What did the Blessed One previously see with regard to those two? How did he see it? Where did he see it? Since you two went there for some purpose and saw it there, explain this thoroughly and examine it well." And thus the Blessed One declared: "Examine them as to what they saw, how they saw it, where they saw it, and why, having gone there for some reason, they claim to have seen it there — explain this well and investigate." The monks then questioned those two thoroughly, examining them as to what they saw, how they saw it, where they saw it, and why they had gone there and seen it there. After the many monks had questioned and examined them thoroughly, the two said: "Venerable ones, the venerable Nandaka did not engage with the nun Utpalavarṇā in the act of mating, which is unchaste conduct. Rather, venerable ones, Nandaka gave us — three times in a row, by striking us with extremely unpleasant and utterly repulsive food of the kind that, when eaten, causes one's stomach to heave — cause to revile the venerable Nandaka by a charge consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part, a charge that would bring about a defeat. But the venerable Nandaka did not engage with the nun Utpalavarṇā in unchaste conduct, the act of mating. Thus, monks, a pure monk is one without a downfall. Why do monks of little account revile, mock, disparage, and slander a pure monk who is without a downfall by leveling against him a charge consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part, a charge that would bring about a defeat?" At that, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this founding case, and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The rule of training to be proclaimed by my hearers in the Vinaya shall be as follows:

"If any monk, out of anger and aversion, with the intention 'by some means I will sever this one from the celibate life,' charges a pure monk who is without a downfall with a defeat-incurring offense by a charge consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part, and later — whether he is asked or not — that same dispute proves to be consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part, and that dispute, being consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part, involves something that was conceived only slightly and barely deliberated upon and taken up as a matter of some concern, and the monk remains in aversion and spoke from aversion — that is an offense requiring the deliberation of the Saṅgha."

Now, "any monk" means a friend, one born of the land, or anyone else of that sort. "Out of anger" means being agitated and upset. "Having become averse" means having become displeased, without having dispelled the agitation. "With the intention of by some means severing this one from the celibate life" means with the thought of severing this one from the monk's way of life by any means. "A pure monk" means Nandaka or anyone else of that kind. "Without a downfall" means without a downfall in that particular matter. As for "consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part" — "what belongs to others" refers to nirvāṇa, and "contrary to their part" refers to the four defeat-incurring phenomena. "Defeat-incurring" means any one of the four. "By a charge" means that what is not the Dharma is stated under the name of the Dharma. "From a charge" means from having made the accusation. "Later" means at a different time. "Whether he is asked" means asked by others. "Whether not asked" means that he himself — having become remorseful, somewhat remorseful, thoroughly remorseful, or extremely remorseful — comes to regret it on his own. "That same dispute" refers to the fourfold dispute that is to be examined: a dispute

arising from a failure to select, a dispute arising from a transgression, and a dispute arising from a matter of procedure.

"Contrary to their part and in conformity with it" means: "contrary to the part of nirvāṇa and in conformity with it, which results in defeat."

As for the expression "that dispute, through something contrary to their part and in conformity with it, took up some phenomenon conceived of as no more than a fleeting thought beyond a mere impulse" — "no more than a fleeting thought beyond a mere impulse" refers to a male or female deer. "Phenomenon" means that what is not the Dharma is stated under the name of the Dharma. "Took up" means having grasped it.

"A monk, moreover, while abiding in aversion" means with the intention of making a false accusation. "If it is said that he spoke out of aversion" means: if one were to say that he made a false accusation. "A saṅghāvaśeṣa" is as before — and therefore it is said to be a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

Now, how does a transgression come about in that regard?

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that results in defeat, comes to form the view that there is no transgression in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that results in defeat, comes to form the view that it is a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that results in defeat, comes to form the view that it is a transgression entailing expiation in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that results in defeat, comes to form the view that it is a transgression to be individually confessed in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that results in defeat, comes to form the view that it is a wrongdoing in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that there is no transgression in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is precisely a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is precisely a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is a transgression requiring individual confession in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is a wrongdoing in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that there is no transgression in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is a transgression requiring individual confession in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression, comes to form the view that it is a wrongdoing in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression requiring individual confession, comes to form the view that there is no transgression in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression requiring individual confession, comes to form the view that there is a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression requiring individual confession, comes to form the view that it is a wrongdoing in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression requiring individual confession, comes to form the very view that it is itself a transgression requiring individual confession, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression requiring individual confession, comes to form the view that it is a misdeed in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that is a misdeed, comes to form the view that there is no transgression in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that is a misdeed, comes to form the view that there is a saṅghāvaśeṣa in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that is a misdeed, comes to form the view that it is a wrongdoing in that act, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that is a misdeed, comes to form the view that it is a transgression requiring individual confession, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

If a monk, having seen another monk committing a transgression that is a misdeed, comes to form the very view that it is itself a misdeed, and then — having shifted his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, and his view — says: "I saw a monk committing a transgression that results in defeat," that becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

There is no transgression when a bell has been rung. There is likewise no transgression from the point at which something has been written in outline on a surface. And there is no transgression if one thinks: "Just as I myself know it, so too does the whole world know it."

There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is deranged, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations. The ninth section of the saṅghāvaśeṣa rules concerned with what is not another's part is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove of the Cool Forest. At that time a severe famine arose, and it became difficult for wandering mendicants in the wilderness to obtain alms. There were among them certain monks who had attained supernormal powers. These monks went to the Jambu tree — the tree from which Jambudvīpa takes its name — and gathered ripe Jambu fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor. They also went to the surrounding groves of myrobalan, bilva, and kapittha trees and gathered ripe fruits from those groves, fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, filled their bowls with them and carried them back; they themselves enjoyed them fully, and when there was any remainder they distributed it among the other monks as well. They went east to Videha and west to Godānīya, and north to Uttarakuru, where they gathered ripe grains of sāli rice that had grown unsown and unplanted, filled their bowls with them and carried them back; they themselves enjoyed them fully, and when there was any remainder they distributed it among the other monks as well. They went among the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings, and they went among the gods of the class of the Thirty-Three, gathering divine ambrosia, filling their bowls with it and carrying it back; they themselves enjoyed it fully, and when there was any remainder they distributed it among the other monks as well. They went to whatever lands were prosperous and flourishing, happy and blessed with good harvests, filled with many people and inhabitants, and gathered there fine prepared foods and pure eatables, filled their bowls with them and carried them back; they themselves enjoyed them fully, and when there was any remainder they distributed it among the other monks as well.

Then the monk Lhaje thought to himself: Right now a severe famine has arisen, and it has become difficult for wandering mendicants in the wilderness to obtain alms. Here there are certain monks who have attained supernormal powers. They go to the Jambu tree — the tree from which Jambudvīpa takes its name — and gather ripe Jambu fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor; and from the surrounding groves of myrobalan, bilva, and kapittha trees they gather ripe fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, fill their bowls with them and carry them back; they themselves enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder they distribute it among the other monks as well. They go east to Videha and west to Godānīya, and north to Uttarakuru, and gather ripe grains of sāli rice that have grown unsown and unplanted, fill their bowls with them and carry them back; they themselves enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder they distribute it among the other monks as well. They go among the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings and among the gods of the class of the Thirty-Three, gather divine ambrosia, fill their bowls with it and carry it back; they themselves enjoy it fully, and when there is any remainder they distribute it among the other monks as well. They go to whatever lands are prosperous and flourishing, happy and blessed with good harvests, filled with many people and inhabitants, and gather there fine prepared foods and pure eatables, fill their bowls with them and carry them back; they themselves enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder they distribute it among the other monks as well. But as for me —

"If I too were to attain supernatural powers, I too would go to the jambu tree — that very tree from which Jambudvīpa takes its name — and gather ripe fruits of the jambu, endowed with fine color, fragrance, and taste. And in the groves round about it — the groves of myrobalan, of bilva, and of kapittha — I would gather ripe fruits of those trees as well, endowed with fine color, fragrance, and taste, fill my bowl with them and carry it back; I myself would enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder I would distribute it among the monks as well. I would go to the Eastern Continent of Videha, and to the Western Continent of Aparagodānīya, and to the Northern Continent of Uttarakuru, and gather grains of unhusked, unsown śāli rice, fill my bowl with them and carry it back; I myself would enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder I would distribute it among the monks as well. I would go among the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings, and among the gods of the class of the Thirty-Three, and gather divine ambrosia, fill my bowl with it and carry it back; I myself would enjoy it fully, and when there is any remainder I would distribute it among the monks as well. I would go to whatever lands are prosperous and flourishing, happy and blessed with good harvests, filled with many people and inhabitants, and gather there fine prepared foods and pure eatables, fill my bowl with them and carry it back; I myself would enjoy them fully, and when there is any remainder I would distribute it among the monks as well. But then, who is there who is able to show me the path to supernatural power?" And so thinking, Devadat went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Devadatta spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please show me the path to supernatural power." Thereupon the Blessed One, having understood in his mind that such a sinful and corrupt desire had arisen in Devadatta, spoke to Devadatta thus: "Son of Gautama, apply yourself strenuously to the higher moral discipline, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well. Son of Gautama, apply yourself strenuously to the higher mind and the higher wisdom, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well." Then Devadatta thought to himself: "The Blessed One will not show me the path to supernatural power." Recognizing this, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One, went to where the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was, and having arrived, spoke to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya thus: "Venerable elder, please show me the path to supernatural power." Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya reflected on the mind of the Blessed One, and recognizing as well that such a sinful and corrupt desire had arisen in Devadatta, spoke to Devadatta thus: "Devadatta, attend to form properly and correctly, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well. Devadatta, attend to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness properly and correctly, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well." Then Devadatta thought to himself: "The elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya too will not show me the path to supernatural power." Recognizing this, he went to where the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrajit, the Venerable Kimbila, the Venerable Nirmala, and the Venerable Gavāmpati

went to where the Venerable Suhastin and the other five hundred elders were staying. Having arrived, he said to them: "May the elders please show me the path to supernatural power." Then the five hundred elders looked carefully into the minds of the Blessed One and of the monks, the elder and the elders, and recognized that such a wicked form of desire had arisen in Devadatta. They spoke to Devadatta as follows: "Devadatta, attend to form properly and correctly, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well. Devadatta, attend to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness properly and correctly, and supernatural powers and other qualities will come to you as well." Then Devadatta thought to himself: "The five hundred elders too will not show me the path to supernatural power. These venerable ones have long walked together with the Blessed One, and for that reason not one of them will show me the path to supernatural power. Who else, then, is there who is capable of showing me the path to supernatural power?"

At that time the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers was dwelling in a cave on Grdhrakūta Hill at Rājagṛha. Then Devadatta thought to himself: "This elder, the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers, has from of old been without guile, without deceit, straightforward and of a straightforward nature, and he is the preceptor of my elder brother Ānanda. The Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers is capable of showing me the path to supernatural power." Recognizing this, he went to where the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers was staying. Having arrived, he prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Devadatta said to the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers: "May the elder please show me the path to supernatural power."

Then the Venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers, without looking into the minds of the Blessed One and of the monks, the elder and the elders, and without taking into account that such a wicked form of desire had arisen in Devadatta, showed Devadatta the path to supernatural power.

Then Devadatta, neither sleeping during the first watch of the night nor the last, striving with diligent effort throughout, and relying upon the first meditative concentration (dhyāna), accomplished supernatural powers through a worldly path. Having done so, from being one he became many; from being many he became one. He experienced both appearance and non-appearance through knowing and seeing. He passed through walls, through embankments, through mountains with his body without obstruction, just as a bird moves through the sky. He rose up through the earth and submerged into it, just as a bird moves through water. He walked upon water without sinking, going along its surface, just as upon the great earth. He traveled through the sky seated cross-legged, just as a winged bird does. He produced smoke and he produced flames, like a great mass of fire. From his body he drew forth great streams of water, like a great cloud. And he reached out and touched with his hand the sun and the moon, great as they are in supernatural power, great in might, and great in splendor.

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "From that Jambu tree by whose name this continent is known as Jambudvīpa, ripe Jambu fruits have fallen — fruits endowed with color and fragrance and taste —

and in the groves of emblic myrobalan, bael fruit, and kapittha that lay nearby, ripe fruits fell from those very trees — fruits endowed with color and fragrance and taste — and with these he filled his begging bowl and carried it away, to enjoy himself and, if any remained, to share the rest among the monks as well. And he went to the Eastern Continent of Videha, and to the Western Continent of Aparagodānīya, and to the Northern Continent of Uttarakuru, where unplowed and unsown rice grains filled his begging bowl, which he carried away to enjoy himself and, if any remained, to share the rest among the monks as well. And he went among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings, and among the gods of the realm of the Thirty-Three, where he filled his begging bowl with divine nectar and carried it away to enjoy himself and, if any remained, to share the rest among the monks as well. And from those lands that were prosperous, flourishing, pleasant, of good harvest, and filled with people and multitudes, he gathered clean and choice prepared foods and dishes, filled his begging bowl with them and carried it away to enjoy himself and, if any remained, to share the rest among the monks as well. What good did all this do? In this land of Magadha, I should find a chief man to follow, he thought — and in this land of Magadha, whoever it is that, if followed, would with little effort cause the common multitude of people to follow as well — that is the chief man I should follow.

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "This young man, the Son of the Enemy, will, when his father has passed, stand as lord and master of his father's royal kingdom. Let me then follow the young Son of the Enemy, for if he follows me, the common multitude of people will follow along with little effort."

Then Devadatta transformed himself into a noble youth of a great elephant's power and entered through the gate of the young Son of the Enemy's house, came out through the window and entered through the window and came out through the gate. He transformed himself into a noble youth of a great horse's power and entered through the gate and came out through the window, and entered through the window and came out through the gate. Then, transforming himself into a shaven-headed monk wearing a patched robe, he entered through the gate of the young Son of the Enemy's house, came out through the window, and entered through the window and came out through the gate — whereupon the young Son of the Enemy recognized him, thinking: "Ah, this is the noble Devadatta!"

Then Devadatta transformed himself into a small golden-hued infant boy and crawled about on the lap of the young Son of the Enemy, and wriggled away, while the young Son of the Enemy embraced him, kissed him, and held him close, and even licked into his mouth — and this too happened thus: Devadatta, overwhelmed by gain and honor and with his mind entirely captivated, swallowed it down. And the young Son of the Enemy also recognized him, thinking: "Ah, this is the noble Devadatta!"

And then the young Son of the Enemy arrived at the vast and wicked view that "the noble Devadatta possesses greater miraculous powers even than the Teacher," and having come to faith in him, he set about performing acts of devotion on account of that faith: in the morning and in the evening he would come with a retinue of some five hundred chariots and pay attendance upon him. He would also offer clusters of food cooked in some five hundred vessels.

Devadatta, too, would seat some five hundred monks in rows for a meal. Then, as a great many monks were out in the early morning — having put on their robes, taken up their bowls and outer cloaks, and entered Rājagṛha on alms-round — while wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, those many monks saw that gain and honor of such a kind had come to Devadatta: that King Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, born of the Licchavis of Magadha, was coming in the evening with a retinue of some five hundred chariots and paying attendance upon him; that he was offering clusters of food cooked in some five hundred vessels; and that Devadatta, too, was seating some five hundred monks in rows for a meal. Having seen this, those monks completed their alms-round in Rājagṛha and attended to the business of eating. Returning from the afternoon alms-round, they set aside their bowls and outer cloaks, washed their two feet, and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, they bowed down with their heads at the Blessed One's two feet and took a seat to one side. Seated to one side, a great many monks addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable One, this morning we many monks, having put on our robes, taken up our bowls and outer cloaks, and entered Rājagṛha on alms-round, while wandering for alms in Rājagṛha, saw that gain and honor of such a kind had come to Devadatta: that King Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, born of the Licchavis of Magadha, was coming in the evening with a retinue of some five hundred chariots and paying attendance upon him; that he was offering clusters of food cooked in some five hundred vessels; and that Devadatta, too, was seating some five hundred monks in rows for a meal. We have heard this, Venerable One."

The Blessed One said: "Monks, do not delight in Devadatta's gain and honor. Why is that? Because Devadatta's gain and honor will be his ruin; Devadatta's gain and honor will be his downfall.

"Monks, consider this: just as a plantain tree laden with fruit is ruined and brought down by that very fruit, so too Devadatta's gain and honor will be his ruin, and Devadatta's gain and honor will be his downfall.

"Consider this as well: just as a bamboo shoot and a reed are ruined and brought down by their fruit when they bear it, so too Devadatta's gain and honor will be his ruin, and Devadatta's gain and honor will be his downfall.

"Consider this further: just as a she-mule, when carrying the young within her womb, is ruined and brought down by that which she carries, so too Devadatta's gain and honor will be his ruin, and Devadatta's gain and honor will be his downfall.

"Monks, for as long as such gain and honor of that kind keep arising for Devadatta, it will be for that foolish man's long-lasting harm, injury, and suffering.

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves as follows: subdue gain and honor; and when gain and honor arise, do not let your minds become thoroughly entangled and abide in them. Monks, you should train yourselves in exactly this way."

The Blessed One had spoken those words, and having spoken them, the Sugata, the Teacher, further declared this:

The plantain is killed by its own fruit;
the bamboo is killed by bearing seed;
the she-mule is killed by what she carries in her womb —
so too is the wicked one killed by honor.

Whatever fame a fool may win
will turn to nothing but his ruin;
it destroys the white virtue of the fool
and brings him crashing down from every height.

Then Devadatta, overwhelmed by gain and honor, his mind utterly addled, was visited by a wicked desire of this sort: "The Blessed One is now elderly, old, and worn; teaching the fourfold assembly — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — must tire him out. If only the Blessed One would entrust the community of monks to me, I would guide the community of monks, and the Blessed One, by applying himself diligently to the practice of dwelling at ease in this very life, would live with far less on his mind."

The very moment he gave rise to this thought, his supernatural powers were utterly lost. Though they were entirely lost, he did not even know that they were lost.

At that time, Kauṇḍinya's son, the venerable monk Moggalla of the Spotted Hair, a hearer of the Blessed One, had lived the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, had cultivated the four divine abodes, had abandoned desire and craving for sense pleasures, and through dwelling long in that cultivation, he had been reborn in the brahma world in accordance with his deeds and station.

At that same time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the great son of Mudgala, was seated in the fearsome forest of Crocodile-Child-Killing Mountain, in the game-haunted wood among the sons of Śuddhodana.

Then Moggalla of the Spotted Hair, from that brahma world, perceived that Devadatta's supernatural powers had been entirely lost. Just as a man of great strength might extend an arm that had been drawn in, or draw in an arm that had been extended, so Moggalla of the Spotted Hair vanished from the brahma world and appeared in the fearsome forest of Crocodile-Child-Killing Mountain among the sons of Śuddhodana, seated before the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Then Moggalla of the Spotted Hair said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, please take note. Devadatta, overwhelmed by gain and honor, his mind utterly addled, has been visited by a wicked desire of this sort: 'The Blessed One is now elderly, old, and worn; teaching the fourfold assembly — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — must tire him out. If only the Blessed One would entrust the community of monks to me; I would then guide the community of monks, and the Blessed One, by applying himself diligently to the practice of dwelling at ease in this very life, would live with far less on his mind.' The very moment he gave rise to this thought, his supernatural powers were entirely lost, and though they were entirely lost, he does not even know that they are lost. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it would be well if you were to go to where the Blessed One is, approach him, and report this matter to the Blessed One in full."

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said nothing in reply to Moggalla of the Spotted Hair and silently consented.

Then Moggalla of the Spotted Hair, having understood from the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana's silence that he had consented, prostrated his head at the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana's two feet and vanished from that very spot.

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, not long after Moggalla of the Spotted Hair had gone, entered into such a meditative absorption that, just as a strong man might stretch out an arm that was bent or draw back an arm that was stretched, so the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana disappeared from the Vulture's Sons and arrived dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka's abode, at Rājagṛha.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived he prostrated his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reported in full to the Blessed One everything that had been spoken in conversation between himself and Moggalla of the Spotted Hair.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One declared to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Son of Maudgala, did Devadatta speak those words only after you had already encompassed his mind with your mind and understood it?" "Venerable sir, it is so. I had already encompassed his mind with my mind and understood it, and it was after that that Moggalla of the Spotted Hair spoke." 

Now, while the Blessed One was speaking these words in conversation with the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Devadatta's companion monks — the four, namely Kokālika, Khaṇḍa the Raven-like, Katamoraka-tiṣya, and Samudradatta — went to where the Blessed One was. The Blessed One saw Devadatta from a great distance. Having seen him, he declared to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Son of Maudgala, Devadatta is coming. Now that fool will proclaim himself a prophet before me — so be silent."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated his head at the Blessed One's two feet and, just as a strong man might stretch out an arm that was bent or draw back an arm that was stretched, so the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana disappeared from the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka's abode, at Rājagṛha, and arrived dwelling among the Vulture's Sons, at the frightening forest on the mountain where the young crocodiles are slain, in the deer park. He entered into such a meditative absorption.

Then Devadatta went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived he prostrated his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Devadatta addressed the Blessed One thus: "At present the Blessed One is old, aged, and worn. Since teaching all four assemblies — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — is a burden, it would be well if the Blessed One were to hand the community of monks over to me. I shall lead the community of monks in full, and the Blessed One, by applying himself to the practice of dwelling at ease in this very life, would live with far less on his mind. That fool Śāriputra and —"

— and Maudgalyāyana's son who keeps the holy life — I would not hand over the community of monks even to those two. As for handing it over to you — a spittle-eater, a leftover-licker — hardly!"

Then Devadatta thought to himself: "The Blessed One has praised Śāriputra's son and Maudgalyāyana's son, while calling me a spittle-eater and a leftover-licker — he has acted against me." And from that moment Devadatta harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, along with intolerance and distrust. Then Devadatta said, "Stay," bowed his head three times in dismissal, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

After Devadatta had gone and not long had passed, the Blessed One understood this in his mind and addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather together into the assembly hall every monk who is dwelling nearby in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Wood." The venerable Ānanda replied, "Reverend sir, I hear and obey," and having assembled into the assembly hall every monk who was dwelling nearby in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Wood, he went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived he prostrated his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Reverend sir, all the monks who are dwelling nearby in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Wood have assembled in the assembly hall and are ready. Blessed One, please consider that the time has now come." Then the Blessed One proceeded to the assembly hall, and having arrived he sat down on the seat that had been prepared at the head of the community of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks thus:

"Monks, these five kinds of teachers exist in the world and appear in existence. What are the five? Here, one kind of teacher, while his own moral discipline is not fully pure, claims: 'My moral discipline is fully pure and without any affliction.' His hearers, knowing this teacher to be wise through long association with him, come to know that he claims his moral discipline to be fully pure and without any affliction even though it is not so. Yet they think: 'If we were to tell others about this teacher, it would displease him; and what would we gain by displeasing him and thereby acting against the teacher? This wise teacher knows himself as he is.' And they think: 'He is sustaining us with robes, alms-food, lodging, and the requisites for illness and medicine.' So the hearers are minded to protect him in the matter of moral discipline as well. Such a teacher expects his hearers to protect him with respect to moral discipline. This is the first kind of teacher who exists in the world and appears in existence.

"Furthermore, here another kind of teacher, while his livelihood is not fully pure, claims: 'My livelihood is fully pure and without any affliction.'

Regarding that teacher, the hearers, through their close association with him, come to know: 'This wise teacher, even though his livelihood is not fully pure, claims: "My livelihood is fully pure and without any affliction." Yet if we were to speak of this teacher's failing to others, he would be displeased with us. And what use is it for someone whose displeasure makes him act badly toward his teacher? This wise teacher knows himself as he is.' And they think: 'He is sustaining us with robes, alms-food, lodging, and the requisites for illness and medicine.' So the hearers are minded to protect him in the matter of livelihood as well. Such a teacher expects his hearers to protect him with respect to livelihood. This is the second kind of teacher who exists in the world and appears in existence.

Furthermore, here another kind of teacher, while his knowledge and vision are not fully pure, claims: 'My knowledge and vision are fully pure and without any affliction.' Regarding that teacher, the hearers, through their close association with him, come to know: 'This wise teacher, even though his knowledge and vision are not fully pure, claims: "My knowledge and vision are fully pure and without any affliction." Yet if we were to speak of this teacher's failing to others, he would be displeased with us. And what use is it for someone whose displeasure makes him act badly toward his teacher? This wise teacher knows himself as he is.' And they think: 'He is sustaining us with robes, alms-food, lodging, and the requisites for illness and medicine.' So the hearers are minded to protect him in the matter of knowledge and vision as well. Such a teacher expects his hearers to protect him with respect to knowledge and vision. This is the third kind of teacher who exists in the world and appears in existence.

Furthermore, here another kind of teacher, while his skill in exposition is not excellent, claims: 'My skill in exposition is excellent and without any affliction.' Regarding that teacher, the hearers, through their close association with him, come to know: 'This wise teacher, even though his skill in exposition is not excellent, claims: "My skill in exposition is excellent and without any affliction." Yet if we were to speak of this teacher's failing to others, he would be displeased with us. And what use is it for someone whose displeasure makes him act badly toward his teacher? This wise teacher knows himself as he is.' And they think: 'He is sustaining us with robes, alms-food, lodging, and the requisites for illness and medicine.' So the hearers are minded to protect him in the matter of skill in exposition as well. Such a teacher expects his hearers to protect him with respect to skill in exposition. This is the fourth kind of teacher who exists in the world and appears in existence.

Furthermore, here another kind of teacher, while he possesses a Dharma and Vinaya that is poorly expounded, claims: 'I possess a Dharma and Vinaya that is well expounded and without any affliction.' Regarding that teacher, the hearers, through their close association with him, come to know: 'This wise teacher, even though he possesses a Dharma and Vinaya that is poorly expounded, claims: "I possess a Dharma and Vinaya that is well expounded and without any affliction." Yet if we were to speak of this teacher's failing to others,

he would be displeased by it, and so they think: 'What is the use of going to this teacher and causing him displeasure through that very displeasure? This wise teacher knows only what he himself knows. He thinks of us like this: in terms of robes, alms-food, lodging, care in sickness, and medicinal requisites.' And so the hearers resolve to protect and guard him through the door of the Dharma and Vinaya as well expounded. Such a teacher expects the hearers to guard what is well expounded in the Dharma and Vinaya. This is the fifth kind of teacher who exists in the world and appears in existence.

O monks, I declare: 'I alone am one whose moral discipline is perfectly pure; my moral discipline is perfectly pure and utterly without affliction.' I do not think that the hearers should guard me through the door of moral discipline, nor do I expect the hearers to guard what pertains to moral discipline.
