O monks, I declare: 'I alone am one whose livelihood is perfectly pure; my livelihood is perfectly pure and utterly without affliction.' I do not think that the hearers should guard me through the door of livelihood, nor do I expect the hearers to guard what pertains to livelihood.

O monks, I declare: 'I alone am one whose knowledge and vision are perfectly pure; my knowledge and vision are perfectly pure and utterly without affliction.' I do not think that the hearers should guard me through the door of knowledge and vision, nor do I expect the hearers to guard what pertains to knowledge and vision.

O monks, I declare: 'I alone am one of excellent instruction; my instruction is excellent and utterly without affliction.' I do not think that the hearers should guard me through the door of excellent instruction, nor do I expect the hearers to guard what pertains to excellent instruction.

O monks, I declare: 'I alone possess a Dharma and Vinaya that is well expounded; my Dharma and Vinaya is well expounded and utterly without affliction.' I do not think that the hearers should guard me through the door of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, nor do I expect the hearers to guard what is well expounded in the Dharma and Vinaya.

O monks, I speak to you having cut through and cut through again, having overpowered and overpowered again. I do not hold you as worthless. Like a potter setting down unfired vessels, I place whatever is essential there. Bear with the paths of my words.

Then Devadatta said to Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyā, Kaṭamorakātiyā, and Samudradatta: 'Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyā, Kaṭamorakātiyā, Samudradatta — come here. While the ascetic Gautama sits by, let us divide the harmonious Saṅgha of hearers and break the wheel as well. If we do so, then after we have died, when the time comes, a great and widely renowned sound of praise will spread in all directions and in all quarters, declaring: "Even though the ascetic Gautama was possessed of such great miraculous power and such great might, Devadatta, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyā, Kaṭamorakātiyā, and Samudradatta divided the harmonious Saṅgha of hearers and broke the wheel."'

Devadatta replied: 'We are not able to do this. Why? Because the hearers of the Blessed One are possessed of great power, great miraculous ability, and the divine eye.

Those who have knowledge of others' minds can see from a great distance, and though someone sits right beside them they may not perceive it that way — yet those knowers will pervade our minds with their own minds, and through their mental consciousness they will come to know us. And so they will come to know our very intentions. Kokālika replied: 'There is one method, however.' Devadatta asked: 'What is that method?' Kokālika answered: 'Come here, and let us go to the elder monks, the venerable ones among our community of monks. Let us ask the elders to regard us with a little kindness, and let us attend upon all the elders with all manner of requisites, saying: "We will relieve you of all concern about every requisite." For the young monks, let us serve and honor them with alms bowl, robe, net, small bowl, belt, the recitation of texts, the reading of texts, the chanting of texts, yoga, and mental application, and let us remain with them in that way.' Devadatta replied: 'If there is such a method as this, let it be done so.'

Then Devadatta began to intrigue with the intention of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. The elder monks of the community immediately came to know: 'Devadatta is intriguing with the intention of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha.' The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, go and admonish Devadatta and anyone else of that kind. Admonish them with these words: "Venerable Devadatta, do not intrigue with the intention of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not take up a dispute that would cause division and cling to it and persist in it. Venerable Devadatta, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha that is harmonious, undivided, rejoicing together, without strife, is most excellent — reciting with one voice, blended together like water and milk — and if it illumines the teaching of the Teacher, you will dwell in contact with happiness. Venerable Devadatta, give up this kind of basis for dividing the Saṅgha." Go and admonish him thus.'

The monks replied: 'As you command, Venerable One,' and having heard the Blessed One, they went to Devadatta and admonished him: 'Venerable Devadatta, do not intrigue with the intention of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not take up a dispute that would cause division and cling to it and persist in it. Venerable Devadatta, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha that is harmonious, undivided, rejoicing together, without strife, is most excellent — reciting with one voice, blended together like water and milk — and if it illumines the teaching of the Teacher, you will dwell in contact with happiness. Venerable Devadatta, give up this kind of basis for dividing the Saṅgha.' They went and admonished him thus.

But though the monks admonished him, he stubbornly clung to that very basis, held to it tenaciously, became attached to it, and continued to assert: 'This alone is the truth; everything else is false.' The monks then reported all of this in full to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: 'Monks, you should admonish Devadatta and anyone else of that kind with a formal act performed through a motion and three announcements. Admonish him in this way: having prepared the seats and struck the wooden signal board, and having properly informed all the monks with the words of inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, one monk shall make the motion and perform the formal act. Let the noble members of the Saṅgha hear. This monk Devadatta has intrigued with the intention of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha —'

— having fully taken up and firmly grasped the dispute that would cause division, and having come forward. Even though many monks admonish him in this matter, even when admonished by many monks in this matter, he tenaciously and supremely grasps at that very position, clings to it, and declares in its regard: "This alone is true; everything else is false." If it suits the moment and is acceptable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant permission. Let the Saṅgha admonish the venerable Devadatta: "Venerable Devadatta, do not intrigue for the purpose of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not sit having fully taken up and firmly grasped the dispute that would cause division. Venerable Devadatta, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha, undivided and harmonious, joyful on all sides, without dispute, one in recitation, blended together like water and milk — if it illumines the teaching of the Teacher, it will abide in the touch of well-being. Venerable Devadatta, abandon this ground of a kind that divides the Saṅgha." This is the motion. The formal act is to be performed as follows.

Let the noble members of the Saṅgha hear. This monk Devadatta, having intrigued for the purpose of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha, has fully taken up and firmly grasped the dispute that would cause division, and has come forward. Even though many monks admonish him in this matter, even when admonished by many monks in this matter, he tenaciously and supremely grasps at that very position, clings to it, and declares: "This alone is true; everything else is false." Therefore, let the Saṅgha admonish Devadatta: "Venerable Devadatta, do not intrigue for the purpose of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not sit having fully taken up and firmly grasped the dispute that would cause division. Venerable Devadatta, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha, undivided and harmonious, joyful on all sides, without dispute, one in recitation, blended together like water and milk — if it illumines the teaching of the Teacher, it will abide in the touch of well-being. Venerable Devadatta, abandon this ground of a kind that divides the Saṅgha." Let the Saṅgha perform the formal act of admonishing Devadatta through a motion and three announcements. Those among the venerable ones who accept and approve of performing the formal act of admonishing Devadatta through a motion and three announcements — let them remain silent. Those who do not accept — let them speak. This is the first announcement of the formal act. In the same way it is repeated a second and a third time.

The Saṅgha has accepted and approved, and the Saṅgha has performed the formal act of admonishing Devadatta through a motion and three announcements. Since no one has spoken, it is accordingly upheld. The monks, having heard from the Blessed One, replied: "Venerable one, we shall act in accordance with your command," and performed the formal act of admonishing Devadatta through a motion and three announcements. Even when admonished through a motion and three announcements, he tenaciously and supremely grasped at that very position, clung to it, and declared: "This alone is true; everything else is false."

Now the four monks who were his accomplices, who followed after him and spoke in his support — Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyāputra, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — said this to the monks: "Venerable ones, whether it be virtue or non-virtue, say nothing whatsoever against this monk. For why is this? Venerable ones, this monk speaks the Dharma; this monk speaks the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and Vinaya and so declares accordingly. This monk speaks with full awareness."

— for he does not speak in ignorance. Whatever this monk approves and accepts, we too approve and accept." This is what they had been saying. At that point the monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, summon Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyāputra, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata, and anyone else of that same kind, and deliver this message to them:

'Venerable Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyāputra, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — you are knowingly acting as companions to a monk who, with full awareness, is undermining the Saṅgha for the sake of dividing it, and who, having taken up and firmly grasped a dispute that leads to schism, remains fixed in that position. Do not align yourselves with him or speak in opposition to the Saṅgha. And do not say to the monks: "Venerable ones, whether it be virtue or non-virtue, say nothing whatsoever against this monk — for this monk speaks the Dharma, this monk speaks the Vinaya; this monk, having fully taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and Vinaya, declares accordingly; this monk speaks with full awareness, not in ignorance; whatever this monk approves and accepts, we too approve and accept." For why is this? Venerable ones, this monk does not speak the Dharma; this monk does not speak the Vinaya. Rather, venerable ones, this monk speaks what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Vinaya. This monk, having fully taken up and firmly grasped what is not the Dharma and not the Vinaya, declares accordingly. This monk speaks in ignorance, not with awareness. Therefore, venerable ones, do not approve and accept what this monk approves and accepts.

Venerable ones, do not seek to divide the Saṅgha; rather, venerable ones, seek harmony in the Saṅgha. Venerable ones, be of one accord with the Saṅgha. A Saṅgha that is harmonious, not divided, rejoices together, does not quarrel, recites with one voice, lives blended as one like water and milk, and illuminates the Teacher's teaching — such a Saṅgha abides in contact with happiness. Venerable ones, abandon this course of aligning with those who speak in opposition and who support the division of the Saṅgha.'"

The monks replied: "Reverend sir, as you command," and having heard the Blessed One, they went to the four monks — Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyāputra, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — who were acting as companions to the schismatic monk and speaking in his support, and said this to them:

"Venerable ones, you are knowingly acting as companions to a monk who, with full awareness, is undermining the Saṅgha for the sake of dividing it, and who, having taken up and firmly grasped a dispute that leads to schism, remains fixed in that position. Do not align yourselves with him or speak in opposition. Do not say to the monks: 'Venerable ones, whether it be virtue or non-virtue, say nothing whatsoever against this monk,' — for why? Venerable ones, this monk does not speak the Dharma; this monk does not speak the Vinaya. Rather, venerable ones, this monk speaks what is not the Dharma

and speaks what is not the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped what is not the Dharma and what is not the Vinaya, and applies designations accordingly. This monk speaks in ignorance, not in knowledge. Therefore, venerable ones, do not desire and consent to what this monk desires and consents to. Venerable ones, do not wish to divide the Saṅgha; rather, venerable ones, wish for the Saṅgha to be in harmony. Venerable ones, be in accord with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha in harmony, undivided, rejoicing together, without quarrel — like a single recitation recited in unison, like water and milk blended into one — will, by making the teaching of the Teacher shine clearly, come to dwell in the touch of happiness. Venerable ones, instruct and admonish those who side with the dividers of the Saṅgha and who speak in opposition, saying: Abandon this conduct of siding with those who divide the Saṅgha and speaking in opposition.

When the monks had gently admonished them in this way, those monks nonetheless forcefully seized that very same position, clung to it with attachment, and continued to apply their designations, saying: "This alone is true; everything else is false." At that point, the monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

Monks, you should admonish Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviya, Kaṭamorakatissaka, and Samuddadatta, and others of that kind, by means of the formal act of admonishment with the triple request. The admonishment is to be carried out thus: having arranged the seats, having sounded the wooden signal board, having duly instructed the monks with the proper words of inquiry, with the entire Saṅgha assembled and in harmony, one monk shall make the formal motion and perform the act.

May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. These monks — Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviya, Kaṭamorakatissaka, and Samuddadatta — have fully taken up and firmly grasped a dispute that will lead them to undermine and divide the harmony of the Saṅgha, and they act as companions to the one who holds it, speaking in opposition. When the monks gently admonished them, though admonished by the monks, they still forcefully seized that very same position, clung to it with attachment, and continued to apply their designations, saying: "This alone is true; everything else is false." If it seems to the Saṅgha that the time is right and that it consents, the Saṅgha should approve. The Saṅgha hereby admonishes the monks Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviya, Kaṭamorakatissaka, and Samuddadatta:

Venerable ones, knowingly do not act as companions to, and do not speak in opposition alongside, a monk who, with full awareness, takes up and firmly grasps a dispute that leads to undermining and dividing the harmony of the Saṅgha. Do not say to the monks: "Venerable ones, whether it be virtue or non-virtue, say nothing whatsoever against this monk" — for why? Venerable ones, this monk speaks the Dharma; this monk speaks the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and the Vinaya, and applies designations accordingly. This monk speaks knowingly, not in ignorance. Therefore, venerable ones, do not say: "We too desire and consent to what this monk desires and consents to" — for why? Venerable ones, this monk does not speak the Dharma; this monk does not speak the Vinaya. Rather, venerable ones, this monk speaks what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped what is not the Dharma and

what is not the Vinaya, and applies designations accordingly. This monk speaks in ignorance, not in knowledge. Therefore, venerable ones, do not desire and consent to what this monk desires and consents to. Venerable ones, do not wish to divide the Saṅgha; rather, venerable ones, wish only for the harmony of the Saṅgha. Venerable ones, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha, undivided and harmonious, rejoices together without dispute, with one recitation and one accord, blended together like water and milk. If you illuminate the teaching of the Teacher, you will abide in contact with happiness. Venerable ones, abandon this — this siding with those who would divide the Saṅgha and speaking in discord." Such was the motion, and the act was carried out by the formal procedure of motion-and-three-announcements.

This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows: "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeva, Kaṭamorakatīṣya, and Samudradatta — these monks, supporting one who has fully taken up and firmly grasped a dispute by which he would corrupt and divide the harmonious Saṅgha, and speaking in discord — the monks have admonished them and given them formal instruction. Even though they have been admonished and given formal instruction by the monks, they still stubbornly cling to and are attached to that very same position, and they apply the designation: 'This alone is true; anything else is false.' Therefore the Saṅgha, addressing Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeva, Kaṭamorakatīṣya, and Samudradatta: 'Venerable ones, you, knowingly, are supporting one who has fully taken up and firmly grasped a dispute by which he would corrupt and divide the harmonious Saṅgha, and you are siding with one who speaks in discord — do not do this. And do not say to the monks: "Venerable ones, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, say nothing at all against this monk." For why? Venerable ones, this monk speaks the Dharma; this monk speaks the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and the Vinaya, and applies designations accordingly. This monk speaks in knowledge, not in ignorance. Therefore do not say: 'We too desire and consent to what this monk desires and consents to.' For why? Venerable ones, this monk does not speak the Dharma; this monk does not speak the Vinaya. Rather, venerable ones, this monk speaks what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Vinaya. This monk has fully taken up and firmly grasped what is not the Dharma and what is not the Vinaya, and applies designations accordingly. This monk speaks in ignorance, not in knowledge. Therefore, venerable ones, do not desire and consent to what this monk desires and consents to. Venerable ones, do not wish to divide the Saṅgha; rather, venerable ones, wish only for the harmony of the Saṅgha. Venerable ones, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha, undivided and harmonious, rejoices together without dispute, with one recitation and one accord, blended together like water and milk. If you illuminate the teaching of the Teacher, you will abide in contact with happiness. Venerable ones, abandon this — this siding with those who would divide the Saṅgha and speaking in discord." If such formal instruction is given by motion-and-three-announcements,

Those venerable ones — Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — who consent to the formal instruction given to them by motion-and-three-announcements should say nothing. Those who do not consent should speak. This is the first recitation of the motion. In the same way it is recited a second and a third time. The Saṅgha, having consented and agreed, hereby gives formal instruction to Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata by motion-and-three-announcements. Since no one speaks, it is accordingly thus accepted.

The monks, having heard from the Blessed One, said, "Venerable ones, we ask that you follow the instruction," and gave formal instruction to Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata by motion-and-three-announcements. Even though they were given that formal instruction by motion-and-three-announcements, those four seized even more tightly upon that very same position, clung to it with attachment, and continued to designate it, saying, "This alone is true; all else is false." Thereupon the monks reported this in full to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, Devadatta is capable of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha of my śrāvakas and of turning the wheel of schism — for there are these four monks who side with the one who speaks in discord, who are his companions and allies: Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata."

Then Devadatta heard it said: "The ascetic Gautama has declared to the monks that Devadatta is capable of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha of his śrāvakas and of turning the wheel of schism — for there are these four monks who side with the one who speaks in discord, who are his companions: Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — and has thus prophesied concerning me." Having heard this, Devadatta said to Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata: "Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata — know this! The ascetic Gautama has prophesied concerning me, saying that Devadatta is capable of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha of his śrāvakas and of turning the wheel of schism — for there are these four monks who side with the one who speaks in discord, who are his companions: Kokālika, Khaṇḍadevi, Kaṭamorakatisya, and Samudradata."

They replied, "Devadatta, if that is so, then excellent!" And as he then set about earnestly striving to divide the Saṅgha on a wide scale, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, regarding this occurrence, this ground, and this occasion, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, said to Devadatta: "Devadatta, is it true that you have taken up and firmly held to a dispute aimed at dividing the harmonious Saṅgha, and are sitting set upon causing a schism?"

"Venerable one, it is not so."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, then censured him, saying that what is not the conduct of an ascetic, what is not in accord, what is not proper, what does not accord with the rules — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth, and so forth — the censure being as before.

Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing the ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, if any monk, for the purpose of dividing the harmonious Saṅgha, strives to cause a schism, and sits having fully taken up and firmly holding to a dispute aimed at causing division, the monks are to address that monk, saying: 'Venerable one, do not strive to divide the harmonious Saṅgha. Do not sit having fully taken up and firmly held to a dispute aimed at causing division. Venerable one, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. Let the Saṅgha be undivided; rejoice together, without dispute; be as one in recitation, blended as water and milk are blended. Illuminating the Teacher's teaching, dwell in the touch of ease. Venerable one, abandon this very ground that would cause division in the Saṅgha.' That monk is to be instructed in these words by the monks.

If, when the monks so instruct him, he abandons that ground, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, he is to be instructed and admonished a second time and a third time for the sake of his abandoning that ground. If, when instructed and admonished a second and third time, he abandons that ground, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, the matter rests with the Saṅgha."

Now, "any monk" refers to Devadatta or anyone else of that kind. "Saṅgha" refers to the Tathāgata's Saṅgha of hearers. "Harmonious" means of one flavor. "For the purpose of division" means for the purpose of making two. "Strives" means makes effort. "Sitting having fully taken up and firmly holding to a dispute aimed at causing division" refers to Kokālika, Khaṇḍadeviyāputra, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta sitting having fully taken up and firmly held to such a dispute.

"That monk" refers to Devadatta. "The monks" refers to those of this teaching. "Saying these words" means that, having gathered, they are to instruct him with the words of instruction as shown before. "When the monks so instruct that monk" means having gathered and instructed him. "If he abandons that ground" means if he fully relinquishes that view. "So much the better" means that would be good. "If he does not abandon it" means if he does not fully relinquish it.

"To be instructed and admonished a second time and a third time" means by the motion-and-three-proclamations act, the instruction is given as shown before. "The instruction" is just that, and "the admonishment" is just that.

"The matter rests with the Saṅgha" means, as before, that this transgression depends on the Saṅgha, and therefore it is said "the matter rests with the Saṅgha."

How does the transgression come about? To whatever small degree a monk strives to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, it becomes an offense throughout. When the monks, having gathered, give instruction, if he abandons that ground, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, there is a grave offense. When instruction is given by the motion-and-three-proclamations act, if he abandons that ground, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, at the conclusion of the motion there is a grave offense. When the first proclamation of the act is being uttered, if he abandons that ground before its completion, so much the better.

If he does not abandon it, at the completion of the first proclamation there is a grave offense. When the second proclamation of the act is being uttered, if he abandons that ground before its completion, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, at the completion of that proclamation there is a grave offense. When the third proclamation of the act is being uttered, if he abandons that ground before its completion, so much the better. If he does not abandon it, there is a grave offense. At the completion of the proclamation, if the instruction is given in a harmonious manner yet contrary to the Dharma, there is no transgression. If the instruction is given in a discordant manner yet in accordance with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If the instruction is given in a harmonious manner and in conformity with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If the instruction is given in a discordant manner and contrary to the Dharma, there is no transgression. If one does not give instruction in accordance with what the Dharma is, what the Vinaya is, and what the Teacher's teaching is, there is no transgression. If, when the proclamation is complete, one does give instruction in harmony and in accordance with what the Dharma is, what the Vinaya is, and what the Teacher's teaching is, the monk incurs a Saṅgha remainder offense. That monk, while remaining seated in that place, must then say the following: "Venerable ones, I have incurred a Saṅgha remainder offense." If he speaks thus, so much the better. If he does not speak thus, from that point onward he will incur the offense of concealment. Therefore, for as long as a monk performs the motion-and-one-proclamation act, the motion-and-two-proclamations act, or the motion-and-four-proclamations act without having confessed and individually confessed that ground, it becomes an offense in every instance. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by pain. This concludes the tenth Saṅgha remainder offense of causing a schism in the Saṅgha.

Then the Blessed One, while remaining on that very seat, wishing to establish the second rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers, declared to the monks: "Monks, there is a small matter of Saṅgha business; please do not yet rise from your seats." The passage beginning with "The blessed buddhas, knowing yet inquiring" and so forth continues as before.

The blessed Buddha then questioned Kokālika, Khaṇḍadrabya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradata, saying: "Kokālika, Khaṇḍadrabya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, Samudradata — you knowingly befriend and act in concert with that monk who, in order to divide the harmonious Saṅgha, stubbornly persists and has taken up and firmly grasped the cause of schism; and siding with him you speak discordantly, saying to the monks: 'Venerable ones, whether good or bad, say nothing at all against this monk. Why is that? Venerable ones, this monk is one who speaks the Dharma, one who speaks the Vinaya; he has rightly taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he designates things accordingly. This monk speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge. Whatever he wishes and accepts, that we too wish and accept.' Is this true?" "Venerable sir, it is not." The Blessed One then censured those monks with words such as: "This behavior — unbecoming of a monk, discordant, unsuitable, not in keeping with the conduct of one who has gone forth" — and so on, just as before.

Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks:

"Monks, seeing these ten benefits, a rule of training for hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so on, just as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

If there is one monk, or two, or many, who are companions to that monk and who side with his discordant speech, and if those monks say to the other monks: 'Venerable ones, do not say anything to this monk — whether in praise or in blame. Why is that? Venerable ones, this monk is one who speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya. He has rightly taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he designates things accordingly. This monk speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge. Whatever he wishes and accepts, that we too wish and accept' — then the monks are to say to those monks: 'Venerable ones, do not say that this monk is one who speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya, that he has rightly taken up and firmly grasped the Dharma and the Vinaya and designates things accordingly, that he speaks with knowledge and not without knowledge, and that whatever he wishes and accepts, you too wish and accept. Why is that? Venerable ones, this monk is not one who speaks the Dharma; he is not one who speaks the Vinaya. Venerable ones, this monk is one who speaks what is not Dharma and speaks what is not Vinaya. He has rightly taken up and firmly grasped what is not Dharma and what is not Vinaya, and he designates things accordingly. This monk speaks without knowledge, not with knowledge. As for whatever he wishes and accepts — venerable ones, do not wish and accept that. Venerable ones, do not seek to divide the Saṅgha; instead, venerable ones, seek harmony within the Saṅgha. Venerable ones, be in harmony with the Saṅgha. May the Saṅgha be harmonious, undivided, rejoicing together, free of dispute — reciting together with one voice, blended like water and milk — and, illuminating the Teacher's dispensation, may you abide in the touch of happiness. Venerable ones, instruct those monks who thus side with the one who divides the Saṅgha and speak discordantly: Abandon this!' When the monks have given that instruction to those monks, if they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, for the sake of abandoning that ground they are to be instructed a second and a third time, and admonished properly. If, upon being properly instructed and properly admonished a second and a third time, they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, that is a saṅghāvaśeṣa."

"That monk" refers to Devadatta. "Companion monks" refers to Kokalika, Khaṇḍadeva, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradata. "Siding with his discordant speech" means holding those same views, those same wishes, and those same intentions. "One, or two, or many" — more than two is many. "If those" refers to those who thus side with him. "The monks" refers to those who follow this Dharma. "Saying thus" means speaking in those words. "Whether in praise" means: do not even engage in what is virtuous.

"Whether it is a misdeed" means: do not even turn him away from a misdeed. "Toward this monk" refers to Devadatta. "Say nothing at all" means: do not say even a word.

Why so? "Venerable ones, this monk speaks the Dharma, this monk speaks the Vinaya; this monk has properly taken up the Dharma and the Vinaya, has embraced it, and continues to apply those designations accordingly" — this means he applies those designations in accordance with what the Dharma actually is, in accordance with what the Vinaya actually is, and in accordance with what the Teacher's teaching actually is. "This monk speaks knowingly, not unknowingly" means he does so having understood the meaning, not without having understood it. "That which this monk approves and accepts, we too approve and accept" — if one says that, it means: whatever grounds Devadatta approves of, we too approve of.

"Those monks" refers to Kokalika, Khaṇḍadeva, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradata. "The monks" refers to those who follow this Dharma. "Saying thus" means: having assembled and admonished them, the admonishment is to be given as was shown before. "When the monks have thus admonished those monks" means: having assembled and given the admonishment. "If they abandon that ground" means: if they relinquish that view. "Well and good" means: in that case it is good. "If they do not abandon it" means: if they do not relinquish it. "They are to be admonished a second and a third time, properly instructed" — this means the admonishment is to be given by means of the motion-and-three-proclamations act, as was shown before. The proper admonishment is precisely that, and the proper instruction is precisely that. "A saṅghāvaśeṣa" — as before, that offense depends upon the Saṅgha, and therefore it is called a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

Now, how does it become an offense? To whatever degree a monk sides with and supports one who has taken up a dispute and holds to it — a dispute that will weaken and divide a harmonious Saṅgha — and who speaks discordant words, in all such cases it becomes a wrongdoing.

If, when a monk has assembled and admonished them, they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, it becomes a grave offense. If they are admonished by the motion-and-three-proclamations act and they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, then at the conclusion of the motion it becomes a grave offense. If, while the first proclamation is being recited and it is not yet complete, they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, at the completion of that recitation it becomes a grave offense. If, while the second proclamation is being recited and it is not yet complete, they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, at the completion of that recitation it becomes a grave offense. If, while the third proclamation is being recited and it is not yet complete, they abandon that ground, well and good. If they do not abandon it, it becomes a grave offense.

If, at the time of the completed recitation, one admonishes them in a concordant manner but contrary to the Dharma, there is no downfall. If one admonishes them in a discordant manner but according to the Dharma, there is no downfall. If one admonishes them in a concordant manner but altered from what is proper, there is no downfall. If one admonishes them in a discordant manner and in a manner altered from what is proper, there is no downfall. If one does not admonish them in accordance with what the Dharma actually is, in accordance with what the Vinaya actually is, and in accordance with what the Teacher's teaching actually is, there is no downfall. If one admonishes them in a concordant manner, in accordance with what the Dharma actually is, in accordance with what the Vinaya actually is, and in accordance with what the Teacher's teaching actually is, then at the completion of the recitation it becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

That monk, while remaining seated on his seat, should declare the following: "Venerable ones, a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression has arisen for me." If he makes that declaration, well and good. If he does not make it, from that point onward a transgression of concealment will arise for him. Therefore, for as long as that monk has not confessed that basis and has not confessed it individually, and continues to act under motions of one, two, and four — performing all of those — it will become a grave offense in all cases. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no downfall. The eleventh saṅghāvaśeṣa, that of the faction, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there were at Reḷe Hill monks who were swift in movement, and together with them Nabso and a reddish-yellow-robed monk who brought disgrace upon households and who engaged in every manner of evil conduct. They consorted intimately with women in their domain. They played with them everywhere. They chattered and made noise in their company. They laughed uproariously, they were arrogant, and they contorted their bodies. They sat together on a single seat. They ate from a single vessel. They drank various intoxicating beverages that made them drunk from a single cup. They gathered flowers and caused others to gather them. They threaded garlands and caused others to thread them. They wore garlands and caused others to wear them. They wore floral ear ornaments and caused others to wear them. They danced and caused others to dance. They sang and caused others to sing. They played musical instruments and caused others to play them. To those skilled in dancing, skilled in singing, and skilled in playing instruments they gave donations drawn from their own shares. They cast off their robes and ran. They leapt. They jumped high. They circled with their thighs. They whirled their arms. They circled like fish. They hurled themselves diving into water. They beat the water with their hands like crocodiles beating their tails. They made the sound of an elephant's cry. They made the sound of a horse's cry. They made the sound of a bull's cry. They made the sound of a peacock's cry. They made the sound of a cuckoo's cry. They made the sound of a clay drum. They made the sound of a conch shell. They made the sound of a great drum. They imitated elephants and caused others to imitate elephants. They imitated horses, they imitated bulls, they imitated buffaloes, they imitated goats, they imitated sheep, they imitated women, they imitated men, they imitated boys, they imitated girls, they imitated crows, they imitated pigeons, and they imitated mynah birds. They caused others to imitate all of these as well. They themselves performed and caused others to perform these and yet other actions that were not proper conduct for monks. Their mode of conduct, their behavior, and their corrupt practices caused monks who had not yet come to Reḷe Hill not to come, and those who had come to be displeased and to abandon their residence on Reḷe Hill. The brahmins and householders living on Reḷe Hill, having become displeased and disgusted, found it difficult even to think of giving alms and rendering service to the resident monks who were the established community there — to say nothing of those who had arrived from elsewhere. Then, at some later time, the venerable Ānanda, while wandering on tour through the districts of Kāśika, came to Reḷe Hill and sat in the forest of Reḷe Hill.

Then the venerable Ānanda, in the morning, having dressed, took up his bowl and robe and entered Reḷe Hill for alms. And just as he had entered Reḷe Hill for alms with only his washed bowl, so too he departed with only his washed bowl — without receiving so much as a single ladle of alms, and without being invited back. Then the venerable Ānanda thought to himself: "In former times this Reḷe Hill was prosperous, flourishing, comfortable, well-provisioned, populous, and full of people — so much so that even a beggar could easily find alms here. Even now this Reḷe Hill is prosperous, flourishing, comfortable, well-provisioned, populous, and full of people. Yet I have entered Reḷe Hill for alms with only my washed bowl, and I depart with only my washed bowl — without receiving so much as a single ladle of alms, and without being invited back. Can it be that some foolish, dull, unclear, and unskilled śrāvakas of the Blessed One, overcome by afflictions, have been speaking indecently to, making lewd overtures to, or touching the women of good family or the young girls of good family in their alms-round territory, the villages of their alms-round territory?"

At that time, some five hundred brahmins and householders of Reḷe Hill were gathered together in their assembly hall for some matter. Then the venerable Ānanda went to the assembly hall of the brahmins and householders of Reḷe Hill, and upon arriving he addressed the brahmins and householders of Reḷe Hill in these words: "Learned ones, in former times this Reḷe Hill was prosperous, flourishing, comfortable, well-provisioned, populous, and full of people — so much so that even a beggar could easily find alms here. Even now this Reḷe Hill is prosperous, flourishing, comfortable, well-provisioned, populous, and full of people. Yet I have entered Reḷe Hill for alms with only my washed bowl, and I have departed with only my washed bowl — without receiving so much as a single ladle of alms, and without being invited back."

When he had spoken these words, the brahmins and householders of Reḷe Hill composed their senses and became attentive. At that time the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Śrotasrota was also present there in that assembly. Then the lay practitioner Śrotasrota took the venerable Ānanda by both hands, led him aside, and said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, please take note. On this Reḷe Hill there are monks who are swift-footed and who loiter about, reddish-yellow monks who bring disgrace upon households and engage in all manner of wicked practices. They keep close company with women, playing and cavorting with them, raising a clamor and din, strutting about and acting arrogantly, presenting themselves in the same seat, begging from the same vessel, drinking various intoxicating drinks from the same cup until they are drunk, picking flowers and giving flowers to be picked, wearing garlands and giving garlands to be worn, wearing floral ear-ornaments and giving them to be worn, playing drums and having drums played for them, dancing —

making music, causing music to be made, giving gifts to skilled dancers, skilled singers, and skilled musicians out of face-saving obligation, exchanging their robes and running about, leaping, jumping high, spinning on their haunches, spinning on their hands, spinning like fish, hurling themselves into the water, beating the water like a small drum, beating the water like a large drum, making the cry of an elephant, making the cry of a horse, making the cry of a bull, making the cry of a peacock, making the cry of a cuckoo, imitating the sound of clay drums, imitating the sound of conch shells, imitating the sound of large drums, performing elephant fights, causing elephant fights to be performed, and likewise performing horse fights, bull fights, buffalo fights, goat fights, sheep fights, women's fights, men's fights, boys' fights, girls' fights, cock fights, quail fights, and pheasant fights, and causing all of these to be performed as well. These and other activities unbecoming of a contemplative they themselves do, and they cause others to do them.

By their manner of conduct, their behavior, and their wrongful practice, those nuns who were not at Ṛleḍiri have not come there, and those who had been there become displeased and abandon the place of Ṛleḍiri. The brahmins and householders living at Ṛleḍiri also become displeased and disgusted, and if they already find it difficult to offer alms and to wish to give to the monks who reside there ordinarily, what need is there to say anything about giving to those who have newly arrived? Therefore, Venerable Ānanda, if it is not troublesome for you, please, out of compassion, present this matter at length to the Blessed One.

The Venerable Ānanda accepted the request of the layman Jālinīprabha by remaining silent. Then, understanding that the Venerable Ānanda had accepted by remaining silent, the layman Jālinīprabha said this to the Venerable Ānanda: Venerable Ānanda, would you kindly permit me to offer a single meal at my home? The Venerable Ānanda accepted the request of the layman Jālinīprabha by remaining silent. Then, understanding that the Venerable Ānanda had accepted by remaining silent, the layman Jālinīprabha, with his own hands, satisfied and delighted the Venerable Ānanda as he sat comfortably, with clean and abundant food and drink, and having satisfied and served him with an abundance of clean and ample food and drink with his own hands, and understanding that the Venerable Ānanda had eaten and set down his bowl after washing his hands, he brought a low seat and sat down in front of the Venerable Ānanda in order to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Venerable Ānanda properly taught the layman Jālinīprabha a Dharmic discourse, established him in it properly, properly encouraged him, and properly gladdened him. Having properly taught the Dharmic discourse, properly established him in it, properly encouraged him, and properly gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the twenty-third section.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having tidied up his lodging as he had customarily used it, took up his begging bowl and robe, and set out walking toward Śrāvastī, traveling gradually along the way, and in due course arrived at Śrāvastī.

Then the Venerable Ānanda set down his begging bowl and robe, washed both feet, and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported in full to the Blessed One everything that had been said in conversation together with the layman Jālinīprabha.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One declared to the Venerable Ānanda as follows: "Ānanda, you are to go with the senior monks to Reḷḍe Mountain and carry out the act of censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. It is to be done in this way. Seat yourself along the way, and appoint a monk as spokesman. A monk-spokesman who possesses five qualities is not to be appointed if not yet appointed, and if already appointed is to be removed. What are the five? He goes by desire, he goes by aversion, he goes by delusion, he goes by fear, and he does not know what has been adjudicated and what has not been adjudicated. A monk-spokesman who possesses these five qualities is not to be appointed if not yet appointed, and if already appointed is to be removed.

A monk-spokesman who possesses five qualities is to be appointed if not yet appointed, and if already appointed is not to be removed. What are the five? He does not go by desire, he does not go by aversion, he does not go by delusion, he does not go by fear, and he knows what has been adjudicated and what has not been adjudicated. A monk-spokesman who possesses these five qualities is to be appointed if not yet appointed, and if already appointed is not to be removed.

The appointment is to be made in this way. After the lodgings have been prepared and the gong struck, the monks are to be properly informed with words of inquiry. Then, with the entire Saṅgha assembled and in harmony, the first one who is willing should be encouraged, saying: 'Venerable one of such-and-such a name, you are to go to Reḷḍe Mountain and speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so regarding the many ways in which they have engaged in conduct unbecoming to a contemplative. Are you willing?' If willing, he should say, 'I am willing.'

After that, one monk makes the motion and the act is carried out. The venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear. If the monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name is willing to go to Reḷḍe Mountain and speak against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so regarding the many ways in which they have engaged in conduct unbecoming to a contemplative, and if it is the right time and the Saṅgha approves, may the Saṅgha grant its consent, and may the Saṅgha appoint the monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name to speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows. The venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear. This monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name has gone to Reḷḍe Mountain and is willing to speak against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so regarding the many ways in which they have engaged in conduct unbecoming to a contemplative. Therefore the Saṅgha appoints the monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name to speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. Venerables, those who consent to the Saṅgha appointing the monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name to speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so should remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and granted its approval, and has appointed the monk-spokesman called such-and-such a name to speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. Thus it is held, since no one has spoken."

"Monks, I shall now establish the rules of conduct for the monk-spokesman. The monk-spokesman is to go to the dwelling of those who have harbored grudges, prepare the lodging, strike the gong, and properly address the monks with words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha has assembled and reached agreement, he shall then speak the censure against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. If those monks do not grant their consent, the act of expulsion from the residence shall be carried out against those very individuals on account of their disrespect. If they do grant their consent, they shall be made to open a gap in the proceedings. If they do not open a gap, the act of expulsion from the residence shall likewise be carried out against those very individuals on account of their disrespect. If they do open a gap, then the censure shall be spoken. If they say, 'We do not see a transgression,' the act of expulsion from the residence shall again be carried out against them on account of their disrespect. If they say, 'We do see the transgression,' then the following shall be declared to them: 'For this very reason the Saṅgha has performed against you two the act of expulsion.' If the monk-spokesman, having duly accepted the rules of conduct for a monk-spokesman as established, fails to put them into practice, he will be in a state of serious fault."

The venerable Ānanda, having heard this from the Blessed One and having received the instruction saying, "Venerable one, as the Blessed One has commanded," went together with the elder monks to Mount Relvde and, sitting along the road, appointed the monk-spokesman.

Now the reddish-yellow monks who were acting in concert with the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so heard that the venerable Ānanda had come there together with the elder monks and, sitting along the road, had appointed a monk-spokesman who would perform the act of expulsion against the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so. Upon hearing this, those monks thought to themselves: "There is nothing that these two venerable ones have practiced, said, or undertaken that we ourselves have not also practiced, said, and undertaken. Therefore, if the expulsion is performed against these two, why should it not also be performed against us? When the venerable Ānanda and the elder monks come here and first perform the act of expulsion against Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so, there will then be grounds for the expulsion to be performed against us as well. We had better take up our bedrolls and belongings and, listening carefully and remaining in place, so that when the venerable Ānanda and the elder monks enter through one door, we can take up our bedrolls and go out through another door and make our way to Śrāvastī without missing our chance."

Then the monk-spokesman went to Mount Relvde, prepared the lodging, struck the gong, and properly addressed the monks with words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha had assembled and reached agreement, and the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so had granted their consent and opened a gap in the proceedings, the monk-spokesman spoke the censure. The two then declared: "Venerable one, we see the transgression." The monk-spokesman said: "For this very reason the Saṅgha has performed against you two the act of expulsion."

Then, as the venerable Ānanda and the elder monks entered through one door, the reddish-yellow monks took up their bedrolls, went out through another door, and set off for Śrāvastī. Those among them who had transgressions to confess confessed them, and those who had various forms of mental conceptuality to restrain restrained them in their minds. They came to dwell together with the monks who were living according to the natural rule, and they also continued to protect and uphold the activities of the Saṅgha.

Thereupon the venerable Ānanda and the elder monks addressed the monks Gro-mgyogs and

performed the act of expulsion against the two of them, Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so, and then set out for Śrāvastī, traveling gradually along the way until they arrived at Śrāvastī.

The two monks, Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so, reflected: "Just as one who has been knocked down by the ground must rise up from that very ground, so too we two should go directly to Śrāvastī and ask forgiveness of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." With that, Gro-mgyogs said to Nab-so: "Nab-so, just as one who has been knocked down by the ground must rise up from that very ground, so too we two should go directly to Śrāvastī and ask forgiveness of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. Let us go and do so." Nab-so replied: "There is no fault in it — come, let us go and ask forgiveness." The two of them agreed on this, and when that same night had passed and the early morning came, they put on their lower and upper robes, took up their bowls and dharma robes, and entered the city of Rete for alms. Having completed their alms round in Rete and eaten their meal, they returned from the midday alms round, put away their lodging things as was customary, took up their bowls and dharma robes, set off toward Śrāvastī, traveling gradually along the way, until they arrived at Śrāvastī.

When the elder monks who were residing there saw those two, they neither engaged them in conversation nor greeted them with a welcome. When the reddish-yellow monks saw those two as well, they likewise neither engaged them in conversation nor greeted them with a welcome.

Then the monks Gro-mgyogs and Nab-so said to the reddish-yellow monks: "Venerable ones, it is fitting that the elder monks do not engage us two in conversation or greet us with a welcome. But why do you not engage us two in conversation or greet us with a welcome? What is there that we two have done, said, or undertaken that you have not done, said, or undertaken?"

Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, that is true. Nevertheless, we too have confessed whatever transgressions were to be confessed, and we too have restrained in our minds the various forms of mental conceptuality that were to be restrained. Now we dwell together with the monks who are living according to the natural rule, and we continue to protect and uphold the activities of the Saṅgha. Therefore from this point on we will no longer share in living together with those who engage in inferior conduct."

Then the two of them said to the monks: "Venerable ones, here among the monks there are some who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear — for with regard to precisely similar transgressions, some monks are expelled while others are not expelled." And they began to make this accusation. Then the monks said to those two: "Venerable ones, you two say there are monks who act out of desire, monks who act out of aversion, monks who act out of delusion, and monks who act out of fear? Venerable ones, it is the monk Ānanda and those elder monks who went to Rete Mountain and performed the act of expulsion against us to whom you are saying this." The few monks said: "Why do monks who know full well that it was the monk Ānanda and those elder monks who went to Rete Mountain and performed the act of expulsion against them still say of those monks that they act out of desire, or say they act out of aversion, act out of delusion, or act out of fear? And why do they say to the monks as well these very words: Venerable ones, here among the monks there are some who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear —

and in this way, from one and the same transgression, some monks perform the act of expulsion while others do not" — thus speaking ill of them, spreading word against them, and slandering them. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should summon the monks Drogo and Napso, and others of that kind, and convey to them the following message. The message to be conveyed is this: Venerable Drogo and Napso, do not say of the venerable monk Ānanda and of those elder monks who went to Rete Mountain and performed the act of expulsion against you that they act out of desire. Do not say that they act out of aversion, out of delusion, or out of fear. And do not say to the monks these words: Venerable ones, here among the monks there are some who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear, and in this way, from one and the same transgression, some monks perform the act of expulsion while others do not. And why not? Because those monks do not act out of desire, they do not act out of aversion, they do not act out of delusion, and they do not act out of fear. Rather, it is you yourselves, venerable ones, who are corrupters of households and practitioners of evil conduct. For it is seen, heard, and well known that you yourselves corrupt households, and it is seen, heard, and well known that you engage in evil conduct. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon this kind of language — the phrases 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' and 'acting out of fear.' Let this message be conveyed to them." The monks replied, "As the Venerable One commands, we will obey," and, having heard it from the Blessed One, they conveyed to the monks Drogo and Napso the following: "Venerable Drogo and Napso, do not say of the venerable monk Ānanda and of those elder monks who went to Rete Mountain and performed the act of expulsion against you that they act out of desire. Do not say that they act out of aversion, out of delusion, or out of fear. And do not say to the monks these words: Venerable ones, here among the monks there are some who act out of desire, some who act out of aversion, some who act out of delusion, and some who act out of fear, and in this way, from one and the same transgression, some monks perform the act of expulsion while others do not. And why not? Because those monks do not act out of desire, they do not act out of aversion, they do not act out of delusion, and they do not act out of fear. Rather, it is you yourselves, venerable ones, who are corrupters of households and practitioners of evil conduct. For it is seen, heard, and well known that you yourselves corrupt households, and it is seen, heard, and well known that you engage in evil conduct. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon this kind of language — the phrases 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' and 'acting out of fear.'" This message was thus conveyed to the two of them. Yet those two stubbornly clung to that very same position and, fixing upon it as supreme and remaining firmly attached, continued to designate it with the words: "This alone is true; everything else is false." At that point the monks again reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should summon the monks Drogo and Napso, and others of that kind, and —

"and others of that same kind — should be addressed by means of the formal act of admonition performed with a motion and three readings. The admonition is to be carried out as follows: having arranged the seats and struck the gong, having duly notified the monks with the words of inquiry, and with the entire Saṅgha assembled and in harmony, one monk is to make a motion and then carry out the act. May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. These two monks, Drogo and Napso, went to the venerable Ānanda and to the elders, the various elders at Rede Mountain, and while seeking to have these two expelled, continued to say to them: 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' 'acting out of fear.' And they also said this to the monks: 'Venerable ones, here there are monks who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear — and thus, from one and the same transgression, some monks expel while others do not expel.' The Saṅgha has therefore addressed these two with a formal act carried out by many monks. Yet even after being addressed by many monks with a formal act, these two cling stubbornly to that very same position, fix upon it as supreme, and remain attached to it, continuing to designate it with the words: 'This alone is true; everything else is false.' If the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, then let the Saṅgha approve this: the Saṅgha shall address the two monks Drogo and Napso, telling them — 'Venerable ones Drogo and Napso, you went to the venerable Ānanda and to the elders, the various elders at Rede Mountain, knowing that they had carried out the act of expelling you, and yet you continued to say to them: "acting out of desire," "acting out of aversion," "acting out of delusion," "acting out of fear." And you also said this to the monks: "Venerable ones, here there are monks who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, who act out of fear — and thus, from one and the same transgression, some monks expel while others do not expel." Do not say such things. And why not? Because those monks were not acting out of desire, nor out of aversion, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear. Rather, it is you yourselves, venerable ones, who are household-despoilers, practitioners of wicked conduct — you are seen and heard and well known as despoilers of households, and you are seen and heard and well known as practitioners of wickedness. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon the verbal usage of the phrase "acting out of desire," and abandon the verbal usage of such phrases as "acting out of aversion," "acting out of delusion," and "acting out of fear."' This is the formal admonition performed with a motion and three readings.' This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows: May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. These two monks, Drogo and Napso, went to the venerable Ānanda and to the elders, the various elders at Rede Mountain, and while seeking to have these two expelled, continued to say to them: 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' 'acting out of fear.' And they also said this to the monks: 'Venerable ones, here there are monks who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear — and thus, from one and the same transgression, some monks expel while others do not expel.' —"

Even though many monks had convened and administered the formal act against these two, they tenaciously clung to that very same position, remaining firmly attached to it, and continued to designate it with the words: "This alone is true; everything else is false." For that reason the Saṅgha wishes to convene and administer to the monks Drogo and Napso, with a formal act by petition and three proclamations, the following charge: "Venerable ones Drogo and Napso, do not say to the venerable Ānanda and to those elders — the elders who went to Rede Mountain knowing full well that they had carried out the act of expelling you — 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' or 'acting out of fear.' And do not say to the monks: 'Venerable ones, here there are monks who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear — and thus, from one and the same transgression, some monks expel while others do not expel.' And why is that? Those monks are not acting out of desire, not acting out of aversion, not acting out of delusion, and not acting out of fear. Rather, venerable ones, it is you yourselves who are corruptors of households and practitioners of wicked conduct — you who are seen, heard, and well-known to have corrupted households, and who are seen, heard, and well-known to practice wickedness. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon this kind of verbal path, namely such words as 'acting out of desire,' 'acting out of aversion,' 'acting out of delusion,' and 'acting out of fear.' — This is the first proclamation of the formal act; the same is then recited a second and a third time."

If the Saṅgha approves and grants permission, then the Saṅgha shall administer to the monks Drogo and Napso the formal act by petition and three proclamations. Let those who approve remain silent; let those who do not approve speak. This is the first recitation of the formal act; and likewise it is recited a second and a third time. The Saṅgha has approved and granted this, and the Saṅgha has administered to the monks Drogo and Napso the formal act by petition and three proclamations. Since no one spoke, so it is held to be.

The monks, having heard from the Blessed One, complied with the venerable one's instruction, and administered to the monks Drogo and Napso the formal act by petition and three proclamations. Even after having been given the formal act by petition and three proclamations, they tenaciously clung to that very same position, remaining firmly attached to it, and continued to designate it with the words: "This alone is true; everything else is false." At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this occasion, and in this connection, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, as before. Likewise the passage beginning "Fully awakened Blessed Ones knowingly commit no offense" follows as before.

"My śrāvakas shall recite the following as a rule for training in the Vinaya: If a great number of monks are residing and dwelling near a village or a settlement, and if those monks are corruptors of households and practitioners of wicked conduct, and if it is seen, heard, or well-known that they have corrupted households, or if it is seen, heard, or well-known that they practice wickedness, then the monks shall address those monks as follows: 'Venerable ones, you are corruptors of households and practitioners of wicked conduct; it is seen, heard, and well-known that you have corrupted households,

and it is seen, heard, and well-known that you practice wickedness. Venerable ones, you are welcome to remain here, but you must depart from this place,' and so they shall be addressed.

If those monks then say to the monks: 'Venerable ones, there are some monks here who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, and who act out of fear. From one and the same transgression, some monks expel, while others do not expel' — then the monks shall say to those monks: 'Venerable ones, do not say that the venerable ones here act out of desire, act out of aversion, act out of delusion, or act out of fear, and that from one and the same transgression some monks expel while others do not. Why? Because those monks do not act out of desire, they do not act out of aversion, they do not act out of delusion, they do not act out of fear. Rather, it is because you yourselves, venerable ones, are corruptors of households and practitioners of wicked conduct — it is seen, heard, and well-known that you have corrupted households, and it is seen, heard, and well-known that you practice wickedness. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon this manner of speaking — saying that there are those here who act out of desire, who act out of aversion, who act out of delusion, who act out of fear — and so they shall be addressed.'

When the monks have so addressed those monks, if they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, they shall be properly addressed and properly instructed a second time and a third time, for the purpose of making them relinquish that ground. If, upon being properly addressed and properly instructed two and three times, they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, that is an offense against the Saṅgha.

The term 'monks' refers to those who move quickly, to novices, and to others of similar standing. The term 'a great number' means more than two. 'Near a village or a settlement' means a market town and the like. As for the phrase 'corruptors of households,' 'households' refers to the households of brahmins and householders. They corrupt such households in two ways: through association and through enjoyment. How through association? They sit together with women on the same seat, they eat from the same vessel, and they drink various intoxicating drinks that lead to intoxication from the same cup — that is how it is through association. How through enjoyment? Through food, drink, clothing, flowers, fruit, and tooth-wood — that is how it is through enjoyment. 'Practitioners of wicked conduct' means practicing degraded conduct. 'Those households' means the households of brahmins and householders. 'Seen' means by way of visual consciousness. 'Heard' means by way of auditory consciousness. 'Well-known' means by way of the other groups of consciousness. 'Practicing wickedness' means practicing degraded conduct. 'By the monks' means by those who belong to this Dharma community. 'In this manner' means addressing them with the words exactly as set forth above. 'When the monks have so addressed those monks' means upon addressing them in that manner. 'If they relinquish that ground' means if they completely abandon that view. 'That is good' means that is well and good.

The words "if they do not relinquish it" mean if they do not completely relinquish it. They are to be admonished a second and a third time, properly instructed. The words "to be properly admonished and properly instructed" mean they are to be admonished by means of a formal act (羯磨, karman) with a motion and three proclamations, just as set forth above. That is what "properly admonishing" means. That is what "properly instructing" means.

The words "the matter rests with the Saṅgha" mean, as before, that the transgression depends on the Saṅgha, and therefore it is said "the matter rests with the Saṅgha."

As for how the transgression arises in that connection: if a monk, knowing full well that certain monks have carried out an act of expulsion against him, goes to them out of desire, goes out of aversion, goes out of delusion, or goes out of fear, he incurs a wrongdoing in every case.

When a monk takes it up and admonishes them, if they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, a serious offence arises. When admonishment is given by means of a formal act with a motion and three proclamations, if they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, a serious offence arises upon the motion. When the first proclamation is recited and, before it is completed, they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, a serious offence arises when it is completed. When the second proclamation is recited and, before it is completed, they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, a serious offence arises when it is completed. When the third proclamation is recited and, before it is completed, they relinquish that ground, that is good. If they do not relinquish it, a serious offence arises.

Once the full proclamation has been completed, if the admonishment is carried out in a concordant and non-Dharmic manner, there is no transgression. If it is carried out in a discordant and Dharmic manner, there is no transgression. If it is carried out in a form that accords with what is concordant and Dharmic, there is no transgression. If it is carried out in a form that accords with what is discordant and non-Dharmic, there is no transgression. If one does not admonish in accordance with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the teaching of the Teacher as it is, there is no transgression. If one does admonish in a concordant manner in accordance with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the teaching of the Teacher as it is, and the full proclamation is complete, then the matter rests with the Saṅgha.

While remaining seated in that place, the monk must declare: "Venerable ones, I have incurred a Saṅgha-remainder transgression." If he so declares, that is good. If he does not declare it, from that point onward the offence of concealment will arise for him.

Therefore, as long as that monk has neither confessed nor individually confessed and yet undergoes a motion, a motion with two proclamations, or a formal act with a motion and three proclamations, he incurs a wrongdoing in every case. For one who is a first offender, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

The twelfth, the Saṅgha-remainder concerning a family-defiling monk, is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the Ghositārāma. At that time the venerable Channa incurred a transgression and did not make amends in accordance with the Dharma. The monks who wished his good, wished his benefit, wished his happiness, wished him to touch happiness, and wished his accomplishment and happiness, spoke to him and reminded him, saying: "Venerable Channa, you have incurred those transgressions — make amends in accordance with the Dharma." When reminded in this way, he replied: "To whom should I make amends for that transgression? If you have incurred a transgression, who would make amends, who would feel remorse? If you have incurred a transgression, who among you would feel remorse?" As the monks spoke to him again and again, he responded in the same vein, saying: "Venerable ones, whether you act virtuously or wickedly, do not say anything to me at all."

"Whether I act virtuously or wickedly, I will say nothing to the venerable ones. Let the venerable ones find a different path of speech toward me. What good would it do if I spoke to you? For you have all gone forth from various castes, various clans, and various households. It is just like the many leaves of various trees that the wind blows together, gathering in one place and resting in one place — in exactly the same way, you too have gone forth from various castes, various clans, and various households. But as for me, awakening has been realized by my noble one." Saying, "Why do monks of lesser aims, when monks speak in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya on the bases of training that fall under what monks are to recite, and on what falls within the sūtras of the Sugata, render themselves not subject to admonishment?" — he would disparage them, dismiss them, and speak ill of them.

On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should approach the monk Channa, and the same should be done with any other such person, and address him with these words: 'Venerable Channa, when monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya on the bases of training that fall under what monks are to recite, and on what falls within the sūtras of the Sugata, do not render yourself not subject to admonishment. Rather, venerable one, make yourself subject to admonishment. When monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, you too should speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. That is to say, each should admonish the other, each should guide and instruct the other, and each should lift the other out of transgressions — it is in just such a way that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, will grow. Venerable Channa, abandon this course of action, namely the practice of rendering yourself not subject to admonishment.' Address him in that way."

The monks, having heard the Blessed One, said "As you command, venerable sir," and approached the venerable Channa and addressed him thus: "Venerable Channa, when monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya on the bases of training that fall under what monks are to recite, and on what falls within the sūtras of the Sugata, do not render yourself not subject to admonishment. Rather, venerable one, make yourself subject to admonishment. When monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, you too should speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. That is to say, each should admonish the other, each should guide and instruct the other, and each should lift the other out of transgressions — it is in just such a way that the retinue of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, will grow. Venerable Channa, abandon this course of action, namely the practice of rendering yourself not subject to admonishment."

When the monks approached and addressed him thus, he seized upon that very same ground with stubborn tenacity, clinging to it with great attachment, and proceeded to designate only that as true and everything else as false. On that occasion the monks reported this again to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should approach the monk Channa, and —"

"Furthermore, in a case such as this, the formal act of admonishment is to be carried out by a motion-and-three-resolutions procedure. It is to be carried out in the following way. Having prepared the seats and struck the gong, the monks are to be properly assembled by means of the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is seated and in harmony, one monk is to make the motion and perform the act.

'Let the venerable Saṅgha hear.
