The monk Channa, having committed a transgression, does not restore it according to the Dharma; and when the monks speak to him in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — citing both the training rules pertaining to what the monks recite and the sūtras belonging to the Sugata — he says: "Venerable ones, do not say anything to me, whether virtuous or not virtuous; and I, whether virtuously or not virtuously, will say nothing to the venerable ones. Venerable ones, do step aside from the path of words toward me. And since I am not in the habit of proclaiming myself while saying, 'What does it matter if you have spoken?' — whenever many monks take him up and admonish him, he clings to that very same ground with stubborn tenacity and great attachment and goes on designating only that as true and everything else as false." If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha give its approval. And let the Saṅgha admonish the monk Channa thus: "Venerable Channa, do not act in such a way that you fail to proclaim yourself; rather, let the venerable one do only what amounts to proclaiming himself. When the monks speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, let the venerable one also speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — that is to say: speaking to one another, explaining and teaching one another, and lifting one another out of transgression. It is in just such a way that the retinue of that Blessed One, that Tathāgata, that arhat, that perfectly and completely awakened buddha, will grow. Venerable Channa, abandon this course of action, namely the practice of rendering yourself not subject to admonishment." This is to be carried out as a formal act by a motion-and-three-resolutions procedure. This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows. "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The monk Channa, having committed a transgression, does not restore it according to the Dharma; and when the monks speak to him in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — citing both the training rules pertaining to what the monks recite and the sūtras belonging to the Sugata — he says: "Venerable ones, do not say anything to me, whether virtuous or not virtuous; and I, whether virtuously or not virtuously, will say nothing to the venerable ones. Venerable ones, do step aside from the path of words toward me. And since I am not in the habit of proclaiming myself while saying, 'What does it matter if you have spoken?'" — having thus made himself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself — whenever many monks take him up and admonish him, he clings to that very same ground with stubborn tenacity and great attachment and goes on designating only that as true and everything else as false. Therefore let the Saṅgha admonish the monk Channa: "Venerable Channa, when the monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya —"

do not make yourself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself when the monks speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. Venerable one, make yourself someone who is indeed in the habit of proclaiming himself. When the monks speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, the venerable one too should speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — that is, by making it a matter of proclaiming oneself to one another, of instructing and guiding one another, and of one lifting the other out of transgression. It is in just such a way that the retinue of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, will grow and flourish. Venerable Channa, abandon this conduct of yours — this extreme of acting as one who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself."

When this request and the formal act with four proclamations has been performed, those venerable ones who consent to the Saṅgha's performing the formal act with four proclamations against the monk Channa should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. This is the first proclamation of the formal act; it is to be repeated a second and a third time in the same way. The Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the Saṅgha has performed the formal act with four proclamations against the monk Channa. Because no one has spoken, it is understood to be accepted accordingly.

The monks, having heard from the Blessed One, replied, "Venerable one, as you command," and proceeded to perform the formal act with four proclamations against the monk Channa. But even as the formal act with four proclamations was being performed, he clung to that very same ground with stubborn tenacity and great attachment, and continued to designate only that as true and everything else as false. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and these circumstances, convened an assembly of monks — and so on as before. The blessed buddhas act while knowing, and so forth — also as before.

The Blessed One then questioned Channa: "Channa, is it true that when the monks spoke to you in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — citing the precepts belonging to the exhortation of monks and citing the sūtras of the Sugata — you made yourself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself?" "Venerable one, it is so." The Blessed One then rebuked him, saying that such conduct is not the way of a renunciant, is not fitting, is not proper, is not in accord with conduct, and is not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Thereupon, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on as before.

"My hearers shall learn this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk here has come to be of a nature that is displeasing to admonish, and when the monks, citing the precepts belonging to the exhortation of monks and citing the sūtras of the Sugata, speak to him in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, he says, 'Venerable ones, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad, and I too will say nothing to you, venerable ones, whether good or bad. Venerable ones, refrain from bringing words my way. And since I am not in the habit of proclaiming myself while saying, "What does it matter if you have spoken?" — thus making himself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself — the monks shall address that monk thus: Venerable one, do not make yourself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself when the monks, citing the precepts belonging to the exhortation of monks

when those belonging to the Sugata's sūtra speak in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, the venerable one should not make himself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself, but should instead make himself precisely someone who is in the habit of proclaiming himself. When the monks speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, the venerable one too should speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya — that is to say, making themselves someone who proclaims to one another, who guides and instructs one another, who lifts one another out of transgressions. It is by such conduct that the retinue of that Blessed One, that Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and completely awakened Buddha will grow. Venerable one, abandon this kind of deed — making yourself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself." Thus shall the monks address him.

When the monks have addressed that monk in this way, if he abandons that position, that is well and good. If he does not abandon it, in order to get him to abandon that position, the address and instruction shall be given a second and a third time, correctly and properly. If upon being correctly and properly addressed and instructed a second and a third time he abandons that position, that is well and good. If he does not abandon it, it is a matter for the Saṅgha to resolve.

Here, the phrase "a certain monk" refers to the aspirant or anyone else of that kind. With regard to the phrase "has become one whose nature is to be difficult to address," the expression "difficult to address" means blocking, not following, not being receptive to the proper path of speech, not acting in accordance with right conduct, not proceeding straightforwardly, obstructing the entire collection of limbs that make up the practice of proper governance, not holding to them, not doing them, not performing them, and holding to what is contrary. The phrase "to him" refers to the aspirant. The phrase "by the monks" refers to the members of this Dharma community. With regard to the phrase "the training precepts belonging to the exhortation," "exhortation" refers to the four factors that constitute defeat, the thirteen matters for the Saṅgha, the two undetermined matters, the thirty matters entailing forfeiture, the ninety matters entailing downfall, the four matters requiring individual confession, the numerous training precepts, and the seven rules for settling disputes. With regard to the phrase "those belonging to the Sugata's sūtra," "Sugata" refers to the Teacher. "Sūtra" means either a sūtra closely connected to him or a correctly compiled sūtra. "In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the discourses and the Māṭṛkā. "In accordance with the Vinaya" means in accordance with the Vinaya itself. The phrase "when they speak" means when they recite it back — that is, when the address is given in accordance with how the Dharma is, how the Vinaya is, and how the teaching of the Teacher is. The phrase "venerable ones, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad" means: do not engage me toward virtue, and do not turn me away from wrongdoing either. The phrase "I too will say nothing to you, venerable ones, whether good or bad" means: I will not engage you toward virtue, and I will not turn you away from wrongdoing either. The phrase "venerable ones, refrain from bringing words my way; and since I am not in the habit of proclaiming myself — what does it matter if you have spoken?" — this means that he establishes himself extensively as someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself. The phrase "when he makes himself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself" means when he establishes himself as precisely that — as one not in the habit of proclaiming himself. The phrase "that monk" refers to the aspirant. The phrase "by the monks" refers to the members of this Dharma community. The phrase "thus" means: having assembled, the monks shall give the address just as was previously shown, in the manner described.

The phrase "the monks shall give that monk the following address" means that he is turned back by the address given after the assembly has convened. The phrase "if that basis" refers to the very discomfort of the instruction. The phrase "he relinquishes it" means that he relinquishes it completely. The phrase "then that is good" means that if it is so, it is well. The phrase "if he does not relinquish it" means that he does not relinquish it completely. The phrase "one should give the address correctly a second and a third time, one should instruct correctly" means: one should give the address by the motion-and-four procedure just as was previously shown, addressing him correctly — and that is what "addressing correctly" is, and that is what "instructing correctly" is.

The phrase "the Saṅgha remains" means that, as before, that transgression depends upon the Saṅgha — therefore it is said that the Saṅgha remains.

Now, how does a transgression come about in this regard? Whenever the monks address a monk with training rules that fall within the scope of what the monks are to admonish, or with matters belonging to the sūtras of the Sugata, speaking in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, and that monk makes himself someone who is not in the habit of proclaiming himself — then in every case an offense is committed.

If a monk, after the assembly has convened and the address has been given, relinquishes that basis, then that is good. If he does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises. If the address is given by the motion-and-four procedure and he relinquishes that basis, then that is good. If he does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises at the time of the motion. When the first recitation of the act is being recited, if he relinquishes the basis before the recitation is complete, then that is good. If he does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises when the recitation is completed. When the second recitation of the act is being recited, if he relinquishes the basis before the recitation is complete, then that is good. If he does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises when the recitation is completed. When the third recitation of the act is being recited, if he relinquishes the basis before the recitation is complete, then that is good. If he does not relinquish it, a grave offense arises.

When the recitation is completed: if the address is given in a manner that is concordant but not in accordance with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If it is given in a manner that is discordant and not in accordance with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If it is given in a manner adjusted to be concordant and in accordance with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If it is given in a manner adjusted to be discordant and not in accordance with the Dharma, there is no transgression. If the address is not given in accordance with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the Teacher's teaching as it is, there is no transgression. If the address is given in a manner concordant with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the Teacher's teaching as it is, then when the recitation is completed, the remainder falls to the Saṅgha.

While remaining seated in that place, that monk shall say the following: "Venerable ones, a transgression belonging to the remainder with the Saṅgha has arisen for me." If he says this, then that is good. If he does not say it, from that point forward the offense of concealment will arise for him.

Therefore, so long as a monk has not confessed and individually confessed that basis, and continues to undergo acts consisting of a motion alone, a motion with two recitations, and a motion with four recitations, in every case an offense is committed. There is no transgression for a first offender, or for one who is insane, or for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is overwhelmed by painful sensations.

Here ends the twenty-fourth fascicle of the Vinaya Vibhaṅga.

The monks, having arisen in doubt, put all their doubts to the Buddha, the Blessed One. The venerable Ānanda, who lives the holy life, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please look upon the fact that this aspirant who lives the holy life declares and proclaims himself to be a relative of the Blessed One before such-and-such practitioners of the holy life." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now —

"In the same way, in times past as well, this very one declared and proclaimed himself to be a relative of mine before such-and-such brahmins and householders. Listen now to how this came about.

Monks, long ago, in times past, in the city of Droṇāvatsara there lived a brahmin named Candrakīrti. He took a wife from his own social class, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and took his pleasure. While they were sporting, rejoicing, and taking their pleasure together, she gave birth to a son, and they named him Sūryacandra. They raised and nurtured him, and he grew to be grown.

Then in the course of time, the brahmin Candrakīrti fell ill and, abandoning his wife and son, was on the verge of death. He had a maidservant, and she thought to herself: 'The brahmin Candrakīrti, served by hundreds of bath-attendants, amassed great wealth and prosperity — yet now that he has fallen ill and abandoned his wife and son, hovering near death, it would not be fitting for me to abandon my master.' With this virtuous intention, and out of affection for her master, she went to a physician and said: 'Good sir, do you know the brahmin called Candrakīrti?' He said that he did. 'Then what is his affliction? He has fallen ill and, abandoning his wife and son, is near death — show me a cure for him.' The physician replied: 'Girl, if he has abandoned his wife and son, who will attend to him?' She said: 'Good sir, show me the cure and I will attend to him.' The physician then inquired into the nature of his illness and prescribed a remedy. The girl then served the brahmin Candrakīrti and nursed him back to health.

The brahmin Candrakīrti reflected: 'When I was struck down by such an illness, and abandoned by my wife and son, hovering between life and death, the very fact that I remained barely alive is due to this girl's power. I must repay her efforts with fitting reward.' Recognizing this, he called the girl to him and said: 'Girl, I know full well that it is through your power that I was not separated from my life when I was struck down by such an illness, abandoned by my wife and son. Tell me — what precious thing shall I give you?' The girl replied: 'Master, if you are pleased with me, I wish to meet with you privately.' He said: 'Girl, what purpose would meeting with me privately serve you? I will give you five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and release you from servitude.' She replied: 'Master, I have been a maidservant for a very long time — I remain a maidservant still. If you are pleased with me, I wish to meet with you privately.' Seeing that she was absolutely insistent on this assignation, he said: 'Girl, when the time comes and your monthly flow has passed, come to me then.' The girl was delighted by these words. She sat counting the days until her monthly flow was over, and when it had passed she went to that brahmin. She took her pleasure with him, and a being entered her womb.

Now the brahmin's wife, a brahmin woman herself, realized that her husband had taken his pleasure with this girl. Overwhelmed by jealousy, she could not bear it, and she struck the girl continually with fists and slaps, and fed her poor food and dressed her in poor, rough clothing. The girl thought: 'What kind of unfortunate being is it that has entered my womb? Ever since it entered my womb, I have been struck continually with fists and slaps, fed poor food, and made to wear poor, rough clothing.' She sat in sorrow over this. When the nine months were complete and she gave birth, a boy was born. He thought to himself:"

"This unfortunate being has entered my womb, and because of that I have come to endure such a condition. If this child is born, I shall have nothing whatsoever from anyone." Knowing this, she placed it in a dustbin and was about to throw it away. At that moment the brahmin saw this and asked: "Girl, what is that?" She answered: "It is nothing, master." He looked at the dustbin, and when he saw there was a baby boy, he said: "Girl, why are you throwing this away? From the time that this unfortunate being entered your womb, up until now, this brahmin woman of mine has been striking you continually with fists and slaps, and feeding you poor food and making you wear poor, rough clothing. It is because if this child were born, I would have nothing whatsoever from anyone. That is why." He said: "Girl, she has done no wrong — it is I who am at fault. Raise this child, and I shall keep count of my debts to it." And he began to suckle it. The brahmin also said to the brahmin woman: "You know that when I was once ill, you and my son abandoned me, and it was this girl who nursed me well with medicine and attendants. Therefore if you now provide this child with what it needs, well and good. If you do not, I will install this one as mistress of the household and make you her slave." The brahmin woman was frightened and thought: "This brahmin is fierce. If I do not act accordingly, he is quite capable of doing exactly that." And so she said: "Brahmin, you took pleasure with a serving girl and this boy is not my son, yet I have not complained even once. From now on I shall not trouble him in the least." Because the boy had been placed in the dustbin, he came to be named Dustbin-born. The brahmin regarded Dustbin-born with the thought: "His mother served as my servant, and this one too has come from me," and so he felt very great affection for him. He and the boy ate together, and wherever he was invited as a guest, he took the boy along with him.

Then in another time the brahmin fell ill. Dustbin-born nursed him with medicines of roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, yet as he nursed him the sick man only grew more gravely ill, and when the time came that he felt he was approaching death and would not last much longer, he summoned his eldest son Nyizla and said: "Son, when I am gone you need not mourn, but your younger brother Dustbin-born will grieve, so you must provide for his needs." And he spoke these words:

All that is gathered reaches its end,
all that is high will come to fall,
all meeting ends in parting,
and all that lives must die.

Such is the nature of things in their season. And so, in due time, Nyizla, Dustbin-born, and others who were dear and close to him carried him to the charnel ground, burned him, and afterward performed the mourning rites and settled in.

Then one day at mealtime, Nyizla called out: "Dustbin-born, come here — eat something." The mother said to him: "Son, how can you eat together with the child of a slave girl?" The son replied: "Mother, I have always eaten and drunk with this younger brother of mine — how can he now be called the son of a slave girl?" The mother said: "Son, because your father was fierce, who dared say a word to him? This one is nothing but the son of a slave girl." When Dustbin-born heard this, he went to his mother and said: "Mother, is it true that I am the son of a slave girl?"

"Son, in this world each person experiences the fruits of their own karma — so whose slave is anyone? Son, go to another land and acquire learning and stay there."

He went to another land, and there he dropped his given name Cholzangpa and proclaimed himself Dawazhiba. In time he eventually made his way to Śrāvastī, where there was a brahmin who was a reciter of texts before an assembly. He went to him step by step, and with his calm and composed deportment and manner of conduct he spoke respectfully and settled at one side. Then the brahmin, welcoming him with words of greeting, gladly enquired: "Ho, brahmin youth, where have you come from?" "I have come from Drojog." "Do you know the community of people dwelling at Drojog?" "And what is the talk of the brahmin Dawadragpa there?" The brahmin youth began to weep. The brahmin asked: "Brahmin youth, why do you weep?" "He was my father." "Then why do you weep?" "He has died." "Brahmin youth, that one born must inevitably die — I am your father's junior friend, so take comfort and I will do everything for you." He replied: "Teacher, for the time being please send away other business and let me read the Vedas." "Son, do not be troubled — for a brahmin, proclaiming one's lineage is precisely that." And so he began to read the Vedas with him, and since he was sharp-witted, steady, and diligent, within a short time he had read through all four Vedas. The brahmin was greatly pleased and gave him his daughter adorned with every ornament as his wife, and also gave him abundant wealth of his own possession. He became known as the brahmin's chief reciter before the assembly and, renowned throughout the entire world as one possessed of the four Vedas, he amassed great household prosperity through generosity, offerings, and acts of service.

Then one day the community of people dwelling at Drojog took provisions and came to Śrāvastī, and there they heard how Cholzangpa had become a brahmin's chief reciter, was possessed of the four Vedas, was renowned throughout the entire world, and had amassed great household prosperity through generosity, offerings, and acts of service. Having heard this they began to deliberate: "Let us go and meet him in person, and spread the good news of Nyizla back at Drojog." And so they went to him. Recognizing him, they said nothing, but then changed their provisions, received payment, and departed for Drojog. When they had rested from the weariness of the road, they said to Nyizla: "In Śrāvastī your younger brother Cholzangpa has become a brahmin's chief reciter, is possessed of the four Vedas, is renowned throughout the entire world, and has amassed great household prosperity through generosity, offerings, and acts of service." Nyizla felt joy arise and said to his mother: "Mother, I hear that Cholzangpa in Śrāvastī has become a brahmin's chief reciter, is possessed of the four Vedas, is renowned throughout the entire world, and has amassed great household prosperity through generosity, offerings, and acts of service." The mother replied: "Son, how could that be so? Who would pay respect to that son of a slave girl through generosity, offerings, and acts of service — would anyone really pay him such respect?" And after that he said nothing more.

Then in time Nyizla's circumstances became straitened, and his mother said to him:

"Son, go to your younger brother. If you do so, he may share his wealth with you." Nyizla replied: "Mother, if he was a slave girl's son then, how can he be a younger brother now?" The mother said: "Son, even so, go — and do not refuse to accept what he offers." Pressed insistently by his mother, he sought out travelling companions and went to Śrāvastī.

Cholzangpa heard that his elder brother Nyizla had arrived there in the company of travelling companions and was staying somewhere in the vicinity. On hearing this, he went out to welcome him, greeted him with words of "Welcome, well come!" and then said: "I have given myself the name Śāntacandra here. Do not call me Cholzangpa." Nyizla replied: "If you are Śāntacandra, who else would anyone call you?"

Śāntacandra then brought Nyizla to his home, attended to him with great honour, provided him with food, and said to his brahmin wife: "Know this: this is my elder brother, called Nyizla. You are to supply him with everything he needs, speak no harsh words to him, and always treat him with respect." She agreed to this.

Now Nyizla was pleasant to live with, whereas Cholzangpa was fierce, proud, and violent, and for even the slightest fault he would beat that wife of his with fists and slaps. The brahmin woman said to Nyizla: "Master, you two were nursed at the same breast and are brothers — why is it that you are pleasant to live with, while this younger brother of yours is fierce, proud, and violent? What is the reason for this?" Nyizla replied: "Sister-in-law, he has not studied the household learning. Master, please grant me that household learning." Nyizla then spoke this verse:

Knowledge is not to be given to just anyone.
One should die with one's knowledge still one's own.
Knowledge is to be given to one possessed of learning, devotion,
and wealth.

The brahmin woman said: "Master, how much wealth must one give?" "Sister-in-law, five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." She then took five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, placed them at his two feet, and said: "Master, please grant the household learning." Nyizla said: "Sister-in-law, bear with me — I will give it when it is time to leave."

The brahmin woman went to the mistress of the house and said: "My lord's son — your elder brother here dislikes being asked about household affairs and will be displeased. Please send him away." He replied: "Good woman, if that is so, then you prepare provisions for the road for sister-in-law here, and I will seek out travelling companions." He then began to seek companions to travel to the stone quarry. The brahmin woman prepared provisions for the road, took five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, placed them at Nyizla's feet, and said: "Master, now is the time of your departure — please grant the household learning." Nyizla said:

"Sister-in-law, at the time when Śāntacandra beats you, recite this learning:

Known to many other people,
known too in other people's homes,
known by the village guard's own kind —
sit apart, O Cholzangpa!

If he asks what these words mean, tell him: if he beats you, you will explain the meaning as well."

"Sister-in-law, these words, which carry the meaning of a secret mantra, will bear fruit by the mere act of reciting them. Take them well to heart so that you will have no cause for regret later."

The brahmin woman memorised those words carefully. Śāntacandra also found travelling companions to go to the stone quarry, divided the kārṣāpaṇas with Nyizla, gave him provisions for the road, and escorted him on his way.

The girl thought: "I should test whether these words of secret mantra are true or false." So when Śāntacandra escorted Nyizla on his way and then returned, she made no preparation whatsoever of food, drink, or water for bathing.

Then Śāntacandra said, "Bless you, bring water — I wish to bathe." His wife replied, "My lord's son, the bathwater has not been prepared." "Very well, Bless you, then bring food — I will eat." "My lord's son, that also has not been prepared." He grew angry and said, "All the while my elder brother was here, I merely kept you at a distance. But your nature is such that you cannot be managed without a beating." With that he rolled up his sleeve and moved to strike her. His wife said, "My lord's son, wait a moment — let me recite the lore of the household." He said, "Speak, then." His wife recited:

Known by many other people,
known even in other people's homes,
known by the village guard's own kind —
sit apart, O Cholzangpa!

When she had spoken, he said, "Bless you, what is the meaning of those words?" His wife replied, "If you strike me, I will tell you the meaning as well." Those words pierced him like an arrow finding its mark, and he cried out in sharp pain, "Do not strike — let it go, and say no more of the meaning!"

O monks, the brahmin known at that time and on that occasion as Śānatacandra — that was none other than myself. The one known at that time and on that occasion as Cholzangpa — that is this Adhyāśaya here. O monks, even at that time this one, before brahmins and householders of that circle, spoke of me as his kinsman and made claims and counter-claims about himself. Even now this one, before those who practise a holy life in that same circle, speaks of me as his kinsman and makes claims and counter-claims about himself. O monks, therefore those who speak of me as their kinsman, claiming kinship with me, must live so as to come under the authority of the long-standing elders among those who lead a holy life, and the middling ones, and the newly ordained, with reverence, with respect, and with fear.

Here ends the thirteenth rule of the Remainder of the Saṅgha, the section on vexing counsel.

O monastics, I have now set forth these thirteen rules of the Remainder of the Saṅgha. Of these, nine are resolved on the first transgression. Four are resolved after three times. A monk who commits any one of these transgressions and, for as long as he knowingly conceals it, shall be required to undergo probation against his will for that same period. A monk who has undergone probation against his will shall thereafter, for up to six days, carry out the acts of appeasing the Saṅgha. A monk who has carried out the acts of appeasing the Saṅgha and then, without obstruction to the restoration, has acted in accordance with the rule and has pleased the minds of the monastic Saṅgha — in whatever place an assembly of twenty monks is present, that monk shall be restored. If, however, an assembly lacking so much as one of the twenty monks performs that monk's restoration, then the restoration is not valid, and those monks too are to be censured. That is the procedure in this matter.

Here ends the complete Remainder of the Saṅgha.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now the venerable Udāyin, in the early morning, having put on his lower robe and taken up his alms bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī on alms round, and as he walked through Śrāvastī on alms round in due course, he came to the house of the householder's wife Bhedā. The householder's wife Bhedā, seeing the venerable Udāyin from some distance away —

— seeing the venerable Udāyin from some distance away, she prepared a seat for him and said: "Venerable Udāyin, please come over here. Welcome, venerable Udāyin. Venerable Udāyin, please be seated on the seat that has been prepared." The venerable Udāyin sat down on the seat that had been spread. Then the householder's wife Bhedā prostrated with her head to the venerable Udāyin's two feet, placed her two knees on the ground opposite his two knees, and sat down to hear the Dharma. The venerable Udāyin then began to teach her pleasant and agreeable teachings on the Dharma.

At that time the mother of Mṛgadhara was walking in the neighborhood of that house, and she heard the sound of the venerable Udāyin's voice ringing out from the house of the householder's wife Bhedā. Hearing it, she thought: "How wonderful — the noble Udāyin is teaching the householder's wife Bhedā pleasant and agreeable teachings on the Dharma, just like a bee drawing out honey. I too shall go and listen to the Dharma being taught to another."

So the mother of Mṛgadhara went to the house of the householder's wife Bhedā. When she arrived, she saw the householder's wife Bhedā sitting with her two knees placed opposite the venerable Udāyin's two knees, listening to the Dharma. Seeing this, she thought: "If some householder, or some wife of a householder, or some faithless son of a householder were to see this, they would certainly conclude that this noble Udāyin had done or was intending to do some sinful act unbecoming of an ascetic — something improper — while alone in a secluded place with the householder's wife Bhedā. It will inevitably lead to the worst outcome. Therefore this is my duty to act on."

So the mother of Mṛgadhara went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, prostrated with her head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the mother of Mṛgadhara addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I was walking in the lane near the householder's wife Bhedā's house when I heard the sound of the venerable Udāyin's voice. Upon hearing it I thought: 'How wonderful — the noble Udāyin is teaching the householder's wife Bhedā pleasant and agreeable teachings on the Dharma, just like a bee drawing out honey. I too shall go and listen to the Dharma being taught to another.' So I went to the lane near the householder's wife Bhedā's house, and I saw the householder's wife Bhedā sitting with her two knees placed opposite the venerable Udāyin's two knees, listening to the Dharma. Seeing this I thought: 'If now some householder, or some wife of a householder, or some faithless son of a householder were to see this, they would certainly conclude that this noble Udāyin had done or was intending to do some sinful act unbecoming of an ascetic, while alone in a secluded place with the householder's wife Bhedā. It will inevitably lead to the worst outcome, and therefore this is my duty to act on.' Venerable One, for this reason, out of compassion, if the Blessed One would be so good as to lay down some reminder for the noble monks so that when noble ones are alone together in a secluded place with a woman, they do not remain seated — that would be excellent, excellent!"

The Blessed One consented to the mother of Mṛgadhara by remaining silent.

Then the mother of Mṛgadhara, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had given his consent, prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from her seat, and departed.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, together with the grounds for the rule and the circumstances of the case, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. The Blessed Buddhas, though they know, enquire — and so forth, also as before.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, asked the venerable Udāyin: "Udāyin, is it true that you behaved in so unseemly a manner?" The venerable one admitted: "It is true, Blessed One." The Blessed One, the Buddha, censured him with such words as: "What is unbecoming of an ascetic, what is unsuitable, what is improper, what is contrary to proper conduct — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth" — and so forth, censuring him thoroughly.

Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, having seen ten benefits with full discernment, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be established" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Further, whatever monk, together with a woman — alone, one with one, in a secluded and screened place — sits down on a seat in a manner conducive to sexual intercourse: if a female lay practitioner (upāsikā) who possesses words of credible testimony then speaks of any one of the three that entails defeat, or the matter that remains for the Saṅgha, or any matter whatsoever that entails an offense — and the monk acknowledges having so sat — he shall be made to incur whichever of the three entailing defeat, or the matter remaining for the Saṅgha, or any offense whatsoever she has declared; and whatever particular matter that female lay practitioner of credible testimony has spoken of, by that same matter the monk shall be made to incur it. This, however, is a matter that is indeterminate."

Now as to the phrase "whatever monk" — this refers to Udāyin, or to anyone else similarly situated.

"Together with a woman" means a woman or a girl who is capable of bearing the Dharma that arises from unchaste conduct.

"Together" means in her company.

"Alone, one with one" means that one with that one.

"In a secluded place" means a place where no other woman, man, or eunuch whatsoever is present.

"Screened" — screened by five things: screened by a wall, screened by a partition, screened by a curtain, screened by dense [vegetation], or screened by darkness of night.

"In a manner conducive to sexual intercourse" means in a manner conducive to unchaste conduct.

"On a seat" means on a surface.

"Sits down" means placing his buttocks within the distance of a fathom.

Now regarding the phrase "if a female lay practitioner who possesses words of credible testimony": "credible" means one who has genuine faith in the Buddha, genuine faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha; who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, who has gone for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha; who is devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dharma and the Saṅgha; who has no anxiety and no doubt regarding the Buddha, regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha, regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; who has seen the truths, obtained the fruit, and is endowed with direct realization; and who, even to preserve her own life, could not knowingly speak a false word.

Regarding the phrase "the three": the word "three" indicates a number.

"Or that entails defeat" —

"Or the Saṅgha's remainder, or any offense whatsoever" — regarding this phrase: "that entails defeat" means any one of the four defeats. "The Saṅgha's remainder" means any one of the thirteen remainder offenses. "Offense" means any one of the ninety offenses.

Now, a laywoman who is endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness is not learned regarding offenses, not learned regarding the grounds for offenses, and not learned regarding the instigation of offenses. Therefore, if a monk sees her doing any of the following — speaking of Dharma in a superior way to men, making bodily contact while sitting on the same seat as a woman, eating from the same vessel, drinking various intoxicating drinks that would cause intoxication in a single cup, digging the earth, cutting green grass, eating at an improper time, or doing any other transgressive act that is accompanied by an intrinsic fault — then whatever she has agreed to among those acts, he is to make her do it.

"Make her do it" means to have her commit it.

"That is an undetermined matter" means that it is a matter that has not been formally settled.

Then how does a transgression arise? If a monk, using the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, accepts her going but accepts neither her standing nor her sitting nor her lying down, then whatever she has accepted, he is to make her do that. If a monk, using the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, accepts her going and her standing but accepts neither her sitting nor her lying down, then whatever she has accepted, he is to make her do that. If a monk, using the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, accepts her going, her standing, and her sitting but does not accept her lying down, then whatever she has accepted, he is to make her do that. If a monk, using the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, accepts her going, her standing, her sitting, and her lying down, then he is to make her do all of them.

If, however, a monk, using the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, does not accept her going, nor her standing, nor her sitting, nor her lying down, then since he is deserving of a punitive act, the Saṅgha should grant him the formal act of having a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness investigate his conduct. This is how it is to be granted: a seat is prepared, the wooden board is struck, and after correctly informing the entire Saṅgha with the words of inquiry, with the entire Saṅgha assembled and in harmony, a single monk makes a motion and the formal act is performed.

"Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear this. The venerable Cāraka has, through the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, declined to accept going, declined to accept standing, declined to accept sitting, and declined to accept lying down. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it is agreeable, let the Saṅgha grant permission, and let the Saṅgha bestow upon the venerable Cāraka the formal act of having a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness investigate his conduct." That is the motion.

The formal act is then to be performed as follows: "Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear this. The venerable Cāraka, through the words of a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness, has declined to accept going, declined to accept standing, declined to accept sitting, and declined to accept lying down. Therefore, let the Saṅgha bestow upon the venerable Cāraka the formal act of having a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness investigate his conduct. If—

those venerable members who consent to the Saṅgha bestowing upon the venerable Cāraka the formal act of having a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness investigate his essential nature — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak. This is the first proclamation of the formal act." It is then to be repeated a second and a third time in the same way. The Saṅgha having consented and agreed, the Saṅgha has bestowed upon the venerable Cāraka the formal act of having a laywoman endowed with the words of a trustworthy witness investigate his essential nature — as indicated by its silence, so it is held.

"O monks, I shall now set forth the rules of conduct that apply to a monk upon whom this act of investigation has been bestowed. One upon whom the act of investigation has been bestowed must not confer the going forth, must not confer full ordination, must not grant residence, and must not install a novice. He must not raise or mention before a monk any matter of damaged moral discipline, damaged view, damaged conduct, or damaged livelihood. He must not be appointed to teach nuns; and if he was previously appointed, he must not teach nuns. He must not establish a schedule of instruction, must not establish the restoration ceremony, and must not establish the invitation ceremony. He must not perform the formal act of a single motion, the formal act of a motion with two recitations, or the formal act of a motion with four recitations. If within the Saṅgha there are other individuals who hold the Vinaya, he must not recite the Sūtra of Individual Liberation. If one upon whom the act of investigation has been bestowed does not properly accept and enter into the rules of conduct that have been prescribed for him, he becomes one who is at variance with those rules."

The first set of undetermined rules is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Bamboo Forest. At that time the monk Śīrika, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl and robes, entered Rājagṛha to collect alms. As he was going through Rājagṛha collecting alms in due order, he came to the place where the householder's wife, the noble Poṣadhā, lived. The noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, saw the monk Śīrika from a great distance, and upon seeing him, she prepared a seat for the monk Śīrika and said these words: "Venerable Śīrika, please come here. Venerable Śīrika, welcome. Venerable Śīrika, please be seated on the prepared seat." The monk Śīrika sat down on the prepared seat. Then the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, bowed her head to the two feet of the monk Śīrika and sat — knees not touching knees — in order to hear the Dharma. The monk Śīrika thereupon began to teach her pleasing and beautiful words of Dharma. At that time the laywoman Sujanā was passing through the vicinity of the noble Poṣadhā's house, and from within the house the laywoman Sujanā heard the sound and resonance of the monk Śīrika's voice. Hearing it, she thought to herself: "How wonderful — the noble Śīrika is teaching pleasing and beautiful words of Dharma to the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, just as a bee draws out honey. I too shall go to hear the Dharma that has been set forth for others." The laywoman Sujanā then went to the place where the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, lived, and there she saw the noble Poṣadhā sitting — knees not touching knees — in order to hear the Dharma from the monk Śīrika.

Seeing this, she thought to herself: "If some householder, or the householder's wife, or some son of the householder who lacks faith were to see this, they would inevitably conclude that the noble Śīrika has done or intends to do some sinful, disgraceful act — something unbecoming of an ascetic — alone in a secluded place together with the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder. Because this would surely lead to the worst outcome, this is something I must act upon." And so the laywoman Sujanā went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, she bowed her head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the laywoman Sujanā addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable one, while I was in the doorway of the householder's house near the noble Poṣadhā's restoration-day enclosure, I heard the sound and resonance of the noble Śīrika's voice. Hearing it, I thought to myself: 'How wonderful — the noble Śīrika is teaching pleasing and beautiful words of Dharma to the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, just as a bee draws out honey. I too shall go to hear the Dharma that has been set forth for others.' And so I went to the place where the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder, was — near the restoration-day enclosure — and there I saw the noble Poṣadhā sitting with the monk Śīrika, knees not touching knees. Seeing this, I thought to myself: 'If some householder, or the wife of the householder, or some son of the householder who lacks faith were to see this, they would inevitably conclude that this noble Śīrika has done or intends to do some sinful, disgraceful act — something unbecoming of an ascetic — alone in a secluded place together with the noble Poṣadhā, wife of the householder. Because this would surely lead to the worst outcome, this is something I must act upon.' Therefore, venerable one, it would be excellent if, out of compassion, the Blessed One were to establish a reminder for the noble ones — so that when noble ones are alone together with a woman in a secluded place, they do not remain seated."

The Blessed One said nothing to the laywoman Sujanā, and by his silence gave his consent. Then the laywoman Sujanā, understanding that the Blessed One had given consent by his silence, bowed her head to the Blessed One's two feet, rose from her seat, and departed.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, in reference to this occasion and this context, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. And "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowing full well, make inquiry" — and so forth, also as before.

The awakened Blessed One then questioned the monk Śīrika: "Śīrika, is it true that you did such an unseemly thing?"

"Venerable one, it is so."

The awakened Blessed One then rebuked him — "What is unbecoming of an ascetic, what is discordant, what is improper, what is contrary to the rule — that is not something a renunciant should do" — and so forth, in full rebuke.

Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be laid down" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers are to observe and uphold this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk sits alone, in private, with a woman in a secluded place where the two of them are sheltered — a place unsuitable for unchaste conduct — and if a trustworthy laywoman then speaks of either of the two matters that are subject to the Saṅgha Remainder or to any of the offenses entailing downfall, and the monk acknowledges having sat there, he is to be made to undergo whatever of those two matters she has spoken of — that is to say, the Saṅgha Remainder or any of the offenses entailing downfall — by the words of that trustworthy laywoman, and whatever matters she has named, he is to be made to undertake the consequences of those matters accordingly. This is an indeterminate matter.

Now, "whatever monk" means a monk such as Śirika or any other of the same kind.

"In the realm of women" means one capable of serving as the basis for an offense involving the giving of unchaste conduct with a woman or a girl.

"Together" means in her company.

"One alone with one" means that one and that one.

"Secluded" means a place where no other woman, man, or person of indeterminate sex is present.

"Where there is shelter" means sheltered by one of five things: sheltered by a wall, sheltered by a screen, sheltered by a curtain, sheltered by something dense, or sheltered by darkness.

"Unsuitable for unchaste conduct" means a place unsuitable for unchaste conduct.

"On a seat" means on a high seat or a low seat.

"Sits there" means he settles his haunches within less than an arm's length of her.

Regarding "if a trustworthy laywoman": "trustworthy" means one who has explicit faith in the Buddha, explicit faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, who has gone for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, who has become one with the Buddha, who has become one with the Dharma and the Saṅgha, who has no wavering and no doubt regarding the Buddha, who has no wavering and no doubt regarding the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, who has seen the truth and attained the fruit and possesses realization, and who is incapable of knowingly speaking a false word even to save her own life.

"The two matters" — the word "two" indicates a stated number.

Regarding "the Saṅgha Remainder or any of the offenses entailing downfall": "Saṅgha Remainder" means any one of the thirteen. "Entailing downfall" means any one of the ninety.

Because a trustworthy laywoman is not learned in what constitutes a downfall, not learned in the grounds for a downfall, and not learned in what constitutes the full commission of a downfall, if she has seen the monk do certain things alongside a woman — speaking of a matter surpassing a human's capacity, or sitting together with a woman on the same seat, or making bodily contact, or eating from the same vessel, or drinking various intoxicating beverages that could lead to intoxication from the same cup, or digging the earth, or cutting green grass, or eating at an improper time, or doing any other act that bears an inherent offense — then whatever she has acknowledged of these, he is to be made to undergo the consequences of that.

"To be made to undergo" means to be caused to assume the consequences.

"This too is an indeterminate matter" means this too is a matter that has not been determined as a specific downfall.

The rules concerning the establishment of a downfall, the manner of inquiring into its essential nature, and the conduct in accordance with the determination of its essential nature are to be understood as before.

The two indeterminate matters are complete.

In summary:
Retaining, losing, establishing —

entering, taking,
begging, upper robe, lower robe —
each article assessed and conveyed at its proper value.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there arose among the monks this situation of having an excess of robes. Some monks were spreading their robes flat on the floor of the shrine hall. Others were rolling them up neatly. Others were rubbing them with a paste of heavy clay. Others were washing their hands and feet with them. Others were using them to discard their tooth-sticks. Others were wearing them to go on alms rounds in the village. Others were laying them out on the rows of food. Others were going about wearing them to visit their preceptors and teachers. Others were wearing them to listen to the Teacher's instructions. Others were wearing them to listen to the Dharma during the day. Others were wearing them to listen to the Dharma at night. When they put on and took off these robes, there was much busyness and much activity, and it caused them to neglect scriptural recitation, reading, chanting, yogic practice, mental application, and the inner stillness of calm abiding of the mind.

A certain monk of few wants said: "Why has this situation arisen among the monks — this excess of robes — such that some monks spread their robes flat on the floor of the shrine hall, others roll them up neatly, others rub them with a paste of heavy clay, others wash their hands and feet with them, others use them to discard their tooth-sticks, others wear them to go on alms rounds in the village, others lay them out on the rows of food, others go about wearing them to visit their preceptors and teachers, others wear them to listen to the Teacher's instructions, others wear them to listen to the Dharma during the day, others wear them to listen to the Dharma at night — and when they put on and take off these robes, there is much busyness and much activity, causing them to neglect scriptural recitation, reading, chanting, yogic practice, mental application, and the inner stillness of calm abiding of the mind?" He rebuked them, expressed disapproval, and spoke against them. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in connection with this founding case and in this context, convened an assembly of the community of monks. The Tathāgata convened the assembly of monks having seen the twofold purpose: namely, so that all my hearers might come to know, and so that I may properly establish a foundation for training in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, inquires knowingly — inquiring knowingly, yet not inquiring unknowingly; inquiring at the right time, not inquiring outside the right time; inquiring when it is purposeful, not inquiring when it is not purposeful. Thus the Blessed One, the Buddha, repels with a fence inquiring when it is not purposeful. And as for the Blessed One, the Buddha, when inquiring with purpose, he knows the right time. Therefore the Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned the monks: "Monks, has this situation of an excess of robes arisen among you — such that some monks spread their robes flat on the floor of the shrine hall, others roll them up neatly, others rub them with a paste of heavy clay, others wash their hands and feet with them, others use them to discard their tooth-sticks, others wear them to go on alms rounds in the village —"

others spread them out among the food dishes; others wear them when going to visit their preceptors and teachers; others use them while receiving the Teacher's oral instructions; others use them while listening to the Dharma during the day; others use them while listening to the Dharma at night — and while you put on and take off robes in this way, you have many duties and many tasks, and you neglect recitation, reading, chanting, yoga, mental application, and the inner calm abiding of the mind. Is this true?" "Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, then censured those who are difficult to support, difficult to satisfy, who have great desires, and who do not know contentment. Then the Blessed One praised being easy to support, easy to satisfy, having few desires, knowing contentment, being restrained, maintaining few possessions, cultivating good qualities, being beautiful in conduct, and knowing measure. Having spoken these praises, he declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits fully and truly, a rule of training in the Vinaya is to be laid down for the hearers. It is this: for the sake of uniting the Saṅgha; for the sake of making the Saṅgha excellent; for the sake of the Saṅgha dwelling at ease; for the sake of cutting off those persons who are shameless and difficult to admonish; for the sake of those who feel shame dwelling at ease; for the sake of those without faith coming to have faith; for the sake of increasing the faith of those who already have faith; for the sake of restraining the defilements of this very life; for the sake of turning back those of future lives; and so that this pure conduct of mine, which brings benefit to the many, widely taught with full exactness among gods and humans, may long endure."

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: When a monk has obtained a robe fabric and it is sturdy and ready to be straightened out, he is to maintain three robes. If he keeps more than that, it is an offense of relinquishment." Thus the Blessed One laid down this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. At that time the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was sitting at the foot of a tree in a forest hermitage near Rājagṛha. Now at the time when the Blessed One had placed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa in charge of the Saṅgha, a certain householder had long been wishing: "Ah, if only I could offer the Elder Mahākāśyapa — who is worshipped by gods and humans — a meal and cover him with a great length of fine cloth, would that not be fitting?" But that wish had not yet been fulfilled. So that householder took a great length of fine cloth and went to where the Venerable Ānanda was. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, do you know at present where the Elder Mahākāśyapa is staying?" "Householder, I have heard that he is sitting at the foot of a tree in a forest hermitage." "When might he come?" "On this very occasion of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony." "Venerable Ānanda, please be aware of this: I have long been wishing — 'Ah, if only I could offer the Elder Mahākāśyapa, who is worshipped by gods and humans, a meal and cover him with a great length of fine cloth, would that not be fitting?' — and I have come bringing that great length of fine cloth. Venerable Ānanda, please be aware of this. We householders have many duties and many tasks,

"Ah, Venerable Ānanda, out of your compassionate regard for me, please present this great length of fine cloth to the Elder Mahākāśyapa, who is worshipped by gods and humans."

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself: "If I accept the great length of fine cloth from the householder, the rule of training may be undermined. But if I do not accept it, that too would obstruct the merit of the householder and obstruct the Elder Mahākāśyapa's receiving a gift. If I were to accept it, there may also be grounds on which the Blessed One would grant permission, since the time is right." And so the Venerable Ānanda accepted the great length of fine cloth from the householder and went to where the Blessed One was. On arriving, he bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported the whole matter to the Blessed One in detail.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, excellent, excellent! You knew what I had permitted. Therefore I now permit monks to keep, for up to ten days without designating it as allowable, a robe that is extra beyond what has been consecrated."

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of those who desire training, those who are respectful toward training, those who have devoted themselves to the training's implements, those of refined virtue, those of fine character, and those of measured conduct, declared to the monks: "Monks, what was stated before was a rule, and this is a permission. My hearers should learn this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: when a monk has received robes and the rains retreat is over, he should keep, for up to ten days without designating it as allowable, a robe that is extra beyond what has been consecrated. If he keeps it beyond that, it is an offence of forfeiture."

The word "monk" refers to one who is in this Dharma. As for the phrase "when a monk has received robes and the rains retreat is over," there are four cases: there may be receiving of robes without the rains retreat being over; there may be the rains retreat being over without receiving of robes; there may be both receiving of robes and the rains retreat being over; and there may be neither receiving of robes nor the rains retreat being over.

Now, what constitutes receiving of robes without the rains retreat being over? It is this: when a monk has washed, wrung, scrubbed, and turned the robes, but the Saṅgha has not yet released the rains retreat. That is what constitutes receiving of robes without the rains retreat being over.

What constitutes the rains retreat being over without receiving of robes? It is this: when a monk has not yet washed, wrung, scrubbed, and turned the robes, but the Saṅgha has released the rains retreat. That is what constitutes the rains retreat being over without receiving of robes.

What constitutes both receiving of robes and the rains retreat being over? It is this: when a monk has washed, wrung, scrubbed, and turned the robes, and the Saṅgha has also released the rains retreat. That is what constitutes the rains retreat being over and the robes being received.

What constitutes neither receiving of robes nor the rains retreat being over? It is any situation other than the foregoing three.

As for "up to ten days," this means up to the end of ten nights. "Extra beyond what has been consecrated" means beyond what has been set apart through consecration. "Without designating it as allowable" means without having examined it. "Keep" means to hold it as one's own. "If he keeps it beyond that" means if he keeps it past that point. "An offence of forfeiture" means that after forfeiting the object, the transgression of the forfeiture offence is to be confessed. That is why it is said to be an offence of forfeiture.


The Vinaya Analysis, twenty-fifth bundle.


Now, how does the transgression occur? It is as follows:

If a monk obtains a robe on the first day of the fortnight, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor designates it as allowable, nor gives it to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

Even if he does not obtain a robe on the first day, should he obtain one on the second day, or the third day, or the ninth day, or up to and including the tenth day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor designates it as allowable, nor gives it to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk obtains one robe on the first day and then obtains another robe on the second day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the first and give away the second, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another; or alternatively, consecrate the second and give away the first, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

Even if he does not obtain a robe on the first or second day, should he obtain one between the third day and the tenth day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the first and give away the second, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another; or alternatively, consecrate the second and give away the first, or designate it as allowable, or give it to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk obtains two robes on the first day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate those two robes, or give them away, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates them, nor gives them away, nor designates them as allowable, nor gives them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

Even if he does not obtain two robes on the first day, should he obtain two robes on the second day, or the third day, or the ninth day, or up to and including the tenth day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate those two robes, or give them away, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates them, nor gives them away, nor designates them as allowable, nor gives them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk obtains two robes on the first day and then obtains two further robes on the second day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the first two and give away the latter two, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another; or alternatively, consecrate the latter two and give away the first two, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk does not obtain robes on the first or second day but obtains two robes any time from the third day up through the tenth day, then that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the first two and give away the latter two, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another; or alternatively, consecrate the latter two and give away the first two, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk obtains many robes on the first day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate those robes, or give them away, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk does not obtain many robes on the first day but obtains many robes on the second day, or the third day, or the ninth day, or any day up through the tenth day, then that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate those robes, or give them away, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk obtains many robes on the first day and then obtains further many robes on the second day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either consecrate the first lot and give away the latter lot, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another; or alternatively, consecrate the latter lot and give away the first lot, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither consecrates, nor gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk does not obtain many robes on the first or second day but obtains many robes any time from the third day up through the tenth day, that monk must, within those very ten days, either give away the first lot, or designate them as allowable, or give them to another. If he neither gives away, nor designates as allowable, nor gives to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offence of forfeiture.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and without having relinquished it or separated himself from it, and without having confessed the transgression, he obtains another robe, that new robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by continuity with the first.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished it but without having separated himself from it, and without having confessed the transgression, he obtains another robe, that new robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by continuity with the first.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished it and separated himself from it, but without having confessed the transgression, he obtains another robe, that new robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by continuity with the first.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished it and separated himself from it, and having confessed the transgression, he then obtains another robe, there is no transgression with respect to that robe.

Likewise, for as long as a monk has not confessed and individually declared a forfeitable article, if he makes use of or takes up any other requisite whatsoever — whether an alms bowl, a Dharma robe, a strainer, a cup, a belt, or any other implement for the livelihood of a renunciant — that too becomes subject to forfeiture by continuity with the first.

There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

This completes the first section on forfeiture through possession.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the following situation arose among the monks — an abundance of Dharma robes. A certain monk who had undertaken the rains retreat obtained a Dharma robe, washed it, mended it, sewed it up, turned it over, bundled it into a roll of patches, and then entrusted it to the monks who were residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis, saying: "Monks, go wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes." And those monks, going wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes, did so without concealing them or causing them to be hidden.

The monks who were residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis then had much work and many tasks with those Dharma robes — drying them, airing them, spreading them out, shaking them, beating them, and storing them — so that they abandoned the recitation of scripture, the reading of texts, chanting, yoga practice, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding of mind.

For this reason, those monks of few concerns censured, criticized, and complained: "Why is it that such an abundance of Dharma robes has come about among the monks? A certain monk who had undertaken the rains retreat obtained a Dharma robe, washed it, mended it, sewed it up, turned it over, bundled it into a roll of patches, and entrusted it to the monks residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis, saying: 'Monks, go wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes.' And those monks go wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes without concealing them or causing them to be hidden. And the monks residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis have much work and many tasks with those Dharma robes — drying them, airing them, spreading them out, shaking them, beating them, and storing them — so that they abandon the recitation of scripture, the reading of texts, chanting, yoga practice, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding of mind."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this grounds for the rule, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and so forth, as before. The Blessed Buddhas, though they know, yet inquire — and so forth, likewise as before.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned the many monks: "Monks, is it true that this abundance of Dharma robes has come about among you — that a certain monk who had undertaken the rains retreat obtained a Dharma robe, washed it, mended it, sewed it up, turned it over, bundled it into a roll of patches, and entrusted it to the monks residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis, saying: 'Monks, go wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes' — and that you, going wandering the provinces wearing upper and lower Dharma robes, did so without concealing them or causing them to be hidden; and that the monks residing there permanently and on an ongoing basis, having much work and many tasks with those Dharma robes — drying them, airing them, spreading them out, shaking them, beating them, and storing them — abandon the recitation of scripture, the reading of texts, chanting, yoga practice, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding of mind?"

"Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, then censured those who are difficult to support, difficult to satisfy, who have great desires, and who do not know contentment. Thereupon the Blessed One praised those who are easy to support, easy to satisfy, who have few desires, who know contentment, who are scrupulous, who use few requisites, and —

who are trained in refinement and elegance, and who know moderation — having uttered such praises, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, seeing precisely ten benefits, the rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, as before. The rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established in this way: if a monk who has received his robes wrings them out because they are damp, and even for a single night separates any one of his three robes from him beyond the boundary, that is an offense entailing forfeiture.

Thus did the Blessed One establish the rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. At that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling in Rājagṛha in a cave of the Saptaparṇī, observing the rules of the restoration ceremony in harmony with the Saṅgha. A great many monks were also seated in harmony in the place of the restoration ceremony on that very fifteenth day of the restoration, waiting above all for the venerable Mahākāśyapa to arrive. Then, as the venerable Mahākāśyapa was going to the place of the restoration ceremony, a noble river swollen with the fine summer floods came rushing over, and a great wave arose and soaked his patched outer robe. The venerable Mahākāśyapa then wrung out that patched robe, aired it, and spread it to dry, and it took him a long while. After squeezing it out, airing it, and drying it, the venerable Mahākāśyapa went to the place of the restoration ceremony, and having arrived, he sat down right where a seat had been laid out for him before the assembly of monks.

Then the great many monks addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa with these words: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, please take note. Here we, a great many monks, have been seated in harmony in the place of the restoration ceremony, waiting above all for the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and yet the venerable Mahākāśyapa has been delayed. Venerable one, here, on the way to the restoration ceremony, a noble river swollen with the fine summer floods came rushing over, and a great wave arose and soaked my patched robe. As I was wringing out that patched robe, airing it, and drying it, it took me quite a long while. Venerable ones, now I, the monk Mahākāśyapa, am old, aged, and advanced in years, and since I am not strong enough to fully manage the patched robe on account of its heaviness, what am I to do?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should grant permission to the monk Mahākāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, and to any others who are similarly situated, to not be separated from their patched robe. It is to be granted in this way: having prepared a seat, striking the wooden signal board, and duly informing the monks with the words of the motion, an assembly of all the monks who are seated in harmony within the boundary — no fewer than a quorum of four monks — shall convene, and the monk Kāśyapa, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, shall bow in order of seniority, then sit on his heels at the edge of the senior monks, join his palms, present his patched robe to the Saṅgha, and speak these words: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me.
