I, the monk Kāśyapa, am old, aged, and advanced in years, and since I am not strong enough to fully manage my patched robe on account of its heaviness, I, the monk Kāśyapa, who am old, aged, and advanced in years, request from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from my patched robe.

May the compassionate venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, grant to me, the monk Kāśyapa, who am old, aged, and advanced in years, permission to not be separated from my patched robe.' This is to be repeated a second and a third time.

After that, one monk shall make the motion and perform the act. 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk Kāśyapa is old, aged, and advanced in years, and since he is not strong enough to fully manage his patched robe on account of its heaviness, this monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, requests from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from his patched robe. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it is agreeable, may the Saṅgha grant permission to the monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, to not be separated from his patched robe. This is the motion. The act shall be performed as follows. May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk Kāśyapa is old, aged, and advanced in years, and since he is not strong enough to fully manage his patched robe on account of its heaviness, this monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, requests from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from his patched robe. Therefore, if the Saṅgha grants to the monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, permission to not be separated from his patched robe, then those venerable ones who consent to granting the monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, permission to not be separated from his patched robe shall remain silent, and those who do not consent shall speak. The Saṅgha, having consented and agreed, has granted to the monk Kāśyapa, who is old, aged, and advanced in years, permission to not be separated from his patched robe. So it is held, since no one has spoken. The Saṅgha has granted to whichever monk permission to not be separated from his patched robe; that monk may travel about wearing the upper and lower robes together with it, and there should be no regret in this.'

At that time the venerable Śāriputra was present in that very assembly and was in agreement. Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the monks: 'Venerable ones, I, the monk Śāriputra, am afflicted with a wind ailment, and since I am not strong enough to fully manage my patched robe on account of its heaviness, what am I to do?' At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, grant to the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, and to any others who are likewise afflicted, permission to not be separated from their patched robes. It is to be granted in this manner: having prepared the lodging, having struck the wooden signal-board, having properly instructed the monks with the words of inquiry, a Saṅgha of not fewer than four monks shall all be present and in agreement in the center of the assembly. The monk Śāriputra shall arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, bow in order of seniority, then sit on his heels at the edge of the senior monks, join his palms, present his patched robe to the Saṅgha, and speak these words: "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the monk Śāriputra, am afflicted with a wind ailment, and since I am not strong enough to fully manage my patched robe on account of its heaviness, I, the monk Śāriputra, who am afflicted with a wind ailment, request from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from my patched robe. May the compassionate venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, grant to me, the monk Śāriputra, who am afflicted with a wind ailment, permission to not be separated from my patched robe." This is to be repeated a second and a third time.

Following that, one monk is to make the motion and perform the formal act. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. The monk Śāriputra is afflicted with a wind ailment, and since he is not strong enough to fully manage his patched robe on account of its heaviness, the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, requests from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from his patched robe. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it is agreeable, may the Saṅgha grant that permission. The Saṅgha grants to the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, permission to not be separated from his patched robe. This is the motion."

The formal act is to be performed as follows. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. The monk Śāriputra is afflicted with a wind ailment, and since he is not strong enough to fully manage his patched robe on account of its heaviness, the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, requests from the Saṅgha permission to not be separated from his patched robe. Therefore, if the Saṅgha grants to the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, permission to not be separated from his patched robe, those venerable ones who consent to granting the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, permission to not be separated from his patched robe should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha, having consented and approved, has granted to the monk Śāriputra, who is afflicted with a wind ailment, permission to not be separated from his patched robe. This is accepted as such, since no one has spoken."

If the Saṅgha grants any monk whatsoever permission to not be separated from his patched robe, that monk may go about wearing both his upper and lower robes, and he should have no regret in this matter.

Then the Blessed One praised those who wish to train, spoke of their virtue, and spoke of the virtues of those who are respectful toward the training, those who are zealous in equipping themselves for the training, those who are thin, those who possess the qualities of thorough purification, those who are graceful, and those who know moderation — and then declared to the monks: "Monks, for this reason what was before was a rule, and this is now a permission. My hearers are to recite this as a basis of training in the Vinaya as follows: Should a monk who has obtained robes take them out to be aired and then separate himself, even for a single night, from any one of his three robes beyond the boundary — except by permission of the Saṅgha — that is an offense requiring forfeiture and confession."

"Monk" refers to one of this Dharma. "Who has obtained robes and takes them out to be aired" — there is the case of one who has obtained robes but has not taken them out to be aired; one who has not obtained robes but has taken them out to be aired; one who has obtained robes and has taken them out to be aired; and one who has not obtained robes and has not taken them out to be aired. These are to be elaborated in four branches as before. "Even for a single night" means even at the end of a single night. "Any one of his three robes" means any one of the patched robe, the upper robe, and the under robe. "Separates himself beyond the boundary" means causing dawn to break elsewhere. "Except by permission of the Saṅgha" means setting aside permission granted by the Saṅgha. "An offense requiring forfeiture and confession" means that after forfeiting that object, the transgression of the forfeiture offense is to be confessed — that is why it is called an offense requiring forfeiture and confession.

As for how a transgression arises in this regard, the intermediate summary in verse:

One dwelling, two dwellings,
a dwelling shared by a group,
encircled by a wall, a fence, or a ditch —
these four constitute a village or homestead.
A way-station, a non-Buddhist establishment, a marketplace,
a shop, a music hall, a battlefield,

a naval vessel, a chariot, a tree grove, a pleasure park —
these are the intermediate summary, complete.

A village having one dwelling, a village having two dwellings, a village having a group of dwellings, a village encircled by a wall, a village encircled by a fence, a village encircled by a ditch — these are to be understood as the four types: a village with a single surrounding area, a village with separate surrounding areas, many villages with a single surrounding area, and many villages with separate surrounding areas. A single household with a single surrounding area, a single household with separate surrounding areas, many households with a single surrounding area, many households with separate surrounding areas. A householder's dwelling with a single surrounding area, a householder's dwelling with separate surrounding areas, many householders' dwellings with a single surrounding area, many householders' dwellings with separate surrounding areas. A tīrthika's dwelling with a single surrounding area, a tīrthika's dwelling with separate surrounding areas, many tīrthikas' dwellings with a single surrounding area, many tīrthikas' dwellings with separate surrounding areas. A marketplace with a single surrounding area, a marketplace with separate surrounding areas, many marketplaces with a single surrounding area, many marketplaces with separate surrounding areas. A shop with a single surrounding area, a shop with separate surrounding areas, many shops with a single surrounding area, many shops with separate surrounding areas. A music hall with a single surrounding area, a music hall with separate surrounding areas, many music halls with a single surrounding area, many music halls with separate surrounding areas. A battlefield with a single surrounding area, a battlefield with separate surrounding areas, many battlefields with a single surrounding area, many battlefields with separate surrounding areas. A military encampment with a single surrounding area, a military encampment with separate surrounding areas, many military encampments with a single surrounding area, many military encampments with separate surrounding areas. A vessel with a single surrounding area, a vessel with separate surrounding areas, many vessels with a single surrounding area, many vessels with separate surrounding areas. A chariot with a single surrounding area, a chariot with separate surrounding areas, many chariots with a single surrounding area, many chariots with separate surrounding areas. A tree grove with a single surrounding area, a tree grove with separate surrounding areas, many tree groves with a single surrounding area, many tree groves with separate surrounding areas. A pleasure park with a single surrounding area, a pleasure park with separate surrounding areas, many pleasure parks with a single surrounding area, many pleasure parks with separate surrounding areas.

By means of these distinctions — traveling on a road and so forth, going straight ahead and so forth, and the distinctions of what is shared and what is not shared among the other boundary-zones — the transgressions of a monk's being separated from and not being separated from his Dharma robes are set forth in extensive detail.

Now, what is a village having one dwelling? It is, for example, the villages of forest-dwellers, Tibetans, and border peoples. And what is the surrounding area of such a village? It is the entire interior, and one arrow's length beyond the exterior — or the distance within which people carry out their threshing, winnowing, weaving, cooking, eating, drinking, and whatever children do. That is the surrounding area of such a village.

If a monk leaves his Dharma robes inside and dawn breaks while he is in the surrounding area, there is no transgression. If he leaves his Dharma robes in the surrounding area and dawn breaks while he is inside, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his Dharma robes inside or in the surrounding area and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village having two dwellings? It is just as with a village having one dwelling — a village having two dwellings is the same in that regard.

What is a village having a collection of dwellings? It is one that is inhabited from many gates on all sides. What is its surrounding area? Each part is separate and distinct. What do they share in common? Nothing whatsoever.

What is a walled village? It is a village that is enclosed by a wall. What is its surrounding area? It is the entire interior, and one fathom beyond the exterior — or the distance within which a cart drawn by six oxen and loaded with bamboo can be covered, and as far as a crow will fly up and alight. That is the surrounding area of such a village. If a monk leaves his Dharma robes inside and dawn breaks while he is in the surrounding area, there is no transgression. If he leaves his Dharma robes in the surrounding area and dawn breaks while he is inside, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his Dharma robes inside or in the surrounding area and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village enclosed by a palisade? It is a village that is enclosed by a palisade. What is its surrounding area? It is the entire interior, and one fathom beyond the exterior — or the distance within which the dust raised by the hooves of goats and sheep being driven out settles, and as far as a person who by nature has a sense of modesty will go to relieve himself. That is the surrounding area of such a village. If a monk leaves his Dharma robes inside and dawn breaks while he is in the surrounding area, there is no transgression. If he leaves his Dharma robes in the surrounding area and dawn breaks while he is inside, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his Dharma robes inside or in the surrounding area and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village enclosed by a moat? It is a village that is enclosed by a moat. What is its surrounding area? It is the entire interior, and one fathom beyond the exterior — or the distance within which a ladder of twelve rungs can lie flat, and as far as the coarse sound of a donkey braying after having been struck with a cloth can be heard. That is the surrounding area of such a village. If a monk leaves his Dharma robes inside and dawn breaks while he is in the surrounding area, there is no transgression. If he leaves his Dharma robes in the surrounding area and dawn breaks while he is inside, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his Dharma robes inside or in the surrounding area and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village having a single surrounding area? It is a village in which there is a single pleasure grove, or assembly ground, or divine abode. What is its surrounding area? Each part is separate and distinct. What do they share in common? The divine abode. If a monk leaves his Dharma robes in the village and dawn breaks at the divine abode, there is no transgression. If he leaves his Dharma robes at the divine abode and dawn breaks in the village, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his Dharma robes in the village or at the divine abode and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

What is a village having separate surrounding areas? It is a village in which there are many pleasure groves, assembly grounds, or divine abodes. What is its surrounding area? Each part is separate and distinct. What do they share in common? Nothing whatsoever.

What is the case of many villages having a single surrounding area? It is the case of villages in which there is a single pleasure grove, assembly ground, or divine abode. What are the surrounding areas of those villages? Each is separate and distinct.

What do they share in common? The divine abode. If a monk leaves his robes in the village and dawn breaks at the divine abode, there is no transgression. If he leaves his robes at the divine abode and dawn breaks in the village, there is likewise no transgression. But if he leaves his robes in the village or at the divine abode and dawn breaks elsewhere, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture.

The venerable Upāli then addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, if a monk entrusts his robes to another monk and sets out traveling the road, what is the surrounding area for those robes?" Upāli continued: "I put it to you that there is a brahmin's field in which stand seven mango trees in full blossom, with abundant fruit and abundant branches, separated from one another by intervals of seven armspans — and for each of those seven mango trees, forty-nine armspans are indicated. That is the surrounding area for the robes of a monk who has set out upon the road. The surrounding area for standing, sitting, or lying down is one armspan in every direction. The surrounding area for traveling straight ahead is likewise one armspan in every direction. The surrounding area for standing, sitting, or lying down in a straight line is also one armspan in every direction."

"Venerable Sir, if a monk goes to a different district and lies down to sleep there, what is the surrounding area for his robes?" Upāli replied: "It extends as far as the hem of the robe has not been separated from him."

If a monk becomes subject to relinquishment of a robe — if he has not relinquished it, not given it up, and not confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another — that other robe as well is to be relinquished by virtue of the same prior continuum. If a monk becomes subject to relinquishment of a robe — if he has not relinquished it, has given it up, and has not confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another — that other robe as well is to be relinquished by virtue of the same prior continuum. If a monk becomes subject to relinquishment of a robe — if he has relinquished it, has given it up, and has not confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another — that other robe as well is to be relinquished by virtue of the same prior continuum. If a monk becomes subject to relinquishment of a robe — if he has relinquished it, has given it up, and has confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another — there is no transgression with regard to that other robe.

Likewise, for as long as a monk who has become subject to relinquishment of an object has not confessed it separately and individually, if he acquires and keeps close at hand any other item — whether an alms bowl, robes, a net, a small bowl, a belt, or any other article used for the livelihood of a renunciant — that too shall be relinquished by virtue of the same prior continuum. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The second category, relinquishment through separation, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, there arose among the monks a situation of having many robes of the following kind: when any monk obtained a blue robe, he would not use it straightaway but would set it aside with the hope, "When I obtain another one like this, I will have the robe made" — and just as with the blue, so too with the yellow, the red, the thick, and the thin.

Monks of few wants began to criticize, to complain, and to grumble: "Why is it that among the monks there arose this situation of having many robes of the following kind — that when any monk obtained a blue robe, he would not use it straightaway but would set it aside with the hope, 'When I obtain another one like this, I will have the robe made' — and just as with the blue, so too with the yellow, the red, the thick, and the thin?"

At that point the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon, on account of this occurrence, on account of this occasion, and in this context, convened the community of monks — and the rest proceeds as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, act as though they do not know" — and the rest, again, is as before.

The Blessed One questioned the many monks: "Monks, is it true that among you such an accumulation of robes has occurred as this — that whenever any monk obtains a blue robe, he does not put it to use straightaway, but sets it aside with the hope, 'When I obtain another one like this, I will have the robe made,' and that just as with the blue, so too with the yellow, the red, the thick, and the thin?"

"Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed One then rebuked great desire, not knowing contentment, being difficult to support, and being difficult to satisfy. Thereafter, the Blessed One praised little desire, contentment, ease of support, ease of satisfaction, the quality of being frugal, simplicity of requisites, refinement of character, beauty, and awareness of warmth — and then addressed the monks:

"Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits in full, a rule of training for the hearers is to be established in the Vinaya" — and the rest proceeds as before. "Let my hearers recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

If a monk whose robe-season has been received has the robe-material raised from storage, and if an out-of-season robe is obtained and he desires it, that monk may take that robe. Having taken it, if it suffices, he should promptly have it consecrated and kept as a robe without delay. If it does not suffice and there is hope that out-of-season cloth will supplement what is lacking, that monk may set that robe aside for up to a month. If he keeps it beyond that, it is an offense requiring forfeiture."

"Monk" refers to one who is a member of this Dharma community.

"Whose robe-season has been received and who has raised robe-material from storage" — here there are four cases: the robe-season received but the robe-material not raised from storage; the robe-season not received but the robe-material raised; the robe-season received and the robe-material raised; and the robe-season not received and the robe-material not raised — these four permutations are as before.

"An out-of-season robe" — one asks: what is the season for robes for a monk, and what is the out-of-season? In a place where the rains retreat is observed, the months from mid-autumn to the end of mid-spring constitute the robe season; beyond that is out-of-season. In a place where the rains retreat is not observed, all times are out-of-season.

"Obtained" means obtained from another.

"If he desires it" means if he seeks it out.

"That monk may take that robe" means he may make it his own.

"If it suffices" means if it is adequate.

"He should promptly have it consecrated and kept as a robe without delay" means he should consecrate it without putting it away and keep it.

"Supplement what is lacking" refers to supplementing what is incomplete in the lower robe, the upper robe, or the outer robe.

"If there is hope of obtaining a robe" means there is hope that a mother, father, sibling, sister, preceptor, or abbot will give a robe to oneself; or hope that a robe will be obtained at the occasion of the five-year festival, the six-year festival, the hair-cutting festival, the dwelling-house festival, or at the time of a great festival.

"That monk may set that robe aside for up to a month" means up to the limit of one month.

"If he keeps it beyond that" means if he goes past that limit.

"An offense requiring forfeiture" means that after having forfeited the article, the offense requiring forfeiture must be confessed. Therefore it is said to be an offense requiring forfeiture.

As for how the offense arises, there is a summary verse:

With doubt and without doubt,
deteriorated and not accomplished,
interrupted, the five robes and the two robes,
combinations, and the measures.

A monk, having obtained a blue robe on a particular date, does not put it into use, thinking, "When I find one like this, I will put the robe into use then" — and so he sets it aside. If on that very same date he then obtains another blue robe that is doubtful, that monk must, within those ten days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find one on the first day, but finds a blue robe on the second day, the third day, or any day up to the tenth, that monk must, within those ten days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find one within those ten days but finds one by the nineteenth day, that monk must, within those twenty days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the twentieth day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find one on the twentieth day but finds one by the twenty-ninth day, that monk must, within that same month, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the thirty-first day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to finding a blue robe applies equally to a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe.

A monk, having obtained a blue robe on a particular date, does not put it into use — having no expectation of finding one like it, he sets it aside — and if on that very same date he then obtains another blue robe that is not doubtful, that monk must, within those ten days, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find one on the first day, but on the second day or any day up to the tenth, or by the nineteenth, or by the twenty-ninth, he finds a blue robe, that monk must, within that same month, either consecrate that robe, or give it away, or make it allowable, or bestow it upon another. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the thirty-first day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to finding a blue robe applies equally to a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe.

A monk, having obtained a blue robe on a particular date, does not put it into use — he sets it aside with expectation regarding that robe — and that expectation he had regarding it has deteriorated, been delayed, and diminished, and then on that very same date he finds another blue robe.

That monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within those same ten days. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find it on the first day of the month but finds a blue robe on the second day of the month, or at any point up to the tenth day of the month, that monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within that same month. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the thirty-first day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to finding a blue robe applies equally to a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe.

A monk, having obtained a blue robe on a particular date, does not put it into use — he sets it aside with expectation, and that expectation he had regarding it has not yet been fulfilled, and has not yet been cut off — and then on that very same date he finds another blue robe. That monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within those same ten days. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find it on the first day of the month but finds one on the second day of the month, or at any point up to the twenty-ninth day, that monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within that same month. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the thirty-first day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to finding a blue robe applies equally to a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe.

A monk, having obtained a blue robe on a particular date, does not put it into use — he sets it aside with expectation — and every last bit of the expectation he had regarding that robe has been entirely cut off. That monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within those same ten days. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If he did not find it on the first day but finds one on the second day of the month, or at any point up to the twenty-ninth day, and does not put it into use but sets it aside with expectation, and every last bit of the expectation he had regarding that robe has been entirely cut off, that monk must consecrate that robe, give it away, make it allowable, or bestow it upon another within those same ten days. If he neither consecrates it, nor gives it away, nor makes it allowable, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eleventh day an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to a blue robe applies equally to a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe.

The venerable Upāli then addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha.

Venerable one, there are several kinds of robes. There are five in the adjacent category: a robe that has an owner, a robe that has no owner, a robe that has been taken back, a robe from a charnel ground, and fifth, a robe that has been cast aside as a rag.

What is a robe that has an owner? Any robe over which a man, a woman, or a person of indeterminate sex has ownership — that is called a robe that has an owner.

What is a robe that has no owner? Any robe over which no man, no woman, and no person of indeterminate sex has ownership — that is called a robe that has no owner.

What is a robe that has been taken back? It is like this: relatives, knowing that one of their kin has fallen ill, has died, or that the right moment has come, cover him with a robe from behind, carry him to the charnel ground, and then take that robe back again and present it to the Saṅgha. That is called a robe that has been taken back.

What is a robe from a charnel ground? Whatever robe has been taken from a charnel ground that has no one claiming ownership over it — that is called a robe from a charnel ground.

What is a robe cast aside as a rag? There are five kinds of robes cast aside as rags: a robe left on a road, one abandoned in a desolate place, one found on a riverbank, one that is excrement-soiled, and fifth, one that is tattered — and "tattered" means one that is thoroughly moth-eaten.

Furthermore, there are another five kinds of robes cast aside as rags: one burned by fire, one carried away by water, one eaten by rats, one eaten by oxen, and fifth, a shroud used for a corpse.

There are also two further kinds of robe: a new robe and a robe used in a particular season. What is a new robe? One freshly woven by a weaver that has not yet been used during any one of the three seasonal periods — that is called a new robe. What is a robe used in a particular season? One that has been used during any one of the three seasonal periods — and "a season" means four months — that is called a robe used in a particular season.

If a monk obtains a new robe, and if that monk is able to cut, stripe, net, sew, and alter it, then from that robe he should make a patched outer robe with two layers of stitching, an inner robe also with two layers of stitching, an upper robe of a single layer, and an under robe also of a single layer.

If a monk unravels the third layer of stitching in a double-stitched patched outer robe, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise. If a monk, intending to restitch it differently from the double stitching, pulls out a layer of stitching, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of pulling it out, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise. If a monk washes a double-stitched patched outer robe, turns it over, and intending to restitch it in that very same manner pulls out a layer of stitching, no offense arises at the moment of pulling it out; but if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

Whatever applies to the patched outer robe applies equally to the inner robe.

If a monk unravels the stitching of a single-layer upper robe, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise. Whatever applies to the upper robe applies equally to the under robe.

If a monk obtains a robe used in a particular season, and if that monk is able to cut, stripe, net, sew, and alter it, then from that robe he should make a patched outer robe with four layers of stitching, an inner robe also with four layers of stitching, an upper robe with two layers, and an under robe also with two layers.

If a monk unravels the fifth layer of stitching in a four-layered patched outer robe, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If a monk unravels a layer of a four-layered patched outer robe intending to rework it into something other than what it was, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If a monk unravels a layer of a four-layered patched outer robe having washed it and turned it around, intending to rework it into that very same garment, no offense arises at the moment of unraveling; however, if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

What applies to the patched outer robe applies equally to the inner robe.

If a monk unravels the third layer of a two-layered upper robe, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If a monk unravels a layer of a two-layered upper robe intending to rework it into something other than what it was, an offense of wrongdoing arises at the moment of unraveling, and if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

If a monk unravels a layer of a two-layered upper robe having washed it and turned it around, intending to rework it into that very same garment, no offense arises at the moment of unraveling; however, if ten days pass, an offense requiring forfeiture will arise.

What applies to the upper robe applies equally to the under robe.

As for a hand-towel or bathing cloth, one may rework it as many layers as one wishes.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, how many strips does a patched outer robe have?" Upāli continued: "There are nine types. A robe with nine strips, one with eleven strips, one with thirteen strips, one with fifteen strips, one with seventeen strips, one with nineteen strips, one with twenty-one strips, one with twenty-three strips, and one with twenty-five strips."

He then explained: a nine-strip robe consists of three panels of three joined pieces each. An eleven-strip robe consists of three panels of three joined pieces plus two additional strips. A thirteen-strip robe consists of four panels of three joined pieces plus one additional strip. A fifteen-strip robe consists of five panels of three joined pieces each. A seventeen-strip robe consists of five panels of three joined pieces plus two additional strips. A nineteen-strip robe consists of six panels of three joined pieces plus one additional strip. A twenty-one-strip robe consists of seven panels of three joined pieces each. A twenty-three-strip robe consists of seven panels of three joined pieces plus two additional strips. A twenty-five-strip robe consists of eight panels of three joined pieces plus one additional strip.

Upāli explained further: a patched outer robe of nine strips, one of eleven strips, and one of thirteen strips — these three are to be made with a board one and a half cubits by three cubits and kept accordingly. A patched outer robe of fifteen strips, one of seventeen strips, and one of nineteen strips — these three are to be made with a board one and a half cubits by four cubits and kept accordingly. A patched outer robe of twenty-one strips, one of twenty-three strips, and one of twenty-five strips — these three are to be made with a board one and a half cubits by five cubits and kept accordingly.

All of these are to be sewn with a running stitch.

"Venerable One, what are the proper dimensions of a patched outer robe?" Upāli replied: "There are three sizes to be known: large, medium, and small. The large is three and a half cubits. The small is two and a half cubits. The medium is whatever falls between those two."

What applies to the patched outer robe applies equally to the upper robe and the under robe. Furthermore, the under robe comes in two forms: one that is five and a half cubits long, and one that is four and a half cubits long. The outermost of the under robes is one that covers three circuits of the body. The outermost of the forfeitable robes is one that covers exactly one cubit all the way around.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and before he has surrendered it, separated himself from it, and confessed the offense he obtains another robe, that robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuity.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and before he has surrendered it, separated himself from it, and confessed the offense he obtains another robe, that robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuity. If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and after he has surrendered it and separated himself from it, but before he has confessed the offense, he obtains another robe, that robe too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuity. If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and after he has surrendered it, separated himself from it, and confessed the offense he obtains another robe, there is no transgression regarding that robe.

Likewise, for as long as a monk, without having confessed the very forfeitable object in question and without having confessed it individually, proceeds to take possession of an alms bowl, a Dharma robe, a net, a cup, a belt, or any other requisite of a renunciant's livelihood, those too become subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuity. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is mentally disturbed, one whose mind is agitated, or one who acts while overcome by painful sensations. This completes the third section, on forfeiture through placing.

At the time when the Blessed One, as a bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, having examined the world through the five examinations — of clan, of region, of time, of lineage, and of mother — transformed his appearance into that of a great elephant and entered his mother's womb, the great earth trembled violently. And those regions between the worlds where the sun and moon, though possessed of such great miraculous power and such great might, cannot make their light felt — those regions plunged in darkness, dense darkness, utter darkness — were at that moment pervaded by a great radiance. The beings born there, who could not even see their own outstretched hands, beheld one another by that light, and those who had understanding knew: "Other beings too have been born here. Other beings too have been born here."

At the time when the Blessed One as a bodhisattva was born from his mother's womb after ten months had passed, the great earth trembled violently. And those regions between the worlds where the sun and moon, though possessed of such great miraculous power and such great might, cannot make their light felt — those regions plunged in darkness, dense darkness, utter darkness — were at that moment pervaded by a great radiance. The beings born there, who could not even see their own outstretched hands, beheld one another by that light, and those who had understanding knew: "Other beings too have been born here. Other beings too have been born here."

On the very day that the Blessed One as a bodhisattva was born, sons were also born to the four great kings. In Śrāvastī, the great king Prasenajit fathered a son named Vimala-datta, and he thought to himself: "When my son was born, the world appeared bright and luminous, so I shall give this youth the name Prasanna-rāja" — and thus he named that son Prasanna-rāja. In Rājagṛha, the great king Mahāpadma fathered a son, and he thought to himself: "When my son was born, the world appeared as though the form of the sun had risen, and since this child is the son of queen Rūpavatī, I shall give this youth the name Rūpavatī-sāra" — and thus he named that son Rūpavatī-sāra. In Kauśāmbī, the great king Śatānīka fathered a son, and he thought to himself: "When my son was born, the world appeared as though the sun had risen, so I shall give this youth the name Udaya" — and thus he named that son Udaya.

In Āryarājya, the great king Mukhyūda-Ananta fathered a son, and he thought to himself: "When my son was born, the world shone with a brilliant radiance, so I shall give this youth the name Prabhasvara" — and thus he named that son Prabhasvara.

Each of the kings thought to himself, "This is the power of my son, this is the power of my son." Yet in truth it was not so, for all of this was the power of the bodhisattva.

On the very day the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was born, five hundred young Śākya men, beginning with Bhadrika, were also born. Five hundred attendants and companions were also born. From five hundred mares, five hundred foals — beginning with the celebrated Kaṇṭhaka — were born. And the gods revealed five hundred treasures.

The Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was prophesied by brahmins and astrologers who read signs and marks: "If this youth remains within the palace, he will become a wheel-turning king who conquers the four quarters, a righteous king of Dharma, possessing the seven precious things. And these seven precious things will be as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the precious minister of war — these are the seven. He will have heroic and courageous sons, endowed with the finest form of limb, a full thousand who utterly vanquish the armies of his enemies. He will govern, without exception, all the great earth that reaches to the ocean's shore, without violence and without harm, unbroken and uncut by weapons, ruling in accord with Dharma, bringing it under his sway in equanimity and establishing it well. But if he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from home into homelessness with sincere and perfect faith, he will become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, renowned throughout the world, endowed with the voice of fame." Such was the prophecy.

When the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, appeared in the world, everywhere near the slopes of the Himālayas, along the banks of the auspicious river by the road of the fortunate chariot, near the hermitage of the yellow-robed sages, a young Śākya prince was born not far away. And the brahmins and astrologers, examining his signs and marks, proclaimed: "If this youth remains within the palace, he will become a wheel-turning king who conquers the four quarters, a righteous king of Dharma, possessing the seven precious things. And these seven precious things will be as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the precious minister of war — these are the seven. He will have heroic and courageous sons, endowed with the finest form of limb, a full thousand who utterly vanquish the armies of his enemies. He will govern, without exception, all the great earth that reaches to the ocean's shore, without violence and without harm, unbroken and uncut by weapons, ruling in accord with Dharma, bringing it under his sway in equanimity and establishing it well. But if he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from home into homelessness with sincere and perfect faith, he will become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, renowned throughout the world, endowed with the voice of fame." And this proclamation was resounded abroad.

The kings of the southern regions also heard the proclamation — that not far from the Himalayas, near a river, beside a road along which fortunate horses traveled, in the hermitage of the yellow-robed seers, a youth had been born among the Śākyas; and that Brahmin soothsayers and mark-readers had declared: if that youth were to remain within the palace, he would become a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), victorious in the four directions, a righteous king endowed with Dharma, possessed of the seven precious treasures. Those seven precious treasures would be as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious gem, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the precious general as the seventh. And he would have in his service a thousand valiant and resolute sons, endowed with the finest physiques, who crush enemy armies utterly. He would govern, without exception, all the great earth that reaches to the ocean's shore, without violence and without harm, unbroken and uncut by weapons, ruling in accord with Dharma, bringing it under his sway in equanimity and establishing it well. But if he were to shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from home into homelessness with sincere and perfect faith, he would become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with the voice of fame renowned throughout the world. Thus did they hear the proclamation.

Having heard it, those kings of the southern regions thought to themselves: if we serve this youth now, he will in due time yield his fruit — so what must we serve in order to serve the youth? They reasoned: we should serve King Śuddhodana, for by serving him we will be serving the youth. And so they began to serve King Śuddhodana, sending messengers with reverential offerings and treasure-chests at the fitting and appropriate times.

Then King Śuddhodana reflected: now that my son has been born, all aims have been accomplished and all purposes fulfilled; therefore I shall name this youth Sarvārthasiddha — "All Aims Accomplished." And he named him Sarvārthasiddha.

Now when the Blessed One was born as a great bodhisattva, and having seen an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, he was moved at heart and went forth into the forest — at that time, King Śuddhodana and the Śākya named Supratibuddha sent two hundred and fifty, two hundred and fifty messengers bearing petitions and supplications, and those messengers came bringing the word of the Blessed One, the great bodhisattva, saying: "Each day the youth sustains himself on a single sesame seed, or a single grain of thick rice, or a single bean of black pulse, or a single bean of green pulse, or a single grain of pine-nut, or a single bean of soybean."

When the kings of the southern regions heard that the youth Sarvārthasiddha had seen an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, had been moved at heart, and had gone forth into renunciation, they thought to themselves: the youth on whose account we were serving King Śuddhodana has now gone forth. And so all of them, with the sole exception of Prasenajit, the king from Kosala, cut off their reverential offerings — their messengers and their treasure-chests — entirely.

At that time, at the court of Prasenajit, king from Kosala, there was a chief minister named Bandhaka, and at the court of King Śuddhodana there was a herald named Ācāra. Whenever Prasenajit, the king from Kosala, dispatched a messenger to King Śuddhodana, he would send the chief minister Bandhaka,

He would perform the royal duties and the royal functions, and then he would gain entry into the household of Ācāra. And whenever King Śuddhodana dispatched a messenger to Prasenajit, king from Kosala, he would send the herald Ācāra. And Ācāra too would perform the royal duties and the royal functions, and then he would gain entry into the household of the chief minister Bandhaka. Now Bandhaka had a wife named Bandhamatī, who was fair of form, pleasing and beautiful to look upon, and charming to men. Ācāra entered into an intimate liaison with Bandhamatī. When Bandhaka came to know that Ācāra had entered into an intimate liaison with Bandhamatī, he thought to himself: I should kill him. But then he thought again: if I were to kill him, the two kingdoms would fall into great conflict, so why should I kill a brahmin on account of a woman's body? And so he let the matter rest in equanimity.

Then Ācāra, sensing in his mind that Bandhaka had taken offense at him, grew afraid, left the house, and took up residence elsewhere. Bandhaka then said to him: Ācāra, why have you abandoned your own home and taken up residence elsewhere? Come here. This is your own home — stay here as comfortably as you wish. Then Ācāra thought to himself: In truth, he has given me his permission, and so he remained there just as before.

The Vinayavibhaṅga. The twenty-seventh fascicle.

Then at another time, Bandhaka, the chief minister, died when his time had come, and Prasenajit, king from Kosala, had all of his wealth placed in his own treasury and vaults on account of his having no son. Bandhamatī sent a letter to Ācāra, saying: When my husband was alive and living, you came to visit me regularly. Now the time has come when he has died, and Prasenajit, king from Kosala, has placed all the wealth into his own treasury and vaults on account of there being no son — will you not now even send a word on my behalf?

Then Ācāra, having heard the contents of the letter, thought to himself: If I were to go there, on account of that very matter people would say: Ācāra went there because he is attached to women, because of a woman. I must therefore devise some skillful stratagem. And so, having performed the royal duties and the royal functions two or three times over, he went to the place where King Śuddhodana was and, having arrived, spoke to King Śuddhodana thus: O King, at the time when the youth who accomplishes all purposes was born, all the kings of the regions beneath the sun bowed down and all of them offered messengers and treasure-chests. Then, at the time when the youth who accomplishes all purposes saw an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, and was moved in heart and went forth into the forest, all those kings of the regions beneath the sun, with the exception of Prasenajit, king from Kosala, cut off the stream of their offerings of messengers and treasure-chests. But Prasenajit, king from Kosala, continued to send messengers and treasure-chests, and dispatched them. Now, to abandon in this way one who has been a steadfast companion would in the future be a great harm — he stands close to us, in connection and continuity, and it is therefore fitting to maintain that companionship. Ācāra, if that is so, you yourself should go as the messenger. O King, as you command, he replied. And so Ācāra took up the treasure-chests and set out toward Śrāvastī, and in due course arrived at Śrāvastī.

Then Ācāra thought to himself:

Since one ought not to rely on those unworthy of reliance, but rather rely on those worthy of reliance, I should first look to the ministers and then, through them, approach the king — so that I may plead on behalf of the bride. And so he began to approach the ministers and said: "Good sirs, surely you know how I was formerly acquainted with the bride? Her husband's time has come, and Prasenajit, king from Kosala, has caused all her wealth to be placed in his own treasury and storehouses on the grounds that she has no son. Therefore I wish to petition the king on her behalf — please, be my allies in this." They agreed to do so.

Then Ācāra went to where Prasenajit, king from Kosala, was to be found, and having arrived, he offered the king salutation and blessings on his long life, took a seat beside him, and two or three times conducted royal business and performed royal services. Then he said to Prasenajit, king from Kosala: "O King, grant me a dwelling."

"Ācāra, where have you been residing until now?"

"O King, I have been staying as a guest-companion in the household of a chief minister's wife."

"Ācāra, go and take up residence in that very place."

"O King, the chief minister's wife — her time has come."

"If she herself has come of age, has her household also come of age?"

"O King, their union has not yet come of age, and yet there is not so much as a seat left in the house."

The king then said to the ministers: "Good sirs, provide Ācāra with a dwelling." And it having come to light that this was on Ācāra's behalf, the ministers said: "O King, does it seem to you that Ācāra has no dwelling? The fact is that Ācāra has come before you together with the bride, and in truth it is on the bride's behalf that Ācāra is petitioning you. O King, Ācāra is the son of a brāhmaṇa chanter who recites before the assembly. A brāhmaṇa cannot be compelled against his will — but if this matter is well settled, then, O King, one who eats pure food will have taken up something good."

Then the king summoned Ācāra and said: "Ācāra, I did not know before how you were acquainted with the bride. Now go, and take the bride, her household, and all her wealth."

"As the king commands," he replied.

Ācāra went to where the bride's house was. When the bride heard that Ācāra had come, she sat in the doorway and began to weep. Seeing this, Ācāra said: "Bride, why do you weep?"

She replied: "When one whose husband I sought has come of age, have you too abandoned me entirely?"

Then Ācāra thought to himself: if I speak in agreement with her, she will weep all the more bitterly — I must cut through this at once. And so Ācāra said to the bride: "Bride, the bodhisattva who practised austerities — he who renounced sixty thousand women such as the queen Grakdzin (Yaśodharā), Saatsoma, and Ridag Kye, and others, and went forth into homelessness — you would not even be worthy of the dust on the soles of his feet."

At that she fell silent and said nothing. Then Ācāra said: "It is not that I abandoned you — I came here for your own sake. I have obtained from the king both you and your household and all your wealth. Will you stay here, or go to the place where the yellow-robed ones dwell?"

She thought to herself: if I go to where the yellow-robed ones dwell, I shall not even obtain my life from the brāhmaṇa woman. And so she said, "I will remain here," and she stayed right there.

At that time Ācāra had two houses: one in Śrāvastī and one in the place of the yellow-robed ones. Now, at the time when the Blessed One, as a bodhisattva, had practised austerities for six years and came to understand that austerities accomplished nothing —

he breathed in as he wished and breathed out as he wished, and was offered abundant food — rice gruel, hot cooked rice, and the like. His body was anointed with clarified butter and grain oil, and bathed with warm water. He then proceeded to a village, where he received from the two daughters of a householder — Gayā and Gayābala — milk mixed with honey, churned sixteen times. Praised by Kāla (Nāgarāja), the black king of the nāgas, he received from a grass-seller grass of golden hue, fashioned a seat of undisturbed grass at the place of awakening, and sat down there cross-legged, held his body upright, set his mindfulness directed inward, and, making his resolve, spoke these words:

Until the undefiled is obtained,
this cross-legged posture I shall not break.
And so, until the undefiled is won,
he broke not his cross-legged seat.

At the midnight hour, the Blessed One subjugated by the power of loving-kindness the host of māras — three hundred thousand million māras together with their retinues of sixty billion — and, having comprehended unsurpassed omniscience, was requested by Brahmā and proceeded to Vārāṇasī, where, in twelve aspects and recited three times, he turned the wheel of Dharma endowed with the Dharma. At that time he tamed the five and the group of five, and five hundred lofty youths of the town. Going to the Karṇaviṣa grove, he established sixty members of Bhadravarga in the truths. Proceeding to the village, he established the two daughters of the householder, Gayā and Gayābala, in the truths. Going to Uruvilvā, he ordained the thousand Jaṭilas and conferred full ordination upon them. Going to the Gayāśīrṣa stūpa, he instructed those thousand monks by means of the three miracles, freed them from the wilderness of cyclic existence, and established them in the utterly supreme and peaceful unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Going to the eastern grove, he established together in the truths the king of Magadha, Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, together with eighty thousand gods, and the many hundreds of thousands of brāhmaṇas and householders who had arisen in Magadha. Going to Rājagṛha, he accepted the Bamboo Grove, and ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana together with their retinue of two hundred and fifty, conferring full ordination upon them. Going to Śrāvastī, he accepted the Jeta Grove and tamed the young-example-of-a-king, Prasenajit of Kosala. Thereafter the buddha, the Blessed One, dwelt at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then Prasenajit of Kosala sent a messenger to King Śuddhodana, saying: "Rejoice, O god! Your son has come to know the nectar, and satisfies beings with that nectar. He dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada." Having heard this, King Śuddhodana sent a messenger before the Blessed One, saying: "It has been long since I have seen my son. I, your father, thirst to see you." That messenger was immediately ordained on the spot. A second messenger was sent, and he too was ordained on the spot. Because the Blessed One had taught the Dharma-Vinaya excellently, each and every messenger sent was ordained on the very spot. Then at another time, when King Śuddhodana heard this, he sat with his arm resting on his knee, lost in his own thoughts.

Chāraka saw this and said: "Your majesty, why do you sit with your cheek resting on your hand, lost in thought?" Chāraka, when the young prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I would send remarkable men as messengers, and each day they would bring back news and report: 'The young Sarvārthasiddha is staying at such-and-such a place.' Now that the young Sarvārthasiddha has taken the nectar of awakening to heart and satisfies beings with that nectar, and I have heard that he dwells at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada — when I send remarkable men as messengers, not one of them returns with news of the young Sarvārthasiddha. Each and every one I send as a messenger settles there on the spot. How then can I sit here with my cheek resting on my hand, lost in thought? 

Chāraka said: "Your majesty, command me. I, too, will go there. I shall go, your majesty, presenting a message before the eyes of your son." 

King Śuddhodana himself then composed a letter in these words:

From the time you lay within the womb
I watched over you with care and love.
Scorched by the burning canopy of affliction,
I remain standing by the Victor's tree.
Now through the branches, twigs, and roots
of disciples you have come to full bloom.
While others rejoice in happiness,
I am left to cling to suffering.
When first you were born into this world
you performed a great and meaningful act,
and the kindred gathered round to embrace you —
so too in that moment you made a solemn vow.
Therefore, now that you have found peace and rank,
turn your compassionate mind toward me
and toward all the host of your kinsmen,
and be pleased to bring the thought of coming.

Having written this, Chāraka took the letter and set out for Śrāvastī. At length he reached Śrāvastī and, as soon as Chāraka had presented the letter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One himself read the letter. Chāraka then asked: "Blessed One, will you come to the land of the Śākyas?" "Chāraka, I will come." And with the same boldness he had shown before, Chāraka said this: "If the Blessed One does not come, I shall drag you there by force."

Then the Blessed One at that time spoke these verses:

For one in whom no net of craving spreads
to lead him anywhere at all —
that buddha, boundless in conduct and without ground,
by whose home shall he be led?

For one in whom no net of craving spreads
to lead him anywhere at all —
that buddha, boundless in power and without ground,
by whose home shall he be led?

For one whose victory is never lost,
over whom the world can win no victory —
that buddha, boundless in conduct and without ground,
by whose home shall he be led?

For one whose victory is never lost,
over whom the world can win no victory —
that buddha, boundless in power and without ground,
by whose home shall he be led?

Chāraka said: "Blessed One, I will go and speak to King Śuddhodana." The Blessed One declared: "Chāraka, messengers of the Victor are not of that kind." "Blessed One, then of what kind are the messengers of the Victor?" "They are those who have gone forth, with shaven heads and wearing the ochre robe." "Blessed One, please grant me permission to return to King Śuddhodana." The Blessed One declared: "Go forth and depart."

For the Blessed One, having been a bodhisattva in all those successive past lives, had never broken a single word of the Dharma spoken by his father, his mother, his preceptor, his teacher, his guru, or those in the role of a guru — and so, the very moment the Blessed One spoke, Chāraka said: "Blessed One, I will go forth." 

The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

"Śāriputra, give Chāraka the going-forth." "This will be for his long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness."

The Venerable Śāriputra, having heard from the Blessed One and replied "As the Venerable One commands," gave Chāraka the going-forth and full ordination. He then recited for him all the rules of conduct — what he should do and what he should not do — including: "Chāraka, from this day forward you shall not sleep under the same roof as a woman," and all the other rules of training.

Chāraka replied to his preceptor, "As the Venerable One commands," prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra with his head to the ground, and departed. He went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One with his head to the ground, and said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I will go to the Śākya settlement."

The Blessed One declared: "Chāraka, you are not to enter the royal palace without announcement. Stand at the gate and say: 'A Śākya monk has come.' If they ask whether there are other Śākya monks as well, say: 'There are other Śākya monks as well.' If they say 'Enter,' then enter. If the young man Sarvārthasiddha asks whether those who have accomplished all aims also wear such robes, say: 'They too wear exactly such robes.' You are not to take up residence in the royal palace. If the young man Sarvārthasiddha asks whether he who has accomplished all aims would also not take up residence in the royal palace, say: 'He would not take up residence there.' If he asks where he would take up residence, say: 'In a hermitage or a temple.' If he asks whether the young man Sarvārthasiddha will come, say: 'He will come.' If he asks how long before he comes, say: 'After seven days have passed.'"

The Venerable Chāraka, having heard from the Blessed One and replied "As the Blessed One commands," prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One with his head to the ground and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Now, when Chāraka set out, it had taken many days to travel to Śrāvastī, but on the return journey, by the power of the buddhas — that power which is the power of the buddhas — and by the power of the gods — that power which is the power of the gods — he reached the Śākya settlement in a single day.

The Venerable Chāraka then went to where King Śuddhodana was, and having arrived, called to the doorkeeper: "Ho there, my good man, go and announce to the king that a Śākya monk has come." The doorkeeper said: "Are there other Śākya monks as well?" Chāraka said: "There are other Śākya monks as well." The doorkeeper announced this to the king, and the king said: "Let the Śākya one enter. Who would turn away a Śākya?"

Then the Venerable Chāraka, recognized by the doorkeeper, went to where King Śuddhodana was, and having arrived, he said to King Śuddhodana: "Great King, the Blessed One sends you greetings."

King Śuddhodana, recognizing Chāraka by his voice, said: "Are you Chāraka? O lord of gods, a person conveys such greetings as this." The king then said: "Is the young man Sarvārthasiddha really wearing such robes as these?" "O lord, yes, he is wearing exactly such robes." The king fell from his lion throne onto the ground, and having been revived with water, he asked: "Will the young man Sarvārthasiddha come?" "O lord, he will come." "How long before he comes?" "After seven days have passed." The king then said to his ministers:

"Wise ones, today let the royal palace and the queen's retinue be swept and cleaned. The young god Sarvārthasiddha will not be taking up residence within the royal palace or among the queen's retinue." "Then where will he take up residence?" "In a hermitage or in a monastery." "What kind of monastery?" Chāraka then described what he had seen — what kinds of monasteries existed in Śrāvastī.

Now at that time King Śuddhodana had, in Kapilavastu, the Pleasure Grove of the Living, the Nyagrodha (banyan) pleasure grove, the Place of Brahmā, and four hundred and ninety-seven other pleasure groves. The king said to his ministers: "Wise ones, today, in each of the three groves — the Living Pleasure Grove, the Nyagrodha Pleasure Grove, and the Place of Brahmā — have them quickly build monasteries like the Jeta Grove, each containing sixteen great halls and sixty dwelling foundations. And let every place in the city of Kapilavastu be kept free of stones, gravel, and weeds."

"Kings accomplish things by their word, gods by their mind, and yogins by the mere arising of intention — all is accomplished. Let the ministers attend to this as though it were a divine command." Having heard this from King Śuddhodana, the ministers caused monasteries like the Jeta Grove — each with sixteen great halls and sixty dwelling foundations — to be built in each of the three pleasure groves: the Living Pleasure Grove, the Nyagrodha Pleasure Grove, and the Place of Brahmā. And every place in the city of Kapilavastu was made free of stones, gravel, and weeds.

Now there are ten things which, by the nature of reality, will infallibly occur during the lifetime of a living and abiding Buddha, the Blessed One. The Blessed One will not pass into complete nirvāṇa so long as: he has not given a prophecy of buddhahood; so long as another sentient being has not yet generated the irreversible mind toward unsurpassed awakening; so long as all those to be tamed by a buddha have not been tamed; so long as one-fifth of his lifespan has not elapsed; so long as he has not established a retreat boundary; so long as he has not indicated the foremost pair of śrāvaka disciples; so long as he has not shown the descent from the gods, illuminating the entire city; so long as he has not displayed the great miracle at Śrāvastī; so long as he has not, together with the śrāvakas, declared their past karmic causes at the great unheated lake; and so long as he has not established both his father and mother in the truths.

The Blessed One then reflected: "The time for taming Great King Śuddhodana and many hundreds of thousands of Śākyas is near at hand. And this — the establishing of both father and mother in the truths — is something the Tathāgata will assuredly accomplish." Having so reflected, the Blessed One then addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, go and announce to the monks: 'The Tathāgata is going to Kapilavastu. Among you, whoever wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata to Kapilavastu and to witness the meeting of father and son — let him take up his robe.'"

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied, "Yes, Reverend One, as commanded," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is going to Kapilavastu. Among you, whoever wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata to Kapilavastu and to witness the meeting of father and son —

let him take up his robe.'" The monks replied to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Yes, Reverend One, as you command," and heard this from him.

Then the Blessed One set out — he who had tamed, surrounded by a retinue that had been tamed; he who was peaceful, surrounded by a peaceful retinue; he who was liberated, surrounded by a liberated retinue; he who had found relief, surrounded by a retinue that had found relief; he who was subdued, surrounded by a subdued retinue; he who was an arhat, surrounded by arhats; he who was free from attachment, surrounded by those free from attachment; he who was beautiful, surrounded by a beautiful retinue.

He was encircled by a herd of bulls as a magnificent bull is by his herd. He was encircled by a host of young elephants as a great elephant is by them. He was encircled by a pride of fanged beasts as a lion is by his pride. He was encircled by a flock of geese as a king of geese is by his flock. He was encircled by a host of birds as a garuḍa is by his host. He was encircled by a group of students as a brahmin is by his students. He was encircled by a throng of the sick as a skilled physician is by them. He was encircled by a troop of soldiers as a hero is by his troop. He was encircled by those who have entered the path as a guide is by those he leads. He was encircled by a company of merchants as a caravan leader is by his company. He was encircled by the full assembly of his retinue as a guild master is by his following. He was encircled by a host of ministers as a king of the citadel is by his ministers. He was encircled by a thousand sons as a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) is by his. He was encircled by a host of constellations as the moon is by them. He was encircled by a thousand rays of light as the sun is by them. He was encircled by a host of gandharvas as Dhṛtarāṣṭra is by his. He was encircled by a host of kumbhāṇḍas as a noble man is by his household. He was encircled by a host of nāgas as Virūpākṣa is by his. He was encircled by a host of yakṣas as Vaiśravaṇa is by his. He was encircled by a host of asuras as Rāhu is by his. He was encircled by a host of the Trāyastriṃśa gods as Śakra (Indra) is by his. He was encircled by a host of Brahmā's realm as Brahmā is by his.

His sense faculties were utterly tamed. His deportment and conduct were undisturbed. He was steady as a great ocean. He was laden with goodness as a rain cloud with water. He was free from arrogance as a great elephant-king. He was well adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being. His body was beautified by the eighty minor marks. His form was adorned by an aura extending a fathom's breadth on every side. He possessed radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns. He was altogether good, moving like a walking mountain of jewels. He was possessed of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three applications of mindfulness that are uniquely his own, and great compassion. He had entered upon the work of benefiting the world. He was the sole protector, uniquely heroic, without a second, uttering no dualities. He dwelt in calm abiding and insight. He made the three kinds of knowledge shine clearly. He was well trained in the three trainings. He was skilled in the basis of the three domains of discipline. He had crossed beyond the four rivers. He was well established in the basis of the four legs of miraculous power (ṛddhi). He had long since thoroughly purified the four means of gathering beings. He was not intimidated by any of the four fearlessnesses. He had abandoned the five limbs and had passed entirely beyond the five destinies. He was endowed with the six limbs and had fully completed the six perfections. He abode in the six constant abidings. He was rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening. He taught the eightfold path. He was skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions. He was endowed with the power of the ten powers. His fame had spread throughout the ten directions. He was supremely distinguished, exercising sovereignty over a hundredfold.

His great śrāvaka retinue included the venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa,

Nadi-Kāśyapa, and the thousand former matted-hair ascetics, along with the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and many others — a great Saṅgha of monks — went before him and proceeded along the way, walking toward the place of the Nyagrodha pleasure grove in the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time King Śuddhodana, on the seventh day, had the entire city of Kapilavastu swept clean of stones, gravel, and weeds, and had it perfumed with incense and strewn with scented powder; flowers of every variety were spread about, and the great accessories of veneration — victory banners and pennants — were all arranged and raised. In the Nyagrodha pleasure grove, the ground was prepared with wide and open seats shaped like crescents. Along every road from the Nyagrodha pleasure grove to the city of Kapilavastu, the way was made beautiful and cleared of all stones, gravel, and weeds; fragrant water was sprinkled along it, many clusters of silk were hung in garlands at intervals, and masses of flowers were arranged. The smoke of sweet-smelling incense wafted thickly, flowers of every variety were spread out, and victory banners and pennants were raised and set in place. King Śuddhodana himself, with his great royal wealth and great royal power, prepared dwelling in the Nyagrodha pleasure grove in just this way, as a fitting abode for the Blessed One.

Then, as the Blessed One was proceeding on his way, he arrived at the bank of the river Rohitaka. There some of the monks washed their hands and feet, some discarded their tooth-cleaning sticks, some drew water, and some bathed.

The Śākyas residing in the city of Kapilavastu heard that the youth of universal accomplishment was coming, and that King Śuddhodana had prepared wide and open seating in the Nyagrodha pleasure grove. Upon hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of Śākyas assembled in the Nyagrodha pleasure grove. Among them, some came stirred by their roots of past virtue. Others came out of curiosity, wondering whether they would see the father bow at the feet of his son first, or rather the son bow at the feet of his father.

Then the Blessed One reflected thus: if the Tathāgata were to enter Kapilavastu on foot, the proud Śākyas would not show great reverence to the youth of universal accomplishment, thinking: "He who formerly, as a bodhisattva, departed from the city of Kapilavastu welcomed by many hundreds of thousands of gods descending from the sky above — now, even though he has realized the unsurpassed wisdom, he has come on foot." Disbelief might arise in them. Knowing this, the Blessed One resolved: I shall enter Kapilavastu by means of miraculous power.

He then spoke to the monks: "Monks, you shall cross the river Rohitaka on foot. The Tathāgata will go by miraculous power." The monks replied to the Blessed One: "As you command, venerable one," and, having listened to the Blessed One, they crossed the river Rohitaka on foot and proceeded directly to the Nyagrodha pleasure grove.

Then, not long after the monastic Saṅgha had departed, the Blessed One gathered his mind, and entering a meditative absorption of the following kind, with his mind perfectly settled in equipoise, he disappeared by miraculous power from the far bank of the river Rohitaka and rose into the sky above, like a king of geese stretching its wings. He proceeded from above the city of Kapilavastu directly to the Nyagrodha pleasure grove, arriving there, and then he remained seated in cross-legged posture in the sky above the Nyagrodha pleasure grove.

There the Blessed One, facing the eastern direction, performed the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

He then entered a meditative absorption on the element of fire. From the body of the Blessed One, the buddha who had entered absorption on the element of fire, rays of light of many kinds blazed forth: blue, yellow, red, white, rose-red, and colors like those of crystal and silver. He then displayed paired miracles: from the lower part of his body fire blazed, while from the upper part cool streams of water flowed; and from the upper part of his body fire blazed, while from the lower part cool streams of water flowed. Just as he performed these things facing the eastern direction, so too he performed them facing the south, the west, and the north. Thus in all four directions he displayed four kinds of miraculous wonder by his supernormal powers.

Then the Blessed One had this thought: if the Tathāgata were to touch his two feet to the feet of King Śuddhodana, the king's skull would split into seven pieces. And if King Śuddhodana were to bow down and touch his head to the Tathāgata's two feet, the haughty Śākyas would think, "Why is one who has become a father touching his head to the feet of his son?" and their lack of faith would arise. Therefore he thought, "I must by all means employ such a miraculous power that King Śuddhodana will bow with his head to the Tathāgata's two feet while remaining in an upright stance, without prostrating his body."
