Having considered this and understood what was needed, the Blessed One remained suspended in the sky at a height of about seven tāla trees, then descended to the height of six tāla trees, then five, then four, then three, then two, then one tāla tree. Then he descended to the height of about seven men's lengths, then six, then five, then four, then three, then two, then one man's length.

Then King Śuddhodana, remaining upright without bowing, bowed his head to the two feet of the Tathāgata. And to make this known to the Śākyas, he spoke these verses at that very moment:

When you were born, the earth trembled violently,
and the shadow of the jambu tree did not shift from your body.
Three times the all-seeing, omniscient one looked —
to your feet, O buddha, I pay homage.

The Blessed One then gathered back the miraculous display he had manifested, went to the Nyagrodha pleasure grove, and took his seat on the cushion that had been prepared before the assembly of the community of monks.

Then King Śuddhodana, and those known as Bṛhad-bhojana, Śvetabhojana, Amṛtabhojana, and many hundreds of thousands of Śākyas bowed their heads to the two feet of the Blessed One and assembled on one side. Some of the Śākyas, joining their palms together in the direction where the Blessed One was, assembled on one side. And some of the Śākyas, upon seeing the Blessed One from afar alone, assembled on one side without saying a word.

Then King Śuddhodana made this request to the Blessed One in verse:

How is it, O hero who once rode upon war elephants,
on horses and in chariots for traveling to the city,
that now across grounds covered with thorns
you walk upon your feet?

The Blessed One declared:

I range across the whole of the earth
by the mount of the legs of supernormal power
and the vehicle of proper giving,
unstung by the thorns of affliction.

The king asked:

O hero, formerly you were resplendent
clothed in the robes of Kāśika silk —
how is it that you endure upon your body
these rough, ochre-colored robes?

The Blessed One declared:

O king, I am adorned by wearing
the sewn cloth robe of the modest sage.
Whoever wears the robe of the Sage (the Buddha)
becomes a beauty in the tranquil forest.

The king asked:

Formerly, steadfast one, you partook of meals
of many flavors from golden vessels —
how is it that you now come
to accept such poor alms food?

The Blessed One declared:

Food of those endowed with Dharma is joy,
accompanied by renunciation and meditative equipoise.
Though I have abandoned craving for food,
I eat for the sake of guiding the entire world.

The king asked:

O noble-minded one, formerly you dwelt in due season
in your immeasurable palace above —
now that you dwell alone in the forest,
how do you become free from cold and discomfort?

The Blessed One declared:

Gautama has abandoned the root and continuance of all fears
together with their latent tendencies.
Dwelling in the forest, freed from the fear of sorrow,
there is nothing there of which I am afraid.

The king asked:

O sovereign of sages, formerly in your city
you always performed the finest ablutions.
Now that you dwell alone in the forest,
how do you bathe with proper water?

The Blessed One declared:

Gautama bathes on the bank of the Dharma-lake, in the waters of merit —
clear, cool, praised by the wise.
One who bathes there is cleansed in body and mind,
and passes beyond the attainments of the Vedas.

The king asked:

O hero, when in your own palace
you bathed with golden and silver vessels,
how is it that you now bathe your body
with water that is warm and turbid?

The Blessed One declared:

Gautama bathes in the river-like stream of moral discipline —
clear and cool, praised by the wise.
One who bathes there is cleansed in body and mind,
and passes beyond the attainments of the Vedas.

Then King Śuddhodana asked:

From where does majesty arise?
From where does fear and dread arise?
From where does disenchantment arise?
Speak to me of these things as I have asked.

The Blessed One declared:

From where majesty arises,
from where fear and dread arise,
and from where disenchantment arises —
listen, and I shall explain them to you.

Were it not for aging, illness, and death,
were those three things not to exist,
then even I would take great delight
in the objects that are so exceedingly pleasant.

The king said:

O hero who brings joy to the Śākya clans,
that you are untouched by the eight worldly conditions —
how excellent it is that you, so nobly born,
have done so nobly well.

Then, with great joy and exuberance, he bowed his head to the feet of the sovereign of sages, surrounded by the Saṅgha of sages, and remained contemplating the Sugata on every side.

Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself: how fortunate I am to have found, in my son, one who has realized such a wealth of excellent qualities.

Thereupon the Blessed One, having discerned the dispositions, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of the assembly of common people, taught the Dharma in such a way that — with the exception of King Śuddhodana himself, and Devadatta (who was sinful, desirous, and more arrogant than arrogance itself) — seventy-seven thousand Śākyans, along with Śuddhodana and others, came to see the truths. From that assembly, many thousands of living beings directly realized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, and some went forth and, by abandoning all afflictions, directly realized the state of arhathood. The greater part of that assembly was established in turning toward the Buddha, alighting on the Dharma, and alighting on the Saṅgha.

King Śuddhodana, so overwhelmed with joy at thinking "my son possesses such great miraculous power, such great might," did not see the truths. Devadatta, due to sinfulness, desire, and arrogance surpassing arrogance, also did not see the truths. And Devadatta, having failed to see the truths and overcome with anger, declared: "If I too were to master this magic of gathering followers in such a way, then the gathering of all the world as followers would depend on me alone."

The Śākyas who had been gladdened and were displaying their joy said to him: "Devadatta, let it go. The Blessed One possesses great miraculous power and great might — do not speak in such a way." And so he fell silent and said nothing further.

On the second day, in the pleasure grove, seats like half-moons were arranged in a spacious area with good open ground. There too the Blessed One, having fully perceived the intentions, latent dispositions, constitutions, and natures of that great multitude of people, taught the Dharma in such a way — with the exception of King Śuddhodana and Devadatta, who was sinful, desirous, and arrogant surpassing arrogance — that seventy-six thousand Śākyas, beginning with one named Breja, came to see the truths. Among that assembly, many thousands of living beings directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some realized the fruit of once-returning; some realized the fruit of non-returning; and some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhathood. Most of that assembly were established in turning toward the Buddha, alighting on the Dharma, and alighting on the Saṅgha.

King Śuddhodana, so overwhelmed with joy at thinking "my son possesses such great miraculous power, such great might," did not see the truths. Devadatta, due to sinfulness, desire, and arrogance surpassing arrogance, also did not see the truths. And Devadatta, having failed to see the truths and overcome with anger, declared: "If I too were to master this magic of gathering followers in such a way, then the gathering of all the world as followers would depend on me alone."

The Śākyas who had been gladdened and were displaying their joy said to him: "Devadatta, let it go. The Blessed One possesses great miraculous power and great might — do not speak in such a way." And so he fell silent and said nothing further.

On the third day, in a spot of open, spacious ground in the pleasure grove at the place of Brahmā, seats like half-moons were arranged. There too the Blessed One, having fully perceived the intentions, latent dispositions, constitutions, and natures of that great multitude of people, taught the Dharma in such a way — with the exception of King Śuddhodana and Devadatta, who was sinful, desirous, and arrogant surpassing arrogance — that seventy-five thousand Śākyas, beginning with one who partook of ambrosia, came to see the truths. Among that assembly, many thousands of living beings directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some realized the fruit of once-returning; some realized the fruit of non-returning; and some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhathood. Most of that assembly were established in turning toward the Buddha, alighting on the Dharma, and alighting on the Saṅgha.

King Śuddhodana, so overwhelmed with joy at thinking "my son possesses such great miraculous power, such great might," did not see the truths. Devadatta, due to sinfulness, desire, and arrogance surpassing arrogance, also did not see the truths.

Then the Blessed One reflected: "Why does King Śuddhodana not come to see the truths?" Considering this, he understood: there are two causes by which one does not see the truths — a mind that is excessively elated, and a mind that is excessively downcast. He thus perceived that the mind of King Śuddhodana, which in his youth had been fulfilled in every aim and had formerly been revered by both gods and men, was now excessively downcast because he thought: "Now I am revered by men, but no longer revered by gods." Then the Blessed One reflected:

"I shall tame King Śuddhodana by teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone." Reflecting thus and perceiving this, the Blessed One then gave rise to a worldly intention.

It is the nature of all buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that when they give rise to a worldly intention, even the tiniest creatures — even worms and beetles — know it through the Blessed One's mind. But when they give rise to a supramundane intention, even pratyekabuddhas do not know it through the Blessed One's mind — how much less then śrāvakas and the rest.

Then Brahmā, Śakra (Indra), and the other gods thought to themselves: "Why has the Blessed One given rise to a worldly intention?" And they saw that the Blessed One wished to teach the Dharma to the divine retinue alone for the sake of taming King Śuddhodana.

Thereupon the gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm, knowing it through the Blessed One's mind, vanished from the divine world — just as a person might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm — and appeared before the Blessed One in the pleasure garden of the Brahma realm. The Blessed One then, by his miraculous power, conjured a magnificent four-gated palace made of four kinds of precious jewels, and appointed the four World-Protecting Kings (the Caturmahārājas) as gatekeepers at the four gates.

The gods of the form realm then circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and took their seats to the right, close by. The gods of the desire realm likewise circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and took their seats to the left, close by.

Now, King Śuddhodana's daily practice was to go three times each day to see the Blessed One and to pay him reverence.

And so the next morning King Śuddhodana rose early and went to where the eastern gate of the palace was. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said to him: "Great King, stop — do not enter. The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone, and no measure of mere humans can fill this place. Handsome one, who are you?" The King replied: "Great King, I am Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great King." Then King Śuddhodana went to where the southern gate of the palace was. Virūḍhaka said to him: "Great King, stop — do not enter. The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone, and no measure of mere humans can fill this place. Handsome one, who are you?" The King replied: "Great King, I am Virūḍhaka, the Great King." Then King Śuddhodana went to where the western gate of the palace was. Virūpākṣa said to him: "Great King, stop — do not enter. The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone, and no measure of mere humans can fill this place. Handsome one, who are you?" The King replied: "Great King, I am Virūpākṣa, the Great King." Then King Śuddhodana went to where the northern gate of the palace was. Vaiśravaṇa said to him: "Great King, stop — do not enter. The Blessed One is teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone, and no measure of mere humans can fill this place. Handsome one, who are you?" The King replied: "Great King, I am Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King."

Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself: "How unfortunate it is that I see the Blessed One teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone." The Blessed One, knowing King Śuddhodana's mind with his wisdom, transformed the palace into the nature of crystal, so that King Śuddhodana saw the Blessed One teaching the Dharma to the divine retinue alone as if they were seated within the reflection of a mirror. Having seen this, the King thought to himself: "There is no woman anywhere who is like this — one for whom all my aims are now as good as accomplished." And so King Śuddhodana's mind became exceedingly elated.

Then the Blessed One drew back the miraculous display he had manifested and began to teach the Dharma to King Śuddhodana. The Blessed One reflected thus: "Why is it that King Śuddhodana does not see the truth?" And he understood that at this very moment King Śuddhodana, out of excessive delight at the thought that "there is no woman anywhere like this — one for whom all my aims are now as good as accomplished," had his mind stream become exceedingly elated.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, attend upon King Śuddhodana." The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied, "Yes, Venerable One, as you command," and having received this instruction from the Blessed One, he went to where King Śuddhodana was.

King Śuddhodana saw the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana while he was still at a considerable distance, and when he saw him he said: "Venerable Maudgalyāyana, please come here. Venerable Maudgalyāyana, it is good that you have come. Venerable Maudgalyāyana, please take your seat on the prepared seat."

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, given the opportunity by the Blessed One, entered into such a meditative absorption that, with his mind thus evenly placed, he became invisible from his own seat and arose into the open sky above the eastern quarter, where he performed the four deportments — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. He then entered into absorption on the fire element, and from the body of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as he rested in absorption on the fire element, there issued forth rays of light of many kinds: blue, yellow, red, white, orange, and those resembling the color of crystal and silver. He also displayed pairs of miraculous feats: flames blazed from the lower part of his body while streams of cool water flowed down from the upper part, and flames blazed from the upper part of his body while streams of cool water flowed down from the lower part. Just as he did in the eastern quarter, so too in the southern, western, and northern quarters — displaying four types of miraculous wonder in each of the four directions. Then, having drawn back the miraculous display, he sat down on the prepared seat.

Then King Śuddhodana said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is there anyone else among the Blessed One's śrāvakas who possesses such great miraculous power, such great might?"

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana at that moment spoke these verses:

The śrāvakas of the Sage (the Buddha) are mighty.
They know the three knowledges and the categories of mind.
Many there are whose defilements are exhausted,
Many who have conquered their foes.

Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself: "Not only is the Blessed One alone great in miraculous power and mighty —"

"And so the śrāvakas, too, possess great miraculous power and great might." With that thought, the mind-stream of King Śuddhodana became calm and composed.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana led King Śuddhodana to where the Blessed One was and arrived there. He bowed his head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

Then the Blessed One, knowing King Śuddhodana's mind with his own mind, understanding his intentions, his latent dispositions, his constitution, and his nature, taught the Dharma to King Śuddhodana as he sat right there upon that seat — shattering with the vajra of wisdom the mountain peak of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), twenty heights high, accumulated from beginningless time, and thereby directly actualizing the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, the king spoke: "Venerable One, through relying upon the Blessed One as my virtuous friend, the Blessed One has done for me what neither my father did, nor my mother, nor any king, nor the gods, nor my forefathers of old, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor the gathering of friends, companions, and kinsmen — you have dried the ocean of blood and tears, you have freed me from the mountains of bones, you have closed the doors to the lower realms, you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, you have drawn my feet out from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed me among gods and humans, you have brought cyclic existence to an end. With the vajra of wisdom you have shattered the mountain peak of the view of the transitory collection, twenty heights high, accumulated from beginningless time, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable One, I have entered the stream. Venerable One, I have entered the stream, and I go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks. I pray to be accepted as a lay practitioner. From this day forth, for as long as I live, from the depths of my heart I take refuge with complete sincerity."

He also spoke these verses:

What a good son does for his father
in return — that benefit —
you have done for me.
My mind has turned toward the higher realms.

What a good son does for his father
in return — that benefit —
you have done for me.
My mind has turned toward liberation.

You have drawn me well out of the lower realms,
and through your effort you have placed me on the path
to the higher realms and to liberation.
You have accomplished this difficult task with excellence.

As a merchant who has found his profit,
I have found the higher realms.
To rely upon virtuous friends —
this is truly excellent.

Then King Śuddhodana, having seen the truth, said to Śuddhodana the White: "Young man, let you govern the kingdom. I, like the royal seer, shall live the holy life. Why would I not give over the kingdom? I have seen the truths. When did the gods see them? This very day. The gods have seen them today, yet it was under the same parasol under which the Blessed One came here that I have seen the truths."

Then King Śuddhodana said to the young men Dronodana and Amṛtodana: "You two young men, let you govern the kingdom. I, like the royal seer, shall live the holy life. Why would I not give over the kingdom? I have seen the truths. When did the gods see them? This very day. The gods have seen them today, yet we had seen them still earlier."

The king said: "Among the sons of these young men, which is the eldest?" He replied: "It is the young man Bhadra." King Śuddhodana consecrated the young man Bhadra as the Śākya king.

At that time the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas —

Each day, without interruption, he attended the royal palace at mealtime, and King Śuddhodana saw those who had gone forth from Rāhula and were practicing austerities, their bodies appearing gaunt and unattractive. Having seen them, he thought to himself: "These great ones have good minds, yet their bodies are not good — it is the fierce austerities that make their bodies appear so unpleasant. If the Blessed One's retinue, however numerous, were to become just like the Blessed One himself in appearance, then the Blessed One would look all the more beautiful."

Then King Śuddhodana assembled the Śākyas and said: "O wise ones, if the young man Sarvārthasiddha had not gone forth, what would he have become?" They replied: "He would have become a divine wheel-turning king." "And what would your sons have become?" "They would have become his divine attendants." "Well then, since the young man Sarvārthasiddha has gone forth and drunk the nectar of the Dharma to his heart's content, and since he nourishes beings with that nectar, why do your sons not serve as his attendants? O king, shall those then be sent forth into the going-forth? Let them be sent forth! O king, if not, the Śākya lineage will be cut off." The king said: "Let one from each household be sent forth." They replied: "We will do as the king has commanded." King Śuddhodana then proclaimed that one Śākya youth from each household was to be sent forth.

At the time when King Śuddhodana made that proclamation, five hundred Śākya youths — Bhadra, Aniruddha, Nandaka, and others — went forth into the going-forth. At the time when the Blessed One sent forth those five hundred Śākya youths, the Blessed One said: "Going forth from a high lineage is a means of gain, and it brings closeness." Because of this, great gain and great honor arose for them.

The Blessed One then considered the matter: "These sons of good family went forth solely for the sake of others — they are attached to others alone," he reflected. He then wished to cut off the gain and honor that had arisen for them. Dwelling at his pleasure in the dwelling place of the Blessed One, he set out in the direction of Śrāvastī, traveling by stages, and arrived at Śrāvastī. There he resided in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Vinayavibhaṅga. The twenty-eighth fascicle.

Then the venerable Udāyin, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and Dharma robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he was wandering through Śrāvastī collecting alms, step by step, he went to the dwelling of the householder's wife Śyāmā. The householder's wife Śyāmā saw the venerable Udāyin while he was still some distance away. Having seen him, she beat her breast and said: "Udāyin! Why have you abandoned me and gone forth?" Udāyin replied: "The bodhisattva, when he went forth, abandoned the queen Gopā, Śaktimatī, Mṛgajā, and sixty thousand other women — that was truly difficult. Yet as for you, who are like a speck of dust, why would I not abandon you? I too, Śyāmā, am going forth." She said: "Very well then. Let me properly conclude the household affairs first." Udāyin came at the right and fitting time on a subsequent occasion and said: "Śyāmā, will you not go forth?" Śyāmā replied: "I have not yet properly concluded the household affairs." Śyāmā said: "In all the time since Kosala was founded, the household affairs have never been fully concluded. Udāyin, let me conclude them well today and I will go forth tomorrow."

Udāyin thought to himself: "Previously I was overwhelmed by those with black begging bowls. If I were now to give ordination to a nun, the group of six would overwhelm me all the more, saying, 'Udāyin has given ordination to a nun.'" Remorse arose in him, and taking up his bowl and robes he set out walking toward Rājagṛha, and journeying gradually along the way he arrived at Rājagṛha. There he accepted the rains retreat and settled in.

The next day Śyāmā properly concluded the household affairs, came to the Jeta Grove, and went among the monks to ask them: "Noble ones, where has he gone? Who is he?" They replied: "He is the noble Udāyin. He has gone to Rājagṛha." Śyāmā began to weep. The monks said: "Śyāmā, why do you weep?" She answered: "At the word of the noble Udāyin I properly concluded the household affairs and came, saying he would give me ordination. He said, 'Come once you have properly concluded the household affairs, and I will give you ordination.' I did conclude the household affairs properly and came — but now he has gone to Rājagṛha. I am neither remaining at home nor have I gone forth." The monks said to her: "Śyāmā, Udāyin went to Rājagṛha for a razor, and the barber will shave your hair there." Then fully ordained nuns who had come to the Jeta Grove to present their confession ceremony saw Śyāmā weeping and asked: "Śyāmā, why do you weep?" She replied: "At the word of the noble Udāyin I properly concluded the household affairs and came, saying he would give me ordination. He said, 'Come once you have properly concluded the household affairs, and I will give you ordination.' I did conclude the household affairs properly and came — but now he has gone to Rājagṛha. I am neither remaining at home nor have I gone forth." The wandering nun said: "Monks, who performs the ordination of nuns? It is nuns who ordain nuns — come here. The noble great Progenitress Gautamī will give you ordination." They led her to the great Progenitress Gautamī and said: "Noble one, this Śyāmā, a householder's attendant, wishes to go forth." The great Progenitress Gautamī gave her the going forth and conferred upon her full ordination.

Udāyin thought to himself: "By my consideration for those with black begging bowls, I did not give ordination to Śyāmā, the householder's wife, and I even obstructed her with a razor, a whip, a sickle, and small sickles. And yet some of those with black begging bowls have gone ahead and ordained her — I will not even meet her now." Remorse arose in him, and reluctantly he accepted the rains retreat. At Śrāvastī an elder monk who had reluctantly accepted the rains retreat, placing his bowl and robes under his arm, performed the invitation ceremony, and the invitation ceremony was performed correctly. The invitation ceremony was performed exceedingly well. With that he set out toward Rājagṛha, and journeying gradually along the way he arrived at Rājagṛha. There the venerable Udāyin was sitting at the gate of the monastery looking along the road, and from quite a distance he saw someone approaching — an elder with hair white as a brahmin-flower, with hanging eyebrows. Udāyin thought: "This monk coming — whoever this elder is," and said aloud: "Welcome, elder. Well come. I prostrate." The other replied: "I prostrate to the teacher." Udāyin perceived: "This is an elder who knows neither preceptor nor abbot." Udāyin had him enter the monastery and asked: "Elder, where have you come from?" He replied: "From Śrāvastī."

Udāyin thought: "If I ask about the householder's wife Subhad­rā right at the start, it will seem rude. I should approach the matter gradually, asking first about other things and then about her." So he spoke: "Venerable one, how is the Blessed One — does he have little trouble, little distress? Is he at ease, free from illness, and abiding in strength? Has he consented to spend the rains retreat at Śrāvastī?" The venerable Udāyin replied: "It is just so. The Blessed One has little trouble, little distress; he is at ease, free from illness, abiding in strength, and has consented to spend the rains retreat at Śrāvastī." "Venerable one, and how is the community of monks, the community of nuns, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen — are they at ease in Śrāvastī, with little trouble, little distress, free from illness, and abiding in strength? Do they wish to see the Teacher? Do they wish to hear the sacred Dharma?" "Venerable Udāyin, it is just so. The community of monks, the community of nuns, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen are dwelling at Śrāvastī with little trouble, little distress, at ease, free from illness, and abiding in strength. They wish to see the Teacher, and they wish to hear the sacred Dharma." "Venerable one, and how are the elder Kauṇḍinya, the elder Mahākāśyapa, the elder Śāriputra, the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the other senior monks — are they dwelling at Śrāvastī with little trouble, little distress, at ease, free from illness, and abiding in strength?" "Venerable Udāyin, it is just so. They are dwelling at Śrāvastī with little trouble, little distress, at ease, free from illness, and abiding in strength." "Venerable one, and are you acquainted with Prasenajit, king of Kosala, the chaplain-brahmin Brahmadatta, the elder Jyeṣṭha, and the householder's wife Mṛgāramatā Viśākhā?" "Venerable Udāyin, yes, I know them." "Then, venerable one, do you know the householder's wife Subhadrā?" "Venerable Udāyin, I know her. She is the former wife of the venerable Udāyin." Then Udāyin said: "You are aware of the situation — the talk that comes with old age. Do you still consider her your householder's wife?" "She has gone forth." "Who gave her the going forth?" "The great lady Gautamī." Udāyin thought: "She still has residual objects of attachment," and said: "Come here, old one — wash your feet." He then massaged the other's feet and gave many rubbings of the hands, hung the other's bowl and robe on a peg and set them up on a high rack, and said: "Old one, this monastery has food and gains. Be pleased to stay here." The elder replied: "Venerable Udāyin, I have come to pay reverence at a shrine and intend to go on; I do not wish to stay here." Udāyin then placed iron door-bolts and a bent key before him and said: "The Blessed One has declared that monks should lodge in the monastery; they should not go without lodging," and with that he disappeared from sight. The elder eventually wandered on gradually and, arriving at Śrāvastī, Udāyin swept out his own monastery room, plastered it well, applied a plaster of fresh cow-dung, shut the door, and lay stretched out on top of a seat with his outer robe on, intoning a recitation in a melodious voice. Then nuns who had come to make an offering arrived and, hearing the melody of his voice, they paid him reverence and said: "Noble Udāyin, where have you been travelling?" Udāyin said: "To Rājagṛha." They went to the residence hall and said to Subhadrā:

"Subhadrā, rejoice! Your teacher has come." "Where is my teacher?" "Udāyin!" "How is he my teacher? Did she read that from his forehead? You scatter-brain — you do not understand. Nuns depend heavily on monks, so go and look to that." Subhadrā took barley flour, bathwater leavings, and oil, and went to Udāyin's monastery. Subhadrā knocked on the door of Udāyin's monastery room, and Udāyin said: "Who is there?" Subhadrā said: "It is I, Subhadrā." "Welcome — the householder's wife Subhadrā has come." "Am I still your householder's wife?" "Then what are you?" "I have gone forth." "Who ordained you?" "The noble great Mātṛkā, Gautamī." "Something of that sort has happened, and it was on that account that I went to Rājagṛha; because I wanted to inquire after you, you have gone forth. You said with your own mouth that you would settle the household affairs properly and come, and I said I would give you the going-forth. When you had settled the household affairs properly and came, you had already entered Rājagṛha, and if the noble one had not given me the going-forth, I would have been neither one who remains in the home nor one who has gone forth." Udāyin said: "Subhadrā, do you think I am going to salt my own hand? Whether the great Mātṛkā Gautamī ordained you or I ordained you, it is fine — come inside and I will teach the Dharma." Subhadrā paid reverence at Udāyin's two feet and sat before him to hear the Dharma. He began to teach her Dharma, and after he had taught her Dharma for a time, he began to call to mind their former conversations, the delight they had shared, their play, and the pleasures they had enjoyed together: "Subhadrā, do you remember how the two of us ate such-and-such food in a grove, a pleasure garden, or some delightful divine residence, and dressed in such-and-such finery, and drank such-and-such drink?" At those words, attachment arose in Udāyin. The more attachment arose in him, the more he became agitated.

Now, women skilled in the ways of men have five qualities unmixed with others. What are those five? They know when a man has become attached and when he has become free of attachment; they know the right time and know the signs of the months; they know when conception has taken place in the womb; they know from whom that conception in the womb arose; and they know whether it is a boy or a girl — if it is a boy, it rests leaning on the right hip, and if it is a girl, it rests leaning on the left hip.

Subhadrā, knowing that Udāyin had become attached, said: "I must step outside for a moment and will return." Udāyin thought: "Does she want to defecate, or does she want to urinate? Let nothing go wrong." And so he said: "Go ahead." Subhadrā went out, broke off an armload of firewood, and began to run. Udāyin was skilled in sounds, and hearing the noise she made, he ran out after her, calling: "Nun, where are you running to with your shaved head?" He ran after her, and as he grabbed her his semen was released. At that, freed entirely from his entanglement, he remained in that very place, like an elephant freed from rut.

Subhadrā, seeing him freed from all entanglement and turned back, understood: "This one is freed from all entanglement." She went to him and said to the venerable Udāyin: "Noble one, if I had consented, I would have become unfit to remain a nun, and you would have become unfit to remain a monk. Sister, the Blessed One (the Buddha) has well declared: 'If one guards oneself, one guards others; if one guards others, one guards oneself.' How does guarding oneself guard others? By cultivating, by habituating, by doing it repeatedly, by protecting continuously, by making it a felt reality, by making it manifest — in this way, guarding oneself guards others. How does guarding others guard oneself? By not acting harshly, by not reviling, by not harming, by caring for others, by being tender toward others, by a mind of loving-kindness — in this way, guarding others guards oneself. Noble one, please pass me that lower robe; I will wash it." Udāyin gave that lower robe to Subhadrā. Subhadrā, seeing the semen on it, felt remorse, thinking: "Had the monk Udāyin previously seen some part of my body, or previously smelled it, or previously touched it, then my not consenting was wrong of me." And as Subhadrā was thinking in this way, her mind became thoroughly inflamed with desire and torn apart, and she poured that semen into the opening of her own womb. Because the ripening of karma (Skt. karman) in sentient beings is inconceivable, a being entered into her.

The nuns who saw this said: "Subhadrā, all of us know you — do you really intend to go to the noble Udāyin on the grounds of the Dharma of good conduct? We never thought that he would put you in such a situation as this." Subhadrā replied: "Sisters, that monk is one of pure moral discipline — from the time he went forth until now, not once has he so much as touched her with his hand." They said: "Even without touching you, if he has put you in such a situation as this, what sort of situation might he have put you in if he had touched you?" At that point, the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that nun has not incurred a defeat. However, let her be set apart in a secluded place, free from any involvement with alms-gathering. And she will give birth to a young son named Kāśyapa (Skt. kāśyapa), who will go forth in my teaching and, having abandoned all afflictions, will directly realize arhathood — namely, the novice monk Kāśyapa, who will become the foremost among those who speak my varied teachings, speak pleasing words, and who possess the confidence born of virtue." The Blessed One then reflected: "The offense that has arisen among the monks came about through a nun who was not a blood relative draping an old garment over herself." Thinking thus, the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this ground of formulation, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks, and so forth as before.

"My śrāvakas, in training in the Vinaya, are to recite this rule as follows: Whatever monk causes a nun who is not a blood relative to drape an old garment over herself, or wrings it out for her, or holds it out for her to step into — that is an offense requiring forfeiture.

Now, 'whatever monk' refers to Udāyin or any other monk of that kind. 'Nun' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Who is not a blood relative' means one who is not a grandmother,

a grandfather, or any other relative up to and including the seventh generation reckoned through both fathers and mothers. Beyond that seventh generation, one is not a blood relative.

"Garment" refers to any one of the seven kinds: woolen cloth, cotton cloth, silk cloth, fine muslin, coarse hemp cloth, kotamba cloth, or linen cloth.

"Old" means one that has been used in any one of the three seasons.

"Drapes it over her" means: places it into water for soaking.

"Wrings it out for her" means: even dips it into dye.

"Holds it out for her to step into" means: even strikes it with the palms of the hands.

"An offense requiring forfeiture" means: the item is to be forfeited and the transgression is to be confessed; therefore it is said to be an offense requiring forfeiture.

As for how the transgression arises: if a monk, perceiving a nun who is not a blood relative as not being a blood relative, drapes an old garment over her, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he wrings it out for her, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he holds it out for her to step into, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he drapes it and also wrings it out; if he drapes it and also holds it out for her to step into; if he wrings it out and also drapes it; if he wrings it out and also holds it out for her to step into; if he holds it out for her to step into and also drapes it; if he holds it out for her to step into and also wrings it out; or if he drapes it, wrings it out, and holds it out for her to step into — in each of these cases it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, uncertain whether a nun who is not a blood relative is or is not a blood relative, drapes an old garment over her, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he wrings it out for her, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he holds it out for her to step into, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he drapes it and also wrings it out; if he drapes it and also holds it out for her to step into; if he wrings it out and also drapes it; if he wrings it out and also holds it out for her to step into; if he holds it out for her to step into and also drapes it; if he holds it out for her to step into and also wrings it out; or if he drapes it, wrings it out, and holds it out for her to step into — in each of these cases it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, perceiving a nun who is a blood relative as not being a blood relative, drapes an old garment over her, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he wrings it out for her, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he holds it out for her to step into, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he drapes it and also wrings it out; if he drapes it and also holds it out for her to step into; if he wrings it out and also drapes it; if he wrings it out and also holds it out for her to step into; if he holds it out for her to step into and also drapes it; if he holds it out for her to step into and also wrings it out; or if he drapes it, wrings it out, and holds it out for her to step into — in each of these cases it becomes a wrongdoing.

If a monk, uncertain whether a nun who is a blood relative is or is not a blood relative, drapes an old garment over her, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he wrings it out for her, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he holds it out for her to step into, it becomes a wrongdoing. If he drapes it and also wrings it out; if he drapes it and also holds it out for her to step into; if he wrings it out and also drapes it; if he wrings it out and also holds it out for her to step into; if he holds it out for her to step into and also drapes it; if he holds it out for her to step into and also wrings it out; or if he drapes it, wrings it out, and holds it out for her to step into — in each of these cases it becomes a wrongdoing.

There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by pain.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. The Blessed One addressed the monks thus: "Monks, this kind of person — one who has gone forth from a high noble family — is close to being surrounded by gains.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those among the Śākyas who had gone forth gained great offerings and great honor, and they became thoroughly devoted to the pursuit of adorning themselves with robes and maintaining extra possessions — carrying extra alms bowls, extra robes, extra nets, extra cups, and extra belts. Although the Blessed One taught them the Dharma again and again, at the proper times, they did not come to see the truths.

Then the Blessed One reflected: "Why is it that these Śākyan monastics do not come to see the truths?" He saw that it was because they were thoroughly devoted to the pursuit of adorning themselves with robes and because they carried extra alms bowls, extra robes, extra nets, extra cups, and extra belts. He thought: "If I were to rebuke these Śākyan monastics, it would be difficult to shame them." Since the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are supremely skilled in taming those who are to be tamed, the Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, during these three months I wish to enter into retreat. Except for a single monk who brings me my alms round, and except at the time of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of that same period, no monk is to come near me. The community of monks, too — venerable ones — during the months of the rains retreat, except for a single monk who brings me my alms round and except at the time of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of that same period, you are to establish as a rule among yourselves: none of you is to approach the Blessed One. Whoever among you during the rains retreat — other than the one who brings the alms round and except on the day of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony — approaches the Blessed One is to be made to undergo a transgression." With that, the rule was established.

When the Blessed One had entered into the three-month retreat, no monk went to him except for the one who brought his alms round and except on the day of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony.

At that time the venerable Upananda had undertaken to observe the rains retreat with the last month added on, while the Blessed One had accepted to observe the rains retreat with the last month added on as well.

Then, when the venerable Upananda had passed through the three months of the rains retreat, he made himself ready with his robes prepared and his robes collected, looking fine and with an attractive retinue, and taking up his alms bowl and robe, he set out toward Śrāvastī, traveling gradually on his way, until at last he arrived in Śrāvastī.

Then the venerable Upananda set down his alms bowl and robe, washed his two feet, and went toward the Blessed One's assembly hall. The six-group monks saw the venerable Upananda from quite a distance. On seeing him, they said: "Venerable ones, right now that one, for the sake of a small matter, will be splitting the community's rule." Others said: "He will be made to undergo a transgression." Still others said: "He is now only beginning to engage in the matter — when the splitting actually occurs, then he will be made to undergo it."

Then the venerable Upananda gently knocked on the door of the Blessed One's assembly hall, and the Blessed One opened the door for him. The venerable Upananda bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side.

Now it is the nature of reality of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to ask a monk who has arrived unexpectedly: "Monk, where have you come from just now?"

The Blessed One, having asked the venerable Upananda "Upananda, where have you come from just now, and where did you commit to spending the rains retreat?" — this being the occasion for mutual rejoicing — the Blessed One expressed his delight, and the venerable Upananda replied: "Venerable One, I have come just now from the provinces. I request permission to spend the rains retreat there in the provinces."

"Upananda, have the monks in the provinces performed the invitation ceremony?"

"Venerable One, they have."

"Upananda, what was the cause, what was the condition, by which you came to have a beautiful retinue, a retinue of fine appearance?"

"Venerable One, if there was someone who had gone forth under my former preceptor, I would say to him: 'Good fellow, come here. Seek out a forest-dweller.' And I would also speak the praises of the forest-dwelling life itself. 'Seek out an alms-goer, one who wears only the three robes, one who makes use of rags from the dust-heap, one who dwells at the foot of a tree.' And I would also speak the praises of tree-root dwelling itself. If he said he would do so, I would have him go forth. If there was someone seeking full ordination, or one who had entered upon a dwelling, or one who had entered upon reading, or one who had entered upon the meaning of what was spoken, or one who had entered upon reflection — I would say to him as well: 'Good fellow, come here. Seek out a forest-dweller,' and I would speak the praises of the forest-dwelling life itself. 'Seek out an alms-goer, one who wears only the three robes, one who makes use of rags from the dust-heap, one who dwells at the foot of a tree,' and I would speak the praises of tree-root dwelling itself. If he said he would do so, I would cause him to take up the reflection. Venerable One, that was the cause, that was the condition, by which I came to have a beautiful retinue, a retinue of fine appearance."

"Upananda, it is excellent, excellent, that you have undertaken this for the benefit of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare and benefit and happiness of gods and humans. Upananda, whoever does not speak in praise of the cultivated qualities of another — that person does not speak in praise of me. Whoever does speak in praise of the cultivated qualities of another — that person speaks in praise of me. And why is that? Because I have long commended, honoured, praised, and extolled those very cultivated qualities.

"Upananda, do you not guard the rule of the Saṅgha?"

"Venerable One, I do not know what the rule of the Saṅgha is, nor what constitutes observing the rule."

"Upananda, here I declared to the monks as follows: 'Monks, during these three months I wish to remain in seclusion within. No monk is to come before me save for one monk who brings my alms-food, and at the time of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of this very period.' And the Saṅgha of monks likewise established this as a rule: 'Reverends, during the months of the rains retreat no one among us is to go to visit the Blessed One save for one monk who brings alms-food and at the time of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of this very period. During the rains retreat, save for one monk who brings alms-food and at the time of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of this very period, whoever among us goes to visit the Blessed One — we will make that person undergo a transgression-producing downfall.' That was the rule that was established.

"Venerable One, I arrived unexpectedly —"

That rule was to be observed by the monks who were permanent residents. But when a monk arrives unexpectedly, both he who arrives unexpectedly and those who are permanent residents must observe the rule of the Saṅgha. Reverend, I shall therefore establish the following standards of conduct for monks who arrive as unexpected visitors: a monk who arrives unexpectedly shall enter the assembly hall and inquire of the monks what rule is in effect at that place. If he asks, that is well. If he does not ask, it becomes a matter involving an offence.

Reverend, be that as it may, I grant to forest-dwelling monks the exemption from forest retreat, so that for a forest-dwelling monk who wishes to pay homage to the Tathāgata there is no inappropriate time to go.

A monk who is an alms-round practitioner, or a content-with-what-is-found alms-round practitioner, or one who does not eat after mealtime, or one who eats at a single sitting, or one who holds to the three robes, or one who dwells at the foot of a tree, or one who dwells in a charnel ground, or one who sits in the open air, or one who uses any seat as it comes, or one who lives without a roof — to such a monk who practises in accordance with his own foundation I grant the exemption from that foundation, so that for a monk who practises in accordance with his foundation there is no inappropriate time to go for the purpose of paying homage to the Tathāgata.

Then the venerable Neyasena rejoiced in and praised what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet in reverence, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then the group of six went to where the venerable Neyasena was, and upon arriving they said this to the venerable Neyasena: "Venerable Neyasena, open the matter. Disclose the matter with regard to these five categories of transgression. The transgression that has arisen for you — confess it in accordance with the Dharma." "I see no transgression." "Did you not break the rule of the Saṅgha? What is the rule of the Saṅgha?" The group of six explained the matter at length, and then the venerable Neyasena said this to the group of six: "Reverends, the Blessed One declared: 'Reverend, be that as it may, I grant to forest-dwelling monks the exemption from forest retreat, so that for a forest-dwelling monk there is no inappropriate time to go for the purpose of paying homage to the Tathāgata. A monk who is an alms-round practitioner, or a content-with-what-is-found alms-round practitioner, or one who does not eat after mealtime, or one who eats at a single sitting, or one who holds to the three robes, or one who dwells at the foot of a tree, or one who dwells in a charnel ground, or one who sits in the open air, or one who uses any seat as it comes, or one who lives without a roof — to such a monk who practises in accordance with his foundation I grant the exemption from that foundation, so that for a monk who practises in accordance with his foundation there is no inappropriate time to go for the purpose of paying homage to the Tathāgata.'"

Then those Śākyan monks who had gone forth thought: "In this way the Blessed One has censured great desire and praised having few desires — which means in effect that the Blessed One has censured us. So let us send our surplus bowls, robes, straining cloths, small bowls, and girdles to the venerable Ānanda and, with minds made pure, go to where the Blessed One is."

Then those monks, taking their surplus bowls, robes, straining cloths, small bowls, and girdles, went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and upon arriving they said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, out of compassion for us, please accept these — our surplus bowls, robes, straining cloths, small bowls, and girdles."

"Venerable ones, wait here until I have asked the Blessed One about this matter." Then the venerable Ānanda went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated at the Blessed One's feet with his head, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, take them and pile them in a great assembly hall, and give them to whichever monk who is in need of such things."

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he collected the surplus bowls, robes, straining cloths, small bowls, and girdles from the Śākya monks who had gone forth, piled them in a great assembly hall, and placed them there.

Then those Śākya monks who had gone forth, abandoning their surplus bowls, robes, straining cloths, small bowls, and girdles — as one abandons sickness, as one abandons a festering wound, as one abandons a thorn — took up the three robes as their full kit, and with pure minds and with few possessions went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with their heads and took their places to one side.

The Blessed One, having fully understood the intention, the latent dispositions, the faculties, and the nature of those monks, then taught the Dharma in such a way that, while those five hundred young Śākya monks remained sitting right there in their seats, he shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection — which had been accumulated since beginningless time — and caused the fruit of stream-entry to be directly realized.

Having seen the truth, they addressed him thus: "Venerable one, through relying on the Blessed One as our spiritual friend, what the Blessed One has done for us is something that our fathers did not do for us, our mothers did not do for us, kings did not do for us, the gods did not do for us, our ancestors of old did not do for us, ascetics and brahmins did not do for us, and the host of loving friends, dear companions, and relatives did not do for us. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, freed us from the mountains of bones, shut the door to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, drawn our feet out of the hells, the animal realms, and the realms of hungry ghosts, placed us among gods and humans, brought cyclic existence to an end, and — shattering with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time — made the fruit of stream-entry directly realized."

Then the monks, having generated doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable one, how wondrous it is that the Blessed One, relying on the venerable Ānanda, arranged for those five hundred young Śākya monks to be established in the having of few desires and the abandonment of great desires, and then settled them in the utterly perfected accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa."

"Monks, now I — free from attachment, free from craving, free from clinging, omniscient, having mastery over all knowable things — how much more wondrous is it that, relying on the noble son Ānanda, I arranged for those five hundred young Śākya monks to be established in the having of few desires and the abandonment of great desires, and settled them in the utterly perfected accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa. For in the past I was possessed of attachment, possessed of aversion, possessed of delusion, possessed of craving, possessed of clinging — subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental unhappiness, and

disturbances — and yet, not yet freed from disturbances, I brought about this: relying on the noble son Ānanda, I established these five hundred young Śākya monks, setting them free from great desires, settling them in having few desires, and placing them in the five higher knowledges. Now hear this.

Monks, in former times, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was a king named Brahmadatta. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and happy; the years were good; it was filled with people and a great multitude; and he caused to be pacified the strife, fighting, quarreling, disputes, tumult, internal conflict, banditry, famine, and disease. He had his only son, dear to him as his own heart, govern the kingdom.

King Brahmadatta had a queen named Brahmavatī and a lotus pond also called Brahmavatī. King Brahmadatta had no son, and desiring a son he made prayers to the water deity, to those of ill form, to Śakra (Indra, king of the gods), to Brahmā, and to still other particular classes of deities — the deities of the pleasure grove, the deities of the forest, the deities of the crossroads, the deities of the triple juncture, the deities who accept torma offerings, the deities born together with one, those in accord with the Dharma, and the deities who always follow in one's train.

Now there is a saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of the cause of making such prayers. But that is not so. If it were so, then each person would have a thousand sons — like a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). In fact, it is from the coming together of three conditions that entry into the mother's womb and dwelling therein occurs. What are those three? The parents are united and have come together; the mother's time has come and she has her monthly sign; and a gandharva (Skt. gandharva) is nearby and ready to enter. It is from the coming together of these three conditions that sons and daughters are born.

Now it happened that while this one was earnestly devoted to the making of prayers, a certain sentient being who had set the aspiration toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening and whose resolve was firm passed away from the hells and entered into the womb of Queen Brahmavatī.

Among women versed in the ways of women, some possess five distinctive qualities. What are these five? They know when a man has come under the influence of desire and when he is free from desire. They know the time and know the monthly sign. They know when a being is dwelling in the womb. They know from what circumstance the entry into the womb has occurred. And they know whether it is a boy or a girl — for if it is a boy, it dwells leaning upon the right hip, and if it is a girl, it dwells leaning upon the left hip.

She, rejoicing and delighted, said to King Brahmadatta: "May the god be pleased. The being that has entered me is certainly going to be a boy, for it is dwelling leaning upon my right hip."

King Brahmadatta too was filled with joy and delight, and he spoke thus: "Ah! Now after so long I see the face of the son I have longed for. He will be born in accord with me and not discordantly. He will perform my deeds. As I have nurtured him, so he will in turn nurture me. He will enjoy his inheritance. He will cause my lineage to continue for a long time. And after we have died and passed on, whether little or much, let us give gifts and make merit, and may this pair, wherever they are born, go there together and follow one after the other" — so he uttered and uttered again a solemn declaration, naming the merit-dedications by name.

Now, knowing that a being had entered, in order to bring the embryo dwelling in the womb to full maturation, she arranged within the upper apartments — when it was cold, the implements appropriate for cold, and

when it was warm, the implements appropriate for warmth — along with foods prepared under medical supervision that were not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too hot, not too pungent, and free of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, heat, and pungency; and she had her attended in every comfort, adorned with necklaces and ornaments upon her body, moving about as though in the pleasure grove of the daughters of the gods, not descending from one couch to another couch, nor from one small seat to another small seat, nor to any lower floor, so that she would hear not even the slightest unpleasant sound, and so that she would remain entirely without harm.

Then at another time, a wish of this kind arose in Queen Brahmavatī: "Oh, may gifts be given and merit be made at the eastern gate of the city of the gods! And may the same be done at the southern gate, the western gate, the northern gate, and the four crossroads at the center — may gifts be given, merit be made, and may all prisoners be freed!" Thereupon King Brahmadatta, upon hearing that such a wish had arisen in Queen Brahmavatī, gave gifts and made merit at the eastern gate of the city. Likewise at the southern gate, the western gate, the northern gate, and the four crossroads at the center, he gave gifts, made merit, and freed all the prisoners.

Again a wish of this kind arose in Queen Brahmavatī: "Oh, may I, together with the gods, go out to sport, rejoice, and make merry in pleasure groves and in the forests of austerities!" Thereupon King Brahmadatta, upon hearing that such a wish of this kind had arisen in Queen Brahmavatī, entered together with Queen Brahmavatī into the pleasure groves and the forests of austerities, and they sported, rejoiced, and made merry.

Again a wish of this kind arose in Queen Brahmavatī: "Oh, may I board a boat together with the gods and enter the water, and sport, rejoice, and make merry in the lovely pond!" Thereupon King Brahmadatta, upon hearing that such a wish of this kind had arisen in Queen Brahmavatī, boarded together with Queen Brahmavatī a boat filled with blue lotus flowers, red lotuses, white night-blooming lotuses, and white day-blooming lotuses, and they entered the water and sported, rejoiced, and made merry in the lovely pond.

And right there in that very boat she gave birth, and a boy was born who remembered his former lives, handsome, beautiful to behold, fair, radiant, of a golden complexion, possessed of a head like a parasol, with long arms, wide forehead, arched brows, and a high-bridged nose. His kinsmen gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — three times seven — a grand birth-celebration was held, and they proceeded to give the boy a name, asking what he should be called. They thought to themselves: "Because this boy was born inside the water, let his name be Jātassara — Born-of-Water." And so his name was given as Jātassara — Born-of-Water.

The young Jātassara was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to hold him in their laps and raise him, two to give him suck, two to bathe and cleanse him, and two to play with him and keep him company. These eight nurses nourished and raised him with milk, yogurt, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other finest provisions of every kind, and caused him to grow swiftly, like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

Then the young Jātassara reflected: "From where did I die and transmigrate to be born here?"

He understood that he had died and transmigrated from the hell realms and been born here. He then wondered: "What action was it that caused those beings to be born in the hells?" He understood that it was because they had been installed in the exercise of royal power as regents for sixty years that they had been born there. He then reflected: "Where have I now been born?" He understood that he had been born among human beings, in the royal lineage. And so he thought to himself: "If I too am installed in the exercise of royal power, that will lead me to be born in the hells — which would be terrible. I should devise some stratagem." And so he presented himself as though he were a fool and sat in that manner.

On the very day that the young Jātassara — Born-of-Water — was born, the sons of five hundred ministers were also born, and each of them was given a name fitting his family lineage. The practice of those ministers was to come every day, just as they went to King Brahmadatta, so too to the young Jātassara. Then in time, those five hundred young men came to be capable of jumping and running. King Brahmadatta then thought: "Even if my son Jātassara had not become a fool, he would by now be capable of just such jumping and running. Yet since this one of mine is a fool, I should at least establish sovereign authority over the kingdom in him for the sake of name and lineage." Then the young Jātassara heard this and thought to himself: "This king will harm me without compunction. I should present myself as mute and sit in that manner." And so he deliberately presented himself as mute and sat thus.

Then in time those five hundred young men came to be capable of speech. King Brahmadatta thought: "Even if my young Jātassara had not become mute, he too would by now be capable of just such speech." At that time the name Jātassara — Born-of-Water — fell into disuse, and the name Young-Mute-Fool, Young-Mute-Fool took hold.

Then at another time King Brahmadatta sat resting his cheek upon his hand, deeply absorbed in thought. The ministers said: "Sire, why do you sit with your cheek resting in your hand, lost in thought?" The king said: "I am lord over a kingdom such as this, yet I have neither son nor daughter. When I am gone the royal line will be cut off. And the one son I do have has become a mute fool. How can I not sit here lost in thought?" The ministers summoned physicians, and having examined him the physicians said: "Sire, this young man's faculties appear clear. There seems to be not the slightest indication of madness. It seems right to put him to the test."

King Brahmadatta summoned executioners and gave them this secret command: "I am banishing this Young-Mute-Fool in plain sight of the common people. You are not to kill him." "As the god king commands." King Brahmadatta then went into his retinue and gave the executioners this order: "I am banishing this young man; take him away." "As the god king commands." With that, the executioners, following King Brahmadatta's instructions, placed the Young-Mute-Fool upon a chariot and led him out from the city of Vārāṇasī.

Then the Young-Mute-Fool, seeing the prosperity and abundance of the city of Vārāṇasī, spoke these words: "Is this Vārāṇasī empty, or is it inhabited?"

The executioners then presented the Young-Mute-Fool to the king, saying: "Your divine majesty, the Young-Mute-Fool spoke words such as these." Thereupon King Brahmadatta took the Young-Mute-Fool upon his lap and spoke these words: "Young man, whom shall I have killed? Whom shall I have put to death? Whom shall I have deprived of life? To whom shall I give what?" Though he spoke these words, the Young-Mute-Fool said nothing at all. King Brahmadatta then said again to the executioners: "I am releasing this young man; take him away." The executioners replied, "As the god king commands," and once again placed the Young-Mute-Fool upon a chariot and led him out from the city of Vārāṇasī.

As they went, the Young-Mute-Fool saw four men carrying a corpse and said: "Is this corpse the body of one who has died, or the body of one still living?" The executioners again presented the Young-Mute-Fool to the king, saying: "Your divine majesty, the young man spoke words such as these." King Brahmadatta again took the Young-Mute-Fool upon his lap and said: "Young man, whom shall I have killed? Whom shall I have put to death? Whom shall I have deprived of life? To whom shall I give what?" Though he spoke these words, the Young-Mute-Fool said nothing at all. King Brahmadatta then said again to the executioners: "I am releasing this young man; take him away." The executioners replied, "As the god king commands," and once again placed the Young-Mute-Fool upon a chariot and led him out from the city of Vārāṇasī.

As they went, the Young-Mute-Fool saw a great heap of grain and said: "If this heap of grain were not eaten from its base at the very start, it would grow great." The executioners again presented the Young-Mute-Fool to the king, saying: "Your divine majesty, the young man spoke words such as these." King Brahmadatta again took the Young-Mute-Fool upon his lap and said: "Young man, whom shall I have killed? Whom shall I have put to death? Whom shall I have deprived of life? To whom shall I give what?" Though he spoke these words, the Young-Mute-Fool said nothing at all.

King Brahmadatta then said again to the executioners: "I am releasing this young man. Wise ones, go now and take the young man quickly into the forest and bury him in the ground there." The executioners replied, "As the god king commands," and once again placed the Young-Mute-Fool upon a chariot, went to a place in the forest, arrived there, and began to dig a pit.

Then at that moment the Mute-Fool spoke these verses:

You who steer the chariot, why do you
Dig a pit with mattock and with spade?
Why is it that you dig this pit?
Tell me quickly when I ask.

The charioteer answered:

The king's own son who does not speak —
The Mute-Fool born — for him the order came:
Bury this one quickly
Here within the forest in a pit.

Then the Young-Mute-Fool thought to himself: "These men are violent, red-handed, given to tormenting and to inflicting great torment, cutting short the lives of others, making their living by taking the lives of others. It may come to pass that they will kill me." Recognizing this and feeling frightened, he said to the executioners: "If the gods would grant me one boon, I would enter the city on my own feet and speak."

The executioners went before the king and reported this in full. The king said: "Young man, if you desire the kingdom, I shall grant even that to you."

Thereupon King Brahmadatta, filled with joy and delight, said to his ministers: "Wise ones, today quickly clear all the streets of every city of stones, gravel, and thorns, and

burn incense, strew perfumed powder, raise victory banners and pennants, and scatter flowers of every kind." For kings accomplish things through the spoken word, and gods through the power of mind, while yogins accomplish everything through the mere arising of intention — and so the ministers, hearing from the king and seeking to fulfill his command as one fulfills a divine command, cleared all the cities of stones, gravel, and thorns, burned incense, strewed perfumed powder, raised victory banners and pennants, and scattered flowers of every kind. Many hundreds of thousands of people from throughout the realm, filled with amazement, gathered together to watch the mute youth with the withered limb enter the city and speak words.

Vinayavibhaṅga, the twenty-ninth fascicle.

Then the mute youth with the withered limb entered the city, went to where King Brahmadatta was, approached him, and touched his two feet. At that moment he spoke these verses:

I am not mute, nor am I lame,
nor am I simple-minded, nor without intelligence.
With words that make things plain and clear
I speak, O lord of men.
I am not mute, nor am I lame,
nor am I simple-minded, nor without intelligence.
With faculties intact, bright and clear,
so am I endowed, O lord of men.

The king said: "Son, why did you neither speak nor walk on your feet? Live, for that one's sake. In my former lives, for sixty years I ruled as regent over men within the kingdom, acting in harmony with my lineage; for sixty thousand years I burned in the hells as a sentient being. Recalling the unbearable, fierce, and terrible suffering of the hells, I do not desire a kingdom, and I will not go to the hells again. Father, I pray you give your permission for me to go forth into renunciation."

The king said: "Son, the ascetics (ṛṣis) who torment themselves with austerities, who perform fire sacrifices and burnt offerings — they do so for the sake of a kingdom. Why would you abandon what lies in the palm of your hand and go forth into renunciation?"

Then the mute youth with the withered limb spoke these verses:

I do not desire the enjoyment of sensual pleasures
won through enmity, conflict, and strife.
I will practice the holy life,
that life made fearful by enmity, conflict, and strife.
I do not desire the enjoyment of sensual pleasures
that resemble the fruit of the kimpā tree.
I will practice the holy life
whose fruit yields the taste of nectar.

The king said: "Every pleasure that one can possibly experience is found in kingship itself. Why would you abandon the kingdom and go forth into renunciation?"

Then the mute youth with the withered limb spoke these verses:

From that which produces suffering,
I do not count pleasure as pleasure.
From that which produces happiness,
I count that suffering as happiness.
Father, grant me leave
to go to the forest of austerities.

The king said: "Son, here you may lie in perfect safety on the upper terrace, amid incense burning and perfumed powder strewn, with flowers of every kind scattered about, and soft, fine bedding well arranged; you will be woken by the sweet sounds of melodious music; you will wear soft garments and eat and drink the finest foods and drinks. Whereas if you go forth in a wilderness, you will always lie beneath trees on beds of grass or leaves, with a mind seized by fear and dread, sleeping alongside savage wild beasts, woken by the cries of jackals, wearing pieces of bark and tree-skin,

eating roots and fruits, and drinking only warm, muddy water — why would you abandon a royal kingdom and go forth?" Then the young prince spoke these verses in reply:

To dwell in the forest, clad in bark and grass,
subsisting on roots and fruits,
dwelling together with fierce wild beasts —
this is the highest good.
For the wise, fearing the world beyond,
do not commit killing, binding, and beating
for the sake of a kingdom —
and so that way is not for me.
Therefore, Father, please grant me leave
to go to the forest of austerity.

The king said: "Son, it is no fault. But first resolve these three doubts of mine, and after that your going forth will not be difficult. When you saw the city of Vārāṇasī in its prosperity and abundance and said, 'Is this Vārāṇasī empty, or is it inhabited?' — from what thought did you speak so? O God, let it live! When a god commands, 'Let it be compressed until it has no entrails,' and yet no one speaks a righteous word asking why this young one should be destroyed — it was from reflecting on that that I spoke."

"Son, it is no fault. When you saw a human corpse being carried by four men and said, 'Is this body the body of one who has died, or the body of one still living?' — from what thought did you speak so? O God, let it live! The body of one who has done wrong action is a dead body, and the body of one who has done good action is a living body — it was from reflecting on that that I spoke."

"Son, it is no fault. When you saw a great heap of grain and said, 'If this heap of grain were sought from the very beginning without being consumed at the base, it would grow large' — from what thought did you speak so? O God, let it live! Those farmers who borrow grain as a loan, who seek it and work, at harvest time offer great heaps of grain to those who lent it, and so those lenders have indeed been seeking repayment from the very beginning. In the same way, when one obtains human existence through the path of the ten virtuous actions, if having obtained it one does not continue to accumulate virtue through the path of virtuous action, then those prior roots of virtue will be cut off; and when the roots of virtue are cut off, one falls away entirely from the happy destinies and comes to rely upon the lower realms — it was from reflecting on that that I spoke."

Then the king, having heard his son's words, took him up with eyes full of tears and spoke: "Keep and bear this discipline as your own practice of the Dharma. I too declare myself your student." Then King Brahmadatta spoke to his ministers: "Wise ones, if the young prince had not gone forth, what would he have become?" "O God, he would have become king." "And what would your sons have become?" "O God, they would have become his servants." "Then why do your own sons not go forth, since he is doing so?" "O God, as your majesty commands, so shall it be done."

At that time, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there dwelt in a hermitage a sage endowed with loving-kindness, possessed of compassion, full of affection, one who loved all sentient beings. The young prince, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, went forth to that sage with great abundance. The sage gave teachings and instructions to the prince, and the prince, through striving, effort, and application, directly realized the five superknowledges (abhijñā).

Then, at another time, the sage passed away in the natural course of things. The young prince Lūgphye cremated the body of that sage upon a pyre of various fragrant woods and performed great offerings and acts of veneration. The young prince Lūgphye then began to care for and provide for all five hundred brahmin youths. The name "young prince Lūgphye" faded from use, and the name "Teacher Lūgphye, Teacher Lūgphye" came to be established.

Then, at another time, the Teacher Lūgphye thought to himself: "Why is it that these five hundred brahmin youths do not directly realize the five superknowledges?" And he reflected: "It is because they remain devoted to and absorbed in the pursuit of grass, bark, sticks, balls, pouring-ladles, filling-ladles as secondary matters, and in the use of leafy greens, wild grains, and the roots of the utpala lotus." Then the Teacher Lūgphye thought: "If I were to rebuke these brahmin youths openly, it would be difficult to accomplish." Since bodhisattvas are supremely skilled in taming those who are to be trained, the Teacher Lūgphye said to the brahmin youths: "Brahmin youths, during these three months of the rains retreat, if any one of you wishes to remain properly settled within, you may come to me only to deliver roots and fruits, a single portion, and for the ceremony of restoration on the fifteenth day of this very period — no one is to approach for any other reason. And among you brahmin youths, during the rains months, no brahmin youth shall go to the teacher except to deliver roots and fruits, a single portion, and for the restoration ceremony on the fifteenth day of this same period." They then established it as a rule: "During the rains months, any brahmin youth among us who goes to the teacher other than to deliver roots and fruits, a single portion, and for the restoration ceremony on the fifteenth day of this same period shall be made to incur a downfall-producing transgression."

When the Teacher Lūgphye had entered into the three-month period of proper settledness, during that time no brahmin youth came near him except to deliver roots and fruits, a single portion, and for the restoration ceremony on the fifteenth day of that same period.

The Teacher Lūgphye, from a considerable distance, caught sight of a deer. Having seen it, he spoke these words: "Deer, come here. Deer, it is good that you have come. You and I are alike — you are content and fully contented with food that fills the belly, and I too am content and fully contented with alms that fill the belly. Those here who remain devoted to and absorbed in the pursuit of leafy greens, wild grains, and the roots of the utpala lotus are not like that."

Then the brahmin youths thought to themselves: "Without a break, our teacher's vow of discipline has become complete — it seems he is now speaking of going about together with deer." Realizing this, they went to where the Teacher Lūgphye was, and having arrived, they prostrated at the two feet of the Teacher Lūgphye and stood to one side.
