Then the Teacher Lūgphye sat in silence, saying nothing. Then the brahmin youths thought: "Our teacher speaks of going about with animals, but does not do so with humans — surely the vow is unbroken," and they rose from their seats and departed.

Then one who observed the deer-vow came to where the Teacher Lūgphye was, and the Teacher Lūgphye saw that observer of the deer-vow from a great distance. Having seen him, he said: "Come here, observer of the deer-vow! It is good that you have come. You and I are alike: you carry a single water-vessel, and I too carry a single water-vessel. You carry a single strip of bark, a single staff, a single ball of dung, a single ladle, and a single cup, and I too carry a single strip of bark, a single staff, a single ball of dung, a single ladle, and a single cup. You are contented and content in every way with alms just sufficient to fill the belly, and I too am contented and content in every way with alms just sufficient to fill the belly. Here, some carry an excess of water-vessels, strips of bark, staffs, balls of dung, ladles, and cups — but not so with us."

Then the brahmin youths thought to themselves: "Our teacher is reproaching great desire and praising fewness of desire — but in substance our teacher is reproaching us. Let us therefore throw our own excess water-vessels, strips of bark, staffs, balls of dung, ladles, and cups into the swift-flowing river, and go to where the Teacher is." And so they threw their excess water-vessels, strips of bark, staffs, balls of dung, ladles, and cups into the swift-flowing river, and went to where the Teacher Lūgphye was, approaching in a manner that showed purity of conduct and restraint of possessions. Having arrived, they bowed their heads to the two feet of the Teacher Lūgphye and stood to one side.

Then the Teacher Lūgphye, having fully understood the intention, the underlying disposition, the temperament, and the character of those brahmin youths, taught the Dharma to them in such a way that those five hundred brahmin youths directly realized the five superknowledges (abhijñā).

Monks, whoever was the Teacher Lūgphye at that time and in that moment — that was I, entering into the conduct of a bodhisattva. Those who were the five hundred brahmin youths at that time and in that moment — they are these five hundred young Śākyas now. He who was the observer of the deer-vow at that time and in that moment is the monk Nyede. And at that time too, through the monk Nyede — son of good family — I led those five hundred young Śākyas away from great desire, established them in fewness of desire, and set them in the five superknowledges. And now too, through the monk Nyede — son of good family — I have led these five hundred young Śākyas away from great desire, established them in fewness of desire, and placed them in the utterly final accomplishment and happiness of nirvāṇa.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of actions that are uniformly dark is uniformly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are uniformly bright is uniformly bright; and the karmic maturation of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are uniformly dark and mixed, and strive after actions that are uniformly bright. Monks, this is how you should train.

This concludes the fourth section, the abandonment of involvement in deceit.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the Blessed One had not yet prohibited the nuns from dwelling in solitary places, the nuns likewise went to dwell in solitary abodes, and through meditative concentration, liberations (vimokṣa), meditative absorption,

and meditative attainment, they experienced states of bliss. Then the nun Utpalavārṇā, together with five hundred attendants, went to that dark forest and arrived there, and leaning against a tree, she sat down in the half cross-legged posture and experienced states of bliss arising from meditative concentration, liberations, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment.

When the other nuns wished to enter Śrāvastī to beg for alms, they said, "Noble Utpalavārṇā, please arise." Some said, "Noble Utpalavārṇā is one of great power and great miraculous ability; she will find her own way to the almshouse first," and saying this, they went on without rousing her. Utpalavārṇā, for her part, arose at the time of the alms round, and seeing that all the nuns had already gone, she thought, "Shall I go now, or shall I simply remain here?" and decided to remain there, and entered meditative absorption on cessation right where she was.

About five hundred rogues, having done their work, arrived in the dark forest, and among themselves they said, "Let two hundred and fifty of us divide up the shares, and two hundred and fifty of us scatter through the forest." So two hundred and fifty of them began to divide the shares, and two hundred and fifty began to scatter through the forest, and in so doing they caught sight of Utpalavārṇā sitting there. Some among them said, "Wise ones, this is a stump." Others said, "No, it is a person." Still others said, "It is a monk." Then one among them who was familiar with the monastic community said, "This is a nun, not a monk. How can one tell? Monks sit in the full cross-legged posture, while nuns sit in the half cross-legged posture." They were struck with wonder, and said, "Wise ones, just look — a single nun has agreed to remain here alone in the night, in such a fearsome forest." They went before their commander, and the commander asked them, "Wise ones, have you seen anything remarkable in this dark forest? It seems a single nun has agreed to remain here alone in the night, in such a fearsome forest. Go and see to it." They went before her, and the commander saw the nun Utpalavārṇā, beautiful of form, lovely to behold, radiant and fair. Having seen her, he was moved to admiration, and from that admiration he said, "Ah, this nun is remarkable on two counts: that she sits through the night like the moon, and that she is beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and radiant and fair." He then began to rouse her, but his men said, "Why are you rousing her? Rather, offer her food." One among them who knew the ways of the monastic community said, "She does not eat at an improper time." The commander said, "Why not?" He replied, "She has given up eating at an improper time." The commander said, "Ah, this nun is remarkable on two counts: that she is beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and radiant and fair, and that she has given up eating at an improper time." Then someone said, "Let her be given wine to drink." The one who knew the ways of the monastic community said, "She has given up intoxicating drink." The commander said, "Ah, this nun is remarkable on two counts: that she is beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and radiant and fair, and that she has given up intoxicating drink." Then someone said,

"I was unable to fulfill my vow at a merit-field such as this by means of alms-begging alone." With that, he offered up one piece worthy of a great cloth and a portion of his alms-food, hung them on the branch of a tree, and said: "Noble one, since there is nothing whatsoever that you do not know, do not see, do not understand, and do not perceive regarding yourself, I offer you these alms-food and this robe," and then he departed.

Utpalavārnā rose early the next morning and, seeing the many tracks left by a large number of people, she reflected on what had happened. Then, seeing that five hundred thieves had come nearby, she wondered whether any one of them had done something improper to her — and she saw that not one of them had. She then saw the great cloth and the alms-food hanging on the branch of a tree, and she thought: "This has been placed here out of devotion by those who have become faithful." Then she thought: "Should I remain here accepting what has been left? It would be eaten up and consumed by monkeys. I am the one who receives the first portion of alms on behalf of the Saṅgha. Now, in such matters, whatever is unsuitable for monks is suitable for nuns, and whatever is unsuitable for nuns is suitable for monks. Therefore I myself shall carry this and go to the Jeta Grove to offer the first portion of alms to the Saṅgha." Having so resolved, she took it and set off for the Jeta Grove.

It was the custom of the Group of Six that at least one of the Group of Six would always be stationed at the gate of the Jeta Grove, leaving no gate unguarded. Ānanda was walking back and forth and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove when he saw Utpalavārnā and said: "Sister, why have you come through the gates of Śrāvastī so early in the morning?" She replied: "I was not in Śrāvastī. Last night I accepted a dwelling in a dark forest." Ānanda said: "If even Ānanda were to enter a dark forest in the daytime, his hair would stand on end. Sister, what is it that you are carrying?" She replied: "About five hundred robbers had gathered there, and out of devotion those faithful ones made an offering to me out of their faith. Sister, you are one who ought to inspire faith even in robbers. But if those companions had caught sight of you, they would have beaten you with many whips and dragged you away as their captive. Now, whoever possesses a great cloth such as this — even with only a little goodness of heart she will strive toward virtue, just as a patched and layered garment is fashioned from fine cloth. Noble one, do you wish to take this great cloth?" "As the residue of a divine dwelling," she said. "Noble one, wait here until I have offered the first portion of the alms-food to the Saṅgha and returned, and after that I will offer you the great cloth." Ānanda thought: "Whoever holds a black begging bowl will be tempted by this and will desire it." And he said: "Sister, bring those who are receiving the first portion of alms-food and come back; until then, stay right here." Ānanda entered the Jeta Grove and, seeing the monks who were receiving the first portion of the alms-food sitting in a huddled little group, he said: "Venerable ones, the donors are weary and burdened under their loads, and yet you sit here huddled together in a small group. Come here! Receive the first portion of alms-food." They took their bowls and came forward. Utpalavārnā offered them the first portion of the alms-food, then shook out the great cloth and offered it to Ānanda. Ānanda said: "May this act of generosity of yours become the adornment of the mind, the provision of the mind, the accumulation of yogic practice, the highest benefit, and the obtaining of robes for gods and humans." Utpalavārnā thought to herself:

"I shall go to the summer dwelling and, whatever may happen, I will go to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One." And so Utpalavārṇā went to where the Blessed One was, approached, bowed her head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side.

At that time Utpalavārṇā's five robes of Dharma had become worn, tattered, and threadbare. There the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have the nuns obtained their rains-retreat robes?" "Venerable one, they have." "Then why have the five robes of Dharma of the nun Utpalavārṇā become worn, tattered, and threadbare?" "Venerable one, this sister is faithful, good, and possessed of virtuous intention. There is nothing she has not offered or fully given away to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to monks she found pleasing. Even today she obtained a great length of cloth and gave it as well to the venerable Ānanda."

"Ānanda, do monks accept surplus robes from nuns who are not their relatives?" "Venerable one, they do." "Ānanda, do monks, when accepting from nuns who are not their relatives, think to themselves, 'Are this one's five robes complete or not?' No — they simply take whatever comes to hand, whereas from a relative they would not accept even what is given."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Give the nun Utpalavārṇā five robes of Dharma from the great monastery." And the venerable Ānanda gave the nun Utpalavārṇā five robes of Dharma from the great monastery.

Then, on account of this occurrence, this case, and this occasion, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks, and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this as the basis of Vinaya training: 'Whatever monk accepts robes from a nun who is not his relative commits an offense requiring expiation.'" Thus did the Blessed One establish this as the basis of Vinaya training for his hearers.

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had taken a wife from his own social class. He played with her, rejoiced with her, and lived in delight together with her. Thinking to himself, "Though my household is rich with many possessions, I have not gathered even the slightest provision for the journey to the world beyond," he rested his chin upon his hand and sat sunk in thought. His wife, seeing this, said: "My lord's son, why do you sit with your chin resting in your hand, lost in thought?" He replied: "My dear, though our household is rich with many possessions, I have not gathered even the slightest provision for the journey to the world beyond. If I were to feed the Buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks with a meal and present each one with a piece of fine robe-cloth, that would carry provision for me on the journey to the world beyond." His wife replied: "My lord's son, let it be so." And so that householder went to where the Blessed One was, approached, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the Blessed One fully instructed that householder with Dharma-endowed words, fully inspired him to embrace the Dharma, fully praised him, and fully gladdened him. With many categories of Dharma-endowed words he fully instructed, fully inspired, fully praised, and fully gladdened him, and then was silent.

Then that householder rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One and joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, would it be permitted for us to offer a noonday meal tomorrow to the Saṅgha of monks together with the Blessed One at our home?" The Blessed One gave his consent by remaining silent, saying nothing.

Then that householder, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One's words. He bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

That very night the householder prepared pure and excellent food and drink, rose early in the morning, spread out the seats, and set out water vessels. Then he sent an invitation to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, the hour of the midday meal has arrived. May the Blessed One now be pleased to know that the time has come." And so the Blessed One was invited for the noon meal.

Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and set out for the dwelling of that householder, surrounded by the assembly of monks and with the Saṅgha of monks going before him. He arrived and took his seat on the seat that had been prepared, at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then that householder, knowing that the Buddha and all the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, satisfied and sustained them with his own hands with pure and excellent food and drink. Having satisfied and sustained them with many kinds of pure and excellent food and drink from his own hands, he then offered to each member of the Saṅgha of monks — the Buddha and all the rest — a single piece of fine woven cotton cloth.

After that the householder took a low seat and sat down in the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One fully instructed that householder with Dharma-endowed words, fully inspired him to embrace the Dharma, fully praised him, and fully gladdened him. With many categories of Dharma-endowed words he fully instructed, fully inspired, fully praised, and fully gladdened him, and then rose from his seat and departed.

That householder then followed behind the Blessed One just a short distance, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and turned back from the presence of the Blessed One. He went toward his own home, and when he had arrived and was on the ground floor beneath the upper chambers, he reflected on the joy of giving and spoke to his wife: "Good woman, let us carry much provision for the journey to the world beyond, and let us rejoice and delight in this." His wife replied: "My lord's son, if you are carrying provision for the journey to the world beyond, I would not withhold my part. But good woman, are not our possessions held in common between us two? My lord's son, it is just so — our possessions are indeed common to us both. Yet for my part, I would also like to invite the Saṅgha of nuns with the great Mistress of Beings (Skt. prajāpatī), Gautamī, at their head, offer them a meal, and present them with robes befitting such great ones. If I do that, then I too will have carried some provision for the journey to the world beyond." The householder said: "Good woman, does giving earlier prevent one from giving later? Do it just the same way." Then the wife of that householder went to where the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī was, arrived, bowed her head to the two feet of the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī, and sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī then properly taught the householder's wife with Dharma-filled words, properly had her take them to heart, properly praised her, and properly gladdened her. Having properly taught, had her take to heart, praised, and gladdened her with Dharma-filled words through many categories, she said nothing more. Then the householder's wife rose from her seat, turned toward the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī, joined her palms in reverence and bowed, and then said the following to the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī: "Noble lady, would it please you to accept a midday meal together with the Saṅgha of nuns tomorrow?" The great Mistress of Beings Gautamī accepted the householder's wife's invitation by remaining silent. Then, understanding from the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī's silence that her invitation had been accepted, the householder's wife rejoiced and expressed her delight at what the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī had said, bowed her head to the two feet of the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī, and departed from the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī's presence.

Then, that very night, the householder's wife prepared pure and choice food and drink, rose early the next morning, arranged seats and set out water, and called out in the morning: "Noble lady, the time is prepared for the midday meal; may the noble lady now be pleased to know that the hour has come." Then the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī, in the early morning, put on her lower robe, took up her bowl and Dharma robe, and, surrounded by the assembly of nuns with the Saṅgha of nuns going before her, went to the dwelling of the householder's wife and, having arrived, took her seat at the head of the Saṅgha of nuns. Then, once the householder's wife perceived that the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī and the rest of the Saṅgha of nuns were comfortably seated, she satisfied and served them with pure and choice food and drink with her own hands. Having satisfied and served them repeatedly with pure and choice food and drink through many rounds with her own hands, she then opened the bundles of robes befitting great ones, took up those robes befitting great ones, and sat down to one side at the edge of the elder's seat.

Then the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī thought to herself: "The Blessed One has prohibited nuns from accepting robes befitting great ones. If we were to accept them now, it would disturb the foundation of the training. But if we do not accept them, it will become an obstacle to the householder's wife's accumulation of merit, and an obstacle to the gain of the Saṅgha of nuns." The nuns then thought: "Ah, if only the noble great Mistress of Beings Gautamī would accept the robes befitting great ones! If she accepts, the Blessed One will surely grant permission for the fitting occasion." Then the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī accepted the robes befitting great ones, expressed her gratitude to the householder's wife, rose from her seat, and departed. She went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī then reported the matter at length to the Blessed One. When she had spoken thus,

The Blessed One then spoke these words to the great Mistress of Beings Gautamī: "Gautamī, it is excellent, excellent, that you have understood what permission I have given. Therefore I hereby grant permission for the nuns to take the robes befitting great ones and to exchange them with the monks."

Then a group of twelve nuns took those robes, went to the group of the Six Monks, and said: "Noble ones, the Blessed One has forbidden the nuns from keeping robes befitting great ones. We have obtained these robes befitting great ones — please accept them and give us your inferior ones in return."

The Six Monks replied: "Sisters, we have no need of nuns' plain cloth robes. At that time too it was we who were foolish, confused, unclear, and unskilled, and we were the ones burdened with that affair — we will not take them."

Other nuns then went to the elders, the senior monks, and said: "Noble ones, the Blessed One has forbidden the nuns from keeping robes befitting great ones. We have obtained these robes befitting great ones — please accept them, and give us your inferior and lesser ones in return."

When those sisters said, "Please present this matter to the Blessed One," the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, exchange is excepted. And the exchange is this: one should exchange to whatever extent, or for as much as, will make the nun pleased."

Then the Blessed One uttered praise for one who is desirous of training, and spoke in praise of respect for training, of keeping equipment for training at hand, of the qualities of one who is disciplined, of subtlety, and of knowing the right measure of warmth. He then addressed the monks with words in harmony with that teaching, consonant with it, rich in its substance, and in accord with its Dharma. Having done so, the Blessed One spoke to the monks:

"Monks, what came before was a prohibition; this is now a permission. My disciples shall establish the following as a rule of training in the Vinaya: If any monk takes a robe from a nun who is not a blood relation — exchange excepted — he commits an offense requiring forfeiture."

Now, as to the phrase "any monk" — this refers to a companion monk or any other of that kind. The phrase "a nun" refers to one who belongs to this very Dharma. The phrase "who is not a blood relation" means that a relation through one's grandmother, grandfather, or up to the seventh degree of cousinship counts as a blood relation; beyond that, one is not a blood relation. The phrase "a robe" refers to whichever of the seven kinds of cloth: wool cloth, linen cloth, silk cloth, fine cotton cloth, coarse woolen cloth, cotton cloth, or hempen cloth. The phrase "takes" means taking it as one's own. The phrase "exchange excepted" means that an exchange has been set aside. The phrase "commits an offense requiring forfeiture" means that having forfeited the object, the transgression — a forfeiture offense — is to be confessed; that is why it is said to be "an offense requiring forfeiture."

As to how the offense arises: if a monk takes a robe from a nun who is not a blood relation while perceiving her as not a blood relation, he commits an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk takes a robe from a nun who is not a blood relation while being uncertain about her, he commits an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk takes a robe from a nun who is a blood relation while perceiving her as not a blood relation, he commits a wrongdoing. If a monk takes a robe from a nun who is a blood relation while being uncertain about her, he commits a wrongdoing.

There is no offense in offering a robe to the Saṅgha or in speaking well of it. There is no offense if one has undertaken full ordination and then abandoned it, or if one is utterly ruined. There is no offense in receiving by purchase, and there is no offense in exchange.

There is a nun of great fame and merit. She placed goods before a monk and said, "Noble one, I have such and such things. Please accept them out of compassion for me," and then she departed without looking back. In such a case there is no offense.

There is no offense for one who is a novice, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by painful sensations.

The fifth section, on the abandonment of taking, is complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha), the Bhagavān, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had taken a wife from his own social rank. He would play with her, delight in her, and take his pleasure in her company. One day he said to his wife, "Dear one, I must pack my things and travel to another region. For a time, young lady, take your delight and your joy and live happily as befits your youth. In your later years apply yourself to accumulating wealth. Dear one, for as long as the great elements of youth give one endurance of cold and heat, one should apply oneself to earning wealth; in old age one may live at ease and in comfort."

The wife thought, "What I am being urged to do is what I myself intend to do," and she said, "Very well, my lord, it shall be as you say."

The householder gave his wife a small provision of food, packed his belongings, and set off for another region.

The wife then thought, "My husband, while he is away in the cold, is being afflicted by cold; in the heat, tormented by heat; suffering from hunger and thirst; harassed by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and venomous snakes. All the effort, the exertion, and the striving he undertakes to acquire wealth and goods — all of that is for my sake. That he should be away from me while doing so is not in keeping with what is right for me." With that thought she went to the market, purchased fine cotton wool, loaded it on a fine pack-frame, had a skilled weaver weave it into a fine pair of cotton cloths, then had those cloths treated with various perfumes and placed them in a fine cloth box, where she kept them.

As for the householder, having completed his business successfully, he made a profit and returned in good time. His wife bathed him and then presented him with that pair of cloths.

The householder thought, "All the mere provisions of food I left her would not have been enough to obtain a pair of cloths like this." He realized this and said to his wife, "Dear one, where did you get this pair of cloths? Please tell me, my lord's son." The householder put them on and asked again, "Dear one, where did you get this pair of cloths? Please explain fully." After eating his meal he asked again, "Dear one, where did you get this pair of cloths?"

At that point she explained the matter to him in full detail. The householder said, "Excellent, dear one! I have been earning wealth and you too have been so diligently preserving it. In no great time our wealth and possessions will grow, increase, and become abundant."

His wife replied, "My lord's son, I obtained this through great hardship. Do not give it to anyone."

Now the householder was a person of faith, a good person with a virtuous disposition. He went to the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. As he was walking along the road he was seen by a wandering peddler of goods, who thought, "This householder is wearing a pair of cloths of such quality — he must be a man who comes by many fine things."

Now the habitual conduct of the Group of Six was that no one among them would ever leave the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended, and so a companion of theirs was walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. He saw the householder and thought to himself, "This householder is wearing a pair of cloths of such quality — he must be a man who comes by many fine things. If I do not steal them from him, I shall not be worthy of the name 'Ānanda.'" So he said to him, "Welcome, householder! Welcome! You have been gone so long, so very long — where have you been wandering, like the moon?" He added, "Noble sir, I have just come back from another region after attending to some business. Householder, have you managed to acquire much wealth?" The householder replied, "Noble sir, just a little." He then said, "Householder, is not the pond turbid? One should understand by the indication of faith. From the fact that you are wearing such a fine pair of cloths, it is evident that you have acquired great wealth. Come here — let me teach you the Dharma."

Now this companion of the Group of Six had a habit of speaking: if he talked of moral discipline, the listeners would think, "We have been born among the gods." If he talked of generosity, the listeners would think, "We should cut off even our own flesh and give it away, again and again." But if he talked of the lower realms, the listeners would come to think, "We have been reborn in the lower realms."

The householder bowed at his two feet and sat down before him in order to hear the Dharma, and the companion of the Group of Six began to teach him Dharma. He spoke to him in such a way as to inspire faith in him, and having inspired faith, the householder said, "Noble sir, I offer you one of these well-made garments."

The companion said, "Good friend, excellent! May this act of giving bring you the ornament of the mind, the furnishing of the mind, the accumulation of yogic practice, the highest aim, and the garments of the gods."

He then said, "Good friend, the Blessed One himself has declared: 'Who knows what tomorrow may bring — even death? Act with resolve this very day. That great host, the lord of death, is no friend of yours.' Good friend, give me the very fine pair of cloths you are now wearing, and from them I shall fashion a patchwork robe stitched in layers, and from my youth onward I shall travel comfortably on the side of virtue."

The householder replied, "Noble sir, do you want them? They are just like the leavings of a divine dwelling." And he added, "Noble sir, it is not that I am unwilling to offer them to you — it is just that these were given to me by my wife."

The companion retorted, "Householder, if I inspire faith in you toward another, are you then entirely under the power of one woman?" And at that, using the opportunity of the moment, he seized the upper robe from him and twisted both his arms, turning his face.

The householder said to him, "Noble sir, what does this mean? Householder" — addressing himself — "there exists a basis for the merit arising from completely giving to you, but there is no basis for the merit arising from using it for oneself. Whenever one obtains something like this, it will be used to make a Dharma robe from it, so it will be used up serving as a Dharma robe. Noble sir, shall I then go naked?"

He replied, "Householder, what use is it for you to wear a garment? Moral discipline, good conduct, and proper behavior — these are sufficient clothing. Naked, those who have lost their sense of shame and their sense of conscience are unpleasant to behold when they go about naked. But for one like you, possessed of a sense of shame and conscience, what is unpleasant about going about naked? Householder, will you not wear a loin cloth?" The householder replied, "Noble sir, I would appreciate that." Then the companion said, "The habitual practice of householders is to wear a loin cloth, carry a wood-bundle, and go about like the backside of a cow. So you too should take a wood-bundle and go off like the backside of a cow."

The people would know that a cow had strayed and come out." And with that, the companion took for himself half the loin cloth that belonged to the householder at that inauspicious midnight hour. When the householder set out carrying a bundle of firewood, going along in the manner of the backside of a cow, a gatekeeper saw him and said, "Householder, just now I saw you wearing a pair of fine garments befitting a great man. Were those stolen by thieves?" "My friend, the thieves did not steal them. Rather, it was the venerable companion who stripped me of them by the law of the mouth." "Householder, it is the custom of the institution of Anāthapiṇḍada to rise early each morning and go with a retinue of five hundred to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and the elder monks. So, householder Anāthapiṇḍada, you rose early this morning and came out of Śrāvastī with a retinue of five hundred — why did you bring so many associates and yet take no precaution against being robbed?" "Oh noble one, are there bandits between the Jeta Grove and the road?" "Not on the road — the bandits are right there in the Jeta Grove itself." "Noble sir, you are like a black wool — since you came through this very gate, none among the Blessed One or the elder monks have made you white. As for me, I have taken upon my own head the dust from the feet of the Blessed One and the elder monks. Yet today, in broad daylight, you stripped a great householder of his fine pair of garments, then shamed the householder and sent him off in a short loin cloth." Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself, "This is my own affair," and he went to the Jeta Grove. When the companion saw him, he said, "Householder, how are you?" The householder replied, "Whether well or not, so be it." "Householder, before, when you were lukewarm toward me, now you burn with fire alone?" "How could I not burn with fire? While others go forth into renunciation in order to abandon desire, the venerable companion has gone forth for the sole purpose of actively increasing desire. What have I done? You came to the Jeta Grove like a householder, and there you seized half the loin cloth by force at midnight and shamed the householder — do you not?" The companion replied, "That is what they say in the world: gods give, and hungry ghosts (pretas) take back. Well, did he hand you a round pill with a ringing sound? Householder, if you cannot bear it, let a rule of training be promulgated. Would I simply throw that away for nothing?" Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, bowed with his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable sir, if these noble ones solicit clothing from those who are not the householder's close relatives or the householder's kinsmen present, then — O Blessed One — it would be fitting for you to institute some reminder for the noble ones so that noble ones do not solicit clothing from those who are not the householder's close relatives or the householder's kinsmen present." The Blessed One said nothing to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and by his silence he consented. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had consented, rose from his seat, bowed with his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and on account of this ground for legislation,

"On this occasion, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks" — and so forth, as before. "The blessed buddhas, while knowing, act as though they do not know" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One asked Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you solicited clothing from someone who was not the householder's or the householder's wife's close relative?" "Venerable one, it is not so." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that what was unworthy of an ascetic, what was improper, what was unsuitable, what was unbecoming of one's conduct — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One spoke to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya thus: 'Whatever monk goes to a householder or to a householder's wife who is not a close relative and solicits clothing — that is an offence entailing relinquishment.'" In this way the Blessed One established that training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The Vinaya Analysis, the thirtieth bundle.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Forty monks from the city of Vaiśālī, who were of like purpose, were travelling and journeying together through the countryside, when they were set upon by bandits. They thought to themselves: "The Blessed One has established the training rule that whatever monk goes to a householder or to a householder's wife who is not a close relative and solicits clothing commits an offence entailing relinquishment. We have no relatives here at all. If we go to Śrāvastī, our fellow practitioners of the holy life there will share clothing with us." So they said to one another: "Shall we travel in broad daylight? Let us rather travel by night under cover of darkness — hide in the bushes during the day and set out on the road at night." So they went to the Jeta Grove by night under cover of darkness. Some monks who were devoted to practice and did not sleep during the first or the last part of the night saw them and said: "You naked vagabonds — this is not your dwelling place, nor is it a temple. Where have you come from?" The venerable ones replied: "We are not naked wanderers." "Then who are you?" "We are monks." "Are there monks like this? What happened to you? Were you set upon by bandits?" "We are indeed the forty monks of Vaiśālī." "Welcome, welcome, venerable ones!" And some of those monks gave them patchwork robes, some gave upper robes, some gave lower robes, and some gave sweat cloths. Thereupon the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, except in the right time — and the right time is this: when a monk's clothing has been snatched away, or destroyed, or burned, or carried off by the wind, or carried off by water — in that case it is the right time." Then the Blessed One praised those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who devote themselves to the means of training. He then addressed the monks with talk that accorded with that, was of greater scope than that, and was in harmony with the Dharma of that. And then the Blessed One spoke to the monks: "Monks, therefore, what was formerly prescribed stands,

this is permitted. And my śrāvakas shall observe this as a rule of training in the Vinaya in the following manner: Furthermore, should any monk go to a householder or to a householder's wife who is not a relative and beg for clothing — except in the right time — he commits an offense of abandonment. And the right time is this: when a monk's clothing has been snatched away, or destroyed, or burned, or carried off by the wind, or carried off by water — in that case it is the right time.

Now, "any monk" means a fully ordained monk or another of that kind. "Householder" means a man. "Householder's wife" means a woman. "Who is not a relative" — a grandmother or grandfather down to the seventh generation of cousins counts as a relative; beyond that is not a relative. "Goes to" means goes into the presence of. "Clothing" means any one of the seven kinds: woolen cloth, linen, silk, cotton cloth, coarse hemp cloth, jute cloth, or cloth of that which grows beneath the sun. "Begs" means makes a request. "Except in the right time" means outside of the appointed time. "Commits an offense of abandonment" means that, having relinquished that object, the transgression of abandonment is to be confessed.

Now, "the right time" as stated — "when a monk's clothing has been snatched away" — means this: the monk's clothing has been taken away by thieves or by deceitful persons. "Or destroyed" means this: the monk's clothing has been ruined or has gone to waste. "Or burned" means this: the monk's clothing has been burned by fire. "Or carried off by the wind" means this: the monk's clothing has been carried off by wind. "Or carried off by water" means this: the monk's clothing has been carried off by water.

Now, how does a transgression arise? It arises on the basis of value, of color, and of measure. How does it arise on the basis of value? If a monk begs for clothing worth five kārṣāpaṇas and receives clothing worth five kārṣāpaṇas, then the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment. In the same way, if he begs for clothing worth ten kārṣāpaṇas, fifteen kārṣāpaṇas, twenty kārṣāpaṇas, or up to fifty kārṣāpaṇas, and receives clothing worth fifty kārṣāpaṇas, then the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment. If a monk begs for clothing worth five kārṣāpaṇas and receives something of greater value, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the greater amount there is no transgression. In the same way, if he begs for clothing worth ten, fifteen, twenty, or up to fifty kārṣāpaṇas and receives something of greater value, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the greater amount there is no transgression. Such is transgression on the basis of value.

How does it arise on the basis of color? If a monk begs for blue clothing and receives blue clothing, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment. Just as with blue, so too if he begs for yellow, red, heavy cloth, or fine cloth, and receives the fine cloth, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment. If a monk begs for blue clothing and receives yellow —

the act of begging for blue constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the yellow there is no transgression. Just as with begging for blue, so too if he begs for yellow, red, heavy cloth, or fine cloth, and in begging for fine cloth he receives heavy cloth — the act of begging for fine cloth constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the higher-quality item there is no transgression. Such is transgression on the basis of color.

How does it arise on the basis of size in cubits? If a monk begs for a five-cubit cloth and receives a five-cubit cloth, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment. Just as with five cubits, so too if he begs for cloth of ten cubits, fifteen cubits, twenty cubits, up to fifty cubits, and receives a fifty-cubit cloth, the act of begging constitutes a wrongdoing, and if he receives it, it becomes an offense of abandonment.

If a monk begs for a five-cubit cloth and receives something larger, the act of begging for the five-cubit cloth constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the larger amount there is no transgression. Just as with five cubits, so too if he begs for cloth of ten cubits, fifteen cubits, twenty cubits, up to fifty cubits — if in begging for the fifty-cubit cloth he receives something larger, the act of begging for the fifty-cubit cloth constitutes a wrongdoing, but in receiving the larger amount there is no transgression. Such is transgression on the basis of size in cubits.

If a monk does not beg for finished cloth but receives pieces of cut cloth, or if he begs for pieces of cut cloth but receives finished cloth, or if he does not beg for finished cloth but receives whole bolts of cloth, large or small — in all these cases there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression for one who acts for the first time, for one who is mentally deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one overcome by pain. The sixth offense of abandonment — that of begging — is hereby complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A thought arose in Ānanda's mind: "All of these laymen have been bound by the training rules established by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, so that henceforth they cannot offer even the price of a needle from anywhere. Since the Blessed One has, in dependence upon the forty village-dwelling monks, relaxed certain training rules, I shall send those forty village-dwelling monks ahead and thereby secure provisions." With that intention he went to where the forty village-dwelling monks were, and he saw them there mending and patching their torn and worn-out robes. He said to them: "Venerable ones, I had heard and imagined otherwise — I had thought in my mind that you forty village-dwelling monks would be enjoying the pleasures of meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and states of meditative entry. I had not thought, venerable ones, that I would find you sitting here mending and patching worn and tattered robes."

The elder monks replied: "We have been undone by thieves, venerable one. Alas, how unfortunate! How very unfortunate!" Ānanda said: "Elder, for whose sake do you grieve? For ours? No — those who have taken without being given what belongs to you will be reborn in complete isolation and will die in complete isolation. It is for their sake that one should grieve."

Then Ānanda said to them: "Venerable ones, why do you not beg for robes? Is there any elder who, having abandoned the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, would think to give to us and do so? Venerable ones, were you not praised, honored, extolled, and highly commended by the Blessed One in various sūtra passages? Elder, we ourselves do not know from whom to beg. Venerable ones, why do you not entrust the task to some knowledgeable monk who can beg for robes on your behalf?"

What knowledgeable elder monk would ruin his own stock of virtue and beg robes on our behalf? Venerable ones, for the moment I myself have resources for even ten people, and furthermore, since each of us six is able to provide for ten, we six together have resources for sixty people. Moreover, if it would not trouble you, we will also beg small and large pieces of cloth on behalf of the young monks. Elder, what trouble is there to us in this? For the time being, let each one beg and obtain three robes apiece. Venerable ones, since we cannot both go on alms round and also beg for robes, let it be done this way: whenever one is invited outside for food, the robes shall be requested at that time."

With this, Ānanda washed his feet outside the monastery, entered inside, and sat down. He thought to himself: "What means could be found to clothe all of Śrāvastī?" Then he thought further: "First I shall go to the street of the poor, and after that to the street of the wealthy. After that I shall go to the palace of King Prasenajit of Kosala, to the household of Queen Kṣullodharā of royal lineage, to the household of Queen Mālagandha, to the household of the layman Anāthapiṇḍada, to the preceptor the sage Jina, to the households of the two elders, to the household of the laywoman Mṛgāramatā, and to the household of the laywoman Sujanā, wife of the householder."

At that time a householder invited the community of monks with the Buddha at their head to another house for a midday meal. Ānanda said to the young monks: "Venerable ones, if tasks are assigned to you, do not refuse but say to them, 'Our preceptors and teachers have a small matter to attend to.'"

The next morning Ānanda sent a young monk to the forty monks of the city to request them to come back, having collected the robes. When the young monk arrived there and saw that they were all in meditative absorption, he thought: "Who in the world, with a heart devoid of compassion, would rouse these ones from their meditative absorption?" He returned to Ānanda and said: "Teacher, those monks are in meditative absorption. No one is able to rouse them from that absorption."

Ānanda said: "Poor fellow, will you realize the exhaustion of defilements with such diligence?" And he said: "I will go myself." He went and struck the door-panel of the meditation hall with his fist. The entire meditation hall shook, and they arose from their absorption and said: "If the forty venerable monks are to beg three robes, should you not station yourselves in a smaller space in our hearts? Come, let us go. Elder Jesa, take your staff and go. Come now — let us go by this very road."

Then those noble ones and Ānanda said: "Venerable ones, we six of the group are like white crows, and so rather than standing in strict order of seniority, let the elders be interspersed at intervals among the others." They went to the street of the poor, turned to face outward, and stood. When the people there saw them they were moved with pity and said: "Noble ones, has no fault occurred? Fair ones, a fault has occurred. What has gone wrong? Have you heard that the forty monks of the city whom the Blessed One praised, honored, extolled, and highly commended in various sūtra passages —"

"Have you heard?" "We have heard. They were beaten by bandits." The people said: "Wise ones, take up bows and arrows! Take up spears and clubs! We will go and seize the bandits!" The group of six said: "It is long since they were beaten, and they have since robbed in other districts. So what shall be done? Give those monks some robes." The people then gave them both new and old robes. But the group of six found those robes too burdensome to carry, so they handed them to some young men and said: "Take these to the monastery right away." The young men carried the robes and set off for the monastery. Then the group of six went to the street of the wealthy, stood there with their bowls held out, and lingered. When the people there saw them they were moved with pity and said: "Noble ones, has no fault occurred?" "A fault has occurred." "What has gone wrong?" "Have you heard of the forty monks of the city whom the Blessed One praised, honored, extolled, and highly commended in various sūtra passages?" "We have heard. They were beaten by bandits." The people said: "Wise ones, take up bows and arrows! Take up spears and clubs! We will go and seize the bandits!" The group of six said: "It is long since they were beaten, and they have since robbed in other districts. So what shall be done? Give those monks some robes." The people then gave them robes befitting persons of high station. The group of six found those robes too burdensome to carry, so they handed them to some young men and said: "Take these to the monastery right away." The young men carried the robes and set off for the monastery. Then the group of six went to the palace of King Prasenajit (Skt. Prasenajit), the king of Kosala, and stood there with their bowls held out. King Prasenajit of Kosala saw them and was moved with pity and said: "Noble ones, has no fault occurred?" "Your Majesty, a fault has occurred." "What has gone wrong?" "Your Majesty, have you heard of the forty monks of the city whom the Blessed One praised, honored, extolled, and highly commended in various sūtra passages?" "We have heard. They were beaten by bandits." The king said to his general Āryajāta: "Go quickly and seize the bandits and recover the stolen goods." The group of six said: "Your Majesty, those bandits struck long ago and have since robbed in other districts. So what shall be done?" "Your Majesty, give those monks some robes." The king gave each of the monks a set of thirteen requisites. The group of six found those robes too burdensome to carry, so they handed them to some young men and said: "Take these to the monastery right away." Those young men carried the robes and set off for the monastery. Then the forty monks of the city said: "Elders, that is enough — release us now." The group of six said: "Venerable ones, do not be so impatient. Did we not say to you from the very beginning: 'Venerable ones, if you will not harm us, we on our part will beg small strips of cloth and large strips of cloth for the sake of the young men'?" Since those monks were known to be of great influence, the group of six, daunted by their authority, said nothing more and stood in silence. Then the group of six went to the house of the queen of the kṣatriya lineage, Varṣatulā; to the house of the queen Mālikā; to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; to the house of the brahmin teacher Kṛtajña; to the house of the two elders; to the house of the lay woman Mṛgāramatā, Migāra's mother;

and to the house of the laywoman Sujanā, wife of the householder, and so on in order, speaking the words as described before. Those households each gave thirteen sets of requisites to each monk.

Then the group of six said: "Venerable ones, if the monks are not arranged in the rows of a hundred, the rows will be left empty. Today, please take your places in the rows. Do not worry — we too will go after collecting alms." The group of six then went to the monastery and gathered forty sets of old rags into a pile and left them there.

When the forty monks came back having finished their meal, the group of six, sitting there among them, said to the attendant monks: "Venerable ones, come here — call just a few of them over." The attendants called them, and the group of six said: "Venerable ones, are we guarding your robes? Take your own robes." The forty monks then began to look at one another, and the group of six said: "Venerable ones, why are you looking at one another? The elders' things are nothing but old rags. Venerable ones, these here — tie them together; they are patched robes. These are stitched-together rags and an upper robe. These are stitched-together rags and a lower robe. These are stitched-together rags and a sweat cloth. If you do not want them, go ahead — you may raise the matter again. Oh well, venerable elders, it is fine even if those are not raised." The monks took those old rags, went off to the hermitage, and stitched and sewed them.

The word spread everywhere: "Each of the forty monks from Vārāṇasī has obtained seven sets of the thirteen requisites." When other monks saw this and were told of it, they said: "Venerable ones, we have heard one thing and seen another. We hear that each of the forty monks from Vārāṇasī has obtained seven sets of the thirteen requisites, venerable ones, and that the old rags have been stitched and sewn up." They replied: "You see — we also heard that they were to be carried off each on their own shoulders." With this, the matter was reported to those monks, and those monks reported it to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, on account of this case, on account of this circumstance, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so on just as before. "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, act as if they do not know" — and so forth, again just as before.

The blessed Buddha then questioned the forty monks from Vārāṇasī: "Monks, is it true that you did not know the proper measure of what you were receiving?" "Blessed One, it is so." The blessed Buddha censured lack of effort, lack of application, and acting without examining, and then, having praised effort, application, and acting with thorough examination, he declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training shall be established for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so on just as before. "My śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should a monk's robe be stolen, destroyed, burned, carried off by the wind, or swept away by water, he may go to a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative and request a robe. If a brahmin or a faithful householder should wish to supply him with many robes at the right time, that monk may accept from them at most one upper robe and one lower robe. To accept more than that is an offense entailing relinquishment.

The word 'monk' here refers to one belonging to this Dharma."

The phrase "robe stolen" means this: a monk's robes have been taken by thieves or by swindlers.

The phrase "robe destroyed" means this: a monk's robes have been ruined or have fallen to pieces through wear.

The phrase "robe burned" means this: a monk's robes have been consumed by fire.

The phrase "robe carried off by wind" means this: a monk's robes have been carried away by the wind.

The phrase "robe swept away by water" means this: a monk's robes have been swept away by water.

The word "householder" means a man. The phrase "householder's wife" means a woman. The phrase "not a relative" means this: one's grandmother, grandfather, and all relations down through the seventh generation of cousins are relatives; beyond that they are not relatives.

The phrase "go to" means to go and approach.

The word "robe" refers to any one of the seven kinds: wool fabric, linen fabric, silk fabric, fine cotton fabric, coarse cotton fabric, hemp fabric, and jute fabric.

The phrase "may request" means to beg for.

The phrase "should wish" means if one genuinely desires it.

The phrase "may accept at most one upper robe and one lower robe" is explained as follows. Upper and lower robes together come in two kinds: the upper and lower robes of a monk, and the upper and lower robes of a layman. The upper and lower robes of a monk consist of a stitched and layered patchwork robe, a plain length of fine cloth of five cubits, and a belt. The upper and lower robes of a layman consist of a large length of cloth of twelve cubits, a smaller length of cloth of seven cubits, and a belt.

The phrase "to accept more than that" means anything beyond those.

The phrase "an offense entailing relinquishment" means that the object in question must be relinquished and then the offense of transgression confessed. That is why it is called an offense entailing relinquishment.

As for how the transgression arises: if a monk has requested the upper and lower robes of a layman and has received them, and he then requests more, the very act of requesting more constitutes a wrong-doing; and should he actually receive more, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment. If a monk has requested the upper and lower robes of a monk and has received them, and he then requests more, the very act of requesting more constitutes a wrong-doing; and should he actually receive more, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.

If a monk has requested the upper and lower robes of a layman and has received them, then even if what he received falls short of the full measure he should not ask for more, and even if there is a surplus it should not be given to him. If a monk has requested the upper and lower robes of a monk and has received them, then even if what he received falls short of the full measure he may ask for more, and any surplus may also be given to him.

Thus, in all cases: if a monk requests more than the upper and lower robes of a layman, or if more than the upper and lower robes of a monk is given, an offense entailing relinquishment arises.

If a monk's robe has become subject to relinquishment and he has neither relinquished it nor separated himself from it, and has not yet confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another robe, that second robe too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the first. If a monk's robe has become subject to relinquishment and he has relinquished it but has not yet separated himself from it, and has not yet confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another robe, that second robe too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the first. If a monk's robe has become subject to relinquishment and he has both relinquished it and separated himself from it, but has not yet confessed the transgression, and then he obtains another robe, that second robe too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the first.

If a monk's robe has become subject to relinquishment and he has relinquished it, separated himself from it, and confessed the transgression, and then obtains another robe, there is no transgression in that case.

Likewise, for as long as a monk, without having confessed and individually confessed the very item subject to relinquishment, proceeds to keep at hand an alms bowl, a Dharma robe, a net, a cup, a belt, or any requisite for a renunciant's livelihood, that too becomes subject to relinquishment by reason of the first. There is no transgression for one who is a novice, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The seventh category, relinquishment of what is fitting to beg, is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now in Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had taken a wife from a family of equal standing. With her he sported, took delight, and enjoyed himself in pleasure. That householder then became attached to another man's wife. His own wife tried to dissuade him, saying, "My lord and master, do not act in this way." But however much she dissuaded him, he did not turn back, and so his wife too began to enter into misconduct with other men. The householder gave himself to other women, and the wife gave herself to other men, and in this way both of them brought their household to ruin. They had a maidservant living with them, and the householder beat that girl with his fists and the flat of his hand, saying, "It is you who have ruined this household." The girl replied, "I would indeed wish to know what has caused this household to fall into ruin. But how could it be right for me to speak ill of my masters?" A close friend, having understood the situation, went to both the householder and his wife and, wishing by some means to bring the two of them to take refuge and to abide by the precepts of training, spoke in praise of moral discipline and spoke words that were no praise of moral laxity. And so that friend brought the two of them to take refuge and to abide by the precepts of training.

Now the householder was fierce, rough, and hot-tempered, and he began to beat the girl again. His wife then said to him, "My lord and master, at such time as you and I did not know karma and the karmic maturation of karma, you might perhaps have struck her in your ignorance. But now, relying on our good spiritual friend, the noble Ānanda, we know karma and its karmic maturation. In this world, beings experience the fruit of their own karma — so who is anyone's slave? Do not beat this girl. You called her a good woman — that was not wrong. Girl, come here. Come, wash yourself." The girl came after washing, and the wife dressed her in a fine robe and said, "Girl, be glad and go about your work."

The girl thought to herself, "This householder, my master, was formerly fierce, rough, and hot-tempered, and again and again he used to beat me with fists and the flat of his hand and give me poor food and poor clothing. But now he has become like a father to me." Then she thought again, "From the time the noble Ānanda began to enter this house, the householder has been like a father to me, so how should I make the noble Ānanda glad? What could I do for him?" And she thought, "If I were to steal a little from here and give it secretly — but then the householder would beat me severely and return me to my former situation." And so she sat and remained where she was.

Then the householder's wife said to the householder:

"My lord's son should know this: the noble Ānanda is our spiritual friend. The noble Ānanda has separated us from defilement, established us in the going for refuge and the bases of training, and again and again he gathers us together through the Dharma. Therefore we too should gather him in with a little material gift." "Excellent, let it be so. But what shall we do?" "We should offer him a fine large cloth." The girl, hearing this, thought to herself, "I shall express my joy to the noble Ānanda."

Now Ānanda, having put on his lower robe early in the morning and taken up his bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī on his alms round, and as he moved through the streets collecting alms in order, he entered that house. The girl had swept the house well and scattered fresh floor coverings, and when she saw Ānanda she prostrated at his two feet and said, "I shall express my delight to the noble Ānanda. The householder here will offer you a fine large cloth."

Ānanda thought to himself, "All those beings on the earth who possess desire — this girl today has put me on a par with every one of them," and he scolded her, saying, "Girl, if this is true, do not take offence at my scolding you. But if it is false, I shall have you severely beaten and put back in your former situation. If the noble one reproaches you at length, then leave — and you will find out for yourself."

She departed and sat down right where a seat had been prepared. Then the householder together with his wife prostrated at his feet, took seats lower than his, and sat before him to hear the Dharma. Ānanda said, "Householder, let me see this fine large cloth that is to be given to me." The two of them began to look at each other and said, "Noble one, who told you what we said to each other in private? Does the noble one also know the minds of others?"

Ānanda replied, "I have eaten from the bowl and my teeth have worn down and my hair has turned white — could something even so small as this be beyond me?" The householder then took the fine large cloth and offered it to Ānanda. When Ānanda saw the fine large cloth he wrung his hands together and twisted his face. The householder asked, "Noble one, why do you wring your two hands? Why do you twist your face?" Ānanda said, "Householder, for you there is indeed merit arising from having given it away completely, but there is no merit arising from having enjoyed it to the full. This fine large cloth is fit only for wiping boots or patching a window — it will end up worn out and finished off on the face of a robe. So what is to be done?" "Give a different, better fine large cloth." "There is no other fine large cloth." "Buy one from the market and give it." "There is no money." "Give it when the time comes." The householder began to look toward his wife's face, and his wife said, "My lord's son, since the noble Ānanda has benefited us, take out a fine large cloth and offer it to him."

The householder then went to the market together with Ānanda, and they arrived at a shop. Ānanda thought to himself, "I shall arouse the merchant's pride, and then he will give a good fine large cloth." So Ānanda said to the householder, "Householder, this merchant is a small trader — he will have no good fine large cloth here. Let us go elsewhere." When the merchant heard this, he brought out a fine large cloth fit for a great person and said, "Noble one, please look at this fine large cloth. If this cloth is of good quality, the price is such and such, this much. Householder, measure it out. Has the householder measured it? Yes, it is measured. When is payment due? Payment is due at such and such a time."

The merchant gave that fine large cloth to the householder, and the householder presented it to Ānanda. Ānanda said to the householder, "Arogy" — a term of address — and spoke these words: "May this act of generosity become an ornament of your mind, a resource of your mind, an accumulation of yogic merit, the attainment of the highest goal, and the attainment of the robes of gods and humans." So saying, he departed.

The householder then fell into reduced circumstances, and when the time came he was unable to pay the price in full. The merchant had him brought before the sun — that is, exposed him publicly — and when the young companions of the householder saw this, they said, "What is this? Have you been drinking melted butter, or have you been struck by plague? You are being held by a creditor. Your father never had debts, and your ancestors never had debts — so where has this debt come from?" He replied, "Those who place their faith in the śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), the sons of the Śākyan, end up like this: whatever is given to them, they do not take it as enough but always beg for more."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, in regard to this occurrence, this basis, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks, and so on as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign ignorance, and so on as before. The Blessed One asked Ānanda, "Ānanda, is it true that, not being satisfied with what was given, you urged for more?" "Venerable one, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that such conduct was unbefitting the way of a śramaṇa, was not in accord with it, was not appropriate, and was contrary to proper conduct — it was not something a person who has gone forth should do. Having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training (Skt. śikṣāpada) for the hearers in the Vinaya," and so on as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a householder, or the wife of a householder, who is not a relative, has set aside funds for the purchase of robes on behalf of a monk, thinking, 'I shall use these funds to purchase such and such a robe, and when the monk of such and such a name arrives, I shall present him in due time with a robe that is suitable' — then if, before the cloth has been procured, some thought arises in that monk and, out of desire for something fine, he goes to that householder or that wife of a householder who is not a relative, and says, 'Venerable one, you have set aside robe-funds on my behalf; please use those funds to purchase for me such and such a robe and present it to me in good time as a robe that is suitable' — if he obtains the robe in this way, it is an offense requiring forfeiture (Skt. nissaggiya pācittika).

"On behalf of a monk" means on behalf of Ānanda, a son of the Śākyans, or anyone else of that kind. "A householder" means a man. "The wife of a householder" means a woman. "Who is not a relative" — grandmothers and grandfathers, and those related within seven generations, count as relatives; beyond that they are not relatives. "Funds for the purchase of robes" means gold or silver. "Such and such a robe" means any one of the seven: a woolen cloth, a linen cloth, a silk cloth, a fine cotton cloth, a coarse cotton cloth, a hemp cloth, or a half-and-half cloth. "Purchase" means having purchased it. "When the monk of such and such a name arrives" means Ānanda, the son of the Śākyans. "I shall present him in due time with a robe that is suitable" means one that is acceptable for use.

"If the monk had not previously been invited" means he had not previously been called as a guest. "Some deliberation arose" means that some consideration of hospitality arose. "Out of a desire for something fine" means for the sake of what is excellent and superior. "Having gone to the presence of the householder or the householder's wife who is not a relative" means having gone directly to them. "If a robe should be obtained" means if a robe is received. "It is an offense entailing forfeiture" means that the thing in question must be forfeited and the offense of transgression confessed; that is why it is said to be an offense entailing forfeiture.

Now, how does the transgression arise? It arises through three things: value, color, and measure in cubits.

How does it arise through value? If a monk has received a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas and then solicits something beyond that, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for what was received before. Just as for a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas, so too for a robe worth ten kārṣāpaṇas, twenty kārṣāpaṇas, or up to fifty kārṣāpaṇas — if a monk has received such a robe and solicits beyond that value, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for what was received before. Such is the arising of the transgression through value.

How does it arise through color? If a monk has received a blue robe and solicits something beyond it, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for what was received before. Just as with blue, so too with yellow, red, heavy, and light — if such a robe has been received and something beyond it is solicited, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for what was received before. Such is the arising of the transgression through color.

How does it arise through measure in cubits? If a monk has received a robe of five cubits and solicits something beyond that, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for what was received before. Just as for a robe of five cubits, so too for robes of ten cubits, twenty cubits, or up to fifty cubits — if such a robe has been received and something beyond it is solicited, the solicitation of the excess constitutes a misdeed, and upon obtaining it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Such is the arising of the transgression through measure in cubits.

If a monk's robe is subject to forfeiture, and he neither forfeits it nor separates himself from it, and without having confessed the transgression he obtains another, that other also falls under forfeiture by continuity with the first. If a monk's robe is subject to forfeiture, and he forfeits it but does not separate himself from it, and without having confessed the transgression he obtains another, that other also falls under forfeiture by continuity with the first. If a monk's robe is subject to forfeiture, and he forfeits it and separates himself from it, but without having confessed the transgression he obtains another, that other also falls under forfeiture by continuity with the first. If a monk's robe is subject to forfeiture, and he forfeits it, separates himself from it, confesses the transgression, and then obtains another, there is no transgression with respect to that.

Likewise, as long as a monk's robe is subject to forfeiture and that matter has not been confessed and individually disclosed, if he takes possession of an alms bowl, a Dharma robe, a net bag, a small bowl, a belt, or any other article of the ascetic's livelihood, those too fall under forfeiture by continuity with the first.

There is no transgression when soliciting a patch and receiving thread along with it, or when soliciting thread and receiving a small or large piece of cloth. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The eighth forfeiture — soliciting in excess beyond what had been entrusted — is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At Śrāvastī, there was a certain householder who had taken a wife from a family of equal rank. He lived with her in play, in delight, and in happiness. But then that householder became attached to another man's wife. Whenever his own wife tried to restrain him from this, no matter how often she did so, he would not turn back — and to the same degree his own wife began to take up misconduct with other men. The householder, for his part, gave himself to other women, and his wife gave herself to other men, and in this way both sides of the household fell into ruin. The couple had a maidservant girl in their house, and the householder began to beat her with fists and slaps, saying that she had caused the household's ruin. The girl said, "I would indeed wish to know what I have done to cause this ruin. And yet, how could it be right for me to speak words that are no praise of my masters? But let a dear friend take note." Hearing this, that dear friend went to both the householder and his wife, and in whatever way would lead them to take refuge and to abide in the foundations of the training, spoke in praise of moral discipline and against the lack of it, until those two were made to take refuge and to abide in the foundations of the training.

The householder was violent, rough, and overbearing, and he began to beat the girl again. At this, the wife spoke to him: "O son of a master, there was a time when you did not know about karma and the ripening of karma, and in those days you could be said to strike blows. But now we have relied upon the noble one Nandika as our virtuous spiritual friend, and through him we know about karma and its ripening. In this world, beings fare according to the fruit of their own karma — so who then is anyone's slave? Do not strike this girl. Good woman, it is not wrong that you are called 'good.' Come, girl, come — wash yourself and come." The girl washed herself and returned, and the wife dressed her in a new robe and said, "Girl, be glad and work joyfully."

The girl thought to herself, "This master of the household, my owner, was formerly violent, rough, and overbearing, beating me again and again with fists and slaps and giving me poor food and poor clothing. But now he has become like a father and mother to me." And she thought further: "From the time the noble one Nandika began to come to this house, this householder has been like a father and mother to me — so what can I do to gladden the noble one Nandika?" She thought: "If I were to steal a little from here, and the householder were to find the shortage, he would beat and harass me greatly and put me back in my former state." And so she stayed where she was, in her place.

The householder's wife then spoke to the householder: "O son of a master, please know this: the noble one Nandika is our virtuous spiritual friend. The noble one Nandika separated us from defilement, established us in the going for refuge and in the foundations of the training, and again and again he gathers us in through the Dharma. Let us gather him in, in return, with some material gift." "Very well — let it be done so. But what shall we do? Let each of us from our own means offer a large bolt of cloth." The girl, hearing this, thought to herself, "I too shall join my joy to the noble one Nandika's."

Now Nandika, in the early morning, having dressed, taken his bowl and his robe, had entered Śrāvastī on the alms round, and as he went gradually along collecting alms, he entered that house. The girl, having carefully swept and cleaned the house and laid out a cloth, saw Nandika and bowed at his two feet, saying:
