"I shall join my joy to the noble one Nandika's. This householder and the householder's wife will each offer you a large bolt of cloth."

Nandika thought to himself, "Among all those on the face of the earth who are possessed of desire, this girl today has gone as far as any of them," and he rebuked her, saying: "Girl, if it is true, do not take offense at the rebuke I give you. But if it is false, then I shall have you given many blows and beatings and left in your former condition. Noble one, if you are given to much abuse, please leave — and you yourself shall come to understand."

She went inside, and as soon as she took her seat on the prepared cushion, the householder together with his wife bowed at his two feet, took lower seats, and sat before him to hear the Dharma.

Nandika said: "Householder, observe what you have done — each of you offering me a large bolt of cloth." The two of them began looking at one another and said: "Noble one, who disclosed to you what we said in secret? Does the noble one know the minds of others too?"

Nandika replied: "I have eaten from my bowl, my teeth are worn down, and my hair has turned white — is even this much not possible for me? Householder and wife, each take a large bolt of cloth and present it to Nandika." They took the large bolts of cloth and offered them to Nandika, and when Nandika saw those large bolts of cloth, he wrung his hands together and turned his face aside.

The householder asked: "Noble one, why do you wring your hands together? Why do you turn your face aside?"

Nandika replied: "Householder, there is merit arising from the renunciation you have made, but there is no merit arising from full enjoyment — these large bolts of cloth are fit only for wiping sandals or patching windows. They will be worn out and come to an end in binding up monastic robes. Then what shall we do? Give other, finer large bolts of cloth." "We have no large bolts of cloth." "Buy some from the market and give them." "We have no money." "Give them when the time comes."

The householder began looking toward his wife's face, and the wife said: "Son of a noble family, since the noble Nandika has shown us kindness, let us borrow large bolts of cloth and offer them to him."

The householder went together with Nandika to the market street and entered a shop. Nandika thought, "I shall provoke the merchant's pride, and then he will give fine, large bolts of cloth," so Nandika said to the householder: "Householder, this merchant is a petty fellow — there will be no fine large bolts of cloth here. Let us go elsewhere."

When the merchant heard this, he displayed large bolts of cloth of a quality befitting something great, and said: "Noble one, look at these large bolts of cloth. These bolts are fine — how much are they? So and so much. Householder, will you measure them?" "Yes, I will measure." "How long a time will you need? About this much time."

The merchant gave those large bolts of cloth to the householder, and the householder offered them to Nandika. Nandika said to the householder, "Excellent!" and added: "By this generosity of yours, may you obtain an ornament of mind, and provisions for the mind, and the accumulation of yoga, and the attainment of the highest aim, and the garments of gods and humans" — and then he departed.

The householder's means had become thin, and he was unable to pay the price within the allotted time, so the merchant brought the householder to court before the sun. When he was brought low, his friends saw him and said: "Have you been drinking melted butter? Or have you been struck by fever? You are being held by a creditor. Your father never incurred debts, nor did your grandfather — so how did this debt come about?"

He replied: "Those who place their faith in the śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), the sons of the Śākyas, come to be like this —

saying that whoever gives something will be unsatisfied with what they have received and will demand more besides."

The monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this origin-case, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, feign ignorance" also proceeds as before. The Blessed One then questioned Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you were unsatisfied with what was given and demanded more?" He replied: "Venerable One, it is not so." The Blessed One then censured the conduct unworthy of a śramaṇa, the conduct not in conformity with the training, the conduct not proper, the conduct not in accord with the rule, declaring that one who has gone forth should not act in such a way. After censuring it in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits, one should establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If, for the sake of a monk, a householder and someone who is not a close relative of the householder's wife each set aside separate cloth-fund contributions, thinking, 'We two, using our separate cloth-fund contributions, will each separately purchase this or that variety of robe and present a suitable robe to the monk so-and-so when he comes' — then, if that monk, without having been invited beforehand, approaches out of desire for something superior that householder and that non-relative of the householder's wife and says: 'Venerable ones, please pool together the separate cloth-fund contributions that the venerable ones have set aside for my sake, purchase this or that variety of robe together, and at the right time present me with a suitable robe' — if he obtains the robe in this way, he commits an offense involving relinquishment (Skt. naihsargika-pācittika)."

Now, the phrase "for the sake of a monk" means: for the sake of Ānanda, the son of the Śākyas, or for the sake of any other monk of that kind. "A householder" means a man. "The householder's wife" means a woman. "Non-relative" means: up to and including a grandmother, grandfather, or seventh-degree cousin by descent — these count as relatives; beyond that, they are non-relatives. "Cloth-fund" means gold or silver. "This or that variety of robe" means any one of the seven: woolen cloth, hempen cloth, silk, fine muslin, coarse cotton, kotamba cloth, or bark cloth. "Purchase" means: let them buy it. "The monk so-and-so comes" means: Ānanda, the son of the Śākyas, comes. "Present a suitable robe at the right time" means: to allow it to be used. "Without having been invited beforehand" means: without having previously been invited as a guest. "A certain thought arising" means: a certain thought of seeking veneration arises. "Out of desire for something superior" means: for the sake of the best and finest. "Approaches that householder and that non-relative of the householder's wife" means: goes into their presence. "Pooling together" means: both together assemble it. "If he obtains the robe" means: if he receives the robe. "He commits an offense involving relinquishment" means: having relinquished the thing, one must confess the transgression — therefore it is called an offense involving relinquishment.

How then does the transgression come about? It depends on the value, the color, and the measure in cubits. As to how it comes about in terms of value —

When a monk has received a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas and then solicits something beyond that amount, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. For what came before, there is no transgression. Just as it is with a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas, so too with robes worth ten kārṣāpaṇas, twenty kārṣāpaṇas, and up to fifty kārṣāpaṇas: when a monk has received such a robe and solicits something beyond that amount, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. For what came before, there is no transgression. Thus it comes about in terms of value.

How does it come about in terms of color? When a monk has received a blue robe and solicits something beyond that, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. For what came before, there is no transgression. Just as it is with a blue robe, so too with a yellow robe, a red robe, a thick robe, and a thin robe: when a monk has received such a robe and solicits something beyond that, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. For what came before, there is no transgression. Thus it comes about in terms of color.

How does it come about in terms of measure in cubits? When a monk has received a robe of five cubits and solicits something beyond that, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. For what came before, there is no transgression. Just as it is with a robe of five cubits, so too with robes of ten cubits, twenty cubits, and up to fifty cubits: when a monk has received such a robe and solicits something beyond that, the act of soliciting the excess constitutes a wrongdoing, and should he receive it, it becomes an offense involving relinquishment. Thus it comes about in terms of measure in cubits.

If a monk's robe is to be relinquished but he has not yet relinquished it, not yet separated himself from it, and not yet confessed the transgression, and he then obtains another robe, that other robe too is to be relinquished by virtue of the continuum of the first. If a monk's robe is to be relinquished and he has relinquished it and separated himself from it, but has not yet confessed the transgression, and he then obtains another robe, that other robe too is to be relinquished by virtue of the continuum of the first. If a monk's robe is to be relinquished and he has relinquished it and separated himself from it, but has not yet confessed the transgression, and he then obtains another robe, that other robe too is to be relinquished by virtue of the continuum of the first. If a monk's robe is to be relinquished and he has relinquished it and separated himself from it, and has confessed the transgression, and he then obtains another robe, in that case there is no transgression.

Likewise, if a monk's robe is to be relinquished, for as long as that item has not been confessed and individually confessed, should he place nearby his alms bowl, his Dharma robe, a net, a small cup, a belt, or any other requisite for a monk's livelihood, all of those too are to be relinquished by virtue of the continuum of the first.

When soliciting a needle-case one receives a companion item, and when soliciting a companion item one receives a small piece of cloth or a large piece of cloth, there is no transgression. There is also no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The ninth offense involving relinquishment — that of soliciting beyond what was individually designated — is complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the thirty-first fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. Ānanda conceived the following idea: all these householders who have restrained themselves by means of the training rules established by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada are, from this time forward, unable to solicit even a single small scrap of cloth from anyone. He thought: there is a brahmin teacher of the summer season who teaches the letters of the alphabet together with me in a school of writing; if I go to him and look, it may even be possible to obtain a little something from him. With this in mind, he went to that person's house, whereupon the doorkeeper stopped him, saying: "Noble one, do not enter."

Ānanda said: "Friend, the Blessed One has taught five kinds of places that are not proper domains for us: the house of a musician, the house of a woman of dissolute ways, the house of a liquor-seller, the royal palace, and —"

"— or the house of an outcaste. Is this a musician's house, a house of dissolute ways, a liquor-seller's house, a royal palace, or the dwelling of an outcaste? Noble one, you have come a great many times. This is not a musician's house, not a house of dissolute ways, not a liquor-seller's house, not a royal palace, and not the dwelling of an outcaste. Rather, it is the house of the brahmin of the summer season. Go inside and let the brahmin of the summer season know that the venerable Ānanda wishes to see him and is waiting at the gate."

The doorkeeper went in and said: "Do you perhaps have the heart of a king of noble form and noble substance? If a poor person begs, then give. If you do not give, I shall see to it that a great barrier is placed between you." The doorkeeper thought: this person speaks without fear and without shame, and if I do not go and tell him, he will make trouble for me — so I had better go and tell him. He went and said: "Venerable lord, the venerable Ānanda wishes to see you, reverend lord, and is waiting at the outer gate."

The brahmin of the summer season said: "Who would stop the venerable Ānanda? Let the venerable Ānanda enter." When Ānanda had entered, the brahmin of the summer season said: "Welcome, venerable Ānanda. Welcome, welcome. Venerable Ānanda, please be seated on this prepared seat." Ānanda sat down before him, and with a high voice, a pleasing voice, and a deep voice began to recite a eulogy of generosity. As Ānanda, joyful and gladdened, recited the eulogy of generosity, the faithful brahmins and householders thought: "Alas, we should cut away even our own flesh and give it away!" And so the brahmin of the summer season said: "Venerable Ānanda, for the rains retreat I offer sixty kārṣāpaṇas. May this gift of healing bring you ornament of mind, equipment of mind, the accumulation of yoga, the attainment of the highest aim, and may you also obtain the enjoyments of gods and humans." Having said this, he departed.

Two monks came from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'The Tathāgata is setting out to tour the Kosala lands; whoever among you wishes to travel to the Kosala lands together with the Tathāgata, let that one perform the robe-work ceremony.'" The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One, replied: "Venerable one, as you command," and announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is setting out to tour the Kosala lands; whoever wishes to travel to the Kosala lands together with the Tathāgata, let that one perform the robe-work ceremony." The monks replied to the venerable Ānanda: "As you command, venerable Ānanda," and heard him.

When the two monks who had come from Śrāvastī heard this, they thought: "We too need to return to Śrāvastī," and became displeased. Ānanda, upon hearing, became distressed, thinking: "An obstacle has arisen to the gain that I was on the verge of obtaining after a hundred or a hundred attempts." He went to the brahmin of the summer season and began to recite the eulogy of generosity with a low voice, an unpleasing voice, and a subdued voice. The brahmin of the summer season said: "Venerable Ānanda, before you recited the eulogy of generosity with a high voice, a pleasing voice, and a deep voice, yet now you use a low voice,

an unpleasing voice, and a voice without depth, to recite the eulogy of generosity. What is the reason for this?" "Friend, it is because when companions meet once in a hundred encounters, a hundred journeys, even that parting comes after no great length of time." The people of Magadha understood by implication. The people of Kosala grasped it when it was stated openly. The people of Pañcāla understood by half a letter. But the people of the west do not understand unless it is said plainly.

The brahmin of the summer season reflected in his mind: "This man has abandoned so vast a fortune of the Śākya clan and gone forth into homelessness — he will not grieve at parting from me, but he grieves at losing sixty kārṣāpaṇas." So he said: "Venerable Ānanda, wherever you may be staying, I shall send you sixty kārṣāpaṇas." "Excellent! In that case," said Ānanda, "one gives and makes merit free of benefit to oneself and free of any affliction." And having said this, he rose from his seat and departed.

Then the Blessed One — himself tamed, his retinue tamed; himself peaceful, his retinue peaceful; himself liberated, his retinue liberated; himself at ease, his retinue at ease; himself subdued, his retinue subdued; himself an arhat, his retinue arhats; himself free of attachment, his retinue free of attachment; himself resplendent, his retinue resplendent — surrounded by a herd of bulls as by a supreme bull among the herd; surrounded by a company of young elephants as by a great elephant; surrounded by a pride of fanged beasts as by a lion; surrounded by a flock of geese as by the king of geese; surrounded by flocks of birds as by Garuḍa (the sky-soarer); surrounded by a company of students as by a brahmin; surrounded by a company of the sick as by a skilled physician; surrounded by troops as by a hero; surrounded by those entered upon the road as by a guide; surrounded by a company of merchants as by a caravan leader; surrounded by a retinue of followers as by a merchant-chief; surrounded by a company of ministers as by a king of the citadel; surrounded by a thousand sons as by a wheel-turning monarch; surrounded by a host of constellations as by the moon; surrounded by a thousand rays of light as by the sun; surrounded by a company of gandharvas (fragrance-eaters) as by Viśvāmitra (guardian of the realm); surrounded by a company of treasure-vases as by a noble man; surrounded by a host of nāgas as by Virūpākṣa (the ill-eyed one); surrounded by a host of yakṣas as by the wealth-giver; surrounded by a host of asuras as by Vemacitrin; surrounded by a company of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three as by Śakra (Indra); surrounded by the company of the brahmin worlds as by Brahmā —

With his faculties supremely tamed, his conduct and behavior unagitated, deep as an ocean of water, full of rain-clouds, free of arrogance as the king of great elephants, his body finely adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being, his form beautified with eighty excellent features, clothed in radiance a fathom wide, possessed of a brilliance surpassing a thousand suns, wholly beautiful as a moving mountain of jewels, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three establishments of mindfulness, and great compassion, devoted to the benefit of the world, sole protector, uniquely courageous, without a second, speaking of no second, abiding in calm abiding and insight, fully illuminating the three knowledges, perfectly trained in the three trainings, skilled in the basis of the three grounds of discipline, having crossed the four rivers, perfectly established in the basis of practice of the four legs of miraculous ability, long purified in the four means of gathering —

not intimidated by the four fearlessnesses, having abandoned the five hindrances, having fully transcended the five destinies, endowed with the six qualities, having perfectly fulfilled the six perfections, abiding in the six constant abidings, rich with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, teaching the eight limbs of the path, skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, endowed with the powers of the ten powers, his renown fully spread throughout the ten directions, supremely excellent above those who command a hundred companies of a hundred —

surrounded by and preceded by great śrāvakas, namely Kauṇḍinya the Omniscient, Śreṇika, Mahānāman, Anupama, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Nandottara, together with many others in the great community of monks, the Blessed One was passing through the region of Kosala and came to Śrāvastī, where he took up residence in the Jeta Grove in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now certain merchants of Śrāvastī had taken up their packs and were setting out for Rājagṛha. If a sufficient number of them were of one mind, the brahmin Varṣatula would cut dice for them, and so Varṣatula said to those who played dice with him: "Whenever the merchants of Śrāvastī come back to Śrāvastī, let them bring word to me." The dice-players passed the message along to the merchants. Those merchants exchanged their goods, received their payment, and went before the brahmin Varṣatula, saying: "What are our obligations toward you upon our return to Śrāvastī?"

Varṣatula entrusted to one of the merchants sixty kārṣāpaṇas and gave him this instruction: "Take these to the Venerable Ānanda and offer them to him." The merchant thought to himself: "This monk whom Varṣatula the brahmin intends to honor is certainly someone of great repute. Let me also do something pleasant for him and provide him with fine robes." And so he went to the Amber Grove, came before the monk, and asked: "Noble monk, what kind of robes are proper for a monk? Good sir, does the Saṅgha accept the gift of a large cloth?"

"The Saṅgha does not accept the gift of a large cloth. I have come to convert the sixty kārṣāpaṇas that Varṣatula the brahmin has sent to the Venerable Ānanda into proper robes for him."

The monk said: "Good sir, accept the proper robes, and as for the matter of your offering the sixty kārṣāpaṇas — there will be an occasion for that."

The merchant thought: "This is just the same matter and nothing else." He went before another monk and asked: "Noble monk, what kind of robes are proper for a monk? Good sir, does the Saṅgha accept the gift of a large cloth?"

"The Saṅgha does not accept the gift of a large cloth. I have come to convert the sixty kārṣāpaṇas that Varṣatula the brahmin has sent to the Venerable Ānanda into proper robes for him."

That monk said: "If you bring it without a seal, your matter of offering the local customs duty will have an occasion."

The merchant thought: "These two answers are in agreement." He went before the brahmin Varṣatula and said: "Varṣatula, have these kārṣāpaṇas sealed. Good sir, take them yourself with confidence."

Varṣatula said: "Though I am grateful for your concern on my behalf, I shall do what is proper." Varṣatula affixed his seal, and the merchant took the coins and went to Śrāvastī. He went to the Jeta Grove and asked the monks: "Noble ones, which is the monastery of the noble Ānanda?"

They showed him which monastery was Ānanda's, and he went there. Finding the noble Ānanda nowhere to be seen, he asked a monk: "Noble sir, where has the venerable Ānanda gone?" The monk replied: "He has gone out for his daytime walk." The merchant said: "The brahmin Varṣatula has sent these sixty kārṣāpaṇas for him. Please keep them, and when he arrives, give them to him. Good sir, have you ever seen anyone carrying a blazing lamp on their head?" The monk thought: "This man is certainly referring to that very person." And so he went to another monk and said: "Noble sir, the brahmin Varṣatula has sent these sixty kārṣāpaṇas for the venerable Ānanda. Please keep them, and when he arrives, give them to him. Good sir, if you were to come without a seal, you would find yourself in a situation of having to pay the local customs duty." That monk thought: "These two are in agreement with each other. I shall go home, and when he arrives there I shall answer him pleasantly with words." He then said: "Noble sir, the householder asks me to convey this message to the venerable Ānanda: 'My storehouse is in a certain corner somewhere; if you wish to take the kārṣāpaṇas, please come,' " and departed.

Ānanda then arrived at the monastery. The monks said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has well spoken when he said that the aspirations of the mind of one endowed with moral discipline are fulfilled, precisely because of the purity of moral discipline. Today you went out for your daytime walk, and today itself the sixty kārṣāpaṇas have been obtained. As for the benefactor who gave sixty kārṣāpaṇas each to the Blessed One's retinue of twelve hundred and fifty — who is such a person? Venerable Ānanda, it is not for the whole Saṅgha but for you alone. And as for the benefactor who gave sixty kārṣāpaṇas to Ānanda — who is such a person? It was sent by the brahmin Varṣatula. Now, if this is merely an outside acquisition — was it weighed? Was it assayed? Was it tested for fraud? By whom was it examined? Was it taken without examination? By whom was it taken? I myself am sitting right in the midst of enemies."

To this the other monk said: "Venerable Ānanda, what is the penalty for you in this? The householder said: 'My storehouse is in a certain corner somewhere; if you wish to take the kārṣāpaṇas, please come.' " Ānanda took his outer robe and set out, walking briskly. The householder, seeing him coming from quite a distance, thought: "This ascetic coming along with such a brisk stride — he cannot be anyone other than the venerable Ānanda." From quite a distance he called out to him: "Are you not the venerable Ānanda?" "I am." "The brahmin Varṣatula has sent these sixty kārṣāpaṇas for you. Please accept them. May this gift of Ārogyasabhiṁ bring you adornment of mind, equipment of mind, a gathering of yogic merit, attainment of the highest aim, and also the enjoyments of gods and men." The noble one said: "Why did you announce the offering in my name? Announce it in the name of the brahmin Varṣatula. What need does this poor man have of it? For it is because you took great pains and you brought it here." "Whoever brought this — please first find a boy to carry it to the marketplace." "Noble sir, I have no boy." "Poor man, having carried it all the way from Rājagṛha to here, are you unable to convey it to the marketplace?" The merchant then said to a boy: "Carry these kārṣāpaṇas and walk behind the noble one, but do not go outside."

"Have this one pay you the wages owed." The boy took the kārṣāpaṇas and walked behind him, and arriving first at the marketplace's opening stall, he said: "Noble sir, please set these kārṣāpaṇas down here." The noble one replied: "Boy, you have been very well trained." He then said to a boy working at a perfume stall: "Good fellow, set these kārṣāpaṇas down here for a moment." "Noble sir, I depend on my teacher." "May you never have to depend on yourself." He then went to another perfume-stall boy and said: "Good fellow, set these kārṣāpaṇas down here for a moment." "Noble sir, my teacher has gone to the back." "May you never enter into such a state." He then went to yet another perfume-stall boy, one who possessed fresh faith, and said: "Good fellow, set these kārṣāpaṇas down here for a moment." "Noble sir, I depend on my mother." "I know you to be a person of faith, but how deeply your faith runs I do not know. If you were to lose your faith, you might even take up a cudgel and drive monks away." The boy was frightened and said: "Noble sir, please set them down." The noble one left the kārṣāpaṇas there, sent the householder's boy back, and departed.

The assembly of merchants then established the rule: "Whoever among us is the last to arrive when the sun has risen shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas." The mother said to the perfume-stall boy: "Son, by all means see to it that you yourself are not fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas."

That night, remorse arose in the noble one, and he thought: "Since that perfume-stall boy possesses fresh faith, there will surely be some occasion on which those kārṣāpaṇas will be taken from him." So the next morning he rose early, brought a boy with him, and went to the marketplace. He saw the perfume-stall boy sitting there opening his stall, and said to him: "Good fellow, give back those kārṣāpaṇas." "Noble sir, the merchants' assembly has established a rule that whoever arrives last among us when the shade of the parasol has shifted shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas. Since I belong to the merchants' assembly, please keep them just for a moment until I return. What poor wretch do you think will fill your belly, and who do you think will crouch folding and unfolding their knees sitting here? If you leave without giving them back, I will have you summoned to trial before King Prasenajit of Kośala for a debt of sixty kārṣāpaṇas."

The perfume-stall boy flew into a rage and flung down the bundle of kārṣāpaṇas, and the seal broke. The noble one said: "Did the seal break? Has it not been untied? Has it not been tampered with? Let it be inspected. Did I entrust it to you after examining it? If you accepted it without examining it, why do you now break the seal?"

The noble one kept the perfume-stall boy detained in this way until the merchants' assembly had pledged sixty kārṣāpaṇas from his household as surety. The mother then said to him: "Son, what have you done? You have now had yourself summoned to trial for sixty kārṣāpaṇas." The boy said: "Those who place their faith in the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, come to this: a sprout of faith no sooner arises than it is caused to wither." It was at this point that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this founding occasion, and this context, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowing yet feigning not to know" — and so forth, also as before.

The Blessed One, the awakened one, questioned the venerable Nanda: "Nanda, is it true that you did something so unbecoming?" "Reverend Sir, I did."

The Blessed One, the awakened one, rebuked him, saying that it was conduct unworthy of a śramaṇa, conduct not in accordance with the way, not fitting, not in conformity with the rule — and that it was not something a person who has gone forth ought to do. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving these ten benefits, one ought to establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "Let my hearers rehearse this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

If a king, or a great minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a townsman, or a villager, or a wealthy person, or a merchant, or a caravan leader, wishing to present a monk with the price of a robe, dispatches it by the hand of a messenger — and if that messenger, carrying those funds, goes to where that monk is and says: 'Venerable one, be pleased to know that a king, or a great minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a townsman, or a villager, or a wealthy person, or a merchant, or a caravan leader, out of respect, sends these funds for robes. Noble one, please accept them out of compassion' — then that monk shall say to the messenger: 'Friend, messenger, monks are not permitted to accept funds for robes. When robes of the right kind are obtainable at the proper time, we will accept them.'

If that messenger then says to that monk: 'Noble one, does someone here act as steward for the noble ones? Does someone here carry out the business of the noble ones?' — then the monk, being desirous of a robe, shall indicate the Ānanda grove keeper, or a male lay practitioner who acts as steward, saying: 'This person is the steward for monks; this person carries out the business of monks.'

The messenger shall then take those robe funds, go to where that steward is, and upon arriving, say to him: 'Friend, steward, be aware — these robe funds: with them purchase such-and-such a robe, and when the monk named such-and-such comes, present him with the robe at the proper time.' The messenger shall instruct and inform him clearly and thoroughly.

The messenger shall then go back to where that monk is and, upon arriving, say to him: 'Noble one, the steward you indicated to me — I have duly informed him. Noble one, go to him, and he will present you with a robe at the proper time.'

The monk who is desirous of a robe shall go to the steward and say: 'Friend, steward, I am in need of a robe. Friend, steward, I am in need of a robe' — prompting him two times, three times. He shall prompt him and remind him. If, having prompted and reminded him two or three times, the robe is obtained, that is well and good. If it is not obtained, he shall remain silent in that quarter up to four, five, or six times. If, remaining silent up to four, five, or six times, the robe is obtained, that is well and good. If it is not obtained, then, making further effort beyond that to obtain the robe — if the robe is obtained, an offense requiring expiation (pācittika) is incurred. If it is not obtained, he should go to the place from which those robe funds came."

"Furthermore, if the reliable messenger sent by venerable persons to convey robe funds on behalf of a senior monk has accomplished nothing for that monk's purpose, the venerable ones should be sent word: 'Know that we have accomplished nothing for that monk's purpose — please do not let your own wealth go to waste.' That is the proper procedure in that case.

'On behalf of a monk' means: on behalf of a son of the Śākyas, Ānanda, or anyone else of that kind.

'A king' means the following: whether a woman who has been anointed with sovereignty over a kingdom — such a one too is a king anointed over the royal class with the crown — or whether members of the royal class, the brahmin class, the merchant class, or the common class have been anointed with sovereignty over a kingdom, such a one too is a king anointed over the royal class with the crown.

'A great minister' means those other than the king — ministers, accountants, and senior officials — who govern the kingdom, who live by mutual agreement on confidential matters, and who maintain their livelihood in dependence on the king.

'Or a brahmin' means a brahmin of pure caste.

'Or a householder' means a wealthy person.

'Or a townsman' means a person of a city.

'Or a country person' means a person of a village.

'Or a man of wealth' means one who is wealthy through his riches.

'Or a merchant' means one who wears a turban.

'By a caravan leader' means one who has gone beyond the agreed number two or three times.

'Into the hands of a messenger' means into the hands of a male, a female, or a eunuch.

'Robe funds' means gold or silver.

'If he says' means if he speaks.

'A suitable robe' means one that is fit for use.

'If the monk, wishing a robe' means if he seeks one.

'The attendant of Ānanda's grove' means one who renders it suitable.

'A layman' means one who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and has taken the five bases of training (the five precepts).

'In a quarter' means in the four quarters. What are these four quarters? They are: the place of calling, the place of residence, the far end of a task, and the place of a task. The place of calling is the potter's workshop and the weaver's workshop. The place of residence is a house or a waterside dwelling. The far end of a task means the far end of sugarcane work, the far end of rice cultivation, and the far end of salt production. The place of a task means a shop or a market.

'He shall remain silent' means through the six modes of prompting. What are these six modes of prompting? They are: when someone says 'Have you come?' — he says 'It is for that reason'; when someone says 'Welcome' — he says 'It is for that reason'; when someone says 'Please sit on this seat' — he says 'It is for that reason'; when someone says 'Please wash your feet' — he says 'It is for that reason'; when someone says 'Please eat food and refreshments' — he says 'It is for that reason'; and when someone says 'Please drink a drink' — he says 'It is for that reason.' If the six modes of prompting are delivered too quickly and without pause, leaving no room for another's words, then it is said that the six modes of prompting have not been completed. If the six modes of prompting are delivered not too quickly, with pauses, and allowing room for another's words, then it is said that the six modes of prompting have been completed.

'After that' means below that point, thereafter.

'If the robe is obtained' means if it is received.

'An offense requiring expiation is incurred' — it is declared that, having abandoned the object, one must confess the offense of expiation; hence it is called 'an offense requiring expiation.'

'He should go to the place from which those robe funds came' means he himself should go there."

Alternatively, "from a messenger who has been prompted" means from a companion or attendant.

"That is the proper procedure in that case" means that is the conforming Dharma in that case.

As for how a transgression arises in that case: if the donor comes to that monk and says, "Noble one, please accept these robes," then that monk must say to the donor, "I have already abandoned these; go and give them to that very person." If the donor then says to that monk, "Noble one, I shall do what is needed to win his acceptance; please take them," then the monk may accept them.

If the monk takes anything at all without having followed that procedure, an offense results in every case.

If a non-human being makes the gift, the messenger is a non-human, and a non-human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a non-human being makes the gift, the messenger is a non-human, and a human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a non-human being makes the gift, the messenger is human, and a non-human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a human makes the gift, the messenger is a non-human, and a non-human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a human makes the gift, the messenger is human, and a non-human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a human makes the gift, the messenger is a non-human, and a human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a non-human being makes the gift, the messenger is human, and a human makes the transaction fit, an offense results. If a human makes the gift, the messenger is human, and a human makes the transaction fit, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and without having relinquished and separated from it and without having confessed the offense he obtains another robe, that one too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuum. If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished it but without having separated from it and without having confessed the offense he obtains another robe, that one too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuum. If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished and separated from it but without having confessed the offense he obtains another robe, that one too becomes subject to forfeiture by reason of the former continuum. If a monk's robe has become subject to forfeiture, and having relinquished and separated from it and having confessed the offense he obtains another robe, in that case there is no offense.

Likewise, for as long as the monk has not confessed and individually confessed that basis, if he keeps nearby an alms bowl, a Dharma robe, a net, a small bowl, a belt, or any other implement of a renunciant's livelihood, that too becomes subject to forfeiture. There is no offense for one who acted for the first time, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feelings.

The tenth forfeiture, the forfeiture by dispatch, is complete.

Summary verse:

Wool alone, two shares,
Six, a cubit's span, the road,
Washing, gold and silver,
Explicit claiming, and buying and selling.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time monks were making and having made seats of wool. When monks made and had made seats of wool, because wool was scarce and precious there became much work and much activity, and they abandoned scriptural recitation, reading, chanting, yoga, mental application, and inner calm abiding of the mind. Those who wanted wool, and those who came for the very purpose of wool, repeatedly made inquiry of brahmins and householders. Other non-Buddhists, who were learned, said of them: "These renunciants, sons of the Śākyan, are ones who take life —

they have not turned back from taking life, have not abandoned it, have not individually abandoned it — and therefore they make and have made seats of wool." Because they made and had made seats of wool, they destroyed and took the lives of many living creatures, hosts of insects that arise within the wool. Whoever thought to give alms to these shaven-headed renunciants — they reviled them, derided them, and spoke ill of them.

On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this as the basis, and on this occasion, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and the rest proceeds as before. "The awakened Blessed Ones, while knowing, act without concealment" — and so forth, also as before.

The awakened Blessed One questioned the monks: "Monks, is it true that you make seats of wool?" "Venerable One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One then rebuked having great desires, not knowing contentment, being difficult to sustain, and being difficult to satisfy. After that, the Blessed One spoke in praise of having few desires, knowing contentment, being easy to sustain, being easy to satisfy, wearing simple robes, using few possessions, having the quality of refinement, being of good appearance, and knowing warmth. Then he declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing these ten benefits clearly, a rule of training is to be established for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk makes a seat of wool commits an offense requiring abandonment.

'Whatever monk' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. 'A seat of wool' refers to two kinds of seat: one that is filled inside and one that is a pad — and here both are intended. 'Makes' is understood in two senses: making anew, and making from what has been obtained — and here 'making anew' is intended. 'If he makes it' — whether he does so himself or has another do it. 'Commits an offense requiring abandonment' means that, having abandoned the item, he is to confess the transgression of an offense requiring abandonment. Therefore it is called 'an offense requiring abandonment.'

In that regard, one may ask: how does a transgression come about? It comes about through bundles, through layers, and through heaps. If a monk separates, destroys, or tears apart bundles of wool, then for as long as he has not made the seat, it is a wrongdoing; once the seat has been made, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment. If a monk separates, destroys, or tears apart layers of wool, then for as long as he has not made the seat, it is a wrongdoing; once the seat has been made, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment. If a monk separates, destroys, or tears apart heaps of wool, then for as long as he has not made the seat, it is a wrongdoing; once the seat has been made, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

If a monk separates, destroys, or tears apart bundles and layers, bundles and heaps, layers and bundles, layers and heaps, heaps and bundles, heaps and layers, bundles and layers and heaps, bundles and layers and heaps — in all their combinations — then for as long as he has not made the seat, it is a wrongdoing; once the seat has been made, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

As for one who obtains a completed seat and makes full use of a completed seat —

There is no offense for one who is refurbishing something old. There is no offense for a first offender, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations. The eleventh section, the abandonment of wool fleece, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, certain monks were making seats entirely of black sheep's wool and were having them made. Now because they were making and having made seats entirely of black sheep's wool, black sheep's wool being rare and costly, this gave rise to much work and many tasks — receiving scriptural transmission, reading, recitation, yoga, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding were being abandoned. Those who desired only black sheep's wool, and those who came for the sole purpose of black sheep's wool, were repeatedly soliciting brahmins and householders. Monks criticize this matter of so little importance: "Why are monks making seats entirely of black sheep's wool and having them made? Because black sheep's wool is rare and costly, this gives rise to much work and many tasks — receiving scriptural transmission, reading, recitation, yoga, mental application, and the practice of inner calm abiding are abandoned. Those who desire only black sheep's wool, and those who come for the sole purpose of black sheep's wool, repeatedly solicit brahmins and householders." They criticized, they raised an outcry, and they spread it about. Thereupon, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this founding case, and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, act as if unknowing — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One addressed the monks: "Is it true, monks, that you have been making seats entirely of black sheep's wool?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One reproached those of great desire, those who do not know contentment, those who are difficult to support, and those who are difficult to satisfy.

Then the Blessed One, having praised those of few desires, contentment, ease of support, ease of satisfaction, frugality, restraint in material things, the quality of refinement, beauty, and knowledge of what is sufficient, addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk makes a seat entirely of black sheep's wool incurs an offense requiring abandonment."

Now, "whatever monk" means one who belongs to this Dharma. "Wool" means sheep's wool. "Entirely of black" means four kinds of black: naturally black, darkened by blue, muddy black, and dark reddish-brown. "Seat" means two kinds of seat: one with an inner frame and a rug; in this context it is the rug that is intended. "Makes" means two kinds of making: making it as something new, and making it from something found; in this context it is making it as something new that is intended. "If he makes it" means whether he does so himself or has another make it. "Incurs an offense requiring abandonment" means that having abandoned that object, the offense requiring abandonment is to be confessed; therefore it is called an offense requiring abandonment. Thus it was taught.

Now, how does the transgression arise? It arises in three ways: through a bundle, through a layer, and through a heap. If a monk separates, destroys, or pulls apart a bundle of nothing but black sheep's wool, then for as long as he does not make a seat from it, it remains a wrongdoing; but once he has made the seat, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment. If a monk separates, destroys, or pulls apart a layer of nothing but black sheep's wool, then for as long as he does not make a seat from it, it remains a wrongdoing; but once he has made the seat, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment. If a monk separates, destroys, or pulls apart a heap of nothing but black sheep's wool, then for as long as he does not make a seat from it, it remains a wrongdoing; but once he has made the seat, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment. If a monk separates, destroys, or pulls apart any combination of bundle and layer, bundle and heap, layer and bundle, layer and heap, heap and bundle, heap and layer, bundle and layer and heap, from nothing but black sheep's wool, then for as long as he does not make a seat from it, it remains a wrongdoing; but once he has made the seat, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

There is no offense for one who uses something already made, who makes full use of something already made, or who makes use of something found. There is no offense for one who is a first offender, who is mentally deranged, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by feeling.

The twelfth offense requiring abandonment, that concerning nothing but black wool, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that monks must not make seats of nothing but black sheep's wool. Thereupon those monks, mixing in some white wool and some coarse wool together with nothing but black sheep's wool, proceeded to make seats and to have seats made. This activity, together with having it done, brought about many tasks and many duties; and they gave up the recitation of scripture, reading, memorization, yoga practice, mental application, and inner calm abiding of the mind. They repeatedly informed brahmins and householders who had come with desires and for that very purpose about these activities, saying: "Why do monks of little purpose make seats of nothing but black sheep's wool mixed with some white wool and some coarse wool, and have such seats made? This activity and having it done brings about many tasks and many duties, and leads them to abandon the recitation of scripture, reading, memorization, yoga practice, mental application, and the inner calm abiding of the mind; and they repeatedly inform brahmins and householders who have come with desires and for that very purpose." Thus they censured them, ridiculed them, and spoke ill of them. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and these circumstances, convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, inquire knowingly, and so forth, likewise as before.

The Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, is it true that when I had declared that monks must not make seats of nothing but black sheep's wool, you proceeded to mix in some white wool and some coarse wool and to make seats of nothing but black sheep's wool, and to have such seats made?"

"Venerable one, it is so." The buddha, the Blessed One, censured those of great desire, of no moderation, who were difficult to sustain and difficult to satisfy.

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of few desires, of moderation, of ease of sustenance, of ease of satisfaction, of restraint, of frugality with requisites, of qualities refined through training, of dignity, and of knowing warmth, and he addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing fully these ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to take up this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk makes a new sitting mat, two parts of it must be made from nothing but black sheep's wool, the third part from white wool, and the fourth part from coarse wool.

If a monk makes a new sitting mat without putting in two parts of nothing but black sheep's wool, without putting in a third part of white wool, and without putting in a fourth part of coarse wool, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment.

Regarding the phrase 'a monk': one who belongs to this Dharma community. Regarding 'mat': there are two kinds of mat, the enclosed kind and the open kind; here the open mat is what is intended. Regarding 'new': there are two kinds of new, new by being newly made and new by being newly obtained; here new by being newly made is what is intended. Regarding 'makes': whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it.

Regarding the phrase 'two parts must be made from nothing but black sheep's wool': 'sheep's wool' means the wool of sheep. 'Nothing but black' means the four kinds of black: naturally black, dark with a bluish cast, mud-colored, and dark brown. Regarding 'the third part from white': 'white' means the wool from the belly, the wool from the back, and the wool from the neck. Regarding 'the fourth part must be made from coarse wool': 'coarse wool' means the wool from the legs, the wool from the head, and the wool from the belly-region. Regarding 'without putting in': without mixing in. 'It is a transgression entailing relinquishment' means that, having relinquished that article, one must confess the offense of transgression; hence it is called a transgression entailing relinquishment.

How does the transgression arise? If a monk makes a sitting mat of ten tolas weight, he must put in five tolas of nothing but black sheep's wool, two and a half tolas of white wool, and two and a half tolas of coarse wool. If a monk makes a new sitting mat without putting in two parts of nothing but black sheep's wool, without putting in a third part of white wool, and without putting in a fourth part of coarse wool, once the mat is completed it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

In the same way as for a mat of ten tolas, if a monk makes a sitting mat of twenty tolas, thirty tolas, forty tolas, or fifty tolas, he must put in twenty-five tolas of nothing but black sheep's wool, twelve and a half tolas of white wool, and twelve and a half tolas of coarse wool. If a monk makes a new sitting mat without putting in two parts of nothing but black sheep's wool, without putting in a third part of white wool, and without putting in a fourth part of coarse wool, once the mat is completed it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk, falling short by even one tola or half a tola of white wool or coarse wool, makes a new sitting mat from nothing but black sheep's wool, it is in every case a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If only black wool is available, if white wool and coarse wool cost the same, or if white wool and coarse wool are scarce or expensive, there is no offense. Likewise there is no offense for one who is a first offender, for one who is deranged, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The thirteenth rule, concerning relinquishment for mixing in two parts, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, something of this kind occurred among the monks: there was an excess of sitting mats. The monks would say of a mat, "This one is far too long," or "This one is far too short," and discard it to have another one made. They would say, "This mat is far too narrow," or "This one is far too wide," or "This one is, in every single respect, full of holes, worn through, and beyond repair," and discard it to have another one made. Because the monks kept making sitting mats and discarding them over and over, they found themselves with an abundance of tasks and an abundance of work to do, and they abandoned the recitation of scripture, reading aloud, chanting, the practice of yoga, contemplation, and the cultivation of inner calm abiding.

Certain monks of few wants complained about this, reproached the others, and made their displeasure known, saying: "Why has this occurred among the monks — this excess of sitting mats — such that they say of a mat, 'This one is far too long,' or 'This one is far too short,' and discard it to have another one made; or say, 'This mat is far too narrow,' or 'This one is far too wide,' or 'This one is, in every single respect, full of holes, worn through, and beyond repair,' and discard it to have another one made? Because these monks keep making sitting mats and discarding them over and over, they have an abundance of tasks and an abundance of work to do, and they abandon the recitation of scripture, reading aloud, chanting, the practice of yoga, contemplation, and the cultivation of inner calm abiding." These monks criticized, censured, and spread the matter widely.

Then those monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Whereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident and in regard to this occasion and circumstance, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed One, buddhas and blessed ones, knowingly caused inquiry to be made — and so forth as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, then asked the monks: "Is it true, monks, that something of this kind occurred among you — that you were saying of a mat, 'This one is far too long,' or 'This one is far too short,' and discarding it to have another one made; or saying, 'This mat is far too narrow,' or 'This one is far too wide,' or 'This one is, in every single respect, full of holes, worn through, and beyond repair,' and discarding it to have another one made?" The venerable ones replied: "It is true, Blessed One."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, then rebuked them for their great wanting, their lack of contentment, their difficulty in being nourished, and their difficulty in being satisfied. After that, the Blessed One praised the virtues of having few wants, contentment, ease of nourishment, ease of satisfaction, conscientiousness, restraint in the use of requisites, diligence, elegance, and sensitivity to warmth. Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten true benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall observe this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk makes a new sitting mat, he is to keep the old one for six years against his will. If a monk, having kept the old sitting mat for fewer than six years — whether he has discarded it or not — makes a new sitting mat, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment." Thus the Blessed One, the Buddha, laid down this rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was then dwelling in a forest dwelling, in a forest grove.

The dwelling place was cold and windy, and the monks who could not manage with a sitting mat for six years found that the cold caused them to fall into a decline in their monastic work. Now, the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, know and yet ask. They know and ask; they know and yet do not ask; they ask at the right time and not at the wrong time; they ask when it is purposeful and do not ask when it is without purpose. And so the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, ward off with a preliminary formality anything that would be purposeless to ask about. In matters where asking would be purposeful, the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, know the right time. And so the Blessed One, the Buddha, asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why have the monks who cannot manage with a sitting mat fallen into a decline in their monastic work?" "Blessed One, it is as you have ordained — that if a monk makes a new sitting mat he is to keep the old one for six years against his will; that if a monk, having kept the old sitting mat for fewer than six years — whether he has discarded it or not — makes a new sitting mat, it is a transgression entailing relinquishment. And so those monks who cannot manage with a sitting mat for six years have been laid low by the cold in their monastic work." The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, a monk who cannot manage with a sitting mat for six years should request a leave regarding sitting mats, for fewer than six years, from the Saṅgha. He should make the request as follows: Having arranged the seats, struck the wooden signal board, properly informed the monks with the words of inquiry, and assembled the entire harmonious Saṅgha, that monk with the hand-robe should place his robe over one shoulder, bow in order of seniority, sit on his haunches at the edge where the seniors are, join his palms together, and speak these words: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such, am unable to manage with a sitting mat for six years. I, the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such, request of the Saṅgha a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years. May the venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, grant me, the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such, a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years out of compassion.' He should make this request in the same way a second and a third time. Those monks should not go to the monk with the hand-robe out of faith or trust alone; rather, the entire Saṅgha should go to him, or else monks appointed by the Saṅgha should be sent, and those sent should have the sitting mat brought before their own eyes, or else the sitting mat should be brought up into the midst of the Saṅgha. If the mat is too long, they should cut it. If it is too short, they should add stuffing. If it is too wide, they should cut it. If it is too narrow, they should add stuffing. If it is frayed and worn through, they should add stuffing. If it is entirely worn through in every part, the flesh is gone, and it cannot be repaired, then one monk should thereafter make a motion and perform the act: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such requests of the Saṅgha a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years, being unable to manage with a sitting mat for six years. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha grant the leave. The Saṅgha grants the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years.' This is the motion."

The formal act is to be performed as follows. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such is unable to manage with a sitting mat for six years and requests of the Saṅgha a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years. For that reason, if the Saṅgha grants the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years, then those venerable ones who consent to granting the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the Saṅgha has granted the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years. Since no one has spoken, it is held to be so."

The Saṅgha having granted a leave regarding sitting mats for fewer than six years to the monk with the hand-robe named such-and-such, that monk should be made to use a sitting mat for fewer than six years, and in this matter there should be no regret.

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke words of praise for those who desire the training, who respect the training, and who are content with the requisites of the training. He then addressed the monks with words that were in harmony with this, that surpassed it, and that were suited to it, and he declared to the monks: "Monks, that which came before was a rule, and this now is a permission. My hearers should take up this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk makes a new sitting mat, he should keep it for six years even if he does not want to. If, within fewer than six years, a monk — whether he has discarded the old sitting mat or has not discarded it — makes another new sitting mat, that is an offense with forfeiture, except when the Saṅgha has granted a leave. As for the phrase 'a monk': this refers to one who follows this Dharma. As for the phrase 'a sitting mat': there are two kinds of sitting mat — the bordered and the unbordered; here the unbordered is intended. As for the phrase 'makes new': there are two senses of new — new by being newly made, and new by being newly acquired; here the sense of newly made is intended. As for the phrase 'makes': whether one makes it oneself or directs another to make it. As for the phrase 'he should keep it for six years even if he does not want to': he should keep it for the full extent of six years. As for the phrase 'if, within fewer than six years': that is, within that full period. As for the phrase 'the old sitting mat': it is whatever sitting mat he already has. As for the phrase 'whether he has discarded it or has not discarded it, makes another new sitting mat': that is the second case. As for the phrase 'except when the Saṅgha has granted a leave': setting aside the case where the Saṅgha has granted leave. As for the phrase 'an offense with forfeiture': having forfeited that object, the forfeiture offense is to be confessed — and therefore it is called 'an offense with forfeiture.'"

As to how transgressions arise in this regard, a summary verse on the intermediate rule:

Beginning two and grasping the later;
beginning two and grasping the earlier;
grasping two and then discarding one;
beginning two and giving both away;
and on the sixth year, no offense —
this is the summation of the sitting mat rule.

If in the very year in which a monk begins a sitting mat he also begins a second sitting mat, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it likewise incurs a wrongdoing; there is, however, no defeat with respect to the first. Even if he does not begin a second sitting mat in that same year, if he begins a second sitting mat in the second year, the third year, the fourth year, or the fifth year, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it likewise incurs a wrongdoing; there is, however, no defeat with respect to the first.

If in the very year in which a monk begins a sitting mat he also begins a second sitting mat and, before completing the first, completes the second, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it incurs a forfeiture-entailing transgression; there is, however, no transgression with respect to the first. Even if he does not complete the second sitting mat begun in that same year, if in the second year, the third year, the fourth year, or the fifth year he begins a second sitting mat and, before completing the first, completes the second, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it incurs a forfeiture-entailing transgression; there is, however, no transgression with respect to the first.

If in the very year in which a monk makes a sitting mat he also makes a second sitting mat, and he then consecrates the first and gives away the second, or keeps the second and gives away the first, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it incurs a forfeiture-entailing transgression; there is, however, no transgression with respect to the first. Even if he does not make a second sitting mat in that same year, if in the second year, the third year, the fourth year, or the fifth year he makes a second sitting mat, and he then keeps the first and gives away the second, or keeps the second and gives away the first, beginning that second one incurs a wrongdoing, and completing it incurs a forfeiture-entailing transgression; there is, however, no transgression with respect to the first.

If in the very year in which a monk begins a sitting mat he also begins a second one and abandons it before completing it, or if he begins it in the second year, the third year, the fourth year, or the fifth year and abandons it before completing it, beginning it in each such instance incurs five wrongdoings; there is, however, no transgression with respect to the first.

If a monk does not make a second sitting mat in that same year, nor in the second year, nor in the third year, nor in the fourth year, nor in the fifth year, but makes one in the sixth year, there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression for one who is a first-time offender, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by pain.

This concludes the fourteenth forfeiture — the forfeiture pertaining to keeping a sitting mat for six years.

The Vinaya Analysis. The thirty-second fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At the time when the Blessed One had fully realized unsurpassed knowledge, the sound rang out everywhere throughout the central land: "A buddha has arisen in the world." Merchants traveling on the northern road heard that a buddha had arisen in the world in the central land, and that those who made offerings to him would gain offerings of tremendous fruit, tremendous benefit, great renown, and wide reach. Upon hearing this, they thought to themselves: "Let us take our loads of goods and travel to Śrāvastī; there we shall accomplish our trade as well as pay homage to the Blessed One." And so five hundred merchants, taking their loads of goods, set out from the northern road and journeyed to the central land. When they had at length arrived at Śrāvastī, they set down their loads of goods and went to where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was. They said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Householder, we wish to behold the Blessed One, the buddha." The knowledgeable Anāthapiṇḍada replied: "Friends, Tathāgatas — arhats, perfectly and fully awakened buddhas — are truly precious to behold. Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and fully awakened buddhas appear as rarely as the udumbara flower blossoms and comes forth." Thereupon the householder Anāthapiṇḍada led those five hundred merchants to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, the Blessed One then taught those merchants with a Dharma-rich discourse, rightly presenting it, rightly establishing them in it, rightly praising it, and rightly delighting them in it. With many categories of Dharma-rich talk he rightly taught, rightly established, rightly praised, and rightly delighted them, and then fell silent.

Thereupon those merchants paid homage to the Blessed One and began to tour the assembly halls of the elder monks. As they moved among the sleeping quarters of the elder monks, those merchants saw that the mats there were worn through in the middle. Seeing this, they said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Householder, why are the mats of these elder monks worn through in the middle?" Anāthapiṇḍada replied: "These great ones for the most part spend the night sitting in meditation." Their minds filled with confident faith, and from that faith which had arisen they offered the monks five hundred great bolts of cloth. The monks then placed those old, worn-out mats in an uncovered storage area of the great hall.

At that time, a certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks to his home at midday, and the Saṅgha of monks went. The Blessed One, however, remained behind in the storehouse and occupied himself with gathering alms. Now, awakened ones, blessed ones, remain in a storehouse and attend to the gathering of alms for five reasons. What are those five? They wish to rest inwardly in meditative composure; they wish to teach the Dharma to the gods; they wish to visit the sick; they wish to inspect the sleeping quarters; and they wish to lay down training rules for the hearers in the Vinaya. In this instance, the Blessed One remained in the storehouse and attended to the gathering of alms because he wished to inspect the sleeping quarters and to lay down training rules for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Then, not long after the Saṅgha of monks had gone, the Blessed One understood what had occurred, took his key, and from one courtyard to another courtyard, from one assembly hall to another assembly hall, from one dwelling to another dwelling, from one walkway to another, he passed along and proceeded gradually until he came to where the great hall was. At that time in the great hall there lay spread upon the floor a great many old, worn, tattered mats, all mixed with dust and grime. The Blessed One beheld those many old, worn, tattered mats, all mixed with dust and grime, lying spread upon the floor. Beholding them he exclaimed, "What a shame!" and, deeply moved, he thought: "The faith-filled brahmins and householders who, squeezing and squeezing out their skin, flesh, and blood, give gifts and make merit — the monks consume what those persons give without any warmth of feeling and without discerning reflection." Then the Blessed One carefully swept and shook out those old mats, dried them and aired them, arranged them without letting them touch the walls, and rinsed his two feet outside the assembly hall. Then he entered the assembly hall in order to rest inwardly in meditative composure.

Then a certain monk who had been gathering alms, having collected his alms, went to where the Blessed One was. Now, awakened ones, blessed ones, when attending to a monk who is gathering alms by performing the customary work of monks — how does one receive food from a monk?

"Did he satisfy the community of monks?" — thus individually gladdening them. It was by this act of individually gladdening them that he gladdened them. The Blessed One, attending to a monk gathering alms, individually gladdens them with the words: "Did you satisfy the community of monks?" And that monk replied: "Venerable One, I gathered alms for Tebo and satisfied the community of monks."

Then, after the Blessed One had taken his meal, he rinsed his two feet outside the assembly hall and entered the assembly hall in order to rest inwardly in meditative composure. Later, in the afternoon, the Blessed One arose from meditative composure and took his seat on the mat that had been spread before the community of monks. Having seated himself, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, I knew that not long after the community of monks had gone out, and so I took the key and went from courtyard to courtyard, from assembly hall to assembly hall, from building to building, from walking path to walking path. As I walked along and came at last to a certain great assembly hall, there in that great assembly hall I saw a great many old mats, crumbling and worn to tatters, scattered on the ground mixed with fine dust. When I saw this I was dismayed, and thinking critically to myself: 'The faithful brahmins and householders who give gifts by squeezing from their very skin, flesh, and blood — who are making merit — these monks use what is given without gratitude and without discerning reflection.' Therefore, monks, it would be well if, with respect to what is given in faith, you were to make use of things with gratitude, to make use of things with renunciation, to make use of things at the right time, to make use of things with discernment, and to make use of things with care."

A summary verse:

With gratitude, and with renunciation,
likewise at the right time, with discernment,
and with care — so should one make use.

Then, having spoken in praise of making use with gratitude, renunciation, timeliness, discernment, and care, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing these ten benefits, one should establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — " and so forth, as before. "My hearers should recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should a monk make a new mat, he is to have it bordered all around with old mat-material one sugata-span wide, so as to dull the brightness of the new color. If a monk makes a new mat without having it bordered all around with old mat-material one sugata-span wide — so as to dull the brightness of the new color — that is an offense requiring relinquishment."

As for the terms of the rule: "A monk" refers to one who follows this Dharma. "A mat" means a specific mat. "New" — there are two kinds of newness: new by being freshly made, and new by having been newly obtained. In this context, newness by being freshly made is what is intended. "Makes" means doing it oneself or causing another to do it. "So as to dull the brightness of the new color" means in order to make the new mat's appearance less striking. "Bordered all around with old mat-material one sugata-span wide" — this applies if he has other old mat-material measuring one sugata-span to border it with. "Sugata" means the Teacher. The sugata-span is one and a half standard forearm-lengths, plus a span.

"Bordered all around" means that there is a raised edge on every side. "Shall be joined" means it shall be attached. "Without joining" means without having attached it. "An offense of abandonment" means that having set that item aside, the transgression of the abandonment offense is to be confessed. That is why it is taught as an offense of abandonment.

Now, how does the transgression come about? If a monk uses a new mat while the old mat has not been bordered all around with a sugata-span of old mat-material — even if only a little portion remains unbordered — then in every case it becomes an abandonment offense. If all parts of the entire old mat have completely worn away, or have fallen into holes, or are in a condition that cannot be repaired, there is no offense. If that much old material is simply unavailable, there is no offense. For one who is a novice practitioner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no offense.

This completes the fifteenth offense of abandonment, concerning the sugata-span.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six said: "Friends, Nandaka and Upanandaka — these fellows with their black alms-bowls anoint their feet with monkey-fat and, when they go out, procure gains; and when they return, they also procure gains from unexpected arrivals, and they become pleasing and agreeable to many people. As for us, we are like tortoises in a dried-up well — we go nowhere and come from nowhere, so how could we ever obtain gains or become pleasing and agreeable to many people? Let us also go out. Where shall we go? Wherever our purpose can be accomplished." They thought: "If we all go, the households that depend upon us for their needs will be taken over by those with black alms-bowls. So let one of us remain while the others go — but who shall remain? Venerable Chāraka." Then they said: "Venerable Chāraka, you stay right here. We shall go." And Chāraka agreed to stay.

The five began to seek a purpose, and seeing an opportunity to travel to Nepal, they went to those travelers and said: "Good sirs, where are you going?" "Noble ones, we are going to Nepal." "Good sirs, we would travel together with you." "Noble ones, Nepal is like the back of a drum — you will not find it to your liking." "Good sirs, even so, since we shall at least see the land, let us go." "Noble ones, if that is the case, then please come along." The group of six set out together with those travelers toward Nepal and eventually arrived there. On the very same day they arrived in Nepal, they became displeased with it, and early the next morning they rose and set out along the road.
