Some merchants saw the group of six and bowed at their feet, saying: "Noble ones, what was Nepal like? Did you not find it to your liking?" "Good sirs, on the very same day we arrived in Nepal, we became displeased with it." "Noble ones, did we not tell you from the very beginning that Nepal is like the back of a drum and that you would not find it to your liking?" "Good sirs, since that is the case, shall you come back now?" "Noble ones, we ourselves did not change our route — it was indeed as we said — but we have other merchant companions who did change their route; we have entrusted our goods to them, so please travel with them." The group of six said:

"Very well, we shall do just so." Now in Nepal there were two groups, the Nepalis and the Doṅros, who were traveling companions. The Nepalis loaded their wagons and set out, and the group of six also joined those companions and departed together. The customary practice of the group of six was this: fearing dust, they would either walk ahead of the companions or walk behind them as a rear party. And so they began walking behind those companions as a rear guard.

After a time, the axle of the merchants' wagon broke. The merchants thought to themselves: "If we repair the wagon axle, the noise will bring brigands, and they will first kill us and afterward steal our goods as well. Let us therefore take what is most precious to us and go." And so they halted in a state of gloom.

The group of six caught up and asked them: "Good sirs, why do you halt in such gloom?" "Noble ones, the wagon axle has broken, and if we repair the wagon axle the noise will bring brigands, who will first kill us and afterward steal our goods as well. Therefore we are going to take what is most precious to us and come along." "Good friends, do you have Nepali wool to spare?" "We do." "If it will not be a burden to you, please hand over a little in exchange for hats, tied sandals, inner upper-garments, silk cloth, whips, fine cords, and so forth." "Noble ones, what use is all this to us? Take everything."

The group of six said: "Friends, dear companions, cloth rags have been found!" And with that they packed all five sets of begging bowls and robes together into one bundle, had four men take ropes on the spot, made up four great heavy loads, and those men took them up and went.

As they were carrying those loads and making their way along, the merchants saw the group of six coming behind them bearing Nepali loads and said: "Noble ones, we had thought we would bring along hired hands — but you yourselves have carried all this wool and come! Noble ones, we will pay you a wage." "Poor fellows, are we your hired hands?" "Noble ones, even so, at least accept some payment." The group of six said: "Friends, dear companions, we have found cloth rags." And laughing at that, they went on.

Among those traveling together there were some non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) making their way along, and they said: "Alas, group of six — where your loads will be destroyed, there your gains will be fulfilled; where your mother's belly was torn open, there your loads will be destroyed and there your gains will be fulfilled." The group of six replied: "Friends, dear companions, if we go together with the companions, many disputes will arise — so we will go ahead of the companions." And saying so, they went on ahead of the companions.

At a certain cliff face, many bandits were posted in ambush to attack travelers. Those bandits spotted them from a great distance, and upon seeing them they grew alarmed and said to one another: "Good sirs, an army with elephants is coming!" And all those posted at the cliff face were frightened and fled into the forest.

Then some among them said: "These are not an army with elephants — this is some kind of female yaks coming." Others said: "These are not female yaks — these are oxen of some kind." Others said: "These are not oxen — these are people carrying loads." As they drew nearer, the bandits said:

"Noble ones, because you carry such loads as these, every man posted at the cliff face was frightened and fled into the forest. Poor fellows, if the bandits come to know that you are afraid of them, they will bind you in broad daylight and drag you off into the forest. Dear friends, if you travel by the main road, you will meet with many thieves, so go by the side road." And saying this, those people sent them off along the side road.

Then some gamblers, who had stationed many lame men to wait and watch for traders carrying dice, saw them coming and said: "Well now, traders carrying dice — why do you come entering the town by a side way?" "Poor men, are we your dice-carrying traders? Who are you?" "We are the group of six nobles. Let us pass." Those men said: "Dear friends, if you enter through the gate of the Jeta Grove, you will meet with many thieves among those with black bowls, so you should enter by the window." And so they entered through a window.

A gatekeeper saw them and said: "Well now, porters — why do you enter the settlement by a side way?" "Gatekeeper, are we your porters?" He asked: "Who are you then?" "We are the venerable group of six." "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome!" They went inside, set down those loads of wool, and the great heaps stood there resembling Mount Meru.

Then the monks said to them: "Venerable ones, carrying such loads as these — do you not attract thieves? Venerable ones, have you really gone to such trouble merely to fill your own mouths? Whatever is offered to us we should in turn give back doubled." The monks then reproached, rebuked, and upbraided them, saying: "Monks — why such paltry little aims? Monks, you fill yourselves by means of the very member by which you should be making others feel ashamed." And the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, on account of this occasion, and in this connection, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The awakened Blessed Ones, knowing full well, act as if unknowing — and so forth, as before. The awakened Blessed One questioned the group of six: "Monks, is it true that you committed such an unseemliness?" "Blessed One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One rebuked them, saying that this was unbecoming for a renunciant, was improper, was unfit, and was contrary to proper conduct — it was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. And after rebuking them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should a monk traveling a road come upon some sheep's wool and desire it, that monk may take it. Having taken it, if there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to a distance of three leagues. If he carries it beyond that, it is an offense requiring expiation.

'Monk' refers to the group of six or anyone else of that sort. 'Traveling a road' means traveling a road in a remote area."

"Sheep's wool" means wool from sheep. "Found" means obtained from another. "If he desires it" means if he seeks it for a purpose. "That monk may take it" means he may pick it up. "If there is no one to carry it" means if there is no one willing to do so. "Up to a distance of three leagues" means up to and not beyond the limit of three leagues. "He may carry it himself" means he himself may carry it. "If he carries it beyond that" means if he carries it further than that. "An offense requiring expiation" means that having set aside that object, one must confess the offense of expiation; and therefore it is called an offense requiring expiation.

Now, how does the offense occur? If a monk has found some sheep's wool and there is no one to carry it, and he carries it himself beyond three leagues, then at half a krośa he incurs a minor offense, and at the full krośa he incurs an offense requiring expiation. If, though there is someone to carry it, he carries it himself, then at the very moment of beginning he incurs a minor offense; at half a krośa he incurs another separate minor offense; and at the full krośa he incurs an offense requiring expiation.

Six very subtle particles make one subtle particle. Six subtle particles make one water particle. Six water particles make one iron particle. Six iron particles make one rabbit's dust particle. Six rabbit's dust particles make one sheep's dust particle. Six sheep's dust particles make one ox's dust particle. Six ox's dust particles make one sunbeam mote. Six sunbeam motes make one liceling. Six licelings make one louse. Six lice make one barleycorn. Six barleycorns make one finger-breadth. Twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit. A cubit and a half plus four cubits makes a human fathom. Four cubits make a bow-length. Five hundred bow-lengths make one krośa. Eight krośas make one league.

Now, a monk dwelling in a remote area who has set out on a road and has found sheep's wool, takes it and, finding no one to carry it: at half the distance of the seventh village measured by a krośa, he incurs a minor offense, and at the village boundary he incurs an offense requiring expiation. If he then sets out from the village on the road to the remote dwelling, he incurs a minor offense at each half krośa, and an offense requiring expiation at each full krośa.

If one carries such wool to make a hat, sandals with straps, an inner garment for the upper body, a broad sash, a whisk, or a small bag and the like, there is no offense. Likewise there is no offense for one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is threatened by pain.

This completes the sixteenth rule, the expiation concerning carrying wool.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks said: "Let us divide the shares among Nandaka and Upananda." The other monks who were to receive shares said: "Our venerable Charka is right here among us — why give a share to him?" "Let it be six shares." Nandaka and Upananda replied: "We shall put those shares to the purpose of our venerable Charka who is staying here." Hearing this, Charka said: "Venerable ones, whatever gains you have obtained there, keep them for yourselves. Whatever gains I have obtained here while staying here shall remain mine." Then Upananda thought to himself: "By staying right here I stand to lose many gains," and he said: "Venerable ones, we are always a group of six — why should we now become a group of five? Let it remain a full group of six. Put forward someone. As for the venerable Charka, since he is not tired, let him be put forward." So Charka divided it into six shares and had his own share placed in his own quarters and set it aside. Then the others said:

"Venerable Charka, take for yourself whatever gains you have obtained — go ahead and divide them up." Charka said: "In all that time I did not obtain so much as a single kakaṇi coin. You have deceived me." Charka thought to himself: "I have obtained a small amount of wool — to whom shall I entrust it for carding? If I entrust it to laypeople, since they have not properly taken up the precepts, all of it will be stolen. If I entrust it to members of the twelve sects, they will charge a fee for keeping it. If I entrust it to Dharmadatta, Dharmadatta is a specialist in the sūtras, and his retinue is likewise made up of sūtra specialists — while they are turning over the words of the sūtras in their minds, time will drag on. If I entrust it to the ascetic Gautamī, the ascetic Gautamī is a holder of the Vinaya, and her retinue too consists of Vinaya holders — while they are deliberating over what is a transgression and what is not a transgression, time will drag on. The great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, is not a renunciant, and her retinue consists of those who are renunciants; since carding wool would not disturb her one-pointed concentration, I shall entrust the wool to her for carding." As he was sitting there thinking these very thoughts, the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, came to where the Blessed One was. At that moment the venerable Charka, seeing her from a considerable distance, said: "Gautamī — the Blessed One has declared well when he said, 'By virtue of pure moral discipline, the aspiration of the mind endowed with moral discipline is fulfilled.' Now indeed I feel: 'Oh, if only the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, would come!' — and here you have come. Please card this small amount of wool I have obtained, and give it back. I bow at the feet of my noble lord, the Blessed One, and upon returning please send two nuns over and have them sent here with it." Charka bound those bundles of wool tightly into two bales with carding rope and placed them against the door panel. Then the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and went into her summer residence, and sent two nuns to him with the instruction: "Go to the venerable Charka and say: 'We have been sent to deliver this wool to you today.'" The two of them went and said: "We come with a message from the noble Gautamī, bearing this wool to deliver to you." Charka said to the two of them: "There are two bales by the door panel — take them and go now." The two of them entered the quarters and began to lift the bales, but were unable to budge them even slightly. The two said: "Venerable one, have you perhaps put some additional rope weights in here?" Charka replied: "Young women, are you two flimsy little girls?" Then with one hand he hoisted up one bale and tossed it onto one of their heads, and with the other hand tossed the other bale onto the other's waist. "My head is broken!" said one. "My waist is broken!" said the other. They went into the summer residence, set the load down in the carrying place, laid it on top of a bed-frame, and sat down. The nuns said to the two of them: "Are you two flimsy little girls?" The two replied: "Whoever among you has strength — let her lift this." They began to lift it but were unable to budge it even slightly, and they said: "Noble ones, has he perhaps put some actual stones in here?" They then undid those two bales, and immediately it turned out to be one enormous great heap. The nuns burst into laughter and said: "The venerable Charka said it was just a little wool — if it were more, what would it be like?" The great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, said:

"Sisters, what shame is there in that for those of you who have shaved heads and tattered armpits? The venerable Charka said it was just a little wool — if it were more, what would it be like?" The great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, said: "Sisters, those ones are of evil conduct and wicked behavior, and by that conduct they incur a transgression against the Blessed One's teaching, causing a downfall. Sisters, the Blessed One has declared that these two are noble persons — those who do not take up a burden they have not assumed, and those who, having taken up a burden, carry it through to the end. Since this burden has been taken up, it must be carried through to the end. Therefore let each of you spin as much as you are inclined to spin, and carry it there and give it."

Those nuns delayed for a long time, and Charka thought: "They have stored that wool at the price of lodging, and it is not lost. I have done something wrong, and that wool of mine has become like something left out in the open at the mercy of the rain." The two nuns spun a load of wool and came bringing it, and said: "Venerable Charka, we have come bringing spun wool — where shall we put it?" Charka thought: "There is still more domain of activity remaining," and said: "Take it into the cell and set it down." Those two set it down and went. Then others also came bringing theirs. And so in due course all of them came bringing theirs.

Then the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, paid homage at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side. At that time the two hands of the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, were red — red and extremely red, just like the hands of a washerwoman.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the great lady Gautamī, mother of beings, in these words: "Gautamī, why have your two hands become red and very red, like the hands of a washerwoman?" "Blessed One, if there is something else to be done here, then something else is being done. How did it come about? The venerable Charka gave me wool to spin." Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do monks cause nuns who are not their relatives to spin sheep's wool?" "Venerable One, he did cause them to spin."

Then the Blessed One reproved this, and the occasion for it, and the circumstances of it, and convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The awakened Blessed Ones, while knowing, caused inquiry to be made — and so forth, also as before.

The awakened Blessed One addressed the venerable Charka: "Charka, is it true that you caused nuns who are not your relatives to spin sheep's wool?" "Venerable One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One censured him, saying that such conduct was not in accordance with the ascetic life, was not fitting, was not proper, was not in conformity with proper conduct, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits fully, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk causes a nun who is not his relative to spin sheep's wool by twisting it, or by combing it, or by spinning it — that is an offense requiring expiation.

Here, 'whatever monk' means one such as Charka or any other of that kind. 'Nun' means one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Who is not his relative' — seventh-degree cousins and closer than that count as relatives,

Beyond that degree, they are not relatives. "Sheep's wool" means the wool of sheep. "By twisting it" means having her twist it, even just to draw it through water. "By combing it" means having her comb it, even just to draw it through dye. "By spinning it" means having her spin it, even just to draw it across the thread. "An offense requiring expiation" means that after forfeiting the article, the transgression requiring expiation is to be confessed — and therefore it is called an offense requiring expiation.

As for how the transgressions arise: if a monk, perceiving a nun who is not his relative as not his relative, has her twist sheep's wool, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her comb it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her spin it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her both twist and comb it, or twist and spin it, or comb and twist it, or comb and spin it, or spin and twist it, or spin and comb it, or twist, comb, and spin it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation.

If a monk, with uncertainty about whether a nun who is not his relative is or is not his relative, has her twist sheep's wool, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her comb it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her spin it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation. If he has her both twist and comb it, or twist and spin it, or comb and twist it, or comb and spin it, or spin and twist it, or spin and comb it, or twist, comb, and spin it, it becomes an offense requiring expiation.

If a monk, perceiving a nun who is his relative as not his relative, has her twist sheep's wool, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her comb it, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her spin it, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her both twist and comb it, or twist and spin it, or comb and twist it, or comb and spin it, or spin and twist it, or spin and comb it, or twist, comb, and spin it, it becomes a wrong deed.

If a monk, with uncertainty about whether a nun who is his relative is or is not his relative, has her twist sheep's wool, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her comb it, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her spin it, it becomes a wrong deed. If he has her both twist and comb it, or twist and spin it, or comb and twist it, or comb and spin it, or spin and twist it, or spin and comb it, or twist, comb, and spin it, it becomes a wrong deed.

There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful feelings.

This concludes the seventeenth forfeiture, the offense requiring expiation concerning having wool spun.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Rājagṛha, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Veṇuvana. Then the headman Topknot Jewel went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the headman Topknot Jewel addressed the Blessed One with these words.

Venerable sir, in former times, long ago, in the royal palace, there was an assembly of the king and his ministers, and among those gathered in agreement, a conversation of this sort arose as a topic of discussion from time to time. The wise ones asked: Is it proper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and do the śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), sons of the Śākyas, take gold as their own? Or is it improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and do the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, not take gold as their own? At that, some spoke up saying: It is proper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do take gold as their own. Others spoke up saying: It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not take gold as their own.

Venerable sir, with regard to those who speak thus, saying that it is proper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own and that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do take gold as their own — if one were to explain things as they do, would one not be maligning the Blessed One and going too far? And would not those people be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, speaking the Dharma, explaining what is consistent with the Dharma? And would it not be the case that for those who speak in accordance with what has been said, there is nothing whatsoever that could rightly be criticized by others on the grounds of consistency with the Dharma?

Headman, those who say that it is proper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own and that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do take gold as their own — in explaining things in that way, they malign from within and go too far. Those people are not speaking in accordance with what I have said, they are not speaking the Dharma, they are not explaining what is consistent with the Dharma. For those who do not speak in accordance with what has been said, there is indeed something that can rightly come to be criticized by others on the grounds of consistency with the Dharma. And why is that?

Headman, it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not take gold as their own. If there is someone for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own, that is not the way of a śramaṇa, and it is not the way of a son of the Śākyas.

Headman, for this very reason I shall state the matter to you two and three times: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not take gold as their own. If there is someone for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own, that is not the way of a śramaṇa, and it is not the way of a son of the Śākyas.

Venerable sir, how wonderful it is that the Blessed One has declared: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not take gold as their own. If there is someone for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own, that is not the way of a śramaṇa, and it is not the way of a son of the Śākyas! How exceedingly well has the Blessed One spoken!

Venerable sir, as to why the Blessed One declared: Headman, for this very reason I shall state the matter to you two and three times — it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver as their own, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not take gold as their own —

If there is someone for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own, that is not the way of a śramaṇa, and it is not the way of a son of the Śākyas — that declaration of the Blessed One is exceedingly good. Venerable sir, I myself think this too: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever is one for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own — that person is surely one for whom the five strands of sensual pleasure are likewise proper.

The Blessed One replied: Headman, it is exactly so. It is exactly so: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever is one for whom it is proper to accept gold and silver and who does take gold as his own — that is not the way of a śramaṇa, and it is not the way of a son of the Śākyas.

Then the headman Cūḷadhanañjaya, having rejoiced in and applauded what the Blessed One had declared, bowed his head to the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Now at that time the venerable Ānanda was seated to one side of the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. Then, not long after the headman Cūḷadhanañjaya had departed, the Blessed One took the matter to mind and spoke to the venerable Ānanda: Ānanda, go to the Kalandaka Grove in the Bamboo Park and assemble in the meeting hall all the monks who are dwelling there in dependence upon that place.

The venerable Ānanda replied, "Yes, venerable sir, as you have commanded," and having heard the Blessed One, he went to the Kalandaka Grove in the Bamboo Park and assembled in the meeting hall all the monks who were dwelling there in dependence upon that place. He then went to where the Blessed One was, approached, paid homage at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: Venerable sir, all the monks who dwell in dependence upon the Kalandaka Grove in the Bamboo Park have assembled and gathered in the meeting hall. The Blessed One should now know that the time has come.

Then the Blessed One went to the meeting hall, arrived, and took his seat upon the mat that had been spread at the head of the assembly of monks. Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the monks: Monks, just now the headman Cūḷadhanañjaya came to me, paid homage at my two feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the headman Cūḷadhanañjaya said this to me: Venerable sir, some time ago, when a former gathering of canopies was assembled — in the royal palace, with the king and ministers all gathered together — there arose in conversation this kind of topic in between: Wise ones, is it proper for monks to accept gold and silver, and do the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas take gold as their own? Or is it improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and do the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas not take gold as their own?

Some there said this: It is proper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do take gold as their own. Others there said this: It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own.

Venerable sir, in that matter, those who said this — that it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and that the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own —

Venerable sir, those who spoke in that way — when they instruct others in that manner — do they not thereby misrepresent the Blessed One, and do they not go to the other extreme? And do they not speak in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, speak the Dharma, instruct others in a teaching that accords with the Dharma, and speak in accordance with what was taught? And is there any teaching that accords with the Dharma, such that they could be faulted by others on the basis of that accord?

Saying this, I then spoke as follows: Village headman, those who say that it is proper for monks to accept gold and silver, and that the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do take gold as their own — when they instruct others in that manner, they do misrepresent me, and they do go to the other extreme. They do not speak in accordance with what I have taught, they do not speak the Dharma, they do not instruct others in a teaching that accords with the Dharma, and they do not speak in accordance with what was taught. For those who do not speak in accordance with what was taught, there will indeed come upon them some teaching by which others may rightly find fault on the basis of accord with the Dharma. And why is that? Village headman, it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas.

Village headman, on account of this very matter I will state it to you a second and a third time: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas.

Having said this, the venerable one now speaks: For whose sake did the Blessed One declare this, saying, "It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own; whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas"? How wonderfully well the Blessed One has spoken! Venerable sir, for whose sake did the Blessed One further declare: "Village headman, on account of this very matter I will state it to you a second and a third time: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own; whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas"? That declaration of the Blessed One is thoroughly excellent. Venerable sir, I myself also think this: it is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — for such a one the five strands of sensual pleasure are likewise fitting.

I then spoke as follows: Village headman, just so, just so. It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas.

Thereupon the village headman Jewel-on-the-Crown, delighted and rejoicing in what I had said, bowed his head to my feet and departed from my presence.

Monks, the village headman Jewel-on-the-Crown, taking up that very point, proclaimed in the presence of the retinue attending the king: "It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. As for any one who finds it proper and does take gold as his own — the five strands of sensual pleasure are likewise certainly fitting for such a one." With these words, speaking the great speech of a thoroughbred bull, he roared the lion's roar rightly and truly in the midst of the assembly.

And monks, I too then spoke thus: "It is improper for monks to accept gold and silver, and the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas do not take gold as their own. Whoever finds it proper and does take gold as his own — that is not the practice of a śramaṇa, and that is not the practice of a son of the Śākyas."

Therefore, monks, from this day forward: those who wish for wood should seek out wood in full; those who wish for grass should seek grass; those who wish for carpentry work should seek carpentry work; those who wish for servants should seek servants in full. But by no category whatsoever shall the taking of gold as one's own be spoken of.

Now, this event had occurred, yet the Blessed One, the Buddha, had not yet at that point established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the group of six monks were accepting gold and silver with their own hands, causing others to accept it for them, piling it into one heap, piling it into two heaps, placing it on thrones, on small thrones, and on tiny seats. Other non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), persons of understanding, remarked: "The śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya have neither turned back nor abandoned, nor have they individually abandoned these things — for in just this way they accept gold and silver with their own hands, cause others to accept it for them, pile it into one heap, pile it into two heaps, and place it on thrones, on small thrones, and on tiny seats."

And brahmins and householders likewise, when they saw others accept gold and silver with their own hands, cause others to accept it for them, pile it into one heap, pile it into two heaps, and place it on thrones, on small thrones, and on tiny seats, persons of understanding said: "What difference is there, what distinction is there, what separation is there between the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya and the brahmins and householders?" They criticized, derided, and reproached, saying: "Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed śramaṇas?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this ground, and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddhas act with full knowledge, feigning otherwise — and so forth likewise as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you accept gold and silver with your own hands and cause others to accept it for you?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One, the Buddha, rebuked them, declaring that what is not in keeping with the conduct of a śramaṇa, what is not concordant, what is not fitting, what is not in conformity with proper conduct — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing the ten benefits, the training rules (śikṣāpada) for the hearers in the Vinaya are to be laid down" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk accepts gold and silver with his own hands, or causes others to accept it for him — that is an offense entailing forfeiture."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to the group of six — or any other of that same kind. "With his own hands" means with one's own hands. "Gold and silver" means silver and gold. "Accepts" means accepting it oneself. "Causes others to accept" means through another person. "An offense entailing forfeiture" means that having relinquished the object in question, the transgression (āpatti) of the offense entailing forfeiture is to be confessed — and that is why it is said to be "an offense entailing forfeiture."

As to how the offense is incurred, it is incurred through eight bases. These are the instructions: "Take this," "Take it from here," "Take this much," — and — "Bring this," "Bring it from here," "Bring this much," — and — "Put this down," "Put it down here," "Put down this much" — and likewise — "Take that," "Take it from there," "Take that much," — and — "Bring that," "Bring it from there," "Bring that much," — and — "Put that down," "Put it down there," "Put down that much."

Regarding these: "Take this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take this silver" or "take this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Take it from here" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take it from this large copper vessel, or from this copper pot, or from this clay vessel, or from this box, or from this leather bag, or from this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Take this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Bring this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "bring this silver" or "bring this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is brought, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Bring it from here" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "bring it from this large copper vessel, or from this copper pot, or from this clay vessel, or from this box, or from this leather bag, or from this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is brought, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Bring this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "bring a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is brought, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Put this down" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "put down this silver" or "put down this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is put down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Put it down here" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "put it in this large copper vessel, or in this copper pot, or in this clay bowl, or in this box, or in this leather bag, or in this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is put down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Put down this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "put down a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is put down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Receive this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "receive this silver or this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is received, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Receive from this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "receive from this large copper vessel, or from this copper pot, or from this clay bowl, or from this box, or from this leather bag, or from this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is received, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Receive this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "receive a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is received, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Take this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take this silver or this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Take from this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take from this large copper vessel, or from this copper pot, or from this clay bowl, or from this box, or from this leather bag, or from this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Take this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "take a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is taken, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Place this" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "place this silver or this gold." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is placed down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Place it there" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "place it in this large copper vessel, or in this copper pot, or in this clay bowl, or in this box, or in this leather bag, or in this basket." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is placed down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

"Place this much" means directing someone in the direction of what is to be obtained, saying "place a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand." The one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is placed down, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

Now, if one directs someone using any of the following expressions — "receive this," "receive from this," "receive this much," "take this," "take from this," "take this much," "place this," "place it here," "place this much," or using the forms "receive that," "receive from that," "receive that much," "take that," "take from that," "take that much," "place that," "place it there," "place that much" — but directs them toward something that is not going to be obtained, then the one who issues such a direction incurs a wrong action, and when it is received, taken, or placed down, it also becomes a wrong action.

If a monk touches silver, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches gold, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches both silver and gold, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If a monk touches beaten silver or beaten gold, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches silver or gold that bears a visible stamp or mark, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches money, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches a precious gem, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches a pearl, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches lapis lazuli, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he touches a precious gem, a pearl, and lapis lazuli together, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If a monk touches silver or gold that passes as legal currency in a region, it becomes a wrong action. If he touches brass and copper —

touching iron, sharp iron, lead, tin, and alkaline water — these entail no offense. In this way the Blessed One thus established the rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the thirty-third fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was in Campā a householder who was faithful, of virtuous intention, and a generous giver. He had a monastery constructed for the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers — one with tall stairways, windows, latticed windows, adorned with balustrades, beautiful and pleasing to behold, fit to serve as a stairway to the heavens. Many monks accepted the invitation to spend the rains retreat there. When the invitation ceremony had concluded, they said: "Householder, we intend to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Teacher and of the elder monks. Please give us robes."

The householder said: "Noble ones, there are no fine robes available here. Let it be known that suitable things are on their way. Wait a while until suitable things arrive, and then fine robes will be measured out and offered to you."

They said: "Householder, if there are no fine robes, then give us coarse ones."

"Noble ones, I am a generous giver — how could I offer you inferior things? If you are willing, please accept cloth-money of kārṣāpaṇas for the robes and depart."

"Householder, the Blessed One has forbidden kārṣāpaṇas, so we will not accept them."

"Noble ones, not to give you anything at all is not right for me, and to give inferior things is also not appropriate." The monks departed, taking only the coarse robes and refusing the kārṣāpaṇas, and in due course arrived at Śrāvastī. There the other monks asked them: "Venerable ones, did you not obtain gains in the form of rains-retreat robes? How is it that you have ended up with inferior robes? Where did you spend the rains retreat?"

"In Campā, at a certain householder's." "Which householder?" "The one known as the generous giver — that is why we did not obtain them."

They then related the matter in full, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thought: "Even faithful brahmins and householders give cloth-money as offerings, and my hearers too desire cloth-money. Let me grant the hearers a small permission in this regard."

Having so reflected, the Blessed One declared: "One may accept it, and once accepted, entrust it to that very donor to keep on one's behalf. Furthermore, a monk may have a lay steward attend to transactions. Since the monks did not know what 'having a lay steward attend to transactions' meant, the Blessed One declared: "An ānanda-garden-dweller or a layman may act as steward. An ānanda-garden-dweller is one who provides requisites. A layman is one who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and has taken the five training precepts."

When monks traveling to another district felt regret, thinking, "Here we have no patron at all," the Blessed One declared: "For as long as that same patron is traveling, staying, living, or dwelling, one may go to him even at great distance without any lapse." When monks had obtained cloth-money for a monastic robe but had no patron and felt regret, not accepting it, the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared:

It should be accepted, and having accepted it, one should stand before a monk and say these words: "Venerable one, please take note. I, the monk called such-and-such, have obtained this unsuitable article. I, the monk called such-and-such, hereby consecrate this unsuitable article. With this unsuitable article I will acquire a suitable article." In the same way one should say this a second and a third time. In this there is no cause for regret.

When faithful brahmins and householders had temples built in border regions, and from time to time alarms arose there and the monks abandoned the temples and fled, those who took without being given, knowing the temples to be empty, ransacked them. The Blessed One declared: "The valuables of the Saṅgha or of a stūpa should be concealed and one should depart." When the Blessed One had declared that they should be concealed, the monks did not know who should conceal them. The Blessed One declared: "A garden-keeper or a layman should conceal them." When those same people who did the concealing then stole the items, the Blessed One declared: "A faithful layman should conceal them. If there is no faithful layman, a novice should conceal them. If there is no novice, the monks themselves should conceal them." When it was necessary to dig a pit for this purpose and they did not know who should dig it, the Blessed One declared: "A garden-keeper or a layman should dig it. If that same person steals from it, the Blessed One declared: A faithful layman should dig it. If there is no faithful layman, a novice should dig it. If there is no novice, the monks themselves should dig it." When the danger has passed, they should retrieve the items in just that manner and present them to the Saṅgha.

"Monks, what I have permitted during times of hardship must not be practiced in times of ease. If it is practiced in ease, it becomes a serious offense. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is endangered by painful sensations."

Here ends the eighteenth section, on the avoidance of touching gold and silver.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the Blessed One appeared in the world, throughout every land the sound went forth that a Blessed One, a buddha, had arisen. His śrāvakas performed miracles of blazing, of radiance, of rainfall, and of lightning. Hearing that those who made offerings to him thereby gained results exceedingly great, benefits exceedingly great, glory exceedingly great, and expansion exceedingly great, a caravan of traders from the northern road said to one another: "Friends, let us go to the central land. There we shall also accomplish great profit. Let us make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha." Those caravan traders of the northern road loaded up their goods, set out for the central land, and journeyed on until they arrived at Śrāvastī.

Now at Śrāvastī there dwelt a learned and skilled accountant. He heard that traders had come from the northern road for mutual benefit, and thought: "If I go and look into this matter, I may gain something." He understood a little by observation and a little by calculation. He went and addressed the caravan leader by clan and by name: "Welcome, you who are called such-and-such! Welcome, welcome! Your mother is called such-and-such. Your father is called such-and-such. Your goods have come to this amount. On such-and-such a day your pack-load will come to ruin."

"Your profit will come to this much," he said. The caravan leader then thought: "Among those disciples of the Blessed One who are reputed to perform the miracles of blazing, shining, raining, and lightning, this man must surely be one of them." With faith he filled a begging bowl with fruits from the northern road's forests and gave it to him, and draped over him a robe the color of a lac-insect larva. The learned man accepted it, put it on, and went among those who practice the holy life. When they saw him they said: "Learned one, how did you come by the robe you slept off your deceit to obtain?" He replied: "Traders came from the northern road for mutual benefit, and there I addressed the caravan leader by clan and by name, and he, out of faith, gave it to me as a gift prompted by his trust." They said: "Learned one, we would have you know that those renunciants who are sons of the Śākyan never inspire heartfelt confidence in anyone who is not primarily a ropemaker, a garland-maker, or an oil-presser. Go, wearing that robe, and split open the hearts of those renunciants who are sons of the Śākyan." And so the learned man, wearing that robe, went to the Jeta Grove.

Now the conduct of the group of six was this: "Here we shall teach the Dharma to whatever brahmins and householders come, defeat our opponents in debate, and proclaim our own fame." And so one or another of the group of six would never leave the gate of the Jeta Grove unguarded. The friend Ānanda, who was pacing and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove, spotted the learned man from a great distance. Ānanda then thought: "This wretched naked ascetic has come wearing a fine robe. If I do not strip it from him, the name 'Ānanda' will mean nothing." He said to him: "Learned one, you are a naked ascetic — how have you come to be wearing such a robe? Have you turned back? I myself have not turned back. Here is what happened: traders came from the northern road for mutual benefit, and there I addressed the caravan leader by clan and by name, and he, out of faith, gave it to me as a gift prompted by his trust." "Wrong! Wrong! In your old age you have practiced corrupt conduct in full. Come, sit down, and I shall teach you the Dharma." The learned man sat before Ānanda, and Ānanda, pleased and delighted, began to deliver a discourse in praise of generosity.

Now the conduct of the group of six was this: when they delivered discourses on moral discipline, the listeners would think, "We ourselves have been born among the gods." When they delivered discourses on generosity, the listeners would think, "Let us cut off our very own flesh and give it away, again and again." When they delivered discourses on the lower destinies, the listeners would think, "We ourselves have been born in the lower destinies." So Ānanda said to the learned man: "Learned one, your teacher is inclined toward the bad. If he truly desired what is good, he would have given you a hundred thousand robes of fine wool, food endowed with a hundred flavors, and a many-windowed multistory palace — yet he has given you none of these. Our teacher, by contrast, is inclined toward the good, and so he has given us a hundred thousand robes of fine wool, food endowed with a hundred flavors, and a many-windowed multistory palace. If you were to go begging while wearing such a robe as that, the faithful brahmins and householders would know that this learned man has practiced corrupt conduct, and you would obtain nothing in alms. Give me your robe and I will give you another one in exchange."

"When I go begging while wearing this robe, the faithful brahmins and householders will see me and say, 'Venerable Ānanda, where did you obtain such a robe?' I shall then tell them, 'A certain learned man gave it to me.' They will thus come to know that the learned man is endowed with faith, and when you go out begging they will fill your bowl with ale and oil and give it to you."

He said, "Venerable Ānanda, please accept it."

Ānanda replied, "Learned man, those who live the celibate life alongside you are of corrupt moral discipline, and having heard your words they may well come again to take it back — that situation could arise. Venerable Ānanda, is this robe under the control of those celibate companions of yours, or is it under my own control? Take it, and it shall not be taken back."

Ānanda took that robe, gave him a different, coarser robe in exchange, and the learned man, having put on that coarse robe, went back to where the celibate practitioners were. When they saw him they said, "Learned man, where did you get that turned head — that sleeping robe?" He replied, "This came about through other means. How so? I gave the robe to Venerable Ānanda, and he in turn gave me this robe." They grew angry and said, "Learned man, the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan — even their living is unwelcome to us. Just as the Group of Six behave one way and others do not, so Ānanda behaves like the Group of Six and others do not. If you had given it to some other senior monk, we would have rejoiced along with you — but you gave it to Ānanda. That one wants to wipe the blood from our wounds with a cloth soaked in blood. If you bring back the robe, well and good. If you do not bring it back, we will expel you from the community of celibate practitioners, overturn your meditation seat, upend your sitting mat, smash your begging bowl, and throw away your water vessel."

Frightened, he went to where Ānanda was. Ānanda, seeing him coming from a great distance, thought, "This learned man is coming with such a gait — he is coming to take back my robe." So he went inside the monastery, closed the door, and sat there. The learned man began knocking at the door, calling out, "Venerable Ānanda! Venerable Ānanda!" but Ānanda said nothing.

The monks said to him, "Learned man, what do you want with Venerable Ānanda?"

He replied, "He has taken my robe."

"Learned man, if you want the robe back, go and take refuge with the Blessed One."

He then went to where the Blessed One was. The Blessed One, seeing the learned man coming from a great distance, declared to the monks: "Monks, look at that learned man coming from afar. Venerable One, as you have commanded — this one has come on account of the robe. If he obtains the robe, well and good. If he does not obtain it, he will vomit blood and die at that very moment."

The learned man then approached and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, Venerable Ānanda has taken my robe. May the Blessed One restore it to me. If the Blessed One does not restore the robe to me —"

"I shall thus be expelled from the celibate community, and my mendicant's staff too shall be taken away. My flat-seated mat shall be overturned, my begging bowl shall be upended, and my staff shall be cast aside."

The Blessed One then declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to where the companion is and say to him: the learned man's robe is to be returned. If it is not returned, there exists such a situation that this learned man will vomit blood and die at that very moment."

The venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, "Venerable One, as you have commanded," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he set out toward where the companion was. The companion, seeing the venerable Ānanda coming from a great distance, thought to himself: "A messenger of this kind has been brought along — he has come so that this one may snatch away my robe."

The venerable Ānanda then said to the companion: "The Blessed One has declared: the learned man's robe is to be returned. If his robe is not returned swiftly, there exists such a situation that this learned man will vomit blood and die at that very moment."

The companion replied: "Venerable Ānanda, I do what the Teacher commands and nothing else. Otherwise, were this naked ascetic, this Nirgrantha, to vomit blood and die — and were learned men, as numerous as sugarcane groves or bamboo thickets or forests of reeds, to fill this whole continent of Jambudvīpa, every last one of them vomiting blood, turning pale, and dying — not a single hair on the companion's body would stir. Nevertheless, begone, and I shall give it."

When the venerable Ānanda had gone, the companion said: "Hey, you naked Nirgrantha, listen! Your lying Teacher, through his false speech, deceived the world and was born in the hell realms, where his tongue is ploughed with five hundred ploughshares. You are an even greater liar than he, so your tongue too shall be ploughed with a thousand ploughshares. And further, if you wear my robe — do you suppose I would then wear your robe? Certainly not, venerable Ānanda."

The companion then folded the robe on all four sides, then folded it again into four layers, placed it on his left hand, and with his right hand slapped it with a crack, so that every fold burst open. He said: "Learned man, stretch out both your hands." The man stretched out both his hands, and the companion, with such force that it would have knocked him down, placed the robe into his hands — and down he fell. The companion jabbed him with his knee and said: "Naked Nirgrantha, go from this Śrāvastī without so much as touching the threshold of its monastery. Venerable Ānanda, if you do not like it, then come — but henceforth you shall not come to the Jeta Grove." That is what occurred for the time being. As for the Buddha, the Blessed One, he was not yet establishing training rules for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the group of six monks were engaging in various scandalous forms of conduct: making general loans, making special loans, distributing capital, distributing profits — and whether for something done returning something done, or for something done returning something not done, or for something not done returning something done, or for something not done returning something not done, giving out funds in all such ways.

Now, how did they make general loans? They would initiate transactions.

They would seek out markets, ready carts and the like, arrange goods for travel to those markets, and seek out accountants, grain measurers, ink, pens, and scribes. That is how they made general loans.

And how did they make special loans? For the sake of one-eighth interest, or one-tenth interest, or one-twelfth interest, they would seek out moneylenders, grain measurers, ink, pens, and scribes. That is how they made special loans.

And how did they distribute capital? They would send out old barley and grain, refined gold, and similar items for the benefit of a community of associates, seeking out measuring vessels, small weights, tips and grain measurers, ink, pens, and scribes. That is how they distributed capital.

And how did they distribute profits? For the sake of a collection of conch shells, they would send out a collection of jewels; for the sake of a collection of jewels, they would send out a collection of pearls; for the sake of a collection of pearls, they would send out a collection of vaiḍūrya, and they would seek out witnesses, grain measurers, ink, pens, and scribes. That is how they distributed profits.

And how did they give for something done returning something done? For marked gold, they would give what was marked. That is how they gave for something done returning something done.

And how did they give for something done returning something not done? For marked gold, they would give what was unmarked. That is how they gave for something done returning something not done.

And how did they give for something not done returning something done? For gold that was unmarked, they would give what was marked. That is how they gave for something not done returning something done.

And how did they give for something not done returning something not done? For gold that was unmarked, they would give what was unmarked. That is how they gave for something not done returning something not done.

Now certain learned non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) said: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan have not turned back, have not abandoned, have not individually abandoned these things. Indeed, those who conduct themselves with marked currency engage in various forms of conduct — making general loans, making special loans, distributing capital, distributing profits — and give for something done returning something done, for something done returning something not done, for something not done returning something done, and for something not done returning something not done."

And brahmins and householders too would say: "Those who conduct themselves with marked currency engage in various forms of conduct — making general loans, making special loans, distributing capital, distributing profits — and give for something done returning something done, for something done returning something not done, for something not done returning something done, and for something not done returning something not done. O learned ones, what difference then is there between the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan and brahmins and householders? What intention is there? What distinction is there? Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed ascetics?" And they reproached them, taunted them, and spoke disparagingly of them.

Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this incident, and in this connection, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and so on as before. And: "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, make inquiry" — and so on as before.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, then questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you engage in various forms of conduct involving marked currency?" "It is true, Venerable One," they admitted. The Blessed One, the Buddha, rebuked them: "That which is not the way of an ascetic, is not fitting, is not proper, is not in accord with the rule — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth." And thus he formally reproached them.

Then the Blessed One, having rebuked them in many ways, spoke to the monks: "Monks, seeing fully the ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so on as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk engages in various forms of conduct involving marked currency commits an offense requiring abandonment.

'Whatever monk' means those of the group of six, or any other of that kind. 'Various forms of conduct involving marked currency' means many types. 'Engages' means if he fully arranges it, if he thoroughly arranges it, if he lends grain, if he lends seed — if he engages in these activities. 'Commits an offense requiring abandonment' means that having abandoned that thing, the offense requiring abandonment must be confessed; it is therefore called an offense requiring abandonment.

As to how the transgression arises: if a monk, desiring gain, fully arranges a transaction in the conventional currency of a region, and for that transaction seeks out carts, oxen, hired men, witnesses, written records, ink, a pen, and a scribe, and gives pledges of dice, stakes, or boat-passage — so long as he does not appropriate the gains, it constitutes a wrong act; but when he appropriates the gains, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

If a monk, desiring gain, thoroughly arranges a transaction in silver or gold, and for that transaction seeks out witnesses, written records, ink, a pen, and a scribe — so long as he does not appropriate the gains, it constitutes a wrong act; but when he appropriates those gains, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

If a monk, desiring gain, lends out barley or grain, and for that transaction seeks out measuring vessels, small ladles, bowls, witnesses, written records, ink, a pen, and a scribe — so long as he does not appropriate the gains, it constitutes a wrong act; but when he appropriates those gains, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment.

If a monk, desiring gain, gives a collection of conch shells in exchange for a collection of jewels, or gives a collection of jewels in exchange for a collection of pearls, or gives a collection of pearls in exchange for a collection of vaidūrya gems, and for such a transaction seeks out witnesses, written records, ink, a pen, and a scribe — so long as he does not appropriate the gains, it constitutes a wrong act; but when he appropriates those gains, it becomes an offense requiring abandonment."

Thus did the Blessed One establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Excellent Hall of the Storeyed Pavilion on the bank of the Monkey Pool. At that time, the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were building houses of six and seven storeys. Just as the houses of the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were, so too were their temples built to six and seven storeys. These being constructed very tall, they were built up and then collapsed. The patrons thought: "While we are alive and living, our temples are collapsing in this way — what will happen to them after we are dead? Let us offer an inexhaustible endowment to the Saṅgha for the purpose of repair." Thinking thus, they took up the inexhaustible endowment and went to the monks' quarters. Having arrived, they said this to the monks: "Noble ones, please accept these inexhaustible endowments for the purpose of repair." The monks said:

"Good sirs, the Blessed One has established a rule of training; therefore we will not accept them." On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "For the sake of the Saṅgha, inexhaustible endowments for repair are to be accepted." Furthermore, the Blessed One declared: "The temple of the monks' Saṅgha is to be built to three storeys. The rains-retreat hall of the nuns' Saṅgha is to be built to two storeys." The monks, having heard this from the Blessed One, accepted the inexhaustible endowments and deposited them in the treasury of the Saṅgha, where they were kept.

The patrons came and said: "Noble ones, why is no repair of the temple being done? There are no kārṣāpaṇas." The monks replied: "Do you think we have consumed the inexhaustible endowments? They are sitting in the treasury of the Saṅgha." The patrons said: "Noble ones, if that is so, it will not be inexhaustible — in fact it will be exhausted. Is it that there is no one among you skilled in investment? Why do you not put them to work?" On that occasion, since the monks said "The Blessed One has established a rule of training; therefore we do not put them to work," the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "For the sake of the Saṅgha, the inexhaustible endowments for repair are to be put to work in investment."

Likewise, when faithful brahmins and householders offered inexhaustible endowments for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the Blessed One declared: "The inexhaustible endowments offered for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are to be invested, and whatever income is generated from them is to be used for offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

When those patrons gave the endowments to certain persons, and after they had done so disputes arose among those persons over the funds, and the monks asked: "Noble ones, why have disputes arisen over your own wealth?" — on that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They are not to be given to such persons."

When those patrons gave the endowments to wealthy persons and, after they had done so, those recipients relied on the powerful and would not repay, and through the influence of superior households they withheld repayment, the Blessed One declared: "They are not to be given to such persons."

When those patrons gave the endowments to poor persons, and those persons in turn were unable to repay, the Blessed One declared: "A pledge deed is to be taken at twice the value of the collateral, written on a tablet with a seal and in the presence of witnesses, and then the endowment is to be given. On that tablet the year, the month, the day, the senior elder of the Saṅgha, the steward, the recipient, the principal, and the names of the returns are to be written. As for whoever is to receive the endowment — even if it be a faithful lay practitioner who has undertaken the five bases of training — it is to be given solely on the basis of a pledge deed. There is no transgression for one acting for the first time, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by sensation."

The nineteenth section, on the abandoning of conduct involving manifest characteristics, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks engaged in various kinds of trading: buying and selling, acquiring and dispensing. How did they acquire? When the harvest was good in the countryside but bad in the city, they would bring goods from the countryside into the city — that is how they acquired. How did they dispense? When the harvest was good in the city but bad in the countryside, they would send goods from the city out to the countryside — that is how they dispensed. How did they buy?

When the price was low, they would buy. That is how they bought. How did they sell? When the price was high, they would sell. That is how they sold.

Other wise non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) remarked: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan have not turned away, have not abandoned, have not each individually abandoned these things — they engage in all manner of buying and selling: acquiring, dispensing, buying, and selling." And brahmins and householders likewise engaged in all manner of buying and selling — acquiring, dispensing, buying, and selling. "Then what difference is there between these ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan and brahmins and householders? What distinction of intent is there? What distinction of conduct is there? Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed ascetics?" They spoke in reproach, spread the word, and gossiped.

The monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, with this as the basis, on this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so on, as before. And the passage "the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ask while knowing," and so forth, is likewise as before.

The Blessed One rebuked the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you engage in all manner of buying and selling — acquiring, dispensing, buying, and selling?"

"It is true, Blessed One."

The Blessed One censured them, saying that this was not befitting an ascetic, was not consonant with right conduct, was not proper, was not in accord with the rule — it is not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then the Blessed One, having censured them in many ways, addressed the monks: "Therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so on, as before.

"My śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk who engages in all manner of buying and selling incurs a transgression requiring abandonment and confession (a pācittika requiring forfeiture)."

Now, "any monk" means the group of six or any other who is likewise so inclined. "All manner of buying and selling" means the many forms thereof. "Engages in" means habitually carrying on acquiring, dispensing, buying, and selling. "Incurs a transgression requiring abandonment and confession" means that, having relinquished the article in question, one must confess the pācittika transgression — that is why it is said to "incur a transgression requiring abandonment."

How does a transgression arise? If a monk, out of desire for gain, buys and then sells: in the buying there is a wrongdoing, and in the selling there is a transgression requiring abandonment and confession. If a monk buys out of desire for gain and sells without desire for gain: in the buying there is a wrongdoing, but in the selling there is no transgression. If a monk buys without desire for gain and sells out of desire for gain: in the buying there is no transgression, but in the selling there is a transgression requiring abandonment and confession. If a monk both buys and sells without desire for gain: in both there is no transgression. When one is purifying something obtained in a prior stream through an arrangement in another district, there is no transgression.

Thus the Blessed One established the rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled House beside the Monkey Pond.

At that time, some merchants who were travelers on the northern road caught sight of a monastery with high gabled porticos, latticed windows, window-lattices, and balustrades adorned with ornamental railings — a sight so captivating to the eye and heart that it was like a stairway to the heavens. Filled with faith, they entered the monastery and said to the monks: "Noble ones, we wish to offer a feast to the Saṅgha." The monks replied: "Bring the requisites for the feast and come." The merchants said: "We are people who have arrived here suddenly. We would like to give you the price; please provide us with rice." When the monks replied that the Blessed One had established a rule of training and that they therefore did not sell rice, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Do not act in such a way. Rather, for those who hold a feast on behalf of the Saṅgha, rice should be given in exchange for a price."

When the monks gave only raw, unhusked rice, the Blessed One declared: "For those who hold a feast at the monastery itself, give it with husking included."

After the Blessed One had established the rule that rice should be given in exchange for a price, many people held feasts and, since rice was given to all of them, the communal stores became exhausted through the consumption of rice. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Do not act in that way. Rather, use that price to purchase other rice. As for old rice, inspect it individually; if there are no living creatures in it, sell it in due season so as to fill the rice-storage bins." There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, or who is mentally deranged, or whose mind is disturbed, or who acts under the duress of painful feelings. This completes the twentieth training rule, the rule concerning buying and selling.

Summary verse:

Two bowls and two garments,
Taking by stealth, a feast, a junior month,
A hermit and heavy cloth,
Something dedicated, and a store set aside.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

Then the venerable Ānanda thought to himself: "All of these householders have been encompassed by the rules of training laid down by the donor Anāthapiṇḍada, so that henceforth it will be impossible to raise any gain from any quarter." While he was thinking this, he saw a group of sixty revelers going into a pleasure garden. The venerable Ānanda thought: "If I cannot secure some gain from them, I do not deserve to bear the name of Ānanda." Now, the habitual conduct of the group of six monks was this: whenever someone spoke about generosity, they would think to themselves that if listeners heard them they would cut off their own flesh piece by piece and give it away; whenever someone spoke about moral discipline, they would think that listeners would imagine they had been born among the gods; and whenever someone spoke about the lower realms of existence, they would think that listeners would be convinced they had been born in those lower realms. And so, carrying a bright, round alms-bowl under his arm, Ānanda went to where that group of revelers was. When he arrived, he spoke words of generosity to one of the revelers in such a way as to arouse full faith in that person's mind. The person's faith was stirred, and he said: "Noble one, why have you come?" Ānanda replied: "Good friend, I need an alms-bowl." The man said: "Noble one, I do not have an alms-bowl, but if you find one for a price I will present it to you when I see you." Ānanda then drew the alms-bowl from under his arm, showed it to the man, and said: "Good friend, this alms-bowl too was obtained for a price." The man asked: "Noble one, how much is its price?"

"Sixty kārṣāpaṇas." "I will present sixty kārṣāpaṇas as the price of this bowl. Good friend, may these sixty kārṣāpaṇas become yours. May this act of generosity become an ornament of your mind, a provision for your mind, an accumulation for your practice of yoga, a means of attaining the supreme goal, and may it make you a worthy vessel among gods and humans."
