In the same way, Ānanda caused each of the sixty revelers to contribute sixty kārṣāpaṇas apiece. Having done so, he departed. All those revelers then gathered together in one place, and one of them said: "Friends, let us rejoice that we have given sixty kārṣāpaṇas as the price of an alms-bowl to the venerable Ānanda, who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who preaches the Dharma, and who is endowed with the confidence of learning and liberation." Another said: "I too gave." Yet another said: "I too gave." And in this way all of them said: "I too gave, I too gave." Then they looked at one another and asked a monk: "Friends, we understand that one monk needs an alms-bowl." They asked a monk: "Noble one, one monk needs an alms-bowl." He replied: "Good friends, only one is needed." At that they began to criticize the community, saying: "These ascetics, sons of the Śākyans, are people overcome by the desire for gain."

This is what had occurred, but the buddha, the Blessed One, had not yet established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One was then dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the group of six monks were accumulating alms-bowls, keeping everything they received, neither using them themselves nor giving them to other monks. Monks of modest means began to censure, disparage, and gossip, saying: "Why do these monks accumulate all the alms-bowls they receive, neither using them themselves nor giving them to other monks?"

The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in connection with this basis, and in regard to this matter, convened the community of monks — and so forth as before. The phrase "although the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know, they pretend not to know" — and so forth as before. The Blessed One interrogated the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you accumulate all the alms-bowls you receive, neither using them yourselves nor giving them to other monks?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying: "This is not befitting a renunciant, not in accord with it, not proper, not consonant with the ascetic life — this is not something a person who has gone forth should do." Having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

A monk may keep an extra alms-bowl for up to ten days. If he keeps it beyond that, it is an offense requiring relinquishment.

The phrase 'a monk' refers to the person under this rule. 'Extra alms-bowl' means one that is in excess of what has been consecrated. 'For up to ten days' means until the end of ten days and nights. 'May keep' means may take as his own."

The phrase "if he keeps it beyond that" means keeping it past that point. The phrase "it is an offense requiring relinquishment" means that after relinquishing that object, the transgression — an offense requiring relinquishment — is to be confessed. That is why it is said to be an offense requiring relinquishment.

Now, as to how the offense comes about, it is as follows. If a monk obtains an alms-bowl on the first day of the fortnight, he must, within those very ten days, either consecrate that bowl, relinquish it, examine it, or give it to another. If he does not consecrate it, relinquish it, examine it, or give it to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If he does not obtain a bowl on the first day, but obtains one on the second day, the third day, the ninth day, or any day up to and including the tenth, he must within those very ten days either consecrate that bowl, relinquish it, examine it, or give it to another. If he does not consecrate it, relinquish it, examine it, or give it to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk obtains one alms-bowl on the first day and then obtains another on the second day, he must within those very ten days consecrate the former and either relinquish the latter, examine it, or give it to another; or alternatively, consecrate the latter and either relinquish the former, examine it, or give it to another. If he does not consecrate, relinquish, examine, or give either of them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If he obtains no bowl on the first or the second day, but obtains one on the third day or on any day up to and including the tenth, he must within those very ten days consecrate the former and either relinquish the latter, examine it, or give it to another; or alternatively, consecrate the latter and either relinquish the former, examine it, or give it to another. If he does not consecrate, relinquish, examine, or give either of them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk obtains two alms-bowls on the first day of the fortnight, he must within those very ten days either consecrate both, relinquish both, examine both, or give both to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If he does not obtain two alms-bowls on the first day, but obtains two on the second day, the third day, the ninth day, or any day up to and including the tenth, he must within those very ten days either consecrate both, relinquish both, examine both, or give both to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk obtains two alms-bowls on the first day and then obtains two more on the second day, he must within those very ten days consecrate the first two and either relinquish the second two, examine them, or give them to another.

Alternatively, he may consecrate the second two and either relinquish the first two, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk does not obtain two alms-bowls on the first or second day but obtains two on the third day or on any day up to and including the tenth, then that monk must within those very ten days consecrate the first two and either relinquish the second two, examine them, or give them to another. Alternatively, he may consecrate the second two and either relinquish the first two, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk obtains many alms-bowls on the first day, he must within those very ten days either consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk does not obtain many alms-bowls on the first day but obtains many on the second, the third, the ninth, or on any day up to and including the tenth, then that monk must within those very ten days either consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk obtains many alms-bowls on the first day and then obtains more on the second day, he must within those very ten days consecrate the first set and either relinquish the second set, examine them, or give them to another. Alternatively, he may consecrate the second set and either relinquish the first set, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk does not obtain many alms-bowls on the first or second day but obtains many on the third day or on any day up to and including the tenth, then that monk must within those very ten days consecrate the first set and either relinquish the second set, examine them, or give them to another. Alternatively, he may consecrate the second set and either relinquish the first set, examine them, or give them to another. If he does not consecrate them, relinquish them, examine them, or give them to another, then when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

If a monk's alms-bowl has become subject to relinquishment and he obtains another without having relinquished the first, without having parted from it, and without having confessed the transgression, then that new bowl too becomes subject to relinquishment by virtue of the continuity of the earlier one.

If a monk's alms-bowl has become subject to relinquishment, and he has relinquished it and parted from it, yet obtains another without having confessed the transgression, that new bowl too becomes subject to relinquishment by virtue of the continuity of the earlier one. But if a monk's alms-bowl has become subject to relinquishment, and he has relinquished it, parted from it, confessed the transgression, and then obtains another, there is no transgression in that new one.

Likewise, for as long as a monk, without having confessed and individually acknowledged an item that has become subject to relinquishment, sets aside another alms-bowl, or a robe, or a net, or a cup, or a belt, or any other requisite of a renunciant's life, that item too becomes subject to relinquishment by virtue of the continuity of the earlier one.

There is no transgression in holding a small alms-bowl, a plain alms-bowl, a large alms-bowl, or an undyed alms-bowl. There is no transgression in any case of holding an alms-bowl for the sake of one who is going forth into renunciation. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, or who is mentally deranged, or who is mentally disturbed, or who is afflicted by pain.

This completes the twenty-first relinquishment concerning the holding of alms-bowls.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now in Śrāvastī there was a young incense-seller who had come upon an alms-bowl that was perfectly bright, well-shaped, and fit for use. A certain mendicant monk, having dressed in his inner robe early in the morning and taken up his alms-bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī to collect alms, and after making his alms-round he went along the main street. The young incense-seller saw him and said, "Noble one, I have found an alms-bowl that is perfectly bright, well-shaped, and fit for use. If you wish, please accept it graciously — I have an alms-bowl for you. Noble one, if any other monk should come seeking an alms-bowl, please do send him to me, and I will give it."

Then that monk, having completed his alms-round in Śrāvastī, went to the Jeta Grove. After eating his meal, while washing his alms-bowl, he said to the other monks, "Venerable ones, on a certain main street there is a young incense-seller who has found an alms-bowl that is perfectly bright, well-shaped, and fit for use. Whichever of you wishes an alms-bowl, go there." Not far away, a certain companion monk was sitting and overheard this. He thought to himself, "If some monk with a black alms-bowl were to hear of this and come running, that would be unseemly — he ought to be reprimanded." And so he said to the monk, "Venerable one, you have eaten food given in faith, and yet you speak of nothing but alms-bowls and robes." The monk thought, "All those in the world who are attached to desire are no different from this companion of mine. For a moment he has reprimanded me, but if some senior monk were to hear of this, he would be reprimanded even more severely." So he said nothing.

The companion then urged him on, saying, "Venerable one, my own preceptor and yours are friends, so do not be troubled by my reproach. Elder, if I too have said something wrong, you may reproach me in return. Venerable one, I was merely trying to set things at ease — for is that bowl not, after all, a bowl? I ask that the elder not speak any further on this matter."

The monk said, "So it may be, venerable one, yet say this much at least: on a certain main street there is a young incense-seller who has found an alms-bowl that is perfectly bright, well-shaped, and fit for use, and he has said that if any monk should come seeking an alms-bowl, please send him. That is all it was."

But that was only enough to set things a little at ease. Then Ānanda put on his patched robe, set out at a measured pace, and went to the market. The young incense-seller saw him coming from quite a distance, walking at that steady pace, and thought to himself: "This wandering ascetic is coming at such a pace — he must be coming to take my alms-bowl." So he picked up the bowl, hid it beneath the hem of his garment, and set it there. When Ānanda saw him hiding it, he said, "Good fellow, is that alms-bowl the property of some low-caste person, that you would hide it away like that?" The young man stretched out his hand, took the alms-bowl, and said, "Good fellow, may this gift of Arogya cause you to become an ornament of mind, a furnishing of mind, a gathering of yogic qualities, an attainer of the highest aim, and a vessel worthy among gods and humans. Noble one, we merchants make our living by seeking profit, and so I will not give this away without payment — I offer it thus, in exchange for a price."

"Good fellow, are you really selling a vessel fit for a sage?" And he also spoke a verse:

If a man of clay were to obtain
a vessel of pure gold,
why would he grieve?
I see in this no deception at all.

"Noble one, you may say much, but I will not give it without payment."

Ānanda said, "Your excessive attachment to this alms-bowl will cause you to be reborn among the hungry ghosts with hollow bellies." While he was speaking to him in this way, a householder arrived from that direction and said, "Homage to the noble one. Homage to the venerable Ānanda."

Ānanda said, "Good fellow, what use is your empty salutation? Noble one, there is something the venerable Ānanda commanded me to do that I have not yet accomplished. Purchase this alms-bowl and give it to him."

That householder said to the young incense-seller, "Good fellow, what is the price of this alms-bowl?" "Such and such an amount." "I give it to you." The young incense-seller gave the alms-bowl to the householder, and the householder in turn presented it to Ānanda.

Ānanda said, "May this gift of Arogya cause you to become an ornament of mind, a furnishing of mind, a gathering of yogic qualities, an attainer of the highest aim, and a vessel worthy among gods and humans."

After the householder had departed, Ānanda said to the young incense-seller, "Poor fellow, did you not realize that Ānanda would be unable to spend the price of an alms-bowl? Your excessive attachment to this alms-bowl will cause you to be reborn among the hungry ghosts with bloated bellies."

"Noble one, what has gone wrong? You have received the alms-bowl, and I have received the price — so be on your way."

Ānanda took the alms-bowl and went to the monastery, where he showed it to the monks and said, "Venerable ones, look — what a bowl I have!" A young monk said, "Elder, do you not already have another alms-bowl?" "I do." "Well then, is it proper for an elder who already has an alms-bowl to go seeking yet another one?" "It was because I was crushed underfoot at the enemies' throats." "Does the elder have enemies?" "Since you yourself cannot bear my having a second alms-bowl, you are clearly my chief enemy."

The monks of few wants began to criticize, censure, and gossip among themselves, saying: "Why do monks seek out another alms-bowl when they already have one?" And so the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident and this occasion —

For this occasion, the convening of the assembly of monks and so forth proceeds as before. Likewise, the passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, while knowing full well, yet inquire" and so forth also proceeds as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that while you already possess an alms-bowl, you went seeking yet another one?" "Venerable sir, it is so." The Blessed One, the Buddha, rebuked him, saying that this was not the way of a renunciant, not befitting, not proper, not in accord with the rules, and not something that one who has gone forth ought to do. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore a monk who already possesses an alms-bowl must not seek out yet another one."

Vinaya Vibhaṅga, thirty-fourth fascicle.

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk who already possesses an alms-bowl must not seek out yet another one, a certain monk who was going on alms-round had his alms-bowl crack slightly. Holding it together, he entered Śrāvastī for alms. He found some flour and pressed it into the crack of the bowl with the bowl itself. Then, finding some moist grain husks, he pressed those in as well. But the moisture caused the flour to become wet and soggy, making the bowl unfit as a vessel, and it became entirely surrounded by flies. At that, some boys and girls said: "The noble one has performed the deed of gaining a great retinue, just like a wealthy man, a merchant, or a caravan leader, and goes about surrounded by flies." When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw this, he said: "Children, why do you mock the noble one in this way?" The householder said: "Noble one, what is this commotion?" The boys replied: "The noble one has performed the deed of gaining a great retinue, just like a wealthy man, a merchant, or a caravan leader, and goes about surrounded by flies." The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to that monk: "Noble one, the Blessed One's teaching adorns all — why do you engage in such frivolous behavior?" The householder replied: "Noble one, what is frivolous about this? Have you not seen him entering the homes of musicians, the homes of dancing girls, taverns, the royal palace, and the homes of outcastes?" The noble one said: "But then why do you let children surround and mock you?" The householder said: "My alms-bowl has cracked." "Then why do you not seek another bowl?" "The Blessed One declared that a monk who already possesses an alms-bowl must not seek out yet another one." "Noble one, this bowl of yours — do you actually possess and own something like this?" At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Whoever has a cracked bowl may have it repaired." Having made this ruling — that a monk whose bowl has cracked may repair it — the monks used the five soft adhesives: sugar, lac resin, monkey fat, fragrant resin, and dark pigment to seal it. But when these came into contact with heat, the bowl leaked again. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Abandon those five soft adhesives and repair it instead with the five hard adhesives." The monks did not know what the five hard adhesives were, and so the Blessed One declared: "They are long lac strips, small lac chips, lac paste, material like the teeth of a water-serpent, and powdered mineral." The monks did not know how much powdered mineral to use, and so the Blessed One declared:

"There are two kinds of powdered mineral: iron powder and stone powder. An iron bowl is to be repaired with iron powder, and an earthenware bowl is to be repaired with stone powder." When these were mixed with water and ground, then sealed in the same way, but the bowls leaked again, the Blessed One declared: "Grind it with sesame oil and seal it." When these were fired too intensely, the seal cracked, and when heated too little, it did not hold, so the Blessed One declared: "Heat it to just the right degree." When they became too rough, the Blessed One declared: "Polish them." When the monks poured water over them and polished them, and they again leaked, the Blessed One declared: "Pour sesame oil and polish them." When earthenware bowls cracked, the Blessed One declared: "Repair them with molasses and clay, then fire them." Thus the Blessed One ruled: "Repair bowls using these five hard adhesives."

Having made this ruling, a monk who was on his alms round dropped an earthenware bowl from his hands and it broke into five pieces. He stuffed those pieces with tow and strung the shards together with thread and went about on his alms round. The Blessed One then declared that there should be no food in a bowl in such a condition, and while he was trying to make it serviceable he kept breaking it apart and rejoining it, so that the entire morning was spent thus. Then the other monks said to him: "Venerable one, is this the whole of your virtuous practice — just tying things back together?" He replied: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has ruled that a broken bowl must be repaired with the five hard adhesives." The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, in many ways expressing praise for those who desire training, who respect training, and who provide the requisites for training, addressed the monks with a discourse consonant with that, containing the substance of it, and appropriate to the occasion. He then declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten genuine benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on, as before — "and my hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should any monk, when his bowl lacks the five adhesives, though it is still usable, seek a new bowl out of a desire for something better, and upon obtaining a bowl, commit an offense entailing relinquishment. That monk shall present that bowl to the community of monks. Whichever bowl is the most inferior among the bowls of that community of monks shall be given to that monk with the words: 'Monk, you must not consecrate this bowl, give it away, or donate it to another; you must use it carefully, little by little, until it finally breaks.' That is the procedure."

The commentary then explains: the phrase "should any monk" refers to one of this Dharma. "Lacks the five adhesives" means that the bowl is incomplete in the five adhesives. "Though it is still usable" means that it is still fit for continued use. "Out of a desire for something better" means either desiring what is superior or desiring it repeatedly. "A new bowl" — there are two kinds of new: new because it is newly made, and new because it is newly acquired; in this context both are intended. "Another" means a second one. "Seek" means he goes about seeking. "Upon obtaining a bowl" means upon actually getting a bowl.

"Is a relinquishment offense" means that having relinquished that article, one must confess the relinquishment offense. That is why it is said to be a relinquishment offense. "That monk" means the particular monk in question. "That bowl" means the bowl that is without an owner. "Should present it to the assembly of monks" means to those monks who are gathered there.

The monk who has the lowest-ranking bowl in that assembly of monks is to be told: "Monk, you should not consecrate this bowl, give it away, or donate it to another. Rather, it is given to you so that you may use it gently and carefully until it breaks completely." Furthermore, the Saṅgha is to appoint a monk who is skilled in distributing ownerless bowls. A monk who is skilled in distributing ownerless bowls but who possesses the following five qualities should not be appointed even if he has not yet been appointed, and should be dismissed if he has already been appointed. What are the five? He goes on account of desire, he goes on account of aversion, he goes on account of delusion, he goes on account of fear, and he does not know what constitutes a proper or improper distribution of an ownerless bowl.

A monk who is skilled in distributing ownerless bowls but who possesses the following five qualities should be appointed even if he has not yet been appointed, and should not be dismissed if he has already been appointed. What are the five? He does not go on account of desire, he does not go on account of aversion, he does not go on account of delusion, he does not go on account of fear, and he knows what constitutes a proper or improper distribution of an ownerless bowl.

He is to be appointed in the following manner. First he is to be asked his willingness: "You who are called so-and-so — are you willing to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha?" If he is willing, he should say, "I am willing." After this, he is to arrange the assembly seats, strike the gong, and duly inform the monks with a formal announcement. Once the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is in harmony, one monk should present the motion and perform the act.

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The monk named so-and-so is willing to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha. If it seems right and the Saṅgha approves, may the Saṅgha grant permission, and may the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha." This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The monk named so-and-so is willing to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha. Accordingly, the Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha. Those venerable ones who consent to the appointment of the monk named so-and-so to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak." Since no one has spoken, the Saṅgha has consented and granted this, and the Saṅgha has thereby appointed the monk named so-and-so to distribute ownerless bowls for the Saṅgha. So it is held, and it is so received.

I shall now establish the rules of conduct for the monk who distributes ownerless bowls. At the time of assembly, the monk who distributes ownerless bowls should announce to the venerable members of the Saṅgha: "Tomorrow I will distribute ownerless bowls to the Saṅgha."

"Tomorrow, when the sounding board is struck, take up your own bowls and enter the Saṅgha hall." This announcement is to be made.

Then, on the following day, the monk who distributes ownerless bowls is to prepare the sitting places, strike the sounding board, and by means of the customary words of inquiry, make the proper announcement to the monks. The monks, for their part, are to take up their own bowls — those that have been consecrated — and enter the Saṅgha hall.

The monk who distributes ownerless bowls is then to take up an ownerless bowl. When the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is in harmony, he is to pay homage at the side of the most senior member, then sit before the senior elder of the Saṅgha and, praising the ownerless bowl according to its actual qualities — saying such things as, "Most venerable, this bowl is very bright, well-shaped, and fit for use; if you wish, please accept it" — offer it. The senior elder of the Saṅgha may accept it if he wishes.

If the senior elder of the Saṅgha accepts that bowl, then whatever bowl belonged to the senior elder is to be offered to the second elder. Whatever bowl belonged to the second elder is to be offered to the third elder. And so on in this manner, until whatever bowl belongs to the second-most-junior member of the Saṅgha is offered to the most junior member.

If the senior elder of the Saṅgha does not accept it, it is to be offered to the second elder. If the second elder does not accept it, it is to be offered to the third elder. If the third elder does not accept it, and if the senior elder of the Saṅgha makes a request, it is not to be given on the first request, nor on the second request. On the third request it is to be given — and the senior elder of the Saṅgha is to confess the transgression and downfall of acting contrary to the Vinaya.

Likewise, if the third-most-junior member of the Saṅgha has not accepted it, it is to be offered to the second-most-junior member. If the second-most-junior member does not accept it, it is to be offered to the most junior member. If the most junior member of the Saṅgha has accepted it, and if the third-most-junior member then makes a request, it is not to be given on the first request, nor on the second request. On the third request it is to be given — and the third-most-junior member of the Saṅgha is to confess the transgression and downfall of acting contrary to the Vinaya.

Whatever bowl is left last in that assembly of monks is to be given to that monk with these words: "Monk, you are not to consecrate this bowl, not to give it away, not to offer it to another. Until it is broken beyond use, make gradual, careful use of it." This is how it is to be given.

If the monk who distributes ownerless bowls, having properly received the rules of conduct he is to observe in every respect, does not put them into practice, he incurs a serious fault.

I shall now set down the rules of conduct for the monk who holds ownerless bowls. The monk who holds ownerless bowls is to keep two bowl-vessels nearby. Into the better of the two he is to place the ownerless bowl, and into the other he is to place his consecrated bowl. Carrying both bowls, he is to go on the alms round. If he receives dry cooked rice, it is to be received into the ownerless bowl. If he receives wet cooked rice, it is to be received into the consecrated bowl.

Upon arriving at the temple, he is to make a maṇḍala, place the ownerless bowl before him, and eat from the consecrated bowl. After eating, the scraping out and wiping away of the smell of food is to be done first with the ownerless bowl and afterwards with the consecrated bowl. Washing, drying, and polishing with a weight are likewise to be done in that same order. If the bowl-vessel has two compartments, the ownerless bowl is to be placed in whichever is the better of the two, and the consecrated bowl is to be placed in the other. If there is only one compartment and the side is good, the ownerless bowl is to be placed at the side and the consecrated bowl is to be placed in the compartment. If the compartment is better, the ownerless bowl is to be placed in the compartment and the consecrated bowl is to be placed at the side.

When firing the bowls, if there are two kilns, the ownerless bowl is to be fired in whichever kiln is the better one, and the consecrated bowl is to be fired in the other. If there is only one kiln and the bottom fires well, the ownerless bowl is to be placed at the bottom and the consecrated bowl is to be placed on top. If placing on top fires well, the ownerless bowl is to be placed on top and the consecrated bowl is to be placed at the bottom.

When traveling on the road, both bowl-vessels are to be carried, and the ownerless bowl is to be placed in whichever of the two is the better one, with the consecrated bowl placed in the other. If there is a porter available, the ownerless bowl is to be entrusted to that person to carry, and the monk himself is to carry the consecrated bowl. If there is no porter at all, the ownerless bowl is to be carried on the left shoulder and the consecrated bowl is to be carried on the right shoulder.

This is for the time being a matter of forfeiture, and it is to be observed for as long as one lives through the proper guarding of moral discipline. If the monk who holds ownerless bowls, having duly taken up all the rules of conduct he is to observe in every respect, does not put them into practice, he incurs a serious fault.

As for the phrase "that is the proper procedure," it means that that is the conforming practice in the matter. As for how a transgression arises: if a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with a single patch, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with two patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with three patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with four patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture.

If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with one patch, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with two patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with three patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with four patches, yet it has not been repaired but remains usable, and while that usable bowl exists he goes seeking another new bowl, then the seeking itself constitutes a misdeed, and if he obtains one it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture.

If a monk's bowl is broken and it is suitable to have it repaired with five patches, then whether it has been repaired or not, whether it remains usable or not, if he goes seeking another new bowl, there is no transgression in the seeking and no transgression if he obtains one. There is likewise no transgression in acquiring one by purchase or by exchange. There is no transgression for one who is acting for the first time, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feelings.

This completes the twenty-second forfeiture concerning the seeking of a bowl.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Ānanda thought to himself: all of these people have been bound by the rules of training laid down by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, so that from now on they are unable to borrow even the value of a single small and coarse piece of cloth from anyone. Let me go and look — it is possible that some among them may still be able to provide something. So early that morning he dressed, took up his bowl and his monastic robe, and entering Śrāvastī through the eastern gate he went on his alms round. In a certain garden he saw about five hundred women dressed in coarse cloth, carrying loads and doing work. He thought: these are people who have work that belongs to others to do — day and night they wear white garments, yet they do not pay the tribute owed to King Prasenajit of Kosala. He then addressed them, saying: "Sisters, may you be well! May you be well!" They made no response but remained at their work. He spoke to them again: "Sisters, this phenomenon called death — unwanted by many people, unloved by many people, disagreeable to many people, unwelcome to the minds of many people — is common to the entire world and will come. When it does, you will be unable to speak even a word from the very first moment."

Then a young woman who desired merit rose from her seat, spread a seat for the venerable Ānanda, and having invited him to sit, she prostrated at his feet and sat before him. Ānanda then said to them: "Sisters, is there among you even a little of the wholesome Dharma rightly undertaken and practiced?" "Noble one, there is nothing at all." "Sisters, that is not good. This young woman has already created and accumulated two wholesome qualities of Dharma. Through the fact that she has generated sincere faith toward me, she has created and accumulated the karma by which she will become wealthy. Through the fact that she rose to greet me, spread a seat, and made prostration, she has created and accumulated the karma by which she will be reborn in a high family."

"If she were to give even a little, that would become for her a cause of great wealth. Sisters, where do your livelihoods come from?" "Noble one, from this very alms-round." "And your robes — where do they come from?" "From this very alms-round." "Do you carry with you even a little provision for the journey to the next world?" "Noble one, there is none at all, none whatsoever." "Sisters, that is not good, not good at all."

"Noble one, toward whom do you bear ill will?" "Toward you. You come here having been ruined in the next world, and you go to the next world continuing to be ruined here." "Noble one, by what means could we send even a little provision ahead of us to the next world?" "Sisters, if you were to present a length of cloth to a mendicant (śramaṇa) of the Śākya lineage who has gone forth, who is endowed with the three collections of scripture, who teaches the Dharma, who possesses the confidence of reasoning and liberation — then that would carry for you a great deal of provision for the journey to the next world." "Noble one, where would we find such a monk?" "Sisters, do you not know that I myself have gone forth from the Śākya lineage, am endowed with the three collections of scripture, teach the Dharma, and possess the confidence of reasoning and liberation?" "Noble one, where would we find a length of cloth to give?"

"Sisters, do you not know this verse:

Do not despise even a little merit,
thinking it will not come to me.
Just as falling drops of water
can fill a great vessel,
so the steadfast, by gathering
merit little by little, become complete.

Can you manage to give so much as one tola of raw wool? I'll accept it." One of them said, "I will give a full tola." Another said, "I will give a quarter tola." And in the same way all of them pledged to give their respective portions.

Ānanda said, "Sisters, give whatever fine-spun wool you have." "Noble one, all of us are burdened with coarse loads. There is one among us, the comfortable one, who carries fine-spun wool." "Sisters, call her." They called her, and Ānanda said to her, "Girl, measure out the fine wool still smaller." She measured it out smaller, and Ānanda said, "Girl, measure it out smaller still." She measured it out still smaller. Ānanda said again and again, "Girl, measure it out even smaller than that." She replied, "Noble one, it cannot be made finer than this." Ānanda said to them all, "Sisters, all of you give exactly this much wool." "Noble one, we cannot accept carrying wool this fine as a load. But can this girl not manage it? You carry it for her sake, and let her carry it for your sake." "Noble one, if that can be done." Ānanda said to her, "Girl, do it — and it will become merit for you. Noble one, this wool is so fine and light; please do not press too hard, but just hold it for now and carry it for a little while." Ānanda said "Arogya" to her, rose from his seat, and departed.

The comfortable one, holding the wool until that moment, then went to the others, they all gathered, and the wool was offered to Ānanda. Ānanda said to them all, "May this gift of Arogya become for you the adornment of mind, the resource of mind, the accumulation for the practice of yoga, the attainment of the highest purpose, and the obtaining of the garments of gods and humans," and he departed.

Then Ānanda took the wool and went to the monastery, where he showed it to the monks and said, "Venerable ones, look at this wool of mine. Elder, the wool is fine. Elder, might you find a weaver capable of weaving a great length of cloth from this wool?" The venerable ones said, "Did you overwhelm Ānanda? If Ānanda has not yet gone forth, Ānanda himself will do the weaving." "Elder, we overwhelmed the elder Gala. There is a weaver living near the fence of Gagemo, and if he obtains this wool, a great length of cloth worthy of a great one will result. Children, it is for the sake of Arogya that you have had my great length of cloth woven," and taking the wool he went to the weaver's house. The weaver saw him from a great distance and spoke these verses:

The wise shine forth even from afar,
like a snow-laden mountain peak.
The unwise are nowhere to be seen,
like an arrow shot into the dark.
Fair-faced one, your fame has filled all of Śrāvastī —
truly, what you have obtained, you have obtained well.
Look at this wool — what a fine thing!
Noble one, the wool is excellent.
This is the wool, and I am the weaver; a great length of cloth worthy of a great one shall result.
Fair-faced one, take it.

Ānanda said, "Noble one, who will give me the weaving fee?" "Fair-faced one, do you really never tire of always receiving a weaving fee? Provide also the provisions for the journey to the world beyond." Then the wife said, "This son of a noble family has praised the two of us from a great distance — take the great length of cloth. Noble one, this wool is exceedingly fine and delicate; please use it gently for this time being." Ānanda said "Arogya" and departed. The weaver completed the great length of cloth in exactly that much time. Ānanda returned there in exactly that much time, and the weaver offered him the great length of cloth. Ānanda took it and went to the monastery, where he showed the great length of cloth to the monks and said, "Venerable ones, look at this great length of cloth of mine. Elder, the great length of cloth is fine. Whoever has a second piece like this should stitch the pieces together from the selvage, overlapping them in sequence, and apply himself wholeheartedly and diligently to the side of virtue. Venerable ones, do you really think in your hearts that Ānanda is incapable of joining two such great lengths of cloth together? Watch how he joins them."

Then Ānanda, early in the morning, having put on his lower robe and taken up his bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī from the west gate for alms. In a certain garden he saw approximately five hundred yoke-loads of wool laid out and spread around, and he thought: "These are persons who have tasks that are their own business. Though day and night they make use of white combed fleece, they do not pay the weaving tax to King Prasenajit of Kosala." Thinking thus, he spoke to them: "Sisters, Arogya, Arogya." They remained there without saying anything, and he spoke to them again: "Sisters, there is something unwelcome to many people, displeasing to many people, disagreeable to many people, and disagreeable to the minds of many people — something that is common to the entire world — namely, the phenomenon called death that is bound to come. At that moment, from the very first, you will be unable to speak a word."

Then a young woman named Sonam Döpa who was present rose from her seat, spread a cushion for Nyadga, sat down beside him, and prostrated at his feet, then sat before him. Nyadga spoke to them: "Sisters, do you have even a little wholesome Dharma that you have properly taken up and are putting into practice?" "Noble one, there is nothing whatsoever." "Sisters, that is not good. This young woman has performed and accumulated two wholesome acts of Dharma. What she has done is this: by generating faith and devotion toward me, she has performed and accumulated karma that will cause her to become wealthy. And by rising to greet me, spreading a cushion, and prostrating before me, she has performed and accumulated karma that will cause her to be born into a high family. If she were to give even a little in generosity, that too would become for her a source of great prosperity. Sisters, where does your food come from? From this very weaving. Where do your clothes come from? From this very weaving. Do you have even a little provisions set aside for the journey to the world beyond?" "Noble one, we have nothing whatsoever of that kind." "Sisters, that is not good, not good at all." "Noble one, toward whom do you bear ill will? It is toward you! You come here broken from the world beyond, and from here you go on broken to the world beyond." "Noble one, by what means might we send ourselves a little provision for when we journey to the world beyond?" "Sisters, if you were to give a great bolt of cloth to a monk of the Śākya clan who has gone forth, who is versed in the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who is endowed with the confidence of reasoning and liberation, then by that act you would carry much provision on the road to the world beyond." "Noble one, where would we find such a monk?" "Sisters, do you not recognize that I myself am one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, versed in the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and endowed with the confidence of reasoning and liberation?" "Noble one, how could we possibly come by a great bolt of cloth?" "Sisters, do you not know the verse:

Do not despise a small merit,
thinking it will not come to me.
Just as a great vessel fills to the brim
drop by drop of dripping water,
so the steadfast, by accumulating
merit little by little, bring it to fullness.

Can you give even a single measure of thread for now? Go ahead and load it." Another said, "I will give half a measure." Another said, "I will give a quarter of a measure." And in the same way all of them promised to contribute each their own portion. Nyadga said, "Sisters, each of you give just a small amount." "Noble one, all of us are the heavy-load carriers here. There is one among us, Dekhenma, who carries the lighter load." "Sisters, call her over." They called to her, and Nyadga said to her, "Girl, spin the thread down finer." She spun it finer, and Nyadga said, "Girl, spin it finer still." She spun it finer still, and again and again Nyadga said, "Girl, spin it even finer than that," until she said, "Noble one, I cannot spin it any finer than this." Then Nyadga said to them all, "Sisters, all of you together give thread of just this fineness." "Noble one, we cannot load thread of this fineness by the measure. Can this girl not manage it? Or if you want it for her benefit, then let her carry it on your behalf." "Noble one, if she is willing." Then Nyadga said to her,

"Girl, do it, and it will become merit for you. Noble one, this thread is very fine, so please load it gradually over a long time and do not pull it too taut — weave it in this present moment." Nyadga said to her, "Bravo," and rose from his seat and departed.

O Fortunate One, that woman loaded the thread by that same time, then went to the others, and all gathered together and offered that thread to Nyadga. Nyadga said to them, "Bravo. May this act of generosity become an ornament of mind, a provision of mind, an accumulation of yogic practice, the attainment of the supreme benefit, and the obtaining of garments for gods and humans." Having said this, he departed.

Then Nyadga took that thread, went to the assembly hall, and showed the thread to the monks, saying, "Venerable ones, look at this thread of mine. Elder, the thread is excellent. Elder, might there be a weaver who could weave a great cloth worthy of it?" "Venerable ones, are you trying to suppress Nyadga? If Nyadga cannot manage this, Nyadga will weave it himself." "Elder, we are not trying to suppress the elder. There is a certain weaver who has just arrived, by the name of Gaga, living nearby. If he could obtain this thread, he could produce a great cloth worthy of something grand. My children, bravo — in effect you have made him weave my great cloth." With that he took the thread and went to the weaver's house, and when the weaver saw him from a great distance, he recited these verses:

The learned shine brilliantly from afar,
like a snow-clad mountain peak.
The unlearned do not shine at all,
like an arrow shot in darkness.
Fair of face, your renown has filled all of Śrāvastī —
what you have found, you have found well.

"Look at this thread. Noble one, the thread is excellent." "This thread here — and I am the weaver — will become a great cloth worthy of something grand." "Fair one, take this as well." "Noble one, who will give me payment for the weaving?" "Fair one, are you not perpetually satisfied with weaving pay? Send along provisions too for the journey to the world beyond." "Noble one, when I was weaving the previous great cloth, the debts I took on at that time have still not come back around." He began to look at his wife's face, and his wife said, "Noble one, even if he wants it, I do not want it." Nyadga laughed and said, "Hey, bare-headed weaver, listen! If I cannot get you to weave this great cloth, I swear by this bare head." The weaver also laughed and said, "Hey, shaven-headed ascetic, listen! If I do weave your great cloth, I swear by this shaven head." Nyadga laughed and went off, and he had a friend at the great palace of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, a man named Yidten Chempa. Nyadga went to visit him, and said to the household servants, "Hey, servants, where has the great one gone?" They said, "Noble one, he has gone to the market." Nyadga went to the market where he was coming, and the great one had entered a certain wine-seller's stall. Nyadga stood at the door of that stall and sent word to the great one that Nyadga was waiting at the door. The great one came out and said, "Venerable Nyadga, I bow to you. I bow to you." Nyadga said, "Great one, I have come about the king's affairs and

thought that I had come with the intention of being diligent in the king's affairs. It never occurred to me that I would find you wandering from wine-seller's stall to wine-seller's stall like this." The great one said, "Noble one, I entered here on the king's business." Nyadga said, "Venerable Nyadga, what is the purpose of your coming?" The great one said, "I have obtained a small amount of raw fiber. Let it first be sent to be woven into a large bolt of cloth. I shall present Venerable Nyadga with that very bolt of cloth." Then he added, "But if it is to be sent, should one not give with faith rather than set aside this act of giving?" The great one then instructed a man: "Hey, servant, go to that weaver Spyicer's house and take this noble Nyadga's large bolt of cloth and present it." Nyadga said, "Rather than having it woven by the weaver Snabo, let it be woven by the weaver Spyicer, who lives beside a certain fence over there, sitting with his loom out in the open." The great one said to that man, "Hey, servant, go to the weaver Spyicer and say these words: the great one says, take this and give it." That man took the raw fiber, went to where the weaver Spyicer was sitting in the open, and said, "Hey Spyicer, the great one says, take this and give it." Spyicer recognized the fiber and said, "It is my turn." The man went back and said to the great one, "The weaver Spyicer says: it is my turn." The great one said, "Hey, servant, go to Spyicer and say: he will not be allowed to take another turn." The man went and said, "Hey Spyicer, the great one says: he will not be allowed to take another turn." Spyicer said, "Hey, servant, if the great one rules in Śrāvastī, I for my part need only leave Śrāvastī. I will not do work that is not my due." The man went back to the great one and said, "Spyicer says: if the great one rules in Śrāvastī, I need only leave Śrāvastī. I will not do work that is not my due." The great one said, "Hey, servant, go to the weaver Snabo and say: take this fiber and weave a large bolt of cloth." Nyadga said, "Let it not be woven by the weaver Snabo, but rather let it be woven by the weaver Spyicer." The great one said to that man, "Hey, servant, go to the weaver Spyicer and say: the great one says, in exchange for a drink of water, take this and weave a large bolt of cloth." Then the noble Nyadga said to that same man, "You wretch, who appointed you as the king's man? You are to be struck with many blows and put to work breaking up the ground and cutting wood." Then the man went and said, "The great one says: in exchange for a drink of water, take this and weave a large bolt of cloth." Spyicer said, "I, who am not of the allotted lot, cannot weave it." The man seized him by the hair, dragged him over, and struck him with his fist. Spyicer began to cry, and the man began to tangle his loom out of order. Spyicer's wife began to cry as well, and

He seized the other by the hair and began to drag him along, saying, "You two have insulted the great one, so come — you two are to be brought before King Prasenajit of Kosala to face a lawsuit in which five hundred kārṣāpaṇas are to be assessed. You are to go to the royal palace." With that, he took the two of them away. The noble one's wife said to Spyicer, "My lord's son, if the two of us are put in prison there will be no one at all to secure our release, and we would have to die there from the torments of the prison. Take this large bolt of cloth."

Spyicer said, "Dear kinswoman, do not be anxious — rather than having us dragged to the royal palace, let us be on our way. I will weave the large bolt of cloth, and I will also give you many combs." She set aside her anxiety and left. Then Spyicer said to his wife, "Good woman, that bolt of cloth must be woven in such a way that it will be of no use either as a loom-weight or as a large bolt of cloth." His wife said, "My lord's son, since that mendicant is such a miserable wretch, if we make the bolt of cloth like that, he will no doubt just leave it behind." So he wove the large bolt of cloth, and while that large bolt of cloth was still hanging free from the loom, Ānanda arrived and took the large bolt of cloth. Spyicer said, "Noble one, please give me a drink of water." Ānanda replied, "You wretch, am I to give you a drink of water? Why did you not send poison? Why did you not send corrosive? The monastic conduct of the mendicants, the sons of the Śākyan, is just words. The conduct of a brahmin is just words. In this way, even with a little payment for the mouth they made him weave; even with a small power of the royal palace they made him weave," — and so he abused, snapped his fingers, and hurled insults.

At that point the monks informed the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in connection with this origin story and on this occasion, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, as before. That the buddha Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign not to know — and so forth as before. The buddha Blessed One asked Ānanda, "Ānanda, is it true that you acted in such an unseemly manner?" "Venerable one, yes, it is." The buddha Blessed One rebuked him, saying that what was unbecoming of a mendicant, discordant, improper, and contrary to deportment was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having rebuked him in many ways, addressed the monks, declaring: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave cloth, soliciting him with thread that the monk himself has obtained — when the cloth is finished, that constitutes a downfall entailing relinquishment.

'Whatever monk' means a son of the Śākyan, Ānanda or any other of that sort. 'Thread that he himself has obtained' means thread solicited with intent — from some, one śrāṇa in weight; from some, half a śrāṇa; from some, two śo; from some, one śo. 'Weaver' means a person who weaves on a loom. 'Who is not a relative': the seventh degree of relation reckoning from the grandmother and grandfather back through collateral lines constitutes a relative; beyond that is not a relative. 'Causes to weave cloth': the seven kinds of cloth are: woolen cloth, hempen cloth, silk cloth, fine cotton cloth, cotton-and-wool cloth, coarse linen cloth, and sun-bleached cloth — any one of these."

"When the cloth is finished" means when the cloth has been obtained. "It is an offense requiring forfeiture" means that after forfeiting that article, the transgression requiring forfeiture must be confessed. That is why it is said to be an offense requiring forfeiture.

Now, as to how the transgression arises: if a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and then directs a weaver who is not a relative to weave cloth, there is a wrong act in the soliciting, and directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and then directs a weaver who is a relative to weave cloth, there is a wrong act in the soliciting, but there is no transgression in directing the relative weaver to weave. If a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and weaves the cloth himself, there is a wrong act in the soliciting, and weaving it himself also constitutes a wrong act.

If a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and then directs both a relative weaver and a non-relative weaver to weave cloth, there is a wrong act in the soliciting; directing the relative weaver to weave incurs no transgression, while directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and then directs himself and a non-relative weaver to weave cloth, there is a wrong act in the soliciting; weaving it himself also constitutes a wrong act, and directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a non-relative and then directs himself and a relative weaver to weave cloth, there is a wrong act in the soliciting; weaving it himself also constitutes a wrong act, but directing the relative weaver to weave incurs no transgression.

If a monk solicits thread from a relative and then directs a non-relative weaver to weave cloth, there is no transgression in the soliciting, but directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a relative and then directs a relative weaver to weave cloth, there is no transgression in the soliciting, and no transgression in directing the relative weaver to weave either. If a monk solicits thread from a relative and weaves the cloth himself, there is no transgression in the soliciting, but weaving it himself constitutes a wrong act.

If a monk solicits thread from a relative and then directs both a relative weaver and a non-relative weaver to weave cloth, there is no transgression in the soliciting; no transgression arises in directing the relative weaver to weave, but directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a relative and then directs himself and a non-relative weaver to weave cloth, there is no transgression in the soliciting; weaving it himself constitutes a wrong act, but directing the non-relative weaver to weave constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture. If a monk solicits thread from a relative and then directs himself and a relative weaver to weave cloth, there is no transgression in the soliciting; weaving it himself constitutes a wrong act, but directing the relative weaver to weave incurs no transgression.

Directing weaving for wages incurs no transgression. For a first offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

The twenty-third forfeiture offense, that of directing weaving, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was a certain householder in Śrāvastī who had taken a wife from an equal family. He took pleasure with her, rejoiced with her, and lived in delight with her.

At another time that householder became attached to another man's wife. When his own wife tried to turn him away from this, saying, "My lord, please do not act in this way," he would not desist no matter how much she tried to dissuade him. And so his wife, for her part, began to take up with other men. The householder then gave himself to other women, and his wife gave herself to other men, and in this way both households fell into ruin. Now there was a maidservant in that household, and the householder began striking her with his fists and the flat of his hand, saying, "You have brought this household to ruin." The maidservant replied, "I do not dispute that this household has fallen to ruin. And yet, how could it be fitting for me to speak ill of my lord and master?"

A friend, hearing this, went to that householder and his wife and, by speaking the praises of moral discipline and the disgrace of moral misconduct in whatever way would cause both of them to take refuge and abide by the precepts of training, managed to establish them in the going for refuge and in the observance of the training precepts.

But the householder, being fierce, impetuous, and violent, began striking the maidservant again. His wife then said to him, "My lord, at the time when you and I did not understand karma and the ripening of karma, that was the time to do the striking. Now we have relied upon the virtuous friend, the noble Ānanda, and we understand karma and the ripening of karma. This being so, since beings in this world live out the fruits of their own karma, who is whose slave? Do not strike this girl. Good woman, I am pleased with what you said. Come here. Go and bathe." The girl bathed and came, and he dressed her in a new garment and said, "Girl, take delight and be at ease in your work."

The girl thought to herself, "This master of the house, my husband's lord, was previously fierce, impetuous, and violent, and he repeatedly struck me with his fists and the flat of his hand and gave me poor food and clothing. Now he has become like a father and mother to me." She then thought further, "From the time that the noble Ānanda began coming to this house, this householder has become like a father and mother to me. How might I do something to please the noble Ānanda?" And she thought, "If I were to steal something from here, even a small thing, this householder, because I am a servant, would beat me many times and leave me in my former condition." So she sat and stayed where she was.

The householder's wife then said to the householder, "My lord, please take note of this: the noble Ānanda is our virtuous friend. It is the noble Ānanda who separated us from our defilements, established us in the going for refuge, and set us in the training precepts. Again and again he gathers us through the Dharma. We for our part should gather him with a small material gift." "Good woman, let it be so." "My lord, I have spread out a soft cushion. From the yarn of that cushion I shall have a master weaver weave a great bolt of cloth, and afterwards I shall present you with that great bolt of cloth." The householder gave the cushion to the weaver, saying, "Good man, weave a great bolt of cloth from this cushion and I will offer it to the noble Ānanda." "So be it."

When the girl heard this she thought, "I shall add to the joy being made ready for the noble Ānanda."

Now Ānanda, rising early in the morning and putting on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe and entered Śrāvastī on the alms round. Going from house to house in due order, he entered that house. The girl had cleaned and swept the house well, and

When the girl saw Ānanda she prostrated at his feet and said, "I shall add to the joy being made ready for the noble Ānanda." Ānanda said, "Girl, what joy do you mean to add for me? This householder will present you with the great bolt of cloth." Ānanda thought to himself, "Of all the beings on the face of the earth who are subject to desire, I know that this girl today has become as agitated as any of them," and he spoke to her thus: "Girl, are you trying to beguile me?" The girl replied, "Why would I try to beguile the noble one?" Ānanda said, "Girl, if it is true, I shall not hold you to blame for any harsh words. But if it is false, I shall have you beaten and dirtied many times over and placed back just as you were before. Noble one, if you do not believe me, there is a weaver in a certain direction — go there and you will find out for yourself."

She went there and said to the weaver, "Good man, whose work is this great bolt of cloth being woven?" "It belongs to the venerable noble Ānanda." "Do you know Ānanda?" "I do not." "He is me." "Good man, be satisfied with this much for now." "Noble one, who will provide the dye?" "That same householder will provide it." "I too shall do a small service for you."

The next morning Ānanda rose early, put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī on the alms round. Going from house to house in due order, he entered the home of the queen Phreṅ ldan ma. She had his seat laid out, and when he had sat down, the queen Phreṅ ldan ma prostrated at Ānanda's feet and sat before him to hear the Dharma. He taught her the Dharma, and she said, "Noble one, have you been invited today, or are you on the alms round?" "I am on the alms round." She thought, "Who might offer him the finest alms?" and she filled his bowl with the best foods and offered them to him. Ānanda accepted them, then went to that weaver and said, "Good man, hold out both hands." When he had held out both hands, Ānanda gave him one morsel of food and said, "Good man, eat this." When he had eaten it, Ānanda said, "Good man, how does the food taste?" "Noble one, it is delicious." "Have you ever before eaten food like this?" "Noble one, never once." "Hold out your bowl." When he held out his bowl, Ānanda poured all the food into it and said, "Good man, weave this great bolt of cloth of mine well. I have done you a small service with a little food, and now for this much in return, complete it. Noble one, if the dye runs out, who will provide it?" "That same householder will provide it."

When the weaver had woven the great bolt of cloth and the dye ran out, he went to the householder's home. As it happened the householder's wife was not there; only the householder was present. The weaver said to the householder, "Householder, the dye for weaving that great bolt of cloth has run out — give me dye." The householder gave it and sent him off. Again when he was weaving and the dye ran out, he once more went to the householder's home. As it happened the householder was not there; only the householder's wife was present. The weaver said to the householder's wife, "Madam, the dye for weaving that great bolt of cloth has run out — give me dye." She gave it and sent him off. Again when he was weaving and the dye ran out, he went to the householder's home. As it happened both the householder and his wife were present. The weaver said to the householder, "Householder, again the dye for weaving that great bolt of cloth has run out — give me dye again."

The householder's wife said, "Weaver, how is that great bolt of cloth coming along?" The householder said to his wife, "My dear, did you also give him dye?" She said that she had. The householder said, "Weaver, how is that great bolt of cloth coming along?" The weaver replied, "Householder, do you think I could finish it today? On the very day that the noble Ānanda came to me and said, 'Weave this much in width and this much in length,' it was on that very day that I began weaving it." The householder's wife thought to herself, "I wonder how that great bolt of cloth is turning out," and went there to see. She saw a great bolt of cloth, fit in every way for a great man. Seeing it, her eyes filled with tears and she said, "She will not give this great bolt of cloth to the noble Ānanda. She will have another great bolt of cloth woven for that purpose," and with that she left.

Ānanda came there from time to time and said, "Weaver, is it ready?" "Noble one, it is ready for me but not for you." "Weaver, what has happened?" He replied, "The householder's wife came and saw the great bolt of cloth, and her eyes filled with tears. She said she would not give this great bolt of cloth to the noble Ānanda, and that she would have another great bolt of cloth woven for that purpose, and then she left." Ānanda said, "Weaver, do you know what a small thing I did for you?" He replied, "Why would I not know? Even now I am still coming and paying my respects at your feet. Weaver, when I come to that house, take this great bolt of cloth and bring it. Have the noble one step back a little, and I too will come around from the other side."

Ānanda went to that house and stood right at the doorway. The householder's wife bowed at his feet and sat before him looking toward the door. The weaver rolled up the great bolt of cloth, took it, and went there. The householder's wife saw him from a great distance and gestured with her hand signaling him not to come. The weaver looked in all four directions and, watching carefully, bowed his head and slipped inside and placed the great bolt of cloth in the lap of the householder's wife. Ānanda without hesitation took it and said, "May this gift bring you adornment of mind, the requisites of mind, the accumulation of yoga, the attainment of the highest purpose, and the obtaining of robes among gods and humans."

The householder's wife said, "Noble one, please return it, giving it back from your own hands to the householder." Ānanda said, "I have made this more auspicious. After this, have the householder take on the banner of a ṛṣi." The householder's wife said, "Noble one, the Blessed One has praised the white color." Ānanda said, "Let him take on the banner of a ṛṣi," and with that he rose and departed.

Vinayavibhaṅga, thirty-fifth fascicle.

The weaver said, "Householder's wife, give me my wages." She said, "Having had even one great bolt of cloth taken from her, would she drive away other wages as well? Go, and ask for your wages from the one to whom you gave the great bolt of cloth." He went to Ānanda's presence and said, "Noble one, give me my wages." Ānanda said, "Go and ask the householder's wife herself." "Noble one, shall I go to the householder's dwelling and say, 'The one to whom you gave the great bolt of cloth — go and ask that one for your wages'?" Ānanda said, "Go, and you shall receive them." The weaver went to her presence and said, "Householder's wife, give me my wages." She said, "My goodness, husband — can you not bear to sit? If you will sit, then sit."

"If you will not sit, she will fasten a copper yoke around your neck and parade you through all of Śrāvastī." The weaver then went to Ānanda's presence and said, "Noble one, the householder's wife said to me, 'My goodness, husband — can you not bear to sit? If you will sit, then sit. If you will not sit, she will fasten a copper yoke around your neck and parade you through all of Śrāvastī.' So please, noble one, give me my wages." Ānanda said, "O householder, if I were to pay the wages of the one who had my great bolt of cloth woven, I would be left without even my alms bowl and robes. Furthermore, reckon it up: add together all the flour, clarified butter, molasses, and the like that you have carried off from me, and count it out." When they reckoned it up, it turned out that he had taken considerably more than was due. Ānanda then had the weaver placed in the sun for a short while and sent him away.

That weaver was in the habit of disparaging the manner of life of the renunciants who were sons of the Śākyans, and the manner of life of the brahmins, saying, "They are like that — they just talk about doing more, yet in practice they do only less." He would mock them, spread false rumors about them, and slander them. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, in this context, and concerning this case, convened an assembly of monks — and so on, as before. The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though fully knowing, feigned not to know — and so on, as before. The awakened Blessed One then asked Ānanda, "Ānanda, is it true that you did something so unseemly?" The Venerable One replied, "It is so, Lord." The awakened Blessed One rebuked him, saying that what was not in keeping with the manner of a renunciant, not befitting, not proper, not in accord with the discipline, was not something to be done by one who had gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having rebuked him in many ways, addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so on, as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Should a monk — on behalf of a monk — cause a weaver who is not a relative to weave cloth for him, and if, before having previously arranged the matter, some thought arises in that monk and he goes to the non-relative weaver and says, 'Venerable weaver, know that this cloth is being woven for my sake. Venerable weaver, please make this cloth wide, long, closely woven, and well finished.' And if, after having said this, that monk gives the weaver wages such as food, provisions of some kind, or a little something to eat in order to obtain the cloth, and the cloth is completed — that constitutes an offense entailing forfeiture.

As for the phrase 'on behalf of a monk': this refers to Ānanda, a son of the Śākyans, or to another of that kind. 'Householder' means a man. 'Householder's wife' means a woman. 'Not a relative' is explained as follows: a grandmother, a grandfather — up to and including the seventh degree of kinship on the mother's side, these are relatives; beyond that, they are not relatives. 'Weaver' means one who weaves. 'For a non-relative' is explained as follows: a grandmother,

a grandfather, and up to and including the seventh degree of kinship on the father's side are relatives; beyond that, they are not relatives. As for the phrase 'from the weaving of cloth': this refers to any one of the seven kinds of cloth — woolen cloth, linen cloth, silk cloth, cotton cloth, coarse wool cloth, hemp cloth, or goat-hair cloth. As for the phrase 'if for that monk': this refers to Ānanda, a son of the Śākyans. As for 'not having previously invited': this means not having previously called him as a guest. As for the phrase 'some thought having arisen': this means that some notion of hospitality has arisen. As for 'going to a non-relative weaver': this means going into his presence. As for the words 'Let the venerable weaver know this — weave this cloth for me': this means presenting oneself as the beneficiary. As for 'wide': this means broad in width. As for 'long': this means long in length. As for 'tightly woven': this means without loose ends. As for 'well finished in weave': this means the warp threads are even, the quality is good, and there are no protruding strands. As for 'something to eat': these are the five kinds of food. As for 'or something as a relish': these are the five kinds of relish. As for 'edible cause': this means what serves as the basis for food. As for 'if that monk': this refers to Ānanda, a son of the Śākyans. As for 'in order to obtain the cloth': this means for the purpose of acquiring the cloth. As for 'when the cloth is completed': this means upon obtaining the cloth. As for 'that constitutes an offense entailing forfeiture': the item is to be forfeited, and then the offense entailing forfeiture is to be confessed — therefore it is said to constitute an offense entailing forfeiture. As for how the offense is incurred: from the moment the monk rises from his seat in order to accomplish his purpose — putting on robes and lower garment, washing his hands and his alms bowl, going out to beg for alms, soliciting the five kinds of relish and the five kinds of food, and giving them to the weaver — until the cloth is not yet obtained, each action constitutes a wrongdoing. When the cloth is obtained, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If, however, someone from some region had previously invited him, saying "Have cloth woven there and you may inspect it," then there is no offense. There is no offense for one who acts for the first time, for one who is mentally deranged, for one who is distracted in mind, or for one who is afflicted by pain.

The twenty-fourth offense, entailing forfeiture — that of causing weaving — is complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain companion of Ānanda — a monk named Dharma, who was conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and eager for the training — as long as he did not know that this other monk was constantly engaging in corrupt conduct, dwelt together with him. But when he came to know that he was constantly engaging in corrupt conduct, he began to live instead with monks of naturally upright character, and by the instruction of the Blessed One he went to pay homage at his feet only at the three proper times of day. Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks that the Tathāgata is setting out to tour the Kosala districts — whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata on the tour of the Kosala districts should prepare their robes." The venerable Ānanda replied, "Reverend one, I shall do as you have commanded," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he spoke to the monks:

"Venerable ones, the Blessed One is setting out to tour the Kosala districts. Whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Blessed One on the tour of the Kosala districts should prepare their robes." When Ānanda heard this, he then spoke to Nandaka: "Venerable Nandaka, take note." And the venerable Ānanda spoke to the monks: "Venerable ones, take note. The Blessed One is setting out to tour the Kosala districts. Whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Blessed One on the tour of the Kosala districts should prepare their robes."
