At this, some said among themselves: "If we stay here, we will have passed through a hundred doorways and will still have to struggle somehow just to fill our bellies. But if we travel together with the Blessed One, the Blessed One has taught that traveling in the retinue of a buddha brings eighteen benefits, and so many hundreds and thousands of living creatures will also be traveling together with the Blessed One. Yet if we do travel with the Blessed One, for a time we will have to drink muddied water, and we shall not be able to find a place in the shade of a tree. So let us take some monks who are good companions, reciting the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha as we go forward — in that way we will travel in comfort and obtain abundant provisions."

Nandaka said: "Master, have you given up a golden begging bowl and taken to going on almsround with an earthen bowl? Is there anyone here among your companions who has the qualities of Dharma — who is conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and eager for the training? That person wants nothing to do with seeing you. Master, of the four means of gathering disciples (saṃgrahavastu) — generosity, kind words, purposeful conduct, and consistency of purpose — that the Blessed One has taught, has the master properly adopted and practiced even a single one? Not in the slightest. That is why you have come to your present situation."

The venerable Dharma had a worn-out patch-robe, and having found a large bolt of cloth he thought: "I will go and request the preceptor to sew a new patch-robe." He took it and went to the presence of Ānanda, and as he was going, a monk on almsround saw him and said: "Venerable Dharma, where are you going?" He replied: "My patch-robe is worn out, and I have found this large bolt of cloth, so I am going to ask my preceptor to sew a new patch-robe." The almsround monk said: "If you are going to have a new patch-robe sewn, give that old patch-robe to me." He agreed, and went to Ānanda's presence and said: "Preceptor, my patch-robe is worn out and I have found this large bolt of cloth, so I ask you to sew me a new patch-robe." Nandaka said: "Master, this is the right moment." Ānanda said: "Venerable Dharma, I myself have a patch-robe, and I will give it to you. There is no need to trouble the preceptor — from this large bolt of cloth I will cut and sew a patch-robe and keep it." Nandaka said: "Venerable Dharma, I have heard with my own ears and seen with my own eyes that you are conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and eager for the training. But I do not know how you could so flout what the preceptor has said, which accords with the Dharma. Could it be that you are accepting something contrary to the preceptor's intention?" At this, the powerful monk said nothing in response to the rebuke, and Ānanda gave him the patch-robe.

He took it and said: "Preceptor, please accept this large bolt of cloth." The venerable Dharma said: "Why would I exchange anything with you? You gave me the patch-robe, so take the large bolt of cloth back for yourself." The other monk thought: "What use have I for this useless article? I will offer this large bolt of cloth to the Saṅgha, and as for this old patch-robe, I will ask the preceptor's permission to give it to that almsman." He then said: "Preceptor, I intend to offer this large bolt of cloth to the Saṅgha, and since an almsman has received this old patch-robe, I wish to give it to him — I ask the preceptor's permission." The preceptor replied: "So be it." The monk offered the large bolt of cloth to the Saṅgha and gave the old patch-robe to the almsman.

The next morning, the almsman came wearing that patch-robe to pay his respects at the preceptor's feet. Ānanda said: "Venerable Dharma, please take note. Let the venerable Ānanda inform the monks: the Blessed One is setting out to tour the Kosala regions. Whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Blessed One on this tour of the Kosala regions should attend to the matter of robes. If we stay here, we will have to pass a hundred doorways and somehow manage to fill our bellies. But if we travel together with the Blessed One, the Blessed One has declared there to be eighteen benefits in traveling together with a buddha, and many hundreds of thousands of living beings will likewise travel with him. Even so, when one travels together with the Blessed One, one will at times have to drink turbid water and will not find shelter at the foot of a shaded tree. But if we go ahead reciting the praises of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, then we shall travel in comfort and abundant gains will also be secured."

The preceptor spoke: "Those eighteen benefits that the Blessed One has declared to attend traveling together with a buddha — for me they amount only to drawbacks. For my part, I shall travel together with the Blessed One himself." Ānanda said: "Then I will go along with you." The other replied: "I am going with the Blessed One himself." Ānanda grew angry and said: "Wicked one! Do you imagine that I gave you the patch-robe out of genuine spiritual regard for you in the Dharma? I gave it to you so that you would travel together with me. If you do not go together with me, I will not let you keep the patch-robe." The venerable Dharma thought: "Having my robe seized is the better option. It would not be right for me to go on a regional tour together with those who are completely given over to vile conduct." And so he returned the patch-robe to him.

Then the Blessed One — himself tamed, his retinue tamed; himself at peace, his retinue at peace; himself liberated, his retinue liberated; himself at ease, his retinue at ease; himself subdued, his retinue subdued; himself an arhat, his retinue of arhats; himself free of attachment, his retinue free of attachment; himself resplendent, his retinue resplendent — surrounded by a herd of bulls as a supreme bull among them, surrounded by a herd of elephants as a great elephant, surrounded by a pride of fanged beasts as a lion, surrounded by a flock of geese as a king of geese, surrounded by a host of birds as a Garuḍa, surrounded by a company of students as a brahmin, surrounded by a crowd of patients as a skilled physician, surrounded by an army of warriors as a hero —

surrounded by a company of travelers as a caravan leader; surrounded by a throng of merchants as a merchant chief; surrounded by a host of attendants as a lord of trade; surrounded by a council of ministers as a king in his fortress; surrounded by a thousand sons as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin); surrounded by a multitude of constellations as the moon; surrounded by a thousand rays of light as the sun; surrounded by hosts of gandharvas as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, guardian of the realm; surrounded by throngs of kinnaras as an āryan; surrounded by hosts of nāgas as Virūpākṣa; surrounded by hosts of yakṣas as Vaiśravaṇa, the giver of wealth; surrounded by hosts of asuras as Vemacitra; surrounded by the assembly of the Thirty-Three as Śakra (Indra, king of the gods); surrounded by the assembly of the Brahmā realm as Brahmā —

His sense faculties utterly tamed; his conduct and comportment untroubled; still as an ocean; bearing moisture like a cloud; free of pride as a great royal elephant; his body beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being; his form made splendid by the eighty minor marks; adorned with a halo of radiance a fathom wide; possessing a luminosity surpassing that of a thousand suns; moving through the world with uninterrupted goodness like a moving mountain of jewels; endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared mindfulnesses; possessing great compassion; entered upon the work of benefiting the world; sole protector; solitary hero; without a second; speaking nothing of duality; abiding in calm abiding and insight, making the three knowledges shine clear; well trained in the three trainings; skilled in the foundation of the three bases of discipline; having crossed the four rivers; well established in the foundation of practice in the four bases of miraculous power; having long since thoroughly purified the four means of gathering beings; knowing no intimidation from the four fearlessnesses; having abandoned the five limbs; having truly passed beyond the five destinies; endowed with the six limbs; having fully perfected the six perfections; abiding in the six constant abidings; rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening; teaching the eight limbs of the path; skilled in the nine absorptions of successive abiding; endowed with the power of the ten powers; his fame having spread and pervaded completely in all ten directions; exceedingly exalted above those who rule over a hundred thousand realms —

He set out to tour the realm of Kośala, preceded by his great śrāvaka retinue: the venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and the remaining thousand former matted-hair ascetics; the venerable Śāriputra, the great Maudgalyāyana, and the many monks of the Saṅgha who accompanied him.

Now, it is the nature of reality that whenever a blessed buddha sets out to tour the realm, he surveys with his entire body, turning in the manner of an elephant, to the right, to see whether anything is out of order or improperly arranged. And so as the Blessed One surveyed to the right in the manner of an elephant with his whole body, he saw the venerable one walking on the tour of the realm clad only in his Dharma robe, with upper and lower robe in place. Having seen this, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have the robes of the monks who are in the rains retreat been successfully obtained?" "Blessed One, they have." "Then why does this monk walk on the tour of the realm wearing his Dharma robe alone, with upper and lower robe in place?" At that point, a detailed account was presented to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, do monks give a robe to a monk and then take it back?" "Venerable One, they do."

Then, with regard to this incident, this founding case, and this circumstance, the Blessed One convened the assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The Blessed Buddhas, while knowing, question for a purpose" also proceeds as before. The Blessed Buddha questioned Dāsaka: "Dāsaka, is it true that you gave a robe to a monk and then took it back?" "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed Buddha then censured him, saying that such conduct was unworthy of a renunciant, improper, unsuitable, out of keeping with the Vinaya, and not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should any monk, having given a robe to another monk, later become angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure either seize it back himself or cause another to seize it back, saying to that monk, 'I do not give you the robe — return it!' — if that monk, having a surplus, gives it back and relinquishes it, he incurs an offense requiring forfeiture."

"Any monk" refers to a son of the Śākyas — Dāsaka or any other such person. "To a monk" means one who is a member of this Dharma community. "A robe" means any one of the seven kinds: wool cloth, hemp cloth, silk cloth, cotton cloth, coarse linen, jute cloth, or sun-bleached cloth. "Having given" means without any need to return it. "Later" means at some other time. "Angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure" means while the anger has not subsided. "Seize back himself" means to do so by one's own hand. "Cause another to seize back" means to have another do so. "That monk" means whichever monk it is. "Having a surplus" means having whatever surplus is available. "Gives it back and relinquishes it" means to hand it over. "If he relinquishes it" means if he has parted from it bodily. "He incurs an offense requiring forfeiture" means that, having forfeited the article, one must confess the offense requiring forfeiture — that is why it is said "he incurs an offense requiring forfeiture."

Now, how does the transgression arise? It arises through bodily action, through verbal expression, through both together, or through others acting on one's behalf.

How does it arise through bodily action? If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure physically grabs, pulls, and carries away the robe without saying verbally to the monk "I do not give you the robe — return it!" — then, for as long as he has not separated the robe's hem from the recipient's body, he incurs a wrongdoing; but when he does cause the robe's hem to separate from the body, he incurs an offense requiring forfeiture. That is how it arises through bodily action.

How does it arise through verbal expression? If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure says verbally "I do not give you the robe — return it!" without laying hands on the robe himself — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, he incurs a wrongdoing;

but when he does cause the robe's hem to separate from the recipient's body, he incurs an offense requiring forfeiture. That is how it arises through verbal expression.

How does it arise through both together? If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure both lays hands on the robe bodily and says verbally "I do not give you the robe, monk — return it!" — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, he incurs a wrongdoing; but when he does cause the robe's hem to separate from the body, he incurs an offense requiring forfeiture. That is how it arises through both together.

How does it arise through others? If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a monk to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, a wrongdoing accrues to each of the two; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, each of the two incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a nun to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, a wrongdoing accrues to each of the two; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, the nun incurs a wrongdoing, while the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a female probationer to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, a wrongdoing accrues to each of the two; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, the female probationer incurs a wrongdoing, while the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a novice monk to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, a wrongdoing accrues to each of the two; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, the novice monk incurs a wrongdoing, while the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a novice nun to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, a wrongdoing accrues to each of the two; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, the novice nun incurs a wrongdoing, while the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a layman to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, great demerit accrues to the layman and the monk incurs a wrongdoing; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, even greater demerit accrues to the layman, and the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture.

If a monk, having given a robe to another monk, later becomes angry, agitated, and wrathful, and in a state of displeasure, sends a laywoman to snatch it back — then, for as long as the robe's hem has not been separated from the recipient's body, great demerit accrues to the laywoman and the monk incurs a wrongdoing; and when the robe's hem is caused to separate from the body, even greater demerit accrues to the laywoman, and the monk incurs an offense requiring forfeiture. That is how it arises through others.

For other purposes, and through implements of the Vinaya, there is no transgression.

How does it arise for other purposes? It is like this: when a preceptor, an abbot, or their attendants are traveling at an improper time toward a dangerous area, toward the bank of a river, or toward the edge of a great precipice, and the abbot or preceptor thinks, "It would not be right if thieves or deceivers were to snatch their robes," and so snatches the robes or causes them to be snatched — that is how it arises for other purposes.

How does it arise through implements of the Vinaya? It is like this: when attendants dwelling together with monks are keeping company with evil friends, evil associates, and evil companions, going along the road with them and associating in evil, and the abbot or preceptor thinks, "It would not be right for these attendants to be in the company of evil friends, evil associates, and evil companions," and so snatches the robes or causes them to be snatched — that is how it arises through implements of the Vinaya. There is no transgression for a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by pain. The twenty-fifth rule, the abandonment of snatching, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At a certain rocky cliff there lived a faithful householder, good and of virtuous intention, who had built a monastery temple for the Saṅgha — one furnished with high entrance steps, with latticed windows, adorned with railings, delightful to the heart and eye, fit to serve as a stairway to the heavens, and fully equipped with large and small seats and furnishings. Sixty monks resided there, and that householder provided them with robes, alms-food, and other necessities. Then at another time, the householder came to possess the Dharma of the season — that is, he passed away — and he had a son. The monks went to that son and said, "Good sir, your father provided the sixty monks with robes, alms-food, and other necessities. Would you also be able to provide the sixty monks with robes, alms-food, and other necessities?" He replied, "Noble ones, some give service to a hundred, some to a thousand, some even to a hundred thousand. But as for me, I can barely sustain myself, so I cannot take this upon my shoulders." Thereupon the monks departed from that temple.

Two men who had gone forth from the household life right there at that same rocky cliff, having wandered for alms, took up residence in that very temple. Travelers heading in the same direction arrived from the north, and they saw that temple from a great distance and went there. Having paid homage to the stūpa with verse, they entered the temple. They found it empty, and they thought, "Have the monks gone inside for proper meditation, or have they gone out on their daytime rounds?" As they were walking around inside, they saw the two newly ordained men, and they said to them, "Noble ones, where have the monks gone?" The two replied, "Good sirs, no monks are residing here. Why? The householder who had this temple built provided the sixty monks with robes, alms-food, and other necessities; then he came to possess the Dharma of the season, and the monks went to his son and said, 'Good sir, your father provided the sixty monks with robes, alms-food,

and other necessities. Can you likewise provide the sixty monks with robes, alms-food, and other necessities?' The son replied, 'Noble ones, some people make offerings to a hundred; some make offerings to a thousand; some even make offerings to a hundred thousand. But as for me, I can barely support myself, so I cannot take this on.' And so those monks departed. As for the two of us, we supported ourselves by going on alms rounds and have remained here in this very temple."

The caravan leader said, "Wise ones, it has long been our aspiration: 'How wonderful it would be if we could have a Saṅgha temple built, and having had it built, provide the monks with what they need.' Now this temple is already built, so we will provide the monks with what they need in this very temple." He then spread out a large bolt of cloth and said, "Wise ones, each of you, donate here whatever you can give." They each gave according to their means, and a great quantity of goods was assembled there. The caravan leader then said to the two newly ordained men, "Noble ones, this is three months' alms-food for sixty monks. This is alms-food for the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth of the fortnight. This is for illness and medicinal supplies. This is for gains. This is a store of robes. Please invite the good monks, for after the rains retreat has passed, we will come here and provide a hundred monks with what they need." Having said this, they departed.

One of the two newly ordained men said, "Who shall keep the Saṅgha's gains?" The other replied, "The younger one." Of the two, the younger one hid the gains away, and then said, "When monks are being summoned from Śrāvastī, who should go there?" The elder said, "The younger one should go." The younger replied, "I am the one who hid the gains, so you go." The elder of the two went to Śrāvastī to summon monks.

Now the conduct of the group of six was this: they thought, "Here, when brahmins and householders come and gather, we shall teach them the Dharma, defeat our opponents, and proclaim our own reputation." So one of the group of six, not wanting to leave the gateway of the Jeta Grove empty, was walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. Venerable Ānanda, walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove, saw from a considerable distance an approaching figure — the elder monk — gray-haired like the flower of the wheat plant, with hanging eyebrows. He thought, "Who is this senior monk coming? I should greet him." So he said, "Welcome, elder. Well come, well come. I pay you homage."

The elder replied, "I pay homage to the teacher." Then Ānanda thought, "Alas — this is merely a newly ordained man; he does not even know who is a teacher and who is a preceptor." Ānanda said to him, "Newly ordained one, where have you come from?" "I have come from a certain rocky mountain temple." "Newly ordained one, is that place a proper temple, or is it a place of poverty? What is a proper temple? What is a place of poverty? Where all requisites are present — that is a proper temple. Where all requisites are lacking — that is a place of poverty." "Previously it was a place of poverty, but now it has become a proper temple." "How did that come about?" Along the road, likeminded companions had gathered together, and they had offered to it three months' alms-food for sixty monks, alms-food for the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth of the fortnight, supplies for illness and medicine, gains, and a store of robes; and saying, "Please invite the good noble monks —

"We too, after the rains retreat has passed, will come here and provide requisites for a hundred monks," they said. The intimate companion replied, "And yet you have come to steal monks." "Indeed so." The elder Prasena, who had arrived in Kosala, King Prasenajit, Queen Mālikā, the Kṣatriya woman Vārsākārī, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the learned brahmin Jīvaka, the elder Vṛddha, the householder's wife, the mother of Mṛgāradhṛtā, Sujanā, other brahmins, and many other faithful householders — all of these had served the monks with every requisite, and each day the elders of the Saṅgha were announcing donations, saying, "May those monks who have not yet come to this place also come, and may those who have come take great delight here." For there, robes, alms-food, lodging, the conditions needed in illness, and the supplies of medicine were all present without any lack, and the Blessed One was personally teaching the Dharma. So here the enjoyment of the Dharma and the enjoyment of material things were both in full abundance. "Therefore, if the monks were to learn that you had come here to steal monks, there would be a procedure to expel you from this residence. So do not say such a thing to any other monk. Rather, we each have a retinue of ten, making sixty of us in all, and we have come out of affection for you." "Teacher, I have come to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and to return thereafter." The intimate companion thought, "If some black-bowl bearer should see this and hear of it and go straight to the Blessed One first, that would not be right." He therefore said, "Elder, have you not heard the saying, 'A god is circumambulated with the mind, not with the body'? And the Blessed One himself declared:

All phenomena are led by the mind,
the mind is their foremost, they move in the mind's wake.

So right here, pay homage at the Blessed One's feet." And taking the elder by the scruff of the neck, he made him bow down, saying, "Do this: 'Homage to the buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha!'" And thus he caused him to bow. "Teacher, I am thirsty. Please drink whatever you need to drink for thirst. Wait right here — I will fill a small thirst-bowl and bring it back to you." Having filled the thirst-bowl and poured it out, he said, "Elder, go now." He escorted him a good distance away, then instructed him, "Do not turn back now," and returned by himself.

Now the way of the Group of Six was this: however small a piece of news they heard, the moment it spread about they would gather together and report it to one another. So the intimate companion went to the temple and said to the Group of Six, "Venerable ones, let us at last put an end to our worries. Have you heard a certain small piece of news?" "We have. At a pleasant temple among rocky crags, a group of like-minded companions arrived from the northern road, and they offered there three months' alms-food for sixty monks, food for the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth of the fortnight, the conditions needed in illness, the supplies of medicine, gains, and a store of robes. Go there." "Should we keep the rains retreat there or not?" "No — consume those provisions there during the rains itself, then come back here and accept a place for the later rains retreat, which is now close at hand."

When those monks arrived and the two elders saw them coming from a great distance, the intimate companion said, "Venerable ones, welcome!"

"Welcome!" the two elders said, and they assigned those monks their lodgings and gave out bedding, high seats, low seats, water pitchers, bowls, water-straining cloths, and crooked keys.

Those monks thought, "Let us now look into the matter for which we have come," and they said, "Venerable elders, show us whatever gains have been accumulated here." The two elders, being of straightforward character, showed them everything: "This is three months' alms-food for sixty monks. This is the food of the eighth. This is the food of the fourteenth. This is the food of the fifteenth. This is the provision for illness. This is the store of medicinal supplies. This is the gain from this source. This is the store of robes."

Those monks said, "Venerable ones, since the two elders are miserly, they are unable to give food in alms, and yet here the two elders have rendered service to the Saṅgha. On account of that, we give the relinquishment." They gave the two elders the relinquishment, and the two elders were glad, saying, "We have received the relinquishment."

Then those monks said, "Venerable ones, if we entrust this to some monk who has a good stomach, he will provide the assembly each day with meals in eighteen varieties, together with many kinds of oily and flavourful side dishes, and well-prepared beverages in abundance." They did entrust it to a monk with a good stomach, and he provided them each day with meals in eighteen varieties, many kinds of oily and flavourful side dishes, and well-prepared beverages in abundance. In a short time all the alms-provisions were spent.

Then the appointed steward sat down to one side of the elders and said, "Venerable ones, a single parasol's share has now arrived for the Saṅgha."

Those monks said, "Venerable ones, those who have not properly undertaken the training observe the ceremonies of the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. We who have properly undertaken the training do not do that — so eat that too." And they ate it.

Again the steward sat down to one side of the elders and said, "Venerable ones, there now remains a single portion of the Saṅgha's provisions for illness and medicinal supplies."

The group of six said, "Venerable ones, for as long as the five aggregates subject to clinging continue to live, we are perpetually ill — so eat that medicine too." And they ate it.

Then they said, "Venerable ones, it is hard to carry an unequal load. Let us divide this store of robe-cloth as well, so that with equal loads we may travel comfortably." And they divided that too.

Again the steward sat down to one side of the elders and said, "Now there is nothing left of the Saṅgha's single parasol's share."

Those monks said, "You two elders claimed there were three months' alms-provisions for sixty monks, yet they have all been exhausted within the rains itself."

The two elders said, "Did we say, 'Make only a continuous succession of meals in eighteen varieties, many kinds of oily and flavourful side dishes, and well-prepared beverages'?"

Those monks said, "The two elders used it themselves before, and now they criticize those who are doing the same. Venerable ones, perform the act of expulsion against these two from this residence." Some said, "Let the two elders request forgiveness at once. If they wait to request forgiveness later, it will be as late as the hair on a louse." The two had just begun to request forgiveness when some said —

Some said, "Venerable ones, these two elders are straightforward by nature — grant them forgiveness." The others said, "The two elders are to be forgiven." Then they said, "This rocky cliff has many who lack faith, and even alms are hard to find here. If there are a few leftovers, give those. But if there are none, we shall depart." The venerable ones replied, "There is nothing at all — you may leave today." And so those monks departed, went to Śrāvastī, and upon arriving there agreed to observe the latter rains retreat.

When the rains retreat had passed, a corresponding group also arrived, and they paid homage to the stūpa with the same verse-recitation, and entered the monastery. Upon entering, they saw the monastery was empty and thought, "Have the monks gone inside to lie down properly, or have they gone out for their daytime activities without delay?" As they were making their way around, they caught sight of those two elders and said, "Noble ones, where have the monks gone? Good sirs, there are no monks here at all." The noble ones said, "Did we not provide alms-food for sixty monks for three months?" The two elders replied, "The monks came, ate everything during the rains retreat, and departed." They asked, "Which monks did you two bring?" The answer was: "The group of six." The noble ones said, "You two went to the great ocean and brought back string-pearls, yet could you not find any monks other than the group of six to bring?"

Those people then condemned the conduct of the śramaṇas (renunciants) who are sons of the Śākyan, and the conduct of brahmins, saying, "The very moment a sprout of faith arises in us, they crush it." They complained, they slandered, and at that very occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One — on account of this incident, this occasion, and this context — convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, just as before. And the passage beginning "The Blessed Buddhas, though knowing, act as if they do not," and so on, also proceeds as before. The Blessed One then asked the group of six monks: "Is it true, monks, that you divided the gains of the rains retreat during the rains retreat itself?" They replied, "It is true, Blessed One." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that such conduct is unworthy of a renunciant — it is not the proper way of a renunciant, it is not fitting, it is not suitable, it is not in accord with the precepts.

Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing these ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, just as before.

The rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be recited as follows: "Therefore, monks shall not divide the gains of the rains retreat during the rains retreat itself. If monks divide the gains of the rains retreat during the rains retreat itself, it shall constitute a serious offence." Thus did the Blessed One establish this rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī, there were the fully ordained nun Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and Dharmadinnā. Of these two, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, though not herself accompanied by a retinue of renunciants, was one possessed of the qualities of a renunciant,

Dharmadinnā, for her part, was accompanied by a retinue versed in the sūtra collection, and that retinue was itself possessed of expertise in the sūtra collection. Both had undertaken to observe the rains retreat together in a single dwelling. When the time came that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī's retinue arose and departed, Dharmadinnā instructed her own retinue, saying to her sisters: "Whatever the Blessed One has permitted to the fully ordained nuns — the going forth, the full ordination, and all the requisites of the fully ordained nun's life — all of this depends upon Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Moreover, the Blessed One has declared that a person who protects the mind of another generates abundant merit. Therefore, for the time being, cultivate the contemplation of impermanence." And her retinue began to cultivate the contemplation of impermanence.

When the time came that Dharmadinnā's retinue arose and departed, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī likewise instructed her own retinue, saying to her sisters: "Over three immeasurable eons, through hundreds and thousands of ascetic deeds, the Blessed One fully perfected the six perfections, and all the unsurpassed knowledge he thereby realized is a cause of benefit for sentient beings. Moreover, the Blessed One has declared that a person who protects the mind of another generates abundant merit. Therefore, for the time being, chant all those passages of the sūtra collection that deal with impermanence." And her retinue began to chant all those passages of the sūtra collection concerned with impermanence.

In this way, the fully ordained nuns, by thus guarding one another's minds, did not flourish in virtuous qualities — like a blue lotus (utpala) growing without water. Now, there was a laywoman named Sāgā who had faith in Dharmadinnā, and she invited her as a guest, providing all necessities. On a later occasion, the laywoman Sāgā came to prostrate at Dharmadinnā's feet. Dharmadinnā said to her: "Good lady, a great many fully ordained nuns have undertaken to keep the rains retreat together in one dwelling, yet because they guard one another's minds, they do not flourish in virtuous qualities — like a blue lotus growing without water. Could you arrange for the nuns' Saṅgha to have a rains retreat dwelling built? The land belongs to the king; for the sake of the land, please petition the king."

Sāgā replied: "Noble one, I have kārṣāpaṇa coins available. As for the land, since it is under the king's authority, please petition the king yourself. As for the construction, I shall provide for it."

The fully ordained nun Dharmadinnā went to Queen Mallikā, and Queen Mallikā said: "Noble one, welcome, welcome. Noble one, for what purpose have you come?" Dharmadinnā replied: "I wish to have a rains retreat dwelling built for the nuns. The land is under the king's authority, and I wish to petition the king for the land. Noble one, please go ahead; I shall petition the king on the noble one's behalf."

Dharmadinnā departed. Then Queen Mallikā went before Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, and said to him: "Your majesty, the fact that the noble Dharmadinnā has come to your palace is a great gain for you. She has come wishing to have a rains retreat dwelling built for the nuns, and she says she has come to petition the king for land that is under your royal authority."

The king said: "If the noble Dharmadinnā wishes to stay here in this very place, she may remain right here and I shall have another palace built. If she does not wish that, she may choose whichever location she pleases and a rains retreat dwelling shall be built there."

Queen Mallikā conveyed the king's reply to Dharmadinnā, saying: "Your majesty offers the noble one this assurance —"

"If the noble Dharmadinnā wishes to remain in this very place, she may stay here and I shall have another palace built. If she does not wish that, wherever she pleases, a rains retreat dwelling shall be built there." This was the message she conveyed.

Dharmadinnā then told the laywoman Sāgalā that King Prasenajit, born of Kosala, had given her this assurance: "If the noble Dharmadinnā wishes to stay here in this very place for the time being, she may remain here and I shall have another palace built elsewhere. If she does not wish that, wherever she pleases, a rains retreat dwelling shall be built there." This was the message she passed on.

Now the King of Kosala, Prasenajit, had two districts: one called Sword-Powered and one called Noble Royal Lineage. The Sword-Powered district had gone off to a military posting, and the wives of those men were spending their time in pleasurable company with other men, so that quarter had become quiet and secluded. Dharmadinnā said: "Let a rains retreat dwelling be built in that direction." The laywoman Sāgalā had the rains retreat dwelling built in that quarter, and the nuns began residing there.

Then the Sword-Powered district returned from the military posting. Those men began dragging their wives back and beating them, and in the streets the sound of the women weeping rose up high and loud, like the sound of horses and elephants.

The nuns said: "Noble one, we are frightened by the summer rains and have taken shelter under the eaves."

Dharmadinnā thought: "I wonder whether any among these women have roots of virtue." She looked and saw that some did. She then thought: "On whom does it depend?" and saw that it depended on herself. She said: "Sisters, in accordance with their capacity to be tamed, one must bear all of this with patience."

Dharmadinnā set a jar of sesame oil to one side and said to the nuns: "Sisters, whatever nail-clippings any of you have, put them all into this jar." Whatever nail-clippings they had, they all poured into the jar.

Then some children came there, and Dharmadinnā gave the boys sesame oil, had them anoint one another's heads with it, and with her own hands she gave them food. To the girls she herself applied the sesame oil, anointed their heads, and with her own hands gave them food. The children took these things and went off to their own homes, and their mothers asked them: "Who gave you these?" They said: "The noble Dharmadinnā did." The wives thought: "In truth, the noble Dharmadinnā has done for us the work of a mother." They were filled with faith in her and thought: "Whenever our husbands go off to the military posting, we shall see our husbands off and then attend upon the noble Dharmadinnā."

On another occasion their husbands departed for the military posting, and Dharmadinnā, knowing it was the right time to tame them, had the temple swept clean, well plastered, coated with a smooth plaster of fresh clay and dung, and arranged with washing materials, water, incense, fragrant smoke, flowers, and mats. She appointed nuns with pleasant voices to remain there. The wives, having seen their husbands off, came into the presence of Dharmadinnā, and Dharmadinnā provided them with washing materials, water for rinsing the hands, incense, fragrant smoke, flowers, and

seating mats, and in a melodious, verse-like voice made prostration to the stupa. She then took her seat in the presence of the community of nuns. The wives too made prostration at her feet and arranged themselves before her in order to hear the Dharma. Dharmadinnā, having fully understood their intentions, habitual tendencies, constitutions, and characters, taught the Dharma in such a way that, without fail, they shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had been accumulated since beginningless time, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, they said: "Noble one, relying on you as our virtuous spiritual friend, what you, noble one, have done for us is something that neither our fathers did for us, nor our mothers, nor the king, nor the gods, nor our ancestors of former times, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor friends and companions, nor any gathering of relatives — you have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed us from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; you have lifted our feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you have established us among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to an end. By shattering with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had been accumulated since beginningless time, we have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Noble one, we have truly entered the path. Noble one, we have truly entered the path. Noble one, we take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the community of monks. We ask to be received as laywomen. From this day forward, for as long as we live, we take refuge from the very depth of our hearts."

Having become filled with faith, they went home to their respective houses, swept them clean, plastered them well, coated them with a smooth plaster of fresh clay and dung, and conducted themselves with peaceful composure. When their husbands returned from the military posting, the husbands thought: "Our wives must be making merry with some elephant-keeper, or cowherd, or someone of that sort." Then they heard that their husbands had arrived. Having heard this, the wives greeted them with gracious and welcoming words, saying "Welcome, dear lords, welcome," and sent them off to their respective homes. Their wives massaged them with scented oils, bathed and cleansed them, dressed them well, and gave them food. The husbands thought: "Such conduct as this has never happened before," and asked them: "Dear ones, if conduct like this is unprecedented, how has it come about?" They replied: "Dear lords, the noble Dharmadinnā has taught us the Dharma in such a way that, however long we continue to revolve in cyclic existence, such afflictions will never again arise among those who wander in saṃsāra." The husbands thought: "The noble Dharmadinnā is one who tames the untamed — and look, she has tamed these women here. Those whom we were unable to tame by killing, binding, beating, and cursing have been tamed by the noble Dharmadinnā through teaching the Dharma. The noble Dharmadinnā has truly benefited us, and for our part we shall look to the king and pay homage to the noble Dharmadinnā."

Dharmadinnā, knowing it was the right time to tame them as well, had the temple swept clean, plastered well, coated with a smooth plaster of fresh clay and dung, and arranged with washing materials, water, incense, fragrant smoke, flowers, and seating mats, and appointed nuns with pleasant voices to remain there. The husbands too, having looked to the king, came into the presence of Dharmadinnā, and

Dharmadinnā gave them washing things, water for rinsing the hands, incense, fragrant smoke, flowers, and betel, and then with a voice of verse offered salutation to the stūpa. She then sat down on the seat that had been prepared before the community of nuns. The husbands as well paid homage at her feet and took their places before her to hear the Dharma.

Dharmadinnā, having fully grasped their intention, their latent tendencies, their elements, and their character, taught the Dharma in such a way as to ensure that through the vajra of gnosis they would shatter the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a personal self), accumulated from beginningless time, and directly realize the fruit of having entered the stream.

Having seen the truths, they said: "Noble one, even our own fathers did not do for us what the noble one has done for us by relying on her as a virtuous spiritual friend. Our mothers did not do it. The king did not do it. The gods did not do it. Our forebears of old did not do it. Ascetics and brahmins did not do it. The assembly of friends, companions, and relatives did not do it. She has dried up the ocean of blood and tears. She has freed us from the mountains of bones. She has closed the doors to the lower destinies. She has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. She has drawn our feet out from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed them among gods and humans. She has brought cyclic existence to an end. Having shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated from beginningless time, we have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Noble one, we have entered the stream. Noble one, we have entered the stream. Noble one, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the community of monks. Please accept us as laymen. From this day forward, for as long as we live, we go for refuge from the depths of our hearts."

Having become filled with faith, they spoke again: "Noble one, since from this day forth we shall not incur the guilt of intentionally taking the life of even a worm or a beetle, and yet we live by the sword, how shall we sustain ourselves?"

Dharmadinnā replied: "Take up bows without strings, arrows without points, and swords made of wood."

And so they took up bows without strings, arrows without points, and swords made of wood.

From the moment they saw the truths, they no longer engaged in sport with weapons, no longer drank ale, and no longer pursued pleasure in the company of other women. As a result, they became wealthy and prosperous through their possessions. Their elephants and horses, being no longer used up, grew thriving, well-hided, flush with flesh and blood.

Now a certain chieftain had turned against Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, and the king sent one regiment there. It was defeated, thoroughly routed, and scattered, and returned. In the same way, a second regiment was sent there, and it too was defeated, thoroughly routed, and scattered, and returned. Then the ministers said to the king: "Sire, the chieftain's forces grow while the king's forces dwindle. If the king himself does not go there, the chieftain will be difficult to overcome."

The king had the drum of proclamation sounded and issued the order: "Let all those within my realm who live by the sword go there."

The king himself also set out, equipped and armed with a four-division fourfold army.

Now in the service of Prasenajit, king of Kośala, there were two guilds, one called the Sword-Mighty and the other called the Noble-Kshatriyas. The guild of the Sword-Mighty were men who went in the van of battle, while

The guild of the Noble-Kshatriyas consisted of men who came from outside, and so when the king looked toward the front of the Sword-Mighty guild, he saw the men marching there to be well-fed, full of flesh and blood, and their elephants and horses likewise well-fed, full of flesh and blood. Seeing this, he said to his ministers, "Wise ones, to whom does this guild belong?" They replied, "Sire, this is the guild called the Sword-Mighty, which marches at the fore." Then when the king looked behind, he saw the men of the Noble-Kshatriyas guild to be haggard, thin, emaciated, lean, and without bodies filled out, and their elephants and horses likewise haggard, thin, emaciated, lean, and without bodies filled out. Seeing this, he said to his ministers, "Wise ones, to whom does this guild belong?" They replied, "Sire, this is the guild called the Noble-Kshatriyas, which follows behind."

The king said, "Wise ones, are they not given equal provisions?" They replied, "Sire, please grant them equal provisions." He had them summoned, and when they came the king said to them, "Wise ones, are you not given equal provisions? I grant you equality. But then why is it that the Sword-Mighty guild is prosperous, full of flesh and blood, whereas you of the Noble-Kshatriyas guild are reduced to wretchedness, thinness, emaciation, leanness, and lack of bodily fullness?" They said, "Sire, if only we too were without bows and bowstrings, without arrows, carrying wooden swords, selling and reselling weapons, then we too would become prosperous, full of flesh and blood. Furthermore, the elephants and horses of those others are wholly unused, while our own horses and elephants are wholly used up."

The king said to them, "Wise ones, is what you say true?" They replied, "Sire, it is." "Then do you wish to be led out there and slaughtered at a cliff?" They replied, "Sire, what shall it be — battle with weapons or battle without weapons?" The king replied in anger, "If you will not fight with weapons, then you yourselves this very day — topple that cliff." And with that, the king turned back.

The guild of the Sword-Mighty went to the presence of Dharmadatta and said, "Noble one, the king has appointed us to a military post. How are we to carry it out?" Dharmadatta said, "Come now. No harm whatsoever will befall any of those of you who go there. In whichever place you are stationed, look to the third lunar day. On whichever day the cliff is to be circumambulated, give them the gift of hearing the Dharma throughout all the watches of that night, and invoke in praise the lord of the Enduring World, Brahmā; the lord of the gods, Śakra (Indra); the Four World-Guardians (the four mahārājas); the twenty-eight great yakṣa commanders; the five great yakṣa commanders called Sena; the nāga king Nandaka; and Priya by name — praise them and rejoice with them."

At these words of the noble Dharmadatta, those men expressed joyful approval and rejoiced aloud. Thereafter, in whichever place they were stationed, the noble one had them recite the third lunar day text. On whatever day the cliff was to be circumambulated, he gave them the gift of hearing the Dharma throughout all the watches of that night, and they praised the lord of the Enduring World, Brahmā; the lord of the gods, Śakra; the Four World-Guardians; and

the twenty-eight great yakṣa commanders, and the five great yakṣa commanders called Sena, and the nāga king Nandaka, and Priya by name — and they offered praise and rejoiced with them.

At that very time, Vaiśravaṇa, the great king and son of a good family, had gathered the yakṣas together, and when he heard the praises being offered, he thought: "Who is this who offers praise using my name?" And he saw that a certain number of his Dharma-brothers had been stationed in an unsuitable place. Seeing this, the five great yakṣa commanders called Sena addressed him: "These Dharma-brothers of mine have been posted in an unsuitable place. Go and drive down that cliff and hurl it upon them — but harm no living creature."

The five great yakṣa commanders called Sena obeyed the great king Vaiśravaṇa and manifested: elephants resembling mountain peaks, horses resembling rhinoceroses, chariots resembling boundless palaces, and men resembling ferocious yakṣas. The cliff-dwellers, looking from a great distance, saw them coming, and were seized with terror. They thought:

When both land and life are threatened,
a person must strive above all to preserve life.
Weighing both with reason one finds:
land can be regained, but lives cannot.

With that, they hung their swords around their necks, departed from the cliff, and were captured. Bound with fetters, they were escorted to Śrāvastī and brought before Prasenajit, the king who had arisen in Kośala, and they were told: "Your majesty, here are the cliff-dwellers, and here are their weapons." The king was pleased and said: "Wise men, keep these weapons for yourselves." They thought: "All of our survival and well-being, all of our prosperity and good fortune in full measure, is entirely due to the power of the noble Dharmadatta. Let us go, then, and offer these weapons to the noble Dharmadatta." And so they took the weapons, went to Dharmadatta, and said: "Noble one, whatever survival and well-being we have, whatever prosperity and abundance of good fortune is ours — all of it is solely due to the power of the noble one. These weapons that the king has given us, we beg the noble one to accept them out of compassion."

He replied: "Children, even among the gods there are those who are poor, so make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha — that will bring you long-lasting benefit, welfare, and happiness."

They then invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of hearers for three months, providing all requisites. In the mornings they made offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; in the afternoons they listened to the Dharma.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the thirty-sixth fascicle.

At another time, some other cliff-dwellers came back to Prasenajit, the king who had arisen in Kośala, and the king commanded the market guild of the warrior class: "Today, drive down those cliff-dwellers." They replied: "Your majesty, we are exhausted, while the guild of those who wield the power of swords is well supplied — why then, at this time, give commands to us and send us on yet another mission?" The king then commanded the guild of those who wield the power of swords: "Today, drive down a great number of cliff-dwellers." They replied: "Your majesty, it is our turn in rotation. We will go today, but should not be sent on the next occasion." They thought: "On that previous occasion, it was through the power of the five great yakṣa commanders called Sena that we drove down those cliff-dwellers.

"Now we ourselves will have to die right there in that place. Let us therefore present robes to those noble ones whom we have hosted for three months with all provisions, and then depart." With that thought, they took up the robes, went to the monastery, and said to the monks: "Venerable ones, the king has sent us to a military posting. Should we happen to perish there, we may come to such an end. Please accept these robes." The monks replied: "Good sirs, the Blessed One has established a training rule that monks must not divide the rains-retreat gains within the rains retreat itself, so we will not accept them." The men said: "Venerable ones, please take them, set them aside, and after the invitation ceremony distribute them." With that, they placed the robes in the monks' lodgings and departed.

The noble ones and the householder Anāthapindada (the giver of food to the unprotected) saw them and said: "Good men, where are you going?" "Householder, we are going to a military posting." "Is it your rotation?" "Householder, it is our rotation." "Then why are you going?" "Word came from His Majesty that we should go today, and that we would not be sent on the next occasion." "I will petition His Majesty on your behalf — wait here a moment." He went before the king and said: "Your Majesty, to which guild did you give the command?" "Householder, a large group of cliff-dwellers has come back; go drive them down." "Is it their rotation, Your Majesty?" "Householder, it is their rotation." "Then why have you given the command?" "They were not to be sent on the next occasion." "But does Your Majesty not know that those men, having no bows with bowstrings, no arrows, and carrying only ceremonial swords made of wood, cannot possibly turn back the cliff-dwellers? Furthermore, they are nothing but sons of the Buddha — they would not incur the sin of intentionally taking the life of even a living worm." The king replied: "It is just as it was before — on that previous occasion too it was through the power of the five great yakṣa commanders called Sena that those cliff-dwellers were driven down. Yet if they go there now, some fault may arise, and that too would reflect badly on Your Majesty. So I did not kill them." "Householder, are they truly nothing but sons of the Buddha?" "Your Majesty, that is indeed so — and through reliance on their good spiritual friend, the noble Dharmadattā, every one of them has directly realized the fruit of stream-entry."

The king of Kosala, Prasenajit, then issued orders to his ministers: "Good sirs, from this day forward you are to issue commands to the noble warrior class. You are not to issue commands to the guild of those who wield the power of swords." He then dismissed that guild of sword-wielders and stood them down.

When the monks performed the invitation ceremony, the monks went before those men and said: "Good sirs, we have performed the invitation ceremony — give us the robes." The men replied: "Venerable ones, we have already offered those robes. Please accept them." The monks went and opened the door of the lodging, and found that the robes had been lying there, permeated with the oiliness and sweetness of the air, wrapped up in mold, and crumbled to dust. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, a robe-keeper monk is to be appointed. One lacking the following five qualities is not to be appointed as robe-keeper monk, and one already appointed is to be removed. What are the five? One who proceeds through desire, one who proceeds through aversion, one who proceeds through delusion,

one who proceeds through fear, and one who does not know what robe-gains have been stored and what have not. A monk who is a robe-keeper and who possesses the following five qualities is to be appointed even if not yet appointed, and one already appointed is not to be removed. What are the five? One who does not proceed through desire, one who does not proceed through aversion, one who does not proceed through delusion, one who does not proceed through fear, and one who knows what robes have been stored and what have not.

He is to be appointed in the following manner. First, consent is to be sought: "You, whose name is such-and-such, are you willing to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during the rains retreat?" If he is willing, he should say, "I am willing." After that, a seat is to be arranged, the gong is to be struck, the monks are to be properly informed with the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, one monk is to make the motion and perform the act.

"May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. If the monk named such-and-such is willing to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat, and if it is timely for the Saṅgha and they consent, may the Saṅgha please grant permission. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named such-and-such to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat. The monk named such-and-such will keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat." This is the motion.

The act is to be performed as follows. "May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named such-and-such to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat. If the appointment of the monk named such-and-such to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat is acceptable to the venerable ones, those who consent to the appointment of the monk named such-and-such to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and permitted; the Saṅgha has appointed the monk named such-and-such to keep the robe-gains of the Saṅgha during this rains retreat. So it is held, in that no one spoke."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who aspire to the training, those who are devoted to the training, those who are equipped with the implements of the training, those who are clean, those who possess the virtues of refinement, those who are beautiful, and those who sense warmth, and he declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, what came before was a rule, and this is a permission. My hearers are to recite this as the basis for training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk, before the last ten days of the last month of autumn have been reached, obtains a robe that has arisen from an urgent occasion and desires it, that monk may accept that robe. Having accepted it, he is to keep it until the time for distributing robes. If he keeps it beyond that, it is an offense requiring relinquishment."

Now the explanatory commentary: "A monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. "Before the last ten days of the last month of autumn have been reached" means up until the invitation ceremony arises on the tenth day. "A robe that has arisen from an urgent occasion" means the five robes that arise from urgent occasions: one given to a sick person, one given on account of a sick person, one given to someone at the point of death, one given on account of someone who has died, and one given to someone who is about to depart. "Obtains" means from another person. "Desires" means if one seeks to make use of it. "That monk" means whichever monk it may be. "That robe" means any one of the seven: a woolen robe, a linen robe, a silk robe, a fine cotton robe, a coarse cotton robe, a hemp robe, or a canvas robe.

"Should be taken" means should be made one's own. "Having taken it, should keep it until the time for distributing robes to monks" means should store it away.

What, then, is the time for distributing robes to monks, and what is the non-time? In a place where the spreading out of mats has not been performed, up through the fifteenth day of the last month of autumn is the non-time for distributing robes; the remainder is the time. In a place where the spreading out of mats has been performed, from the fifteenth day of the last month of autumn onward up through the fifteenth day of the middle month of spring is the non-time; the remainder is the time.

"Should one keep it beyond that" means should one keep it in excess of that. "It is an offense requiring forfeiture" means that having forfeited that article, the transgression requiring forfeiture must be confessed; therefore it is called an offense requiring forfeiture.

As to how a transgression arises in that regard: however much a monk makes gains of the rains retreat his own during the rains retreat, or keeps them beyond the time for distributing robes, in every case it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If one makes one's own any of the five robes arising from an urgent occasion, and the donor gives them from his own hand, there is no transgression. If a monk has been appointed to oversee the storing of robes, and a donor comes saying, "Noble ones, please accept these; I am here with these robes and will distribute them from my own hand," there is no transgression. For one who is a beginner, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for one afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

This completes the twenty-sixth forfeiture arising from urgent occasions.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Not far from Śrāvastī there was a cliff-face, and there dwelt a wealthy householder of great possessions and abundant resources. He was a man of faith, of good character, and of virtuous intention, and so he dedicated an assembly hall to the Saṅgha: a lofty building with high doorways, with latticed windows, adorned with balustrades, captivating to heart and eye, fit to serve as a stairway to the higher realms. In that assembly hall sixty monks performed the rains retreat and the invitation ceremony, and when they had departed the householder set guards there, saying, "Let no one steal the chairs and benches."

Now at another time sixty other monks were traveling through the countryside and arrived at that cliff-face, seeking lodging. A man spoke to them, saying, "Noble ones, why do you not stay in the assembly hall? Where is the assembly hall? Noble ones, it is right here in this hermitage." The monks went there, and the guards saw them and welcomed them with words of greeting. They assigned them their quarters, provided chairs, benches, cushions, bedding, and water vessels and the like, then borrowed a broom and said, "Noble ones, please wash first, and in the meantime I will inform the householder." The man went to the householder and said, "Be pleased, householder! Sixty monks have suddenly arrived at your assembly hall." The householder, gathering himself with reverence, spoke to his household members: "Wise ones, let those monks of the Saṅgha who have come to my assembly hall be satisfied with well-prepared drinks, sugar, molasses, treacle, grapes, and pomegranates." The householder prepared those well-mixed drinks and went to the assembly hall. The monks had washed and arranged themselves each according to his own deportment. The householder, seeing those monks from a distance, saw the assembly hall as if it were filled with a lake of lotuses.

Moved by a surge of deep faith, his being transformed, he spoke these verses:

Whether it be a village or a hermitage,
a valley or an open plain,
wherever noble ones take up their abode,
that very ground becomes a place of joy.

He then prepared the well-mixed drinks, and with his own hands satisfied that community of monks. He himself took up a vessel and, together with the community of monks, offered prostrations before the stūpa, then entered the assembly hall and sat to one side among the elders. The elder of the Saṅgha explained the merit of giving, and the householder then prostrated to his feet and said: "Would the noble Saṅgha graciously consent to take the midday meal tomorrow at my home?" The monks accepted, and after prostrating to the householder's feet, departed.

The next day the householder satisfied the monks with alms food, and even outside mealtimes he poured out drinks for them, and the monks in turn taught the Dharma. Later, in the same manner, after the elder of the Saṅgha had explained the merit of giving, the householder sat to one side among the elders and said: "Noble ones, this assembly hall has not been built for my own benefit, nor for the benefit of my relatives; it has been offered precisely for the sake of noble ones such as yourselves. Please accept it and take up the rains retreat here. I shall see to it that noble ones are supplied with all requisites and want for nothing."

The monks replied: "Householder, in Śrāvastī the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dharma, is dwelling in person, and from time to time one hears reports that some great monk has directly realized arhatship, and that another great monk has announced the attainment of the interval before the unlovely state. The king is greatly devoted to the teaching; and the queen Mālyā (Phreng ldan ma), the royal ladies of the Kṣatriya summer assembly, the teacher Bla mkhyen the sage, Byid the elder, the laywoman Sāgā, the mother Mṛgadhāriṇī (Ri dags 'dzin gyi ma), and many other faithful ones are also there — so both material abundance and great Dharmic abundance are to be found there. For these reasons we intend to go there."

The householder replied: "Noble ones, Dharmic abundance depends on noble ones themselves, while material abundance depends on me. Please be of good cheer — not the slightest insufficiency will occur." The elder of the Saṅgha then said: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught that one should foster the faith of the faithful and show compassion toward one's benefactors. Let us therefore remain here." And so they agreed to stay there.

Blo brtan pa then proceeded to examine the assembly hall thoroughly, both inside and outside, and found it to be abundantly endowed with flowers and abundantly endowed with fruits — a most delightful place. The elder of the Saṅgha said: "Friends, since this assembly hall is so abundantly endowed with flowers and fruits and is so very delightful, if we were to accept the early rains retreat here we would not be able to enjoy all its flowers and fruits to the full. We must therefore definitely accept the late rains retreat." And so they agreed to observe the late rains retreat there.

Now, as that householder had only this one assembly hall, everything he intended to give or do as an act of generosity he gave and did in that very assembly hall. In that rocky place too there was no other assembly hall, and so those who dwelt among the crags likewise directed everything they intended to give or do as an act of generosity to that same assembly hall.

Since there was no other assembly hall in the vicinity of those crags, all those who dwelt among the crags likewise directed everything they intended to give or do as an act of generosity to that same assembly hall, and so the monks who had accepted the rains retreat there received abundant gains.

Now the wayward ones whose conduct belonged to the last month of autumn gathered together right after the invitation ceremony and began to deliberate among themselves, saying: "What could we do so that we might enjoy ourselves and live comfortably all year round without needing to exert ourselves?" They thought to themselves: "We should destroy these monks, the sons of the Śākyas." But others said: "Even if they recite a hundred door-panels' worth of begging, it is hard for them to fill their bellies. If they have nothing at all, why should we stay here as long as that?" Then one among them who knew about monks spoke up and said: "What do you know? Those monks have plenty." "How so?" "Well, the householder to whom this assembly hall belongs is a man of faith, a good man with wholesome intentions. And as he has only that one assembly hall, everything he intends to give or do as an act of generosity he gives and does in that very assembly hall. Here among these crags too there is no other assembly hall, and so those who dwell among the crags likewise direct everything they intend to give or do as an act of generosity to that same assembly hall. And in the vicinity of these crags as well there is no other assembly hall, and so those who dwell in the vicinity of the crags likewise direct everything they intend to give or do as an act of generosity to that same assembly hall. Therefore the monks who have accepted the rains retreat here have received abundant gains. If you don't believe me, go and see for yourself — it will become plain to your own eyes." "Very well then, if that is the case, you go ahead and see for yourself directly, and we will come later." He replied: "Good, do it that way. I will go." And with that he adjusted his robes and set out.

Then, singing in verse, he paid homage to the stūpa and entered that assembly hall. As soon as he stepped into the gatehouse, he found an elder sitting there. The wayward one bowed at his feet and began to question him: "Noble one, this assembly hall — so captivating, so delightful — this stairway to the higher realms: to whom does it belong?" "Good-looking one, it belongs to a certain great householder." "Noble one, is this an assembly hall, or is it destitute?" "Good-looking one, what is an assembly hall like, and what is destitution like?" "Noble one, where the requisites are complete and well-furnished — that is an assembly hall. Where the requisites are absent — that is destitution." "Good-looking one, then this is indeed an assembly hall and not destitution, for here the requisites are complete and well-furnished; it is not a place where requisites are absent." "Noble one, those who eat food do not eat any mere dust, and those who wear clothes do not wear any mere tree bark — so do you not have even a little clothing?" The elder, being of a straightforward nature, took the wayward one by the hand, led him into his room, and said: "Good-looking one, look at those stacked piles of cloth lying there." "Noble one, are these yours, or do they belong to the Saṅgha?" "Good-looking one, these belong to me personally." "Noble one, then without any ambiguity you are an elder of the Saṅgha, or a Dharma-preacher." "Good-looking one, I am neither an elder of the Saṅgha nor a Dharma-preacher. The fact is, I am a newly admitted novice of the Saṅgha."

The noble one said: "Good-looking one, is there not even a little Saṅgha lodging here? There are many such things — for now, you may also obtain the seven items among my own personal belongings. And you should come and meet that noble one too, and ask him this: here in this monastery, those to whom no one pays reverence — are they washed in the vessels of a potter, or are they washed in bronze vessels? Good-looking one, have you seen these lodging rooms?" "Noble one, I have." "Good-looking one, these lodging rooms are full and stocked with bronze vessels."

The wayward one thought: "I have been thoroughly tricked — now I shall go." And the wayward one said: "Noble one, the full decline of your virtuous side is the full decline of my own purpose; and so it is for my sake as well that I shall come — yes, now I shall come." "Good-looking one, do as you will then."

The wayward one made obeisance at the feet of that elder who had entered old age, and departed. Then that wayward one went to those thieves and said: "Lotus-eyed ones, a great ship laden with all manner of goods lies grounded on dry land — rob it! Rob it!"

At that, one of them said: "It is well known that the sixty monastics staying there are masters of archery and nothing less — we cannot overpower them in the same way. When they go to hear the Dharma at night, that is when we should strike." Others said: "On what day does their Dharma-hearing take place?" He replied: "It falls on the eighth and the fourteenth — the eighth has already passed, so it will occur on the fourteenth."

They counted the days on their fingers, keeping track one by one, until at last the fourteenth arrived. The Saṅgha's elder recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra (the sūtra of individual liberation), the Saṅgha performed the restoration ceremony, and the Dharma-preacher ascended the lion throne and began to speak these words:

He who steers the chariot of taming the best of men,
the Tathāgata who cuts the bonds of all fettered attachments,
skilled in the stilled and the very stilled, with pacified faculties —
as he entered Śrāvastī he spoke in accord with his word.

Just as he began to speak, those wayward ones beat upon the door. The monks, becoming aware, asked: "Gentlemen, who are you?" "Noble ones, we are sons of good families." The monks thought: "A crowd of people has surely come down from the rocky crags to hear the Dharma — we must not cause them to miss it; let us open the door." So they opened it, and those men entered.

When they were just about to strike, the monks said: "Gentlemen, you announced yourselves as sons of good families — and now you intend to attack us?" Those men replied: "Noble ones, we have two names: outwardly we are called sons of good families, and inwardly we are called thieves. It is a disgrace that you address us by that name." Those wayward ones then beat and drove away those monks.

The beaten monks deliberated together: "The Blessed One has declared that these and all the rest must be beaten as well. For now, this householder has had gifts given to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions — what more is there to do? He has had gifts given to us — what more is there to do? If we were to go to Śrāvastī itself, those there who lead the holy life (brahmacarya) in the same manner as ourselves would provide us with robes and we would not be in want." So they resolved.

How should they travel? "We shall travel covered by night and move in dense concealment by day." And so they departed without even looking back at the householder.

When in the course of time they finally reached Śrāvastī, and the monks who were devoted to practice without sleeping in the first or last watch of the night saw those monks wandering alone at the threshold of the gate, they said:

"You naked, disheveled fellows — what do you want here? This is neither your monastery nor your dwelling place."

They replied: "Venerable ones, we are not naked men." "Then who are you?" "We are monks." "Are such as you monks? What are those who have been stripped by robbers like? What are your names?" "We live by the Buddha. We live by the Dharma. We live by the Saṅgha."

"Welcome, venerable ones, welcome!" the monks said, and opening the gate they let those monks enter. Some gave them outer robes, some gave them lower garments, some gave them sweat-cloths, some gave them alms bowls, some gave them water-strainers, and they shared everything equally according to each one's proper share.

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, a forest-dwelling monk may leave any one of the three robes in another's dwelling." After the Blessed One had declared that a forest-dwelling monk might leave any one of the three robes in another's dwelling, those monks went there and spent the night, and some brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, why do you sleep here? We have left robes here. Noble ones, do you think we would steal your robes? If you have no worry about that, please feel free to go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One may not spend the night there."

They went back, and as dawn was breaking they went out in stages. Some women who were sleeping there alone said: "Noble ones, why have you come here in the middle of the night? We have left robes here. Noble ones, do you think we would steal your robes? If you have no worry about that, please feel free to go."
