At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One may not be there at dawn."

Later they went there and were waiting in the courtyard for dawn to break, and at that point they fell into the power of robbers, tricksters, lions, tigers, and leopards. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One may be there at dawn inside the monastery." When monks needed to go beyond the boundary for the sake of Saṅgha business, stūpa business, or personal affairs and said, "We have left robes in another's dwelling," and then did not go, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A forest-dwelling monk may be separated from that robe beyond the boundary for up to six nights at the most."

When the group of six monks intentionally remained separated beyond the boundary for seven nights, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and so forth as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though fully knowing, act as if they did not know" — and so forth also as before. The awakened Blessed One then questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, I declared that a forest-dwelling monk may be separated from that robe beyond the boundary for up to six nights at the most — is it true that you intentionally remained separated beyond the boundary for seven nights?" "Venerable One, it is true."

The awakened Blessed One then rebuked them, saying that this was unbecoming of a renunciant, discordant, unseemly, and contrary to proper conduct — and that it is not something one who has gone forth should do. Having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

When a number of monks are dwelling in a forest lodging that is known to be dangerous — known as a place of danger from thieves and rogues, known as a place of fearsome creatures where there are various distinct terrors — and when the latter rains retreat has commenced, if a forest-dwelling monk so wishes, he may place any one of the three robes in a household. Should a circumstance arise that requires the forest-dwelling monk to go beyond the boundary, that forest-dwelling monk may remain separated from that robe beyond the boundary for up to six nights at the most. To exceed that and remain separated is an offense entailing relinquishment."

Now, as for the term "monk" — this refers to one who is a member of this Dharma community. "A number" means two or more. "Lodging" refers to a temple or monastic hall. "Forest" is defined as follows: six subtle particles make one subtle particle; six subtle particles make one water particle; six water particles make one iron particle; six iron particles make one rabbit-hair particle; six rabbit-hair particles make one sheep-wool particle; six sheep-wool particles make one ox-hair particle; six ox-hair particles make one dust-mote visible in a sunbeam; six sun-mote particles make one nit's egg; six nit's eggs make one louse; six lice make one barleycorn; six barleycorns make one finger-breadth; twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit; one and a half cubits make one fathom; four cubits make one bow-length; five hundred bow-lengths make one league — and from that distance onward is "forest."

"Known to be dangerous" means known to be a place of danger from thieves and rogues. "Known as a place of fearsome creatures" means known as a place dangerous on account of lions, tigers, and leopards. "Where there are various distinct terrors" means known as a place of various distinct terrors on account of wasps, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and venomous snakes.

"When the latter rains retreat has commenced" means when one has undertaken to remain for the latter portion of the rains retreat. "A forest-dwelling monk" refers to whichever monk it may be. "If he so wishes" means if he desires it for a purpose. "Any one of the three robes" means whichever he wishes from among the lower robe, the upper robe, and the outer robe. "In a household" means in a place where there is a main road, a market street, a crossroads, or a junction. "May place" means may store it there.

"Should a circumstance arise that requires the forest-dwelling monk to go beyond the boundary" means if a circumstance arises that requires him to go beyond the boundary for the sake of the Saṅgha, or of a stūpa, or of an individual. "That forest-dwelling monk" refers to whichever monk it may be. "Up to six nights at the most" means within the limit of six days and nights. "May remain separated from that robe beyond the boundary" refers to the robe that was placed there.

"Should he remain separated beyond that" means if dawn breaks while he is beyond that limit.

"It is a transgression requiring forfeiture" means that after forfeiting that article, the transgression that requires forfeiture must be confessed. That is why it is said to be a transgression requiring forfeiture.

Now, how does the transgression come about? It is as follows: if a forest-dwelling monk remains separated from any one of his three Dharma robes beyond the boundary, in every case it becomes a transgression requiring forfeiture. The eight obstacles in this regard are these: the danger of a king, the danger of thieves, the danger of fire, the danger of water, the danger of a lion, the danger of a tiger, the danger of humans, and the danger of non-humans. If any one of these is present nearby, there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is mentally deranged, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one afflicted by feelings.

This completes the twenty-seventh rule, concerning forfeiture through remaining separated for seven nights.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that monks should store their heavy rains cloth. Thereupon, monks who had accepted the invitation for the earlier rains retreat thought: "Our own time has come," and they would go searching for it, saying: "Why should we not store it?" Monks who had accepted the invitation for the later rains retreat also thought: "Our own time has come," and they would store it, saying: "Why should we not go searching for it?" Because some searched too quickly and others stored for too long, much activity and busyness arose, and they abandoned the recitation of scripture, the chanting of liturgy, the practice of yoga, mental work, and the inner mental calm abiding. The few monks of modest aims said: "The Blessed One has declared that monks should store their heavy rains cloth — so why do they cause so much activity and busyness by searching too quickly and storing for too long, thus abandoning the recitation of scripture, the chanting of liturgy, the practice of yoga, mental work, and the inner mental calm abiding?" They criticized them, spread the matter abroad, and spoke against them. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, with this as the basis and in this context, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. "The blessed buddhas, though knowing, would ask" — and so forth, also as before.

The Blessed One then asked the monks: "Monks, when I declared that monks should store their heavy rains cloth, is it true that you were searching too quickly and storing for too long?" "Lord, it is true."

The Blessed One then rebuked those who are hard to support, hard to satisfy, who have great desires, and who do not know contentment. He then praised the qualities of being easy to support, easy to satisfy, having few desires, knowing contentment, being refined, well-trained, excellent in conduct, and being warmly regarded, and spoke to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before.

"Let my hearers recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: When one month of the hot-season months remains, a monk should seek out his heavy rains cloth. After the rains have ended, he may store it for up to half a month thereafter.

If a monk seeks out his heavy rains cloth before one month of the hot-season months remains, or

or stores it for more than half a month after the rains have ended, that is an offence entailing forfeiture.

"By a monk" means: by one who upholds this Dharma. "When one month of the hot-season months remains" means: when the rains retreat is about to be established within one month. "The heavy rains cloth" means: a garment for when rain has fallen. "Should seek it out" means: from another. "He may store it for up to half a month after the rains have ended" means: for half a month after the invitation ceremony has been performed. "If a monk seeks out his heavy rains cloth before one month of the hot-season months remains" means: prior to that time. "Or stores it for more than half a month after the rains have ended" means: beyond that limit. "That is an offence entailing forfeiture" means: having forfeited the item, the transgression that is an offence entailing forfeiture must be confessed. That is why it is said to be an offence entailing forfeiture.

As to how the transgression is incurred: it applies either to the earlier or the later rains retreat. Those who have committed to observing the earlier rains retreat incur an offence entailing forfeiture if they keep the cloth for too long. Those who have committed to observing the later rains retreat incur an offence entailing forfeiture if they seek it out too soon. Thus, in all cases, a monk who seeks it out too soon or keeps it too long incurs an offence entailing forfeiture. There is no transgression for a first-time offender, for one who is mentally deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feelings.

The section on forfeiture of the rains cloth, the twenty-eighth, is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling among the Śākyas in the Śākya market-town called Sakkara. At that time a householder, out of his own faith, his own initiative, and his own generosity, had a monastery built and offered it to the venerable Śāgata personally. After residing in that monastery for a time, the venerable Śāgata took up his bowl and his Dharma robe and departed to travel through the region. When the householder heard that the noble Śāgata had resided in that monastery for a time, then taken his bowl and Dharma robe and gone traveling through the region, he donated that monastery to the Saṅgha.

Then the venerable Śāgata, having wandered the region as he pleased, set out traveling toward the Śākya market-town of Sakkara. As he journeyed along, gradually making his way, he arrived at Sakkara, and there he heard that the householder had donated the monastery to the Saṅgha. Hearing this, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head to the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Śāgata addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Bhante, here a householder, out of his own faith, his own initiative, and his own generosity, had a monastery built and offered it to me personally. After I had resided in that monastery for a time, I took my bowl and Dharma robe and went traveling through the region. That householder then heard that the noble Śāgata had resided in that monastery for a time, taken his bowl and Dharma robe, and gone traveling, and upon hearing this he donated the monastery to the Saṅgha. Bhante, what am I now to do in this matter?"

"Śāgata, come here. Go to where that householder is, and when you have gone to him, say these words to him: 'Householder, would you do me even a small discourtesy in body or in speech?'"

The venerable Śāgata replied, "As you command, Bhante," received these words from the Blessed One, went to where that householder was, and when he had arrived, spoke these words to the householder: "Householder, would you do me even a small discourtesy in body or in speech?" The householder replied, "Noble Śāgata, I would not show you even the slightest discourtesy in body or in speech."

Thereupon the venerable Śāgata went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Śāgata addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Bhante, I went to where that householder was, and when I had arrived, I said to the householder these words: 'Householder, would you do me even a small discourtesy in body or in speech?' And he replied: 'Noble Śāgata, there is not even the slightest discourtesy on my part toward your body or your speech.'"

Now at that time the venerable Ānanda was seated to one side of the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and assemble all the monks who are lodging nearby with their foxes into the meeting hall."

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Bhante," received these words from the Blessed One, assembled all the monks who were lodging nearby with their foxes into the meeting hall, then went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Bhante, all the monks who were lodging nearby with their foxes have assembled in the meeting hall and are ready. May the Blessed One now know that the time has come."

Then the Blessed One went to where the meeting hall was, and having arrived, sat down on the seat that had been arranged in front of the community of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, when one has made a gift to one person and then makes a gift to another single person, that is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use. Likewise, when one makes a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to two persons and then makes a gift to another single person, that is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use. Likewise, when one makes a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to a great many persons and then makes a gift to another single person, that is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use. Likewise, when one makes a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to the Saṅgha and then makes a gift to another single person, that is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use. Likewise, when one makes a gift to two others, or to a great many others,"

"or to the Saṅgha — that too is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use.

"Monks, when the Saṅgha has split and divided into two factions dwelling on opposite sides, and one makes a gift to one faction and then makes a gift to the second faction — that is not a proper gift, nor a proper reception, nor is it fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to a single person and does not make a gift to another single person — that is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use. Likewise, when one does not make a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to two persons and does not make a gift to another single person — that is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use. Likewise, when one does not make a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to a great many persons and does not make a gift to another single person — that is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use. Likewise, when one does not make a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use.

"Monks, when one has made a gift to the Saṅgha and does not make a gift to another single person — that is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use. Likewise, when one does not make a gift to two others, or to a great many others, or to the Saṅgha — that too is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use.

"Monks, when the Saṅgha has split and divided into two factions dwelling on opposite sides, and one has made a gift to one faction and does not make a gift to the second faction — that is a proper gift, a proper reception, and it is fit for use.

"Monks, therefore: the former gift is a gift, and the latter is not. A king has authority over the land; an owner has authority over lodgings; a monk has authority over his bowl and robes. A donor and a patron may make offerings intended as their own acts of giving, but they may not give away on their own what belongs to another.

"Monks, let the monastery be returned to the monk named Grācin. Those monks then returned the monastery to the venerable Grācin. This matter had arisen, but the Blessed One had not yet established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

"The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A mendicant had established a certain householder in the refuges and set him in the training precepts, and on a later occasion that mendicant praised to the householder the seven bases of meritorious action that arise from material things. The householder said: 'Noble one, I too shall do a little merit through bases of meritorious action arising from material things. Please let it be so.'"

"What should be done?" The mendicant said, "Offer a feast of offerings to the Saṅgha of monks, with the Buddha at their head." "So it shall be. But do you have some spare cloth?" "Noble one, my means are slender, yet I will offer a single pair of cloth." "Noble one, please invite in my name, for tomorrow at midday, the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head."

At the time of assembly, that mendicant invited, in that householder's name, the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head, to another house at midday. The monks then said: "Mendicant, you have made the household into a devotee. But tell us — has the householder offered a feast with a gift-offering, or a feast without a gift-offering?" "Venerables, it is with a gift-offering. However, since that householder's means are slender, he is offering a single pair of cloth."

Ānanda heard this and thought: "Whoever offers a single pair of cloth to the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head — from that, something great is surely bound to arise. If I do not take that pair of cloth, I will no longer be known by the name Ānanda." Having thought this, the next morning Ānanda put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and went to that householder's house. When he arrived, he saw that the householder was making preparations for the feast. He asked the householder: "Householder, what are you doing?" "Noble one, I am preparing a feast." "Householder, the Blessed One has declared — and this was well spoken — that for those sentient beings who during the period of morning conduct themselves well in body, speech, and mind, a good morning will be close at hand for them at that time; and for those sentient beings who during the period of midnight and the period of dawn conduct themselves well in body, speech, and mind, a good midnight and a good dawn will be close at hand for them at those times. Householder, do you have a little cloth to give?" "Noble one, my means are slender, yet I will offer a single pair of cloth." "Householder, let me see what that pair of cloth is like."

The householder showed it, and seeing how fine it was, Ānanda said: "Householder, for you there is merit arising from having given it away completely, but there is not even a fraction of merit arising from having fully enjoyed it yourself. The Blessed One's retinue numbers twelve hundred and fifty, and it takes twelve hundred and fifty pairs of cloth to satisfy them. With this single pair, only one collar of a robe can be completed at most. The Blessed One has moreover taught that when food is obtained it should be shared even down to the last grain on a lotus leaf, and when cloth is obtained it should be shared even down to what would suffice for the wick of a lamp. So if you do not share it, you will derive no enjoyment from this either."

The householder then said: "Noble one, what means is there by which I may have merit arising from having given it away completely and also merit arising from having fully enjoyed it myself?" Ānanda replied: "Householder, if you were to make an offering of this pair of cloth to one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation — then you would have both the merit arising from having given it away completely and the merit arising from having fully enjoyed it yourself." The householder said: "Noble one, one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan —

who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation — who is there?" Ānanda replied: "Householder, I myself have gone forth from the Śākya clan, I possess the Three Baskets, I proclaim the Dharma, and I have the confidence of reasoning and liberation." At this, the householder began to offer the pair of cloth to Ānanda, saying: "Noble one, please accept this pair of cloth." But Ānanda said: "Householder, do you not know how to give a gift? Whenever a feast is held in offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, let there be someone at the elder's side rejoicing in it, and then give it to me." The noble one replied: "Very well," and having listened to him, the householder thereafter held a feast in offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and then said: "Please rejoice in this pair of cloth at the elder's side. Please do rejoice." Having caused him to rejoice, he gave it to Ānanda. The monks then said to the monastery's attendant: "Receive that pair of cloth from Ānanda." The attendant said to Ānanda: "Hand over that pair of cloth. Is it to be carried to the assembly hall and given there?" The attendant replied: "No — this has been offered to the Saṅgha." Ānanda said: "Why do you not offer your own bowl and robe to the Saṅgha? This was given to me." Then the Blessed One, having spoken words of appreciation, rose from his seat and departed, and the almsman, startled, remained right there. That almsman, having realized that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha had not gone far after departing, said this to the householder: "Householder, the thunder has sounded in one place while the rain has fallen in another." The householder asked: "Noble one, what should I do?" He replied: "Venerable Ānanda has said to me that for you, householder, there exists merit arising from having given it away completely, whereas merit arising from having fully enjoyed it yourself does not exist even once — for the Blessed One's retinue numbers twelve hundred and fifty, and to fulfill their needs would require twelve hundred and fifty pairs of cloth, so for now this will have to be exhausted on the mere borders of the robes. Moreover, the Blessed One himself has declared that if a gain of food arises, it should be shared even with those as small as flies on a lotus leaf; and if a gain of cloth arises, it should be shared even with those fit only to be wicks for oil lamps. If it is not divided, then this too will not become something you have fully enjoyed." I then said to him: "Noble one, what means is there by which I may have both the merit arising from having given it away completely and the merit arising from having fully enjoyed it myself?" And venerable Ānanda said to me: "Householder, if you were to make an offering of this pair of cloth to one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation — then you would have both the merit arising from having given it away completely and the merit arising from having fully enjoyed it yourself." I then said to him: "Noble one, who is there who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation?" Venerable Ānanda said to me: "Householder, I myself have gone forth from the Śākya clan, I possess the Three Baskets, I proclaim the Dharma, and I have the confidence of reasoning and liberation." And so I began to offer the pair of cloth to venerable Ānanda, saying: "Noble one, please accept this pair of cloth." But venerable Ānanda said: "Householder, do you not know how to give a gift?

"When the feast for the monastic Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is being offered, let those at the far edge among the elders express their rejoicing, and then give it to me." Since I did exactly as he said, what fault have I committed in this matter?" The almsman went to the monastery, and the monks said to him: "Whatever is in conformity with almsmanship — if a householder generates faith and makes an offering, the thunder rolls in one place and the rain falls in another." He said: "What fault is there in that? It was like this: one person went there and said these words: 'Householder, if there is merit arising from your full gift, then there is not even a trace of merit arising from full use. The Blessed One's retinue of twelve hundred and fifty receives twelve hundred and fifty pairs of cloth, so this need only be entirely used up for the purpose of robes. And the Blessed One has said that if food is received it should be divided even to the size of a pula leaf, and if cloth is received it should be divided even to what is fit for a lampwick — and if you do not divide it, then this too will not come to be used by you.'" Saying this, he spoke thus: "Noble one, what means is there by which merit arising from my full gift to you may come to be, and merit arising from your full use of it may also come to be?" Then he said: "If you were to offer this pair of cloth to someone who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation, then in that case it would become for you both merit arising from full giving and merit arising from full use." He then asked: "Who is there who has gone forth from the Śākya clan, who possesses the Three Baskets, who proclaims the Dharma, and who has the confidence of reasoning and liberation?" To this he replied: "I myself have gone forth from the Śākya clan, I possess the Three Baskets, I proclaim the Dharma, and I have the confidence of reasoning and liberation." And so he began to offer that pair of cloth to him. At that point the other said: "Householder, do you not know how to give a gift? When the feast for the monastic Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is being offered, let those at the far edge among the elders express their rejoicing, and then give it to me." Since he did exactly as he was told, what fault does he have? Why do certain monks of little sense, knowing full well that a gain has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, yet direct it to be dedicated to themselves personally, and then berate, slander, and speak ill of the matter?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in connection with this ground case, and in these circumstances, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and so on as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, act as though they do not know — and so on as before.

The Blessed One then addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that, knowing full well that a gain has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, you directed it to be dedicated to yourself personally?" "Venerable sir, it is not so." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying: "That which is unworthy of an ascetic, not befitting, not allowable, and not in accord with proper conduct — such is not to be done by one who has gone forth." Having rebuked him in this way, the Blessed One then addressed the monks in many ways:

"Monks, seeing clearly these ten benefits — and so on as before — a rule of training for hearers in the Vinaya is to be established." The rule of training is to be recited by my hearers in the Vinaya in this way: "Furthermore, whatever monk, knowing that a gain has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, directs it to be dedicated to himself personally — that is an offense entailing forfeiture."

The phrase "whatever monk" refers to Ānanda, son of the Śākyas, or any other who is of that kind. "To the Saṅgha" means to the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. "Dedicated" means that it has been set apart and assigned. "A gain" — there are two kinds of gain: gain in robes and gain in food; in this context, gain in robes is understood to be intended. "Knowing" means either that one has come to know it oneself, or that others have told one of it. "Directs it to be dedicated to himself personally" means that one causes it to be offered to oneself. "An offense entailing forfeiture" means that after forfeiting that article, the offense of transgression is to be confessed — therefore it is said to be "an offense entailing forfeiture."

Vinaya Analysis, the thirty-seventh fascicle.

Now, how does the transgression come about?

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one person to be dedicated to himself personally, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to two persons to be dedicated to himself personally, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to many persons to be dedicated to himself personally, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the Saṅgha to be dedicated to himself personally, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one person to be dedicated to one other person, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one person to be dedicated to two other persons, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one person to be dedicated to many other persons, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one person to be dedicated to the Saṅgha, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to two persons to be dedicated to one other person, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to two persons to be dedicated to two other persons, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to two persons to be dedicated to many other persons, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to two persons to be dedicated to the Saṅgha, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to a gatehouse to be dedicated to a staircase platform, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to a staircase platform to be dedicated to a gatehouse, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one particular buddha image to be dedicated to a second buddha image, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one particular stūpa to be dedicated to another stūpa, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the first step of a stūpa's stairway to be dedicated to the second step of the stairway, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression. The same applies likewise to the second step, the third step, the fourth step, and on up to the topmost of all the steps.

In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression. The same applies likewise to the second, third, and fourth harmikās.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the vase of the stūpa to be dedicated to the finial shaft, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the finial shaft to be dedicated to the lowest umbrella disc, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, there is no transgression. The same applies likewise to the second, third, and fourth umbrella discs, and on up to the topmost of all.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the topmost of all the umbrella discs to be dedicated to the rain cover, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, however, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the rain cover to be dedicated to the topmost of all the umbrella discs, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the reliquary vase of the stupa to be dedicated to the harmikā, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to the harmikā to be dedicated to the flower chamber, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. In the case of a loan given as a Dharma gift, there is no transgression.

If a monk directs a gain dedicated to one portico to be dedicated to another portico, the act of directing it constitutes a wrong act, and upon receiving it, it likewise remains a wrong act only. If one has searched and it cannot be found, there is no transgression.
