If one has searched and it cannot be found, there is no transgression.

There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is mentally disturbed, whose mind is agitated, or who is afflicted by painful feelings.

This completes the twenty-ninth section: the abandonment of redirecting what has been dedicated.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. At that time the venerable Pilindavatsa was residing there together with his attendant monks. Certain medicines that had been taken into storage, received from others, mixed with powdered food, blended together, and absorbed into the body such that no distinction was apparent — these they ate at the proper time and also at improper times, and no distinction in their manner of eating was apparent. A few monks of little concern said: "Why do monks eat medicines that have been taken into storage, received from others, mixed with powdered food, blended together, and absorbed into the body such that no distinction is apparent, both at the proper time and at improper times, with no apparent distinction in the manner of eating them?" They criticized them, threw it in their faces, and spoke disparagingly.

Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in light of this founding incident and on this occasion, assembled the community of monks — and so forth as before. And the passage beginning "The Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, though knowing, feign not to know" — and so forth as before.

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Pilindavatsa and his attendant monks: "Monks, concerning medicines that have been taken into storage, received from others, mixed with powdered food, blended together, and

consumed through one's own bloodstream — those that cannot be distinguished even when separated — may one eat them both in season and out of season, and is it true that no distinction in eating them is apparent?" "Venerable sir, it is so."

The Blessed One, the buddha, then censured those who are difficult to heal, difficult to satisfy, who have great desires, and who know no contentment. Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who are easy to heal, easy to satisfy, of few desires, of contented nature, of cultivated virtue, of gracious conduct, and who are discerning in what is fitting. He then addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing these ten benefits, a training rule is to be established for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to take up this training rule in the Vinaya in the following manner: The Blessed One has permitted medicines for use as individual remedies for sick monks, namely: clarified butter, grain oil, honey, and molasses. If a sick monk so desires, he may himself consecrate these for seven days and use them while keeping them in storage. If he uses them beyond that, it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

The phrase "the Blessed One" refers to the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha. The phrase "monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. "For the sick" means for those who are ill. "Beneficial" means agreeable or suitable. "For individual use as remedies" means fitting and appropriate. "Medicines that have been permitted" means those that have been explicitly taught. "Clarified butter" means butter that has been melted and clarified. "Grain oil" means oil derived from grain. "Honey" means the honey of bees. "Molasses" — the expression "the head of molasses" — means molasses itself. "A monk" refers to whichever monk it may be. "A sick person" means one who is ill. "If he so desires" means if he seeks it for that purpose. "Himself" means by his own hand. "Consecrated for seven days" means within seven days and nights. "He may use them while keeping them in storage" means he may take and consume them himself. "If he uses them beyond that" means beyond seven days. "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment" means that the article is to be relinquished and the transgression — the falling — is to be confessed; hence it is said to be a transgression entailing relinquishment.

Now, how does this transgression arise? If on the first day of the lunar fortnight a monk obtains a medicinal remedy for the sick, that monk should consume it, give it away, or bestow it upon another within those very seven days. If he neither consumes it, nor gives it away, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Even if he does not obtain it on the first day, but obtains it on the second, the third, or up through the seventh day, that monk should likewise consume it, give it away, or bestow it upon another within those seven days. If he neither consumes it, nor gives it away, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk obtains a medicinal remedy on the first day and then obtains another medicine on the second day, that monk should consume the earlier one within those seven days and give away or bestow upon another the later one; or alternatively, he may consume the later one and give away or bestow upon another

the earlier one. If he neither consumes it, nor gives it away, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

Just as described for the first and second days, the same applies through the sixth day: if a monk obtains a medicinal remedy on any day up to and including the sixth, and then obtains yet another on any day up to and including the seventh, that monk should consume the earlier one within those seven days and give away or bestow upon another the later one; or alternatively, he may consume the later one and give away or bestow upon another the earlier one. If he neither consumes it, nor gives it away, nor bestows it upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk obtains two medicinal remedies on the first day, that monk should consume both of those medicines within those seven days, or give them away, or bestow them upon another. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Even if he does not obtain them on the first day, should he obtain two medicinal remedies on the second day, or the third day, or on any day up to and including the seventh, that monk should consume both of those medicines within those seven days, or give them away, or bestow them upon another. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk obtains two medicinal remedies on the first day and then obtains two more on the second day, that monk should consume the first two within those seven days and give away or bestow upon another the latter two; or alternatively, he may consume the latter two and give away or bestow upon another the first two. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Just as described for the first and second days, the same applies through the sixth day: if a monk obtains two medicinal remedies on any day up to and including the sixth, and then obtains two more on any day up to and including the seventh, that monk should consume the first two within those seven days and give away or bestow upon another the latter two; or alternatively, he may consume the latter two and give away or bestow upon another the first two. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk obtains a great many medicinal remedies on the first day, that monk should consume all of those medicines within those seven days, or give them away, or bestow them upon another. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Even if he does not obtain them on the first day, should he obtain a great many medicinal remedies on the second day, or the third day, or on any day up to and including the seventh, that monk should consume all of those medicines within those seven days, or give them away, or bestow them upon another. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

If a monk obtains a great many medicinal remedies on the first day of illness, and then on the second day obtains yet another great many, that monk should, within those same seven days, either consume all the earlier medicines and give away or bestow upon another the later ones, or else consume all the later medicines and give away or bestow upon another the earlier ones. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Just as it is with the first and second days, so too if he obtains a great many medicinal remedies on any day up to and including the sixth, and then on any day up to and including the seventh obtains yet another great many, that monk should, within those same seven days, either consume all the earlier medicines and give away or bestow upon another the later ones, or else consume all the later medicines and give away or bestow upon another the earlier ones. If he neither consumes them, nor gives them away, nor bestows them upon another, then at the dawn of the eighth day it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment.

Now, as for any medicines that have been taken into personal keeping from that stock, or received as gifts from it, or mixed with powdered food, or mixed together with one another, or absorbed into one's own body-stream, such that they can no longer be distinguished as separate — these should be relinquished to the residents of the monastery or to the novices.

As for any medicines that have not been taken into personal keeping from that stock, have not been received as gifts from it, have not been mixed with powdered food, have not been mixed together with one another, and have not been absorbed into one's own body-stream, such that they still cannot be distinguished as separate — these the monk may consecrate for seven days by his own act of dedication and then make use of them as stored provisions. The consecration is to be performed as follows. Having washed his hands, taking the medicines into his hands, and sitting in the presence of a fellow practitioner of the celibate life, he should recite these words:

Venerable one, please give heed. I, the monk known as such-and-such, hereby consecrate these suitable medicines for seven days, for the sake of myself and my fellow practitioners of the celibate life.

He should repeat this a second time and a third time. As much as he consumes he should also report to his fellow practitioner of the celibate life, saying: Today I have consumed one day's portion; I will continue to consume the remainder. He should continue to make this report in the same way up to and including the seventh day. If anything remains after that, all of it should be relinquished to the residents of the monastery or to the novices.

If a monk's medicinal remedies have become subject to relinquishment, and he has neither relinquished them, nor separated himself from them, nor confessed the transgression, and then obtains further medicines, those too become subject to relinquishment through the continuity of the earlier one. If a monk's medicinal remedies have become subject to relinquishment, and he has relinquished them but has not separated himself from them, and has not confessed the transgression, and then obtains further medicines, those too become subject to relinquishment through the continuity of the earlier one. If a monk's medicinal remedies have become subject to relinquishment, and he has relinquished them and has separated himself from them, but has not confessed the transgression, and then obtains further medicines, those too become subject to relinquishment through the continuity of the earlier one. If a monk's medicinal remedies have become subject to relinquishment, and he has relinquished them, separated himself from them, and confessed the transgression, and then obtains further medicines, there is no transgression with regard to those.

Likewise, to whatever extent a monk's medicinal remedies have become subject to relinquishment, and he has neither relinquished them nor individually relinquished them, and has neither confessed nor individually confessed the transgression, if he then obtains an alms-bowl, or a monastic robe, or a net, or a bowl, or a belt, or

or any other requisite for a renunciant's livelihood, these too shall be subject to relinquishment by continuity with the earlier one. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations. This completes the thirtieth rule on relinquishment through hoarding. The rules entailing relinquishment are complete.

Summary verse:

Knowingly, and with seeds,
without appointment, and repeatedly,
water, a house, and deliberately,
many guests, a thief, a feast.

Summary verse:

False accusation of a monk, slander,
causing regret, and teaching,
recitation, accepting bad lodging, and Dharma
for the sake of a friend's face, and disparagement.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. At that time the venerable Śāriputra was staying at Rājagṛha in the Hot Springs pleasure grove. Brahmins and householders of faithful disposition went to where the venerable Śāriputra was, and having approached him, asked: "Venerable Śāriputra, where is the Blessed One dwelling?" If the Blessed One was in the Bamboo Forest, Śāriputra would say: "He is dwelling on Vulture Peak." If the Blessed One was on Vulture Peak, Śāriputra would say: "He is dwelling in the Bamboo Forest." If the Blessed One was in the cave of Pippala, Śāriputra would say: "He is dwelling in the cave of Mṛgāra's Mother." If the Blessed One was in the cave of Mṛgāra's Mother, he would say: "He is dwelling in the cave of Pippala." When they then sought the Blessed One and did not find him, they returned, wearied and exhausted and worn in body, to where the venerable Śāriputra was. Śāriputra asked them: "Friends, did you see the Blessed One?" "Venerable Śāriputra, we did not see him." Thereupon he laughed, and they said to him: "Venerable Śāriputra, do you not deliberately mislead us? That is indeed what you are doing." They reproved him, they raised their hands against him, they spoke harsh words to him. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, in the morning, put on his lower robe, took his bowl and monastic robe, and went to Rājagṛha for alms. Having gone on alms round in Rājagṛha and completed the meal, on returning from the after-meal alms round he went to the Hot Springs pleasure grove, to the dwelling of the venerable Śāriputra. The venerable Śāriputra saw the Blessed One from a great distance. Seeing him, he prepared a seat for the Blessed One, set out water for washing the feet together with a footstool, went to receive him, and took the monastic robe, saying: "Welcome, Blessed One. It is good that the Blessed One has come. Let the Blessed One be seated on the prepared seat." And so he said it. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Then the Blessed One himself washed his two feet, left a small remainder of water in the water vessel, and said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you see that I have left a small remainder of water in the water vessel?" "Venerable one, I see it." "Śāriputra, in just that way, whoever among those who are not utterly deluded speaks deliberate falsehood, without shame, without modesty, without remorse — I say that their conduct as a renunciant is of little worth." Then the Blessed One poured out that small remainder of water on the ground and said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you see that I have poured out that small remainder of water on the ground?" "Venerable one, I see it." "Śāriputra, in just that way, whoever among those who are not utterly deluded speaks deliberate falsehood, without shame, without modesty,

without remorse — I say that their conduct as a monk is overturned." Then the Blessed One tilted that water vessel on the ground and said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you see that I have tilted the water vessel on the ground?" "Venerable one, I see it." "Śāriputra, in just that way, whoever among those who are not utterly deluded speaks deliberate falsehood, without shame, without modesty, without remorse — I say that their conduct as a renunciant is tilted." Then the Blessed One turned that water vessel upside down on the ground and said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you see that I have turned the water vessel upside down on the ground?" "Venerable one, I see it." "Śāriputra, in just that way, whoever among those who are not utterly deluded speaks deliberate falsehood, without shame, without modesty, without remorse — I say that their conduct as a renunciant is turned upside down."

"Śāriputra, consider this example. Take a royal elephant — one born from the finest stock, in the prime of youth, sixty years old, with tusks as long as chariot-shafts, with a broad chest, trained for battle, having entered the field of combat — who does his work with his two forefeet, his two hindfeet, his two knees, his haunches, his tail, his two flanks, his back, his two sides, his neck, his two ears, and his two tusks, and does his work, routing the enemy's forces and the enemy's army; yet who guards his trunk. The elephant-rider thinks to himself: 'This royal elephant — born from the finest stock, in his prime, sixty years old, with tusks as long as chariot-shafts, with a broad chest, trained for battle, having entered the field of combat — does his work with his two forefeet, his two hindfeet, his two knees, his haunches, his tail, his two flanks, his back, his two sides, his neck, his two ears, and his two tusks, routing the enemy's forces and the enemy's army; yet he guards his trunk. The royal elephant has not yet given his life utterly.'

"Śāriputra, when a royal elephant — born from the finest stock, in the prime of youth, sixty years old, with tusks as long as chariot-shafts, with a broad chest, trained for battle, having entered the field of combat — does his work with his two forefeet, his two hindfeet, his two knees, his haunches, his tail, his two flanks, his back, his two sides, his neck, his two ears, and his two tusks, and with his trunk as well, routing the enemy's forces and the enemy's army, the elephant-rider thinks to himself: 'This royal elephant — born from the finest stock, in his prime, sixty years old, with tusks as long as chariot-shafts, with a broad chest, trained for battle, having entered the field of combat — does his work with his two forefeet, his two hindfeet, his two knees, his haunches, his tail, his two flanks, his back, his two sides, his neck, his two ears, his two tusks, and with his trunk as well, routing the enemy's forces and the enemy's army; and he does not guard his trunk. The royal elephant has given his life utterly.' Śāriputra, I say that there is nothing whatsoever that such a royal elephant will not do.

"Śāriputra, in just that way, when one who is not utterly deluded speaks deliberate falsehood, without shame, without modesty, without remorse — I say there is not even the slightest evil deed that such a person will not commit."

Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these two verses:

One who, embodied, speaks falsehood
has transgressed the one Dharma,
and being without any regard for the world beyond,
there is no evil such a person will not do.

Better to swallow iron balls
blazing like tongues of flame,
than for one who is without discipline, who holds no genuine restraint,
to eat the alms food of a realm.

"Rāhula, why do you think people hold up a mirror? It is for this reason, venerable one: to examine one's own reflection, feature by feature. In just the same way, Rāhula, you too should examine again and again every bodily action you intend to perform: 'Is this bodily action that I intend to perform one that would harm myself or others — non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering? Or is this bodily action one that would benefit myself and others — virtuous, productive of happiness, ripening in happiness?' Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the bodily action you intend to perform is one that would harm yourself or others — non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering — then, Rāhula, you must abandon that bodily action. But, Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the bodily action you intend to perform is one that would benefit yourself and others — virtuous, productive of happiness, ripening in happiness — then, Rāhula, you should go ahead and carry out that bodily action.

"Rāhula, while you are actually performing a bodily action, you should examine it again and again: 'Is this bodily action that I am performing one that would harm myself or others — non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering? Or is this bodily action one that would benefit myself and others — virtuous, productive of happiness, ripening in happiness?' Rāhula, if, while examining it in this way, you understand that the bodily action you are performing is one that would harm yourself or others — non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering — then, Rāhula, you must stop that bodily action. But, Rāhula, if you understand that the bodily action you are performing is one that would benefit yourself and others — virtuous, productive of happiness, ripening in happiness — then, Rāhula, you should continue and complete that bodily action.

"Rāhula, having performed a bodily action — one that is past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed — you should examine it again and again: 'Was this bodily action that I performed one that harmed myself or others — non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering? Or was it one that benefited myself and others — virtuous, productive of happiness, ripening in happiness?' Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the bodily action you performed — now past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed — was one that harmed yourself or others, was non-virtuous, productive of suffering, ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should disclose and confess that bodily action openly before the Teacher, before those who practice the holy life, and before the wise, and from that point forward you should strive to restrain yourself. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that —"

If you understand that the bodily action you performed — now past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed — was one that benefits yourself and others, is virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, with that very joy and delight you should train day and night, continuing to abide abundantly in mindfulness and vigilance.

Rāhula, as for whatever verbal action you are intending to perform, you should again and again examine it carefully: "Is this verbal action I intend to perform one that will harm myself or others, being non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering? Or is this verbal action one that will benefit myself and others, being virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness?" Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the verbal action you intend to perform will harm yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should abandon that verbal action. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the verbal action you intend to perform will benefit yourself and others, is virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, you should carry out that verbal action.

Rāhula, as for whatever verbal action you are in the midst of performing, you should again and again examine it carefully: "Is this verbal action I am performing one that will harm myself or others, being non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering? Or is this verbal action one that will benefit myself and others, being virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness?" Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the verbal action you are performing will harm yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should abandon that verbal action. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that this verbal action will benefit yourself and others, is virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, you should continue to carry out that verbal action.

Rāhula, as for whatever verbal action you have already performed, you should again and again examine it carefully: "Is this verbal action I performed — now past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed — one that harmed myself or others, being non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering? Or is this verbal action one that benefited myself and others, being virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness?" Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the verbal action you performed — now past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed — was one that harmed yourself or others, was non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should disclose and confess that verbal action openly before the Teacher, before those who practice the holy life, and before the wise, and from that point forward you should strive to restrain yourself. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the verbal action you performed — now past, exhausted, ceased, dissolved, and transformed —

was beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, with that very joy and delight you should train in it day and night, and you should dwell at length in mindfulness and vigilance.

Rāhula, since the mind arises in dependence on past formations, what of that mental action? Examine again and again whether the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on past formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, or whether that mental action is beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness.

Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on past formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should abandon that mental action. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on past formations is beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, you should pursue that mental action.

Rāhula, since the mind arises in dependence on future formations, what of that mental action? Examine again and again whether the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on future formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, or whether that mental action is beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness.

Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on future formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should abandon that mental action. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on future formations is beneficial to yourself and others, and ripening in happiness, then, Rāhula, you should pursue that mental action.

Rāhula, since the mind arises in dependence on present formations, what of that mental action? Examine again and again whether the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on present formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, or whether that mental action is beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness.

Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on present formations is one that harms yourself or others, is non-virtuous, productive of suffering, and ripening in suffering, then, Rāhula, you should abandon that mental action. Rāhula, when you examine it in this way, if you understand that the mental action that has arisen from your mind in dependence on present formations is beneficial to yourself and others, virtuous, productive of happiness, and ripening in happiness,

then, Rāhula, you should carry out that mental action.

Rāhula, all the ascetics and brahmins (śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas) who at the present time examine and thoroughly purify their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions, and who dwell much in that purification — they all examine and thoroughly purify their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions in just this way, and dwell much in that purification. All the ascetics and brahmins who in the past examined and thoroughly purified their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions, and dwelt much in that purification — they all examined and thoroughly purified their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions in just this way, and dwelt much in that purification. All the ascetics and brahmins who in the future will examine and thoroughly purify their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions, and will dwell much in that purification — they all will examine and thoroughly purify their bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions in just this way, and will dwell much in that purification.

Therefore, Rāhula, you should train in this way: examine and thoroughly purify your bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions, and dwell much in that purification. Rāhula, you should train in just this way.

The Blessed One thus declared these words, and having so spoken, the Sugata, the Teacher, spoke yet further:

If one holds in mind the Buddha's teaching,
Then in bodily action, verbal action,
And mental action, examine them thoroughly,
And dwell therein at length, O Rāhula.
This is the work of the ascetic's life;
Train yourself in this, O Rāhula.
If you train yourself accordingly in this,
You will become virtuous and free of wrong.

Then the Blessed One, having duly instructed the venerable Rāhula with words full of Dharma, having caused him to retain them, having duly praised him, and having caused him to rejoice fully, rose from his seat and departed.

This, for now, is what occurred. As yet the Blessed One, the Buddha, was not establishing rules of training for his śrāvaka disciples in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in Śrāvastī there was a certain Śākyan monk named Laghuvaggiya, who was most fond of talk and was devoted to following after the speech of others. At that time a young brahmin student who desired secret formulas and was seeking a teacher of them traveled southward from the middle country. There was a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their ancillary sciences and who served as a teacher to brahmin communities dwelling in various regions. The young student went to that brahmin, and upon arriving, bowed his head to the ground with a calm and gentle bearing, and sat to one side. The brahmin then addressed the student with the customary words of welcome, saying: "Young man, from where have you come? And what do you wish?" The student replied: "I have come from the middle country and wish to sit at the feet of the learned master. For what purpose? In order to recite the Vedas." The brahmin said: "Well then, young man, so be it. You are a brahmin." And so the student began to study the Vedas in the presence of that brahmin.

Now this was the general conduct of the students: whenever they were not reciting, some would go down to the riverbank to bathe, some would go to look about the town, and some would go to gather firewood for the sacred fire. One day it happened that, while they were not reciting and had gone to gather firewood for the sacred fire, along the road they fell into casual conversation of this kind. "Ho, you of the Kautsas! You of the Vātsas! You of the Śāṇḍilyas! You of the Bharadvājas! You of the Pañcas! You of the Upapañcas! Let each of you be asked from which region you have come." Then one student said: "I have come from the east." Others said: "We have come from the southern road." Yet another said: "I have come from the west." And another said: "I have come from the northern road." Then that one student said: "I have come from the middle country." The others replied: "Good sirs, though we have seen and heard of all regions, we have neither seen nor heard of the middle country." And they spoke this verse:

In the east dwell the clear-minded,
on the southern road the crooked,
in the western lands the deceitful,
on the northern road the harsh of tongue.

Then they asked: "Young man, what is the middle country like?" "Good sirs, the middle country is the finest of all regions. It is endowed abundantly with rice, garlands of sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo; pervaded by hundreds of wandering mendicants; filled with the people of the centre; shunned by the people of the borderlands; frequented by the wise. There flows a river named the Gaṅgā, famed as a place of good fortune, merit, auspiciousness, purity, and the very essence of cleanliness, with cool moisture rising from both its banks, renowned as the abode of the sages, into which flow nine hundred and eight streams. There, when the sages perform austerities, they ascend by means of their own bodies to the higher realms. Ho, young man, ask him about this another time. Are there those counted as learned in the middle country?" "Good sirs, did I not say at the very outset that the middle country is filled with the people of the centre, shunned by the people of the borderlands, and frequented by the wise?" "Young man, you did say that." "In the middle country there are those like this: for example, are there the finest of speakers, comparable to our own teacher?" "Good sirs, in the middle country there are finest-of-speakers who speak eloquently, such that even our teacher would be unable to look them in the face." When that student had thus praised the middle country to them in this way, all of them came to wish to go there. Then those students gathered firewood for the sacred fire, and taking up loads of firewood, went to where the brahmin's house was. Having arrived, they set down the loads of firewood to one side, went to where the brahmin was, and addressed him thus: "Honoured teacher, please know that this student has so praised the middle country that all of us have come to wish to go there." The brahmin said: "Children, is everything one hears to be journeyed to? Regions are pleasing to hear about, so one should listen, but one need not go." "Teacher, from what this student has said, there are in the middle country the finest of speakers who speak so eloquently that even our teacher would be unable to look them in the face." "Children, do I claim that I alone upon this earth am a speaker and that there is no other? The earth holds many precious things, and so the ground is filled with magnificent beings."

"Master, I too shall one day see that region, draw near to its shores, pay reverence to those foremost speakers, silence my opponents, proclaim my own renown, and secure my gains. Let us go to the middle country." The brahmin, feeling affection for his students and having but a small retinue, said to those young men: "Children, if that is your wish, then gather your carrying straps, bark strips, staffs, ladles, cups for pouring, and balls of provisions, and set out for the middle country." They gathered those things, and together with that brahmin they set out nobly for the middle country. As they traveled, he silenced some opponents and yoked them to his own debating chariot; some he struck on the head with clay pots filled with ash; some he abandoned from a great distance, like a crow driven from a burial ground; some he received with parasols, victory banners, and flags; and some he accepted as students outright. In this way, gradually traveling through villages and market towns, through hamlets and trading posts, silencing opponents as he went, he arrived at Śrāvastī.

The Vinaya-vibhaṅga, the thirty-eighth fascicle.

At Śrāvastī, a brahmin with a very large retinue heard the news: "A brahmin debater has come from the southern road." On hearing this, he said to his own followers: "Learned ones, take note. I have heard that a brahmin debater has come to Śrāvastī from the southern road. If he wishes to debate on some great branch of learning, you should engage in debate with him. If he wishes to debate on some other great branch of learning, then you should engage in debate with him as well. If for now you are able to defeat him, all the better. If you are unable to defeat him, send him into the community of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas. If the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, defeat him, then we brahmins shall be the foremost. And if he defeats the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, then throughout all the directions and their quarters a vast and glorious wave of auspicious renown will arise for us: that a debater who came from the southern road was defeated right here at Śrāvastī."

The brahmin who had come from the southern road rose early in the morning, wrapped his robes tightly about him, took a torch of grass in his hand, and entered Śrāvastī. The young brahmins of Śrāvastī said to him: "Master, why have you wrapped your robes about you?" "So that all I have heard and retained does not burst out and escape." "If that is the case, it would be fitting to wrap yourself with a board of copper instead." "And why do you carry a torch of grass?" "To walk with the lamp of knowledge into the darkness of a world that does not know." He then went about and debated with whichever learned persons he encountered in any branch of learning, leaving every one of them without eloquence; and when he had rendered them all speechless, they said to him: "Master, are you only capable of defeating your opponents' positions?" He replied: "Is there any opposing position at all that I have failed to defeat?" They said: "There is. There are the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who are not long arisen, yet they are keenly committed to making the four classes pure in exposition, in imputation, and in thorough refutation. Please go and debate with them for a time." "And where are they?" "Right here in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada." "Who among them is the foremost speaker?" "They are all learned —"

"— though their conduct is exemplary indeed. But the foremost speaker among them is called the śramaṇa Lakṣaṇa, a son of the Śākyas." "And where is he?" "Right here in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada."

As they were conversing in this way, Lakṣaṇa, the son of the Śākyas, happened to pass right by. The brahmin youths said to the brahmin: "Master, set aside the other śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas — please engage in debate with this Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyas." The brahmin looked at him and said: "He bears the mark of a teacher, so he is indeed the foremost speaker." He then approached him and said: "Ho, monk! I have gathered a few letters from my master. I wish to settle some matters in discussion with you." The brahmin replied: "No offence, brahmin. As for me too, whenever the thought arises in my mind that I should sharpen my treatise for debate, you should likewise come here and do the same." "When?" "Tomorrow." "At what place?" "In a certain pleasant grove." "Very well," said the monk, and departed.

The brahmin then spent the whole night turning over his own position and his opponent's position, thinking: "If he says such-and-such, I shall reply thus," until all the night watches had passed. Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyas, reflected: "If I were simply to defeat the brahmin straightaway, I would still need to pass through a hundred gateposts and find a way to fill my belly. But if the brahmin defeats me, my garland of renown will be no more."

Early the next morning the brahmin rose and went to the grove, where he waited a long time. Realising that the other was not coming, he entered Śrāvastī. Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyas, had also let the appointed time for the debate slip by, and entered Śrāvastī on his alms round. The brahmin saw him and said: "Ho, monk! You did not come to that grove." Lakṣaṇa replied: "I never agreed to come to any particular grove. I said we should settle our discussion tomorrow in a certain pleasant grove." "Brahmin, I have completely forgotten." The brahmin thought: "I spent the whole night turning over my position and my opponent's position, and when day broke this monk said he had forgotten entirely. He must either be a great minister of state, or someone whose mind is undisturbed by learning." So he said: "Ho, monk, let it be tomorrow." "Very well, brahmin."

The following day the brahmin rose early again and went to that grove, where he waited a long time. Realising that the other was not coming, he entered Śrāvastī again. Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyas, had likewise let the appointed time for debate slip by and had entered Śrāvastī on his alms round. The brahmin saw him and said: "Ho, monk! You did not come to that grove." Lakṣaṇa replied: "Brahmin, are my activities confined to that alone? I must attend upon my Teacher, receive his teachings, take part in the recitation of texts, and teach the Dharma to whatever brahmins and householders come and arrive." The brahmin said: "Monk, do you not deliberately slight me?" "That is indeed the case." At that moment Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyas, indicated a direction with a gesture and gave a sign. Having given that directional gesture and that sign, he deliberated and, not going there himself —

— other tīrthikas and persons of knowledge were saying: "These ascetics (śramaṇas), sons of the Śākyans, are liars who have not turned away from lying, who have not abandoned it and individually abandoned it. They indicate a direction and give gestures and signs; having indicated a direction and given gestures and signs, they deliberate and yet do not go there." They were reviling him, throwing abuse at him, and speaking ill of him. On account of this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this occasion, and in this context, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The buddhas, the blessed ones, knowingly put a question — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One, the buddha, questioned Lakṣaṇa, son of the Śākyans: "Lakṣaṇa, is it true that you indicated a direction and gave gestures and signs, and then, having indicated a direction and given those gestures and signs, you deliberately did not go?" "Venerable one, that is so." The Blessed One, the buddha, rebuked him, saying that this was not the conduct of an ascetic, was not fitting, was not proper, was not in accordance with the rule, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. After rebuking him in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

If one speaks a deliberate lie, it is a transgression.

'Deliberately' means after having examined the matter. As for 'if one speaks a lie,' false speech has nine modes. It also has eight modes, seven modes, six modes, five modes, four modes, three modes, and two modes.

What are the nine modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of a defeat (pārājika) without grounds; of a matter remaining before the Saṅgha; of a transgression; of something requiring individual confession; bringing up a matter involving a fault; falsely accusing another of a lapse in moral discipline, a lapse in view, a lapse in ritual conduct, or a lapse in livelihood.

What are the eight modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of a defeat without grounds; of a matter remaining before the Saṅgha; of a transgression; of something requiring individual confession; bringing up a matter involving a fault; and falsely accusing another of what one has not seen, not heard, or only suspected.

What are the seven modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of a lapse in moral discipline, a lapse in view, a lapse in ritual conduct, or a lapse in livelihood without grounds; and falsely accusing another of what one has not seen, not heard, or only suspected.

What are the six modes of false speech? A monk who wishes to speak falsely thinks: "I shall speak a lie." While speaking the lie he thinks: "I am speaking a lie." Having spoken the lie he thinks: "I have spoken a lie." And a monk speaks falsely concerning what he has not seen, not heard, or only suspected.

What are the five modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of a defeat without grounds; of a matter remaining before the Saṅgha; of a transgression; of something requiring individual confession; and bringing up a matter involving a fault.

What are the four modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of a lapse in moral discipline, a lapse in view, a lapse in ritual conduct, or a lapse in livelihood without grounds.

What are the three modes of false speech? Falsely accusing another of what one has not seen, not heard, or only suspected.

As for a further set of three modes of false speech: when wishing to speak falsely, one thinks: "I shall speak a lie." While speaking the lie, one thinks: "I am speaking a lie." Having spoken the lie —

Having spoken the lie, one thinks: "I have spoken a lie." What are the two modes of false speech? While speaking the lie, one thinks: "I am speaking a lie"; and having spoken the lie, one thinks: "I have spoken a lie." There is no single solitary mode of false speech standing alone.

Among instances of false speech: there is false speech that constitutes a defeat; there is false speech that results in a remainder for the Saṅgha; there is false speech that constitutes a grave offense; there is false speech that constitutes a transgression; and there is false speech that constitutes a misdeed.

What is the false speech that constitutes a defeat? It is this: a monk who does not possess them falsely claiming, as though he did, superhuman qualities of a noble person.

What is the false speech that results in a remainder for the Saṅgha? It is this: a monk who has become angry and filled with aversion, thinking "By whatever means I shall drive this one from the celibate life," falsely accusing a pure monk who is free from transgressions, groundlessly, with a matter that would constitute a defeat.

What is the false speech that constitutes a grave offense? It is this: a monk who deliberately, in the midst of the Saṅgha, teaches what is not Dharma as Dharma, teaches what is Dharma as not Dharma, teaches what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and teaches what is Vinaya as not Vinaya.

What is the false speech that constitutes a misdeed? It is this: when a monk, at each half-month when the sūtra of individual liberation is being recited, is asked "Are you pure in this regard?" and, not being pure, remains silent without saying a word.

What is the false speech that constitutes a transgression? It is this: all other instances of false speech apart from those four kinds of false speech just described constitute transgressions.

As for what is meant by "transgression": it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, states of misfortune, and states of wrong descent. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and not individually confessed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. Therefore it is called a transgression.

Now, how does one incur a transgression? The intermediate rule states:

Not forgotten, and of two minds,
Perception is the last condition.

When a monk has not seen, not heard, not known, or not perceived something, yet alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it; I have heard it; I have known it; I have perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has seen something yet forgotten it, or has heard, known, and perceived it yet forgotten it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and I have not forgotten it; I have heard, known, and perceived it and I have not forgotten it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has seen something yet has doubt about it, or has heard, known, and perceived it yet has doubt about it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and I have no doubt about it; I have heard, known, and perceived it and I have no doubt about it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he perceives what he has seen as not seen, perceives what he has heard, known, and perceived as not perceived, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and

altered view, says: "I have seen it; I have heard it, known it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has not heard something yet has seen, known, and perceived it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it, but I have not heard it, not known it, and not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has not known something yet has seen, heard, and perceived it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have known it, but I have not seen it, not heard it, and not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has not perceived something yet has seen, heard, and known it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have perceived it, but I have not seen it, not heard it, and not known it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has seen something and has also forgotten it, and has heard, known, and perceived it and has also forgotten it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it and I have not forgotten it either; I have not heard it, not known it, and not perceived it, and I have not forgotten those either" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has seen something yet has doubt about it, and has heard, known, and perceived it yet has doubt about it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it and I have no doubt about it; I have not heard it, not known it, and not perceived it, and I have no doubt about those either" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has seen something and perceives it as seen, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it, but I have heard it, known it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has heard something and perceives it as heard, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not heard it, but I have seen it, known it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has known something and perceives it as known, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not known it, but I have seen it, heard it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When he has perceived something and perceives it as perceived, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not perceived it, but I have seen it, heard it, and known it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk alters his perception with respect to what he has seen, heard, known, and perceived, and with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it; I have not heard it; I have not known it" —

"I have not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not seen something and has not forgotten that he has not seen it, and has not heard it, not known it, not perceived it, and has not forgotten that either, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and have forgotten that; I have heard it, known it, and perceived it, and have forgotten that too" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not seen something and has no uncertainty about that, and has not heard it, not known it, not perceived it, and has no uncertainty about that either, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and I am uncertain about that; I have heard it, known it, and perceived it, and I am uncertain about that too" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk perceives what he has not seen as seen, and perceives what he has not heard, not known, and not perceived as perceived, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it; I have not heard it; I have not known it; I have not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has seen something but has not heard it, not known it, and not perceived it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not seen it, but I have heard it, known it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has heard something but has not seen it, not known it, and not perceived it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not heard it, but I have seen it, known it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has known something but has not seen it, not heard it, and not perceived it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not known it, but I have seen it, heard it, and perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has perceived something but has not seen it, not heard it, and not known it, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have not perceived it, but I have seen it, heard it, and known it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not seen something and has not forgotten that, and has not heard it, not known it, not perceived it, and has not forgotten that either, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and have forgotten that; I have heard it, known it, and perceived it, and have forgotten that too" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not seen something and has no uncertainty about that, and has not heard it, not known it, not perceived it, and has no uncertainty about that either, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it and I am uncertain about that; I have heard it, known it, and perceived it, and I am uncertain about that too" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not seen something and perceives it as not seen, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have seen it; I have not heard it, not known it, and not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not heard something and perceives it as not heard, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view —

— says "I have heard it; I have not seen it, not known it, and not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not known something and perceives it as not known, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have known it; I have not seen it, not heard it, and not perceived it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

When a monk has not perceived something and perceives it as not perceived, and then alters his perception and, with acceptance, desire, reasoning, thought, and altered view, says: "I have perceived it; I have not seen it, not heard it, and not known it" — everything he has said constitutes a transgression.

However extensively a monk alters his perception and then speaks, everything constitutes a transgression. However, there is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is deranged, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is overcome by painful feelings. The first transgression regarding false speech is complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha), the Bhagavān, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the group of six monks addressed the other monks in terms of their physical defects, calling them things such as: big-ears, bald-heads, loose-limbed ones, stumpy-fingered ones, hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with goiters, mutes, deaf ones, scab-covered ones, flat-footed ones, impudent ones, droopy-lipped ones, and big-heads. By speaking of monks in terms of their physical defects and conducting themselves in this way, those monks became dejected, humiliated, and despondent, and they abandoned the recitation of scripture, the reading of texts, oral repetition, yoga practice, mental cultivation, and the inner calm abiding of the mind, and they remained in a state of much suffering and mental discomfort.

Some monks of few wants said: "Why do these monks address other monks in terms of their physical defects, calling them big-ears, bald-heads, loose-limbed ones, stumpy-fingered ones, hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with goiters, mutes, deaf ones, scab-covered ones, flat-footed ones, impudent ones, droopy-lipped ones, and big-heads — mocking them, jeering at them, and speaking ill of them?" Those monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, in view of this occasion and this context, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and what follows is as before. The statement "The blessed buddhas, while knowing, act as though they do not know" and what follows is also as before.

The Blessed One censured the group of six monks, saying: "Is it true, monks, that you have been addressing other monks in terms of their physical defects, calling them big-ears, bald-heads, loose-limbed ones, stumpy-fingered ones, hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with goiters, mutes, deaf ones, scab-covered ones, flat-footed ones, impudent ones, droopy-lipped ones, and big-heads, and conducting yourselves in this way?" "It is true, Venerable One." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that this was not the conduct of a renunciant, was not appropriate, was not fitting, and was not in accord with proper discipline — it was not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

"Monks, long ago in a time past, there lived a householder on a rocky cliff. He took a wife of equal birth, and with her he played, rejoiced, and lived in happiness. To them a daughter was born, and they raised and nurtured her until she grew up. That householder was a farmer, and he himself went to plow the fields.

A son of another householder, separated from his parents, came from the forest carrying a load of firewood. He set it down beneath a tree near that field and rested, and he said to him, "Uncle, why do you plow the field yourself? You who could do the work of the village in the village — why do you do the work of the forest in the forest? I have no son, and I have no brothers. Uncle, lend me the yoke and let me plow while you rest a while." And with that he began to plow.

The householder came, bringing food for the young man, and called out, "Nephew, come here and eat." The two of them ate, and then the householder's son said, "Uncle, I do not know your household — you should go home. Stay and I will finish the plowing by evening." The householder departed, and the young man plowed for a little while longer; then, toward evening, he turned the two oxen loose in the direction of the field boundary, took up a load of grass, and began heading toward that rocky cliff. The householder, going to meet him, led him back to the house.

The householder's son tethered the oxen to their post, spread out fodder, calmed them with a gentle motion, and laid grass before the two oxen. The householder thought, "This boy has been of great benefit to me. I will give him my daughter as his wife." He said to the young man, "Nephew, work here happily — I will give you this daughter as your wife." The young man began to build a house. Then one of the oxen bolted into the field, and when he tried to drive it back he could not, so he struck it and hurled a piece of wood at it; this broke one of its horns, and from that event the ox was named Broken-Horn. On another occasion the ox again bolted into the field, and when he tried to drive it back he could not, so he struck it and hurled a clod at it; this cut off its tail, and from that the ox was named Stump-Tail. And so, having been given the names Broken-Horn and Stump-Tail, the ox was thereafter called simply Broken-Stump.

At another time the householder's son said to the householder, "Uncle, keep the promise you made." The householder said to his wife, "Good woman, make preparations for the bridal sendoff — we will send the daughter as a bride." The wife replied, "My lord, this daughter has never been given to anyone at all — how shall we send her as a bride?" He said, "I have promised her to another." "To whom?" "To this young householder." The wife said, "It seems wrong to give our daughter to this one, who is as white and vacant as a white gourd and has never achieved anything of his own. Let her be given where she will have clothing to wear and food to eat." He said, "My dear, this young man has been of great benefit to me — and even if he were to leave, I would still have to plow the fields myself." The wife replied, "I cannot give my daughter to this good-for-nothing." The householder thought, "If I say to the young man, 'I will not give you my daughter,' he will leave this very day and I will be left in suffering." So he put the matter off.

Again the householder's son said to the householder, "Uncle, keep the promise you made." He replied, "Nephew, I must provide a feast for all my many relatives — first go and harvest the rice." The young man harvested the rice and came back saying, "Uncle, now send the bride." He replied, "Nephew, I also need sugar cane for the feast — first go and procure the sugar cane." He went and procured the sugar cane, and returned saying, "Uncle, now send the bride." He replied,

"Nephew, I also need loads for the feast — first go and procure the grain." He went and procured the grain as well, and returned saying, "Uncle, now send the bride." The householder said, "Nephew, the earlier rice is used up — go and harvest more rice first."

The householder's son thought to himself: "These three tasks are by their very nature impossible to complete all at once, so he is simply stringing me along. I will go into the assembly of common people, make him acknowledge his promise publicly, and if he still refuses to give her, I will have him brought to court from the royal palace." So he went into the assembly of common people and said to him there, "Uncle, send the bride." The householder was irritated and said, "Good people, if this man is doing the work of my stomach — that is, working as my farm laborer — should I really give him my daughter?" The householder's son thought to himself: "I have received neither the kārṣāpaṇas nor the girl. I will do him some injury and be on my way." So he ploughed the fields with those oxen that very day, flogged them many times with a whip, tied them in the hot sun to a dry post, and left.

Now, by the nature of reality, in the early age when the world was first established, animals too could speak. So those oxen said to him: "Hey, you — you have been just like a father and mother to us. You always tended us well with comfort and care. Why then, today, did you plough the fields, flog us many times with a whip, tie us to a dry post in the hot sun, and leave? Did we do you some wrong?" "You have done me not the slightest wrong. It is your master who has wronged me." "And what did he do?" "He promised to give me his daughter and has not given her." "Then why don't you go to the royal palace?" "I have no witnesses." "Go — we will testify as witnesses." "But can you speak in human language?" "We cannot. But here is what you should do: petition the king with a declaration of truth. We will be tied up for seven days without anyone giving us grass or pouring us water. On the seventh day, send us toward a place with abundant grass and abundant water. Then, before the king, speak these words of truth: 'If I am telling the truth, may these oxen neither eat grass nor drink water.' We, for our part, for as long as the king has not yet come to believe, will neither eat grass nor drink water."

The householder's son went to the royal palace and petitioned the king: "Sire, a certain wealthy householder promised to give me his daughter and then refused." The king said, "Do you have any witnesses?" "I do, Sire." "Are they men?" "They are not men." "Who, then?" "Sire, they are oxen." "Can they speak in human language?" "They cannot, Sire. But this is what I will do: I will petition by a declaration of truth. I myself will tie up those oxen for seven days, give them no fodder and pour them no water, and on the seventh day I will send them toward a place of abundant fodder and abundant water. At that time I will petition before Your Majesty with these words of truth: 'If I am not lying, may these oxen neither seek fodder nor seek water.' And for as long as Your Majesty has not yet come to believe, they will neither seek fodder nor seek water." The king instructed his ministers, "Good people, do as he has said." They tied up those oxen and left them. Then Khaṇḍarūpa said, "Has the sun risen in the west?"

"Why do they not release us?" The others said, "No — we must petition before that householder's son in this way, with words of truth: 'We will remain tethered in the stable for seven days, receiving no fodder and no water, and on the seventh day we will be sent toward a place of abundant fodder and abundant water. At that time, you must petition before the king with these words of truth: If I am not lying, may these oxen neither eat fodder nor drink water.' And we have pledged that for as long as the king has not yet come to believe, we will neither eat fodder nor drink water."

Khaṇḍarūpa said, "If they were let free, what need is there even to mention grass — they would eat stones."

The others said, "That householder's son is like a father and mother to us. Do not act in that way."

Khaṇḍarūpa said, "It is true that he is like a father and mother to us, yet he calls me Khaṇḍarūpa — and that I do not like at all. In fact, I would rather rip out his belly."

Now the householder's son came to the oxen from time to time and asked them, "Dear oxen, how are you faring?" They replied, "We are faring well — it is you who are not faring well. What harm has Khaṇḍarūpa done? He says, 'If I were let free, what need even to mention grass — I would eat stones.' Well then, should we flee? No — rather do not flee: instead, punch this Khaṇḍarūpa on the nose, and if he should try to eat grass or drink water, we will seize him by the nose with our horns and hold his head up toward the sun. And you, at that moment, tell everyone: 'The fifth world-guardian sun is also among the four great ones' — pointing up at the sun."

When the boy began to punch Khaṇḍarūpa on the nose, Khaṇḍarūpa cried, "Wise ones, look at this — he is matching himself up to my height!" The others said, "He is adorning you with an ornament — be silent."

Then on the seventh day, the king assembled together with the ministers, and the oxen were sent toward a place of abundant fodder and abundant water. At that moment Khaṇḍarūpa reached out to take a mouthful of grass, and those oxen seized him by the nose with their horns and held his head up, gazing at the sun. The king said to the ministers, "Wise ones, why are these oxen gazing at the sun and standing still?" At that one minister said, "Your Majesty, in effect they are making a petition to the deity: not merely that the four great ones are ours alone, but that the fifth world-guardian sun with its canopy is yet another set of four great ones." The king was filled with wonder and instructed the ministers, "Wise ones, let the non-humans resolve the dispute over the four great ones, and give this householder's son the householder's daughter." The householder's son defeated that householder and was given his daughter.

Monks, even those creatures born in the animal realm, when led by humans into court and made to act and speak, will plot to kill — to say nothing of human beings. Therefore a monk must not lead a fellow monk into court through human testimony and make him act and speak so.

Monks, in times gone by, long past, in a certain rocky mountain gorge there lived a householder who was a wagon-driver, and he had two bulls named Bādagāyeda and Sārī. From among those two, in the spring month a dappled calf

followed by two dappled ones. Now, the calf of Bādagāyeda was a hornless bull, and the calf of Sārī was a striped one, and so he named one Bādagāyeda Hornless and the other Sārī Striped. In time, those two grew into great bulls.

On another occasion, some wagon-drivers gathered at a drinking party and fell to boasting. "Good sirs," they said, "whose bulls are the finest?" One of them said, "Mine are the best." Another said, "Mine are the best." The wagon-driver in question also said, "Mine are the best." The others said, "How do you know?" He replied, "Load the wagon heavily on the lowest road, stake five hundred kārṣāpaṇas as the wager, and drive the two bulls — that will settle it." So they loaded the wagon heavily on the lowest road, staked five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and that day drove those two bulls. The wagon-driver began to urge them on: "Go, Bādagāyeda Hornless! Go, Sārī Striped!" But those two bulls stood motionless and would not budge. He then began to beat them with his hands. The other wagon-drivers said, "You have lost — do not harm the cattle; release those two bulls and pay the forfeit." And so he was made to pay five hundred kārṣāpaṇas.

Then that wagon-driver, furious with the two bulls, flogged them many times with a whip and tied them to a dry post in the sun. Now, by the very nature of reality, in a world not long established animals too were still able to speak in human language. So the two bulls said to him, "You treat us as though we were your own father and mother — have we ever done you any wrong? Why then do you flog us many times and tie us to a dry post in the sun?" He replied, "You two deliberately feigned weakness, and it has cost me a forfeit of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." The two replied, "You brought the forfeit on yourself by your own tongue. What has come to pass? We two — one named Bādagāyeda and the other named Sārī — why do you call us by those ugly epithets, Hornless and Striped? Be that as it may. Now load the wagon twice as heavily on the lowest road, stake twice that amount in kārṣāpaṇas as the wager, and drive us two. Or do you also wish to be made to pay another forfeit? Do not call us by ugly names — give us our proper names — and we will pull the wagon."

On another occasion those wagon-drivers again gathered at a drinking party and fell to boasting. "Good sirs," they said, "whose bulls are the finest?" One said, "Mine are the best." Another said, "Mine are the best." That same wagon-driver also said, "Mine are the best." The others said, "Good fellow, do you also wish to be made to pay a forfeit again?" He replied, "What harm is there to you? Load the wagon twice as heavily on the lowest road, stake a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, and drive the bulls." So they loaded the wagon twice as heavily on the lowest road, staked a thousand kārṣāpaṇas as the wager, and drove those two bulls. The wagon-driver began to urge them on: "Go, Bādagāyeda! Go, Sārī!" And those two swiftly, with all speed, hauled that load across the plain. The wagon-driver received the forfeit of a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, and then the gods spoke these verses:

When the load is heaviest
and when the road runs lowest,
those two bear the burden there
and draw the wagon forward.
If pleasant words are spoken —

they carry even the heaviest load
and are rewarded for it as well,
and both are glad at heart.
Therefore speak what is pleasing,
and never what is displeasing.
When pleasant words are spoken,
virtue arises and no wrongdoing remains.

Monks, even those creatures born in the animal realm — when humans treat them with taunting speech and habitually address them in that way, it severs the stream of loving-kindness toward them. How much more so is this true in the case of human beings. Therefore a monk must not habitually address another monk with speech that demeans him by reference to his human origins.

Then the Blessed One, having rebuked this conduct in many ways, addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk speaks with the intent to demean another by his human origins commits a transgression."

Now, "speaks with the intent to demean another by his human origins" means: with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, one utters speech — words, phrases, designations, expressions, utterances, definitive statements, verbal routes, vocal sounds, verbal actions, and vocal communications. "Commits a transgression" means: it burns, torments, and causes one to fall into the states of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the realms of ruin and wrong descent. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the virtuous qualities. It is for this reason that it is called "committing a transgression."

Now, as to how the transgression occurs, the summary verse states:

By birth, by craft, by occupation,
by bodily signs — five categories of internal transgressions —
along with the secondary afflictions,
and the act of mockery is the last.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the brahmin caste" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a wrongdoing for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the warrior caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the warrior caste" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a wrongdoing for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the noble class and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the noble class" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a transgression for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the common people and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the common people" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a transgression for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the warrior caste (kṣatriya) and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you?
