If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the householder caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the householder caste — and so, venerable one, you should practise the crafts proper to you, namely: tilling fields, tending cattle, and trading" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a transgression for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the common people's caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the barbers' caste —

and so, venerable one, you should practise the crafts proper to you, namely: cutting hair, trimming nails, shaving beards, dressing wounds, and whatever other crafts belong to barbers" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a transgression for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the carpenters' caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? You, venerable one, have gone forth from the carpenters' caste — and so, venerable one, you should practise the crafts proper to you, namely: beds, small beds, chairs, stools, door-panels, and whatever other crafts belong to carpenters" — whether the monk who says this is tonsured or not, it constitutes a transgression for that monk.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the basket-weavers' caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? The Vinayavibhaṅga, the thirty-ninth section.

If a monk, with the intention of demeaning another by his human origins, goes to one who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says to him: "Venerable one, where is the conduct of a renunciant in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin in you? shooting great arrows — techniques of handling, stances, top-knot combat, cutting, slashing, thrusting, striking at range, striking with a sound, striking a vital point, striking without missing, and striking with great force — and whatever other activities belong to the warrior-noble caste you should also perform." Whether or not the monk himself has gone forth from the warrior-noble caste, it is a misdeed for that monk.

Whether or not the monk himself is bald-headed, it is a transgression for that monk.

Venerable one, you are like a corpse" — and insults him with such insults and the like — whether or not the monk himself is bald-headed, it is a transgression for that monk.

If there happen to be many persons with such a name, and in answering the one spoken to he says "Which is the monk Saṅgharakṣita?" and says "It is the one who went forth from the brahmin caste" — and similar preceding statements of that kind — there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who acts for the first time, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by acute sensations.

The second transgression of demeaning by human origins is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks were everywhere engaging in slander against the monks. When they engaged in slander everywhere, some monks became humiliated, downcast, and dispirited, and ceased studying, reading, reciting,

and meditation, mental application, and inner calm abiding. In this way the group of six monks also severed the continuum of virtuous qualities that the others had been diligently cultivating and accumulating over a long time. Those monks then reported this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, why do monks engage everywhere in slander against monks?" — reviling them, deriding them, and speaking ill of them.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and this circumstance, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so on, as before. "The blessed buddhas, knowing yet feigning not to know" — and so on, also as before.

The blessed Buddha questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you engaged everywhere in slander against monks?" "Venerable sir, we did." The blessed Buddha then censured them, declaring that such conduct was unbecoming for a renunciant, unsuitable, improper, and not in accord with discipline — it was not something a fully ordained monk should do.

"Monks, in times long past there was a lioness who was pregnant and dwelling in a certain forest. Now the habit of lionesses is this: when the time of giving birth arrives, they assemble a great store of meat and then give birth. This lioness followed after a large herd of cattle and, while still nursing her young shortly after giving birth, a calf that was following at the herd's rear — a calf being tended by its mother, who would not go far — was killed by the lioness, who took its flesh and returned to her den.

Now that calf, wishing to drink its mother's milk, kept following after the lioness, and the lioness thought: 'This calf too should be killed.' But then she thought again: 'If my own cub comes to follow this calf, then this calf will become a companion to my cub — I will not kill it.'

The lioness gave birth, and a male cub was born to her. The lioness began nursing both her own cub and that calf together, and in time both of them grew large. Then at another time the lioness grew old, and as the moment of her death approached she spoke to them: 'You two are nursing-companions, having suckled at the same breast. Slanderers, those who sow division, will fill the entire world. After I am gone, you two must not listen to any of them.' And having said this, she spoke these words:

All that has been gathered comes to its end,
and those who have risen high are brought to fall.
Whatever has met together must part,
and whatever lives must die.

And so it was that her time came, and she passed away in accordance with the nature of things.

The lion grew large by slaying the finest of wild beasts, eating their excellent flesh, and drinking their rich blood. And that noble bull calf also grew large by eating fine grasses in the lion's protected domain and drinking clean water. The king of wild beasts, that lion, had in his retinue an old fox — utterly greedy, a scavenger living on scraps — who always followed behind. Now the lion, having slain the finest of wild beasts and eaten their excellent flesh and drunk their excellent blood, would rest there contentedly, and because of this the other smaller predators of that vicinity dared not approach. So that old fox ate and drank the scraps of meat and the remnants of blood left behind after the lion had slain the finest of wild beasts and eaten their excellent flesh and drunk their excellent blood, and thereby became fat in hide, flesh, and blood."

Now at a certain other time, the lion slew the finest of wild beasts and ate their excellent flesh and drank their excellent blood, then went straight home to his pride and sat playing and resting with the finest of stallions. The leftover meat was eaten by the other smaller predators, and the old fox thought to himself: "I must watch where this lion goes." So he followed along behind him, and when he saw him sitting and playing with the finest of stallions, the fox thought: "This stallion has become an obstacle to my food supply. I must drive these two apart." And the old fox went and sat before the stallion with his ears laid flat. The stallion said: "Uncle, do the hot winds not blow?" The fox replied: "Indeed, hot winds blaze fiercely. But what of it? This lion here says: 'Where has that stallion gone, my means of gathering meat? When I cannot find other flesh, I shall eat this stallion.' " The stallion said: "Uncle, when we were both at our mother's deathbed, we two were brothers who nursed at the same teat, and she gave her last testament saying that after she was gone, you two must not listen to slanderers, those who sow division and fill the world with their scheming. Do not say such things." The fox replied: "Stallion, if you will not now listen to my words spoken for your benefit, you will come to ruin." The stallion said: "Uncle, how would that come about?" The fox replied: "Stallion, this lion will come forth from his lair, shake himself, yawn wide, survey the four directions, and then roar the lion's roar three times before coming toward you. When that happens, know that it is I he means to kill."

Then the fox went and sat before the lion with his ears laid flat. The lion said: "Uncle, do the hot winds not blow?" The fox replied: "Indeed, hot winds blaze fiercely. But what of it? This stallion here says: 'Where has that ancestral lion of mine gone? I shall slash open his belly in revenge for the killing of his mother.' " The lion said: "Uncle, when we were both at our mother's deathbed, we two were brothers who nursed at the same teat, and she gave her last testament saying that after she was gone, you two must not listen to slanderers, those who sow division and fill the world with their scheming. Do not say such things." The fox replied: "Lion, if you will not now listen to my words spoken for your benefit, you will come to ruin." The lion said: "Uncle, how would that come about?" The fox replied: "Lion, this stallion will come forth from the herd, shake himself, make a buzzing sound, paw the ground, snort with fury, and then come toward you. When that happens, know that it is I he means to kill."

Now although both of them naturally behaved in exactly these ways all the time, on no occasion had they ever taken it as a sign directed against them. But then at another time, the lion, king of wild beasts, came forth from his lair, shook himself, yawned wide, surveyed the four directions, roared the lion's roar three times, and then went toward the stallion. The stallion too came forth from the herd, shook himself, made a buzzing sound, pawed the ground, snorted with fury, and then went toward the lion. Those two had always naturally behaved in exactly those ways all the time, and on no prior occasion had they ever taken it as a sign directed against them — but now, at the very moment when the seed of division had been planted in their minds, they took it as such.

The stallion thought, "He is going to kill me," and the lion thought, "He is going to kill me." The lion raked the stallion's chest with his claws, and the stallion gored open the lion's belly with his horn, and both fell dead at the same moment. Then the god spoke in verse:

Those who look upon what is good
should not keep company with the wicked.
See how the fox drove apart
the lion and the stallion who were dear to one another.

Monks, even animals born into animal destinies will, when slander is practiced among them, think to kill one another — how much more needless to say this of human beings. Therefore, monks, a monk must not practice slander against a fellow monk. If a monk does practice slander against a fellow monk, it will bring about serious conflict.

Monks, in a time long past, in a certain forest there lived a lioness with her cub and a tigress with her cub. The lioness went out to her hunting ground, and while her cub was wandering about it came upon the tigress's den. The tigress saw it and thought, "I shall kill this one," but then thought again, "No — this one can become a companion and younger friend to my own cub; I will not kill it," and she began to suckle it. The lioness, having ranged through her hunting ground, returned home. When she could not find her cub she began to search for it, and she found the cub being suckled by the tigress. The tigress, seeing the lioness, was frightened and began to flee. The lioness called out to the tigress, "Sister, do not flee! Let us dwell together. In this way, when you go out to your hunting ground I will tend to your cub, and if you should go out to the hunting ground, I will tend to your cub as well." The two began to live together, and together they named the lion cub Goodfang and the tiger cub Goodshoulder, and in time those two grew up. Then, at another time, the lioness and the tigress both fell ill, and as the time of their death drew near they spoke to their two sons: "You two are brothers who have suckled at the same breast — but those who carry slander, those who drive apart with divisive words, fill the world with discord. After we two have passed away, you must not listen to anyone of that kind." Then they said:

All that has been gathered comes at last to exhaustion,
all that has risen high must in the end fall.
All meeting ends at last in parting,
and all that lives must in the end die.

And so it was that they met the nature of impermanence. The lion used to go out, kill the finest game animals, eat the best flesh and drink the best blood, and then return swiftly, directly to the lair. The tiger used to go out to the hunting ground, kill game animals with great effort, eat flesh and drink blood, and then return only after a long time. Then on one occasion the tiger hid his leftovers and ate from them, and returned quickly. The lion said to the tiger, "Before this, you always came back after a long time, yet today you have come back quickly — what is the reason for this?" The tiger said, "I had hidden some leftovers and I ate from those and came back." The lion said, "You hide leftovers?" The tiger said, "Yes." The lion said, "As for me, I kill the finest game, eat the finest flesh, and drink the finest blood, and then go home without a second thought." The tiger said, "You have great strength, that is true —

but I cannot do likewise." The lion said, "Let us go out together." And so the two of them set off together.

Now, an old fox — exceedingly cunning, a eater of leftovers — was in the retinue of that lion, king of wild beasts, and was always following along behind him. This fox thought, "This tiger has become a rival for my food supply, so I must drive these two apart." With that in mind, the old fox went and sat before the lion with its ears drooping down. The lion said, "Uncle, are hot winds not rising?" The fox said, "Hot winds, blazing fiercely, are indeed rising. What is wrong? This tiger here keeps saying, 'Where has that lion gone, the root of my strength? Because he made me eat leftovers, I shall surely kill him.'" The lion said, "Uncle, our two mothers, at the moment of their deaths, told you two that you were brothers who had nursed at the same breast. Slanderers and troublemakers who split households fill the world, and they left a testament saying that after the two of them passed away you two should never listen to anyone like that — so do not say such things." The fox said, "Elder, if you do not listen to words spoken now for your own benefit, you will come to ruin." The lion said, "Uncle, how will it come about in sequence?" The fox said, "Elder, this tiger will come out from his lair, screech like a bird, crouch low, look out in all four directions, then give three tiger roars and come before you — and when that happens, you should know that he intends to kill you. After that, go and sit before the tiger with your ears drooping down." The tiger said, "Uncle, are hot winds not rising?" The fox said, "Hot winds, blazing fiercely, are indeed rising. What is wrong? This lion here keeps saying, 'Where has that tiger gone, the root of my strength? He shall surely be killed.'" The tiger said, "Uncle, our two mothers, at the moment of their deaths, told you two that you were brothers who had nursed at the same breast. Slanderers and troublemakers who split households fill the world, and they left a testament saying that you two should never listen to anyone like that — so do not say such things." The fox said, "Elder, if you do not listen to words spoken now for your own benefit, you will come to ruin. Elder, how will it come about in sequence?" The fox said, "Elder, this lion will come out from his lair, screech like a bird, crouch low, look out in all four directions, then give three lion roars and come before you — and when that happens, you should know that he intends to kill you."

Now, although by their natures these two always behaved in just this way, not once had they ever taken it as a sign. But on another occasion, the lion king of wild beasts came out from his lair, screeched like a bird, crouched low, looked out in all four directions, gave three lion roars, and went before the tiger. The tiger too came out from his lair, screeched like a bird, crouched low, looked out in all four directions, gave three tiger roars, and went before the lion. Although these two had always done exactly this, they had never once taken it as a sign — but now, the moment the seed of discord had been planted in their minds, they took it as a sign, and the lion thought, "He intends to kill me," and the tiger likewise thought, "He intends to kill me."

Then the lion thought further, "I am endowed with great strength, whereas the tiger is not like that, so he cannot attack me — let me investigate more closely." And with that thought he spoke in verse:

With a splendid grove of trees and water,

With skill and strength endowed,
To attack one with fine fangs is not right.

Then the tiger also spoke in verse:

With a fine grove and water,
And endowed with skill and strength,
To attack one with fine flanks is not right —
One with fine fangs should not do so.

The lion said, "Who told you this?" The tiger replied, "This fox did." The tiger then said, "And who told you?" The lion replied, "This fox did."

The lion reflected, "This one is trying to drive a wedge between the two of us." And with that he struck the fox dead with a blow of his paw. Then a god spoke in verse:

Do not abandon a friend on account of another's words,
But examine well what others say.
Those who seek occasion to divide
Are slanderous persons — do not trust them.
The fox, born a village-dweller, spoke falsehood
And sought to part good friends — look at that!
Now that this slanderer has been slain,
See how friends rejoice in happiness.

Monks, even these creatures born in the animal realm were willing to kill when slander was practiced against them — what need is there to speak of human beings? Therefore, monks, a monk must not engage in slander against a fellow monk. If a monk slanders a fellow monk, it becomes a serious transgression.

Then the Blessed One, having censured this conduct in many ways, addressed the monks and said: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk engages in slander, it is a transgression."

The phrase "if a monk engages in slander" means: with the intention of slandering a fellow monk, one speaks — using speech, words, terminology, sounds, declarations, definitive expressions, the avenue of words, the sounds of words, verbal actions, or verbal expressions.

The phrase "it is a transgression" means: it scorches, it burns, it causes one to fall into the bad rebirths of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, into wretched destinies and downfalls. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and individually confessed, it obstructs wholesome dharmas — therefore it is called a transgression.

How does one come to incur a transgression in this matter? A summary verse:

Clan, craft, livelihood,
Sign, illness, the five categories of transgression,
The minor afflictions,
And mockery — that is the last.

If a monk, with the intention of slandering, goes to one who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says: "Venerable one, a certain monk said to you, 'Where is the conduct of an ascetic in you, venerable one? Where is the conduct of a brahmin? You, venerable one, are one gone forth from the brahmins'" — and if he names a monk saying, "The monk's name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such" — then the utterance of the name constitutes a full offense, and the utterance of clan and lineage constitutes a minor offense of slander.

If a monk, with the intention of slandering, goes to one who has gone forth from the warrior caste (kṣatriya) and says: "Venerable one, a certain monk said to you, 'Where is the conduct of an ascetic in you, venerable one? Where is the conduct of a brahmin? You, venerable one, are one gone forth from the warrior caste'" — and if he names a monk saying, "The monk's name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such" — then the utterance of the name constitutes a full offense, and the utterance of clan and lineage constitutes a minor offense of slander.

A monk, with the intention of sowing discord, goes to one who has gone forth from the brahmin caste and says: "Venerable one, a certain monk said to you, 'Venerable one, where is the conduct of an ascetic in you? Where is the conduct of a brahmin? The venerable one has gone forth from the brahmin caste —

the venerable one ought to practice his own proper occupation, which is this: the conduct and deportment of a brahmin, cleanliness, proper behavior, taking up ashes, taking up a water vessel with a spout, hand gestures, a topknot, the recitation of hymns of praise, the exclamation "Kye!", the Veda of invocations, the Veda of oblations, the Veda of poetry, the Veda of protection, performing fire sacrifices, directing others to perform fire sacrifices, reciting texts, directing others to recite texts, giving and receiving, and whatever other occupations belong to brahmins." Which monk? His name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such. If he says these words, naming the name constitutes a downfall, while stating the clan and lineage constitutes an offense.

A monk, with the intention of sowing discord, goes to a monk and says these words: "The venerable one has a monk who says to him: 'Where is the conduct of a śramaṇa in the venerable one? Where is the conduct of a brahmin? The venerable one has incurred a defeat, a Saṅgha remainder, a transgression, a downfall requiring individual confession, or a downfall.'" Which monk? His name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such — if these words are spoken, stating the name constitutes a transgression, while stating the clan and lineage constitutes a downfall.

A monk, with the intention of sowing discord, goes to a monk and says these words: "The venerable one has a monk who says to him: 'Where is the conduct of a śramaṇa in the venerable one? Where is the conduct of a brahmin? The venerable one is wrathful, holds grudges, is deceitful, speaks at the wrong time, is envious, is miserly, is dishonest, is crafty, is without shame, is without embarrassment, desires evil, and holds wrong views.'" Which monk? His name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such — if these words are spoken, stating the name constitutes a transgression, while stating the clan and lineage constitutes a downfall.

A monk, with the intention of sowing discord, goes to a monk and says these words: "The venerable one has a monk who says to him: 'Where is the conduct of a śramaṇa in the venerable one? Where is the conduct of a brahmin?'" — and reviles him with insults such as "The venerable one is like a corpse," and so forth. Which monk? His name is such-and-such, his clan is such-and-such, his lineage is such-and-such — if these words are spoken, stating the name constitutes a transgression, while stating the clan and lineage constitutes a downfall.

In the same way, however much a monk speaks divisive words among monks with the intention of sowing discord, whether true or false, in all cases it constitutes a transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one overcome by feelings of pain.

This concludes the third transgression of sowing discord among monks.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks, knowing that a dispute had been lawfully settled by the harmonious Saṅgha, said: "This dispute has not been settled by arbitration, has not been properly settled by arbitration — it must be settled by arbitration again."

"This dispute has not been investigated, has not been properly investigated — it must be investigated again. This dispute has not been pacified, has not been properly pacified — it must be pacified again." In this way they again cause weariness with the act. When monks repeatedly pacify disputes, they have many duties and many things to do, and this causes them to neglect recitation of scripture, reading, chanting, meditation practice, contemplation of meaning, and the inner calm abiding of the mind.

Monks of few concerns — why should monks, knowing that a dispute has been lawfully settled by the harmonious Saṅgha, saying "This dispute has not been settled by arbitration, has not been properly settled by arbitration — it must be settled by arbitration again; this dispute has not been investigated, has not been properly investigated — it must be investigated again; this dispute has not been pacified, has not been properly pacified — it must be pacified again," again cause weariness with the act? — reproach them, revile them, spread slander about them.

At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this occasion and this circumstance, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddhas, knowing full well, act without feigning ignorance — and so forth as before.

The Blessed Buddha reprimanded the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you, knowing that a dispute has been lawfully settled by the harmonious Saṅgha, again cause weariness with the act?"

"Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed Buddha censured them: "This is not in conformity with the conduct of a renunciant, is not befitting, is not appropriate, is not in accord with proper conduct — it is not something to be done by one who has gone forth."

Having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Therefore, having seen ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If any monk, knowing that a dispute has been lawfully settled by the harmonious Saṅgha, again causes weariness with the act, he commits a transgression."

"Any monk" refers to the group of six or any other of that sort. "The Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. "Harmonious" means harmonious in intention. "Lawfully" means in accordance with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the teaching of the Teacher as it is. "Dispute" refers to the four disputes: dispute for the sake of quarreling, dispute for the sake of teaching, dispute on account of transgressions, and dispute on account of affairs. "Settled" means pacified and brought to rest. "Knowing" means either recognizing this oneself or having been told by others. "If he again causes weariness with the act" means if he does so again. "He commits a transgression" means it burns him, boils him, and causes him to fall into the hells of sentient beings, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower realms, and into the states of wrong downfall. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and individually confessed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — that is why it is said "he commits a transgression."

As to how this becomes a transgression:

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting as a quarrel undertaken for some other purpose, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of not advising, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of causing a downfall as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression.

If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of fighting, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk, perceiving a quarrel undertaken for the sake of an act as a quarrel undertaken for the sake of a transgression, perceives what has been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he is doubtful about what has been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he commits a transgression. If he perceives what has not been purified by confession as having been purified by confession, and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he is doubtful about what has not been purified by confession and yet again causes weariness with that act, he incurs a wrongdoing.

These are the five kinds of persons: one who is present from the beginning, one who performs the act, one who presents a motion, one who states a view, and one who arrives suddenly. Of these, who is the person present from the beginning? It is one who knows the beginning, the middle, and the end of that quarrel. Who is the person who performs the act? It is one who has performed an act in order to bring that quarrel to peace. Who is the person who presents a motion? It is one who has presented a motion in order that act to be performed. Who is the person who states a view? It is one who has stated his own view with respect to that quarrel. Who is the person who arrives suddenly? It is one who does not know the beginning, the middle, or the end of that quarrel.

Of these, the first three persons — the one present from the beginning, the one who performs the act, and the one who presents a motion — if those three, knowing that the quarrel has been resolved in accordance with the Dharma by a harmonious Saṅgha, yet again cause weariness with that act, they commit a transgression. The last two persons — the one who states a view and the one who arrives suddenly — if those two, knowing that the quarrel has been resolved in accordance with the Dharma by a harmonious Saṅgha, yet again cause weariness with that act, they incur a wrongdoing. There is no transgression for one who is acting for the first time, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations. The fourth transgression of causing weariness is complete.

The blessed Buddha (Bhagavān) was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Cārkāśa was skilled in the science of signs and marks. One morning he put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and Dharma robe, and went out to beg alms in Śrāvastī. He went to the homes of brahmins and householders, taught the Dharma, and having taught the Dharma, asked the daughter-in-law: "Sister, what is your daughter-in-law like?" She replied: "Noble one, she is like a rabbit struck by an arrow." Cārkāśa said: "Sister, do you consider that a fault of hers? She has flesh wounds, pimples, moles, red marks, and curling hairs from the tops of her breasts down to her navel and from her navel down to her waist — that is her fault." After that, he went to the daughter-in-law's room and asked: "Sister, what is your mother-in-law like?" She replied: "Noble one, her faults are that she is polished smooth as fine silk, yet lazy, incapable of effort, fierce, harsh, and given to abuse." Cārkāśa said: "Sister, do you consider that a fault of hers?"

She has, in those very regions from the tops of her breasts down to her navel and from her navel down to her waist, the definite marks of auspicious signs: vases full to the brim, marks of good fortune, and swastikas. These, therefore, are her qualities." Afterwards, he went to the daughter-in-law's room and asked: "Sister, what is your mother-in-law like?" "Noble one, she is just as a daughter or younger sister would be described." "Sister, those are not her qualities. For she has, in those very regions from the tops of her breasts down to her navel and from her navel down to her waist, the definite marks: vases full to the brim, marks of good fortune, and swastikas. These, therefore, are her qualities."

Then on another occasion, when those women were massaging, rubbing, and bathing one another, they began examining each other's private bodily marks. They observed auspicious and inauspicious marks exactly as the venerable Cārkāśa had described them. When a quarrel broke out among them, they began to speak against one another: "You too were speaking with her, or you were doing such and such with other men." "How shameful!" "But then, how would other men know the auspicious and inauspicious marks in the private regions of your body? If that is so, why does she not speak? You too were speaking with her, or you were doing such and such with other men." "How shameful!" "But then, how would other men know the auspicious and inauspicious marks in the private regions of your body?"

When they then sought forgiveness from one another, each asked the other: "Who told you?" "It was the noble Cārkāśa." "And who told you?" "It was the noble Cārkāśa." They then denounced him, saying: "The noble Cārkāśa deliberately set us against each other." They spoke ill of him, cast blame upon him, and slandered him. Filled with doubt, when the elder monks went on their alms round, those women asked them: "Noble ones, what kind of monk is the noble Cārkāśa, the bhikṣu?" "Sisters, he is a monk who went forth from a family of chanters and is endowed with moral discipline." "Noble ones, if he is a monk endowed with moral discipline, how did he come to examine flesh wounds in the private regions of women's bodies?" They replied: "Sisters, he knows the science of reading bodily marks, and through that knowledge he discerned these things." "Noble ones, would you really reveal everything he was looking for?" And so they denounced him, cast blame upon him, and slandered him.

At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then reflected: "Since all these slight faults and whatever else has arisen have come about from monks teaching Dharma in the domain of women, a monk must not teach Dharma in the domain of women." Having so reflected, he declared: "A monk must not teach Dharma in the domain of women."

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not teach Dharma in the domain of women, when monks went out on alms rounds, the women of those households said to them: "Noble ones, please teach us the Dharma." The monks replied: "Sisters, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The women then said: "If you will not teach us the Dharma, we will not offer you alms." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Dharma may be taught in five statements: 'Sisters, form is impermanent; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent.' " When monks went on alms rounds and the women of those households said, "Noble ones, please teach us the Dharma," the monks taught them the Dharma in those five statements: "Sisters, form is impermanent; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent." But the women said: "Noble ones, please teach us more Dharma." The monks replied: "Sisters, the Blessed One has for the time being permitted only that much." The women then said: "Noble ones, very well — we will also offer you a little in the way of alms." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Dharma may be taught in six statements: 'Sisters, the eye is impermanent; the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are impermanent.' " When monks went on alms rounds and the women of those households said, "Noble ones, please teach us the Dharma," the monks taught them in those six statements: "Sisters, the eye is impermanent; the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are impermanent." But the women said: "Noble ones, please teach us more Dharma." The monks replied: "Sisters, the Blessed One has for the time being permitted only that much." The women then said: "Noble ones, very well — we will also offer you a little in the way of alms." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "With a man present, you may teach Dharma to whatever extent you wish." When monks went on alms rounds and the women of those households said, "Noble one, please teach us the Dharma," the monks replied: "Sisters, bring along some man and come." The women asked: "Noble ones, what need is there of a man?" The monks replied: "Sisters, the Blessed One has laid down a rule of training that with a man present, one may teach Dharma to whatever extent one wishes." The women said: "Noble ones, that is good — we too will be very well concealed and well guarded, and the noble ones will be able to teach the Dharma without fear." So they brought a man and came, and the monks taught as much Dharma as they wished and then departed.

Now when the group of six monks went on alms rounds, they said to the women of those households: "Sisters, sit down — we will teach you the Dharma." The women replied: "Noble ones, please bring a man and wait just a short while." The group of six said: "What need is there of a man? There is a dog, a monkey, a calf, an old man lying on his back, a cripple, and a boy sitting here — what more of a man do you need?" And having said this, they taught them the Dharma and departed.

When senior monks of long standing went on alms rounds and the women of those households said to them, "Noble ones, please teach us the Dharma,"

the senior monks replied: "Sisters, bring a man and then come back." The women said: "Noble ones, is there not a dog, a monkey, a calf, an old man lying on his back, a cripple, and a boy right here?" The senior monks said: "Sisters, we do not teach the Dharma in the presence of a man like that. Who then is it that teaches you the Dharma in the presence of a man like that?" The women replied: "It is the group of six." And that is why it was said that the circumstances of those monks were as they were.

The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should seat a trustworthy man and then teach the Dharma as one wishes." The Blessed One had declared: "In the presence of women, one should teach the Dharma using five or six sentences." But when the group of six were teaching the Dharma using five sentences, they would deliberately proceed to a sixth sentence, and when teaching using six sentences, they would deliberately proceed to a seventh. The monks said to them: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that one should teach the Dharma using five or six sentences in the presence of women. When you teach the Dharma using five sentences, do you deliberately proceed to a sixth, and when teaching using six sentences, do you deliberately proceed to a seventh?" They replied: "Venerable ones, for whomever five sentences are appropriate, six are also appropriate; and for whomever six are appropriate, seven are also appropriate. Does teaching six or seven sentences consume all the food or drain all the drink? By what reason should it be prohibited?" The monks said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that in the presence of women one should teach the Dharma using five or six sentences — so why, when you teach the Dharma using five sentences, do you deliberately proceed to a sixth, and when teaching using six sentences, do you deliberately proceed to a seventh?" And they reproached them, rebuked them, and spoke ill of them, and the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in accordance with the precedent and the origin story, convened the community of monks — and so forth as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, pretended not to know" — and so forth as before.

The awakened one, the Blessed One, asked the group of six monks: "Monks, I declared that in the presence of women one should teach the Dharma using five or six sentences. Is it true that when you teach the Dharma using five sentences, you deliberately proceed to a sixth, and when teaching using six sentences, you deliberately proceed to a seventh?" They replied: "Blessed One, it is true." The awakened one, the Blessed One, rebuked them: "That is not in keeping with the conduct of a renunciant, it is not in accord, it is not proper, it is not consistent with the rule — such a thing should not be done by one who has gone forth." Then the Blessed One rebuked them in many ways and addressed the monks: "Monks, in light of this, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training should be established for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before.

"My hearers should recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk who, in the presence of women, teaches the Dharma using more than five or six sentences — unless a trustworthy man is present — commits a transgression."

Now, "any monk" refers to a member of the group of six or any other such person. "In the presence of women" means in the presence of a woman or a young girl who is capable of understanding fully the meaning of teachings spoken well or spoken poorly.

"More than five or six sentences" means that when teaching the Dharma using five sentences, one intentionally lets it spill over into a sixth; and when teaching the Dharma using six sentences, one intentionally lets it spill over into a seventh.

"The Dharma" refers to what has been spoken by a buddha or explained by a śrāvaka of a buddha. "Teaching" means expounding. "Unless a trustworthy man is present" means setting aside the case where a trustworthy man is present.

"Commits a transgression" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower rebirths, and the miserable states. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome Dharmas. Therefore it is said to be "a transgression."

As to how a transgression arises in this matter: if a monk is teaching the Dharma to women on an upper floor, he should teach the Dharma using five or six sentences. If while teaching with five sentences he intentionally lets it spill over into the sixth, he commits a transgression. If while teaching with six sentences he intentionally lets it spill over into the seventh, he commits a transgression. If, after teaching, he enters the middle level of the building and she follows behind him, saying, "Noble one, please teach the Dharma," he should respond, "Sister, the Dharma has already been taught to you." If she then says again, "Noble one, please teach the Dharma here as well," then here too he should teach using five or six sentences. If while teaching with five sentences he intentionally lets it spill over into the sixth, he commits a transgression. If while teaching with six sentences he intentionally lets it spill over into the seventh, he commits a transgression. The same applies equally to the ground floor, the entranceway, and the staircase landings.

When a woman of discerning character asks one question after another in order to settle a point, to learn, to request recitation, to inquire about a specific matter, to estimate the time, or to discuss offerings, there is no transgression. There is no transgression when a monk speaks as much as he wishes to say in response to a prohibition, or when he speaks in an abbreviated way or speaks quickly. There is no transgression for a first offender, for someone who is mad, for someone whose mind is disturbed, or for someone afflicted by painful sensations.

The fifth transgression concerning teaching is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks were reciting the Dharma in verse together with persons who had not received full ordination. This caused a high and loud noise to arise at the edge of the garden — a sound like the clamor of a great common crowd — like brahmins reciting their brahminic formulas, or like astrologers speaking in the place of calculation, and it became widely known. The Blessed One, at the edge of the garden, heard that high and loud noise, that sound like the clamor of a great common crowd. Having heard it, he addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is this high and loud noise at the edge of the garden — this sound like the clamor of a great common crowd — like brahmins reciting their brahminic formulas, or like astrologers speaking in the place of calculation?" "Venerable sir, the group of six monks are reciting the Dharma in verse together with persons who have not received full ordination. This has caused a high and loud noise to arise at the edge of the garden — a sound like the clamor of a great common crowd — like brahmins reciting their brahminic formulas, or like astrologers speaking in the place of calculation. That is what has become known."

"Ānanda, are monks reciting the Dharma in verse together with persons who have not received full ordination?" "Venerable sir, they are."

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and this founding case and this circumstance, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth as before. "The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, while knowing, act as though unknowing" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One then rebuked the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you are reciting the Dharma in verse together with persons who have not received full ordination?" "Venerable sir, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that this was not in keeping with the way of a renunciant, was not appropriate, was not fitting, was not in accord with proper conduct, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having rebuked them in many ways, spoke to the monks:

"Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk recites the Dharma in verse together with a person who has not received full ordination incurs a transgression."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to the group of six or any others of that kind. "Together with a person who has not received full ordination" — those who have received full ordination are of two kinds: monks and nuns; anyone other than these has not received full ordination. "In verse" means with simultaneous words, with words spoken first, with simultaneous syllables, or with syllables spoken first.

How is it simultaneous words? When a teacher recites "Avoid all evil" and the attendant at the same moment recites "Avoid all evil" — that is simultaneous words. How is it words spoken first? When, before the teacher has yet recited "Avoid all evil," the attendant recites "Accomplish all that is wholesome" — that is words spoken first. How is it simultaneous syllables? When the teacher recites the syllable "a" and the attendant at the same moment also recites "a" — that is simultaneous syllables. How is it syllables spoken first? When the teacher has not yet recited the syllable "a" and the attendant recites "a" first — that is syllables spoken first.

"The Dharma" refers to what has been spoken by a buddha or explained by a śrāvaka of a buddha. "Reciting" means leading someone in memorization. "Incurs a transgression" means it causes one to burn, to fall, and to descend into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, evil destinies, and places of miserable rebirth. Moreover, if that transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome phenomena; hence it is said to incur a transgression.

As for how the transgression arises: if a monk, perceiving a person who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous words, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, perceiving a person who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using words spoken first, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has not received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous words, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has not received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using words spoken first, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, perceiving a person who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous syllables, he incurs a transgression.

If a monk, perceiving a person who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using syllables spoken first, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has not received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous syllables, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has not received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using syllables spoken first, he incurs a transgression.

If a monk, perceiving a person who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous words, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, perceiving a person who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using words spoken first, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous words, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using words spoken first, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, perceiving a person who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous syllables, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, perceiving a person who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using syllables spoken first, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using simultaneous syllables, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt about whether a person who has received full ordination has not received full ordination, recites the Dharma with that person using syllables spoken first, he incurs a wrongdoing.

There is no transgression for one who stammers, or for one who speaks quickly. There is no transgression for one who causes another to join in a recitation, or for one who causes another to inquire into it. There is no transgression for one who publicly announces and then gives a Dharma transmission. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, or for one who is insane, or for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations. This completes the sixth section on transgressions related to recitation.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the forty-first fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Because certain monks had not abandoned their afflictions and were not free from attachment, they were causing the expulsion of offences in the Saṅgha, and some had gone astray in their conduct as they aged. When monks who were masters of the sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkā heard of this, they caused those offenders to restore the transgressions in accordance with the Dharma, and while those monks were observing their rehabilitation and conducting themselves in a manner to be approved, at the time of the Saṅgha's alms round, faithful brahmin householders said: "Those who understand what is precious also examine what lies nearby and gather up those precious things." And the elder monks who were undertaking the alms round on behalf of the Saṅgha also began the alms gathering for the Saṅgha. But the group of six, those pot-bellied ones, ate and remained seated. When others reproached them, the group of six heard this and said: "Friends, do you think that these others are providing for the Saṅgha with the Dharma of good conduct? Not so — these ones are the ones doing the work of those who have been suspended." When asked, "What have these others done?" the group of six replied, "They have done what should not be done with the hand, and they have done such and such." And they spoke ill of the circumstances even of those who were elders among the monks, saying: "If the situation of even the senior elder monks is like this, what will become of the situation of the middle monks and the junior monks?" They disparaged them, they spread slander, and they spoke maliciously against them.

Now the monks who were performing the restoration ceremony were, in the late afternoon, anointing the stūpas of the Blessed One's hair and nail relics with a soft, fragrant ointment. At that time the group of six questioned their fellow residents and attendants, saying: "Novices, where have your preceptors and teachers gone?" Those attendants replied: "They have gone to do meritorious deeds — they are anointing the stūpas of the Blessed One's hair and nail relics with a soft, fragrant ointment. You too should perform such meritorious deeds." The group of six then said: "Do you suppose they are anointing the stūpas of the hair and nail relics because they are people of good conduct? Not so — these are the ones doing the work of those who have been suspended." When asked what those monks had done, the group of six replied: "They did what should not be done with the hand, and they did such and such." And when the monks who had been performing the restoration ceremony arose from that transgression, the group of six then directed the novices: "You novices, do this and that." But those novices replied: "Why don't you do it yourselves? It is not fitting for us to do it." The group of six said: "If it is fitting for you to do it in this way, then why is it not fitting?" The novices replied: "Even so, we have already repaired that transgression in accordance with the Dharma." The group of six asked: "Who told you that?" The novices replied: "The group of six told us."

Thereupon certain monks of little consequence began to reproach, revile, spread slander, and speak maliciously against those monks, saying: "Why do these monks report infractions involving degrading offenses to one who has not received full ordination?" This matter was then reported by the monks to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared that this should be answered with the following words:

Who is without fault,
who is the person who does no wrong,
who will never be utterly bewildered,
who is said to be ever steadfast —
it is one liberated through perfect knowledge,
the fully awakened Buddha, the supremely knowing one.
That one is without fault,
that one is the person who does no wrong,
that one will never be utterly bewildered,
that one is said to be ever steadfast.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this as the occasion, and in these circumstances, convened an assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. And as before: the Blessed Buddhas know and yet feign not to know — and so forth. The Blessed Buddha then questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you reported an infraction involving a degrading offense to one who had not received full ordination?" They replied: "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that such conduct is unworthy of a renunciant, is not in accordance with the rules, is not fitting, is not in harmony with proper discipline, and is not something that one who has gone forth should do. After rebuking them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks and said that, seeing the ten benefits, he would establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk who reports an infraction involving a degrading offense to one who has not received full ordination commits a transgression." Thus did the Blessed One establish this rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

At Śrāvastī, a monk acted impulsively and —

There was a nun named Gsalma who behaved in households in such a way that the congregation of ordinary people would come to know of it and lose faith. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you shall appoint a monk to make individual announcements in households, doing so alongside the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma. A monk who lacks the following five qualities shall not be appointed to make individual announcements in households, and if he has already been appointed he shall be removed. What are the five? He goes with desire, he goes with aversion, he goes with delusion, he goes with fear, and he does not know which households have been informed and which have not. A monk who possesses the following five qualities shall be appointed to make individual announcements in households, and if he has already been appointed he shall not be removed. What are the five? He does not go with desire, he does not go with aversion, he does not go with delusion, he does not go with fear, and he knows which households have been informed and which have not.

"He shall be appointed in the following manner. Having prepared the seat and struck the gong, one shall properly inform the monks using the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, one shall first ask for consent. 'Venerable monk, called such-and-such, do you consent to making individual announcements in households, together with the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma? If you consent, say: I consent.'"

After that, one monk shall make the motion and perform the formal act. "Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear this. The impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma have been behaving in households in such a way that the congregation of ordinary people would come to know of it and lose faith. The monk called such-and-such wishes to make individual announcements in households together with the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma. If it is the right time and the Saṅgha approves, may the Saṅgha grant permission. The Saṅgha is appointing the monk called such-and-such to make individual announcements in households. The monk called such-and-such will make individual announcements in households together with the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma. This is the motion.

"The formal act shall be performed as follows: Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear this. The impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma have been behaving in households in such a way that the congregation of ordinary people would come to know of it and lose faith. The monk called such-and-such wishes to make individual announcements in households together with the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma. For that purpose, the Saṅgha is appointing the monk called such-and-such to make individual announcements in households. The monk called such-and-such will make individual announcements in households together with the impulsive monk and the nun Gsalma. Those venerable ones who consent to the appointment of the monk called such-and-such to make individual announcements in households shall remain silent; those who do not consent shall speak. The Saṅgha has consented and granted permission, and the Saṅgha has appointed the monk called such-and-such to make individual announcements in households. Since no one has spoken, it is taken to be so."

"Monks, I shall now establish the rules of conduct for a monk who makes individual announcements in households. The monk who makes individual announcements in households shall speak as follows: 'Venerable ones, hear this. There are those who disgrace households —

— those who disgrace households are of the following kind. Consider, for example, a prosperous rice field upon which an overwhelming hailstorm descends: that very rice is utterly ruined, wasted, and rendered unfit in an improper manner. Or again, consider a prosperous sugarcane field in which a disease called the red blight appears: that very sugarcane is utterly ruined, wasted, and rendered unfit in an improper manner. In just such a way, venerable ones, you should take note of the standard demonstrated by this monk and this nun. For this monk and this nun are, like a scorched barley-seed, possessed of a quality that makes them unfit to remain in this Dharma and Vinaya. Look to the elder monks, the elders: to the Blessed One, and to the Elder Kauṇḍinya, and to Vāṣpa, and to Aśvajit, and to Bhadrika, and to the Elder Yaśas, and to Vimala, and to Gavāmpati, and to Subāhu, and to Śāriputra, and to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and to Mahākauṣṭhila, and to Mahākappina, and to Mahākātyāyana, and to Nadī Kāśyapa, and to Nadāśvajit Kāśyapa, and to Gayā Kāśyapa, and to Kubjita Kāśyapa, and to Mahā Kāśyapa, and to Nandaka, and to Kimbila, and to Bhadrapāla, and to Rāhula, and to Svāgata, and to Upananda, and to Doṣāpratiyāta Rāhula, and to Sthavira, and to Upasthāyin, and to Vīmāṃsaka, and to Mahāpanthaka, and to Yaśodatta, and to those and all the other elder monks among the elder monks — look to them!'

When the monk who makes individual announcements in households has gone out to make individual announcements in households, and a certain monk, having quickly heard that the Saṅgha has appointed the monk called such-and-such to make individual announcements in households, goes to him and says: 'Are you going to go and expose us in households? You should comply with the lawful instruction of the Saṅgha. If you do such and such, your belly shall be split open and your intestines shall be used to wind around the Jetavana, and as for your head, there is no reason why it should not be hung, like a vessel of sesame oil, at the gate of the Jetavana.' And having immediately denounced himself to the monks, saying: 'It was I who said to him: if you do such and such, your belly shall be split open and your intestines shall be used to wind around the Jetavana, and as for your head, there is no reason why it should not be hung, like a vessel of sesame oil, at the gate of the Jetavana — and therefore I am unwilling to go and make individual announcements in households' — at that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, that foolish person is capable of killing an individual, but he is not capable of killing the Saṅgha. Therefore the Saṅgha should make individual announcements in households. It should be done as follows: it should be carried out as a single-motion act of the Saṅgha. And it should be done in this way: having arranged the seats and struck the wooden signal-board, and having duly informed the monks with the proper words of inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, one monk should make the motion: "Venerable Saṅgha, please hear this. The monk called such-and-such and the nun called such-and-such have behaved in households in such and such a way as to cause the multitude of common people to become faithless and aware of it. The monk called such-and-such and the nun called such-and-such, having caused the multitude of common people to become faithless and aware of it by behaving in households in such and such a way, and the monk called such-and-such and the

nun called Gsal ma are eager to be proclaimed separately in households — if there is no one who is willing, and if the time is right for the Saṅgha and it consents, let the Saṅgha grant its permission. Let the Saṅgha separate the monk such-and-such and the nun Gsal ma, and wherever someone sees the monk called such-and-such and the nun called such-and-such behaving in households in such and such a way as to cause the multitude of common people to become faithless and aware of it, let that person, in that very household, take note of the extent of what this monk and this nun have been shown to be. This monk and this nun, like a burned-out grain-stalk, have qualities that make them unfit to be planted in this teaching and discipline. Look to the Blessed One and to the elder monks, the elders." This is the motion.

The Blessed One then declared that they were to be proclaimed separately in households that were known, and so they went about proclaiming separately in households. While they were proclaiming separately in households both in those that were known and those that were unknown, there came a time when they were reduced to want in their alms-rounds, and the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "They may proclaim separately in households that are known, but they shall not proclaim separately in households that are not known. Therefore, this is subject to the permission of the Saṅgha."

Thereupon the Blessed One, having spoken words of praise for those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who have proper equipment for training, and having given a teaching that was in accord with that, that was its greater part, and that was endowed with qualities befitting it, declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore what came before was the rule, and this is the permission. My hearers are to recite the following as the foundation of training in the Vinaya: furthermore, if any monk discloses a grave offense to one who has not received full ordination, except with the permission of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing expiation."

The term "any monk" refers to the group of six, or any others of that kind. The phrase "one who has not received full ordination" is explained as follows: those who have received full ordination are of two kinds — fully ordained monks and fully ordained nuns; anyone other than these has not received full ordination. The term "grave offense" is explained as follows: grave offenses are of two kinds — those that provoke a defeat, and those that provoke the remainder of the Saṅgha's offenses. Why are these called grave? Because of their very nature and because of the provocation they entail. The phrase "discloses it" means to speak it. The phrase "except with the permission of the Saṅgha" means that the Saṅgha's permission is set aside. The phrase "it is an offense entailing expiation" means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the states of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, into the wretched realms, and into states of wrong downfall. Furthermore, if that offense is not confessed and not individually confessed, it obstructs virtuous qualities — therefore it is said to be an offense entailing expiation.

As for how the transgression arises: if a monk, perceiving as unknown the households that are unknown, proclaims separately to a monk, an offense entailing expiation arises. If a monk, being of two minds about whether the households that are unknown are unknown, proclaims separately to a monk, an offense entailing expiation arises. If a monk, perceiving as unknown the households that are known, proclaims separately to a monk, a wrong deed arises. If a monk, being of two minds about whether the households that are known are unknown, proclaims separately to a monk, a wrong deed arises. When the announcement is made publicly by drum, there is no transgression.

When drawn as a picture on a surface, and thereafter, there is no transgression. If one thinks, "Just as I myself know it, so too does everyone in the world know it," there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, who is mentally disturbed, or who is overwhelmed by painful sensations. The seventh offense of declaring disgraceful conduct is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was residing at Vaiśālī, in the Peaked House in the Monkey Pool. At that time five hundred fishermen were encamped along the banks of the delightful river. Among them there were two nets called the Standard Net and the Great Net. Sometimes they would cast the Standard Net, and sometimes they would cast the Great Net.
