When there were no fish to be bought, they would cast the Standard Net; and when there were fish to be bought, they would cast the Great Net. Then on a certain occasion a festival arose at Vaiśālī, and they cast both nets together — two hundred and fifty men casting the Standard Net, and two hundred and fifty men casting the Great Net. Those who had cast the Standard Net piled up great heaps of fish, tortoises, frogs, young crocodiles, catfish, and many other creatures, like great mounds of sesame, thick rice porridge, pine needles, and beans heaped up together. Those who had cast the Great Net caught a creature that had entered the delightful river from the great ocean — a huge creature of the crocodile-fish species, as large as a donkey lying down — and they began to haul it in. When they hauled it, it awoke, and carrying the two hundred and fifty fishermen along with the Great Net, it plunged off in the direction of the current. Those fishermen called out to the other two hundred and fifty fishermen: "Friends, the Great Net and we ourselves are being carried away — turn back and help!" Hearing this, the other two hundred and fifty fishermen also hurried over and applied themselves to the same task, yet even so all five hundred fishermen, together with the Great Net, were carried off in the direction of the current and could not hold it. Helpless, they called out on all sides: "Friends, the Great Net and we are being carried away — come to our aid, turn back!" Herdsmen tending cattle and livestock who had not witnessed the event, woodcutters, grass cutters, those who earned their living on the roads, those who earned their living by detours, and many hundreds of thousands of other living beings turned back, and by battering and striking it with their bodies the net was torn and badly torn, until that creature of the crocodile-fish species was pulled from the water onto dry land. It had eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes. Among its heads, some resembled the head of an elephant, some the head of a horse, some the head of a she-camel, the head of a donkey, the head of a bull, the head of a monkey, the head of a lion, the head of a tiger, the head of a bear, the head of a yak, the head of a snake, the head of a cat, the head of a goat, the head of a sheep, the head of a deer, the head of a buffalo, the head of a pig, and the head of a dog. Word spread everywhere among the five hundred fishermen along the banks of the delightful river that the Great Net had caught a huge creature of the crocodile-fish species — as large as a donkey lying down — that had entered the delightful river from the great ocean, that it had been pulled from the water onto dry land, and that it had eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes. Hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered on the banks of the delightful river.

Some were struck with wonder at the sight. Others were stirred by the roots of virtue they had planted in former lives. The six teachers, Pūraṇa and the rest, who were dwelling and residing in Vaiśālī, were likewise seized with curiosity and came there. The great crowd of people was filled with amazement, staring wide-eyed, and those with discernment began to examine and discuss it: "Some of the heads on this creature resemble the head of an elephant," they said, "and then they went on to examine it further. Others said, "Some of the heads resemble the head of a dog, and then from that they examined further."

Now, since the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess not even the slightest trace of unknowing, unseeing, ignorance, or failure of clear comprehension — from that point up to the Blessed One causing those five hundred fishermen to go forth and receiving their full ordination, all of this is to be set out in full in the manner already taught in the earlier section on the fourth case of defeat.

Then at another time, those five hundred monks on the banks of the delightful river, delighting in, striving at, and applying themselves to their practice of robes and bowl, dwelling alone in seclusion, heedful, composed, and self-contained — for the sake of that very purpose on account of which young men of good family shave off hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from home into homelessness through faith in nothing but the truth — had in that very lifetime, through their own direct knowledge, directly realized and accomplished the supreme pinnacle of the holy life, and had come to understand: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is nothing more beyond this existence." They had become arhats, free from attachment to the three realms, with minds equal toward a clod of earth and toward gold, equal in their regard for sky and for the palm of a hand, who, like sandalwood set out for use, had split open the cave of existence through insight, and who had attained insight, direct knowledge, and individual perfect understanding. They had turned their backs on existence, on the gains of desire, and on honors, and were worthy of veneration, reverence, and open praise by the gods — both those with faculties and those accompanied by their lesser faculties.

At that time there was a terrible famine in the wilderness, and even parents found it exceedingly difficult to feed their own children — to say nothing of what had come to pass for wandering beggars who had difficulty obtaining food. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, now there is a terrible famine in the wilderness; wandering beggars find it difficult to obtain food, and even parents find it exceedingly difficult to feed their own children — still less what has come about for beggars. Therefore, monks, come here and, with such invitation as is fitting, with such words of welcome as are fitting, and with such companionship as is fitting, agree to spend the rains retreat in the village of Śoṅgyeday on the outskirts of Vaiśālī. I too shall accept the invitation to spend the rains retreat here in this very village of Odmachen, together with the venerable Ānanda who is attending me. It would not be proper for all of you to be troubled by going on alms rounds."

The monks replied, "Venerable sir, we shall do as you have commanded," and having heard this from the Blessed One, they accepted the invitation to spend the rains retreat in the village of Śoṅgyeday on the outskirts of Vaiśālī, with such invitation as was fitting, with such words of welcome as were fitting, and with such companionship as was fitting. The Blessed One too accepted the invitation to spend the rains retreat in that very village of Odmachen together with the venerable Ānanda who was attending him.

Thereupon those five hundred monks thought to themselves: "Since the Blessed One has given this instruction, there is no relative of ours here, but our relatives are settled in the fishermen's village. Let us go to the fishermen's village, visit our relatives, and spend the rains retreat in the environs of the fishermen's village for a year, along with the leaves and —

— flowers and leaf-huts for the rains retreat, without fail."

Then those five hundred monks on the bank of the delightful river thought to themselves: "In the past, when we went to the fishermen's village and visited our relatives, we proclaimed to one another's relatives qualities that were not genuine. Now let us proclaim to one another genuine qualities." With that thought, those five hundred monks went to the fishermen's village, visited their relatives, and formally undertook the rains retreat in the environs of the fishermen's village, making leaf-huts of leaves and flowers.

When their relatives came to visit them, the monks said to those relatives who had come: "Relatives, those relatives in whose village a community of monks has undertaken the rains retreat in a place worthy of offerings in such a manner as this — those relatives have obtained good fortune indeed. For this monk has attained the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of no-self in what is suffering, the perception of disenchantment with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of fault, the perception of abandonment, the perception of freedom from attachment, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of the bloated corpse, the perception of the festering corpse, the perception of the livid corpse, the perception of the gnawed corpse, the perception of the devoured corpse, the perception of the blood-stained corpse, the perception of the scattered corpse, the perception of the skeleton, and the perception that individually examines emptiness. This monk has attained the first meditative concentration, the second, the third, and the fourth; loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning; the domain of miraculous powers, the divine ear, thorough knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of all defilements. This monk is accomplished in the eight liberations of an arhat. This monk is one who is liberated in both respects."

The relatives said to them: "Noble ones, have you yourselves attained such an accumulation of qualities?" "We have." The world delights in qualities, and so the relatives, taking even from their own children, resolved to give alms to the monks.

Now, while a buddha, a Blessed One, is alive, dwelling, living, and abiding, it is by the very nature of things that there are two great assemblies of śrāvakas: the first is at the time of approaching the rains retreat at the full moon of the middle summer month, and the second is at the full moon of the middle autumn month. Those who, having received instruction at the time of approaching the rains retreat at the full moon of the middle summer month, undertake the rains retreat in villages, towns, districts, and royal residences — when the full moon of the middle autumn month comes around, they report what they have attained and undertake to mix together in fellowship for the sake of attaining what they have not yet attained.

Then those monks who had undertaken the rains retreat in the villages surrounding Vaiśālī, when the three months of the rains had passed, possessed of Dharma-robes and holding their Dharma-robes, thin, humble, lean, and dried out, their bodies fallen away, with their almsbowls —

— holding their Dharma-robes, they wandered and walked toward that place, Vaiśālī. As they wandered and walked along, stage by stage, they arrived at the town of Vaiśālī. And the Venerable Ānanda saw those very many monks from a great distance. Seeing them, and delighted with those who dwell in the holy life (brahmacarya), he welcomed them with warm and friendly words, and took their almsbowls, Dharma-robes, carrying-straps, head-cloths, round pouches for pouring over the head, vessels of oil and grain, hats, worn-out sandals, and leather sandals, and spoke these words as well: "Welcome, venerable ones! Come, come! Venerable ones, from where have you come here just now? Where did you undertake the rains retreat?" "Venerable Ānanda, we have come here from the village of Spongbyed. We undertook the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed." "Venerable ones, did you undertake the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed in comfort and ease? Were you not wearied by the alms-round?" "Venerable Ānanda, we did indeed undertake the rains retreat in the village of Spongbyed in some comfort and ease, but we were wearied by the alms-round." "Venerable ones, it appears to be so. For thus, harassed and exhausted by the alms-round, you have become thin, humble, lean, and dried out, your bodies fallen away, your skin, flesh, and blood depleted."

Now those monks who had undertaken the rains retreat in the villages surrounding the fishermen's village — they too, when the three months of the rains had passed, possessed of Dharma-robes and holding their Dharma-robes, their complexions, skin, flesh, and blood full and flourishing, holding their almsbowls and Dharma-robes, wandered and walked toward that place, Vaiśālī. As they wandered and walked along, stage by stage, they arrived at the town of Vaiśālī. And the Venerable Ānanda saw those very many monks from a great distance. Seeing them, and delighted with those who dwell in the holy life, he welcomed them with warm and friendly words, and took their almsbowls, Dharma-robes, carrying-straps, head-cloths, round pouches for pouring over the head, vessels of oil and grain, hats, worn-out sandals, and leather sandals, and spoke these words as well: "Welcome, venerable ones! Come, come! Venerable ones, from where have you come here just now? Where did you undertake the rains retreat?" "Venerable Ānanda, we have come here from the fishermen's village. We undertook the rains retreat in the fishermen's village." "Venerable ones, did you undertake the rains retreat in the fishermen's village in comfort and ease? Were you not wearied by the alms-round?" "Venerable Ānanda, we undertook the rains retreat in the fishermen's village in full comfort and ease, and we were not wearied by the alms-round either." "Venerable ones, it appears to be so indeed. For thus, free from the trouble of the alms-round, your complexions, skin, flesh, and blood have become full and flourishing."

"Venerable ones, right now there is a terrible famine, a place of desolation fit for wandering ascetics, where food is hard to come by, and parents find it difficult even to feed their own children — to say nothing of wandering mendicants, how much more would anything further be needed. Here then, venerable ones, what was the cause and what was the condition for your having been free from the trouble of the alms-round?"

"Venerable Ānanda, among us, in the presence of our relatives, we proclaimed one another's genuine qualities, each the qualities of the other, saying: 'This monk has the perception of impermanence, and the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of selflessness in what is suffering, and the perception of what is adverse in food, and —'"

the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of danger, the perception of abandonment, the perception of freedom from attachment, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of the bloated, the perception of the festering, the perception of the worm-infested, the perception of the gnawed, the perception of the eaten, the perception of the blood-smeared, the perception of the scattered, the perception of bones, and the perception that individually examines everything as empty. This monk had attained the first meditative concentration (dhyāna), the second, the third, and the fourth, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-return, the domain of supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of previous lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the attainment of the exhaustion of all defilements. This monk was one who meditates on the eight liberations of an arhat. This monk was one liberated in both respects.' In this way they proclaimed one another's genuine qualities. Was this proclamation genuine or not genuine? It was genuine. Venerable ones, is it permissible to declare the supreme human Dharma — a truth — to one who has not received full ordination? It may be permissible, and it may be impermissible; yet we spoke as we did. Why do monks of few virtues censure, rebuke, and slander other monks, saying they declared the supreme human Dharma — a truth — to one who has not received full ordination? At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident and with this as the basis of the case, assembled the community of monks — and so forth, exactly as before. The Awakened Blessed Ones, though knowing, cause it to be asked — and so forth, also as before. The Awakened Blessed One questioned the monks who were dwelling on the banks of the delightful river: "Is it true, monks, that you declared the supreme human Dharma — a truth — to one who has not received full ordination?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Awakened Blessed One rebuked lack of effort, lack of application, and acting without due reflection. Then the Blessed One praised effort, application, and acting with due reflection, and declared to the monks: "Monks, having rightly seen the ten benefits, one should lay down the rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, exactly as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, whatever monk declares the supreme human Dharma — a truth — to one who has not received full ordination, that constitutes a transgression.

Now, 'whatever monk' refers to one who belongs to this teaching. 'One who has not received full ordination' — full ordination here is of two kinds: a fully ordained monk and a fully ordained nun; anyone other than these has not received full ordination. 'The supreme human Dharma' (uttaramanuṣyadharma) means the nirvāṇa of human beings — the state attained by humans, but not attained by those who are neuter, hermaphrodites, or persons of indeterminate sex; and as for hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, that goes without saying.

"Superior" means: the form realm is superior to the desire realm, and the formless realm is superior to the form realm. Alternatively, "the human Dharma" refers to the five hindrances, and "the superior" refers to the abandonment of those hindrances. "True" means that the thing in question is genuinely real. "If one speaks" means if one utters it. "That constitutes a transgression" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the states of woe — into the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, the lower destinies, and the realms of utter downfall. Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and not individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and that is why it is said to constitute a transgression.

Now, as to how a transgression comes about, the intermediate summary states:

Without altering one's perception, in hermitages
and in households, spreading out one's seat,
claiming one's own distinguishing marks,
and presenting oneself as superior.

If a monk, without altering his perception, his patience, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I have seen the gods" — that constitutes a transgression. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "I have seen them" — that constitutes a transgression. Even if he says "I have seen the carrion-eaters of the charnel ground" — that constitutes a misdeed.

If a monk, without altering his perception, his patience, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I have heard the voice of the gods" — that constitutes a transgression. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "I have heard their voice" — that constitutes a transgression. Even if he says "I have heard the voice of the charnel-ground carrion-eaters" — that constitutes a misdeed.

If a monk, without altering his perception, his patience, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I am going to visit the gods" — that constitutes a transgression. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "I am going to visit them" — that constitutes a transgression. Even if he says "I am going to visit the charnel-ground carrion-eaters" — that constitutes a misdeed.

If a monk, without altering his perception, his patience, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "The gods are coming to see me" — that constitutes a transgression. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "They are coming to see me" — that constitutes a transgression. Even if he says "Even the charnel-ground carrion-eaters are coming to see me" — that constitutes a misdeed.

If a monk, without altering his perception, his patience, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I converse with the gods, I speak with them as they arrive, I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a transgression. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "I converse with them, I speak with them as they arrive, I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a transgression. Even if he says "I converse with the charnel-ground carrion-eaters, I speak with them as they arrive —

I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a transgression. If a monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "The gods converse with me, they speak with me as they arrive, I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a downfall. From nāgas and yakṣas, continuing in the same way down through putrefying corpses — if he says "I converse with them, I speak with them as they arrive, I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a downfall. Even if he says "I converse with the charnel-ground carrion-eaters, I speak with them as they arrive, I take delight in them individually, and I dwell together with them constantly" — that constitutes a transgression. If a monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "While still in the process of attaining, I have attained the perception of impermanence" — that constitutes a downfall. From the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, continuing in the same way down through the perception that individually discerns emptiness — if he says "I have attained it" — that constitutes a downfall. If a monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "While still in the process of attaining, I have attained the first meditative concentration" — that constitutes a downfall. Likewise for the second, third, and fourth, continuing in the same way down through claiming "I am an arhat, one who meditates on the eight liberations, and one who is liberated from both sides" — that constitutes a downfall.

Consider the following case: a great many monks are dwelling in a remote forest hermitage, and they are being harmed there by non-human beings. Among them there is a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and these non-human beings do not harm that monk. If another monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I too am dwelling in that remote forest hermitage, and the non-human beings there do not harm me" — that constitutes a downfall.

Consider the following case: a great many monks have been invited as guests to households and are being fed there, and in that place striped seats have been set out for them. Among them there is a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and a striped seat is offered in close attendance to that monk. If another monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I too have been invited as a guest to that household and have eaten there, and a striped seat is offered in close attendance to me as well" — that constitutes a downfall.

Consider the following case: a great many monks dwelling in a hermitage, relying on a small sign, a particular characteristic of the cause of calm abiding, suppress afflictions through a worldly path, such that attachment to sense pleasures and malicious intent do not arise pervasively in their mindstream. If a monk, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "I too am dwelling in that remote forest hermitage,

and while dwelling there, relying on a slight grasp of the particular characteristic that is a cause of calm abiding, through a worldly path I suppress afflictions, such that attachment to sense pleasures and malicious intent do not arise pervasively in my mindstream either" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who sees the gods" while not saying "That monk is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. If he says "There exists one who sees them" — ranging from the nāgas and yakṣas down through decomposing corpses, as before — while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And even if he says "There exists a monk who sees the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who hears the sounds of the gods" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. If he says "There exists one who hears their sounds" — ranging from the nāgas and yakṣas down through decomposing corpses, as before — while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And even if he says "There exists a monk who hears the sounds of the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who goes in order to see the gods" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. If he says "There exists one who goes to see them" — ranging from the nāgas and yakṣas down through decomposing corpses, as before — while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And even if he says "There exists a monk who goes to see the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk to whom the gods come in order to be seen" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. If he says "There exists one to whom they come to be seen" — ranging from the nāgas and yakṣas down through decomposing corpses, as before — while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And even if he says "There exists a monk to whom the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground come in order to be seen" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who converses together with the gods, speaks with them pleasantly, rejoices with each of them individually, and dwells together with them constantly" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And ranging from the nāgas and

and ranging from the yakṣas, just as before, down to the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground — saying "There exists a monk who converses together with them, speaks with them pleasantly, rejoices with each of them individually, and dwells together with them constantly" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. And even saying "There exists a monk who converses together with the flesh-eaters of the charnel ground, speaks with them pleasantly, rejoices with each of them individually, and dwells together with them constantly" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who has attained the perception of impermanence" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. Just as with the perception of impermanence, so also ranging through those who have, just as before, attained the perception of individual analysis of emptiness — saying this while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

If a monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who has attained the first meditative concentration" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall. Just as with the first meditative concentration, so also ranging through those who have, just as before, attained the second, the third, and the fourth, down to the monk who meditates on the eight liberations of an arhat and who is liberated in both ways — saying this while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

Now, in the following case: many monks are dwelling in a remote wilderness hermitage, and there non-human beings are harming them. In that place, there is a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, and the non-human beings there do not harm him. Then another monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk dwelling in that remote wilderness hermitage whom the non-human beings there do not harm" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

Here is another case: a great many monks are invited as guests to households and eat there, and in those places striped cushions are spread out for them. There, a monk who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat is made to clear away the striped cushions from that place. Then another monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk who is invited as a guest to that household and eats there, and in that place too is made to clear away the striped cushions" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

Here is another case: a great many monks dwelling in a hermitage, relying on even a slight degree of the characteristic mark of the cause of calm abiding, suppress the afflictions through a worldly path, such that attachment to desirable objects and ill will do not arise throughout their mental continuum. Then another monk, presenting himself in a certain way, without having altered his perception, his forbearance, his desire, his reasoning, his discursiveness, or his view, says "There exists a monk dwelling in that remote wilderness hermitage who, relying on even a slight degree of the characteristic mark of the cause of calm abiding, suppresses the afflictions through a worldly path, such that attachment to desirable objects and ill will do not arise throughout his mental continuum" while not saying "That is myself" — that constitutes a downfall.

This completes the eighth offense of speaking a superhuman quality of a person.

The Vinaya Analysis (Skt. Vibhaṅga), the forty-second fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka, in the Cool Forest. At that time, the venerable Gyabu Norné was appointed to arrange lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food. He was a person of faith, of good and virtuous intention, and he was diligent in the work of serving the Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma. There was nothing at all that he did not offer or fully give to the buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to the monks he approved of. Having offered and given in full in this way, his three robes were poor, made of patched cloth, and thoroughly worn out. The monks said: "Venerable ones, this venerable Gyabu Norné is a person of faith, of good and virtuous intention, and he is diligent in the work of serving the Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma. There is nothing at all that he has not offered or fully given to the buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to the monks he approved of. Having offered and given in full in this way, his three robes are poor, made of patched cloth, and thoroughly worn out. If the Saṅgha were to obtain some large bolts of cloth, let them be given to the venerable Gyabu Norné." Having said this, when the Saṅgha did obtain large bolts of cloth, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "If the request is made and then given, it will be unimpeachable. This is how it should be done: having prepared the seats, strike the gong, and having properly informed the monks with the words of the inquiry, once the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, let one monk make the request: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. This venerable Gyabu Norné, being a person of faith and of good and virtuous intention, is diligent in the work of serving the Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma. There is nothing at all that he has not offered or fully given to the buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to the monks he approved of.

Having thus offered and fully given in that way, his three robes are poor and patched and utterly worn out, while the Saṅgha is abundantly supplied with large bolts of cloth. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha grant this, and let the Saṅgha bestow a large bolt of cloth upon the venerable Gyabu Norné. This is the motion.

Later, after the Saṅgha had given him the large bolt of cloth, two monks — the monk Dzawo and the monk Salékye — who had had a connection with the venerable Gyabu Norné across many lifetimes, stood before the assembled monks and spoke critically, saying: "These venerable ones are in this manner, out of personal friendship, dedicating to an individual all the gains obtained by the Saṅgha at once. How could the Saṅgha's acquisition of gain possibly succeed in this way?" They reviled them, they stirred up trouble, and they spread malicious talk. At that time the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One assembled the Saṅgha of monks on account of this occurrence, this basis of discussion, and this occasion — and so forth, just as before. The passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, make inquiry" likewise proceeds just as before.

The awakened Blessed One then addressed the monk Dzawo and the monk Salékye: "Is it true, monks, that after having first properly consented, you subsequently said 'The venerable ones dedicated to an individual what had been dedicated as Saṅgha gain, doing so out of personal friendship,' and spoke in condemnation?" "Venerable One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One then rebuked them, declaring: "This is not the conduct of an ascetic; it is not fitting; it is not proper; it is not in accordance with the Vinaya; this is not what those who have gone forth should do." Then the Blessed One, having rebuked them in many ways, addressed the monks:

"Monks, therefore, perceiving ten genuine benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, just as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk, having first properly consented and thereafter saying 'The venerable ones, acting out of personal friendship, dedicated to an individual what had been dedicated as Saṅgha gain' — if he speaks in such a way, it is a transgression."

Now, the phrase "whatever monk" refers to either Dzawo or Salékye, or any other monk of similar conduct. The phrase "having first properly consented" means having previously offered assent. The phrase "thereafter" means at some other time. The phrase "saying the following" means if he says these words. Regarding the phrase "acting out of personal friendship," who counts as a monk's friend? The preceptor's friend is his co-resident; the co-resident's friend is the preceptor. The teacher's friend is the attendant; the attendant's friend is the teacher. The friend of one who shares the same preceptor is one who shares the same preceptor. The friend of one who shares the same teacher is one who shares the same teacher. A close companion's friend is a close companion. The phrase "Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the word "acquisition," there are two kinds of acquisition: acquisition of robes and acquisition of food. In this context, it is intended to mean acquisition of robes. The phrase "dedicated" means established within the Saṅgha. The phrase "dedicated to a person of mine" means for my own benefit. The phrase "it causes a downfall" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, and into the states of wrong falling. Furthermore, for as long as that downfall has not been confessed and individually confessed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. Therefore it is said to cause a downfall. As for how the downfall arises in that case: if a monk, having first made a small amount of preliminary and suitable preparation, subsequently says the following — "Venerable ones, having acted out of personal friendship, they have dedicated to the Saṅgha an acquisition, and I have dedicated it to a person of mine" — in every such case a downfall arises. If it is true that, having acted out of personal friendship, they dedicated the Saṅgha's acquisition and that he dedicated it to a person of his own, there is no downfall. There is no downfall for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is overcome by painful sensations. The ninth downfall-producing rule, that of calumny, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that the Prātimokṣa sūtra was to be recited each fortnight. When the monks were reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra every fortnight, the group of six, when the four defeats were being recited, remained completely silent. When the thirteen rules entailing suspension were being recited, they spoke as follows: "Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?" Likewise, when the two indefinite rules, the thirty rules involving forfeiture and downfall, the ninety downfall-producing rules, the four rules requiring individual confession, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for settling disputes were being recited, they again said: "Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?" The monks replied: "Venerable ones, we do not recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra for your sake; we recite it by the scriptural command of the Teacher. If it causes you suffering and mental discomfort, why do you engage in higher conduct? Why, with so little benefit, monks — when the four defeats are recited, you remain utterly silent; yet when the thirteen rules entailing suspension are recited, you say: 'Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?' "

And when the two cases of indeterminate offence, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules entailing confession, the four rules requiring individual acknowledgment, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes are recited, they speak in just the same way: "Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?" And so speaking, they disparage, they mock, and they slander. It was in this context that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, for this reason, and on this occasion, convened a gathering of the monastic Saṅgha — and all the rest proceeds as before. And the passage beginning "The blessed buddhas knowingly do what is uncharacteristic" also proceeds as before. Then the Blessed One rebuked the group of six monks: "Monks, when the four defeats are recited, you remain utterly silent; yet when the thirteen rules entailing suspension are recited, you say: 'Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?' And likewise, when the two cases of indeterminate offence, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules entailing confession, the four rules requiring individual acknowledgment, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes are recited, you speak in just the same way: 'Venerable ones, while there are cases where the matter is determined and the person can be clearly identified, why do you tear open our healed wounds? What use is it to those who have recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm?' Did you truly say this?" "Venerable One, we did."

The blessed Buddha then reproved them: "That which is not the conduct of a contemplative, that which is not fitting, not proper, not in accord with proper conduct — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth." Having thus reproved them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, having seen ten good reasons, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and all the rest proceeds as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Furthermore, if any monk, while the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited every half-month, says: 'What use is it to those, venerable ones, who cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm — that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the Prātimokṣa sūtra, which is recited every half-month, to be recited at all?' — if he denigrates the training in this way, it is a transgression."

The phrase "furthermore, if any monk" refers to the six groups of monks, or to any other such individual. The phrase "every half-month" means every half-month. The phrase "the Prātimokṣa sūtra" refers to: the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha, the two undetermined cases, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules entailing confession, the four rules to be confessed individually, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes.

The phrase "the sūtra" means either a discourse composed in connection with it, or else a properly compiled discourse. The phrase "while it is being recited" means while it is being formally taught. The phrase "says thus: 'What use is it to those, venerable ones, who cause the monks regret, anxiety, and harm — that these minor and trivial rules of training cause the Prātimokṣa sūtra, which is recited every half-month, to be recited at all?' — and denigrates the training in this way" means that with the intent to denigrate the training, one gives utterance through speech, words, common expressions, sounds, statements, definitive terms, the course of words, the sound of words, vocal action, and verbal communication.

The phrase "it is a transgression" means it causes one to be burned, scalded, and cast down into the hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of ruin. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression remains unconfessed and unacknowledged individually, it acts as an obstruction to wholesome phenomena — and it is for that reason that it is called a transgression.

As to how a transgression comes about in detail: when the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause the monks regret?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause the monks anxiety?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause harm to monks?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks distress?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks thorough distress?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks complete distress?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks regret?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks manifest displeasure?" — that is a transgression. When the four rules entailing defeat for a monk are being recited, if one says, "What use is it to recite these, venerable ones, which cause monks to wander in distraction?" — that is a transgression.

In the same way, when the thirteen rules entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha are being recited, and the two undetermined rules, and the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, and the ninety rules entailing confession, and the four rules to be confessed individually,

and the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes are being recited, if one says, "What use is it, venerable ones, to recite these, which cause monks remorse, mental distress, harm, anguish, deep anguish, thorough anguish, longing, manifest displeasure, and wandering in distraction?" — that is a transgression.

In the same way, when the monk's basic rules, the minor rules, the origin narratives, the supplementary sections, the fifth portion of the Vinaya, the sixth portion of the Vinaya, the Vinaya mātṛkā, and the other sūtras belonging to the Vinaya are being recited, if one says, "What use is it, venerable ones, to recite these, which cause monks remorse, mental distress, malicious intent, anguish, deep anguish, thorough anguish, longing, manifest displeasure, and wandering in distraction?" — that is a transgression.

When sūtras other than those belonging to the Vinaya are being recited, if one says, "What use is it, venerable ones, to recite these, which cause monks remorse, mental distress, harm, anguish, deep anguish, thorough anguish, longing, manifest displeasure, and wandering in distraction?" — that is a misdeed.

There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful feelings.

This concludes the tenth transgression entailing defeat in respect of the training — the undermining of the training.

A summary verse:
Scorning the seed, causing another to instruct,
the seat, the hammock, and the expulsion,
implanting that harm will come later —
these are arranged in two successive groups.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, an old, inexperienced, foolish, dim-witted, and unskilled carpenter caused a tree to be felled and had it used for building the Saṅgha's assembly hall.

The deity who had dwelt in that tree, being of exceedingly surpassing radiance, came to where the Blessed One was at the break of dawn that very night. Having arrived, she prostrated her head at the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. By the power of that deity's radiance, the entire Jeta Grove was suffused with a great, broad light. Sitting to one side, that deity addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, an old, inexperienced, foolish, dim-witted, and unskilled carpenter has cut down the tree that was my abode, my grove, my protection, my refuge, my ally, my resting place, my ground, and my support, and has had it used for building the Saṅgha's assembly hall. Venerable One, the winter nights are long; now in the latter part of winter, up until the eighth day, the morning frost rises with an unbroken sheen — and Venerable One, my children and little ones are young: how shall I manage for them?"

Then the Blessed One spoke to a deity: "Deity, grant this deity her dwelling in your own abode." That deity, by the command of the Teacher, granted the other deity her dwelling in his own abode.

Then, after that same night had passed, the Blessed One took his seat on the prepared seat before the assembly of monks. Having taken his seat, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, last night a deity of exceedingly surpassing radiance, at the break of dawn, came to where I was. Having arrived, she prostrated her head at my two feet and sat to one side. By the power of that deity's radiance, the entire Jeta Grove was suffused with a great, broad light. Sitting to one side, that deity addressed me thus: 'Venerable One, an old, inexperienced, foolish, dim-witted, and unskilled

person cut down the tree that was my home, my island, my protector, my refuge, my ally, my resting place, my foundation, my support — and has given it over for the building of a Saṅgha hall. Venerable One, the winter nights are long. At the time of the latter part of winter, in the days up to the eighth, the unmelted frost lifts in the early morning, and I do not know what I shall do for my children and infants when they are small.' On hearing this, the monks said: 'Alas, the monks who are disciples of the Śākyan are like this — they will be utterly ruined through virtuous qualities,' and they blamed them, derided them, and spoke disparagingly of them. That is ugly and unseemly."

Then the Blessed One reflected thus: "Whatever fault of any kind has arisen here, it has come about from monks cutting down trees." Having reflected thus, he addressed the monks: "Monks, for that reason a monk must not cut down a tree. If he does, it becomes an offence of grave consequence."

The Blessed One was dwelling in a pastoral district, in the finest forest of that pastoral region. The Blessed One having declared that a monk must not cut down a tree, the carpenters among the monks, having no timber, sent back refusals of work. The Blessed Ones, though knowing, act as though unknowing, and so the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why did the carpenter monks send back refusals of work?" "Venerable Blessed One, having declared that a monk must not cut down a tree, the carpenter monks, having no timber, sent back refusals." "Ānanda, I shall establish rules of conduct for the carpenter monks. When a carpenter monk is about to cut down a tree after seven or eight days, he should first make a maṇḍala at the foot of that tree, offer incense, flowers, and a torma, recite the third chapter of a tantra, proclaim its virtues, establish the paths of the ten virtuous actions, and also recite the discouragement of the paths of the ten non-virtuous actions. He should say this: 'Whatever deity dwells in this tree, let that deity seek another abode. This tree will be made to perform service for a stūpa, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.' After that, after seven or eight days, that tree may be cut down. If it shows signs of change, it must not be cut. But if it does not show signs, it may be cut. If a carpenter monk does not properly receive and follow the rules of conduct so established, it becomes an offence of grave consequence."

Now this was a matter that arose before the time: the Blessed One did not yet at this period establish rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group-of-six monks were themselves cutting down trees and causing them to be cut down, digging up green grass and causing it to be dug up, picking flowers and causing them to be picked. When other tīrthikas (non-Buddhist adherents) of learning learned of this, they said: "These monks who are disciples of the Śākyan themselves cut down trees and cause them to be cut down, dig up green grass and cause it to be dug up,

pick flowers and cause them to be picked. Brahmins and householders likewise, with their own hands, cut down trees and cause them to be cut down, dig up green grass and cause it to be dug up, pick flowers and cause them to be picked. So what difference is there between these ascetic disciples of the Śākyan, and these brahmins and householders? What intention is there? What distinction is to be made? Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed ascetics?" And so they criticized them, mocked them, and spoke ill of them. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this original ground, and this occasion, convened the assembly of the community of monks, and so forth, just as before. And "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign not to know," and so forth, also just as before. The awakened Blessed One questioned the group-of-six monks: "Monks, is it true that you yourselves, with your own hands, cut down trees and cause them to be cut down, dig up green grass and cause it to be dug up, and pick flowers and cause them to be picked?" "Venerable One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One then reproved them, declaring that this conduct is unbecoming of a renunciant, not in accordance with the teaching, not proper, not in keeping with the rules. Then, having reproved them in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya," and so forth, also just as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If one destroys or causes the destruction of a seed-community or the dwelling of a sentient being, there is a transgression. A seed-community is to be understood as five kinds of seeds: root seeds, stem seeds, node seeds, joint seeds, and the fifth, seeds that are themselves seeds proper.

What are root seeds? They include bladder campion, white turmeric, ginger, water lily roots, white atis root, and whatever else, when a root is planted, grows from that root itself.

What are stem seeds? They include the kañcana tree, the kapittha, the aśvattha (sacred fig), the udumbara (cluster fig), the nyagrodha (banyan), and whatever else, when a stem is planted, grows from that stem itself.

What are node seeds? They include sugarcane, cane grass, bamboo, sea-born plants, and whatever else, when a node is planted, grows from that node itself.

What are joint seeds? They include ārdaka, sarjaka, phaṇīnarjaka, bhustrina, jambhārī, and whatever else, when a joint is planted, grows from that joint itself.

What are seeds that are themselves seeds? They include rice, barley, wheat, large black lentils, small black lentils, mustard, and whatever else, when a seed is planted, grows from that seed itself.

As for the dwellings of sentient beings: the sentient beings in question are ants, flat insects, small insects, sesame-eating insects, snakes, scorpions, insects called treṃapuka, and trailataka. Their dwellings are trees and the like.

As for destroying or causing the destruction of these: this refers to uprooting, trampling, cutting, piercing, scraping, or causing to be scraped.

A transgression: this means a hell being, an animal,

a hungry ghost, an evil destiny, a bad rebirth, burning, scorching, and falling — it causes one to fall into these. Furthermore, so long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. For that reason it is called a transgression, so it is said.

Now, as for how one incurs a transgression in this regard, the intermediate rule states:

The five seeds and what damages them,
cutting trees, grass roots,
green plants, walking on vegetation, a line of grass,
fish scales, mushrooms, and dampness itself.

If a monk, thinking "May the seeds be damaged, may the seeds be utterly ruined," causes the five kinds of seeds to be put into fire, and the seeds are damaged and utterly ruined, he incurs five transgressions. If the seeds are not damaged and not utterly ruined, he incurs five wrongdoings.

The same analysis is to be applied in full to blue lotus, lotus, and the like.

If a monk, with the intention of causing vegetation to wither or to deteriorate, throws salt, a caustic substance, something heavy, or a needle in the direction of the vegetation, and the vegetation does wither and deteriorate, he incurs a transgression. If the vegetation neither withers nor deteriorates, he incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to stick it in, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing vegetation to wither or to deteriorate, scatters hot water, fruit juice, or legumes in the direction of the vegetation, and the vegetation does wither and deteriorate, he incurs a transgression. If the vegetation neither withers nor deteriorates, he incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to discard them, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing vegetation to wither or to deteriorate, walks through the vegetation, and the vegetation does wither and deteriorate, he incurs a transgression. If the vegetation neither withers nor deteriorates, he incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to walk there, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing vegetation to wither or to deteriorate, drags a branch, a bundle of kindling, or a rake through the vegetation, and the vegetation does wither and deteriorate, he incurs a transgression. If the vegetation neither withers nor deteriorates, he incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to drag it, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing cotton plants to wither or to deteriorate, walks through the area where cotton plants are growing, and the cotton plants do wither and deteriorate, he incurs a wrongdoing. If the cotton plants neither wither nor deteriorate, he still incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to walk there, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing cotton plants to wither or to deteriorate, scatters hot water, fruit juice, or legumes in the area where cotton plants are growing, and the cotton plants do wither and deteriorate, he incurs a wrongdoing. If the cotton plants neither wither nor deteriorate, he likewise incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to discard them, there is no transgression.

If a monk, with the intention of causing cotton plants to wither or to deteriorate, pours brine, applies a caustic substance, applies a heavy substance, or drives stakes into the area where cotton plants are growing, and the cotton plants do wither and deteriorate, he incurs a wrongdoing. If the cotton plants neither wither nor deteriorate, he still incurs a wrongdoing. If his intention was merely to drive in stakes, there is no transgression.

If a monk severs the sap-channel of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk pulls out the roots of a living tree, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk strips the bark of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk scrapes away the cambium of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk extracts the heartwood of a living tree, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk plucks the fresh leaves of a living tree, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk plucks the yellowed leaves of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk plucks the unopened flowers of a living tree, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk plucks the opened flowers of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk plucks the unripened fruit of a living tree, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk plucks the ripened fruit of a living tree, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk draws out fish scales, for as long as he has not removed them from water onto dry land, he incurs a wrongdoing; once he removes them from water onto dry land, he incurs a defeating offense. If a monk removes a fish nest, for as long as he has not removed it from water onto dry land, he incurs a wrongdoing; once he removes it from water onto dry land, he incurs a defeating offense.

If a monk picks mushrooms, he incurs a wrongdoing. If a monk picks puffball mushrooms, he incurs a wrongdoing.

If a monk disturbs a mold-covered earthen vessel, a spout, a pill, a piece of cloth, or the lining of a garment, he incurs a wrongdoing. If he makes it usable and then uses it, there is no transgression.

For one who is a novice, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is tormented by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

This completes the eleventh chapter on the defeating offenses of destroying seeds and growing things.

Here begins the Vinaya, volume Ja.

The Vinaya Analysis, the forty-third fascicle.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove of the Cool Forest. At that time, the venerable Gyabu Norgé had been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food. A friendly monk and a youth born of the earth — the venerable Gyabu Norgé — had harbored animosity toward one another across many lifetimes, and when the friendly monk and the youth born of the earth, together with a companion, were gathered in conversation, the venerable Gyabu Norgé arrived there. The two said to the companion: "Venerable companion, if you too were appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food, you too would be as highly regarded by us as the venerable Gyabu Norgé." The companion replied to the two of them: "You two — knowing full well which monk has been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food — are you affronting him to his face?" The two replied: "What, are we not even at liberty to whisper among ourselves?"

The monks of few wants criticized them, asking why monks who knew full well that a certain monk had been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food would affront him to his face, would slander him openly, and would speak ill of him behind his back. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, let the case of the venerable Youthful One and the Born-of-the-Earth — or of any others like them — be also classified as the offense of affronting to the face. The procedure for classifying it shall be as follows: after the lodgings have been arranged, the wooden sounding board has been struck, and the monks have been properly assembled by the prescribed summons, and when the entire Saṅgha is seated in harmony, one monk shall make the following motion: 'Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The venerable Youthful One and Born-of-the-Earth, while knowingly affronting to his face the monk — namely the venerable Gyabu Norgé — who has been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food, if the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha approve it. The Saṅgha hereby classifies the venerable Youthful One and Born-of-the-Earth as having committed the offense of affronting to the face.' This is the motion."

Now at the time when the Saṅgha had classified the two of them under the offense of affronting to the face, those two were again seated together with the venerable companion in conversation, when the venerable Gyabu Norgé arrived there once more. The two said to the companion: "Venerable companion, if you too were appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food, you would be as highly regarded among us as the likes of certain others." The companion replied to the two of them: "You two — knowing full well which monk has been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food — are you affronting him sideways, behind his back?" The two replied: "What, did we even mention anyone by name or clan?" The companion said: "If speaking ill behind someone's back is to be permitted without naming a name or a clan, then I could speak ill behind the back of everyone in the entire world without naming names or clans."

The monks of few wants criticized them, asking why monks who knew full well that a certain monk had been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food would speak ill of him behind his back, would slander him openly, and would speak ill of him to his face. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, let the case of the venerable Youthful One and the Born-of-the-Earth — or of any others like them — also be classified as the offense of speaking ill behind the back. The procedure for classifying it shall be as follows: after the lodgings have been arranged, the wooden sounding board has been struck, and the monks have been properly assembled by the prescribed summons, and when the entire Saṅgha is seated in harmony, one monk shall make the following motion: 'Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The venerable Youthful One and Born-of-the-Earth, while knowingly speaking ill behind the back of the monk — namely the venerable Gyabu Norgé — who has been appointed by the Saṅgha to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food, if the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha approve it. The Saṅgha hereby classifies the venerable Youthful One and Born-of-the-Earth as having committed the offense of speaking ill behind the back.' This is the motion."

Now at the time when the Saṅgha had classified the two of them under the offenses of affronting to the face and speaking ill behind the back, those two proceeded to affront the venerable Gyabu Norgé to his face and to speak ill of him behind his back, and —

Some monks of little virtue asked: "Why do monks, knowing full well that the Saṅgha has harmoniously appointed a certain monk to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food, affront him to his face, speak ill of him behind his back, spread rumors, and disparage him?" The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, with this as the basis for the rule, and on this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. The Blessed Buddhas act with full knowledge — and so forth, as before. The Blessed Buddha addressed the two monks, the Youthful One and Born-of-the-Earth: "You two, did you knowingly affront to his face and speak ill behind the back of the monk Gyabu Norgé, whom the harmonious Saṅgha had appointed to allocate lodgings and to oversee the distribution of food?" They replied: "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed Buddha then rebuked them: "That which is not the conduct of an ascetic, not in accord with the teachings, not fitting, not in harmony with the precepts — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth." And so the Blessed One rebuked them in many ways. He then declared to the monks: "Monks, seeing precisely ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth, as before. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If one affronts to the face or speaks ill behind the back, it is an offense entailing a transgression."

Now, "if one affronts to the face or speaks ill behind the back" means: with the intention of affronting or of speaking ill behind the back, one utters speech — words, terms, names, sounds, expressions, definitive statements, linguistic formulations, vocal sounds, and verbal declarations.

"It is an offense entailing a transgression" means: it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, states of woe, bad destinies, and downfall states. Furthermore, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome phenomena. Thus it is said to be an offense entailing a transgression.

As to how the transgression comes about: if a monk affronts to his face a monk who has been classified by the Saṅgha and formally appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has not been released from that appointment — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has been classified by the Saṅgha and formally appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has been released from that appointment — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has been classified by the Saṅgha but not appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has not been released from that appointment — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has been classified by the Saṅgha but not appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has been released from that appointment — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes an offense entailing a transgression.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has not been classified by the Saṅgha but who has been appointed as one of twelve persons and has not been released from that appointment — it becomes a misdeed. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has not been classified by the Saṅgha, who has not been appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has been released from that appointment — it becomes a misdeed. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has not been classified by the Saṅgha, who has not been appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has not been released from that appointment — it becomes a misdeed. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed.

If a monk affronts to his face a monk who has not been classified by the Saṅgha, who has not been appointed as one of twelve persons, and who has been released from that appointment — it becomes a misdeed. If one speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed. If one both affronts him to his face and speaks ill of him behind his back — it becomes a misdeed.

There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, who is mentally disturbed, or who is overwhelmed by painful feelings. The twelfth rule entailing a transgression through affronting is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Kauśāmbī in the grove of Ghaṇṭā. At that time the venerable Dundubha, having incurred a transgression, was not making amends for it in the proper manner. The monks who sought his welfare, who sought his benefit, who sought his happiness, who wished to reach happiness, who sought his accomplishment and happiness, said to him: "Venerable Dundubha, a transgression has arisen for you — make amends for it in the proper manner." He replied: "Who, when a transgression has arisen, will then make amends? When a transgression has arisen for you, who will make amends for it? Who will feel remorse? When a transgression has arisen for you, who will feel remorse? If a transgression arises for any of you venerables, do not come before me — go before someone else. You venerables have gone forth from various castes, various clans, and various households. Just as leaves from various trees, carried by the wind, fall together and settle together, so too have you gone forth from various castes, various clans, and various households — whereas my noble one has fully understood awakening."

When he made the monks who were instructing him stop up their ears in this way, some monks of few wants began to criticize, complain, and murmur, saying: "Why does a monk make the monks who are instructing him stop up their ears?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should count the monk Dundubha, and others like him, among those who stop up their ears against instruction. The counting is to be done in this way: having arranged seats and struck the wooden gong, having properly informed the monks with the words of inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in concord, one monk should make the motion: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The venerable Dundubha, having incurred a transgression, does not make amends for it in the proper manner. If the monks who seek his welfare, seek his benefit, seek his happiness, wish to reach happiness, and seek his accomplishment and happiness speak to him about this matter, and if he stops up his ears against the monks' instruction — if the time has come for the Saṅgha and if the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha grant it: the Saṅgha hereby counts the venerable Dundubha among those who stop up their ears against instruction.' This is the motion."

When the venerable Dundubha had been counted among those who stop up their ears against instruction, he thought to himself:

"Whatever fault has come upon me arose from my having spoken words to those monks." He recalled that someone had said:

A person endowed with wisdom
should guard all four aspects of speech.
Look at the fire burning the forest above —
observe how it is seized by the one who makes a sound.

He considered that this had been well said. Yet when the monks spoke to him he said nothing at all; he stopped up his ears against the monks' instruction. And when monks of few wants blamed him, reproached him, and spoke critically of him, saying, "Why do you, venerable, say nothing at all when the monks address you, and instead stop up your ears against their instruction?" — at that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should count any monk such as Dundubha, or any other like him, who says nothing at all and stops up his ears against instruction, among those who stop up their ears against instruction. This is how it is to be done: having prepared the assembly hall and struck the wooden signal board, having duly informed the monks with the motion formula and with the entire Saṅgha present and in agreement, one monk shall make the motion: 'Let the noble Saṅgha hear. The venerable Dundubha, though a transgression has arisen, will not rectify it in accordance with the Dharma. When monks who seek his welfare, seek his benefit, seek his happiness, wish to reach happiness, and seek his accomplishment and happiness raise this matter with him, he stops up his ears against the monks, saying nothing at all. If the time has come for the Saṅgha and if the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha grant it: the Saṅgha hereby counts the venerable Dundubha among those who stop up their ears against instruction.' This is the motion."

When the Saṅgha had then counted the monk Dundubha among those who both stop up their ears against instruction and say nothing at all and stop up their ears — he then stopped up his ears against instruction and said nothing at all. When monks of few wants blamed him, reproached him, and spoke critically of him, saying, "Why do you, venerable, stop up your ears against the monks' instruction and say nothing at all, stopping up your ears?" — at that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, in reference to this matter, on this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and everything else proceeds as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though they know, pretend not to know" — and so forth, also as before. The awakened one, the Blessed One, asked the monk Dundubha: "Monk, is it true that you stop up your ears against the monks' instruction and say nothing, stopping up your ears?" "Blessed One, it is so." The awakened one, the Blessed One, rebuked him: "What is not the conduct of a renunciant, what is not in accordance, what is not fitting, what is not conforming — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth."
