Having thus rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, perceiving ten benefits, a rule of training is to be laid down for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and everything else as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Stopping up one's ears against instruction is an offence."

As for the phrase "stopping up one's ears against instruction" — it means expressing, with the intention of stopping up one's ears against instruction, a speech, a word, a conventional expression, a sound, an utterance, a definitive statement, a path of words, the sound of words, a verbal action, or a verbal communication.

As for the phrase "is an offence" — it means hell-beings,

animals, hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, the miserable states, and the states of falling — it burns one, it scorches one, it causes one to fall. Moreover, for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. For that reason, it is called a transgression.

As for how it becomes a transgression: a monk comes before another monk and says, "Venerable sir, did you see a monk — one who had shaved his hair and beard not long ago, wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe, with an alms-bowl repaired with a hemp-leaf patch or bound around the neck with a withy, coming along with a bowl of melted butter, or a bowl of grain oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl of molasses?" And in reply the other monk says, "Venerable sir, I did not see a monk coming in that manner with a bowl of melted butter, or a bowl of grain oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl of molasses — rather, I saw a monk coming along on two feet." Should he speak in that way, it becomes a transgression.

A monk comes before another monk and says, "Venerable sir, did you see a nun — one who had shaved her hair not long ago, wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe, with an alms-bowl repaired with a hemp-leaf patch, coming along with a bowl of melted butter, or a bowl of grain oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl of molasses?" And in reply the other monk says, "Venerable sir, I did not see a nun coming in that manner with a bowl of melted butter, or a bowl of grain oil, or a bowl of honey, or a bowl of molasses — rather, I saw a nun coming along on two feet." Should he speak in that way, it becomes a transgression.

The same applies accordingly to a novice monk, a novice nun, and a female novice.

A monk comes before another monk and says, "Venerable sir, did you see a layman coming along with a load of sugarcane, or a load of bamboo, or a load of reeds, or a load of wood, or a jar of melted butter, or a jar of grain oil, or a jar of honey, or a jar of molasses?" And in reply the other monk says, "Venerable sir, I did not see a layman coming with a load of sugarcane, or a load of bamboo, or a load of reeds, or a load of wood, or a jar of melted butter, or a jar of grain oil, or a jar of honey, or a jar of molasses — rather, I saw a layman coming along on two feet." Should he speak in that way, it becomes a transgression.

A monk comes before another monk and says, "Venerable sir, did you see a laywoman whose garments were all blue, or all yellow, or all red, or all white, coming along with a jar of melted butter, or a jar of grain oil, or a jar of honey, or a jar of molasses?" And in reply the other monk says, "Venerable sir, I did not see a laywoman coming in that manner with a jar of melted butter, or a jar of grain oil, or a jar of honey, or a jar of molasses —

rather, I saw a laywoman coming along on two feet." Should he speak in that way, it becomes a transgression.

Whatever another monk asks, if a different answer is given to any of it, it becomes a transgression in every case. If one says nothing at all in response to any of those categories and simply ignores it by turning a deaf ear, that becomes an offense.

Now, someone fleeing from an executioner who is about to kill him comes to a monk and asks, "Noble one, did you see the one who is about to kill me?" If it is cold weather, the monk should say to the executioner, "Friend, enter the warm room and light a fire." If it is hot weather, he should say, "Friend, enter the cool room. Drink some water. Rest a while." If the executioner then says, "I am not cold. I am not hot. I am not thirsty. I have not stopped. I am asking about the one who is to be killed," the monk should look at his own fingernails and say, "I see my fingernails." He should look at the sky and say, "I see the sky." If the executioner then says, "I am not asking about your fingernails. I am not asking about the sky. I am asking about the one who is to be killed," then that monk, having looked in the four directions, should call to mind that all formations are without self, and then say, "In the ultimate sense, I see no sentient being." In so saying there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who speaks with care and for one who holds to wholesome remedies. There is no transgression for a novice, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The monks then made a request to the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable One, please look into the matter of the instances of turning a deaf ear by ignoring instructions, and of turning a deaf ear by saying nothing, that have been assigned in the case of those who live the holy life in the same community with the senior venerable ones and who do not listen to their words."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now, but in times gone by as well, this very failure to listen to the words of good spiritual friends led, through wrongful conduct, to suffering. Listen to this.

Monks, in a time long past, in a certain pond there lived one turtle and two geese. Then on another occasion, a drought lasting twelve years arose and began to dry up the pond. It is the nature of things that in the early age of the world, when it had not yet been long established, even animals could speak. So the two geese said to the turtle, 'Friend, the two of us are going to another pond.' The turtle said, 'Friends, take me with you and go.' The two geese said, 'How shall we take you and go?' The turtle said, 'I will grip the middle of a stick in my mouth, and the two of you take hold of each end and lift off.' The two geese said, 'Since you are one who wants to talk and cannot guard your words, we will not carry you — the two of us will not go with you.' The turtle said, 'I will guard my words.' So the two geese took the turtle and flew up into the sky above, and as they were passing over a rocky cliff, some boys and girls saw them and called out, 'Look, everyone! Two geese are carrying a turtle!' At that, the turtle was pleased with himself. Then as they passed over another rocky cliff, once more some boys and girls saw them and called out, 'Look, everyone! Two geese are carrying a turtle!' The turtle thought to himself, 'I must hold my dignity for as long as I am able,' and said, 'It is not the two geese who are carrying me — I am going of my own accord!' And with that he lost his grip on the stick and fell to the ground. Those below seized him and caused him suffering through wrongdoing. At that moment a god spoke these verses:

Those who wish to benefit a friend
and speak words of counsel — whoever does not hold to them
will fall and come to grief,
like the turtle that let go of the stick.

Monks, the eldest of the two geese at that time and on that occasion was myself. The other goose at that time and on that occasion was Ānanda. The turtle at that time and on that occasion was this very Dundupā. Even then, this one did not listen to the words of his good spiritual friends and, acting wrongly, fell into suffering. And now too, not listening to the words of those who live the holy life, he has been placed in the category of one who wears a censure on his ear — for saying nothing when a censure is pronounced is itself counted as wearing a censure on one's ear. This completes the thirteenth offense that occasions the wearing of a censure on the ear.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a certain householder invited the community of monks, with the Buddha at its head, to another house at midday. The community of monks went and took their seats. The Blessed One, however, remained behind in the building and engaged in his alms round. The Blessed One, the Buddha, had five reasons for remaining in the building and engaging in his alms round. What are those five? He wished to enter into inner composure; he wished to teach the Dharma to the gods; he wished to visit the sick; he wished to inspect the lodgings; and he wished to establish rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. In this instance, the Blessed One remained in the building and engaged in his alms round because he wished to inspect the lodgings and to establish rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Then, not long after the community of monks had departed, the Blessed One perceived this in his mind, took up his key, and passed from courtyard to courtyard, from shrine hall to shrine hall, from room to room, from walking-path to walking-path through the monastery, and proceeded on his way. Eventually he came to the shrine hall of a great house. At that time, in the shrine hall of that great house, very many bedding articles and cushions had been left out without cover, and a great unseasonable storm-cloud had gathered. The Blessed One saw the many bedding articles and cushions left uncovered in the shrine hall of that great house, and the great unseasonable storm-cloud that had massed. Having seen this, he exclaimed, "Ah!" and was displeased. He reflected thus: "Devout brahmin householders and laymen squeeze and press out skin and flesh and blood to give their gifts and make merit, and yet the monks enjoy these things without warmth of feeling and without discernment." Then the Blessed One, through his miraculous power, held back that great unseasonable storm-cloud. Through the exercise of that miraculous power it came to hover in the sky overhead like a water-pot, remaining at the edges while the greater part of it stayed still, directed toward the Blessed One. The Blessed One then covered those many bedding articles and cushions so they were protected, took up his summer robe of fine cloth, wishing to cool himself, and sat down upon the steps. Then the Blessed One, through his miraculous power, withdrew that very intervention that had held back the great unseasonable storm-cloud. When the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous power, thunder rolled and rain fell, filling every valley and plain to satiation. The Blessed One then cooled his body and washed both feet, and went into the shrine hall in order to enter into inner composure. Then a monk who had been out gathering alms returned with his alms,

went to where the Blessed One was. It is the natural way of buddhas, of Blessed Ones, to gladden individually each monk who has been out gathering alms by asking, "Monk, how was the food you gathered? Did you satisfy the community of monks?" And so the Blessed One did gladden that monk who had been out gathering alms by asking him, "Monk, how was the food you gathered? Did you satisfy the community of monks?" The monk replied, "Venerable One, the food was gathered in abundance, and the community of monks was satisfied."

Then, after the Blessed One had taken his meal, he washed both feet on the steps outside the shrine hall and went inside for the sake of entering into inner composure. Later that afternoon the Blessed One arose from inner composure and took his seat upon the prepared throne before the community of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, not long after the community of monks had departed, I took the key and went from pleasure garden to pleasure garden, from shrine hall to shrine hall, from dwelling to dwelling, from walking path to walking path, going about in a wandering way, gradually making my rounds, until I came to where a certain great shrine hall was. There I saw a great many beds and seats in that great shrine hall left uncovered, while a great unseasonable storm-cloud had gathered. Seeing this, I was displeased and thought to myself: 'The faithful brahmins and householders who give gifts, pressing out as it were their very skin, flesh, and blood in order to make merit — the monks consume what is given through faith carelessly, without mindfulness and without due reflection.' Therefore, monks, it is well if you consume what is given through faith with warmth, consume it with restraint, consume it in proper time, consume it with examination, and consume it with frugality."

The summary verse reads:

With warmth and with restraint,
likewise in proper time, with examination,
and with frugality one should consume.

Then, after the Blessed One had spoken in praise of consuming with warmth, with restraint, in proper time, with examination, and with frugality, he addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing these ten benefits, one should establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers," and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk leaves uncovered and unprotected — without collecting them or causing them to be collected — a seat cushion, a small seat, a mat with a cover, a mat with a fringe, a rug, or a cushion belonging to the community, and then departs from that place, that constitutes a transgression." Thus did the Blessed One establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

Now, a large number of monks who were of one purpose set out together to travel through a region, and when they had come to a certain cliff-face they began to make their lodging there. At that cliff-face there was a shrine hall, and someone said to them there, "Noble ones, will you not stay in the shrine hall? It would not be right to stay outside — we rely on your being of one purpose with us. If you were to stay in the shrine hall, being of one purpose might cause them to abandon us and go." That man said, "Noble ones, please go in and sleep in the shrine hall. At the time when your companions of one purpose arrive, I will come and rouse you, noble ones."

They went into the shrine hall, arranged their bedding, and lay down. Meanwhile, the caravan had set out, the last ox already loaded and on its way. Then that man awoke, went to the monks, and said to them, "Noble ones, the companions of one purpose have set out — come quickly! For as long as they are still stretching their limbs, discarding their tooth-sticks, and rolling up their bedding, the purpose is still shared. Follow along behind them." And as they were walking along behind, they were set upon by robbers, and in due course the monks arrived at the shrine hall. When they were seen by the monks there, the monks said to them, "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How have you fared? Did you travel well, venerable ones?" They replied, "We fared poorly. What has happened?" They said, "Venerable ones, we have been attacked by robbers." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "The matter is to be entrusted to the resident monks."

Having declared that it was to be entrusted to the resident monks, the Blessed One went on to speak of the following situation. In Śrāvastī, two householders were lodging together who had a quarrel with each other, one of them being a man of faith and the other faithless. The faithful one thought, "What is the use of prolonging this quarrel? Let me settle it, take leave of the household, and go forth." And so he went to the Jeta Grove and took ordination as a monk under a monk there. The faithless householder asked someone, "Where has that householder called Śīlabhadra gone?" The man replied, "He has gone forth." "Where?" "Into the community of the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyan." The faithless man thought, "Is that a city without danger? I shall go there too and do him harm." Now, in this world there are friends, enemies, and those who are indifferent, and so another man went to that monk and said, "That householder is hostile to you." The monk thought, "Whatever faults led me to go forth — those very faults have now followed me." He went to his preceptor and said, "Preceptor, the very faults for which I went forth have followed me here. Please send me away." "My son, where will you go?" "To Rājagṛha." "Then go." And so the monk departed for Rājagṛha.

The hostile householder arrived at the Jeta Grove and asked a monk, "Noble one, has the monk called such-and-such gone forth?" "He has." "Where has he gone?" "To Rājagṛha." The man thought, "Is that a city without danger? I shall go there too and do him some harm." And so he also departed for Rājagṛha.

A monk travels at proper times and not at improper times, while a layman travels both at proper times and at improper times. The monk had entered a cliff-face shrine hall, and when that householder caught sight of him, he thought, "If I say even a word to him here, his many monk companions will do me harm. Let me get to know him better tomorrow." Then the monk rose early in the morning and said to the monks, "Venerable ones, I am going — please keep this bedding for me," and he entrusted his bedding to them. The monks asked, "Where are you going?" "To Rājagṛha." "Venerable one, that road is dangerous — do not go by this road. There is another road; go by that one instead." He went by that other road.

The householder also rose early in the morning, went to the shrine hall, and asked a monk, "Noble one, where has the monk called such-and-such gone?" "To Rājagṛha." "Which way did he go?" "He went by such-and-such a road." The man followed after him, and when the monk saw him approaching, he said to him:

"Handsome one, be at peace!" The man replied, "Now I will make you be at peace!" — and with that, the householder beat the monk severely, smashed his alms bowl, tore his robes, and finally left him for dead. The monk barely survived; he recovered from near death and made his way back to that very shrine hall. When the monks saw him, they asked, "Venerable one, why have you come to be in such a state?" He then related the whole matter in detail to the monks, and added, "If I had not done as the venerable ones instructed me, I would not have come to be in such a condition." The monks thereupon reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Except in such circumstances." Then the Blessed One, having praised the desire for training, respect for training, and the placing of training above all else, spoke words in harmony with this, further elaborating upon it, and in accordance with it and what was most germane to it, he addressed the monks and declared:

"Monks, what came before was the rule; what is now established is the permission. My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk leaves behind, without covering, a seat — whether a high seat, a low seat, a cushioned seat stuffed with wool, a reclining seat, a mat, or a square cushion — belonging to the Saṅgha, either by abandoning it himself without putting it away, or by having another abandon it without having it put away, and who departs from there without entrusting it to a monk who is present — except in such circumstances, he incurs a transgression."

"Now, 'whatever monk' refers to one who is a member of this community. 'Of the Saṅgha' means of the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. 'A high seat' means precisely a high seat. 'A low seat' means precisely a low seat. 'A cushioned seat stuffed with wool' means one filled with wood-wool. 'A reclining seat' means precisely a reclining seat. 'A mat' means something spread out as a mat. 'A square cushion' means something four-cornered. 'Without covering' means without having it wrapped up. 'He abandons it himself' means by his own act. 'Having another abandon it' means by the act of another. 'Without putting it away himself' means by his own neglect. 'Without having it put away' means through another's neglect. 'A monk who is present' means whatever monk happens to be staying there. As for 'without entrusting,' entrusting is of five kinds: 'Watch over this shrine hall,' or 'Look after the shrine hall'; 'Watch over this lodging,' or 'Collect the bedding'; and 'Fasten the lock' — that last makes the fifth. If no monk is available, one may entrust it to a novice. If no novice is available, one may entrust it to a layman. If no layman is available, one should look in all four directions, hide the key, and then depart. If a monk is encountered along the road, one should say, 'I have hidden the key in such-and-such a place — please go and take charge of it.' 'Departs from there' means having left the vicinity behind. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Blessed One being present: 'Venerable one, what constitutes the vicinity of a monk's lodging?' Upāli said, 'I was born as a brahmin and was shown seven mango trees — each abundantly blossoming, richly fruiting, and lavishly branched, and spaced seven fathoms apart from one another — and it was indicated that among those seven trees there are forty-nine fathoms: that is the vicinity of a monk's lodging.' 'Except in such circumstances' means: with such conditions being duly set aside. 'He incurs a transgression' means: he is burned, scorched, and caused to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts, into bad destinations, into lower states of existence."

Furthermore, for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it creates an obstruction to virtuous qualities. That is why it is called a "causing of a downfall." Now, how does one come to incur such a downfall? Consider the following. If a monk leaves the Saṅgha's bedding and furnishings unattended and then departs, for as long as he has not removed what lies within the vicinity it constitutes a wrongdoing, and once he has removed the vicinity it becomes a downfall-causing offence.

If, while on the road, a monk recalls, "I have left such-and-such a piece of Saṅgha bedding or furnishing in such-and-such a place," and if he thinks, "My fellow practitioners of the pure life who are skilled will come to gather it," then that monk must generate the intention, expressed also in words, "I shall not do so again henceforth," and must properly confess that transgression according to the Dharma.

If, while on the road, he sees another monk approaching and thinks, "He will gather it," he should say to that monk: "Venerable one, please gather the piece of Saṅgha bedding and furnishing that I have left in such-and-such a place." And that monk must also generate the intention, expressed also in words, "I shall not do so again henceforth," and must properly confess that transgression according to the Dharma. The other monk, for his part, having accepted the request, must respectfully go and collect it. If he does not collect it, he incurs a serious offence.

If, upon arriving at the destination, a monk recalls, "I left a piece of Saṅgha bedding or furnishing in such-and-such a place," and if he thinks, "My fellow practitioners of the pure life who are skilled will come to gather it," then that monk must generate the intention, expressed also in words, "I shall not do so again henceforth," and must properly confess that transgression according to the Dharma.

If, upon arriving at the destination, he sees another monk about to set out, and thinks, "He will gather it," he should say to that monk: "Venerable one, please gather the piece of Saṅgha bedding and furnishing that I have left in such-and-such a place." And that monk must also generate the intention, expressed also in words, "I shall not do so again henceforth," and must properly confess that transgression according to the Dharma. The other monk, for his part, having accepted the request, must respectfully go and collect it. If he does not collect it, he incurs a serious offence.

If a monk has left the Saṅgha's bedding and furnishings unattended and then enters a temple, thinking either "I will now settle my unsettled mind" or "I will liberate my already settled mind," and enters it properly for the purpose of inward composure — and if he then rises from that meditative absorption at the first night-watch or at the midpoint of the watch — then, if the bedding and furnishings have not been put in order, it constitutes a wrongdoing; and if they have been put in order, it becomes a downfall-causing offence.

If a monk has left the Saṅgha's bedding and furnishings unattended and then enters a temple, thinking either "I will now settle my unsettled mind" or "I will liberate my already settled mind," and enters it properly for the purpose of inward composure — and if he then rises from that meditative absorption at the middle night-watch, or at the final night-watch, or before dawn breaks, or at dawn's breaking, or before sunrise, or at sunrise, or when an eighth part of the sun has risen, or when a quarter of the sun has risen, or before midday, or at midday, or when a quarter of the day remains, or when an eighth of the day remains, or before sunset, or at sunset, or before the stars have appeared, or when the stars have appeared — then, if the bedding and furnishings have not been put in order, it constitutes a wrongdoing; and

if it is in disarray, it constitutes a defeat.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend One, there are two kinds of disarray of bedding and furnishings: disarray caused by wind, and disarray caused by rain. What is disarray caused by wind? It is when things have been scattered and blown from one layer to a second. What is disarray caused by rain? It is when things have been soaked and muddied from one layer to a second."

Summary verse: teaching the Dharma, the invitation of guests, the assembly hall and hearing the Dharma, sitting and both of them together, an image and the sick, a seat and five and one becoming two, going behind another and accompanying, recitation and requesting, the offering of a seat and the cutting off of food, fumigation and entrusting, fire and water likewise. Brahmins and faithful householders came to the monks and said: "Noble ones, please teach the Dharma." The monks replied: "The Blessed One resides here. Go to the Blessed One today — the Blessed One will teach." The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, the Teacher is but one; for now he teaches the Dharma to gods, or to nāgas, or to yakṣas, or to gandharvas, or to human beings — whoever is teaching it, you too should teach." Upon hearing them say that the Blessed One had not permitted this, the monks appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it — monks too shall teach the Dharma."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks too should teach the Dharma, when monks were teaching the Dharma while standing and were surrounded by a great crowd of ordinary people, the faithful brahmins and householders said: "Have these ones come to offer gifts?" Thereupon the monks appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Sit down and teach the Dharma."

When monks took up their own individual seats and were walking along, and those without faith saw them and began to jeer, asking whether they were parading about like a troupe of musicians, the monks appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it — seats of the Saṅgha shall be placed in readiness." When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One had permitted seats of the Saṅgha to be placed in readiness, he donated five hundred thrones to the Saṅgha. When all of them were teaching the Dharma simultaneously and a commotion arose, the monks appealed to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One person shall teach the Dharma."

Since they did not know who among them should teach, the Blessed One declared: "Beginning from the elders of the Saṅgha and extending down to the most recently ordained, each shall teach the Dharma in turn."

When all of the most recently ordained were teaching the Dharma and all of the elders became discomfited, the Blessed One declared: "Let the elders sit apart and teach the Dharma."

When the elders of the Saṅgha became discomfited, the Blessed One declared: "Let two or three seats be arranged separately for the elders, and let the Dharma be taught from there."

When the Dharma teacher in that arrangement too became discomfited, the Blessed One declared: "Let two or three seats be arranged separately for the elders and a lion throne set up."

When the Dharma teacher found it difficult to ascend, the Blessed One declared: "If the direction is fixed, steps shall be made by the novices."

If the direction is not fixed, wooden steps shall be made.

When the Dharma teacher became discomfited by spitting, the Blessed One declared: "A spittoon shall be set out."

When insects gathered there, the Blessed One declared: "A cover shall be placed over it."

When the monks did not know what to place as a cover, the Blessed One declared: "Sand or ash shall be placed over it."

When it became foul-smelling, the Blessed One declared: "It shall be cleaned and dried from time to time."

When those seats, being arranged in a single row only, extended so far that those at the far end could not hear, the Blessed One declared: "The seats shall be arranged in two forms: either in the shape of a crescent moon or in the shape of a small pond."

When faithful brahmins and householders invited the monks as guests to another home and the monks did not accept, the faithful brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, at the time when a buddha had not appeared in the world, the non-Buddhists were worthy recipients of offerings. But now the Blessed One has appeared in the world, and you are the worthy recipients of offerings. If you do not accept, shall we pass from this world to the next without any virtuous roots?" Hearing this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Accept the invitation."

When those hosts wished to borrow seats after the monks had eaten and the monks refused to lend them, the Blessed One declared: "Lend the seats."

After the monks had eaten and were leaving, taking the seats with them, the hosts said: "Noble ones, please go, and we shall bring them back to you." The monks, out of reluctance, did not leave the seats behind, and the Blessed One declared: "Leave them."

When the hosts said: "Noble ones, we are thirsty — please wait here a moment until we depart," the monks did not stay, and the Blessed One declared: "Stay."

When because of circumstances like these the seats were not being brought back to them, the Blessed One declared: "Take them back."

After the Blessed One had declared they should take them back, the monks did not know by whom they should be taken back, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who are staying shall strike a small wooden sounding board and then take them back."

When faithful brahmins and householders came to the monastery and invited the monks as guests and the monks did not accept, the Blessed One declared: "Accept the invitation."

After the monks had eaten, when those hosts wished to borrow seats and the monks refused to lend them, the hosts said: "Noble ones, we have offered you a meal — will you not lend us your seats?" The Blessed One then declared: "Lend the seats."

When the hosts left those seats right there and departed, and some thieves stole them by taking what had not been given, the Blessed One declared: "A monk shall be appointed as guardian."

When a thief entered into the midst of those people and they said to him: "Noble one, do you need anything?" he replied: "I need nothing — I am guarding these seats." They said: "Noble one, do you think we are stealing your seats? If you have no suspicion, then be at ease and go." At this, the Blessed One declared: "One shall not enter into their midst but shall sit to one side. If one is a reciter, one shall recite and should also direct attention to that. If one is a meditator, one shall also sit to one side, cultivate mental application, and direct attention to that as well. When the time comes to leave, one shall strike the sounding board."

When those rattan seats became unfit for use on account of mother-of-pearl inlay, oil, excrement, and urine, the monks discarded them. The Blessed One then declared: "They are not to be discarded. Those that have become unfit on account of mother-of-pearl inlay shall be cleaned with water. Those that have become unfit on account of oil shall be cleaned with ash. Those that have become unfit on account of excrement and urine shall be cleaned with earth, or with cleaning substances, or with dung." The Blessed One then declared: "One shall listen to the Dharma."

After this declaration, when the monks remained without any shade and the sun grew hot, the Blessed One declared: "A canopy shall be erected." When wind and rain came and the monks abandoned their resting places and departed, and this became improper, the Blessed One declared: "A shelter shall be made." But they did not know who was to make the shelter, and when whoever happened to be sitting there made it, and all the comfortable resting places at the end of the elder monks' section had been laid out but the senior monks could not make the shelter themselves, the Blessed One declared: "At the end where the elder monks sit, the juniors shall make the shelter; and at the end where the junior monks sit, the elders shall make it." When, after making the shelter, they put everything together in one heap and this became improper, the Blessed One declared: "They shall be arranged each according to its match."

When the monks afterwards failed to listen to the Dharma, the Blessed One declared: "One shall sit either draped or in the open." When listening to the Dharma in this way, faithful brahmins and householders set out lion thrones adorned with jewels and decorated with cloth of gold and silver, and the monks, feeling discomfort, did not sit on them. The Blessed One then declared: "They are lay robes. One shall press them down with the thought of impermanence and take one's seat — one should feel no discomfort in this." When monks neither sheltered the seats of the Saṅgha nor abandoned them right there, and this became improper, the Blessed One declared: "Those too shall be sheltered."

A certain householder had two temple residences, one in a forest monastery and one at the edge of a town. In the town-edge temple there were many resting places, while in the forest temple there were few. On one occasion a festival took place at the forest temple, and the forest monks went to borrow resting places from the town-edge temple, but the town monks refused to give them. The Blessed One declared: "They shall be lent." However, if rain was falling or was expected to fall, they were not to be lent. When wind and rain fell along the road and the resting places were damaged, the Blessed One declared: "One shall take shelter beside a tree or at the foot of a wall, covering oneself with a single cloth." When they covered themselves with fine cloth, the Blessed One declared: "One shall cover oneself with coarse cloth." When the festival was over and the monks, thinking that the temple also belonged to that householder, did not return the resting places, the Blessed One declared: "They shall be reclaimed by authority." When it was not clear whose they were, the Blessed One declared: "One shall write an inscription stating 'This resting place belongs to the forest temple of such-and-such a householder' or 'This belongs to the town-edge temple,' and it shall be used in accordance with however the resting place has been designated."

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One in these words:

When the Blessed One was residing at the old-age home, the old-age home was honored; and when the Blessed One was not residing at the old-age home, the old-age home was without honor. The householder therefore addressed him: "If the Blessed One would permit it, I would have a statue of him made, seated in the shade of a rose-apple tree, to be placed there." The Blessed One declared: "Permission is granted; let it be done." And so he had a statue made, seated in the shade of a rose-apple tree, and it was placed at the old-age home.

When wind and rain came, the monks abandoned it and left, and faithful brahmins and householders reproached them saying, "You have even abandoned the Teacher." The Blessed One then declared: "A layman or a novice monk shall be invited to attend to it." When there was no layman and no novice monk available, the Blessed One declared: "The monks shall generate the perception of the Teacher and invite him in." When monks fell ill and no one was attending to them, the Blessed One declared: "The sick shall be attended to three times a day." When the Blessed One had given this instruction to attend to the sick three times a day, and it was not known who should do the attending, the Blessed One declared: "Beginning from the elder of the Saṅgha down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, all shall attend to the sick."

When the Blessed One had thus instructed that the sick be attended, the elder monks went to see the sick but did so standing up, and the sick became distressed. The Blessed One declared: "One shall sit and attend to the sick." When the Blessed One had instructed that one should sit to attend to the sick, the monks each took their own seats and went to the sick, and faithless people remarked: "Do these noble ones go about like wandering minstrels?" At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One shall not carry one's seat along; rather, the sick attendants shall arrange seats." When the group of six monks went to attend to the sick, they lingered there for a long time engaged in chatter, and the attendants of the sick said to them: "Venerable ones, the business of caring for the sick is quite ruined now; please come later." Those monks replied: "Then do that, and also check on the bedding, for in that way you will receive the six possessions of a deceased monk." They further said: "Otherwise, do not ruin the care of the sick; go now, and we shall attend to it ourselves." The attendants then left without entrusting anything to the sick, and the group of six also departed. When wind and rain came, the sick were unable to get their bedding under cover, and things became disordered. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, care of the sick shall not be entrusted to these five: one who is shameless, one who is himself ill, one who is aged and frail and feeble, one who cannot endure the exertion of attending the sick, and anyone who has not received full ordination."

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the forty-fourth bundle.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, if two monks are on one seat-frame, which of them should get up to give way? The one who got up last." "If both rise at the same time, the junior one." "If both are equally junior, both together shall give way." When ācāryas and preceptors go for a walk, the monks who reside with them and the attendants who dwell in the monastery do not grow in wholesome qualities — like lotuses without water. The Blessed One declared: "The resident monks and attendants shall follow behind the ācāryas and preceptors." When ācāryas and

preceptors carry their own seat-frames and go out for a walk, while the resident monks and attendants walk along with arms stretched out. The Blessed One declared: "The resident monks and attendants shall carry the seat-frames of the ācāryas and preceptors."

When those ācāryas and preceptors are pacing back and forth and sweeping, the resident monks and attendants stand by with arms stretched out. The Blessed One declared: "The resident monks and attendants shall take up the broom and assist the ācāryas and preceptors with small tasks from the heart. If appointed to sweep in their place, there is no transgression."

When the ācāryas and preceptors are sewing robes, the resident monks and attendants stand by offering small assistance. The Blessed One declared: "The resident monks and attendants shall thread the needle and assist the ācāryas and preceptors with small tasks. If appointed to do the sewing in their place, there is no transgression."

When resident monks and attendants, having received scriptural transmission from their ācāryas and preceptors, recite those texts in the presence of those very teachers — the Blessed One declared: "Monks who are learning recitation shall, having received the scriptural transmission, sit within hearing distance, free from any distraction, and recite it within range of the teacher's voice. Monks who are practitioners of renunciation shall receive the instructions and then go apart to a secluded place and give rise to contemplation."

When those resident monks and attendants go off on an assigned task, having taken leave of their ācāryas and preceptors, and other work then arises for them at the place they have gone to, and they come back again asking permission — the Blessed One declared: "If other work arises for those who have gone there, they shall not return again and again to ask permission; rather, they shall do that work right there. That single leave-taking they gave at the outset counts as permission for everything."

When they carried seat-frames there and then came back without bringing the seat-frames with them — the Blessed One declared: "They shall bring the seat-frames back when they return."

When they had gone ahead earlier carrying seat-frames, and a circumstance arose for the ācāryas and preceptors such that those teachers would not be coming — the Blessed One declared: "They shall ask the ācāryas and preceptors whether they are going for a walk or not. If they say they are going, the seat-frames shall be sent. If they say they are not going, the seat-frames shall not be sent."

A certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal at another house. A certain young monk, earnestly devoted to virtue, thought to himself: "Today I need not go out on alms-round. Until the time set by the shadow of the sundial arrives, I shall apply myself to virtue." With that thought he took up his seat-frame, went outside, and proceeded. The monks had gathered early and set out, having closed the door of the assembly hall. He too, having marked the time, came when he should — but when he arrived he saw that the door of the assembly hall was closed. He thought: "It is better for me to miss the meal; if I am with a transgression it will not do." So he fasted. And for as long as there was energy in his body he continued to apply himself to virtue. When the energy finally left his body, he lay down and reclined.

The monks then said to him: "Venerable one, do you suppose this food and this meal belong to someone else? Why did you go so far in your effort toward virtue that you could not manage even that much to eat? Who ate? You did not eat?" "I did not eat." "Why?"

He then explained the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks should ascertain the time and, rather than entering another house too early in the assembly, they should beat the gong and then enter. Teachers of discipline and preceptors should each keep watch over their own assemblies. If someone arrives unexpectedly, the senior elder of the Saṅgha should look after that person. If a monk arrives to find the door closed, he should place his mat near a wall or at the foot of a tree and depart. A monk should not out of hesitation cut his meal short. If a monk cuts his meal short out of hesitation, it becomes a transgression."

Brahmin householders and faithful laypeople came to the monastery, sat down on the seats, and then left, abandoning them there. Since no one had put those seats away, the place became disordered. The Blessed One declared: "Whoever sees them should put them away."

Elderly monks who were bent with age and frail, and sick monks who were too weak for physical effort, saw the seats left uncovered and were unable to put them away themselves. The Blessed One declared: "They should inform the monastery steward, and he in turn should respectfully put them away."

The monks left the bedding and furnishings of their quarters unprotected, entrusted them to a single monk, and went out for alms-round. Others too entrusted their things to that same monk, and while he had gone out on alms-round, wind and rain came and he was unable to cover them. The Blessed One declared: "A great many monks should not entrust their things to a single monk. If such circumstances arise, he should beat the gong, and all the monks who are present should respectfully come and cover the things. Those who hear the gong should go with due care."

A monastery situated in a forest caught fire, and the fire spread to a village, to a town, to the royal palace, and to the surrounding countryside. The monks' walking grounds, the paths through the walking grounds, the cloister, the storeroom, the gatehouse, and the monastery itself were consumed in the fire. The monks each retrieved their own bowls and robes, but the bedding and furnishings of the Saṅgha burned. A householder came and asked the monks: "Noble ones, was nothing spared? Nothing at all? And what of the Saṅgha's bedding and furnishings?" "Those burned." "Nothing was spared? Was it like that — nothing of ours burned either?" Then he said: "Alas, they could not even manage to save the Saṅgha's furnishings."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "The Saṅgha's furnishings too should be carried out. While they are carrying out the Saṅgha's furnishings, the individual monks' personal furnishings, their bowls, and their robes burned, and those individuals were left destitute."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Since individuals will be destitute but the Saṅgha will not, first carry out the individuals' bowls and robes, and after that carry out the Saṅgha's."

As they were being carried out, those who take what is not given stole them. The Blessed One declared: "A monk should be stationed there as a guard." They posted monks who were powerful, and the Blessed One declared: "Appoint one with modest strength." Those guards were made to enter when the fire was too intense to endure. The Blessed One declared: "If the fire is too intense to endure, they should not enter, and even if the things burn, they should have no regrets about it."

While a monastery was situated in the midst of heavy hail,

when a torrent of thick rain fell from the hillside above, water entered the monastery and reached the village, the town, the royal palace, and the surrounding district. When it reached the walking grounds, the walking paths, the covered hall, the gateway buildings, and the monastery itself, the monks each took out their own bowls and robes, and carried off the Saṅgha's furnishings. When the householders came and asked the monks, "Noble ones, what did you not take out?" they answered, "We did not take out anything." "Then what about the Saṅgha's furnishings?" "Those we did take out." "And whatever you did not take — was it like that? We too did not take out anything of our own." One of them then said, "Alas, we did not even dare to remove the Saṅgha's furnishings" — and on that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The Saṅgha's furnishings too should be removed." While they were removing those Saṅgha furnishings, some people took the individual monks' furnishings, their bowls, and their robes, and those monks were left destitute. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Since an individual may be left destitute but the Saṅgha will not be, first remove the individual monks' bowls and robes, and only after that carry out the Saṅgha's." As they were being carried out, those who take what is not given stole them. The Blessed One declared: "A monk should be stationed there as a guard." They posted monks who were powerful, and the Blessed One declared: "Appoint one with modest strength." Those guards were made to enter when the water was too intense to endure. The Blessed One declared: "If the water is too intense to endure, they should not enter, and even if the things are swept away, they should have no regrets about it." There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is mad, who is mentally disturbed, or who is beset by painful sensations.

The fourteenth rule on furnishings transgressions is complete.

Summary verse: the southern road; not discarding; discarding without asking; discarding by force; the well; taking; the covered hall; the walking path; and placing a heavy load — these are the last.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Two monks — one senior and one junior — came from the southern road to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the Blessed One's feet. The senior monk was assigned to a monastery that had furnishings; the junior monk was assigned to a monastery that had none. The junior monk, being industrious, gathered much grass and laid out bedding about knee-high. The senior monk thought, "I shall go and see what kind of monastery the junior fellow has been assigned to," and went there. When he saw how excellent a bed had been laid out, he thought, "For as long as I am busy looking after the furnishings, going tomorrow will be delayed — I shall just stay here." So he handed over the monastery that had the furnishings to the monk in charge of lodgings there, and the two of them spent the night in that monastery, then rose early the next morning and departed. As that region was an oily, greasy land, fleas had bred in the grass that had been spread out, and the entire interior and exterior of the monastery became infested with fleas.

At that time a certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks, with the Buddha at the head, to another house for a midday meal. The Saṅgha of monks went and took their seats. The Blessed One, however, remained among the material things that had arisen and concentrated on obtaining alms food.

The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remain among material things that have arisen for five reasons, and it is for those five reasons that they set about obtaining alms food. What are the five? They wish to place themselves properly in inner composure; they wish to teach the Dharma to the gods; they wish to look after the sick; they wish to inspect the lodgings; and they wish to establish, in the Vinaya, the rules of training for the hearers. In this particular instance, the Blessed One remained among the material things that had arisen and set about obtaining alms food because he wished to inspect the lodgings and because he wished to establish in the Vinaya the rules of training for the hearers.

Then, not long after the Saṅgha of monks had departed, the Blessed One perceived this in his mind, took up the key, and went from courtyard to courtyard, from monastery to monastery, from room to room, from walking-ground to walking-ground, passing through them one by one in succession, until he came to that particular monastery building. There the Blessed One saw that the entire interior and exterior of the monastery was overrun with fleas. And having seen this, he uttered the exclamation "Ah me!" and, with disapproval in his heart, he thought: "Faithful brahmin and householder donors give and give again, squeezing out skin and flesh and blood to make their gifts and to make merit — and these monks enjoy it all without feeling gratitude and without individual discernment." Then the Blessed One thought to himself: "I should by all means perform such a display of miraculous power as would cause the fleas to go off to one side and the ground to become clear to one side." And so the Blessed One performed just such a display of miraculous power as would cause the fleas to go off to one side and the ground to become clear to one side.

Then, with his two hands adorned with a web of fingers — bearing the marks of the wheel, the auspicious knot, and the swastika hook, and arisen from many hundreds of meritorious deeds — the Blessed One carefully gathered up those fleas and set them to one side in a cool place. Then the Blessed One swept out the monastery, sweeping it thoroughly, cast the sweepings outside the monastery building, washed his two hands and feet, and entered the monastery in order to settle into inner composure.

Then the monk who had been gathering alms, having received the alms food, came to where the Blessed One was. Now it is the nature of things that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, always delight each monk individually who is gathering alms by asking: "Monk, how was the alms round? Did the monk satisfy the Saṅgha of monks?" And because this is how they individually delight them, the Blessed One individually delighted the monk who had been gathering alms by asking: "Monk, how was the alms round? Did the monk satisfy the Saṅgha of monks?" And he replied: "Venerable One, the alms round was good, and the Saṅgha of monks was satisfied." Then the Blessed One performed the act of eating, washed his two feet at the threshold of the monastery building, and entered the monastery in order to settle into inner composure. Then in the afternoon the Blessed One rose from inner composure and took his seat on the mat that had been spread out before the assembly of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, here, not long after the Saṅgha of monks had departed, I understood what had happened, took the key, and went from courtyard to courtyard, from monastery to monastery, from room to room, from walking-ground to walking-ground,

going from place to place in order, until I came to one particular monastery building and saw that it was entirely covered inside and out with grass droppings. Seeing this, I was displeased, and reflected: "The faithful householders and brahmins who, squeezing and squeezing their very skin, flesh, and blood, give gifts and make merit — the monks are consuming what those people have given without feeling any warmth of gratitude, without discerning it individually." Thinking thus, I declared: "Monks, it would be good if you were to make use of what is offered in faith in these five ways: with warm gratitude, with restraint, in a timely manner, with discernment, and without excess."

The summary verse runs:

With warm gratitude and with restraint,
likewise in due time and with discernment,
and making use without excess —

Then, after the Blessed One had spoken in praise of making use with warm gratitude, restraint, timeliness, discernment, and without excess, he addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing these ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: 'Whatever monk spreads out a grass mat or a leaf mat in the Saṅgha's monastery building, or causes one to be spread, and then departs without gathering it up or causing it to be gathered up — this constitutes a transgression.'" Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Now, a great many monks were traveling together on a regional tour when they came to a certain rocky mountain. There they went to a householder and asked him to lend them lodging, and the householder said: "I will lend it on a pledge: if you will accept an alms meal from me, I will lend it." The monks replied: "Householder, we depend on mutual agreement. If we reach agreement, we will stay and eat." The householder asked: "Are there any beds or seats here? Noble ones, there are none." Many laymen and novices were present with those monks, and they gathered a great deal of grass and spread out mats reaching to about knee height. During the night or at dawn, the group departed, and those monks left without removing the mats. The householder thought: "If the noble ones are still here, I will prepare a canopy to their measure and check on them," and went there, only to see that the monks had departed before dawn. When the householder and his wife went to remove those mats, they had already rotted away by morning.

Then yet another great many monks were traveling together on a regional tour and came to that same rocky mountain. There they went to that householder and asked him to lend them lodging, and the householder said: "Noble ones, I will lend it on a pledge: if you do not spread out your own adequate mats, I will lend it." The monks said: "Householder, where shall we sleep? There is nowhere here for us to lie down — no bed, no seat. Noble ones, how are we to sleep on the bare ground?" The householder replied: "It seems that fellow practitioners of your own pure conduct came here, spread out their own adequate mats, and departed without removing them, and when I and my family went to remove them in the morning, they had completely rotted away."

Those monks passed the night on the bare ground and rose early the next morning and departed. Traveling onward by stages, they eventually arrived at Śrāvastī. When the other monks there saw them, they said: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How did you fare on the journey?" "How did we fare? We passed the night turning from side to side on the bare ground." "Where did you stay in that rocky place?" "At a certain spot." "In whose courtyard?" "At a certain householder's." Then some of the monks said: "As for us, we came having slept on the mats laid out in that householder's courtyard." "And where did you leave those mats?" "We left them right there." At this, they said that the householder was blaming them — and on that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "One may discard mats at other people's houses as well." Having so declared, the Blessed One went on.

When a large company of monks traveling together on tour went to a certain rocky place, a householder there, for the benefit of wandering ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins who arrived unexpectedly, had fetched a great quantity of grass from far away and spread out mats. The monks went to that householder and asked him to lend them lodging, and the householder said: "Noble ones, I have fetched a great quantity of grass from far away for the benefit of wandering ascetics and brahmins who arrive unexpectedly, and I have spread out these mats — please sleep here." They slept there, and then, before dawn, without asking the householder, they discarded the mats and departed. The householder rose early the next morning and, seeing that they had gone and left the mats behind, he thought: "So they have gone. If they have discarded them in a clean place, I will pick them up." He went and looked, but seeing that they had been discarded in an unclean place, he did not pick them up.

Then another large company of monks, also traveling together on tour, came to that same rocky place. They went to that householder and asked him to lend them lodging. The householder said: "Noble ones, please be seated. Householder, are there any chairs or seats here?" "Noble ones, there are none." "Householder, how are we to sleep on this bare ground?" "Noble ones, for the benefit of wandering ascetics and brahmins who arrived unexpectedly, I had fetched a great quantity of grass from far away and spread out mats — but fellow practitioners of your own pure conduct came, slept there, and then before dawn, without asking me, discarded those mats in an unclean place and departed. They slept on the bare ground there and left." Traveling onward by stages, these monks eventually arrived at Śrāvastī. When the other monks there saw them, they said: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How did you fare on the journey?" They replied: "How did we fare? We spent the night on bare ground turning from side to side until dawn came." "Where did you stay in that rocky place?" "At a certain spot." "In whose courtyard?" "At a certain householder's." Then some of the monks said: "As for us, we came having slept on the mats laid out in that householder's courtyard." "And where did you leave those mats?" "We discarded them outside." At this, they said that the householder was blaming them — and on that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "One should ask the householder if he is present, and if he says 'Please discard them,' then one may discard them. If he says 'Do not discard them,' then one may not discard them."

At a certain cliff-face there was a monastery that had no bedding. The monks there had gathered much grass from a great distance and laid out grass mats for the benefit of monks who might arrive unexpectedly.

A large group of monks traveling together on a tour of the countryside came to that cliff-face, entered the monastery, and asked the resident monks: "Venerable ones, is there any bedding here?" They replied: "There is. We ourselves gathered much grass from a great distance and laid out mats for the benefit of monks who might arrive unexpectedly — please sleep here tonight." Those monks slept there, and early the next morning they rose before dawn and were about to discard the mats. The resident monks said to them: "Venerable ones, do not discard these mats. We gathered much grass from a great distance and laid them out for the benefit of fellow celibates who arrive unexpectedly." The visiting monks replied: "Venerable ones, you have just now made yourselves liable to a transgression." "How have we made ourselves liable to a transgression?" At that, those monks abused them and forcibly threw away the mats and left.

Another large group of monks traveling together on a tour came to that same monastery, and finding themselves short of bedding, the resident monks said to them: "Venerable ones, does this monastery have no bedding? We gathered much grass from a great distance and laid out mats for the benefit of fellow celibates who might arrive unexpectedly — yet when other celibates traveling together on tour came to this monastery, slept on those mats, rose early the next morning, and were about to discard them, and we said 'Do not discard them,' those monks abused us and forcibly threw them away and left." These monks too then slept on the bare ground, rose early the next morning, and departed.

In due course, as they continued on their tour, they arrived at Śrāvastī. When the monks there saw them, they said: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How was your journey?" They replied: "How was our journey? We spent the whole night on the bare ground, turning this way and that, and so the night passed." "Venerable ones, at which cliff-face did you stay?" "At a certain monastery." Then some of the monks said: "As for us, we came having slept on the mats in that monastery." "And where did you leave those mats?" "The senior monks there kept telling us not to, but we forcibly threw them outside and left." And so they were blaming those fellow celibates.

On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not discard them in that way; one should ask the monks who are present."

A large group of monks traveling together on tour spent the night beside a well, and they gathered much grass and laid out grass mats. Not far from them a brahmin also spent the night. The monks traveling together rose early the next morning and departed, and the returning group of traveling companions also arrived. The brahmin, having concluded his business with that group, returned together with them, and that same group then spent the night at that very well on the mats just as they had been laid out. Together with that group there also came some naked ascetics (Jainas), and those ascetics slept on the very same mats on which the monks had been sleeping. Then one of the naked ascetics said:

"It has been seized by a knowing being." Another naked ascetic said: "You ate a great many sugar-cane joints, and so you have been seized by a mental proliferation of desire." He looked at the mat and, seeing that it was full of insects, said: "Who was it who slept on this mat? Not far from them, the brahmin who had been sleeping there heard this being said, and he said: "It was the monks, the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan, who slept on this mat." The naked ascetics then said: "O wise ones, the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan consider themselves experts in the world, and yet they do not even know enough to discard a grass mat in an open place like this." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Grass mats are to be discarded even when in open country."

After the Blessed One had declared that grass mats were to be discarded even in open country, a large number of monks were traveling together as a company through a region. They stopped for a night at a place in the open country, and that company rose before dawn. As long as the monks were in the act of discarding the mats, the company waited, but then they went ahead. As the monks followed behind and traveled along, they were attacked by bandits. Eventually the group continued traveling and arrived at Śrāvastī. The monks there, seeing them, said: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How was your journey? Did you travel comfortably?" The venerable ones replied: "Venerable ones, we did not travel comfortably. We were attacked by bandits." "Who? How did this come about?" They then recounted the circumstances to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "They are not to be discarded in every case without exception; rather, one should gather them up and proceed."

Then, monks who worked with dyes would spread out grass on the ground in their dye-yards to dry their robes, and they would not discard that grass, and insects came to appear there. The Blessed One declared: "The grass is to be discarded." Other monks who wished to work with dyes said: "Venerable ones, do not discard this grass — we too wish to dry robes here." But the monks did not give it to them. The Blessed One declared: "Give it to them." When those monks had dried their robes there in one place or another, they would not discard the grass, saying, "We did not spread it out." The Blessed One declared: "One should ask them whether they intend to discard the grass or not. If they say they will discard it, then give it to them. If they say they will not discard it, then do not give it to them."

When monks were walking in their walking-places and the ground there was rough and heated the soles of their feet, the Blessed One declared: "Grass is to be laid down there." When the grass had been laid down and insects appeared there, the Blessed One declared: "Discard it." When they would discard it every single day, the Blessed One declared: "It is not to be discarded every single day; rather, one should examine it from time to time. If one is going out completely, then one should gather it up before departing."

When monks in their walking-places would set down bundles of grass on the ground and insects appeared there, the Blessed One declared: "Tie them with cord and hang them from the trees and leave them there."

When monks set down heavy objects on the ground and insects appeared in those places, the Blessed One declared: "Put them on a rack."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who respect training, and who are furnished with the requisites of training, and in accordance with that, and going further,

Having delivered a discourse containing teachings related to that matter, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, what came before was a rule, and this is a permission. My hearers are to recite the following as a training basis in the Vinaya: Furthermore, whatever monk lays down or has laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha and does not gather it up himself, or does not have it gathered up, and departs from there without entrusting it to a monk who is present — except in such circumstances — commits an offense."

The phrase "whatever monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. The phrase "of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. The phrase "in the assembly hall" refers to any place suitable for the four modes of conduct — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The phrase "a bundle of grass" refers to grass. The phrase "a bundle of leaves" refers to leaves. The phrase "lays down" means doing so oneself. The phrase "has laid down" means having another do so. The phrase "does not gather up himself" means doing so oneself. The phrase "does not have it gathered up" means through another. The phrase "a monk who is present" means whichever monk is there at that place. The phrase "without entrusting" means without delegating. The phrase "departs from there" means having left the immediate vicinity.

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Reverend one, what is the immediate vicinity of a bundle? I, Upāli, was born a brahmin, and in the case of seven mango trees, each abundantly flowered, abundantly fruited, and abundantly branched, standing at intervals of seven fathoms from one another — those trees having been shown to have forty-nine fathoms between them — that is the immediate vicinity of a bundle."

The phrase "except in such circumstances" means that such circumstances have been set aside. The phrase "commits an offense" means it causes one to burn, to be scorched, to fall into the states of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, evil destinies, and states of ruin. Furthermore, as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome phenomena — and therefore it is called "commits an offense."

As to how one incurs that transgression: if a monk lays down or has laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha, and does not gather it up himself, and does not have it gathered up, and departs without entrusting it to a monk who is present — then for as long as he has not left the immediate vicinity, it constitutes an infraction; when he leaves the immediate vicinity, it becomes a downfall-offense.

If while walking along the way a monk recollects: "I laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha" — and if he thinks: "Skilled practitioners of the celibate life will gather it up" — then that monk should generate the thought "I will not do so again in the future" and also state it in words, and that transgression is to be confessed according to the Dharma.

If, while walking along the way, one sees another monk going in that direction, and one thinks: "He will gather it up," then one should say to him: "Venerable one, I placed a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves somewhere in the direction of the assembly hall of the Saṅgha — please gather it up." That monk should generate the thought "I will not do so again in the future" and also state it in words, and that transgression is to be confessed according to the Dharma. That monk, for his part, should respectfully accept the charge and gather it up. If he does not gather it up, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

If, having gone there, one recalls: "I laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha" — and if one thinks: "Skilled practitioners of the celibate life will gather it up" —

That monk should generate the thought "I will not do so again in the future" and also state it in words, and that transgression is to be confessed according to the Dharma. If, having gone there, he sees another monk approaching and thinks "That one will gather it up," he should say to him: "Venerable one, I myself laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha — please gather it up." That monk should generate the thought "I will not do such a thing again in the future" and also state it in words, and that transgression is to be confessed according to the Dharma. That monk, for his part, should respectfully accept the charge and gather it up. If he does not gather it up, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

If a monk has laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha, or has had one laid down, and has neither gathered it up himself, nor had it gathered up, nor entrusted the matter to a monk who was present — and then, thinking either "I will now settle my mind, which has not yet been settled" or "I will liberate my mind, which has already been settled," he enters within in order to practice proper meditation, and then rises from that meditative absorption at the first watch of the night or at the midpoint of the first watch: if harm has not resulted, it is an offense of wrongdoing; if harm has resulted, it constitutes a downfall.

If a monk has laid down a bundle of grass or a bundle of leaves in the assembly hall of the Saṅgha, or has had one laid down, and has neither gathered it up himself, nor had it gathered up, nor entrusted the matter to a monk who was present — and then, thinking either "I will now settle my mind, which has not yet been settled" or "I will liberate my mind, which has already been settled," he enters within in order to practice proper meditation, and then rises from that meditative absorption at the middle watch of the night, the last watch of the night, before dawn appears, after dawn has appeared, before the sun has risen, after the sun has risen, when an eighth part of the sun's course remains, when a quarter part remains, at the midpoint before noon, past the midpoint, when a quarter of the sun's course remains, when an eighth part remains, before the sun has set, or after the sun has set, or before the stars have appeared, or after the stars have appeared: if harm has not resulted, it is an offense of wrongdoing; if harm has resulted, it constitutes a downfall.

The venerable Upananda (Nyeba Khor) asked the Blessed One the Buddha: "Venerable One, what kinds of harm arise from a bundle?" He replied: "There are two kinds of harm from a bundle: harm from wind and harm from rolling. What is harm from wind? It is when it is blown from one layer up to a second layer. What is harm from rolling? It is when it rolls from one layer down to the point of a second layer." On ground that is rocky or sandy, where such harm of that kind does not arise, there is no downfall. For a person who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no downfall. The fifteenth rule entailing a downfall concerning bundles is complete.

The Blessed One the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Udāyin was encouraging young, newly ordained monks, saying: "Venerable ones, come here! Go traveling through the provinces! There we will overcome our opponents, proclaim our own reputations, and acquire gains. As for yourselves, do not be preoccupied with your alms bowls, Dharma robes, nets, begging cups, belts, recitation of scriptural transmission, reading, oral recitation, yoga, or mental activities." Upon hearing this, those monks asked their preceptors and abbots: "Venerable abbots, we are going to travel through the provinces. With whom should we go?"

"Venerable ones, Udāyin is a person of thoroughly bad conduct — he will be a burden to you." But those monks dismissed these words, saying, "The abbot, the venerable Udāyin, dwells among us like a father and mother — why would he be a burden to us?" And so they disregarded what their preceptors and abbots had said and set off to travel through the provinces together with him.

When Udāyin had passed beyond the outer boundary, he said to them: "Venerable ones, why do you set out to travel through the provinces without having established lodgings? Come here — settle down first!" And with that he had them sit in a row before him and made them find lodging.

He assigned some of them carrying-poles, some he assigned alms bowls, some he assigned shoulder-bags, some he assigned begging cups, some he assigned round balls for washing the head. Then, stretching out both his arms himself, wearing nothing but a sweat-cloth, he walked along putting on airs before the world. They came to a rocky cliff, and there those monks rested beside a well. Now at that cliff there was a monastery, and the wooden sounding board was struck. Hearing it, those monks said: "Teacher, the sounding board has been struck at the monastery — let us go in." Udāyin said: "Those who have nothing but black-stained alms bowls have struck the work-sounding board, meaning that we, who are tired, will have to work. That is how it will be." "Teacher, is it not perhaps the sounding board for gains? If so, we will receive something when we go to that boundary district." "The teacher has great fame and much merit — he will receive; but who will give anything to us? If there are gains today, take them for me." As soon as they entered, the sounding board for lodgings was struck, and the monks said: "Venerable ones, claim lodgings!" Those monks said: "There is one among us who is senior to us all." "Who is that?" "It is the teacher Udāyin." "Then claim lodgings for him too." And so those monks claimed lodgings.

Now the venerable Udāyin was sitting there engaged in idle talk — whose is this rocky cliff, whose is this monastery, whose is this shrine, whose is this pleasure grove, whose is this park, whose is this well, whose is this field, whose are these cattle, whose are these buffalo — and so he sat on in idle talk. Those monks thought to themselves: "The teacher Udāyin is going to stay here for a long time." So they conferred among themselves and, making up the venerable Udāyin's bed, they set out together the foot-water and the foot-washing cloth at one side, washed his two feet, entered the fire room, and went to sleep.

The venerable Udāyin, for as long as he had a partner in idle talk, stayed on and on; but when there was no longer a partner for his idle talk, at the time when his line of sight was cut off — at dusk — he came to the monastery and began calling out: "Venerable ones! Venerable ones!" The monks said to him: "Venerable Udāyin, why do you call out like someone who has fallen into thick mud?" Udāyin said: "Are some of my young disciples here? Has anything happened to any of them?" Hearing that, they said: "Teacher, do not call out. A bed has been spread in the outer room of the lodging-house; foot-water and foot-washing cloth have also been set there — go and sleep there." Udāyin said: "Venerable ones, at whose request did you wash your feet?" "Teacher, you were delayed for a long time, so we conferred among ourselves and washed our own feet."
