Udāyin was furious and said: "Get out of the monastery! Go to those who provide lodging to people who have no respect and no sense of station like this, and take up residence with them!" And with that he drove them out of the monastery.

Those monks, having arrived that night with no covering overhead, were in danger. The next morning they rose early and said: "Teacher, we pay our respects. We are leaving." "Where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Stay — I will nurse you when you are sick." "Teacher, since you made us sick in the first place, nursing the sick would only be fitting." With that they departed for Śrāvastī.

When the monks there met them, they said: "Venerable ones, welcome, welcome! How was your journey? Was the road comfortable?" "We arrived in the middle of the night without any overhead shelter, having set out at dawn, and so we fell ill." "Why is that?" The monks recounted the whole matter in detail, and those monks, over this trifling affair, condemned and upbraided and reviled Udāyin, saying: "Why does a monk expel other monks from the Saṅgha's monastery?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, on account of this occasion, and in relation to this matter, convened the assembly of monks — and all that follows is as before. The passage beginning "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though they know, yet ask" is likewise as before. The Blessed One then questioned Udāyin: "Udāyin, is it true that you expelled a monk from the Saṅgha's monastery?" "Blessed One, it is so." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that what is not in keeping with the conduct of a renunciant, not in accord with propriety, not fitting, and not in conformity with the rule is not something that one who has gone forth should do. The Blessed One then rebuked him in many ways, and having done so, he addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and all that follows is as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, in anger, disturbed and enraged, displeased and resentful, expels a monk from the Saṅgha's monastery or causes him to be expelled, commits an offense."

Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The Blessed One was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a certain monastery of the earth, and in it a sick monk was staying. Seeing that heavy five-colored storm-clouds had gathered, the monks said to him: "Venerable one, since five-colored storm-clouds have gathered, the monastery may collapse — come out." "I am unable to get up on my own." The monks, out of reluctance to act and regretting it afterward, did not bring him out. Rain fell, the monastery collapsed, and it fell upon that monk, and he died at his appointed time. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who are well-furnished with the requisites of training, and then addressed the monks with a teaching that accorded with that theme, that surpassed it, and that was endowed with the qualities appropriate to it. He then said to the monks: "Monks, therefore, the earlier rule was established, and now this is permitted. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, in anger, disturbed and enraged, displeased and resentful, expels a monk from the Saṅgha's monastery or causes him to be expelled — except in a circumstance such as this — commits an offense."

The phrase "whatever monk" refers to Udāyin or to any other monk of the same kind. "In anger, disturbed and enraged, displeased and resentful" means being angry and overwhelmed by the force of that anger.

The phrase "of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. The phrase "from the monastery" means from a place where it is suitable to perform the four bodily comportments: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The phrase "a monk" means one who belongs to this Dharma. The phrase "expels" means doing so oneself. The phrase "causes him to be expelled" means through another. The phrase "except in a circumstance such as this" means that such a circumstance has been set aside. The phrase "commits an offense" means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the wretched destinations — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower rebirths, and the states of utter downfall. Furthermore, for as long as the offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. That is why it is said "commits an offense." As for how an offense is incurred: whenever a monk, in anger, disturbed and enraged, displeased and resentful, expels a monk from the Saṅgha's monastery or causes him to be expelled, in every such case an offense is committed. There is no offense for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by feeling. This completes the sixteenth offense of expulsion.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Udāyin kept encouraging young monks, saying: "Come here, venerable ones — travel through the provinces, go about the countryside, and we will cut down our opponents, spread our own fame, acquire gains, and you yourselves need not be troubled by the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the net, the cup, the belt, reciting scriptures, reading, chanting, yoga, or mental work." Those monks went to their preceptors and teachers and said: "Venerable preceptors, we are going to travel through the provinces. With whom?" "With the venerable Udāyin." The preceptors replied: "Venerable ones, he is a person of wretched habits who indulges in them everywhere — he will be a bad influence on you." But those monks dismissed the preceptors' words as worthless and set off through the countryside together with him. When Udāyin had passed beyond the outer boundary, he said: "Venerable ones, why do you travel through the provinces without having established a dwelling? Come, let us settle somewhere." He then had them sit cross-legged before him and assigned them their lodgings. He gave some of them a water-strainer, some a vessel for the alms bowl, some a razor case, some a cup, some a pill-box for pouring together, and then, stretching out both arms and carrying nothing but a sweat-cloth, walking along loftily with the world at his back, they all went to a rocky cliff. There they rested beside a certain well. Near that place there was a monastery on the cliff, and the wooden signal-board was struck. Hearing it, those monks said: "Teacher, the signal-board has been struck at the monastery — let us go in." Udāyin said: "Those who have nothing better to do than strike the work signal-board on account of their black alms bowls will find that we who are weary will end up having to do the work. Is that signal-board for gains, teacher? If so, we will get our share when we go to the boundary. As for the teacher, since he is of great fame and merit, he will receive some — but who will give any to us? For today, if there are any gains, take my share as well." When they arrived and the signal-board for lodgings had been struck, the monks said: "Venerable ones, take your lodgings." Those monks replied: "There are some who are even senior to us."

"Who is it?" "It is the teacher Charka." "Then take his lodging as well." So they had claimed the lodging. The venerable Charka was also sitting there engaged in conversation about possessions, asking: "Whose is this cliff? Whose is this temple? Whose is this shrine? Whose is this garden? Whose is this pleasure grove? Whose is this well? Whose is this field? Whose are these cattle? Whose are these buffaloes?" — and so he sat on, deep in talk about possessions. Those monks thought: "The teacher Charka is going to be delayed for a long time." So they conferred with one another, spread the venerable Charka's bed, set out the foot-water and the foot-ointment in one place, washed both his feet, and then entered the fire-room and lay down to sleep.

The venerable Charka remained sitting for as long as his conversation about possessions had a partner; but when his conversation about possessions no longer had a partner — at the time when the last light of evening had faded — he came to the temple and began calling out: "Venerable ones! Venerable ones!" The monks said to him: "Venerable Charka, why do you call out like a man who has entered a thicket of dense reeds?" Charka said: "Are there some of my younger ones here? Has any one of them perhaps fallen ill?" When they heard this, they said: "Teacher, do not call out. In the lodging room we have spread your sleeping mat, set out the foot-water and the foot-ointment, and washed your feet — go and sleep there." Charka said: "Venerable ones, whose feet did you wash by asking whom? The teacher was delayed for a long time, and so you conferred with one another and washed your own feet." Charka grew angry and said: "I have a small matter to settle with you — open the door." When they did not open the door, he grew angry, struck the door panel with his fist, and shook the entire fire-room. They were frightened and thought: "He is a man of great strength. If the Saṅgha's temple were to collapse, that would be wrong — let us open the door." So they opened the door, and he entered and threw himself down in their midst, jabbing some of them with his elbow and others with his knee. They said: "Teacher, forgive us! Forgive us!" Charka said: "Let the harm go to whoever caused it." The monks said among themselves: "Venerable ones, this man is powerful. There exists the possibility that he might deprive us all, entirely, of our lives — therefore let us leave." So they went outside. That night, lying exposed with no covering overhead, they were in danger of the cold.

In the morning they rose early and said: "Teacher, we pay homage to you. We are leaving." "Where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Wait, and I will nurse you sick ones." "Teacher, because you have made us who were not sick into sick ones, nursing the sick is only fitting." And so they departed for Śrāvastī.

The monks said to those who arrived: "Welcome, venerable ones. Welcome. Have you traveled comfortably? How did you travel?" "We were struck with cold in the night by the teacher Charka." "Why?" They then related the matter in full, and the monks of few wants began to reproach, criticize, and complain: "Why do monks, knowing full well that monks were already present earlier in the Saṅgha's temple, come later, use the threat of harm as a pretext, then press in afterward and lie and sit down on seats?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this basis of rule, and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and so on, as before. The passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, though they know full well, act as though they do not know" also proceeds as before. The blessed Buddha then addressed the venerable Charka: "Charka, is it true that, knowing full well that monks were already seated earlier in the Saṅgha's temple, you came later, used as your pretext the very fact that whoever would cause harm would go away, then pressed in afterward and lay or sat down on a seat?" "Blessed One, it is true." The blessed Buddha then rebuked him, saying: "That is not the way of a contemplative, it is not fitting, it is not appropriate, it is not in conformity with the rule — it is not something one who has gone forth ought to do." The Blessed One rebuked him in many ways and then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so on, as before. "My hearers shall proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, knowing full well that monks were already seated earlier in the Saṅgha's temple, comes later, uses as his pretext the very fact that whoever would cause harm would go away, then presses in afterward and lies or sits down on a seat — that is an offense."

Now, the phrase "whatever monk" refers to Charka or any other monk of the same sort. "Of the Saṅgha" means the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. "In the temple" means any place where it is suitable to perform the four bodily deportments: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. "Monks" means those who belong to this Dharma. "Were already seated" means were present there earlier. "Knowing full well" means either that he himself was aware of it or that others informed him. "Comes later" means arrives after them. "Whoever would cause harm" means whoever will not be able to rest comfortably. "Would go away" means that person will depart from that place to somewhere else. "Uses as his pretext" means using nothing other than that as his reason. "Presses in afterward" means having overwhelmed them by means of that harm. "On a seat" means on a resting place. "Lies down" means reclines the body. "Sits down" means places himself on his haunches. "An offense" means it scorches, torments, and causes one to fall into the bad destinations — into the hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of ruin. Furthermore, for as long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome factors of virtue — therefore it is said to be an offense.

As for how the offense is incurred: whenever a monk, knowing full well that monks were already seated earlier in the Saṅgha's temple, comes later, uses as his pretext the very fact that whoever would cause harm would go away, then presses in afterward and lies or sits down on a seat — in every such instance the offense is incurred.

Verses summarizing the intermediate rules:

The bad guest, the meritorious, the cold and the warm,
The impure, the washed-clean, the medicinal,
Suitable for practice, the recitation,
The fearful, together with the fearless.

The blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At that time the venerable Charka was saying to various newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here. Go out to tour the provinces. We shall also cut down our opponents there, and spread our own renown, and secure gains — and you will also obtain alms bowls, Dharma robes, nets, cups, belts, and texts for recitation, and —"

— and reading, recitation, yoga practice, and mental cultivation without distraction." Having thus encouraged them, those monks went to their teachers and preceptors and said: "Venerable preceptors, we are going on a tour of the provinces. With whom? With the venerable Charka."

The elder monks replied: "Venerable ones, that one habitually practises every kind of base conduct. He will bring shame upon you."

The young monks answered: "The venerable Charka is like a father to us. Why would he bring shame upon us?" And having thus dismissed the words of their seniors as empty, they set out on the provincial tour together with him.

When Charka had passed beyond the outer boundary markers, he said: "Venerable ones, why are you setting out on a provincial tour without having established a residence? Come here — settle down first." He had them sit cross-legged before him and assigned them their lodgings. He assigned some of them a leather bag, some an alms bowl, some a copper vessel, some a cup, some a communal ball of medicinal pills. Then, with both arms extended and wearing nothing but a sweat-cloth, he went about making himself known to the world. They proceeded to a certain cliff-face, and there they rested beside a well. At that place there was a monastery on the cliff, and its signal gong was struck. On hearing it, the monks said: "Teacher, the gong has been struck at the monastery — let us enter."

Charka said: "Those who have no work — idlers — strike the gong for the sake of work. People such as we who are weary would only be required to do tasks there. That kind of place exists."

The monks replied: "Teacher, is it not the gong for the receipt of gains? If that is what it is, if we go to the boundary we shall obtain them."

"The teacher has great fame and merit, so he will obtain them. But who would give to us? If there happen to be gains today, take his share as well." When they entered, the gong for the distribution of lodgings was struck, and the monks said: "Venerable ones, select your lodgings."

Those monks said: "There is someone elder than us."

"Who is that?"

"The teacher Charka."

"Then take his share as well." And so they selected lodgings.

Now the venerable Charka was also there, sitting and engaging in gossip: "Whose cliff is this? Whose monastery? Whose shrine? Whose pleasure grove? Whose park? Whose well? Whose field? Whose cattle? Whose buffalo?" — sitting there engaged in such gossip.

Those monks, for their part, thought: "The teacher Charka is going to be delayed for a long while." So they consulted one another, and having prepared the venerable Charka's sleeping place and set out washing-water and foot-ointment all in order, they said to one another: "Venerable ones, today we have eaten poor food, so we cannot recite. For now, let us cultivate mental application." They entered a room with a meditation platform, sat cross-legged, and began to practise meditative concentration.

The venerable Charka, for his part, sat on and on as long as he had conversational partners for his gossip. When at last there was no one left to talk with, and at the time when sight was failing in the dusk, he came to the monastery and began calling out: "Venerable ones! Venerable ones!"

The monks said to him: "Venerable Charka, why are you calling out like someone plunging into the middle of a thick swamp?"

Charka replied: "If some of my young charges are lodged here, have any of them fallen ill?"

On hearing this, they replied: "Teacher, do not call out. The caretaker of the lodgings has spread out your sleeping mat in the inner chamber, along with washing-water and —"

"— and foot-washing water has also been set out. Go and sleep there. Today, as we were seeking poor food, our recitation fell behind, so for the time being we are doing meditation here in this waiting hall." Charka said: "Venerable ones, did the Blessed One (the Buddha) not declare that one who does not read has no wisdom? Come, apply yourselves to recitation." With that he seated the two of them together and had them recite through the night.

In the morning they rose early and said: "We pay homage to the teacher. We are leaving. Where are we going? To Śrāvastī." "Stay — I shall nurse those among you who are ill." "Teacher, since you made us, who were not ill, into sick people, and then nursed the sick, that is quite enough nursing." And with that they set off for Śrāvastī.

When the monks there greeted them — "Venerable ones, welcome, welcome! How did the journey go? How did it go in comfort?" — they replied: "Our teacher Charka kept us reciting through the entire night." "How did he keep you reciting?" And the monks there recounted it all in detail to the resident monks.

Now at that point certain monks of small virtue began to censure, ridicule, and reproach, saying: "Why does a monk, out of deliberate intention, exalt himself over other monks?" On the occasion of this censure and reproach, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "However little a monk exalts himself over another monk, that becomes a transgression in every case."

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the forty-fifth fascicle.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time the venerable Charka was urging newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come! Let us go touring the provinces. There we shall also silence our adversaries, spread our own fame, and acquire gain. And as for you — be free from distraction in alms-bowl, in robe, in nets, in small bowls, in girdles, in recitation of scripture, in reading, in oral recitation, in yoga, and in applying the mind." Having so exhorted them, those monks went to their teachers and preceptors and said: "Venerable preceptors, we are setting out to tour the provinces." "With whom?" "With the venerable Charka." "Venerable ones, that one habitually engages in bad conduct, and he will bring harm upon you." "But venerable preceptors, the venerable Charka is to us as a father and mother in his manner of dwelling — why would he bring harm upon us?" And with that they dismissed what had been said to them, and set out on tour through the provinces together with him.

When Charka was outside and the boundary time had passed, he said: "Venerable ones, why do you set out on tour without establishing a lodging-place? Come — observe the practice of the dwelling." And he had them sit down in a row before him and set them to keeping the lodging. He assigned some of them a strainer, some a vessel for the alms-bowl, some a cylindrical container, some a small bowl, and some a bottle for pouring medicines over the head. Then, stretching out both his arms and wearing nothing but a sweat-cloth, he went about exalting himself before the world, while they, having arrived at a certain cliff, were resting by a well when a gandhī (a wooden sounding board) was struck at a monastery there upon the cliff.

On hearing it they said: "Teacher, the gandhī has been struck at the monastery — let us go in." Charka said: "Those who have nothing but a blackened alms-bowl will strike the work-gandhī, and we who are weary will have to do work — such a situation will arise." "Teacher, is it not the gandhī for receiving gifts? If it is, then if we go to the boundary we shall obtain something."

"Teacher, you are of great renown and great merit, so you will obtain it — but who will give it to us? If today there is something to be had, then take our share as well." When they had gone there, after a little while the lodging-gandhī of that place was struck, and the monks said: "Venerable ones, take your lodgings." They replied: "There is someone among us who is even more senior." "Who is it?" "It is Teacher Charka." "Then take his share as well." And so they accepted the lodging.

Now Venerable Charka was still there, passing the time in idle chatter: "Whose is this cliff? Whose is this temple? Whose is this shrine? Whose is this pleasure grove? Whose is this park? Whose is this well? Whose is this field? Whose are these cattle? Whose are these buffalo?" — so he sat about in idle talk. The others thought to themselves, "Teacher Charka is going to be delayed for a long time," and so they consulted one another, prepared Venerable Charka's bed, set out the foot-water and the foot-washing basin together, and said to one another: "Venerable ones, today we have eaten our fill of good food — let us for a while chant together in pairs." And so they began chanting together in pairs.

Venerable Charka, for as long as his idle chatter found an answering companion, sat on and on. But when his idle talk found no more partner, he came to the monastery at the time when the light was failing, and asked them: "Venerable ones, what are you doing?" "Teacher, today we went seeking good food, and for a while we are chanting together in pairs." Charka said: "Venerable ones, did the Blessed One not declare that one who does not meditate lacks wisdom? Come here, all of you — sit in meditation!" And with that he ushered them into the back room, sat them down cross-legged, and kept them awake through the entire night.

In the morning they rose early and said: "Teacher, we pay homage to you. We are leaving." "Where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Wait — I will nurse the sick ones among you." "Teacher, you who made those of us who were not sick fall ill are now proposing to nurse the sick — that is quite something!" And with that they set off for Śrāvastī.

When the monks met them, they said: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! How was your journey? How did you travel?" "We traveled well enough. Our Teacher Charka kept us awake the whole night." "How did he keep you awake?" And they then recounted the whole affair in detail to the monks.

Thereupon, certain monks of little virtue began to criticize, defame, slander, and speak ill of him, saying: "Why does a monk deliberately set out to make himself equal to senior monks?" When the monks brought the matter before the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Whenever a monk makes himself out to be equal to even a slightly more senior monk, it becomes a transgression in every case."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time Venerable Charka was urging the newer and newer monks: "Come, venerable ones — travel through the provinces. There we shall crush our opponents, proclaim our own renown, and also secure gains. As for yourselves, you need not trouble yourselves with your alms-bowls, your robes, your nets, your bowls, your waistbands, reciting scripture, reading, chanting, yoga, or mental application." And when those monks made request of their teachers and preceptors: "Preceptors, we are going to travel through the provinces — with whom shall we go?"

"Venerable ones, Venerable Charka is a person of thoroughly bad conduct — he will bring disgrace upon you."

But those monks dismissed their words as no words at all, saying, "Preceptor Venerable Charka abides toward us just as a father and mother would — why would he bring disgrace upon us?" And they went off to travel through the provinces together with him.

When Charka had passed beyond the outer boundary, he said, "Venerable ones, why do you set out to travel through the provinces without having first established a base? Come here — settle down." And he had them sit down in a row before him and established a base.

He assigned to some among them a small bag; to some, an alms-bowl vessel; to some, a small pot; to some, a cup; and to some, a round water vessel for pouring over the head. Then, with both arms extended and wearing nothing but a sweat cloth, he went about the world presenting himself with an air of superiority. When they arrived at a rocky cliff, they rested there beside a well. Now at that cliff there was a monastery, and the wooden sounding board was struck. When they heard it, they said, "Teacher, the sounding board has been struck at the monastery — let us enter."

Charka said, "Those who have nothing but black alms-bowls are striking the work sounding board, and we who are tired would then have to do work — that is the sort of situation it would be." They said, "Teacher, might it not be the gains sounding board? If so, we will get something when we go to the boundary." Charka replied, "The teacher has great renown and great merit, so he will receive something — but who is going to give to us? If there are any gains today, he should take them for himself as well." They went in.

After some time had passed there, the sounding board for lodging was struck, and the monks said, "Venerable ones, claim your lodgings." Those monks replied, "There is someone among us who is more senior." "Who is that?" "It is Teacher Charka." "He should claim for himself as well." And so they did claim their lodgings.

Venerable Charka remained there, passing the time in idle gossip: "Whose is this rocky cliff? Whose is this monastery? Whose is this shrine? Whose is this grove? Whose is this pleasure garden? Whose is this well? Whose is this field? Whose are these cattle? Whose are these buffalo?" — and so he remained in idle chatter.

Those monks thought to themselves, "Teacher Charka is going to hold us up for a long time," and so they consulted one another. They spread out Venerable Charka's bedding, set out foot-water and foot-ointment in one place, and said to one another, "Venerable ones, the cold season has now arrived — let us go into the fire room and sleep." And they went into the fire room and slept.

As long as Venerable Charka had a counterpart in his idle gossip, he remained there; but when there was no longer anyone to reciprocate his idle talk, he came to the monastery at the time when his sight failed him in the dark, and began calling out, "Venerable ones! Venerable ones!"

The monks said to him, "Venerable Charka, why do you call out like someone who has entered deep into a thicket of mud?"

Charka said, "Some of my young ones were here — have any of them perhaps fallen ill?"

When they heard this, they said, "Teacher, do not call out. In the inner chamber of the lodging, the bed has been made up and foot-water and foot-ointment have been set out — sleep there. As for us, the cold season has now arrived and we have gone into the fire room to sleep. Venerable ones, if you should come down with a blood disorder or a bile disorder, how would we be able to nurse you for that long? Come out." And with that he drove them outside without any shelter, doused them with cold water, and fanned them with a cooling fan in the middle of the night.

At dawn, when night had lifted, those monks said, "Teacher, we pay homage to you. We are here. Where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Then stay, and we shall nurse those among you who are sick." "Teacher, you have made healthy monks into sick ones, so it is only fitting that you nurse those who are ill." And with that, they set off for Śrāvastī. When they arrived, the monks greeted them saying, "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! Have you traveled comfortably? How was your journey?" "Our teacher Chārkā struck us with blows in the middle of the night." "How did he strike you?" And so they recounted the whole affair in detail to the monks there.

Some monks of little account began to criticize, denounce, and reproach, saying, "Why does the monk Chārkā deliberately humiliate his fellow monks?" And so the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, to whatever degree a monk humiliates another monk, that act becomes an offense in every case."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Chārkā would urge newly ordained monks, saying, "Come, venerable ones — come and go on circuit through the provinces. There we shall silence our opponents, proclaim our own reputation, and secure offerings. And as for you, you need not trouble yourselves with alms bowl and robe, with nets, with bowls, with belts, with receiving transmissions, with recitation, with chanting, with yoga, or with mental practice." When those monks were thus encouraged, they went to their preceptors and teachers and said, "Preceptors, we are going on circuit through the provinces." "With whom?" "With the venerable Chārkā." "Venerable ones, he lives by improper conduct, and he will bring humiliation upon you." "Preceptors, the venerable Chārkā abides toward us as a father and mother would — why would he bring humiliation upon us?" And dismissing their words, they set off on circuit together with him.

When Chārkā had led them out beyond the outer boundary, he said, "Venerable ones, why are you going on provincial circuit without having settled your lodgings? Come, take your lodgings now." And having made them sit down before him on their haunches, he assigned them their lodgings. To some he assigned a gourd; to some he assigned an alms bowl; to some he assigned a gourd dish; to some he assigned a small bowl; to some he assigned a broad-spouted jug for pouring liquid over the head. Then, stretching out both arms and wearing nothing but a sweat-cloth, he went about the world in haughty display.

They made their way to a rocky cliff, and while they were resting beside a well there, they heard the wooden board being struck at a temple on top of the cliff. They said, "Teacher, the board is being struck at the temple — let us go in." Chārkā said, "Those who have nothing but black alms bowls will strike the work-board, and we who are weary will have to do labor — such will be our situation." "Teacher, is this not the board for receiving offerings? In that case, if we go to the boundary, we shall obtain some." "The teacher is famous and has great merit, so he will receive them — but who will give them to us? If today there happen to be any offerings, then take some for me too."

When they went there, as soon as they arrived the board for announcing lodgings was struck. The monks said, "Venerable ones, take your lodgings." They replied, "There are those among us who are senior." "Who are they?"

"The teacher Charka!" "Then take his lodgings." And they took those lodgings.

Now the venerable Charka was there at that time, sitting engaged in various conversations — asking whose was this rocky slope, whose this monastery, whose this temple, whose this pleasure grove, whose this park, whose this well, whose this field, whose these cattle, whose these buffalo. Thinking "The teacher Charka will be delayed a long while," the monks conferred among themselves and, having prepared the venerable Charka's bed and set out his foot-water and foot-ointment together in one place, they said to one another, "Venerable ones, the evening hour is now upon us; let us enter the dormitory and sleep." And they entered the dormitory and slept.

The venerable Charka, for as long as his various conversations had a partner to keep them going, sat on and on in conversation; and when at last the conversations had no partner left, then at the hour of dusk he came to the monastery and began calling out: "Venerable ones! Venerable ones!" The monks said to him, "Venerable Charka, why do you call out like one who has entered deep into a thicket of reeds?" Charka said, "If some young disciples of mine are lodged here, might one of them not have fallen ill?" When they heard this, they said, "Teacher, do not call out. In the main lodging-house a bed has been prepared for you, and foot-water and foot-ointment have been set out — go and sleep there. We, for the evening hour has come upon us, have entered the dormitory and are sleeping. Venerable ones, if you were to be afflicted by wind or phlegm, how could we attend upon your illness for so long? Come inside." And with that they brought him inside, covered the windows, lit a fire, closed the door, wrapped him in as many blankets as there were, piled them on top of him, and sat with him.

When dawn broke the next morning, they said, "Teacher, we pay you homage. We are leaving." "Where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Stay, and I will nurse your sick ones among you." "Teacher, you have made us, who were not sick, into sick men — enough of nursing the sick!" And they departed for Śrāvastī.

The monks said to them when they arrived, "Venerable ones, welcome, welcome! Have you traveled comfortably? How did you travel?" "The teacher Charka tormented us through the night from the very first watch." "How did he torment you?" And they recounted the whole incident to the monks in full.

Then certain monks who were men of little virtue began to scold, saying, "Why do monks, with deliberate intent, set themselves up as superior to other monks? They make disparaging remarks, they spread reproaches, they speak slander." With that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Whenever a monk sets himself up as superior to another monk even to the slightest degree, it shall everywhere constitute an offense."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Charka was saying to the newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here. Go on a circuit of the district; we shall there demolish our adversaries, proclaim our own fame, and secure offerings. And you, do not trouble yourselves with alms-bowl, robes, net, cup, girdle, textual study, recitation, chanting, yoga, or mental application."

He also encouraged them, saying, "You should also attend to the sick among you." When the monks came to know that he engaged in all manner of base conduct, none of them were willing to go on a circuit of the district with him, and so he went alone. On his circuit he came to a shrine built into a rocky cliff. That shrine had no shelter for defecation and no shelter for urination, and so the monks would place their chamber-pots there, defecate and urinate in them, and leave them behind. When Charka entered that shrine, and when the monks came to know that he engaged in all manner of base conduct, not one of them waited upon him. He thought to himself, "I shall make these black-bowl men displeased," and so he climbed up onto the shrine. When he saw that chamber-pots had been placed there, he said, "Is this shrine made of bronze?" and seizing those pots by their rims with his toes, he hurled them outside. During the night, when the monks rose and could not find their pots, they defecated and urinated at the mouth of a fox's den. Then when dawn broke at the end of the night, faithful brahmins and householders arrived, and he said to them, "Wise ones, look at how these monks of base conduct who carry black alms-bowls have fouled every shrine with their defecation and urination." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Whenever a monk sets himself up as superior to another monk even to the slightest degree, it shall everywhere constitute an offense."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Charka was saying to the newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here. Go on a circuit of the district; we shall there demolish our adversaries, proclaim our own fame, and secure offerings. And you, do not trouble yourselves with alms-bowl, robes, net, cup, girdle, textual study, recitation, chanting, yoga, or mental application. You should also attend to the sick among you."

When the monks came to know that he engaged in all manner of base conduct, none of them were willing to go on a circuit of the district with him, and so he went alone. On his circuit he came to a shrine built into a rocky cliff. When Charka entered that shrine, and when the monks came to know that he engaged in all manner of base conduct, not one of them waited upon him. He thought to himself, "I shall make these black-bowl men displeased," and so he swallowed a purgative pill, entered the hot room, and sat there. While he was sitting there, he began to have loose bowels. Now the Blessed One had instructed that sick monks should be attended to three times a day, and so elder monks came to inquire after his illness. They asked him, "Venerable one, are you at ease?" He said, "I am at ease." The elders sat a while and then began to leave. He said, "Elders, please wait just a moment." They sat a while again and began to leave, and once more he said, "Elders, please wait yet another moment. Venerable ones, have I not deliberately set myself up as superior?"

When he said, "You there with the black bowl, you should not be displeased in that way," the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "However much a monk sets himself up as superior over another monk, in every case that becomes a transgression."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Chārka began urging the newer monks, saying: "Venerable ones, come here, let us go on the alms round together. There we will also silence our opponents, proclaim our own fame, and secure offerings. And you too should concern yourselves with the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the net bag, the bowl stand, the belt, the recitation of scriptures, the reading, the chanting, the yoga practices, and the mental contemplations without distraction. You should also nurse the sick among you." When the monks came to understand that this was reprehensible conduct being practiced throughout, no one wished to go with him on the alms round, and so he went alone. Going along on his rounds, he came to a certain temple built into a rocky cliff. In that temple there dwelled only ascetic monks. When Chārka entered that temple, the monks learned that he was one who engaged in such reprehensible conduct throughout, and so not a single monk attended to his needs. He then thought to himself, "These ones with the black bowls should be made displeased," and he saw that the temple was already half-completed. So the venerable Chārka went to the householder who was the patron of that place, arrived there, and said: "Householder, why do you not complete the temple? Has not the Blessed One himself said,

Enter quickly into virtue,
turn the mind away from evil deeds.
If one makes the offering of merit,
the mind comes to delight in evil.

Noble one, I have the kārṣāpaṇa coins but I have no laborers." The householder said: "Has not the Blessed One declared that monks should do building work? If the noble one is willing to do the building work, that would be excellent." So Chārka went to the temple and struck the wooden sounding board (gaṇḍī). The Blessed One had praised striking the gaṇḍī to summon monks, and so the monks came when the gaṇḍī was struck. Then, as the monks saw how many planks the venerable Chārka had begun to shape, those monks too began to shape planks. Chārka set those monks to producing planks all day long, and they said: "Venerable ones, this temple was formerly suited to yoga practice, but now it has become suited to building work. We are going to Śrāvastī." They went to Śrāvastī, and when they arrived the monks said to them: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! We are glad to see you, but we are not glad that you have come away. If that temple was suited to yoga practice, why did you abandon that temple and come here?" They replied: "Venerable ones, that temple was formerly suited to yoga practice, but now it has become suited to building work." "How so?" "The venerable Chārka came there and started the building work." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "However much a monk sets himself up as superior over another monk, in every case that becomes a transgression."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At that time the venerable Chārka said to various newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here and go on a district round with me. There we shall also silence our opponents, proclaim our own fame, and secure gains. And you yourselves need not be troubled with the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the strainer, the bowl-stand, the belt, studying scripture, recitation, chanting, yoga, or mental application. You shall also nurse those among you who are sick." Having thus encouraged them, when the monks came to know that this was base conduct that he was habitually practising, none of them were any longer inclined to go on the district round with him. So he went on the district round alone, and arrived at a temple set in a rocky cliff. In that temple there were only monks who engaged in recitation. When Chārka entered that temple, knowing from the monks that this was base conduct that he habitually practised, none of them ministered to his needs. He then thought: "I will make these monks with their black alms bowls displeased." Now that temple had already been half built, and so the venerable Chārka went to the householder who was its patron and, having gone there, said: "Householder, why do you not complete the temple? Has not the Blessed One also said:

Engage swiftly in what is virtuous,
and turn the mind away from evil deeds.
If one offers up merit,
the mind will come to delight in evil."

"Noble one, I have the kārṣāpaṇa coins, but I have no workmen." "Householder, has not the Blessed One said that monks should do building work in return?" "If the noble one is willing to do building work in return, that would be excellent." Chārka went to the temple and struck the gaṇḍī. The Blessed One had said that one should respond to the gaṇḍī, and so the monks responded to the gaṇḍī. When they saw how many planks the venerable Chārka was beginning to set in place, the monks too began setting planks in place. Chārka had those monks doing the plank-work from morning until midday, and then they said: "Venerable ones, this temple was formerly suited to recitation, but now it has become suited to building work. Go to Śrāvastī." Those monks went to Śrāvastī, and the monks said to them: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! We are glad to see you, but we are not glad that you have come away. If that temple was suited to recitation, why did you abandon that temple and come here?" "Venerable ones, that temple was formerly suited to recitation, but now it has become suited to building work." "How so?" "The venerable Chārka came there and started the building work." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "However much a monk sets himself up as superior over another monk, in every case that becomes a transgression."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At that time the venerable Chārka said to various newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here and go on a district round with me. There we shall also silence our opponents, proclaim our own fame, and secure gains. And you yourselves need not be troubled with the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the strainer, the bowl-stand, the belt, studying scripture, recitation, chanting,

chanting, meditation, and mental application. You shall also tend to the sick among you." Having thus urged them with enthusiasm, when the monks came to know that this was the conduct of one who takes up an inferior dwelling place and practices accordingly, none of them were willing to go on the district round together with him. So Chārka went on the district round alone and came to a monastery built into a cliff face. That monastery was a place of danger, for it was frequented by robbers. When Chārka entered that monastery, the monks came to know that this was the conduct of one who takes up an inferior dwelling place, and so not a single monk rendered him any service. He thought to himself, "I shall make these black-bowled ones unhappy," and so he opened the gate and sat down in the gateway. The duty monk said, "Venerable Chārka, I am going to close the gate — please sit over to this side." Chārka replied, "You close your own cell door properly and sit down," and he did not give way so the gate could be closed. The monks, being in a place of danger with the monastery gate unclosed, spent the night in fear and alarm, and in that state they passed the night until dawn. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "However much a monk sets himself up as superior over another monk, in every case that becomes a transgression."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At that time the venerable Chārka said to various newly ordained monks: "Venerable ones, come here and go on a district round with me. There we shall also silence our opponents, proclaim our own fame, and secure gains. And you yourselves need not be troubled with the alms bowl, the Dharma robe, the strainer, the bowl-stand, the belt, studying scripture, recitation, chanting, meditation, and mental application. You shall also tend to the sick among you." Having thus urged them with enthusiasm, when the monks came to know that this was the conduct of one who takes up an inferior dwelling place and practices accordingly, none of them were willing to go on the district round together with him. So Chārka went on the district round alone and came to a monastery built into a cliff face. That monastery was a place without danger. When Chārka entered that monastery, the monks came to know that this was the conduct of one who takes up an inferior dwelling place, and so not a single monk rendered him any service. He thought to himself, "I shall make these black-bowled ones unhappy." And since that monastery was without danger, the monks went out to relieve themselves, and while they were out, Chārka barred the gate, laid out his bedding in the gateway, and went to sleep. When the monks went out again in the night to relieve themselves, they said, "Venerable Chārka, we are going outside — please move over to this side." Chārka replied, "Go outside from the back corner of each of your own cells." The monks, needing to relieve themselves, had some of them relieve themselves in the courtyard, and others relieve themselves beside the pond. Then at dawn brahmin householders who were devotees arrived at the monastery, and Chārka said to them, "Wise ones, just look at how these black-bowled ones of inferior dwelling and conduct have befouled the entire monastery with their excretions." At that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"If a monk demeans another monk even slightly, he commits an offense in all cases. Moreover, monks, there are these six further places that are not to be assigned: the gatehouse, the base of the steps, the corridor, the lumber storage building, the fireroom, and the refuse pit. There is no offense for one who is a beginner, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by pain."

Thus the seventeenth rule on suppression-offenses is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the Venerable Ānanda encouraged the newer monks, saying, "Venerable ones, come here and let us go on a wandering tour of the region. There we can also refute our opponents, proclaim our own renown, and acquire material gains. And you yourselves need not be burdened with alms-bowl, robes, net, bowl-stand, waistband, recitation, reading, chanting, yoga, or mental work. You will also serve as nurses for those among you who are ill." When the monks came to know that this dwelling was a place of corrupt conduct all around, none of them felt any enthusiasm for going on the wandering tour with him. Then a wandering ascetic said, "Venerable Ānanda, I will go on the wandering tour with you." The monks said to that wandering ascetic, "That wandering ascetic is one who practices corrupt conduct everywhere — it will demean you." The wandering ascetic replied, "I am a man of years past, and there remains not even a little that he needs to look after for me in the way of lodging, recitation, reading, chanting, yoga, or mental work — so what can he do to me?" And having made nothing of those monks' words, he set off on the wandering tour together with Ānanda.

When Ānanda had passed beyond the outer boundary, he said, "Wandering ascetic, carry this waterpot for a while." The wandering ascetic replied, "Venerable Ānanda, have you not seen the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha? What use is this worthless implement?" Ānanda said, "Wandering ascetic, if you refuse to carry it, do you think you are more learned than I?" The wandering ascetic replied, "I may not be learned, but I speak what is reasonable." Ānanda thought, "I will make this wandering ascetic uncomfortable," and the two of them continued on their wandering journey. Eventually the two arrived at a rocky cliff, and while they rested beside a well there, a wooden sounding board was struck at a monastery on the top of that rocky cliff. Upon hearing it, the wandering ascetic said, "Venerable Ānanda, the sounding board is being struck at the monastery — let us go." Ānanda said, "At such a place as this, those who have no black-bowled ones strike the work-board and we weary ones will have to do the work — that is the kind of place it will be." The wandering ascetic said, "Venerable Ānanda, is it not the sounding board for material gains?" Ānanda replied, "If that is so, when we arrive at the boundary we will receive them." "But Venerable Ānanda, you have great renown and merit, so you will receive them — who will give to me?" Ānanda said, "Go, and if there are material gains, collect them on my behalf as well."

So the wandering ascetic went, and shortly thereafter the sounding board for lodging was struck. The monks said, "Wandering ascetic, receive a lodging." He replied, "There is one who is older than I." "Who is that?" "The Venerable Ānanda." "Then receive it on his behalf as well." So he received the lodging.

Meanwhile the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there engaged in worldly conversation,

"Whose is this rocky cliff? Whose is this temple? Whose is this shrine? Whose is this pleasure grove? Whose is this garden enclosure? Whose is this well? Whose is this field? Whose are these cattle? Whose are these buffalo?" — so he sat there engaged in worldly conversation.

The wandering ascetic thought to himself, "The Venerable Ānanda is going to be delayed for a long time," and so he spread out Ānanda's bedding on the upper floor, set out the foot-washing water and the foot-wiping cloth in one place, washed his own two feet outside the temple, and then went down to the lower room, made up his own bed, and lay down to sleep.

The Venerable Ānanda, for as long as he had company in his worldly conversation, remained sitting. When at last his companions in conversation had gone and the time came when the lamps were extinguished, he came to the temple and began calling out, "Wandering ascetic! Wandering ascetic!" The monks said to him, "Venerable Ānanda, why do you call out like someone plunging into a thicket of reeds?" Ānanda said, "There is a wandering ascetic friend of mine here — has he been troubled?" The wandering ascetic heard this and said, "Venerable Ānanda, do not call out. I have made up your bed on the upper floor, set out the foot-washing water and the foot-wiping cloth in one place — go up there and rest." Ānanda said, "Wandering ascetic, there is a little door lamp — open the door." "Venerable Ānanda, I am exhausted; I will open it tomorrow morning." "Wandering ascetic, I will keep the lamp burning with you through the entire night until dawn — open it." "Venerable Ānanda, I am exhausted; I will not open the door for you."

Ānanda climbed up to the upper floor, washed his two feet, entered the lodging room, and called out, "Wandering ascetic!" The wandering ascetic replied, "What is it, Venerable Ānanda?" Now Ānanda was skilled in acoustics, and he directed a chair-leg to a point directly above the wandering ascetic's forehead — in such a way that if he pressed down hard enough, the chair-leg would break through the ceiling and come down onto the wandering ascetic's forehead — and he pressed down with great force. It struck the wandering ascetic's forehead and broke the skin of his forehead.

The wandering ascetic said, "Venerable Ānanda, I forgive you. I forgive you." "Hey, wandering ascetic, what are you saying?" The wandering ascetic thought to himself, "If I make a sound, he will claim seniority and take away my bed as well," and so he said nothing more and lay still.

The next morning he rose early and said, "Venerable Ānanda, I pay homage to you. I am leaving." "Wandering ascetic, where are you going?" "To Śrāvastī." "Wandering ascetic, stay — I will nurse you in your illness." "Venerable Ānanda, you have made someone who was not ill into someone ill, and now you offer to nurse him in his illness — what a fine nurse that would be!" And with that he departed for Śrāvastī.

The monks said to him, "Venerable wandering ascetic, welcome, welcome! How have you fared on your journey?" "Noble ones, how have you fared? The Venerable Ānanda has broken my forehead." "How did he break it?" And he then recounted the whole incident in full to the monks.

The monks of few wishes then reproached Ānanda, saying, "Why does a monk knowingly press down heavily on a chair or a chair-leg that is projecting out into the open space above the assembly's temple, and sit and lie there?" They reproached him, spoke out against him, and complained of it. Then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in connection with this case, and on this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before.

The phrase "the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign ignorance" and so forth proceeds as before. The Blessed One questioned the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you, knowing that a chair or a chair-leg was projecting out into the open space above the assembly's temple, pressed down heavily upon it and sat and lay there?" "Reverend One, it is so." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that this was not in keeping with the conduct of a renunciant, was not fitting, was not proper, was not in accord with the discipline — this is not something one who has gone forth should do. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits and so forth, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and this proceeds as before. "My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, knowing that a chair or a chair-leg is projecting out into the open space above the assembly's temple, presses down heavily upon it and sits or lies there — that is a transgression."

Now as for the phrase "whatever monk": this refers to a son of the Śākyas such as Ānanda, or to anyone else of that kind. "Of the assembly" means the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. "Temple" means any place suitable for the four modes of deportment — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. "Into the open space above" means into the space above the building. "Projecting out" means projecting over a thatched or leafed roof. "Chair" means a chair proper. "Chair-leg" means a chair-leg proper. "A leg projecting out" means a leg that protrudes. "Knowing" means that he himself has understood it, or that others have told him. "Presses down heavily" means that he presses upon it with force. "Sits" means that he rests upon it with his haunches. "Lies" means that he stretches his body out upon it. "A transgression" means that it scorches, torments, and causes one to fall into bad rebirths: the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of wrongful falling. Furthermore, for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs wholesome phenomena — hence it is said to be a transgression.

As for how the transgression is incurred: to whatever extent a monk, knowing that a chair or a chair-leg is projecting out into the open space above the assembly's temple, presses down heavily upon it and sits or lies there — in all such cases a transgression is incurred. If, however, the seat is covered with a flat board, covered with a small flat board, covered with a flat plank, covered with a plank that has a raised portion, or if the seat tilts and gives way, there is no transgression. If a footrest has been installed, or if a brace has been put in place, there is likewise no transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is beset by painful sensations. The eighteenth transgression concerned with sitting when a leg is projecting out is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the park of Ghositārāma. At that time the venerable Udāyin, knowingly, was watering grass, dung, and earth with water containing living creatures, and was having others water them. The monks said to him: "Venerable Udāyin, do not knowingly water grass, dung, and earth with water containing living creatures, and do not have others water them." Udāyin replied: "Has anyone counted these and entrusted them to me? If I were to go to the great eastern ocean, what harm would there be?"

"What harm would there be in going to the great southern ocean? What harm in going to the great western ocean? What harm in going to the great northern ocean? What harm in going to a river, a lake, or a pond?" The monks rebuked him, saying: "Monks, why do you, for such a trivial matter, reproach, humiliate, and speak ill of a monk who knowingly waters grass, dung, and earth with water containing living creatures, and has others water them?" This matter was then reported by the monks to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, in relation to this origin-story and in this connection, convened the assembly of monks, and so on, just as before. And the passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowingly do remarkable things" proceeds likewise as before.

The Blessed One then questioned the venerable Udāyin: "Udāyin, is it true that you knowingly watered grass, dung, and earth with water containing living creatures, and had others water them?" "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked him: "That is not the conduct of a renunciant; it is not fitting, not proper, not in accordance with the rule. What has gone forth from the household life ought not to do such a thing." Having thus rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on, just as before.

"My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk knowingly waters grass, or dung, or earth with water containing living creatures, or has others water them, incurs a transgression."

Now, as to the words of this rule: "Whatever monk" refers to Udāyin or anyone else of that kind. "Knowingly" means either that he himself has recognized it, or that others have told him. "Containing living creatures" — living creatures are of two kinds: those that are visible to the eye, and those that are caught by a water-strainer. "With water" means with water itself. "Grass" means grass itself. "Dung" means dung itself. "Earth" means earth itself. "Waters" means doing it oneself. "Has others water" means having another do it. "Incurs a transgression" means it burns him, scorches him, and causes him to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, into the states of misfortune. Moreover, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. That is why it is said to be a transgression.

Now, as to how a transgression arises in each case: If a monk, perceiving water that does contain living creatures as containing living creatures, waters grass, dung, or earth with it, or has others do so, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, being uncertain about water that does contain living creatures, waters grass, dung, or earth with it, or has others do so, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, perceiving water that does not contain living creatures as containing living creatures, waters grass, dung, or earth with it, or has others do so, he incurs a misdeed. If a monk, being uncertain about water that does not contain living creatures, waters grass, dung, or earth with it, or has others do so, he incurs a misdeed.

If a monk pours out a large bucketful of water containing living creatures, he incurs as many transgressions as the number of living creatures that are killed, and as many misdeeds as the number of living creatures that are not killed.

If a monk cuts through a large bucketful of water containing living creatures, he incurs as many transgressions as the number of living creatures that are killed, and as many misdeeds as the number of living creatures that are not killed. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, who is mentally disturbed, or who is overcome by feeling. The nineteenth transgression regarding conduct involving living creatures is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the Ghośita Park. The Group of Six were residing in temples that had been built by others, and while they were living there in those places, they began to mock Nanda and Upananda, saying: "This temple has fallen into disrepair. This one has cracks. This one has deteriorating joints. This one has a deteriorating surface. This one is like a widow's house." The monks then said to them: "Venerable ones, you are living in temples that were built by others, you cannot so much as set up a stone yourselves, and yet you taunt others." When those words were spoken, the Group of Six became filled with arrogance and began to say to one another: "These black-bowled ones, Nanda and Upananda, are pressing down hard on us by saying, 'You are living in temples built by others, you cannot so much as set up a stone yourselves, and yet you taunt others.' Come now — let us commission the building of a temple such as those temples that black-bowled ones have never commissioned before. If all of us apply ourselves to manual labor, the black-bowled ones will constantly be looking for an opportunity against us, and they will find the opportunity to say that all of the Group of Six have taken to manual labor. And then at the households where we beg, they will point out our faults to the lay supporters and set them against us. Therefore, among ourselves there is one who is learned, whose conduct is clear, and who is capable of threading a needle, drawing the awl through: we should go to him and rouse his enthusiasm. Let us go to the one among us who is learned, whose conduct is clear, and who is capable of drawing an awl through to thread a needle — the venerable one who is learned, whose conduct is clear, capable of drawing an awl through to thread a needle — and rouse his enthusiasm for going to that one." So they went to that one who was of like mind and said: "Venerable one, these black-bowled ones press down hard on us by saying, 'You are living in temples built by others, you cannot so much as set up a stone yourselves, and yet you taunt others.'" And pressing down on him exceedingly hard, those among us thought to themselves: "These black-bowled ones press hard on us by saying, 'You are living in temples built by others, you cannot so much as set up a stone yourselves, and yet you taunt others — come here! Let us commission a temple such as those temples that black-bowled ones have never commissioned before.' If all of us apply ourselves to manual labor, the black-bowled ones will be constantly looking for an opportunity against us, and they will find the opportunity to say that all of the Group of Six have taken to manual labor."

"Moreover, at those households where we go for alms, they will find fault with us for being a burden and turn people against us. Therefore, if we could manage to go to whichever one among us is learned, whose conduct is pure, who is able to thread a needle — and rouse his enthusiasm — that would be the right course of action. For this reason, whichever one among us is learned, whose conduct is pure, who is able to thread a needle: the Venerable Dundubhissara is learned, his conduct is pure, and he is able to thread a needle — so let us go to him and rouse his enthusiasm."

So they thought to themselves: "We should rouse the Venerable's enthusiasm for the sake of the temple, and we will entreat you — use this limb to overwhelm the black-bowled ones." Dundubhissara said: "That is a good plan; let it be done so." They went away in good spirits.

Now the Venerable Dundubhissara, having washed both feet outside the temple, entered the temple, sat down, and entered into the thought: "By whatever means it may be, let the Saṅgha's temple be accomplished." He began to reflect on who might be devoted to whom, and he thought to himself: "For the time being, the world with its gods is devoted to the Blessed One. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Śāriputra. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Aniruddha. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Aśvaśāvaka. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Bhadrika. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Vāṣpa. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Mahānāman. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Pūrṇa. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Vimala. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Gavāmpati. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Ānanda. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Sundarananda, the son of the Blessed One's younger sister. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Rāhula, the son of the Blessed One. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Nandaka. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Nanda. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Upananda. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Śīghragāmin. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka. One great householder is devoted to the Venerable Nābhasa — so it will not be possible to engage those. But in Kauśāmbī there dwells a brahmin who is wealthy, with abundant possessions and great resources, whose domain of dependents is broad and extensive — yet he is a miser, of narrow eye, one who would not give so much as a scrap to a crow, a man who hoards all his goods. But he possesses much silver and gold, and if he could be made to engage, the Saṅgha's temple would be accomplished."

Having entered into this thought, he passed the night with great effort. In the morning he put on his lower robe, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Kauśāmbī for alms. After passing through two or three houses for alms and collecting a small amount of flour, he began to enter the brahmin's house — and the doorkeeper stopped him, saying: "Noble one, stay there! Do not enter!"

He said:

"Fair one, the Blessed One has taught five kinds of places that are not our proper domain: the dwelling of musicians, the dwelling of a woman of loose conduct, the dwelling of a liquor seller, the dwelling of an outcaste, and the royal palace. Now, is this house a dwelling of musicians? Or is it a dwelling of a woman of loose conduct? A liquor seller's dwelling? An outcaste's dwelling? Or the royal palace? Why then do you stop me?" The doorkeeper said: "Noble one, you may well have much to reproach, yet this is not a dwelling of musicians, nor a dwelling of a woman of loose conduct, nor a liquor seller's dwelling, nor an outcaste's dwelling, nor the royal palace. Rather, this is the house of a certain great brahmin."

The Venerable Udāyin thought: "Where there is not even the chance of a face-to-face meeting, what else can there be?" And so, blocked at the gate, he sat absorbed in thought. Just then it happened that the son of a householder arrived there, and with him entered a company of twelve gathered for celebration, with dance, song, and the music of cymbals. As the doorkeeper began to examine them one by one, and his attention was turned away from the gate, the Venerable Udāyin seized the opportunity to enter, and once inside, he set about purifying the ground of attachment through his conduct.

When that brahmin saw him, he said: "The Venerable Udāyin has come. Please be seated on this cushion." Udāyin sat down purposefully, but finding no opening for conversation, he spoke: "Brahmin, permit me to have this small amount of alms-flour I obtained kneaded and offered." The brahmin instructed his daughter: "Daughter, gather the noble one's alms-flour and offer it." As the daughter began to knead it, the Venerable Udāyin started to inspect the flour. The brahmin asked: "Noble one, what are you examining?" "A living creature." "If one is present, what should be done?" "It must not be eaten." "If it were to be consumed, what fault would there be?"

"Brahmin, the Blessed One has taught that one who habitually resorts to killing, practices it repeatedly, and does it many times will, after the dissolution of this body at death, be reborn in a miserable realm, an evil destiny, a place of downfall, in the hells. And even if one were to come to a state equal to that of human beings, one would be short-lived." And he went on to teach extensively the ten paths of non-virtuous and virtuous action, and so forth.

The brahmin thereupon became filled with sincere faith, and himself filled a vessel with clean, pure food and drink, and said: "Noble one, out of compassion please accept this."

The Venerable Udāyin thought: "If I accept it, it will be like boiling something in a wooden vessel — what began as first will become last for me." Knowing this, he said: "Brahmin, let this small amount of alms-flour I obtained be fully enjoyed as it is. How could I take what is offered in faith and discard it?"

The brahmin said: "Noble one, it is the custom among us brahmins that if we obtain something inferior and then come by something superior, we set aside the inferior and enjoy the superior fully. What fault could that be for you?"

"Brahmin, we have properly undertaken the rules of training, whereas you brahmins have not properly undertaken the rules of training, and so you brahmins may do as you please. As for us, the Blessed One has proclaimed for us the four noble lineages. What are the four? The noble lineage of being content with whatever robe one happens to have; the noble lineage of being content with whatever alms-food one happens to receive; the noble lineage of being content with whatever lodging and bedding one happens to have;

and the noble lineage of delighting in renunciation and delighting in meditation. That brahmin, becoming filled with deep faith, said: "Noble one, please visit this household of yours from time to time." "Brahmin, that gatekeeper of yours is like the staff of Yama, the Lord of Death — do not let anyone past him; keep good watch at the gate, and then he will be no obstacle to me." The brahmin called the gatekeeper over and gave him careful instructions: "Ho there, steward! This household is one where a noble one comes to visit — see that you do not bar him. And instruct the household staff as well: you are not to show disrespect to anyone the noble one wishes to visit." The venerable Dundubhissara thought to himself: "This brahmin has become faithful. Nevertheless, if some black-bowled one were to enter here, that person would cause endless trouble — I must find a skillful approach." So he said to the gatekeeper: "Ho there, steward! Did you see how that brahmin became so full of faith toward me?" "Yes, noble one, I saw it." "Then let only me enter here, and do not allow any other black-bowled one inside. If you let some black-bowled one enter, I will have you brought before a great court." "Noble one, please proceed with full ease of mind. While you yourself are away and have not yet arrived, how much more would that mean that a black-bowled one of another sort might enter — that goes without saying." The venerable Dundubhissara arose with a glad heart and departed, and from then on he would go to that brahmin's house from time to time. And when the brahmin repeatedly made the same invitation over and over, the venerable Dundubhissara would not accept it but simply gave him teaching on the Dharma of generosity and took his leave.

This is the Vinaya Analysis, the forty-sixth fascicle.

Then on another occasion the venerable Dundubhissara praised to that brahmin the seven bases of merit-making arising from material things, and explained them fully at length. The brahmin said: "Noble one, I too would like to perform some basis of merit-making arising from material things." "Then do so, brahmin." "Noble one, what should I do?" "Have a temple built for the Saṅgha." The brahmin thought: "I have paid court to the noble Dundubhissara in many ways, and each time he did not accept — yet now he has accepted, and this too must be for the sake of the Saṅgha." Struck with wonder, he said: "Venerable sir, I have the kārṣāpaṇa coins, but I have no helper in the work of merit. You have acted as my helper in merit — in this way please have the noble Saṅgha supervise me with the work of building by entrusting it to their hands." The householder went to the temple, sat down at the far edge among the elders, and said: "Noble ones, I wish to build a temple for the noble Dundubhissara. For that purpose, out of affectionate care for me, I entreat the noble Saṅgha to appoint the noble Dundubhissara to supervise the building of my temple, entrusting it to his hands."

Now within the Saṅgha there was the venerable Śāriputra, who acted as the Saṅgha's presiding elder. He thought: "Even without being appointed by the Group of Six, he already tends to exalt himself over the monks — if he were appointed as supervisor, he would exalt himself over the monks all the more." And so the venerable Śāriputra said to Dundubhissara: "Venerable Dundubhissara, when I had the enclosure wall of the Jeta Grove built, no one appointed me as supervisor by entrusting it to their hands. And when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had the enclosure wall of the Ghositārāma built, no one appointed him as supervisor by entrusting it to their hands either."

"If you too wish to undertake the building of a temple, proceed without being appointed."

The venerable Dundubhissara thought: "Those of the black-bowled ones do not even like to see us — how could they entrust anything into our hands?" So he went to that brahmin and, having obtained kārṣāpaṇa coins, went to the brickmakers and said: "Good sirs, can you in a single day provide the bricks for a three-storied temple?" They replied: "Noble one, give us the kārṣāpaṇas and we shall return and supply them." He gave them the kārṣāpaṇas. He went to the tilers and said: "Good sirs, can you in a single day complete the roofing of a three-storied temple?" "Noble one, give us the kārṣāpaṇas and we shall return and do the work well." He gave them the kārṣāpaṇas. He went to the carpenters and said: "Good sirs, can you in a single day set the timbers for a three-storied temple?" "Noble one, give us the kārṣāpaṇas and we shall return and fix them in place." He gave them the kārṣāpaṇas. He went to the plasterers and said: "Good sirs, can you in a single day plaster a three-storied temple?" "Noble one, give us the kārṣāpaṇas and we shall return and plaster it." He gave them the kārṣāpaṇas. He went to the painters and said: "Good sirs, can you in a single day paint a three-storied temple?" "Noble one, give us the kārṣāpaṇas and we shall return and paint it." He gave them the kārṣāpaṇas. Then Dundubhissara went to the labourers' quarter, hired many labourers, and came to the temple site, and in a single day had the three-storied temple completed. Yet in building it he left no space for doorways, no space for pillars, no windows, and no space for drains — he had it built all solid throughout, in the very same uniform way.

He then went to the brahmin and said: "Brahmin, your temple is finished. Come, offer it to the Saṅgha."
