The brahmin replied: "Noble one, today I have not made preparation of food; tomorrow I shall make preparation of food and come." The Blessed One reflected: "This temple will collapse today itself. If it were to collapse without ever having been properly used, this brahmin, who has vomited hot blood, would come to such a pass as to die." Having reflected thus, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks in these words: 'Although I have instructed you, monks, not to accumulate virtue and to confess wrongdoing, nevertheless, whichever among you dwells in a state of meditative attainment and has entered into and obtained a particular absorption — let that one, by means of that meditative state and that absorption, spend the first watch of the night in that brahmin's temple.'" The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One, replied: "As you command, venerable sir," and he said to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has spoken thus: 'Although I have instructed you, monks, not to accumulate virtue and to confess wrongdoing, nevertheless, whichever among you dwells in a state of meditative attainment and has entered into and obtained a particular absorption — let that one, by means of that meditative state and that absorption, spend the first watch of the night in that brahmin's temple.'"

Those monks, saying to the venerable Ānanda, "As you command," listened to the venerable Ānanda and, whichever among them dwelt in a state of meditative attainment and had entered into and obtained a particular absorption, by means of that meditative state and that absorption spent the first watch of the night in that brahmin's temple.

Then, at the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One went there, and the Blessed One aroused a worldly intention. It is the nature of reality of the blessed buddhas that if they arouse a worldly intention, then even insects and worms come to know the Blessed One's mind and thoughts; whereas if they arouse a supramundane intention, then even pratyekabuddhas cannot know the Blessed One's mind and thoughts — to say nothing of śrāvakas and others.

Then Brahmā and Śakra (Indra) and the other gods thought to themselves: "Why has the Blessed One aroused a worldly intention?" And they perceived that the Blessed One intended to teach the Dharma to the gods at the middle watch of the night in that brahmin's temple.

Then Śakra and Brahmā and the rest of the gods, having understood the Blessed One's mind and thoughts, vanished from the divine world — just as a person stretches out a bent arm or bends back an outstretched arm — and appeared before the Blessed One. They prostrated with their heads at the Blessed One's two feet and stood to one side. The Blessed One then taught them the Dharma. They rejoiced and expressed their delight in what the Blessed One had declared, prostrated with their heads at his two feet, and vanished on the spot.

The Blessed One also passed the middle watch of the night there and then departed.

At the last watch of the night, a five-colored cloud gathered and discharged rain upon that temple — exactly as much rain as would fill it to the brim, as if it were a vessel filled with rinsing water — and by that water the entire temple was flooded to such a depth that it collapsed. The Group of Six heard that the temple had thus collapsed entirely. Hearing this, they fled in terror.

The brahmin, the following day, loaded a carriage with pure and fresh food and provisions, came to the temple, and asked the monks: "Noble ones, where is my temple?" Now there was an elder among the Group of Six who bore a grudge against them, and he said: "Brahmin, your temple is as flat as if a she-fox had been rolling in it. Take care not to dash your forehead against the doorpost as you enter."

The brahmin thought: "I dedicated such an enormous mass of wealth to this temple, and yet it has collapsed without ever having been used at all." He fainted and fell to the ground.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to that brahmin and say this to him: 'Many gods and humans, having dedicated temples to the Tathāgata, have caused them to be put to use — those the Tathāgata has not left unused. As for your temple here, the elder monks fully made use of it in the first watch of the night, and the Blessed One himself together with Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods also fully made use of it at the middle watch of the night. Therefore, you have obtained a fine acquisition indeed.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Blessed One," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he went to where that brahmin was, and said to him the following: "Brahmin, the Blessed One has declared: 'Many gods and humans, having dedicated temples to the Tathāgata, have caused them to be put to use — those the Tathāgata has not left unused. As for your temple here, the elder monks fully made use of it in the first watch of the night, and the Blessed One himself together with Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods also fully made use of it at the middle watch of the night. Therefore you have obtained a fine acquisition indeed.'"

The brahmin asked, "Venerable Ānanda, did the Blessed One make full use of my temple?"

"Brahmin, he did make full use of it."

"Venerable Ānanda, if the Blessed One has made full use of my temple, then I would gladly cause to be built for the Blessed One one such temple for each and every parasol — just like this one. But where are those good spiritual friends of mine?"

He had heard that the Group of Six monks had questioned the brahmin in that manner, and so he quickly and hastily arrived. That brahmin then presented each of them with a large bolt of fine cloth and furnished them with all manner of requisites as well. The monks then said to them, "It was the Group of Six who had a temple like this one built." The Group of Six responded, "Even though we did indeed cause all that wealth of that brahmin to be wasted in just that way, nevertheless he has now presented each of us with a large bolt of fine cloth and furnished us with all manner of requisites. In this way we have won that brahmin's admiration."

The monks of few wants asked why monks who boasted by means of the very limb that should be a cause for shame, criticizing and disparaging and backbiting — why they acted thus. And at that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this basis, and this occasion, convened the community of monks, and so forth, just as before. And it is likewise just as before regarding the passage beginning "The blessed buddhas know yet feign not to know," and so forth. The Blessed Awakened One then questioned the Group of Six: "Monks, is it true that you have done something so unseemly?"

"Blessed One, it is true."

The Blessed Awakened One declared, "It is unseemly," and proceeded to censure them. Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, for that reason, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, just as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should a monk undertake to have a large temple built — measuring it from when the site is examined with an eye to the gateway recess, the foundations, and the extent of the area for windows and light — the successive courses of bricks, including the plaster, are to be laid two or three. If more than that are laid, it is an offense. 'A monk' refers to one of the Group of Six or any other who is similarly disposed. 'A temple' is any place suitable for the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. 'Large' is large in two senses: in terms of what it is to be given and in terms of measure — and in this context both are intended. 'Undertake to have it built' means either by oneself or through another."

"The door socket and the lintel" means that a door socket and a lintel are to be installed. "With the perception of how much space for light" means with the perception of how much space is to be left at the beginning for windows and for drainage openings. "From the inspection of the ground, the successive courses of bricks together with the plaster, two or three" — "successive courses of bricks" means layers of bricks stacked one upon another; "together with the plaster" means together with the clay plaster; "are to be laid" means are to be placed; "if more than that are laid" means if more than that are placed.

"It is an offense" means: it causes one to be burned, scorched, and to fall into the bad destinations of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts (pretas), the lower realms, and the states of ruin. Moreover, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually confessed, it obstructs wholesome Dharma qualities — and that is why it is said to be an offense. As for how the offense arises: if a monk lays even so much as a single course of bricks beyond two or three, it becomes an offense in every case. If the construction is of stone alone, or of brick alone, or entirely of wood, or if the donor says "Build it and then we shall see" or "We shall look into it once it is complete," there is no offense in that.

The monks then petitioned the Blessed One, the Buddha: "The venerable Śāriputra observed the venerable Udāyin trying to appoint himself as the presiding officer of the assembly." The Blessed One said: "Monks, not only now — in the past as well, this one forestalled that one from being consecrated as king of the birds. Listen carefully to this.

"Monks, once upon a time, long ago, in the Himalayan foothills there was a great assembly of birds gathered together. As the proper time had come to appoint a king of the birds, the birds began to harm one another. They said: 'Friends, let us consecrate as king of the birds one among us who is able to govern us with judgment and to benefit us. Whom shall we consecrate as king of the birds?' Not far away there sat an old owl, and the birds said: 'Let us consecrate this old owl as king of the birds.' Not far from there sat an old myna bird. The birds said: 'First let us also ask the old myna bird about this,' and they went to the myna and asked.

The old myna bird spoke in verse:

That you birds would consecrate the owl as king —
this does not please me.
Look at his face when he is not angry;
what will he do when he is angry?

The birds did not consecrate the owl, and they consecrated that very old myna bird as king of the birds. Monks, the one who at that time, in that age, was the old myna bird is this very Śāriputra. The one who at that time, in that age, was the old owl is this very Udāyin. And just as at that time Śāriputra forestalled Udāyin from being consecrated as king of the birds, so now too Śāriputra has forestalled Udāyin from being appointed as presiding officer.

There is no offense for one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by feeling."

The twentieth offense pertaining to a temple is complete.

Summary verse: Not appointed, the sun setting, food and Dharma-robes, those of shared purpose, the boat, and the two solitary places — these are what the nun enabled. Intermediate summary verse: the discourse teaching joy, the six groups, the road sūtra, the corpse sūtra, the three treasuries, the noble trader, the perception of no self, the life-giver, the horse, and the aspiration prayer.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the noble nun, the great hearer, the elder among elders, along with others of her kind, accepted the rains retreat at Śrāvastī, in the nuns' retreat hall in the royal pleasure grove — namely Kulamātā, Nandā, Madavā, Paṭhācārā, Droganāsa, Sukhā, Candā, Gautamī Śyāmā, Utpalavaṇṇā, the nun Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the great mistress of beings, and still others besides — all these noble nuns, great hearers, elders among elders, accepted the rains retreat at Śrāvastī, in the nuns' retreat hall in the royal pleasure grove.

Then the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred nuns, went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, she bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, fully and properly with Dharma-endowed words; he led her to fully receive it; he fully praised her; he made her fully rejoice. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed words, he fully instructed, fully led her to receive it, fully praised her, made her fully rejoice, and then urged her saying, "Gautamī, it is your time — you may go."

Then the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, delighted and gladdened by what the Blessed One had declared, bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

After the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī had gone, the Blessed One reflected on it before long, and then declared to the monks: "Monks, I am now old, aged, advanced in years, and it would be wearisome for me to teach the fourfold assembly — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Therefore, monks, from this day forward, let the elder monks, in turn, teach the nuns."

Thereupon the elder monks taught the nuns in turn. But the venerable Ānanda, when his turn came around, was unable to teach the nuns.

Then the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred nuns, went once more to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, she bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One again instructed the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, fully and properly with Dharma-endowed words; he led her to fully receive it; he fully praised her; he made her fully rejoice. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed words, he fully instructed, fully led her to receive it, fully praised her, made her fully rejoice, and then urged her saying, "Gautamī, it is your time — you may go."

Then the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, delighted and gladdened by what the Blessed One had declared, bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

After the great mistress of beings, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī had gone, the Blessed One reflected on it before long, and then declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, those elder monks who teach the nuns in turn —

"Venerable one, most of the elder monks do teach the nuns in turn, but the venerable Ānanda, even when it is his turn, is unwilling to teach the nuns." Now at that time the venerable Ānanda was sitting right there in that assembly and heard this.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, you should instruct the nuns. Ānanda, you should teach the nuns. Ānanda, you should speak to the nuns words endowed with Dharma. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, whether it is I or you who instructs them is fitting; whether it is I or you who teaches them is fitting; and whether it is I or you who speaks words endowed with Dharma to the nuns is fitting."

The venerable Ānanda, saying nothing, accepted the instruction from the Blessed One in silence. Then the venerable Ānanda, delighted and gladdened by what the Blessed One had declared, bowed his head to the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then, when that same night had passed, the venerable Ānanda, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having gathered alms throughout Śrāvastī and completed the business of the meal, he returned from his alms round for the afternoon meal, put down his bowl and outer robe, washed his two feet, and entered the assembly hall in order to settle into inner stillness.

Then, when the venerable Ānanda had risen from his inner stillness in the cool of the morning, he took up his sitting cloth and, accompanied by a wandering monk walking behind him, went to where the nuns' rains-retreat quarters were in the royal pleasure grove.

The nuns saw the venerable Ānanda from a great distance. Seeing him, they prepared seats for the venerable Ānanda and said these words: "Venerable Ānanda, come! Venerable Ānanda, welcome! Venerable Ānanda, please be seated on the seat that has been prepared." The venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat.

Then those nuns bowed their heads to the two feet of the venerable Ānanda and took their places to one side. When they had taken their places to one side, the venerable Ānanda spoke to those nuns as follows:

"Sisters, ask your questions, and let there be talk endowed with Dharma. Among you, those who understand everything, let them say, 'We understand everything.' Those who do not understand everything, let them say, 'We do not understand everything.' Whoever speaks and fully understands the meaning of what is said, let that one take it exactly as it is. Whoever speaks and does not fully understand the meaning of what is said, let that one ask of oneself: 'What is the meaning of what the venerable Ānanda has said? What is it like?'

"Venerable Ānanda — for whatever reason the venerable Ānanda has said, 'Sisters, ask your questions, and let there be talk endowed with Dharma; among you, those who understand everything, let them say, We understand everything; those who do not understand everything, let them say, We do not understand everything; whoever speaks and fully understands the meaning of what is said, let that one take it exactly as it is —

whoever speaks and does not fully understand the meaning of what is said, let that one ask of oneself: 'What is the meaning of what the venerable Ānanda has said? What is it like?' — that very declaration has gladdened us and filled us with joy. We shall say: 'Venerable Ānanda, speak the Dharma, and among us those who understand everything shall say, We understand everything; those who do not understand everything shall say, We do not understand everything; whoever speaks and fully understands the meaning of what is said shall take it exactly as it is; whoever speaks and does not fully understand the meaning of what is said shall ask the venerable Ānanda himself: Venerable Ānanda, what is the meaning of what the venerable Ānanda has said? What is it like?'"

"Sisters, do you rightly see the inner sense base of the eye as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, do you rightly see the inner sense bases of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen with right wisdom, truly as it is, that these six inner sense bases are without self, and our minds too are devoted to them in just that way — as being without self."

"Sisters, excellent! Excellent! Indeed, the meaning of what was said is this: these six inner sense bases are to be seen truly as they are — as being without self.

"Sisters, do you rightly see the outer sense base of visible forms as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, do you rightly see the outer sense bases of sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mental phenomena as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen with right wisdom, truly as it is, that these six outer sense bases are without self, and our minds too are devoted to them in just that way — as being without self."

"Sisters, excellent! Excellent! Indeed, the meaning of what was said is this: these six outer sense bases are to be seen truly as they are — as being without self.

"Sisters, with respect to eye-consciousness — the eye-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the eye and visible forms — do you rightly see that eye-consciousness as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, with respect to mind-consciousness — the mind-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the mind and mental phenomena — do you rightly see that mind-consciousness as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen with right wisdom, truly as it is, that these six groups of consciousness are without self, and our minds too are devoted to them in just that way — as being without self."

"Excellent, sisters! Excellent!" he said. "That being so, these six groups of consciousness are to be seen truly as they are — as being without self.

Sisters, with respect to eye-consciousness — the eye-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the eye and forms, and from the coming together of these three there arises eye-contact — do you rightly see that eye-contact as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, with respect to ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — the mind-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the mind and mental phenomena, and from the coming together of these three there arises mind-contact — do you rightly see that mind-contact as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen with right wisdom, truly as it is, that these six groups of contact are without self, and our minds too are devoted to them in just that way — as being without self."

"Excellent, sisters! Excellent!" he said. "That being so, these six groups of contact are to be seen truly as they are — as being without self.

Sisters, with respect to eye-consciousness — the eye-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the eye and forms, and from the coming together of these three there arises contact, and from contact as condition there arises feeling: the feeling that arises from eye-contact — do you rightly see that feeling as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, with respect to ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — the mind-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the mind and mental phenomena, and from the coming together of these three there arises contact, and from contact as condition there arises feeling: the feeling that arises from mind-contact — do you rightly see that feeling as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen with right wisdom, truly as it is, that these six groups of feeling are without self, and our minds too are devoted to them in just that way — as being without self."

"Excellent, sisters! Excellent!" he said. "That being so, these six groups of contact are to be seen truly as they are — as being without self.

Sisters, with respect to eye-consciousness — the eye-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the eye and forms, and from the coming together of these three there arises contact, from contact as condition there arises feeling, and from feeling as condition there arises craving: the craving that arises from eye-contact — do you rightly see that craving as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Sisters, with respect to ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — the mind-consciousness that arises in dependence upon the mind and mental phenomena, and from the coming together of these three there arises contact, from contact as condition there arises feeling, and from feeling as condition there arises craving: the craving that arises from mind-contact — do you rightly see that craving as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my very self'?"

"Venerable Ānanda, we do not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen, just as it is, with genuine wisdom, that these six groups of craving are without self, and our minds are devoted to that understanding — that these six groups of craving are indeed without self."

"Excellent, sisters, excellent! He said: The meaning of this is that one should look at these six groups of craving exactly as they are — as being without self.

"Sisters, consider this example: an oil lamp burns in dependence upon the oil and the wick. The oil of that oil lamp is impermanent. The wick, the flame, and the vessel are also impermanent. Now, sisters, if someone were to say: 'Even though the oil is absent, and the wick, the flame, and the vessel are absent, the light that depended on them would nonetheless remain — permanent, stable, everlasting, of a nature that does not change, abiding as suchness' — would such a statement be well spoken?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it would not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, the oil of that oil lamp is impermanent, and the wick, the flame, and the vessel are also impermanent. When the oil is absent, and the wick, the flame, and the vessel are absent, the light that depended on them will not arise at all. That is why."

"Sisters, in the same way, if someone were to say of these six impermanent internal sense bases: 'Whatever pleasure and mental happiness arises in dependence on these six impermanent internal sense bases — that is permanent, stable, everlasting, of a nature that does not change, abiding as suchness' — would that statement be well spoken?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it would not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, from the very beginning we have seen, just as it is, with genuine wisdom, that these six internal sense bases are impermanent, and our minds are devoted to understanding that when those phenomena arise, such phenomena come to arise, and when those phenomena cease, such phenomena come to cease, subside, cool, and pass away."

"Excellent, sisters, excellent! He said: The meaning of this is that one should look at these six internal sense bases as being impermanent — as things such that when those phenomena arise, such phenomena come to arise, and when those phenomena cease, such phenomena come to cease, subside, cool, and pass away — seeing them exactly as they are.

"Sisters, consider this example: a great tree possessed of roots, a trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit — its roots are impermanent, its trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit are also impermanent. Now, sisters, if someone were to say: 'Even though the tree's roots, trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit are all absent, the shadow that depended on them would nonetheless remain — permanent, stable, everlasting, of a nature that does not change, abiding as suchness' — would that statement be well spoken?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it would not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it is like this: a great tree possessed of roots, a trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit — its roots are impermanent, and its trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit are also impermanent. If those roots are absent, and the trunk, heartwood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit are absent, then the shadow that depended on them would not arise at all, in any way whatsoever. Sisters, in just the same way, these six outer sense sources are impermanent. If someone were to say: 'These six outer sense sources are impermanent, yet the pleasure and mental ease that arose in dependence on them would remain — permanent, stable, everlasting, of a nature that does not change, abiding as suchness' — would that statement be well spoken?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it would not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, because from the very beginning we have seen, through authentic wisdom and in accordance with the correct view, that these six outer sense sources are impermanent — and our minds, too, are so inclined: that when such and such phenomena arise, such and such phenomena come to arise; and when such and such phenomena cease, such and such phenomena come to cease, to be pacified, to be cooled, and to subside."

"Excellent, sisters! Excellent! What was said means this: one should see with clear insight that these six outer sense sources are impermanent, and that when such and such phenomena arise, such and such phenomena come to arise; and when such and such phenomena cease, such and such phenomena come to cease, to be pacified, to be cooled, and to subside. That is how one should look at things exactly as they are.

Sisters, wise people here come to understand the full meaning conveyed by a simile — so listen now to a simile. Sisters, it is like this: a skilled butcher, or a butcher's skilled apprentice, slaughters a cow with a sharp butcher's knife. Without damaging the inner mass of flesh and without damaging the outer mass of hide, he slices through, cuts apart, and pierces all the inner channels — the interior blood vessels, the interior lungs, the interior liver, and all the interior veins — slicing through them all, cutting them apart, striking through them, and piercing them, before once again wrapping the whole in the cow's own hide. Now, sisters, if someone were to say of that cow: 'This cow is still joined to its hide; it is not separated from it' — would that statement be well spoken?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it would not."

"Why is that?"

"Venerable Ānanda, it is like this: the skilled butcher, or the butcher's skilled apprentice, slaughtered the cow with a sharp butcher's knife. Without damaging the inner mass of flesh and without damaging the outer mass of hide, he sliced through, cut apart, and pierced all the interior blood vessels, the interior lungs, the interior liver, and all the interior veins — slicing through them all, cutting them apart, striking through them, and piercing them — and then wrapped the whole in the cow's hide. That cow, Venerable Ānanda, is not joined to its hide; it is separated from it."

"Sisters, this simile has been given in order to convey a meaning clearly, so let it be understood in this way:

"Sisters, here is the meaning that is to be understood: 'The cow' is a designation for this gross physical body, composed of the four great elements, born from the impure seed of one's parents, built up by cooked grain and warm food, subject to constant anointing, washing, massaging, rubbing, dispersal, and disintegration. 'The inner mass of flesh' is a designation for the six inner sense bases. 'The outer mass of hide' is a designation for the six outer sense bases. 'The interior blood vessels, the interior lungs, the interior liver, and the interior veins' are a designation for attachment bound up with delight. 'The skilled butcher or the butcher's apprentice' is a designation for a noble śrāvaka who is endowed with learning. 'The knife' is a designation for the weapon of wisdom. Sisters, a noble śrāvaka endowed with learning, with the weapon of wisdom, slices through, cuts apart, strikes through, and pierces all the engagements, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and enwrappings without exception.

"Sisters, therefore you should train yourselves in this way: that toward those phenomena which are prone to arouse attachment, your minds shall not become attached — in order to abandon attachment; that toward those phenomena which are prone to arouse aversion, your minds shall not become aversive — in order to abandon aversion; that toward those phenomena which are prone to arouse delusion, your minds shall not become deluded — in order to abandon delusion.

"Sisters, therefore you should train yourselves in this way: you shall dwell in continuous contemplation of the arising and passing away of the five appropriated aggregates. You shall dwell in continuous contemplation of the arising and ceasing of the six sense bases of contact. You shall dwell with minds firmly established in the four foundations of mindfulness. And when you dwell with minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness, you shall cultivate, develop, and repeatedly practise the seven limbs of awakening. Thus shall you train.

"Sisters, by the cause of cultivating the seven limbs of awakening, by the cause of developing them, by the cause of practising them repeatedly, and by the cause of taking them thoroughly to heart, your minds shall become free from attachment and fully liberated from the defilement of desire, free from attachment and fully liberated from the defilement of becoming and from the defilement of ignorance. Sisters, when you are fully liberated, there shall arise in you the knowledge and vision of liberation: 'Our birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, the task is done; we know that there is nothing further beyond this existence.' Sisters, thus shall you train."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having thoroughly instructed those nuns with Dharma-connected discourse, having made them take it to heart, having praised them, and having filled them with joy, rose from his seat and departed.

Then the great Progenitrix Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred nuns, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet with her head, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly taught the great Progenitrix Gautamī with Dharma-connected discourse, made her take it to heart, praised her, and filled her with joy.

Then, having thoroughly instructed her with Dharma-connected discourse in many ways, made her take it to heart, praised her, and filled her with joy, he urged her: "Gautamī, it is your time — go now."

Then the great Progenitrix Gautamī, delighting and rejoicing in what the Blessed One had declared, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with her head, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Not long after the great Progenitrix Gautamī had gone, the Blessed One, having reflected on the matter, spoke to the monks: "Monks, if the noble son Ānanda were to counsel and thoroughly instruct those five hundred nuns well, and they were to pass away in this very life without having attained liberation and finality, I see not a single conditioning factor among the conditioning factors by which, possessed of those factors, they would come again to this world. Monks, consider this illustration: when the waxing moon falls on the fourteenth day, people dispute over the moon, saying 'is it full, or is it not yet full?' And because it is not yet full, it has not reached finality. In just the same way, if Ānanda were to counsel and thoroughly instruct those five hundred nuns well, and they were to pass away in this very life without having attained liberation and finality, I see not a single conditioning factor among the conditioning factors by which, possessed of those factors, they would come again to this world."

Thus the Blessed One prophesied that those five hundred nuns would be non-returners.

Then the Blessed One spoke a second time to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, you should guide the nuns. Ānanda, you should give instruction to the nuns. Ānanda, you should speak words connected with Dharma to the nuns. And why? Because whether I or you counsel the nuns, whether I or you instruct the nuns, whether I or you speak Dharma-connected words to the nuns, it is equally fitting."

The venerable Ānanda said nothing, and in silence accepted it from the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Ānanda, delighting and rejoicing in what the Blessed One had declared, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Then, when that very night had passed, the venerable Ānanda dressed in the early morning, took up his bowl and robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having made his alms round in Śrāvastī and completed the meal, he returned from the alms round for the later meal, put away his bowl and robes, washed his two feet, and entered the assembly hall in order to settle properly into meditation. Then the venerable Ānanda rose from that period of inward settling in the assembly hall, took up his outer robe, and went to the place in the royal garden where the monks and nuns had their rains retreat dwelling.

Those nuns, from quite far away, saw the venerable Ānanda coming. Seeing him, they made ready seats for the venerable Ānanda, and said these words: "Venerable Ānanda, please come here. Venerable Ānanda, welcome."

"Venerable Ānanda, please be seated on the prepared seat." The venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. Then those nuns bowed their heads at the venerable Ānanda's feet and took their places to one side. Having taken their places to one side, the venerable Ānanda thoroughly instructed those nuns with Dharma-endowed discourse, thoroughly guided them in taking it up, thoroughly encouraged them, and thoroughly gladdened them. With many categories of Dharma-endowed discourse he thoroughly instructed them, thoroughly guided them in taking it up, thoroughly encouraged them, and thoroughly gladdened them; then he rose from his seat and departed.

Then the great Progenitress Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred nuns, went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's two feet and took their places to one side. Having taken their places to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly instructed the great Progenitress Gautamī with Dharma-endowed discourse, thoroughly guided her in taking it up, thoroughly encouraged her, and thoroughly gladdened her. With many categories of Dharma-endowed discourse he thoroughly instructed her, thoroughly guided her in taking it up, thoroughly encouraged her, and thoroughly gladdened her; then he urged her, saying: "Gautamī, it is now your time — you may go."

Then the great Progenitress Gautamī, rejoicing and delighting in the Blessed One's words, bowed her head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then, not long after the great Progenitress Gautamī had gone, the Blessed One, having reflected on the matter, declared to the monks: "Monks, the noble son Ānanda gave excellent instruction and excellent guidance to those five hundred nuns, and they attained liberation and reached the final consummation. If he were to pass away at this time, they would have no one to point out the path — and look upon this: it is the culmination of suffering.

"Monks, it is just as when, on the full-moon night that is precisely the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, people do not make two things of the moon by saying 'Is it the new moon?' or 'Is it not the new moon?' — for this reason, being the full moon, it has reached its consummation. In exactly the same way, the noble son Ānanda gave excellent instruction and excellent guidance to those five hundred nuns, and they attained liberation and reached the final consummation. If he were to pass away at this time, they would have no one to point out the path — this itself is the culmination of suffering."

In this way, the Blessed One then gave the highest prophecy to those five hundred nuns.

Now this took place at a time when the Blessed One, the Buddha, had not yet established training rules for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya. The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Blessed One had declared: "Monks shall teach nuns in rotation, elder by elder." When it came to the turn of the group of six monks to teach the nuns, they taught them a little, and then behaved with them in an overly familiar manner — playing about, making noise, leaning on them, acting distracted, and moving their bodies. Those among them who were possessive behaved with the nuns in this overly familiar way — playing about, making noise, leaning on them, acting distracted, and moving their bodies. Those who were not possessive withdrew to their own walking-meditation paths and

settled at their meditation places and gatehouse cells, saying: "These people are displaying to us every sort of misconduct of this kind." They scorned them, denounced them, and spread word against them. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The group of six shall not be appointed as teachers of nuns."

Having thus declared that the group of six shall not be appointed as teachers of nuns, those monks appointed one another and proceeded to teach the nuns — and the very same fault arose again. The Blessed One then declared: "One shall not teach nuns without having been appointed."

Those monks then went outside the boundary and appointed one another, and proceeded to teach the nuns — and the very same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "One appointed outside the boundary shall not teach nuns."

Those monks then, within the boundary, obtained the consent of the sick monks and sent the remaining monks off on errands, and then appointed one another and proceeded to teach the nuns — and when that very same fault arose again, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not, within the boundary, obtain the consent of the sick monks, send the remaining monks off on errands, and then appoint one another to teach nuns. Instead, the appointment of a teacher for the nuns is to be made thus: on the very day of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, a teacher for the nuns shall be appointed.

The appointment is to be made in this manner. First, willingness is to be ascertained: 'You, called so-and-so — are you willing to be teacher of the nuns? If you are willing, say: I am willing.' After that, one monk shall make a formal motion and perform the act. The venerable Saṅgha, please hear. This monk called so-and-so is willing to be teacher of the nuns. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and if it consents, let the Saṅgha grant approval, and let the Saṅgha appoint the monk called so-and-so as teacher of the nuns, so that the monk called so-and-so may teach the nuns. This is the motion.

The act is to be performed thus. The venerable Saṅgha, please hear. The monk called so-and-so is willing to be teacher of the nuns, and for that purpose the Saṅgha appoints the monk called so-and-so as teacher of the nuns, so that the monk called so-and-so may teach the nuns. Those venerable ones who consent to the appointment of the monk called so-and-so as teacher of the nuns — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the Saṅgha has appointed the monk called so-and-so as teacher of the nuns. Since no one has spoken, so it is held to be."

Having declared that teachers of nuns are to be appointed in this way, the Blessed One then declared: those monks — whether experienced or inexperienced, whether obscure or unskilled — were appointed without distinction. And now, for the time being, that one who has not disciplined himself should discipline others — that is impossible. That one who has not calmed himself should calm others — that is impossible. That one who has not crossed out of the mire himself should free others from the mire — that is impossible. And that one who has not himself fully passed into nirvāṇa should lead others to fully pass into nirvāṇa — that too is impossible. Therefore the Blessed One declared:

A nun who possesses five qualities should be appointed as an instructor. What are the five? She possesses moral discipline; she is learned; she is like a senior elder (sthavira) and a regent; she is proficient in the language of the city; and she has not shamed any nun through bodily contact — or, if she did once cause shame, she has properly remedied that transgression in accordance with the Dharma.

How does she possess moral discipline? She has not committed any of the four defeats. That is how she possesses moral discipline.

How is she learned? She has fully recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra at length and has mastered it. That is how she is learned.

How is she like a senior elder and a regent? She has been fully ordained for twenty years or more. That is how she is like a senior elder and a regent.

How is she proficient in the language of the city? The palace and its environs are called the city, and she is proficient in the language of that place. That is how she is proficient in the language of the city.

How has she not shamed a nun through bodily contact? She has not drawn close to a nun's body with her own body. That is how she has not shamed a nun through bodily contact.

One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed as an instructor of nuns.

After the Blessed One declared that one who possesses these five qualities should be appointed as instructor of nuns, the group of six monks — without having been appointed at all — went on instructing nuns. Some monks of few wants then censured, complained of, and disparaged them, saying: "Why do these monks instruct nuns without having been appointed?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, in relation to this incident and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, just as before. The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, act with full knowledge — and so forth, just as before.

The Blessed One then rebuked the group of six monks: "Monks, I have said that one should not instruct nuns without having been appointed. Is it true that you were instructing nuns without having been appointed?" They replied: "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed One, the buddha, censured them, saying that this was not proper conduct for a renunciant, not consonant with right conduct, not fitting, not in accordance with proper form, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, having seen these ten benefits, one should lay down a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth, just as before. "My śrāvakas should recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk instructs nuns without having been appointed by the Saṅgha commits a transgression."

Thus did the Blessed One lay down that rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time there was a brahmin residing at Śrāvastī who had taken a wife from an equal family, and he would play with her, make merry with her, and enjoy himself with her. She bore him children one after another, and then in due course his wife became pregnant. The brahmin then placed his hand under her arm, feeling tender in his heart as he sat with her.

Not far from there an old woman was sitting, and she saw this and said to him, "Brahmin, why do you sit holding your hand under her arm, so troubled in your heart?" The brahmin replied, "Every child my wife has borne has died in due time. And now that a being has entered into my wife's womb and another child is about to be born, that one too will die in due time, and so I shall have much grief and go on in sorrow." The old woman said, "When the time comes for your wife to give birth, let me know."

Then, at another time, when his wife's time to give birth arrived, the brahmin summoned that old woman and she came. As soon as the birth took place, a boy was born. The old woman bathed the boy, wrapped him in white cloth, filled his mouth with clarified butter, and gave him into the hands of a young girl. She said to the girl, "Take this boy to the crossroads of the great road, and if any renunciant or brahmin should notice him, bow at his feet with reverence and humility, and say to him: 'This boy pays homage at the feet of the noble ones.' At sunset, if he is still alive, bring him back home; but if he has died, leave him there."

The girl was diligent, and being capable, she took the boy and went to the crossroads of the great road and sat there. Now the daily practice of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) was to rise early in the morning and go to the riverbank for ritual contact with the water, and so the tīrthikas who were going to the riverbank for this purpose came by that spot. The girl bowed at their feet with reverence and humility and said, "Noble ones, this boy pays homage at the feet of the noble ones." They replied, "May he live long! May he be sustained for a long life! May the heartfelt wishes of both his parents be fully accomplished!"

Then the elder monks — the senior monks — having put on their lower robes in the early morning and taken up their bowls and outer robes, set out for alms in Śrāvastī. The girl bowed at the feet of the venerable elders with reverence and humility and said, "Noble ones, this boy pays homage at the feet of the noble ones." The venerable elders replied, "May he live long! May he be sustained for a long life! May the heartfelt wishes of both his parents be fully accomplished!"

The girl then carried the boy along the path leading to the Jeta Grove, and the Blessed One — having also put on his lower robe in the early morning, taken up his bowl and outer robes — was on his way into Śrāvastī for alms. The girl bowed most reverently and humbly at the feet of the Blessed One and said, "Blessed One, this boy pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One." The Blessed One declared, "May he live long! May he be sustained for a long life! May the Dharma-endowed heartfelt wishes of both his parents be fully accomplished!"

When the girl looked at sunset, she saw that the boy was still alive, so she took him and came home. They asked her, "Is the boy alive?" The girl said, "He is alive." They asked, "Where did you hold him?" "At a pleasant crossroads on the great road." They asked, "What name shall be given to the boy?" "Since this boy was held on the great road, let his name be Mahāpanthaka — Great Road — and so that became his name."

The boy Mahāpanthaka was raised and grew up. When he had grown up, he mastered writing, arithmetic, calculation, finger-counting, casting up accounts, carrying forward, setting down, dividing, and reading. And at that time, in accordance with brahmanic customs of conduct,

conduct, cleanliness, daily practice, the taking of ash, the taking of a water vessel fashioned like a bird, the taking of clay, hand gestures, topknot wearing, the recitation of praises, the utterance of the sacred syllable kye, the Vedic science of definitive expression, the Vedic science of sacrifice, the Vedic science of poetic composition, the Vedic science of polity and protection, and the six duties of brahmins — performing sacrifice, officiating at the sacrifices of others, reciting the Vedas, teaching others to recite them, giving gifts, and receiving gifts — he became a brahmin learned in the Vedas and the ancillary sciences of the Vedas, one who had reached the far shore of those disciplines, able to set forth his own position clearly and to refute the positions of others.

At that time the brahmin Mahāpanthaka had some five hundred young brahmin students reciting brahminic sacred formulas. Then at a certain time that brahmin was amusing himself, rejoicing, and sporting together with his wife, and his wife conceived. When the time came for her to give birth, that brahmin summoned the old woman, and she came. In due course the birth took place, and a boy was born. The old woman bathed the boy, wrapped him in white cloth, filled his mouth with clarified butter, and placed him in the hands of a girl, saying to her: "Girl, hold this boy at a pleasant crossroads on the great road. If any ascetic or brahmin happens to pass by, bow down with veneration and reverence at his feet, and say to him: 'Noble one, this boy pays homage at the feet of the noble ones.' At sunset, if he is still alive, bring him home. If he should die, leave him there on the spot." Now that girl was foolish and lazy, so she took the boy and went and sat down on a side path.

It was the custom among non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to rise before dawn and go to touch the riverbank. So a group of tīrthikas who were setting out to touch the riverbank arrived there. The girl bowed down to them with veneration and reverence at their feet, and said: "Noble ones, this boy pays homage at the feet of the noble ones." They said: "May he have a long life. May he be sustained for a long time. May the wishes in the hearts of both his parents be completely fulfilled." The girl looked at sunset and saw that he was still alive, and so she took him and came home. They asked the girl: "Is the boy alive?" The girl said: "He is alive." They asked: "Where did you hold him?" "On a pleasant side path." They asked: "What name shall be given to the boy?" "Since this boy was held on a side path, let his name be Cūḷapanthaka — Little Road." And so that became his name.

The boy Cūḷapanthaka was raised and grew up. When he had grown up, when he was put to writing, if he said the syllable sid he would forget dhāṃ, and if he said dhāṃ he would forget sid. His teacher said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, I have many other brahmin students to teach, and I am unable to teach Cūḷapanthaka to read. Mahāpanthaka, with just a little instruction, is able to retain a great deal; but this Cūḷapanthaka, when he says sid he forgets dhāṃ, and when he says dhāṃ he forgets sid." The brahmin thought: "Not every brahmin is learned in letters and syllables. This one may yet become a brahmin of the Vedas." And so he gave him to a reciter to read the Vedas. But when that one said oṃ he forgot bhū, and when he said bhū he forgot oṃ. So the reciter said to the brahmin:

"Brahmin, I have many other brahmin students to teach, and I am unable to teach Cūḷapanthaka to read. Mahāpanthaka, with just a little instruction, is able to retain a great deal; but this Cūḷapanthaka, when he says oṃ he forgets bhū, and when he says bhū he forgets oṃ." The brahmin thought: "Not every brahmin reads the Vedas. Whether learned or unlearned, whether pure or impure, whatever is born a brahmin is by that very birth a god — so this one will at least belong to the brahmin caste alone." Since the younger was the very least of offerings and the very least of the little, his name came to be Cūḷapanthaka, meaning "Little Road." Wherever that brahmin was invited as a guest for any small occasion, he would take Cūḷapanthaka along with him.

Then at another time the brahmin fell ill, and though he was attended with medicines derived from roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, he only grew worse. He summoned Mahāpanthaka and said to him: "Son, after I am gone you need not grieve. Take care of your younger brother Cūḷapanthaka and provide him with what he needs." Then, having said:

All that is accumulated comes at last to exhaustion;
the lofty must fall in the end;
all meeting ends in parting;
and the end of the living is death —

he passed away in accordance with the law of his time. The two of them wrapped him in robes of blue and yellow and red and white, carried him to the charnel ground, and cremated him. After that they performed the mourning rites and departed.

Vinayavibhaṅga, the forty-seventh fascicle. Now that brahmin Mahāpanthaka dwelt beside a certain tree in a village between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove, where some five hundred brahmin students were assembled and being taught the secret brahmin recitations. The Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having completed their Vinaya duties, were traveling through the Kosala regions with a retinue of five hundred and came to Śrāvastī. When the great assembly of ordinary people at Śrāvastī heard that the noble Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were journeying through the Kosala regions with a retinue of five hundred and had arrived at Śrāvastī, many hundreds of living beings began to go forth from home into homelessness. When Mahāpanthaka saw them going forth, he said: "You who are wise, where are you going?" They replied: "The noble Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have come to Śrāvastī while traveling through the Kosala regions, and we are going to meet them." Mahāpanthaka said: "Those two have abandoned the highest caste and gone forth under the śramaṇa Gautama of the second caste — what is the point of seeing them?" But there was among the brahmin students one who had faith, and he said: "Teacher, please do not speak so. Those two are great beings. If the Teacher were to hear the Dharma from them, there is indeed a basis on which the Teacher's mind could come to genuine confidence." Mahāpanthaka thought: "I shall investigate. For now, when the brahmin students stop their recitation I too shall go." The students' custom was that whenever they paused from recitation, they would sometimes walk toward the town and sometimes go down to gather firewood. Then one day it happened that they stopped reciting and went down to gather firewood, and at that very time Mahāpanthaka himself set out toward the Jeta Grove.

A monk was walking and sitting beneath a tree at the gate of the Jeta Grove. The brahmin saw him from quite a distance, went over to him, and said: "O monk, please speak a few words of the Buddha's teaching."

The monk thought: "This brahmin is a disputant, so I cannot speak expansively to him for his benefit." He therefore taught the brahmin extensively on the ten pathways of virtuous action and the ten pathways of non-virtuous action.

The brahmin said: "O monk, I myself have fallen short in my own affairs, and if you too are failing in the domain of virtue, that is not good. As for me, I shall go — but I will return again later." With that, he departed.

Then on another occasion, the brahmin students stopped their recitation and went down to gather firewood, and Mahāpanthaka set out alone along the great road toward the Jeta Grove. The monk saw the brahmin from quite a distance. Seeing him, he thought: "Earlier I taught this brahmin extensively on the ten pathways of virtuous action and the ten pathways of non-virtuous action. Now I shall teach him extensively on the twelve links of dependent origination in their forward order and in their reverse order."

The brahmin went to where the monk was, arrived, and bowed his head to the monk's two feet, then sat to one side. When he had sat to one side, the monk taught the brahmin extensively on the twelve links of dependent origination in their forward order and in their reverse order.

The brahmin, filled with faith, said: "O monk, I request to go forth under you."

The monk thought: "This brahmin is a disputant — if I ordain him, he will be a credit to the teaching." And so he said: "Brahmin, do so."

The brahmin said: "O monk, I am a brahmin of good repute, and if I go forth here without preliminary steps, I will be set apart from my community. Let it be done properly."

The monk led the brahmin away to a suitable place, had him go forth, and conferred upon him full ordination. Then he said: "Good sir, the tasks of a monk are two: meditative concentration and recitation. Which of the two do you wish — concentration or recitation?"

Mahāpanthaka replied: "Preceptor, I shall do both. By day I shall recite, and at night I shall meditate." "Son, do so."

Then the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, through recitation and oral study by day, came to master all three collections of scripture. He became one possessed of the three collections, a Dharma preacher, endowed with the eloquence of knowledge and liberation.

Through meditation by night, he attained progressively refined states of mental application, recognized the moving and unmoving aspects of the fivefold wheel of cyclic existence for what they are, and, overwhelmed by the very nature of all formations — their deterioration, their downfall, their dispersion, their disintegration — he abandoned all afflictions. Thus, noble sons, for the sake of which one shaves off hair and beard, dons the ochre robe, and goes forth from home into homelessness in genuine faith — that supreme end of the holy life — he realized directly through his own direct knowledge in this very life itself. Having accomplished it, he understood: "My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is no further existence beyond this."

He became an arhat freed from attachment throughout the three realms — mind equal to earth and gold, equal to sky and the palm of one's hand — and with his wisdom he split open the hollow of the gateway of ignorance. Endowed with knowledge —

— endowed with direct knowledge and individual perfect understanding, he turned his back on the gains and honors of existence and desire, and became a worthy recipient of worship, esteem, and open praise from the gods who possess both gross and subtle sense faculties.

Now, at the very time when the venerable Mahāpatha had gone forth on the great path, the livelihood that went with the lesser path had grown thin, had been fully exhausted, and had been completely used up, and so he began to sustain his life with great hardship. Then the venerable Mahāpatha thought to himself: "Whatever I ought to obtain through learning, that I will obtain; and I will go to Śrāvastī and attend upon the Blessed One."

So the venerable Mahāpatha set out toward Śrāvastī, traveling through the Kosala countryside with a retinue of five hundred. While in Śrāvastī, a great gathering of common people heard that the noble Mahāpatha was traveling through the Kosala countryside with a retinue of five hundred and had arrived at Śrāvastī. Having heard this, a crowd of common people began streaming out, and a traveler on the lesser path saw them and asked: "Good people, where are you going?" They replied: "The noble Mahāpatha, traveling through the Kosala countryside with his retinue of five hundred, has arrived at Śrāvastī — that is where we are going." The traveler on the lesser path thought: "These people are neither his brothers nor his relatives, yet they go to him like that. If he were my elder brother, why would I not go in the same way?" And so the traveler on the lesser path also set out to see the noble Mahāpatha.

When the venerable Mahāpatha saw him, he asked: "Traveler, are you well?" "I am well, noble one." "How are you faring?" "With great hardship, noble one." The venerable Mahāpatha said: "How is it that you have not yet gone forth?" The traveler on the lesser path replied: "Noble one, I am among the poorest of the poor, the least of the least — could someone like me go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One?" The venerable Mahāpatha looked to see whether he had even a small root of virtue, and saw that he did. He asked himself who it depended upon, and saw that it depended on himself alone. He then said: "Traveler, in the scriptural teaching of the Lord of Sages (the Buddha), birth is not what is cherished, nor lineage, nor learning — in the scriptural teaching of the Lord of Sages what is cherished is practice. So if you wish, go forth."

"Noble one, I will go forth."

The venerable Mahāpatha gave that traveler on the lesser path the going-forth and full ordination, and then began to have him recite the following verse:

Do no evil with body, speech, or mind,
and be free from the wish to grasp hold of all the world.
With mindfulness and vigilance,
do not approach whatever suffering brings harm.

Yet even in three months he had not managed to learn it. Cowherds and other herdsmen heard it and learned it, and he went to them with respect and humility, bowed before them, asked them about it, and they taught it to him.

Just as it is the natural way of things that during the lifetime of the Blessed One, the buddhas — while living, present, and abiding — there were two great assemblies of hearers: one at the time of the rains retreat near the middle month of summer, and the second on the middle month of autumn. And so too it was for the great hearers. Those who, near the middle month of summer, had received instructions for the rains retreat and had undertaken the rains retreat in villages, towns, districts, and royal palaces — these would, at the time of the full moon of the middle month of autumn, report what they had attained.

And so, in order to attain what had not yet been attained, they would inquire further of the venerable Mahāpanthaka. Those attendants who had undertaken the rains retreat in the districts — once the three months of the rains retreat had passed, having made and received their rains-retreat robes and taking up their bowls and robes — they set out and went to where the venerable Mahāpanthaka was. They prostrated at his feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, some of them reported what they had attained. Others sought recitations and inquiries in the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.

Now among them, those who were utterly wretched — the most wretched of the wretched, the most petty of the petty — they attended upon the Group of Six, grew close to them, and rendered them service. And so the venerable Panthaka too, attending upon the Group of Six, growing close to them, and rendering them service — his companion said to the venerable Panthaka: "Panthaka, these others who share one and the same preceptor with you are also seeking recitations and inquiries from the preceptor. You too should go and for a time seek recitations and inquiries from the preceptor."

Panthaka replied: "I have read nothing at all. In three months I learned one verse, and even that I could not master. How then should I seek recitations and inquiries?" His companion said: "Did not the Blessed One declare that the stain of secret teachings is not to be recited? Come now, why could you not at least master one verse? Go and seek."

Panthaka went and said: "Preceptors, please give me for a time some recitations." The venerable Mahāpanthaka thought to himself: "Is this one now asking out of his own initiative, or has he been sent by someone else?" Seeing that he had been sent by another, Mahāpanthaka thought: "Is this one to be tamed by criticism, or is he to be tamed by praise?" Seeing that he was to be tamed by criticism, Mahāpanthaka seized him by the neck, expelled him outside the Jeta Grove, and said: "You are nothing but utterly wretched — the most wretched of the wretched, the most petty of the petty. You went forth into the Blessed One's teaching, and to what end? Stay right here."

Panthaka thought: "Now I am neither a wanderer nor a brahmin," and he began to weep. The Blessed One saw the venerable Panthaka weeping outside the Jeta Grove. Then, moved by great compassion, the Blessed One went to where the venerable Panthaka was and, coming to him, spoke to him thus: "Panthaka, why are you weeping outside the Jeta Grove?"

Panthaka replied: "Blessed One, my preceptor seized me by the neck, expelled me outside the Jeta Grove, and said: 'You are nothing but utterly wretched — the most wretched of the wretched, the most petty of the petty. You went forth into the Blessed One's teaching, and to what end? Stay right here.' And so now I am neither a wanderer nor a brahmin."

Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke this verse:

What a fool praises
and what a wise one criticizes —
here it is the wise one's censure that is supreme;
it is not the fool's praise.

Then the Blessed One declared:

"My son, your preceptor completed the six perfections through many hundreds of thousands of difficult deeds performed over three immeasurable eons, and thereby fully accomplished this scripture of the Lord of Sages — and yet he did not truly establish it in practice. Now I, having completed the six perfections through many hundreds of thousands of difficult deeds performed over three immeasurable eons, and thereby fully accomplished this scripture of the Lord of Sages — can you read it from the Tathāgata?" Panthaka replied: "Blessed One, I am wretched, supremely wretched, insignificant, supremely insignificant."

Then the Blessed One spoke this verse on the occasion:

One who knows a fool to be foolish —
in that very knowing, he is wise.
A fool who fancies himself learned:
he, here, is the truly foolish one.

It is not possible, it is not the right occasion, for the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to teach the Dharma word by word. There being no such occasion, the Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have Panthaka taught to recite."

The venerable Ānanda began to have Panthaka recite, but Panthaka was unable to do so. The venerable Ānanda then said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, for my part I would attend upon the Teacher, I would retain what I hear, I would have assemblies recite, I would teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who come — and so I find no point in being asked to have Panthaka recite."

The Blessed One then gave him just the two words, "Dispel the dust! Remove the stain!" — and Panthaka could not retain even those two words. The Blessed One, thinking "I shall purify his karma," then addressed the venerable Panthaka: "Panthaka, can you clean the sandals and strapped shoes of the monks?" He replied: "Blessed One, I can manage that." "Then go and clean the monks' sandals and strapped shoes." Panthaka began to clean the monks' sandals and strapped shoes, but the monks would not hand them over to him. The Blessed One then said: "Monks, let Panthaka clean the sandals and strapped shoes — for it is in order to purify his karma. And have him learn the recitation of these two words as well."

As Panthaka was cleaning the monks' sandals and strapped shoes, the monks also taught him the recitation of the two words, "Dispel the dust! Remove the stain!" He learned them, and at another time he came to know those two words by heart.

Then, at the break of dawn one night, the venerable Panthaka reflected: "When the Blessed One said 'Dispel the dust! Remove the stain!' — was he speaking with inner dust in mind, or outer dust in mind?" As he was thinking this, three verses he had never heard before arose clearly in his mind:

This "dust" here — desire is not physical dust;
"Dust" is the name for desire, not for grime.
Those wise ones who have fully cast off that dust
will become heedful in the teaching of the Sugata.

This "dust" here — aversion is not physical dust;
"Dust" is the name for aversion, not for grime.
Those wise ones who have fully cast off that dust
will become heedful in the teaching of the Sugata.

This "dust" here — delusion is not physical dust;
"Dust" is the name for delusion, not for grime.
Those wise ones who have fully cast off that dust
will become heedful in the teaching of the Sugata.

With joy, with effort, and with

with striving, ever advancing, attaining an excellence of mental application, knowing this very wheel of saṃsāra in its five parts — moving and unmoving — and being overwhelmed by the very nature of reality of all formations: their decay, their falling away, their dispersal, and their dissolution, and having abandoned all afflictions —

noble sons, for whatever reason one shaves hair and beard, dons saffron robes, and with sincere faith goes forth from home into homelessness: that supreme culmination of the holy life, in that very life, one directly realizes and accomplishes through one's own direct knowledge, and understands: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is no further existence beyond this." And one becomes an arhat, free from attachment, beyond the three realms, with a mind equal toward a clod of earth and gold, equal toward the sky and the palm of the hand, having set sandalwood aside — one's door of faculties has been burst open by gnosis — having attained gnosis, direct knowledge, and individual discriminating awareness, turned away from becoming, from gain through desire, and from honor, and become worthy of being venerated, revered, and proclaimed by gods with and without their retinues.

The venerable Lāmpa was seated cross-legged, and when the venerable Lāmachenpa saw him, since arhats know without deliberating, and since seeing does not require engagement, the venerable Lāmachenpa took the venerable Lāmpa by both hands and said: "Lāmpa, first recite your lessons, and after that go into meditative concentration."

The venerable Lāmpa extended his arm like an elephant's trunk, and the venerable Lāmachenpa, turning to look back, saw this, and said: "Venerable Lāmpa, have you realized such an accumulation of qualities?" "I have."

Everywhere it was heard proclaimed that the Blessed One had fully ordained the lesser Lāmpa. In Rājagṛha, a young man named Tsojezhönnu (who tended to the living) heard that the Blessed One had fully ordained the lesser Lāmpa, and he thought: "If the Blessed One comes to Rājagṛha, the monastic Saṅgha of monks, led by the Buddha — with the exception of the venerable Lāmpa — will be invited to other homes for the midday meal."

Other learned non-Buddhist (tīrthika) thinkers began to slander, dismiss, and speak ill of this, saying: "This ascetic Gautama says, 'My teaching is deep, appears deep, is hard to see, hard to realize, beyond examination, not the domain of logic, subtle, to be known by the wise and discerning' — yet he fully ordains those of this sort: a lesser Lāmpa, a greater, a lesser, and an even lesser — how can his teaching be deep?" And they mocked, derided, and disparaged.

The Blessed One, considering that the great śrāvakas, like Mount Meru, were spoken of by the crowd of ordinary people as "producing unwholesomeness," intended to proclaim the elder's qualities. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell Lāmpa from the Tathāgata's own lips, saying as I say: 'Teach the nuns.'"

The venerable Ānanda, having heard from the Blessed One, replied "As you command, Venerable One," and went to where the venerable Lāmpa was. Having arrived, he said to the venerable Lāmpa: "Venerable Lāmpa, the Blessed One has commanded, 'Teach the nuns.'"

The venerable Lāmpa reflected:

He thought: "Why has the Blessed One set aside the elder monks and commanded me?" Then, understanding that the Blessed One wished to proclaim his qualities, he thought: "I must fulfil the Teacher's intention completely," and said: "Venerable Ānanda, I shall do as the Blessed One has commanded."

Two nuns coming to offer the restoration ceremony arrived at the Jeta Grove. The two of them said: "Who has been appointed as our teacher of nuns?" The monks said: "The venerable Lāmpa." They replied: "Is it the noble great Lāmpa, or the venerable Lāmpa?" The monks answered: "The venerable Lāmpa." The two said: "Brothers, look at that despised woman's territory — he could not even learn a single verse in three months — and yet he is to teach the nuns, who are versed in the second and third Piṭakas, who proclaim the Dharma, who possess knowledge and the eloquence of liberation. We shall go and see how he manages to teach the nuns." So saying, they went to where the venerable Lāmpa was, and arriving there, they prostrated with their heads at the venerable Lāmpa's feet and said: "Venerable Lāmpa, please attend. The community of nuns of the pleasure grove of the king prostrates with their heads at the feet of the community of monks of the Jeta Grove. Are there few hardships? Are there few difficulties? Is movement easy? Are you alive? Do you have strength? Are you at ease? Are you free of fault? Do you dwell in comfort?" So they inquired after his health. "We request teachings and instructions every fortnight. We request that you preside over the ceremony and the restoration. Please know this request as well. It is convenient." The two of them said: "It is convenient," knowing even that much, and they went off toward the summer dwelling. When the nuns saw them, they said: "Who has come as our teacher of nuns?" The two replied: "The noble Lāmpa." The nuns asked: "Is it the noble great Lāmpa?" They answered: "Not the noble great Lāmpa — it is simply Lāmpa." Those nuns said: "Sisters, look at that despised woman's territory — he could not even learn a single verse in three months — and these nuns are versed in the second and third Piṭakas, who proclaim the Dharma, who possess knowledge and the eloquence of liberation. How is he going to teach the nuns? And we — just as the Blessed One has overpowered us — not one of those ninety-six wonders has overpowered any woman's territory at all."

When the groups of twelve nuns heard that the noble Lāmpa was coming as teacher of the nuns in this way, they said: "Sisters, by all means, from this point forward, however little we have heard, let us not teach even a single thing to a nun" — meaning, let that child of the womb-eater be displeased. Then they said: "Sisters, six of us shall prepare a lion throne from branches twelve cubits long, and six of us shall enter Śrāvastī and proclaim to the great crowds in the main roads, the market streets, the crossroads, and the junctions: 'Tomorrow our teacher of nuns, a great śrāvaka of such quality, is coming; among you, whoever has not yet seen the truths — let that person know they will have to wander in saṃsāra for a very long time.' Let this be announced!" Six of those women prepared the lion throne from branches twelve cubits long, and six of them entered Śrāvastī and went through the main roads, the market streets, the crossroads, and

the junctions, and proclaimed to the great crowds of people: "Tomorrow our teacher of nuns, a great śrāvaka of such quality, is coming; among you, whoever has not yet seen the truths — let that person know they will have to wander in saṃsāra for a very long time." When this proclamation was made, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered there — some drawn by curiosity, and some stirred by the roots of virtue they had planted in the past.

Then the Venerable Lampā, when that very night had passed, dressed in her inner robe at dawn, took up her bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished her almsround through Śrāvastī and completed the business of her meal, she returned from the afternoon almsround, set aside her bowl and outer robe, washed both feet, and entered the assembly hall in order to settle properly into inner equipoise. Then the Venerable Lampā rose from her inner settling, took up her patchwork robe, and went to where a certain wandering monk walking behind was staying, and to the nuns' rain-retreat quarters — the king's pleasure grove.

When the great crowd of people saw her, they said among themselves: "Who is this teacher of nuns? Is she a former wandering ascetic, or is she a wandering monk who follows behind?" Then they said: "Have you ever heard that some wandering monk following behind teaches nuns? No — this very former wandering ascetic is herself the teacher of nuns." Then others said: "If she takes three months to read a single verse and still cannot master it, how will she teach nuns who are masters of the second and third collections of scripture, Dharma proclaimers, possessed of the confidence of knowledge and liberation? These wretched little female ascetics are going to humiliate us — let us leave!" But others said: "Whatever she does, let us wait a while and watch."

Then the Venerable Lampā entered the midst of that assembly and went to where the lion throne had been prepared.
