When she saw the lion throne made from branches twelve cubits long, she thought: "Was this prepared by those of faithful mind, or by those of presumptuous mind?" — and she perceived it had been prepared by those of presumptuous mind. Then the Venerable Lampā, stretching out a hand like an elephant's trunk, pressed down the lion throne just as it had been set in place, and seated herself upon the lion throne in such a manner that some among the crowd could see her and others could not.

Then the Venerable Lampā entered meditative absorption (samādhi) of this kind: as she settled her mind in equipoise, she became invisible from her own seat and rose manifest into the sky above the eastern direction, performing the four modes of conduct — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. She also entered absorption upon the fire element, and from the body of the Venerable Lampā as she remained in absorption upon the fire element there came forth rays of light of various kinds — blue ones, yellow ones, red ones, white ones, crimson ones, and ones resembling the color of crystal and silver. She displayed also paired miracles: from the lower part of her body flames blazed forth while from the upper part of her body streams of cool water poured down; from the upper part of her body flames blazed forth while from the lower part streams of cool water poured down. Just as she did in the eastern direction, so likewise in the south, the west, and the north —

Having displayed in each of those four directions four forms of miraculous display, the Venerable Lampā withdrew the manifestation of those miracles and took her seat upon a lion throne that had been arranged in front of the assembly. Seated there, the Venerable Lampā addressed the nuns, saying: "Sisters, I took up a single verse for three months. For seven days and nights I shall delight in analyzing the meaning of that verse by means of other words, other letters, and other words and letters combined.

"Sisters, in that verse: the word 'body' indicates what the Blessed One taught — that the three bodily non-virtues are not to be committed. The word 'speech' indicates what the Blessed One taught — that the four verbal non-virtues are not to be committed. The words 'by mind' indicate what the Blessed One taught — that the three mental non-virtues are not to be committed. The words 'abstaining from evil' indicate what the Blessed One taught — that all evil whatsoever is not to be done. The words 'for all the world' indicate what the Blessed One taught — namely, all the appropriated aggregates (skandhas). The word 'clinging' indicates what the Blessed One taught — the three kinds of clinging: the clinging of attachment, the clinging of aversion, and the clinging of delusion."

By as much as the Venerable Lampā had analyzed even half the meaning of the verse, twelve thousand living beings saw the truths. Some of them actualized the fruit of stream-entry; some actualized the fruit of once-returning; some actualized the fruit of non-returning; and some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and actualized arhatship itself. Some generated the mind set upon the awakening of a hearer; some generated the mind set upon the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; and some generated the mind set upon unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. The greater part of the assembly was directed toward taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Then, having directed the greater part of that assembly toward taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the Venerable Lampā rose from her seat and departed.

Now, those monks who were walking about and standing near the gate of the Jeta Grove, upon seeing the Venerable Lampā approaching from a great distance, said among themselves: "Venerable ones, if the Venerable Lampā has not failed to inspire confident faith in a great multitude of people today, since it is painful to speak of something openly disappointing, let us ask the attendant monk who is following behind her." And so they said to the monk who was following behind her: "Venerable one, how great a multitude of people did the Venerable Lampā inspire with confident faith today?"

He replied: "As for who it was that inspired faith — it was the one who, at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Sages (Ṛṣipatana), recited three times and turned the wheel of Dharma in twelve aspects, endowed with the Dharma. Whatever the Blessed One did then, that same thing today the Venerable Lampā has continued in turn. By as much as the Venerable Lampā had analyzed even half the meaning of the verse, twelve thousand living beings saw the truths. Some of them actualized the fruit of stream-entry; some actualized the fruit of once-returning; some actualized the fruit of non-returning; and some went forth, abandoned all afflictions, and actualized arhatship itself."

Some aroused the mind set upon the awakening of a śrāvaka. Some aroused the mind set upon the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. And some aroused the mind set upon the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. The greater part of the assembly was established in going for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Among those of my śrāvakas who are skilled in transforming minds, Lampā is supreme. One who lacks qualities such as these is therefore excluded."

Thereupon the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of desiring the training, of reverence for the training, and of equipping oneself with the requisites of the training, gave a discourse to the monks in accordance with that praise, going further into it and suited to it. He then addressed the monks: "Therefore, what was formerly prescribed is prescribed, and this is now permitted. My śrāvakas are to learn this as a rule of the Vinaya training: if any monk, without having been appointed by the Saṅgha, teaches a nun, then — unless he possesses qualities such as these — he commits a transgression.

"As for the phrase 'any monk,' this refers to the group of six and anyone else of that kind. 'By the Saṅgha' means by the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. 'Without having been appointed' means without the act of the motion and the second proclamation. 'Nun' refers to a nun of this Dharma community. 'Teaches' refers to the higher moral discipline, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. 'Unless he possesses qualities such as these' means excepting one who does possess such qualities and is accordingly established. 'Commits a transgression' means he is scorched, cooked, and fallen into the lower realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of wrong falling. Moreover, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas. Therefore it is said 'commits a transgression.'

"As to the question of how a transgression arises: if a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha outside the boundary but not within the boundary, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he too commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, yet the appointment was not made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was indeed made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, yet the entire Saṅgha is not present and in harmony, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, yet he does not possess moral discipline, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline, yet he is not learned,those who make the appointment incur an offense,

and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned, yet he is not like a senior elder acting as a deputy, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned and is like a senior elder acting as a deputy, yet he does not know the local dialect, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned and is like a senior elder acting as a deputy and knows the local dialect, yet he has been expelled by a nun through physical contact and has not properly reversed that transgression according to the rule, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned and is like a senior elder acting as a deputy and knows the local dialect, and he has not been expelled by a nun through physical contact, or even if he has been expelled, he has properly reversed that transgression according to the rule, yet he is unable to recite in full the eight rules entailing defeat, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned and is like a senior elder acting as a deputy and knows the local dialect, and he has not been expelled by a nun through physical contact, or even if he has been expelled, he has properly reversed that transgression according to the rule, and he is able to recite in full the eight rules entailing defeat, yet he is unable to recite in full the eight weighty rules, those who make the appointment incur an offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he commits a transgression. If a monk is appointed by the Saṅgha within the boundary but not outside the boundary, and the appointment was made on that very fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and the entire Saṅgha is present and in harmony, and he does possess moral discipline and is learned and is like a senior elder acting as a deputy and knows the local dialect, and he has not been expelled by a nun through physical contact, or even if he has been expelled, he has properly reversed that transgression according to the rule, and he is able to recite in full the eight rules entailing defeat and is also able to recite in full the eight weighty rules, then those who make the appointment incur no offense, and if that appointed monk teaches a nun, he likewise incurs no offense.

The subsequent rule regarding teaching nuns runs as follows. "Sisters, is your community of nuns assembled? Is it pure? Is it in harmony? Is there no offense? Is it the case that no one who has not been appointed by the Saṅgha teaches you? The person who teaches you is one who comes from the Saṅgha. No monk whatsoever will be dispatched to teach you without appointment. Your instruction and guidance come from the Saṅgha. Sisters, practice with heedfulness" — this much he is able to teach.

The monks then made a request to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, please look upon the fact that twelve groups of nuns, intending to harm the venerable Lampā, instead brought him benefit. And not only that — monks, even in times past, those same groups, though intending to harm him, ended up bringing him benefit. Listen to this.

Monks, long ago in a time gone by, there lived a brahmin dwelling in a rocky mountain fastness. He took a wife of equal birth, and together they sported, took pleasure, and enjoyed themselves in delight, and a son was born to them. Now, sensual pleasures are like salt water — the more one partakes of them, the greater one's thirst becomes — and so he again and again sported, took pleasure, and enjoyed himself in delight with her, until twelve sons were born, and he settled them all into his household.

In time, his wife passed away, and the brahmin, now old and stricken with grief, was afflicted in both eyes and became blind. His twelve daughters-in-law were thoroughly dissolute, and whenever their husbands went out of the house, they would revel in merriment with other men. The brahmin, being skilled in the sounds of voices, would think, 'This is the voice of my sons; this is the voice of other men.' Thus, hearing the voices of other men, he reproached his daughters-in-law. They thought to themselves, 'This brahmin has set himself against us to do us harm — let us do him an injury,' and so they served him coarse grain husks and dishwater.

The brahmin said to his sons, 'Sons, your wives have served me coarse grain husks and dishwater.' The sons then said to their wives, 'Why did you serve father coarse grain husks and dishwater?' They replied, 'It is on account of father's pure merit that when a vessel of thick śāli rice is offered to him it turns to coarse husks, and when broth is offered it turns to dishwater. Why would it be otherwise?' The sons said, 'If you doubt us, we shall demonstrate it right before your eyes.' They said among themselves, 'We must bring to fulfillment the plan we made with our husbands,' and so they summoned a potter and said to him, 'Good man, can you make a single pot with two separate compartments inside?' He replied, 'I can,' and he made a pot with two compartments. Into one compartment of the pot they put coarse grain husks, and into the other they put thick śāli rice. Into one compartment of another pot they put whey, and into the other they put rich broth. They stirred everything together and then spoke to the husbands: 'Young masters, shall we first serve father, or shall we serve the young masters first?' They replied, 'Serve father first, and after that give us ours.'

They then opened one compartment of a pot before the fathers-in-law and gave them coarse grain husks, and from another pot opened one compartment and gave the husbands the broth they had skimmed off the boiling whey. After that, they opened one compartment of another pot and filled it with the thick śāli rice broth, and opened one compartment of yet another pot and filled it with whey soup, which they gave to the husbands. The sons then said to their father, "Father, it is on account of your merit that, right before our very eyes, one compartment of a pot was given over to thick śāli rice and another compartment to fresh whey broth to stir together, while into your mouth went coarse grain husks and boiled dregs. The women have done no wrong."

The brahmin then thought to himself, "I built up all these provisions through a hundred hardships of my own hands — why has my merit now been exhausted?" And so, without their noticing, he secretly went in great numbers through their pantry, feeling about by hand, and when his hands came upon pots that each had two compartments inside, he hid those pots away. When the sons arrived and came in, he said to them, "Look at the exhaustion of my merit," and he showed them those pots and then spoke in verse:

In other men's houses,
a single pot has but a single mouth.
For us who are without fortune,
a pot with two compartments inside still has but a single mouth.

They then struck those daughters-in-law soundly, and the daughters-in-law thought to themselves, "This brahmin has set himself against us to cause us harm. We must kill him." And so a snake-charmer came by that way, and they asked him, "Good man, do you have a snake?" He replied, "What kind of snake do you want — a dead one or a live one?" They said, "A dead one." He thought, "What do these people want with a dead snake? It seems clear they want to kill this brahmin." Now, it is the nature of things that the venom of an enraged snake travels to two places — the head and the tail. So he took a black snake and made it angry, then cut off its head and tail and gave them only the middle part of the body. They made a broth of the snake flesh and said to the brahmin, "Father, will you drink some snake broth?" The brahmin thought, "Why would they be offering me snake broth? It seems clear they want to give me some poison." But then he thought, "Whatever happens, I will drink it," and they poured out for him the snake broth, and he drank it. The fumes of it cleared the film from his eyes, and the brahmin's sight became clear. He thought, "I must find a way to make this even more potent," so he threw himself down on the ground and said, "I am near death, I am near death." They thought, "May he die quickly," and said, "Father, drink some more and you will recover." He said, "I'll drink it," and they poured him yet more of the snake broth. He drank it again, and its fumes cleared the film from his eyes even further. His eyes saw as clearly as before, and he sat there saying nothing.

Now, those daughters-in-law, in the time when the brahmin had previously been blind, had treated him with contempt and behaved carelessly — and they began to carry on in exactly the same way as before. The brahmin then rose, took up his staff, and said, "What are you thinking? Do you suppose that I cannot see?"

"Now, the fumes of that snake-flesh broth have struck my eyes and cleared away every last film, so that I see everything clearly, just as in former times. Daughters-in-law, from this day forward, conduct yourselves with care."

O monks, the brahmin who lived at that time and in that age was none other than the elder Lampa himself. The twelve daughters-in-law who lived at that time and in that age are these very twelve communities of nuns. Even then, instead of intending to harm him, they acted for his benefit alone.

Then the monks addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend Blessed One, see how by teaching the elder Lampa with just a few words of instruction, you drew him out of the wilderness of cyclic existence and established him in the utterly final attainment — in nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed state of bliss and peace."

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, not only now — even thus, in times long past, I set him upon the great lord of mastery by guiding him with just a few words of instruction. Now listen well.

O monks, long ago in a past age, in a certain mountain gorge, there lived a wealthy householder of great riches and abundant possessions, whose holdings were broad and extensive. He took a wife from a family of equal rank, and with her he played, rejoiced, and sported in happiness. As they were playing, rejoicing, and sporting in happiness together, a son was born to them. The householder then said to his wife: 'My dear, debtors who steal and plunderers who take our wealth have arisen, so I shall take up a cargo and set out to sea on the great ocean. Act accordingly, O son of a noble lord.' The householder then thought: 'If I were to entrust a large sum of kārṣāpaṇas to this wife of mine, she would turn and consort with another man.' So he gave her only a small quantity of kārṣāpaṇas.

Now, in that mountain gorge there also lived a merchant, and this merchant happened to be the householder's intimate younger friend. The householder therefore placed a large sum of kārṣāpaṇas in the merchant's hand and said: 'If my wife falls short of food and clothing, supply her with whatever food and clothing she needs.' Having said this, he took up his cargo and went out upon the great ocean — and right there, in that very place, he came to grief through misfortune.

The wife raised and nurtured their little son through the strength of her kinsmen and through the labor of her own hands. When the boy had grown, he asked his mother: 'Mother, what work did my father and grandfather do?' The mother thought: 'If I tell him, "They sailed great ships upon the great ocean," then this one too will go out upon the great ocean, and he too will come to grief through misfortune in that very place — such a danger would arise.' So instead she said: 'Son, your father and grandfather carried on trade right here in this very place. Mother, give me the kārṣāpaṇas, and I shall trade here as well.' The boy said: 'Mother, where would you get kārṣāpaṇas? You nurtured and raised me through the strength of your kinsmen and the labor of your own hands — how could you have an abundance of kārṣāpaṇas? However, this merchant is your father's intimate younger friend; go to him, obtain kārṣāpaṇas from him, and set to work.'

The boy went to the merchant. Now, another man had been pressing the merchant three times over the matter of a failed trade, and while the merchant was sitting there being pestered by him, a servant girl came out from inside his house carrying a dead rat on a piece of cloth, and she started to throw it away. At that moment, the merchant said to that man: 'Anyone with ability can make a livelihood from even this dead rat.'

When the boy heard this, he thought:

'This merchant is a great man, and therefore he will not go about boasting of what has happened here; I can certainly take this dead rat for myself without missing my chance.' The boy followed right behind that servant girl, and when she threw down the piece of cloth, the boy picked up the dead rat and went off to the marketplace. Now, in a certain shop there was a cat tied up, and when the boy showed the dead rat to that cat, the cat lunged toward it. The shopkeeper said to the boy, 'Give that dead rat to this cat.' The boy replied, 'How can I give it without a price? Give me a price and I will give it.' The shopkeeper filled the boy's cupped hands with beans and gave them to him.

The boy thought: 'If I eat these up, that will cut off my capital.' So he soaked the beans and roasted them, filled a pot with cool water, and went to the rocky hills to a place where the woodcutters would come to rest, and he sat down there. When the woodcutters arrived, the boy said to them, 'Good fellows, set down your loads of wood and rest a while.' The woodcutters set their loads down, and the boy gave each of them a small portion of beans and let them drink of the cool water. The woodcutters said, 'Young man, where are you going?' 'I am going to sell wood.' 'However far ahead we go, we still come back the same day — if you go now, when will you return?' And each of them gave him a piece of wood. One piece from each of them thus made up the boy's load of wood, and he carried it away and came back. He sold those pieces, bought beans with the proceeds, roasted them, filled a pot with cool water, and went again to that same place and sat down. Those woodcutters came along as well, and he said to them, 'Good fellows, set down your loads of wood and rest a while.' The woodcutters set their loads down, and again he shared beans among them and let them drink their fill of cool water. They said to him, 'Young man, stay here every single day with beans and water, and we will bring you the price of a load of wood and give it to you.' The boy began to do just that, day after day, and then he said to them, 'Good fellows, do not take your loads of wood to the market; leave them in my storehouse, and I will reckon the price for you and pay it all at once.' They left their loads of wood at his house.

On another occasion, a famine lasting seven days came upon the land, and the boy sold that wood and earned a great many profits. Then the boy thought: 'Among the trades, this one — selling wood — is a dead end; for even if one lives by sandalwood, one lives by wood alone. I should set up a provisions stall.' He set up a provisions stall and traded in it with honesty and fairness, so he earned a great many profits there as well.

Then he thought again: 'Among the trades, selling provisions is a dead end. I should set up a perfume and incense stall.' He set up a perfume and incense stall and traded in it with honesty and fairness, and there too he earned a great many profits.

Then he thought again: 'Among the trades, selling perfume and incense is a dead end. I should set up a jewellery stall.' He set up a jewellery stall and traded in it with honesty and fairness, and he surpassed every jeweller there was, so that his name came to be known as 'Byi-dbyi-pa — the Rat Boy, the Jeweller.'

The jewellers all said, 'This Rat Boy has surpassed us all —

they will find a way to send him into the great ocean, and when things go wrong there he will suffer — let us stir up his pride.' Saying this, one of them went and stood not far from him and began to speak idle words of provocation. 'Wise friends, consider this example: a man who has ridden an elephant dismounts to ride a horse, and having ridden a horse dismounts to ride a donkey, and having ridden a donkey goes on foot. In just the same way, this Rat Boy here — while his forebears sailed great ships across the ocean — now ekes out a hard living by mere small trade in goods.' When he had said this, Rat Boy heard it.

Rat Boy said, 'Wise friends, what is that you say? My forebears sailed great ships across the ocean, and now they are dead, and I earn my living in hardship through petty trade?'

Rat Boy went home and asked his mother: 'Mother, is it true that my forebears sailed great ships across the great ocean?' His mother thought: 'He must have heard this from someone. I should not let him down, for it would not be in keeping with my own character to speak false words to him.' And so she said, 'Son, it is true.'

Rat Boy said, 'Mother, give me your blessing to enter the great ocean myself.'

His mother said, 'Son, stay right here.'

Rat Boy said again and again that he would go, and his mother, knowing that the time had come when she must yield, gave her consent.

Rat Boy announced to the great assembly of merchants: 'Whoever among you wishes to go with the caravan-leader Rat Boy into the great ocean — without casting lots, without a lottery, without squabbling, without wrangling — let him prepare provisions for the voyage into the great ocean.'

Then some five hundred merchants prepared their provisions for the voyage into the great ocean.

Thereafter the caravan-leader Rat Boy performed rites of good omen, auspiciousness, and blessing, and loaded many cargoes onto wagons, onto draft animals, onto riding horses, onto mules, onto she-camels, onto oxen, and onto donkeys, and set out for the great ocean together with those merchants.

Now in that company there were five men: one who gathered, one who resolved disputes, one who bailed, one who drew water, and one who read the winds. The gatherer was the one who prepared food and drink. The one who resolved disputes was the one who settled all quarrels and conflicts as they arose. The bailer was the one who caulked and repaired the ship. The one who drew water was the one who drew up water. The one who read the winds was the one who observed the constellations.

In due course they arrived at the shore of the ocean. When those merchants saw the great ocean they were frightened, and no longer felt eager to board the great ship. The caravan-leader Rat Boy said to the wind-reader, 'My dear captain, proclaim the praises of the great ocean exactly as they are.'

Then the wind-reader began to proclaim: 'Hear, O wise merchants of Jambudvīpa! In this great ocean there are great and precious jewels of such kinds as these: gems, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, mother-of-pearl, the essence of stones, conch, carnelian, and right-whorled shells. With such precious things as these, each one of you may bring perfect happiness and contentment to yourselves, your fathers and mothers, your sons, your wives, your male servants and female servants, your workers, those who live on your charity, your friends and companions, your ministers, your relatives and kinsmen by blood, and, from time to time, to renunciants and

brahmins, in order to rise to a high station, to become one of the fortunate, to attain a pleasant karmic maturation, and to go to a higher realm in the next life — let such a one enter the great ocean. Now, it is the way of the world that the many ordinary folk who board the great ship are driven by desire for wealth; and when they and the ship were beyond what could be endured, the ship's captain considered: "Now I should cry out — what shall I say to turn them back?" Thinking this, he spoke to the one who held the wind-rope: "Proclaim inside the hold a fitting proclamation about the great ocean, not as praise but as it truly is." Then the one who held the wind-rope began to make the proclamation: "Wise merchants of Jambudvīpa, listen! In this great ocean there are such great and terrible dangers as these: the danger of great fish, the danger of fish-swallowing great fish, the danger of fish-swallowing-fish-swallowing great fish, the danger of great waves, the danger of whirlpools and eddies, the danger of the water-monster the kumbbhīra, the danger of the young-child-killing water-monster, the danger of striking against mountains that have risen up from within the water, and the danger of black winds. And here there will also come dark-clad and white-clad pirates who steal wealth, and they will in every way separate each and every one of you from your lives. Therefore, whoever among you is unwilling to be parted from all of these — yourself, your father and mother, your sons, your wife, your male servants and female servants, your workers, those who live on your charity, your friends and companions, your ministers, your relatives and kinsmen by blood — let that one not enter the great ocean." Now, it is the way of the world that the brave are few and those who have gone before are many; so the great mass of ordinary folk turned back. The ship having become bearable, thereafter the one who held the wind-rope made three cries of proclamation. Then, releasing one cable and then the second, and releasing up to the third, the great ship caught a great favorable wind and was well held; set in motion by the force and power of the wind, it moved like a great cloud, borne forward by a following wind, and in due course arrived at the jewel island. Then the one who held the wind-rope began to make proclamation: "Wise merchants of Jambudvīpa, listen! Right here on this jewel island there are stones and pebbles resembling precious gems — examine them carefully and closely, so that when you return to Jambudvīpa you will have no regrets; take the gems in just that way. Right here on this jewel island there are she-demons called Young Cranes; they will in every way bring men to ruin right here through improper conduct — so be wary, and do not consort with them. Right here on this jewel island there are fruits that cause intoxication; whoever eats them will remain senseless for seven days — do not eat them. Right here on this jewel island there are non-humans dwelling here, and they cannot tolerate your staying longer than seven days; after seven days they will send such a wind as this — one that carries away even a great ship as though it had never been built — so do not tarry beyond that either." When the merchants heard this, they gathered their minds and stayed with vigilance. They examined and examined the gems carefully, and the great ship — filled, for instance, with sesame, great heaps of rice, pine,

lentils and the like — departed from the jewel island, and, carried by a favorable wind, arrived in Jambudvīpa. In the same way, seven times over, the great ship was successfully completed and came to Jambudvīpa.

Then the navigator Byidhyigpālam's mother said to him, "Son, build a house." He replied, "Mother, should I not first pay off the debts and build under that?" His mother said to him, "Son, your father never had debts, nor did your grandfather — so how did you come to have debts?" He said, "Mother, I alone know," and he had four rats made from the four precious gems, filled a chest with gold, placed those four rats at the four sides of the chest, and went to that merchant.

That merchant was sitting there praising him, saying: "O wise ones, whatever grass or hemp or anything at all that the navigator Byidhyigpālam picks up turns into gold — see how meritorious and greatly renowned he is!" — and so the merchant sat there singing his praises. While the merchant was speaking those praises, someone came to the door and announced that the navigator Byidhyigpālam was standing at the gate. The merchant said, "Let the navigator Byidhyigpālam enter! Who would turn the navigator Byidhyigpālam away?" The navigator Byidhyigpālam then entered inside and said to the merchant, "Merchant, this is the principal, and this is the profit — please accept them." The merchant said, "Navigator, I cannot recall having given you even the smallest thing." The navigator said, "It is I who should remind you," and he reminded him. The merchant asked, "Whose son are you? You are the son of some great householder." The merchant said, "Then you are the son of my dear younger friend. When your father was passing away, he entrusted many kārṣāpaṇas into my hand — it is I who was to give them to you." With that, the merchant received him with a welcome offering of a golden vessel filled with water, and gave him his youngest daughter, adorned with every ornament, as the wife of the navigator Byidhyigpālam.

O monks, he who was the merchant at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself. He who was the navigator Byidhyigpālam at that time and on that occasion is this very Lampā. At that time too, by giving him a little instruction, I established him in the mastery of great lordship. And now too, by giving him a little instruction, I have drawn him out from the wilderness of saṃsāra and established him in the utterly final accomplishment — in the nirvāṇa of unsurpassed bliss and peace.

The Vinaya Analysis, the forty-eighth fascicle. The monks requested of the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, what action did the elder Lampā perform such that by the karmic maturation of that action he was brought low, supremely low, and utterly, supremely diminished?" The Blessed One declared:

O monks, it is Lampā himself who, having performed and accumulated a collection of karmas, having converted the conditions — dwelling close by like a flame — performed and accumulated those actions that are inevitably bound to arise. Who else could experience separately the karma that Lampā himself performed and accumulated? O monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas). As it is said in verse:

Even if a hundred aeons pass,
the karmas one has gathered do not perish;
when the assembly and the time arrive,

they ripen as fruits for those who bear a body.

O monks, in a former time, in the past, during this very good aeon, when the lifespan of living beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, appeared in the world. He resided near Vārāṇasī together with a retinue of twenty thousand monks. In that Blessed One's scriptural collections, this very Lampā became a monk who was master of the three baskets of scripture, yet due to his Dharma-miserliness he did not teach even a single four-line verse to anyone.

Now there was also a pig-dealer who lived on a certain rocky cliff. At a festival time that arose on those cliffs along both banks of a river, the pig-dealer thought: "If I were to slaughter the pigs here and now, there would not be enough buyers for that much meat, so I should bring them alive and slaughter and sell them on the spot." With this in mind, he tied the blind pigs one to another in a line, loaded them onto a boat, and set off. While the pigs were being conveyed, the boat capsized, and there they suffered in an improper manner.

When the pig-dealer was carried along by the current, about five hundred pratyekabuddhas were encamped on the bank of that river. One of those pratyekabuddhas had gone down to the riverside for water, and seeing the pig-dealer he thought: "Is this one dead, or alive?" He stretched out his hand, which was like an elephant's trunk, pulled the man out, spread sand over him, laid him face-down upon it, and departed.

When all the moisture had drained from the man through the sand, he regained his perception (saṃjñā), rose up, and saw a human footprint. He followed after it, and presently, seeing the five hundred pratyekabuddhas, he began to wait upon them with leaves, fruits, and tooth-wood. They, in turn, gave him the remainders from their almsbowls. And whenever those pratyekabuddhas sat cross-legged in meditative concentration, he too would sit to one side and enter meditative concentration cross-legged. Through this he developed the meditative absorption of non-perception, and was reborn among the gods of non-perception.

O monks, at that very time and in that very era, the monk who had become master of the three baskets in the scriptural collection of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, and who had become a pig-dealer — that was this very monk Lampā. The karma of his never having taught even a single four-line verse to anyone out of Dharma-miserliness, of his having slaughtered pigs, and of having been born here from among the gods of non-perception — by the ripening of that karma he became one who was given to, supremely given to, lowly and supremely lowly.

O monks, thus there are these and other faults in meditating without instruction. Therefore a monk should not engage in meditative concentration without instruction; if he does, it will lead to transgression.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Śrāvastī as long as he wished, set out toward Rājagṛha and, traveling gradually, arrived at Rājagṛha and took up residence there in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park. In Rājagṛha there was a physician named Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta, who heard that the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagṛha while traveling gradually and was residing in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park. He went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

Sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta with Dharma-endowed words, guiding him rightly, establishing him rightly, exhorting him rightly, and gladdening him rightly. With many categories of Dharma-endowed words he instructed him rightly, established him rightly, exhorted him rightly, and gladdened him rightly, and then said nothing more. Then Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, and with palms joined in the direction of the Blessed One, bowed and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "May the Blessed One please consent to accept, together with the Saṅgha of monks, a midday meal at my dwelling tomorrow. The Blessed Buddhas are difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, so Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta is unable to say to the Blessed Buddhas, 'Except for the Venerable Lamba.'" The Blessed One said nothing, and by that silence he granted the request to Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta. Then Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that the request had been granted, rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One's words, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One. He went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Venerable Ānanda's feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta spoke to the Venerable Ānanda thus: "Venerable Ānanda, please know this: I have invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a midday meal at my dwelling tomorrow, excepting the Venerable Lamba. May your virtuous qualities, Jīvaka, flourish accordingly." Then Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta rejoiced and delighted in what the Venerable Ānanda had said, bowed his head to the Venerable Ānanda's feet, and departed. Not long after Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta had left, the Venerable Ānanda understood the situation, went to where the Venerable Lamba was, and upon arriving spoke to the Venerable Lamba thus: "Venerable Lamba, please know this: Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta has invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to a midday meal at another household tomorrow, excepting the Venerable Lamba alone. May the virtuous qualities of the Venerable Ānanda flourish accordingly." Then, that very night, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta made preparation of pure and fine food and drink, and rising early the next morning, spread out seats, set out water for the hands, and invited the Blessed One with the words: "Venerable One, since you have graciously agreed to come at midday, may the Blessed One please bear in mind that the time has now arrived." Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe and took up his bowl and outer robe, and, surrounded by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to and arrived at the dwelling of Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta. He took his seat on the seat that had been prepared, at the head of the Saṅgha of monks. When he had taken his seat, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, set down the pitcher of water. Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta has a golden pill called bhṛṅgāra; he is sitting to one side of an elder. The Blessed One has not yet accepted the water."

Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta addressed him: "Why does the Blessed One not accept the water?"

The Blessed One declared: "The assembly of monks has not yet fully gathered."

Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta asked: "Blessed One, who is absent?"

The Blessed One declared: "The monk Lāmpa."

Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta said: "Blessed One, I did not invite him."

The Blessed One declared: "Jīvaka, did you not invite the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha?"

"Blessed One, I did invite them."

"Then is Lāmpa outside the assembly of monks?"

"Blessed One, no."

"Go then and call him." Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta thought to himself: "I will call him at the Blessed One's word, yet I will do so respectfully and not presumptuously." So he sent a messenger, with the instruction: "Go and call him."

Now the Venerable Lāmpa had entered into a meditative absorption of such a kind that, as his mind rested in equipoise, two thousand two hundred and fifty monks appeared, sitting there as his emanations. The messenger went and called out "Lāmpa, Lāmpa," and a great many monks answered "Here!" The messenger returned and said to Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta: "I went there and called out 'Lāmpa, Lāmpa,' and at the Kalandaka grove in the Bamboo Grove, just as the monks had been filling the space before, so again the monks were filling the space, and a great many of them answered 'Here!' Which of them was I to call?"

Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Go, and tell the true Lāmpa to come."

He went and said: "Let the one who is the true Lāmpa please come."

Then the Venerable Lāmpa withdrew the miraculous display of his supernatural power, went there, and took his seat in his own proper place. Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta then began to serve the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha, but he served the Venerable Lāmpa without the special respect he was showing the others.

The Blessed One reflected: "Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta is receiving the words of this great hearer, who is like Mount Meru. I should have his qualities proclaimed." And so, since the Venerable Ānanda was the one who customarily received the Blessed One's bowl, the Blessed One did not pass it to him. For by established custom, so long as the Blessed One has not yet accepted his bowl, the senior monks do not accept theirs.

The Venerable Lāmpa then thought: "Why is it that the Blessed One and the senior monks are not accepting their bowls? I understand: it is in order to proclaim my own qualities." Thinking thus that he should fulfil the Teacher's intention completely, the Venerable Lāmpa rose halfway from his seat, extended his arm like an elephant's trunk, and took up the Blessed One's bowl. Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta, who was sitting to one side of the elder, saw this and thought: "I wonder which elder this is who is displaying such a miraculous marvel?" He followed after the bowl, and after a short while recognized that it was the Venerable Lāmpa. Upon recognizing him, he fainted and fell to the ground. Water was sprinkled on him and he revived. He then touched the two feet of the Venerable Lāmpa, begged his forgiveness, and spoke in verse:

Sandalwood is always cool, fragrant, and full of virtue;
The blue lotus always breathes a fresh and stainless scent;
Like the light of vaiḍūrya, ever bright and pure;
The sins of childish ordinary beings are ever constant,
Like the markings of an incomparable gourd, unchanging.
Noble persons always possess compassion.
The patience of arhats is steadfast indeed.
The Venerable Lāmpa then said: "Jīvaka, I forgive you."

The Blessed One gave his approval, rose from his seat, and departed.

The monks then addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable sir, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta — when he failed to recognize the qualities of the Venerable Lāmpa, he strove in disrespect, and when he did recognize those qualities, he touched his two feet and begged forgiveness. Please observe this." The Blessed One said: "Monks, this is not the only time. In the past as well, whenever he did not recognize this one's qualities he strove in disrespect, and whenever he did recognize them he touched his two feet and begged forgiveness. Listen now.

Monks, long ago in times past, a caravan leader drove five hundred pack-horses northward and traveled to the central lands. A horse that knew nothing entered the womb of a mare, and from the very day it entered, all those horses ceased to whinny. The caravan leader thought: "Has some illness come upon my horses? Why do they not whinny?" Then at a later time a foal was born from that mare, and from the very day it was born, all those horses no longer even made the effort to snort. The caravan leader thought: "This foal is an unfortunate creature; because of its fault my horses have fallen ill." He therefore always rode the mare yet gave her neither grass nor fodder.

Eventually he arrived at a place called Ultimately Worshipped, and there the rains season came upon him. He thought: "If I travel now, the horses' hooves will become sore and they will be unfit for the caravan, so I shall stay here through the rains." He stayed there through the rains season, and the craftsmen living there served him, each in accordance with their own craft. When the time came for him to depart, the craftsmen came to see him off, and he distributed shares among them. Among them was a potter who had also served him with the work of his craft. The potter's wife said to him: "My lord, the caravan leader is about to leave — ask him for something." The potter took up a lump of clay and stood before the caravan leader. When the caravan leader saw him, he said: "Alas, master, you have come too late — I have already distributed everything I had."

The caravan leader's mind turned with ill omen toward that foal, and he said to the potter: "As it happens, I have a foal. If you want it, take it and go." The potter replied: "No matter — I shall make pots and it will break them." Just then the foal began to lick the potter's two feet with its tongue, and the potter was moved with affection for it, took it with him, and went home.

His wife said to him: "My lord, did you get anything from him?" "I got this foal." "No matter — you shall make pots and it shall break them." Then the foal began to lick the wife's two feet with its tongue as well, and she too was moved with affection for the foal.

When the foal walked among the fired and unfired pots, it did not break a single one, and the potter said to his wife: "This is a fine foal — it walks with full awareness." On another occasion the potter took up a basket and went to fetch clay, and the foal followed close behind him of its own accord. When the potter had filled the basket with clay, the foal offered its back; and so the potter loaded the basket of clay onto the foal's back, and it carried it home for him. The potter then said to his wife: "My dear, this is a fine foal indeed — from now on I shall no longer need to haul clay myself. I shall dig the clay over there, and you can load it here." His wife said "Excellent!" and gave the foal fodder of grass and beans.

Now at that time in Vārāṇasī there reigned a king named Brahmadatta, and under his rule the kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and joyful; the harvests were good and the land was filled with many people. Battles, strife, quarrels, and civil unrest were entirely at peace; it was free from thieves, famine, and disease. He caused the land to abound in rice, garlands of sugar cane, cattle, and buffalo, and as a righteous king ruling by the Dharma, he ruled his righteous kingdom.

Now when the time came for that king's horse-master to make his round of inspections, the kings of the lands under the sun heard that King Brahmadatta's horse-master had arrived on his tour of inspection, and they sent word to him: "Either submit to an accounting of tribute, or else come out to the pleasure grove outside Vārāṇasī. If you do not, you shall be chained and dragged away by the neck." King Brahmadatta refused to render any tribute to them, yet out of fear he did not go out to the pleasure grove either, and so he sat confined within his city.

In time the merchant caravan leader arrived in Vārāṇasī, and King Brahmadatta heard that a certain merchant caravan leader had driven five hundred trading horses northward and come to Vārāṇasī. He summoned his ministers and said to them: "Wise ones, for as long as I remain shut up here, go today and seek out the horse-master." They went to the caravan leader, and when they saw those horses they said among themselves: "Wise ones, these horses are clearly all broken by the horse-master, yet the horse-master himself is nowhere to be seen here." Then they saw the mare and said: "Wise ones, if the horse-master were to follow this mare, he would be nowhere in sight." They went to the caravan leader and asked him: "Caravan leader, have you sold any horse to someone, or given one away?" The caravan leader replied: "I have not sold any at all, but it is the case that I gave away a foal at a place I took to be inauspicious, thinking it unlucky, to a certain potter." They said to one another: "Wise ones, this caravan leader is a fool — he cast away what was of the highest value and drove the dregs here." They reported to the king and went to the place of the inauspicious omen, and then they went to the potter and asked him: "What use is this foal to you?" The potter said: "It fetches clay for me." They said: "We shall give you a donkey; give us this one." The potter said: "This is what I need." They said: "We shall give you a cart with four oxen." The potter said: "This is what I need." They said: "Consider it today, and we shall come again tomorrow," and they departed.

Now it is in the nature of reality that when the world had not long been established, even animals could speak. So the foal said to the potter: "What is it they want? They want you. Why will you not give me away?"

"Does your heart truly believe that as long as I live I shall carry clay for you and eat chaff and grain husks? I must be consecrated as a king of the warrior-noble class (kṣatriya), anointed on the crown of my head, and I must eat rich and excellent food piled high and brimming over in vessels of gold. If they call me a mere foal, you should say to them in rebuke: 'What do you know of horses?' And if they offer a price, say to them: 'Then give a hundred thousand in gold, or give as much gold as this right haunch of mine can carry.'"

The next day they came and asked the potter: "Dear friend, have you considered, sir?" "I have considered." "Then give us this foal. Are you not ashamed to have them say you know nothing of horses?" They thought to themselves: "This simpleton — does he know whether this is a horse or not? It was this very horse that told him to say this to them, so it must be so." And so they said: "Whether it is a horse or a foal, give it to us for a price." The potter said: "Then give a hundred thousand in gold, or give as much gold as this right haunch of mine can carry." They thought: "This one is powerful; he will be able to carry a great many things. A situation like this will arise." So they said: "We shall give a hundred thousand in gold."

They sent word to King Brahmadatta saying: "We have purchased the horse-knower for a hundred thousand in gold." King Brahmadatta sent word back to them: "Whatever price you paid to obtain him, you will be reimbursed that same amount."

They took their hundred thousand in gold, led the horse-knower away, and arrived at Vārāṇasī. They placed him first in the royal stable and gave him hay and fodder, but he would not eat. The king said: "Have you brought your horse-knower to me sick?" They replied: "He is not sick, Your Majesty. He is wounded in this way" — and then the horse-trainer spoke these verses:


When swift-going ones are timely fit and watered well,
but a potter keeps them — head gone dry, mere bone and skin —
think then of eating self-healed, re-grown roots.
In that time, did many think of you?

Here, where a swift one carries a thousand loads,
and the king has supplied the finest mounts for riding —
why you do not eat: ask that of me, and I shall tell.


Then the most swift, upright, and steadfast one,
with impatience and disturbance, the swiftest of the swift,
having calmed himself from that and reflected well,
spoke to the wise horse-trainer, that excellent man:


"Here you yourself know my very qualities.
I am not unknown to you as I truly am.
If scorned by the wise, I will not move upon this earth —
to die here quickly would be better for me.
Even if scorned long by base people,
if my qualities are yours, that is no scorn.
But if for even a moment a wise person scorns me —
if that peace itself, that quality, is scorned —"


The horse-trainer said to the king: "Your Majesty, he is not sick. The reason is this: the proper ceremonial reception has not been performed for him, and so he does not wish to eat hay and fodder. How should his reception be performed?" "Your Majesty, for half a yojana and three quarters in his wake, let it be made beautiful, and let the city itself be made beautiful. Let a royal kṣatriya consecration army with its four divisions be assembled to greet him. In whatever direction he is placed, let that direction be screened with panels of copper. Let the eldest prince hold over his head a white parasol with a hundred ribs. Let the eldest princess fan off the insects with a golden fan adorned with jewels."

Let the king's chief queen present food of fine provisions bound with fresh butter from a golden vessel. Let the king's chief minister discard the dregs with a golden ladle of copper.

The king said, "In that case, this one is the king, and I am not the king."

The trainer said, "Your Majesty, it is not possible to perform that reception for him at all times. It shall be done in this way for seven years. After the seven years have passed, he will become obedient. Whatever has already passed cannot now be undone, but let what remains be carried out. Let the king screen in whatever direction he is placed with panels of copper. Let the eldest prince hold over his head a white parasol with a hundred ribs. Let the eldest princess fan off the insects with a golden fan adorned with jewels. Let the chief queen present food of fine provisions bound with fresh butter from a golden vessel. Let the chief minister discard the dregs with a golden ladle of copper."

The earth-lord became attached to the trainer with his retinue,
holding the finest fragrant ointment,
and the earth-lord's queen, with fresh butter and fine provisions,
filled the vessel and took it for the swift and excellent one.

When the king wished to go to the pleasure grove, a horse of fine breeding was presented to him, and as the king mounted from behind, he whispered to the trainer, "Will this one not kick?" The trainer replied, "Your Majesty, it will not kick. It thought: if the king were to have difficulty mounting, that would not be right, and so it lowered its hindquarters for that reason."

The king mounted and rode off. As they were going, a body of water arose and the horse would not cross it. The king whispered to the trainer, "Is it not afraid?" The trainer said, "Your Majesty, it is not afraid. It thought: if the king were to be splashed by the water from its tail, that would be improper, and so it does not cross for that reason."

The king had the horse's tail placed inside a golden tube, and then the horse crossed over.

The king went to the pleasure grove and was sitting there at ease, when the kings of the southern regions heard that King Brahmadatta had gone to the pleasure grove. They came and seized the gates of the city.

When King Brahmadatta heard that the kings of the southern regions had seized the city gates, he mounted the horse of fine breeding. Between Vārāṇasī and the pleasure grove there lay a pool called Brahmasaras, covered with blue lotuses, pink lotuses, kumuda water-lilies, and white lotuses. The horse of fine breeding thought to itself: "For me to abandon one who has been consecrated as the crown of the kṣatriya royal lineage, leaving him in harm's way, in distress, and in danger — that would not accord with my nature." And so the horse of fine breeding placed its hooves upon the lotus petals and entered Vārāṇasī through the window.

The king was delighted and said to his ministers, "O wise ones, what shall be given to one who has saved the life of a king consecrated as the crown of the kṣatriya royal lineage?" They replied, "Your Majesty, half the kingdom." The king said, "This is an animal — what use has it for half the kingdom? Rather, taking it as the occasion, let us for seven days give gifts, accumulate merit, and hold an out-of-season kumuda festival." And so, taking that as the occasion, the king gave gifts for seven days, began to accumulate merit, and for seven days held an out-of-season kumuda festival.

Then the caravan leader asked the people, "O wise ones, why has this out-of-season kumuda festival come about?" And they told him:

"From the place called Consecrated-by-the-King, a horse trainer had come here after purchasing the horse that knows everything from a potter for a hundred thousand in gold. He then saved this king's life, and the king, taking that as the occasion, gave gifts for seven days, accumulated merit, and held an out-of-season kumuda festival."

The caravan leader thought, "Has that foal become the horse that knows everything? I must go and see." He went to where the horse was, and the horse that knows everything said, "Lord of the caravan, what did those five hundred horses fetch? A hundred thousand in gold. And I alone gave that potter a hundred thousand." At this, the caravan leader fainted and fell to the ground. When water was sprinkled on him he recovered his senses, and prostrating at the two feet of the horse that knows everything, he begged his forgiveness.

Monks, he who was the caravan leader at that time and on that occasion is none other than the youth Jīvaka who nurtured the young. And he who was the horse that knows everything at that time and on that occasion is none other than this very Lāmpa. Even then, when he did not recognize that one's qualities, he fell into disrespect toward him; and when he came to recognize those qualities, he prostrated at his two feet and begged forgiveness. Even now, whenever he does not recognize this one's qualities, he falls into disrespect toward him; and whenever he comes to recognize those qualities, he prostrates at his two feet and begs forgiveness.

The monks then addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable One, what action did Lāmpa perform, such that through the karmic maturation of that action the Blessed One has declared him the foremost among those skilled in transforming minds?"

The Blessed One declared: "It was through the power of an aspiration. Where was that aspiration made? Monks, long ago, when this one had gone forth under the teaching of the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, the preceptor from whom he had gone forth was declared by the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa to be the foremost among those skilled in transforming minds. Yet this one, having lived the holy life throughout his entire life without gaining even a portion of the accumulation of virtuous qualities, made at the time of his death this aspiration: 'Throughout my life I have lived the holy life under the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, he of unsurpassed qualities, Kāśyapa, yet I have not gained even a portion of the accumulation of virtuous qualities. By the root of virtue of this holy life I have lived throughout my life, may the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, just as he declared the brahmin youth who is my preceptor to be foremost, prophesying: "Brahmin youth, at a future time, when human lives last a hundred years, there shall appear a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one, named Śākyamuni" — just as my preceptor was declared foremost among those skilled in transforming minds under that Blessed One, so too may I be declared foremost among those skilled in transforming minds by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the chief of the Śākya kings.' Having begun to plant that aspiration, it is through the power of that aspiration that the Tathāgata has now declared him the foremost among those skilled in transforming minds.

Monks, thus it is that the karmic maturation of deeds that are wholly dark is wholly dark;

the karmic maturation of deeds that are wholly bright is wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon deeds that are wholly dark and mixed deeds, and strive for deeds that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train yourselves accordingly.

There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is mentally disturbed, one who is distracted, or one who is overcome by painful feeling.

The twenty-first rule entailing transgression for teaching without having been appointed is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One addressed the venerable Nanda: "Nanda, you are to instruct the nuns. Nanda, you are to teach the nuns. Nanda, you are to speak to the nuns with Dharma-infused words." Having given this command, the five hundred nuns of the Utpalāvarṇā circle went to where the venerable Nanda was, and having arrived they prostrated with their heads at the venerable Nanda's feet and sat to one side. The venerable Nanda thought to himself, "Women's domain is of little wisdom," and so he taught them the Dharma in brief, summarizing the meaning, the words, and the letters. Since she — Utpalāvarṇā — was endowed with wisdom, she kept asking deeper and deeper questions, and the venerable Nanda gave answers; and he taught them the Dharma until the time when the sun had set. Then they prostrated with their heads at his feet, rose from their seats, and departed. Now, as they were going, the gates of Śrāvastī had been closed, and the nuns went in search of a gate. The gatekeeper said, "The gates are closed." They said, "Open them — the keys are at the royal palace." Thinking to themselves, "We should stay right here," they went to a pleasure grove that was not far from Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One then gave the order that trees should be assigned in order of seniority, and they began assigning the trees in order of seniority. At that point, as the nuns were calling out to the gatekeepers at the trees with loud cries, calling out phrases in a foreign tongue — "A-ye, a-ya, ha-ḍe, a-ga, e, a-ga, ha-ḍe!" — about five hundred villains wishing to attack Śrāvastī arrived and, hearing that loud, great outcry, said to one another: "Friends, stay still for a moment here at Śrāvastī! Friends, before the retinue of the venerable lady hears this, let us destroy them." Now Utpalāvarṇā thought to herself: "Could something terrible be about to happen without being known?" When she saw those approximately five hundred villains who wished to destroy them, she conjured up the army of a noble warrior, beat the great battle drum, and they said, "Friends, we are surrounded by the army of a noble warrior and are about to be captured — it is not right; let us flee!" Realizing this, they fled. Utpalāvarṇā then said to the nuns: "Sisters, about five hundred villains intent on destruction came here, and I frightened them off so they fled. Now gently, gently, quietly tap the gate and open it." Early the next morning they rose and entered Śrāvastī. When brahmins and householders saw them, they said, "It is excellent that the renunciants who are disciples of the Śākya son both mix with the Dharma and practice pure conduct beyond that." But there were a few monks who censured, disparaged, and criticized: "Why do the monks teach the nuns until sunset?" And in that circumstance the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis for a rule, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, exactly as before. The passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, act as though unknowing" also proceeds exactly as before. The blessed Buddha asked the venerable Nandaka: "Nandaka, is it true that you were teaching the nuns until sunset?" "Reverend one, it is so." The blessed Buddha reproached lack of diligence, lack of application, and acting without examination. Then the Blessed One spoke words of praise for diligence, application, and examined conduct, and declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers, and so forth, exactly as before. My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk who has been appointed by the monastic Saṅgha teaches nuns until sunset commits an offense."

The word "monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. The phrase "by the monastic Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. The phrase "who has been appointed" refers to appointment by a motion and a dual-act procedure. The phrase "until sunset" means up to the moment when sunset falls. The phrase "nuns" refers to those belonging to this Dharma. The phrase "teaches" refers to instruction in higher moral discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The phrase "commits an offense" means: it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the lower realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and wrong rebirths. Furthermore, as long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome qualities. That is why it is said to be an offense.

As to how the offense comes about: if a monk, when it is indeed sunset, perceives it as sunset and teaches a nun, he commits an offense. If a monk, when it is sunset, is uncertain about it and teaches a nun, he commits an offense. If a monk, when it is not yet sunset, perceives it as sunset and teaches a nun, he commits a wrong act. If a monk, when it is not yet sunset, is uncertain about it and teaches a nun, he commits a wrong act.

Teaching that happens to be heard at night, teaching at the door of a temple, sitting without having closed the door, a temple or a summer dwelling located within a city, and teaching after going to another household — in all these cases there is no offense. For one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, and for one who is afflicted by painful feelings, there is no offense.

The monks, having doubts, asked the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Reverend one, please look upon the nun of lotus-blue complexion who fully protected five hundred nuns from the terror of bandits." The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now — in the past as well she fully protected a great many like-minded companions from the terror of lions. Listen to this, monks. Long ago, in time past, a householder dwelt on a rocky cliff. He took a wife of equal family, and together with her he played, rejoiced, and enjoyed pleasures. He said to his wife: 'Good woman, I must take up provisions and travel to another region.' His wife replied: 'My lord's son, I too shall come.' The householder said:

"Who will serve as your attendant on the road? Stay here — I am not taking you." At this she began to weep, and those who lived by selling curds asked the householder: "Why, my lord, has she been caused to cry?" The householder replied: "Because I said I am not taking her." They said: "Why will you not take her?" The householder said: "Who would serve as her attendant there?" They said: "We will serve as her attendants there." So the householder took her along, and together with those like-minded companions they spent the night on a forest road. Those like-minded companions, exhausted from the journey, lay down to sleep, while the householder's wife kept watch. Just then a lion came and, seizing a sickle stalk, threatened them; and as they fled, a god spoke these verses:

Not only men are skilled
in every task and undertaking —
in this or that endeavor, too,
a woman proves herself adept.

Monks, she who was the householder's wife at that time and occasion is none other than this very Utpalā of the blue-lotus complexion, and those five hundred like-minded companions at that time and occasion are these very five hundred nuns. At that time also she fully protected many like-minded companions from the terror of a lion, and now likewise she has fully protected five hundred nuns from the terror of bandits. Here ends the twenty-second offence entailing expiation until sunset, the offences of the Teacher.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, you should teach the nuns. Ānanda, you should instruct the nuns. Ānanda, you should address the nuns with Dharma-connected discourse." Having so declared, the great sovereign lady of living beings, Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred nuns, went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, she bowed her head to the two feet of the venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. The venerable Ānanda then taught the Dharma to her with deep and profound meanings, words, and letters. But the domain of women, on account of their flickering wisdom, cannot receive the signs, and out of fear they are unable to inquire. Thereupon, the great sovereign lady of living beings Gautamī, delighted and rejoicing in what the venerable Ānanda had said, bowed her head to the two feet of the venerable Ānanda, rose from her seat, departed, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the great sovereign lady of living beings Gautamī addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend One, when the noble Ānanda teaches the nuns the Dharma with deep and profound meanings, words, and letters, the domain of women, on account of their flickering wisdom, cannot receive the signs, and out of fear they have no occasion to inquire. The Blessed One has declared that giving is a cause of fearlessness. If the Blessed One would permit it, the nuns might do what would bring delight to the monks." The Blessed One declared: "In that case, so be it — let the nuns do what would bring delight to the monks." The Blessed One having declared "Let the nuns do what would bring delight to the monks," they did not know how to go about it. The Blessed One then declared: "The five things to be planted — roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits — and the five things to be eaten — unhusked grain, cooked rice, small cakes, meat, and oil — and the alms bowl, the Dharma robes,

nets, bowls, ladles, straining cloths, small straining pouches, and cloth strips — with these things let the nuns do what would bring delight to the monks.

A certain nun carried some milk porridge and went to the Jeta Grove. Now the practice of the group of six was this: they thought to themselves, "Here, when brahmins and householders come and arrive, we shall teach the Dharma, we shall refute opponents, and we shall proclaim our own reputations." And so one or another of the group of six would not leave the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended. Ānanda rose early in the morning, set aside his tooth-stick, put on a red-and-yellow patched robe, and was walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. When Ānanda saw that nun, he asked her: "What is it you have brought?" "Milk porridge." "For whom are you pouring it?" "For the noble Ānanda." "If Ānanda were to receive milk porridge as well, he would always in return teach the Dharma to the nuns." In the same way, when some nuns brought yoghurt porridge and others brought it in a bucket, Ānanda said: "I, Ānanda, am thinking to teach the nuns the excellent Dharma — I, Ānanda, am not at all thinking to teach the nuns for the sake of a mere trifle of food."

Now, certain monks of few wants reproached, dismissed, and criticized the monks, saying: "Why do the monks say to the other monks: 'The monks teach the nuns for the sake of a mere trifle of food'?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on this occasion, in regard to this matter, and in this context, convened the community of monks, and so on as before. "The Blessed Buddhas, knowing fully, inquire" — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddha inquired of Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that the monks say of the other monks: 'The monks teach the nuns for the sake of a mere trifle of food'?" "Venerable One, it is not so." The Blessed Buddha then censured what was not the way of the ascetic, what was discordant, what was improper, what was inconsistent with the discipline, declaring: "This is not something that one who has gone forth should do." Then, having censured it in many ways, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing the ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk says to other monks: 'Monks teach the nuns for the sake of a mere trifle of food' — that is an offense.

'Whatever monk' refers to a son of the Śākyas such as Ānanda, or another of that kind. 'To other monks' means to those belonging to this Dharma. 'Says as follows' means if he says such a thing. 'Monks' refers to those of this Dharma. 'For the sake of a mere trifle of food' refers to the five things to be planted and the five things to be eaten. 'To the nuns' means to those of this Dharma. 'Teaches' — the term for teaching here refers to the higher moral discipline, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. 'That is an offense' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall — into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, into the wretched states, and into the downward fall."

Furthermore, if that transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and that is why it is called a downfall.

As for how one incurs the downfall: whenever a monk says to the monks even the slightest thing, such as, "Monks, he teaches the nuns for the sake of even a trifle of food," in every such case he incurs the downfall. If it is true that he teaches the nuns for the sake of a little food, there is no downfall. There is no downfall for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by feeling. The twenty-third downfall — teaching for the sake of a mere trifle of food — is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a merchant who took a wife from among those of equal rank, and with her he made merry, delighted, and lived in joy. When he came to old age, his relatives had dwindled away, his wealth was exhausted, and his resources were spent. He said to his wife: "Good woman, I am no longer able to acquire wealth now; I will go forth into homelessness." His wife replied: "My lord's son, I too shall go forth." "Do so, then," he said, and he brought his wife to the great Prājāpatī Gautamī (the chief nun, foster-mother of the Buddha) and said: "Noble lady, this my attendant wishes to go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya; may the noble lady grant her the going forth and confer upon her the full ordination." The great Prājāpatī Gautamī granted her the going forth and conferred the full ordination. She then said to the merchant: "My lord's son, the world of women is to be lived through existence; visit from time to time." The merchant also went to the Jeta Grove and went forth under a monk. Word spread that the merchant of Śrāvastī had gone forth, and because of his great renown and great merit, his robes, alms food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and requisites were all supplied.

Then at another time, wearing a patched robe of red and yellow, he went to that nun's summer dwelling.
