That nun prostrated with her head at his two feet, sat before him, and looked again and again at his patched robe. The monk said: "Sister, do you desire this patched robe?" She replied: "Like the remnant of a divine dwelling." He thought: "I will give her this patched robe and sew myself another." And so he gave her that robe and went away.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the monks: 'The Tathāgata is setting out to tour through Kosala — whichever of you wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata, let him take his robes.'" The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One, respectfully replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is setting out to tour through Kosala — whichever of you wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata, let him take his robes."

Then the Blessed One, tamed, with a retinue that was tamed; peaceful, with a retinue that was peaceful; liberated, with a retinue that was liberated; at ease, with a retinue that was at ease; subdued, with a retinue that was subdued; an arhat, with a retinue of arhats; free from attachment, with a retinue free from attachment —

beautiful, with a retinue that was beautiful; like a supreme bull surrounded by a herd of cattle; like a great elephant surrounded by a throng of elephant calves; like a lion surrounded by a throng of fanged beasts; like a king of geese surrounded by a flock of geese; like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of birds; like a brahmin surrounded by a throng of students; like a skilled physician surrounded by a throng of patients; like a hero surrounded by a troop of warriors; like a guide surrounded by a throng of travelers on the road; like a caravan leader surrounded by a throng of merchants; like a merchant chief surrounded by a throng of followers; like a king of a fortress surrounded by a throng of ministers; like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a throng of a thousand sons; like the moon surrounded by a host of stars; like the sun surrounded by a host of a thousand rays; like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a throng of gandharvas; like a noble man surrounded by a throng of attendant vessels; like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a throng of nāgas; like Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a throng of yakṣas; like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a throng of asuras; like Śakra (Indra) surrounded by the assembly of the Thirty-Three gods; like Brahmā surrounded by the assembly of the Brahmā realm —

his faculties perfectly subdued; his deportment and conduct undisturbed; still as an ocean; full of moisture like a cloud; free from arrogance like the lord of elephants; beautifully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being; his body rendered magnificent by the eighty minor marks; his form adorned with an aura of a fathom's breadth; possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns; utterly good like a moving mountain of precious gems; endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion; together with the all-knowing Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāman, Vimalakīrti, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Nandaka, and other great śrāvakas —

surrounded by the great community of monks, he set out to tour through Kosala.

Now, it is the nature of things that when buddhas, Blessed Ones, set out on tour, some monks travel along fully robed, with upper and lower robes. Knowing this, the Blessed One turned and surveyed the whole of his body from the right side with the gaze of a great elephant, and he saw that very monk traveling along fully robed, wearing both his upper and lower robe. Having seen this, he spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have the monks who kept the rains retreat obtained their share of robes?"

"Blessed One, they have."

"Ānanda, then why does this monk travel along fully robed, wearing both upper and lower robe?"

The venerable Ānanda explained the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One then said: "Ānanda, do monks give robes to nuns who are not their relatives?"

"Venerable sir, they do."

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, when a nun is not a relative, a monk does not think, 'Are this one's three robes complete, or are they not complete?' He simply takes whatever he can get, and even if he gives to a relative he will not accept anything in return."

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis for the ruling, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, as before. And "The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, though knowing, feign not to know," and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One questioned that monk: "Monk, is it true that you gave a robe to a nun who was not your relative?" "Venerable sir, it is so." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that it was unbecoming of a renunciant, not in accord with proper conduct, not fitting, not in harmony with the rule — it was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits, a rule of training in the Vinaya is to be established for the hearers," and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk gives a robe to a nun who is not his relative incurs a transgression.

Now in this rule, 'whatever monk' refers to one of this Dharma. 'Nun' likewise refers to one of this Dharma. 'Who is not his relative' means: a grandmother, a grandfather, and those related by descent down to the seventh generation are relatives; beyond that they are not relatives. 'A robe' means any one of the seven kinds: woolen cloth, linen, silk, coarse cotton cloth, cotton flannel, hemp cloth, or jute cloth. 'Gives' means even without being asked. 'Incurs a transgression' means it causes one to be burned, scorched, and to fall into the bad destinies — into the hells as sentient beings, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into misfortune, and into ruin. Furthermore, as long as the transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome qualities. That is why it is said to incur a transgression.

As for how a transgression is incurred: if a monk gives a robe to a nun who is not his relative, perceiving her as not his relative, he incurs a transgression. If a monk gives a robe to a nun who is not his relative while feeling uncertain about the matter, he incurs a transgression. If a monk gives a robe to a nun who is his relative, perceiving her as not his relative, he incurs a fault. If a monk gives a robe to a nun who is his relative while feeling uncertain about the matter, he incurs a fault.

There is no transgression in giving to one whose robe has been lost or destroyed, in giving to one who speaks well, in giving a robe as a gift to the community of nuns, in giving to one undertaking full ordination, in giving in exchange for a price, or in giving in exchange for something else. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feelings.

The twenty-fourth defeat-incurring rule concerning giving of robes is complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the forty-ninth fascicle.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. The nun Bhadā had five sets of Dharma robes, all poor and patched and worn out. She found a large bolt of cloth and sat absorbed in thought, wondering to herself who might sew it into Dharma robes for her. The nuns said to her: "Sister, why do you sit absorbed in thought?" "Sisters, my five Dharma robes are poor, patched, and worn out, and now that I have found a large bolt of cloth, I do not know who might fashion it into Dharma robes for me." "Sister, could you not go begging with a golden vessel? Your own monk, the noble Cāraka, is a close friend of yours." Bhadā replied:

"He will not make her Dharma robes." The nuns asked: "Have you ever entrusted him with anything?" "I have never entrusted him with anything." "Well, would he not remove your sandals at the sound of the water bell? Go and ask him — he will do it." Bhadā went to the presence of the venerable Cāraka, bowed her head to his two feet, and sat before him. The venerable Cāraka, seeing her large bolt of cloth, said to her: "A person who possesses such a large bolt of cloth should have a patched robe made from fine linen, and then, with something even a little smaller at heart, should press forward toward virtue." Bhadā replied: "Noble one, it is not that I would not offer you this large bolt of cloth. Rather, my five Dharma robes are poor and the patches are worn out, and so I ask you to sew my patches and give them back to me." Cāraka thought to himself: "Even if I were to sew just one now, from all the twelve groups, all those whose Dharma robes need sewing would bring them to me, and how could I ever sew so many? On the other hand, if I do not sew them, I will not even be given the loan of a needle and thread. Therefore I must sew in such a way that, just as with what is boiled in a wooden vessel, what comes first becomes last." So thinking, he said to her: "Leave it and go." Bhadā left it and departed.

The six monks came there, and seeing the large bolt of cloth said: "Venerable Cāraka, whose is this large bolt of cloth?" "It belongs to me — it is for the one whose Bhadā she is." "In that case, cut it into whatever sizes are fitting." "Do it that way." They measured out and cut the large bolt of cloth, rendering it worn through. Then Cāraka took the patches and five-colored thread and went for a walk. He went there, and on the patches he stitched in embroidery — with five-colored thread — the image of himself embracing Bhadā around the neck, and brought it back to the assembly hall. He folded the patches and placed them on the Dharma robe rack.

When Bhadā also came, Cāraka said: "Bhadā, I have sewn your patches, so now you may come." He held the folded patches out and laid them on Bhadā's shoulders, saying: "For now, do not unfold them until the color has been set. You will incur a downfall." Bhadā, with the folded patches still draped just so on her shoulder, tossed them into the summer residence, and the nun Kṣemā said to her: "Bhadā, do look at how the noble Cāraka has sewn your patches." Bhadā said to her: "The noble Cāraka said: 'For now, do not unfold them until the color has been set — you will incur a downfall.'" And so she did not show them.

Bhadā went into the summer residence, and the nuns said to her: "Bhadā, do look at how the noble Cāraka has sewn your patches." Bhadā said: "The noble Cāraka said: 'For now, do not unfold them until the color has been set — you will incur a downfall.'" Some of her fellow nuns were sitting behind her and, thinking "What downfall could there be in this?", snatched the patches away, opened them, and looked. The nuns saw, stitched in embroidery with five-colored thread, Cāraka embracing Bhadā around the neck, and they burst out laughing, saying: "Bhadā, the noble Cāraka has been holding you for quite a long time!" When the great mother of beings, Gautamī, heard this, she said: "Sisters, if you are bald-headed and have your armpit hair shaved, what is there to laugh about?" They said: "Noble one, look at how in such and such a manner the noble Cāraka has done something unseemly."

At the point where the six groups of nuns, who habitually engaged in every kind of misbehavior, were saying that transgressions committed together with them would destroy the teaching of the Blessed One, the nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this originating circumstance, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, just as before. And the passage "The blessed buddhas, though knowing, make deliberate inquiry" — and so forth — likewise proceeds just as before. The blessed Buddha then addressed the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you made robes for a nun who is not a blood-relation?" He replied: "Blessed One, I confess it." The blessed Buddha censured what is not the manner of a contemplative, what is not fitting, what is not proper, what does not accord with the rule, saying: "This is not something that one who has gone forth should do." Then, having censured this in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, since the ten benefits are clearly seen, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, just as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk makes a robe for a nun who is not a blood-relation commits a transgression.

As for the word 'whatever monk' — this means Cāraka, or any other who is of that sort. As for the word 'nun' — this means one who belongs to this Dharma community. As for 'not a blood-relation' — grandmother and grandfather down to the seventh cousin are blood-relations; beyond that they are not blood-relations. As for the word 'robe' — any one of the seven kinds: woolen cloth, linen cloth, rough cotton, fine cotton, soft wool, hemp cloth, and silk. As for 'makes' — this means sewing. As for 'commits a transgression' — it causes burning, it causes scalding, it causes falling into the hells, into the animal realm, into the hungry ghost realm of evil destinies, and into lower realms of misfortune. Furthermore, as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs wholesome qualities. It is for this reason that it is said to be a transgression.

How does one come to transgress? If a monk, perceiving a nun who is not a blood-relation as not being a blood-relation, makes a robe for her, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, with doubt in his mind, makes a robe for a nun who is not a blood-relation, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, perceiving a nun who is a blood-relation as not being a blood-relation, makes a robe for her, a misdeed is incurred. If a monk, with doubt in his mind about a nun who is a blood-relation, makes a robe for her, a misdeed is incurred. For one who is a first offender, for one who is deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for one afflicted by pain, there is no transgression.

The twenty-fifth transgression concerning making robes is complete.

The blessed Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The six groups said: "These friends Nandika and Upanandika, who go about with black begging bowls whose feet are smeared with monkey fat — when they go out, they acquire gains; when people come to them, they acquire sudden gains, and they also become pleasing and agreeable to many people. We, by contrast, are like tortoises in a dry well: we go nowhere, no one comes to us from anywhere, and so we obtain no gains, and people find us neither pleasing nor

agreeable. So let us go too." "Where shall we go?" "Let us go on a country tour. Let us visit the sisters." So early in the morning they put on their lower robes, took their bowls and outer robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Then they went to the nuns' rains-retreat residence, approached the group of twelve, and said: "Sisters, look after us — we are going on a country tour." At this the nuns wept. The six groups said: "Sisters, why do you weep? If you leave on a country tour, the Jeta Grove will become empty for us." The six groups said: "Sisters, the Blessed One dwells there with a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty — would you really say the Jeta Grove will become empty for us?" The nuns replied: "When we do not even wish to see those monks with their black bowls coming, offering their seats, or teaching the Dharma, how could it be otherwise?" Nandika said: "Sisters, then let us all go together." Upanandika said: "Is it proper for nuns to travel together with monks?" Nandika said: "It is perfectly proper, entirely proper — where has it been forbidden, and by whom? Prepare plenty of provisions for the road." They prepared plenty of provisions for the road.

The six groups, early in the morning, put on their lower robes, took their bowls and outer robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having completed their alms round in Śrāvastī, they went to the nuns' rains-retreat residence, and there the group of twelve said to them: "Reverend ones, please come and eat." As the monks kept borrowing food from them, the nuns ate up all the provisions they had prepared for the journey. Then the monks said: "Sisters, please see how many provisions you had prepared." The nuns said: "Those were the very things you consumed." The six groups said: "How can such a small amount of provisions suffice for a country tour? On the road you will become especially hungry — prepare more provisions." The nuns prepared more provisions, and then set out on the country tour together with the six groups.

Now a mendicant also set out on the country tour with them. The monks said to him: "These mendicants are of bad conduct and engage in bad behaviour — do not travel on the country tour with them. It will bring you into ill repute." The mendicant replied: "I am a man of advanced years. I receive nothing from these people — no transmission of scripture, no reading, no recitation, no thorough questioning, no meditation practice, no mental training of any kind. What use are they to me?" And with those words he dismissed what they said as meaningless, and set out on the country tour together with the six groups.

When they had gone beyond the boundaries of the settlement, the monks said: "Nanda, Nandika — let us, for as long as we can, travel under the guise of others' behavior. Come, let us travel under the guise of our own proper behavior." So first Nanda sat down, then Nandā sat beside him, then the monk who was Nanda's companion sat, then the nun who was Nandā's companion sat, then Nanda's novice sat, then Nandā's novice sat. In the same way Nandika, together with Gupta-nandā and the others, were arranged in paired order, and they proceeded.

Now a brahmin was traveling in that direction. Seeing them, he understood: "This one is a renunciant, this is his wife, this is his son, this is his daughter-in-law, this is his grandson, and this is his grandson's wife." When Nandika heard this, he said: "You poor wretch — a yoke-pin is pressing down on your head! This is not my wife, this is not his son —"

"This is not his daughter-in-law — this is my grandson, and this is my grandson's wife." The monk who was collecting alms thought to himself: "It would be better to die than to go wandering about on the road together with these people of the group of six who practice all manner of misconduct." He then turned back and went to the Jeta Grove.

When the monks saw him, they said: "Venerable, how was your journey? How comfortable was the travel?" He said: "Venerables, the group of six who practice all manner of misconduct cause damage by means of transgressions that bring ruin upon the Blessed One's teaching." What had happened? He then recounted the matter in full to the monks. Those monks of few wishes censured, rebuked, spread word abroad, and complained, saying: "Why do monks engage the road in harmony with nuns, having joined their purposes together?"

Then on that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident and on account of this basis, convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, just as before. "The blessed buddhas, the Bhagavāns, though knowing, ask" — and so forth, just as before.

The Blessed One then questioned the group of six: "Is it true, monks, that you have joined your purposes together with nuns and engaged the road in harmony with them?" "It is true, Blessed One." The Blessed One declared: "That which is contrary to the conduct of a wandering ascetic, discordant with it, improper, and inconsistent with propriety — this is not to be done by those who have gone forth." And he rebuked them.

Then, having rebuked them through numerous synonyms, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, having seen ten benefits in their fullness, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be established" — and so forth, just as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: 'Whatever monk engages the road in harmony with a nun, having joined his purpose together with hers, commits a transgression.'" Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A large number of nuns at Rājagṛha had undertaken the rains retreat in the nuns' rains-retreat dwelling at the king's pleasure grove. When the three months of the rains season had passed, they set out to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One at Śrāvastī, and they began to seek a traveling companion for the journey to Śrāvastī. When they found a traveling companion that included a monk, they said: "Sisters, this traveling companion includes a monk. We should seek another companion without a monk." They began to seek another companion without a monk, but after searching for a long time they could not find a traveling companion without a monk. So they said: "Sisters, even if we were to wait a very long time, we will find no traveling companion without a monk. Let us proceed with this very companion, keeping only to the fore." And they set off with that companion, walking just ahead.

That companion traveled very far ahead. As the nuns were following behind, they were set upon by bandits, and eventually they arrived at Śrāvastī and came to the nuns' rains-retreat dwelling. When the nuns there saw them, they said: "Sisters, how was your journey? How comfortable was the travel?" "Sisters, we were attacked by bandits."

"Sisters, just as the Blessed One has fully sent us forth, even those ninety-six wondrous ones have never fully sent forth any woman into the world." When this was said, the nuns reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, except in a time of necessity."

When monks and nuns traveling together as companions were afflicted with shortage of alms-food, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Provisions for the road are to be sent." When the Blessed One had declared that provisions for the road were to be sent, they did not know by whom to send them, and the Blessed One declared: "A novice monk is to send them. If there is no novice monk, a novice nun is to send them. If there is no novice nun, then the monks are to send provisions for the road to the nuns, and the nuns are to send provisions for the road to the monks. The monks are to instruct the nuns in receiving; and the nuns are to instruct the monks in receiving."

When monks were traveling on a journey and fell ill, and the nuns abandoned them and went on, the Blessed One declared: "Nuns must also carry the monks." When the nuns were holding the monks by the foot-side and the monks were holding the nuns by the head-side, attachment arose among the nuns, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks are to hold from the foot-side, and nuns are to hold from the head-side."

When they had arrived in a village and all remained there, they became afflicted with shortage of alms-food. The Blessed One declared: "Not all are to remain; medicine and food there are to be prepared well, one monk is to be left behind, and the rest are to set out. The same applies equally to the nuns."

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire the training, who have respect for the training, and who embrace the training as their resource, and then addressed the monks with words endowed with qualities consonant with this, abundant in this, and appropriate to this, and declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, what was prescribed before was a rule, and this is a permission. Let my hearers proclaim this as the training-basis in the Vinaya: a monk who, having arranged to travel together with a group of nuns as companions, sets out on a journey — except in a time of necessity — commits a transgression. The time of necessity is this: it is a road that is known to require traveling with companions and is known to be dangerous, or is known to be frightening due to various perils. In such a case, that is the time of necessity.

"As for the phrase 'a monk' — this refers to the Group of Six or any other such person. 'Together with nuns as companions' means those of this same Dharma community. 'Having arranged' means having given a signal. 'On a journey' means on a road through the wilderness. 'Sets out' means goes. 'Except in a time of necessity' means setting aside the time of necessity. 'Commits a transgression' means it scorches, sears, and causes one to fall into the hells as a sentient being, into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower realms, into the state of ruin."

Furthermore, as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs one's wholesome qualities. It is for this reason that it is said to be a transgression.

As for the time of necessity mentioned there: the phrase "to travel with a shared purpose" means that one cannot travel without a shared purpose. The phrase "known to be accompanied by suspicion" means known to be feared because of thieves and deceivers. The phrase "known to be accompanied by danger" means known to be feared because of lions, tigers, and bears. The phrase "known to be accompanied by the kind of danger that is frightening on account of various different dangers" means known to be accompanied by the kind of danger that is frightening on account of various different dangers such as mosquitoes, long-beaked insects, wind, sun, and venomous snakes.

Now, how does the transgression occur? If a monk sets out together with nuns as companions with even the slightest shared purpose and enters upon a journey, an offense is incurred at every half league, and a transgression is committed at every full league. If a monk sets out together with nuns as companions and enters upon a journey from a village to a monastery, an offense is incurred at every half league of the seven intervals measured by a village league, and a transgression is committed at every full league. If a monk sets out together with nuns as companions and enters upon a journey from a monastery to a village, an offense is incurred at every half league of the seven intervals measured by a village league, and a transgression is committed at every full league.

There is no transgression for one who is a first-time offender, for one who is mentally disturbed, for one whose mind is agitated, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

The twenty-sixth transgression, concerning setting out on a journey together with a nun, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Group of Six said: "Friends, Upananda — these ones with their black bowls, their feet smeared with monkey grease — when they go out they manage to acquire gains, and when they come back they acquire unexpected gains as well, and many people become pleased and delighted with them. We, by contrast, are like turtles in a dry well: we go nowhere and come from nowhere, so how could we ever acquire gains and have many people be pleased and delighted with us? We too shall go out. Where shall we go? We shall go wandering through the provinces. Look, sisters!" And so, early in the morning, having put on their lower robes and taken up their bowls and outer robes, they entered Śrāvastī on alms round, then went to the nuns' rains-retreat quarters and, going among the assembly of the twelve groups, said: "Sisters, look at us — we are going wandering through the provinces." The nuns wept. The Group of Six said: "Sisters, why are you crying? If you go wandering through the provinces, the Jeta Grove will become empty for us." The Group of Six said: "Sisters, the Blessed One resides there with a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty. Are you really saying the Jeta Grove will become empty for us?" The nuns said: "You ones with the black bowls — we do not even enjoy seeing you. Why would we look forward to your coming, offering seats, and teaching the Dharma?" Upananda said: "Sisters, then let us go together." They replied: "Has not the Blessed One laid down the training rule that it is a transgression for a monk to set out on a journey together with nuns as companions, except in a time of necessity?" Upananda said: "That rule was laid down for travel by land; we shall go by boat." Bhaddā Moggallanā said:

Bhaddā Moggallanā said: "Is it proper for nuns to travel by boat together with monks?" Upananda replied: "Perfectly proper. Entirely proper. Where has it been prohibited? Who prohibited it? Prepare plenty of provisions for the journey." They prepared plenty of provisions for the journey.

The group of six monks, early in the morning, put on their lower robes, took up their bowls and outer robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having made their alms round in Śrāvastī, they went to the nuns' rains-retreat quarters. The group of twelve nuns said to them: "Please, masters, lend us a little food." When those nuns lent them food, the monks ate all the provisions the nuns had prepared for the journey. Then the monks said: "Sisters, check and see how many provisions you have prepared for the journey." The nuns replied: "They are the ones you asked for." The group of six said: "How can that much food suffice for travel through the provinces? You will go quite hungry along the road — prepare many more provisions for the journey." The nuns prepared many more provisions and set out to travel through the provinces together with the group of six.

Now a certain mendicant who was also going that way along with them, having observed them, came to understand: "This is the monk, this is his wife, this is his son, this is his daughter-in-law, this is his grandson, and this is his grandson's wife." Upananda overheard this and said: "You pauper — I'll press your skull down with my knee and say: this is my wife, this is my son, this is my daughter-in-law, this is my grandson, and this is my grandson's wife."

A certain wandering mendicant also set out to travel through the provinces together with them. The monks said to him: "These wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) here are of corrupt conduct — do not travel through the provinces with them. It would be too much for you." The mendicant said: "I am old, and I cannot get from them even a little recitation of scripture, reading, oral instruction, thorough questioning, meditation practice, or mental cultivation — what possible use am I to them?" And with those words he dismissed their talk and embarked on a boat together with the group of six.

When they had gone beyond the boundary markers, the monks said: "Dear Upananda, for as long as we are on the way, let us follow the conduct of others. Come, when we return let us follow our own conduct." They arranged it as follows: first Nanda sat, then Nandā, then Nanda's companion, then Nandā's companion, then Nanda's novice, then Nandā's novice nun. In the same way, Upananda together with Sthūlanandā and the others were arranged in alternating pairs and set off.

The other wandering mendicant who was travelling with them saw this and said: "I recognize now: this is the monk, this is his wife, this is his son, this is his daughter-in-law, this is his grandson, and this is his grandson's wife." Upananda heard this and said: "You pauper — I'll press your skull down with my knee and say: this is my wife, this is my son, this is my daughter-in-law, this is my grandson, and this is my grandson's wife."

The mendicant thought to himself: "Better I should die than travel by boat with these ones who practise utter depravity." He therefore turned back and went to the Jeta Grove.

When the monks saw him, they said: "Venerable ones, did the mendicant travel comfortably? Venerable ones, how did he travel comfortably? The fully depraved group of six, through the transgression of defilement, ruin the teaching of the Blessed One." What was done? At that point he explained it fully to the monks. Those few monks of modest desires thereupon censured, upbraided, and rebuked them, asking: "Why do the monks travel together as companions of the nuns who share their destination and board a single boat?" That occasion moved the monks to present the matter before the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and

this occasion, convened an assembly of monks, and so forth, as before. "The Blessed Buddhas, though knowing, act as though they do not know" — and so forth, as before. The Blessed Buddha questioned the group of six: "Monks, is it true that you traveled together as companions of nuns who shared your destination and boarded a single boat?" "It is true, Blessed One." The Blessed Buddha censured them: "That is not the conduct of a renunciant, it is not fitting, it is not proper, it is not in accordance with the discipline. This is not something one who has gone forth should do." And so he censured them. Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing these ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya should be established" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk travels as a companion of nuns who share his destination and boards a single boat, going upstream or downstream, commits a transgression." Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, a certain householder had a temple built across the river for the sake of the Saṅgha, in the garden on the far bank by the riverside, and having done so he invited both communities of the Saṅgha to come and consecrate it. A certain nun who was earnestly devoted to what is wholesome thought to herself: "Today I need not go out for alms. Until midday approaches, I shall apply myself to what is wholesome, and after that, knowing the right time, I will go." Having applied herself to what is wholesome until midday was near, she then, knowing the right time, went to the bank of the river. By then the monks had already boarded the boat, and the boatman said to her: "Noble one, board the boat." She replied: "Good sir, please go ahead; I will go on another boat when it is loaded." The boatman came back again and again, saying: "Noble one, board the boat." And she replied again: "Good sir, please go ahead; I will go on another boat when it is loaded." The boatman departed and, having poled the boat across the river, entered into the midst of a large crowd and sat there. The nun called out to him again and again, but the boatman gave her no reply, and she remained there waiting. When midday had passed, she returned to the summer dwelling and, for as long as vigor had not left her body, she applied herself to what is wholesome. When her bodily vigor was spent, she lay down to rest. The nuns then arrived and said to her: "Noble one, is it perhaps that you think the food belongs to another, or that the meal belongs to another?" She asked: "What happened?" "You lay down to rest — and for as long as you lay resting, the food was eaten." "Who ate it?" "You did." "She did not eat it." "Then why did you lie down to rest?" She then recounted the circumstances in detail to the nuns, and the nuns reported the matter to the monks. The monks presented it before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said: "Monks, therefore, crossing straight across is excepted." Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, who are content with the requisites of training, and addressed the monks with words appropriate to this and consistent with it, saying:

Then, having spoken words of praise appropriate to this and consistent with it, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, therefore, the earlier rule stands as a rule, and this is permitted. My hearers are to promulgate this as the basis of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, having made arrangements together with a nun who shares his aim, and having boarded the same boat, travels upstream or downstream — excepting crossing straight across — commits a transgression.

Now, 'whatever monk' means one of the group of six, or any other of that kind. 'A nun who shares his aim' means one who is of this teaching. 'Having made arrangements' means having agreed by signal. 'The same boat' means a flat-bottomed vessel, a canoe, or a vessel with a prow. 'Having boarded' means having embarked. 'Travels upstream' means going in the direction opposite the current. 'Travels downstream' means going in the direction of the current. 'Excepting crossing straight across' means that crossing straight across is set aside. 'Commits a transgression' means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, evil rebirths, and states of perdition. Furthermore, for as long as the transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome factors of the Dharma. That is why it is said to commit a transgression.

How does the transgression accrue? For every half league that a monk, having made arrangements together with a nun who shares his aim, boards the same boat and travels upstream or downstream, he incurs a misdeed; and for every full league, a transgression.

If a monk, having made arrangements together with a nun who shares his aim, boards the same boat and travels from a village to a wilderness, then for each half league of the seven intervals measured by the distance of a village, he incurs a misdeed; and for every full league, a transgression.

If a monk, having made arrangements together with a nun who shares his aim, boards the same boat and travels from a wilderness to a village, then for each half league of the seven intervals not divided by the distance of a village, he incurs a misdeed; and for every full league, a transgression.

There is no transgression in the case of one who veers off from turbulent water, veers off from a place where the light is cut off, veers off from whirlpools, where the rudder has broken, where the mast has broken, or where the helmsman will not obey instructions. There is no transgression if either bank is nearby with any one of the eight impediments at hand. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by pain.

The twenty-seventh transgression making rule concerning boarding a boat together with a nun is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. Then the venerable Udāyin, having dressed in the morning, took up his bowl and robe and entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he wandered through Śrāvastī on alms-round in due order, he came to the house of the householder's wife Bhadā. The householder's wife Bhadā saw the venerable Udāyin from a great distance, and seeing him she prepared a seat for the venerable Udāyin and spoke these words: "Venerable Udāyin, come here! Welcome, venerable Udāyin! Venerable Udāyin, please be seated on the seat that has been prepared." The venerable Udāyin looked inside and sat down.

The householder's wife Bhadā likewise prostrated herself at the feet of the venerable Udāyin, then sat down facing away from him. Udāyin taught her the Dharma to such and such an extent, and then he began to recall their former conversations, their flirtations, their pleasures, and the enjoyments they had shared together: "Bhadā, do you remember how the two of us spent time in such and such a pleasure grove, such and such a meeting place, such and such a divine dwelling — how we wore such and such fine clothes, how we ate such and such foods, how we drank such and such drinks, how such and such a bed was spread out, how such and such an oil lamp was lit, and how the two of us did such and such things there?" Bhadā replied, "I remember."

Now, an almsman who had come on his morning alms-round, his robe arranged and bowl and outer robe in hand, had entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he was going through Śrāvastī on his alms-round in due order, he came to the very house of the householder's wife Bhadā. The householder's wife Bhadā saw him, and she thought: "If I were to rise and offer alms, I would lose the venerable Udāyin's discourse." So she waved him away with her hand. When Udāyin saw Bhadā gesturing with her hand, he said to her: "Bhadā, while I am sitting right here before you, are you making hand signals to another man?" Bhadā replied: "Noble one, I was not signaling to another man. An almsman has arrived and I thought: if I were to rise and offer alms, I would lose the noble one's words — so I gestured to him to go on." Udāyin said: "Bhadā, do you really think I have been speaking to you in your heart about the Four Noble Truths? It is like this: if I were to obtain a hundred pleasures through the work of my own hands, could you not then give gifts and make merit?" Bhadā called the almsman back, and filling his bowl with clean and pure provisions and food, she gave it to him, and he took it and departed.

The venerable Udāyin, having finished the business of his meal, went to the assembly hall. The almsman thought: "I will speak to the venerable Udāyin and, upon hearing him, generate the highest joy." So he said to him: "Venerable Udāyin, rejoice! Today I have eaten your alms-food." The almsman said: "You know — did she call you first, or did she signal you to go away with her hand, and then I caused her to call you back afterwards?" "What did she give?" "She filled the bowl with clean and pure provisions and food and gave it. Venerable Udāyin, that is yours." Then the venerable Udāyin remained as he had been sitting. "While you were alone with a woman, in a secluded private place, sitting on a seat — perhaps it was proper, perhaps it was not, perhaps it was improper yet still possible — I was sitting there like that. Almsman, today you ate my alms-food; if you cannot bear it, let a rule of training appear to have been laid down through me — do you think I simply cast it aside?" At that point he told the monks what had occurred, and the monks of few desires rebuked him: "Why do monks sit alone in a secluded private place with a woman?" They criticized him, spread word of it, and spoke against it. Then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this basis of rule, and on this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before.

"The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, knowing, do such and such" — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One said to the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you sat alone together with a woman in a secluded private place that was sheltered?" "Indeed so, O Blessed One." The Blessed One censured him, saying that this was unworthy of a renunciant, was not in accord with propriety, was not fitting, was not in keeping with proper conduct, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having censured him in many ways, spoke to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing fully ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before — "and my hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk sits alone together with a woman in a secluded private place that is sheltered, it is a transgression."

Now, "whatever monk" means Cāraka or anyone else of that kind. "With a woman" means a woman, or a girl, one who can bear the characteristic factor that arises from improper conduct. "Together" means in her company. "Alone" means just the two of them. "Secluded" means a place where no other woman, man, or eunuch is present. "Sheltered" means sheltered by one of five things: sheltered by a wall, sheltered by a screen, sheltered by a curtain, sheltered by dense foliage, or sheltered by darkness. "Sitting" means on a seat, that is, upon a surface. "Sits" means places his buttocks within the span of one fathom.

"It is a transgression" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into bad destinations — hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, lower realms, and states of ruin. Moreover, as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities; therefore it is called a transgression.

As to how the transgression comes about: however slightly a monk sits alone together with a woman in a secluded private place that is sheltered, in every case it becomes a transgression. Sitting in a doorway, entering under a curtain, sitting without the door being shut, or when some are entering and others are leaving — in those cases there is no transgression. There is no transgression for a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations. The twenty-eighth transgression concerning sitting alone is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At a time when a female attendant had gone forth and was acting as the duty officer, the nuns in the morning, having dressed and taken their bowls and robes, went out for alms. The female attendant sat in the temple sweeping and cleaning. The venerable Cāraka also in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robes, entered Śrāvastī for alms, and while wandering for alms in Śrāvastī he went to the place where the nuns' summer residence was. The female attendant, who was sweeping in the nuns' summer residence, saw the venerable Cāraka from a considerable distance, and upon seeing him she spoke thus:

"Welcome, noble Cāraka, welcome!" she said, and setting her broom to one side, she prostrated at the feet of the venerable Cāraka and stood before him. Cāraka then taught her the Dharma to some fitting degree, and they began to recall former conversations, jests, pleasures, and enjoyments they had shared. "Do you remember, attendant, how you arranged our lodgings in such-and-such a park, assembly hall, and divine dwelling, wearing such-and-such garments, eating such-and-such food, drinking such-and-such drink, arranging such-and-such bedding, lighting such-and-such lamps of grain-oil, and how the two of us did such-and-such things there?" The attendant replied, "I remember."

Now there was an elderly sick nun who was sitting there, and she thought to herself: why are these two, even though they have not yet been taken as bride and groom, speaking to each other in this way?

The attendant then said, "Noble one, please go now. The nuns are about to arrive, and since the summer residence has not yet been swept, the nuns will reproach me." She took up her broom and Cāraka departed. The attendant then began to sweep the temple. When the nuns returned and saw this, they said to her: "Attendant, how is it that you have swept this summer residence so thoroughly?" The attendant replied, "Sisters, from the moment you went for alms until now, she has not been sitting on the ground." The elderly sick nun heard this and said to the nuns: "It is true that the attendant was not sitting on the ground from the moment you went for alms until now — for the noble Cāraka had come, and she was standing with him, and even though they have not yet been taken as bride and groom, they were speaking to one another."

The nuns then asked the attendant, "Attendant, is it true that you did this?" "Sisters, it is true." The nuns then rebuked her, saying, "Why does a monk stand alone with a nun in a secluded place apart from others?" — censuring her, denouncing her, and spreading the word. Those nuns then reported the matter to the monks, and those monks of few wants, asking why a monk would stand alone with a nun in a secluded place apart from others — censuring, denouncing, and spreading the word — reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, on account of this incident and this occasion and in this context, convened the community of monks, and so forth, just as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, ask" — and so forth, also as before. The awakened Blessed One then asked the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you were standing alone with a nun in a secluded place apart from others?" "Blessed One, it is so." The awakened Blessed One then rebuked him, saying that what is not in accord with the conduct of a renunciant, not fitting, not proper, not in keeping with the training — that is not something one who has gone forth should do. The Blessed One then rebuked him in many ways, and having done so, declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, just as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk stands alone with a nun in a secluded place apart from others commits a transgression."

"Whatever monk" refers to Śārcā or any other of that kind. "With a nun" refers to one who belongs to this very Dharma. "Together" means together with that one. "Alone with one" means with that specific one. "Secluded" means a place where there is no other man, woman, or person of indeterminate sex. "In a sheltered place" means sheltered by one of five things: sheltered by a wall, sheltered by a screen, sheltered by a curtain, sheltered by something dense, or sheltered by darkness. "Stands" means stands within the distance of one outstretched arm. "Commits a transgression" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinations of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and those who have fallen wrongly into lower states of existence. Furthermore, for as long as the transgression remains unconfessed and has not been individually confessed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and therefore it is said to "commit a transgression."

As to how a transgression comes about in this: whenever a monk stands, however briefly, alone in a sheltered secluded place together with a nun, in every such case a transgression is committed. However, if one stands in a doorway, enters to take medicine, stands without closing the door, or while some persons are entering and others are leaving, there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is insane, who is mentally disturbed, or who is afflicted by physical sensations.

The twenty-ninth transgression involving standing alone is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa was in Śrāvastī, dwelling in Mṛgāramātṛ's mansion in the eastern garden. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his sitting, putting away his grinding stone, and went to where the Blessed One was. Having gone there, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa as follows: "Kāśyapa, you are now old, aged, and advanced in years. These hempen lower robes and rags from the rubbish heap that you wear are heavy. Kāśyapa, come to the Saṅgha's assembly hall, and those who are invited as guests by individual persons — take those invitations for yourself. As for the cloth dyed with woad by householders, let that become of inferior color and worn out." The venerable Mahākāśyapa said nothing and accepted the word of the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, rejoicing in and delighting at the words the Blessed One had spoken, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed.

Now at that time, there was a certain householder in Śrāvastī in whom this aspiration had long arisen: "Ah, if only I could invite the elder, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, honored by gods and humans, to another home and offer him a meal — how fitting that would be!" That householder then heard that the Blessed One had entrusted the noble Mahākāśyapa to the Saṅgha. Having heard this, he went to where the venerable Mahākāśyapa was, and having arrived, prostrated with his head at the feet of the venerable Mahākāśyapa and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahākāśyapa instructed that householder thoroughly with a Dharmic discourse, established him firmly in it, encouraged him rightly, and gladdened him fully. Having in many ways instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened him thoroughly with a Dharmic discourse, he fell silent. Then that householder thought to himself:

"If I were to invite the noble Mahākāśyapa alone to another household, there might well be a situation where he would not consent. Therefore, I shall invite him together with three others and myself, making four."

Then that householder rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the venerable Mahākāśyapa, joined his palms in reverence, made a bow, and spoke these words to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "May the noble Mahākāśyapa graciously consent to come to my dwelling tomorrow at noon, together with three others and himself, making four." The venerable Mahākāśyapa, without saying a word, consented to that householder's request by his silence. Then that householder, understanding that the venerable Mahākāśyapa had consented through his silence, prostrated with his head at the feet of the venerable Mahākāśyapa, went to his own dwelling, and said to his wife: "My good woman, there has arisen in me for a long time a wish of this kind: 'How wonderful it would be if I were to invite the elder Mahākāśyapa — honored by gods and humans — to another house and offer him a meal!' And so tomorrow I have invited him, together with three others, to another house at noon, and he has consented through his silence. Therefore prepare a great abundance of food and drink."

That householder's wife, having heard this from the householder, prepared whatever foods were to be served cold on that very day, and whatever foods were to be served warm she prepared the following morning. The householder then rose early in the morning and thought: "If seats are arranged on the lower level of the floor, when the mendicants come and go they will be disturbed by the stirring of dust. If seats are arranged on the upper level, they will be troubled there by flies swarming about them. Therefore, let seats be arranged on the middle level." Having thought this, he arranged seats on the middle level and sent word to the venerable Mahākāśyapa, urging him: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, if you would be so kind as to come as invited at noon, please know that the time has now arrived."

The Blessed One had declared that one should go at the time agreed upon by the one who extended the invitation. So the venerable Mahākāśyapa, early in the morning, put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, went to that householder's dwelling, ascended to the middle level, and sat down upon the seat that had been prepared there. Then that householder prostrated with his head at the feet of the venerable Mahākāśyapa and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahākāśyapa instructed that householder thoroughly with a Dharmic discourse, established him firmly in it, encouraged him rightly, and gladdened him fully.

Then the nun Sthūlanandā, in the early morning, put on her lower robe, took up her alms bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms, and as she went about collecting alms in due order she entered that very house and spoke these words: "O auspicious and healthy one, please give alms."

That householder said: "Noble lady, today the noble Mahākāśyapa — honored by gods and humans — has been invited to my dwelling, and a meal has been prepared for him. Please come back a little later."

Sthūlanandā replied: "He is one who went forth from among other non-Buddhists — the most given away, the most inferior of those given away. As for me, I went forth from among the Śākya women, I possess the three scriptural collections, I preach the Dharma, and I am endowed with the eloquence of reasoning and liberation. You are feeding that one and not giving alms to me?"

When the venerable Mahākāśyapa heard this, he thought: "If much demerit were to arise in him on account of this, that would not be right." And so he cleared his throat.

Since the venerable Mahākāśyapa possessed a voice resonant as a great bell, its sound filled the entire house. When Sthūlanandā heard that voice, she said: "The one called 'Nāga' is right here."

Upon hearing this, the householder said: "So now it turns out that this is the very one who went forth from among other non-Buddhists — the most given away, the most inferior of those given away — and now he is being called 'the one named Nāga.'" Scolding her in this way, he began to descend from the middle floor. Sthūlanandā, hearing the sound of his footsteps coming down — thud, thud — thought: "If this householder descends with such force, he will surely do me harm." Terrified, her arms hanging limp, she began to flee. The householder called out: "Shaven-headed śramaṇī! Nun! Elder among nuns! Do not run — stay where you are! Why are you fleeing? You shall not enter my house again." Sthūlanandā replied: "May your house become a mud-hole and a prison! May outcastes enter your house! We nuns have received from the king the right to complete immunity through the queen's retinue. To whatever extent anyone lays a hand on us, to that same extent she will have both his hands cut off at the wrists." The householder replied: "Shaven-headed śramaṇī! Nuns, elder nuns — it is the nuns who have received from the king the right to immunity through the queen's retinue. You, who practice every kind of bad conduct, have not received it."

Then the householder turned back and, with clean and excellent food and drink, satisfied and sustained the venerable Mahākāśyapa with his own hands. In many ways he satisfied and sustained him with clean and excellent food and drink, and having served him thus, when he understood that the venerable Mahākāśyapa had finished eating and had washed his hands and set down the bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the venerable Mahākāśyapa in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa duly instructed that householder with talk endowed with Dharma, duly guided him, duly encouraged him, and duly gladdened him. Having in many ways duly instructed, guided, encouraged, and gladdened him with talk endowed with Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.

He went to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable Blessed One, today, because I had been assigned by you to the Saṅgha, today I was called 'one who went forth from among other non-Buddhists, the most given away, the most inferior of those given away,' and today I was also called 'the one named Nāga.' Venerable One, for a long time I have been a forest-dweller, and I have also spoken in praise of forest-dwelling; I have been an alms-round practitioner, and I have also spoken in praise of the alms-round; I have been one who wears rag-robes, and I have also spoken in praise of wearing rag-robes. Kāśyapa, if you truly see the purpose in it, then while being a forest-dweller, praise forest-dwelling; while being an alms-round practitioner, praise the alms-round; while being one who wears rag-robes, praise wearing rag-robes. Venerable One, there are two reasons: for my own well-being in this life, and —"

— and so that it may serve as a light for people of future generations. Those elder monks who went forth long ago, who practised the holy life purely, who were praised by the Teacher, who were skilled in the conduct befitting the holy life and were revered by the wise — those who are now passed away — they long ago became forest-dwellers and also spoke praise of forest-dwelling; they became alms-round practitioners and also spoke praise of the alms-round; they became wearers of rag-robes and also spoke praise of wearing rag-robes. Hearing of them and of what they did in that way, people will strive to practise accordingly, and it will bring them long-term benefit, healing, and happiness. Kāśyapa, it is excellent, excellent, that you have long been engaged in benefiting the many, in bringing happiness to the many, in showing compassion to the world, and in working for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans. Kāśyapa, whoever speaks dispraise of those qualities of training that someone has cultivated is speaking dispraise of me; and whoever speaks praise of those qualities of training that someone has cultivated is speaking praise of me. And why is that? Because I have long honoured, esteemed, praised, and highly extolled those very qualities of training. Therefore, Kāśyapa, since you are a forest-dweller, speak praise of forest-dwelling; since you are an alms-round practitioner, speak praise of the alms-round; since you are a wearer of rag-robes, speak praise of wearing rag-robes. Kāśyapa, you should train in this way."

This much occurred at that time; the Blessed One, the buddha, had not yet at this time established a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the fiftieth fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A time of scarcity arose, and faithful brahmins and householders arranged alms for the elder monks, monk by monk. The group of six monks, in the early morning, having arranged their robes and taken up their bowls and monastic robes, entered Śrāvastī for alms and went to the households of the twelve groups. Those households said, "Noble ones, please be seated and receive your meal. Who will give?" They replied, "We will provide it. Who will give tomorrow?" Again they said, "We will provide it." The group of six monks then said, "Sisters, that alone is not enough for us to live on. It is like this: the faithful brahmins and householders who arranged alms for the elder monks — if you were to arrange for those provisions to be diverted to us, then we could live." The nun Sthulanandā said, "Noble ones, is it proper to do so?" The group of six monks replied, "Are we to starve and die? It is perfectly proper. It is entirely fitting." Then where was it prohibited? And by whom was it prohibited?

Thereupon the nun Sthulanandā, in the early morning, having arranged her robes and taken up her bowl and monastic robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms and went to the house where the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya's alms had been arranged, and said these words: "For whom have you arranged alms?" They replied, "Noble lady, for the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya." Sthulanandā said, "You would gain far greater merit if you arranged alms for one who went forth from the Śākya clan, who is possessed of the three scriptural collections, who teaches the Dharma, and who has the gift of eloquence in reasoning and in liberation." They replied, "Noble lady, one who went forth from the Śākya clan, who is possessed of the three scriptural collections,

who teaches the Dharma, and who has the gift of eloquence in reasoning and in liberation — who might that be?" Sthulanandā replied, "The noble Ānanda went forth from the Śākya clan, is possessed of the three scriptural collections, teaches the Dharma, and has the gift of eloquence in reasoning and in liberation." They said, "Very well," and the alms that had been arranged for the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya were redirected and arranged for Ānanda. Similarly, all the alms that had been arranged for the elder monks were redirected and arranged for the group of six monks.

In the early morning the group of six monks donned their robes, took up their bowls and outer robes, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. When they returned carrying alms in bowls that had been claimed by others, the monks who saw this said, "Oh! The group of six monks has taken bowls that belong to others." The group of six monks said, "May the laywoman who arranged alms on our behalf be free from illness." The monks said, "Is it right for you knowingly to eat food that was arranged by a nun?" The group of six monks replied, "It might be right, or it might not be right — but are we to starve to death? Why do you monks of little account reproach us, saying that monks are eating food arranged by a nun?" And so they heaped criticism on them, reviled them, and spoke harshly. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this origin, and on this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and the rest follows as before. The passage beginning "The blessed buddhas knowingly inquire" also follows as before. The blessed Buddha asked the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you knowingly ate food arranged by a nun?" They replied, "Venerable One, it is true." The blessed Buddha reproved them, saying that this was not the conduct of one who has gone forth, not in accordance with proper deportment, not fitting, not in keeping with the rule, and not something that one who has gone forth ought to do. He then reproved them in many ways, and declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and the rest follows as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk knowingly eats food arranged by a nun commits a transgression."

Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a householder who engaged in two kinds of livelihood at the borders of his estate: trading and farming. He ploughed a field in a remote area, sowed seeds, and having made a shelter near that field and taken his provisions, he departed to another district.

A wandering almsman was travelling through the countryside. He arrived in Śrāvastī and, while wandering about there, caught sight of the shelter beside the field. He thought, "This direction is secluded and peaceful — I should stay right here." He began to stay in that very place, and having collected alms in Śrāvastī, he took up residence there.

There no human noise disturbed it, and no wild animals or birds came near. The gods, moreover, had sent rain in good season at the proper times, and so that field had become exceedingly abundant. The householder, for his part, had brought his affairs to a successful conclusion and returned home in joy and good fortune.

Then the householder stored away his goods, bathed, and ate his meal. His wife said to him, "My lord's son, you sowed seed in that remote field and then departed for another district — I wonder whether even a bare return on the seed was managed. You should go and see." The householder went there, and when he saw how extraordinarily abundant the field's harvest had become, he thought to himself, "I built no shelter here, I left not a single watchman, and yet this field has become so supremely abundant — what can be the cause?" He looked about and, catching sight of human footprints, followed them and made his way straight to the shelter. There he found a monk who lived on alms, sitting cross-legged. He thought, "It is through this one's power that the field has become so supremely abundant." He said aloud, "Noble one, are you dwelling in this shelter?" The monk replied, "Yes, householder." The householder said, "Noble one, this field is mine. Please make free use of whatever flowers, fruits, and thorn-wood you wish. And would the noble one be so good as to come to my home tomorrow to receive alms?" The monk replied, "Householder, I am one who wanders for alms alone, and I shall go only where alms are offered" — and with that he declined the invitation. The householder then bowed his head to the monk's two feet, took his leave, went to where his home was, and when he arrived he said this to his wife: "Good woman, make ready the food-vessels. The harvest of that field has become exceedingly abundant." His wife thought, "He is making excuses to me," and she said, "My lord's son, you built no shelter there and left not a single watchman — what excuse is there to be made to me?" The householder replied, "Good woman, do you think I am making excuses to you? Believe it as a fact: the harvest of that field has become exceedingly abundant." His wife asked, "For what reason?" The householder replied, "When I arrived near that field I found a monk who lives on alms sitting in the shelter, and through that one's power the field has become so supremely abundant." His wife said, "In that case, why did you not invite him to come for alms tomorrow?" The householder replied, "I did invite him, but the monk said with his own lips, 'Householder, I am one who wanders for alms alone, and I shall go only where alms are offered,' and so he declined." His wife said, "One must bow to his feet and invite him in that way." The householder replied, "Very well, then you prepare the food while I go there, bow to his feet, and invite him." He went, bowed his head to the monk's two feet, and said, "Noble one, would you be so good as to come to my home tomorrow to receive alms?" The monk replied, "Householder, I go only where alms are wandered for." The householder said, "Noble one, it would not be right for you to decline to come to my home for alms." The monk, recognizing that the householder knew how to receive him properly, said nothing further and accepted. The householder, understanding from the monk's silence that he had accepted, bowed to his feet, took his leave, went to where his home was, arrived, and spoke to his wife:

"Dear one, I have invited that alms-wandering monk to come tomorrow at midday. He accepted without a word of refusal, so please prepare clean and wholesome food in readiness." The householder's wife then prepared whatever foods were cold right away that same day, and whatever foods needed to be warmed she prepared the following morning.

When the monks who wander for alms had set out on their rounds, another alms-wanderer approached that monk and said, "Fellow alms-wanderer, come this way — I am going for alms." The monk replied, "A householder has invited me as a guest, so I know the time I must go. You go ahead." The other said, "May you be well-provided-for, alms-wanderer, and may your alms-round bring great merit. But do be mindful of the proper measure of food. As for me, I too shall be timely about it."

The nun Sthulanandā, having dressed herself in her undergarment that morning, taken her bowl and robe, and entered Śrāvastī to wander for alms, had gone gradually through her round and entered that very house, where she said, "Auspicious lady, please give alms, good and wholesome." The householder's wife said, "Noble one, I have invited an alms-wanderer and it would be wrong if he were kept waiting and his meal cut off. I am busy — please depart for now." Sthulanandā said, "If she brings that alms-wanderer along with her when she comes, will you give alms to her?" The woman replied, "Yes, I will." "And who will give to this wandering mendicant who follows behind?" "I will." "And who will give to those who guard the shrine?" "I will."

Sthulanandā then thought to herself: "The alms-wanderers have been making their rounds and will be coming back out soon, so the one now just entering must be that monk." With this thought she went and stood at the city gate. The monk himself had thought: "Today I need not wander for alms myself, so let me devote myself to the wholesome and keep to the proper time before going." Having thus minded the time, he dressed in his undergarment, took his bowl and robe, and set out to wander for alms in Śrāvastī. Sthulanandā saw him and thought, "This is that alms-wanderer." She approached and asked him, "Noble one, did Sumagadhā not invite you? Sister, she sent an invitation to you." "Noble one, I spoke your praises at that house." He replied, "Sister, did I ask you to speak my praises to anyone?" "Noble one, you gave no such instruction."

The monk thought to himself: "This food has been arranged by a nun interfering in the matter. It would be better that I cut off the meal than that I incur a transgression." So he turned back. Sthulanandā said, "Noble one, I did not enquire about your lineage, I did not enquire about your name, and yet I spoke your praises — would that not have been sufficient?" The alms-wanderer replied, "Sister, if your first statement was true, then the latter is false; and if the latter is true, then the first is false." With these words he turned back, went to the very same spot, and for as long as the glow had not left his body he devoted himself to the wholesome; and when the glow had left his body he spread out his outer robe and lay down.

Other alms-wanderers then came to him and said, "If the food belongs to someone else — do you think the stomach that holds it is also someone else's? What have you done? You could only pursue the wholesome up to a certain point, and then you ate food equal to that measure." He said, "Who ate it?" "You ate it." "I did not eat it." "Then why did you spread out your robe and lie down?"

He then gave a full account of the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is an offense except when previously invited to a home."

The Blessed One then spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who are content with the provisions of training. He addressed the monks with words consonant with that theme, words in which that theme was paramount, words adorned with qualities fitting that theme, and then he declared to the monks:

"Monks, the former rule was provisional; this one is now permitted. My hearers shall recite this training rule of the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk knowingly eats food that has been prepared through the involvement of a nun — except when previously invited to a home — commits a transgression."

Now, "whatever monk" means one of the group of six, or any other person of that kind. "Knowingly" means either being aware of it himself or having been told by another. "A nun" means one belonging to this Dharma. "Prepared through involvement" refers to two kinds of involvement: involvement through moral discipline and involvement through learning. "Food" means the five kinds of hard food and the five kinds of soft food. "Eats" means when it passes down the throat. "Except when previously invited to a home" means setting aside prior invitations to a home as guests.

"Commits a transgression" means it burns, scalds, and causes one to fall into the wretched states — into the hells of sentient beings, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into misfortune, and into wrong states of falling. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. Therefore it is said to be a transgression.

As for how a transgression comes about in this case, it is as follows. A number of monks had been invited as guests to another household. A nun arrived there and questioned the host: "Which monks did you invite?" "The venerable so-and-so and so-and-so and others." "What kind of food will you give?" "Threefold-enhanced rice." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them clean white flour." "What kind of ghee will you give?" "Goat ghee." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them cow's butter." "What kind of salt will you give?" "Transforming salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them rock salt, sea salt, or ocean salt." "What will you pour as a drink?" "Thick brew." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should pour them clear strained liquid." "What condiment will you give with the rice?" "Lentil broth seasoned with salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should pour them cooked broth, boiled broth, or yogurt soup." "What soup will you give?" "Bean-sprout broth from wild peas." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them bean soup, wild-legume broth, or pea broth."

"What condiment will you give with the side dish?" "Lentil broth seasoned with salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them roasted meat, grilled meat, and various kinds of meat." "What drink will you pour?" "Sugar-water." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should pour them fermented grain drink, liquorice water, or warm mild drink." "What rice porridge will you give?" "Coarse rice porridge or bran porridge." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should give them sālu-rice porridge." "What pulse broth will you pour?" "Wild-pea broth." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should pour them black-gram pulse broth." "What poultry will you give?" "Just roasted condiment." "That is not suitable. Those monks are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats; you should pour them various kinds of meat, grain-spirit condiment, yogurt, and warm milk." Having thus arranged all this, if a monk knowingly eats it, it becomes a transgression. If it is true that they are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats, there is no transgression.

Now, when a great many monks had been invited as guests to another household, a monk who had not come asked: "Which monks did you invite?" "Such-and-such elders and others." "What food did you give?" "Triple-measure rice." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them refined flour." "What clarified butter did you give?" "Goat clarified butter." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them cow butter." "What salt did you give?" "Fermented salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them rock salt, sea salt, or ocean salt." "What drink did you pour?" "Coarse drink."
