"That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should pour them strained clear drink." "What condiment did you give with the rice?" "Lentil broth seasoned with salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should pour them cooked broth, boiled broth, or yogurt soup." "What soup did you give?" "Wild-pea broth." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them grain-spirit soup, side-dish soup, or dried-pulse soup." "What condiment did you give with the side dish?" "Lentil broth seasoned with salt." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them roasted meat, grilled meat, and various kinds of meat." "What drink will you pour?" "Sugar-water." "That is not suitable.

"Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should pour for them flower-petal water, cardamom water, and warm soft porridge." "What kind of grain porridge did you give?" "Coarse grain porridge and husked-grain porridge." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should give them sālu rice porridge." "What legume dish did you serve?" "A legume dish of rough wild-pea broth." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should serve them a legume dish of fine wild-pea broth." "What was served as poultry?" "Boiled seasoning." "That is not suitable. Those monks are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā; you should serve them various kinds of meat, together with boiled seasoning, yogurt, and warm milk."

Having arranged all this, if a monk knowingly eats it, it becomes an offence. If they truly are holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā, there is no offence. There is no offence for one who is a novice, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations. The offence of eating food that a nun has arranged — the thirtieth — is complete.

Summary verse: repeatedly; a single dwelling and resting place; flour and provisions and stored food; assembled and out of season and placement and the rest; swallowing from the mouth and receiving.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka grove of the Bamboo Forest. The habitual practice of the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana was to travel at various times through the hell realms, to travel through the animal realm, to travel through the realm of hungry ghosts, to travel through the realm of gods, and to travel among humans. Having passed through those realms, they would come to Jambudvīpa and, to the four assemblies, they would speak of the sufferings of the beings in the hell realms — the lifting, the cutting, the slicing, the cleaving, and so on — and of the sufferings of the animals who eat one another and so on, and of the sufferings of the hungry ghosts such as hunger and thirst and so on, and of the sufferings of the gods such as death and transmigration, downfall, dispersal, and destruction and so on, and of the sufferings of humans such as seeking and craving and so on. By speaking of all these things, those among whom they were dwelling who were companions and those who were practicing the holy life but had no delight in it — those people they would take in hand and lead to where the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were. Having arrived, they would make an effort to introduce them thoroughly to the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana, and would make an effort to instruct them rightly and thoroughly. And the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana would in turn introduce them thoroughly and instruct them rightly. When the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana had thus introduced them thoroughly and instructed them rightly, those people came to delight in the holy life and to distinguish ever-greater excellence in it. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were surrounded and attended upon by the four assemblies.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana come to be surrounded and attended upon by the four assemblies?" "Reverend one, the habitual practice of the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana is to travel at various times through the hell realms, to travel through the animal realm, to travel through the realm of hungry ghosts, to travel through the realm of gods, and

to travel among human beings. The two of them would travel through all those realms and then come to Jambudvīpa, where they would describe to the four assemblies the sufferings of hell-beings — being dragged, pierced, cut, and burned, and the like; the sufferings of animals — devouring one another, and the like; the sufferings of hungry ghosts — hunger and thirst, and the like; the sufferings of gods — death and transmigration, falling from their station, scattering, and destruction, and the like; and the sufferings of humans — striving and craving, and the like. By thus proclaiming these sufferings, they would lead those among their companions and attendants who had no delight in the holy life to the presence of the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana, and there they would present them properly for ordination and instruct them properly. And the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana would in turn properly ordain them and properly instruct them. Once they had been properly ordained and properly instructed by the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana, those persons would take delight in the holy life and would aspire to ever higher distinctions. Reverend one, that is the cause and that is the condition by which the Venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana come to be surrounded and attended upon by the four assemblies.

Ānanda, monks the like of the monk Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana — monks like Śāriputra and like the great Maudgalyāyana — do not arise in every age. It is for this reason that the Blessed One grants permission for the Wheel of the Five Sections to be painted in the gatehouse."

Then the Blessed One declared: "Let the Wheel of the Five Sections be painted in the gatehouse." But the monks did not know how it was to be painted, and the Blessed One declared: "Paint the five destinies: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of gods, and the destiny of humans. Since the monks did not know where each was to be placed, the Blessed One declared: "At the bottom, paint the destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Paint also the eastern continent Videha, the western continent Godānīya, the northern continent Uttarakuru, and Jambudvīpa. In the center, paint attachment, aversion, and delusion. Paint a figure of the Buddha indicating the pure maṇḍala of nirvāṇa. Paint also the beings born by spontaneous birth, dying and being reborn in the manner of a continuous thread of silk. Around the rim, paint the twelve links of dependent origination arising in forward order and in reverse order, and depict the whole as held within impermanence. The two verses are also to be composed and extracted:

Strive and lift yourselves up,
Enter upon the Buddha's teaching.
Like a great elephant in a muddy swamp,
Conquer the army of the lord of death.
Whoever shall practice with true diligence
This discipline of the Dharma
Will, having utterly abandoned the round of birth,
Make an end of suffering.

This too is to be painted."

Then, having declared that the Wheel of the Five Sections was to be painted in the gatehouse, the Blessed One gave the instruction, and the monks had the Wheel of the Five Sections painted in the gatehouse. Brahmins and

householders came and asked, "Noble ones, what is this that has been painted?" And the monks replied, "We ourselves do not know." Thereupon the Blessed One declared, "A monk shall be appointed to explain it to the brahmins and householders who come and gather there." Having declared that a monk was to be appointed, the Blessed One further said that if they were to appoint monks regardless of qualification — whether immature, confused, unclear of mind, or unskilled — and those monks did not know the matter themselves, how could they possibly explain it to the brahmins and householders who came and gathered there? Therefore the Blessed One declared, "Appoint one who is capable."

Now, in Rājagṛha there lived a householder who had taken a wife from among his equals in rank, and with her he played, rejoiced, and lived in happiness. A son was born to them. Then the man said to his wife, "Dear one, robbers have come and seized our wealth and stolen our possessions. I will therefore load up a ship and set out upon the great ocean. Lady, please do so as I have said." He loaded up the ship and set out upon the great ocean, and right there he met with suffering in a manner that was unrighteous. His wife then nurtured, tended, and raised the boy through the power of her own kinship bonds and the strength of her hands. She had him instructed in letters and script, and he became exceedingly skilled in worldly tales and narratives.

The boy then went together with his companions to the grove of Nalendra and entered the temple. There he saw the Wheel of the Five Sections painted in the gatehouse, and he asked a monk, "Noble one, what is this that has been painted here?" The monk replied, "Dear friend, these are the five destinies: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans."

The boy asked further, "Noble one, what karma did these beings perform so that, through the ripening of that karma, they were born in the hells and now experience such sufferings as being hoisted up, chopped, cut apart, and hacked?" The monk replied, "Dear friend, these beings extensively habituated themselves to and repeatedly practiced the paths of the ten non-virtuous actions, and through the ripening of that karma they were born in the hells, where they now experience such sufferings as being hoisted up, chopped, cut apart, and hacked."

"And noble one, what karma did these beings perform so that, through the ripening of that karma, they were born among animals and now experience such sufferings as devouring one another?" The monk replied, "Dear friend, these beings habituated themselves to and repeatedly practiced even the slightest and most minor paths of the ten non-virtuous actions, and through the ripening of that karma they were born among animals, where they now experience such sufferings as eating one another."

"And noble one, what karma did these beings perform so that, through the ripening of that karma, they were born among hungry ghosts and now experience such sufferings as hunger, thirst, and the like?" The monk replied, "Dear friend, these beings habituated themselves to and repeatedly practiced miserliness, and through the ripening of that karma they were born among hungry ghosts, where they now experience such sufferings as hunger, thirst, and the like."

"Noble one, then what karma did these beings perform so that, through the ripening of that karma, they were born among the gods and now experience the pleasures of the gods?"

The monk replied, "Dear friend, these beings thoroughly took up, habituated themselves to, and repeatedly practiced the ten paths of virtuous karma to the greatest degree, and through the ripening of that karma they were born among the gods, where they now experience the pleasures of the gods."

"Noble one, then what karma did these beings perform so that, through the ripening of that karma, they were born among human beings and now experience only minor pleasures?"

The monk replied, "Dear friend, these beings thoroughly took up, habituated themselves to, and repeatedly practiced the ten paths of virtuous karma to a lesser degree, and through the ripening of that karma they were born among human beings, where they now experience only minor pleasures."

"Noble one, for my part, I have no wish for the three destinies — the hells, the animals, and the hungry ghosts. Of the two destinies, the gods and human beings, I do wish for those. Noble one, what karma must I perform so that I may be reborn among the gods?"

"Dear friend, there is a way. Go forth before the Blessed One and live the holy life of celibacy. If in this very lifetime you come to comprehend all things as they truly are, that itself will be the end of your suffering. But if you pass away still possessing the remaining bonds of clinging, you will be reborn among the gods."

"Noble one, for how long?"

"Dear friend, for as long as you live."

"But if I cannot manage even that, is there some other means?"

"There is. What is it? Dear friend, offer a midday meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and you will be reborn among the gods."

"Noble one, how many kārṣāpaṇas would it take to offer such a midday meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha?"

"Dear friend, five hundred kārṣāpaṇas."

"Noble one, that I can manage," said the youth, and he bowed at the monk's feet, departed, and went straight to his own home. There he said to his mother, "Mother, today I went to the Añodā Grove and there I saw a wheel painted with five sections, showing the five destinies — the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and human beings. Mother, do you wish your wicked son to be reborn among the gods?"

"My child, if all sentient beings wish to be reborn among the gods, what need is there even to speak of you? Mother, give me five hundred kārṣāpaṇas so that I may offer a midday meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha."

"My child, I raised you, nurtured you, and brought you up with the strength of my kinship and the labor of my own hands — where would I find the wealth of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas?"

"Mother, I shall go and work for wages."

"My child, you are very young; you are not able to work for wages."

"Mother, I can manage."

She, seeing it was the right moment, gave her consent. The boy went and stood in the laborers' market. When brahmins and householders came to take other laborers, no one took him, and he remained there until the sun had set, then came home at nightfall. His mother, seeing him return, asked, "My child, did you find work for wages today?"

The boy answered, "Mother, no one took me."

"My child, that is just how laborers are — laborers go to the laborers' market with their hair disheveled and wearing soiled clothes, and sit there waiting. So if you too wish to work for wages, dishevel your hair, put on soiled clothes, go to the laborers' market, and sit there."

The next day he disheveled his hair, put on soiled clothes, went to the laborers' market, and sat there waiting. A merchant who was building a house came to the laborers' market seeking workers. He took the other laborers but did not take the boy. The boy spoke up: "Sir, I too will work for wages."

The merchant said, "My child, you are far too young — you cannot work for wages."

The boy replied, "Will you pay me my wages up front?"

The merchant said, "Wages are paid at the end."

The boy said, "I will work from today. If you are satisfied, then please pay me my wages."

The merchant took the boy on, and the boy began working for wages at the merchant's house. While the other laborers worked slowly, the boy worked swiftly and with speed. They said to him, "Young fellow, why do you not work slowly?"

The boy replied, "Uncles, because in a previous life I behaved badly, I was born into a poor household, and that is why I am now working for wages. If I work slowly and then die and pass on from here, what will become of my destiny? What will my fate in future lives be?"

They said to him, "Young fellow, you are newly broken in, and there is indeed a place where one ends up as the very last among all — that is what you are like."

Now the boy was skilled in worldly tales and stories, and so he told those laborers stories as he went along swiftly and quickly. The other laborers, fearing they would miss the stories, hurried along swiftly after him, and that day the laborers accomplished a great deal of work.

It was the householder's custom to inspect all the work done by his hired men at the close of each day. The merchant came in the evening and examined all the work, and seeing that twice the usual amount had been done, he asked his foreman, "Did you bring in any additional laborers?"

The foreman said, "I did not."

The merchant asked, "Then why was so much work accomplished today?"

The foreman replied, "May the householder's son be well! Because this boy is skilled in worldly tales and stories — he tells worldly tales and stories and works swiftly and with speed — the other laborers, fearing they will miss the stories, go along swiftly after him and work, and so today a great deal was accomplished."

The merchant then began to pay the boy double wages. The boy said, "Sir, are you giving me both days' wages all at once?"

"No," said the merchant, "I am giving you a bonus because I am pleased with you."

The boy replied, "If you are pleased with me, then for as long as I work in your service, please hold my wages in your own hand."

The merchant agreed: "So be it."

When the merchant's house was completed and the boy's wages were counted, they came to no fewer than five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and the boy began to weep. The merchant said, "My child, why do you weep? Have I cheated you?"

"Sir, you are a great man — how could you cheat me? It is rather this: I worked for wages to earn five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, thinking I would offer a meal to the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — and be reborn in the realm of the gods. Since I have not yet obtained that, I will have to go elsewhere and work again for wages."

The merchant was a man of faith, and so he said, "My child, I myself will make up the full amount."

"Father, I fear I shall not be reborn among the gods."

"My child, do you have sincere faith in the Blessed One?"

"I do."

"Then go and present your request to the Blessed One."

The boy went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder's son addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I worked for wages in the service of a great merchant in order to earn five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. Since I did not obtain them myself, and since the merchant has made up the full amount on my behalf, may I accept them? Blessed One, that merchant is a man of faith — please accept."

"Blessed One, I fear I shall not be reborn among the gods."

"You will be reborn there."

The boy prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed.

Then the householder's son received the five hundred kārṣāpaṇas from the merchant and went to his mother. He said: "Mother, please use these five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to prepare a meal and invite the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — for the noon meal tomorrow."

"My child, I have no utensils whatsoever, no servants, and no lodging. That same merchant has abundant utensils, servants, and lodging, and he is a man of faith — go and make the arrangements with him."

The boy went to the merchant and said: "Father, in our household there are not even a few utensils, servants, or lodging. Please prepare the meal yourself, and I will be present to invite the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — for the noon meal."

The merchant, being a man of faith, thought to himself: "It would be excellent if the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — were to take their noon meal at my newly built house." He then said: "Very well, my child — go and invite the monastic Saṅgha, the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, for the noon meal tomorrow, and I will prepare the food."

The householder's son then placed the five hundred kārṣāpaṇas in the merchant's hands, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, sat to one side of the elder, and said: "Blessed One, tomorrow I have invited the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — for the noon meal." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent and saying nothing to the householder's son.

Then the householder's son, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had accepted, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed.

That same night the merchant prepared the food, rose early the next morning, arranged the seats, set out water vessels, and sent an invitation to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable sir, we invite you; may it please you, Blessed One, to remember that the time has now come." Then the Blessed One, in the forenoon, dressed in his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, was surrounded by the assembly of monks, and went ahead of the monastic Saṅgha toward the merchant's house.

The group of six monks asked: "Whose house is it that the monastic Saṅgha — the community of monks with the Buddha at its head — has been invited to?"

"It is that of a certain very prominent householder's son."

The group of six monks said: "He is just a hired laborer — what could he possibly offer? As we go along from house to house, let us eat at the homes we pass through and take food there on loan."

So as they went, going from house to house, they said to the householders: "Noble ones, please prepare seats for us."

"So be it," they said, and they ate their fill along the way. Then the Blessed One proceeded to the spot where the merchant's invitation had been laid, arrived there, and was seated in the place of honor prepared ahead of the monastic Saṅgha of monks. The group of six monks, having eaten their fill from house to house along the way as they went, arrived there and sat down in their places as well. Then the householder's son, having ascertained that the monastic Saṅgha — the Buddha and the monks — was comfortably seated, satisfied them and nourished them with his own hands, with pure and delightful food and drink. As he went about serving them, the group of six monks, when their turn came, he saw that they were not eating. Seeing this, they sat before the Blessed One and said: "Blessed One, here certain noble ones, when their turn comes, are not eating. We fear that we may not be reborn among the gods." The Blessed One declared: "Good man, if you will be reborn among the gods even by enjoying the merit of lodging, what need is there even to speak of the merit of enjoying food?"

Then the Blessed One, with a Dharma-endowed discourse, rightly instructed that householder's son, rightly led him to take it to heart, rightly praised him, and rightly gladdened him. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed discourse, he rightly instructed him, rightly led him to take it to heart, rightly praised him, and rightly gladdened him. Then he rose from his seat and departed.

Now some five hundred merchants had come from the great ocean to Rājagṛha, and since a festival had arisen in Rājagṛha, they found they could sell nothing at all. There was among them a merchant who knew about monks, and he said: "Friends, take note. In the household where the monastic Saṅgha — the Buddha and the monks — was invited for their midday meal, it is possible that some leftover food and drink remains in excellent condition. Go there and seek it for a price." On hearing this, the others said: "We hear there is a great prominent merchant's house where the monastic Saṅgha — the Buddha and the monks — was given their midday meal." So they took their goods and went there, and said: "Merchant, we are around five hundred merchants who have come from the great ocean to Rājagṛha. A festival has arisen here in Rājagṛha and we have found nothing to sell. We are now hungry. Since your house was the one where the monastic Saṅgha — the Buddha and the monks — was given their midday meal, if there is any food and drink remaining in excellent condition, please give it to us in exchange for a price." The merchant said: "Good friends, let us see," and went to the householder's son and said: "Son, around five hundred merchants have come from the great ocean to Rājagṛha, and since a festival has arisen in Rājagṛha they have found nothing to sell. They are hungry and have come here seeking food and drink. If there is a good quantity remaining, please give it to them in exchange for a price." The boy said: "Father, I will not give it for a price — but I will give it freely as a gift. Let them come." The merchant had those merchants seated, and the boy satisfied them with food and drink. Having thus satisfied themselves in body, those merchants gave voice to this utterance, saying aloud: "Merchant, the householder in whose house the monastic Saṅgha — the Buddha and the monks — was given their midday meal, and who has also satisfied us five hundred merchants with food and drink, that merchant has found good gains indeed." The merchant said: "Good friends, this is not my food — it is the food of this householder's son." They asked: "Whose son, and of which householder?" The merchant replied: "Of a great and prominent householder."

Their caravan leader said: "In that case, this boy is the son of my younger friend." Others said: "In that case, he is our nephew." Still others said: "In that case, he is our grandson." The caravan leader then said: "Many can take from one, but one cannot take from many." With that he set down a foundation, placed his jewels there, and said: "Good friends, let each of you place here whatever you wish to offer in full." Some placed one jewel, some placed two, and some placed many, and so a great heap of jewels was assembled there. The caravan leader then said to the boy: "Son, take these." The boy said: "Good friends, I did not give for payment." The caravan leader said: "We are not paying you a price. Rather, since a single jewel alone can procure a hundredfold of food such as this, we do this from the joy we feel toward you, placing ourselves under the power of that joy." The boy said: "I wonder whether I might not be reborn among the gods." The caravan leader said: "Do you have faith in the Blessed One?" "I do," said the boy. "Then go and make your request to the Blessed One."

Then the boy went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that householder's son addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, I gave food and drink to some five hundred merchants, and they, placing themselves under the power of the joy they felt toward me, are about to give me something in return — should I accept it? Beautiful One, please tell me. Blessed One, I wonder whether I might not be reborn among the gods." The Blessed One declared: "Son, this is but the flower — take it. Other fruits will come." So the boy took those jewels.

Now in Rājagṛha there was a guild-master without a son who died in due time, and the men of wealth, the guild-masters, and the caravan leaders assembled together and said: "Good friends, whom shall we consecrate as guild-master of the city? It should be whichever being among us is renowned for great merit." They said: "How shall we know?" And they replied: "Let seeds of various colors be poured into an unglazed clay vessel, and whichever one can grasp seeds of only a single color — that person we shall consecrate as guild-master." They poured seeds of various colors into an unglazed clay vessel and began to reach in to grasp them. All the others grasped seeds of various colors, but that householder's son grasped only seeds of a single color. Then those assembled said: "How are we to consecrate this hired-man's son as guild-master?" Yet they performed the test three times in this same manner, and each time all the others grasped seeds of various colors, while the householder's son grasped only seeds of a single color. Then those assembled said: "Good friends, non-human beings have declared it so by a fourfold sign: this very householder's son is to be consecrated as guild-master." And so they consecrated that boy as guild-master of the city.

The guild-master thought to himself:

"This being is renowned for his great merit and power — I should form a connection with him." And so that guild-master gave his own daughter, adorned with all her ornaments, in marriage to this guild-master of the city. And because of that, the household became exceedingly wealthy with abundant goods and possessions, and his name became instantly renowned — he was called "Instantly Renowned."

Then the guild-master Instantly Renowned thought to himself: "All this magnificent wealth and prosperity in my household has come about through my reliance on the Buddha, the Blessed One — it was born from my having invited the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, to another house and offering them a midday meal." And so the guild-master Instantly Renowned went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed the guild-master Instantly Renowned with Dharma-endowed words, rightly showing him, rightly establishing him, rightly uplifting him, and rightly gladdening him. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed words, he rightly showed him, rightly established him, rightly uplifted him, and rightly gladdened him — and then he fell silent.

Then the guild-master Instantly Renowned rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, may the Blessed One be pleased tomorrow to accept a midday meal together with the Saṅgha of monks at my home." The Blessed One gave his consent to the guild-master Instantly Renowned by remaining silent.

Then the guild-master Instantly Renowned, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been granted, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That same night, the guild-master Instantly Renowned prepared food and drink, clean and fine, made everything ready, and early the next morning rose, arranged seats, set out water vessels, and issued this formal invitation: "Blessed One, may you graciously lend your presence — reverend sir, we request your attendance for the midday meal. Blessed One, may it please you to consider that the time has now come." Then the Blessed One, in the morning, having donned his lower and upper robes and taken up his bowl, came surrounded by the assembly of monks, preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, and went to where the guild-master Instantly Renowned's residence was. He arrived and took his seat on the seat that had been arranged in the foremost place among the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the guild-master Instantly Renowned, knowing that the Buddha together with the Saṅgha of monks had been seated comfortably, with his own hands satisfied and refreshed them with food and drink, clean and fine. In many ways, with food and drink clean and fine, he satisfied and refreshed them with his own hands. Then, knowing that the Blessed One had finished the midday meal and had set aside his bowl, he took a low seat and sat — he and his wife — before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, having thoroughly understood the minds, the latent dispositions, the temperaments, and the natures of the guild-master Instantly Renowned and his wife, taught the Dharma in such a way as to utterly shatter with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection — the view of a self in the perishable aggregates — held by the two of them, and thereby bring about the fruit of stream-entry directly before their eyes.

Having seen the truth, they supplicated:

"Venerable One, such benefit as the Blessed One has bestowed upon us, relying on the Blessed One as our good spiritual friend — this our father did not do for us, nor our mother, nor the king, nor the gods, nor our forebears of former times, nor śramaṇas and brahmins, nor the host of our loving friends, companions, and relatives. The ocean of blood and tears has been dried up; we have been freed from the mountains of bones; the doors to the lower realms have been sealed shut; the doors to the higher realms and liberation have been thrown open; we have been lifted out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; we have been placed among gods and humans; saṃsāra has been brought to its end. With the vajra of gnosis you have shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, and we have obtained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable One, we have entered the stream! Venerable One, we have entered the stream! Venerable One, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept us as lay practitioners. From this day forward, for as long as we live, we take refuge with our whole heart."

Then the Blessed One rightly instructed, established, exhorted, and gladdened the guild-master Instantly Renowned with a Dharma-endowed discourse. He rightly instructed him, rightly established him, rightly exhorted him, and rightly gladdened him with Dharma-endowed discourses in many ways, and then rose from his seat and departed.

Now, this took place at a time when the Blessed One, the buddha, had not yet established for the śrāvakas the rules of training in the Vinaya.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga. The fifty-first bundle.

Then the Blessed One, having remained in Rājagṛha as long as he wished, set out on a tour of the countryside in the direction of Vaiśālī. The Blessed One, traveling on tour through the villages, came to Vaiśālī and resided in Vaiśālī in the Lofty Hall by the bank of the Monkey Pond. The householder Fierce Energy heard that the Blessed One, traveling on tour through the villages, had come to Vaiśālī and was residing in Vaiśālī in the Lofty Hall by the bank of the Monkey Pond. Having heard this, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One rightly instructed, rightly established, rightly exhorted, and rightly gladdened the householder Fierce Energy with a Dharma-endowed discourse. He rightly instructed him, rightly established him, rightly exhorted him, and rightly gladdened him with Dharma-endowed discourses in many ways, and then said nothing further.

Then the householder Fierce Energy rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, directed his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, may it please you to accept tomorrow the midday meal together with the Saṅgha of monks at my dwelling." The Blessed One consented to the householder Fierce Energy by remaining silent. The householder Fierce Energy, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had consented, departed from the Blessed One's presence and said to those who sustained themselves on dairy produce:

"Wise ones, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, has consented to come. Prepare abundant pure and excellent food." They prepared abundant pure and excellent food.

Then, the next morning, the householder Fierce Energy rose early, arranged seats, set out water for washing, and invited the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, it is time — may the Blessed One know the hour has come." The group of six said, "Gavämpati and Nandita, go on ahead to the households of those who are going home." And so they did. When those two saw a certain alms-gatherer, they said, "Come — enter into the households of those who are going home." They led him away, and having entered Vaiśālī ahead of the others, they went to the households of those who were going home. Then those householders said, "Noble ones, please eat." The group of six said, "We have been invited as guests." By whom? "By the householder Fierce Energy." The householders said, "Noble ones, in that case, please eat the mango pulp." "So be it," and they ate the mango pulp. The alms-gatherer did not eat, so they said to him, "Noble one, you too should eat the mango pulp." He replied, "I observe the one-session rule." They said to him, "Then pass through and eat there at his place." He filled a small bowl and went there. The Saṅgha of monks was seated. The Blessed One remained in the store-room and was engaged in obtaining alms. Blessed ones, buddhas, engage in the practice of obtaining alms while remaining in the store-room for five reasons. What are those five? They wish to establish themselves inwardly in proper composure; they wish to teach the Dharma to the gods; they wish to attend to the sick; they wish to inspect the lodgings; and they wish to establish training rules for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya. In this instance, the Blessed One remained in the store-room and engaged in the practice of obtaining alms because he wished to establish training rules for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

Then, when the householder Fierce Energy saw that the Saṅgha of monks was comfortably seated, he served and satisfied them from his own hand with abundant pure and excellent food and drink. Then the householder Fierce Energy sat down before the alms-gathering monk. The monk thought to himself: "This householder will come to know that I ate mango pulp as follows — for as long as he finds no fault with me, I should speak to him." And so he said this to the householder Fierce Energy: "Householder, it was not only I who ate mango pulp — these members of the group of six also ate mango pulp." The householder said, "Noble one, why do you say that not only did I eat mango pulp but these members of the group of six also ate mango pulp?" Embarrassed, the monk said, "Noble one, does it seem to you that I have no mango pulp?" He then said to those who sustained themselves on dairy produce: "Wise ones, open the pots of mango pulp." They opened them. Then the monk who had been gathering alms took the alms and went to where the Blessed One was. He went there, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat to one side.

It is the nature of awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, to gladden each monk who has been gathering alms by asking, "Monk, how did the alms-gathering go? Did you satisfy the monastic Saṅgha?" And so, in keeping with this, the Blessed One gladdened the monk who had been gathering alms by asking, "Monk, how did the alms-gathering go? Did you satisfy the monastic Saṅgha?"

The monk then reported: "Venerable one, the alms-gathering went well, and the monastic Saṅgha was satisfied — for the householder Dragshuljen had provided a full meal for the monastic Saṅgha." He then reported the entire matter in detail to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the householder Dragshuljen has provided a dwelling for the monastic Saṅgha."

Then, having completed the meal, the Blessed One rinsed both feet outside the temple hall and entered the temple hall to rest in inner composure. Thereafter, rising from inner composure, he took his seat on the cushion prepared before the monastic Saṅgha.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident and this occasion and this circumstance, convened the monastic Saṅgha — and so forth, as before. It is the nature of awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, to inquire with full knowledge while feigning not to know — and so on as before. The Blessed One then questioned the monks: "Monks, is it true that you ate repeatedly?"

"Venerable one, it is true."

The Blessed One censured them, saying that such conduct was unbecoming of a renunciant, not in keeping with propriety, not permissible, not in accord with proper conduct, and was not the deed of one who has gone forth into renunciation. Having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: eating repeatedly is an offense entailing a downfall." Thus did the Blessed One lay down the training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was residing in Vaiśālī, in the Monkey Pond Pavilion, in the multi-storied dwelling.

A certain sick monk went to a physician's residence, and when the physician saw him, he said, "Good friend, show me your condition and I will give you medicine." The noble one replied, "Please ask the Blessed One." The physician said, "Good friend, this medicine of mine — if you do not use it for your livelihood, you will not recover from your illness." The monk said, "Good friend, the Blessed One has laid down a training rule." The physician replied, "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; taking this very circumstance as the occasion, he will certainly grant permission. Let there be such a case."

The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted except in times of illness."

"Monks, when tasks for the stūpa or tasks for the Saṅgha have been performed, and the monks are hungry, have collapsed in exhaustion, are lying down, and are unable to muster energy for wholesome pursuits, if brahmins and householders who are full of faith arrive at the temple hall and say, 'Noble ones, if you are truly dedicated to the teaching, why do you lie collapsed in sleep and fail to rouse yourselves for wholesome pursuits?' and the monks reply, 'Good friends, we are hungry — please report this to the Blessed One.' The physician had said, 'Good friend, the Blessed One has laid down a training rule.'"

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with the exception of times of work, this rule stands."

Then it occurred that other monks, while travelling on the road, became hungry, collapsed in exhaustion, lay down, and were unable to muster energy for wholesome pursuits. Brahmins and householders full of faith arrived and said to them, "Noble ones, if you are truly dedicated to the teaching, why do you lie collapsed in sleep and fail to rouse yourselves for wholesome pursuits?" The monks replied, "Good friends, we are hungry. Please report this to the Blessed One." The brahmins and householders said, "But the Blessed One has laid down a training rule." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with the exception of times of travel, this rule stands."

After that, the Blessed One resided in Vaiśālī as long as he wished, and then, setting out on a wandering journey in the direction of Śrāvastī, he arrived at Śrāvastī and dwelt there in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now there was a householder in Śrāvastī whose customary practice was to observe the precepts on the eighth and fourteenth days of the month, and as long as the monks who had been invited to his home had not eaten, he himself would not eat. This householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another home. The Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha departed. The householder sent a servant to the temple hall, saying, "Go and invite the monks, for the meal is ready." The servant went to the temple hall, but not a single monk was to be seen, so he returned and reported: "Householder, there are no monks there — I did not see even one." The householder said, "Go to where the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was invited, invite the monks from there, and tell them the meal is ready." The servant went there, and when he arrived he saw that the monks had already eaten and were coming out. He said to them, "Noble ones, please come — a great householder requests you to come for a meal. What do you say?" The monks replied, "We have already eaten." The servant returned and told the householder: "Householder, from the mouths of the monks came these words: 'We have already eaten.'" The householder said, "Go, enter the house, and on behalf of the householder tell them to come, that a meal is ready and a great length of cloth will be offered." The servant went and said: "Noble ones, on behalf of the householder I am told to say: please come, the meal is ready, and a great length of cloth will be offered." The monks replied, "We decline." The servant returned and told the householder: "Householder, from the mouths of the monks came these words: 'We decline.'" Thereupon the householder, establishing the fact that the Saṅgha he had invited had not eaten the meal he had prepared, cut off the food. And the neighbouring households said among themselves: "Even if you give cloth to these ascetics (śramaṇas), sons of the Śākyas, they will not make use of it — this householder has cut off their food because the monks did not eat." They criticized the monks, jeered at them, and spoke ill of them. When the monks reported all of this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with the exception of the time of cloth-giving, this rule stands."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are devoted to training, and who devote their resources to training, and he addressed the monks in words befitting that theme, in harmony with it, in its fullness, and endowed with the Dharma appropriate to the occasion. He then declared to the monks:

"Monks, therefore the former rule stands as a prohibition, and this is now permitted. My hearers should take up this training rule as a foundation for discipline as follows: eating repeatedly except at the permitted times is an offense that causes downfall. The permitted times are these: the time of illness, the time of work, the time of a journey, and the time of cloth-giving — those are the permitted times.

'Eating repeatedly' means eating again and again. 'Except at the permitted times' means setting aside those designated times. 'An offense that causes downfall' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the lower states of wretched existence — into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into miserable destinies, into states of ruin. Furthermore, so long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome qualities. That is why it is said to be an offense that causes downfall.

Of those permitted times, 'the time of illness' means this: when a monk cannot sustain himself on a single meal. 'The time of work' means this: when a monk has performed even the slightest service — such as dusting with a cloth or sweeping the floor — for the Saṅgha or for a stūpa. 'The time of a journey' means this: when a monk has traveled half a league or half of that and then returns. 'The time of cloth-giving' means this: when a monk has received even a small bolt of cloth or a large bolt of cloth.

Now, as to how a downfall may occur in connection with cloth-giving: there are four cases — being invited with cloth, being invited without cloth, being invited with cloth and also with the price of cloth, and being invited without cloth and without the price of cloth.

In the first case: if a monk has been invited with cloth and is then invited to another place also with cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both, and no offense in eating at both.

In the second case: if a monk has been invited with cloth and is then invited to another place without cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance of the second becomes a wrong act and the eating of it becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

In the third case: if a monk has been invited with cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth and also with the price of cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

In the fourth case: if a monk has been invited with cloth and is then invited to another place without cloth and without the price of cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance of the second becomes a wrong act and the eating of it becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and is then invited to another place also without cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both."

If a monk has been invited without cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth and also with the price of cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and is then invited to another place also without cloth and without the price of cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited with cloth and also with the price of cloth and is then invited to another place also with cloth and also with the price of cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

If a monk has been invited with cloth and also with the price of cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth only, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

If a monk has been invited with cloth and also with the price of cloth and is then invited to another place without cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited with cloth and also with the price of cloth and is then invited to another place without cloth and without the price of cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and without the price of cloth and is then invited to another place also without cloth and without the price of cloth, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and without the price of cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and without the price of cloth and is then invited to another place without cloth only, that monk should accept the first invitation and decline the second, or else give it away to another. If he accepts both and eats at both, the acceptance becomes a wrong act and the eating becomes an offense that causes downfall — but there is no offense in regard to the first.

If a monk has been invited without cloth and without the price of cloth and is then invited to another place with cloth and also with the price of cloth, that monk should accept both invitations and eat at both. There is no offense in accepting both and no offense in eating at both.

There is no offense for one who is a beginner, for one who is mentally deranged, for one who is disturbed in mind, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This completes the thirty-first offense that causes downfall, concerning eating repeatedly.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At a certain rocky cliff, a householder was living, and he had established a dwelling place for the śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions. In that dwelling, he provided whatever was needed by way of alms to whichever śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions resided there.

Now at the time when the Blessed One had displayed the great miracle at Śrāvastī, defeating the non-Buddhist adherents (tīrthikas) and bringing delight to gods and humans alike, and gladdening the hearts of the wise — at that very time the remaining tīrthikas took up residence in the outlying regions.

On another occasion, sixty naked ascetics arrived at that rocky cliff and went before that householder, saying, "Venerable one, may we obtain the Dharma! May we obtain the Dharma!" The householder replied, "Noble ones, have you gone forth?" They said, "We have gone forth." The householder said, "You are welcome. Please stay in the dwelling place I have established for the śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions, and I shall provide you with whatever you need by way of alms." They took up residence there, and the householder provided them with what they needed by way of alms.

There was at Śrāvastī a certain householder of faith who came with a caravan and arrived at that rocky cliff. He entered the shop of that householder and came to know that householder as his associate. That householder of faith began to make offerings to the naked ascetics, but he did not send them to the other householder's door. Instead he sent word to them, saying, "Friends, come here — I will make offerings to worthy recipients." Since the householder was a person of faith, he thought to himself, "They may well be disciples of the Blessed One — let me go and see." When he went there, he saw that the naked ascetics were nothing but shameless and without modesty, and he felt that to speak unpleasantness openly would be painful, so he said nothing and simply sat there.

After the naked ascetics had eaten and left, the householder said to the other man, "Friend, is the seed good and the field good?" He replied, "Friend, if the seed is good, the field is nothing but naked ascetics who are shameless and without modesty, who hold wrong views, who are as barren as a salt plain, who have severed connections, who are wicked — it is nothing but evil ground." The householder said, "Friend, is there some other good field?" He replied, "There is — the disciples of the Blessed One." The householder said, "If they would come here, I would provide them with whatever they need by way of alms."

That householder then turned his caravan around, sold his goods, and went to Śrāvastī. He deposited the proceeds of his goods in a warehouse and went to the Jeta Grove. Now the group of six monks had the habit of thinking, "Here we will also teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who come and arrive, we will defeat opponents, and we will proclaim our own fame." For this reason, some member of the group of six always kept the gate of the Jeta Grove from being left unoccupied. So the venerable Nandaka rose early in the morning, discarded his tooth-stick, put on a reddish-yellow patched robe, and was pacing and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove.

When Nandaka saw the householder while he was still far off, he said, "Welcome, householder, welcome! From where have you come after so long a time, arriving like the moon that has been hidden away?" The man replied, "Noble one, at a certain pleasant rocky cliff there is a great householder who has established a dwelling for the śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions, and he wishes to see the disciples of the Blessed One."

Nandaka thought: "If any black-bowl-bearer hears of this, he will rush there very quickly. So if I disparage this householder, I will certainly not tell any black-bowl-bearer about it." And so he said to the householder: "Don't you think your heart is occupied with nothing beyond thoughts such as 'who will give us food along the road?' and 'who will give us robes?' — do you ever think of meditation or recitation?" The householder thought: "Among those who are possessed of desire, there is none worse than Nandaka. Now he has disparaged me. If I were to tell others who are monks by nature, they would disparage me far more widely." And so he sat in silence, saying nothing.

Nandaka, having disparaged the householder, then went to the group of six and said: "Venerable ones, for however long we are in want, let us put an end to that want." They asked him: "Have you heard something?" He replied: "Yes. At a pleasant rocky cliff there is a great householder who has established a dwelling for the śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions, and he supplies those who stay there with robes and alms-food as needed. Let us go there." They asked: "Will all of us go?" Nandaka replied: "Only six will go." And so those six set out, traveling to that pleasant rocky cliff.

The naked ascetics there said: "Let those who know how to conduct themselves according to custom come." And those naked ascetics left a single naked guard at the dwelling and departed elsewhere.

The group of six continued on their way and, arriving at that cliff, went to the householder and said: "Householder, are you well? Are you well?" The householder said: "Who are you?" They replied: "We are disciples of the Blessed One." The householder said: "How wonderful! We too have been wishing to see disciples of the Blessed One, and here you have come. Noble ones, please stay in the dwelling I have established for the śramaṇas and brahmins of the four directions, and I will supply you with alms-food and whatever you need." The group of six then asked: "Is there any bedding — chairs or small seats?" The householder said: "There is none." The group of six replied: "Householder, we do not make our beds on the ground." The householder then searched for bedding there and sent chairs and small seats to the dwelling.

The naked guard said: "Hey, śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), sons of the Śākyas! This is not your temple, and it is not your dwelling — where do you think you are going?" The group of six replied: "What is this so-called person of understanding saying? Don't say 'this is not our temple and this is not our dwelling.' If we stay, then we stay and that is all. If we do not stay, we will cut off your major limbs." The naked man thought: "There are six of these, and I am alone. There is nothing I can do to them. It would not be right if they harmed me." And so, frightened, he fled.

The group of six then went to the householder's house every single day to eat. Then on another occasion, the householder had some business to attend to at a different cliff, and he said to the group of six: "Noble ones, I have some business at another cliff and I am going there. While I am away, please conduct yourselves in my absence as you would in my presence, until I return." The group of six replied:

"So be it." The householder then said to his servant: "Serve the noble ones just as you have been serving them, until I return." And he went off to that cliff.

The group of six continued to go there every single day and eat as before. Then they said among themselves: "Friends and companions, for how long shall we keep to the conduct of others? It is time to show our own conduct." They said: "So be it." And then they said: "Friends and companions, look, look at how beautiful are the eyes of this woman, her ears, her teeth, her lips, her breasts, her waist, her thighs, and her feet!" The woman, overcome with shame, withdrew into a room and sat there.

When the householder returned from that cliff, he asked his servant: "Did the almsmen come and receive food as usual?" The servant replied: "Almsmen of this sort — there were none whatsoever — but that is not the point. I have heard words from your almsmen that I have never heard before from jesters, musicians, or the sons of dancers." The householder thought: "Women's sense-objects are what men think about. Those naked wanderers who entered — when people see them, desire arises. But as for these śrāvakas of the Blessed One, who are well clad in the lower robe and well clad in the Dharma robe, I cannot find this pleasing." So he said to the servant: "Do you find pleasure in those naked wanderers? How could you take pleasure in the śrāvakas of the Blessed One, who are well clad in the lower robe and well clad in the Dharma robe?" His wife then spoke: "My lord's son, if you do not trust me, I shall make it plain before your very eyes."

The householder thought: "Better to investigate." He stayed away for a few days, and then said to the group of six: "Noble ones, I have a little business again at that cliff, and I shall go there. Please conduct yourselves in my absence as you would in my presence, until I return." The group of six replied: "So be it."

When the householder had gone into a room and was sitting quietly, the group of six likewise entered his house and made themselves at home. Then his wife began to serve them, and the group of six said: "Friends and companions, look, look at how beautiful are the eyes of this woman, her ears, her teeth, her lips, her breasts, her waist, her thighs, and her feet!"

The householder heard this and thought: "It would not accord with my character to cut off their alms just like that, on the spot. I must find a skilful approach." So that day he carried out one load and left it out. The group of six said: "Friends and companions, the domain-talk is stinging." Then they said: "Venerable ones, the one load we were in the habit of giving to the hungry — from this day forward, it will no longer be given." The next day he carried out a second load and left it out, and they said: "Friends and companions, the domain-talk is stinging." Then they said: "Venerable ones, the other load that we used to leave at the base beneath the alms bowl — that too will no longer be left from this day forward." And so in this way, gradually, he began to give only coarse grain and rough boiled gruel, and they said: "Friends and companions, the domain-talk is stinging." And they said further: "What is there here to sting about? Even were we to pass through a hundred doorways, it is hard to achieve a full belly. Now here we are, sitting in the cool shade, and you begin with coarse grain and rough

boiled gruel, and you refuse even that?"

Now the naked ascetic wandered around and, catching sight of the naked ascetics, said: "Wise ones, our domain has been taken — drive them back!" They replied: "Where have you been staying, and where did you come from here?" He said: "I was chased away from there." "By whom?" "By the monks, the sons of the Śākyas." They asked: "How many sons of the Śākyan monks came?" He said: "Six." They replied: "We have sixty men — surely we can beat those six soundly and drive them out! Come, let us go. When we call out the signal 'Wise ones, gather!' let ten of us rush upon each of the six groups and beat them thoroughly." They said: "Let us first ask the householder." Agreed. So they went to the householder and said: "Householder, to whom have you offered the lodging?" The householder replied: "I have offered it to no one in particular; whoever is staying there, I supply them with alms food as needed." They said: "Householder, then remain in the middle for now." And they went off to the lodging and said to the group of six: "Ha! Monks, sons of the Śākyas — where did you come from that you have settled here? This is neither your temple nor your lodging — come out! If you come out, well and good; if you do not come out, we will cut you down to size in no small way." The group of six replied: "Ha! What is it these naked scruff-napes are saying? 'This is neither your temple nor your lodging — come out!' they say. Let them not say it! If they are settled here, they are settled. If they do not vacate, we will cut them down to size in no small way." The naked ascetics then called out the signal "Wise ones, gather!" and ten naked ascetics rushed upon each member of the group of six and began to beat them. The group of six said: "Dear ones, companions, brothers in the holy life — it would be unseemly for us to come to grief; protect your eyes and your ears." Then they said: "Scruff-napes, you dare — press in properly from this side!" and they showed their buttocks and such, and had them beaten. When the naked ascetics grew weary and could no longer strike, the group of six called out: "Venerable ones, press in harder!" and each member of the group of six, extending an arm, knocked five naked ascetics to the ground, and withdrawing an arm, knocked five more naked ascetics to the ground, and then began to beat them severely, saying: "Dear ones, companions, it would be unseemly for a root downfall (pārājika), a defeat, to arise — guard the root downfall!" With that, the group of six thoroughly pummelled and thrashed those ascetics with switches, fists, clods of earth, and sticks, and as they were being beaten, the naked ascetics were dragged out of the lodging. Brahmins and householders who saw this said: "Look, look, wise ones! The monks are fighting — it will cause a downpour of rain!" The group of six said: "Dear ones, companions, the domain-talk is still burning and has not yet died down — come, let us go to Śrāvastī." And so they went to Śrāvastī.

A disputant from the south, whose pursuit was to fling challenges at the world, named Acara, came to Śrāvastī and, wishing to have a debate, wishing for the implements of debate, went to the venerable Kauṇḍinya and said: "Oh monk, I have taken a few letters from my teacher, and therefore I wish to settle a discussion with you together." The venerable Kauṇḍinya replied: "Brahmin, I have no wish to debate with you — go away."

Then that world-challenger went to where the venerable Rāṣṭhapāla, Bhadra, Revatī, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāṃpati, and Subāhu were, and said to them: "Oh monks, I have taken a few letters from my teacher, and therefore I wish to settle a discussion with you together." They replied: "Brahmin, we have no wish to debate with you — go away."

Then that world-challenger went to where the venerable Śāriputra was and, having arrived, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Oh monk, I have taken a few letters from my teacher, and therefore I wish to settle a discussion with you together."

The venerable Śāriputra considered: does this one have any roots of virtue at all? He saw that he did. He considered: on whom does this depend? He saw that it depended on himself. He considered: can one such as this be tamed through debate? He saw that he could. He considered: how long will it take for him to be tamed? He saw that after seven days he would be tamed. And so the venerable Śāriputra said: "Brahmin, come here — let it be so." On that first day he engaged him in debate and dismissed him with the remainder still unresolved. The following day as well he dismissed him with the remainder unresolved. And so it continued through to the seventh day, dismissing him each time with the remainder unresolved.

Meanwhile, the report spread throughout all quarters that the world-challenger Acara from the south had come, and that he and the noble Śāriputra had been debating for seven days now, and that neither had defeated the other. Hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered there — some drawn by curiosity, some stirred by their roots of virtue from former times.

The venerable Śāriputra then considered: have those who can be tamed through debate gathered? He saw that they had. And so the venerable Śāriputra defeated that world-challenger, crushed him completely, dismissed him with not the slightest remainder left unresolved, and thus cut down the world-challenger and wanderer Acara. That one, having then become filled with faith, said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if I may obtain the going forth and full ordination in the Dharma and Vinaya well proclaimed by the Blessed One, and thereby the full status of a monk, I will practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." The venerable Śāriputra gave him the going forth and performed the full ordination.

Having thus gone forth, that one dwelt in solitude, in seclusion, in heedfulness, in application, and in self-surrender. And for the sake of which a son of good family shaves off hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and with perfect faith goes forth from home into homelessness — that supreme culmination of the holy life — he realized directly, actualized it with his own direct knowledge in that very life itself, and came to know: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is no knowing of another existence beyond this." He became an arhat: freed from attachment to the three realms, with a mind equal toward a clod of earth and gold, equal toward the sky and the palm of the hand, one who, like sandalwood placed upon an altar, had burst through the shell of the egg of ignorance by means of knowledge, one who had attained the higher knowledges, the superknowledges, and the individual perfect realizations, who had turned his back on continued existence, gain, and honor, and who was worthy of worship, veneration, and homage by the gods together with Indra and his retinue.

Then the assembly was filled with wonder, saying: "The venerable Śāriputra has defeated a challenger such as this."

Then the venerable Śāriputra, knowing the intentions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and natures of those in the assembly, taught the Dharma in such a way that many hundreds of thousands of living beings saw the Truths. Some of them directly realized the fruit of stream-entry (Skt. srotāpatti). Some directly realized the fruit of once-returning. Some directly realized the fruit of non-returning. And some went forth into homelessness, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized the state of arhathood. Having taught the Dharma in this way, the great majority of those in the assembly were established as ones who had turned toward the Buddha, who had arrived at the Dharma, and who had come to rest in the Saṅgha.

The venerable Śāriputra had finished off the wandering brahmin Carakā, a challenger belonging to the school of the world-hurlers, in the morning session, and in the afternoon the six groups arrived at Śrāvastī. The monks said to them: "Welcome, venerable ones, welcome! Where have you come from?" The venerable Śāriputra replied that he had come from the south, where he had finished off the challenger from the school of the world-hurlers, a wandering brahmin named Carakā who had come seeking a debate and the materials of debate, and had emerged victorious from the contest.

The six groups said: "How wonderful it is that the venerable Śāriputra, endowed with a twofold assembly, a general of the Dharma, one who follows in the wake of the wheel of Dharma, should have finished off a single challenger. Even if the venerable Śāriputra had not finished him off, the Blessed One was present nearby, so that would be no great wonder. But as for us six men defeating sixty naked ascetics — that is truly wonderful! We did so by teaching the Dharma to their bodies with the knowledge that struck at whatever branch of learning they took up. Whether they live or die, if they are alive now, they may either live a little longer or be on the verge of death."

Then the monks of few desires rebuked them, saying: "Why do the monks use the very limb by which they should feel shame as a source of pride?" — criticizing them, reviling them, and speaking ill of them. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident and in light of this occasion and these circumstances, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. The awakened Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign ignorance — and so forth, as before — until the awakened Blessed One questioned the six groups: "Monks, did you truly do such an unseemly thing?" They replied: "Blessed One, we did." The awakened Blessed One rebuked them, saying that such conduct was not in keeping with the practice of a renunciant, was not appropriate, was not fitting, was not in conformity with proper conduct, and was not something that one who has gone forth should do.

Having rebuked them in numerous ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: A monk who has dwelt for a day in a single dwelling place shall eat but one portion of alms food. Should he eat more than that, it constitutes a transgression." Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Then that householder took his carrying-net and went to that very cliff, and entered the shop of that householder. The householder began to weigh out goods for the naked ascetics. But Śāriputra did not send anyone on behalf of that householder; instead he gave to those friends who were worthy recipients of gifts.

He called out, "Come here!" and since that householder was a man of faith, he thought to himself, "These must indeed be hearers of the Blessed One — let me go and have a look." He went over, and upon seeing that the naked ascetics were beings devoid of shame and modesty, he felt that to speak ill of them openly would be unkind, and so he said nothing and sat in silence.

When they had eaten and departed, that householder said to the other householder, "Friend, is your field good and your seed good?" The other householder replied, "Friend, if the seed is good, the field itself — inhabited by naked ascetics who are without shame and modesty, who hold corrupt views, who haunt charnel grounds smelling of salt and bones, who are wholly given over to evil — is a soil that is thoroughly foul." The first householder said, "Friend, is there a better field than that?" The other replied, "There is — the hearers of the Blessed One."

The first householder said, "Friend, do not even speak their name!" The other said, "But have they come here?" "They have. They are the group of six." "And what have they been doing?" "Such and such things." The other replied, "Friend, you have taken worthless pebbles from a great ocean." The first householder said, "Are there other fine hearers of the Blessed One?" "There are. If you were ever to see the Venerable Śāriputra, the great Maudgalyāyana, Nāgasamudra, Apratihata, and other great hearers of the Blessed One, there would be such grounds for you to develop genuine faith." The first householder said, "If they were to come here, I would provide them with whatever alms food they require."

That householder then thought to himself, "Now I shall go and make a request to the Blessed One." So that householder converted his goods into money and, taking the proceeds, set out in the direction of Śrāvastī, and in time arrived at Śrāvastī. He then hid his carrying-net in the shop and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

Seated to one side, that householder addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, at a certain steep cliff there is a great householder who provides lodging for the renunciants (śramaṇas) and brahmins of the four directions. He supplies all who dwell there with whatever alms food they need. If it please the Blessed One — out of compassion for him — to send some monks there so that he may see the hearers of the Blessed One, that would be excellent."

The Blessed One said nothing to that householder — which was his consent.

Then that householder, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then the Blessed One considered which monk would be able to tame that householder along with his retinue and the assembly of people dwelling at that cliff, and he saw that it was the monk Śāriputra who would tame them. The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, tend to the great householder at that steep cliff, together with his retinue and the assembly of people dwelling at the cliff."

The Venerable Śāriputra replied, "Venerable One, I shall do as commanded," and having received the instruction from the Blessed One, he set out with a retinue of five hundred, wandering stage by stage in the direction of that cliff. Journeying in stages, he arrived at that cliff and entered the lodging house of that householder.

The householder heard that the Venerable Śāriputra had arrived at that cliff with a retinue of five hundred and had entered his lodging house. Upon hearing this, he went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Śāriputra proceeded to instruct that householder thoroughly with Dharma-endowed discourse, to lead him to full understanding, to uplift him completely, and to fill him with great joy. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed discourse, he thoroughly instructed him, led him to full understanding, uplifted him, and filled him with joy, and then fell silent.

Then that householder rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and facing the direction where the Venerable Śāriputra was, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra with these words: "Would the Venerable Śāriputra be so gracious as to accept tomorrow's midday meal together with the community of monks?" The Venerable Śāriputra accepted by remaining silent, and the householder, understanding from his silence that he had accepted, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra and departed from his presence.

That very night the householder made preparations, readying clean and pure food and drink.
