Rising early the next morning, he spread out seats, set out water for washing, and sent word to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, if you would be so kind as to arrive at the midday hour, may the Venerable Śāriputra please take note that the time has now come."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, in the early morning, dressed himself and, taking up his bowl and robes, set out surrounded by the assembly of monks with the community of monks before him, and went to the home of that householder. Having arrived, he sat upon the seat that had been spread at the head of the community of monks. The householder, perceiving that the Venerable Śāriputra and the community of monks were comfortably seated, satisfied and refreshed them from his own hands with clean and pure food and drink. Having in many ways satisfied and refreshed them from his own hands with clean and pure food and drink, and seeing that the Venerable Śāriputra had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set down his bowl, the householder took a low seat and sat before the Venerable Śāriputra in order to hear the Dharma.

Seated there, the householder said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, please teach the Dharma. For your sake, householder, let a seat be spread in this spacious open area. And tomorrow the noble Śāriputra will teach the Dharma to the great assembly of people here at this cliff. Make a proclamation: 'Let those among you who wish to hear the Dharma come forward.'"

The Venerable Śāriputra gave his thanks, rose from his seat, and departed. Since that householder was the most renowned person at that cliff, he had seats spread in a spacious open area and caused this proclamation to be made to the great assembly of people at that cliff: "Tomorrow the noble Śāriputra will teach the Dharma here. Let those among you who wish to hear the Dharma come forward. And any among you who does not come to see the truths there shall be doomed to wander in saṃsāra for a very long time."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra went to that place and sat upon the seat that had been spread at the head of the community of monks.

Many hundreds of thousands of living creatures had also gathered there — some out of curiosity, and some impelled by the roots of virtue they had planted in former lives. The Venerable Śāriputra, having understood the intentions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and dispositions of that assembly, taught the Dharma in such a way that the householder together with his retinue, along with twenty thousand living creatures, saw the truths directly. Some among them actualized the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti); some actualized the fruit of once-returning; some actualized the fruit of non-returning; some went forth from home life, and by abandoning all afflictions, actualized arhatship itself; some aroused the mind of awakening directed toward the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; some aroused the mind of awakening directed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and some aroused the mind of awakening directed toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete buddhahood. Having thus taught the Dharma, the greater part of that assembly was established in devotion to the Buddha, in reliance upon the Dharma, and in refuge in the Saṅgha.

Since the Venerable Śāriputra had taught the Dharma for a very long time, the sun had passed its zenith and the wind had come to blow at his back. The householder then said: "Venerable Śāriputra, please stay for this reason at my dwelling place, and I shall see to your needs by providing you with almsfood." Śāriputra replied: "Householder, it is on account of you yourself that the Blessed One will establish a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya — and so I must go."

Thereupon the Venerable Śāriputra, while still unwell, finished his meal and departed from that cliff, making his way toward Śrāvastī, traveling on gradually until at last he arrived at Śrāvastī. There the monks who were staying with the Venerable Śāriputra and those who were in his retinue asked him: "Venerable ones, how was the journey — comfortable? Was it somewhat comfortable? Or somewhat uncomfortable?" They replied: "It was somewhat comfortable, and somewhat uncomfortable." "What was comfortable? The fact that the preceptor accomplished the training of so many beings to be tamed — that was comfortable. And what was uncomfortable? The fact that the preceptor, though unwell, left that cliff in the heat of midday — that was uncomfortable."

When this was reported, the monks brought the matter before the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, except in case of illness, it is permitted for a monk to carry someone on his back." Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of those who desire training, who revere training, and who are devoted to the requisites of training, addressed the monks accordingly, with words in full accord with and consonant with that topic, befitting the occasion, and declared to the monks:

"Monks, what was formerly established remains as a rule, and what follows is now permitted. My śrāvakas are to learn this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: a monk who is not ill and who has spent the night in a single lodging place shall eat one portion of almsfood. To eat more than that is an offense.

The phrase 'who has spent the night in a single lodging place' means: one who has spent the night in the lodging place of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). 'A monk' means a monk of this Dharma. 'Who is not ill' means with the exception of one who is ill. 'Shall eat one portion of almsfood' means one meal. 'To eat more than that' means to eat a greater amount. 'Is an offense' means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of misfortune. Furthermore, as long as such a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome dharmas.

Therefore it is said to be an offense. How does a transgression come about in this regard? If one stays there and eats there, staying there incurs a fault and eating there incurs an offense. If one stays there but eats elsewhere, staying there incurs a fault but eating elsewhere incurs no offense. If one stays elsewhere but eats there, staying elsewhere incurs no offense but eating there incurs an offense. If one stays elsewhere and eats elsewhere, neither incurs an offense.

If an assembly, or relatives, or a donor says, "Stay right here," there is no offense. There is no offense for one who is a beginner, for one who is mentally deranged, for one who is disturbed in mind, or for one who is troubled by painful sensations.

Here ends the thirty-second offense, that of eating while staying in a single lodging place.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the fifty-second fascicle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When a group of like-minded monks had come up along the northern road to Śrāvastī, the Six-Group monks heard of this and said among themselves: "Friends, Nandaka, we have heard that a group of like-minded monks has come up along the northern road to Śrāvastī. If we can manage to accomplish even a small thing, let us go out to meet them. If they say, 'Give us some alms food,' we shall say, 'Having a full belly will do.' If they say, 'Give us some robes,' we shall take them." And so those monks went out and said, "Friends, come and sit down; we shall teach the Dharma." Those monks paid homage at their feet and sat down in front of them to hear the Dharma. The Six-Group monks then taught them the Dharma, after which those monks said, "Noble ones, please accept alms food right here." The Six-Group monks replied, "Friends, having a full belly will do."

The Six-Group monks came again and again to teach the Dharma, and again and again the like-minded monks said, "Noble ones, please accept alms food right here," and again and again the Six-Group monks replied, "Friends, having a full belly will do."

Then on another occasion the like-minded monks said to one another, "Knowledgeable ones, there is no grass here for the oxen. Let us go to another rocky hillside for a while, let the oxen graze and rest there, and when we have turned the wagons around and are ready to depart, then we shall set out for Śrāvastī." So they drove the oxen to a rocky hillside so that the oxen might graze there.

The Six-Group monks, rising early the next morning, went out to teach the Dharma as before. But after a while, when the like-minded monks were nowhere to be seen, those monks sat down troubled and disheartened. Then a certain man came and said, "Noble ones, why do you sit there so troubled and downcast?" The Six-Group monks replied, "Friend, some like-minded companions of ours were staying in this direction, and they have gone away without so much as a glance toward us." The man replied, "Noble ones, they have not gone away for good. It is just that their oxen had no fodder, so they have gone to a certain rocky hillside to graze the oxen, and they will come back here again." "Friend, may you be well," said the Six-Group monks, and they went to that rocky hillside.

When they arrived, the like-minded monks saw them approaching from a great distance and spoke these verses:

Do not go to a rugged mountain.
Even if you go, do not stay long.
Just as rugged mountains are,
So too is dwelling on a mountain.

One who dwells first on a mountain
Is like refined gold being polished;
But when one begins plotting harm to people,
That mountain becomes just what it is.

When the like-minded monks heard this, they said, "Noble ones, why do you reproach us?"

"Friends, you are our companions, and it is because we care for you that we have set aside our own virtuous pursuits to teach you the Dharma — and yet you have come here without so much as a glance back at us. Noble ones, it is not that we have all come here on our own account for all our purposes. The fact is, our oxen have no price here, and so we are here tending our oxen. As soon as we have sold our goods and set out, we shall return again to Śrāvastī. Friends, do stay — let us teach you the Dharma."

At that, the like-minded monks prostrated at the feet of the Six-Group monks, took seats lower than theirs, and sat down before them to hear the Dharma. The Six-Group monks taught them the Dharma, and when they had done so, the monks said, "Noble ones, please take alms right here."

"Friends, eating one's fill is enough."

Then the merchant leader said, "Wise ones, the noble ones have said that eating one's fill again and again is sufficient — but these people have no food; they are short of food. Let food be given to them."

"So be it," they agreed, and they served each of the Six-Group monks a portion the color of a silk-worm larva.

Then the Six-Group monks said, "Friends, you say again and again to take alms — but let us see what kind of alms are actually being given." One of the Six-Group monks took up a vessel the size of a cooking-pot and said, "Pour in here." The like-minded monks thought, "This vessel is enormous; if it is filled, there will be enough alms to fill all their bellies." And so they filled that vessel from their provisions and offered it.

The other Six-Group monks did the same, one after another, each taking up a vessel the size of a cooking-pot. And when the like-minded monks had filled all six such vessels from their provisions and offered them, all the provisions the like-minded monks had for the journey were exhausted. Then the like-minded monks said, "Noble ones, we came here with a small amount of provisions for the return journey — and all of that has been consumed. Let us send this man along with some kārṣāpaṇas to Śrāvastī together with the noble ones; let the noble ones purchase our provisions, prepare them, and send them back to us along with someone to escort them. Friends, please do this."

The like-minded monks sent a man behind the Six-Group monks with kārṣāpaṇas. The Six-Group monks went to a temple hall and said to the man, "Good fellow, do this task." He did it. Then they said, "Good fellow, do this other task as well." He did that too. The Six-Group monks kept the man busy with one errand after another until the sun went down. Then they dismissed him afterward, saying, "Now go and make the purchases."

The man bought the provisions himself and, as he was making his way back through the dense outskirts of Śrāvastī, he was attacked by bandits, and he arrived alone back among the like-minded monks.

When the like-minded monks saw him, they asked, "What have you brought?" He replied, "Nothing." "Why not?" "I was set upon by bandits." They said, "Did the noble ones not send someone to escort you?" He replied, "Wise ones, in truth it was they themselves who did this to me — they kept me running errands alone from morning until the sun went down, then sent me off saying, 'Now go and make the purchases.' I bought the provisions myself, and as I was making my way back through the dense outskirts of Śrāvastī, I was attacked by bandits."

At this the like-minded monks criticized and rebuked the Six-Group monks, saying: "The conduct of a śramaṇa (ascetic) among the Śākya sons is mere words; the conduct of a brahmin is mere words — for they say, 'I will help,' yet do nothing but harm." And they spread the story abroad.

They slandered them in this way. Now, this is how things stood at that time: the Blessed One, the buddha, had not yet established the training rules for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now in Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had taken a wife from among his social equals. He took pleasure with her, was delighted with her, and lived with her in joy and happiness. A daughter was born to them on the right side, and they raised her and brought her up until she was grown. When the time came to find suitors for all the other girls of her age, none came to ask for this girl, because she was a daughter born on the right side.

There was another householder in Śrāvastī who had likewise taken a wife from his social equals. His first wife passed away through the ripening of her own karma. He took a second, and she too passed away. In the same way, he took wife after wife up to the seventh, and each of them passed away. Because of the karma that would lead to him being slandered, this householder came to be called "the wife-killer" — the one who kills his wives. Whenever someone came to ask for a daughter for him, the girl's family refused to give her, saying: "Why should we give our daughter away? We will not." When he sought to arrange a match through female go-betweens, those women too said: "Why should we send her to your house when you only destroy us?"

The householder fell into utter despair and began to mend the fence around his house himself. One day a friend, a younger companion of his, came by and saw him and asked: "What are you doing?" The householder replied: "I am mending the fence." The friend asked: "Why are you mending the fence yourself?" The householder said: "I took one wife, and she passed away through the ripening of her own karma. I took a second, and she too passed away. In the same way, up to the seventh — each one passed away." The friend said: "Why don't you seek another?" The householder answered: "When I try, they refuse to give a girl, saying, 'Why should we give our daughter away? We will not.'" The friend said: "Why not seek through female go-betweens?" The householder replied: "I tried, and those women too said, 'Why should we send her to your house when you only destroy us?'" The friend said: "Why not seek the girl born on the right side? They will not refuse her. Go and ask — since that family is utterly weary of her, they will give her." The householder went to the home of the father of the right-side daughter and greeted them, saying: "May all be well, may all be well." They said: "What have you come to ask?" He replied: "I have come to ask for the girl — to ask for a bride." "Which girl?" "The one born on the right side." Since they were utterly exhausted by her, they said: "We will give her." He said: "When will you send her as a bride?" He replied: "In several days' time." The friend said, "Let it be so," and left.

Then that younger friend was seized by regret, thinking: "I have done something wrong by urging my friend to seek the right-side daughter. She is of ill omen, and if she causes my friend's death, that would be terrible." He went to the householder and said: "Have you obtained the right-side daughter?" The householder said: "I have." Then the friend spoke these verses:

Chewing a twig of lac-tree wood,
lying down showing the back at nightfall,
sleeping heavily, drinking curds,
and taking to wife a right-side daughter —
even the peaceful deteriorate from their peace.
As when dropping strikes a pit,
as iron falls upon stone,
you too may be slain by a wife —
and since she is a right-side daughter,
let us see which of you two prevails.

"Friend, that woman is of ill omen, and it would be terrible if she were to cause your death. Instead, take my own sister, a left-side daughter."

The householder said: "Friend, I cannot abandon her now. Nevertheless, let some arrangement be made in this matter."

The mother of the right-side daughter then began preparing a wedding feast. Now, the house was one that members of the group of six frequented, and so the group of six divided the morning alms route among themselves, took up their bowls and robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Going about their rounds in due order, they entered that very house. As they were about to receive their portions, the porters who were carrying loads saw them, and said: "Sister, is your marriage ceremony soon upon you?" She replied: "Noble ones, your elder sister is about to be given in marriage, and we are preparing her wedding feast." The group of six said: "Sister, might we receive a little something?" She said: "Noble ones, who would give to you? This is yours — it belongs to you yourselves." The group of six said: "Sister, never mind what may be stored away in the back — let all that be. Just see what you can give us right now." She relaxed her guard, and those porters filled every bowl with loads of food, and the group of six collected all her food and departed.

After a while the householder arrived, and his wife said: "Noble sons who are recipients of gifts came along, and they took all the food and left. Please tell him who is to be the husband to stay just a few more days while the wedding feast is prepared for your friend." The householder said: "Good woman, he cannot stay. Just send the girl off as a bride, and later provide food to the relatives." His wife said: "Noble son, he is a wife-killer, and so no one else would give him a daughter. He should leave, and she will stay." The householder went to the man and said: "My son, whatever food we had prepared, the recipients of gifts have consumed it. Now, please stay just a few more days while food is prepared for the relatives." He replied: "I will not stay. If this very day you send the bride and give her to me, I will take her as my wife. If you do not give her, I will take another wife and abandon your daughter." The householder went to his wife and told her: "Good woman, the husband says: 'If this very day you send the bride and give her to me, I will take her as my wife. If you do not give her, I will take another wife and abandon your daughter.'" His wife said: "Noble son, he is a wife-killer, and so who else would give him a daughter?" But she then began preparing the wedding feast.

The husband took the friend's sister, a left-side daughter, as his wife. The mother of the right-side daughter, having prepared the food, again said to the householder: "Noble son, now go to that husband and invite him to come and receive his bride." The householder went to him and said: "My son, now come and receive your bride." He replied: "You caused me to miss that day, and so now I will not take her."

The householder seized that husband, crying out and dragging him to the royal palace, and the husband defeated the householder in that proceeding.

The mother of the right-side daughter sat weeping, saying: "He has not taken my daughter." Meanwhile, on the last day of that period, certain neighbors were speaking critically of the practice of the śramaṇas among the sons of the Śākyas — speaking critically of the śramaṇa's way of life and of the brahmin's way of life — saying: "In this manner, they create obstacles for a daughter who has already been given away." And they mocked them openly.

While they were speaking critically in this way, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then, as before, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks in relation to this occurrence, this basis of deliberation, and this occasion, and so forth. As before: "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, knowingly bring things to light" — and so forth as before. The Blessed One questioned the group of six, saying: "Monks, is it true that you have done something so unseemly?" "Venerable one, we have." The Blessed One rebuked them for conduct unworthy of the śramaṇa's way, for conduct unsuitable, improper, and inconsistent with the rules — declaring that what has been gone forth into the renunciant life should not be done. Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training is to be established in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

When a large number of monks have gone to houses, if faithful brahmins and householders press upon those monks flour and the like, and lumps of food, repeatedly and in due time, and if those monks desire to accept, they may take two or three bowlfuls. Having taken two or three bowlfuls, they should go out to the park outside, share with the monks who are staying there, and eat together themselves. That is the proper procedure."

The word "monks" refers to the group of six. "A large number" means more than two — that is what "a large number" means. "To houses" means to the houses of brahmins and householders. "Have gone" means having departed. "Those monks" means those same monks. "Faithful brahmins and householders" — "faithful" means those with faith directed toward the buddha, toward the Dharma, and toward the Saṅgha; those who have gone for refuge to the buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha. "Flour and the like" means flour and fine flour. "Lumps of food" means cooked cakes. "Repeatedly and in due time" means offered again and again. "If they desire" means if they seek it. "Those monks" means whatever monks there may be. "They may take two or three bowlfuls" — there are three kinds of bowl: large, medium, and small. The large one is that into which, when a thick rice gruel cooked in a small vessel of the Magadha measure, together with legumes and vegetables, is poured, the edge of the rim alone does not reach to the navel of the thumb. The small one is that into which, when a thick rice gruel cooked in a full small Magadha vessel, together with legumes and vegetables, is poured, the edge of the rim alone does not reach to the navel of the thumb. The medium is between those two. "If one takes more than that" means more than that amount. "It constitutes a transgression" — it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of misfortune. Furthermore, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome dharmas — therefore it is said to constitute a transgression.

"Having taken two or three full alms-bowls, go to the pleasure grove outside, and share with whatever monks are gathered there" — this means: go to the temple outside the house, and give to whatever monks are gathered there as well.

Now, how does a transgression arise in this matter? If a monk takes three large alms-bowls, the act of taking constitutes a wrongdoing, and the act of eating constitutes a transgression. If a monk takes two large and one medium, the act of taking constitutes a wrongdoing, and the act of eating constitutes a transgression. If a monk takes two large and one small, the act of taking constitutes a wrongdoing, and the act of eating constitutes a transgression. If a monk takes two medium and one large, the act of taking constitutes a wrongdoing, and the act of eating constitutes a transgression. Whatever amount a monk takes in alms that exceeds two and a half small measures, in all such cases it constitutes a transgression. There is no transgression for whatever a donor does of their own accord. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is mentally disturbed, one whose mind is agitated, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The thirty-third transgression — that of taking more than three alms-bowls' worth — is complete.

A summary verse:

One seat, and giving up water likewise,
Fermented foods, permitted foods,
Let go, excessive gruel,
And the group of sour foods — these are gathered here.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the pleasure grove of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, I eat only one meal per sitting. Since I eat one meal per sitting, I live on little, am little troubled, am little afflicted, am light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and I dwell in comfort." "Monks, come now, you too eat one meal per sitting. When you eat one meal per sitting, you will live on little, be little troubled, be little afflicted, be light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and dwell in comfort."

The monks came to eat one meal per sitting. But when they ate one meal per sitting, if they saw their preceptor they would rise, and if they saw their abbot, their teacher, or someone like a teacher they would also rise — and because they would not eat saying "We have given this up," they became emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies lost their fullness.

The blessed buddhas act knowingly yet feign ignorance, and so the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, I said to the monks, 'Monks, I eat one meal per sitting. Since I eat one meal per sitting, I live on little, am little troubled, am little afflicted, am light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and dwell in comfort. Monks, come now, you too eat one meal per sitting. When you eat one meal per sitting, you will live on little, be little troubled, be little afflicted, be light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and dwell in comfort.' Now, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which the monks have become emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies have lost their fullness?"

"Reverend monks, the Blessed One has declared: 'Monks, I eat one meal per sitting. When I eat one meal per sitting, I live on little, am little troubled, am little afflicted, am light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and dwell in comfort. Monks, come now, you too eat one meal per sitting. When you eat one meal per sitting, you will live on little, be little troubled, be little afflicted, be light of movement, live with vitality and strength, in happiness, without blame, and dwell in comfort.'

"After the Blessed One declared this, the monks began seeking out the single-meal practice. Yet in their pursuit of the single-meal practice, when they saw their preceptor, abbot, teacher, or one who is like a teacher, they would rise to their feet. Having done so, they would say, 'We have given this up,' and would not seek to eat — and because they did not eat, they became emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies lost their fullness. Reverend one, this is the cause, this is the condition, by which the monks have now become emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies have lost their fullness."

Then Ānanda said: "Therefore, reverend one, one should eat a satisfying sufficiency without giving up food entirely, and when eating has commenced, one should not rise to one's feet upon seeing one's preceptor, abbot, teacher, or one who is like a teacher."

The Blessed One then declared: "One should eat a satisfying sufficiency without giving up food entirely, and when eating has commenced, one should not rise to one's feet upon seeing one's preceptor, abbot, teacher, or one who is like a teacher."

But having heard this, the monks gave up food as completely as water, renouncing even leaves, pulse, roots, and dried provisions, saying "We have given these up" — and because they would not eat, they became emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies lost their fullness.

Now the buddha, the Blessed One, knowing full well, asked the venerable Ānanda this question: "Ānanda, I have declared that one should eat a satisfying sufficiency without giving up food entirely, and that when eating has commenced, one should not rise to one's feet upon seeing one's preceptor, abbot, teacher, or one who is like a teacher. What then is the cause, what is the condition, by which the monks have now become emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies have lost their fullness?"

"Reverend Blessed One, after you declared that one should eat a satisfying sufficiency without giving up food entirely, and that when eating has commenced one should not rise to one's feet upon seeing one's preceptor, abbot, teacher, or one who is like a teacher — the monks gave up food as completely as water, renouncing even leaves, pulse, roots, and dried provisions, saying 'We have given these up,' and would not eat. This is the cause, reverend one, this is the condition, by which the monks have now become emaciated, feeble, lean, thin, and their bodies have lost their fullness."

"Ānanda, therefore these are the five planted things by eating which one will not come to give up food, and these are the five cooked foods by eating which one will come to give up other foods.

"What are the five planted things by eating which one will not come to give up food? They are: roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits that are cultivated. These are the five planted things by eating which one will not come to give up food.

"What are the five cooked foods by eating which one will come to give up other foods? They are: cooked grain, hot cooked rice, meat, oil-rich food, and sweet food. These are the five cooked foods by eating which one will come to give up other foods."

After finishing the five planted things, one should eat the five cooked foods; and after eating the five cooked foods, one should not partake of the five planted things. A monk who eats the five cooked foods and then partakes of the five planted things incurs a serious offence.

The Blessed One had declared, "The five planted things will not lead to giving up food, whereas the five cooked foods will lead to giving up other foods." But they refused to eat from the hands that had handled those things, and from the alms-bowls that had been touched by them, saying "We have given those up." And so those monks became emaciated, weak, haggard, gaunt, and their bodies wasted away.

Now, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know and yet set things in motion, and so the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, I have declared that the five planted things will not lead to giving up food, whereas the five cooked foods will lead to giving up other foods. So then, what is the cause, and what is the condition, by which monks have now come to be emaciated, weak, haggard, gaunt, and with bodies wasted away?"

The venerable Ānanda replied: "Blessed One, you declared, 'The five planted things will not lead to giving up food, whereas the five cooked foods will lead to giving up other foods,' and so they refuse to eat, saying 'We have given those up,' from the hands that have handled such things and from the alms-bowls that have been touched by them. That is the cause, Blessed One, and that is the condition by which monks have now come to be emaciated, weak, haggard, gaunt, and with bodies wasted away."

"Ānanda, that being the case, one should speak of giving up in terms of five causes, and one should speak of not giving up in terms of five causes.

"What are the five causes by which giving up is to be declared? They are: having food, having someone to present food, having food that has been begun, having food that has been relinquished, and falling away from one's deportment.

"How is there 'having food'? By there being the five planted things and the five cooked foods. That is how there is having food.

"How is there 'having someone to present food'? By there being a woman, a man, or a person of the third sex. That is how there is having someone to present food.

"How is there 'having food that has been begun'? By there being an undertaking of all five planted things and all five cooked foods. That is how there is having food that has been begun.

"How is there 'having food that has been relinquished'? By there being a relinquishment of the five planted things and the five cooked foods. That is how there is having food that has been relinquished.

"How is there 'falling away from one's deportment'? By rising from the seat on which one had been sitting. That is how there is falling away from one's deportment.

"By these five causes, giving up is to be declared.

"What are the five causes by which not giving up is to be declared? They are: having no food, having no one to present food, having no food that has been begun, having no food that has been relinquished, and not falling away from one's deportment.

"How is there 'having no food'? By there being no five planted things and no five cooked foods. That is how there is having no food.

"How is there 'having no one to present food'? By there being no woman, no man, and no person of the third sex. That is how there is having no one to present food.

"How is there 'having no food that has been begun'? By there being no undertaking of all five planted things and all five cooked foods. That is how there is having no food that has been begun.

"How is there 'having no food that has been relinquished'? By there being no relinquishment of the five planted things and the five cooked foods. That is how there is having no food that has been relinquished.

"How is there 'not falling away from one's deportment'? By not having risen from the seat on which one had been sitting.

That is how there is not falling away from one's deportment. By those five factors, the food is to be declared as not having been relinquished.

Furthermore, by five factors food is to be declared as having been relinquished, and by five factors it is to be declared as not having been relinquished. What are the five factors by which it is to be declared as having been relinquished? Relinquishing by means of what is suitable; relinquishing by means of something mixed with what is suitable; relinquishing by means of something that has not been stored; relinquishing by means of something mixed with what has not been stored; and falling away from one's deportment. By those five factors, the food is to be declared as having been relinquished. What are the five factors by which it is to be declared as not having been relinquished? Relinquishing by means of what is not suitable; relinquishing by means of something mixed with what is not suitable; relinquishing by means of something that has been stored; relinquishing by means of something mixed with what has been stored; and not falling away from one's deportment. By those five factors, the food is to be declared as not having been relinquished.

Furthermore, by five words without a remainder, the food is to be declared as having been relinquished, and by five words with a remainder, it is to be declared as not having been relinquished. What are the five words without a remainder? The words "Release it," "Give it," "Take it away," "It has been eaten," and "It is enough." By those five words without a remainder, the food is to be declared as having been relinquished. What are the five words with a remainder? The words "Release it for now," "Give it for now," "Take it away for now," "It has been eaten for now," and "It is enough for now." By those five words with a remainder, the food is to be declared as not having been relinquished.

After the Blessed One declared that a monk must not eat food that has been relinquished, the group of six went ahead and ate both food that had been relinquished and food that had not been relinquished. Then monks of few wishes, on learning that the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not eat food that has been relinquished, reproached them, saying: "Why do these monks eat food both when it has been relinquished and when it has not been relinquished?" They rebuked them, spread the matter abroad, and spoke critically. At that, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though already knowing, made inquiry — and so forth as before. The buddha, the Blessed One, then questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, when I declared that a monk must not eat food that has been relinquished, did you truly eat both food that had been relinquished and food that had not been relinquished?" "Venerable One, it is so." The buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them, saying: "That which is not in keeping with the practice of a renunciant, not in accord, not fitting, not consonant with the rules — such conduct is not to be done by one who has gone forth." Then, after reproaching them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers is to be established in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, having eaten and being satisfied, accepts further food from what has been relinquished, or undertakes to eat it, or eats it — he commits a transgression.

Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain householder invited the buddha along with the monastic Saṅgha of monks to another home for the midday meal.

There were very many monk attendants for very many sick monks, and those attendants, having eaten themselves, stored away the leftover almsfood from the sick monks' full bowls. The sick monks were unable to eat, and the monk attendants, for their part, would not eat it either, saying, "We have already relinquished it." There being no one from the enclosure nor any novices present, they piled up great mounds of food in the enclosure, and when crows came to eat there, a great clamor of crows arose.

The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know yet feign not to know. And so the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is the cause of this great clamor of crows that has arisen in the enclosure?"

"Blessed One, a certain householder invited the buddha along with the monastic Saṅgha of monks to another home for the midday meal. There were very many attendants for very many monks who were bathing, and those attendants, having bathed themselves, stored away the leftover almsfood from the bathing monks' soaking bowls. The bathing monks had not yet had a chance to bathe, and the monk bathing-attendants, for their part, would not use it either, saying, 'We have already relinquished it.' There being no one from the enclosure nor any novices present, they piled up great mounds of food in the enclosure, and when crows came to scavenge there, a great clamor of crows arose."

Then the Blessed One thought to himself: "I should grant a further permission, both so that the monks may remain in comfort and so that the donors' act of giving may be fully enjoyed." Having thought thus, he said to the monks: "Monks, therefore I permit you to eat with a further permission as what has been additionally made."

When the Blessed One had declared that eating with a further permission was permitted, the monks did not know how to make the further permission. The Blessed One then declared: "If a monk has finished eating and relinquished his meal — having made it complete and final — and if any person who has themselves finished eating and fully made things complete then finds food and wishes to eat, that monk should join his two hands together, receive it, and eat. But if a monk has finished eating and has not relinquished, yet has not fallen from proper conduct, or if a monk has finished eating and has relinquished and has not fallen from proper conduct, one should sit before that person in a squatting posture and say these words: 'Venerable one, please pay attention. I, the monk called such-and-such, am one who has sought and relinquished, and having made things complete and final, I seek to find and eat what has been additionally prepared. Please grant it to me with the further permission.' Then, after that person has eaten two or three mouthfuls, he should say: 'That will do for you — now go.' And with that the further permission is made.

In that regard, if the monk has finished eating and has not relinquished, and has not fallen from proper conduct, he himself, having eaten two or three mouthfuls, makes the further permission. In that regard, if the monk has finished eating and has relinquished, and has not fallen from proper conduct, he should hand it over without eating it himself, saying 'That will do for you — now go,' and thereby the further permission is made. If one eats without doing this, it becomes a serious transgression.

In five cases it should be said that the further permission has not been made: what are the five? When it is done outside the boundary, in a direction where the person cannot be reached, from behind, from the side, and when one leads the other into a lapse from proper conduct. In those five cases it should be said that the further permission has not been made.

In five cases it should be said that the further permission has been made: what are the five? When it is not outside the boundary, in a direction where the person can be reached, not from behind,

not from the side, and when one does not lead the other into a lapse from proper conduct. In those five cases it should be said that the further permission has been made.

Furthermore, in five cases it should be said that the further permission has not been made: what are the five? When it is outside the boundary, in a direction where the person cannot be reached, at the base of the alms bowl, from above, and when one leads the other into a lapse from proper conduct. In those five cases it should be said that the further permission has not been made. In five cases it should be said that the further permission has been made: what are the five? When it is not outside the boundary, in a direction where the person can be reached, not at the base of the alms bowl, not from above, and when one does not lead the other into a lapse from proper conduct. In those five cases it should be said that the further permission has been made.

What one person has made as a further permission may be eaten by many, and in this one should have no regret.

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of those who desire the training, who are respectful toward the training, and who are equipped with the requisites of the training, addressed the monks with words suited to this occasion, words of greater import, words endowed with qualities befitting it, and then declared to the monks: "Monks, the foregoing was a rule, and this is a permission. My hearers should establish the following as a training rule in the Vinaya: If a monk, having already eaten and having set aside the remainder, makes an appointment or eats food without having made a further permission, it is a transgression.

As for the phrase 'a monk,' this refers to the group of six or to anyone else of that kind. The phrase 'having already eaten and having set aside the remainder' means from what has been fully and completely consumed. The phrase 'without having made a further permission' means without making it additional, without discarding it and without having fully released it. The phrase 'makes an appointment or eats food' refers to the five kinds of foods to be appointed and the five kinds of foods to be eaten. The phrase 'eats' means swallowing it down the throat. The phrase 'it is a transgression' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the lower destinies of the hell-beings, animals, the wretched hungry ghosts, the miserable states, and the lower rebirths. Furthermore, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome Dharmas — and for that reason it is said to be a transgression.

As for how a transgression arises in this case: if a monk, perceiving as set aside what has been set aside, makes an appointment or eats food without having made a further permission, it is a transgression. If a monk, with doubt about what has been set aside, makes an appointment or eats food without having made a further permission, it is a transgression. If a monk, perceiving as set aside what has not been set aside, makes an appointment or eats food without having made a further permission, it is a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt about what has not been set aside, makes an appointment or eats food without having made a further permission, it is a wrongdoing.

The venerable Upāli (Nyeba Khor) asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, how should something like a hard food be set aside?" The venerable Upāli is the one who tilts his face upward. "Venerable one, how should something like a soft food be set aside?" The venerable Upāli is the one who extends the five fingers forward. There is no setting aside for what the venerable Upāli has drunk down the throat. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is overcome by feeling.

The transgression relating to the one-seat meal is the thirty-fourth. It is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was a householder in Śrāvastī who had taken a wife of equal family and was sporting and rejoicing together with her.

sporting and rejoicing together with her. When he reached old age, his relatives were exhausted, his wealth was exhausted, and his possessions were depleted. He said to his wife, "Good woman, in my old age I am unable to acquire wealth, so I shall go forth into homelessness. My lady, please do likewise."

He went to the Jeta Grove, approached a certain monk, prostrated at his two feet, and said, "Noble one, I wish to go forth — please give me the going forth." The monk replied, "Good sir, I myself have gone forth and am newly ordained, so it is not appropriate for me to give the going forth." The man said, "Noble one, since I have come to you first of all, please entrust me to some other monk." There was a monk whose preceptor was a forest-dweller who practiced meditative concentration in a hermitage, so that monk led him to the preceptor and said, "Preceptor, this son of good family wishes to go forth and receive full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya. For the sake of compassion, preceptor, please give him the going forth and please confer full ordination." The preceptor replied, "My son, the Blessed One has declared that it is not appropriate for monks to give the going forth and confer full ordination in a remote place and then fail to guide and teach the ordinand." The man said, "Preceptor, please just give the going forth and full ordination; I myself will read to him and teach him." The monk then gave him the going forth and conferred full ordination, and said, "Good sir, this person is your teacher, so you will read and receive instruction from him. As for whatever conduct is to be practiced, ask him about it and do it accordingly."

When he was reading and receiving instruction from the teacher, this newly entered elder forgot things repeatedly and kept incurring downfalls, so the teacher made him sit cross-legged before him and would put him through the confessing of downfalls. The newly entered elder thought, "My teacher constantly makes me sit cross-legged before him and puts me through confessing downfalls. I wonder what means there might be for me to make him sit cross-legged before me and put him through confessing downfalls."

A householder invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to another house at midday. The community of monks headed by the Buddha went, the Blessed One ate the midday meal, and then began to teach the Dharma to that householder. The monk said to the newly entered elder, "Elder, come over here — walk along in the manner of laypeople going home." The two of them walked along in the manner of laypeople going home. The people there said, "Noble ones, please take the midday meal. Householder, we two have already eaten." He replied, "Take what is left over and eat the surplus." He looked at the newly entered elder's face and said, "Elder, would you like some?" "I would." The two of them accepted what was given, departed, and went to the Jeta Grove. The monk said to the newly entered elder, "Elder, would you wash the bowls, or else go into the assembly hall and eat the surplus?" The newly entered elder said, "Please allow me to eat the surplus." The monk began washing the bowls, and the newly entered elder took the alms-bowl and entered the assembly hall, where he made himself eat the surplus from his own bowl but did not make the monk eat the surplus from his own bowl.

The monk washed the bowls, entered the assembly hall, and said, "Elder, were you permitted to eat the surplus?" He replied, "You were permitted." The monk sat down and ate. When he had eaten, the newly entered elder said, "Teacher, please open the confession session." He opened it. The newly entered elder said, "A downfall has occurred for you; please restore it according to the Dharma."

He replied, "I see no downfall." The newly entered elder said, "You ate food designated as a meal and as eatables without having made it into surplus." He replied, "Did I not ask you whether I might make you eat the surplus?" The newly entered elder said, "I permitted it for myself." He replied, "Newly entered elder, no downfall will attach to me, but there will indeed be a case of this very kind in which you yourself will incur a downfall." He then reported the matter to the monks. Some monks of few wishes, asking why monks would knowingly seek out an opportunity against a monk who had already eaten and had set aside his food, with the thought "By any means, let this monk commit an offense," and taking that very thought as their motivation, would serve him food not made into surplus, saying "Venerable one, eat this, take this of this" — these monks criticized, rebuked, and condemned him, saying "How can they offer, at such a time, food and eatables not made into surplus?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One — "on this occurrence, with this as the basis, and on this occasion, assembled the community of monks" — and so forth, as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though omniscient, act as though unaware" — and so forth, also as before. The buddha, the Blessed One, questioned that monk: "Monk, is it true that you knowingly sought out an opportunity against a monk who had already eaten and set aside his food, thinking 'By any means, let this monk commit an offense,' and taking that very thought as your motivation, served him food not made into surplus, saying 'Venerable one, eat this, take this'?" He replied, "It is true, Blessed One." The buddha, the Blessed One, reproved him, saying that what is not the manner of a contemplative, what is not concordant, what is not proper, what is not in keeping with the rule — such conduct is not to be performed by one who has gone forth into homelessness. Thereupon, the Blessed One reproved him in many ways and then declared to the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, the training rule for śrāvakas in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, knowingly seeking out an opportunity against a monk who has already eaten and set aside his food, with the thought 'By any means, let this monk commit an offense,' and taking that very thought as his motivation, says 'Venerable one, eat this, take this' — if he offers food and eatables not made into surplus, it is a downfall-producing act.

Now, 'whatever monk' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Knowingly' means either by his own recognition or by another's informing him. 'Monk' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Who has already eaten and set aside his food' means one who has finished eating completely and conclusively. 'Seeking out an opportunity' means seeking a fault. 'With the thought "By any means, let this monk commit an offense"' means thinking 'By any means, let this monk be made to incur a downfall.' 'Taking that very thought as his motivation' means no other motivation than that. 'Venerable one, eat this, take this' refers to food designated as a meal and as eatables. 'Not made into surplus' means not having made it into surplus, not having discarded it, not having fully relinquished it. 'Food designated as a meal and as eatables' refers to the five kinds of meal-foods and the five kinds of eatables. 'If he offers' means if he offers again and again. 'A downfall-producing act' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells among sentient beings, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, into the state of ruin and wrong falling."

Furthermore, it is taught that so long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obscures the wholesome qualities — and for that reason it is called a downfall-producing act.

As for how a downfall arises in this case: if a monk, knowing even slightly that another monk has eaten his meal and has set aside the remainder, seeks an occasion with the thought, "By whatever means may I bring about an offense for this monk," and, using just that intention as the condition, then says to the venerable one, "Eat this! Take this!" — offering food designated as a meal and as eatables that has not been made into surplus — a downfall-producing act arises in every instance. For one who is a first-time offender, for one who is mentally deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by feelings, there is no downfall. The thirty-fifth downfall-producing rule concerning offering to one who has set aside the remainder is complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the fifty-third fascicle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, the monk Devadatta, together with a great many monks, gathered inside a pleasure hall and was eating food. A monk of few duties reproached them, saying, "Why do you monks gather inside a pleasure hall to eat?" He slandered them, spread it about, and criticized them. On that occasion, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One convened the community of monks on account of this occurrence, this ground for discussion, and this occasion — and so forth, as before. As for the passage "the Blessed Buddhas, though knowing, nevertheless act with feigned ignorance" — this too is as before. The Blessed One questioned Devadatta: "Devadatta, is it true that you gathered together with a great many monks inside a pleasure hall and ate food?" "It is true, Reverend One." The Blessed One rebuked him in the manner of: "This is not the way of a monastic practitioner; it is not fitting, not proper, not in keeping with the rule — this is not to be done by one who has gone forth." Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, having seen the ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Eating while gathered together is a downfall-producing act." Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

A great many monks who were ill went to a physician's quarters. The physician, upon seeing them, said, "Handsome ones, prescribe medicine for us." They replied, "Noble ones, you yourselves should present what is to be given. Who will provide it? We shall accept it." "Is it for the entire Saṅgha?" "No — it is for as many monks as are sick." The handsome physician said, "The Blessed One has established a rule of training against eating while gathered together." They replied, "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate; making this itself the condition, there may well be a case in which he would grant permission." Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, excepting the time of illness."

Then, when the monks had performed work for the Saṅgha and for the stūpa, they grew weak from hunger, lay down exhausted, and were unable to engage in virtuous endeavors. Some faithful brahmins and householders came to the monastery, saw them, and asked, "Noble ones, if you are wholly devoted to the Teaching, why do you lie down exhausted and fail to engage in virtuous activities?" They replied, "We are hungry." "Why do you not request food? Who will provide it? We ourselves will provide it."

"Will you feed the entire Saṅgha?" "No, we will feed only you." When they said, "Good friends, the Blessed One has established a training rule concerning eating communally," the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, excepting the time of work."

When monks who were companions were traveling together along a road, they came to a certain cliff-face and said, "Good friends, wait here for a little while as we go out on alms round to this cliff-face." The companions said, "Noble ones, there is danger of bandits in this area behind us. Come this way, and we ourselves will provide alms." "Will one person give to all?" "No, some will give to four, and others to five." When they said, "Good friends, the Blessed One has established a training rule concerning eating communally," and those monks thereby greatly curtailed their eating, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, excepting the time of travel on the road."

When a great many monks who were companions boarded a boat together and were sailing through a region, they came to a certain cliff-face and said, "Good friends, wait here for a little while as we go out on alms round to this cliff-face." The companions said, "Noble ones, there is danger of bandits behind us here on the river. Come this way, and we ourselves will provide alms." "Will one person give to all?" "No, some will give to four, and others to five." When they said, "Good friends, the Blessed One has established a training rule concerning eating communally," and those monks thereby greatly curtailed their eating, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, excepting the time of being on board a boat."

The Blessed One then proclaimed that a topknot festival, a great festival, and a five-yearly festival should be held. On that occasion a great assembly of monks gathered, and faithful brahmins and householders said to the monks, "Noble ones, come and accept the midday meal." The monks replied, "Will you feed the entire Saṅgha?" "Noble ones, where would we find sufficient resources to feed the entire Saṅgha? As it is, some will feed twenty, and others thirty." When they said, "Good friends, the Blessed One has established a training rule concerning eating communally," the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, excepting the time of a great assembly."

There was a time when King Rūpiṇīhṛdaya had not yet seen the truths, and during that time he had assigned the sustenance of the Kundū-tsho grove to an individual called Kundū-tsho. When he came to see the truths, the Kundū-tsho grove sustenance was taken away and offered to the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Blessed One. The maternal uncle of King Rūpiṇīhṛdaya, a man named Kundū-tsho, had gone forth from the household life and the king said, "Noble ones, this is my maternal uncle. So long as he does not engage in corrupt conduct, please allow him to stay alone. When he comes to engage in corrupt conduct, I myself will then expel him too." And so King Rūpiṇīhṛdaya supplied that Kundū-tsho with whatever food he needed. The monks practiced diligently without sleeping in the early and late watches of the night, and Kundū-tsho, seeing this, became very devoted. He then said to the monks, "I too shall provide you with the midday meal. Do proceed in this way."

"Would it be for the entire Saṅgha?" "No, my lady. Just as the king has been providing me with whatever food I need, I myself do not have the means to provide the midday meal for the entire Saṅgha. Rather, I shall provide the midday meal for twenty or twenty-five monks."

The monks then said that the Blessed One had laid down a training rule concerning eating in company, whereupon the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Therefore, it is an offence except at the time of the meal of ascetics."

The Blessed One then spoke in praise of those who desire the training, who are devoted to the training, and who have gathered the requisites for the training, and he addressed the monks with a discourse in accord with that theme, more extensive than that, and containing Dharma points appropriate to it. He then declared to the monks: "Monks, what was laid down before stands as a prohibition, and this is now a permission. My hearers shall recite this training rule of the Vinaya as follows: Eating in company is a transgression except at the appointed time.

The appointed times are these: the time of illness; the time of work; the time of travel; the time of boarding a boat; the time of a great assembly; and the time of the meal of ascetics. These are the appointed times.

Eating in company means eating together in an irregular manner. Except at the appointed time means the appointed time being set aside. Transgression means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinations of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the miserable states of wrong descent. Furthermore, so long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs wholesome qualities. That is why it is called a transgression.

The times are these. The time of illness means this: a sick monk is unable to sustain himself on one meal. The time of work means this: a monk who has performed work for the Saṅgha or for a stūpa, even so much as waving a cleaning cloth or laying out a single maṇḍala mat. The time of travel means this: a monk who has traveled half a yojana or half of that and then returned. The time of boarding a boat means this: a monk who has boarded a boat, traveled half a yojana or half of that, and then returned. The time of a great assembly means: a crowd. The time of the meal of ascetics means this: if renunciants who have gone forth from other traditions outside this one are present there, they too count under the designation 'ascetics,' and that is the appointed time for them. The expression these are the appointed times means: in those cases that is the conforming circumstance.

Now, how does a transgression arise in those cases? If a monk, perceiving it to be within the boundary when it is within the boundary, eats in company, he incurs a transgression. If a monk eats in company while doubtful about whether it is within the boundary, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, perceiving it to be within the boundary when he is actually outside the boundary, eats in company, he incurs a wrong deed. If a monk eats in company while doubtful about whether he is outside the boundary, he incurs a wrong deed.

Where there are two distinct dwelling places — the base dwelling and the household dwelling — those who are eating at the base dwelling must ask whether monks have come from the household dwelling; if they eat without asking, they incur a wrong deed. Those who are eating at the household dwelling must likewise ask whether monks have come from the base dwelling; if they eat without asking, they incur a transgression.

Eating three portions and accepting a single additional portion; completing three full servings but not completing one full serving; receiving even a small morsel of additional food, even so much as a single pinch of salt or a single lump of it; having fixed and separate dwellings; and

If the donor says, "I am giving this to those who are gathered here," there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a novice practitioner, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This completes the thirty-sixth rule among the transgressions related to eating in a group.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gave forth into the going forth and conferred full ordination upon seventeen young men from the village of Upananda and the like. Those seventeen then put on their lower robes in the morning, took up their bowls and Dharma robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.

Now, the realm of women is one where craving operates. Seeing the monks, the women beat their chests and said, "What did those who begot these men gain? These were men who, the very moment they were born, could not fill their mouths with briny gruel, could not be set on a hip and carried along. What have they accomplished?" The group of seventeen, feeling humiliated, said, "It is bad enough that we have cut off our food — and now on top of that we must hear words of such shameful reproach. This is not fitting." From that very spot they turned back, and having cut off their food in that way, as long as there was any vigor left in their bodies they exerted themselves on the side of virtue. When the vigor in their bodies was exhausted, they spread out their robes and lay down.

Seeing them, a dear friend said, "Alas, O group of seventeen! Could it be that the food belongs to someone else — do you perhaps think your stomachs belong to someone else too? No matter how much effort you make toward the side of virtue, you have eaten only as much as suffices for that effort." "Who ate?" "You did." "We did not eat." "Then why are you lying with your robes spread out?" They then recounted the whole matter in full.

Some women from the city, being fond of pleasure gardens, took food and drink and went outside Śrāvastī to the Jeta Grove to share and eat and drink there. Seeing them, the group of seventeen made themselves comfortable in their bellies, and recited these verses:

"O Protector, your many excellent teachings
circulate throughout this world of the moving and the still.
The sage who has no sensation of hunger in his body —
that is your most excellent teaching."

The women then said, "Noble ones, if you are asked — do you wish?" "We do." The women gave food and drink to the group of seventeen, and after they had eaten, the monks paired up and began to walk back and forth reciting their texts.

Seeing them reciting their texts, a dear friend said, "How remarkable — the group of seventeen has applied themselves with great diligence!" The venerable Ānanda then presented the truth of the matter to the Blessed One. He said, "When a donor and a patron give food to a recipient, they bestow five things: they give life, they give complexion, they give strength, they give ease, and they give eloquence — and this brings happiness." The Blessed One declared this, and it is well spoken: if one eats, one will be endowed with eloquence; if one does not eat, one will not. "Did you eat?" "We ate." "Was it fitting for you to eat at an improper time?" "If food is not found at the proper time, are we then to starve and die?" "Monks who are of small account — why do they eat and take up food at an improper time?" — at this, people began to reproach them, to rail at them, to spread gossip and slander. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, with this matter in mind, and

On this occasion and in this context, the convening of the assembly of monks, and so forth, proceeds as before. Likewise, "The blessed buddhas, though knowing, perform a purposeful inquiry" and so forth also proceed as before. The blessed Buddha then questioned the group of seventeen monks: "Monks, is it true that you received solid food and consumables and ate them at an improper time?" "Venerable One, it is true." The blessed Buddha then censured them, saying that this was unworthy of a contemplative, not in accord, not fitting, not in keeping with proper conduct — this is not something one who has gone forth ought to do. Thereupon the Blessed One, having censured them in many ways, spoke to the monks:

"Monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers," and so forth, as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk receives solid food or consumables or eats them at an improper time incurs a transgression."

"Whatever monk" refers to the group of seventeen or any other monk of that kind. "At an improper time" means there are two improper times: before the dawn has risen, and after noon has passed. "Solid food or consumables" means the five kinds of solid food and the five kinds of consumable food. "Receives or eats" means having swallowed it down the throat. "Incurs a transgression" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the hells, into the realm of animals, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into states of woe, and into states of wrong descent. Moreover, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas — therefore it is called "incurring a transgression."

As for how one incurs the transgression: when a monk, perceiving an improper time as an improper time, receives or consumes solid food or consumables, he incurs a transgression. When a monk, in doubt about whether it is an improper time, receives or consumes solid food or consumables, he incurs a transgression. When a monk, at a proper time but perceiving it as an improper time, receives or consumes solid food or consumables, he commits a wrongdoing. When a monk, at a proper time but in doubt, receives or consumes solid food or consumables, he commits a wrongdoing. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

The thirty-seventh transgression, eating at an improper time, is complete.

The blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Kāḷa was dwelling in dependence upon a certain village or hamlet. In the early morning he put on his inner robe, took up his alms bowl and Dharma robe, and entered that very village or hamlet, guarding his body with great care, restraining his faculties thoroughly, and setting his mindfulness close at hand, he went on alms round. If he obtained cooked wet rice, he received it in his alms bowl; if he obtained cooked dry rice, he received it in the vessel of his alms bowl. Then, having made his alms round through that village or hamlet, he went to the temple. The wet cooked rice he ate directly; the dry cooked rice he dried out, filled an unbaked earthen vessel with it, and set it aside. Then, should wind arise, or bad weather come, or rain fall, or hail descend — whenever such things occurred, when wind had arisen, bad weather had come, rain had fallen, or hail had come — at such a time he would rinse the dry cooked rice with hot water, eat it, and then enter into meditative concentration, liberation, and

liberation, and meditative absorption, experiencing the bliss of entering into samādhi.

It is the nature of reality for blessed buddhas, while they are alive, living, and well, to feel compassionate concern for those who are amenable to guidance, and so from time to time they would go down into the hells, range through the animal realm, range through the realm of hungry ghosts, range through the realm of the gods, range through the provinces, range along the riverbanks, range through the mountains, range through the charnel grounds, and go to the temples. With that purpose in mind, the Blessed One decided to go to the temple, and he said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata is going to the temple. Any of you who wishes to go to the temple together with the Tathāgata should take your robes.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Lord," listened to the Blessed One, and then said to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is going to the temple. Any of you who wishes to go to the temple together with the Tathāgata should take your robes."

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the monastic Saṅgha going before him, set out walking to the temple. He went directly to the temple of the venerable Kāḷudāyin. At that time, in the temple of the venerable Kāḷudāyin, a very great quantity of dry cooked rice was lying stored. The Blessed One saw the very great quantity of dry cooked rice lying stored in the temple of the venerable Kāḷudāyin. Having seen it, he said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, to whom does all this stored dry cooked rice belong?"

"Lord, this is the practice of the venerable Kāḷudāyin: whatever village or hamlet he dwells near, he rises early in the morning, takes his bowl and robes, and enters that very village or hamlet keeping his body well restrained, his sense faculties thoroughly subdued, and mindfulness closely established, and goes on his alms round. If he receives wet cooked rice, he takes it in the vessel of his alms bowl; if he receives dry cooked rice, he takes it in the vessel of his alms bowl. Having completed his alms round through that village or hamlet, he goes to the temple. The wet cooked rice he eats directly; the dry cooked rice he fills an unbaked earthen vessel with and sets aside. Then, should wind arise, or bad weather come, or rain fall, or hail descend — whenever such things occur, when wind has arisen, bad weather has come, rain has fallen, or hail has come — at such a time he rinses the dry cooked rice with hot water, eats it, and then experiences the bliss of entering into meditative concentration, liberation, and meditative absorption. Venerable sir, the monks eat stored food — that is his practice."

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this instance, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha — and all that followed proceeded as before. "The blessed buddhas, though knowing, act as if unaware" — and so on, as before. The Blessed One then questioned the venerable Kāḷudāyin: "Kāḷudāyin, is it true that you keep stored provisions and eat stored food?"

"Lord, it is true."

The Blessed One then censured lack of effort, lack of application, and conduct without examination.

Then the Blessed One praised effort, application, and conduct with examination, and declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits in full, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: 'Furthermore, should any monk receive stored provisions or stored food and then eat or consume them, it is a transgression.'"

"Furthermore, any monk" refers to the venerable Kāḷudāyin or any other of like kind.

"Stored provisions and stored food" refers to the five types of provisions and the five types of food.

"Stored" means stored in one of two ways: food received in the morning and kept until the afternoon, or food received in the afternoon and kept beyond the allotted time.

"Eat or consume" means to swallow at the throat.

"Transgression" means: it burns, scalds, and causes one to fall into hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into miserable destinies, and into states of ruin. Furthermore, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome phenomena — and therefore it is called a transgression.

As to how a transgression arises in this matter: if a monk perceives stored provisions as stored provisions and then eats or consumes them — provisions or food — a transgression arises. If a monk, acting with uncertainty regarding stored provisions, eats or consumes them — provisions or food — a transgression arises. If a monk perceives what is not stored as if it were stored provisions and then eats or consumes them — provisions or food — a misdeed arises. If a monk, acting with uncertainty regarding what is not stored provisions, eats or consumes them — provisions or food — a misdeed arises.

If a monk stores an alms bowl, a small alms bowl, a scraper, a cup, a salt pouch, a bowl-container, a robe, a crystal, a high seat, a low seat, a ladle, a water vessel, a ball, a key, or a hooked key, and then eats what has been set aside using these — in all such cases a misdeed arises.

If a monk uses stored mouth or stored hands to eat or consume provisions or food, a misdeed arises.

If a monk stores flowers or fruits, and eats as much as has been stored — in all such cases a transgression arises.

If a monk drinks water to quench thirst without rinsing the mouth first, a misdeed arises.

For one who is a novice practitioner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for one afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

The thirty-eighth transgression concerning stored provisions is complete.

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Mahākāḷa was one who observed all the charnel-ground practices: his alms bowl was from the charnel ground, his Dharma robe was from the charnel ground, his alms-rounds were at the charnel ground, and his dwelling and bedding were at the charnel ground.

How was his alms bowl from the charnel ground? In this way: when relatives would throw into the charnel ground a skull of one who had died and whose time had come, the venerable Mahākāḷa would fire-harden it at the tip of a flame, consecrate it, and carry it as his alms bowl — and in this way his alms bowl was from the charnel ground.
