How was his Dharma robe from the charnel ground? In this way:

when relatives would throw into the charnel ground the garments of one who had died and whose time had come, the venerable Mahākāḷa would wash them, wring them out, turn them over, consecrate them as his Dharma robe, and carry them — and in this way his Dharma robe was from the charnel ground.

How were his alms-rounds from the charnel ground? In this way: when relatives would throw into the charnel ground the five foods of one who had died and whose time had come, the venerable Mahākāḷa would take them up and eat them — and in this way his alms-rounds were from the charnel ground.

How was his dwelling and bedding from the charnel ground? In this way: the venerable Mahākāḷa dwelt in the charnel ground — and in this way his dwelling and bedding were from the charnel ground.

When ordinary people had enough to eat, the venerable Mahākāḷa's sinews, skin, flesh, and blood would become full, and he would not go again and again into the village on alms-rounds. When ordinary people did not have enough to eat, the venerable Mahākāḷa would become lean, feeble, emaciated, dried out, and without bodily nourishment, and he would go again and again into the village on alms-rounds. Taking this pattern as a distinguishing sign, people began to think: "When ordinary people have enough to eat, this noble Mahākāḷa's sinews, skin, flesh, and blood become full, and he does not go again and again into the village on alms-rounds. But when ordinary people do not have enough to eat, this noble Mahākāḷa becomes lean, feeble, emaciated, dried out, and without bodily nourishment, and he does go again and again into the village on alms-rounds — surely this noble Mahākāḷa must be eating human flesh?" And everywhere the report spread: "The noble Mahākāḷa eats human flesh."

Now in Śrāvastī there lived a brahmin who had taken a wife of equal caste, and he sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed her company. And from their sporting, delight, and enjoyment together, a daughter was born; they reared and raised her, and she grew up. Then at another time that brahmin's hour came, and his relatives wrapped him, adorned with blue, yellow, red, and white garments, and carried him to the charnel ground. They cremated him and withdrew into a grave-pit, and his wife and daughter sat together at the edge of the pit. The venerable Mahākāḷa sat there looking into the pit. The daughter saw the venerable Mahākāḷa sitting and staring into the pit, and seeing this she said to her mother: "Mother, this noble Mahākāḷa is sitting there watching intently, like a female crow eyeing carrion."

Then the Blessed One (the Buddha) said to the monks: "Monks, a brahmin's daughter spoke, and having spoken in that way, she uttered a rough verbal act against the great śrāvaka who is like Mount Meru — and because of that, that brahmin's daughter will become a female crow eyeing carrion for five hundred lifetimes." And everywhere the report spread: "The Blessed One has prophesied that that brahmin's daughter will become a female crow eyeing carrion for five hundred lifetimes."

The brahmin woman heard that the Blessed One had prophesied that her daughter would become a female crow eyeing carrion for five hundred lifetimes. Thereupon the brahmin woman took her daughter and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, she prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with her head and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, may you grant pardon to this daughter."

"She did not speak harsh words with a mind of intense hatred." The brahmin woman said, "Can I swear an oath about something? If this daughter of mine had spoken harsh words with a mind of intense hatred, there would be grounds for her to be reborn in the hells. Such a place of rebirth would indeed exist."

Now at Śrāvastī, some brahmin boys heard that the venerable Mahākṛṣṇa ate human flesh, and they said to one another: "Friends, is this really true or not? Or is it false? We have invited the venerable Mahākṛṣṇa to a meal. Let one of us pretend to be dead, and we will carry him to the charnel ground." They decided among themselves: "Let whichever one of us plays the corpse be the one carried there." One of them said, "You play the dead one." He replied, "But won't I be eaten?" They said, "We will protect you." So he pretended to be dead, and they anointed him with oil and sesame butter, wrapped him in a winding cloth, laid him out in a curled position, and began to leave Śrāvastī. Now the venerable Mahākṛṣṇa had entered Śrāvastī on his alms round, and when he saw them, he thought: "It would not do if a fox were to eat these five foods and my meal were cut off." Recognizing this, he quickly began to walk back, and the brahmin boy who was pretending to be dead became frightened and started crying out, "I am being eaten! I am being eaten!" The other brahmin boys grabbed sticks and came running quickly, saying to him: "You, a noble one, bearing the standard of a sage — do you engage in such vile and wicked conduct as this?" He replied, "What? I did not eat human flesh. Good sirs, did you see me pick up a blade and cut and eat flesh?" They said, "Then why did you come running so quickly?" He answered, "Good sirs, it occurred to me: if this fox eats these five foods and my meal is cut off, that would not be right — that is why I came so quickly." They asked, "Noble one, have you eaten the five foods? You did not seek human flesh?" He replied, "That is so — everywhere the report has gone around that the venerable Mahākṛṣṇa eats human flesh."

At this point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen came about because the monks did not allow the food to be received. Therefore, if the monks allow the food to be received and it is eaten with them as witnesses, that itself shall serve as the proof." Thinking thus, he declared: "Therefore, monks, you shall allow the food to be received and then eat it."

When the Blessed One had declared that the monks should allow the food to be received and eat it, they did not know how receiving was to be done. The Blessed One then declared: "There are five kinds of receiving. What are the five? Receiving with the body, body to body; receiving through what is connected with the body, body to body; receiving with the body into what is connected with the body; receiving through what is connected with the body into what is connected with the body; and the fifth is the ritual of placing. How is it done body to body with the body? It is when one gives with the body and the other receives with the body.

That is how it is done body to body through what is connected with the body. How is it done body to body with the body through what is connected with the body? It is when one gives by means of an alms bowl and the other receives with the body. That is how it is done body to body through what is connected with the body. How is it done into what is connected with the body with the body? It is when one gives with the body and the other receives into an alms bowl. That is how it is done into what is connected with the body with the body. How is it done into what is connected with the body through what is connected with the body? It is when one gives by means of an alms bowl and the other receives into an alms bowl. That is how it is done into what is connected with the body through what is connected with the body.

How is the fifth, the ritual of placing, performed? Monks, there are people of a region called "the Reviled," and they revile their mothers, they revile their fathers, and they revile their brothers and sisters. Any monk who goes there should draw a circle and say, "Place it here," and whatever those people place there, one should declare it received; and at the time of the unpleasant sound from the north, having blessed it, one should eat it and need not feel regret about this. That is how the fifth, the ritual of placing, is performed.

When faithful brahmins and householders offered fruits to the monks, the monks did not accept them. Those people then said: "Noble ones, before the Blessed One came into the world, other non-Buddhists were indeed worthy recipients of gifts. Now the Blessed One has come into the world and you are the worthy recipients of gifts. If you do not accept, shall we, who are deprived of the means of planting wholesome roots, pass from this world to the next world in that state? Please accept." At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They may be accepted; and having accepted them, they may be rendered allowable and eaten."

Not knowing how many ways of rendering allowable there were, the Blessed One declared: "There are five ways of rendering allowable. What are the five? Rendering allowable by fire; rendering allowable by a blade; rendering allowable by a fingernail; rendering allowable by aging; and the fifth is rendering allowable by having a wound made by a bird's beak."

There are also a further five ways of rendering allowable. What are the five? Rendering allowable by removal of the seed part; by having been processed; by being cut; by being pierced; and the fifth is the absence of the nature of a seed.

The Blessed One having declared that fruits were to be received and eaten, not knowing how they were to be received, the Blessed One declared: "There are five ways of receiving with the hand extended. What are the five? A flat stone slab; a bed; a low seat; a mat; and the fifth is the base of an alms bowl."

As the monks were making each fruit allowable one by one, it took a very long time, and the Blessed One declared: "If a pile is made and touched by fire in two or three places, the whole becomes allowable. A blade and a fingernail are applied one by one."

When the laypeople distributed the fruits unevenly, the Blessed One declared: "Let the novices be put in charge of the distribution." When the novices also distributed unevenly, the Blessed One declared: "Let the monks wash their hands, receive the fruits, and then distribute them." Yet again it became uneven, and the Blessed One declared: "The portions for distribution — the best, the middling, and the last — should each be done separately." When those in charge of distributing had subsequently all obtained their shares, the Blessed One declared: "The share of the one doing the distribution is to be set aside by the abbot and the preceptor." When those shares turned out to be good ones, the Blessed One declared:

Those seated near them are to be served. When those people kept getting up repeatedly and coming forward to receive many shares, the Blessed One declared: "Those who do not rise from their seats are to be allowed to receive as much as they are able." When it became uneven again and those same people were made to receive, the Blessed One declared: "Those who are able to receive without rising from their seats are to be told that their reception is complete. Those who are unable to receive without rising from their seats are to be made to receive again." When the householders said, "Noble ones, we too shall make the distribution," and the monks were unwilling, the Blessed One declared: "Let them be made to distribute." When those householders took first and the monks took afterward, the Blessed One declared: "The monks are to take first, and the householders afterward." When what the monks had received from the other monks was then made subject to distribution again, the Blessed One declared: "Whatever has been received from monks — the reception of that is final. Whatever has been received from laypeople is to be made subject to distribution." When distributing, the laypeople distributed first and the monks distributed afterward; and then the monks discarded the remaining portions, saying that they had been stored. The Blessed One declared: "The monks are to distribute first and the laypeople afterward, and the following day it is to be distributed to the Saṅgha."

When faithful brahmins and householders offered to the Saṅgha jars of clarified butter, jars of grain oil, jars of honey, and jars of molasses, the monks did not accept them, and the Blessed One declared: "They are to be accepted, and once accepted, distributed to the Saṅgha." When the robes of those monks became soiled with oil, the Blessed One declared: "They are to be distributed with grass or leaves placed in between." When those monks grew tired from holding and standing with the jars, the Blessed One declared: "They may be set down." When those same jars were overturned as they were being set down, the Blessed One declared: "They are to be set upon a base." When some creatures ate from those jars and then those jars were returned to the monks, the monks said: "Noble ones, if clarified butter, grain oil, honey, and molasses are to be offered, surely the jars should not also be offered — you yourselves should make use of the jars." The monks accepted the jars and sat down. The Blessed One declared: "Those jars are to be placed in a deep pond for seven or eight days, and when fish, turtles, frogs, crocodiles, or young animals have licked every last bit from them, or when a dog-owner's dogs have licked them clean, they are to be brought inside a suitable room and put to use." The Blessed One having declared that the contents were to be received and eaten, the monks did not know how to say when something had and had not been properly received. The Blessed One declared: "In five circumstances it is to be said that something has not been properly received, and in five circumstances it is to be said that it has been properly received. What are the five circumstances in which it is to be said that something has not been properly received? They are: receiving while sitting outside the boundary; receiving from a direction from which one cannot reach it; receiving from the side; receiving from behind; and receiving with the hands cupped downward. These are the five circumstances in which it is to be said that something has not been properly received."

What are the five circumstances in which it is to be said that something has been properly received? They are: not sitting outside the boundary; receiving from a direction from which one can reach it; not receiving from the side; not receiving from behind; and not receiving with the hands cupped downward. These are the five circumstances in which it is to be said that something has been properly received.

The Blessed One declared that food which had been properly received was to be eaten. But the group of six monks ate both what had been properly received and what had not been properly received. Some monks with little needs rebuked, scorned, and criticized them, saying: "Why do the monks eat both what has been properly received and what has not been properly received, even though the Blessed One has declared that food which has been properly received is to be eaten?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and this occasion and this circumstance, convened the Saṅgha of monks — and so on as before. The Blessed Buddhas, knowing full well, inquire — and so on as before. The Blessed Buddha questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, when I have declared that food which has been properly received is to be eaten, is it true that you ate both what had been properly received and what had not been properly received?" "Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed Buddha rebuked them, saying that this was not the conduct of a contemplative, was not appropriate, was not fitting, was not in accordance with the code — it was not something for one who has gone forth to do. Having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be laid down" — and so on as before. "My hearers shall train in the Vinaya according to this rule of training: any monk who eats food that has been put into his mouth without it having been properly received commits an offense."

Thus did the Blessed One lay down that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Now, monks dwelling in forest hermitages had no one to formally receive water and tooth-cleaning sticks on their behalf, and so they abandoned their forest lodgings and moved into lodgings on the outskirts of villages.

The Blessed Buddhas, knowing full well, inquire. The Blessed Buddha questioned the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why have the monks dwelling in forest hermitages abandoned their forest lodgings and moved into lodgings on the outskirts of villages?" "Venerable One, it is because the Blessed One laid down the rule of training: any monk who eats food that has been put into his mouth without it having been properly received commits an offense. Since the monks dwelling in forest hermitages have no one to formally receive water and tooth-cleaning sticks on their behalf, they have abandoned their forest lodgings and moved into lodgings on the outskirts of villages."

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, water and tooth-cleaning sticks are excepted. Furthermore, where there are intelligent elephants, intelligent monkeys, or intelligent bears, and these animals offer fruits to the monks — if the monks, out of scrupulousness, do not accept them — the Blessed One declared: since wherever there is something to be received there is also something to be formally received, therefore what has been placed by such animals is to be said to have been properly received. One should not be scrupulous about that."

Then the Blessed One, together with those who delight in the training and who hold the training in respect —

having praised those who dedicate their requisites to the training and who honor the training with respect, the Blessed One then addressed the monks with words consonant with that theme, excelling in that theme, and bearing qualities befitting that theme. He declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, what was formerly prescribed remains prescribed, and what is now permitted is permitted. My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: 'Furthermore, any monk who, having not received food formally, eats it by placing it in his mouth — excepting water and tooth-cleaning sticks — commits an offense.'"

"Any monk" refers to any of the six groups or anyone else of that same kind. "Having not received formally" means that it has not been formally given by any man, woman, or person of the third sex. "Food placed in the mouth" refers to the five kinds of staple food and the five kinds of soft food. "Eats it" means swallowing it down the throat. "Excepting water and tooth-cleaning sticks" means that water and tooth-cleaning sticks are set aside. "Commits an offense" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the bad destinations — into the hell-beings, animals, the woeful realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the realms of wrong fall. Furthermore, so long as such a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous qualities. Therefore it is said to "commit an offense."

As to how a transgression arises in this regard: if a monk, perceiving food not formally received as not having been formally received, accepts or eats staple or soft food, a transgression arises. If a monk, eating staple or soft food with doubt about whether or not it was formally received, accepts or eats it, a transgression arises. If a monk, perceiving food that has been formally received as not having been formally received, accepts or eats staple or soft food, a misdeed arises. If a monk, having doubt about food that has been formally received, accepts or eats staple or soft food, a misdeed arises. There is no transgression for one who acts for the first time, for one who is mad, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is overcome by painful sensations.

The monks then asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what action did the great elder Nāgasena perform, such that through the ripening of that karma he went forth before the Blessed One, came to possess all the charnel-ground practices, abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship, and yet — even after attaining arhatship — was falsely accused?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the great Nāgasena himself accumulated a mass of karma, whose conditions were fully set, which remained close like a flame, and which was certain to arise — karma he himself had performed and accumulated. Could anyone else experience the ripening of karma performed and accumulated by the great Nāgasena himself? Monks, karma performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma performed and accumulated ripens within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources:

Even were a hundred eons to pass,
the karma gathered is not lost.
When the conditions and the time arrive,
for those with bodies it bears its fruit.

Monks, long ago in a time past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there resided a pratyekabuddha (solitary buddha) called Teacher. He was surrounded and attended before by many hundreds of thousands of hosts of gods, and from amidst a great charnel ground he entered Vārāṇasī for alms. In that great charnel ground there dwelt a fierce yakṣa, who was there devouring a human corpse. When Teacher the pratyekabuddha entered that great charnel ground, the fierce yakṣa, through the power of the gods, fled from that great charnel ground, and —"

The human corpse that had been left there was eaten by foxes and other animals. The fierce yakṣa then thought: "This renunciant has become an obstacle to my food. I shall do him dishonor." He placed a human hand into the pratyekabuddha's alms bowl, and throughout all of Vārāṇasī the report spread that this renunciant ate human flesh.

The pratyekabuddha, that great being, thought: "If this fierce and afflicted yakṣa is gravely harmed and ruined, that would be wrong. I will offer him a place to abide." And out of compassion for him, the pratyekabuddha rose up into the sky above, spreading out like a king of geese with wings extended, and began to perform miracles — blazing with fire, shining with light, raining down water, and flashing lightning. Ordinary folk are quick to fix their minds upon miraculous powers, and so the fierce yakṣa, like a great tree cut down at the root, fell prostrate before the pratyekabuddha's feet and spoke these words: "True field of offerings, I beseech you to descend! I beseech you to descend! Please draw me out by the collar from where I have sunk in the mire of affliction. I uttered false and dishonoring speech against you. And throughout all of Vārāṇasī the report spread that this renunciant does not eat human flesh — that I had uttered false dishonoring speech against him."

Out of compassion for the fierce yakṣa, the pratyekabuddha descended from the sky above. Then the fierce yakṣa removed the human hand from the alms bowl and cast it on the ground. He bowed with joined hands at the pratyekabuddha's feet and made this aspiration: "Whatever karma there is in having harmed such a true and perfect field of offerings — may the root of virtue of whatever offering I have made, even though it is not equal to that karma of harm, bring me to attain such qualities as would please a Teacher far more exalted than a hundred thousand billion pratyekabuddhas, without causing him displeasure or offense."

Now monks, the fierce yakṣa of that time, of that occasion, is none other than this very Mahākāla. Through the karmic maturation of having falsely slandered the pratyekabuddha, he was tormented in the hells for many lifetimes. Then through the remainder of that same karma, he was slandered falsely for five hundred lifetimes. And even now, having attained the state of an arhat, he is still slandered falsely.

Through the karmic maturation of the karma of having made an offering and set an aspiration, he went forth in my presence, abandoned all afflictions, and directly actualized the state of an arhat. He pleased me, the Teacher who am far more exalted than a hundred thousand billion pratyekabuddhas, and did not cause me displeasure or offense. And due to the habitual tendency formed by having dwelt in that charnel ground, even now he is wholly endowed with the charnel ground.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is itself mixed. Therefore monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and actions that are mixed, and strive after actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train yourselves in this way.

The intermediate summary verse:

Wholly endowed with the charnel ground,
the cowherd and the daughter,
the brahmin who was struck, and the five who received gifts,
and five others including the case of the fruit,
the water and the tooth-cleaning wood with permission given,
the elephant, the monkey, and the bear —
these are set alongside the former conduct.

This concludes the thirty-ninth rule entailing defeat for eating without having received the food properly.

The Vinaya Analysis, the fifty-fourth fascicle.

When the Blessed One Śākyamuni was wandering on tour among the Śākyas, he came to the Śākya settlement and there, in the Nyagrodhā pleasure grove at the Śākya settlement, he took up residence. Śākya Mingchen heard that the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Śākyas, had come to the Śākya settlement and was residing there in the Nyagrodhā pleasure grove. Upon hearing this, he set out from the Śākya settlement, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving, prostrated with his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed Śākya Mingchen rightly with Dharma-endowed words, roused him rightly, gladdened him rightly, and delighted him rightly. In many ways the Blessed One rightly instructed, rightly roused, rightly gladdened, and rightly delighted him with Dharma-endowed words, and then fell silent.

Then Śākya Mingchen rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with his palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, and said to the Blessed One: "Would the Blessed One please permit me to shelter the community of monks together with myself under a canopy-shade tomorrow?" The Blessed One gave permission to Śākya Mingchen by remaining silent.

Then Śākya Mingchen, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that permission was granted, prostrated with his head to the Blessed One's two feet, withdrew from the Blessed One's presence, went to his own home, and said to his household servants: "Good people, the Blessed One and the community of monks will come in the wake of one another. Make preparations early in the morning for excellent food to be served for the canopy-shade meal." The group of six, having risen early the previous evening, said: "Friends, let us go look in on the households that are going to serve as alms-round houses." They did so, and went to the households. Those households said to them: "Noble ones, please accept your meal here today." The group of six replied: "We have been invited." "By whom?" "By Śākya Mingchen." "In that case, please accept the meal tomorrow." "Very well."

Then Śākya Mingchen rose early in the morning, arranged seats, set out water vessels, and invited the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable one, please think to honor us with the canopy-shade meal; Blessed One, please bear in mind that the time has come." Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and robes, and, surrounded by a gathering of monks, with the community of monks spreading out before him, went and arrived at the dwelling place of Śākya Mingchen. He took his seat on the seat that had been prepared at the head of the community of monks. Then Śākya Mingchen, knowing that the Buddha and the rest of the community of monks were comfortably seated, himself served them with his own hands with ample and clean food and drink, satisfying them and filling them. Having in many ways served, satisfied, and filled them with ample and clean food and drink and set down their bowls, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal and set aside his bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One rightly taught Śākya Mingchen with words that accord with the Dharma, rightly led him to take hold of it, rightly praised him, and rightly gladdened him. In many ways, with words that accord with the Dharma, he rightly taught him, rightly led him to take hold of it, rightly praised him, and rightly gladdened him. Then, rising from his seat, he departed.

Śākya Mingchen then followed close behind the Blessed One, step by step, and having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, he circumambulated the Blessed One three times, withdrew from the Blessed One's presence, and went to a lower part of the estate of that fine house above, where he practiced the meditation on generosity. Those who lived by selling curds then cleared away his sleeping quarters and gathered up the food.

The group of six said, "Friends, since the midday hour has come and Ānanda's meal supply has run out, it would not be right to go empty-handed," and they had sixty portions of food prepared at the households they regularly visited for alms, then went to the house of Śākya Mingchen. When they arrived, they saw that no food had been prepared there and no sleeping quarters had been arranged. The group of six then said to those who lived by selling curds, "Good sirs, he invites the community of monks headed by the Buddha and takes only a small portion from his heart for himself, and yet he does not prepare even the midday meal, nor does he arrange sleeping quarters. Could it be that he intends to cut short the midday meal of the community of monks headed by the Buddha?"

Those men said, "Noble ones, have you been asleep? The community of monks headed by the Buddha took their midday meal and have already departed."

The group of six said, "Would they then cut off our meal?" The men said, "Noble ones, we told Śākya Mingchen to wait just a little while, for the time of mixing the curds, and then we went and told Śākya Mingchen, 'Noble sir, the group of six has just now arrived and has asked for a serving.'" Śākya Mingchen said, "Give them whatever small amount of leftovers there is today." They went and said, "Noble ones, please be seated and take your meal," and as they began to serve, the group of six said, "Śākya Mingchen, with great shamelessness, obtained permission from the Blessed One to take the midday meal together with the community of monks at his own home — but if food like this is suitable for inviting the community of monks headed by the Buddha, then Ānanda too should invite the community of monks headed by the Buddha every single day. This poor man — with whatever he has today — go, householder, to the great lady's house and fetch milk; go to the great lady's house and fetch curds; go to the great lady's house and fetch butter; go to the great lady's house and fetch fish; go to the great lady's house and fetch meat; go to the great lady's house and fetch dried meat" — and in this way, having gathered for themselves such begged food from other households, they ate it there, then left and went to the monastery.

The monks said to them, "Venerable ones, where did you eat your meal?" "Right there." "We did not see you there." The group of six said, "We arrived late." "And what sort of food did you eat?" The group of six said, "Milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat." The monks said:

"We have not obtained such food." The group of six said, "Where would a poor man find such food? We took it from the households we visit and ate it there." "Is it permissible to take such begged food from other households and eat it for your own benefit?" "It may be permissible or it may not be permissible — but are we to starve and die? Monks of little account — why do you censure, denounce, and speak ill of monks who take such begged food from other households for their own benefit and consume it?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this instance, and on account of this occasion, summoned the community of monks — and so forth, as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though fully knowing, feign not to know" — and so forth, as before — and the Blessed One questioned the group of six: "Monks, I have spoken of certain foods proper for monks to receive as alms — namely milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat. Is it true that you took such begged food from other households for your own benefit and ate it?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One then rebuked them, saying that this was not the conduct of a renunciant (pravrajyā), not in keeping with it, not proper, not in accord with proper conduct, and therefore not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten good qualities, a rule of training shall be laid down for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever foods the Blessed One has named as proper for monks to receive as alms — namely milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat — if a monk takes such begged food from other households for his own benefit and accepts or eats it, it is an offense entailing a downfall.

Thus did the Blessed One lay down that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya."

Then a sick monk asked a physician, "Good friend, please prescribe medicine for me." "Noble one, drink milk." "Good friend, who will give me milk?" "Noble one, beg for it from households." "Good friend, the Blessed One has laid down a rule of training." "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — if you take that very circumstance as the condition and make the request, a solution will be found."

At that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted in time of illness." And in the same way, the same procedure as before was followed until permission was granted for other monks as well to beg milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat from households.

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of those who delight in training, who are respectful toward training, and who take training as their provision, addressed the monks with a discourse in keeping with that theme, more extensive than that, and adorned with qualities befitting it, and then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, the former was the rule, and this is now the permission. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

The foods that may be begged by monks, as declared by the Blessed One, are these: milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat. Should any monk who is not ill beg such foods from the households of others for his own sake, and then receive or eat them, he commits a transgression (āpatti).

The phrase "as declared by the Blessed One" refers to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha. The phrase "by monks" refers to those who follow this Dharma. The phrase "foods that may be begged — begged" is an explicit designation. "That is to say, milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat" — these are the beggable foods. "Should any monk" refers to the group of six, or any other monk of similar disposition. "Who is not ill" means excepting one who is sick. "For his own sake" means dedicated to himself. "Such foods" means milk, curds, butter, fish, meat, and dried meat. "From the households of others" means from the households of brahmins and householders. "Beg" means to ask for and receive. "Receive or eat" means to swallow down the throat. "Commits a transgression" means it causes one to be burned, to be scorched, and to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the evil destinies. Furthermore, as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs all virtuous qualities. Therefore it is said to be a transgression.

As for how the transgression arises: if a monk who is not ill begs and eats while not ill, begging constitutes a minor offense and eating constitutes a full transgression. If a monk who is not ill begs and then eats while ill, begging constitutes a minor offense and eating involves no transgression. If a monk who is ill begs and then eats while not ill, the begging involves no transgression but eating constitutes a full transgression. If a monk who is ill both begs and eats while ill, there is no transgression in either case.

When a monk is going on alms round and approaching households, and as he is leaving a woman's domain carrying food, if the monk remains silent without saying anything and the woman in her domain asks, "Noble one, what do you wish?" he should respond that it has been given, and whatever he desires he may take — no transgression arises from this. No transgression arises from whatever the donor does out of kindness. When curds are being offered, no transgression arises from begging whey and fresh curd. No transgression arises for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one threatened by painful sensations.

The fortieth rule entailing transgression through begging food is now complete.

A summary verse: living creatures in bedding and seat; standing, naked, an army; two nights prepared and stirred, going about; striking, stealing, and taking up a bad dwelling.

The Blessed One was dwelling in Kauśāmbī, in the garden called Ghositārāma. The venerable Udāyin knowingly used water containing living creatures. The monks said to him: "Venerable Udāyin, do not knowingly use water containing living creatures." He replied: "Has someone counted them and entrusted them to me? Why should I not go to the great eastern ocean? Why not to the great southern, western, or northern ocean? Why not to rivers, lakes, and marshes?" And he went on blaming, disparaging, and rebuking the monks, saying: "Why do monks of little purpose tell monks knowingly to use water containing living creatures?" At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and

this occasion, he convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, exactly as before. "The awakened Blessed Ones, knowing full well, inquire," and so on, again as before. The Blessed One questioned the venerable Udāyin: "Udāyin, is it true that you knowingly used water containing living creatures?" "It is true, Venerable One." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that conduct unbecoming a contemplative, conduct that is not in harmony, not fitting, not in accord with proper comportment, is not something one who has gone forth should do. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers," and so on, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk knowingly uses water containing living creatures incurs a transgression.

As for 'whatever monk': this means Udāyin or any other like him. 'Knowingly' means either he himself has recognized it or others have told him. 'Containing living creatures': living creatures are of two kinds — those that are visible to the naked eye and those that are caught by a straining cloth. 'Uses water': the uses of water are of two kinds, internal and external. Internal use consists of bathing, drinking, spitting out tooth-wood, and washing hands and feet. External use consists of washing the alms bowl, washing the small bowl, washing robes, doing dyeing work, plastering cracks in a shrine hall, twisting thread, and smearing a plastered surface with clay. 'Incurs a transgression' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells as sentient beings, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, and into the states of wrong descent. Furthermore, as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — therefore it is said to incur a transgression.

As to how a transgression comes about in this regard: if a monk, perceiving water that contains living creatures as containing living creatures, uses it, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, entertaining doubt about water that contains living creatures, uses it, he incurs a transgression. If a monk, perceiving water that contains no living creatures as containing living creatures, uses it, he incurs a wrong deed. If a monk, entertaining doubt about water that contains no living creatures, uses it, he incurs a wrong deed.

If a monk consumes clarified butter, grain oil, honey, the scum of molasses, milk, yoghurt, or butter that contains living creatures, he incurs a transgression. If a monk drinks salt, grain salt, whey, or gruel that contains living creatures, he incurs a transgression. If a monk partakes of food that has been prepared or served with living creatures in it, he incurs a transgression.

One who is a first-time offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by feelings — for these there is no transgression.

The forty-first transgression, concerning the use of water containing living creatures, is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The venerable Cāraka, knowing well the proper time, dressed in his lower robe in the early morning, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. In Śrāvastī there was a young man, a seller of incense, who had not long been married. As this young man was arranging his goods for display, the thought arose in him — an improper mental engagement — thinking, "I shall go and enjoy myself together with my young wife." And he began gathering his goods back up. The venerable Cāraka, seeing this, thought, "While other merchants are now spreading out their wares, why is this incense-seller gathering his in?" And reflecting further, he understood: "He has not long been married, and he wishes to go and enjoy himself with his young wife." Thinking, "I shall go there and put his hope of that to an end," he went first to that man's house, sat down on a seat, and spoke these words: "Come here, daughter, sit down, and let me teach you the Dharma." The young woman prostrated at his feet and sat before him to hear the Dharma. He then began to teach her the Dharma.

After some time the incense-seller arrived and said to his wife, "Offer alms to the noble Cāraka and request that he depart." The venerable Cāraka said, "Good man, having thoroughly exhausted what is on the side of my own virtue, I have come here to teach the Dharma. Do you not wish to hear the Dharma? Sit and listen to the Dharma." And pressing him to stay, he sat him down. As long as the venerable Cāraka was freeing that man from his entanglement with desire, he continued to teach the Dharma.

Then that man began to revile and slander, saying, "The conduct of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyans is mere word; the conduct of brahmins is mere word. Look at how this one has no power even over his own wife." He went on to criticize, mock, and slander, saying, "Why do monks, on a flimsy pretext, enter into the houses of those who seem to lie down negligently, pressing in at a later hour and sitting on a seat there?" When the monks heard this criticism, mocking, and slander, they reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks in connection with this incident, this occasion, and this case — and so on as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, act though already knowing — and so on as before. The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you entered the house of one who seems to lie down negligently, pressed in at a later hour, and sat on a seat there?" "Reverend One, it is true." The Buddha, the Blessed One, censured him, saying that such conduct — unworthy of an ascetic, discordant, improper, and contrary to the rules — is not to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having censured him in many ways, addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, the training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be established" — and so on as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, knowingly, enters the house of one who seems to lie down negligently, pressing in at a later hour, and sits on a seat there, incurs a transgression.

Now, 'whatever monk' means Cāraka or any other of that kind. 'Knowingly' means either he himself is aware of it or others have told him. 'The house of one who seems to lie down negligently' means a woman is one who lies down with a man, and a man is one who lies down with a woman. 'House' means the house of a brahmin or a householder."

"Pressing in at a later hour" means entering afterward. "On a seat" means on the ground. "Sits" means placing one's haunches within the span of a cubit's length. "Incurs a transgression" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinations of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong falling. Furthermore, so long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome qualities — and for that reason it is called "incurring a transgression."

As to how the transgression comes about: if a monk, knowingly and even slightly, sits on a seat in the house of one who seems to lie down negligently, pressing in at a later hour, he incurs a transgression in all cases. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The forty-second transgression — sitting in the house of one who seems to lie down negligently — is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Cāraka perceived a jewel-like opportunity, and that morning he put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and his Dharma robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.

In Śrāvastī there was a young perfume-seller who had not long before taken a wife, and when he spread out his wares he gave rise to inappropriate mental engagement, thinking, "I shall go to enjoy myself with my wife." He began to gather his wares back together. The venerable Cāraka saw this and thought, "While other merchants are spreading out their goods, why is this young perfume-seller gathering his in?" He understood: "This man took a wife not long ago and wishes to go and enjoy himself with her." He thought, "Let me go and watch." So he went first to the man's house and stood upright behind the door panel.

After this the young perfume-seller arrived and led his wife inside the room. The woman saw Cāraka standing alone outside, and she said to her husband, "The noble Cāraka, the son of the lord, is standing behind the door panel." The young perfume-seller said, "The noble Cāraka is standing in the temple experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, and entry into meditative absorption." Having said this, he sported with his wife, and when he had finally disengaged from his entanglement with her, he then saw Cāraka — and he reviled and abused and slandered him, saying, "The wanderers who are Śākya-sons speak of the conduct of a wanderer in words only, and of the conduct of a brahmin in words only — yet in this very way he has no restraint over his own wife!" He censured, disparaged, and criticized, saying, "Why do monks of little substance stand in solitary shelter in the house of one who seems to lie down negligently, knowingly?"

At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then convened the assembly of monks in connection with this incident, this basis, and this occasion — and so on as before. "The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, although they know, feign not to know" — and so on also as before. The Blessed One then questioned the venerable Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you knowingly stood in solitary shelter in the house of one who seems to lie down negligently?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One then said that the conduct was unbecoming of a wanderer, not in accordance with it, not befitting —

not in accordance with it, not befitting of one who has gone forth. In this way he rebuked him. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing the ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, knowingly standing in solitary shelter in a house where one who seems to lie down negligently dwells — commits an offense.

'Whatever monk' refers to Cāraka or any other of that kind. 'Knowingly' means that he himself is aware of it, or that it has been reported to him by others. 'One who seems to lie down negligently' — a woman lies down with a man, and a man lies down with a woman. 'In a house' means in the house of a brahmin or householder. 'Solitary' means a place where no woman, no man, and no person of indeterminate sex is present. 'In shelter' means sheltered by five things: sheltered by a wall, sheltered by a screen, sheltered by a curtain, sheltered by something dense, and sheltered by darkness. 'Standing' means standing within a fathom's distance. 'Commits an offense' means it burns him, scorches him, and makes him fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower realms, into states of wrong view. Furthermore, for as long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and for that reason it is said to 'commit an offense.'

As to how one incurs the offense in this case: however little a monk knowingly stands in solitary shelter in a house where one who seems to lie down negligently dwells, in all such cases he commits an offense. There is no offense for one who acts for the first time, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This is the forty-third offense concerning standing in the house of one who seems to lie down negligently — complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the Kalandakas. Then a great many merchants of Rājagṛha went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One and seated themselves to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened the great many merchants of Rājagṛha with a Dharma-endowed discourse. Having thoroughly instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened them in many ways with a Dharma-endowed discourse, he fell silent.

Then the great many merchants of Rājagṛha, delighted and rejoicing in what the Blessed One had declared, prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from the Blessed One's presence, and went to where the venerable Ānanda was. Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the venerable Ānanda and seated themselves to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda thoroughly taught, established, encouraged, and gladdened the great many merchants of Rājagṛha with a Dharma-endowed discourse. In many ways he thoroughly taught, established, and encouraged —

and gladdened them thoroughly, and then fell silent.

Then the great many merchants of Rājagṛha rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, bowed with their palms joined toward the venerable Ānanda, and said to him:

"Venerable Ānanda, after the Blessed One has completed the rains retreat, where will he travel? Wise ones, please ask the Blessed One this. Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, so we have no way to make this request of the Buddha Blessed One ourselves. And for us as well, since the Buddha Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, we ourselves cannot make the request to the Buddha Blessed One."

"Venerable Ānanda, if even the venerable Ānanda finds that the Buddha Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, and therefore the venerable Ānanda too is reluctant to make the request to the Buddha Blessed One, then how does the venerable Ānanda know by signs, or how does he know from his words, where the Blessed One will travel after completing the rains retreat and going in a particular direction? How does he know by signs? How does he know from his words?"

"Wise ones, after the Blessed One has completed the rains retreat, he faces toward the direction in which he intends to travel, and while seated he gazes in that direction and speaks words of praise about those people. The venerable Ānanda observes which direction the Blessed One gazes toward while seated, and about whose people he speaks words of praise. Wise ones, the Blessed One is now gazing toward Kosala while seated, and he speaks words of praise about the people of Śrāvastī."

They expressed their delight and rejoicing at what the venerable Ānanda had said, prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the venerable Ānanda, and departed. And they thought to themselves: "After completing the rains retreat, the Blessed One will travel to Śrāvastī." And so they made preparations for the journey to Śrāvastī.

Then the Blessed One completed the rains retreat. When the three months of the rains had passed, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata is going on tour through the Kosala lands. Whichever of you wishes to go on tour through the Kosala lands together with the Tathāgata, let him complete the business of his robe-making.'"

The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One and heeding his word, announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is going on tour through the Kosala lands. Whichever of you wishes to go on tour through the Kosala lands together with the Tathāgata, let him complete the business of his robe-making."

The great many merchants of Rājagṛha heard the venerable Ānanda announce to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is going on tour through the Kosala lands. Whichever of you wishes to go on tour through the Kosala lands together with the Tathāgata, let him complete the business of his robe-making." Having heard this, they went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly taught, established, encouraged, and gladdened the great many merchants of Rājagṛha with a Dharma-endowed discourse.

Then, after he had thoroughly taught, established, encouraged, and gladdened them through many categories of Dharma-endowed discourse, he said nothing further. Thereupon the great many merchants of Rājagṛha rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, joined their palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, may it please you to accept from us food and alms-food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal requisites for as long as you travel with the monastic Saṅgha of monks from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī." The Blessed One granted this to the great many merchants of Rājagṛha by his silence. Then the great many merchants of Rājagṛha, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had granted their request, expressed their delight and approval at the Blessed One's word, prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One, and departed from his presence.

Thereupon the great many merchants of Rājagṛha went to where the venerable Ānanda was, arrived, prostrated with their heads at his two feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the great many merchants of Rājagṛha said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, how far does the Blessed One travel each day on the road?" "Sirs, he travels the distance a wheel-turning king travels." "Venerable Ānanda, and how far does a wheel-turning king travel?" "Sirs, a wheel-turning king travels ten leagues along the roads." Accordingly, at every ten leagues those merchants prepared encampments for the retinue of the Blessed One together with the monastic Saṅgha of monks. Whatever foods were cold they prepared that very day in advance; whatever foods needed to be warm they prepared fresh each day.

Then the Blessed One — himself tamed, attended by a retinue of the tamed; himself at peace, attended by a retinue of the peaceful; himself liberated, attended by a retinue of the liberated; himself at ease, attended by a retinue of the at-ease; himself subdued, attended by a retinue of the subdued; himself an arhat, attended by a retinue of arhats; himself free of attachment, attended by a retinue free of attachment; himself glorious, attended by a retinue of the glorious — surrounded by a herd of bulls as a supreme bull among bulls; surrounded by a troop of young elephants as a great elephant; surrounded by a pride of fanged beasts as a lion; surrounded by a flock of geese as a king of geese; surrounded by a host of birds as a garuḍa; surrounded by a throng of disciples as a brahmin; surrounded by a crowd of the sick as a skilled physician; surrounded by troops of warriors as a hero; surrounded by those who have entered the path as a guide who knows the terrain; surrounded by a caravan of merchants as a caravan leader; surrounded by a retinue of followers as a merchant chief; surrounded by a company of ministers as a king of a citadel; surrounded by a host of a thousand sons as a wheel-turning king; surrounded by a host of stars as the moon; surrounded by a host of a thousand rays as the sun; surrounded by a throng of gandharvas (celestial musicians) as Yakṣa-guardian-of-the-realm; surrounded by a host of vessels as a noble man; surrounded by a host of nāgas as one of ill-favored eye; surrounded by a host of yakṣas as the yakṣa Wealth-Giver —

surrounded by a host of asuras as Vemacitrin; surrounded by a host of the Thirty-Three as Śakra (Indra, king of the gods); surrounded by a host of the Brahmā realm as Brahmā; his senses most thoroughly tamed; his manner of movement and conduct undisturbed; still as an ocean; full of moisture like a cloud; free of pride like the king of elephants; well-adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being; his form beautifully graced with the eighty minor marks; his body adorned with a radiance of one fathom; possessed of a light exceeding that of a thousand suns; good in every way like a moving mountain of jewels; endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared bases of mindfulness, and great compassion —

together with those great śrāvakas: Kauṇḍinya the All-Knowing, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Yaśodā, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and others; and moreover surrounded by a very large community of monks and with them walking ahead, he set out from Śrāvastī wandering through the countryside and the gardens there.

A knowing man who shared the same purpose and was traveling along with them fell upon a time of poverty and was overcome with hunger. He thought to himself: "What means is there by which I might not be overcome by hunger?" He then thought again: "If I seek refuge with the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, that will allow me to travel the road in comfort." Realizing this, he went to where the monks were and said to them: "Your teacher is one devoted to the good. He plows his field with a golden plow, and so he provides you with food of a hundred flavors, a hundred thousand garments of fine cloth, and five hundred multi-storied houses. Thus for the time being, even in this very life, you dwell in contact with happiness, and when you pass away from here you will be reborn among the gods. Our teacher is devoted to the bad. He plows his field with a sesame-stalk plow, and so he has provided us with nothing but nakedness, rough garments, food fit for insects, wandering from place to place, and sleeping on the ground. Thus for the time being, even in this very life, we dwell in contact with suffering, and when we pass away from here we will be reborn among the hell-beings."

The monks thought: "This knowing man has developed faith," and they said to him: "Knowing man, how do you get by?" "With difficulty," he replied. The monks asked: "Would you like the leavings from the monks' bowls?" The knowing man thought to himself: "If I do not eat the leavings from the monks' bowls, I shall die of starvation." And so he said: "I would." The monks said: "Knowing man, sit in sight of the monks while they eat, and the monks will give you the leavings from their bowls." The knowing man sat in sight of the monks while they ate, and the monks gave him the leavings from their bowls. He took up his begging bowl with the leavings and rushed away. As he was coming out carrying his begging bowl and hurrying off, the caravan leader saw him and said: "Knowing man, who gave you that load?" He replied: "Those monks are your field of merit, and I am their field of merit, so they gave it to me." The caravan leader said: "Knowing man, if the monks gave it to you out of compassion, would you then say that you are their field of merit? If the Blessed One were to hear this —"

— which would be just the kind of occasion on which the Blessed One would establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers. He said this, and the caravan leader too burst out laughing.

Then, coming along that same road, there arrived some fellow travelers going in the same direction, and with them came a certain knowing man traveling together. He saw the other knowing man and said: "Knowing man, have you eaten?" He replied: "I have." "From whom?" He replied: "These householders of the Śreṣṭhī family supply me with what I need." The other said: "Knowing man, you are one who does not understand what has been done for you. Are these the Śreṣṭhī householders of yours? From among them, it seems that a group of five hundred are on the point of passing beyond sorrow, and have you, knowing man, seen even a single one of them pass beyond sorrow?" And he spoke these verses:

Why does the wicked one not press his face into the earth?
Why does he not split his tongue into a hundred pieces?
Why do the secret parts of your body
Not receive hailstones of vajra, short spears, and arrows?

Just as a jackal that eats the leavings of a lion
And yet desires to kill the lion itself,
So too do you devour the scraps of the one endowed with the ten powers,
While daring to disparage the one with the ten powers.

Wherever and in whomever one takes close refuge,
Rather than gaining a livelihood like this base creature,
The wise who understand things are there friends and enemies alike
And are omniscient —

Those people who do not understand what has been done for them
Are considered far worse than dogs.
For even a dog, it seems, understands what a human has done for it,
While people of serpent-kind spread their venom.

Now this had come to pass for the time being: the Buddha, the Blessed One, had not yet established rules of training in the Vinaya for the hearers. Then the Blessed One, wandering on a tour through the Kosala provinces, arrived at Śrāvastī.

In Śrāvastī, in a park, there were some five hundred courtesans laden with loads of indigo, encamped and settled there. They saw the Buddha, the Blessed One — adorned and resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a great being, endowed with the qualities of an embodied being of that kind, like a man freshly gilded, like a lamp resting in a golden vessel, like a golden mountain in motion, like a golden offering-tree adorned with jewels of every sort — renowned, radiant, fearless, stainless, possessed of a completely pure mind. And seeing him, it was like this: just as a sentient being who has accumulated roots of virtue, upon first seeing a buddha, gives rise to mental well-being — as one does through having trained the mind in calm abiding for twelve years, or as a poor person seeing a treasure, or as someone without a child obtaining a child, or as one delighting in royal sovereignty and being consecrated in royal sovereignty — and since none of those other things produce such mental well-being, they went to where the Blessed One was, came to him, and bowed their heads to his two feet, placing them on top. They took their seat to one side.

Having taken their seat to one side, the Blessed One understood their intention, their latent disposition, their temperament, and their nature, and then taught Dharma in such a way that he would by all means shatter with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection and directly actualize for them the fruit of stream entry. Having seen the truths, they said: "Venerable Blessed One, what you have done for us here is something that our fathers did not do, our mothers did not do, the king did not do, the gods did not do, our ancestors of old did not do, ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins did not do, and neither did the assembly of relatives, friends, and kinsmen — you have dried up an ocean of blood and an ocean of tears.

You have freed us from the mountains of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to higher rebirths and liberation, lifted our feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed us among gods and humans. You have brought cyclic existence to its end. With the vajra of gnosis you have shattered the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, and we have attained the fruit of stream entry. Venerable Blessed One, we have entered the stream. Venerable One, we take refuge in the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept us as laywomen. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, we take refuge with all our heart."

Then they thought: "If the Blessed One were to go to Śrāvastī, we would have no opportunity there. Let us invite the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to take a midday meal here." So those noble daughters rose from their seats, bowed with joined palms turned toward the Blessed One, and addressed him thus: "May the Blessed One please consent to accept tomorrow's midday meal for himself together with the Saṅgha of monks."

The Blessed One gave his consent to those noble daughters by remaining silent. When they understood from his silence that consent had been granted, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One, departed from his presence, went to where the venerable Ānanda was, bowed their heads to his feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those noble daughters said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, we wish to invite the buddha and so forth — the Saṅgha of monks — to the midday meal. Venerable Ānanda, how many kārṣāpaṇas will it take to provide a midday meal for the buddha and so forth, the Saṅgha of monks?"

The venerable Ānanda said: "Five hundred kārṣāpaṇas."

They each contributed one kārṣāpaṇa and said: "Venerable Ānanda, since we lack the equipment, the servants, and the dwelling facilities, please arrange the food yourself, and we will come and serve." "Set down the kārṣāpaṇas." They placed the kārṣāpaṇas all in one place and departed.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the fifty-fifth fascicle.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One was traveling through the Kośala lands and had arrived at Śrāvastī. Having heard this, he went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One taught the householder Anāthapiṇḍada thoroughly with a Dharma-endowed discourse, guided him to proper reception of it, praised him properly, and filled him with proper joy. With many categories of Dharma-endowed discourse he taught him thoroughly, guided him to proper reception, praised him properly, and filled him with proper joy, and then fell silent.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms turned toward the Blessed One, and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, may you consent to accept tomorrow's midday meal at my home together with the Saṅgha of monks?"

The Blessed One said: "Householder, I have already been invited first by five hundred noblewomen."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, rejoicing and delighting in what the Blessed One had declared, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet, departed from the Blessed One's presence, went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the venerable Ānanda's feet and sat down to one side. Seeing those coins, he asked: "Venerable Ānanda, to whom do these coins belong?"

The venerable Ānanda replied: "Approximately five hundred noblewomen invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to another house at noon tomorrow, and they left these coins behind. Mix these coins with your own coins, prepare the food and drink in advance, and send it here."

He took those coins, went away, mixed them with his own coins, prepared the food and drink, and sent it to the Jeta Grove.

The venerable Ānanda sent word to them: "The food has been prepared; come now and serve the Saṅgha of monks, beginning with the Buddha." They arrived and said: "Venerable Ānanda, you are our spiritual friend — come, you too should partake."

As the venerable Ānanda began to partake, two naked wandering women came. When they tried to offer food to those noblewomen, the noblewomen said: "This food belongs to the prince."

The two naked women then said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable one, we, the prince's wives, are in need — please give us food." And they offered food to him.

The venerable Ānanda said: "Sit, and I will give it to you." The two sat down. One was an old woman; the other was a young woman.

The venerable Ānanda, without thinking carefully, began to serve them, and he gave one portion to the old woman and two portions to the young woman.

The old woman, having eaten her single portion, said to the young woman: "How many portions did you receive?"

She replied: "I received two."

The old woman said: "The prince gave me just one portion and you two portions — it must be that he is looking after you. Make preparations for his sake."

The young woman replied: "He has renounced his extensive royal retinue and gone forth. How could he concern himself with someone as stained and defiled as me?"

The old woman said: "Men have desires for various women — the prince is surely looking after you. Make preparations for his sake."

Some monks of few wants then asked why the venerable Ānanda was giving food and provisions with his own hand to naked male wanderers and naked female wanderers. They began to criticize him, to mock him, and to speak ill of him. Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, in connection with this incident, with this occasion, and in this context, convened the Saṅgha of monks, and so forth, as before.

The passage beginning "The Blessed Buddhas, though they know, yet ask" and so forth also follows as before.

The Blessed Buddha then asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you gave food and provisions with your own hand to naked male wanderers and naked female wanderers?"

"Blessed One, it is so."

The Blessed Buddha then admonished and thoroughly rebuked acting without diligence, without care, and without reflection.

The Blessed One then praised acting with diligence, with care, and with reflection, and declared to the monks: "Monks, it is for this reason that, having directly seen the ten benefits, the rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers shall be established thus" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya thus: Whatever monk gives food or provisions from his own hand to a naked male wanderer or a naked female wanderer, he commits an offense."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma. "To a naked male wanderer or a naked female wanderer, from his own hand" means hand to hand. "Food and provisions" refers to the five kinds of food and the five kinds of provisions. "Gives" means without the need for it to be consumed first. "Commits an offense" means he is scorched, he is burned, he falls into the woeful states of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the downfall realms. Furthermore, as long as the offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome dharmas — therefore it is said "he commits an offense."

As to how the offense is incurred: however many times a monk gives food or provisions from his own hand to a naked male wanderer or a naked female wanderer, in each and every instance he commits an offense.

If one wishes to free a relative, a sick person, or someone under the influence of wrong view from that condition, there is no offense. If one breaks the food into pieces and gives it, or has another person give it, there is no offense. For one who is a beginner, or who is mentally disturbed, or whose mind is agitated, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no offense.

The forty-fourth offense in the category of offenses incurred through giving to the naked is complete.

The Blessed Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The king of Kosala, Prasenajit, sent a battalion against a rebel force, and it was defeated and thoroughly routed, and returned. A second battalion and a third were sent, and they too were defeated and thoroughly routed and returned. The ministers then spoke to Prasenajit, the king of Kosala: "Your Majesty, the rebel's forces are growing while our forces are diminishing. If Your Majesty does not go there in person, it will be very difficult to overcome the rebel. We beg Your Majesty to go there in person."

Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, then had it proclaimed by drum throughout his realm: "All those who dwell here and live by the sword shall march. Whoever does not go shall pay a fine of five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." The fourfold army with the host of the royal forces set out, and the six monks said: "Friends, let us go and watch the fourfold army of dear Nandika and great Upananda march." They went and took up a position right along the road. When the elephant corps came, the six monks called out to them: "Ho there, friends! Noble ones, we are coming to help defeat the rebel against Prasenajit, the king of Kosala!" "You poor wretches — can the likes of these elephants subdue a rebel? Your elephants are like pigs, while the rebel's elephants are like heaped-up mountains. Even if you go forward, there is no coming back. Go home today, offer sesame water to your parents, and then depart!" Those soldiers all went away with these words taken to heart, and stood still.

Then the cavalry corps came, and the six monks called out to them: "Ho there, friends! Where are you going?"

"Noble ones, we are coming to help defeat the rebel against Prasenajit, the king of Kosala!" "You poor wretches — can horses like these subdue a rebel? Your horses are like donkeys, while the rebel's horses are like young elephants. Even if you go forward, there is no coming back. Go home today, offer sesame water to your parents, and then depart!" Those soldiers all went away with these words taken to heart, and stood still.

Then the chariot corps came, and the six monks called out to them: "Ho there, friends! Where are you going?" "Noble ones, we are coming to help defeat the rebel against Prasenajit, the king of Kosala!" "You poor wretches — can chariots like these subdue a rebel? Your chariots are like broken-down carts, while the rebel's chariots are like palaces. Even if you go forward, there is no coming back. Go home today, offer sesame water to your parents, and then depart!" Those soldiers all went away with these words taken to heart, and stood still.

Then the infantry corps came, and the six monks called out to them: "Ho there, friends! Where are you going?" "Noble ones, we are coming to help defeat the rebel against Prasenajit, the king of Kosala!" "You poor wretches — can men like these subdue a rebel? Your men are like blades of grass, while the rebel's men are like fierce yakṣas. Even if you go forward, there is no coming back. Go home today, offer sesame water to your parents, and then depart!" Those soldiers all went away with these words taken to heart, and stood still.

Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, arrived and said: "Why have you all gone off and stood still with these words taken to heart, refusing to advance?" They replied: "Your Majesty, how can we prevail? These shaven-headed wanderers with their great patched robes of rough cloth — these nine of them who go about begging — the ones known as the noble six monks — wise friends, they are merely reckless wanderers, yet what harm have their words done you? Go on, depart!" Having considered the matter, Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, thought: "These monks will cause me trouble again and again." He then spoke to a man: "Head-steward, come here. Go to where the Blessed One dwells and, conveying my words, bow your head at the Blessed One's two feet and inquire after his health: 'Is the Blessed One experiencing little affliction? Little distress? Is he at ease in his movements? Does he live and thrive? Does he abide in strength and comfort? Is he free from any offense?' Then present this request on behalf of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala: 'It would be well if, out of compassion, the Blessed One would establish a minor rule whereby the noble ones would not go about in the manner of armed soldiers, so that they might be mindful of not doing so.'" That man replied: "Your Majesty, as you command," and, having received these words from Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, that man addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend sir, Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, bows his head at the Blessed One's two feet and inquires after the Blessed One's health: 'Is the Blessed One experiencing little affliction? Little distress? Is he at ease in his movements? Does he live and thrive? Does he abide in strength and comfort? Is he free from any offense?' And this is the message he conveys: 'Head-steward, may Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, and you be well.'"
