"Reverend sir, on behalf of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala: Reverend sir, when these noble ones go about in the manner of armed troops, alas — if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would be so good as to establish a minor rule by which he would cause those who go about in the manner of armed troops to bear in mind that they should not do so, that would be excellent." Such was his message.

The Blessed One said nothing to that man, granting his request by silence. Then that man, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that the request had been granted, bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and this circumstance, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, just as before. "The blessed buddhas do such-and-such knowingly" — and so forth, also just as before.

The Blessed One questioned the Group of Six: "Monks, is it true that you went about in the manner of armed troops?" "Reverend sir, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked them: "This is not in keeping with the conduct of a contemplative; it is not fitting; it is not appropriate; it is not in accord with proper conduct — it is not something to be done by one who has gone forth." Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, just as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk goes about in the manner of armed troops commits an offense."

"Whatever monk" refers to the Group of Six or any other who is similarly disposed.

Regarding the word "army": an army may have one division, two divisions, three divisions, or four divisions. What is an army of one division? A corps of elephants. What is an army of two divisions? A corps of elephants and a corps of cavalry. What is an army of three divisions? A corps of elephants, a corps of cavalry, and a corps of chariots. What is an army of four divisions? A corps of elephants, a corps of cavalry, a corps of chariots, and a corps of infantry.

"In the manner of armed troops" means with evident delight in engaging in battle.

"Goes about" means goes.

"Commits an offense" means it causes one to be scorched, afflicted, and cast down into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, evil destinations, and states of ruin. Furthermore, for as long as the offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of virtuous qualities — and therefore it is said to "commit an offense."

How does one incur a downfall in this case? Whatever monk goes about even to the slightest degree in the manner of armed troops incurs a downfall in every instance.

A monk who is on his alms round when troops pass by, who is sitting in the colonnade of a monastery when troops arrive there, who has been summoned by a king, a queen, a prince, a minister, a city official, a village headman, or a district official — for him there is no offense. For one who is beset by any one of the eight obstacles and remains in that proximity, there is no offense. For a first offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations, there is no offense.

The forty-fifth offense involving viewing troops is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. Even though the stone-quarry man had not yet come, the king had set up camp there on that very spot, and his ministers said: "Divine lord, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is renowned as one of great power whose good fortune has fully ripened.

"If he were to come, his power would be such that the stone-quarry man would indeed arrive, and there would be a situation of that kind." The king sent a letter to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saying that he wished to see the householder, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to him. Even so, since the stone-quarry man had not yet arrived, Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Householder, do the boys not remember? Divine lord, the boys do not remember — and yet in this way they wish to see the noble ones." Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, sent a letter to the Saṅgha saying: "I wish to see the noble ones of the Saṅgha." The liturgical master read the letter aloud in the midst of the Saṅgha, and announced that whoever wished to go there should draw a lot. When the lots were drawn, the elder monks said: "We are old and cannot endure the journey, so we are unable to go." The junior monks said: "If the Dharma must be taught there, we have heard little and cannot teach the Dharma — so should we draw water instead? Or are we likewise unable to go?" The group of six monks said: "Friends Nandika, as long as the Blessed One lives and we are alive, the teaching endures. When the Blessed One passes into nirvāṇa and our own time comes, it will be said that the teaching has declined. For as long as we live, we have cherished the teaching." They drew lots and went there. Setting out along the road, they taught the Dharma to the king and inspired the king with sincere faith. They taught the Dharma to the queen, to the princes, to the ministers, and to the leaders of the city, and inspired the great multitude of ordinary people with sincere faith. Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, said to his ministers: "I will take the stone-quarry man on a tour," and set out with both the noble ones and the group of six monks. The group of six monks said: "Friends Nandika, for as long as we can, let us abide by the conduct of others rather than our own conduct — let us march like a great army." And they went and stationed themselves along the road. When the elephant corps arrived, those soldiers said: "Noble ones, make way, make way! Why? The elephant corps is coming." "Are creatures like these elephants? They look more like pigs." And they seized them by their tusks and threw them to one side. When the cavalry arrived, those soldiers said: "Noble ones, make way, make way! Why? The cavalry is coming." "Are creatures like these horses? They look more like donkeys." And they seized them by their tails and threw them to one side. When the chariot corps arrived, those soldiers said: "Noble ones, make way, make way! Why? The chariot corps is coming." "Are creatures like these chariots? They look more like broken-down carts." And they seized them by their axle-poles and threw them to one side. When the infantry corps arrived, those soldiers said: "Noble ones, make way, make way! Why? The infantry is coming." "Are creatures like these men? They look more like scarecrows." And they seized them by their collars and threw them to one side, and those soldiers fell into a rage and stood there in fury. When Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, arrived, he said: "Wise ones, why are you standing there in fury without moving? Divine lord, how could we prevail?"

"These mendicants who are seeking large bolts of cloth to tie around their heads — nine of them are coming, are they not? And who are they?" "Noble ones, those are the six-group monks. Since they are dissolute mendicants, what harm can what they say do to you? Leave it be." Now Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, thought to himself: "These fellows will keep provoking me again and again," and recognizing this, he said to one of his men: "My good man, come here. Go to where the Blessed One is, and in my name bow your head to the Blessed One's two feet and ask after his health, saying: 'Is the Blessed One experiencing little discomfort, little distress? Are you vigorous and in good health? Do you dwell in touch with strength and ease? Are you free from any impropriety?' Then speak these words: 'Blessed One, on behalf of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, who bows his head to the Blessed One's two feet — these noble ones have been going about fully armed and remaining in the midst of an army for a very long time. Alas! For the sake of compassion, it would be good if the Blessed One would establish some means of remembrance for the noble ones so that, having gone about fully armed, they would no longer remain in the midst of an army for so very long.'" The man replied, "As the lord commands," and, having heard these words from Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, he went to where the Blessed One was. He arrived and bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, then sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, he spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, bows his head to the Blessed One's two feet and asks after the Blessed One's health: 'Is there little distress, little discomfort? Are you vigorous? Do you live in good health? Are you endowed with strength? Do you dwell in touch with ease? Are you free from any impropriety?'" Then: "My good man, may Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, be well. Blessed One, on behalf of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala: these noble ones have been going about fully armed and remaining in the midst of an army for a very long time. Alas! It would be good if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would establish some means of remembrance for the noble ones so that, having gone about fully armed, they would no longer remain in the midst of an army for so very long." The Blessed One said nothing to the man, and by that silence gave his assent. The man, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that assent had been given, departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this circumstance, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and all the rest is as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowing yet feigning not to know" — and so forth, also as before. The awakened one, the Blessed One, rebuked the six-group monks: "Monks, is it true that you went about fully armed and remained in the midst of an army for a very long time?" "Blessed One, it is so." The awakened one, the Blessed One, criticized their conduct, saying: "This is not the proper conduct of a mendicant, it is not fitting, it is not suitable, it is not in accord with proper conduct, and it is not something that one who has gone forth should do." Having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten genuine benefits, a rule of training is to be established for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a circumstance such as this arises for a monk — that is, going about fully armed — that monk may remain within that army for up to two nights. If he remains beyond that, it constitutes a transgression."

As for "a monk" — this refers to one of the group of six, or to any other such person.

As for "an army" — an army may have one division, two divisions, three divisions, or four divisions. What is a one-division army? It is a host of elephant troops. What is a two-division army? It is a host of elephant troops and a host of cavalry. What is a three-division army? It is a host of elephant troops, a host of cavalry, and a host of chariot troops. What is a four-division army? It is a host of elephant troops, a host of cavalry, a host of chariot troops, and a host of foot soldiers.

As for "armed" — this refers to one who delights in doing battle.

As for "going about" — this means for whatever reason one travels.

As for "if a circumstance such as this arises" — this means if one is summoned by a king, a queen, a prince, a minister, a city magistrate, a town dweller, or a country dweller.

As for "that monk" — this means whichever monk it may be.

As for "within that army" — this means within that armed force.

As for "may remain for up to two nights" — this means he may remain for a period of no more than two nights.

As for "if he remains beyond that" — this means if he remains past that point.

As for "it constitutes a transgression" — this means it causes him to be scorched, burned, and made to fall into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of ruin. Moreover, so long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities of virtue. Therefore it is said to constitute a transgression.

Now, how does the transgression arise? For however much time beyond two nights a monk remains within an army, a transgression arises in every case. There is no transgression, however, for one who is told to stay by a king, a queen, a prince, a minister, a city magistrate, a town dweller, or a country dweller. There is no transgression if, through any one of the eight impediments, one is constrained to remain nearby. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by pain.

This completes the forty-sixth transgression: remaining within an army.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. Now, although Prasenajit of Kosala had not come to see him for some time, he spoke to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying: "Householder, do you not think of the boys? By 'the boys' I mean that I wish to see the noble ones." King Prasenajit of Kosala sent a letter to the community of monks saying that he wished to see the noble ones. The rector of the community read the letter in the midst of the Saṅgha, and announced that whoever wished to go there should cast a lot. The elder monks among the monks said: "We are old and cannot endure the journey, so we are unable to go." The junior monks said: "If the Dharma must be taught there, we have heard little and are unable to teach the Dharma — so should we draw water or is it also impossible for us to go?" The group of six said: "Friends, Nandaka and Upananda — as long as the Blessed One lives and we are alive, the teaching will endure. When the Blessed One passes into nirvāṇa and our time comes, it will be said that the teaching has declined. Therefore for as long as we are alive, you must cherish the teaching."

"Take your tooth-sticks," they said, and taking their tooth-sticks, the monks went there and taught the Dharma to the king, causing the king to develop faith. They also taught the Dharma to the queen, the young princes, the ministers and counselors, and the captains of the city districts, thereby inspiring faith in the great multitude of people assembled there.

King Prasenajit of Kosala said to his ministers: "Today, prepare for battle, and have the rocky crags surrounded." As they began to set the formation, the group of six said: "Friends Nandaka and Upananda, for however long we remain, let us conduct ourselves according to others' standards of deportment rather than our own. Let us go and experience firsthand the sight of the finest victory banners of the great-bellied ones, the finest troops, and an army arrayed and drawn up for battle." So they went into the midst of the elephant corps and asked: "O wise ones, what are you doing?" The soldiers replied: "Noble ones, we are setting up the formation." The group of six said: "You poor fellows — elephants decked out like these: do you put them in this direction, or turn them this way?" And seizing the elephants by their tusks, they flung them all to one side.

Then they went into the midst of the cavalry and asked: "O wise ones, what are you doing?" The cavalry replied: "Noble ones, we are setting up the formation." The group of six said: "You poor fellows — horses like these: do you place them in this direction, or turn them this way?" And seizing the horses by their tails, they flung them all to one side.

Then they went into the midst of the chariot corps and asked: "O wise ones, what are you doing?" The chariot drivers replied: "Noble ones, we are setting up the formation." The group of six said: "You poor fellows — broken-down chariots like these: do you place them in this direction, or turn them this way?" And seizing the chariots by their axle-poles, they flung them all to one side.

Then they went into the midst of the infantry and asked: "O wise ones, what are you doing?" The soldiers replied: "Noble ones, we are setting up the formation." The group of six said: "You poor fellows — slackers like these: do you place them in this direction, or turn them this way?" And seizing the soldiers by their necks, they flung them all to one side.

Then the group of six, placing themselves directly in front of the troops at no great distance from the rocky crags, let out a sudden shout. When the troops heard it they thought: "The rocky crags have broken free from the fort and are sliding down!" Terrified and panic-stricken, they began to flee. The group of six, moving swiftly, came and stood before the city district captains and asked: "O wise ones, why are you fleeing?" They replied: "Noble ones, the rocky crags have broken free from the fort and are sliding down!" The group of six said: "You poor fellows, that was just a little trick of ours. If the rocky crags had truly borne down on you and you had realized it, by the very next morning you would all have been seized by the neck and carried off to the crags. Do not be afraid — turn back." The troops went off to one side and stood there, coming to their senses.

Shortly thereafter, King Prasenajit of Kosala arrived and said: "O wise ones, have you not yet set the battle formation?" They replied: "O King, how could we prevail? As it is, there are these śramaṇas with their shaved heads, wrapped in great bolts of cloth, who are a match for us and number nine to our one." The king asked: "Which śramaṇas?" They answered: "Noble sire, it is the group of six." The king said: "O wise ones, these are merely wandering śramaṇas — what harm could their words do to you? Now set the battle formation today." King Prasenajit of Kosala thought to himself:

Realizing that these men would be a persistent source of trouble for him, the king spoke to one of his attendants: "Come now, go to where the Blessed One is, and in my name bow your head at the Blessed One's two feet and inquire after his health: 'Is the Blessed One free from illness? Free from affliction? Active and vigorous? Living in comfort? Dwelling in a state of strength and ease? Free from anything unseemly?' Then speak these words: 'From King Prasenajit of Kosala comes this message: these noble ones dwell for a very long time within the army, they go to where the battle formation is being drawn up, and they experience the sight of victory banners at their finest, the finest of troops, and the army in full battle array. It would be excellent if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would please establish some rule by which these noble ones, even when dwelling for a very long time within the army, would not go to where the battle formation is being drawn up, would not experience the sight of victory banners at their finest, the finest of troops, and the army in full battle array — so that they may be mindful of this.'"

The man replied, "As you command, Sire," and having received these words from King Prasenajit of Kosala, he went to where the Blessed One was. Upon arriving, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the man addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, King Prasenajit of Kosala bows his head at the Blessed One's two feet and inquires after his health: 'Is the Blessed One free from illness? Free from affliction? Active and vigorous? Living in comfort? Dwelling in a state of strength and ease? Free from anything unseemly?'" The Blessed One replied, "May King Prasenajit of Kosala be well." Then the man continued: "From King Prasenajit of Kosala comes this message: these noble ones dwell for a very long time within the army, they go to where the battle formation is being drawn up, and they experience the sight of victory banners at their finest, the finest of troops, and the army in full battle array. It would be excellent if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would please establish some rule by which these noble ones, even when dwelling for a very long time within the army, would not go to where the battle formation is being drawn up, would not experience the sight of victory banners at their finest, the finest of troops, and the army in full battle array — so that they may be mindful of this."

The Blessed One said nothing to the man, and by his silence gave consent. The man, understanding that the Blessed One's silence was his consent, then bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this origin, and this occasion, convened the assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, act as though unknowing" also proceeds as before.

The awakened Buddha, the Blessed One, then questioned the group of six: "Monks, is it true that you dwell within the army, go to where the battle formation is being drawn up, and experience the sight of victory banners at their finest, the finest of troops, and the army in full battle array?" They replied, "Venerable One, it is true." The awakened Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them: "What is not the conduct of a śramaṇa, what is not in keeping with it, what is not appropriate, what is not in accord with proper conduct — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth." Having thus rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks:

"Monks, therefore, having seen the ten benefits clearly, a rule of training is to be established for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so on, as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk, while dwelling within that army for two days, goes to witness a battle formation in action, or experiences the sight of the finest victory banners, the finest of troops, or the army drawn up in full battle array, he commits a transgression."

The term "monk" refers to the group of six, or any other who is of that same kind. "Two days" means up to and including two days. As for "army" — an army may have one division, two divisions, three divisions, or four divisions. What is a one-division army? A host of elephants. What is a two-division army? A host of elephants and a host of cavalry. What is a three-division army? A host of elephants, a host of cavalry, and a host of chariots. What is a four-division army? A host of elephants, a host of cavalry, a host of chariots, and a host of infantry.

"While dwelling within it" means while staying there. "Goes to witness a battle formation in action" means going to watch a formation set for battle. "The finest of victory banners" — there are four kinds of victory banners: the banner of the horse standard, the banner of the sea-monster (makara), the banner of the lion, and the banner of the nāga. "The finest of troops" refers to the fourfold host of divisions: elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. As for "experiences the sight of the army drawn up in full battle array" — a formation takes four shapes: like the face of a grain, like the form of a chariot, like a crescent moon, or like the wings of a garuḍa.

"Commits a transgression" — it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the evil destinations of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the lower realms. Moreover, so long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas. It is for this reason that it is said "commits a transgression."

How precisely does one commit a transgression in this regard? If a monk goes to watch a formation being stirred into action by armored elephants, he commits a transgression. If the elephants are unarmored, it is a misdeed. If a monk goes to watch a formation being stirred into action by armored cavalry, he commits a transgression. If the cavalry is unarmored, it is a misdeed. If a monk goes to watch a formation being stirred into action by equipped chariots, he commits a transgression. If the chariots are unequipped, it is a misdeed. If a monk goes to watch a formation being stirred into action by armored infantry, he commits a transgression. If the infantry is unarmored, it is a misdeed. If a monk goes to a formation when it is being stirred into action, he commits a transgression. The same applies to experiencing the sight of the finest victory banners, the finest of troops, and the army drawn up in full battle array.

If any one of the eight impediments is present, no transgression is incurred. Likewise, no transgression is incurred for one who is a beginner, one who is mentally deranged, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by feeling.

Here concludes the forty-seventh transgression: the transgression of experiencing the divisions of an army.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had given going forth and full ordination to the group of seventeen, including Upananda and others — youths who were young members of the Śākya clan — those seventeen proceeded to rely upon, attend, and pay homage to the group of six monks.

Then Chāraka said: "Let the seventeen come here and do such and such." They replied: "Are you our preceptor or our abbot? You are not." At that, he said: "You fools, what else would you do?" and struck one of them. Thereupon all of them fell to the ground on their backs and began to cry out, "We have been struck! We have been struck!"

The monks said: "Venerable Chāraka, why do you strike the youths?" Chāraka replied: "Venerable ones, when I struck just one of them, they all fell to the ground and wept." The monks then said to the seventeen: "Venerable ones, when only one of you was struck, why did all of you fall to the ground and cry?" They replied: "If we had not cried out, all of us would have been beaten."

The monks censured, criticized, and reproached them, saying: "Why do monks, over a trifling matter, beat other monks in rage, disturbance, and indignation?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and this context, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth, as before. The section beginning "The Blessed Buddhas, knowing full well, inquire as if unaware" also proceeds as before.

The Blessed One questioned the venerable Chāraka: "Chāraka, is it true that, acting in rage, disturbance, and indignation, you struck a monk?" He replied: "Reverend one, it is true." The Blessed One then censured him, declaring that such conduct was unworthy of a renunciant, was not appropriate, was not suitable, and was not in accordance with the rule — that this is not something to be done by one who has gone forth. And so the Blessed One censured him in many ways.

He then addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits in their entirety, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established," and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to uphold this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, should any monk, acting in rage, disturbance, and indignation, strike a monk, he commits a transgression.

'Furthermore, should any monk' refers to Chāraka or any other who is of that kind.

'Acting in rage, disturbance, and indignation' means being angry and overcome by the force of anger.

'A monk' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.

'Should strike' means should he strike.

'He commits a transgression': this burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower rebirths, and the miserable destinies. Moreover, for as long as the transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. Therefore it is said: 'he commits a transgression.'

As for how a transgression comes about in this case: it may be through inner grasping, through outward projection, or through the possession of both together.

How does it come about through inner grasping?

If a monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, strikes a fellow monk with one finger, he incurs one transgression. If he strikes with two, three, four, or five fingers, he incurs two, three, four, or five transgressions respectively. If he strikes with a fist, an elbow, a shoulder, the head, the chest, the back, the hip, the thigh, the knee, the shin, or even with the big toe of his foot, he incurs a transgression in each case. That is how a transgression comes about through inner grasping.

As for how it comes about through outward projection: if a monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, shoots an arrow at a fellow monk, he incurs a transgression. Just as with an arrow, so too with an iron arrow, an arrow tipped halfway with iron, a dart with a pointed tip, a dart with serrated teeth, a four-edged dart, a dart shaped like the petal of a karāvīra flower, a dart with a hollow tip, a wheel, a single-pointed vajra, a heavy arrow, a single-pointed blade, a bolt of Chinese bamboo, or even a handful of mustard seeds that he throws — for as many mustard seeds as strike the body, he incurs that many transgressions; and for as many mustard seeds as fail to strike the body, he incurs that many offenses of wrongdoing. That is how a transgression comes about through outward projection.

As for how it comes about through the possession of both together: if a monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, strikes a fellow monk with a sword, he incurs a transgression. Just as with a sword, so too with a hatchet, a single-edged blade, a double-edged blade, a spear, a thrown spear, a curved knife, a grass stalk, or even a broom — for as many bristles of the broom as strike the body, he incurs that many transgressions; and for as many bristles as fail to strike the body, he incurs that many offenses of wrongdoing. That is how a transgression comes about through the possession of both together.

There is no transgression for one who is being restrained by others, or who is performing a ritual striking as part of the practice of a vidyā mantra. There is likewise no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is mentally deranged, one whose mind is disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful feelings.

The thirty-eighth transgression concerning striking is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gave forth-going and full ordination to seventeen young men — novices born in Nīpa — together with their near attendants. Once they had been ordained, those novices began to consort with, associate with, and pay service to the group of the Six Monks.

Then Chanda said to them: "You seventeen, come here and do this and that." They replied: "Are you our preceptor or our abbot? We will not do it." At this he mocked them, saying: "You dolts, what else do you do?" — and he made a threatening gesture as though to strike one of them. At once all of them fell to the ground and began to weep. The monks said: "Venerable Chanda, why did you threaten to strike the young men?" Chanda replied: "Venerable ones, I made a threatening gesture as though to strike one of them, and they all fell to the ground and wept." The monks then said to the seventeen: "Venerable ones, he only made a threatening gesture toward one of you — why did you all fall to the ground and weep?" They replied: "If we had not wept, there would have been no one to report what he struck and why."

Then the monks of few desires censured and rebuked those monks, saying: "Why do monks stirred by anger and rage, their minds displeased, make threatening gestures toward fellow monks?"

The monks reported this matter of abusive speech to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this as the basis and occasion, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, while knowing, make inquiry" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One addressed the venerable Chanda: "Chanda, is it true that, stirred by anger and rage, your mind displeased, you made a threatening gesture as though to strike a monk?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One censured him, saying that what is not the proper conduct of a monk, what is not fitting, not suitable, not in accord with the discipline, is not something a person who has gone forth ought to do. Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing the ten benefits rightly, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, makes a threatening gesture as though to strike a monk — even with the flat of the hand — commits an offense.

Now, the phrase 'whatever monk' refers to Chanda or to any other who is likewise. The phrase 'stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased' means overcome by anger and overwhelmed by the force of that anger. The phrase 'toward a monk' means toward one who belongs to this Dharma. The phrase 'makes a threatening gesture as though to strike' means positions himself to strike. The phrase 'even with the flat of the hand' means even if it is merely a threatening gesture with the flat of the palm. The phrase 'commits an offense' means it causes him to be burned, scorched, and cast down into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of miserable rebirth. Furthermore, for as long as the offense is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous qualities — and for that reason it is said to commit an offense.

Now, one may ask: how does it become an offense? It does so through being seized internally, through being cast externally, or through both together. How so through being seized internally? If a monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, makes a threatening gesture as though to strike a monk with one finger, he commits one offense. If he makes a threatening gesture with two, three, four, or five fingers, he commits two, three, four, or five offenses respectively. If he makes a threatening gesture with the fist, with the elbow, with the shoulder, with the head, with the knee, with the back, with the hip, with the thigh, with the knee-joint, with the ankle, or even with the big toe of the foot, he commits an offense in each case. That is how it occurs through being seized internally.

How does it occur through being cast externally? If a monk, stirred by anger and rage, his mind displeased, makes a threatening gesture as though to shoot an arrow at a monk, he commits an offense. Just as with shooting an arrow, so too with an iron arrow, a half-iron arrow, a three-pointed dart, a dart with tooth-like points, a four-cornered dart, a dart shaped like the petals of a karavīra flower, a dart shaped like a bird's heart, a discus, a single-pointed vajra, a large arrow, a single-pointed weapon, a bamboo thorn — and even if he makes a threatening gesture with a palmful of white mustard seeds, he commits as many offenses as there are mustard seeds he threatens with. That is how it occurs through being cast externally.

Now, how does it occur through both together?

If a monk, overcome with rage and agitation, in a state of anger and discontent, makes a threatening gesture toward another monk with a sword, he commits a transgression. Just as with a sword, so too with a cleaver, a single-edged blade, a double-edged blade, a spear, a thrown spear, a knife, and a grass thorn — and even if he makes a threatening gesture with a broom, he commits as many offenses as there are thorns in it. Just as with a broom, so too with a bunch of iron needles and a coil of rope — if he makes a threatening gesture, it is the same. That is how it occurs through both together.

There is no offense for one who is a first offender, who is insane, who is mentally disturbed, or who is afflicted by feelings.

The forty-ninth offense of threatening is complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A monk named Dharma who dwelt together with Ānanda was a person of conscience, given to remorse, restrained, and desirous of training. For as long as he did not know that a certain individual was engaging in misconduct throughout his dwelling, he continued to live together with that person. But when he came to know that the person was engaging in such misconduct, he then began to live together with those monks who were of naturally proper conduct. In accordance with the word of the Blessed One, he would go at the three times of day simply to bow at that person's feet.

Dharma went to the other monk and requested permission to use his parasol. When Ānanda heard this, he said, "My son Dharma, take my mat as well and go. Has the ācārya too gone to use a parasol? Foolish one, do you wish to examine me separately? What practice of yoga is there that I do not know? I do not investigate the ācārya separately." Having thus said, "Has the ācārya too gone to use a parasol?" and having requested a seat, Dharma departed.

Dharma took that monk's mat and went out to use it during the day. He placed the mat at the foot of a tree and sat down in a secluded spot and began to arouse mental application. Afterward Ānanda came and, seeing Dharma from a distance — for they were far apart — said, "Ācārya, I have placed the mat at the foot of a tree; go there and sit." Ānanda went there and sat down covering his head. Not finding what he wished for there, he rose from the mat and began to look in all four directions. Then a girl was seen cutting shadow-grass at the edge of the Jeta Grove, and he called out to Dharma, "Dharma, make the girl stop cutting shadow-grass."

Dharma said to him, "Ācārya, think of the meaning of the Jeta Grove sūtra. Foolish one, have you come to rely on the literal edge of a sūtra passage? Did the Blessed One not say, 'I will not even discard a blade of grass belonging to the Saṅgha'? I shall go myself and turn her away. The ācārya knows."

Ānanda went and said, "Girl, why are you cutting the shadow-grass of the Jeta Grove?" The girl smiled. Ānanda grabbed her by her limbs and her trunk and let out a cry. Then he went to Dharma and asked, "My son Dharma, did you see anything at all?" "Ācārya, I saw everything except the actual penetration." "My son Dharma, do not tell anyone. Ācārya, for as long as you have not seen a monk of naturally proper conduct, I will not tell anyone." Ānanda said, "If I were to conceal the offense of misconduct of your preceptor, would you not conceal mine?" Dharma replied:

When Dharma said, "Even if you, ācārya, conceal it, I will not conceal it," the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The monks rebuked, derided, and murmured against him, saying, "Why do certain monks knowingly conceal a monk's offense of serious misconduct?" The monks then informed the Blessed One, and thereupon the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks on account of this occurrence, this basis, and this occasion — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddhas knowingly feign not to know — and so forth as before.

The Blessed One questioned the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you knowingly concealed a monk's offense of serious misconduct?" "Blessed One, it is so." The Blessed One censured him, declaring that what is not the way of the ascetic life, what is not proper, what is not fitting, what does not accord with the rule — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One censured him in many ways and spoke to the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, I will establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk knowingly conceals a monk's offense of serious misconduct commits a downfall.

Now, 'whatever monk' means a son of the Śākyas such as Ānanda or anyone else of that kind. 'Knowingly' means having recognized it himself or having been told by others. 'A monk's' means one belonging to this Dharma community. 'Offense of serious misconduct' refers to two kinds of serious misconduct: that which leads to defeat (pārājika), and that which leads to a formal act of the remaining Saṅgha. Why are these called serious misconduct? Because of their essential nature and their arising. 'Conceals' means having covered it over. 'Commits a downfall' means it burns him, scorches him, and causes him to fall into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, evil destinies, and states of ruin. Furthermore, as long as the offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas — therefore it is said to commit a downfall.

How does one come to commit a downfall in each case? If a monk sees another monk committing an offense that leads to defeat, and generates in his mind the intention to conceal it from that monk, then until dawn has not yet broken it is a misdeed, and when dawn breaks it becomes a downfall. If a monk sees another monk committing an offense requiring a formal act of the remaining Saṅgha, and generates in his mind the intention to conceal it from that monk, then until dawn has not yet broken it is a misdeed, and when dawn breaks it becomes a downfall. If a monk sees another monk committing an offense that itself constitutes a downfall, and generates in his mind the intention to conceal it from that monk, then until dawn has not yet broken it is a misdeed, and when dawn breaks it also remains a misdeed. If a monk sees another monk committing an offense requiring individual confession, and generates in his mind the intention to conceal it from that monk, then until dawn has not yet broken it is a misdeed, and when dawn breaks it also remains a misdeed. If a monk sees another monk committing a misdeed offense, and generates in his mind the intention to conceal it from that monk, then until dawn has not yet broken it is a misdeed, and when dawn breaks it also remains a misdeed.

For me, this basis does not touch upon ease,

if it would become an obstacle to the ascetic's rules and to the holy life, there is no transgression. For me, if this basis would cause division of the Saṅgha, or disturbance of the Saṅgha, or the Saṅgha becoming two, or the Saṅgha becoming separate, there is no transgression. For one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or who is mentally disturbed, or who is afflicted by feelings, there is no transgression. The fifty offenses of concealing a basis of bad conduct are complete.

The Vinaya Analysis, the fifty-sixth bundle. In summary: ease, fire, and intention; not yet fully ordained, Dharma, and speech; a novice whose complexion has changed; precious things and the hot season.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A monk named Dharma was dwelling together with Ānanda — a monk who was conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and desirous of training. For as long as he did not know that the other was engaging in all kinds of bad conduct, he dwelt together with him. When he came to know that the other was engaging in all kinds of bad conduct, he then began to dwell together only with those monks who were of naturally good conduct, and by the Blessed One's scriptural authority he would go to pay homage at his feet at the three times of day alone.

Upananda said to Ānanda: "Look, teacher Dharma has lodged a complaint before the community of monks, the Saṅgha of the Buddha and the rest. I too should do him some definite harm." Ānanda replied: "This monk is conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and desirous of training — what harm could you do him? What must certainly be done is to cut off his food." "That can be done."

A householder invited both Ānanda and Upananda to a meal. Upananda thought: "Today I shall cut off this Dharma's food." Dharma went to Ānanda's place and said: "Preceptor, I request leave to go on alms-round." Ānanda said: "Dharma, today a householder has invited us to a meal — come here and eat your meal right here." Dharma replied: "Was I ever invited before together with the preceptor?" Upananda said: "Dharma, I have heard from others and seen from others — if I know you to be conscientious, remorseful, restrained, and desirous of training, did your preceptor cause you to take possession of improper things? Why then do you cut off the words of one who has the qualities of a preceptor? Has the Blessed One not said in the Vinaya that when an ācārya or preceptor instructs, one must comply, and that if one does not comply it becomes a misdeed?" Silenced by the eloquent censure of that monk, Dharma sat without saying anything. Then he said: "I shall come, having taken my bowl and water-pot." Ānanda replied: "What use is the bowl and water-pot there? There you will get the water strained from washing the vessels — come along then." Dharma set out together with both of them. A noble one engaged in alms-round saw him and said: "Dharma, where are you going?" "I am going where I have been invited." "Know moderation in food." Dharma said: "Whether I will eat a meal or have my food cut off, there is no telling." He entered Śrāvastī together with those two. The two went along the street and took their place in the market. Upananda went to that householder's house, ate his meal, and returned. After that, Ānanda too went to that householder's house and ate his meal, sitting there. Dharma said to Upananda: "Teacher, it is midday — you should leave." Upananda replied: "Everything there is already prepared, so go there — there is nothing else to do apart from eating — go straight at midday."

Dharma stood up and began measuring the shadow with both feet. Ānanda said: "You fool — do you have not even a little trust in our training? Do you think that by traveling by a middle route we will eat at the wrong time? It is not comfortable for me to speak or sit together with you; it would be more comfortable for me to speak or sit alone. Off you go!" Dharma thought: "If I had come carrying my bowl and water-strainer, I would have been going out on alms-round — but now there is nothing at all to be done." So he went to the temple, and for as long as there was color in his body he strained toward virtue, and when the color faded from his body he lay down and rested. The monks then said to him: "Venerable Dharma, is the food someone else's — is the meal also someone else's? Why, for something as small as being unable to strain toward virtue, did you eat that much food?" Dharma replied: "Who ate? Did you not eat? — I did not eat." Because he expanded on that occasion in that way, and because monks of little understanding were rebuking monks, saying they had intentionally cut off a monk's food, hurling insults, and speaking ill of them, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, because of this occurrence, with this as the grounds, and in this context, convened the community of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddhas, though knowing, made inquiry — and so forth as before.

The Blessed Buddha then questioned Ānanda: "Ānanda, you yourself were seeking a fault and thinking 'I shall find a fault with this monk' — taking that very intention as the condition, you spoke to the monk thus: 'Venerable, come here; go to the householders' homes, and I will have them give you as much lodging and food as you wish' — and then, without actually having them give it to him, you said after that: 'Venerable, it is not comfortable for me to speak or sit together with you; it would be more comfortable for me to speak or sit alone — off you go!' — and you set about cutting off his food. Is that true?" "Reverend, it is so."

The Blessed Buddha then rebuked him, saying that such behavior — contrary to the conduct of an ascetic, not befitting, not suitable, not in conformity with discipline — is not to be done by one who has gone forth. After rebuking him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing ten benefits in their true form, a rule of training is to be laid down in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth as before. My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, seeking a fault and thinking 'I shall find a fault with this monk,' takes that very intention as the condition and speaks to the monk thus: 'Venerable, come here; go to the householders' homes, and I will have them give you as much lodging and food as you may desire for alms' — and then, without having them give it to him, says thereafter: 'Venerable, it is not comfortable for me to speak or sit together with you; it would be more comfortable for me to speak or sit alone — off you go!' — commits an offense.

Here 'whatever monk' refers to Śākyamuni's son Ānanda or another of that kind."

"Seeking a fault, thinking 'I shall find a fault with this monk'" means: thinking "I shall cause this monk's alms to be cut off by any means."

"Taking that very thing as the condition" means: not something else.

"To the monk" means: to one who belongs to this Dharma.

"Saying thus" means: having spoken in these words.

"Venerable, come here; go to the householders' homes" means: to the homes of brahmins and householders.

"Lodging and food as alms for you there" — "lodging" refers to the five kinds of lodging, and "food" refers to the five kinds of food.

"Saying 'I will have them give you as much as you may desire'" means: as much as is sufficient.

"Without having them give it to him, says thereafter: 'Venerable, it is not comfortable for me to speak or sit together with you; rather, it would be more comfortable for me to speak or sit alone — off you go!'" means: having said exactly those words.

"Commits an offense" means: it burns, scorches, and casts one down into the hells, the animal realm, the preta realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of miserable downfall. Furthermore, so long as that offense is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs one's virtuous qualities. Therefore it is said to commit an offense.

As to how a downfall arises in this case: however slight the intention with which a monk causes a monk's alms to be cut off, a downfall arises in every instance. There is no downfall when one causes it to be done for the sake of someone who is ill, or when it is done following a physician's instruction. There is no downfall for a first offender, for one who is mentally deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one overwhelmed by painful sensations.

The fifty-first offense — that of causing alms to be cut off — is complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha), Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then a great many merchants of Śrāvastī went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Blessed One fully taught those many merchants of Śrāvastī with words of Dharma, fully led them to take it up, fully praised them, and fully gladdened them. With many explanations he fully taught, fully led them to take it up, fully praised them, and fully gladdened them with words of Dharma, and then fell silent.

Then those many merchants of Śrāvastī, having rejoiced and expressed their delight at what the Blessed One had declared, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, departed from the Blessed One's presence, and went to where the Venerable Ānanda was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Venerable Ānanda's feet and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda fully taught, fully led to the taking up, fully praised, and fully gladdened those many merchants of Śrāvastī with Dharma talk. With many explanations he fully taught, fully led them to take it up, fully praised them, and fully gladdened them with Dharma talk, and then fell silent.

Then those many merchants of Śrāvastī rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, turned toward the Venerable Ānanda with palms joined in reverence, and spoke to the Venerable Ānanda thus:

"Venerable Ānanda, after the Blessed One has accepted the rains retreat, where will he go? Wise ones, please ask the Blessed One. Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, and so we do not dare to ask the Blessed One directly. Wise ones, for me too, since the Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, I am unable to ask the Blessed One. Venerable Ānanda, if even the Venerable Ānanda, because the Blessed One is difficult to approach and difficult to bear with, does not venture to ask the Blessed One — then how does the Venerable Ānanda know by signs or by words where the Blessed One will go after accepting the rains retreat? How does he know by signs? How does he know by words?"

"Wise ones, whichever direction the Blessed One, having accepted the rains retreat, intends to travel, toward that direction he faces and sits, and he also speaks in praise of those people. Venerable Ānanda, which direction does the Blessed One face as he sits? Of which people does he speak in praise?" "Wise ones, the Blessed One faces toward Magadha as he sits, and he speaks in praise of the people of Rājagṛha."

Those merchants, delighting in and rejoicing over what the Venerable Ānanda had said, bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and departed. They then thought to themselves: "The Blessed One, having accepted the rains retreat, will journey to Rājagṛha." And so they made preparations to travel to Rājagṛha.

Then the Blessed One accepted the rains retreat, and when all three months of the rains had passed, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is setting out to tour the lands of Magadha. Whoever among you wishes to travel with the Tathāgata to tour the lands of Magadha should attend to the business of his robe.' "

The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Yes, Venerable One, as you command," and having heard the Blessed One, he announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is setting out to tour the lands of Magadha. Whoever among you wishes to travel with the Tathāgata to tour the lands of Magadha should attend to the business of his robe."

The merchants of Śrāvastī heard the Venerable Ānanda making this announcement to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is setting out to tour the lands of Magadha. Whoever among you wishes to travel with the Tathāgata to tour the lands of Magadha should attend to the business of his robe." Having heard this, they went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One fully taught, fully led to the taking up, fully praised, and fully gladdened those many merchants of Śrāvastī with Dharma talk. With many explanations he fully taught, fully led them to take it up, fully praised them, and fully gladdened them with Dharma talk, and then fell silent.

Then the very many merchants of Śrāvastī rose from their seats, arranged their robes over one shoulder, joined their palms toward the Blessed One, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, for as long as the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, travels from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha, may it please you to accept from us food, alms-rounds, lodging, medicine for the sick, and all requisite supplies." The Blessed One said nothing to the very many merchants of Śrāvastī, and by that silence he consented. Then, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had consented, the very many merchants of Śrāvastī rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One's word, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then the very many merchants of Śrāvastī went to where the venerable Ānanda was, arrived there, bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Ānanda, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the very many merchants of Śrāvastī said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, how great an entourage does the Blessed One travel with?" The venerable Ānanda replied: "Good sirs, it is like a wheel-turning king." They asked: "Venerable Ānanda, and how great an entourage does a wheel-turning king travel with?" The venerable Ānanda replied: "Good sirs, a wheel-turning king travels along the roads with a retinue extending ten leagues in every direction." With that measure of ten leagues in every direction, they arranged provisions for the assembly accompanying the Blessed One together with the community of monks. Whatever cold foods there were, they prepared in advance on that very day; whatever hot foods there were, they prepared fresh each day.

Then the Blessed One set out, his retinue tamed, surrounded by a tamed retinue; he who was at peace, surrounded by a retinue that was at peace; he who was liberated, surrounded by a liberated retinue; he who had found relief, surrounded by a retinue that had found relief; he who was subdued, surrounded by a subdued retinue; an arhat, surrounded by arhats; he who was free of attachment, surrounded by those free of attachment; one who was beautiful, surrounded by a beautiful retinue. Like a supreme bull surrounded by a herd of bulls; like an elephant surrounded by a host of young elephants; like a lion surrounded by a host of fanged beasts; like a king of geese surrounded by a flock of geese; like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of birds; like a brahmin surrounded by a host of students; like a skilled physician surrounded by a host of patients; like a hero surrounded by a host of troops; like a land-surveyor surrounded by a host of those who have entered the path; like a caravan leader surrounded by a host of merchants; like a merchant chief surrounded by his retinue; like a king of a citadel surrounded by a host of ministers; like a wheel-turning king surrounded by a host of a thousand sons; like the moon surrounded by a host of stars; like the sun surrounded by a host of a thousand rays; like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas; like a noble man surrounded by a host of attendants; like the nāga Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas; like Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a host of yakṣas; like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of asuras; like Śakra (Indra) surrounded by the host of the Thirty-Three Gods; like Brahmā surrounded by the host of the Brahmā realm —

— with faculties perfectly tamed; with conduct and deportment untroubled; steady as an ocean of water; laden with moisture like a rain-cloud; free from arrogance like the king of elephants; well adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being; his body beautifully ornamented with the eighty minor marks; his form resplendent with a radiance extending a fathom in all directions; possessed of a brilliance surpassing a thousand suns; auspicious in every direction like a moving mountain of jewels; endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unmixed applications of mindfulness, and great compassion —

together with those great śrāvakas: Jñānakoṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and the rest — and further, surrounded and attended in front by a very great community of monks, the Blessed One set out to stroll and walk in the direction of Rājagṛha.

The venerable Ānanda had gone on ahead in a direction serving the same purpose. When he saw a fork in the path, he waited there until the Blessed One arrived. After the Blessed One had come, the Blessed One spoke: "Ānanda, why do you wait here?" "Venerable One, this is a forking of paths. The straight path has the danger of lions, while the winding path is safe. By which shall I go?" "Ānanda, take the straight path — the Tathāgata is free from the danger of lions."

Then the Blessed One began proceeding along the straight path, and as he traveled along that road he came to a cliff. From that cliff two young boys came out onto the road and sat there playing. One of them held in his hand a large drum called a ṭaha, and the other held a bow. When those two saw the Blessed One, they said: "May the Blessed One come this way. Welcome, Blessed One. Where does the Blessed One go along this fearsome path? But the Blessed One should not be frightened — the two of us will escort the Blessed One."

Then, filled with faith, one of them beat the ṭaha drum, and the other, filled with faith, twanged the bow. As the two of them began to walk before the Blessed One, the Blessed One thought to himself: "These two boys are generating roots of virtue." Knowing this, the Blessed One spoke to those two boys: "Boys, go back — the Tathāgata is free from the danger of lions."

Those two prostrated with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the Blessed One's presence, and the Blessed One smiled.

By the nature of reality, whenever the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, smile, rays of light — blue, yellow, red, white, rose-pink, crystal-clear, and silver-hued — issue from their mouths. Some of those rays descend downward and some ascend upward. Those that descend downward pass into the hells: the Cold Hell, the Black-Line Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Wailing Hell, the Great Wailing Hell, the Hot Hell, the Intensely Hot Hell, the Avīci Hell, the Blistering Hell, the Bursting-Blister Hell, the Chattering-Teeth Hell, the Crying-Out Hell, the Groaning Hell, the Cracked-Like-an-Utpala-Flower Hell, the Cracked-Like-a-Lotus Hell, and the Greatly Cracked-Like-a-Lotus Hell — and upon whatever hot hells there are, those rays cause a cool refreshing rain to fall;

and upon whatever cold hells there are, those rays cause a warm and gentle rain to fall. By this, the particular torments of those sentient beings are cut off without interruption, and those beings think to themselves: "O wise ones, have we died and passed on from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?" In order to arouse faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When they behold the emanation, they think: "O wise ones, we have neither died and passed on from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere. It is thus: by the power of this being we had never seen before, our particular torments have been cut off." Having developed sincere faith in their minds toward the emanation, they exhaust the karma that had consigned them to experience the hells, and then take rebirth among those gods and humans who are vessels for the truths, in whatever place that may be.

Those rays that travel upward enter among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Heaven Free from Strife, the Joyful Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Emanations, the Heaven of Wielding Power over Others' Emanations, the Heaven of Brahmā's Retinue, the Heaven of Brahmā's Ministers, the Great Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Minor Light, the Heaven of Boundless Light, the Heaven of Radiant Light, the Heaven of Minor Virtue, the Heaven of Boundless Virtue, the Heaven of Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven of Great Fruit, the Heaven of No Perception, the Heaven of Neither Torment nor Ease, the Heaven of Auspicious Appearance, the Heaven of Clear Vision, and the Heaven of Akaniṣṭha — and there they proclaim the words: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness. And they also recite these two verses:

Strive and bring forth,
enter upon the Buddha's teaching.
Like a great elephant at a house of mud,
crush the armies of the Lord of Death.
Whoever dwells with utmost heedfulness
and practices in this taming Dharma
shall utterly abandon the round of birth
and make an end of suffering at last.

Then those rays, having pervaded the great trichiliocosm, follow along behind the Blessed One, trailing after him. If the Blessed One intends to prophesy past karma, the rays dissolve at his back. If he intends to prophesy future karma, they dissolve at his front. If he intends to prophesy rebirth in the hells, they dissolve at the soles of his feet. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they dissolve at his heels. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost, they dissolve at his great toes. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a human, they dissolve at his knees. If he intends to prophesy sovereignty as a wheel-turning monarch of great power, they dissolve at his left palm. If he intends to prophesy sovereignty as a wheel-turning monarch, they dissolve at his right palm. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a god, they dissolve at his navel. If he intends to prophesy the awakening of a śrāvaka, they dissolve at his mouth. If he intends to prophesy the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they dissolve at his hair-tuft between the brows. And if he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they dissolve at his crown protrusion.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and dissolved into his crown protrusion.

Thereupon the venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and asked the Blessed One:

Blazing with a thousand varied hues,
these rays have issued from the Blessed One's face
and lit up all directions on every side,
like a sunshade spreading wide its canopy.

And he spoke further in verse:

Free from agitation, free from timidity, and entirely rid of pride,
the Buddha has become the supreme cause for wandering beings.
The Victor who has subdued his foes, beyond all cause for conflict —

whose hands are white as a conch shell's whorls, who smiles not without cause — for that reason the Teacher, knowing the right moment by his own wisdom, the Sage (muni), the bull of the herd, lord among ascetics and lords of birth, we pray that he dispel with words that are firm, and with the holy and virtuous, the doubts that have arisen in those assembled beings who listen with attentiveness. Like a king of mountains standing firm in the salt sea, the buddha protectors do not smile on a sudden impulse. We who are gathered as an assembly of beings wish to hear the reason why those who are firm now display a smile.

The venerable one — the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition. Venerable one, what then is the cause of this smile? What is the condition?

The Blessed One declared: Ānanda, it is exactly so. It is exactly so. Ānanda, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition.

Ānanda, did you see those two boys, those two young children, who were pelting the Tathāgata with sand?

Venerable one, I did see them.

Ānanda, by virtue of this root of virtue and this wholesome conduct, those two boys will not fall into evil states for thirteen aeons. The two of them will take rebirth among gods and humans, passing through cyclic existence, and when they reach their final existence, their final dwelling, their final form, their final body, it is through that very karma, that very root of virtue, and that very wholesome conduct that they will go forth and directly realize solitary awakening. One will become a pratyekabuddha named Drum Sound, and the other will become a pratyekabuddha named Fearless Giver.

Then the Blessed One consented to pass the night at a certain secluded forest hermitage outside any town. The Blessed One gave the instruction that a hollow tree should be surrounded by elderly monks in succession. The group of six, having obtained the hollow tree, feeling cold, set fire inside the hollow tree, and a snake that was rapidly spreading its venom within the hollow tree was stirred up by the smoke, climbed up to the branches above, and hung there.

The group of six, seeing it hanging there, said among themselves, "It has appeared! It has appeared!" The attendants (doṇmthun), hearing this, thought, "A lion has appeared!" and, terrified, fled in all four directions.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: Ānanda, why have the attendants fled in all four directions?

Venerable one, the Blessed One gave the instruction that a hollow tree be surrounded by elderly monks in succession. The group of six, having obtained the hollow tree, feeling cold, set fire inside the hollow tree, and a snake that was rapidly spreading its venom within the hollow tree was stirred up by the smoke, climbed up to the branches above, and hung there. The group of six saw it hanging there and said, "It has appeared! It has appeared!" The attendants, hearing this, thought, "Has a lion appeared?" and, terrified, fled in all four directions.

The Blessed One declared: Ānanda, go and tell the attendants that the Tathāgata is free from the fear of lions, and bid them return.

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having heard this from the Blessed One, went to where the attendants were and said, "Friends, the Tathāgata is free from the fear of lions — return!" And they returned.

The monks then addressed the Blessed One: Venerable one, the group of six caused the attendants to flee in terror —

— and the Blessed One saw them as they fled in all four directions and breathed a sigh. Monks, not only now, but in times past as well, these same ones caused a great herd of wild animals to flee in terror in all four directions, and I breathed a sigh then too. Listen to this.

Monks, long ago in times past, beside a certain pond there was a grove of bilva trees, and in that grove of bilva trees there lived six hares. From that grove a bilva fruit fell into the pond and made a loud splash. The six hares heard the sound and, being small creatures, were terrified and began to flee.

As they fled, some foxes saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The hares replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the foxes too began to flee.

As they fled, some deer saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The foxes replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the deer too began to flee.

As they fled, some boars saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The deer replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the boars too began to flee.

As they fled, some buffalo saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The boars replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the buffalo too began to flee.

As they fled, some rhinoceroses saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The buffalo replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the rhinoceroses too began to flee.

As they fled, some elephants saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The rhinoceroses replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the elephants too began to flee.

As they fled, some bears saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The elephants replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the bears too began to flee.

As they fled, some hyenas saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The bears replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the hyenas too began to flee.

As they fled, some wolves saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The hyenas replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the wolves too began to flee.

As they fled, some tigers saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The wolves replied, "There was a great crash!" And so the tigers too began to flee.

As they fled, some lions saw them and asked, "Friends, why do you run?" The tigers replied, "There was a great crash!" And so those lions too began to flee.

Now, not far from the foot of a mountain, there sat a lion with a mane like a crown. He saw those lions fleeing and said to them, "Friends, all of you have the strength of claws and the strength of fangs and nothing else — so why do you flee?" The lions replied, "There was a great crash!" The lion said, "Friends, where did this great crash come from? I myself do not know where such a crash comes from." Then that lion spoke:

"You who are wise, do not flee! Let us investigate where this crashing noise has come from." With these words he questioned the tigers: "Who told you this?" The tigers replied, "The wild yaks did." He questioned the wild yaks: "Who told you this?" The wild yaks replied, "The bears did." He questioned the bears: "Who told you this?" The bears replied, "The elephants did." He questioned the elephants: "Who told you this?" The elephants replied, "The rhinoceroses did." He questioned the rhinoceroses: "Who told you this?" The rhinoceroses replied, "The buffalo did." He questioned the buffalo: "Who told you this?" The buffalo replied, "The boars did." He questioned the boars: "Who told you this?" The boars replied, "The deer did." He questioned the deer: "Who told you this?" The deer replied, "The foxes did." He questioned the foxes: "Who told you this?" The foxes replied, "The hares did." He questioned the hares: "Who told you this?" The hares replied, "Come, and we shall show you directly the very fear we saw; and we shall point out where that crashing noise came from." And so they led that lion to the grove of bel trees and said, "The crash came from here." Now, at that very moment, another bel fruit dropped into the pool, and the sound "crash!" arose. Then that lion said, "You who are wise, this is merely a crashing sound — do not be afraid!" And at that, all of them breathed a sigh of relief.

Then the god spoke these verses:

Do not go by what is widely reported;
see for yourself with your own direct perception.
A bel fruit falling in the forest grove —
look how it left all four-footed creatures without their wits!

Monks, the lion with a mane like a crown who at that time and on that occasion relieved from terror the great assembly of animals that had fled in the four directions — that was none other than myself. And the six hares who at that time and on that occasion caused the great assembly of animals to be seized with terror — those were the Group of Six. Monks, thus even in times past these same ones caused the great assembly of animals to be seized with terror and flee in the four directions, and I relieved them; and now too these same ones have, in concert, caused terror and flight in the four directions, and I have relieved them.

This, then, is something that has occurred. For the time being, the Blessed One, the Buddha, will not for the time being set down a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the Group of Six and tell them this: 'None of you are to go before the Group of Six. The Tathāgata himself will come before the Group of Six.'" The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having listened to the Blessed One he went to the meeting place of the Group of Six and said, "You who are wise, the Tathāgata has declared: 'None of you are to go before the Group of Six. The Tathāgata himself will come before the Group of Six.'" Such was his announcement.

Then the Tathāgata himself went before the Group of Six. And when he arrived, a certain lion with a mane like a crown came roaring and flung itself down before the Blessed One,

the Blessed One emanated five lions with manes like crowns in the palm of his right hand. Smelling their scent, the lion became frightened and began to flee, whereupon the Blessed One emanated fire in all four directions. That lion saw fire blazing, fiercely blazing, blazing all around in every direction, the flames merging into one continuous conflagration, and saw that only at the very feet of the Blessed One was there peace. The lion then touched its head to the two feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One's hands bore the wheel, the auspicious symbol, the swastika, and the webbing between the fingers — born of many hundreds of merits, bestowing relief from all fears. With these hands he stroked the lion's head and spoke: "Fair-faced one, because you acted with past misdeeds you were born in the realm of animals. You are now engaged in fierce cruelty, in striking and slaying with blood-red paws; you take the lives of others, you lead others to take life, you live by killing the lives of others. When you die and pass on from here, what will your destiny be? What will your birth be? What will your next life be? Fair-faced one, know this: all formations are impermanent, all phenomena are without self, nirvāṇa is peace." Having thus taught the Dharma in these three sayings, he declared, "Fair-faced one, place your mind in manifest faith in me, and through that you will be freed from attachment to the animal realm of birth."

When monks touched that lion, it let out a roar. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, do not touch the lion. Why is that? Because, monks, a lion is difficult to endure and difficult to approach. Therefore, monks, a monk must not touch a lion. If a monk touches a lion, it will become a serious offense."

Then the king of beasts, that lion, thought to himself: "Since I have heard the Dharma in these three sayings before the Blessed One, it is not fitting for me to go on eating food." And so he entered upon a fast. Because the metabolism of those born in the animal realm is acute, when he had grown feeble from hunger he placed his mind in manifest faith in the Blessed One, and when his time came he passed away and was born among the gods of the Four Great Kings. It is the natural condition of a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods that, not long after birth, three thoughts arise: from where did I pass away, where have I been born, and by what karma was I born? He saw that he had passed away from among the animals, that he had been born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, and that he had been born by having placed his mind in manifest faith in the Blessed One.

Then that formerly-a-lion son of the gods thought to himself: "Since I abide in my dwelling place and approach the Blessed One in order to see him and pay homage to him, this is not in keeping with my manner of conduct. Rather, without relying on my dwelling place, I will approach the Blessed One simply to see him and pay homage to him."

Then the formerly-a-lion son of the gods, his ear-ornaments and earrings swaying, wearing pure and stainless garlands and necklaces, his body adorned with garlands and bracelets, filled a basket with divine blue lotuses, pink lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses — streaming down through the night with their colors brilliantly surpassing all — and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he scattered the flowers as an offering before the Blessed One, bowed his head to the two feet of the Blessed One in homage, and sat to one side. And so it was that through the radiance of the formerly-a-lion son of the gods, all the places of the uninhabited wilderness monastery were suffused with a great and spreading light.
