Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, the latent tendencies, the temperament, and the intrinsic nature of the formerly-a-lion son of the gods, taught the Dharma in such a way as to lead one to a thorough individual discernment of the noble Four Truths — the very Dharma by hearing which the formerly-a-lion son of the gods, while still seated on that same seat, shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, he solemnly proclaimed three times: "What the venerable Blessed One has done for me — this, my father has not done, my mother has not done, the king has not done, the gods have not done, my forebears of former times have not done, ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins have not done, and the assembly of friends, companions, and kinsmen has not done. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, you have liberated me from mountains of bones, you have closed the doors to the lower realms, you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, you have lifted my feet from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and you have placed me among gods and humans."

Then he spoke further in verse:

By your supremely mighty power,
I — though laden with many faults —
have had the trail of lower realms blocked off,
been richly endowed with merit,
had the path to the higher realms opened before me,
and attained as well the trail to nirvāṇa.

Relying on you, utterly pure one,
today I have obtained an eye free of defects and clean,
attained the noble sublime station of peace and joy,
and shall cross to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Among beings worshipped by gods, demigods, and humans,
free of birth, old age, and death,
the one who sees existence as empty — supremely rare:
the Sage. Today there is the fruit of having seen you.

Then, with a garland hanging loosely down in grief,
he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, and joy arose within him.
Having circumambulated to the right, honoring the Foe-Destroyer,
he departed through the sky in the direction of the divine world.

Then the formerly-a-lion son of the gods became like a merchant who has found great profit, like a farmer who has obtained an abundant harvest, like a hero who has been completely victorious in battle, like a sick person who has been wholly freed from all illness — and in the very same attire in which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One, he departed for his own abode.

Now those monks who were devoted to striving and remained without sleeping in the first watch and the last watch of the night saw, in the presence of the Blessed One, a vast and spreading radiance fill the space around them. Seeing it, with minds full of doubt, they waited until dawn had broken and then asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what was this? Was it Brahmā, lord of the world of the imperceptible realm? Or was it Śakra (Indra), king of the gods? Or the four world-guardian kings? Or some other son of the gods of great wealth and great power who came to behold the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the lord of the imperceptible realm, Brahmā, did not come to behold me. Nor was it Śakra, king of the gods. Nor the four world-guardian kings. Nor any other son of the gods of great wealth and great power. Monks, do you see that lion, the king of beasts, to whom I taught the Dharma in three statements? Yes, Blessed One, we see him. Monks, he died and passed on from there, was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, and last night he came to me. I taught him the Dharma, he saw the truth, and then he departed for his own abode."

The monks, having arisen with doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, to cut through every one of their doubts: "Venerable One, what karma did the formerly-a-lion son of the gods perform by virtue of whose maturation he was born among lions? And what karma did he perform by virtue of whose maturation he was born among the gods of the Four Great Kings?"

And what karma did he perform by virtue of whose maturation he saw the truth and then departed for his own abode?

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, formerly the very one who was the son of the gods named Lion had performed and accumulated deeds that constitute a collection of karma, that transform conditions, that abide close like light, that will without fail come to arise. Whatever karma the former son of the gods named Lion performed and accumulated — by whom else could it be experienced? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, whatever virtuous and non-virtuous karma has been performed and accumulated ripens solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Actions do not perish even in a hundred aeons;
when the assembly and the time are met,
for those who possess a body,
they will assuredly come forth as their fruit.

Monks, in a former time now passed, in this very good great aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher — a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans — a Blessed One, a buddha by the name of Kāśyapa. He was accompanied by twenty thousand monks and dwelled in dependence upon the deer park of Ṛṣivadana near the city of Vārāṇasī.

At the time before the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa had appeared in the world, there was in Vārāṇasī a brahmin with a very great retinue — one who had reached the far shore of the Vedas and their ancillary branches, and who had become teacher to brahmins dwelling in various lands. He was greatly honored, revered, respected, and venerated by the entire world.

But when the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa had appeared in the world, no one thereafter showed him any honor, revered him, respected him, or venerated him. When the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa was seated before a retinue of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma, that brahmin with his very great retinue passed by that way, and the brahmin saw the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa seated before a retinue of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma. Having seen him, he said: 'This ascetic teaches the Dharma to his retinue as fearlessly and as unabashedly as a lion, while these hearers listen to the Dharma like little timid deer.'

The fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa heard this. Having heard it, he declared to that brahmin: 'Brahmin, you have uttered coarse verbal karma. Come and confess the transgression through the door of confession, for if you do, that karma of yours will become attenuated, utterly exhausted, and brought to its final end.' The brahmin confessed the transgression through the door of confession, went for refuge in the presence of the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa, and took up the bases of training.

Monks, at that time, in that era, whoever it was who spoke of the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa as a lion — and whoever engaged in all that conduct — that very one was this same son of the gods, the former Lion.

By the karmic maturation of that conduct — having referred to the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa as a lion — he was born among lions for five hundred lifetimes, and even up to the present he has continued to be born among lions. By the karmic maturation of that action through which he aroused faith and devotion toward me, he passed away when his time came and was born among the gods of the Four Great Kings. And by the karmic maturation of the action of going for refuge in the presence of the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa and taking up the bases of training, he saw the Truths in my presence, and having seen the Truths, he went to his own abode.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and actions that are mixed, and strive after actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train in this way.

Then, as the Blessed One was wandering on tour through Magadha, he arrived at Rājagṛha and dwelt there in the Kālandaka Bamboo Grove in the Jeta Grove of the Cool Forest. At that time, the Group of Six monks were amusing themselves by throwing fire at one another, making moon shapes, making sun shapes, and making wheel-of-sickle-fire shapes. Certain wise non-Buddhists who saw this said: "These ascetics, sons of the Śākyan, amuse themselves by throwing fire at one another, making moon shapes, making sun shapes, and making wheel-of-sickle-fire shapes — just like these small boys who amuse themselves by throwing fire at one another, making moon shapes, making sun shapes, and making wheel-of-sickle-fire shapes. Wise ones, what difference is there between these small boys and these ascetics, sons of the Śākyan? What intention is there? What distinction is to be made? Who would think to give alms or render service to these shaven-headed ascetics?" And they reviled them, spoke disparagingly of them, and gossiped about them. At that juncture, the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this ground, and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The awakened Blessed Ones, though they know, feign not to know — and so forth, as before. The awakened Blessed One asked the Group of Six: "Monks, is it true that you were amusing yourselves by throwing fire at one another, making moon shapes, making sun shapes, and making wheel-of-sickle-fire shapes?" "Venerable One, it is so." The awakened Blessed One censured them, saying that this was not the way of an ascetic, was not in conformity with the rule, was not fitting, was not in accord with proper conduct, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One censured them in many ways, and spoke to the monks as follows: "Monks, therefore, having seen the ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya thus: 'Furthermore, whatever monk touches fire or causes another to touch it incurs a transgression.'" Thus did the awakened Blessed One lay down that training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya.

"Monks, henceforth they are not to offer incense at stūpas enshrining the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, nor to light lamps there. They are not to offer warm water to their preceptors and masters. They are not to perform bowl-making work. They are not to perform dyeing work."

The awakened Blessed Ones act knowingly, and so the awakened Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why is it that the monks henceforth are not to offer incense at stūpas enshrining the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, nor to light lamps there? Why are they not to offer warm water to their preceptors and masters? Why are they not to perform bowl-making work? Why are they not to perform dyeing work? Reverend Blessed One, you have laid down a training rule in the Vinaya to the effect that whatever monk touches fire or causes another to touch it incurs a transgression — and so, from now on, those monks will no longer offer incense at stūpas enshrining the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, nor light lamps there. They will not offer warm water to their preceptors and masters. They will not perform bowl-making work. They will not perform dyeing work."

"Ānanda, therefore, the time must be blessed. Let the time be blessed." The Blessed One spoke the words "Let the time be blessed," but as they did not know how to bless the time, the Blessed One declared: "One should bless the time by means of acts that accord with the Dharma in relation to the Teacher, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, one's preceptors, one's masters, and those who share in the holy life."

Now, when monks were performing bowl-making work and dyeing work, they would repeatedly forget and touch fire, and when remorse arose in them on account of this, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Bless the time for a long duration."

A certain monk came to suffer from a disease of wind and bile. He went to a physician and asked: "Good sir, prescribe medicine for me. Noble one, please provide a remedy. Good sir, the Blessed One has laid down a training rule. Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — in just this way, if he were to make that very condition the occasion and then permit it, such a circumstance would come about." At this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Except in the case of illness."

Then the Blessed One uttered praise of wanting to train, of reverence for training, and of immersion in the requisites of training, and addressed the monks with words fully in accord with that, more extensive than that, and endowed with a teaching appropriate to that. He then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, what was stated before is the rule, and this that follows is the permission. My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya thus: 'Furthermore, whatever monk who is not ill touches fire for his own sake, or causes another to touch it, incurs a transgression.'"

"Whatever monk" refers to one of the six classes or any other of that sort. "Who is not ill" sets aside the case of illness. "For his own sake" means for his own benefit. "Touches fire" means by his own hand. "Causes another to touch it" means through another person. "Incurs a transgression" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling in the hells, among animals, among hungry ghosts, in states of woe, and in states of utter downfall.

Furthermore, it is said that for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome phenomena of virtue. For that reason, it is called a downfall. As to how a downfall arises in this context: if a monk uses fire to play a game of spinning a wheel of fire with another person, it becomes a downfall. If he makes a moon shape with fire, it becomes a downfall. If he makes a sun shape with fire, it becomes a downfall. If he makes a sickle or a wheel of fire, it becomes a downfall. If a monk wishes to light a fire, he should do so after first performing the consecration at the proper time. If he lights a fire without having performed the consecration at the proper time, it becomes a downfall. If a monk wishes to extinguish a fire, he should do so after first performing the consecration at the proper time. If he extinguishes a fire without having performed the consecration at the proper time, it becomes a downfall. If a monk wishes to stir up or draw out firewood, he should do so after first performing the consecration at the proper time. If he stirs up or draws out firewood without having performed the consecration at the proper time, it becomes a downfall. If a monk wishes to stoke or draw out kindling, he should do so after first performing the consecration at the proper time. If he stokes or draws out kindling without having performed the consecration at the proper time, it becomes a downfall. If a monk wishes to stoke or draw out fire-embers, he should do so after first performing the consecration at the proper time. If he stokes or draws out fire-embers without having performed the consecration at the proper time, it becomes a misdeed. If a monk throws hair, fur, bones, or nails into a fire, it becomes a misdeed. If a monk throws saliva, mucus, vomit, or phlegm into a fire, it becomes a misdeed. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is in danger due to feeling.

This concludes the fifty-second downfall pertaining to touching fire.

The Vinaya Analysis, the fifty-seventh fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Chāraka, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship. The venerable Udāyin had gone to Kauśāmbī and was sitting at leisure. The seasons of swift travel and of the rains retreat had arrived. Nanda and Upananda were residing within the Saṅgha. At that time the seventeen groups, being wicked and domineering, were masters of sūtra, masters of Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkā as well, and so they said: "Venerable ones, we have long been slandered by the six groups. Just as Nanda and Upananda have been slandered, so too others have not been slandered in that same manner. And just as Upananda has been slandered, Nanda has not been slandered in the same way. So let them come here. Let us perform the act of removal from residence." Then one among them said: "Brothers, his brother Nanda is skilled in debate, and so we are unable to perform the act of removing Upananda from residence. Let us provoke an altercation." Saying this, they went to where Nanda was and said: "Homage to the elder. Venerable ones, take notice — the elder's robes have become soiled. My friend, since you have grown old, the monks who dwell with you and the attendants too despise you for your old age, and from now on they refuse to perform the work of the robes. We shall wash the elder's robes; please hand them over." Nanda gave his robes to the seventeen groups. They in turn said:

"Elder, let us wash all the robes at once. Please hand over every one of your robes." Nanda, in his fondness for old worn things, put on his old rags and handed all his robes over to the seventeen groups. The seventeen groups took those robes and set about altering them, then prepared a meeting place, struck the gong, and went before Nanda, saying: "Elder, there is some business of the Saṅgha. The gong has been struck; please come." Nanda replied: "My boys, given my circumstances, how can I go before the Saṅgha? I offer my assent to whatever lawful business the Saṅgha has to conduct."

Then, when the whole Saṅgha had assembled and was sitting in harmony, the monk who was stirring up trouble sat down off to one side, near the elder, and goaded Nanda, saying: "Venerable Nanda, do you recall saying something like this — that you would disembowel the seventeen groups and festoon the Jeta Grove with their entrails?" The elders replied: "What use is there in cutting open those whose wounds have healed? That is a matter of the past." But those monks pressed Nanda into a quandary, saying: "The Blessed One established rules of training for hearers in the Vinaya only with reference to past events," and so doing they carried out the act of suspending him from residence.

Once the act of suspending Nanda from residence had been carried out, he went to his elder brother Nanda and began to weep. Nanda said: "Nanda, why do you weep?" Nanda replied: "Those who carry black begging bowls have carried out the act of suspending me from residence." Nanda said: "May those who have carried out the act of suspending my younger brother from residence be expelled from village, city, province, and all three realms. Nevertheless, I shall go and beg forgiveness from those who have carried out the act of suspension, even if there is no village or city for them to go to. Let them stay, and I shall ask their pardon." In this way they had performed the act solely in a spirit of contention.

As for whoever had not been present there — "It was I." The elder Nanda offered his assent. "Did I know that they were carrying out the act of suspending my younger brother from residence? I would not offer my assent to a Saṅgha act of that kind. I have not offered my assent. My assent was given wrongly."

Why is it that monks of small account, after offering assent on behalf of a monk to a lawful act of the Saṅgha, then afterward become angry, turbulent, and aggressive, are displeased, and make it a practice of renunciation, saying: "Monk, take back your assent — it will not be given to you" — insulting him, dismissing him, and speaking against him? The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this context, convened the assembly of monks, and so on, all as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowing, inquire for a purpose," and so on, also as before.

The awakened Blessed One asked Nanda: "Nanda, is it true that, after you offered assent on behalf of a monk to a lawful act of the Saṅgha, you then afterward became angry, turbulent, and aggressive, were displeased, made it a practice of renunciation, and said, 'Monk, take back your assent — it will not be given to you'?" "Venerable Sir, it is true." The awakened Blessed One rebuked him, saying that such conduct was unworthy of a renunciant, was discordant, was improper, was contrary to discipline, and was not something to be done by one who has gone forth. Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One —

addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, I establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Should any monk, having offered assent on behalf of a monk to a lawful act of the Saṅgha, afterward become angry, turbulent, and aggressive, be displeased, make it a practice of renunciation, and say, 'Monk, take back your assent — it will not be given to you,' he commits a transgression."

Now, "any monk" means Nanda, son of the Śākyas, or another of similar kind. "Of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. "To a lawful act" means to a lawful ecclesiastical act. "On behalf of a monk" means on behalf of one who holds this Dharma. "Having offered assent" means having given his assent. "Afterward" means at another time. "Angry, turbulent, and aggressive, and displeased" means angry, overwhelmed by the force of anger. "Makes it a practice of renunciation" means makes it a practice of withdrawal. "Says" means utters the following words. "Monk, take back your assent — it will not be given to you" — "says" means speaks those words.

"He commits a transgression" means he burns, scorches, and falls into the hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of misfortune. Moreover, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome factors of Dharma — and therefore it is said that he commits a transgression.

As for how a transgression arises in this case: whatever and however much a monk, having offered assent on behalf of a monk to a lawful act of the Saṅgha, afterward becomes angry, turbulent, and aggressive, is displeased, makes it a practice of renunciation, and says, "Monk, take back your assent — it will not be given to you" — in every such instance he commits a transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a novice in the training, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations.

The fifty-third offense, of withdrawing assent, is complete.

Summary verse:
Listening to Dharma, and with a sign,
sickness, a monk of evil conduct,
two done in agreement,
bowing before, and the novice.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Faithful brahmins and householders came to the monastery and said to the monks: "Noble ones, please teach the Dharma." The monks replied: "Good people, come before the Blessed One today, and the Blessed One will teach you the Dharma." They said: "Noble ones, the Teacher is solitary and at present teaches the Dharma to the gods, or to nāgas, or to yakṣas, or to humans — please enquire. And do you yourselves also teach the Dharma." "Good people, the Blessed One has not given permission for that," the monks said. They then made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I give permission for monks also to teach the Dharma." Having declared that monks too should teach the Dharma, from that time onward they taught the Dharma during the day.

Now, those who lived by the fruit of merit, having listened to the Dharma by day, would tell those who lived by the fruit of toil at night: "Noble ones, the āryas teach lovely and lovely teachings of the Dharma, presenting the Dharma like the nectar of bees — like bees making honey, they offer and dispense what is like the nectar of the Dharma." Those who lived by the fruit of toil replied: "For those among you who hear the Dharma, the arising of a buddha is fruitful. But then why do you yourselves not listen to the Dharma?" "We who live by the fruit of merit listen to the Dharma by day. But we who live by the fruit of toil — if we do not do our work by day, we will go hungry and die. If the noble ones were to teach the Dharma at night, then we too would listen." At that point the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Teach the Dharma at night." They taught the Dharma every night, and they grew weary. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not teach the Dharma every single night." They taught until midnight, and yet they grew weary again. The Blessed One declared: "Teach the Dharma on the eighth day and the fourteenth day of the month."

When they were teaching the Dharma on the eighth and the fourteenth, an alms-seeker came to the temple to hear the Dharma, and the monks taught until midnight. That person thought: "It is not yet time to leave — I shall stay right here." He went to a corner, sat down cross-legged, and remained there. The laypeople who had come likewise lay down right there, and the duty monk began to extinguish the lamps. They called out: "Noble one, please do not put out the lamps, and we will provide sesame oil." The duty monk kept the lamps burning and went off. The laypeople remained there, and they said: "A great elder among the noble ones taught lovely and lovely teachings of the Dharma. A great elder among the noble ones taught most lovely and lovely teachings of the Dharma."

At that moment an elderly monk who was forgetful and had been sleeping dreamed in his sleep that he was lying together with a former old acquaintance, and he began to mutter something or other. The laypeople said: "Wise ones, who is this layman muttering like that?" They moved over toward him. When they saw that the elderly monk had been sleeping in the back and was muttering something or other, they said: "Wise ones, even the condition of the old ones is like this — as for these young ones who have gone forth, what will their condition be like?" And they gave rise to lack of faith.

The alms-seeker arose early in the morning and went to the forest dwelling. The ascetic monks saw him and asked: "Venerable one, did those who practice the holy life teach lovely and lovely teachings of the Dharma and inspire faith in the great assembly of people?" He replied: "The ones who practice the holy life taught lovely and lovely teachings of the Dharma and inspired faith in the great assembly of people — indeed, the many. But one elderly monk caused the great assembly of people to lose faith." "How did that come about?" He then related the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it in full to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen here is the fault of monks sleeping together with those who have not received full ordination."

Thinking that the fault had arisen from sleeping in the light, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a monk must not sleep together with one who has not received full ordination, and must not sleep in the light either. Whoever does so incurs an offense requiring expiation."

Now this is what had first come about. For the time being, the buddha, the Blessed One, did not yet establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers. The venerable Śāriputra had two novices named Grasp-Sound and Spur-On. When a monk arrived unexpectedly, the venerable Grasp-Sound, who had gone out during the day, had his cell assigned to the newly arrived monk. That monk then took out Grasp-Sound's bowl and robes and set them to one side. When the venerable Grasp-Sound returned from his daytime activities, he saw that his own bowl and robes had been taken out and set to one side, and he sat absorbed in thought. Presently the novice Spur-On arrived and said: "Venerable Grasp-Sound, why do you sit so absorbed in thought?" Grasp-Sound replied: "The cell I went out to during the day has been assigned to a monk who arrived unexpectedly, and he has taken out my bowl and robes and set them to one side. Now that a five-colored cloud has gathered, I do not know where my bed is to be laid." Spur-On said: "Venerable Grasp-Sound, why sit absorbed in thought? Just spread your bed wherever it suits you." Grasp-Sound replied: "Venerable Spur-On, you are possessed of great miraculous powers and great strength — you can conjure a mat not made of leaves and arrange a bed. What am I to do?"

At that time some faithful brahmins and householders had applied fragrant ointment to the outer walkway of the Blessed One. The venerable Grasp-Sound thought: "It is impossible and out of the question that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would relieve themselves at an improper time, so that place will be free. Let me go and sleep there." And so he went, rested his head on the footrest of the outer walkway, and lay down. That night a five-colored cloud gathered and began to pour down rain. Not far from that outer walkway there was the nest of a serpent — chief among those whose venom spreads swiftly — and when the rainwater flowed in, that serpent, the swift-spreading chief, lunged toward the outer walkway where the Blessed One had been.

Since it is the very nature of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, never to be forgetful, the Blessed One reflected: "If that serpent chief, whose venom spreads swiftly, were to find Grasp-Sound, it would leave nothing but his name behind. The Śākyas are proud people: if young Grasp-Sound of good character had not gone forth, he would have become a genuine king. Now that he has gone forth, the unprotected act at this untimely hour will cause faithless people to hear of it and scorn the teaching." Comprehending this, the Blessed One stretched out his hand — like an elephant's trunk — took Grasp-Sound up, and laid him down to sleep in his own sleeping quarters.

It is impossible and out of the question for a buddha, the Blessed One, to sleep in the same place as one who has not received full ordination. So the Blessed One spent much of that night in walking back and forth and in sitting in the open air.

In the morning, when it was yet early, the elder monks arose and came to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One,

It is the nature of all buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that when they wish to establish a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya, they welcome the monks who arrive in the future but do not turn away the monks who are already present. Now, the elder Prompting-One went to bow at the feet of the Blessed One, and as he approached he saw that the venerable Grasp-Sound was lying in the Blessed One's sleeping quarters. Seeing this, he roused the venerable Grasp-Sound by making a snapping sound with his fingers and said, "Venerable Grasp-Sound, where are you sleeping?" Grasp-Sound awoke and, realizing at once that he was lying in the Blessed One's sleeping quarters, rose with all haste and descended from the Blessed One's bed. Then Prompting-One said, "Venerable Grasp-Sound, if the Blessed One had not been mindful of you, a serpent whose venom spreads with terrible speed would have left nothing of you but a name."

Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, these novices have no mother, no father, and no other community of friends and companions. You alone are their companions in the holy life, and these novices stand at the very gateway to the state of an arhat. If you do not look after them fully, who else will? Therefore, monks, I allow sleeping in the same place for up to two nights with one who has not received full ordination."

Then a monk fell ill with dysentery, and while relieving himself in the dark he soiled both his legs and lay down with them stretched out. The next morning his fellow monk, who had been residing there with him, and some attendants came and asked him, "Preceptor, are you well?" He replied, "I am not well." "How are you unwell?" He explained the situation in full detail. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "In that case, let a lamp be lit." A lamp was lit, but from remorse the monk would not sleep, and that very situation became an offense. The Blessed One declared, "He should sleep, and need not feel remorse in this matter."

When monks who were nursing the sick felt remorse and would not sleep, they too became ill. The Blessed One declared, "They too should sleep." When those who were caring for them grew lax in their duties, the Blessed One declared, "Those who have not received full ordination may also sleep there." When, after two nights, they were made to leave and this caused harm to the patient, the Blessed One declared, "They may sleep there a third night as well." When the patient felt remorse, the Blessed One declared, "He should sleep and need not feel remorse in this matter." When the nursing monks felt remorse and would not sleep, the Blessed One declared, "They should sleep and need not feel remorse in this matter."

When elder monks fell ill and, though they rose and tried to receive their own food, they were unable to eat, the Blessed One declared, "Their attendants should hold the bowl with them, receive the food, and sit together and eat." Even if those attendants were juniors, they too should do likewise in that fashion. When there were no fully ordained monks present, the Blessed One declared, "Those who have not received full ordination may receive the food." Just as juniors and those without full ordination serve as attendants to the elders, so too the elders should serve as attendants to the juniors and to those without full ordination.

When moonlight or sunlight came in and monks, out of remorse, would not sleep, the Blessed One declared, "These are not considered conventional transgressions; they should sleep and need not feel remorse in this matter."

The Blessed One declared, "One should not sleep together with a person who has not received full ordination in the same place for more than two nights." When monks expelled those who had not received full ordination from the monastery, those persons were then set upon by thieves, by wrongdoers, by lions, by tigers, and by leopards. The Blessed One therefore declared, "They should not be expelled from the monastery." When monks expelled them from the cloister, the Blessed One declared, "They should not be expelled from the cloister; rather, they should be set aside in a nearby area."

There was a monk who had a novice with him, and a wicked monk came to that monastery and said to the novice, "Novice, where do you sleep?" The novice replied, "Right here, at this doorway." The novice's preceptor heard this, and he asked the novice, "What did you say?" The novice replied, "He was asking me where I sleep." The preceptor then had the novice sleep in his own cell, and the preceptor himself passed the night walking and sitting.

The next morning, the monks who were staying together and the attendants came and asked, "Preceptor, are you well?" He replied, "I am not well." They asked, "Why?" and he explained the whole matter in detail. They then said, "Preceptor, the Blessed One has declared that there are two kinds of noble persons: one who does not take up a burden that has not been assumed, and one who brings to completion a burden that has been assumed. Wishing to bring to completion this burden that has been assumed, we will do so." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"If a wicked monk enters among those who have not pledged to remain and can be expelled for the time being, he should be expelled. If he cannot be expelled, take the novice and go to another monastery. If a wicked monk enters among those who have pledged to remain and can be expelled for the time being, he should be expelled. If he cannot be expelled, place the novice in the care of a friendly monk. If there is no friendly monk, they may pass three months together in the same place. After the invitation ceremony, if the wicked monk can then be expelled, he should be expelled. If he cannot, take the novice and go to another monastery."

When monks were traveling on the road, novices also traveled with them, and when monks expelled those novices after two nights had passed, sending them outside the agreed fellowship, those novices were then set upon by thieves, by wrongdoers, by lions, by tigers, and by leopards. The Blessed One declared, "Rather than expelling them outside, let there be two agreed fellowships." When two agreed fellowships were formed, those in the smaller fellowship were set upon by thieves, by wrongdoers, by lions, by tigers, and by leopards. The Blessed One declared, "If the agreed fellowship is too small to be divided into two, then the monks should keep vigil without sleeping." When the monks kept vigil the entire night without sleeping, they became exhausted. The Blessed One declared, "They need not keep vigil the entire night; they should keep vigil for three watches, or two, or one, or at the very least at the time of the breaking of dawn." Even so they became exhausted, and the Blessed One declared, "They may sleep, and they need not feel remorse about this."

When monks, while traveling on the road, abandoned novices by the roadside and went on, those novices were then set upon by thieves, by wrongdoers,

by lions, by tigers, and by leopards. The Blessed One declared, "They should be sent on ahead." Those novices became hungry early in the morning, and the Blessed One declared, "They should be given food on loan." When those novices went begging for food even in the morning hours and the monks said to them, "We already gave you food on loan this morning — are you begging again?" the Blessed One declared, "Since novices have a large constitution of fire, food should be given to them even in the morning hours."

Now the venerable Ānanda had two novices named Thorn and Great One. He was sleeping together with those two in a single dwelling for more than two nights. The monks said to him, "Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has declared that a monk may not sleep in the same dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights. You should not sleep in a single dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights." Ānanda replied, "If two nights are permissible, then three nights should be permissible as well. What harm is there in drinking spirits on the third night, or eating from a common pot?" The monks of few desires began to rebuke him, to protest, and to reproach him, saying, "The Blessed One has declared that a monk may not sleep in a single dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights — so why do those monks deliberately transgress beyond two nights?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One convened the community of monks in regard to this incident, in regard to this basis, and in regard to this occasion — and so forth, just as before. The Blessed Ones who are buddhas act knowingly, and so forth — also just as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, reproved Ānanda, saying, "Ānanda, since I have declared that a monk may not sleep in a single dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, is it true that you deliberately transgress beyond two nights?" "Revered One, it is so." The Blessed One, the Buddha, then formally censured him: "That which is not the way of a contemplative, which is not in accord with propriety, which is not fitting, and which is not in conformity with proper conduct — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth." Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, one should establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, just as before. "My hearers should recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk sleeps in a single dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights commits an offense."

Now, "whatever monk" means a son of the Śākyas — Ānanda or any other of that kind. "Together with one who has not received full ordination" — those who have received full ordination are two: a monk and a nun. Anyone other than those two has not received full ordination. "More than two nights" means having passed beyond two nights. "Sleeping in a single dwelling" — there are four kinds of dwelling, consisting of all fully covered and all fully enclosed; all fully covered and mostly enclosed; mostly covered and all fully enclosed; and mostly covered and mostly enclosed — sleeping in any of these such that one witnesses the breaking of dawn. "All fully covered and all fully enclosed" means a building or dwelling

the surrounding cloister, or multi-storied buildings. "All fully covered and mostly enclosed" refers to structures with ten doorways or twelve doorways. "Mostly covered and all fully enclosed" refers to four-sided cloisters. "Mostly covered and mostly enclosed" refers to three-sided cloisters and surrounding colonnades.

"It causes a transgression" means it scorches, burns, and causes one to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, and into states of utter downfall. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of virtuous qualities — and that is why it is said to cause a transgression.

Now, how does a transgression come about? If a monk, perceiving a person who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, sleeps together with that person in a single dwelling for more than two nights, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, being of two minds about whether a person has received full ordination, sleeps together with that person in a single dwelling for more than two nights, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, perceiving a person who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, sleeps together with that person in a single dwelling for more than two nights, a wrongdoing is incurred. If a monk is of two minds about a person who has received full ordination and sleeps together with that person in a single dwelling for more than two nights, a wrongdoing is incurred. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by feeling, there is no transgression. This concludes the fifty-fourth rule entailing a transgression: sleeping in a single dwelling together with one who has not received full ordination.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, gave rise to a pernicious view of the following kind while facing death: "Those things that the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors — I understand that practising them does not constitute an obstruction." Many monks heard that the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, had given rise, while facing death, to a pernicious view of that kind — namely, that those things the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors are not obstructive when practised, and that this is how he understood the Dharma as taught by the Blessed One. Upon hearing this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, you should approach the monk Ariṭṭha — and any others who are like him — and speak to him as follows. You are to say: 'Venerable Ariṭṭha, do not say: "Those things that the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors — I understand that practising them does not constitute an obstruction." Do not slander the Blessed One. Slandering the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. The Blessed One has declared in many ways that the factors which obstruct are indeed obstructive, and that practising them leads to obstruction. Ariṭṭha, abandon this pernicious view of yours.'"

The monks replied, "Venerable one, we will do as you have commanded," and having heard the Blessed One, they approached Ariṭṭha and said: "Venerable Ariṭṭha, do not say: 'Those things that the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors — I understand that practising them does not constitute an obstruction, and that this is how the Blessed One taught the Dharma.' Do not say this.

Do not slander the Blessed One. To slander the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One has not said any such thing. The Blessed One has declared in many ways that the factors which obstruct are indeed obstructive, and that practising them leads to obstruction. Ariṭṭha, abandon this pernicious view of yours.'"

Even though the many monks admonished and instructed him in this way, he clung tenaciously to that very same view, grasped it firmly, and continued to maintain: "This alone is true; everything else is false." Thereupon the monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you must admonish and instruct the monk Ariṭṭha and anyone else who is like him by means of the formal act with a motion and three proclamations. The admonition is to be carried out as follows: prepare the seat, strike the wooden sounding board, properly assemble the monks with the formal summons, and when the entire Saṅgha is seated in harmony, one monk shall make the motion and perform the act. 'Let the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The monk Ariṭṭha has given rise to a view of this pernicious kind: that those things which the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors do not constitute an obstruction even when practised — this, he says, is how I understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it. Many monks have admonished and instructed him, yet even when admonished and instructed he has clung tenaciously to that very pernicious view, grasped it firmly, and continued to maintain: "This alone is true; everything else is false." If the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, then let the Saṅgha grant approval, and let the Saṅgha admonish the monk Ariṭṭha: Ariṭṭha, do not say that those things which the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors do not constitute an obstruction even when practised — that is how I understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it. Do not say such a thing. Do not slander the Blessed One. To slander the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One has not said any such thing. The Blessed One has declared in many ways that the factors which obstruct are indeed obstructive, and that practising them leads to obstruction. Ariṭṭha, abandon this pernicious view of yours.' This is the motion. The formal act is to be performed as follows: 'Let the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The monk Ariṭṭha has given rise to a view of this pernicious kind: that those things which the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors do not constitute an obstruction even when practised — this, he says, is how I understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it. Many monks have admonished and instructed him, yet even when admonished and instructed he has clung tenaciously to that very pernicious view, grasped it firmly, and continued to maintain: "This alone is true; everything else is false." Therefore, let the Saṅgha admonish the monk Ariṭṭha: Ariṭṭha, do not say that those things which the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors

do not say that this is how I understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. Those things which the Blessed One has taught in many ways as obstructive factors are indeed obstructive; when one engages in them, obstruction arises. Ariṭṭha, abandon this pernicious view of yours, which is of just such a kind." If, after the Saṅgha has admonished him with a formal act of censure by motion and three proclamations, those venerable monks who consent to the Saṅgha performing this formal act of censure by motion and three proclamations toward the monk Ariṭṭha should remain silent, while those who do not consent should speak. This is the first recitation of the motion. It is to be repeated in the same way a second and a third time. When the Saṅgha has consented and allowed it, the Saṅgha shall have performed the formal act of censure by motion and three proclamations toward the monk Ariṭṭha. Since no one has spoken, this is accordingly upheld. The monks, having heard the Blessed One, replied: "Venerable sir, we will act as the Blessed One has commanded," and carried out the formal act of censure toward Ariṭṭha by motion and three proclamations. Yet even when censured by motion and three proclamations, he continued to cling tenaciously to that very same view, grasped it firmly, and went on asserting: "This alone is true; everything else is false." At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you shall perform the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning his pernicious view, and similarly toward anyone else of that kind. It is to be done as follows. Having prepared seats, the drum is to be struck, and the monks are to be duly assembled with the words of summons. When the entire Saṅgha is seated and united, one monk shall make a motion and the act shall be performed. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. In the monk Ariṭṭha there has arisen a pernicious view of just such a kind — that those things which the Blessed One has taught as obstructive factors do not constitute an obstruction even when practised; this, he says, is how he understands the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it. Many monks have admonished and instructed him, yet even when admonished and instructed by many monks he has clung tenaciously to that very pernicious view, grasped it firmly, and continued to assert: 'This alone is true; everything else is false.' The Saṅgha is to censure the monk Ariṭṭha by motion and three proclamations. Even when censured by motion and three proclamations, if he still clings tenaciously to that pernicious view, grasps it firmly, and asserts 'This alone is true; everything else is false,' then, if the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha approve this. The Saṅgha shall perform the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning his pernicious view. For as long as the monk Ariṭṭha does not abandon this pernicious view in every aspect and in every way, the Saṅgha shall not speak with him, shall not converse with him, and shall treat him with contempt and utter contempt, as one treats an outcaste." This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. In the monk Ariṭṭha there has arisen a pernicious view of just such a kind —

— that those things which the Blessed One has taught as things that obstruct the path, when one relies on them, do not obstruct the path — saying: "I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in just this way."

Now, though this monk Ariṭṭha was admonished by a great many monks, he stubbornly clung to and held fast to that very form of the pernicious view, and having attached himself to it, he continued to declare: "This alone is true; all else is false." And though the Saṅgha admonished him by means of a motion and a threefold act, he still stubbornly clung to and held fast to that very form of the pernicious view, and having attached himself to it, continued to declare: "This alone is true; all else is false."

Therefore the Saṅgha shall perform the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning this pernicious view. For as long as the monk Ariṭṭha does not abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind in every aspect and in every way, the Saṅgha shall not speak with him, shall not converse with him, and shall treat him with contempt and utter contempt, as one treats an outcaste.

Those venerable ones who consent to the Saṅgha performing the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning this pernicious view, and who consent that for as long as the monk Ariṭṭha does not abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind in every aspect and in every way, the Saṅgha shall not speak with him, shall not converse with him, and shall treat him with contempt and utter contempt as one treats an outcaste — let those venerable ones remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak.

This is the first recitation of the act. The same is recited a second and a third time.

The Saṅgha having consented and approved, the Saṅgha performed the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning this pernicious view, and for as long as the monk Ariṭṭha does not abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind in every aspect and in every way, the Saṅgha shall not speak with him, shall not converse with him, and shall treat him with contempt and utter contempt, as one treats an outcaste. Since no one spoke, it is held to be so confirmed.

The monks, having heard from the Blessed One and received his instruction, then performed the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning this pernicious view, and for as long as the monk Ariṭṭha did not abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind in every aspect and in every way, they did not speak with him, did not converse with him, and treated him with contempt and utter contempt, as one treats an outcaste.

Those monks having performed the act of reproach against the monk Ariṭṭha for not abandoning this pernicious view, and having thus refused — for as long as he did not abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind in every aspect and in every way — to speak with him or converse with him, treating him with contempt and utter contempt as one treats an outcaste, yet he stubbornly clung to and held fast to that very form of the pernicious view, and having attached himself to it, continued to declare: "This alone is true; all else is false." At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, with this incident as the occasion, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, as before.

"The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, act with knowledge" — and so forth, as before.

The Blessed One then questioned Ariṭṭha: "Ariṭṭha, is it true that you have said: 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that the very things the Blessed One has declared to be impediments are not, when one engages in them, actual impediments'?"

"Venerable One, that is not so."

The Blessed One then proceeded to rebuke him as one who conducts himself in a manner unbecoming of an ascetic, as one who acts in a way that is not fitting, not suitable, and not in accordance with proper conduct — this is not something that one who has gone forth should do. And so, having rebuked him in this way and through many expressions, the Blessed One then declared to the monks:

"Therefore, monks, seeing the ten benefits clearly, I shall establish a rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before.

"Let my śrāvakas recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should any monk say: 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that the very things the Blessed One has declared to be impediments are not, when one engages in them, actual impediments' — then the monks shall address that monk thus: 'Venerable friend, do not say such a thing. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One does not say any such thing. Venerable friend, the impeding factors are indeed impediments — so the Blessed One has declared through many expressions — and if one engages in them, they become impediments. Venerable friend, abandon this pernicious view of just such a kind.' When the monks address him in this way, if he abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, he shall be addressed a second time and a third time, correctly and with full instruction, so that he may give it up. If, upon being so addressed and instructed a second and a third time, he abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not, it constitutes a transgression."

Now, the phrase "any monk" refers to Ariṭṭha or anyone else of that kind. The phrase "says thus" means when he utters such words. As for the phrase "the things the Blessed One has declared to be impediments," the term "impeding factors" (antarāyika dharmas) refers to: the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha, the two indefinite rules, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules entailing simple confession, the four rules entailing acknowledgment, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes — all of which the Blessed One has taught. The phrase "even if one engages in them" means even if one practices them extensively. The phrase "they are not actual impediments" means he claims they do not obstruct one's standing as an ascetic. The phrase "thus by the Blessed One" refers to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha. The word "Dharma" refers to what has been spoken by the Buddha and explained by the śrāvakas. The word "taught" means fully and explicitly taught.

The phrase "if he says, 'I know this'" means "if he says, 'I know all of this.'" The phrase "to that monk" refers to the one showing signs of death. The phrase "the monks" refers to those belonging to this Dharma community. The phrase "in these words" means he is to be admonished, delivering the admonition exactly as previously taught. The phrase "when the monks admonish that monk in these words" means when they deliver the admonition. The phrase "if he abandons that ground" means if he entirely relinquishes that view. The phrase "that is good" means that is excellent. The phrase "if he does not abandon it" means if he does not relinquish it entirely. The phrase "he should be correctly admonished and correctly instructed a second and a third time" means that one should admonish him by means of the motion and the fourfold formal act, exactly as previously taught; that which is "correct admonition" is precisely that, and that which is "correct instruction" is precisely that.

The phrase "it entails a downfall" means: it burns, it scorches, it causes one to fall into the lower rebirths — into the hells, into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies and bad destinies. Moreover, for as long as that downfall has not been confessed and individually confessed, it obstructs all wholesome qualities; therefore it is said to "entail a downfall."

Now, as to how a downfall arises: if a monk says even so much as this — that those things which the Blessed One has taught as impediments would not be impediments even if one practiced them — then on every occasion this constitutes an offense.

When monks admonish him with the introductory act and he abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, it becomes an offense.

When he is admonished by the motion and fourfold formal act and he abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, it becomes an offense at the point of reading the motion.

When the first recitation of the formal act is being read and he has not completed it but abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, the offense arises upon completion of the reading.

When the second recitation of the formal act is being read and he has not completed it but abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, the offense arises upon completion of the reading.

When the third recitation of the formal act is being read and he has not completed it but abandons that ground, that is good. If he does not abandon it, then when the reading is completed: if the admonishment is delivered in a manner that is discordant and contrary to the Dharma, there is no downfall. If it is delivered in a manner that is discordant yet in accordance with the Dharma, there is no downfall. If it is delivered in a manner that is concordant and conforms to the Dharma, there is no downfall. If it is delivered in a manner that is discordant and contrary to the Dharma in a corrected form, there is no downfall. If it is not delivered in accordance with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the teaching of the Teacher as it is, there is no downfall. But if it is delivered in a manner concordant with the Dharma as it is, the Vinaya as it is, and the teaching of the Teacher as it is, then upon completion of the reading it entails a downfall.

That monk, while still seated in his place, must declare: "Venerable ones, a downfall entailing a fall has arisen for me." If he makes that declaration, that is good. If he does not, from that point onward an offense of concealment will arise for him.

Therefore, for as long as a monk has not confessed and individually confessed that downfall, performing the motion and the fourfold formal act on every occasion, it becomes an offense in each instance.

For one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is overwhelmed by painful feeling, there is no downfall.

Here ends the fifty-fifth downfall entailing a fall, that of not relinquishing the view.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the formal act of expulsion was performed against Ariṭṭha from that residence, he wept and went to his friend. His friend said, "Ariṭṭha, why are you weeping?" Ariṭṭha replied, "Those with black bowls have performed the formal act of expelling me from the residence." His friend said, "May those who performed the formal act of expelling Ariṭṭha from the residence be expelled from village, town, province, and all three realms. Yet as for those against whom the formal act of expulsion from the residence was performed, is there no village or hamlet? Please ask permission to stay." And so his friend conversed with Ariṭṭha, spoke of his coming, provided him with lodging, provided him with enjoyment, and slept together with him in one dwelling.

Then a monk rebuked them, saying, "Monks, why, for a trifling matter, do you converse with, speak of the coming of, provide lodging to, provide enjoyment to, and sleep together in one dwelling with that person who has been spoken about — one who has not acted in accordance with the Dharma and who has not relinquished that form of a wicked view — doing so knowingly?" He reproached them, raised a clamor against them, and spread word against them. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident and this basis and this occasion, convened the community of monks — and all the rest is as before. The phrase "the Blessed Buddhas knowingly make it appear as though they do not know" and so forth is also as before.

The Blessed One then questioned Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you, knowingly, conversed with, spoke of the coming of, provided lodging to, provided enjoyment to, and slept together in one dwelling with that person who has been spoken about — one who has not acted in accordance with the Dharma and who has not relinquished that form of a wicked view?" He replied, "Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed One then thoroughly censured him, saying, "That which is not the manner of a monastic, not in conformity, not proper, not in accord with the rule — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth." And so the Blessed One censured him in many ways. He then addressed the monks, declaring, "Therefore, seeing ten benefits and with the intention of establishing a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and all the rest is as before — "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, whatever monk, knowingly, converses with, speaks of the coming of, provides lodging to, provides enjoyment to, and sleeps together in one dwelling with that person who has been spoken about — one who has not acted in accordance with the Dharma and who has not relinquished that form of a wicked view — that is a downfall."

Now, "whatever monk" means a son of the Śākyas, namely Ānanda or anyone else of that kind. "Knowingly" means that he himself has come to know it, or that others have told him. "The person who has been spoken about" means Ariṭṭha. "Has not acted in accordance with the Dharma" means has not acted in conformity with the Dharma. "Has not relinquished that form of a wicked view" means whatever that form of view was. "Converses with" means providing scriptural recitation. "Speaks of the coming of" means providing visits with a purpose in mind. "Provides lodging" means providing a place to stay. "Provides enjoyment" and so on means receiving service from him and making it one's own. "Sleeps together in one dwelling" means covering and surrounding all four sides of the dwelling,

fully covered and mostly surrounded, mostly covered and fully surrounded, and mostly covered and mostly surrounded — sleeping there until dawn breaks. "Fully covered and fully surrounded" refers to a residential building, a surrounding cloister, and a multi-storied structure. "Fully covered and mostly surrounded" refers to buildings with ten doors and buildings with twelve doors. "Mostly covered and fully surrounded" refers to cloisters open on all four sides. "Mostly covered and mostly surrounded" refers to cloisters open on three sides and surrounding walkways.

"Constitutes a transgression" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower rebirths, and the states of misfortune. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities — and for that reason it is said to constitute a transgression.

As to how the transgression comes about: if a monk, knowing even a little, converses with a person of whom it has been said that he has not acted in accordance with the Dharma and has not relinquished that form of a wicked view, a transgression is incurred. If one speaks of his coming, a transgression is incurred. If one provides him lodging, a transgression is incurred. If one shares enjoyments with him, a transgression is incurred. If one sleeps with him until dawn breaks in any of the four kinds of dwellings, a transgression is incurred. However, if one is ill, or if one wishes to be separated from that form of wicked view, there is no transgression. For one who is a beginner, who is insane, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations, there is no transgression.

This concludes the fifty-sixth transgression of the section on abandonment, in full.

The Vinaya Analysis, the fifty-eighth fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. There were two novices in Ānanda's retinue named Kṣudraka and Mahaka. While they had not yet become free from attachment, the monks would sit beside them on benches, play with them, touch them playfully, sport with them, make noise with them, and engage in laughter, pride, and bodily movements. Afterward, those two novices restrained whatever transgressions required restraint and confessed whatever transgressions required confession, and through enthusiasm, effort, and striving, having abandoned all afflictions, they directly realized the state of arhathood and also manifested supernormal powers.

On another occasion, when Kṣudraka and Mahaka were picking and arranging flowers, they saw some monks traveling through the sky by supernormal power. The two said: "Who are you?" Those monks replied: "We are such-and-such by name." The two then said: "You once did such-and-such together with us." The monks replied: "That is so. However, we restrained whatever transgressions required restraint and confessed whatever transgressions required confession, and through enthusiasm, effort, and striving, having abandoned all afflictions, we directly realized the state of arhathood and also manifested supernormal powers."

At that point a wicked view of the following kind arose in Kṣudraka and Mahaka: that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has said are obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions —

When they said "We understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it" — at that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you are to summon the novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka, and likewise any others of that kind, and admonish them. The admonition is to be given in these words: 'Kṣudraka and Mahaka, do not say this: that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and that we understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. Do not slander the Blessed One. It does not go well for one who slanders the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not say any such thing. The Blessed One has stated in many ways that those sensual pleasures which are obstructions are indeed obstructions, and that to engage in them will become an obstruction. Kṣudraka and Mahaka, abandon this kind of wicked view.' That is how the admonition is to be given."

The monks replied "Venerable ones, we will carry out the instruction as commanded," and they went to the two novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka and admonished them: "Kṣudraka and Mahaka, do not say this: that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and that we understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. Do not slander the Blessed One. It does not go well for one who slanders the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not say any such thing. The Blessed One has stated in many ways that those sensual pleasures which are obstructions are indeed obstructions, and that to engage in them will become an obstruction. Kṣudraka and Mahaka, abandon this kind of wicked view." That is how they summoned and admonished them.

Now when the many monks summoned and admonished the two novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka in this way, those two, even though thus summoned and admonished, clung tenaciously to that very wicked view, held fast to it, and continued to assert: "This alone is true; everything else is false." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you are to summon the novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka, and likewise any others of that kind, and admonish them by the act of formal inquiry with a quorum of four. The procedure is as follows: having prepared the seats and struck the gong, after duly informing all the monks with the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, the two novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka are to be removed from hearing range and placed within sight range, and then a single monk is to make a motion and the formal act is to be carried out. The motion is to be stated thus: 'Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear. The following wicked view of this kind has arisen in these two novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka: that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and saying that they understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. When the many monks summoned and admonished these two, even though thus summoned and admonished, they clung tenaciously to that very wicked view, held fast to it, and continued to assert: "This alone is true; everything else is false."

If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha is willing, let the Saṅgha grant its consent. The Saṅgha's novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka are hereby admonished: "Kṣudraka and Mahaka, do not say this — that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and that you understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One did not say any such thing. Kṣudraka and Mahaka, the Blessed One has said in many ways that sensual pleasures that obstruct are indeed obstructions, and that to engage in them is to create obstruction. Therefore, Kṣudraka and Mahaka, abandon this wicked view of such a kind." This is the motion, and the formal act is performed with the motion-and-three-proclamations.

This is the motion.

Thereafter, one monk should address these two and say: "The Saṅgha is about to perform the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations in regard to you two. The motion has already been made. You two are hereby admonished to abandon this wicked view of such a kind. If, when thus admonished, you abandon that position, well and good. If you do not abandon it, then the formal act that follows shall be performed."

The formal act is to be performed as follows. Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear. In these two novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka there has arisen a wicked view of this kind: that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and they have said that they understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. When the many monks summoned and admonished these two, even though thus summoned and admonished, they clung tenaciously to that very wicked view, held fast to it, and continued to assert, "This alone is true; everything else is false." Therefore, the Saṅgha's novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka are hereby admonished: "Kṣudraka and Mahaka, do not say this — that those sensual pleasures which the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions are, even when engaged in, not in fact obstructions, and that you understand the Dharma as the Blessed One has taught it in this way. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One did not say any such thing. Kṣudraka and Mahaka, the Blessed One has said in many ways that sensual pleasures that obstruct are indeed obstructions, and that to engage in them is to create obstruction. Therefore, Kṣudraka and Mahaka, abandon this wicked view of such a kind." The formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations is hereby performed in this way. Those venerable ones who consent to the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations being performed in regard to the novices Kṣudraka and Mahaka should remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak. This is the first proclamation.

Thereafter, one monk should address these two and say: "The Saṅgha has also performed the first proclamation of the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations in regard to you two. You two are hereby admonished to abandon this wicked view of such a kind. If, when thus admonished, you abandon that position, well and good. If you do not abandon it, then the second proclamation shall follow."

After the second proclamation has likewise been made, one monk should again address these two and say: "The Saṅgha has also performed the second proclamation of the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations in regard to you two. You two are hereby admonished to abandon this wicked view of such a kind."

If, when thus admonished, you abandon that position, well and good. If you do not abandon it, then the third proclamation shall follow.

After the third proclamation has likewise been made, one monk should again address these two and say: "The Saṅgha has now also performed the third proclamation of the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations in regard to you two. You two are hereby admonished to abandon this wicked view of such a kind."

If, when thus admonished, you abandon that position, well and good. If you do not abandon it, the closing declaration shall then be made. The Saṅgha having consented and approved, one should declare: "The Saṅgha has performed the admonishment of the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla by means of the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations. Since they have said nothing in reply, it is understood that they maintain their position accordingly."

The monks then replied to the Blessed One: "Venerable ones, we shall act according to the Blessed One's instruction." And in compliance with the Blessed One's word, they performed the admonishment of the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla by the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations.

When the monks performed this admonishment of the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla by the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations, the two of them, even when thus admonished, stubbornly clung to and became firmly attached to that very same wicked view, and continued to assert: "This alone is true; all else is false." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you shall perform upon the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla, who will not relinquish this wicked view, and upon any others of such a kind, the formal act of expulsion. This is how it shall be done: Having arranged the seats and struck the signal board, the monks shall be properly convened with the words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in concord, the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla are to be removed from the hearing range and placed within sight, and then one monk shall put the motion and carry out the formal act.

Venerable Saṅgha, please hear this. This wicked view of such a kind has arisen in the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla — namely, that they have declared: 'We understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One to mean that those things which the Blessed One called obstructions are not, when indulged in, actually obstructions.' Even when admonished by a great many monks, these two clung stubbornly to and became firmly attached to that very same wicked view, asserting, 'This alone is true; all else is false.' And even when the Saṅgha admonished these two by the formal act of motion-and-three-proclamations, they still clung stubbornly to and became firmly attached to that very same wicked view, asserting, 'This alone is true; all else is false.'
