If the Saṅgha is ready and consents, the Saṅgha shall approve. The Saṅgha hereby expels the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla, who will not relinquish this wicked view. Henceforth, you two novices must not refer to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, as your Teacher. You must not follow in the footsteps of whatever brahma-faring master-like figure you may encounter. Whatever permission you had to sleep overnight together with monks and novices in the same dwelling up until the second night — that too you no longer possess. You deluded ones are hereby expelled; go elsewhere." This is the motion.

Following that, a single monk shall address the two of them in these words: "You two — the Saṅgha is about to perform the act of one motion and three proclamations concerning you. On account of that motion, you two must relinquish this wicked view of such a kind." When he has so addressed them, if they relinquish that ground, so much the better. If they do not relinquish it, the act shall then proceed as follows.

The act is to be performed in this way. "Venerable members of the Saṅgha, please hear. Regarding these two novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla, there has arisen in them a wicked view of this kind: they have declared, 'We understand that the teaching which the Blessed One gave — namely, that those things he described as obstructions do not in fact obstruct one who indulges in them — is what the Blessed One truly taught.' Many monks then took hold of these two and admonished them. Although the two were taken hold of and admonished, they seized upon that same wicked view with even greater tenacity and clung to it, asserting thereafter, 'This alone is true; all else is false.' Even though the Saṅgha now performs the act of one motion and three proclamations concerning these two, even after the Saṅgha performs this act of one motion and three proclamations, they seize upon that same wicked view with even greater tenacity and cling to it, asserting thereafter, 'This alone is true; all else is false.' Therefore, the Saṅgha hereby expels the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla, who will not relinquish this wicked view. Henceforth, you two novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla must not refer to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, as your Teacher. You must not follow in the footsteps of whatever brahma-faring master-like figure you may encounter. Whatever permission you had to sleep overnight together with monks and novices in the same dwelling up until the second night — that too you no longer possess. You deluded ones are hereby expelled; go elsewhere." If the Saṅgha performs the act of expulsion, those venerable ones who consent to the expulsion of the novices Ariṭṭha and Mahāpāla, who will not relinquish this wicked view, shall remain silent. Those who do not consent shall speak. This is the first proclamation of the act.

Following that, a single monk shall address the two of them: "You two — the Saṅgha has performed the act of one motion and three proclamations, and the first proclamation of the act has also been made. You two must relinquish this wicked view of such a kind." When he has so addressed them, if they relinquish that ground, so much the better. If they do not relinquish it, the second proclamation of the act shall then be made.

After the second proclamation has been made, a single monk shall again address the two of them: "You two — the Saṅgha is performing the act of one motion and three proclamations, and the second proclamation of the act has also been made. You two must relinquish this wicked view of such a kind." When he has so addressed them, if they relinquish that ground, so much the better. If they do not relinquish it, the third proclamation of the act shall then be made.

After the third proclamation has been made, a single monk shall again address the two of them: "You two — the Saṅgha is performing the act of one motion and three proclamations, and the third proclamation of the act has also been made. You two must relinquish this wicked view of such a kind." When he has so addressed them, if they relinquish that ground, so much the better. If they do not relinquish it, the conclusion shall then be performed.

With the Saṅgha's consent and permission, the Saṅgha has performed the act of one motion and three proclamations, the act of suspension, against the novices Thorny and Great-One. Since no one has spoken against it, this is held to be so.

The monks, having heard from the Blessed One and saying, "Reverend sir, we accept the command," performed the act of suspension by one motion and three proclamations against Thorny and Great-One. When the act of suspension had been performed against the two of them, they went weeping to their companion, and the companion said: "Thorny and Great-One, why do you two weep?" The two of them replied: "Those who carry black begging bowls have performed the act of suspension against us two." The companion said: "May those who performed the act of suspension against you two be themselves suspended from village, from town, from province, and from the three realms. But as for those against whom the act of suspension has been performed, are there no villages and towns? Stay here, and ask for forgiveness." And he settled those two close by, kept company with them, and had the two sleep together with him in one dwelling.

Then a few monks said: "Why, monks, do monks knowingly settle close by these novices against whom the act of suspension has been performed, keep company with them, and sleep together with them in one dwelling?" They rebuked them, pointed it out, and spread word of it. At that occasion, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and in connection with this matter and this occasion, summoned the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, knowingly ask — and so forth as before as well.

The Blessed One asked Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you knowingly settle those suspended novices close by, keep company with them, and sleep together with them in one dwelling?" "Reverend sir, it is so." The Blessed One then censured this as not the conduct of a renunciant, as not in accordance with what is fitting, as not appropriate, as not in conformity with the discipline, and as something that one who has gone forth ought not to do.

Then, having censured it in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten good reasons, a rule of training for the hearers is to be established in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If any novice should say, 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One to be such that those things he declared to be obstructions are not, when engaged in, obstructive' — then the monks shall say to that novice: 'Do not say this, novice. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. To misrepresent the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not say this. Venerable novice, the Blessed One has declared in many ways that the things which obstruct are indeed obstructions — and if one engages in them, they become obstructions. Novice, relinquish this wicked view of such a kind.'"

When the monks have so spoken to that novice, if he relinquishes that ground, so much the better.

If he does not relinquish it, in order that he may relinquish that ground, he is to be admonished and instructed correctly a second time and a third time. If, when admonished and instructed correctly a second and third time, he relinquishes that ground, so much the better. If he does not relinquish it, the monks shall say to that novice: "From this day forward, novice, you shall not say of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, that he is your Teacher. You shall not follow after any accomplished elder in the holy life (brahmacarya), as one follows a preceptor. And the permission you previously had to sleep in the same lodging together with monks for up to two nights — that too you shall have no more. Foolish one, you are expelled; go elsewhere." This is how the admonition is to be given. Furthermore, any monk who knowingly gives lodging to a novice who has been expelled in this way, or associates with him, or sleeps with him in the same lodging, commits a transgression.

Now, "a novice" means one of a thorny type, one of a major type, or any other such kind. "Speaking thus" means when one says such words. Regarding "things the Blessed One has declared to be obstructions": "desires" here means the five qualities of desire. "Even if one engages in them" means even if one pursues them extensively. "They will not become obstructions" means they will not become obstructions to the way of the ascetic. "Thus declared by the Blessed One" refers to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha. "Dharma" means what has been spoken by the buddha or explained by a śrāvaka. "Taught" means thoroughly taught. "If he says 'I know'" means if he says "I know all of it." "To that novice" refers to the thorny type and the major type. "The monks" means those who belong to this Dharma community. "Speaking thus" means that one takes the matter up and admonishes as was shown before. "When the monks have so spoken to that novice" means when the admonition has been properly given. "If he relinquishes that ground" means if he utterly relinquishes that form of view — if so, so much the better. "If he does not relinquish it" means if he does not utterly relinquish it. "He is to be admonished and instructed correctly a second time and a third time" means that the admonition is to be given by means of a motion-and-three-proclamation act, just as was shown before — and that is what correct admonition means, and that is what correct instruction means. "To that novice" refers to the thorny type and the major type. "The monks" means those who belong to this Dharma community.

"From this day forward, novice, you shall not say of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, that he is your Teacher. You shall not follow after any accomplished elder in the holy life as one follows a preceptor. The permission you previously had to sleep in the same lodging together with monks for up to two nights — that too you shall have no more. Foolish one, you are expelled; go elsewhere." This is to be administered by means of a motion-and-three-proclamation act of expulsion, just as was shown before.

"Furthermore, any monk" refers to a son of the Śākyas or any other such person. "Knowingly" means having come to know it himself, or having been told by others. "A novice who has been expelled in this way" is as described, of the thorny or major type. "Gives lodging" means provides a place of residence. "Associates with him" means sharing the begging bowl and

the robe, the net bag, the bowl, the belt, the recitation of texts aloud, reading, chanting, and the giving of instruction through intentional questioning.

"Sleeping together in one dwelling" refers to sleeping until dawn in any of the four kinds of dwelling: one that is fully enclosed and fully surrounded on all sides; one that is fully enclosed and mostly surrounded; one that is mostly enclosed and fully surrounded; or one that is mostly enclosed and mostly surrounded. "Fully enclosed and fully surrounded" refers to a proper dwelling hall, a cloistered courtyard, and a multi-storied building. "Fully enclosed and mostly surrounded" refers to a building with ten doors or one with twelve doors. "Mostly enclosed and fully surrounded" refers to a cloister open on four sides. "Mostly enclosed and mostly surrounded" refers to a cloister open on three sides and an open-sided courtyard cloister.

"It entails a transgression" means that it causes one to burn, to be scorched, and to fall into the hell-beings, the animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of ruin. Furthermore, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and for that reason it is called a transgression.

As for how exactly a transgression arises in this context: if a monk, knowing even something of this, nonetheless provides lodging for a novice who has been expelled in such a way, a transgression arises. If he associates with him, a transgression arises. If he sleeps with him in the same dwelling, a transgression arises. There is no transgression for one who wishes to be separated from that person, whether on account of illness or on account of a view that is corrupt and evil. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is mentally disturbed, whose mind is distracted, or who is overcome by painful sensations.

Here ends the fifty-seventh transgression in the category of transgressions concerned with harboring expelled persons.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Veṇuvana. At that time, dwelling in Rājagṛha were two nāga kings named Parvata and Manāpa. Through their power, the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha, its streams, its lakes, and its ponds were caused by the gods to flow with excellent water at the proper seasons, and the harvests were exceedingly abundant. When the Blessed One had tamed the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, those two, on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day of each lunar fortnight, would come to the terraced slopes of Mount Meru and pay homage to the Blessed One. Then the nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa thought to themselves, "Since the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda come on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days to the terraced slopes of Mount Meru and pay homage to the Blessed One, while we two remain here and have not paid homage to the Blessed One, let us go and pay homage to him." So the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed with their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Having stood to one side, the Blessed One established the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa in the going-for-refuge and in the bases of training. When the Blessed One had established those two in the going-for-refuge and in the bases of training, those two became exceedingly elevated in body and in possessions. When those two had become exceedingly elevated in body and in possessions, they thought, "Let us go forth into the great ocean." And so those two went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived,

they bowed with their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Having stood to one side, the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable Blessed One, when you established the two of us in the going-for-refuge and in the bases of training, we two became exceedingly elevated in body and in possessions. If the Blessed One would permit it, we two would enter the great ocean." The Blessed One declared: "O lords of nāgas, you two are kings born in Magadha, dwellers in the heartland of the refined form — Kalandaka's grove in Veṇuvana. You should present your request to the king of Magadha, born of the refined form, the essence of Kalandaka's grove." Those two thought: "In effect, the Blessed One has not given us permission to go into the great ocean."

During the nights when those two would attend upon the Blessed One, they would attend him in the manner befitting a celestial palace; and during the days when they would attend upon the Blessed One, they would attend him in the manner befitting a householder. Then the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, of the refined form, went to where the Blessed One was dwelling at the Kalandaka grove in the Bamboo Forest. Now, the kṣatriya lineage is by nature proud, and so the king remained on the road and said to a certain impure-edged one: "Go inside and look at who is attending upon the Blessed One." That impure-edged one, having respectfully heard from the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, the words "As your lord commands," went to where the Blessed One was, and saw two householders attending upon the Blessed One. Having seen this, he went back to where the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, was, and said to him: "Your Majesty, two householders are attending upon the Blessed One — they seem to be dwelling in the realm of the gods; they did not bend their knees." The king thought: "Those two householders are dwellers in my own realm; if they see me, they will surely rise to their feet." And so he went to where the Blessed One was.

The two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa saw the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, from a considerable distance. Having seen him, those two addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, should we first pay homage to the sacred Dharma, or should we pay homage to the king?" "O two nāga kings, first pay homage to the sacred Dharma. The Blessed buddhas themselves hold the sacred Dharma in reverence, and the arhats too place the Dharma first."

Thereupon the Blessed One, on this occasion, declared these verses:

All the buddhas of the past,
and all the buddhas yet to come,
and the buddhas now dwelling in the present, many as they are, who dispel sorrow —
every one of them abides, has abided, and will abide
in reverence toward the sacred Dharma.
And they cause others likewise to abide in reverence.
This is the very nature of buddhahood.

Therefore, one who desires what is good for oneself,
who aspires to great distinction,
should, in recollecting the teaching of the buddhas,
hold the sacred Dharma in deep reverence.

Those two did not rise to their feet before the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra. The king became angry and thought: "These two householders are dwellers in my own realm, yet they do not rise to their feet before me." And with that, he bowed with his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, Bimbisāra, king of Magadha, whose body was shaped by noble craftsmanship and whose heart was full, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, please teach the Dharma."

The Blessed One then spoke these verses on the occasion:

One who lacks delight, who harbors aversion, who is agitated — such a one cannot come to know all the sacred Dharma taught by the perfectly and completely awakened one. But one who restrains the impulse toward wrongdoing, who dispels the mind of delight and its absence, and who abandons here the mind that broods with hostility — that one will come to know the well-spoken teaching.

The king thought to himself: "Through these two householders, my audience with the Blessed One for hearing the Dharma has also come to an end." Then Bimbisāra, king of Magadha, bowed with his head to the feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from the Blessed One's presence, and as he departed from the Bamboo Grove, he gave instruction to those who lived by dairy produce: "When these two householders have departed from the presence of the Blessed One, tell them this from the king's mouth: 'The two of you are not to remain in my territory.'" Having said that, the king departed.

Those who lived by dairy produce replied, "As the king commands," and remained there. Then the two nāga kings, Parvata and Manāpa, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from his presence, and when the two of them had departed from the Bamboo Grove, the king's dairymen said to them: "You two householders, this message has come from the king's mouth: 'The two of you are not to remain in my territory.'"

Upon hearing these words, Parvata and Manāpa thought: "The aspiration we have long held has now been fulfilled with little difficulty." Knowing this, right there and then they generated a great effulgence of water in all directions and entered into the small streams. From the small streams they entered into the large streams. From the large streams they entered into the small rivers. From the small rivers they entered into the great rivers. From the great rivers they entered into the great ocean. And at the moment the two of them entered the great ocean, their bodies and wealth rose to heights of Dharmic excellence exceedingly great.

Now at the very moment the two of them entered the great ocean, the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha also began to dry up. The gods no longer sent the waters flowing well in season into the cascades, the lakes, and the ponds. The harvests too became utterly ruined. The king then thought: "In this Rājagṛha there used to dwell two nāga kings named Parvata and Manāpa. Through their power, the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha, the cascades, the lakes, and the ponds had waters flowing well in season, and the harvests were most abundant. Now the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha have begun to dry up, the gods no longer send the waters flowing well in season into the cascades, the lakes, and the ponds, and the harvests have become utterly ruined. Has it happened that the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa have fallen ill, died, fled, or been seized by some serpent enemy? For this buddha, this Blessed One, is omniscient and all-seeing —"

— for he is one who has attained supreme mastery of knowledge and of all that is to be known. I shall go to the buddha, the Blessed One, and ask."

Then Bimbisāra, king of Magadha, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Venerable one, in this city of Rājagṛha there dwell two nāga kings named Parvata and Manāpa. Through their power, the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha, the cascades, the lakes, and the ponds have had waters flowing well in season, sent by the gods, and the harvests have been most abundant. But now the five hundred hot springs of Rājagṛha have begun to dry up, the gods no longer send the waters flowing well in season into the cascades, the lakes, and the ponds, and the harvests have become utterly ruined. Has it happened that the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa have fallen ill, died, fled, or been seized by some serpent enemy — or has none of this occurred?"

"Great King, the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa have not fallen ill, have not died, have not fled, and have not been seized by a serpent enemy. It is you yourself who drove them away."

"Venerable one, I do not even recall having seen the nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa — how then could I have driven them away?"

"Great King, I shall remind you of it."

"Venerable one, may the Blessed One please do so."

"Great King, what did you say to those two householders at that time?"

"Venerable one, when those two householders departed from the presence of the Blessed One, I told the men who were living off curds to spread the word: 'The moment those two householders leave the Blessed One's presence, let it be announced from the king's mouth that the two of you are not to remain in my domain.' That is what I ordered."

Then the Blessed One declared: "Great King, those two householders were none other than the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa."

The king asked: "Venerable one, where did those two go at that time?"

"They entered the great ocean."

The king said: "Venerable one, Blessed One, then my domain has been harmed."

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, your domain will not be harmed — provided that you offer forgiveness to those two."

The king said: "Venerable one, they have entered the great ocean and I am here. How shall I offer them forgiveness?"

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, those two will come here to bow at my feet on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth days of the month. You also should come here on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth, and I will show you those two so that you may offer them forgiveness."

"Venerable one, should I then touch their two feet?"

"Great King, you need not touch their feet. When one bows at the feet of those of low birth, one is grasped by the hand of the chief men — therefore extend your right hand and offer forgiveness to the two lords of the nāgas, saying: 'May you forgive.'"

Then at another time the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving they bowed their heads to the Blessed One's two feet and stood to one side. At that same time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha also went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side.

The Blessed One gave a signal. Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha, whose body was well-formed and refined, extended his right hand and said: "May the two lords of the nāgas forgive." The two replied: "Great King, we forgive." The two lords of the nāgas then said: "If you would forgive us, please invite us to your land." The two replied: "Great King, at the time when we entered the great ocean, our bodies and wealth became exceedingly and manifestly exalted — and so if we were now to come here, there would simply be no place fitting for the two of us. The king said: "Two lords of the nāgas, in that case my land is not worthy of you." The two replied: "Great King, your land will not be unworthy — for if you cause two shrines to be built, one for the mountain and the other for the pleasant grove, and if you install there the sustenance and livelihood of the two of us, and if every six months you cause a festival to be held, then the two of us will also come in person at those times and fulfill our former obligations."

Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha caused two shrines to be built — one for the mountain, the other for the pleasant grove — and had festivals held there every six months. Whenever a festival took place, great crowds of common people from all six great cities would come and gather together in harmony.

Then at another time, when the festival of the two nāga kings Parvata and Manāpa came around in Rājagṛha, a dancer also arrived in Rājagṛha from the southern road. He thought to himself: "What means might there be to greatly delight the crowds of common people and also obtain abundant gain?" He then thought further: "If I were to recite the praises of a great person, then the crowds of common people would be greatly delighted and abundant gain would come about as well."

At that time, most of the great crowd of common people had come to have faith in the Blessed One. The dancer thought: "For now, this world with its gods has faith in the Blessed One — so if I recite the praises of the Blessed One, the buddha, the crowds of common people will be greatly delighted and abundant gain will come about. Therefore I shall recite the praises of the Blessed One, the buddha." And so he went to the assembly of those who rejoiced and spoke:

"Noble ones, at the time when the Blessed One, still a bodhisattva, dwelled in the Tuṣita heaven, he surveyed the world through the five kinds of examination — looking at lineage, family, land, time, and woman — and then purified the six gods of the desire realm three times. He transformed his form into the appearance of a great elephant and, with full awareness, entered the womb of his mother. At that very time this great earth shook violently. And those interspaces of the world where the light of the sun and moon — so great in their supernatural power, so great in their might — cannot reach, those that are darkened by an enveloping darkness, a thick darkness, an obscuring darkness, those too were at that moment pervaded by a vast illumination. Sentient beings born there who could not even see their own extended hands — even they, by that light, saw one another, being and being, and those endowed with understanding said: 'Other sentient beings too are born here.'"

those endowed with understanding said: "Other sentient beings too are born here. Other sentient beings too are born here." And at the time when the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was born from his mother's womb after ten months had passed, at that time too this great earth shook violently. And those interspaces of the world where the light of the sun and moon — so great in their supernatural power, so great in their might — cannot reach, those that are darkened by an enveloping darkness, a thick darkness, an obscuring darkness, those too were at that moment pervaded by a vast illumination. Sentient beings born there who could not even see their own extended hands — even they, by that light, saw one another, being and being, and those endowed with understanding said: "Other sentient beings too are born here. Other sentient beings too are born here."

And on the very day when the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was born, sons too were born to the four great kings. In Śrāvastī, the son of the great king Rib-kyi 'phur-tshang-byin was born, and that king thought to himself: "When my son was born, the world appeared brilliantly illuminated, bright as brightness itself; therefore I shall name this youth Bright Victor." And so he gave that son the name Bright Victor. In Rājagṛha, a son was born to the great king Padmamahā, and he thought: "When my son was born, the world appeared as though the form of the sun had risen, and since this boy is the son of the queen Gzugs-can, I shall name this youth Essence of Form." And so he gave that son the name Essence of Form. In Kauśāmbī, a son was born to the great king of the Hundred-Armed Army, and he thought: "When my son was born, the world appeared as though the sun had risen; therefore I shall name this youth Risen." And so he gave that son the name Risen. In the noble kingdom, a son was born to the great king Mu-khyud-mtha'-yas, and he thought: "When my son was born, the world became illuminated by a supreme light; therefore I shall name this son Supreme Light." And so he gave that son the name Supreme Light.

And on the very day when the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was born, five hundred young Śākyas headed by Bzang-ldan were also born, and five hundred attendants headed by 'Dun-byed were born. From five hundred mares, five hundred foals headed by Bsngags-ldan were born. And the gods revealed five hundred treasures nearby. The Blessed One, the bodhisattva, was then examined by brahmins who were readers of omens and by specialists in marks, and they prophesied: "If this youth remains within the palace, he will become a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) victorious in all four directions — a righteous king, a king endowed with Dharma, possessed of the seven precious things. Those seven precious things will be as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious queen, the precious householder, and the precious general — these are the seven. He will have brave and bold sons of supreme form, a full thousand of them, who utterly vanquish enemy armies. And he will settle the entire great earth reaching to the ocean's edge, without injury and without harm, without cutting down and without the sword, by means of Dharma, in harmony and accord, well established and at peace."

"If he shaves his hair and beard, dons ochre robes, and goes forth from home into homelessness with perfect faith, then he will become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened Buddha, renowned throughout the world, possessed of a fame that resounds everywhere" — such was the prophecy.

And at the time when the Blessed One, still a bodhisattva, was born into the world, everywhere near the face of the snowy mountains, beside a river, by a road where fortunate travelers passed, not far from the hermitage of the golden-robed ascetics, a young son was born among the Śākyas. The brahmin astrologers and sign-readers proclaimed: "This is how the prophecy was spoken." And the kings of the regions under the sun, hearing that near the face of the snowy mountains, beside a river, by a road where fortunate travelers passed, not far from the hermitage of the golden-robed ascetics, a young son had been born among the Śākyas, and that the brahmin astrologers and sign-readers had proclaimed it so — hearing this, those kings of the regions under the sun thought to themselves: "If we attend upon the youth, in due time it will bear fruit. Whom should we attend upon? We should attend upon the youth." And so they considered: "We should attend upon King Śuddhodana, for attending upon him is the way to attend upon the youth." So they began to attend upon King Śuddhodana, and at the proper seasons they sent messengers and gifts, honouring him.

Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself: "When my son was born, every purpose was fulfilled and every undertaking accomplished. Therefore I shall give this youth the name Sarvārthasiddha, Fulfiller of All Purposes." And so the name Sarvārthasiddha was requested and bestowed.

Then, when he was led to pay homage to the deity of the Śākyas, a yakṣa named Śākyavardhana, "Increaser of the Śākyas," the young Śākya proved capable, and when he bowed before that deity, he was named Śākyamuni, "Capable One of the Śākyas," and also "God above Gods."

And at the time when the Blessed One, still a bodhisattva, grew into maturity in body, having mastered all branches of learning, and having engaged in the sports of youth, he beheld an old man, a sick man, and a dead man, and his mind turned away. He went into the forest and for six years practised austerities. During that time King Śuddhodana and the Śākya nobleman Śākya Legs-par-Rab-rtogs dispatched two hundred and fifty men in shifts, two hundred and fifty at a time, to seek an audience with the Blessed One the bodhisattva, and each day those men went to request an audience with him.

And at the time when the Blessed One the bodhisattva had practised austerities for six years, he recognised that asceticism was of no benefit whatsoever, and he breathed in as he wished and breathed out as he wished, and he partook of abundant food — boiled rice, warm gruel, and so forth. He anointed his body with butter and grain oil, and bathed his body with warm water.

Then he went to the nearby village, where two village girls — Sujātā and Balavijayā — offered him milk mixed with honey that had been churned sixteen times. Praised by Kāḷanāgarāja, the black nāga king, he accepted bundles of golden-coloured auspicious grass from a grass-seller, and went to the place of awakening. Arriving there, he himself spread a seat of undisturbed grass, sat down cross-legged, drew his body upright, settled his mindfulness, and dwelt there, uttering from his heart this resolve:

Until I attain the undefiled,
this cross-legged seat I shall not break.

And at the time when the Blessed One, at midnight, subdued by the power of loving-kindness the māras and demons — thirty million and sixty million — together with their retinues,

— please teach extensively how the Blessed One attained, in full and complete manifestation, unsurpassable perfect and complete awakening.

Ānanda said: What use is that to you?

The dancer said: Noble one, I would set it to the art of dance.

Ānanda said: You pauper — would you embellish it as our Teacher is embellished? Be off with you and say no more.

Then the dancer went to the assembly of Ānanda's attendants, asked the same question, and they too gave the same reply. Then he went in turn to the assemblies of the quick-walkers, the Nabhasos, the Undaos, and the Charkas, asked the same question, and every one of them, each in their own way, gave the same reply and did not teach him.

Then the dancer went to the twelve assemblies of nuns, and first he asked the nun Bhaumadharā, saying the same thing. Bhaumadharā replied: What use is that to you?

The dancer said: I would set it to the art of dance. What fee is appointed for her? I offer it.

Now Bhaumadharā was one of great learning, endowed with the three scriptural collections, possessed of the confidence that comes from reasoning and liberation. She therefore taught him in full — from the time when the Blessed One, dwelling as a bodhisattva in Tuṣita Heaven, surveyed the world through the five modes of vision, looking at family, lineage, region, time, and woman, and having looked upon the world, caused the six gods of the desire realm to purify themselves three times completely; then, transforming the appearance into that of a great elephant, he knowingly entered into his mother's womb; and at that very moment the great earth shook and trembled violently, and the dark and darkening darkness that pervades the interworld spaces — where the sun and the moon, though of such great miraculous power, of such great might, cannot make their light felt — that darkness too was at that time pervaded by a vast radiance, so that the sentient beings born there, who could not even see their own hands outstretched, by that light could see one another, and knowing this said: "O wise ones, another sentient being has been born here! O wise ones, another sentient being has been born here!" — down to the time when, at midnight, the Blessed One subdued by the power of loving-kindness the māras and demons — thirty million and sixty million — together with their retinues, and fully attained unsurpassable perfect and complete awakening — all of this exactly as it is extensively told in the sūtra of the manifest arising up to the perfect and complete awakening.

Then the dancer set it to the art of dance, and then he thought: By this I am able to increase the faith of the masses of ordinary people who already have faith — but what means is there by which even those who have no faith might come to have faith?

So he ingratiated himself with the six groups of monks, following close behind them one after another. At a certain moment, the venerable Undao had finished eating and set aside his main dish, and found some leftover food and scraps and wished to eat them, and he rubbed his hands together and was about to take that leftover food, when the venerable Charka, who was eating his gruel, was approached by Undao, who sat down on his haunches before him and said: Venerable Charka, please take note. I, the monk Undao — having sought, found, and completely and utterly exhausted my main dish and food — have found and sought some leftovers, and if you would leave a little more, please give it to me.

Charka ate two or three mouthfuls from it, then said: Take what remains for yourself and be gone.

When the dancer saw this, he thought: By this I shall be able to bring even those without faith to faith. And then he departed.

Vinayavibhaṅga, the fifty-ninth fascicle.

Then the dancer, in Rājagṛha, went to Giriva, the nāga king of the mountains, and —

On the day when the festival of Delightful Twain had begun, the great clay drum was beaten from a high seat, and when a great multitude of common folk had gathered there and sat together in harmony, the dancer performed, in elaborate dance, all the enactments of that time when the Blessed One, dwelling as a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita realm, surveyed the world through the five surveys — of clan, lineage, region, time, and woman — and having looked upon the world, caused the six gods of the realm of desire to purify themselves three times; and then, having transformed his appearance into that of a great white elephant, entered with full awareness into his mother's womb. At that very moment the great earth trembled violently, and those dark interspaces of the world — the regions between world-systems — where the light of the sun and moon, great as their supernatural power is, mighty as their might is, does not reach, so that those places are wrapped in thick, blinding darkness, those very places were pervaded by a vast radiance. The sentient beings born there, who could not even see their own hands stretched out before them, saw one another by that light, and those with wisdom understood: "Yet another sentient being has been born here, yet another sentient being has been born here." And then, enacting the events from the sūtra — as it extensively describes them — up to the time when the Blessed One, at the midnight hour, subdued Māra (Skt. māra) who had come with a retinue of thirty million demons and sixty million attendants, by the power of loving-kindness, and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, the dancer staged all of this extensively as dance. The faithful among the great multitude of common folk grew yet more fervent in their faith, and called out: "Eamo! Well danced! Eamo! Well danced!" And the dancer gained great material reward.

Then the dancer thought again: I have increased the faith of those among the common folk who already had faith. Now I should also bring to faith those who have no faith yet. After that, one dancer dressed himself in the costume of Charka, and another dancer dressed himself in the costume of Undao. The one dressed as Undao filled a bowl with ashes, placed two or three lumps of raw sugar on top, then sat cross-legged in front of the one dressed as Charka who was eating a meal, and said: Venerable Charka, please take note. I, the monk Undao, having sought, found, and completely and utterly exhausted my main dish and food, have now sought and found a little more; if you would leave some over, please give it to me. The one dressed as Charka then took the two or three lumps of raw sugar and ate them, and the one dressed as Undao poured the ashes from the bowl over his own head, saying: Take what is yours and be gone. At this, the entire great multitude of common folk burst into loud laughter, crying out "Ha! Ha!" Those who had no faith grew fervent in their faith, and called out: "Eamo! A madman's trick! Eamo! A madman's trick!" And the dancer gained great material reward.

Then those among the great multitude of common folk who were faithful said: Look here, friends! This dancer has enacted the time when the Blessed One, dwelling as a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita realm, surveyed the world through the five surveys — of clan, lineage, region, time, and woman — and having looked upon the world, caused the six gods of the realm of desire to purify themselves three times,

having transformed his appearance into that of a great white elephant and entered, fully conscious, into his mother's womb — and at that very moment the great earth trembled violently, and those regions of the world between worlds where these two — the sun and the moon, great as they are in their miraculous power and their might — cannot reach with their light, and which remain in utter, impenetrable, pitch-black darkness: those regions too were at that moment pervaded by a great radiance, so that the sentient beings born there, who could not even see their own hands stretched out before them, could now see one another by that light, and knew: "Friends, yet another sentient being has been born here! Friends, yet another sentient being has been born here!"

From that point up to the time when the Blessed One, in the middle watch of the night, with the power of loving-kindness (Skt. maitrī) subdued the māra host — thirty million demons together with sixty million attendants — and fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening: all of this in its entirety, exactly as it is described at length in the sūtra on his manifest arising, was set to dance with great elaboration and performed.

And those among the faithful in the great crowd of common folk said: "Friends, look! This dancer has elaborated upon and enacted, at great length and with all its details, the dance of the Blessed One's entry into the bodhisattva's conduct — the dance called 'Unpleasant Sound.' " And their faith grew manifestly stronger.

Those among the great crowd of common folk who had no faith said: "Friends, look! This dancer has elaborated upon and enacted all of this at great length as a madman's trick — parodying what the six groups of loose wandering monks (Skt. śramaṇa) do that is not to be done." And they laughed.

In time the six groups came to hear that it was being said the dancer had imitated them. They said: "We shall make this dancer unwelcome. We will go and take counsel with our sisters." And they went to the community of twelve groups of nuns and said: "Sisters, let us discuss together whatever we can recall of the dance-performance called 'Unpleasant Sound,' which depicted the Blessed One's entry into the bodhisattva's conduct." And so they went together with those nuns to a pleasure garden and began their deliberations.

In time, having forgotten nothing at all, those nuns fetched ornaments and costumes from the royal palace, set up a tent-canopy not far from the dancer, had a close companion bind his head in a cloth and beat a great clay drum — while the watching crowd streamed out from among the common folk and gathered there. The dancer also arrived at that spot.

When he saw something that resembled the dance of gods, he thought to himself: "Can these be gods performing a dance? Or are they nāgas? Or yakṣas? Or gandharvas (Skt. gandharva)? Or kinneras (Skt. kiṃnara)? Or great serpents?" And realizing what he saw, he was filled with amazement.

The six groups, having performed their dance, changed out of their costumes and departed. The dancer thought: "Who are these people?" and followed along behind them. In time they entered the Ōmā Grove, and the dancer waited at the gate. In time, one named Acharka came out through the gate, his shoulder-cloth draped about him, as though anointing himself. The dancer said to him: "Noble one, did you perform that dance?"

Acharka replied: "We are going to make you unwelcome. You, a pauper, make your living by our arts alone, and yet you imitate us — so wherever you go to dance, we will go there and outbid you, and you will find that neither the great clay drum nor any other equipment will need to be carried for us."

The dancer replied: "Noble one, that is our livelihood — please be patient."

Acharka said:

"If you give everything you earn to us, we will be patient."

He thought: "These ones will keep pestering me again and again, so I will give." And having given all his earnings to them, he sat there with a heavy heart.

After a while, his younger companion arrived and asked him: "Friend, why do you sit with such a heavy heart?"

He replied: "I have been cut down by a penalty."

"By whom?"

"By the śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), the sons of the Śākya."

"Why?" He then gave a full account of what had occurred, and said that the code of conduct of the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya is merely words, and the code of the brahmins (Skt. brāhmaṇa) is merely words — for even against dancers they impose penalties, they condemn them, they disparage them, they slander them. And they condemned, disparaged, and slandered the monks, saying: "Why do monks — monks of small worth — do such an unseemly thing?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about from monks wearing householders' clothing. Therefore a monk should not put on householders' clothing." Having so reflected, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks regarding this incident, this case, this occasion — and so forth, as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though they already know, cause enquiry to be made" — and so forth, also as before.

The Blessed One questioned the group of six: "Monks, is it true that you did something so unseemly?" "We did, Venerable One."

The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that what is not proper conduct for one who has gone forth — what is not fitting, not appropriate, not in accordance with the rule — that should not be done by one who has gone forth. Then the Blessed One, having rebuked them in many ways, addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, having seen ten benefits fully and correctly, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas" — and so forth as before.

"My śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya thus: If a monk obtains a new robe, he shall mar its appearance by dyeing it in one of the three discolouring colours — blue-black, red, or ochre. If a monk wears a new robe without having marred its appearance with one of the three discolouring colours — blue-black, red, or ochre — he commits an offence."

As to the terms of this rule: "a monk" refers to the group of six. "Robe" means any one of the seven kinds: woollen cloth, hemp cloth, silk cloth, muslin cloth, coarse linen cloth, cotton cloth, or a cloth made of a mixture of these. "New" — there are two kinds of new: what is new in the sense of being freshly made, and what is new in the sense of being newly obtained. In this context, it is intended as newly made. "Obtains" means from another. As to "one of the three discolouring colours — blue-black, red, or ochre": blue-black means indigo; red means lac; ochre means tree-bark. "Shall mar its appearance" means to make its colour unattractive.

"If a monk wears a new robe without having marred its appearance with one of the three discolouring colours — blue-black, red, or ochre" means if he wears it. "He commits an offence" means it causes him to be scorched, to be scalded, to fall — to fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of utter downfall.

Furthermore, so long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities. For that reason it is said to cause one to fall. As to how the transgression comes about: whenever a monk obtains any new cloth at all — even a bowl-cover will do — he must mar its appearance with one of the three discolouring colours, blue-black, red, or ochre, whichever is suitable. If a monk uses a new cloth without having marred its appearance with one of those three discolouring colours — blue-black, red, or ochre — he incurs a transgression in every instance. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations.

This is the fifty-eighth rule giving rise to transgression, concerning the wearing of robes without marring their appearance, and it is complete.

As an interlude verse:

The Vulture Peak, the casting away,
music, the great Licchavi assembly,
the melodious lute, she who holds the deer —
these are the proper collection here.

The Blessed One, the buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak. Then one morning the Blessed One donned his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and his Dharma robe, and came down from Vulture Peak. The venerable Ānanda followed close behind him. As they proceeded to Rājagṛha for alms, the Blessed One saw that in that direction a radiance of water had fallen and was shimmering and glowing, for a treasure hidden there by people of the first aeon had been caused to rain down by a god. Having seen this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, that is a swiftly spreading serpent-venom." The venerable Ānanda replied, "Blessed One, it is indeed a fierce serpent-venom." "Ānanda, it is a swiftly spreading serpent-venom." "O Sugata, it is indeed a fierce serpent-venom."

Now nearby, not very far away, there was a man who was living by gleaning leftover curds, with only a stump remaining of his crops and roots. He heard this exchange and thought: "I can see the swiftly spreading serpent-venom, but I cannot see any fierce serpent-venom. What then might the fierce serpent-venom of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan be like? I myself wander through this area day and night, and if I were to be seized by some fierce serpent-venom it would be terrible — how would I escape?" And so he went over to that spot. When he arrived, he saw a treasure shimmering and glowing, and he thought: "The fierce serpent-venom of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan is beautiful! The fierce serpent-venom of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan is truly excellent! With a fierce serpent-venom such as this, even seizing one's own unloved father and mother would be easy. Even seizing one's children, one's wife, one's maidservants, one's workers, those who live by gleaning curds, one's friends and companions, one's ministers, one's relatives, and one's dearest kin by blood — even all of that would be easily done." And so that man wrapped up the treasure in bundles of leaves and carried it home step by step, bit by bit.

Now at the time when Ajātaśatru, king born of the noble lady Vaidehī, who had come from Māgadha, had been surrounded and misled by the evil companion Devadatta, and his righteous father, the Dharma-king Bimbisāra, had been separated from his life — when Ajātaśatru himself had been bound with the diadem and installed as the sovereign lord of royal dominion — at that time he commanded those who lived by gleaning leftover curds: "Wise ones, go and look — whatever assemblies there are, whatever provisions there are, whatever it is by which people live: examine all of this." Then those men who lived on gleaned curds, following the royal command, obeyed King Ajātaśatru, born of the noble lady Vaidehī from Māgadha, and

When those men who lived by gleaning the king's leftover curds were wandering through the quarters, they saw that man making his household prosperous. They said to him: "My friend, you are poor — you survive by selling roots and fruits, root and branch alike, and by stringing together a meager living. Whence has this household prosperity of yours come? Have you found a treasure?" He replied: "I have indeed found a treasure. I have this prosperity now, but previously, when there was a king who did not act in accordance with the Dharma, I did not bring it forth. Now, however, a king who does act in accordance with the Dharma has arisen, and that is why I am building up my household prosperity. As for the king Rūpaṣeṇahṛdaya, his palace, his retinue, and the people of the realm are pleased with him — but he is not one who acts in accordance with the Dharma. As for King Ajātaśatru, the palace, his retinue, and the people of the realm are not pleased with him — and yet he is a king who acts in accordance with the Dharma." They replied: "My friend, if King Rūpaṣeṇahṛdaya, who acts in accordance with the Dharma, does not in fact act in accordance with the Dharma, and if the one who killed his own father turns out to be the one who acts in accordance with the Dharma — do you know who we are?" He replied: "I know. You are men who live on the king's leftover curds, and through your very eyes the king will come to see."

They said: "My friend, do not deceive us with lies. Take half of the treasure you found for yourself, and give the other half to us." He replied: "I have found a treasure, and it is indeed mine — nevertheless, be satisfied with a gift of a third." They thereupon seized him, bound both his arms behind his back, strung a cord through his collar, and brought him before the king, saying: "Your majesty, this man has found a treasure." The king said: "My friend, do you know who I am? I pay homage to you — the four guardians of the world do guard the world. You yourself are the fifth guardian of the world, a kṣatriya king anointed on the crown, who protects living beings." Then: "My friend, do not deceive me with lies about the treasure you found. Speak the truth — take half for yourself and give half to me." He said: "Your majesty, I have found a treasure." Then: "My friend, since you found a treasure, give me a third of it." He said: "Your majesty, I have found a treasure." The king grew angry and said to his ministers: "Wise ones, what is the punishment for one who has interrupted three times the word of a kṣatriya king anointed on the crown?" They replied: "Your majesty, the punishment is death." The king said: "Wise ones, let this man be banished completely. Let his relatives be made to crawl on their bellies. And let all his wealth be presented to the royal palace." Then the ministers, saying "As your majesty commands," and obeying King Ajātaśatru — son of the noble lady Vaidehī, born in Māgadhā — had that man's relatives thrown into prison, and all his wealth was presented to the royal palace. As for the man himself, he was bound around the neck with red karavīra blossoms by men dressed in dark blue garments bearing swords in their hands, and was being led away to the place of execution. As he went he called out:

"Ānanda! A snake's venom spreads swiftly.
O Blessed One, a snake's venom is fierce.
Ānanda! A snake's venom spreads swiftly.
O Sugata, a snake's venom is fierce."

Now that king's custom was such that, when a man condemned to death was questioned, he would give a different answer — and as long as one had not yet petitioned the king, the execution would not be carried out for the time being. So the ministers said to the king:

"Your Majesty, when that man is questioned by others, he gives a different answer." The king said, "Bring him here." The ministers brought him, and the king asked, "My dear man, what are you saying?" He replied, "Ānanda! A snake's venom spreads swiftly. O Blessed One, a snake's venom is fierce. Ānanda! A snake's venom spreads swiftly. O Sugata, a snake's venom is fierce." The king said, "My dear man, what is the meaning of what you have said? Your Majesty, please grant me fearlessness." The king said, "It is granted." The man then recounted the matter in full, and spoke these words: "If a swift-spreading snake's venom had seized me, then I alone would have met my appointed time. But it was a fierce snake's venom that seized me, and on account of that, I and all my kinsmen and all my wealth have been made to suffer unjustly."

Now at that time the king of Magadha (Skt. Magadha), Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, had not long before come to faith in the Blessed One, and so he said, "My dear man, do you have sincere faith in the Blessed One?" The man replied, "Your Majesty, I do have sincere faith." Then the king of Magadha, Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, was moved to tears and said, "My dear man, what happened to you was done by you yourself — go now." The king then gave orders to the jailers: "Release this man's kinsmen, and return to him all his wealth." The jailers released his kinsmen and returned all his wealth.

Then that man thought to himself: "Whatever prosperity and good fortune I have in my home, all of it is owing to the Blessed One. I shall therefore invite the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks to another house and offer them a midday meal." So the man went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One fully instructed that man with a Dharma teaching, fully established him in it, fully praised him, and fully gladdened him. With many words he fully taught him with a Dharma teaching, fully established him in it, fully praised him, and fully gladdened him, and then said nothing further.

Then that man rose from his seat, bowed with joined palms turned toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Would the Blessed One kindly consent to accept tomorrow, together with the Saṅgha of monks, a midday meal at my dwelling?" The Blessed One consented to the man's request by his silence. Knowing from the Blessed One's silence that the invitation was accepted, the man prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

That very night the man made the preparations, and in the morning rose early, set out the seats, placed water vessels, and invited the Blessed One with the words: "Venerable one, may the Blessed One please be mindful that the time for the midday meal has now come." Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his begging bowl and robe, and surrounded by an assembly of monks, with the Saṅgha of monks proceeding before him, went to the place where that man's dwelling was, arrived there, and took his seat on the prepared seat at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then, perceiving that the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably settled, the man served them with pure and choice drink and food from his own hand, satisfying them fully. In many different ways he served pure and choice drink and food from his own hand, filling them to contentment. Then, perceiving that the Blessed One had finished his meal and set aside his bowl, he bowed with joined palms, and taking a seat lower than the Blessed One's, sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood that man's thoughts, latent tendencies, temperament, and nature, taught the Dharma in such a way that, as that man sat there together with his wife, the peak of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection — twenty heights high — was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was directly realized. Having seen the truth, the man said in petition: "Venerable one, through relying on the Blessed One as my virtuous friend, what the Blessed One has done for me here is something my father did not do, nor did my mother, nor did the king, nor did the gods, nor did my ancestors of old, nor did the ascetics and brahmins, nor did the assembly of friends, companions, and relatives. You have dried the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed me from the mountain of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; you have drawn my feet out of the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm; you have placed me among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to an end. The peak of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection — twenty heights high — accumulated since beginningless time, has been shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry has been obtained. Venerable one, I have directly entered the stream. I have directly entered the stream. Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. I humbly request to be received as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I take refuge with faith from the depths of my heart."

Then the Blessed One instructed that man with a Dharma-endowed discourse, correctly establishing him, correctly uplifting him, and filling him with joy. Then he rose from his seat and departed.

Now at this point the awakened Blessed One had not yet established a rule of training for the hearers within the Vinaya. The awakened Blessed One was residing in Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka's Grove of the Bamboo Forest.

The venerable Śārika dressed in the early morning, took his begging bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. As he was making his alms-round, he saw a place where archery was being practiced, and went there. There was no archery master, but some boys were standing about, and he asked them: "Boys, what are you doing?" They replied: "Noble one, we are learning archery." Śārika said: "Good, boys — you have surpassed the highest craft! Boys, practice shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, throwing the lasso, shooting a great arrow, cutting, piercing, bending back, the single-pointed vajra shot, and casting a single-pointed weapon." And they began to practice shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, throwing the lasso, shooting a great arrow, cutting, piercing, bending back, the single-pointed vajra shot, and casting a single-pointed weapon.

Śārika clasped his two hands together and turned his face aside. They said: "Noble one, why do you clasp your two hands together and turn your face aside?" Śārika said: "Even your teacher does not know this — how should you be expected to understand it?" They said: "Noble one, do you know something of this?" Śārika said: "Boys, what is the craft or occupation on earth that I do not know?" They said: "Noble one, please perform shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, throwing the lasso, shooting a great arrow, cutting, piercing, and bending back." So Śārika performed shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, and throwing the lasso in a manner that no one else could replicate, and, binding himself with a belt and taking up a round shield, he also performed cutting, piercing, and bending back. They were filled with amazement and said: "Noble one, excellent! Excellent!" Śārika said: "Boys, you should train in the craft in this way — or else seek another teacher! What use is it to stand about like husks of fruitless grain?" And with that he departed.

Presently their teacher arrived and said: "Boys, why are you standing about? Do your shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, throwing the lasso, shooting a great arrow, cutting, piercing, bending back, the single-pointed vajra shot, and casting a single-pointed weapon!" They clasped their two hands together and turned their faces aside, saying: "Master, you yourself still know nothing of this — how are we supposed to look at you?" The teacher said: "Boys, when something unprecedented like this has occurred, has someone come here?" They replied: "Yes." "Who?" "The noble Śārika. He performed shooting to the left, shooting to the right, footwork, gripping the bow, throwing the lasso, shooting a great arrow, cutting, piercing, bending back, the single-pointed vajra shot, and casting a single-pointed weapon in such a way that no one could match it." He also said to them: "He has trained with the very one from whom a bodhisattva would train in the fundamentals of archery. Were he not gone forth into renunciation, he would become the supreme archery master throughout all of Jambudvīpa. Still, whatever I know, learn that from me, and for the rest learn from others."

The teacher thought to himself: "He will keep coming back to challenge me — I had better go to him." And so he went to Śārika and said: "Noble Śārika, have you come to the place where we practice our archery?" Śārika said: "I have." "Noble one, did you discipline the boys somewhat?" Śārika said: "I disciplined them." He said: "Noble one, those boys are my livelihood — please do not discipline them further. You are a poor man; you live by our craft. Will you not give us even a small fee for our service?" Śārika replied: "Noble one, I am destitute." Śārika said: "Poor man, if you do not pay, I shall come back again and again and discipline them." The teacher thought: "If I do not pay his fee, he will keep coming back and disciplining the boys." And so he sold all his archery equipment, paid him his fee, and sat with his heart deeply troubled.

After a time, the teacher's younger friend came and asked: "Friend, why do you sit with your heart so troubled?" He replied: "I have been fined." "By whom?" "By the śramaṇas (wandering renunciants), the sons of the Śākyas." "Why?"

He then recounted the matter in full detail, and the younger friend found the deportment of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, to be worthy of reproach, and the deportment of the brahmins likewise to be reproach-worthy. In this way he began to revile them, saying: "Even the teachers of archery impose fines," and he spread slander, heaping scorn and insults upon them.

Now at that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, had not yet established rules of training in the Vinaya for the hearers. The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at the Veṇuvana.

The venerable Śāraka dressed himself in his robes in the early morning, took up his bowl and Dharma robe, and entered Rājagṛha on alms round. As he was going about collecting alms, he came upon a performance ground and entered it. There was no music teacher present; only some boys were gathered there. He asked them: "Boys, what are you doing?" They replied: "Noble one, we are learning music." Śāraka said: "Well done, boys — you have surpassed the master craftsmen. Boys, try performing the six-beat, the sage-style, the earth-holding, the clear-minded, the encircling-ear, the middle-style, and the Keśika." They began to perform the six-beat, the sage-style, the earth-holding, the clear-minded, the encircling-ear, the middle-style, and the Keśika. Then Śāraka clasped his two hands together and turned his face away. They said: "Noble one, why do you clasp your two hands together and turn your face?" Śāraka said: "Even your teacher still does not know it — how would you ever come to know it?" They said: "Noble one, do you know something of it?" Śāraka said: "Boys, is there any craft or professional art on earth that I do not know?" They said: "Noble one, please then perform the six-beat, the sage-style, the earth-holding, the clear-minded, the encircling-ear, the middle-style, and the Keśika for us, quickly, without delay." Śāraka then performed the six-beat, the sage-style, the earth-holding, the clear-minded, the encircling-ear, the middle-style, and the Keśika in such a way that no one else could have done it. They were filled with wonder and said: "Noble one, excellent! Excellent!" Śāraka said: "Boys, you should train in the craft to that standard — otherwise, go find yourself another teacher; there is no point in you sitting here tossing about worthless chaff." And with that, he departed.

Presently their teacher arrived and said: "Boys, just sit and do as you please — perform the six-beat, the sage-style, the earth-holding, the clear-minded, the encircling-ear, the middle-style, and the Keśika." They clasped their two hands together and turned their faces, saying: "Even our teacher still does not know it — how could we come to know it?" The teacher said: "Boys, if there was a transformation of this kind, never seen before, then someone must have come here." They said: "Indeed, someone did come." "Who?" "Noble Śāraka. He performed the six-beat and the rest in a manner that no one else could, to such a degree that no song or dance could match him." The teacher said to them: "The bodhisattva too trained in music at the very performance ground where Śāraka trained in music. If Śāraka had not gone forth into renunciation, he would have become the supreme master of music throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa. Nevertheless, let each of you learn from him whatever he knows, and learn the remainder from someone else."

The teacher then thought to himself: "This man will keep coming here and putting me to shame. I had better go to him." He went to Śāraka and said: "Noble Śāraka, have you come to our performance ground?" Śāraka replied: "I have." "Noble one, did you discipline the boys even a little?" Śāraka replied: "I disciplined them." The teacher then said:

"Noble one, you are my livelihood — do not discipline the boys too harshly. You are a poor man; we make our living by the performing arts. Will you not give us even a small fee for your stay?" Śāraka replied: "Noble one, I am destitute." Śāraka said: "Poor man, if you will not pay, I shall come again and again and discipline them." Śāraka thought to himself: "If I do not pay this man his fee for lodging, he will come again and again and discipline the boys." So he sold all his musical instruments, paid the man his lodging fee, and sat there deeply troubled.

After some time, a younger friend of his came to visit and asked him: "Friend, why do you sit so troubled?" He replied: "I have been fined." "By whom?" "By the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyans." "Why?" The man then recounted what had happened in full. Now the conduct of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyans, was a subject of talk, and the conduct of the brahmins was a subject of talk. People were criticizing them, saying that even masters of music impose fines, and they were mocking them and speaking ill of them.

Now this was a time when the Blessed One, the buddha, had not yet established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. Then the Blessed One, having stayed as long as he wished in Rājagṛha, set out wandering on tour in the direction of Vaiśālī, and in due course arrived at Vaiśālī, where he took up residence in the excellent multi-storied dwelling on the bank of the Monkey Pool. In the morning, the venerable Ānanda put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Vaiśālī for alms. At the same time, a great many young Licchavī boys came out of Vaiśālī. Outside the city they set aside all their ornaments in one place and began to play. Ānanda saw them and, thinking the ornaments were the property of a yakṣa, took them all and went on his way. The young Licchavī boys of Vaiśālī then seized Ānanda — some by the hands, some by the feet, some by his outer robe — saying: "Noble one, why do you steal our ornaments?" A senior Licchavī who saw the young Licchavī boys of Vaiśālī seizing Ānanda and raising their fists said: "Boys, why do you raise your fists against the noble Ānanda?" They replied: "He has stolen our ornaments." He said: "Noble Ānanda, why did you take the boys' ornaments?" Ānanda replied: "I found them and thought they were a yakṣa's property." The senior Licchavī said: "If these seem like a yakṣa's property to you — these are the ornaments of young men — please return them without taking them." Ānanda set them down, and then went to the monastery with his outer robe soiled with dust. The monks said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, why are you soiled with so much dust?" Ānanda replied: "May the senior Licchavī be well. I found what I took to be a yakṣa's property and had to set it down."

Now this too was a time when the Blessed One, the buddha, had not yet established a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. The Blessed One was residing at Vaiśālī in the excellent multi-storied dwelling on the bank of the Monkey Pool. The Group of Six, in the morning, put on their lower robes, took up their bowls and outer robes, and entered Vaiśālī for alms. Along the way, there were pleasure gardens belonging to the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, and the Licchavīs said:

"Dear friends, the Blessed One obtained these pleasure gardens from the gods of the thirty-three who belong to the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī — come and look at what those gardens are like." So they entered there. And in the gardens there were various kinds of supplies of this sort: bathing lotions, tooth-cleaning twigs, unguents, combs, incense, emblic myrobalan, hair-washing preparations, lutes, milk, mahātī, woolly blankets, and sughoṣaka instruments — all laid out. And those who were there said, "Dear friends, shall we bathe first, or shall we sing and dance?" Those others replied, "We have been singing and dancing for a long time — let us sing and dance again." And so they began to sing and dance.

Now whatever sound of music had been performed in the pleasure garden of King Śuddhodana, that very sound was the sound of the music performed on the battlefield of King Ajātaśatru, the son born of Vaidehī. When they struck up that music, the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī heard it. Hearing it, they were startled and said, "Good people, the patricide has raised his army and come upon us without warning!" They armed themselves and began to rush out.

The Group of Six had also left that pleasure garden just then. Seeing the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī arming themselves and rushing out, the Group of Six asked them, "Good people, where are you going?" They replied, "The patricide has come, and we are heading out to meet him in battle." "Where is he?" "Just now," they said, "the sound of the music performed on the battlefield of King Ajātaśatru, the son born of Vaidehī, arose here." The Group of Six said, "Good people, is that so? We were the ones who were making merry — surely you are not fleeing in such a panic because of us?" The Licchavīs said, "Noble ones, was it your musical instruments that produced that sound?" The Group of Six replied, "We were the ones who made that sound." The Licchavīs said, "Noble ones, the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were alarmed, and it is not right that they be harmed on your account — please turn back." They turned back.

Then the monks said to the Group of Six, "Venerable ones, why did you turn back?" The Group of Six replied, "Venerable ones, we killed those men." "Who did?" "The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī did." "Why?" They gave a full account of the circumstances. A few of the monks who were modest said, "Why do monks do something so unseemly?" and they rebuked them, insulted them, and spoke against them. Then those monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, on account of this occasion, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, just as before. "The blessed buddhas, while knowing, ask questions" — and so forth again, just as before.

The blessed Buddha questioned the Group of Six: "Monks, is it true that you did such an unseemly thing?" "It is true, Reverend One." The blessed Buddha rebuked them, saying that what is improper for a monk, what is incongruous, what is unfitting, what is contrary to the discipline — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth. Having rebuked them in this and in many ways, the Blessed One then declared to the monks:

"Monks, seeing the ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the discipline is to be established" — and so forth, just as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the discipline as follows: 'Furthermore, whatever monk takes with his own hand, or causes to be taken, a precious object or what is regarded as a precious object, he commits an offense.'" Thus did the Blessed One establish this rule of training for the hearers in the discipline.

Thereafter, the Blessed One stayed in Vaiśālī as long as he wished, and then set out wandering by stages toward Śrāvastī. Traveling on stage by stage, he arrived at Śrāvastī and there dwelt in the eastern park, in the mansion of Mṛgāramātṛ.

Now Mṛgāramātṛ Sāgā heard that the Blessed One had been traveling through the Kośala regions, had arrived at Śrāvastī, and was staying there at her own mansion. Hearing this, she adorned herself with all her ornaments and came forth from Śrāvastī to where the Blessed One was. Being a person of modesty, however, she removed her ornaments, bundled them up, and gave them into her daughter's hands. She then went before the Blessed One, bowed her head to his two feet, and sat down to one side. Not far from where she sat there was a branch of a campaka tree in full blossom. She saw it and thought to herself: "I shall pluck flowers from this and scatter loose petals over the Blessed One — that will be a fine offering." So she set aside the bundle of ornaments to one side, plucked flowers from that campaka branch, scattered the loose petals over the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One taught her the Dharma at length, after which she bowed to his feet and departed — and in that very spot she forgot and left behind the bundle of ornaments.

The venerable Ānanda saw that she had left the ornaments behind and departed, and he thought to himself: "Although the Blessed One has not yet permitted it, this could serve as a cause through which something of this nature might come to be permitted." So the venerable Ānanda had the ornaments stored away, then went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head to his two feet, and sat down to one side.
