Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend One, Mṛgāramātṛ Sāgā forgot her ornaments and departed, and it occurred to me: 'Although the Blessed One has not permitted it, this could serve as the very cause through which what is to be permitted might come to be permitted in such a case.' So I had those ornaments stored away."

"Ānanda, it is well that you perceived what I am going to permit. Well done! Ānanda, for that reason, when staying in the park of the pleasure grove or when staying within a dwelling, with the exception of those places: since it is in the nature of women to be attached to ornaments, the next day Sāgā remembered the ornaments and said to her daughter: 'Daughter, where are the ornaments?' The daughter replied: 'Lady, you left them there yourself.' She said: 'Go and retrieve them.' Her sons, hearing this, said: 'Mother, do you not know they are in the storeroom? How could they have been taken and brought back?' Sāgā said to her sons: 'Children, she is not one who would squander wealth.' Then the daughter went to the venerable Ānanda, and the venerable Ānanda said: 'Daughter, why have you come?' The daughter said: 'Noble one, the lady left her ornaments behind.' The venerable Ānanda said:

'They are here. Take them and go.' The daughter took them and went back to Sāgā and said: 'Lady, here are your ornaments, recovered and returned.' Sāgā said to her sons: 'Children, she has brought back the ornaments. Did I not say she is not one who squanders wealth?' Her sons then asked the daughter: 'Daughter, which noble one hid them away?' The daughter said: 'The noble Ānanda.' They said: 'Because the noble Ānanda saw them, they were simply safeguarded. But if the Group of Six had seen them, there would have been a situation in which what was there would have been consecrated as a finder's fee.' Then they thought: 'Now we shall test whether our mother squanders wealth or not.' They filled some bags with dinars to the size of grain heaps and threw them at a crossroads. People passing by from there, seeing them, abandoned them completely and would not pick them up, saying: 'These spread snake-poison swiftly.' Then those sons said: 'There are bags filled with dinars sitting there, heaped like grain — why does no one take them?' The people replied: 'These spread snake-poison swiftly; they are not bags of grain heaped up with dinars, and so we do not take them.' Then those sons came back and said to their mother: 'Mother, you are indeed not one who squanders wealth.' And everywhere the reputation spread: 'It is true — Sāgā, the mother of Mṛgārin, is not one who squanders wealth.' A monk belonging to the Ānanda community saw a bag fallen there that was filled with dinars heaped like grain, and a man came in that direction. The monk said to the man: 'My dear friend, is not this grain-like bag yours?' 'It is, noble one.' 'Take it and go.' The man took it and went away quickly. Then another man came, his head covered in dust, weeping, and said: 'Noble one, did you see a bag like a heap of grain?' The monk said: 'A man took it and went away.' That man, not finding the bag, went mad and distraught, searching here and there, and was suffering grievously through improper conduct. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'In the same way, one must not speak rashly but should ask that person: What kind of bag like a heap of grain? And ask whether it was a weighing-merchant's.'

If the description matches the marks, one should give it back. If the description does not match the marks, one should not give it back. When they had left it there and gone away, others stole it. The Blessed One declared: 'In the same way, one should not simply leave it and go. Rather, one should conceal it with earth or a covering of leaves beside the path along which people travel.' When they had abandoned it entirely and gone, the Blessed One declared: 'One should not abandon it completely, but should go there and remain for seven or eight days. If the owner comes and describes the marks correctly, one should give it back. If the owner does not come, then after that it should be placed in and kept in the Saṅgha's treasury. If the owner comes after six months have passed and describes the marks correctly, one should give it back. If the owner does not come, then after that the property should be sold for a fair price and the proceeds kept. Should the owner arrive at that time, one should say to him: "This property of yours was sold here; please be satisfied with that." If he is satisfied, that is good. If he is not satisfied, one should give it back to him. If he makes trouble, one should say: "Is it not the case that we who have carefully preserved it deserve some gratitude? Take it and go." Accordingly, it must not be left outside in what belongs to the assembly hall or remain in what belongs to the residential quarters.'

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who have secured the requisites for training. He then addressed the monks with words appropriate to the occasion, more pronounced on that point, and bearing on Dharma-teachings suited to it, and declared to the monks: 'Monks, therefore what was stated before is a prescribed rule, and this is a permissive allowance. My hearers should recite the following as a training rule in the Vinaya:

Whatever monk receives with his own hand, or causes another to receive, a precious object or what is spoken of as precious, while sitting in what belongs to the assembly hall or sitting in what belongs to the residential quarters — except for sitting in what belongs to the assembly hall or sitting in what belongs to the residential quarters — commits a transgression.

As for the phrase "whatever monk": this refers to the six groups and others of the same kind. As for "a precious object or what is spoken of as precious": a precious object means a jewel, a pearl, beryl, white crystal, coral, gold, silver, the essence of stone, spug, the red one, and the right-coiling one. What is spoken of as precious means all weapons used in battle and all implements used in music. "With his own hand" means hand to hand. "Receives" means he himself does so. "Causes to receive" means another does so. "Sitting in what belongs to the assembly hall" means outside the assembly hall. "Sitting in what belongs to the residential quarters" means inside the assembly hall. "Except for" means leaving aside sitting in what belongs to the assembly hall or sitting in what belongs to the residential quarters. "Commits a transgression" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the miserable realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the places of wrong rebirth. Furthermore, so long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of virtuous Dharma-factors — therefore it is called a transgression. "A monk" means one who belongs to this Dharma. As for "sitting in what belongs to the assembly hall or in what belongs to the residential quarters, a precious object or'

a precious object' — thinking, "I wonder whose this is, and who will take it?" — one should take it up with such a thought in mind. As for "that being the proper procedure": that means that is the conforming Dharma-procedure for that situation.

Now, how does a transgression arise in this case?

As the intermediate summary verse states:

Jewels and necklaces, lutes,
Conches and bows and arrows,
Statues together with reliquaries —
These are the last of the earlier rules.

If a monk takes a jewel — if he takes one that has been strung, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one that has not been strung, it incurs a misdeed. Just as with jewels, so too with pearls, beryl, quartz crystal, coral, silver, gold, gemstone essences, turquoise, red gems, and right-spiraling shells — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as a tiny chip of a jewel, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes a necklace, it incurs a transgression. Just as with a necklace, so too with bracelets, armlets, a garland hung about the neck, and a shoulder ornament — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as a string of seeds, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes a lute — if he takes one fitted with strings, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one without strings, it incurs a misdeed. Just as with a lute, so too with the vīṇā, the Balari, the Mahātī, and the Sughoṣaka — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as a mouthpiece, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes a conch — if he takes one that produces sound, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one that does not produce sound, it incurs a misdeed. Just as with a conch, so too with the great drum, the paṭaha drum, and the clay drum — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as a single-faced clay drum, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes a bow — if he takes one fitted with a bowstring, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one without a bowstring, it incurs a misdeed. Just as with a bow, so too with a sword, a curved sword, a double-edged sword, a spear, a throwing spear, and an iron hook — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as a little bow, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes an arrow — if he takes one fitted with an arrowhead, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one without an arrowhead, it incurs a misdeed. Just as with an arrow, so too with an iron arrow and an arrow whose head is half made of iron — all are the same. Even if a monk takes so much as something fashioned to resemble an arrow, it incurs a misdeed.

If a monk takes a statue — if he takes one with relics, it incurs a transgression; if he takes one without relics, it incurs a misdeed. If one takes it while holding the perception that it is the Teacher, there is no transgression. Likewise, for one who is a novice, or who is mad, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by painful sensations — there is no transgression.

The monks, having become uncertain, requested the Blessed One, the Buddha, to resolve all their doubts: "Venerable One, what could the mother of Mṛgāra's lord have done such that, through the ripening of that karma, one would never lack for wealth?" The Blessed One declared: "O monks, it is because the mother of Mṛgāra's lord herself performed and accumulated actions that bring results, that transform conditions completely, that abide like a flame, and that are certain to mature — that those actions performed and accumulated by the mother of Mṛgāra's lord herself will be experienced individually by whoever the person may be. O monks, actions that are performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and non-virtuous actions that are performed and accumulated ripen in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases that have been appropriated. And:

Even over a hundred eons, actions do not perish —
When the assembly and the time have come together,

They will ripen as fruits for those who bear a body.

O monks, in this very same great and good eon, at a time long past when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher, a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One by the name of Kāśyapa. When the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa had performed all the deeds of a buddha and had passed beyond sorrow into the expanse of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates, at that time there was a king named Kṛkī whose kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and at peace, blessed with good harvests, filled with many common folk and people, in which battles, strife, quarrels, and domestic unrest had been thoroughly stilled, and which was free of thieves, famine, and disease, abounding in rice paddies, rows of sugarcane, and herds of cattle and buffalo. He was a righteous king who governed a righteous kingdom. By his authority, a stūpa was built with four kinds of precious substances, one league in breadth and half a league in height, in honor of the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa. At that place there was a single elderly woman who had taken refuge and accepted the precepts, and she dwelt there paying homage and making offerings at the stūpa of the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa.

Then one spring day, when the trees were blossoming and bearing abundant fruit, and groves resounded with the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, cuckoos, wagtails, and birds of paradise, King Kṛkī came to the pleasure garden accompanied by his retinue of queens. The king then quickly and swiftly entered Vārāṇasī. The queen's retinue had begun their bathing, hanging garlands of pearls on the branches of the mango trees, when they heard that the king had quickly and swiftly entered Vārāṇasī. In a rush, they forgot the garlands of pearls and left them behind, and entered Vārāṇasī. The elderly woman noticed those garlands of pearls and hung them on a bamboo pole, keeping them there. Since women by nature are fond of adornments, the next day she remembered the jewelry and reported it to the king. The king sent his men of the yogurt-provision to that place, and they saw the garlands of pearls hung on the bamboo pole. They questioned the elderly woman: "Who hung these garlands of pearls on the pole and left them here?" The old woman said, "I did." They presented the garlands of pearls to the king. The king said to his men of the yogurt-provision, "Where did you find these?" They said, "We found them where an elderly woman had hung them on a bamboo pole." The king said, "Call that elderly woman." They called her and said, "Your Majesty, this is that elderly woman." The king said, "Is it true that you hung these garlands of pearls on the bamboo pole and left them there?" The old woman said, "Your Majesty, it is not so." The king said, "Did you not feel any desire for them?" The old woman said, "Your Majesty, since I have taken refuge before the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, and have accepted the precepts, how could I give rise to a mind of desire for another's belongings?" The king was delighted, and he gave her those very garlands of pearls as a gift.

"Take them — they are yours." The old woman took those garlands of pearls, sold them, and with the proceeds made offerings and acts of veneration at the stūpa of the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa. She prostrated, touching her head to his two feet, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue, may I never suffer the destruction of wealth." 

Monks, the elderly woman of that time and occasion was none other than this very Sāgā, the mother of Mṛgadhārin. Because she made that aspiration at that time, through the karmic maturation of that action, she came never to suffer the destruction of wealth.

Monks, it is thus: the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright; and the karmic maturation of mixed actions is itself mixed. Monks, therefore, abandon actions that are wholly dark and mixed, and seek out actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train accordingly.

Here ends the fifty-ninth transgression-producing rule belonging to the category of forfeiture.

The Vinayavibhaṅga (the Exposition of Monastic Discipline), sixtieth fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the Kalandakas. In Rājagṛha there were three hot springs. At the first, the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra (the Handsome King of Sound Craft), bathed. At the second, the royal consorts and their retinue bathed. At the third, the townspeople and country folk bathed.

The king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra, thought to himself: "I have served the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of hearers, in many ways and with all kinds of requisites — yet I have not served them with a bath. Let me invite the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of hearers, to bathe." Having formed this intention, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed with his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra, addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Venerable sir, here in Rājagṛha there are three hot springs. At the first, I myself bathe. At the second, my consorts and their retinue bathe. At the third, the townspeople and country folk bathe. Venerable sir, wherever I myself bathe, may the noble ones also bathe; and when the noble ones are bathing, may I remain to one side, and when I am bathing, may the noble ones be pleased to use me as an attendant. And wherever my consorts and their retinue bathe, may the noble women also bathe; and when the noble women are bathing, may my consorts and their retinue remain to one side, and when my consorts and their retinue bathe, may the noble women be pleased to accept their attendance."

The Blessed One granted this by remaining silent and saying nothing to the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra. Then, knowing that the Blessed One had granted the request by his silence, the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra, bowed with his head to the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The group of six monks had the idea: "Nandā and Upanandā — since the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra, is a man of faith, let us go see what his faith is like by going to bathe." So they went there to bathe, and they said: "Nandā and Upanandā, if we all bathe at once we will finish quickly. Let two bathe while four assist, then let the next two bathe while four assist."

Then the next two were to bathe while four assisted. "Very well," they agreed, and so two of them began to bathe while the four sat assisting them.

Now at that time the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra, whose name was Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra, had also come to that place to bathe. He spoke to one of his attendants from among his private guard: "Go inside — go now and see who is bathing." The man replied, "As my lord commands," and obeying the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra, he went there and looked. He saw that the group of six monks were bathing, then returned to the king's presence and said: "Sire, the noble group of six monks are bathing." The king said: "Set up a chair and let us wait." A chair was set up and the king sat down.

After a long time had passed, the king again spoke to one of his private guard: "Go inside — go now and see who is bathing." The man replied, "As my lord commands," and obeying the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra, he went there and looked. He saw again that the group of six monks were still bathing, then returned to the king's presence and said: "Sire, those same noble members of the group of six are still bathing." The king again remained seated in the very same chair.

After yet another long time had passed, the king once more spoke to one of his private guard: "Go inside — go now and see who is bathing." The man replied, "As my lord commands," and obeying the king of Māgadha, Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra, he went there and looked. He saw that even now the group of six monks were still bathing, then returned to the king's presence and said: "Sire, even now those same noble members of the group of six are still bathing." The king said: "Wise ones — they have kept me waiting here a very long time indeed. Bring water, then, and let me bathe with the royal consecration bathing." They brought water, and the king bathed right there with the royal consecration bathing. Then he proceeded to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed with his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence without hearing any Dharma teaching at all.

Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why did King Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra leave without hearing any Dharma?" "Venerable One, King Bimbisāra of Rūpasāra was kept waiting by the group of six monks." "Why? Let that occasion be explained in full."

Then the Blessed One reflected thus: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about from monks bathing. Therefore monks should not bathe." Having so reflected, he declared: "Therefore monks shall not bathe."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks were not to bathe, the monks no longer bathed, and their bodies became smeared with the filth of dirt and began to smell foul. When brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, who are these foul-smelling ones?" the monks replied: "We are." "Noble ones, why do you not bathe?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." "Do you think you will become pure by carrying around your filth?" At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing once a fortnight."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks might bathe once a fortnight, the hot season arrived, and the monks, overcome with heat, became pale and wan, emaciated,

without gaining comfort for their bodies. Faithful brahmins and householders said to them: "Noble ones, why have you become so pale and haggard, emaciated, feeble, and thin, without gaining comfort for your bodies?" The monks replied: "We are overcome with heat." "Why do you not bathe?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during the hot season."

Some monks then fell ill and went to a physician to ask him: "Good sir, we are sick. Please prescribe medicine for us." He said: "Noble ones, bathe every day and you will recover." "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted it." "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate; making this very circumstance the occasion, he will surely grant permission. Such a situation will come to pass." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of illness."

After the monks had done work for the Saṅgha and for the stūpas, they were standing about covered in mud and filth when faithful brahmins and householders arrived and asked them: "Noble ones, why are you standing about covered in mud and filth? What harm is there in bathing?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of work."

When monks had been out travelling and returned from their journey, they were prostrated with exhaustion from the heat and lay down to rest, and faithful brahmins and householders arrived and asked them: "Noble ones, if you are devoted to the Teaching above all else, why are you lying down prostrated and not exerting yourselves in virtue?" The monks replied: "We have been travelling, and being overcome with heat we have lain down prostrated and are unable to exert ourselves in virtue. What harm is there in bathing?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of travel."

Wind arose and the monks became covered in dust, and as they were standing there just as they were, faithful brahmins and householders arrived, saw them, and asked: "Noble ones, why are you standing about covered in dust? What harm is there in bathing?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of wind."

Rain fell and the monks became thoroughly drenched and were standing there just as they were when faithful brahmins and householders came to the temple hall and asked them: "Noble ones, why are you standing about soaked through by the rain? What harm is there in bathing?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of rain."

A muddy rain fell and the monks' bodies became blotched and streaked, and as they were standing there just as they were, faithful brahmins and householders came to the temple hall and asked: "Noble ones, why are you standing about with your bodies blotched and streaked? What harm is there in bathing?"

"The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit bathing, except during times of muddy rain."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who revere training, and who are furnished with the requisites for training, and having addressed the monks with words in accord with this, rich in this meaning, and with teachings befitting it, he declared to the monks: "Monks, what was stated before is a rule, and what follows is a permission. My hearers should uphold this as a training basis in the Vinaya in the following manner: if one bathes more frequently than once a fortnight as taught by the Blessed One — except at permitted times — it is a downfall. The permitted times are these: the last two half-months of the hot season; the first half-month of the rains seasons; these three half-months constitute the hot season. The remaining times are: the time of illness; the time of work; the time of travel; the time of wind; the time of rain; and the time of muddy rain. These are the permitted times."

As for the phrase "as declared by the Blessed One" — it is by the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha.

As for "once a fortnight as declared for bathing" — it refers to each half of the lunar month.

As for "if one bathes more frequently than that" — it means bathing more often than once per fortnight.

As for "except at permitted times" — the times are set out here.

As for "it is a downfall" — it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and into wrong downfalls. Furthermore, for as long as the downfall is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous phenomena. Therefore it is said to be a downfall.

As for "the permitted times are these: the last two half-months of the hot season; the first half-month of the rains seasons; these three half-months constitute the hot season" — the last two half-months of the hot season refers to those two half-months during which the rains retreat draws near: from the first day of the middle summer month up to the fifteenth of that same middle summer month, those two half-months. As for "the first of the rains seasons" — it refers to the first month of those who have undertaken the rains retreat: from the sixteenth day of the middle summer month up to the fifteenth of the last summer month, that one month.

As for "the time of illness" — it is as follows: when a monk is unable to sustain life without bathing.

As for "the time of work" — it is as follows: when a monk sweeps even a small section of the Saṅgha's or a stūpa's grounds, or plasters even a small circle of the mandala-floor.

As for "the time of travel" — it is as follows: when a monk has traveled one league or half a league and returned.

As for "the time of wind" — it is as follows: even when the wind has stirred the hem of one's robe.

As for "the time of rain" — it is as follows: even when two or three drops of rain have fallen on the body.

As for "the time of muddy rain" — it is as follows: even when a muddy rain has stirred the hem of one's robe and two or three drops of rain have fallen on the body.

As for "these are the permitted times" — in each case, that is the corresponding permitted condition.

Now, how does a transgression arise? If a monk bathes using a consecration bath in the form of an empowerment (abhiṣeka), he must at that time bless it accordingly.

If one bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk bathes using an immersion bath, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed using a consecration bath in the form of an empowerment, then bathes using an immersion bath, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed using an immersion bath, then bathes using a consecration bath in the form of an empowerment, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk bathes in cold water, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk bathes in warm water, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed in cold water, then bathes in warm water, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed in warm water, then bathes in cold water, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk bathes in a slow-flowing river, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk bathes in a swift-flowing river, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed in a slow-flowing river, then bathes in a swift-flowing river, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

If a monk, having bathed in a swift-flowing river, then bathes in a slow-flowing river, he must bless it as a permitted time. If he bathes without having blessed the permitted time, then for as long as the water has not reached the navel it is an offense of wrongdoing, and once the water reaches the navel it becomes a downfall.

Some monks, when crossing a river, felt regret afterward. The Blessed One declared: "There is no need for regret in such a case. If one wished to bathe, one should have blessed it as a permitted time and then bathed."

Some monks, thinking the ground was dry, entered the water, and having fallen in there, regret arose in them. The Blessed One then declared:

"There is no need for regret in such a case. If one wished to bathe, one should have blessed it as a permitted time and then bathed."

Likewise, when monks fell into water through inattentiveness while walking about, or when water was thrown onto someone who had fainted, regret arose in them. The Blessed One declared: "There is no need for regret in such a case. If one wished to bathe, one should have blessed it as a permitted time and then bathed. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by feeling, there is no downfall."

This completes the sixtieth offense pertaining to bathing.

Summary verse:

An animal, regret, a finger,
shooting alongside another, causing fright,
concealment, no support, no ground,
and traveling without a man — these are the cases.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Cāraka, in the early morning, having put on his lower robe and taken up his bowl and outer robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having made his alms round there, he saw an archery training ground and entered it. The archery master being absent, some boys were gathered there. He asked the boys: "Boys, what are you doing?" They replied: "Noble one, the archery master Cāraka told us: 'Boys, excellent! You have set your eyes on mastering the supreme craft. Shoot to the left, shoot to the right, and release five arrows.' " And they had begun to shoot to the left, to shoot to the right, and to release five arrows. He then twined his two hands together and contorted his face.

They asked: "Noble one, why do you twine your two hands together? Why do you contort your face?" Cāraka said: "Even your own master does not know this — could you come to know it by watching?" They replied: "Noble one, does he have some knowledge of this?" Cāraka said: "There is no craft and no field of work on earth that I do not know." They said: "Noble one, please be so kind as to demonstrate — shoot to the left, shoot to the right, and release five arrows." Cāraka said: "Bring a bow." They offered a bow. Cāraka said: "This bow is like a bow of wool-felt. Bring another bow." They offered a second and a third, and Cāraka said: "These too are like bows of wool-felt. Bring your master's bow." They offered the master's bow, and Cāraka said: "This one seems to have some measure of tension." He then bent the bow as if it were a bow of wool-felt, drew the string taut, and sent forth its resonant twang, whereupon a flock of crows began to fly about in the sky above. Cāraka said: "Which shall it be — shall I pierce this crow in the tail and bring it down by the mouth, or pierce it in the mouth and bring it down by the tail?" They replied: "Noble one, please pierce it in the tail and bring it down by the mouth." Cāraka shot one arrow into the sky to the east, then one arrow each into the sky to the south, the west, and the north, and the crow, turning its beak upward, began to fly. Cāraka then shot a single arrow after it, piercing it in the tail so that it came out through the mouth, and the crow fell to the ground. Those boys were struck with wonder and stood there, deeply impressed.

Cāraka said: "Boys, you must train in the craft in this manner, or else seek another master — what is the point of sitting about tossing up the husks of something fruitless?" Having said this, he departed.

Those boys stood there deeply impressed, and after some time their master arrived. He asked: "Boys, why do you stand there so deeply impressed? Shoot to the left —

to the right, shoot five arrows — those hands will spin and the face will turn." The master said: "Boys, when a transformation of this kind, unseen before, has occurred here, could it be that someone has come? Who was that noble Cāraka, and what did he do?" "He shot five arrows, pierced this crow in the tail, and brought the arrow out through its mouth." The master said: "Boys, wherever the bodhisattva has trained in the archer's stance, and in that very stance this one too has trained — if he does not go forth into the renunciant life, he will become the supreme master of archery throughout all of Jambudvīpa. Yet for now, learn from me what I know, and learn the rest from others."

He then thought: "Again and again this one will become my equal, and so I wish to be displeased with him." He therefore said to those boys: "Boys, do you wish the renowned and widespread sound and assemblage of Cāraka's fame to be celebrated in every direction and quarter?" They replied: "We do." He said: "When the noble Cāraka goes on his alms round, take the carcass of this crow, fix it on the tip of a long bamboo pole, follow directly behind the venerable Cāraka, and proclaim to all people: 'Look — the noble Cāraka shot five arrows thus, piercing this crow in the tail and bringing the arrow out through its mouth!' And even if you are told to turn back, do not turn back."

The next day, the venerable Cāraka rose in the morning, put on his lower garment, took up his bowl and his monastic robe, and went on his alms round in Śrāvastī. When those boys saw him, they fixed the carcass of the crow to the tip of a long bamboo pole, followed directly behind the venerable Cāraka, and proclaimed to all people: "Look — the noble Cāraka shot five arrows thus and pierced this crow in the tail, bringing the arrow out through its mouth!"

When Cāraka saw them he said: "Boys, why do you try to exalt me? Turn back!" But when they did not turn back, they kept up that proclamation, and the brahmins and householders, the learned ones, began to say: "These śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), sons of the Śākyans, are killers — they do not refrain from killing, have not abandoned it, have not individually abandoned it. O learned ones, look — these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyans, kill in just this way: even the hide of a sentient being is of no use to them, nor its flesh, nor its sinews, nor its bones, yet they kill like this. Who would think to give alms to these tonsured śramaṇas?" They reviled them, made a great outcry, and spoke ill of them. At that juncture the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, in connection with this event, this occasion, and this circumstance, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign not to know" — and so forth, as before.

The awakened Blessed One asked Cāraka: "Cāraka, is it true that you did this unseemly thing?" "Venerable one, it is so." The awakened Blessed One then formally rebuked him, declaring: "This is not the conduct of a śramaṇa, it is not fitting, it is not proper, it is not in accord with the training — this is not what one who has gone forth should do." Then, having rebuked him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing these ten benefits fully, I establish the rule of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk intentionally kills a living being belonging to the animal realm incurs a transgression."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to Cāraka or anyone else of that kind. "Intentionally" means after having deliberated. "A living being belonging to the animal realm" means a crow or any other creature of that kind. "Kills" means causes the cessation of its life. "Incurs a transgression" — this is said because it scorches, burns, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the wretched states of existence. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities of the Dharma — and therefore it is called a transgression.

As for how the transgression comes about, a summary verse:

Seized by oneself, or launched from without,
or involving both together —
these are the fully gathered categories.

How does "seized by oneself" apply? When a monk, with the intention to kill a living being belonging to the animal realm, thinking, "May this action that I am now undertaking bring about its death," presses it with one finger, and if through that very undertaking it does indeed die, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time but dies thereafter from that cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time and does not die thereafter from that cause either, then the monk commits an offense through that earlier act of effort itself.

In the same way as with one finger — pressing with the thought "May this action that I am now undertaking bring about its death" — so too with two fingers, or three, or four, or five, or with the fist, or the elbow, or the shoulder, or the head, or the hip, or the thigh, or the knee, or the shin, or the heel, or the sole of the foot, or even with the big toe — if through that very undertaking it dies, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time but dies thereafter from that cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time and does not die thereafter from that cause either, the monk commits an offense through that earlier act of effort itself. Such is the case of "seized by oneself."

How does "launched from without" apply? When a monk, with the intention to kill a living being belonging to the animal realm, thinking "May this action that I am now undertaking bring about its death," shoots it with an arrow, and if through that very undertaking it dies, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time but dies thereafter from that cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time and does not die thereafter from that cause either, the monk commits an offense through that earlier act of effort itself.

In the same way as with an arrow — with the thought "May this action that I am now undertaking bring about its death" — so too with an iron arrow, or a half-arrow tipped with iron, or a blunt-ended shaft, or a small blade with teeth like a saw, or a quadrangular blade, or a blade shaped like a karṇikāra leaf, or a blade shaped like a bird's heart, or a discus, or a single-pointed vajra, or a large arrow, or a single-pointed weapon, or even with the fruit of a cypress tree — if through that very undertaking it dies, the monk incurs a transgression.

If it does not die at that time but dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it neither dies at that time nor dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a wrongdoing through that very earlier act of undertaking. That is how it is with what is hurled outward.

As for how it applies when both factors are present: when a monk, with the intention to kill a living creature belonging to the animal realm, undertakes an action with the thought "May this undertaking that I now begin cause it to die at this time," and pierces it with a sword — and if through that very undertaking it does die at that time, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time but dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it neither dies at that time nor dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a wrongdoing through that very earlier act of undertaking.

Just as with a sword, so too — with the thought "May this undertaking that I now begin cause it to die at this time" — if one pierces it with a knife, or a single-edged blade, or a double-edged blade, or a lance, or a throwing spear, or a pointed digging tool, or a whip, or even with a grass arrow, and through that very undertaking it dies at that time, the monk incurs a transgression. If it does not die at that time but dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a transgression. If it neither dies at that time nor dies afterward from that same cause, the monk incurs a wrongdoing through that very earlier act of undertaking. That is how it applies when both factors are present.

There is no transgression for a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by intense feeling.

This concludes the sixty-first section on the transgressions of killing animals.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had completed the going forth and full ordination of the assembly of the seventeen groups — including Neighboring Monastery and so forth, and the novice Sāra — those groups began to associate with, draw close to, and pay homage to the Group of Six.

Thereupon the venerable Chāraka said to the seventeen groups: "All seventeen groups, come here. Do such-and-such." They replied: "Are you our preceptor? Are you our abbot? Why should we do anything for you?" Chāraka said: "Fools! Then what else would you do?" And grabbing them by their collars, he drove them out. They then said to some venerable monks: "Whatever reproach we have suffered at the hands of the Group of Six has come about entirely because we had little learning. We wish to take hold of more learning, and therefore henceforth we shall have no need whatsoever to inquire of the Group of Six." Saying this, they went to a certain monk and said: "Venerable one, please give us a reading." He told them that it would be beneficial for them, and they began to read in his presence.

A companion said: "Venerable Chāraka, the seventeen groups are no longer associating with us, drawing close to us, or paying homage to us." Chāraka said: "I drove them away, and now they have begun to take hold of learning. Venerable Chāraka, you have prodded a sleeping snake with a stick for us! As long as those fools have little learning, they will associate with us, draw close to us, and pay homage to us. But when they have gained much learning and become holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātr̥kā, and have become fierce and able to overpower others, then at that time they will set their minds on harming us." Chāraka said: "I will make sure that they do not manage to take hold of learning at all, and —"

"— and even cause them to fall away from the learning they have already taken hold of. Go in that way." So Chāraka went to their dwelling and spoke thus: "Ho there, you seventeen groups! Have you been applying yourselves with great diligence?" They replied: "We have." "And what does diligence accomplish?" "It accomplishes the taking hold of learning." "And what does taking hold of learning accomplish?" "It accomplishes great learning." "And what does great learning accomplish?" "It accomplishes the full ripening of the faculties." "And what does the full ripening of the faculties accomplish?" "It accomplishes entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements." "So you expect to attain entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements, do you? Venerable Chāraka — have we perhaps committed actions of immediate retribution, or severed the roots of virtue?" "You have neither committed actions of immediate retribution nor severed the roots of virtue. And yet, have you not heard what the Blessed One declared: that any monk who confers full ordination upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty — that person will not have attained valid full ordination, and those monks will be subject to censure? Since you received full ordination without having reached the age of twenty, how do you expect to attain entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements?"

When they heard this they became troubled and fell into despondency. Then their preceptor arrived, and he said: "Young ones, why have you become troubled and despondent? Come here and take hold of learning!" They replied: "Preceptor, what does taking hold of learning accomplish?" "It accomplishes great learning." "And what does great learning accomplish?" "It accomplishes the full ripening of the faculties." "And what does the full ripening of the faculties accomplish?" "It accomplishes entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements." They said: "Preceptor, we expect to attain entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements — but have we committed actions of immediate retribution, or severed the roots of virtue?" He replied: "You have neither committed actions of immediate retribution nor severed the roots of virtue. However, since the Blessed One has declared that any monk who confers full ordination upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty — that person will not have attained valid full ordination, and those monks will be subject to censure — since you received full ordination without having reached the age of twenty, you will attain entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements?" They said: "Preceptor, we expect to attain entry into certainty and the exhaustion of the defilements, but since we received full ordination without having reached the age of twenty we fear we cannot." He said: "Have you not also heard what the Blessed One declared: that for a first offender there is no transgression? Since you are first offenders, you have indeed received full ordination. Come then, and receive the scriptural transmission." Furthermore: "Who was it that aroused this remorse in you?" "It was Venerable Chāraka." The monks then censured him: "Why does a monk with so little purpose deliberately arouse remorse in monks?" — they reproached him, mocked him, and disparaged him. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and these circumstances, convened the assembly of monks — and all that follows is as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, ask" — and so forth, likewise as before. The Buddha, the Blessed One, then questioned the venerable Chāraka: "Chāraka, is it true that you deliberately aroused remorse in monks?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Buddha, the Blessed One, censured him, saying: "That which is contrary to the conduct of a contemplative, which is not in accord with what is proper, which is not fitting, which is not in conformity with the code — that is not something a person who has gone forth should do." Having thus censured him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing these ten benefits, a rule of training should be established for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, having deliberately formed the intention 'By whatever means, let this monk not experience even a moment of happiness,' and making that very thought the condition, arouses remorse in a monk — that is an offense.

Now, 'whatever monk' means Chāraka, or any other of the same kind.

'Deliberately' means having thought it through.

'By whatever means, let this monk not experience even a moment of happiness' means: 'Let him feel displeasure in mind, even for just a moment.'

'Making that very thought the condition' means: not for any other reason.

'In a monk' means: in one belonging to this Dharma.

'Arouses remorse' means: if he causes in the mind even a little remorse, or full remorse, or intense remorse.

'An offense' — this burns him, scorches him, and causes him to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the states of misery, and the lower destinies. Furthermore, for as long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas — therefore it is said to be an offense.

As to how this becomes an offense: a monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall such-and-such a king, or a wealthy man, or a great merchant, or a great caravan leader?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was in an earlier time, and you, venerable one, are a latecomer; since you did not receive full ordination properly, but received full ordination improperly, you must receive full ordination again.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall such-and-such a great lunar eclipse or solar eclipse?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was in an earlier time, and you, venerable one, are a latecomer; since you did not receive full ordination properly, but received full ordination improperly, you must receive full ordination again.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall such-and-such a good year or a bad year?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was in an earlier time, and you, venerable one, are a latecomer; since you did not receive full ordination properly, but received full ordination improperly, you must receive full ordination again.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, where did you receive full ordination?' When the other replies, 'In such-and-such a place,' the first monk says, 'That place had its boundary improperly demarcated and the central area was not properly determined; since you did not receive full ordination properly, but received full ordination improperly, you must receive full ordination again.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense."

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, who was your preceptor? Who was your instructor?' When the other replies, 'Such-and-such a person was my preceptor, and such-and-such a person was my instructor,' the first monk says, 'Both of them are of defective moral discipline; since you did not receive full ordination properly but received full ordination improperly, you must receive full ordination again.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, where are you going?' When the other replies, 'I am going there,' the first monk says, 'That place is a dangerous pass; a defeat-entailing transgression has arisen for you, Venerable one.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, did you take the robes of your instructor and your preceptor?' When the other replies, 'I did take them,' the first monk says, 'You, Venerable one, took them with the intention to steal; thus a defeat-entailing transgression has arisen for you.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

A monk goes somewhere with the intention of arousing remorse in another monk, and says, 'Venerable one, did you proclaim in the midst of the Saṅgha, "All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are without self; nirvāṇa is peace"?' When the other replies, 'I did say that,' the first monk says, 'You, Venerable one, proclaimed a superhuman quality of a human being; thus a defeat-entailing transgression has arisen for you.' Whether or not remorse arises in the monk, the one who spoke is guilty of an offense.

For another purpose, and when Vinaya implements are used, there is no offense. How is it for another purpose? It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall some great king, wealthy man, merchant, or caravan leader?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was long ago, and so the Venerable one does not recall it; the Venerable one received full ordination properly.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall some great lunar eclipse or solar eclipse?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was long ago, and so the Venerable one does not recall it; the Venerable one received full ordination properly.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, do you recall some great good year or bad year?' When the other replies, 'I do not recall,' the first monk says, 'That was long ago, and so the Venerable one does not recall it; the Venerable one received full ordination properly.' In that case there is no offense. That is how it is for another purpose.

How is it when Vinaya implements are used? It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, where did you receive full ordination?' When the other replies, 'In such-and-such a place,' the first monk says, 'That place had its boundary properly demarcated and the central area was properly determined; the Venerable one received full ordination properly.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, who was your preceptor and who was your instructor?' When the other replies,

'My preceptor is such-and-such a person, and my instructor is such-and-such a person,' the first monk says, 'Both of them are monks endowed with moral discipline, and if you pay them proper respect, great merit will arise for you, and you will have served the Venerable one in a way that brings full completion.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and says, 'Venerable one, did you take the Dharma robes of your preceptor and instructor?' When the other replies, 'I did take them,' the first monk says, 'Do not take them with a mind of theft. See to it that a transgression leading to defeat does not occur.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and asks, 'Venerable one, are you going to such-and-such a region?' When the other replies, 'I am going,' the first monk says, 'That region is dangerous territory — do not go there. You are a celibate practitioner of pure conduct; do not cause those who are wise to become suspicious of a place where there is no grounds for suspicion, and do not cause them to become doubtful about a matter that gives no cause for doubt.' In that case there is no offense.

It is as follows. A monk goes to another monk and asks, 'Venerable one, did you, in the midst of the Saṅgha, speak these words: "All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are without self; nirvāṇa is peace"?' When the other replies, 'I did speak them,' the first monk says, 'Do not speak of superhuman qualities. See to it that a transgression leading to defeat does not occur.' In that case there is no offense.

That is how it is when Vinaya implements are used.

For one who is at the beginning of their practice, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for one afflicted by painful sensations, there is no offense.

The sixty-second section, on transgressions that generate regret, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had caused the group of the Seventeen — including those born near him, the youths of the Sārpaka clan — to go forth and receive full ordination. Whenever any one of those Seventeen was assigned a monastic duty, they would all band together to do it. Once, late one night, a teaching arose in that very monastery, and they all gathered together and made noise. The next day, when a teaching arose at the Saṅgha's heating chamber, they all gathered there as well and made noise. The day after that, the duty of monastery overseer fell to one of the Seventeen, and on that day too they all decorated the monastery and took their seats. Then, when the overseer was about to make noise, one of the Seventeen thought, 'I shall sleep soundly. Why should sixteen men not be able to make the noise on their own?' And so, each one in turn had exactly that same thought, and all sixteen others went off separately to sleep. The overseer, left alone by himself, got up in the last part of the night, collected the lamp stands, opened the doors, swept and plastered the monastery, announced the time, arranged the seats, spread incense smoke around the precincts of the stūpa, and then stood atop the monastery and began to strike the gaṇḍī. The sixteen, awakened by the sound of the gaṇḍī, came out of their own quarters carrying their bowls, and they saw that one overseer running to and fro by himself. They said to one another, 'Venerable ones, this one is running to and fro all alone — did none of us come to his aid?' One of them said, 'The thought came to me —

'I was exhausted and slept — surely the sixteen of them could have managed without my help.' In the same way, another said the same, and yet another said the same, until all of them had said the same thing. Then the sixteen said to one another, 'Venerable ones, if it is our custom always to be the first to go to any immediate task, then our not having helped him was wrong on our part — he will reproach us for it. Let us ask his forgiveness as soon as we have finished eating.' And so, after eating, they began to ask his forgiveness. The younger ones touched their heads to his two feet, and the elders embraced him around the neck, saying, 'Venerable one, please forgive us.' But he sat there in complete silence. One who was a particularly close friend of his then tickled him, and he began to laugh, and said, 'I forgive you.' They thought, 'That is a good method,' and one after another the rest also tickled him, until finally, midway through all of them tickling him, the breath reversed upward and he died at that moment. They stood there in shock and began to grieve. The monks said to them, 'Hey, you group of seventeen — why are you standing there in shock and grief?' They replied, 'We were formerly a group of seventeen, but now we are a group of sixteen; a pleasant companion in the holy life has been lost, and a defeat transgression has occurred.' The monks said, 'That is wrong,' and departed. The sixteen also departed together, deeply troubled and sunk in remorse. Other monks saw them sitting there having sunk into themselves in silence, and those monks began to mock those monks, saying, 'These venerables of the group of seventeen blazed up like straw-fire — flaring up in an instant and dying out in an instant; for a little while they were boisterous, and now for a little while they sit sunk in silent remorse.' Though they were tormented inwardly by the fire of grief and fully mocked, they said nothing and sat silent, sunk in remorse. The overseer saw them sitting sunk in remorse and said, 'Group of seventeen, why are you sitting here sunk in remorse?' They replied, 'Do we still count as the group of seventeen? Why would we?' They then explained the incident in detail.

Now, as for why monks of little sense were reproaching monks by poking them with fingers, snapping at them, and talking back at them on that occasion, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and these circumstances, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth as before. The awakened, Blessed Buddhas, though fully knowing, feign not to know — and so forth as before. The awakened Blessed One then questioned the group of seventeen: 'Monks, is it true that you were poking with fingers?' 'Venerable one, it is so.' The awakened Blessed One then formally rebuked them, declaring that this was conduct unbecoming a renunciant (pravrajyā), not in accordance with proper conduct, not allowable, not consistent with the rules. He then rebuked them in many ways, and having done so, he addressed the monks: 'Therefore, monks, having seen ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth as before.' My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

"Whoever tickles with fingers commits a transgression." As for the phrase "tickles with fingers," this refers to performing any bodily action, bodily conduct, or bodily movement with the intention of tickling with fingers. As for the phrase "commits a transgression," this means being burned, scorched, and cast down into the bad destinations and wrong rebirths — namely, hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts in the lower realms. Moreover, for as long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome phenomena. Therefore it is said to be a transgression.

As for how a transgression comes about in this matter: if a monk tickles another monk with one finger, a transgression is incurred. If he tickles with two, three, four, or five fingers, a transgression is likewise incurred. If he uses his fist, elbow, shoulder, head, chest, back, waist, thigh, forearm, or even the big toe of his foot to tickle, a transgression is likewise incurred. If one exposes a wound, a sore, a blister, a mole, or a hair follicle, there is no transgression. For one who is a novice, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by feelings, there is no transgression.

The sixty-third transgression rule, that of tickling, is complete.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Upananda, from among the group of seventeen, had directly realized arhatship by abandoning all afflictions, he thought to himself: "Do these companions of mine in the holy life (brahmacarya) have even a little wholesome root?" He saw that they did. "On whom does it depend?" He saw that it depended upon himself. And so, keeping in view the taming of those other sixteen, he went along following behind them one after another. They said to him: "Venerable ones, let us go to the bank of the river to fetch water, and let us bathe there." And so, taking water vessels and water pots, they went to the bank of the river. Then they said: "Venerable ones, shall we simply bathe, or shall we splash the water?" They said: "Let us splash the water, and then bathe afterward." So they splashed the water, and setting their robes aside in a single pile they began to bathe, entered the water, and proceeded to come up to the surface and then sink down below; to go from this bank to the far bank and return from the far bank to this bank; to go with the current and go against the current; to make sounds like great kettledrums upon the water and sounds like a one-sided clay drum; to scatter and hurl sprays of water; to make circles and vajra-like patterns in the water; to make whirlpools, eddies, and swirling currents in the water; and to make a commotion, splashing about, and twisting their bodies in the water.

Venerable Upananda, knowing full well, bathed, crossed the river, put on his robe, and sat apart. At that time, King Prasenajit (Skt. Prasenajit) of Kosala was seated at the upper floor of his palace with Queen Mālinī and happened to see the group of seventeen playing and frolicking in the water. Having seen this, he said to Queen Mālinī: "Mālinī, look, look at the beauty of the monks of good conduct!" Queen Mālinī replied: "Your Majesty, that is not so remarkable —

it is not so remarkable that they practice the holy life in the freshness of their youth. What is truly remarkable is that even though the god has reached the age of old age, he still has no such thoughts!"

The king, embarrassed, sat in silence.

Now, Venerable Upananda thought to himself: "I wonder whether some among the group of seventeen have become displeased." And looking over, he indeed saw that King Prasenajit of Kosala, seated at the upper floor of his palace, had become displeased. Seeing this, he said to the seventeen: "Venerable ones, King Prasenajit of Kosala has become displeased. Come out at once, and let him be pleased."

At that, they came out of the water. While they were putting on their robes, Venerable Upananda entered a meditative absorption (samādhi) born of loving devotion, and in that way all of them, along with their water-pots and water-vessels, rose up into the sky above, soaring like the king of swans with wings spread wide, and departed.

The shadow of them moving through the sky above fell upon the upper floor of King Prasenajit of Kosala's palace, and Queen Mālinī looked up and saw them soaring through the sky above like the king of swans with wings spread wide. She said to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Your Majesty, look, look at the beauty of these men of virtue!"

The king replied: "Mālinī, it cannot happen and it is not the occasion for arhats whose defilements are exhausted to play about in the water with frivolous splashing. That simply cannot be."

Queen Mālinī said: "Your Majesty, has he not heard the Blessed One say this: 'When I see a monk seated here, he may be with attachment, with aversion, and with delusion; yet that very same one, when he rises, I see to be free of attachment, free of aversion, and free of delusion'? Has he not heard the Blessed One declare: 'Monks, therefore, the mind is like lightning, and meditative absorption is like a vajra — by means of wisdom the afflictions are destroyed'? The king has heard too little of this." And so the king sat in silence.

Then Queen Mālinī also reflected: "It cannot happen and it is not the occasion for arhats whose defilements are exhausted to play about in the water with frivolous splashing. That simply cannot be."

Thereupon Queen Mālinī said to a certain man: "Good sir, come here. Go to where the Blessed One is, and when you have gone, bow your head at the feet of the Blessed One, and convey these words of mine: 'Venerable One, these noble ones have been playing about in the water with frivolous splashing, and the king has become displeased in his heart. It would be well, Blessed One, if you would be pleased to establish some rule by means of which the noble ones will not engage in such frivolous playing about in the water, so that they will remember to refrain.' Please present this petition."

The man replied: "As my lady commands," and, having listened to Queen Mālinī, he went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, he spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, Queen Mālinī bows her head at the feet of the Blessed One. May the Blessed One and Queen Mālinī be well. Venerable One, Queen Mālinī conveys this message: 'These noble ones have been playing about in the water with frivolous splashing, and the king has become displeased in his heart. It would be well, Blessed One, if you would be pleased to establish some rule by means of which the noble ones will not engage in such frivolous playing about in the water, so that they will remember to refrain.'"

The Blessed One gave his consent by remaining silent and saying nothing to the man.

Then that man, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this ground for legislation, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, make inquiry" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One questioned the seventeen groups of monks: "Monks, did you truly engage in frivolous splashing about in the water?" "Venerable One, it is true, we did." The Blessed One rebuked them, declaring that this was not in keeping with the conduct of a renunciant, not fitting, not proper, and not in conformity with the discipline; it was not something that one who has gone forth should do. Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, perceiving ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If one plays in the water, it is a downfall."

"Playing in the water" means: if, with the intention of playing in the water, one performs a bodily action, a bodily movement, or a physical gesture. "It is a downfall" means: it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the wretched states — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of ruin. Furthermore, as long as the downfall has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of virtuous qualities. Therefore it is called a downfall.

Now, how does one incur the downfall? It arises from nine bases — that is, from the intention that one ought to play, that one ought to get others to play, that one ought to frolic, that one ought to get others to frolic, that one ought to enjoy oneself, that one ought to get others to enjoy themselves, that one ought to be boisterous, that one ought to splash about frivolously, or that one ought to move one's body about.

As for how the downfall arises from the intention that one ought to play: if a monk, with the intention of playing in the water, rises from his seat, puts on his lower robe, puts on his outer robe, sets out, then lays aside his outer robes, puts on a bathing cloth, enters the water, and goes down under — a downfall is incurred. If one comes up to the surface, a downfall is incurred. If one's intention is merely to cool oneself, there is no downfall. If one goes from the near bank to the far bank, a downfall is incurred. If one comes from the far bank to the near bank, a downfall is incurred. If one's intention is to cross over, there is no downfall. If one strokes along with the current, a downfall is incurred. If one strokes against the current, a downfall is incurred. If one's intention is to learn swimming, there is no downfall.

If one beats a large drum over the water, beats a one-headed clay drum over the water, performs a dance over the water, goes in circles over the water, performs the vajra posture over the water, or stirs up turbulence in the water, a downfall is incurred. Even striking the water with the palm of the hand is a misdeed.

If a monk beats a large drum over the water using a pot, a pitcher, a ball, or a bowl — or beats a one-headed clay drum — even striking the water with the palm of the hand constitutes a misdeed.

If a monk beats a large drum over the water with peas, sesame, or dry grass, or beats a one-headed clay drum — even striking the water with the palm of the hand constitutes a misdeed. If one's intention is merely to measure or count, there is no downfall.

Such, then, is the analysis of the intention that one ought to play.

The same applies to the remaining intentions, such as the intention to poke at something with a point. There is no downfall for one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by painful sensations. This completes the sixty-fourth rule on downfalls concerning playing in water.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the sixty-first fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At a certain time, the venerable Unobstructed, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship and was experiencing the bliss of liberation. In that moment, this thought arose in his mind: "The Blessed One has done what is beneficial for me. That Sugata (well-gone one) has done what is good for me — for the Blessed One has dispelled the many qualities of suffering in me; the Blessed One has established the many qualities of happiness in me; the Blessed One has dispelled the many evil and non-virtuous qualities in me; the Blessed One has established the many virtuous qualities in me. What then should I do so that I might truly repay the Blessed One, serve him, and honor him greatly?"

Then this thought arose in him again: "All the countless hardships that the blessed buddha-Blessed Ones underwent through three immeasurable eons to perfect the six perfections and thereby realize unsurpassed omniscience — all of this was for the sake of sentient beings. I too, therefore, should do something, however small, in the work of taming beings."

Then the venerable Unobstructed rose from his meditative settling, early in the morning while it was still dawn, took his robe and bowl, went to where the Blessed One was, and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, then sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Unobstructed addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable sir, I wish to go on a wandering tour of the regions."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the mind of the venerable Unobstructed with his own mind, spoke to the venerable Unobstructed in these words: "Unobstructed, go — and those sentient beings who have not crossed over, lead them across; those who have not been liberated, liberate them; those who have not breathed easy, bring them relief; those who have not passed beyond sorrow, cause them to pass beyond sorrow."

Then the venerable Unobstructed, rejoicing and delighting in the words spoken by the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That same evening passed, and when morning came, the venerable Unobstructed dressed himself, took up his bowl and his Dharma robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms, made his meal, and when he returned from the alms round for the meal, prepared his dwelling and provisions as befitted his needs, then took his bowl and Dharma robe and set out on his tour of the regions.

At a certain rocky cliff, there lived a householder who had taken a wife from an equal family and lived with her in play, in joy, and in delight. He had two sons and one daughter. He settled the two sons in their own households and gave the daughter in marriage. At a later time, that householder himself passed away, and the daughter's husband also died, so she began residing in the household of her two brothers, living in merriment together with other men.

Now at that rocky cliff, those two brothers of hers were well-known as men of prominence. Whenever the two of them quarreled with someone, the adversary in the quarrel would say, "You two may speak —

your sister carries on in merriment with other men." The two brothers went and said to their sister: "Sister, when we quarrel with people, they say, 'You two may speak — but your sister carries on in merriment with other men.'" The sister replied: "Both brothers, I am a person of moral discipline; it is false people who slander me."

At a later time, a being entered into her, and signs of a child dwelling in the womb appeared. The two brothers then said to her: "Sister, you yourself said, 'I am a person of moral discipline; it is false people who slander me' — so where did this come from?"
