The sister replied: "Both brothers, this is a being with a prominent forehead who has forcibly entered my womb."

At a later time she gave birth, and a boy was born. When her relatives gathered and assembled to give the boy a name, they thought: "Since before this boy was even born, the word 'prominent-forehead one' was repeatedly uttered on his account, let the boy's name be Prominent-Forehead." And so the boy's name was given as Prominent-Forehead. His mother too came to be known by the name "Mother of Prominent-Forehead," and the two brothers settled her in another place.

Now the venerable Anaghata was roaming and wandering through the countryside, and coming to that rocky cliff he sought lodging there. Some boys who were playing and gathered there said to him: "Noble one, go seek lodging from Mother of Prominent-Forehead — she will offer you lodging." It is the nature of arhats that knowledge and vision do not arise through deliberation, so he went there and sought lodging. She offered him lodging, spread a seat, and said: "Noble one, please sit here." He sat down there, and she brought water to wash his feet and came saying: "Noble one, allow me to wash your feet." The venerable Anaghata said: "I do not have my feet washed by a woman." She thought: "Those who have gone forth must have taken up a discipline of this kind," and she brought foot-anointing oil, came forward, and said: "Noble one, allow me to anoint your feet." The venerable Anaghata said: "I do not have my feet anointed by a woman." She thought: "Those who have gone forth must have taken up a discipline of this kind," and she brought food, came forward, and said: "Noble one, please take a meal." The venerable Anaghata said: "I do not eat at an improper time." She thought: "Those who have gone forth must have taken up a discipline of this kind," and she spread his bed. The venerable Anaghata sat cross-legged on that bed, held his body upright, and remained with mindfulness directed forward and present.

She came before him and began to display the wiles of a woman, the tricks of a woman, the coquetries of a woman, and all the artifices of a woman, whereupon the venerable Anaghata subdued his senses. She thought: "This tiresome creature — let him sleep for now, and at midnight I shall go." At midnight she went and again began to display the wiles of a woman, the tricks of a woman, the coquetries of a woman, and all the artifices of a woman, whereupon the venerable Anaghata subdued his senses. She thought:

"Even if I had to travel a very great distance to be with a man like this and enjoy his company, what means is there to bring him under my power?" She thought: "The touch of a woman's body is a poison — if I embrace him, he will come under my power." And so she began to embrace him, whereupon the venerable Anaghata, like a king of geese spreading his wings without obstruction, rose up into the sky above and began to perform miracles — blazing, shining, raining down water, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary people are quickly seized with wonder at miracles, and so the woman, like a tree cut at the root, fell prostrate at the feet of the venerable Anaghata and said: "Worthy one who dwells in merit, please come down. Please come down. Please draw me out from the very depths of this mire of affliction." Out of compassion for that woman, the venerable Anaghata descended from the sky above. The woman then bowed her head to the feet of the venerable Anaghata, took a very low seat, and sat before him to hear the Dharma. The venerable Anaghata, having understood her disposition, her latent tendencies, her temperament, and her character, taught her the Dharma in such a way that, remaining right there on that seat, she shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that had been built up since beginningless time, directly realized the fruit of stream-entry, and rightly distinguished the Four Noble Truths one by one.

Having seen the truths, she said: "Venerable Anaghata, what you have done for me is something that neither my father did for me, nor my mother, nor a king, nor the gods, nor my forebears of former times, nor śramaṇas and brahmins, nor friends, companions, and kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed me from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to higher states and to liberation; you have drawn my feet out of the hell realms, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you have placed me among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to its end. You have shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, and I have obtained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable Anaghata, I have entered the stream. Venerable Anaghata, I have entered the stream. Venerable Anaghata, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a laywoman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with all my heart."

"Venerable Anaghata, please grant permission to offer a midday meal here tomorrow. Sister, it shall be accepted on one condition: only if it is offered with the door properly closed." She said: "It shall be offered with the door bolted." That very night she made the food ready, and early the next morning she rose, arranged the seat, bolted the door, and at the midday hour, having understood that the venerable Anaghata was comfortably seated, she satisfied and strengthened him with her own hands, serving him with pure and well-prepared foods and drink. In many ways she served him with pure and well-prepared foods and drink, satisfied him with her own hands, and having satisfied him —

Having perceived that the venerable Anaghata had finished eating, washed his hands, and set down his bowl, she took a low seat and sat down before the venerable Anaghata to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, her two brothers got into a quarrel with a man. That man said: "Do you two have anything to say? Your sister, that woman of wondrous and diverse offerings, has not even let go of the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas — and now that the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has entered her mouth, she still cannot get enough of it." The two brothers thought: "Every bit of contempt we two have suffered from people is the doing of this one. We shall go and kill her." Drawing their swords from their scabbards, they ran off toward where she lived.

Many hundreds and thousands of living creatures, some drawn by curiosity, others spurred on by roots of virtue accumulated in former lives, followed along behind those two.

Then the venerable Anaghata said: "Sister, I am going out — bolt the door." He came out, and she bolted the door.

Then the venerable Anaghata rose up into the sky above like a king of geese spreading his wings, and began to perform miracles: blazing, shining, making rain fall, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary people are quickly captivated by miracles, and so those two fell at the feet of the venerable Anaghata like trees cut down at the root, and said: "O true and worthy recipient of offerings, please come down. Come down. Please, we pray you, draw us out by the collar from the swamp of affliction in which we are sunk." Out of compassion for those two, the venerable Anaghata descended from the sky above.

The two of them then paid homage at the feet of the venerable Anaghata and stood to one side. The venerable Anaghata, having penetrated the intention, the latent tendencies, the constitution, and the natural disposition of that entire assembly, taught the Dharma accordingly. For twenty thousand living beings, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and they directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Some directly realized the fruit of once-returning. Some directly realized the fruit of non-returning. Some, going forth and abandoning all afflictions, directly realized arhatship itself. Some generated the mind set upon the awakening of a hearer. Some generated the mind set upon solitary awakening. Some generated the mind set upon the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening of a buddha. Having thus taught the Dharma, the great majority of that assembly came to take refuge in the Buddha, to take refuge in the Dharma, and to take refuge in the Saṅgha.

Then the venerable Anaghata properly instructed that assembly with a discourse in accordance with the Dharma, properly established them in it, properly praised them, and having gladdened them thoroughly, he rose from his seat, departed, and went off to another rocky crag. Not far from that crag there was a pleasure grove, and he accepted it as his lodging for the night. He sat down there in cross-legged posture.

Now about five hundred bandits who wanted to plunder the rocky crag had also entered that pleasure grove. One of the bandits, thinking the venerable Anaghata was a tree stump, laid arrows upon him and began to pull them back. The venerable Anaghata said: "Friend, your ear-ornament is catching on your robe — take care and draw slowly, so your robe does not tear." The bandit said: "Who are you?" "A śramaṇa."

"Whose śramaṇas?" "The śramaṇas of the Śākya's sons." He said: "Friends, we see a bad omen in this — let us kill him." Now the military commander among them had previously been a servant in the household of the venerable Anaghata, and had trained in the very same sword-fighting ground where the venerable Anaghata had trained, and had become skilled at cutting with the sword. At the time when the venerable Anaghata had gone forth, this man too had joined the bandits and had risen to become the military commander of the five hundred bandits. Recognizing the venerable Anaghata by his voice, he said: "Is this not the noble Anaghata? Handsome man, people know him as such." He said: "Friends, do not kill this one. He is a renunciant of excellent fortune, and by the power of his name merchants have returned safely with great ships from the great ocean. How is this known? If we obtain nothing at all just now, we can kill him afterward, but if we do obtain something, let us not kill him — wait a while." So they posted four bandits as his guards, with the instruction "See that this one does not escape," and then entered the rocky crag with the intention of plundering it.

The venerable Anaghata said to those four guards: "Good people, stand down your weapons for a moment." They said: "You will flee." "If four of you are stationed here, how can I flee?" They stood down their weapons and took up their posts, and the venerable Anaghata, penetrating their minds, latent tendencies, constitutions, and characters, then and there, while they remained seated on that very spot, shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had been built up since beginningless time, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. In this way he taught them the Dharma.

Having seen the truth, they said: "Venerable one, relying upon you as a virtuous spiritual friend, what you have now done for us — this has been done for us by neither father nor mother, neither king nor gods, neither ancestors of old nor śramaṇas and brahmins, nor by the assembly of relatives, friends, and kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, freed us from the mountains of bones, shut the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, lifted our feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed us among gods and humans. You have brought our wandering in saṃsāra to an end. With the vajra of gnosis you have shattered the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, and we have obtained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, we have entered the stream. Venerable one, we have entered the stream. Venerable one, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. We beseech you to accept us as lay practitioners. From this day forward, for as long as we live, we go for refuge with wholehearted sincerity from the very core of our hearts." "Noble one, will our other companions also obtain Dharma such as this?" "All of you who have a basis for it will obtain far more than you."

The venerable Anaghata blessed things so that not even a single dog would be roused at that rocky crag, and the bandits completed their plunder and returned. They said to the four men: "Where is the renunciant? What is he doing?" "We have completed our work and returned, so let us pay him our respects." The venerable Anaghata said to them: "Good people, stand down your weapons and take your seats — I will teach you the Dharma."

"Noble one, will our captors not come?" "They will not come." They removed their armor and took their seats before the venerable Anaghata to hear the Dharma. The venerable Anaghata, having thoroughly understood their minds, their habitual tendencies, their temperaments, and their characters, taught the Dharma in such a way that, right there as they sat upon their very seats, he shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a self within the aggregates), which had been piled up from beginningless time — and thereby directly actualized for them the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, they said: "Venerable one, we have relied upon you as our spiritual friend, and what you have done for us is something our fathers never did for us, our mothers never did, kings never did, the gods never did, our ancestors of old never did, ascetics and brahmins never did, and neither did friends, companions, or the circle of our kindred. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears. You have delivered us from the mountains of bones. You have closed the gates of the lower destinies. You have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. You have drawn our feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and set us among gods and humans. You have brought cyclic existence to its end. From beginningless time the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection had been heaped up — you have shattered it with the vajra of wisdom, and we have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, we have entered the stream. Venerable one, we have entered the stream. Venerable one, we go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept us as lay practitioners. From this day forward, for as long as we have life, we go for refuge with heartfelt, wholehearted joy.

Noble one, we will no longer incur the fault of taking what is not given — not even so much as a sesame husk belonging to another. As for these goods, what use are they to us? Good sirs, leave them right there on the spot." "Noble one, will our captors not come? Did even a single dog awaken there?" "Leave them there on the spot." So they went and set all those goods back where they had been.

Then a deity who had faith in the venerable Anaghata spoke at that rocky crag: "Everything that has been left unharmed is through the power of the noble Anaghata. The noble Anaghata is dwelling in this garden — come hear the Dharma today." Thereupon many hundreds of living creatures — some drawn by curiosity, some stirred by the roots of virtue from former lives — came forth and went to where the noble Anaghata was. They bowed their heads to his two feet and took their places before the noble Anaghata to hear the Dharma.

The venerable Anaghata, having thoroughly understood the minds, habitual tendencies, temperaments, and characters of that assembly, taught the Dharma in such a way that twelve thousand living creatures, right there as they sat upon their very seats, shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection — and directly actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Some directly actualized the fruit of once-returning. Some directly actualized the fruit of non-returning. Some went forth into renunciation and, having abandoned all afflictions, directly actualized arhatship. Some aroused the mind of awakening oriented toward the awakening of a śrāvaka. Some aroused the mind of awakening oriented toward solitary buddhahood. Some aroused the mind of awakening oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete buddhahood. In this way the Dharma was taught, and the greater part of that assembly turned toward the Buddha, arrived at the Dharma, and came to rest in the Saṅgha.

Then those five hundred sons of good family said this to the venerable Aniruddha: "Venerable Aniruddha, if we could obtain the going forth into renunciation and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, attaining the status of monks, we would practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." "Good friends, come then! The Blessed One will perform your going forth and your full ordination, and you will attain the status of monks." Then the venerable Aniruddha led those five hundred sons of good family to where the Blessed One was. At that time the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw the venerable Aniruddha coming from a great distance. Having seen him, he said to the monks: "Monks, do you see the monk Aniruddha approaching from a great distance?" "Venerable One, we see him." "Monks, this Aniruddha comes to the Tathāgata carrying a gift, and there is no such gift for the Tathāgata other than one such as this, from those who are to be trained."

Then the venerable Aniruddha went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Aniruddha said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, these five hundred sons of good family wish to obtain the going forth into renunciation and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, attaining the status of monks. May the Blessed One, out of compassion, be pleased to give them the going forth, and be pleased to confer full ordination upon them." The Blessed One said to them: "Come, monks!" — granting them the going forth — "Come, monks! Practice the holy life." And at the very conclusion of the Blessed One's words, they found themselves with their heads shaved and wearing patched robes, their hair and beards grown as if for seven days, their hands occupied with begging bowl and water-pot, and they were just as a monk who has been fully ordained for a hundred years.

And it was also said:

When the Tathāgata spoke the word "Come,"
those bodied ones, wearing shaved heads and patched robes,
straightaway found their faculties perfectly stilled,
and by the Buddha's intention their bodily forms were clothed.

Then the Blessed One gave them this instruction: "Sons of good family, dwelling alone in solitude, with heedfulness, with ardor, with the self fully surrendered — you who have shaved your hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth from home into homelessness in genuine faith, in order to realize in this very life, through your own direct knowledge, the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life — should realize and accomplish it, knowing: 'My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What was to be done has been done. I know no other existence beyond this.'" And they became arhats (Skt. arhat), free from attachment, released from the three realms, their minds equal toward a clod of earth and gold, equal toward the sky and the palm of the hand, like sandalwood set aside, their faculties fully stilled. With the three knowledges (vidyā) they had split open the shell of the egg of ignorance, and they had attained the knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the analytical discriminations. They turned their backs on continued existence, on the gains of desire, and on honor. They became worthy of worship, of reverence, and of direct praise by the gods together with Indra and their retinues.

The monks asked the venerable Aniruddha: "Venerable Aniruddha, how did you fare comfortably along the way?" "Venerable ones, I fared somewhat comfortably and somewhat with difficulty." "How was it comfortable?"

"How was it difficult?" "The work of taming that was done — that was the comfortable part. The killing of the young deer at Hadapo — that was the difficult part." "Why?" Then he spoke of that at length.

The monks said: "Venerable Aniruddha, is it proper for you, who have not ceased, to lie in one dwelling together with a woman? Because it is not proper, a fault has arisen." The monks of little want asked: "Why do the monks reproach, rebuke, and criticize, saying that monks lie in one dwelling together with a woman?" Then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this instance, and on account of this occasion, assembled the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, act as though they do not know" also proceeds as before. The Blessed One then asked the venerable Aniruddha: "Aniruddha, is it true that you lay in one dwelling together with a woman?" "Blessed One, it is so." The Blessed One censured lack of effort, lack of application, and unconsidered conduct. Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of effort, application, and considered conduct, addressed the monks:

"Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits in full, a rule of training is to be laid down for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk lies in one dwelling together with a woman commits a transgression.

Now, 'whatever monk' means one who belongs to this Dharma. 'Together with a woman' means a woman or a young girl who is capable of engaging in or has engaged in unchaste conduct. 'Together' means with such a one. 'In one dwelling' means in all four types of enclosed and surrounded spaces: those that are fully enclosed and fully surrounded, those that are fully enclosed and mostly surrounded, those that are mostly enclosed and fully surrounded, and those that are mostly enclosed and mostly surrounded. 'Fully enclosed and fully surrounded' refers to a dwelling room, a surrounding corridor, and a multi-storied building. 'Fully enclosed and mostly surrounded' refers to structures with ten doors or twelve doors. 'Mostly enclosed and fully surrounded' refers to corridors with four sides. 'Mostly enclosed and mostly surrounded' refers to corridors with three sides and surrounding walkways. 'If he lies' means if he lies down after nightfall. 'Commits a transgression' means it burns, scorches, and causes falling into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, and into the miserable states of falling. Furthermore, so long as the transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome Dharmas — and therefore it is called a transgression."

Now, as to how a transgression comes about: if a monk lies in an upper room while a woman lies in the middle room below, that monk must draw up the ladder, or block the door with a firm lock, or station a monk as guard. If he does not draw up the ladder, or does not block the door with a firm lock, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the upper story while a woman lies in the middle story, that monk must draw up the ladder, or block the door with a firm lock, or station a monk as guard. If he does not draw up the ladder —

or does not block the door with a firm lock, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the middle room while a woman lies in the upper room above, that monk must draw up the ladder, or block the door with a firm lock, or station a monk as guard. If he does not draw up the ladder, or does not block the door with a firm lock, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the lower room while a woman lies in the middle room, that monk must draw up the ladder, or block the door with a firm lock, or station a monk as guard. If he does not draw up the ladder, or does not block the door with a firm lock, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the main dwelling while a woman lies in the corridor, that monk must block the door with a firm lock, or station a monk as guard. If he does not block the door with a firm lock, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the corridor while a woman lies in the main dwelling, that monk must block the door from the outside, or station a monk as guard. If he does not block the door from the outside, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies in the gatehouse while a woman lies on a staircase, that monk must block the door from the inside, or station a monk as guard. If he does not block the door from the inside, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a monk lies on a staircase while a woman lies in the gatehouse, that monk must block the door from the outside, or station a monk as guard. If he does not block the door from the outside, or does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it becomes a transgression.

If a householder keeps guard, there is no transgression.

If a monk lies in a cowshed or a livestock shelter, that monk must screen off that area with planks, or boards, or curtains, or station a monk as guard. If he does not screen off that area with planks, or boards, or curtains, and does not station a monk as guard, then from that time until dawn it constitutes a wrongdoing, and when dawn breaks it likewise constitutes a wrongdoing. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful feelings.

The monks became uncertain, and in order to resolve all their doubts they put a question to the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, what action did the long-lived Anāgata perform, such that through the ripening of that action he was born into a household of wealth, great riches, and abundant possessions, and then, having gone forth into the teaching of the Blessed One and abandoned all mental afflictions, he directly realized arhatship and performed such a vast work of taming beings?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was by the long-lived Anāgata himself that this accumulation of karma was obtained.

conditions fully transformed, abiding nearby like light, and arising without fail — these were performed and accumulated. Through the very unobstructedness of karma performed and accumulated, who else but oneself would experience it? Monks, karma performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even through a hundred aeons, karma does not perish.
When the conditions and the time have gathered,
it will bear fruit for embodied beings without fail.

Monks, in this very same great and excellent aeon, long ago, when the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher — the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One — Kāśyapa appeared in the world. At that time this one had gone forth in the teaching of that Blessed One and was serving as an abbot in a temple on a certain rocky cliff. Together with him there were five hundred co-residents and attendants. Nearly all the people living in that community on the rocky cliff had deep faith in him.

On another occasion, when some time had passed, his co-residents and attendants asked him: "Venerable Abbot, have you attained any accumulation of excellent qualities?"

He replied: "I have attained none at all."

They asked: "What aspiration, then, did the Abbot make?"

He said: "I made this aspiration: May I go forth in the canonical words of the Blessed One — the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One — who was prophecied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, to the brahmin youth his teacher, saying: 'O brahmin youth, in a future time, when the lifespan of human beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One, to be called Śākyamuni.' Having gone forth in the canonical words of that one who was thus prophesied as being certainly destined, and having abandoned all mental afflictions, may I directly realize arhatship."

His co-residents and attendants then said: "May we too, in reliance on the Abbot, go forth in the canonical words of that Blessed One and, having abandoned all mental afflictions, directly realize arhatship."

When the community of people living on that rocky cliff heard of this, in the manner of what a noble one had said, they went to him and asked: "Noble One, have you attained any accumulation of excellent qualities?"

"None at all," he replied.

They asked: "What aspiration, then, did the noble one make?"

He said: "I made this aspiration: the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, prophesied with certainty to the brahmin youth his teacher, saying: 'O brahmin youth, in a future time, when the lifespan of human beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One, to be called Śākyamuni.' Having gone forth in the canonical words of that one who was thus prophesied as certainly destined, and having abandoned all mental afflictions, may I directly realize arhatship."

They then said: "May we too, in reliance on the noble one, go forth in the canonical words of that Blessed One and come to see the truths directly."

"Monks, the monk who at that time was chanting the text — that is this one who has not yet passed away, Māgandha. Through the karmic maturation of the act of chanting that text with proper doctrinal understanding, he was born into a wealthy household of great possessions and abundant riches, and going forth in my teaching he abandoned all mental afflictions and directly realized arhatship. The five hundred companions and attendants who were with him at that time — those are these five hundred monks. Through the power of the aspiration they made on that occasion, relying on this one who has not yet passed away, they went forth in my teaching, abandoned all mental afflictions, and directly realized arhatship. The assembly of people who were dwelling on that cliff face at that time — those are the assembly of people now dwelling on this cliff face. Through the power of the aspiration they made on that occasion, relying on this one who has not yet passed away, they have come to see the truths in my scriptures.

"Venerable Māgandha, what act did he perform whose karmic maturation was the possession of the divine eye?"

"Monks, in this very excellent great aeon that has already come to pass, when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher — a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One buddha — named Saṃsāra-Destroyer. Having performed all the deeds of a buddha, he passed into the nirvāṇa realm of nirvāṇa without remainder through the exhaustion of the aggregates. Then King Mañjuśrī had a jeweled stūpa for him built from four kinds of precious materials, one league in breadth and half a league in height, and he also arranged a festival in his honor. When the time of the festival arrived, five hundred men wishing to defeat a band of robbers came there. There, at the frayed boot of the robber chieftain, not far away there was a bathhouse, in which a lamp was burning with a small, dim flame. The robber chieftain saw it, entered that bathhouse, and began to repair his boots. As he worked, the lamp was burning with a small, dim flame, and he trimmed the wick of the lamp, whereupon the lamp blazed with a very bright, clear light. As soon as he could see the image before him, he was filled with very great faith, made an offering with a coin, and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue of mine, may I come to possess the divine eye.'

"Monks, the robber chieftain of that time is this monk Māgandha. Through the karmic maturation of the act of trimming the wick and generating faith, he came to possess the divine eye."

"Venerable Māgandha, what act did he perform whose karmic maturation was the Blessed One proclaiming him foremost among those who possess the divine eye?"

"That too was through the power of aspiration. Where was that aspiration made? Monks, in this very excellent great aeon that has already come to pass, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher — a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One buddha — named Kāśyapa, and he dwelt in dependence near Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park of the Forest of Sages."

In that teaching, a certain monk who had gone forth and been ordained by him was pointed out by the Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, as supreme among those possessing the divine eye. Yet throughout that one's entire life he had practiced the holy life without attaining any accumulation of virtuous qualities whatsoever. Then, at the time of his death, he made this aspiration: "Throughout my entire life I practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, the unsurpassed field of offerings, Kāśyapa, yet I did not attain any accumulation of virtuous qualities. By this root of virtue — my practice of the holy life throughout my entire life — may the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, who pointed out the brahmin youth Lama as supreme, and who prophesied with certainty: 'Brahmin youth, in a future time, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who are to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Blessed One buddha, named Śākyamuni' — may I, just as this preceptor was pointed out by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa as supreme among those possessing the divine eye, likewise be pointed out as supreme among those possessing the divine eye by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the chief of the Śākya kings." Having set down that aspiration, through its power he has now been pointed out by the Tathāgata as supreme among those possessing the divine eye.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of actions that are purely dark is itself purely dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are purely bright is itself purely bright; and the karmic maturation of mixed actions is itself mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are purely dark and mixed, and strive for actions that are purely bright. Monks, this is how you should train.

Here ends the sixty-fifth rule concerning lying down together with a woman.

The Blessed One buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had fully ordained and administered full ordination to the group of seventeen — including Upananda and others, the young men born in Sara — those seventeen then attended, associated with, and paid homage to the group of six. Then Charka said to them: "You seventeen, come here and do this and that." They replied: "Are you our teacher or preceptor? We will not do it." Charka said: "You fools! Who else is there to do it?" And he seized them by the neck and drove them away. They then said: "Venerable ones, everything in which we were looked down upon by the group of six came about because of our scant learning. Let us go and acquire learning. From now on let us not ask the group of six anything at all." They went to a certain monk and said: "Venerable one, please grant us recitation." That monk said to them, "This is a means," and they began to receive recitation from him. Upananda said: "Venerable one, Charka — the seventeen — no longer attend us, no longer associate with us, no longer pay us homage." Charka said:

"I drove them away and they have now begun to acquire learning. Venerable Charka, you have beaten sleeping snakes with a stick! As long as these fools remain of scant learning, they will attend us, associate with us, and pay us homage. But once they become learned — once they master the sūtras, master the Vinaya, master the mātṛkā — they will become fierce and will overcome others, and then they will think to harm us." Charka said: "I shall arrange it so that they will not understand what they do not yet understand, and will lose even the understanding they already have."

The seventeen monks lit a lamp in the fire-room and began their recitation. Then the Venerable Charka wrapped himself in an animal skin with the fur turned outward, entered the fire-room, extinguished the lamp, and cried: "A spirit! A spirit!" At that, the seventeen were seized with terror and fled out of the fire-room, and they gathered in a corner.

Their teacher saw them and said: "Young men, why do you sit here in silence without doing your recitation?" They said: "Teacher, we were frightened by a non-human being." He thought: "The Jeta Grove is never empty, for five hundred yakṣas clad in blue robes dwell there always — and here there may well be a non-human being. Some rogue with a black begging bowl, a scoundrel who roams about everywhere, has terrified these lads." He said: "Young men, do you wish to catch that non-human being?" They said: "We do." He said: "Young men, place lamps at the four corners of the fire-room, and set a lamp in the middle on top of an earthenware pot, then recite. If it comes and extinguishes the lamp in the middle and cries 'A spirit! A spirit!', bar the door, uncover the lamps at the four corners of the fire-room, and seize it."

They did as instructed. Before long, the Venerable Charka wrapped himself in an animal skin with the fur turned outward, entered the fire-room, extinguished the lamp in the middle, and cried: "A spirit! A spirit!" They barred the door, uncovered the lamps at the four corners of the fire-room, seized him, and began to beat him. He cried: "Charka! Charka!" They said: "Did you think that by crying 'It is Charka — he is our friend' in your heart's distress we would release you? We will not release you until the warmth of death leaves your body." They said: "Venerable ones, even killing a very great non-human being brings only a heavy offence — so we confessed our transgression and then beat him thoroughly." They pummeled him soundly and let him go.

Charka crept away, dragging himself back to his own dwelling. The next day he lay on a couch while others rubbed and massaged his body with oil and ghee. The monks said to him: "Venerable Charka, what is wrong with you?" Charka said: "Venerable ones, for having done just a small wrongful thing, such a misfortune as this has befallen me." "What did you do?" He then recounted the whole matter in full. The monks said to him: "Is it fitting for you to frighten monks? Because it is not fitting, exactly this kind of misfortune has befallen you. Why do monks who care so little for the Dharma reproach, abuse, slander, and denounce other monks for frightening them?"

The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, in connection with this incident, this founding case, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the Saṅgha of monks — and so on as before.

The blessed buddhas, though knowing, act as if they do not know:

And so on as before, with the five-part formula. The Blessed One, the Buddha, then questioned the venerable Charka: "Charka, is it true that you frightened a monk?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One then censured him, saying that what is not the way of a contemplative, what is not fitting, what is not proper, what is not in accordance with the training — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth. After censuring him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits with full discernment, a rule of training for the hearers is to be established in the Vinaya," and so on as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk frightens a monk, or causes another to frighten a monk — even if it was only intended as a joke — commits a transgression.

As for the phrase 'whatever monk': this refers to Charka or anyone else of that kind. 'A monk' means one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Frightens' means does so himself. 'Causes another to frighten' means through someone else. 'Even if it was only intended as a joke' means even if it was only intended as a prank. 'Commits a transgression': this means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of ruin. Moreover, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome phenomena — and therefore it is said to 'commit a transgression.'

As for how a transgression arises in this context: when a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces appearances — such as a hungry ghost, a flesh-eater, a skeleton, or a rotting corpse with black crows, or like a burning post or charred timber — unpleasant forms of that kind, and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a transgression against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces sounds — such as a hungry ghost, a flesh-eater, a skeleton, or a rotting corpse making sounds like those of a lion, a tiger, a bear, an owl, a leopard, or a fox — unpleasant sounds of that kind, and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a transgression against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces smells — such as those of a hungry ghost, a flesh-eater, a skeleton, or a rotting corpse: the smell of excrement and urine, or a smell like that of a goat or goat's bile — unpleasant smells of that kind, and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a transgression against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces tactile sensations — such as those of a hungry ghost, a flesh-eater, a skeleton, or a rotting corpse: a burning touch, a stinging touch, a touch like being slapped — unpleasant tactile sensations of that kind, and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' —

then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a transgression against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces pleasant visual forms — such as those of gods, nāgas, gandharvas (dri za, scent-eaters), yakṣas, kinaras (mi 'am ci, half-human beings), or great serpents; or of kings, great ministers, brahmins, householders, the wealthy, merchants, or caravan leaders — and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a misdeed against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces pleasant sounds — such as those of gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinaras, or great serpents; sounds like those of the vīṇā, the flute, the paṇava drum, the mahāti, or the sughoṣaka — and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a misdeed against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces pleasant scents — such as those of gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinaras, or great serpents; scents like those of agaru, sandalwood, saffron, or the leaves of the tamāla tree — and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a misdeed against that monk.

When a monk, with the intention of frightening another monk, produces pleasant tactile sensations — such as those of gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinaras, or great serpents; sensations like the touch of silk, of fine cotton cloth, of fine linen, of taffeta, of dukūla fabric, or of kauṭamba cloth — and then asserts, 'These will carry you off; these will kill you; these will deprive you of your life' — then, whether fear arises in the other monk or not, he commits a misdeed against that monk.

However, when one speaks of the hells, of the animal realm, of hungry ghosts, of gods, or of humans for the purpose of generating weariness and disenchantment, there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression in the case of one who is a novice, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations.

The sixty-sixth section on transgressions involving frightening is complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the sixty-second bundle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had ordained and fully ordained seventeen groups of young men, beginning with those in his own inner circle, such as Saṃprasanna. At that point those seventeen groups began to associate with, befriend, and pay reverence to the group of six monks. A certain householder had invited the buddha and the Saṅgha of monks to his home for a midday meal, and the buddha together with the Saṅgha of monks set out. The group of six monks and the group of seventeen followed along behind.

Now, along the road there was a pond full of water. The group of six monks said to the group of seventeen: "O group of seventeen, if you and we are truly well matched, come, little ones — let us see who can sink and stay under the water the longest." The seventeen replied, "So be it," and all of them entered the water. Then one of their companions came up out of the water, hid the robes of the group of seventeen under a clump of earth, and left them there. The group of six monks quickly came up out of the pond, put on their robes, and left. When the group of seventeen surfaced, the group of six were nowhere to be seen. "It would not be right for them to have beaten us," the seventeen said, and they too ducked back under the water. They came up again and again and looked around, but still the group of six were nowhere in sight. Thinking, "They must still be beneath the water," the seventeen said to one another, "Venerable ones, the group of six have hidden our robes and gone off." Since not a single robe was to be found, they said, "Venerable ones, they have made fools of us." So they came up out of the pond and stood to one side.

The venerable Śāriputra and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a retinue of five hundred, were traveling through the Kosala regions on a teaching tour and had arrived at the Jeta Grove. Upon arriving, they found the Jeta Grove empty, and the two of them said to one another, "Where has the Saṅgha of monks gone, headed by the Buddha? A householder must have invited them." They said, "Let the two of us also go there and take our meal." So the two of them set off.

As they went, the venerable Śāriputra saw the group of seventeen playing by the bank of the pond. Seeing this, he said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Look at the state of your disciples." The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied, "Since they do not heed my words, what am I to do?" The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then said to the group of seventeen, "Young ones, it is not right that the hour is already past midday — cross the water and come along." They said, "Preceptor, the group of six monks have hidden our robes." The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana wondered, "Did they carry them off, or did they hide them here on the spot?" Perceiving that the robes had in fact been hidden right there, he retrieved them and gave them to the monks. The group of seventeen put on their robes and set off.

When the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived and began to settle the monks, the group of seventeen likewise stirred the monks into commotion. The monks said to them, "Venerable ones, the venerable Śāriputra and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana have come here having carried out their work of guiding beings; it is fitting that those two should settle the monks for a while. What have you done that you now come here and create a disturbance among the monks?" The seventeen replied, "Venerable ones, if our preceptor has failed to look after us, we shall be cut off from food." Whereupon they explained the matter in full.

The monks who had little desire then censured, reproached, and criticized them, saying: "Why do monks hide the robes of other monks?" This situation was then reported to the Blessed One by the monks. Thereupon the Blessed One convened the Saṅgha of monks in relation to this incident, this founding case, and this situation — and the rest proceeds as before.

"The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, though they know, act as though they do not know" — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One then questioned the group of six monks: "Is it true, monks, that you hid the robes of other monks?" "Venerable One, it is not true." The Blessed One censured them, saying: "This is not the conduct of a renunciant, it is not in accordance with what is fitting, it is not proper, it is not in keeping with the discipline — this is not something one who has gone forth should do." Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, having seen the ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "Let my hearers recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk whatsoever who hides, or has another hide, the alms bowl, robe, straining cloth, cup, belt, or any other requisite belonging to the livelihood of a renunciant belonging to a monk, a nun, a probationer, a novice monk, or a novice nun — he commits a transgression."

Thus did the Blessed One establish this training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Then it happened that one monk placed robes in the keeping of another monk's hands, and a frightening situation arose. That monk hid his own robes but did not hide the robes of the other monk, and those who take what is not given stole them, leaving that monk destitute. The monks then informed the Blessed One of this, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, with the exception of such a circumstance."

Thereupon the Blessed One, having praised those who desire the training, who are respectful toward the training, and who are well-disposed toward the training, addressed the monks with a discourse containing what is foremost in that spirit, in accord with it, and consonant with it. Then he addressed the monks: "Monks, whereas the former was prescribed, this is now permitted. Let my hearers recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk whatsoever who hides, or has another hide, the alms bowl, robe, straining cloth, cup, belt, or any other requisite belonging to the livelihood of a renunciant belonging to a monk, a nun, a probationer, a novice monk, or a novice nun — except in such a circumstance — commits a transgression."

Now in the phrase "any monk whatsoever," this means a son of the Śākyas, a friend of virtue, or anyone else of that kind. "A monk, a nun, a probationer, a novice monk, or a novice nun" means those who belong to this Dharma. "Alms bowl" means the alms bowl itself. "Robe" means any one of the seven kinds. "Straining cloth" means the vessel for the alms bowl. "Cup" means a water cup. "Belt" means a strap, a twisted cord, a broad band, or a small strap. "Any other requisite belonging to the livelihood of a renunciant" means anything else besides those enumerated. "Hides" means by oneself. "Has another hide" means through another. "Except in such a circumstance" means setting aside such a circumstance as that. "Commits a transgression" means: it causes one to burn, to be scorched, and to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of the hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, into the states of wrong downfall. Moreover, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and therefore it is said that one commits a transgression.

Now, how does a transgression come about? When a monk, even to the slightest degree, hides — or has another hide — the alms bowl, robe, straining cloth, cup,

a belt, or any requisite for the livelihood of a renunciant — hides it or causes another to hide it — in every case this constitutes a transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one who has a disturbed mind, or for one who is afflicted by feeling. This concludes the sixty-seventh transgression, that of concealment.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the venerable Charka had abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship, the venerable Undana departed for Kauśāmbī, and he went about very bent and stooped; both Nābhasa and the two others arrived at their time. Ānanda and Upananda were both present within the Saṅgha. At that time the venerable Upananda had grown old. He dwelt together with Ānanda, but since none of his attendants obeyed him and his robes had become soiled, and since he was unable to wash and reverse them himself, it occurred to him to devise a means. So he gave out those robes to those who dwelt with him and to his attendants: to some he gave an under-robe, to some an upper robe, to some a lower robe.

They said to him: "Preceptor, shall we wash these, turn them, and return them?" He replied: "Children, since I am old, these are now yours." And so, out of their own longing for them, they washed those robes well and turned them well.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'The Tathāgata is about to journey to the Kośala regions. Whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata to the Kośala regions — let him perform the robe transaction.'"

The venerable Ānanda, having listened to the Blessed One and replied "Reverend Sir, as you command," announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Tathāgata is about to journey to the Kośala regions. Whoever among you wishes to travel together with the Tathāgata to the Kośala regions — let him perform the robe transaction."

Upon hearing this announcement, the monks took up their robes and went to a certain monk and said: "Venerable one, we entrust these robes of ours to you for the time being. We are going on the road-tour together with the Blessed One." That monk asked: "Is your preceptor also going?" They said: "He is not going." He replied: "Then entrust them to him today himself. It is not right for me to cause a break within my own circle."

They then went to their preceptor and said: "Preceptor, we entrust these robes to you for the time being. We are going on the road-tour together with the Blessed One." The preceptor replied: "Venerable ones, even if I were a monk of good moral discipline bound with grass, I would still act according to the proper time — I have no wish to keep them. Entrust them to the hand of some other monk who is your friend."

They said: "Preceptor, who is a better friend to us than you? We place them in your very hands." The preceptor said: "In that case, take a good mark and set them down. When I return, each one of you can easily take your own." They set those robes there and went off on the road-tour together with the Blessed One.

The preceptor, opening one bundle, took out a patched under-robe, and wearing it exactly as soiled as it was, he wore and wore it, then put it back into that very bundle.

In the same way he took out an upper robe from a second bundle, wore it, and in this manner made use of all the robes, wearing each until it was thoroughly soiled, then folded them back exactly as they had been and set them down.

In due time the Blessed One completed his tour of the provinces and departed for Śrāvastī. A householder heard that the Blessed One had made a provincial tour together with the Saṅgha of monks and had come to Śrāvastī, and he invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks who had just arrived on short notice for a meal at midday. The monks thought: "We left our travel robes here. Let us wear our other robes and go." They went to where their friend was, pulled out the bundles of robes and looked at them — but the robes had become so soiled they could not recognize them. The monks said: "Preceptor, are these our robes?" The friend said: "Venerable ones, I did tell you: 'Even if I were bound with grass, I — a monk who keeps moral discipline — would keep my appointed duties. Take a good mark and set them down; when I return, each of you can easily take his own.' Did I not say that?" Just then one monk recognized his own robes by their distinctive marks and said: "Venerable ones, these robes are mine — and the preceptor has been using them." The friend said: "Poor fellows, do not be upset." They replied: "Venerable ones, our travel robes are far better than these — let us simply put on our travel robes and go." And so they put on their travel robes and came. When the other monks saw them, they said: "Venerable ones, you left your robes packed away — why have you come wearing your travel robes?" They replied: "We did leave them packed away." "Then why were you not wearing those?" They then recounted the whole matter in full, and some monks of few desires criticized, rebuked, and condemned: "Why does a monk give his robes to a fellow monk and then use them shamelessly in the meantime?"

Those monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and this founding case and these circumstances, convened the Saṅgha of monks — and so forth as before. The phrase "The blessed buddhas, though knowing, make enquiry" — and what follows — likewise proceeds as before. The blessed Buddha then questioned the son of the Śākyas, the friend: "Friend, is it true that you gave robes to a monk and then used them shamelessly in the meantime?" "It is true, Venerable One." The blessed Buddha rebuked him: "What an unworthy act, what is not in keeping, not proper, not consonant with the ascetic life — this is not something one who has gone forth should do." And he rebuked him in many categories.

He then addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a training rule is to be established for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk gives a robe to a fellow monk and then uses it shamelessly in the meantime commits an offense.

'Whatever monk' means a son of the Śākyas such as the friend, or anyone else of that kind. 'To a fellow monk' means to one who belongs to this Dharma community. 'Robe' means any one of the three: the patched under-robe, the upper robe, or the lower robe. 'Gives' means gives without retaining possession. 'In the meantime' means at some other time thereafter."

"Shamelessly" means without having received permission. "Uses" means wears it. "Commits an offense" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad rebirths of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong falling. Furthermore, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and that is why it is said to "commit an offense."

Now, one may ask: how exactly does the offense arise? If a monk gives so much as a small amount of robe to a fellow monk and then uses it afterwards without having received permission, in every such case an offense is committed. If, however, the giving was pleasurable, welcomed, and agreeable to the recipient, and upon hearing of it the recipient feels great delight, then no offense is incurred. No offense is incurred either for one who acts for the first time, for one who is mentally deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful sensations. The sixty-eighth training rule among those that cause downfall through the livelihood supported by giving is now complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. At that time the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. Not very far from there was a pond called the Stone-Walled Pond, and beside it the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo used to spend the daytime. During the time when, relying on the virtuous friend of the complexion of a blue lotus — the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana — he had gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya and had attained the victory of an arhat, he recognized this and, filled with faith, would go again and again to pay his respects to the Blessed One and to the elder monks and nuns of the Saṅgha. More particularly, seeing that the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo, although he had brought himself to meditate on the eight liberations of an arhat, had set aside the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, and entering into meditative absorption, and was instead striving diligently in the tasks of the Saṅgha's communal affairs — perceiving this as something difficult to do — he would go again and again to observe him.

Then on another occasion, after paying homage at the feet of the Blessed One and of the elder monks, he went to where the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo was, arrived there, and with his head bowed to the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo's two feet, sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.

At that time two monks — a friend and one born of the earth — found a rag used for sweeping. Both of them had been going after the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo life after life, and had constantly been striving to find fault with him. The friend said: "Born of earth, where should we launder this sweeping rag?" The one born of the earth replied: "The Stone-Walled Pond has little traffic and a clean surrounding, so let us go there." The two of them took the sweeping rag and went to the Stone-Walled Pond, washed it there, and laid it out in the sun to dry.

At that time a corner of the venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo's monastic robe was blown by the wind and touched the head of the nun of the complexion of a blue lotus. The friend saw this, and said: "Born of earth, a Saṅgha remainder has arisen here — Gyabu Norgyalpo has had physical contact with the body of the nun of the complexion of a blue lotus. Go and report this to the monks." The one born of the earth replied: "Venerable friend, at this moment, if we two first perform the act of suspension while remaining in the assembly — would you actually want to carry out the act of suspension while remaining in the assembly?" The friend said:

"Venerable one born of earth, at that time it was not in accordance with truth on your part, whereas on my part it is in accordance with truth. Did not the Blessed One say that the term 'lanu' refers to hair and garments connected with it? How could there be any falsehood here, venerable one? Come now — let us go and report this to the monks." The one born of earth, having been deceived by his friend and thus won over, the two of them went to the temple and spoke to the monks: "Venerable ones, we two have witnessed a Saṅgha remainder arising through physical contact between Venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo and the nun of the complexion of a blue lotus. In whose faith or trust should we two now place reliance?" The monks said: "Venerable ones, are you two bundling together gods and humans alike, and likewise abiding together among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals? Or are you two making a baseless accusation under a Saṅgha remainder charge against the monk who is an arhat, accomplished in the eight liberations, absorbed in meditation, displaying the miraculous powers supreme among human qualities?" The two replied: "Venerable ones, we two have not erred in this matter. Surely, what our own eyes have seen — should we gouge out those eyes? The Blessed One has commanded: examine carefully what you two saw, how you saw it, and where you saw it; on what basis did you two go there, and thereby see it — discuss this thoroughly and investigate it." The monks then questioned the two thoroughly: what did you see, how did you see it, and where did you see it, and why, having gone there, did you see it there — they discussed and investigated this thoroughly. When a great many monks had discussed and investigated it thoroughly, the two said: "Venerable ones, there was no Saṅgha remainder of physical contact between Venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo and the nun of the complexion of a blue lotus. Rather, we two spoke against Venerable Gyabu Norgyalpo out of desire, out of aversion, out of delusion, and out of fear." The monks of few wants thereupon criticized them, asking why monks would make a baseless Saṅgha remainder accusation against a monk who is pure and free from transgression. They rebuked them, cast them out, and spoke against them. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this origin of the rule, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and all the rest follows as before. "The blessed buddhas, though fully knowing, feign inquiry" — and so forth, as before. The blessed Buddha then addressed the friend and the one born of earth: "Monks, is it true that you two, aroused to anger and filled with aversion, made a baseless Saṅgha remainder accusation against a monk who is pure and free from transgression?" "Venerable sir, it is so." The blessed Buddha then censured them, saying that this is conduct unworthy of a renunciant, not in accord, not fitting — such behavior is not what one who has gone forth should do. He rebuked them accordingly.

Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall lay down a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and all the rest follows as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Should any monk, aroused to anger and filled with aversion, make a baseless accusation under a Saṅgha remainder charge against a monk who is pure and free from transgression, he commits a transgression."

Now, "any monk" means a friend, or one born of the soil, or anyone else of that kind.

"Aroused to anger" means being disturbed and agitated.

"Filled with aversion" means having become mentally displeased — that is, the disturbance has not yet become manifest.

"A monk who is pure" means the venerable Gyadbu Nor, or anyone else of that kind.

"Free from transgression" means free from transgression in respect of that particular basis.

"Baseless" means without any of the three bases — the basis of what was seen, the basis of what was heard, and the basis of what was suspected.

"Under a Saṅgha remainder charge" means under any one of the thirteen. This is something that is not Dharma, yet is spoken of by the name of Dharma.

"He makes an accusation" means he slanders another.

"He commits a transgression" — this means it burns him, it scorches him, it causes him to fall into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong descent. Moreover, for as long as that transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome dharmas. For this reason, it is called "a transgression."

Now, how does a transgression come about in this matter? When one makes a baseless accusation against a pure person, a transgression arises through ten bases, whereas through five bases no transgression arises.

How does a transgression arise through ten bases? When, with respect to what one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected, one shifts one's perception and alters one's acceptance, intention, understanding, thought, and view — and then declares, "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspect it" — every single utterance constitutes a transgression.

When one has heard something and remembers it, and when one suspects something and remembers it, yet one shifts one's perception and alters one's acceptance, intention, understanding, thought, and view — and then says, "I heard it and I have not forgotten it," "I suspect it and I have not forgotten it" — every single utterance constitutes a transgression.

When, trusting in what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; when, not trusting in what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; when, on the basis of what one has heard, one suspects it and then says "I saw it"; when, on the basis of what one has heard, one does not suspect it and then says "I saw it"; and when, on the basis of what one suspects, one suspects and then says "I saw it" — every single utterance constitutes a transgression. In this way, a transgression arises through ten bases.

How does no transgression arise through five bases? When, with respect to what one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected, one does not shift one's perception and does not alter one's acceptance, intention, understanding, thought, and view — and yet says, "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspect it" — no transgression arises.

When one has heard something and has forgotten it, and when one suspects something and has forgotten it, yet one does not shift one's perception and does not alter one's acceptance, intention, understanding, thought, and view — and then says, "I heard it and I have forgotten it," "I suspected it and I have forgotten it" — no transgression arises. In this way, no transgression arises through five bases.

Just as making a baseless accusation against a pure person results in a transgression through ten bases and no transgression through five bases, in the same way, making a baseless accusation against a pure person whom one has treated as impure likewise results in a transgression through ten bases and no transgression through five bases.

When one makes a baseless accusation against an impure person, however, a transgression arises through eleven bases, and no transgression arises through six bases. How does a transgression arise through eleven bases? When, with respect to what one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected, one shifts one's perception and alters one's acceptance, intention,

desire, understanding, thought, and view, and then says "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspected it," then everything one has said constitutes a transgression. If one saw it and then forgot it, heard it and then forgot it, or suspected it and then forgot it, and then, having shifted one's perception, acceptance, desire, understanding, thought, and view, says "I saw it and have not forgotten it," "I heard it and have not forgotten it," "I suspected it and have not forgotten it," then likewise everything one has said constitutes a transgression. If, believing what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; if, not believing what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; if, having doubts about what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; if, having no doubts about what one has heard, one says "I saw it"; or if, having suspected something, one says "I saw it" — all of these constitute transgressions. In this way a transgression arises through eleven bases.

How does no transgression arise through six bases? When, with respect to what one has not seen, not heard, and not suspected, one does not shift one's perception, acceptance, desire, understanding, thought, or view, and yet says "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suspected it," no transgression arises. If one saw it and then forgot it, heard it and then forgot it, or suspected it and then forgot it, and yet, without shifting one's perception, acceptance, desire, understanding, thought, or view, says "I saw it and have not forgotten it," "I heard it and have not forgotten it," "I suspected it and have not forgotten it," no transgression arises. In this way no transgression arises through six bases.

Just as a baseless accusation against an impure person results in a transgression through eleven bases and no transgression through six bases, so too a baseless accusation against an impure person whom one has treated as pure likewise results in a transgression through eleven bases and no transgression through six bases.

There is no transgression when an announcement has already been made publicly. There is likewise no transgression from the point at which it has been inscribed as a painted image on a wall, if one thinks: "Just as I know it, so too does the entire world." There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one who has a disturbed mind, or for one who is overwhelmed by painful feelings.

This completes the sixty-ninth transgression-producing offense, that of making a baseless accusation.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Rājagṛha there lived a weaver named Spyi-cer. He took as his wife the daughter of a weaver from Śrāvastī, and he repeatedly struck that young woman with his fists and the flat of his hand. A certain old woman lived in the neighboring dwelling, and the young woman went to the old woman and said: "Mother, this husband of mine repeatedly strikes me with his fists and the flat of his hand, and I am fleeing." The old woman replied: "Daughter, so long as you have not borne a son for him, he will strike you. But once you have borne him a son, he will come to love you. Do not flee; stay." And the old woman then said this to the weaver Spyi-cer:

"My son, if this young woman should flee because you repeatedly strike her with your fists and the flat of your hand, that would not be right. From now on, do not strike her." Yet the weaver Spyi-cer, though the old woman had spoken to turn him back in this way, could not be restrained, and thereafter he went on repeatedly striking that young woman with his fists and the flat of his hand.

Then on another occasion, that weaver drank liquor at a tavern, and in his intoxication he went home and beat that young woman severely. The young woman thought to herself: "Before I have borne him a son, if he kills me in the meantime, that would not be right. Even though I have no son, it is better for me to flee and go." And so, once she knew that the weaver had fallen asleep, she slipped out the very moment the front door was opened and fled.

Now a monk who had undertaken to spend the rains retreat in Rājagṛha was traveling up to Śrāvastī to pay his respects at the feet of the Blessed One — and he too had come out the moment the front door was opened and set off. The young woman saw this monk and asked him: "Noble one, where are you going?" The monk replied: "Sister, I am going to Śrāvastī." The young woman said: "I too am going to Śrāvastī. Let me travel together with the noble one." "Do so then." And the young woman set out, traveling along together with that monk.

Now when the weaver Spyi-cer had slept off his intoxication and woke up, he found the young woman nowhere to be seen, and he went to the old woman next door and asked: "Mother, the young woman is nowhere to be found." The old woman said: "My son, did I not say to you from the very beginning that you should not strike her, for if she were to flee it would not be right? She has apparently fled and gone. Ask the gatekeeper." The weaver went and asked the gatekeeper: "Hail, doorkeeper — did a young woman come out through this gate?" The gatekeeper replied: "She came out the very moment the front gate was opened and went." The weaver climbed up onto a rampart and looked out ahead, and when he saw that she had gone only a great distance away, he came down quickly and gave chase. He was gaining on them, but then he saw that she was traveling together with a monk, and he thought: "I am alone, and these two are two together. If I were to seize her, both of them together might turn on me and beat me — that kind of situation could arise. I will seize her when I find some companions." And so he followed along behind the two of them.

In time they came to a rocky cliff, and at that cliff some five hundred weavers were encamped. The weaver Spyi-cer went to them and said: "Good friends, if you are kinsmen of mine, then help me — a śramaṇa (Skt. śramaṇa), a son of the Śākyas, has taken away my wife." And he incited them to shoot arrows in that direction.
