The weavers, being entirely without discernment, grabbed up about five hundred shuttles from their looms, came out from the cliff, and beat the monk severely. They also broke his almsbowl, smashed his bowl and his ladle, tore his robes, and thinking him dead, they left him there.

The young woman said to the monk: "Noble one, have you not received from the king the privilege of being exempt from prosecution as a youth? Go to the king and speak. Ask that the hands and feet of these men be cut off." The men, frightened, began to beg the monk's forgiveness and said: "Noble one, please forgive us." The monk's heart was gentle as butter, and he said: "I forgive you." But the young woman said: "Even if the noble one forgives, I do not forgive." Then the men said to the young woman: "Sister, you are a kinswoman of ours — you too should forgive." The young woman replied: "I may forgive you, but I cannot forgive the weaver Spyi-cer here —

I will have his hands and feet cut off." The men said to the weaver: "Forgive him as well." The young woman replied: "I will forgive him on a pledge — if he promises never to beat me again, I will forgive him." The weaver said: "I will never beat you again." The young woman said: "If that is so, then I forgive you."

The monk then gradually made his way to Śrāvastī. When the other monks saw him, they said: "Welcome, venerable one, welcome! How was your journey? Venerable ones, how was your journey?" He replied: "Fellow monks, the weavers almost cost me my life and my companion along with it." When asked why, he recounted the whole episode in detail. The monks then said to him: "Is it fitting for a man without a male companion to travel on the road together with a woman? Precisely because it is not fitting, this kind of trouble arose." And the monks, because of the small number of things at stake, nevertheless reproached him, saying: "Why does a monk travel on the road together with a woman without a male companion?" They blamed him, threw it in his face, and spoke ill of him. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One — seeing that this incident had occurred, that this was the originating circumstance, and that this was the occasion — convened the assembly of monks, and so forth, just as before. The Blessed Buddhas, knowing yet feigning not to know, and so forth, likewise as before. The Blessed Buddha questioned that monk: "Monk, is it true that you traveled on the road together with a woman without a male companion?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed Buddha then reprimanded him, saying that such conduct was unworthy of a wandering ascetic, was not in keeping with the rule, was not proper, was not in conformity with the discipline, and that one who has gone forth should not act in this way. After rebuking him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya," and so forth, just as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk travels on the road together with a woman without a male companion — even if only as far as a village — commits an offense.

Now, 'whatever monk' refers to one of this kind or any other similar case. 'Without a male companion' refers to the specific situation. 'Together with a woman' refers to a woman or a young girl who is capable of engaging in unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse. 'Travels on the road' means traveling on a path through a wilderness. 'Even as far as a village' means even as far as the distance of one krośa. 'Commits an offense' means it causes one to burn, to be tormented, and to fall into a hell-being existence, into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts, into evil rebirths, and into downfall states. Furthermore, for as long as that offense is neither confessed nor individually confessed, it obstructs virtuous qualities — and therefore it is said to 'commit an offense.'

As to how the offense arises: however little distance a monk travels on the road together with a woman without a male companion, in all cases he commits an offense. If a village is separated from a wilderness by seven krośas, and a monk travels from the village into the wilderness, then for every half-krośa he incurs a wrongdoing, and for every full krośa he commits an offense. And if he travels from the wilderness to the village, likewise for every half-krośa he incurs a wrongdoing, and for every full krośa he commits an offense. However, when a monk goes ahead to show a woman the way, when a woman who has lost the path shows a monk the way,

when a monk who is unable to travel is led by a woman, there is no offense. There is no offense for one who is a beginner, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is threatened by feelings of pain.

This completes the seventieth rule entailing a wrongdoing, concerning traveling together with a woman.

A summary verse:

Theft, and those under twenty,
Digging, hospitality, training,
Fighting, not speaking, traveling,
Disrespect, drinking liquor at the wrong time.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk had accepted the rains retreat at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka. When the three months of the rains retreat had passed, that monk, having obtained his robe-cloth and received his robe, took up his alms bowl and robes and set out to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, seeking companions for the journey to Śrāvastī. He saw some merchants who were dice-players and said to them, "Wise ones, where are you going?" They replied, "Noble one, we are going to Śrāvastī." He said, "Wise ones, I too will go to Śrāvastī together with you." They replied, "Noble one, please do so." But then they thought it would be inconvenient, felt regret, and said to him, "Noble one, we are merchants who play dice: we travel at the right time and at the wrong time, we travel ahead and we travel out of the way, so it would not be fitting for you to travel together with us." He said, "Are you going empty-handed, or will you be carrying loads?" They replied, "We will be going with loads." He said, "Since you will be going with loads, why can I not go behind you, going empty-handed?" They replied, "If you will do so, then go ahead in this direction and wait for us there until we arrive." He went on ahead and waited there. In due course the dice-playing merchants arrived and set out together with him. After some time they reached a certain cliff, a haunt of dice-players, and the dice-playing merchants, fearing bandits who cut off travelers, began to make their way by a side road, while that monk went on ahead. As they were traveling by the side road, some dice-players spotted them and said, "Hey, you dice-playing merchants, where are you going?" Seeing the monk going ahead, the dice-players said, "Wise ones, do not harm these dice-playing merchants — but that Śākyan śramaṇa going ahead has wronged us, so let us kill him." They beat that monk severely, smashed his alms bowl, broke his wooden dish and his spoon, tore his robes, and threw him aside thinking he was dead. The dice-playing merchants then said to the monk, "Noble one, since you have obtained from the king the protection due to a young man of rank, go before the king and speak, and let him have the hands and feet of these dice-players cut off." The dice-players, terrified, began to beg forgiveness of the monk and said, "Noble one, we beg you to grant us your forgiveness." The mind of the monk was like butter, and he said, "I forgive you." The dice-playing merchants said, "Even if the noble one forgives them, we do not." The dice-players said, "You too should forgive." The dice-playing merchants replied, "We will forgive under this pledge: if you dice-players, however many you are, prevent us merchants, however many we are, from being robbed by dice-players, then we too will forgive." The dice-players granted this to the merchants. The monk eventually arrived at Śrāvastī, and the monks spoke to him saying:

"Welcome, venerable one, welcome! How was your journey? Was the journey comfortable for the venerable one?" He replied, "The dice-players struck and beat me terribly." He then recounted the whole episode in detail. The monks said to him, "Is it fitting for you to travel the road together with a like-minded thief? It is precisely because it is not fitting that such faults and harms as these have come about." Monks of few concerns — why do they censure, rebuke, and reproach monks, saying, "Why should monks travel the road together with a like-minded thief?" At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then convened the community of monks regarding this incident, this origin story, and this occasion — and the rest is as before. "The blessed buddhas, though fully knowing, act as if they do not know" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One then asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you traveled the road together with a like-minded thief?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked him, saying that this was not the conduct of an ascetic, was not in accord with the training, was not proper, was not in conformity with the rule, and was not what one who has gone forth should do. The Blessed One rebuked him again and again in many ways. He then declared to the monks, "Therefore, having seen the ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and the rest is as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule of the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk travels the road together with a like-minded thief — even as far as a single village — commits a transgression.

Now, in this rule, 'whatever monk' means one who is of this Dharma or of another community of the same kind. 'Together with a like-minded thief' — 'thief' refers to those bandits who raid and plunder villages, and merchants who cheat at dice. 'Travel the road' means to travel along a path leading through a wilderness. 'Even as far as a single village' means even as far as a single league. 'Commits a transgression' means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, into the lower realms and the states of wrong falling. Furthermore, so long as the transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome dharmas — therefore it is said to be a transgression.

As for how the transgression arises: however little a monk may travel the road together with a like-minded thief, he commits a transgression in every case. Among seven villages separated from one another by a league: if a monk travels from a village to a wilderness hermitage, at every half-league he incurs a fault, and at every full league he commits a transgression. Likewise, if he travels from a wilderness hermitage to a village, at every half-league he incurs a fault, and at every full league he commits a transgression. There is no transgression if one joins a thief in order to drive him away, if one is led onto the road by a thief when one has lost one's way, or if one is led away by a thief when one is unable to go on one's own. There is no transgression for one who is a novice, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful feelings.

The seventy-first transgression, that of traveling the road together with a thief, is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gave going forth and full ordination to the group beginning with Upāli and other young novices — seventeen groups in all. Then, at the hour of the predawn watches of the night, those newly ordained were overwhelmed by the distress of hunger and wept.

At the hour of the predawn watches of the night, the Blessed One heard the sound of a great many young children crying inside the grove. Having heard it, he addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, who are these many young children crying inside the grove at this hour of the predawn watches?"

"Venerable one, it is those whom the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gave going forth and full ordination — the group beginning with Upāli and the other young novices, seventeen groups in all. They are weeping, overwhelmed by the distress of hunger at this predawn hour."

"Ānanda, do monks give full ordination as monks to persons who have not yet reached the age of twenty?"

"Venerable one, they do."

"Ānanda, a person who has not reached the age of twenty is by nature unable to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, sun, horseflies, mosquitoes and biting insects, contact with venomous snakes, harsh words spoken by others, ill treatment that comes upon one, and all the bodily feelings of suffering that arise — unbearable, rough, hot, disagreeable, life-threatening — nor is such a person able to endure defilements or be willing to regard them with resolve, or to accept and bear them."

"A person who has reached the age of twenty is by nature able to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, sun, horseflies, mosquitoes and biting insects, contact with venomous snakes, harsh words spoken by others, ill treatment that comes upon one, and all the bodily feelings of suffering that arise — unbearable, rough, hot, disagreeable, life-threatening — and is able to endure defilements, to regard them with resolve, and to accept and bear them."

Thereupon the Blessed One convened an assembly of monks on account of this occurrence, this basis for the teaching, and this occasion — and so forth, as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, knowingly establish what has been observed — and so forth, as before.

The Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, is it true that you give full ordination as monks to persons who have not yet reached the age of twenty?"

"Venerable one, it is true."

The Blessed One then censured the lack of effort, the lack of care, and the conduct of acting without examination. He then praised effort, care, and conduct undertaken with examination, and addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth, as before. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk gives full ordination as a monk to a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty commits a transgression. That person does not thereby become fully ordained, and those monks are to be censured. This is the proper procedure in such a case.

As for the phrase 'whatever monk': this refers to one who belongs to this Dharma, or to anyone else who is similarly situated. As for 'person': this is whoever is to be made a monk.

As for the phrase "who has not yet reached the age of twenty": this means one who has not yet reached the full age of twenty.

As for the phrase "gives full ordination as a monk": this is done by means of the motion-and-three-proclamations procedure.

As for the phrase "commits a transgression": this causes one to be burned, scorched, and cast down into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower destinies, and into the downward falls. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous qualities of Dharma — and for that reason it is said that one commits a transgression.

As for the phrase "that person does not thereby become fully ordained": this refers to whichever person that may be.

As for the phrase "those monks are to be censured": this refers to whichever monks were present on that occasion.

As for the phrase "this is the proper procedure in such a case": this means that this is the Dharma in accordance with what is appropriate.

Now, how does the transgression arise? In the first case: the candidate has not reached the age of twenty, perceives himself as not having reached the age of twenty, and when the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" he answers, "I have not reached the age of twenty." If the monks then proceed to give that person full ordination as a monk, that person is not fully ordained from the very outset, and there is a transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company, and this also becomes a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the second case: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, perceives himself as not having reached it, and when the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" he answers, knowing and remembering without any doubt, "I have not reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, that person is not fully ordained from the very outset, and there is a transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company, and this also becomes a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the third case: the candidate has not reached the age of twenty, yet perceives himself as having reached it, and when the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" he answers, "I have reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, the going-forth and the full ordination arise for that person then and there, establishing him in the state of a monk; there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company, and it does not become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the fourth case: the candidate has not reached the age of twenty, yet perceives himself as having reached it, and when the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" he answers, knowing and remembering without any doubt, "I have reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, the going-forth and the full ordination arise for that person then and there, establishing him in the state of a monk; there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company, and it does not become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the fifth case: the candidate has not reached the age of twenty, and he does not know, does not remember, and has no doubt about it; and the monks either do not ask him or, having asked, he gives no answer. If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, the going-forth and the full ordination arise for that person then and there, establishing him in the state of a monk; there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company, but this does become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the sixth case: the candidate has reached the age of twenty but perceives himself as not having reached it; the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and he replies, "I have not reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company from the very beginning, establishing him in the state of a monk; but this does become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the seventh case: the candidate has reached the age of twenty but perceives himself as not having reached it; the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and he replies, "I know it, I remember it, I have no doubt about it — and I have not reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company from the very beginning; but this does become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the eighth case: the candidate has indeed reached the age of twenty and perceives himself as having reached it; the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and he replies, "I have reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company from the very beginning, and this does not become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the ninth case: the candidate has indeed reached the age of twenty and perceives himself as having reached it; the monks ask him, "Have you reached the age of twenty?" and he replies, "I know it, I remember it, I have no doubt about it — I have reached the age of twenty." If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company from the very beginning, and this does not become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

In the tenth case: the candidate has reached the age of twenty; he does not know, does not remember, and has no doubt about it; and the monks either do not ask him or, having asked, he gives no answer. If the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk, there is no transgression for accompanying him and making use of his company from the very beginning; but this does become a serious offense against the Saṅgha.

Now, the first and second persons among these are those who were confused from the outset and were therefore not properly fully ordained from the beginning. If they participate together with persons who are properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or if they take part in Saṅgha acts, they are dwelling by stealth and are persons fit to be expelled.

Concerning a person who was given full ordination while under twenty years of age yet perceived himself as having reached twenty: if his relatives come and approach and ask, "Has the one called so-and-so been fully ordained?" and he is said to be not yet twenty, then the months he spent in the womb and any intercalary months must also be counted. If when these are included the total is complete, then that is good. If it is still not complete, either the ordination boundary must be changed or the full ordination must be performed again. If neither the boundary is changed nor the full ordination is performed again, and he participates together with persons properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or takes part in Saṅgha acts, he is dwelling by stealth and is a person fit to be expelled.

Concerning a person who was fully ordained at the age of nineteen: if he later comes to recall that his years were not complete, he must count the months spent in the womb and any intercalary months as well.

If the years are complete, then all is well. If they are not complete, the ordination boundary must be changed or the full ordination must be performed again. If neither the boundary is changed nor the full ordination is performed again, and he participates together with persons properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or takes part in Saṅgha acts, he is dwelling by stealth and is a person fit to be expelled.

If he comes to recall a single year, then the full ordination performed in that manner is a proper full ordination, for it is rare that a person who has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya actually attains the status of a monk.

Concerning a person who was fully ordained at the age of eighteen: if he later comes to recall that his years were not complete, he must change the ordination boundary or be fully ordained again. If neither the boundary is changed nor the full ordination is performed again, and he participates together with persons properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or takes part in Saṅgha acts, he is dwelling by stealth and is a person fit to be expelled. If he comes to recall a single year, he must count the months spent in the womb and any intercalary months as well. If they are complete, then all is well. If they are not complete, the ordination boundary must be changed or the full ordination must be performed again. If neither the boundary is changed nor the full ordination is performed again, and he participates together with persons properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or takes part in Saṅgha acts, he is dwelling by stealth and is a person fit to be expelled. If he comes to recall two years, then the full ordination performed in that manner is a proper full ordination, for it is rare that a person who has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya actually attains the status of a monk.

Concerning a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, who does not know, does not recall, and is in doubt regarding the full ordination he received: he must come to know, come to recall, and dispel his doubt. When he has come to know, to recall, and has dispelled his doubt, he must count the months spent in the womb and any intercalary months as well. If they are complete, then all is well. If they are not complete, the ordination boundary must be changed or the full ordination must be performed again. If neither the boundary is changed nor the full ordination is performed again, and he participates together with persons properly established in their natural state in the restoration ceremony two or three times, or takes part in Saṅgha acts, he is dwelling by stealth and is a person fit to be expelled.

Concerning a person who has reached the age of twenty but who, perceiving himself as not yet having reached twenty, receives full ordination: that full ordination is a proper full ordination from the very beginning. Concerning a person who has reached the age of twenty and who, perceiving himself as having reached twenty, receives full ordination: that full ordination too is a proper full ordination from the very beginning. There is no transgression for a first offender, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by feeling.

The seventy-second offense — that of performing full ordination for one who has not yet reached the age of twenty — is complete.

Here begins the Vinaya, the fifteenth volume.

Here begins the Analysis of the Vinaya, the sixty-third fascicle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the group of six monks were digging the ground with their own hands, having others dig, turning over the soil, having others turn it over, and pulling up plants.

— having others drag it away. Then other non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who were knowledgeable said: "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyan, dig the ground with their own hands, have others dig, turn over clods of earth, have others turn them over, pull up plants, and have others drag them away. And yet brahmins and householders also dig the ground with their own hands, have others dig, turn over clods of earth, have others turn them over, pull up plants, and have others drag them away. If that is so, what difference is there, what distinction is there, what separateness is there between these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyan, and brahmins and householders? Who would think to give alms to these shaven-headed śramaṇas?" And so they reproached them, disparaged them, and spoke ill of them.

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this occasion, assembled the community of monks — and all the rest proceeds as before. "The blessed buddhas, though already knowing, feign not to know" — and so forth, also as before. Then the Blessed One rebuked the group of six, saying: "Monks, is it true that you dig the ground with your own hands, have others dig, turn over clods of earth, have others turn them over, pull up plants, and have others drag them away?" "Venerable One, it is true." The Blessed One rebuked them, saying that this is not proper conduct for a śramaṇa, not in accordance with what is fitting, not allowable, not in conformity with proper conduct, and that this is not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be established" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk digs the ground with his own hands or has it dug — this is an offense producing a downfall.

Now, 'whatever monk' refers to one of the group of six or anyone else of that kind. 'With his own hands' means hand to hand, by one's own hand. 'Ground' refers to two kinds of ground: ground with intrinsic nature and ground without intrinsic nature. 'Ground with intrinsic nature' means ground that has consolidated over three months with the falling of rain, or ground that has consolidated over six months without the falling of rain. 'Ground without intrinsic nature' is anything other than that.

'Digs' means doing so oneself. 'Has it dug' means having another do so.

'An offense producing a downfall' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, states of misfortune, and states of ruin. Furthermore, as long as the downfall has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the arising of virtuous qualities — and therefore it is called an offense producing a downfall.

Now, how does the downfall come about? If a monk digs ground that has intrinsic nature, it becomes an offense producing a downfall. If he digs ground without intrinsic nature, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk breaks apart compacted earth, breaking apart what is hard becomes an offense producing a downfall, while breaking apart what is loose becomes a wrong deed. If a monk drives a stake into the ground, it is an offense producing a downfall; if he extracts a stake from the ground, it is a wrong deed. If a monk draws a line in the ground, it is a wrong deed. If the intention is merely to demonstrate or show something, there is no downfall.

If a monk removes clay that is adhered to the ground, it becomes a wrong deed. If he removes clay alone, without it being adhered to the ground, there is no downfall. If a monk causes a bank to collapse, causing what is hard to collapse becomes an offense producing a downfall, while causing what is loose to collapse becomes a wrong deed. If a monk walks through mud, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk lifts a ladle, a pot, or a ball that is connected with mud, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk demolishes a wall, demolishing what is hard becomes an offense producing a downfall, while demolishing what is loose becomes a wrong deed. If a monk removes the mortar of a wall, removing what is hard becomes an offense producing a downfall, while removing what is loose becomes a wrong deed. If a monk drives a stake into a wall, it becomes an offense producing a downfall; if he extracts a stake from a wall, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk removes clay adhered to a wall, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk draws a line on a wall, it becomes a wrong deed. If the intention is merely to demonstrate or show something, there is no downfall. If a monk causes salt deposits to crumble from a wall, it becomes a wrong deed. If a monk digs stony ground, and there is considerably more earth than stones, it becomes an offense producing a downfall. If there are considerably more stones than earth, it becomes a wrong deed. If he merely moves stones alone, there is no downfall. If a monk digs sandy ground, and there is considerably more earth than sand, it becomes an offense producing a downfall. If there is considerably more sand than earth, it becomes a wrong deed. If he merely digs sand alone, there is no downfall. If a monk has no implement suitable for the workmanship of hand-crafts and the arrangement of stars, and he inserts his finger into the earth to a depth of about four finger-widths, there is no downfall. There is no downfall for one who is a novice at the act, for one who is mad, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is overcome by painful sensations. The seventy-third offense producing a downfall, that of digging the earth, is complete.

When the Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was wandering on tour among the Śākyas and came to the Śākya settlement, he stayed at the Nyagrodha Park in that Śākya settlement. The great Śākya noble Mahānāman heard that the Blessed One, the buddha, was wandering on tour among the Śākyas and had come to the Śākya settlement, staying at the Nyagrodha Park there. Upon hearing this, he thought to himself: "I have many times invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, to my house for a midday meal, providing complete requisites on some occasions but not on others. Now let me invite the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, for four months with all complete requisites."

Then Mahānāman the great Śākya went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly taught Mahānāman with Dharma-endowed speech, caused him to thoroughly grasp it, thoroughly praised him, and thoroughly delighted him. Having in many ways thoroughly taught, caused to grasp, thoroughly praised, and thoroughly delighted him with Dharma-endowed speech, he fell silent. Then Mahānāman the great Śākya rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in homage toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, consent to accept from me, for four months, robes, almsfood, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medical requisites." The Blessed One consented to Mahānāman the great Śākya by remaining silent. Then Mahānāman the great Śākya, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from the presence of the Blessed One, and had a suitable infirmary constructed, had medicines for the sick stored there, had restorative medicines stored that were appropriate for any time of day, appropriate for specific periods, for seven days, and for lifetime use, had root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, and fruit medicines stored, had both clarified and unclarified butter stored, had both clarified and unclarified grain oil stored, had cows, female buffaloes, and she-goats kept there, had all requisites stored, and had physicians and attendants for the sick stationed there. He also supplied the monks with all requisites.

Now the group of six spoke among themselves, saying, "Dear friend Upananda, let us find a way to obtain such fine lodgings and food as these," and they went and questioned the physician: "Good sir, look and see what illnesses we have." The physician thought to himself, "These are slovenly ascetics who are speaking agreeably with me because they want to eat," and so he said to them, "Noble ones, you are indeed exhausted from the road — please apply an oil massage, and after that take a steam bath." They said in reply, "Dear friend Upananda, this physician is a great physician skilled in illness, in the causes of illness, and in bodily constitution — the kind a king would need. If all of us were to begin doing as he says at the same time, we would be caught quickly. Let two of us first apply the oil massage while four attend to the sick. After that, let two more apply the oil massage while four attend to the sick. After that again, let two more apply the oil massage while four attend to the sick." Proceeding in this manner, while two were beginning to apply the oil massage and four were attending to the sick, a full month passed. Then, after the second pair began to apply the oil massage and four attended to the sick, the second month passed. Then again, after another pair began to apply the oil massage and four attended to the sick, the third month passed. In the fourth month all assembled and began eating, and when the four months had elapsed, Mahānāman the great Śākya invited the Blessed One to a concluding meal, and Upananda sent a message to the attendant in charge of utensils: "Good sir, prepare broth, soups, and meat dishes for me today." The attendant said, "Noble one, four months have passed and Mahānāman the great Śākya has invited the Blessed One to the concluding meal — has your business still not been finished?" Upananda replied, "The poor Mahānāman, with great generosity, has invited the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks with all requisites for four months. If an invitation of this kind is a proper way to invite the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, then Upananda too would be delighted to invite the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks for as long as life lasts." The attendant said, "Although you have eaten nothing but meat and flesh soups for four months, still you criticize others. Elder, elder — those who have not taken so much as a single piece of āmalaka fruit in four months, they are truly the ones who practice austerity."

On the occasion when monks with few wants criticize other monks, saying "Why do monks beg so excessively?" — reviling them, taunting them, and speaking ill of them — the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks must not beg excessively.

"Monks, once upon a time, long ago in a past age, there was a hermit (ṛṣi) dwelling in a forest hermitage far from any village. His hermitage was abundantly endowed with flowers, abundantly endowed with fruits, and abundantly endowed with hedges and enclosures. Not very far from that hermitage there was a great pond, and in that pond dwelt a young nāga. Whenever the hermit sat cross-legged in meditation, the young nāga would emerge from that great pond and coil his body seven times around the hermit's body, then rear up and spread a great hood above him, and remain there thus.

"Whenever the hermit rose, the young nāga would uncoil his body from the hermit's body, adorn himself with shoulder ornaments, earrings and ear-hoops, garlands and ornaments of various jewels, and ointments, and then sit before him with palms joined together and serve the hermit with every requisite. Yet from the touch of the nāga's body, the hermit had become pale and wan, emaciated, weak, thin, and had lost his bodily health.

"On another occasion, a different hermit who was wandering and travelling through that region came to the hermitage of that first hermit and said to him: 'O hermit, this hermitage of yours is abundantly endowed with flowers, abundantly endowed with fruits, and abundantly endowed with hedges and enclosures — so why have you become pale and wan, emaciated, weak, thin, and lost your bodily health?'

"The first hermit replied: 'That is so. Although this hermitage of mine is abundantly endowed with flowers, abundantly endowed with fruits, and abundantly endowed with hedges and enclosures, there is nonetheless a fault here.'

"The other asked: 'What fault is there here?'

"The first hermit said: 'In this great pond there dwells a young nāga. Whenever I sit cross-legged in meditation, the young nāga emerges from that great pond and coils his body seven times around my body and rears up with a great hood above me and remains there thus. Whenever I rise, he uncoils his body from my body, adorns himself with shoulder ornaments, earrings and ear-hoops, garlands and ornaments of various jewels, and ointments, and sits before me with palms joined together and serves me with every requisite. Yet from the touch of his body I have become pale and wan, emaciated, weak, thin, and have lost my bodily health.'

"The second hermit said: 'Would you wish that the young nāga not come to you again from now on?'

"The first hermit said: 'I would.'

"The second hermit said: 'The next time the young nāga comes and serves you with every requisite, ask him for the jewel that rests upon his head. Nāgas are miserly by nature and will not give it, and so he will cease to come again.'

"On another occasion, when the hermit was sitting cross-legged in meditation, the young nāga emerged from the great pond just as before, coiled his body seven times around the hermit's body, reared up with a great hood above him, and remained there thus. When the hermit rose, the young nāga uncoiled his body from the hermit's body and adorned himself with shoulder ornaments, earrings and ear-hoops,

necklaces of various jewels, and garlands, anointed with perfume. He pressed his palms together, sat before the hermit, and served him with every requisite. Then the hermit said to him, "Young nāga, give me that jewel which rests upon your head." The young nāga replied, "I must ask my parents." The hermit said, "Very well, do so."

The young nāga went and asked both his parents: "Father and Mother, if the hermit asks me for the jewel, shall I give it to him?" The two of them replied, "It is through the power of this jewel that we obtain our food, drink, perfume, garlands, and ornaments, so do not give it away."

Then the young nāga emerged from the pond and sat before the hermit, and the hermit said to him, "Young nāga, give me that jewel which rests upon your head." And so the young nāga spoke these verses:

Food and drink, and likewise clothing too —
all these are accomplished through this jewel's power.
That is why I will not give this jewel to you.
By asking too much you have become a source of anger.
By asking too much you have become loathsome to me,
like a sharp sword honed with sesame oil.
If you come to my dwelling henceforth,
beat me on the head with a stone!

So he spoke, and disappeared along a road unseen. Monks, if even those creatures born in an animal realm, when pushed too far, take themselves off along a road unseen, what need is there even to speak of human beings? Therefore, monks, a monk must not make excessive demands.

Monks, in yet another story from the distant past, there was a hermit dwelling in a forest hermitage without any village nearby. His dwelling was excellent — richly adorned with flowers, abundant in fruit, and splendid with encircling groves. Many birds lived there, and they raised their calls, for sound is a thorn in meditative concentration, and so that hermit was unable to attain one-pointedness of mind on account of the many birds' noise.

Then another hermit who was wandering through the countryside came to that hermit's dwelling and said to him, "O hermit, this dwelling of yours is excellent — richly adorned with flowers, abundant in fruit, and splendid with encircling groves. Have you here attained one-pointedness of mind?" He replied, "That is true — my dwelling is excellent, richly adorned with flowers, abundant in fruit, splendid with encircling groves — yet there is a fault here as well." The other said, "And what fault is there?" He replied, "Many birds live here and raise their calls, and sound is a thorn in meditative concentration, so on account of the many birds' noise I have not been able to attain one-pointedness of mind."

The other said, "Would you wish that these birds no longer come here?" He answered, "I would." Then the other said, "On the twenty-ninth night of the month, kindle a grass-torch and go to the foot of the trees and say these words: 'Eat your eggs! Eat your young!' and they will come no more."

He began to do exactly as instructed. The birds, however, thought to themselves, "Has this hermit gone mad?" — and the birds caused their young to grow wings, and then they departed and came no more, until finally every last one of them had gone off along a road unseen.

Monks, if even those creatures born in an animal realm, when pushed too far, take themselves off along a road unseen, what need is there even to speak of human beings?

Therefore a monk should not push others too far. If one pushes too far, it becomes a cause of conflict.

Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this case, and this occasion, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, act with full knowledge" — that too proceeds as before.

The Blessed One addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that one who has been invited as a guest for four months treats that as his own entitlement and then claims even more than that as his entitlement?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One rebuked this as conduct unworthy of a contemplative, conduct that is not conformable, not fitting, not in accord with proper standards, and conduct not to be performed by one who has gone forth. Then, having rebuked it in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten advantages clearly, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: A monk may accept an invitation as a guest for four months and treat it as his own. If he claims more than that as his entitlement, it is an offence." In this way the Blessed One established that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed as long as he wished in the land of the Śākyas, set out wandering toward Rājagṛha, travelling in stages, and in the course of that gradual journey arrived at Rājagṛha, where he dwelt in the Bamboo Grove, in the place of the Kalandakas.

Now the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, the man of noble form and heart, heard that the Blessed One, while wandering among the Śākyas, had arrived at Rājagṛha and was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove at the place of the Kalandakas. Upon hearing this, he thought to himself: "The great Śākya name — the Blessed One together with the assembly of monks — has been invited for four months with all provisions by those great Śākyas. I too have many times invited the Blessed One together with the assembly of monks to other houses for a midday meal, but I have never once invited them for four months with all provisions. I should invite the Blessed One together with the assembly of monks for four months with all provisions."

Then the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, guided, inspired, and gladdened the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, with a Dharma-filled discourse. Having in many ways instructed, guided, inspired, and gladdened him with a Dharma-filled discourse, the Blessed One became silent.

Then the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, may you please consent to the assembly of monks receiving from me, for four months of the season, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal requisites."

The Blessed One consented to the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, by remaining silent. Then the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet, and departing from the Blessed One's presence, had a suitable infirmary built and had suitable medicines placed there as well. He had placed there medicines that are beneficial when taken at pleasant times, medicines for specific hours of the day, seven-day medicines, medicines to be kept for life, root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, and fruit medicines. He had clarified butter both rendered and unrendered placed there. He had grain-oil both rendered and unrendered placed there. He had cows, female buffaloes, and she-goats placed there. He had all requisites placed there. He had physicians and sick-attendants placed there as well.

Now, the husband of the sister of the venerable Pilindavatsa heard that when the Blessed One was wandering through the Śākya territories and had arrived at Rājagṛha, he was residing in Rājagṛha at the Veṇuvana, the abode of the Kalandakas. Having heard this, he thought to himself: "The great Śākya clan has invited the Blessed One together with the community of monks for four months with all requisites. I too have on many occasions, at the lunchtime hour, invited the Blessed One together with the community of monks to another household and offered a meal, yet not once have I invited them with all requisites. Let me invite the Blessed One together with the community of monks for four months with all requisites."

Then that brahmin went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One fully instructed that brahmin with a Dharma-filled discourse, fully guided him, fully inspired him, and fully gladdened him. Having in many ways fully instructed, guided, inspired, and gladdened him with a Dharma-filled discourse, the Blessed One became silent.

Then that brahmin rose from his seat, and bowing with joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, may you please consent to the assembly of monks together with the Blessed One receiving from me, for four months of the season, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal requisites."

That brahmin had previously been invited by the king who had arisen in Magadha, Bimbisāra. The brahmin then thought: "The noble Pilindavatsa is my kinsman; if I invite him, he will likely grant permission." And so he went to where the venerable Pilindavatsa was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the venerable Pilindavatsa's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Pilindavatsa fully instructed that brahmin with a Dharma-filled discourse, fully guided him, fully inspired him, and fully gladdened him. Having in many ways fully instructed, guided, inspired, and gladdened him with a Dharma-filled discourse, the venerable Pilindavatsa became silent.

Then that brahmin rose from his seat, and bowing with joined palms toward the venerable Pilindavatsa, addressed the venerable Pilindavatsa in these words:

"Would the noble one permit me to provide robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal requisites for four months?"

The venerable Pilindavatsa replied, "I shall ask the Blessed One."

Then the venerable Pilindavatsa went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Reverend sir, my son-in-law came to where I was, and said to me, 'Would the noble one permit me to provide robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal requisites for four months?' What response shall I give him?"

The Blessed One declared, "In that case, with the exception of individual invitations, a monk may accept an individual invitation as his own."

Now some other monks who had arrived later thought, "We were not invited by the king, so let us go on alms-round," and understanding this, they went on alms-round. The king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, was sitting at the base of a belvedere atop the Finework Pinnacle Palace, and seeing those monks wandering on alms-round, he said to his ministers, "Wise ones, why are these noble ones going on alms-round?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it appears that the reason they have come is this: those monks who arrived at the same time as the Blessed One were invited by the king, but we who arrived later were not invited by the king — thinking this, they went on alms-round." The king said, "In that case, the noble ones shall be invited again and again."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "In that case, with the exception of repeated invitations, a monk may accept a repeated invitation as his own."

The monks then thought, "King Bimbisāra has many duties and many affairs, while we have few duties and few affairs; so let us go on alms-round" — and thinking this, they went on alms-round. The king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, was sitting at the base of the belvedere atop the Finework Pinnacle Palace, and seeing those monks wandering on alms-round, he said to his ministers, "Wise ones, why are these noble ones going on alms-round?" They explained the situation in full, and the king said, "In that case, the noble ones shall be invited at the appointed time."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "In that case, with the exception of a timely invitation, a monk may accept a timely invitation as his own."

King Bimbisāra then invited the Blessed One along with a display of his going forth, and the following day a great many monks went on alms-round. The king of Magadha, Bimbisāra, was sitting at the base of the belvedere atop the Finework Pinnacle Palace, and seeing those monks wandering on alms-round, he said to his ministers, "Wise ones, why are these noble ones going on alms-round?" They explained the situation in full, and the king said, "In that case, the noble ones shall always be invited."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "In that case, with the exception of a standing invitation, a monk may

accept a standing invitation. Then the Blessed One praised the desire to train, reverence for the training, and providing requisites for the training, and addressed the monks with words in accord with this, bearing this meaning at length, and befitting this occasion. He then declared to the monks: "Monks, what came before was a rule; this is a permission. My hearers shall recite this rule for training in the Vinaya thus: a monk may accept an invitation for up to four months. To accept beyond that is an offence. Except in the case of an individual invitation, a repeated invitation, a timely invitation, and a standing invitation — for in those cases it is the proper occasion. This is the rule."

The analysis of terms is as follows. "A monk" refers to one who possesses this teaching. "For four months" means up to four months. "An invitation" means one that has been extended. "May accept" means it is to be taken up. "To accept beyond that" means to go beyond that limit. "An offence" means it burns, it scorches, it causes one to fall into the bad rebirths of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong descent. Moreover, for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome Dharmas — and for that reason it is called an offence.

"An individual invitation" is as follows: monks invited separately, one by one. "A repeated invitation" is as follows: monks invited again and again. "A timely invitation" is as follows: monks invited with urgency. "A standing invitation" is as follows: monks invited on a permanent basis. "Except" means set aside. "For in those cases it is the proper occasion" means that in those cases it is the conforming rule.

Now, how does an offence come about? If a monk accepts even a little beyond an invitation for four months, it becomes an offence in every instance. If a monk is invited for an unwholesome purpose and requests alms-food, the requesting is a wrong act and the eating is an offence. If a monk is invited for a wholesome purpose and requests something unwholesome, the requesting is a wrong act and the eating too is a wrong act.

When a monk is on alms-round and a woman brings food from her household, the monk may say, "Sister, that is sufficient; I do not want it." If the woman says, "Venerable one, what does the noble one wish for?" he should state what has been extended to him and may take whatever he desires. There is no offence for one who is a beginner, or who is mentally deranged, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by feeling.

This is the seventy-fourth offence entailing removal from the invitation, the one of remaining at a distance.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the Kalandaka squirrels. At that time, when the Blessed One was establishing a rule of training common to all hearers in the Vinaya, he assembled both orders of the Saṅgha. This too, therefore, is a rule of training common to all hearers established by the Blessed One in the Vinaya, and for this one he assembled both orders of the Saṅgha. The Blessed One then declared to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, go and release a monk among the monks into the midst of the nuns and deliver this message: 'Sisters, the Blessed One has established the following rule of training common to all hearers in the Vinaya: a monk may accept an invitation for four months; if he accepts beyond that, it entails a transgression. Excepted are individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations — for these it is timely. The Blessed One having thus established this rule, you too should train in this training.' Convey this instruction."

The Venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Blessed One commands," received these words from the Blessed One, went to where the Venerable Lāmpa was, and instructed him: "Venerable Lāmpa, go and, addressing the nuns, deliver this message: 'Sisters, the Blessed One has established the following rule of training common to all hearers in the Vinaya: a monk may accept an invitation for four months; if he accepts beyond that, it entails a transgression. Excepted are individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations — for these it is timely. The Blessed One having thus established this rule, you too should train in this training.'"

The Venerable Lāmpa replied, "As the Venerable Ānanda commands," received these words from the Venerable Ānanda, and set out for the nuns' rains retreat dwelling. As he arrived, the group of six saw him and asked, "Venerable Lāmpa, where are you going?"

The Venerable Lāmpa thought to himself, "These ones also seem not to have heard this. I should tell them as well." And so he said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has established the following rule of training common to all hearers in the Vinaya: a monk may accept an invitation for four months; if he accepts beyond that, it entails a transgression. Excepted are individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations — for these it is timely. The Blessed One having thus established this rule, you too should train in this training."

They replied: "We are monks who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs. We will not train in this training on the basis of your words — you are childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled." And with these words they heaped on him the epithets of being childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled.

The Venerable Lāmpa then continued on his way, and as he went the group of twelve nuns saw him and asked him, "Venerable Lāmpa, where are you going?"

He said: "Sisters, know this: the Blessed One has established the following rule of training common to all hearers in the Vinaya: a monk may accept an invitation for four months; if he accepts beyond that, it entails a transgression. Excepted are individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations — for these it is timely. The Blessed One having thus established this rule, you too should train in this training."

They replied: "We are nuns who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs. We will not train in this training on the basis of your words — you are childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled." And with these words they heaped on him the epithets of being childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled, and departed.

The venerable Lamba thought to himself: "What is the use of speaking to these nuns who engage in all manner of bad conduct? I shall now go and not speak of this to anyone other than the great Progenitress Gautamī." And so he went to where the great Progenitress Gautamī was, and upon arriving, spoke to her as follows:

"Gautamī, know this well. The Blessed One has established the following as a common training rule in the Vinaya for śrāvakas: 'A monk may accept invitations for up to four months. If he accepts beyond that, it entails a transgression. Excepted are individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations — for these it is timely.' This rule the Blessed One has established, and you too should train in this training."

The great Progenitress replied: "Venerable Lamba, the Blessed One has established that training rule in the Vinaya as a common rule for śrāvakas — namely, that a monk may accept invitations for up to four months, that to accept beyond that entails a transgression, and that individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations are excepted, for those it is timely. That rule which the Blessed One has so established — this I accept with head, speech, and mind alike.

"Venerable Lamba, consider this example. Suppose some young women of the warrior caste, or of the brahmin caste, or of the merchant caste, or of the common people's caste — well bathed, well anointed, with hair and nails well trimmed, desiring white garments — were to be given a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of jasmine, or a garland of atimukta flowers. They would receive it with delight, taking it up with both hands, and place it as an adornment upon their noble heads. In just the same way, Venerable Lamba, the rule which the Blessed One has established in the Vinaya as a common training rule for śrāvakas — that a monk may accept invitations for up to four months, that to accept beyond that entails a transgression, and that individual invitations, repeated invitations, timely invitations, and standing invitations are excepted, for those it is timely — that rule too I accept with head, speech, and mind alike."

The venerable Lamba then conveyed this and returned. When the venerable Ānanda saw him, he asked: "Venerable Lamba, did you convey this to the nuns?" He replied: "I conveyed it, and this is what happened: they heaped upon me the epithets of being childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled." "Who did?" "The group of six." "Why?" At that, he recounted the matter in full. The few monks who had little desire asked why the monks were conveying to the venerable ones that they should train in this training — and when that was done, those nuns said: "We are nuns who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs — we will not train in this training on the basis of your words, you who are childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled." And so they reviled them, spread it about, and gossiped. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident and this occasion and this context, convened the assembly of monks — and the rest proceeds as before.

"The awakened blessed ones, though knowing, act as though they do not know" — and so forth, continuing as before. The Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned the group of six, saying: "Monks, is it true that when monks conveyed to the venerable ones that they should train in this training, those monks said: 'We hold the sūtras, we hold the Vinaya, we hold the māmakīs — we will not train in this training on the basis of your words, you who are childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled'?" "Blessed One, it is true." The Buddha, the Blessed One, then condemned them, saying: "That which is not the manner of a renunciant, not befitting, not proper, not in accord with the rule — that is not what one who has gone forth should do." Then, having condemned them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be laid down" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows. Whatever monk, when monks convey to the venerable one that he should train in this training, says to them: 'I hold the sūtras, I hold the Vinaya, I hold the māmakīs — I will not train in this training on the basis of your words, you who are childish, confused, obscure, and unskilled' — that constitutes a transgression. And any monk who wishes to know everything should also train in that training. He should inquire of those who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs — and in that matter, that is the proper procedure."

"Whatever monk" refers to the group of six or anyone else of that kind. "When monks" refers to those who follow this Dharma. "Convey to the venerable one that he should train in this training" refers to whatever training it may be. "To them" refers to those monks. "Says" means when one says the following. "Those who hold the sūtras" means those who hold all the sūtras. "Those who hold the Vinaya" means those who hold all the Vinaya. "Those who hold the māmakīs — we will inquire of them" means those who hold all the māmakīs. "Childish" — by "childish" is meant one who thinks harmful thoughts, speaks harmful words, and performs harmful deeds. "Confused" — by "confused" is meant one who does not hold the sūtras, does not hold the Vinaya, does not hold the māmakīs. "Obscure" — by "obscure" is meant one who is obscure regarding the sūtras, obscure regarding the Vinaya, and obscure regarding the māmakīs. "Unskilled" — by "unskilled" is meant one who is unskilled in the sūtras, unskilled in the Vinaya, and unskilled in the māmakīs. "Says that he will not train in this training on the basis of your words" means when one says exactly that. "That constitutes a transgression" — it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of misfortune. Furthermore, as long as the transgression is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous qualities — and therefore it is said to constitute a transgression. "Any monk who wishes to know everything should also train in that training. He should inquire of those who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs — and in that matter, that is the proper procedure" means: in that matter, that is the conforming practice. Now, how does a transgression come about in this matter?

If a monk, to whatever small degree, instructs others saying, "Venerable one, you should train in this training," and those addressed respond: "I will not train in this training on the word of someone who, until he has inquired of those who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the māmakīs, is childish, confused, unclear, and unskilled" — in all such cases a transgression is incurred. If they say, "I will not train in this training on the word of someone childish" — a transgression is incurred. If they say, "I will not train in this training on the word of someone confused" — a transgression is incurred. If they say, "I will not train in this training on the word of someone unclear" — a transgression is incurred. If they say, "I will not train in this training on the word of someone unskilled" — a transgression is incurred. However, if one is genuinely and truly childish, confused, unclear, and unskilled, there is no transgression. There is likewise no transgression for one who is a beginner, who is mad, whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful sensations. The seventy-fifth transgression concerning the abandonment of placing oneself close to the training is hereby complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the Venerable Charka, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship. The Venerable Udāyin had gone to Kauśāmbī and was there sitting in a small, depressed state of mind. Āvāsin and Nāgasamāla had arrived at their time of death. Nanda and Upananda were sitting within the Saṅgha. At that moment, the group of seventeen — who were hostile, domineering toward others, holders of the sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the māmakīs — said among themselves: "Venerable ones, the group of six has been opposing us for a long time. Just as Nanda and Upananda have opposed us, no one else has done so in the same way; and just as Upananda has opposed us, Nanda has not done so in the same way. We should therefore carry out an act of expulsion against them from this place." They then said, "This one's elder brother is skilled in debate — summon him. Let us take counsel." They entered the deliberation hall, shut the door, and began to deliberate. Upananda, however, listened through a window, and having overheard them he challenged them, saying: "Alas, you group of seventeen — what are you deliberating? Some of my fellow practitioners of celibacy have passed fully into nirvāṇa; some are merely sitting in a low-spirited state; some have arrived at their time of death. Do you really think, then, that now you will carry out an act of expulsion from this place? Do you imagine you will now overwhelm and suppress us? We too shall deal you a great defeat." And he challenged them with these words: "Have you not heard the verse — Even if the elephant's rope be dried out by the sun and wind, and even if one falls from the elephant's neck-yoke, still five hundred sheep should be driven along." Hearing this, they thought: "He has overheard our deliberations and will go and report to others." So they entered the fire-house and began to deliberate there. Upananda crept there as well, listened, and challenged them there in the same way. They then assembled in the upper chamber and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the middle story and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the middle story and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the lower chamber and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the residence hall and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the corridor and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the corridor and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the residence hall and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the gatehouse and began to deliberate,

while Upananda sat in the stairwell and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the walking-meditation path and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the cells and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the cells and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the walking-meditation path and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled in the hermitage grounds and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat among the shrubs and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They assembled among the shrubs and began to deliberate, while Upananda sat in the hermitage grounds and listened, and challenged them there likewise in the same way. They set out along the road, deliberating as they went, while Upananda followed along behind and listened, and having challenged them there likewise in the same way, the monks said to him: "Venerable ones, we are unable to carry out the act of suspension against him from this place; let us ask his pardon." And so they said to him: "Venerable Upananda, please grant us your pardon." Upananda said: "Pardon is granted." They then asked him: "How did you know what we were deliberating?" Upananda said: "When you entered the assembly hall and deliberated, I listened through the window. When you entered the fire house and deliberated, I listened by crouching down. When you assembled in the upper chamber and deliberated, I sat in the middle story and listened. When you assembled in the middle story and deliberated, I sat in the lower chamber and listened. When you assembled in the residence hall and deliberated, I sat in the corridor and listened. When you assembled in the corridor and deliberated, I sat in the residence hall and listened. When you assembled in the gatehouse and deliberated, I sat in the stairwell and listened. When you assembled in the stairwell and deliberated, I sat in the gatehouse and listened. When you assembled in the walking-meditation path and deliberated, I sat in the cells and listened. When you assembled in the cells and deliberated, I sat in the walking-meditation path and listened. When you assembled in the hermitage grounds and deliberated, I sat among the shrubs and listened. When you assembled among the shrubs and deliberated, I sat in the hermitage grounds and listened. When you set out along the road and deliberated as you went, I followed along behind and listened." They said to him: "Is it right for you to sit eavesdropping like that?" Upananda replied: "If I had not been sitting and listening while you deliberated, you would have carried out an act of suspension against me."

Monks of little account — why did the monks come to fight, to slander one another, to be at odds, to quarrel? It is while sitting in that very assembly that these monks, thinking "Whatever they say, I will listen and then traduce them accordingly," take that very intention as their occasion to sit in silence listening as a spy, then condemn them, denounce them, and spread malicious talk about them. At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then, on account of this incident and this basis for legislation,

"On this occasion the Saṅgha of monks was convened" — and so forth, as before. "The blessed buddhas, knowing full well, nevertheless inquired" — and so forth, likewise as before.

The Blessed One, a buddha, then asked Ānanda, the son of the Śākyas: "Ānanda, when monks have come to fight, to slander one another, to be at odds, to quarrel, and are sitting in that assembly — is it true that you sat listening as a spy, saying nothing, having taken as your occasion the very thought, 'Whatever these monks say, I will listen and then traduce them accordingly'?"

"Venerable One, it is so."

The Blessed One then rebuked him, saying that this is unworthy of a renunciant, that it is improper, inappropriate, and contrary to proper conduct — it is not something one who has gone forth ought to do.

After rebuking him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya shall be laid down" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Furthermore, whatever monk, when monks have come to fight, to slander one another, to be at odds, to quarrel, and are sitting in that assembly — taking as his occasion the very thought, 'Whatever these monks say, I will listen and then traduce them accordingly' — sits listening as a spy, saying nothing: that is an offence entailing a downfall."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to Ānanda, the son of the Śākyas, or to any other who is similarly situated.

"Monks" refers to those who are of this Dharma.

"Have come to fight, to slander one another, to be at odds, to quarrel, and are sitting in that assembly" refers to those who are stationed on one side or the other of a dispute.

"Taking as his occasion the very thought, 'Whatever these monks say, I will listen and then traduce them accordingly'" means: with such an intention, thinking to counter and press against the other side in that or this manner as a counteragent.

"Taking that very thing as his occasion" — meaning no other occasion.

"Sits listening as a spy, saying nothing" means sitting with ears pricked, uttering not a word.

"Offence entailing a downfall" — it burns, it scorches, it causes one to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the realm of hungry ghosts, into the lower rebirths, into the states of misfortune. Furthermore, for as long as that downfall is not confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome qualities. That is why it is called "an offence entailing a downfall."

Now, how does the downfall occur?

If monks are holding a deliberation in an upper chamber and a monk also ascends there, that monk should make a sound with his heel, the sound of a sandal, or a cough. If he does not make the sound of a heel, the sound of a sandal, or a cough, then for as long as he hears voices but has not yet understood the meaning, it amounts to a wrongdoing for that monk. Once he understands the meaning of what is being said, it becomes an offence entailing a downfall.

If monks are walking along and holding a deliberation in a hall, a lower room, a dwelling, a corridor, a gatehouse, a terrace, a walkway, a park, or on a road, and a monk follows behind them — that monk should make the sound of a heel, the sound of a sandal, or a cough. If he does not make the sound of a heel, the sound of a sandal, or a cough, then for as long as he hears voices but has not yet understood the meaning, it amounts to a wrongdoing for that monk. Once he understands the meaning of what is being said, it becomes an offence entailing a downfall.

There is no offence in the following cases: when one is not intentionally concealed; when one is in a state of doubt;

when one listens with the intention of bringing about a reconciliation, there is no offence. There is no offence for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The seventy-sixth offence entailing a downfall, arising from eavesdropping, is complete.

The Vinaya Analysis, the sixty-fourth fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. At the time when the venerable Chārcā had directly realized arhatship by abandoning all afflictions, the venerable Udāyin had gone to Kauśāmbī and was staying quietly and humbly there. The pair Mahānāma and Anuruddha had each arrived at their appointed time. The pair Nandika and Ānanda were at that time within the community, and the assembly of the group of seventeen — being contentious, overbearing toward others, masters of the sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkā — said the following: "Venerable ones, for a long time the group of six has been lodging formal accusations against us. Just as Nandika and Ānanda have lodged accusations against us, yet no one else has done the same against them; and just as Ānanda has lodged accusations, Nandika has not done the same in return — therefore let us carry out the act of formal expulsion against them from this place."

Then some among them said: "Nandika's elder brother Ānanda is skilled in debate, and so we are not able to carry out the act of formal expulsion against him." Others among them said: "When one person speaks, two should not listen; but when the assembly speaks, the assembly is like a king — so if he were to say even a little, that would be the moment to carry out the act of formal expulsion against him."
