Having thus arranged the meeting place, they struck the gaṇḍī bell and duly conveyed the matter to the monks in the proper form of invitation, and when the entire community was seated together in harmony, the instigator sat to one side of an elder and said: "Reverend Ānanda, do you recall saying words such as these — that the belly of the assembly of the group of seventeen should be split open and their entrails used to encircle the Jeta Grove?"

Ānanda replied: "Venerable ones, that matter is past — what is the use of speaking of a healed wound? Let it be."

They said: "The Blessed One established the rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya solely on the basis of past occurrences." And when Ānanda began to respond in counter, they said: "Whoever offers a counter-response shall also be formally expelled."

Ānanda thought to himself: "Given the way these people are behaving, if they were to carry out the act of formal expulsion against me as well, that would not be good." Since the winter season had arrived, he put on a woolen cloak, propped that cloak up against the base of a wall, and without saying a word, rose from his seat and left.

Then they said: "Venerable ones, speak your opinion!" — and in his absence they carried out the act of formal expulsion against Ānanda. After the act of formal expulsion had been carried out, he went weeping to his elder brother. Ānanda said: "Ānanda, why are you weeping?" He replied: "Those who carry black alms-bowls have carried out the act of formal expulsion against me from this place."

Ānanda said: "May those who have carried out the act of formal expulsion against my younger brother be expelled from village, from town, and from all three realms. Yet for those against whom an act of formal expulsion has been carried out — is there no village, no town? Stay on, and afterward request pardon. For they have performed this act in a spirit of pure antagonism."

"Who was there at the time?" Ānanda said: "It was I. I heard the sound of a teacher from where I was sitting, to the side of an elder."

Ānanda said: "At the moment when they were saying, 'Whoever offers a counter-response shall also be formally expelled,' I thought to myself:

"If they proceed in this manner, they will end up performing an act of formal expulsion against me as well while I remain here — that would not be good." And so, since the winter season had arrived, he put on a shawl, stood that shawl against the wall, rose from his seat without saying a word, and departed.

Monks of little worth then censured him, gossiped about him, and spread adverse talk, saying: "Why is it that when a discussion fully in accord with the Dharma of the Saṅgha has taken place and a proper determination has been reached, monks simply rise from their seats without a word and walk away?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks regarding this occurrence, this basis of discussion, and this occasion — and so forth, as before. The phrase "The blessed buddhas, with full knowledge, perform inquiry" — and so forth, also as before — and the blessed Buddha questioned the Śākya's son Nanda: "Nanda, is it true that when a discussion fully in accord with the Dharma of the Saṅgha had taken place and a proper determination had been reached, you rose from your seat without saying a word and departed?"

"Reverend one, it is so."

The blessed Buddha then rebuked him: "That is not the conduct of a renunciant, it is not fitting, it is not proper, it is not in accord with proper conduct — it is not what one who has gone forth should do." And so the Blessed One reproached him in many ways. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing these ten benefits, one should establish rules of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk, when a discussion fully in accord with the Dharma of the Saṅgha has taken place and a proper determination has been reached, rises from his seat without saying a word and departs — that is a transgression." Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

Now, there were monks who were seriously ill and unable to remain seated for long, and their attendant monks were also neglecting the care of the sick; and monks who were waiting upon others were also neglecting the business of the Saṅgha. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, one should speak to the seated monk and then depart."

After the Blessed One had declared that one should speak to the seated monk and then depart, a certain monk left his bowl and robes at another household and went away, and while he was there a fire broke out. As that monk had set out to leave and had gone halfway along the road, the thought arose in him: "I have not spoken to the seated monk." So he turned back, and by the time he had spoken to the seated monk who was there seated, his bowl and robes had been burned. He then arrived there, and the householder said: "Noble one, why have you come so late? On account of that, your bowl and robes are burned. Had you come more quickly, your bowl and robes would not have been burned." And that monk found himself in a state of loss and hardship. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, except in circumstances such as these."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are devoted to training, and who are equipped with the implements of training, and addressed the monks with words in accord with that, exceeding that, and befitting it. The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore the former rule stands as it was established, and this is now the permitted exception:

My śrāvakas shall recite this as the rule and basis of training in the Vinaya: "Furthermore, whatever monk, when a Saṅgha proceeding that possesses the qualities proper to the Saṅgha arises for the purpose of settling a matter, departs from his seat without saying a word and goes away, and does not speak to a sitting monk — that constitutes a transgression, except in such circumstances."

The phrase "whatever monk" refers to a son of the Śākyas, such as Gavampati, or any other of like kind. The phrase "of the Saṅgha" refers to the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas. The phrase "when a Saṅgha proceeding that possesses the qualities proper to the Saṅgha arises for the purpose of settling a matter" refers to when a formal act has arisen by single motion, by motion and one proclamation, or by motion and three proclamations. The phrase "departs from his seat without saying a word and goes away" means that he leaves while still within earshot of the assembly. The phrase "does not speak to a sitting monk" refers to whatever monk is sitting there at that time. The phrase "except in such circumstances" means that such circumstances have been allowed as an exception. The phrase "constitutes a transgression" means it causes one to be burned, scorched, and to fall into states of woe — namely the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, unfortunate destinies, and lower rebirths. Moreover, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the arising of virtuous qualities, and for that reason it is said to constitute a transgression.

Now, how does the transgression occur? Whatever monk, as soon as a Saṅgha proceeding that possesses the qualities proper to the Saṅgha has arisen for the purpose of settling a matter, departs from his seat without saying a word and goes away, and does not speak to a sitting monk — for as long as he has not yet gone beyond earshot of the assembly, it constitutes a wrongdoing; once he has gone beyond earshot, it constitutes a transgression. For one who is a beginner, one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by pain, there is no transgression. The seventy-seventh transgression, that of going away without speaking, is complete.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Grove of the Bamboo Forest. At that time, a certain monk, the black son of the lord of the great elephant god, was sitting together with a large number of monks in the meeting hall, having gathered there in harmony for the purpose of settling some dispute regarding the question "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Teacher," when one party alone was causing disruption in the Saṅgha, one party alone was causing discord in the Saṅgha, and they were holding to their dispute and arguing, not allowing the matter to come to its conclusion, not showing respect, not deferring to seniority, and intending to speak out again. That monk then began to rebuke, deride, and slander a small number of monks, saying: "Why do you monks — though so few — object to a large number of monks who are sitting together in harmony at the meeting hall for the purpose of settling a dispute, namely the question 'This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Teacher,' when one party alone is causing disruption in the Saṅgha, one party alone is causing discord in the Saṅgha, holding to their dispute, arguing, not allowing the matter to come to its conclusion, not showing respect, not deferring to seniority, and intending to speak out again?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, concerning this basis, and regarding this circumstance, convened an assembly of the monks — and so forth, as before. "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, knowing fully, act without error" — and so forth, as before. The Buddha, the Blessed One, then addressed the black son of the lord of the great elephant god: "Monk, you —

"This is the Dharma. This is the Vinaya. This is the teaching of the Teacher" — sitting in the waiting room in order to bring some dispute to rest, and having reached agreement, one alone turns the Saṅgha away, and one alone causes the Saṅgha to be at odds: holding to the dispute, arguing while seated there, not allowing the matter to come to its conclusion, not showing respect, not deferring to seniority, and intending to speak out again — is this true?" "Venerable sir, it is so." The Buddha, the Blessed One, censured him, declaring that this was improper conduct for a renunciant, not in accordance with harmony, not fitting, not in keeping with the rule — this is not something that one who has gone forth ought to do. Then, having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing fully the ten benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If one does not show respect, it is an offense."

Now, "not showing respect" means not showing respect in either of two ways: toward the Saṅgha and toward individual persons. The Saṅgha here means the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata, and also what goes by the conventional designation of Saṅgha. Individual persons means one's preceptor and one's teachers. "It is an offense" means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, states of misery, and wrong destinations. Furthermore, as long as that offense has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the wholesome qualities — and that is why it is called an offense.

As for how one incurs the offense in practice: if the Saṅgha instructs a monk, "Be seated," and he does not sit, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Do not be seated," and he sits, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Go," and he does not go, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Do not go," and he goes, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Take a lodging," and he does not take it, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Do not take a lodging," and he takes it, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Take the assembly hall," and he does not take it, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Do not take the assembly hall," and he takes it, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Speak," and he does not speak, he incurs an offense. If the instruction is "Do not speak," and he speaks, he incurs an offense. If he gives a Dharmic admonishment in a proper and harmonious manner, there is no offense. The same applies when the instruction comes from those who bear the conventional designation of Saṅgha.

If a preceptor instructs a monk, "Be seated," and he does not sit, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Do not be seated," and he sits, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Go," and he does not go, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Do not go," and he goes, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Take a lodging," and he does not take it, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Do not take a lodging," and he takes it, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Take the assembly hall," and he does not take it, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Do not take the assembly hall," and he takes it, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Speak," and he does not speak, it is a misdeed. If the instruction is "Do not speak," and he speaks, it is a misdeed. If he gives a Dharmic admonishment in a proper and harmonious manner, there is no offense. The same applies when the instruction comes from teachers. There is no offense for one who is a beginner, for one who is mentally disturbed, for one who is mentally troubled, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This completes the seventy-eighth section on transgressions arising from disrespectful conduct.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

On the hill of Crocodile Child-Slayer there lived a householder named Wise One, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, of extensive property, with vast and wide holdings, endowed with the wealth of the son of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the son of Vaiśravaṇa in riches. He took a wife from among women of equal birth and sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed pleasure with her. To him was born a daughter who was beautiful in form, pleasing to behold, and lovely. He raised and nurtured her, and she grew to maturity. The householder thought to himself: "I will not give this daughter away on account of her beauty, nor on account of her craft. I will give her only to one who is equal to me in lineage and in wealth, or better."

He heard that in Śrāvastī there lived a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, of extensive property, with vast and wide holdings, endowed with the wealth of the son of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the son of Vaiśravaṇa in riches, and that this man was equal to him in lineage and in wealth, indeed surpassing him in the manner of his wealth. So he gave his daughter in marriage to the son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī. And the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took her as a wife for his son, the wealthy Śrī.

The householder Wise One would sport with her, delight in her, and enjoy pleasure with her, and a sentient being entered her womb. From the very day that the sentient being entered her womb, a hundred afflictions befell the householder Wise One. As the one dwelling in the womb continued to develop and grow, so too did great afflictions — a hundred in number — befall the householder Wise One again and again.

The householder Wise One thought: "I shall go and sit in the pleasure garden." He instructed his stewards: "O wise ones, if some great harm should befall me, give the signal. If it does not come, do not give it." Having given this instruction, he went and sat in the pleasure garden.

Then at a later time his wife gave birth, and a boy was born. On the very day he was born, a thousand afflictions befell the householder Wise One. Then a man came running at full speed toward where the householder Wise One was, and the householder Wise One, seeing the man coming running at full speed from a great distance, thought: "Could it be that some great harm has come upon me?" And he said to the man: "My dear fellow, why do you come running in such a way?" The man replied: "Your son has been born — rejoice!" Wise One said: "My dear fellow, though my son has caused me hundreds upon hundreds of afflictions, still it is good that a son has come."

His relatives assembled and gathered together, and thinking to give the boy a name, they reflected thus: "Since his father uttered the words 'it is good that he has come,' let this boy's name be Legs-'ongs," that is, Welcome. And so his name was given as Welcome.

As Welcome continued to grow and develop, the wealth, grain, silver, gold, servants both male and female, workers, and stewards in the household of the householder Wise One became utterly exhausted.

Then at another time the householder Wise One's time came, and his wife's time came as well.

That house too burned down. Every form of storehouse, every form of field, every form of wealth, every form of grain — all of it burned down. Some of the townspeople had taken up bundles of goods and set out for other lands: some met with the wreck of a great ship on the vast ocean; some found that their goods were not what they had supposed; some met with suffering in that very place through improper means; and some settled there and gave nothing in return. Some of the relatives too met their time; some fled; and some settled there, giving nothing in return. Male servants, female servants, workers, and wage-earners — some met their time, some fled, and some settled there, giving nothing in return.

One old female servant of the householder Wise One, who alone had remained to attend to Welcome's needs, sent the boy Welcome off to school to learn letters and writing. That old woman reflected: "The householder Wise One's household, rich in so many possessions, has become utterly exhausted and spent — I wonder whether this has come about through my own lack of merit, or through Welcome's lack of merit. Let me look into this." And so, however many times she registered a crop in Welcome's name, it was consumed and ruined; and however many times she registered one in her own name, it thrived. From this she concluded: "This is a being without good fortune. Because of his ill returns, the householder Wise One's household, rich in so many possessions, has been ruined through improper means. Because of his ill returns, I too will surely end up suffering through improper means — there can be no doubt this situation will arise. What then is to be done with him?" And she thought: "I must flee." That old woman therefore gathered up whatever few precious things remained and fled.

Dogs entered the empty house, ate whatever food was left, and began to fight. A man of leisure who happened to be passing through that direction heard the sound of dogs fighting in the house and thought: "Has the householder Wise One's house become empty? Why are dogs fighting and lingering here like this? Let me go and see." He entered, and finding that nearly all the dogs were fighting with one another and not a single person was present — the place entirely deserted — he took whatever remained of the leftover scraps and went on his way.

After him, Welcome came from the school, thinking to eat a meal. He entered the house and found it empty. He called out, "Mother, mother!" but no one answered. Not far from there was the house of a relative, and he went inside — only to find that the people of that house had gotten into a quarrel. When the quarrel subsided, they said to one another: "Friends, when I used to see you before, you were dear to my heart — but now, seeing you, I could kill you." The others said the same to one another, and then they thought: "Let us see whether someone else has come here." Looking, they saw that Welcome had arrived, and they said: "Friends, this is not Welcome — this is Misfortune-come! Because of his ill returns, a quarrel has broken out among us." And so they drove him out, and he went elsewhere. In that place too things went just the same way: they said the same words and drove him out and sent him away. He entered among the destitute, and even those destitute ones, finding their hands empty and

their begging bowls empty, returned — and those people said: "Friends, in the past, whenever we entered somewhere, we would return with full hands and full begging bowls; yet today we have come back with hands empty and begging bowls empty. What is the reason for this?" They said to one another: "Some ill-starred sentient being has entered our midst, and that is why we have come back with hands empty and begging bowls empty." They said again: "Let us investigate, then split into two groups and go in separately." So they divided into two groups and went. Those among whom Welcome had entered returned with hands empty and begging bowls empty, while the others all returned with hands full and begging bowls full. Those people then said: "This ill-starred sentient being has entered our midst, and that is why we have come back with hands empty and begging bowls empty." And so they split once more into two groups and went in separately — and again the same thing happened. They divided into two groups again and again, and still it turned out the same. After this had gone on in just this way, at a certain point Welcome and yet another hungry wanderer entered together as a pair; yet when they separated, Welcome came back with hands empty and begging bowl empty, while all the others came back with hands full and begging bowls full. Those people then declared: "This ill-starred sentient being has entered our midst, and that is why we have come back with hands empty and begging bowls empty." And so they beat Welcome soundly and drove him away.

Now in Śrāvastī there lived a householder friend of Togden, the younger brother of the householder Togden. This man had taken up a net and gone to the bank of a river where children came to kill crocodiles. There he saw Welcome walking along the road, holding his begging bowl in hand, and recognizing him by his very appearance, he called out to him: "Child, are you not the son of the householder Togden?" Welcome answered that he was. The man said: "Where have your father and mother gone?" Welcome replied: "Their time has come." The man said: "And what has become of his house, his storerooms, his fields, his wealth, his grain?" Welcome said: "All of it was burned by fire." The man asked: "And the people of the town who took their belongings and went to other lands — where did they go?" Welcome said: "Some were lost in the great ocean when a large ship was wrecked. Some lost their goods along the way. Some suffered misfortune right there through wrongdoing. And some stayed where they were but did not give so much as a word." The man asked: "And his relatives — where did they go?" Welcome said: "Some met their time. Some fled. Some stayed right there but did not give so much as a word." The man asked: "And his servants, male and female, his workers, and those who lived on a share of yogurt — where did they go?" Welcome said: "Some met their time. Some fled. Some stayed right there but did not give so much as a word."

Hearing this, the householder sat weeping, and then he said: "Child, let me go together with you to Śrāvastī." Welcome said: "Father, and what would be the point of my going there?" The man said: "Child, there in Śrāvastī lives the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the giver of food to the shelterless. His son has taken your younger sister as his wife, and if you go there, she will be able to provide for what you need." Welcome said: "Father, let us go." The householder gave Welcome two kārṣāpaṇas and said: "Child, until I can arrange my affairs and join you, stay here for a while and live on these two coins." But Welcome tossed those two kārṣāpaṇas into the fold of his robe and set them aside, and through the force of his karmic maturation he forgot them both entirely.

That householder traded his goods, received the price, and led Welcome away; and Welcome departed together with him. After they had traveled some distance, a quarrel broke out among the members of their party, and even the oxen began to fight. The men said to one another: "Friends, in the old days, whenever we saw each other our hearts were gladdened, yet now, whenever we see one another we fall to quarreling, and even the oxen fight the moment they catch sight of each other. Could it be that some misfortune has come upon us?" And when they looked and saw that Welcome had joined them, they said: "Friends, this is not Welcome — this is Misfortune! It is on account of his karma that we have fallen to quarreling and the oxen have begun to fight." And they started to drive him away. Then the householder said: "Friends, this is my younger brother's son, my friend's child — do not drive him away." But they replied: "Householder, you may do as you like within your own party, but we cannot travel with him. If he goes, we will not go." So the householder said to Welcome: "Child, follow behind us and come along, and I will set food aside for you." As Welcome followed behind them and arrived at each stopping place, the householder would indeed set food aside for him — but some portions he placed on the ground covered with grass, and others he placed on the branches of trees covered with leaves. The food left covered with grass on the ground was eaten by foxes, and the food placed on branches covered with leaves was eaten by birds and monkeys, so that Welcome received only a little and mostly went without. He thus dragged himself onward in the most wretched misery.

Now, it is an impossibility, a thing that cannot occur, that a being in his last existence — one who has not yet attained the exhaustion of all defilements — should die and have his stream cut off midway before the appointed time. Since that was impossible, Welcome eventually arrived at Śrāvastī, and there he sat resting at the mouth of a well just outside the city. The younger sister of Welcome, who had become the daughter-in-law of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the giver of food to the shelterless, sent her maidservant carrying a water jug to draw water at that well. The maidservant recognized Welcome by his appearance and said to him: "Young master, are you not Welcome, son of the householder Eloquent (Rtogs ldan), from the hill country where they kill sea-monster children?" He replied: "Yes, I am your mistress's brother." The maidservant asked: "Young master, where have your father and mother gone?" He said: "They have passed away." "And the house, the storerooms, the fields, the wealth, the grain — where are they all?" "Everything was burned in a fire." "And the townspeople who took their goods and went to other regions — where are they?" "Some perished when a great ship was wrecked on the ocean. Some lost their goods and came back empty-handed. Some were afflicted right there by unjust mistreatment. Some stayed right there and will not send even a word." "And the relatives — where are they?" "Some have passed away. Some fled. Some stayed right there and will not send even a word." "And the servants, the maidservants, the workers, the hired hands — where are they?" "Some have passed away. Some fled. Some stayed right there and will not send even a word."

When the maidservant heard all this, she sat there bathed in tears. Then she said to Welcome: "Young master, wait here just a moment while I go and tell your elder sister." She went and said to her mistress: "Mistress, your brother has arrived." The mistress asked: "In what state has he come?" The maidservant replied: "Mistress, he has come with matted hair, filthy and tattered, carrying a beggar's bowl." The mistress then sent a set of garments and some kārṣāpaṇas by the hand of that maidservant and said:

"Tell Young Master the following, and ask him to eat this first and be satisfied. Then later, if he happens to meet his nephews and nieces, he will be able to give them whatever kārṣāpaṇas may be needed, and so your kinsmen will not be disappointed in you." The maidservant went there, offered the garments and the kārṣāpaṇas to Welcome, and said: "Young master, your elder sister conveys this message: please eat this first and be satisfied, and then later, if you happen to meet your nephews and nieces, you will be able to give them whatever kārṣāpaṇas may be needed, and so your kinsmen will not be disappointed in you." Having said this, she departed.

Welcome thought to himself: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has a large circle of kinsmen and dependants, and I too formerly had a large circle of kinsmen. If I go there now, they will press me with questions and detain me a long time, and I shall end up dying of hunger in the meantime. Let me first go borrow somewhere to eat and drink my fill, and only then go there, so that I may greet each of my assembled kinsmen with ease and gladness." With that thought, he went to the house of a brewer and drank as much fermented drink as would intoxicate him. He became intoxicated and went into a park and lay down to sleep.

Now in Śrāvastī there were men whose task it was to clear the parks, and they would sweep through the park and rouse anyone they found sleeping. If a person woke up, they would say to him: "Sir, have you not heard that in Śrāvastī the men who clear the parks sweep through and drive away those who are found sleeping there? Get up and be gone!" But if a person did not wake up, they would beat him and drag him out. Those park-clearers arrived at that spot and, finding Welcome lying asleep, they shook him with their feet. When he did not wake up, they beat him and dragged him away. When at last Welcome did wake up, he saw that he himself had been beaten, and he sat there in the very same filthy rags he had been wearing.

His sister wondered why her brother had been detained so long, and so she sent a maidservant, not a close attendant but a lower servant, to go and have a look. When the girl went and looked, she saw that he had been beaten, and she returned and reported to the mistress: "Mistress, the young master has been beaten and is sitting there just as he was before." The sister thought to herself: "He is a being of ruined fortune. His karmic retribution has already caused the householder of discernment to squander his many riches through improper conduct. Now, if I were to take him into my house, his karmic retribution would likewise bring suffering upon my husband's household through improper means — there would come to be such a situation." And so she abandoned him entirely.

Welcome too, his mind obscured by karma, forgot all this and entered into the company of wandering beggars. And those beggars — their hands were empty and their begging bowls were empty when they came back. They said: "Friends, whenever we used to enter our usual places, we would come back with hands full and bowls full. Today we have come back with empty hands and empty bowls. What is the reason for this?" They said among themselves: "Some being of ruined fortune has joined our company, and that is why we have come back with empty hands and empty bowls." And they said further: "Let us investigate — we will divide into two groups and go." They divided into two groups and set out; and whichever group Welcome had joined returned with empty hands and empty bowls. Then those in the other group also split into two and set out, and whichever group Welcome had joined returned with empty hands and empty bowls.

They too returned with empty hands and empty bowls. Again those in that group split into two and set out, and the very same thing happened. And so it continued, time after time — until eventually Welcome and another beggar entered together alone, and when they separated, Welcome came back with empty hands and empty bowls, while all the others came back with hands full and bowls full. Then those beggars said: "This being of ruined fortune has joined our company, and that is why we have come back with empty hands and empty bowls." And they beat Welcome severely, broke his head with a begging bowl, and drove him away, saying: "You bringer of ill fortune, be gone from here!"

Now the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to come at midday to another house. He gave instructions to those in his household who were to prepare the curds and provisions: "Good people, until the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha has been served at midday, do not let any beggar enter. Serve them afterward." When the beggars then began to press their way in, the doorkeepers turned them back. The beggars said: "Hey, good steward! This house is known by the name of our patron — the householder Sudatta — as Anāthapiṇḍada, the Provider of Food for the Friendless. So why do you turn us away?" But the doorkeepers replied: "Good people, look here — has that ill-fated one not crept in among us?" They looked, and when they saw that Welcome had indeed entered among them, they said: "There is the bringer of ill fortune!" They beat Welcome severely, broke his head with a begging bowl, seized him by his hands and feet, dragged him off, laid him on a heap of rags, and said: "You bringer of ill fortune — sit there!" And Welcome sat upon that heap of rags, weeping.

Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and, surrounded by the assembly of monks and preceded by the Saṅgha of monks, set out in the direction of the dwelling-place of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One saw Welcome sitting upon that heap of rags with his head split open, blood trickling down, weeping. Upon seeing this, the Blessed One spoke to the monks: "Monks, even a being who is in his last existence can be reduced to such a condition as this. Let him be satiated with existences, let him be satiated with the requisites of existence."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, you shall leave the remains of your bowl for Welcome." The Blessed One then went to the dwelling-place of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, arrived there, and took his seat upon the prepared throne at the head of the Saṅgha of monks. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, knowing that the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, satisfied and strengthened them from his own hand with many varieties of pure and choice foods and provisions. Having satisfied and refreshed them with many varieties of pure and choice foods and provisions from his own hand, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished his midday meal and had set aside his bowl, he took a seat lower down and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. And the Venerable Ānanda forgot to leave the remains of his bowl for Welcome.

Since the buddhas and Blessed Ones are by their very nature incapable of forgetfulness, the Blessed One himself left the remains of his bowl for Welcome. Then, when the Venerable Ānanda began to take away the Blessed One's bowl, he remembered that the Blessed One had told him to leave the remains of the bowl for Welcome, and he began to weep. The Blessed One said to him, "Ānanda, why do you weep?" "Venerable sir, I forgot to leave the remains of the bowl for Welcome, and in so doing I have broken the Blessed One's command." The Blessed One replied, "Ānanda, you have not broken my command. It is rather that Welcome's own karmic obscuration caused you to forget to leave him the remains of the bowl. Now go, Ānanda, and call Welcome."

So Ānanda went and called out, "Welcome! Welcome!" Many voices answered, "Here!" and each of them thought, "Whom does the Blessed One, teacher of the three worlds, have in mind today?" The Venerable Ānanda returned and asked, "Venerable sir, when I called out 'Welcome! Welcome!' many voices answered 'Here!' — which one am I to bring?" The Blessed One replied, "Go and call out these words: 'Welcome — the son of the householder Wise One, the hunter who slays crocodile cubs — come here!'"

The Venerable Ānanda went and called out those very words. Welcome, hearing his own name called, then spoke these verses:

The name "Welcome" has slipped away —
from where could I come here now?
What was ill-fated has been exhausted,
and what is good has truly come.
Those who take refuge in you —
their protector is the Omniscient One.
Those who delight in your words,
those noble ones — they are the truly welcome.
As for me, I am bereft of good fortune:
abandoned by all kin and companions,
having reached a harsh and fearful state,
I am tormented by the sting of grief.

The Venerable Ānanda led him back and presented him, saying, "Venerable sir, this is Welcome." The Blessed One said, "My son, will you eat the remains of the Blessed One's bowl?" "I ask this of the Blessed One." The Blessed One gave him the remains of the bowl. When Welcome saw how little there was, he thought to himself, "Even though the Blessed One, teacher of the three worlds, has thought of me in a hundred ways, he has left only a small amount of bowl-scraps for me." The Blessed One, knowing his thought with his own mind, said, "My son Welcome, even if you were to eat food in quantities the size of Mount Meru and drink in quantities the size of the great ocean, as long as you were not yet satisfied, the remains of the Tathāgata's bowl would still not be exhausted."

Welcome ate the remains of the Blessed One's bowl. When he was satisfied, he began to gaze at the Blessed One's face. The Blessed One asked, "My son Welcome, are you satisfied?" "Blessed One, I am satisfied." "Now drink the last drop of water, and it will vanish." He took it, and it vanished.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then asked, "Blessed One, who is this?" The Blessed One replied, "Householder, this is Welcome — the son of the householder Wise One, the hunter who slays crocodile cubs." "Blessed One, then he is my younger brother's companion's son!" "Householder, he is indeed."

Then the Blessed One gave a discourse of thanks, rose from his seat, and departed. That being of final existence followed step by step behind the Blessed One, and went with him to the monastery, where the Blessed One took his seat on the throne laid out before the community of monks. Welcome, too, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side.

The Blessed One, thinking to himself, "I should now purify this one's karma," then spoke to Welcome. "Welcome, do you have any kārṣāpaṇas?" "Blessed One, I have none." The Blessed One said, "Son, look in the fold of your robe." Welcome looked, and saw that there were exactly two kārṣāpaṇas. He said, "Blessed One, there are." The Blessed One said, "Son, go to the Joyful Grove, to Prince Duṃba's enclosure, and bring back some blue utpala lotuses."

Welcome replied, "As the Blessed One commands," and having received the instruction from the Blessed One, he set off toward the Joyful Grove where Prince Duṃba was. Prince Duṃba, seeing him coming from a great distance, thought to himself, "This troublemaker — wherever he comes from, his arrival will surely bring harm to me. Some such situation will arise." And so he said, "Troublemaker, do not enter the Joyful Grove!"

Welcome then spoke in verse:

I do not seek the utpala for myself,
nor do I need the lotus for my own sake.
I am the messenger of him who is renowned
as all-knowing — the Lord of Sages.

Duṃba replied in verse:

If the Sage, the peaceful one himself,
the object of worship for gods and men,
if you are the messenger of that supremely worthy
object of veneration, then come forward.

Duṃba asked, "Are you the messenger of the Buddha?" Welcome answered, "I am indeed the Buddha's messenger." "What have you come for?" "I have come for some utpala lotuses." "Go — take as many as you wish."

Welcome took up a load of blue utpala lotuses and went before the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Welcome, distribute them among the monks." Welcome began to distribute the blue utpala lotuses among the monks, but the monks did not accept them. The Blessed One then said, "Monks, all fragrant things are beneficial to the eyes, and it will also serve to purify this one's karma — please accept them." The monks then took the flowers.

Now, Welcome's previously exhausted capacity for perceiving blue had been restored, so as he sat there at the edge of the elder's assembly, he saw the monks holding the blue utpala lotuses in their hands. And upon seeing them, his capacity for perceiving blue, which had been so long exhausted, manifested fully once again.

The Blessed One then said, "Welcome, why have you not gone forth?" "Blessed One, I will go forth." The Blessed One gave him the going forth (pravrajyā) and conferred full ordination (upasaṃpadā) upon him, and then gave him instruction.

Having thus gone forth, living alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, diligence, and dwelling in earnest — in that very way in which the sons of good family, having cut their hair and beard and donned the ochre robes, go forth from home into homelessness out of genuine faith — he realized and directly accomplished, through his own direct knowledge, the unsurpassed pinnacle of the holy life, and in that very life he achieved it: "My birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done."

He became one who knows: "There is no further existence beyond this." He became an arhat, freed from attachment, beyond the three realms — one whose mind is equal toward clay and gold, equal toward the sky and the palm of the hand. As when sandalwood is placed upon a blade, his awareness split open the sheath of ignorance. He attained gnosis, the superknowledges, and the individual perfect understandings. He turned his back on the gains and honors of existence and worldly desire. And he came to be worshipped, revered, and openly praised by the gods, both those with power and those under their sway.

Then, when the venerable Svāgata attained arhatship and experienced the joy and bliss of liberation, he spoke these verses:

He who sees things as they truly are
bound me with the lasso of his skillful means.
As a great aging elephant is drawn from the mud,
with his compassion he drew me from the mire of suffering.

Formerly, I was of ill arrival;
after him, of ill arrival I remained.
Now, by the power of your words, O Mighty Sage,
I have become truly of good arrival.

I, like iron in the presence of the omniscient one,
heard your supreme speech —
and now I have attained a body like gold,
undefiled and without outflow.

Whether seeking material riches, or the higher realms, or liberation,
it is excellent to rely upon a spiritual friend
who always wishes one's genuine benefit.

This is the sixty-fifth fascicle of the Vinayavibhaṅga.

Now, at the time when the venerable Svāgata had gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, other learned non-Buddhist adherents (tīrthikas) were saying: "The ascetic Gautama's teaching is entirely beautiful in all respects." But then, seeing that even fools like Svāgata and others were being admitted into it, they spoke in disparagement, saying: "How can his teaching be beautiful in all respects?" They sneered, gossiped, and spread slander.

The Blessed One considered: "These common crowds speak slightingly of a great śrāvaka who is like Mount Meru. If his virtues are to be proclaimed, where should it be done? It should be done in the very place where he was born and where he fell." And so the Blessed One so considered.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'The Tathāgata is going on a begging round through the village of the Aṅgas. Whoever among you wishes to go on the begging round through the Aṅga village together with the Tathāgata, let them take their robes.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having listened to the Blessed One, he announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One is going on a begging round through the Aṅga village. Whoever among you wishes to go on the begging round through the Aṅga village together with the Blessed One, let them take their robes."

Then the Blessed One — tamed, with a tamed retinue; at peace, with a peaceful retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue; at ease, with an at-ease retinue; restrained, with a restrained retinue; an arhat, with a retinue of arhats; free from attachment, with a retinue free from attachment; resplendent, with a resplendent retinue — surrounded by a herd of bulls as by a supreme bull among the herd; surrounded by young elephants as by a great elephant; surrounded by a pride of fanged beasts as by a lion; surrounded by a flock of geese as by a king of geese; surrounded by flocks of birds as by a garuḍa; surrounded by students as by a brahmin —

surrounded by a throng of the sick as by a skilled physician; surrounded by a troop of warriors as by a hero; surrounded by a company of travelers as by a guide who knows the terrain; surrounded by a host of merchants as by a caravan leader; surrounded by an assembly of retinue as by a merchant lord; surrounded by a throng of ministers as by a king of a fortress; surrounded by a company of a thousand sons as by a wheel-turning king; surrounded by a multitude of stars as by the moon; surrounded by a thousand rays of light as by the sun; surrounded by a host of gandharvas as by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, guardian of the realm; surrounded by a host of kinnaras as by a noble man of excellence; surrounded by a host of nāgas as by Virūpākṣa; surrounded by a host of yakṣas as by Vaiśravaṇa, the giver of wealth; surrounded by a host of asuras as by Prahrāda of the copper mountain; surrounded by the throng of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three as by Śakra; surrounded by the assembly of the Brahmā realms as by Brahmā —

his senses supremely tamed; his deportment and conduct unagitated; still as a deep ocean; laden with water as a cloud; free from arrogance as a lord among great elephants; beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being; his body splendidly embellished with the eighty minor marks; his body ornamented with a halo a fathom in breadth; possessed of a radiance surpassing a thousand suns; wholly excellent in every direction as a moving mountain of precious gems; endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of exclusive mindfulness, and great compassion —

with the great śrāvakas Kauṇḍinya the All-Knower, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāma, Śrāvaka, Pūrṇa, Nirmala, Gavāṃpati, and Subāhu, and others, together with a great multitude of the Saṅgha of monks surrounding him and preceding him, he was traveling on a tour of inspection through the country of the sons of the Mallas when he arrived at Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain and took up residence in a fearsome forest thicket on that mountain, in the wilderness haunted by wild beasts.

The brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain heard that the Blessed One, while traveling on a tour of inspection through the country of the sons of the Mallas, had arrived at Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain and was residing in a fearsome forest thicket on that mountain, in the wilderness haunted by wild beasts. Having heard this, they gathered together in groups from assembly to assembly, from district to district, came forth from Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived there, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain with a Dharma-laden discourse in the proper manner. By means of many kinds of Dharma-laden discourse he instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened them thoroughly, and then fell silent.

Then the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain rose from their seats, folded their hands toward the Blessed One in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, would the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks be so gracious as to accept a meal from us tomorrow?"

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent and saying nothing to the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain. Then the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had consented, bowed their heads to the Blessed One's feet, and departed from his presence.

That very same night the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain prepared pure and excellent food and drink, and rising early the next morning they arranged seats and set out water vessels. They then invited the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable one, if it pleases you, the time has come. May the Blessed One be so gracious as to consider that the hour is right."

Then the Blessed One, in the morning, dressed in his lower robe and, taking up his bowl and outer robe, went surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, and proceeded to the place where the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain had invited him. He arrived there and took his seat on the prepared throne at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain, seeing that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, served and satisfied them with pure and excellent food and drink from their own hands, in many and various kinds. Having served them and satisfied them abundantly with pure and excellent food and drink of many kinds from their own hands, when they saw that the Blessed One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, they took lower seats and seated themselves before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Having seated themselves, the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has tamed malevolent nāgas and malevolent yakṣas such as Sogatama and others dwelling in the wilderness and such places — so too, Venerable One, this nāga Āmra-Riverbank has long harbored resentment toward us who have no quarrel with him, he seeks to compete with those who do not compete with him, he causes harm to those who do no harm, and he ruins the harvest of crops. Ah, may the Blessed One out of his compassionate care subdue this nāga Āmra-Riverbank for us."

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent and saying nothing to the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain. Then the Blessed One instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain thoroughly with a Dharma-laden discourse in the proper manner. By means of many kinds of Dharma-laden discourse he instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened them thoroughly, then rose from his seat and departed.

The Blessed One then proceeded to the place where the monastery was and arrived there, taking his seat on the prepared throne at the head of the Saṅgha of monks. Having seated himself, the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'Whichever of you wishes to tame the nāga Āmra-Riverbank, take a toothstick.' Then distribute toothsticks to the Saṅgha."

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard the Blessed One's words, he announced to the monks: "Whichever of you wishes to tame the nāga Āmra-Riverbank, take a toothstick." He then began to distribute toothsticks to the Saṅgha. But the Blessed One did not take a toothstick, and the elder monks, the senior elders, reflected to themselves —

— wondered to themselves why the Blessed One had not taken a toothstick. Perceiving that the Blessed One wished to proclaim the virtues of the venerable Śubhāṅga, they likewise refrained from taking toothsticks.

The venerable Śubhāṅga thought to himself: "Why have the Blessed One and the elder monks, the senior elders, not taken toothsticks?" Perceiving that they wished to proclaim his virtues, he resolved to fulfil the intention of the Teacher. He rose halfway from his seat, extended his arm like the trunk of a great elephant, and took a toothstick.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, which elder monk took a toothstick?"

"Venerable One, it was the venerable Śubhāṅga."

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, go to the monk Śubhāṅga and tell him this: 'That nāga is venomous — guard the faculties of your body.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard the Blessed One's words, he went to the venerable Śubhāṅga and said: "Venerable Śubhāṅga, the Blessed One has declared: 'That nāga is venomous — guard the faculties of your body.'"

The venerable Śubhāṅga replied: "Venerable Ānanda, I obey the Teacher's command. Yet even if this entire Jambudvīpa were filled to the brim with nāgas like Āmra-Riverbank — as a grove of sugarcane, a thicket of reeds, or a forest of rushes — they could not so much as stir a single tip of my hair. How then could they obstruct the faculties of my body? For I have thoroughly and repeatedly cultivated all four bases of miraculous power in the presence of the Blessed One, having practised them again and again."

Then the venerable Śubhāṅga, when that very night had passed, dressed himself in the early morning, took his almsbowl and robes, and entered the lane of Crocodile-Child-Killer to go on almsround. Having made his almsround through the lane of Crocodile-Child-Killer, he went to the dwelling of the nāga Āmra-Riverbank.

The nāga Āmra-Riverbank saw the venerable Śubhāṅga coming from afar. Upon seeing him, the nāga thought: "Has this ascetic heard that I am deadly? Why else would he come to my abode? For the moment, this is sudden — let him come." Then the venerable Śubhāṅga set his water-strainer and almsbowl to one side, shook out his patchwork robe, washed his two feet, rinsed his two hands, drew water, plucked leaves that had fallen there, sat down, and began to attend to his meal.

When the venerable Śubhāṅga had finished his meal, he reflected: "A venomous nāga, if not provoked, is not a fit subject for taming. Since this one is venomous, I shall provoke it." He washed his almsbowl, and poured the bowl-washing water into the nāga's pond. The nāga Āmra-Riverbank was disturbed by this, and thought: "This ascetic arrived and even ate his fill here, yet I let it pass. Now he insults me and pollutes my abode with his bowl-washing water. This ascetic is clearly not someone who dwells at peace." Enraged, the nāga rose up into the sky above, unleashed a great crash of thunder, and began to rain down upon the venerable Śubhāṅga all manner of weapons: single-pronged vajras, discuses, great arrows, single-pointed spears, and the like.

The venerable Śubhāṅga entered into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, and those weapons were transformed into divine flowers — blue lotuses, lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses — and fell upon the body of the venerable Śubhāṅga. The nāga Āmra-Riverbank then began to rain down a shower of flaming arrows, and the venerable Śubhāṅga, entering into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, caused those flaming arrows to be transformed into divine mandāra flowers, which fell upon his body. The nāga Āmra-Riverbank then began to rain down a shower of burning embers, and the venerable Śubhāṅga, entering into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, caused those embers to be transformed into powdered divine aloe wood, powdered sandalwood, powdered costus, and powdered tamāla leaves, which fell upon his body. The nāga Āmra-Riverbank then released smoke by the power of his rage, and the venerable Śubhāṅga likewise dispelled it by the power of his miraculous ability. The nāga Āmra-Riverbank then kindled fire by the power of his rage, and the venerable Śubhāṅga entered into meditative equipoise within the element of fire. Then, from the great radiance that arose through the combined power of the nāga Āmra-Riverbank's rage and the venerable Śubhāṅga's miraculous ability, the brahmin householders of Crocodile-Child-Slaying Mountain said to one another: "Friends, this is the Blessed One taming the nāga Āmra-Riverbank."

Then the Blessed One said to the monks: "Among my śrāvaka monks who again and again enter into meditative equipoise within the element of fire, this — namely the monk Śubhāṅga — is the foremost."

When the nāga Āmra-Riverbank had exhausted all his weapons and began to flee, the venerable Śubhāṅga manifested fire on all sides, so that the nāga Āmra-Riverbank saw everything blazing, burning intensely, and flaring up on every side into a single mass of flame — with only the space at the feet of the venerable Śubhāṅga appearing calm. The nāga then went to where the venerable Śubhāṅga was, approached him, and said: "Venerable Śubhāṅga, why do you do this to me? It is I who am subject to aging — it is not fitting that I should challenge you; rather, it is you who have challenged me. Had I not attained such a gathering of qualities, you would this very day have left nothing of me but a name." Śubhāṅga said: "Venerable Āmra-Riverbank, what shall I do? Tell me." "Come now, fair one. Go into the presence of the Blessed One, take refuge, and take up the training precepts."

Then the venerable Śubhāṅga placed the nāga Āmra-Riverbank into his almsbowl, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Sitting thus to one side, the venerable Śubhāṅga said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, here is the nāga Āmra-Riverbank." The Blessed One then spoke: "Fair one, formerly, through your misdeeds, you have now been born in the wretched animal realm of existence — violent, red-handed, given to harm and extreme harm, robbing others of their lives, inciting the killing of others' lives, living by the slaying of others' lives. When you pass from here, what will your destiny be? What will your rebirth be? What will your future life be?"

The Blessed One declared: "Fair one, come here, take refuge before me, undertake the training precepts, and grant fearlessness to the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain." The nāga replied: "Venerable sir, I take refuge before the Blessed One, I accept the training precepts, and from this day forward I grant fearlessness to the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain."

Then the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain, taking up many female birds as gifts, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed their heads to the two feet of the Blessed One, and sat to one side. Sitting thus to one side, the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, has the Blessed One tamed the nāga Āmra-Riverbank?" The Blessed One declared: "I did not tame the nāga Āmra-Riverbank. The monk Subhāṅga tamed the nāga Āmra-Riverbank." They then said: "Venerable Subhāṅga — who tamed the crocodile-child-killing mountain householder — is Subhāṅga, the son of the wise householder." And then some said: "He is the son of our father's brother." Others said: "He is our nephew." Others said: "He is our maternal uncle." And still others said: "He is the son of our younger friend." And they offered him many female birds as gifts.

Then the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One together with the monastic Saṅgha of monks be pleased, through the venerable Subhāṅga's merit, to accept our offering of a canopy meal for seven days." The Blessed One consented to the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain by remaining silent. Then the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed their heads to the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Now on the crocodile-child-killing mountain there was a brahmin, the younger companion of the wise householder, who was a snake-charmer. He had fled to Śrāvastī out of fear of the nāga Āmra-Riverbank, and the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, had appointed him as superintendent of the royal elephant stables and installed him there. He had gone back to the crocodile-child-killing mountain on some business, and there he heard how the venerable Subhāṅga, son of the wise householder, had tamed the nāga Āmra-Riverbank. On hearing this, he went to where the venerable Subhāṅga was, arrived there, bowed his head to the two feet of the venerable Subhāṅga, and sat to one side. Sitting thus to one side, that brahmin said to the venerable Subhāṅga: "Venerable Subhāṅga, would you be pleased to accept my canopy meal tomorrow at my home?" The venerable Subhāṅga replied: "Brahmin, the brahmins and householders of the crocodile-child-killing mountain have invited me — on account of me — to a canopy meal for seven days for the Buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks. I cannot come." The brahmin said: "If you will not accept now, then when you come to Śrāvastī, please accept my almsfood first of all." The venerable Subhāṅga said: "So be it." And he rose and departed.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed as long as he wished at the crocodile-child-killing mountain, set out wandering on tour toward Śrāvastī, and travelling on by stages he arrived at Śrāvastī and took up residence in the Jeta Grove there, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada (Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada — "feeder of the destitute").

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One had set out wandering on tour toward Śrāvastī through the region of the Aṅga people and had arrived at Śrāvastī and was residing in the Jeta Grove, in his own park. Having heard this, he came out from Śrāvastī, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Sitting thus to one side, the Blessed One instructed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with a Dharma-filled discourse, rightly showing him, rightly causing him to take hold of it, rightly encouraging him, and rightly delighting him. In many and various ways, with a Dharma-filled discourse, he rightly showed, rightly caused him to take hold, rightly encouraged, and rightly delighted him, and then fell silent.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, joined his palms and bowed in the direction of the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, would you kindly consent — together with the monastic Saṅgha of monks — to accept tomorrow a canopy meal at my residence?" The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by remaining silent, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The brahmin Sarpaskandhin heard that the Blessed One had set out wandering on tour toward Śrāvastī through the region of the Aṅga people and had arrived at Śrāvastī and was residing in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Having heard this, he went to where the venerable Subhāṅga was, and having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the venerable Subhāṅga's feet and sat down to one side. Sitting thus to one side, the venerable Subhāṅga instructed that brahmin with a Dharma-filled teaching, rightly showing him, rightly causing him to take hold of it, rightly encouraging him, and rightly delighting him. In many and various ways, with a Dharma-filled teaching, he rightly showed, rightly caused him to take hold, rightly encouraged, and rightly delighted him, and then fell silent.

Then that brahmin rose from his seat, joined his palms and bowed in the direction of the venerable Subhāṅga, and said this to the venerable Subhāṅga: "Venerable Subhāṅga, would you kindly consent to accept a canopy meal at my residence tomorrow?" The brahmin replied: "Inquire of the Blessed One."

Then the venerable Subhāṅga said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, that brahmin has come to me and requests, by way of a word of invitation, that I go elsewhere for tomorrow's canopy meal — may I be lent out?" The Blessed One declared: "The prior invitation shall be honored." The venerable Subhāṅga consented to that brahmin by remaining silent. Then that brahmin, understanding that the venerable Subhāṅga had consented by remaining silent, prostrated with his head at the venerable Subhāṅga's feet and departed from the venerable Subhāṅga's presence.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, that very night, had pure and excellent food and drink prepared in advance,

In the morning, rising early, seats were arranged and water vessels set out. Then an invitation was sent to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, we request that you be pleased to attend the canopy meal; may the Blessed One be pleased to come at the appropriate time." Then, in the early morning, the Blessed One dressed, took up his alms bowl and robes, and, surrounded on all sides by the assembly of monks, with the monastic Saṅgha going before him, proceeded to the place of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's canopy meal and arrived there. He took his seat in the place prepared, at the head of the monastic Saṅgha. That brahmin, meanwhile, had also prepared pure and excellent food in advance for the venerable Subhāṅga. And so the venerable Subhāṅga too, in the early morning, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl and robes, and went to that brahmin's place of the canopy meal, arriving there and sitting down upon the seat that had been laid out.

Then that brahmin, seeing that the venerable Subhāṅga was seated comfortably, satisfied him with pure and excellent food. The brahmin then thought: "The venerable Subhāṅga has eaten the excellent food and will be unable to digest it." And so he said to the venerable Subhāṅga: "Venerable Subhāṅga, will you drink some digestive drink tomorrow?" Subhāṅga replied: "I will drink." Then the brahmin dipped his finger into a large vessel of elephant liquor and stirred it into a cup of plain water, and offered this to the venerable Subhāṅga. Now, arhats do not bring into action knowledge and vision that they have not deliberately applied; and so the venerable Subhāṅga drank it. Having offered his words of thanks, he rose from his seat and departed.

Then, as he was passing through Śrāvastī along a street covered with a reed awning, the rays of the sun struck his body, and right there, overcome by the force of the liquor, he collapsed to the ground. Since it is the nature of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to be free from forgetfulness, the Blessed One emanated a clump of leaves that were not real leaves and covered him with it.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, knowing that the Blessed One and the rest of the monastic Saṅgha were seated at ease, with his own hands satisfied them and served them in abundance with pure and excellent food and drink. In many ways and on many occasions he satisfied them and attended upon them with pure and excellent food and drink by his own hand. Knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal and set aside his alms bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, with Dharma-endowed words of instruction, properly taught, properly guided, properly encouraged, and properly gladdened the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. In many ways, with Dharma-endowed words of instruction, he properly taught, properly guided, properly encouraged, and properly gladdened him. Then, having given words of thanks, he rose from his seat, departed, and went in that direction.

Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn the supernatural feat he had performed, addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, is this not the very monk named Subhāṅga who tamed the nāga on the shore of the Āmra stream? Monks, what do you think — is this monk Subhāṅga now capable of taming even a baby snake?" "Venerable one, certainly not." "Monks, in that case, such faults as these, and others besides, arise from drinking intoxicants. Therefore, monks, those who call me their teacher shall not drink anything intoxicating — not so much as a drop on a blade of grass — nor shall they cause others to drink."

Then the Blessed One caused the venerable Subhāṅga to awaken and asked him: "Subhāṅga, why has this come to pass?" "Blessed One, I did not think. Sugata, I did not think."

Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall and, having arrived, took his seat on the prepared throne before the community of monks. Having seated himself, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, it is on account of seeing ten benefits that a rule of training in the Vinaya is to be established for the hearers" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: if one drinks grain liquor or prepared liquor that causes intoxication, it is an offense entailing a downfall.

What is meant by grain liquor? It is a drink made from grain, a drink made from flour, or a drink made from fermented mash. What is meant by prepared liquor? It is a drink made from roots, a drink made from wood, a drink made from leaves, a drink made from flowers, or a drink made from fruit. When both are mixed together, that is called grain liquor and prepared liquor. What is meant by 'if one drinks it'? It means swallowing it down the throat. What is meant by 'an offense entailing a downfall'? It burns one, scorches one, and causes one to fall into the hells, into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts, into bad rebirths, into states of ruin. Furthermore, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs wholesome qualities — and for this reason it is said to entail a downfall.

Now, how does a downfall come about? If a monk drinks something possessing the color that causes intoxication, and the smell that causes intoxication, and the taste that causes intoxication, and the sensation that causes intoxication, and having drunk it becomes intoxicated, it constitutes an offense entailing a downfall. If having drunk it he does not become intoxicated, it constitutes a minor offense. If a monk drinks something possessing the color that causes intoxication, and the smell that causes intoxication, and the taste that causes intoxication, and having drunk it becomes intoxicated, it constitutes an offense entailing a downfall. If having drunk it he does not become intoxicated, it constitutes a minor offense. If a monk drinks something possessing the color that causes intoxication and the smell that causes intoxication, and having drunk it becomes intoxicated, it constitutes an offense entailing a downfall. If having drunk it he does not become intoxicated, it constitutes a minor offense. As for drinking something that possesses only the color that causes intoxication, unmixed with anything else — there is no offense in that, for it has become merely brine.

If a monk drinks grain liquor, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If he drinks prepared liquor, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If he drinks grain liquor and prepared liquor together, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If a monk drinks the yeast of grain liquor, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If a monk eats grain husks, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If a monk eats grain stalks, it is an offense entailing a downfall. If a monk eats the sediment of liquor, it is a minor offense. If a monk eats flowers or fruits that cause intoxication, it is a minor offense. There is no offense in drinking boiled liquor, in carrying it on a physician's prescription for someone with a mouth ailment, or in using it to rinse the body along with threads. There is no offense for one who acts for the first time, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

The monks, having doubts, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubts: "Venerable one, what action did the venerable Subhāṅga perform such that by the ripening of that action he was born into a household of great wealth with abundant riches and many enjoyments? What action did he perform such that by the ripening of that action he entered among the hungry and came to be known by the name Subhāṅga — 'Auspicious' — only in name? What action did he perform such that by the ripening of that action he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and, having abandoned all afflictions, directly realized the state of an arhat?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was this very Subhāṅga, the son of good family, who accumulated those actions."

Actions that transform conditions, that abide like a flame, that will unfailingly come to be — these were performed and accumulated. Since the one called Subhāṅga himself performed and accumulated those actions, who else could experience them individually? Monks, actions that are performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth; they do not ripen in the element of water; they do not ripen in the element of fire; they do not ripen in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous actions that are performed and accumulated ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even across a hundred aeons,
actions do not perish.
When the conditions and the time are met,
their fruits will surely come to be for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago in times gone by, there lived in a certain mountain cliff-dwelling a householder who was wealthy, of great possessions, and with many enjoyments. One day, accompanied by his retinue, he went to a pleasure garden. Now, in an age when no buddhas arise in the world, pratyekabuddhas — solitary buddhas — arise: beings who feel compassion for the lowly and the poor, who delight in remote dwelling-places, who are solitary like a rhinoceros, and who have become worthy recipients of offerings for the world. Such a solitary buddha, a great being, was wandering for alms near that mountain cliff-dwelling. The householder, seeing the solitary buddha from a great distance, instructed those among his household who lived by their share of dairy food: "Wise ones, drive away this renunciant!" But none of them were willing to drive the solitary buddha away. So the householder, annoyed, rose from his seat, seized the solitary buddha himself by the neck, drove him out, and said: "You wretched beggar — go off among the starving!"

And he hurled him into a heap of dirty rags.

The great being, that solitary buddha, then reflected: "This afflicted householder has acted extremely badly. If he is ruined and harmed by this, it would be wrong." Wishing to extend a hand to him from this condition, the solitary buddha, spreading his wings like a king of swans, rose manifest into the sky above, and began to perform miraculous feats — blazing, radiating, bringing rain, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary people are swift to place their trust in supernatural power, and so the householder fell prostrate at the feet of that solitary buddha, like a great tree cut at its root, and said: "O true worthy one, please come down, please come down! Please extend a hand to pull me, sunk in the mud of afflictions, up from my depths!"

Out of compassion for that householder, the solitary buddha descended from the sky above. The householder made offerings to him, prostrated with his head at his feet, and offered this aspiration prayer: "Whatever root of virtue there is in these offerings made to undo the harm I have done to one who is such a true worthy one — may it not be in accord with that portion of the action of harm. By this root of virtue, may I be born into a household of wealth, great possessions, and many enjoyments, and may I attain qualities of such a kind that one can please and not disappoint a Teacher far more supremely excellent than this one."

Monks, that householder of that time and place is none other than this Subhāṅga. Because he made offerings to that solitary buddha and offered that aspiration prayer, by the karmic maturation of that action he has now been born into a household that is wealthy, of great possessions, and with many enjoyments.

By the karmic maturation of that action — the action of having done harm and of having uttered the word "Nyeong" — he was tormented for an aeon in the great hell of Avīci. Then, by the remaining force of that very same action, he wandered for five hundred lifetimes in the state of hunger, being gnawed by starvation, bearing the name "Nyeong." Even to this day he has taken birth among the hungry ghosts and carries the name "Nyeong."

Now, as for the action of having done harm to one who was a perfectly worthy recipient of offerings — instead of coming to accord with that portion of the action, he offered an aspiration prayer to attain qualities of such a kind that one can please and not disappoint a Teacher supremely more excellent than this one. By the karmic maturation of that action, he went forth into my teaching, and by abandoning all afflictions he has directly realized arhatship. He has pleased me, the Teacher who is supremely more excellent than a hundred thousand billion pratyekabuddhas, and has not caused me disappointment.

Monks, what action did the venerable Subhāṅga perform, such that by its karmic maturation the Blessed One has again and again proclaimed him foremost among those who enter meditative absorption in the fire element? This too came about through the power of aspiration. And where was that aspiration made?

Monks, long ago, in a time past, during this very excellent great aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One Kāśyapa. He dwelt near Vārāṇasī, in the deer park in the forest of the Seer who speaks truth. This one went forth into that Teacher's teaching, and the monk by whom he was ordained was again and again proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the perfectly complete buddha Kāśyapa, foremost among those who enter meditative absorption in the fire element.

Now, having practiced the holy life under that Teacher for as long as his life lasted, this one attained not even a portion of the accumulation of qualities. Then, at the time of his death, he offered this aspiration prayer: "Throughout my life I have practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly complete buddha, the unsurpassed recipient of offerings, Kāśyapa, and yet I have attained not even a portion of the accumulation of qualities.
