By this root of virtue of having practiced the holy life for as long as I lived, may the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly complete buddha Kāśyapa, give a prophecy to the brahmin youth Lama, saying: 'Brahmin youth, in a future time, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha and Blessed One called Śākyamuni.' And may I then go forth into the teaching of that prophesied one, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhatship — and just as my preceptor here was proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly complete buddha Kāśyapa, foremost among those who enter meditative absorption in the fire element again and again, may I likewise be proclaimed by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas,

foremost among those who enter meditative absorption in the fire element again and again." Having begun to make this aspiration, by the power of that aspiration he has now been proclaimed by the Tathāgata as foremost among those who enter meditative absorption in the fire element again and again.

Monks, that being so, the karmic maturation of actions that are entirely dark is entirely dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are entirely bright is entirely bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are entirely dark and those that are mixed, and strive for actions that are entirely bright. Monks, you should train accordingly.

Here ends the seventy-ninth rule entailing a transgression through drinking intoxicants.

Summary verse:
Śiva, the matted-hair ascetic, the jewel merchant,
the physician, the Saṅgha, the ladder and the food,
the eaten thing, the one turned harmful, the fierce woman,
the youth, the alms bowl, and the powerful ones.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. On a rocky hillside, a brahmin was living there who had taken a girl from Śrāvastī as his wife. He sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed pleasures with her. A daughter was born to them, and he raised and nurtured her until she grew up.

Business requiring the brahmin's presence in Śrāvastī arose, and he set out in a carriage, riding in dignity. His daughter saw him and said, "Father, where are you going?" The brahmin said, "To Śrāvastī, daughter." The daughter said, "Father, I will come too." The brahmin said, "Daughter, you are on the verge of attaining the highest good, so if someone were to touch your hands or feet, it would be unpleasant for us — stay right here." The daughter began to weep, and her mother said, "Daughter, why do you cry?" The daughter said, "Father is going to Śrāvastī but does not wish to take me there." The mother said, "Take the noble lord's daughter along as well, and she will see her relatives." The brahmin said, "Daughter, she is about to attain the highest good, so if someone were to touch her hands or feet, it would be unpleasant for us — let her stay here." The mother said, "If she travels together with the noble lord's son, she will be well concealed and well protected." So the brahmin had his daughter mount the carriage and set out in dignity.

Because the daughter was of a curious and inquisitive nature, she asked her father: "Father, whose park is this? Whose lotus pond is this? Whose temple is this? Whose pleasure grove is this? Whose well is this? Whose assembly hall is this?" The brahmin said, "Daughter, this is the dwelling place of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan." The daughter said, "Father, let us go there." The brahmin said, "Daughter, in this dwelling place reside those who have gone forth from many different classes and lineages — if someone were to touch your hands or feet, it would be unpleasant for us — come back, let us go on." And they rode away in dignity.

Now, near the town, a large number of brahmin wives and householders' wives who wished to visit the assembly hall had come out to the outskirts of Śrāvastī. They saw that brahmin and said to him, "Welcome, welcome! You have come well. Where have you been for so long?" The brahmin said, "If I were to come just as you all do, where would I be going? I have come to visit the assembly hall in the Jeta Grove."

"Bring this daughter-in-law of yours along as well today. Show her too the assembly hall." And so that girl went together with them to the Jeta Grove.

Now the practice of the group of six was this: "When brahmins and householders come and arrive here, we will teach them the Dharma, defeat our opponents, and spread our own fame." Because of this, one or another of the group of six would always be standing at the gate of the Jeta Grove, never leaving it unattended. The venerable Charka had risen early in the morning, before dawn, had thrown away his tooth-stick, put on his patched robe of reddish-yellow, and was walking back and forth and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove.

Now in the six great cities, there was no one among the inhabitants — whether by lineage, clan, family line, name, physical appearance, craft, or livelihood — whom the group of six did not know or had not seen or heard of or recognized or understood. And so the venerable Charka, seeing from a great distance that large gathering of brahmin wives and householders' wives, called out to them saying: "Welcome, mother of so-and-so! Welcome, wife of so-and-so! Welcome, daughter-in-law of so-and-so! Welcome, daughter of so-and-so! Welcome, sister of so-and-so! You have come well, you have come well! Why do you wander about for so long, like the moon?"

They replied: "Venerable Charka, when the Blessed One so excellently proclaimed that the eight inopportune states are not the time for a person to live the holy life, we find ourselves in a ninth inopportune state — being burdened with the busyness of household life."

Charka said: "Sisters, have you not heard someone recite these words:

When a king afflicted by poison and the like
leaves his duties undone,
both he himself and those duties
come to utter ruin.
And even those very duties,
before they are fully accomplished,
death — the enemy of the world —
will come to take him away."

They said: "Venerable Charka, it is for that very reason that we have come to the pleasure garden to enter the Jeta Grove, to view the assembly hall, and to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and the venerable elder monks."

Charka said: "Sisters, if that is why you have come, then it is excellent — for the Blessed One has also taught that one should draw out what is essential from this body that is without essence. Excellent, excellent! But sisters, go ahead and ask me how one should view it, as one views a spectacle. Sisters, where do you intend to enter?"

"Venerable Charka, we all wish to enter through the main gate and view the assembly hall."

"Sisters, the Blessed One has said:

If a person of wisdom, with a genuinely devoted mind,
takes even a single step toward the stūpas of the buddhas,
even a hundred thousand times the weight in gold
of the river Jambū would not equal that merit."

"That too is excellent! Sisters, have you found some monk who will show you the assembly hall?"

"Noble one, shall we enter with a lamp-holder in hand, or should we look for someone else? Venerable Charka, why look for another monk, having passed you by? Who is there who surpasses you? Please show it to us yourself."

Then the venerable Charka thought to himself: "If I show them the assembly hall, my store of virtue will be entirely depleted. But if I do not show it to them, I will not receive the alms of the one who was burned."

The Blessed One had declared: "Those who lack faith are to be established in perfect faith, tamed, grasped, and properly set in place." Recognizing this, Charka resolved to commit them firmly to virtue and to show them everything in full. He took up various offerings — flowers, incense, and the like — held the lamp-holder in his hand, and began to show them the hall in proper sequence.

"Sisters, this is the Blessed One's perfume chamber, where the Blessed One three times by day and three times by night surveys the world with a buddha's eye, discerning: who has fallen away, who has grown, who has been harmed, who has become distressed, who has become unhappy, who has become harmed and distressed and unhappy, who is inclined toward the lower realms, who is falling toward the lower realms, who has fallen into the lower realms — and raises such beings from the mire of the lower realms and places them in the higher states, liberation, and its fruit. Those sunk in the mire of desire he draws out by the hand. Those bereft of the wealth of the noble ones he places in the sovereignty of the noble wealth. The worlds adorned by the arising of buddhas he causes to be endowed with fruit. The roots of virtue not yet produced he causes to be produced; roots of virtue already produced he causes to ripen; and those that have ripened he causes to be liberated." With this knowledge and vision he acts, even as it is said:

A being venomous as a sea-monster's lair
may yet pass beyond the appointed time —
but the loving-kindness of a buddha toward those to be tamed
does not pass beyond the appointed time.

As a mother ceaselessly attends her only beloved child
and watches over its life,
so too the Tathāgata attends upon those who are to be tamed
and watches over their lives.

The compassion residing in the mind-stream of the omniscient one
is a mare who seeks her foal to be tamed and does not tire.
Loving-kindness toward those wasted by existence and the lower realms
is like the love of a cow for her wasted calf.

"This is the assembly hall of the venerable Kauṇḍinya. It was here that the Blessed One, when the world was in the darkness of ignorance, without a guide, without a full guide, first cleansed the eye of Dharma of the one whose Dharma-eye he purified with the collyrium-stick of the eye of gnosis — the Blessed One who, being the foremost among those who are elders, those who are like regents, those who have long since gone forth, those who visibly practice the holy life, and those who bear aloft the victory banner of the patched robe, is prophesied supreme. It is his stream. And here too, because the Blessed One set in motion the wheel of Dharma endowed with the Dharma — the wheel that no ascetic, brahmin, god, māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world is able to turn back, the wheel that is for the benefit of the many, for the welfare of the many, for their happiness, out of compassion for the world, for the good and benefit and happiness of gods and humans — turning it thrice, in twelve aspects, seek to pay proper reverence at his feet.

"This is the assembly hall of the venerable great Kāśyapa. He was a brahmin like a great sāla tree in its prime — one who abandoned the unsatisfied accumulation of a thousand and went forth; one endowed with six hundred million particles of gold; one possessed of eighty small granaries of golden rice —"

— one who owned eighteen villages of servants; one who owned sixteen villages of dependents; one endowed with a beautiful fair-skinned body surpassing even gold — who cast all that aside as one casts away the ash of dried spittle, and who, in the last watch of the night, took up a patched robe of stitched cloth worth a hundred thousand, going forth for the sake of whatever arhats dwelled in the world, dwelling in the forest to cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna), liberation, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment — one at whose very sight even rutting bull elephants are freed from their pride; one who, having accepted the undertaking to make Bumangs a place of offering, received the vows of a monk (bhikṣu); one whom the Blessed One likewise proclaimed among monks — "Among my monk-disciples who are of few desires, who are content, and who speak of the virtues of training, the foremost is this one: the monk Mahākāśyapa" — one praised by the Blessed One. Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Śāriputra — the one who attained the highest fruit; one who, at the age of sixteen, having read the grammar of the Indra tradition, refuted all opponents; one who went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One; one whom the Blessed One proclaimed the foremost among those of great wisdom and great eloquence; one of whom the Blessed One declared that all the world together does not amount even to a sixteenth part of him, and whom the Blessed One praised in verse:

Whatever wisdom all the world may hold,
the gods included — all of it combined
would not suffice to be one sixteenth part
of Śāriputra's wisdom, it is said.

And even if this entire world with its gods
were equal to Śāriputra in his wisdom,
still it would not suffice to be one sixteenth part
of the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana — one who was heir to an uncrowned kingdom among the Manadons and went forth; one by whose miraculous powers the palace called Vijayanta belonging to Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, was shaken three times, rocked completely, and shaken thoroughly with his right big toe; one by whose miraculous powers the Blessed One traveled to the world-realm Prabhāvatī in seven days and nights; one whom the Blessed One proclaimed the foremost among those of great miraculous powers and great might. Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Aniruddha — one who went forth from among men of good fortune; one who is the son of the Blessed One's father's brother, whose very name, when properly proclaimed, causes merchants who are sailing across the great ocean in well-built vessels to arrive safely; one whom the Blessed One proclaimed the foremost among those possessing the divine eye. Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Ānanda — one who for a long time served the Blessed One; one who attended close at the feet of the Buddha, the Blessed One; one truly praised by the Teacher; one who lived the pure life of Brahmā; one truly honored by the wise; one who went forth from among the sons of the Blessed One's father's brothers; one whom the Blessed One proclaimed the foremost among those of great learning, those who retain what they have heard, and those who accumulate learning. Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Nandana — one who went forth from a son born of the Blessed One's younger brother Śru, who, had he not gone forth, would have become a wheel-turning king of great power.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Śrākāvin — one whom the Blessed One proclaimed the foremost among those who restrain the gates of the senses. Seek to pay proper reverence at his feet here as well.

This is the assembly hall of the venerable Nandaka. This is that of Aniruddha. This is that of Chanda. This is that of Lāghava. This is that of Nabasa. This is my assembly hall. Shall we look at this one too? Noble one, having looked at all the assembly halls, shall we not then look at the assembly hall of the noble Cāraka? We very much wish to look at this assembly hall of the noble Cāraka. Sisters, do as you wish.

Now, the venerable Cāraka was one who had indulged in sensual pleasures, and so in his assembly hall the floor was smeared with a paste of black beans, the walls were variegated and neatly painted, beds stuffed with the wool of young lambs were laid out, jars filled with drink were set in place along with vessels containing them, and within the store-room there were various provisions in abundance.

The venerable Cāraka spoke to the very many wives of brahmins and householders who had come to his assembly hall: "Sisters, who is going to serve the drink? Or will you simply drink? Noble one, does a river flow backwards? Whatever it is we would ask of you, do you in turn grant it to us. Give us what we lack." "Sisters, what do you lack?" "Noble one, the hearing of Dharma." "Sisters, the Blessed One has well declared that six things arising in the world are wonderful and rare. What are these six? The Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha; the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata; being human; being born in a central land; having no deficiency in one's faculties; and having aspiration toward wholesome things. Therefore, this aspiration toward wholesome things that has arisen in you is like the arising of a buddha. Excellent! Excellent! Sisters, be seated, and I shall teach you the Dharma." They bowed at his two feet and sat before him to hear the Dharma, and he began to teach them the Dharma.

Vinaya Analysis, the sixty-sixth fascicle.

Now that girl, being by nature fond of spectacle, was looking at pictures and wandered off elsewhere. The others, having heard the Dharma, bowed at the two feet of the venerable Cāraka and departed from the assembly hall. The girl, unaware that the others had left, remained in the very entrance hall, looking at pictures. When the venerable Cāraka had seen the others out and was about to enter the assembly hall, he saw that girl sitting in the entrance hall and said to her: "Girl, have you not gone?" She gave a smile, and Cāraka accosted her and laid hold of her limbs and extremities — he groped her all over. The girl wept, came out, and went to her father, saying: "Father, the ascetic Cāraka has violated my person." The brahmin thought to himself: "If I say even a little about this now, I am alone, and —"

"These many people will become a source of harm to me — that is the kind of situation this will turn into. When I have found allies, I shall have this arrow reversed." Between the Jeta Grove and Śrāvastī there stood a great roadside tree, and beneath it a brahmin sat giving instruction in the secret brahmanical recitations to some five hundred brahmin youths. That brahmin said to them: "Wise ones, the ascetic Cāraka has violated my young daughter. You are fellow practitioners of brahmanical celibacy with me — help me!" The brahmins, being utterly without hesitation, took up their staves and went there. The venerable Cāraka was standing and walking near the gate of the Jeta Grove, and they seized him and began to drag him away, yet they could not move him at all. The Blessed One, knowing the moment ripe for taming, caused Cāraka's strength to wane, and then they were able to drag the venerable Cāraka back and forth and carry him off.

The venerable Cāraka thought to himself: "Surely the Blessed One is aware that I have come to harm, to distress, and to discomfort?" And he reflected: "Since the Blessed One is aware of this, and since this is the last instruction he will give on this matter, it is better to let myself be led away."

Now the Blessed One, knowing that King Prasenajit of Kosala lay sleeping on the floor of his upper chamber, roused him with a snapping of fingers and declared: "Great King, you should investigate carefully and not be hasty." The Blessed One roused King Prasenajit of Kosala, who lay sleeping on the floor of his upper chamber, a second time and a third time with a snapping of fingers, and declared: "Great King, you should investigate carefully and not be hasty."

The brahmins, meanwhile, brought the venerable Cāraka to the gate of the royal palace. At the gate of the royal palace, a great crowd of common people raised a loud uproar and clamor: "The brahmins have seized the ascetic Cāraka and brought him to the king's gate!" King Prasenajit of Kosala, lying on the floor of his upper chamber, was awakened by the noise of the crowd, and he said to his night attendants: "Wise ones, why is this crowd of common people making such a loud uproar and clamor?" They replied: "Your divine majesty, the reverend Cāraka, a brahmin's daughter, a brahmin, and some five hundred brahmin youths have all come and are gathered in a tumultuous crowd at the palace gate."

King Prasenajit of Kosala thought to himself: "It is with this in mind that the Blessed One declared to me, 'Great King, you should investigate carefully and not be hasty.'" And he understood it clearly.

Now it is the custom in Śrāvastī that whenever a great dispute arises, drums are beaten and conch shells are blown. So King Prasenajit commanded his night attendants: "Wise ones, beat the great drum and blow the conch!" They beat the drum and blew the conch, and the assembly gathered together with the king. The king said: "Let that brahmin and the reverend Cāraka be brought inside." When the two had come in, the king said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, what do you say?" "Your divine majesty, the ascetic Cāraka has violated my young daughter." The king said: "Reverend Cāraka, the brahmin says this of you — what do you say?"

"Your divine majesty, I have committed no sinful act against her."

The king said to his ministers: "Wise ones, how is this to be examined?" The ministers said: "Your divine majesty, the Blessed One has declared your majesty himself to be foremost among those possessed of confident eloquence. Therefore let your majesty's own mouth resolve this case."

The king said: "Wise ones, how is this to be known? The eye-consciousness can perceive visible forms, but let the queen's attendants examine the girl. Let the girl be sent in among the queen's attendants and let them investigate her." They sent the girl in among the queen's attendants, and the queen Phrenldanma took the girl onto her lap and said: "Girl, speak truthfully. If the venerable Cāraka violated you and deprived you of your maidenhood, then since he is one who has gone forth from the home of a brahmin reciter, he will fall down into the hearth-pit of your household. But if you remain unharmed and possessed of moral discipline, and you falsely slander a monk, you will be reborn in the great hells." The girl said: "My lady, he did not deprive me of my maidenhood. This is what he did: he suckled me and pressed my limbs and body — he pressed them all over." The queen Phrenldanma said: "Girl, for a matter as small as that you have thrown the entire royal court into turmoil. Do not fathers suckle their daughters and press their limbs and body all over?"

Then the elderly women examined the girl, and as far as they could determine, her maidenhood was unharmed. They reported to the king: "Your divine majesty, this girl's maidenhood is unharmed." The king said to his ministers: "Wise ones, what should be done here?" The ministers said: "Your divine majesty, the venerable Cāraka should be punished." The king said: "Wise ones, then today let this brahmin be placed in a house of lac and burned with fire. Let that girl also be tied to the two hind legs of a wild colt. And let those five hundred brahmin boys have their hands and feet cut off." The venerable Cāraka said: "Your divine majesty, if through any act of mine that many sentient beings were to be harmed, then truly, your divine majesty, you would have expelled me from the teaching of the Blessed One." The king said: "Wise ones, then today release those five hundred brahmin boys, but place this brahmin in the house of lac and burn him with fire, and let that girl be tied to the two hind legs of a wild colt." The venerable Cāraka said: "Your divine majesty, if through any act of mine even a single tiny ant were harmed, then truly, your divine majesty, you would have expelled me from the teaching of the Blessed One." The king said to his ministers: "Wise ones, observe the power of discriminating analysis that a hearer of the Blessed One possesses even without being free from attachment. If the brahmins were to overcome the venerable Cāraka, he would be slain by even a single stone. Wise ones, now let everyone disperse!" They were dispersed, the drum was beaten, the curtain was drawn, and the multitudes of common people scattered in all directions.

Then the king, the queen Phrenldanma, and the venerable Cāraka sat together, and the king said to the queen Phrenldanma: "Phrenldanma, see how the venerable Cāraka's insolence of what kind has thrown the entire royal court into turmoil." The queen Phrenldanma then said to the venerable Cāraka: "Venerable Cāraka, because of you, the fully ordained nun Utpala-colored, the novice nun Kulabyeda, the novice nun Cirika, and —"

"— and many others besides, all of whom have abandoned every affliction and directly realized arhatship: do you feel no remorse even now, having created such ugliness in the midst of the retinue gathered around the king?"

The venerable Cāraka replied: "Phrenldanma, I shall conduct myself in such a way that, as I continue wandering in saṃsāra, I will no longer engage in such afflictions." So saying, he rose from his seat and departed.

Ashamed, he was unable to come before the Blessed One, and so he went instead to where the venerable Śāriputra was, and when he arrived he said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Preceptor, please teach me the Dharma in such a way that, as I continue wandering in saṃsāra, I will no longer engage in such afflictions."

The venerable Śāriputra considered the matter, wondering whether any outstanding transgressions had not yet arisen. Seeing that there remained certain ones still outstanding, he had him confess those transgressions that were to be confessed, and had him restrain those transgressions that were to be restrained through restraint. Then he gave him this instruction: "Attend to your mind in such and such a way, and practise with vigilance."

Thereupon the venerable Cāraka, dwelling alone in seclusion, vigilant, ardent, and fully composed, directly realized in that very lifetime — through his own direct knowledge — that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from home into homelessness with faith in what is true alone. He understood: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. Beyond this present existence there is nothing further to know." He became an arhat, free from attachment beyond the three realms, a mind equanimous toward clay and gold alike, equanimous toward sky and the palm of a hand, cutting through the filth at the gateway of consciousness like sandalwood applied there, attaining the higher knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the individual analytical wisdoms, turning his back on acquisition of existence, desire, and respect, worthy of veneration, worthy of honor, and worthy of being addressed directly by the gods together with Indra and his retinue.

Then, as the venerable Cāraka the arhat was experiencing the joy and bliss of attainment and liberation, he thought: "The Blessed One has been of benefit to me; the Sugata has done me good. For the Blessed One has removed from me many phenomena of suffering; the Blessed One has established for me many phenomena of happiness; the Blessed One has removed from me many forms of evil and unwholesome phenomena; the Blessed One has established for me many forms of wholesome phenomena. What then should I do so that by it I may have repaid the Blessed One, requited him, and repaid him fully?"

He then reflected further: "All that the blessed buddhas have come to know through unsurpassed omniscience — completing the six perfections across three incalculable eons by means of countless hundreds and thousands of hardships — all of that was for the benefit of sentient beings. So I, too, shall bring benefit to sentient beings."

He then thought: "Has the Blessed One ever indicated anyone as supreme among those lay people who inspire faith?" And he saw that the Blessed One had not.

Wondering who might be the right person, he saw that it was himself. He then thought: "Good — by this I shall perfectly fulfill the intention of the Teacher."

As for the time ripe for taming, in Śrāvastī there lived a brahmin who had faith in Śiva and rendered him devoted service. The venerable Śāraka reflected: "This brahmin is ripe for taming," and went to him. The brahmin, for his part, continued rendering devoted service to Śiva, calling out "Ho, brahmin! Brahmin!" as he sought him. The venerable Śāraka said: "I am a brahmin." The brahmin replied: "A brahmin has a topknot, but you are a shaven-headed ascetic." The venerable Śāraka said: "Even so, I am a brahmin, and my Teacher is the foremost of brahmins. Do you have faith in this Śiva?" He replied: "I do." The venerable Śāraka said: "Then let us speak of Śiva. How is it that I am a brahmin and my Teacher is the foremost of brahmins?" Śiva spoke: "Noble Śāraka, that is just so — you are indeed a brahmin, and your Teacher is indeed the foremost of brahmins."

The brahmin then thought: "For a long time I have rendered devoted service to Śiva, and yet he has never shown himself, even in a dream. But when the venerable Śāraka speaks a word, he responds in speech. Ah — the venerable Śāraka must be of great miraculous power and great might!" So the brahmin said: "Venerable Śāraka, why have you come?" Śāraka replied: "For your sake — to tame you. Venerable Śāraka, please remain here for this purpose and accept alms in this place." The venerable Śāraka stayed right there and accepted alms, and then the brahmin together with his wife sat down before the venerable Śāraka to hear the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having penetrated the brahmin's intentions, latent tendencies, constitution, and natural disposition, taught the Dharma in such a way that, while that brahmin and his wife sat right there on their seat, the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection was shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was actualized. He taught just in this way.

Having seen the truth, that brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, through relying on the venerable Śāraka as my spiritual friend, what the venerable Śāraka has done for me is something that neither my father did, nor my mother, nor a king, nor the gods, nor my ancestors of former times, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor friends, companions, or the circle of relatives and kin. He has dried up an ocean of blood and tears. He has liberated me from mountains of bones. He has closed off the doors to the lower realms. He has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. He has drawn my feet out from hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts. He has placed me among gods and humans. He has brought cyclic existence to its end. The twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, has been shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry has been attained. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. I have entered the stream! Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the monastic Saṅgha. May I be received as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with heartfelt sincerity."

The brahmin then said: "Venerable Śāraka, please consent to accepting my alms-food, robes, lodging, provisions in illness, and medicinal requisites for as long as you live." The venerable Śāraka replied: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the path of caring for others' benefit;

he must also work for the benefit of other brahmins." So saying, he declined to accept.

Then the venerable Śāraka tamed and established both households of brahmins in Śrāvastī.

The venerable Śāraka reflected: "Who is now ripe for taming?" He perceived that in Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who had faith in Śiva and paid homage to Śiva. The venerable Śāraka thought: "That brahmin is now ripe for taming," and went to him. The brahmin paid homage to Śiva and then called out, searching for a brahmin: "Ho, brahmin! Brahmin!" The venerable Śāraka said: "I am a brahmin." The brahmin replied: "How can a shaven-headed one like this be a brahmin?" The venerable Śāraka said: "What does a brahmin look like?" The brahmin replied: "A brahmin has matted hair." Thereupon the venerable Śāraka transformed himself into one with matted hair. When the brahmin was filled with wonder at this, he said: "Venerable Śāraka, why have you come?" Śāraka replied: "For the sake of taming you yourself." "Venerable Śāraka, then please stay right here and take your meal." The venerable Śāraka stayed there and ate. Then the brahmin, together with his wife, sat down before the venerable Śāraka to hear the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having understood that brahmin's mind, his latent tendencies, his temperament, and his nature, taught the Dharma in such a way that, as the two of them sat right there together, the vajra of gnosis shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection that had been accumulated since beginningless time, and they directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin said: "Venerable one, in relying upon you, the venerable Śāraka, as my virtuous spiritual friend, what you have done for me is something my father never did, my mother never did, no king ever did, no gods ever did, no ancestors of old ever did, no ascetics or brahmins ever did, no friends, companions, or circle of relatives ever did: you have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, freed me from mountains of bones, closed the doors to the lower rebirths, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and set me among gods and humans, brought cyclic existence to its end. Through the vajra of gnosis you have shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection accumulated since beginningless time, and I have obtained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable Śāraka, I have entered the stream! I have entered the stream! Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. May I be received as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with heartfelt sincerity." "Venerable Śāraka, please consent to accepting my alms-food, robes, lodging, provisions in illness, and medicinal requisites for as long as you live." The venerable Śāraka replied: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the path of caring for others' benefit; he must also work for the benefit of other brahmins." So saying, he declined to accept.

Then the venerable Śāraka tamed and established both households of a second brahmin in Śrāvastī.

The venerable Śāraka reflected: "Who is now ripe for taming?" He perceived that in Śrāvastī there was a miserly brahmin whose wife was fond of jewels. The venerable Śāraka thought: "That brahmin is ripe for taming," and so the venerable Śāraka disguised himself as a jewel-merchant and went to that brahmin's house, calling out: "Jewels for sale! Jewels for sale!" The brahmin's wife heard this and said: "What price are you selling the jewels for?"

The venerable Śāraka said: "These jewels are costly, yet I give them for a small price." So saying, the venerable Śāraka made the appearance of the jewel-merchant vanish and sat there in his own monk's robes. The brahmin was filled with wonder and said: "Venerable Śāraka, why have you come here?" "For the sake of taming you." "Then, venerable Śāraka, please stay right here for that purpose and accept meals." The venerable Śāraka stayed there and accepted meals, and that brahmin together with his wife sat before the venerable Śāraka to listen to the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having thoroughly understood that brahmin's disposition, latent tendencies, constitution, and temperament, then taught the Dharma in such a way that, as that brahmin and his wife sat there on that very seat, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and they manifestly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, I have relied upon the venerable Śāraka as my virtuous spiritual friend, and what the venerable Śāraka has done for me is something that neither my father did for me, nor my mother, nor the king, nor the gods, nor my forebears of old, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor my beloved ones, friends, and circle of relatives. He has dried up the ocean of blood and tears. He has delivered me from the mountains of bones. He has closed the doors to the lower destinies. He has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. He has lifted my feet free from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts. He has placed me among gods and humans. He has brought cyclic existence to its end. The twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, have been shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and I have obtained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, with all my heart I go for refuge wholeheartedly and with full sincerity."

"Venerable Śāraka, please agree to accept for as long as I live my alms food, robes, lodging, medicines for illness, and medicinal requisites." The venerable Śāraka said: "One who has gone forth has entered upon a life of benefiting others, and so one must also benefit other brahmins," and with that he declined to accept.

Then the venerable Śāraka tamed and established both households of a third brahmin in Śrāvastī.

The venerable Śāraka reflected: "Who is now ripe for taming?" He perceived that in Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who was sick. Physicians had treated him with cold medicines, warm medicines, and sweating treatments, and he had grown disgusted with them all. He had instructed his doorkeeper: "Do not let any physician inside." The venerable Śāraka thought: "The time has come to tame that brahmin," and so the venerable Śāraka disguised himself as a physician and went to stand at that brahmin's gate, announcing that a physician had come. The doorkeeper said: "The brahmin has instructed me not to let any physician inside, and so I am posted here for just that reason." The venerable Śāraka said: "Go and tell the brahmin: a physician has come who says he will heal you not with medicine and not with painful treatment, but with secret mantras."

The doorkeeper went and reported all of this to the brahmin, and the brahmin said: "Let him in." The venerable Śāraka entered, and healed the brahmin with secret mantras. Then the venerable Śāraka put aside the guise of a physician and sat in his own appearance. The brahmin was filled with wonder and said: "Venerable Śāraka, why did you come here?" "For the sake of taming you." "Then, venerable Śāraka, please remain right here and accept our hospitality." The venerable Śāraka stayed there and took his meals, and the brahmin together with his wife sat before the venerable Śāraka to hear the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having thoroughly understood that brahmin's disposition, latent tendencies, temperament, and character, taught the Dharma in such a way that, while the brahmin and his wife sat right there on their seats, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) — accumulated since beginningless time — were shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was actualized.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, by relying on the good friend that is the venerable Śāraka, the venerable Śāraka has done something for me that my father never did, my mother never did, the king never did, the gods never did, my ancestors of old never did, neither ascetics nor brahmins, neither friends nor companions nor a host of kinsmen — he has dried the ocean of blood and tears, freed me from mountains of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, and lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and set me among gods and humans, and brought cyclic existence to an end. The twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, have been shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry has been attained. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with a sincere and open heart."

"May the venerable Śāraka please accept, for as long as I live, my alms-food, robes, lodging, remedies for sickness, and medicinal requisites." The venerable Śāraka replied: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the path of caring for others, and so one must also benefit other brahmins," and with that he accepted.

At that time the venerable Śāraka tamed and established both brahmin households in Śrāvastī. The venerable Śāraka thought: "When the time has come to tame someone," and in Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and abundant resources, with extensive and vast holdings — yet miserly, small-eyed, one who would not even give a scrap to a crow, grasping at every possession. At his gate some five hundred brahmin boys were reciting brahmanical sacred texts. The venerable Śāraka thought: "The time has come to tame that brahmin," and so, looking toward the one to be tamed, whenever the venerable Śāraka entered that place for alms, he repeatedly received nothing there at all. Having emerged empty-handed, as the venerable Śāraka came out that brahmin saw him and said: "Hey, ascetic, you keep going in there again and again — do you get anything at all?"

The venerable Śāraka, thinking of that brahmin's wealth of faith, said: "Brahmin, if you yourself have nothing, what is there to give?" The brahmin, stung by this, replied: "Ascetic, you should give to all the household folk together." The venerable Śāraka said, "That is the means," and departed.

Now one of the brahmin boys who was familiar with the monk's ways said to that brahmin: "Do you know, sir, what the teacher meant when he said 'that is the means'?" The brahmin replied: "I do not know." The boy said: "What the teacher said — 'receive it with joy' — that is what he meant by 'that is the means.'" The brahmin asked again: "And what, sir, did the teacher mean by 'all the household folk together'?" The brahmin replied: "I do not know." The boy said: "By 'all the household folk together' is meant the noble Gautama of the warrior clan, together with his retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks. In this way the teacher has effectively invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha."

The brahmin said: "Have I not seen brahmins endowed with the three Vedas? Why then should I give to these shaven-headed ascetics?" The boy replied: "The ascetic, by using the teacher's name today, will tomorrow invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to the teacher's home gathering." The brahmin asked: "Why would he do such a thing?" The boy replied: "Teacher, if you do not trust me, please send a brahmin boy to observe." So he sent a brahmin boy, and when the venerable Śāraka had assembled the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, the boy sat off to one side at the edge of the gathering and heard an elder brahmin inviting the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another home at midday, using that brahmin's name. The brahmin boy, having heard this, came back and reported to the brahmin: "It is just as I said, sir. The venerable Śāraka has, using the teacher's name, invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to tomorrow's home gathering. Please make preparations for the meal."

The brahmin said: "Have I not seen brahmins endowed with the three Vedas? Why then should I give to these shaven-headed ascetics? Let them go eat at the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's almshouse." Then the next morning, when the monks doing water purification arrived at that brahmin's house and said: "Brahmin, where shall we set the water?" the brahmin replied: "At the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's home gathering." Likewise, when those doing the purification of cooked food arrived and said: "Brahmin, where shall the meal be arranged?" the brahmin replied: "At the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's home gathering."

Now the Blessed One had declared: "Whoever has been invited as a guest should go ahead of time and see to what has not yet been prepared." So the venerable Śāraka rose early in the morning and the noble one encountered the householder Anāthapiṇḍada on the road, who said: "Venerable Śāraka, where are you going?" He replied: "A brahmin made use of my name to invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another home at midday, so I am going there." The householder said: "That brahmin is without faith. It would not be right for the midday gathering of the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to be cut off — I shall come as well."

The two of them went there together. When they arrived, the brahmin was sitting in a state of despondency. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to him: "Brahmin, you have invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another home at midday — why then are you sitting in despondency? What harm is there in preparing the food?" The brahmin replied: "Have I not seen brahmins who are masters of the three Vedas? I give to those shaven-headed ascetics (śramaṇas). You, go eat a meal at my home." The householder said: "Brahmin, do you think I have no wealth? I would be glad to go on serving the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for as long as I live, with almsfood, robes, lodging, medicine for illness, and medicinal requisites. But I speak now for your own benefit. Do not sit in despondency — prepare the food. For the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha has been honored, revered, regarded as supreme, and worshipped by King Prasenajit of Kośala, by Queen Mallikā, by the noblewomen of the Kṣatriya clan, by the divine seer Brahmadatta, by those of the old families, by myself, and moreover by a great number of brahmins and householders. If, because of you, the midday gathering of the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha were to be cut off, the king would certainly do you harm, and it would come to such a pass that you would be submerged in water up to your neck and put to death." The brahmin was afraid and thought: "That is indeed what would happen." He said: "Householder, the food has not been prepared — what shall I do now?" The householder replied: "Brahmin, there is nothing in Śrāvastī that money cannot buy. Bring kārṣāpaṇas (silver coins), and I will prepare the food." The brahmin asked: "Householder, how many kārṣāpaṇas will be enough to provide a midday meal for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha?" The householder replied: "Five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." The brahmin gave the householder five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada added further kārṣāpaṇas of his own on top of those and prepared the food.

The brahmin then said: "Householder, I have no serving bowls either." The householder Anāthapiṇḍada replied: "Brahmin, do not sit there in despondency on account of the serving bowls — those will come along with the containers belonging to the ascetics."

Then the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha arrived and was seated. The brahmin saw the monks rinsing out their bowls, and thought: "Well then, I need not rinse out the vessels myself either." He became filled with faith. He said to the venerable Śāraka: "Venerable Śāraka, you are my good spiritual friend. Please do the honors, and then invite those present afterward to take their meal." After the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha had eaten, the Blessed One gave a teaching of thanksgiving, rose from his seat, and departed.

Then the brahmin said: "Venerable Śāraka, now please remain and oversee the matter of the food." Śāraka stayed on, and the brahmin served out the food and attended to all the affairs of the meal. Then the brahmin together with his wife sat before the venerable Śāraka to hear the Dharma, and the venerable Śāraka, having thoroughly understood his disposition, latent tendencies, constitution, and temperament,

Thus, while the brahmin and his wife were seated right there on that very seat, the venerable Śāraka taught the Dharma in such a way that the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was actualized.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, by relying on the good spiritual friend, the venerable Śāraka, and by the venerable Śāraka's doing what he has done for me in this way — this has not been done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by a king, nor by the gods, nor by my forebears of old, nor by wandering ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins, nor by friends, companions, and the company of my kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears. You have freed me from the mountains of bones. You have closed the doors to the lower realms. You have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. You have withdrawn my feet from the hells, from the animal realm, and from the realm of hungry ghosts, and have placed me among gods and human beings. You have brought saṃsāra to an end. The twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, has been shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, with all my heart I joyfully take refuge."

"Will the venerable Śāraka please accept, for as long as I live, my alms-food, robes, lodging, provisions in illness, and requisite medicines?"

The venerable Śāraka said: "One who has gone forth has entered into a life of benefiting others. Therefore one must also benefit other brahmins." So saying, he accepted.

At that time the venerable Śāraka, while living in Śrāvastī, trained and established both members of five brahmin households.

The venerable Śāraka reflected: "When the time has come to tame someone" — and there was in Śrāvastī a brahmin whose wife was beautiful to behold, lovely and fair — "and that brahmin, being extremely attached to her, would not allow anyone to enter the house," the venerable Śāraka thought: "Now is the time to tame this brahmin." He went to that brahmin's house, and when he arrived, the brahmin happened to be urinating. Seeing the venerable Śāraka, the brahmin said: "Ascetic, wait — do not enter."

The venerable Śāraka then blessed the brahmin's stream of urine so that it did not cease, and entered inside. He also blessed the brahmin's wife so that whatever was on her belly within appeared visible from the outside. Then the venerable Śāraka came back out.

The brahmin said: "Venerable Śāraka, did you see my wife?" He replied: "I saw her — just as you see her, so did I see her."

The brahmin then went in and looked, and seeing her in an ugly and repulsive light, said to her: "Brahmin woman, did you not say something to the venerable Śāraka?"

She said: "I said nothing at all — he entered, cursed me, and left. Please go ask his forgiveness."

The brahmin went and said: "Venerable Śāraka, I beg you to forgive me regarding my wife."

The venerable Śāraka said: "I forgive."

Things returned to being as they were before, and the brahmin, now filled with faith, said: "Venerable Śāraka, why did you come?"

"It was for the sake of taming you yourself." "Venerable Śāraka, for that reason please remain right here and accept the offering of food." The venerable Śāraka stayed and accepted the offering of food, and then the brahmin together with his wife sat before the venerable Śāraka to listen to the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having fully understood the brahmin's intention, his habitual tendencies, his constitution, and his character, taught the Dharma in such a way that, as that brahmin and his wife sat right there on that very seat, the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) — accumulated since beginningless time — was shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was directly realized.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, by relying on you, the venerable Śāraka, as my spiritual friend, you have done for me what neither my father did, nor my mother, nor a king, nor the gods, nor my ancestors of former times, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor my loving friends and companions, nor the circle of my kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed me from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to higher rebirths and liberation; you have drawn my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you have placed me among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to its end. The twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated since beginningless time, has been shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with all my heart and with perfect sincerity. And please, venerable Śāraka, grant permission to offer you — for as long as you live — alms-food, robes, lodging, provisions in sickness, and medicinal requisites."

The venerable Śāraka said: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the practice of caring for others' welfare, so one must also care for the welfare of other brahmins as well." Saying this, he accepted.

Now at that time the venerable Śāraka, while at Śrāvastī, tamed and settled both members of a brahmin's household — the sixth such household he had tamed.

Then the venerable Śāraka thought: "When the time has come to tame someone" — and there in Śrāvastī there was a brahmin whose wife was beautiful, lovely, and attractive. That brahmin had gone outside to gather flowers and firewood. The venerable Śāraka thought: "The time has come to tame that brahmin," and went to the brahmin's house. When the brahmin's wife saw the venerable Śāraka at the door, she went inside, and the venerable Śāraka also entered the house. She went into a room, and the venerable Śāraka followed her into that room as well. She came out of the room and began to climb a staircase to the upper story, and the venerable Śāraka also followed her up the stairs. She kicked the ladder away, and the venerable Śāraka fell to the ground and entered into the meditative absorption of cessation. She thought: "Has he died?" She came down and tried to rouse him, but he could not be moved. The brahmin arrived and asked: "What is this?" The brahmin woman explained the whole matter at length, and he said: "What you did to him in this way was wrong. This man is one who has gone forth from the household of a brahmin reciter, a close friend of King Prasenajit, and the teacher of Queen Mallikā —

"They have obtained from the king the dismissal of the youth, and so our king has had them made to prostrate at his feet — such a situation will arise in which they must die." The brahmin woman touched the two feet of the venerable Śāraka and said: "Noble one, there is nothing that you do not know, nothing that you do not see, nothing that you do not understand, nothing that you do not recognize — please grant your forgiveness." And as she begged forgiveness, the venerable Śāraka rose and said: "Forgiven."

The brahmin was astonished, and he said: "Venerable Śāraka, why have you come?" "For the purpose of taming you yourself." "Then, venerable Śāraka, please stay right here and accept the service of meals." The venerable Śāraka stayed there and accepted the service of food.

The brahmin, together with his wife, sat before the venerable Śāraka in order to hear the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having thoroughly understood that brahmin's disposition, latent tendencies, constitution, and temperament, taught the Dharma in such a way that while that brahmin and his wife sat there on that very seat, the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection was shattered by the vajra of wisdom, and they directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, the brahmin spoke: "Venerable one, in reliance upon you, my virtuous spiritual friend, and through what you, venerable Śāraka, have done for me — what neither my father did for me, nor my mother, nor the king, nor the gods, nor my ancestors of old, nor the ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins, nor the assembly of loving friends, companions, and relatives — you have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, you have freed me from the mountains of bones, you have closed the doors to the lower realms, you have opened the doors to the higher states and to liberation, you have drawn my feet out from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, you have placed me among gods and humans, you have brought cyclic existence to its end, and by the vajra of wisdom you have shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, with heart and core I go for refuge with full sincerity."

"Venerable Śāraka, please accept for as long as life lasts: my alms-round offerings, robes, lodging, provisions for illness, and medicinal requisites." The venerable Śāraka said: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the practice of benefiting others. I must also benefit other brahmins," and he did not accept.

Then the venerable Śāraka, while at Śrāvastī, tamed and established both members of the brahmin's household — the seventh — and placed them in the teaching.

The venerable Śāraka thought: "When the time for taming has come" — there in Śrāvastī there lived a brahmin whose wife was beautiful, lovely, and charming. That brahmin had gone outside to fetch flowers and fuel for the fire, and the venerable Śāraka thought: "It is time to tame that brahmin," and he went to that brahmin's home. The brahmin woman, swollen with pride in her beauty, her youth, her lineage, and her wealth, would not even offer a word.

The venerable Śāraka, reflecting upon the exhaustion of her prior karma, spoke this verse:

Old rope frays and breaks away,
yet a small new rope she will not weave.

Seeing her adorned with heedlessness,
he wept with tear-filled face.

Having spoken thus, he departed. The brahmin woman, furious and thinking "He has insulted me," put on soiled clothes, lay down upon a broken bed, and remained there. When the brahmin returned and saw her, he said, "Brahmin woman, what is wrong?" She scolded him and said, "If you lack the means to give food and clothing even to a single person standing at your own door, what is the use of your having taken a wife? That ascetic Śāraka insulted her." The brahmin said, "Good woman, he is one who has gone forth from a family of brahmin cantors; you should be patient with him." The brahmin woman said, "However much you speak, brahmin, whatever the case may be, if he lives, I shall not." Since one driven by desire will stop at nothing, however wicked the act, the brahmin tucked a sword under his arm. When the venerable Śāraka, still some distance away, saw him coming, he wondered what his state of mind might be, and he saw that the man was coming with murderous intent. The venerable Śāraka then manifested through his miraculous power a thicket of leafless shrubs, entered into it, and remained there. The brahmin said, "Venerable Śāraka, open the door." The venerable Śāraka said, "If you have come with good intentions, why would I not open? Throw down the sword." The brahmin thought, "I have been found out; he means to kill me," and so he threw down the sword. The venerable Śāraka said, "Throw down that murderous mind as well." The brahmin thought, "This is a great master indeed; he has even read my mind," and he became filled with faith. The venerable Śāraka then withdrew the miraculous transformation he had wrought and remained as before. That brahmin prostrated at the two feet of the venerable Śāraka and sat before him to receive the Dharma. The venerable Śāraka, having thoroughly understood that brahmin's intentions, latent tendencies, elements, and natural disposition, taught the Dharma to him in such a way that, even while seated on that very seat, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and he actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he said:

"Venerable one, in relying upon you, the spiritual friend, venerable Śāraka, what you have done for me here is something my father never did for me, my mother never did for me, the king never did for me, the gods never did for me, my forebears never did for me, ascetics and brahmins never did for me, and friends, companions, and kinsmen never did for me. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed me from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; you have drawn my feet out from among the hell-beings, the animals, and the hungry ghosts; you have placed me among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to its end. By the vajra of gnosis you have shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection — accumulated since beginningless time — and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream."

"Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I take refuge with wholehearted sincerity."

Then the brahmin said: "Venerable Cāraka, have you come to perform my wedding ceremony?" "Yes." "And what did the venerable Cāraka say to my brahmin wife?" The venerable Cāraka replied: "I said this to her:

Wearing out what is old, making no new store,
seeing one adorned with careless ease,
one weeps with a face drenched in tears."

"Venerable one, what is the meaning of that verse?"

"Brahmin, long ago in times past, a festive gathering took place at a cliff in the mountains. There many householders' wives, adorned with their own ornaments, went to the pleasure garden, and a beggar woman saw them and lamented in sorrow at her own wretched state. Now, when buddhas do not appear in the world, inferior pratyekabuddhas (solitary buddhas) arise — those with compassion for the poor and destitute, fond of remote and isolated lodgings, solitary as a rhinoceros, become worthy fields of offering for the world. One such pratyekabuddha went to that place in order to benefit beings. The beggar woman saw his beautiful body and his beautiful mind, and when she found a small amount of begged food, she thought: 'Because I have not made offerings to such a worthy field of offering as this, I have ended up in a condition like this — let it not continue so. If this Blessed One will accept a little alms from me, I shall give it to him.' Out of compassion for her, that pratyekabuddha accepted his bowl, and she gave the food to him. Then, out of compassion for her, he rose up into the sky above like a king of geese spreading its wings, and began to perform miraculous feats — blazing, shining, causing rain to fall, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary people are quickly moved to faith by miraculous displays, and so she fell prostrate at the feet of that pratyekabuddha, like a tree cut down at its root, and made this aspiration: 'By the karmic maturation of this act of mine, may I never experience suffering.' Brahmin, the beggar woman of that time and place was your own wife. Through the karmic maturation of the offering she made to the pratyekabuddha, she has now been born as she is. And I, having reflected that the karmic maturation of her act has been exhausted, said:

Wearing out what is old, making no new store,
seeing one adorned with careless ease,
one weeps with a face drenched in tears.

Venerable Cāraka thus urged me by way of meaning to attend to my own wife. Venerable Cāraka, will you permit me to invite you for the midday meal tomorrow at my wedding?" The venerable Cāraka accepted by his silence, without saying a word. Then the brahmin, understanding that the venerable Cāraka had accepted by his silence, departed.

The brahmin woman, for her part, felt remorse, thinking: "It was wrong of me to send someone to kill the brahmin Cāraka — what if the brahmin has killed the venerable Cāraka?" When the brahmin returned, his wife said: "My lord's son, did you kill the venerable Cāraka?" The brahmin replied: "He is a great being — who could kill him?" The wife said: "Then did you at least not invite him?" The brahmin replied: "I have invited him to come for the midday meal tomorrow at another house. Now make ready the food."

The brahmin woman prepared the cold dishes that very day, and the hot dishes she prepared for the following morning. The venerable Cāraka, for his part, rose early the next morning, donned his robe, took up his alms bowl, and went to the brahmin's house. When he arrived, he sat down on the seat that had been set out. Then the brahmin, together with his wife, knowing that the venerable Cāraka was seated at ease, satisfied him and served him from their own hands with pure and choice food and drink. Again and again, with pure and choice food and drink in abundance, they satisfied him and served him from their own hands. When the venerable Cāraka had finished eating and had washed his hands and set aside his bowl, the brahmin woman took a seat lower than his and sat down before the venerable Cāraka to hear the Dharma. The venerable Cāraka, having understood her mind, her latent tendencies, her temperament, and her character, taught the Dharma in such a way that, while she sat upon that very seat, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and she directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, she spoke: "Venerable one, by relying on you, my virtuous friend, and through what you, venerable Cāraka, have done for me — this has not been done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by a king, nor by the gods, nor by my ancestors of old, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by the assembly of friends, companions, and kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, you have freed me from the mountains of bones, you have closed the doors to the lower rebirths, you have opened the doors to higher states of existence and liberation, you have lifted my feet from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and you have placed me among gods and humans, you have brought cyclic existence to its end. By the vajra of gnosis, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, accumulated from beginningless time, have been shattered, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a laywoman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with wholehearted and sincere devotion."

She then said: "Please, venerable Cāraka, grant permission for as long as you live to accept almsfood, robes, lodging, the requisites of the sick, and medicinal provisions from me." The venerable Cāraka replied: "One who has gone forth has entered upon a way of life dedicated to benefiting others, and so one must bring benefit to other brahmins as well" — and saying this, he accepted.

At that time the venerable Cāraka had tamed and established both brahmin households in Śrāvastī. Then the venerable Cāraka reflected: "I wonder whether the time has come to tame someone." In Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who was wealthy, with great riches and great resources, with wide and extensive landholdings, yet miserly and tight-fisted — one who would not even give a torma offering to a crow — clinging to all his possessions. This man had assigned a tenant farmer to work a rock-face, and after sealing the storage barns he gave his wife only enough food to sustain herself, then went off to that rock-face and supervised the tenant farming work himself.

The venerable Cāraka thought: "The time has come to tame that brahmin." He gathered alms and went to that brahmin's house, and said: "Brahmin woman, please offer water for the alms bowl."

She offered him a bowl of rice gruel, and the ladle filled up in the same way as before. The brahmin woman said: "Noble one, my husband is miserly and tight-fisted, one who would not even give a torma offering to a crow, who clings to all his possessions — please do not come again."

The venerable Cāraka said: "No matter; tomorrow I myself will come with sixty others."

The following day the venerable Cāraka did indeed come there himself with sixty others, and she offered them rice gruel in the same way. And so it went, day after day, himself and sixty others going once each day to eat alms at that brahmin's house. Now, hear what the neighbors and acquaintances of ours have to say: that brahmin woman — with goods that the brahmin earned by the labor of his own two hands — was eating together with the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan. They gossiped, spread slander, and spoke ill of her.

One brahmin youth had gone from Śrāvastī to that rock-face on some errand. The brahmin, catching sight of that youth from a great distance, called out to him and asked: "Brahmin youth, where have you come from?" He replied: "From Śrāvastī." The brahmin asked: "Have you heard any news of my household?" He answered: "I have. In Śrāvastī the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is the first house for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan, and the house of the preceptor is their second house. Sixty śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyan, come every day to seek alms."

The brahmin thought: "This is aimed at me, the miser, as a rebuke — I should ask someone else as well." So he moved on and sat down along the road. Before long another brahmin youth, going on some errand from Śrāvastī to that rock-face, came by. The brahmin, seeing that youth from a great distance, questioned him: "Brahmin youth, where have you come from?" He replied: "From Śrāvastī." "Have you heard any news of my household?" "I have. In Śrāvastī the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is the first house for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan, and the house of the preceptor is their second house. Sixty śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyan, come every day to seek alms."

The brahmin thought: "Since this one and that one agree, it must indeed be so. If my wife has been consuming my goods in this way, this is not to be borne — I shall go home." He returned home and said to the brahmin woman: "Wicked brahmin woman! I earned these goods by the labor of my own two hands. Are you eating them together with those shaven-headed śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyan? Do you not see brahmins who are masters of the three Vedas? Instead you give to those bald śramaṇas!" And he began to beat her.

She said: "Brahmin, look and see — has she broken the seals on the storage jars that you left in her care? Or, rather, examine each one carefully." The brahmin examined the jars one by one, and when he saw that every seal remained intact just as before, he said to his wife: "Where did you find so much food?" She replied: "A little rice gruel came into this ladle, and when I cooked some legumes along with the gruel, that gruel alone was enough to feed sixty monks and myself as well."

The brahmin asked: "Why did this happen?" She replied: "I shall make this evident to you directly." The following day, when the venerable Cāraka came there himself with sixty others, she offered alms just as before, and then said: "Brahmin, do you see?" That brahmin was filled with sincere faith and said:

The venerable Cāraka said: "Brahmin, will you permit me to come to your home tomorrow for the midday meal?" The venerable Cāraka replied: "Brahmin, is this really how it is done? One invites a guest with proper food and summons him with proper cooked food." Since the venerable Cāraka said nothing further to that brahmin, the brahmin accepted and departed.

Then, understanding that the venerable Cāraka had accepted in silence, that very night the brahmin prepared clean and pure provisions and cooked food in readiness. The venerable Cāraka also, the following morning, dressed himself in his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and went to where the brahmin's house was. Arriving there, he sat down upon the seat that had been spread for him.

Then, perceiving that the venerable Cāraka was seated at ease, the brahmin satisfied and served him with his own hands, offering clean and pure provisions and cooked food. Again and again he satisfied and served him with his own hands with clean and pure provisions and cooked food. When the venerable Cāraka had finished eating, had washed his hands, and had set down his bowl, the brahmin took a low seat and sat down before the venerable Cāraka in order to hear the Dharma.

The venerable Cāraka, having thoroughly understood that brahmin's intention, latent tendencies, constitution, and character, taught the Dharma to him in such a way that, right there as the brahmin sat together with his wife upon that very seat, the peak of the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) — accumulated since beginningless time — was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry was actualized.

Seeing the truth, he said: "Venerable one, through relying on you as a virtuous friend, the venerable Cāraka has done for me what neither my father has done, nor my mother, nor the king, nor the gods, nor my ancestral forebears, nor any ascetics or brahmins, nor any assembly of friends, companions, or kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed me from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower realms; you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; you have lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you have placed me among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to an end. The twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time has been shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and the fruit of stream-entry has been obtained. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with sincere and heartfelt devotion."

The venerable Cāraka said: "Will you please accept, for as long as I live, my alms food, robes, lodging, the requisites for illness, and medicinal supplies?" The venerable Cāraka replied: "One who has gone forth has entered upon a life of benefiting others; therefore one must also benefit other brahmins." Saying this, he did not accept.

At that time the venerable Cāraka, while in Śrāvastī, tamed and established both members of nine brahmin households.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh fascicle of the Vinayavibhaṅga.

The venerable Cāraka thought: "Who is now ripe for taming?" There is in Śrāvastī a brahmin who has taken a wife from an equal family, and who sports with her, takes delight in her, and lives in enjoyment with her. A son was born to them, and they raised and nurtured him until he grew up. That brahmin's wife was fierce, arrogant, coarse, given to outbursts, and sharp-tongued.

She was a quarrelsome person who was constantly fighting and brawling with her own relatives, and so she came to be known by the name Tummo Tummo, meaning "the fierce one, the fierce one."

On another occasion, a festival arose in Śrāvastī, and the brahmin spoke to his son: "My son, your mother here is so fierce that she constantly brawls with others. It has come to a point where we might face such a situation as being thrown into prison and put to death. For now, until the festival is over, go and stay somewhere else at another cliff-face, and afterward return. You go and ask your mother." The son then said to his mother: "Dear mother, for the sake of a small errand, I am going to a certain pleasant cliff-face." The fierce woman replied: "Go to the place where her first garment has gone." The brahmin also said: "I too shall go." The fierce woman said: "Go to a place from which you will never return." As the two departed, the fierce woman addressed the maidservant, saying: "Girl, start carrying loads, and eat the coarser food." The girl began to carry loads and set to doing so, whereupon the venerable Cāraka thought: "This is the time to tame the fierce woman," and early that morning he dressed in his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and monastic robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he went along on his alms round he approached the fierce woman's home to enter, and when the fierce woman saw him approaching she said to the maidservant: "Girl, drive this ascetic away." The girl drove him away, but the venerable Cāraka entered the house first, before the maidservant, and then the maidservant entered afterward. When the fierce woman saw this again she said to the maidservant: "Girl, did you not drive this ascetic away?" The girl replied: "I did drive him away." "Then how did he enter? Drive him away again and shut the door." The girl drove him away, shut the door, and entered, but the venerable Cāraka had already entered before her. When the fierce woman saw this again she said to the maidservant: "Girl, did you not drive this ascetic away and shut the door?" The girl replied: "I drove him away and shut the door." "Then how did he enter from somewhere?" Thereupon the fierce woman said: "Ascetic, what are you begging for?" The venerable Cāraka said: "For food." The fierce woman replied: "If you had come as the eldest son you would not be refused food. Why should I not give you food?"
