The venerable Cāraka then appeared in the form of the eldest son, and the fierce woman said: "Even if you make your hands and feet turn yellow, I will not give you food." The venerable Cāraka then appeared with his hands and feet turned yellow, and the fierce woman said: "Even if you look with eyes like a bowl you will not be given food." The venerable Cāraka then appeared with eyes like a bowl, and the fierce woman said: "Even if you hover in the sky spinning about like a bell swinging in a hawk, you will not be given food." The venerable Cāraka then appeared hovering in the sky spinning about like a bell, and the fierce woman said: "Even if you split yourself evenly into two pieces, you will not be given food." The venerable Cāraka then appeared splitting himself evenly into two pieces and falling to the ground, whereupon the maidservant said: "My lady, among the many afflictions that you have inflicted, this is the most afflicting of all. This ascetic is a companion of the younger brother of King Prasenajit of Kosala, and the teacher of Queen Mallika. Even though I am a lowly servant from very far away, I serve as nothing but a slave, while my lady will face a dousing with a golden water-pot right there in the royal palace." The fierce woman was frightened and thought: "It will come to that," and she said:

"Girl, dig a pit and hide him," she said. The girl began to dig and hide him, but when she did so, the Venerable Cāraka had entered into meditative absorption on the cessation of arising, and she was unable to move him.

Then the fierce woman touched the Venerable Cāraka's two feet and said: "Noble one, there is nothing that you do not know, nothing you do not see, nothing you are unaware of, nothing you do not fully cognize. Please grant me your forgiveness, and I offer you a gift of firewood." The Venerable Cāraka rose and showed an ordinary appearance, whereupon the fierce woman thought: "If he agrees to accept a gift of firewood, these loads of firewood are far too large — I will lose out. I should make another, smaller load instead." She began to burn a smaller load of wood, but that burning caused all the stacked firewood to catch fire. The fierce woman then thought: "I will not give him this firewood. I will give him just one piece from the original load." She began to pull out one piece, whereupon all of the firewood came along with it.

The fierce woman said: "Noble one, does the reverend one want all this firewood?" The Venerable Cāraka said: "I do." The fierce woman said: "Please accept it." The Venerable Cāraka said: "Sister, if you give it entirely, feed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. Today, invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another house at noon, go there yourself with a pit dug for the purpose, and serve them with your own hand."

The fierce woman said: "Noble ones, since everyone knows me as a fierce woman, how could I possibly go there?" The Venerable Cāraka said: "Sister, I will have you brought in." Then the fierce woman took up those loads of firewood and began to enter the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, but the doorkeeper said: "Fierce woman, why have you come here? Do not enter." The Venerable Cāraka said: "Good man, let her in." The doorkeeper let the fierce woman inside.

She then saw the great Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and she began to chop the firewood. The Venerable Cāraka said: "Without chopping it, offer it with gladness." The fierce woman said: "It will not be enough." The Venerable Cāraka said: "Offer it — it will be enough." And so he blessed it in such a way that, after the entire Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha had been fully satisfied, there was even more left over than before. The fierce woman served the entire Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with firewood until they were satisfied. Then the Blessed One gave thanks and rose from his seat and departed.

The fierce woman said: "Venerable Cāraka, you are my spiritual friend. Please come here. Come into my home and take your midday meal there." The Venerable Cāraka went to the fierce woman's home. She gave food to the Venerable Cāraka, and the fierce woman sat before the Venerable Cāraka in order to hear the Dharma. The Venerable Cāraka, having fully understood her intention, her latent dispositions, her constitution, and her natural temperament, then taught the Dharma in such a way that, as she sat right there on that very seat, the peak of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection — twenty peaks high — was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and she directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, she said: "Venerable one, it is in dependence upon my spiritual friend, the Venerable Cāraka, that this has come about. What the Venerable Cāraka has done for me is something that my father has not done, my mother has not done, the king has not done, the gods have not done, my forebears of former times have not done, ascetics and brahmins have not done, and the assembly of friends, companions, and kinsmen has not done.

The ocean of blood and tears has been dried up. From the mountains of bones have I been freed. The doors to the lower realms have been closed. The doors to the higher realms and to liberation have been opened. From the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts have my feet been lifted out. Among gods and humans have I been placed. Cyclic existence has been brought to its end. The peak of the view of the transitory collection — twenty peaks high — accumulated since beginningless time, was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I be received as a laywoman. From today forward, for as long as life endures, I go for refuge from the depths of my heart, with wholehearted joy."

Then the Venerable Cāraka instructed her rightly with Dharma-filled discourse, established her rightly in it, praised her rightly, and gladdened her rightly — and then rose from his seat and departed.

Thereafter Tummo swept her own house well, arranged the furnishings neatly, anointed the walls properly, scattered flowers, and sat in a demeanor of tranquility.

The brahmin, returning after the market day had passed, settled in the pleasure garden and said to his son: "Son, go and see where your mother Khrimön has been placed — where she is — and bring her out."

The son went to the house, and from a considerable distance Tummo saw her son. She said: "Son, welcome! Welcome! Come here, rest a while. Has your father come?"

The son said: "Yes, he is in the pleasure garden and staying there."

After the son had eaten, he went to his father, and the father asked: "Son, is the household well?"

The son said: "Father, such a manner of conduct as mother's — I have never before seen the like of it. She is there in a state of complete tranquility."

When the brahmin entered the house, from a considerable distance Tummo saw him and said: "My lord's son, welcome! Welcome! Please be seated."

He sat down and thought: "A thing like this has never happened before — what can have brought this about?" And he spoke this verse:

"Thus unlike what was before,
you appear to me reversed and strange —
have you become afflicted with madness,
or have you somehow become intoxicated?"

Tummo replied in verse:

"My lord, I am not mad,
nor have I become intoxicated.
I have, in the teaching of the Buddha,
come to see the noble truths.

My lord's son, the noble Cāraka has taught me the Dharma in this way: that henceforth, as long as I wander in cyclic existence, I shall no longer indulge in all those afflictions as before."

The brahmin was filled with wonder and thought: "The one whom I could not tame with beatings, with bonds, and with abuse — the Venerable Cāraka has tamed her with Dharma-teaching. Since it is by teaching the Dharma that he tamed her, the noble Cāraka has done great benefit for me. The noble Cāraka has done much good for me. Let me go and tomorrow invite the noble Cāraka to another household for the midday meal."

At that time he went to where the Venerable Cāraka was, arrived there, and with his head paid homage at the two feet of the Venerable Cāraka, then sat to one side.

Having sat to one side, the Venerable Cāraka duly instructed that brahmin with Dharma-filled discourse, established him rightly in it, praised him rightly, and gladdened him rightly. In many ways he duly instructed with Dharma-filled discourse, established him rightly in it, praised him rightly,

and gladdened him rightly — and then said nothing further. Thereupon that brahmin rose from his seat, bowed with joined palms toward the Venerable Cāraka, and said to the Venerable Cāraka: "Would the Venerable Cāraka be so kind as to accept tomorrow's midday meal at my home?" The Venerable Cāraka, by remaining silent, accepted the invitation from that brahmin.

Then that brahmin, understanding that the Venerable Cāraka had accepted by remaining silent, paid homage with his head at the two feet of the Venerable Cāraka and departed. That very night the brahmin prepared clean and excellent food and drink. The Venerable Cāraka too, early the following morning, dressed, took up his bowl and robe, and went to that brahmin's home, arriving there and sitting down on the seat that had been laid out.

Then that brahmin, seeing that the Venerable Cāraka was seated comfortably, with his own hands satisfied and fortified him with clean and excellent food and drink. When he had with his own hands satisfied and served him in many ways with clean and excellent food and drink, and when he knew that the Venerable Cāraka had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin took a lower seat and sat down before the Venerable Cāraka in order to hear the Dharma.

The Venerable Cāraka, having comprehended that brahmin's intention, latent dispositions, constitution, and nature, taught the Dharma in such a way that, even as that brahmin sat right there on that seat, the twenty mountain peaks of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and the fruit of stream-entry was directly realized.

Having seen the truth, that brahmin said: "Venerable one, by relying on you, the good friend, the Venerable Cāraka, what the Venerable Cāraka has done for me — this has not been done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by a king, nor by the gods, nor by the ancestors of old, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by the gathering of friends, companions, and kinsmen. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears, you have freed me from the mountains of bones, you have closed the doors of the lower destinies, you have opened the doors of the higher realms and liberation, you have drawn my feet out from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and you have placed me among gods and humans. You have brought cyclic existence to its end. The twenty mountain peaks of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time have been shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and the fruit of stream-entry has been obtained. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. I ask to be received as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I go for refuge wholeheartedly and with full sincerity.

"May the Venerable Cāraka be so kind as to accept my alms food, robes, lodging, the requisites of the sick, and medical supplies for as long as I live."

The Venerable Cāraka said: "One who has gone forth has entered upon the path of benefiting others, and so must also benefit other brahmins," and by saying this he declined.

The brahmin said: "If the Venerable Cāraka will not accept, then I shall lay out a brahmin's seat for him. May the Venerable Cāraka come and make use of it."

The Venerable Cāraka, by remaining silent, accepted from that brahmin. The Venerable Cāraka duly instructed him with Dharma-filled discourse, established him rightly in it, praised him rightly, and gladdened him rightly, then rose from his seat and departed.

At that time the Venerable Cāraka had tamed and established ten brahmin households in Śrāvastī. The Venerable Cāraka reflected that the time had come to tame certain others. In Śrāvastī there were about five hundred young brahmin householders together with their wives, who had taken up their seats, their food, their perfumes, and many garlands, and had come to a park to amuse themselves. The Venerable Cāraka thought, "Now is the time to tame these people," and went to where they were.

They said to him: "Venerable Cāraka, you are the son of a brahmin family of distinguished lineage — why then have you gone forth among these śramaṇas, these sons of the Śākya, who eat anything and everything?"

The Venerable Cāraka then performed a blessing in this way: whatever garlands they were wearing became garlands of entrails; whatever burdens they were carrying became ox-hides; whatever meat they had became the flesh of cattle; whatever drink they had became beer. Then the Venerable Cāraka showed them his alms bowl and said: "O wise ones, look here — in my alms bowl there are entrails, ox-hide, beef, and beer. Or rather, is it not the case that you yourselves are wearing garlands of entrails upon your heads, eating ox-hide and beef as your food, and drinking beer as your beverage? You are all eaters of anything and everything."

They looked at one another, and seeing that all of them had garlands of entrails upon their heads, that all their burdens had turned to ox-hides, that all their meat had turned to beef, and that all their drink had turned to beer, they said: "Noble Cāraka, remove this curse from us! We beg you to grant us your pardon."

The Venerable Cāraka said: "I forgive you." Thereupon everything reverted to its former state.

They were filled with wonder, and said to him: "Venerable Cāraka, why have you come? You have come for our sake, to tame us. Please sit down and teach us the Dharma."

They took their seats before the Venerable Cāraka in order to hear the Dharma. The Venerable Cāraka, having fully understood the dispositions, latent tendencies, temperaments, and natures of those brahmins together with their wives, taught the Dharma as follows: while those brahmins and their wives remained seated right there, he shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had towered over them, and he taught in such a way that they directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, they spoke: "Venerable Cāraka, by relying upon the virtuous friend that is the Venerable Cāraka, you have done for us what our fathers did not do, what our mothers did not do, what a king did not do, what the gods did not do, what our ancestral forebears did not do, what śramaṇas and brahmins did not do, and what the assembly of friends, companions, and kinsmen did not do. You have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; you have freed us from the mountains of bones; you have closed the doors to the lower destinies; you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; you have lifted our feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; you have placed us among gods and humans; you have brought cyclic existence to an end. With the vajra of wisdom you have shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had been accumulating since beginningless time, and we have obtained the fruit of stream-entry — Venerable Cāraka, we have entered the stream. We have entered the stream, Venerable Cāraka. We take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. We pray that you receive us as lay practitioners."

"From this day forward, for as long as we live, we take refuge wholeheartedly and with complete trust." The brahmins then said, "Venerable Cāraka, we pray that you accept our alms, our robes, our lodgings, our provisions for sickness, and our medicinal requisites for as long as we live." The venerable Cāraka replied, "One who has gone forth (pravrajyā) has entered upon the path of benefiting others, and so one must also benefit other brahmins." With these words he accepted.

Those brahmins said, "If Venerable Cāraka will not accept our offering, we have prepared a seat for a sage — please, Venerable Cāraka, come and enjoy it." Since the venerable Cāraka said nothing in response to the brahmins, he accepted. Then the venerable Cāraka instructed them completely with Dharma-filled discourse, established them fully in it, praised them fully, and filled them with complete joy. Then he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time the venerable Cāraka tamed and settled more than five hundred brahmin households in Śrāvastī on both sides. Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, among my śrāvaka monks who inspire faith in householder families, the foremost is this monk Cāraka the Black."

Now the venerable Cāraka thought: "When the time has come to tame someone" — there was in Śrāvastī a brahmin who, by means of secret spells, had brought a non-human being under his control and was having it draw his carriage — the venerable Cāraka thought, "The time has come to tame that brahmin." And so, in order to tame that brahmin, when the brahmin had brought the non-human being under control through secret spells, had it harnessed to a carriage and was driving outside Śrāvastī, the brahmin descended from the carriage and began to urinate. At that moment the venerable Cāraka blessed things so that the brahmin's stream of urine did not stop; then the venerable Cāraka drew out his spike of secret spells, and the non-human being fled and was gone.

When the brahmin stood up and saw that the non-human being had fled, he said, "Who has drawn out my non-human being's spike?" The venerable Cāraka said, "I have." "Why, though you are a brahmin, do you practise dealings with non-human beings?" The brahmin said, "Who then will serve me?" The venerable Cāraka showed him his alms bowl and said, "This will serve you." The brahmin said, "What can that accomplish?" The venerable Cāraka said, "Whatever you wish for and whatever you desire — all of it will come to be accomplished." And just then, whatever the brahmin wished for and whatever he desired, all of it was accomplished through that alms bowl. The brahmin was filled with wonder and said, "Venerable Cāraka, how does this come about?" The venerable Cāraka replied, "I know the science of the alms bowl." The brahmin said, "Venerable Cāraka, please give me that science of the alms bowl." The venerable Cāraka spoke in verse:

The science should not be given to just anyone.
One should die while still possessing the science.
It may be given for the sake of wisdom with respect,
or for the sake of the Dharma, reverence, or wealth.

The brahmin said, "I will be devoted to you." The venerable Cāraka replied, "I do not accept service from householders; I accept service only from one who has gone forth." The brahmin said, "Then I will go forth." The venerable Cāraka said, "Go forth then," and so he ordained him.

He gave him full ordination and transmitted the instructions. Having thus gone forth, that one dwelt alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, with earnestness, having surrendered himself. Dwelling alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, with earnestness, having surrendered himself, he came to understand, noble sons, why it is that one shaves hair and beard, dons the ochre robes, and with genuine faith goes forth from home into homelessness — that the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, in that very lifetime, is to be directly realized and achieved through one's own direct knowledge, so that one comes to know: "My births are exhausted, the holy life has been lived, the task is done, there is no knowing of another existence beyond this one." He became an arhat, free from attachment, beyond the three realms, with a mind equal toward clods of earth and gold alike, with a mind like the sky and like the palm of the hand, his wisdom having split open the hollow of the doorpost like a wedge of sandalwood. He attained the knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the individual perfect understandings. He turned his back on gains born of existence and desire, and on honors. He became one worthy of worship, of reverence, and of praise by the gods together with Indra and his retinue.

The venerable Cāraka considered: "The time has come to tame this wrestler." A single wrestler from a certain region had gone about the districts defeating wrestlers and came to Śrāvastī, where he sat at the city gate with his legs stretched out, and to each person who came by he announced: "Either come wrestle me in a contest of strength, or go kneel before me." Among the great crowds of common people who had gathered, not one challenged him to a contest of strength, nor did anyone go to kneel before him. The venerable Cāraka thought: "The time has come to tame that wrestler." The venerable Cāraka went in that direction and asked, "Who is this?" The crowd of common people replied: "This wrestler has been announcing: 'Either come wrestle me in a contest of strength, or go kneel before me.'" The venerable Cāraka said to the wrestler: "Shall I wrestle with you myself, or shall I have you wrestle together with the three wrestlers I have already defeated?" The wrestler replied: "Let me wrestle together with those three wrestlers you have defeated." The venerable Cāraka said: "I have defeated the wrestler of attachment, I have defeated the wrestler of aversion, I have defeated the wrestler of delusion — now go wrestle with them together." Having thus tamed the wrestler, Cāraka ordained him, gave him full ordination, and transmitted the instructions.

Having thus gone forth, that one dwelt alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, with earnestness, having surrendered himself. Dwelling alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, with earnestness, having surrendered himself, he came to understand, noble sons, why it is that one shaves hair and beard, dons the ochre robes, and with genuine faith goes forth from home into homelessness — that the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, in that very lifetime, is to be directly realized and achieved through one's own direct knowledge, so that one comes to know: "My births are exhausted, the holy life has been lived, the task is done, there is no knowing of another existence beyond this one." He became an arhat, free from attachment, beyond the three realms, with a mind equal toward clods of earth and gold alike, with a mind like the sky and like the palm of the hand, his wisdom having split open the hollow of the doorpost like a wedge of sandalwood. He attained the knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the individual perfect understandings. He turned his back on gains born of existence and desire, and on honors. He became one worthy of worship, of reverence, and of praise by the gods together with Indra and

Brahma, together with all the surrounding gods, he became one worthy of worship, of reverence, and of open praise.

Now that fierce woman took her son's wife into her household. Some time later, the fierce woman's own time came, and her husband's time came as well. Her son had gone abroad on some business of recitation, and so his wife remained behind. That daughter-in-law, indulging in fine and pleasant food and clothing, became tormented by afflictions, and she said to her serving-maid: "Girl, go and find me some man who is sturdy and well-built, some worthy fellow of whatever sort you can find, and bring him so that I may enjoy pleasure with him." The serving-maid replied: "My lady, your father-in-law and mother-in-law were seers of truth. If you were to come to a household such as this one of a sage, how could it be fitting to behave in such a way? Would you bring ill repute upon the household of a sage?" She replied: "Bah! What business of yours is what I think? Just go and bring someone back. If you do not bring someone, I shall have you severely punished." The girl thought: "This woman, this glutton's daughter, is set on filling the sage's household with filth — and I cannot prevent it. I had better fetch someone myself." So she went to the marketplace, and there she saw a sturdy, well-built man who was a captain of bandits. She said to him: "Good sir, would you dare to enjoy pleasure together with my mistress?" He replied: "I would dare." She brought him and presented him to her mistress, and he and the mistress began to enjoy pleasure together.

The venerable Carka used to come there from time to time, and he saw them. The venerable Carka thought: "This woman is one who pursues desire," and he spoke to her words that were not praise of desire. She thought: "The noble Carka is skilled at knowing the minds of others — he sees through me. If he is not killed, he will tell my husband, and he will come to harm me. I must have him killed." So she said to the captain of bandits: "The noble Carka is skilled at knowing the minds of others — he sees through us. If he is not killed, he will tell my husband, and he will come to harm us. You must kill him." The captain of bandits replied: "I will not kill him. He is a close friend of King Prasenajit of Kosala, and he is the teacher of Queen Mālikā. If I were to kill him, the king would have me put into a house of lac and burned to death — that is the kind of situation it would be." She said: "If you kill him, so much the better. If you do not kill him, you are never to enter her house again." Since those who cling to desire will stop at no evil deed, the captain of bandits said: "If he is skilled at knowing the minds of others, how am I to kill him?" She said: "We shall use a stratagem," and she sent a messenger to the venerable Carka at an unsuitable time with the message: "Venerable Carka, I am in distress — would you be so kind as to come and see me?" Now since arhats do not exercise their knowledge and vision without first reflecting, the venerable Carka too entered without prior reflection, taught her the Dharma, and then began to leave. As he did so, she said: "Noble one, I am so glad to see you — please stay just a little while," and she detained the venerable Carka until it was very late into the night. Meanwhile the captain of bandits drew his sword from its scabbard and stood waiting at the door. Then, as the venerable Carka came out,

The captain of bandits, his mind devoid of compassion and utterly heedless of the world to come, severed the venerable Carka's head at the neck and threw him to the ground. An old woman witnessed him standing there having killed that noble one, and she said: "Who is this ruffian?" The captain of bandits replied: "Don't tell anyone. I could treat you the same way right now." Frightened, she dared not speak immediately, and thinking that someone might come later to avenge this great one, she sat there in silence saying nothing. The two of them — that merciless pair, heedless of the world to come — hid the venerable Carka's body beneath a pile of cloth and left it there.

That same day, at the restoration ceremony (poṣadha), the elder took his seat at the edge of the assembly and said: "Has anyone taken the venerable Carka's leave? The venerable Carka is absent." Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, that foremost among the faithful laypeople has been killed. Gather the robes and make offerings to his body."

Now the Blessed One, together with the noble one, came out through the gate of Śrāvastī, and as he did so he emitted a light like the radiance of gold, so that all of Śrāvastī shone with a brilliance like refined gold. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, thought: "Why has all of Śrāvastī come to shine with a radiance like refined gold?" And then he thought: "I hope the Blessed One has not decided to depart," and so, together with his queen's retinue, he took the key of Śrāvastī, opened the gate, and the Blessed One proceeded into Śrāvastī. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, thought: "Why has the Blessed One come into Śrāvastī at this unusual hour?" Buddhas, blessed ones, are difficult to approach and difficult to endure, so he was unable to ask the Blessed One about it. The Blessed One, accompanied by the Saṅgha of hearers, went forward, and Prasenajit, king of Kośala, together with his queen's retinue, followed along behind the Blessed One step by step until they arrived at the place where the pile of cloth lay.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, uncover that foremost among the faithful laypeople who has been hidden here." When he was uncovered, those who, through relying on the venerable Carka, had seen the noble truths (āryasatya) made this request: "He is our spiritual friend — Blessed One, do you permit us to make offerings to his body?" The Blessed One did not give permission. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, requested: "He was my dear companion — Blessed One, do you permit me to make offerings to his body?" The Blessed One did not give permission. Queen Mālyavatī requested: "He was my teacher — Blessed One, do you permit me to make offerings to his body?" The Blessed One gave permission. Then Queen Mālyavatī had the venerable Carka's body wrapped in white cloth and anointed with perfumed water, adorned it all around with garments of many colors, placed it within, and left it there. Then the Blessed One, accompanied by the Saṅgha of hearers, went forward, and the king together with the queen's retinue followed step by step behind. They set the body down in a spacious open spot, and Queen Mālyavatī heaped all manner of fragrant wood into a pyre, burned it, quenched the pyre with milk,

They placed those bones in a golden urn, and had a bodily reliquary stupa built at a great crossroads in the middle of the road. They raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and made offerings with fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powder, and cymbals. They prostrated at his feet, and then the Blessed One gave praise and departed. The Blessed One then went to the temple and sat upon the seat that had been prepared for him before the Saṅgha of monks. Having sat down, the Blessed One spoke to the monks: "Monks, this fault and others arise from monks entering a village at an improper time. Therefore, monks, having clearly seen these ten benefits, a rule of training for hearers is to be established in the Vinaya," and so on, as before. "My hearers are to proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: whatever monk enters a village at an improper time incurs a transgression." Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training for hearers in the Vinaya.

Then there was an occasion when monks who were seriously ill could not remain sitting for long, when monk-attendants were neglecting the care of sick monks, and when monks doing service were neglecting the work of the Saṅgha. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, one should speak to the monks who are seated and then depart." After the Blessed One had given the instruction that one should speak to the seated monks before departing, it happened that a monk had left his alms bowl and robe at another household, and a fire broke out there, and as the monk set out to go there, he had gone half the way when the thought arose: "I have not spoken to the seated monks." He turned back, and for as long as it took him to speak to the seated monks, his alms bowl and robe were burned, and he then went there. The householder said: "Noble one, why have you come so late? That is why your alms bowl and robe have burned. If you had come quickly, your alms bowl and robe would not have burned." The monk was then at a loss, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, except in such circumstances." Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who are furnished with the necessities for training, and addressed the monks with words that were in accord with this, that were in large measure devoted to it, and that were endowed with teachings consonant with it. He then spoke to the monks: "Monks, therefore the former rule remains as it was established, and this is now permitted. My hearers are to proclaim this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: whatever monk enters a village at an improper time and does not speak to the seated monks incurs a transgression, except in such circumstances. As for the term 'whatever monk,' this refers to one of this kind or similarly to any other. 'At an improper time' means at one of two improper times: before dawn has broken, and after midday has passed. 'A village' means any place where there are streets, crossroads, and intersections. 'Enters' means goes into. 'Does not speak to the seated monks' means to whatever monk is seated there. 'Except in such circumstances' means with those circumstances granted as an exception. 'Incurs a transgression' means —" and here follows a descent into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (pretas), the lower destinies,

— lower destinies, the states of wrong rebirth — it burns, it scorches, it causes one to fall. Furthermore, for as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous qualities. Therefore it is said to be a transgression. As for how a transgression arises in that case: if a monk, perceiving an improper time as an improper time, enters a village, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, having doubt about an improper time, enters a village, a transgression is incurred. If a monk, perceiving a proper time as an improper time, enters a village, a misdeed is incurred. If a monk, having doubt about a proper time, enters a village, a misdeed is incurred. For one who is a beginner, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, and for one afflicted by feelings, there is no transgression.

Queen Mallikā spoke to Prasenajit, the king of Kosala: "The god has granted to the monks the complete abandonment belonging to a young man, and to the nuns the complete abandonment belonging to a queen's retinue. The noble Cāraka was my younger companion and my teacher. If so renowned a monk as that can be killed by force, who would heed any command given to other monks less renowned?" The king said: "Who ordered the noble Cāraka's death and who killed him? What punishment shall be given?" Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, commanded his men who lived by wages: "Wise ones, speak now — who ordered the noble Cāraka to be slain, and who slew him?" They set out to find them in that direction, and there they saw an old woman. But she had not yet seen them, and the old woman spoke to the local people: "The one who was foremost among the faithful householders of this area — that revered one was killed by such and such persons." When they heard this they said: "What is the old woman saying?" The old woman replied: "Nothing at all." They seized her and interrogated her: "Tell us who killed him." She said: "A brahmin's daughter ordered the killing, and a bandit captain carried it out." They pressed her further: "Is it only those two?" She replied: "There are also five hundred accomplices." The king's men seized the brahmin's daughter, the bandit captain, and the five hundred accomplices, presented them to the king, and said: "Your Majesty, the noble Cāraka was ordered to his death by this brahmin's daughter, and killed by this bandit captain. This one here is the leader of these five hundred accomplices." The king said: "Wise ones, today let this brahmin's daughter be bound to the legs of a wild colt. Let this bandit captain be put into a house of lac and burned. Let the hands and feet of these five hundred accomplices be cut off." And so his men bound the brahmin's daughter to the legs of a wild colt, put the bandit captain into a house of lac and burned him, and cut off the hands and feet of the five hundred accomplices.

The monks were filled with doubt, and to resolve all their doubts they asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, what deed had the venerable Cāraka done that by the karmic ripening of that deed, though he had no enmity and had caused no harm, he came to be killed by those two, those two also came to be killed, and the five hundred accomplices came to have their hands and feet cut off?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, they themselves had gathered that accumulation of karma.

They had performed and accumulated deeds that are inevitably altered by conditions and that arise like light shining in proximity to something. As for the karma they themselves had thus performed and accumulated, who else would experience it separately? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even for a hundred aeons
karma does not perish.
When the time and conditions meet,
it surely ripens for embodied beings.

Monks, in a time long past, in a previous age, when King Brahmadatta was ruling his kingdom in Vārāṇasī, a time of hardship arose, and non-Buddhist seers prophesied that a famine would come lasting twelve years. King Brahmadatta had a proclamation announced: "Let those who have provisions for twelve years remain; let those who do not, depart." Now in front of the king's crier there was a group of about five hundred brahmin boys who were being trained in secret brahmin recitations. These brahmin boys said to him: "Teacher, we have no provisions for twelve years, and so we must go." He replied: "Boys, stay — I will provide you with what you need."

In a dream, King Brahmadatta saw his own intestines coiled around the entire city. Having seen this, he became terrified, thinking: "Surely this means I will either lose my kingdom, or my life will be cut short, or both." He recounted the dream to the crier, and the crier thought to himself: "His Majesty has had a fine dream, but I must not let it become an obstacle to the brahmin boys' livelihood — I should interpret it badly." And so the crier said to the king: "Your Majesty has had a terrible dream; it means you will certainly lose your kingdom, or your life will be cut short, or both." The king said: "What is to be done?" The crier replied: "Your Majesty should offer a great sacrifice of bulls." The king said: "So be it." The crier had a great many thousands of bulls assembled, and when the king came out and saw them, the bulls let out a tremendous lowing. Seeing and hearing them, the king was moved with compassion, and he said to the crier: "Should all of these be slaughtered?" The crier thought: "The king does not wish them all killed," and so he replied: "Your Majesty, not all of them need be killed." Just then a male servant mounted a female servant, and the crier said: "Your Majesty, these two — this man and this woman — shall be killed." The brahmin boys stretched out their hands and, pointing, said: "These are the ones." When those two were led away to be killed, their minds were shaken, and they made a solemn resolve: "We two, who have no enmity and have done no harm, are being killed — and all of this is the doing of that crier and those five hundred brahmin boys. In every future life in which we two are born, may we kill this crier even when he bears us no enmity and has done us no harm, and may we cause those five hundred brahmin boys to have their hands and feet cut off."

Monks, the one who at that time and on that occasion was King Brahmadatta — that one is none other than the present King Prasenajit of Kosala. The one who at that time and on that occasion was the queen of King Brahmadatta — that one is none other than the present queen Mālinī. The one who at that time and on that occasion was the crier — that one is none other than the present monk Śārika. The five hundred brahmin boys of that time and occasion — those are none other than the present five hundred men with withered hands. The one who at that time and on that occasion was the male slave — that one is none other than the present captain of bandits. The one who at that time and on that occasion was the female slave — that one is none other than the present brahmin girl. And through the karmic maturation of the deed by which that crier and those five hundred brahmin boys had the male slave and the female slave killed, even though those two bore no enmity and had done no harm, even now this captain of bandits and this brahmin girl have caused Śārika and the five hundred men with withered hands to be killed, even though those bore no enmity and had done no harm.

Venerable ones, what action did the long-lived Śārika perform such that through its karmic maturation he was born into a household of wealth, great riches, and abundant possessions? And what action did he perform such that he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, and by abandoning all afflictions he directly realized arhatship? And what action did he perform such that even upon attaining arhatship he passed into nirvāṇa by the sword?

The Blessed One declared: Monks, it was the noble son Śārika himself who gathered the accumulation of karma, thoroughly transformed the conditions, and abided like a flame — those deeds were performed and accumulated so that they would inevitably arise. And those things performed and accumulated by Śārika himself — who else could experience them individually? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even were a hundred aeons to pass,
karma once performed does not perish;
when the conditions and the time are met,
embodied beings receive its fruit.

Monks, in a past time long ago, when no buddhas had appeared in the world, a pratyekabuddha — humble, impoverished, compassionate, delighting in remote dwelling places, solitary as a rhinoceros horn — arose in the world as a worthy field of offerings. Now, at a certain cliffside there dwelt a hunter, and not far from that cliff there was a small lake that served as a home for many deer and birds. Day after day that hunter would set out hunting, would lay down many snares and nets, all in order to drive away the deer and birds, to torment them, and to cause them suffering in improper ways. And those hunting devices, those snares and nets, were effective.

Then at some point, as a pratyekabuddha was wandering through that region, he arrived at that cliff. Having agreed to spend the night at a divine abode, he rose early in the morning, donned his lower robe, took up his begging bowl and monastic robes, and entered that cliff area on his alms round. Having made his rounds there for alms, he thought: "This divine abode has a great deal of activity and bustle during the day — I shall eat my alms food in some peaceful place outside the cliff." So he departed from the cliff, thinking "This is peaceful, this is peaceful," and went toward the direction of that small lake. When he arrived there, he set down his begging bowl and water vessel side by side, washed his two feet, and rubbed his two hands together, and drew water.

He gathered some fallen leaves, sat down, performed the act of eating, rinsed his two hands, washed his mouth, and set down the begging bowl and water vessel exactly as they had been. He washed his two feet, leaned against the base of a tree, and sat cross-legged in the manner of the king of serpents coiled in repose, remaining there in tranquil deportment. That day, not a single animal was taken by the human hunter.

Then the next morning the hunter rose early, went to that small lake, and began searching through his hunting grounds, his traps, and his snares, but did not see a single animal. He thought to himself: "If my hunting grounds, traps, and snares are of any use, then what is the reason that not a single animal has been caught there?" So he began to circle the perimeter of that small lake, and seeing a human footprint, he followed it, tracing it step by step. He then saw the pratyekabuddha seated in tranquil deportment, and thought: "Those who have gone forth, with their minds so peaceful, delight in dwelling in such places as this. If I do not kill this one, he will surely cut off my livelihood. By all means I must kill him." With a mind utterly devoid of compassion, that one who had cast aside regard for the next world filled his arrow with poison all the way to the notch, so that it resembled the curve of a bow, and shot it into a vital point of that pratyekabuddha.

That great pratyekabuddha thought: "It would not be right for this afflicted hunter to become deeply wretched and degenerate. Now I must pull him out of this by hand." So, spreading his wings like the king of geese, he rose into the sky above, blazing and brilliant, sending down rain and flashing lightning, displaying miraculous feats. Since ordinary persons quickly fix their minds upon miraculous displays, that hunter fell at the feet of the pratyekabuddha, as if a great tree had been cut off at the root, and said: "O true field of merit, please descend! Please descend! I beg you, pull me out by the collar from the mire of affliction into which I have sunk." Out of compassionate concern for that hunter, the pratyekabuddha descended from the sky above.

Then the hunter, making him free from the arrow's pain, dressed the wound smoothly and said: "Noble one, please accept this reconciliation. If it would be fitting to dress the wound with a gold poultice here, I will apply that as well." The pratyekabuddha thought: "Whatever was to be obtained by means of this body of pus has already been obtained. Therefore, now I shall enter into the expanse of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates." He rose once more into the middle of the sky, right before that hunter, displayed various miraculous feats, and then passed fully into nirvāṇa in the expanse of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates.

The hunter was a man of wealth, so he gathered all the finest fragrant woods, stacked them into a pyre, and burned the body. He quenched the remains with milk, placed the bones in a golden urn, and had a bodily reliquary stūpa built at the crossroads of a great highway. He raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and made offerings of perfumes, garlands, incense, powders, and musical instruments. He prostrated at the feet of the stūpa and uttered this aspiration: "Whatever virtue roots exist in these offerings I have made — offered in a manner disproportionate to the harm I did to such a true field of merit — by this virtue may I not be reborn in accordance with the karma of that harmful act.

"May I be reborn in a household that is wealthy, with abundant riches, and great prosperity."

Monks, the hunter who lived in that time and age is none other than Śārka. Because of the karma of having pierced the pratyekabuddha with a poisoned arrow, he was tormented for an aeon in the Great Hell of Unceasing Torment, and through the remaining force of that same karma he was reborn for five hundred lifetimes as a wild animal on the shore of that very lake, and met his end by the blade at each appointed time. Even now, although he has attained the state of an arhat, he will pass fully into nirvāṇa by the blade. As for the one who made offerings and uttered that aspiration, he has now been reborn in a household that is wealthy, with abundant riches, and great prosperity.

Venerable Śārka — what karma did he perform, such that through its maturation his body at the appointed time was concealed beneath a heap of silken cloth, that he gladdened the Teacher and caused him no distress of mind, that the Teacher along with the Saṅgha of hearers and the royal consort with her retinue made bodily offerings to him at the appointed time of his passing, and that he thus came to obtain such an assembly of virtuous qualities?

Monks, Śārka himself assembled and accumulated actions that were acquired, had their conditions fully transformed, abided like a flame, and were bound to arise without fail. The karma that Śārka himself performed and accumulated — who else would experience it individually? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas):

Actions, though it be a hundred aeons,
do not perish or go to waste.
When the time and conditions meet,
beings indeed receive their fruits.

Monks, in times gone by, in ages past, when no buddhas had appeared in the world, solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas) of lesser station arose in the world — those who had compassion for the poor and destitute, who delighted in remote and secluded dwellings, who lived alone like a rhinoceros horn, and who had become fields of merit for the world. In a certain snowy valley five hundred pratyekabuddhas dwelt. One of them fell ill, and the others said to him: "Please go and seek out a physician and have the treatments performed." He went to another rocky crag and that night agreed to take shelter in the enclosure of a potter's workshop. That very night he fell ill and passed away at the appointed time.

The potter, seeing him there, thought to himself: "This renunciant has passed away at the appointed time inside this enclosure, among the fired and unfired pots. Since the world values cleanliness, if people come to know of this, no one will buy any vessel." So he hid the pratyekabuddha's body beneath a heap of silken cloth and left it there.

The other pratyekabuddhas thought: "Where has our companion in the holy life gone?" They looked, and when they saw that he had passed fully into nirvāṇa, they came straightaway through the sky carrying fragrant sandalwood and descended into the potter's enclosure. When the potter saw them he asked: "Noble ones, where are you going?" They replied: "We are going to make offerings to our companion in the holy life." The potter said: "Did he also obtain an assembly of virtuous qualities such as yours?" They replied: "He did." The potter said: "I have shown him disrespect, and I wish to now pay him proper honor — please wait just a moment." He went and spoke to the king.

The king said to the god: "A renunciant who had gone forth at my enclosure and had perfected his ascetic practice has passed away; please pay him honor." The king came out together with his queen and their retinue, and he had the body of the pratyekabuddha heaped up with fragrant sandalwood and cremated. Once the pyre had been doused with milk, the bones were placed in a golden urn, and at a crossroads on the great highway he had a bodily stupa built. He raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and offered worship with fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powders, and musical instruments.

The potter prostrated at the feet of the pratyekabuddha's remains and made this aspiration: "Whatever the root of virtue is in this act of making offerings, which does not correspond to the weight of my karma in having caused harm to one who was a true field of merit — by this may I not fail to please and gladden a Teacher who is supremely exalted beyond even this one, and at the hour of my own death may the Teacher together with the Saṅgha of hearers, and together with a retinue of queens, perform bodily worship over me."

Then the Blessed One said: Monks, at that time and at that occasion the potter is this very monk Śārikā (Cārka). By the karmic maturation of concealing the body of that pratyekabuddha under a heap of rags, he is now, at the hour of his own death, concealed under a heap of rags. And by the karmic maturation of having made offerings to the body of that pratyekabuddha and having made that aspiration, he has now, through a Teacher supremely exalted beyond a hundred thousand myriads of pratyekabuddhas, pleased me, the Teacher, and not caused me distress; and at this hour of his death, the Teacher together with the Saṅgha of hearers and together with the queen and retinue of a king have performed bodily worship over him.

As for what action the venerable Cārka performed that, by its karmic maturation, the Blessed One proclaimed him the foremost among those of household faith — it was through the power of aspiration. Where was that aspiration made? Monks, long ago in the past, in this very excellent great aeon, when the life span of beings was twenty thousand years, there arose in the world the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, Kāśyapa. He dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at the Grove of Seers (Ṛṣipatana) near Vārāṇasī. In his teaching this one had gone forth, and the monk by whom he was ordained — that monk was proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, as the foremost among those of household faith.

Now this one practiced the holy life throughout his entire life and did not attain so much as a single virtuous quality, and at the time of death he made this aspiration: "Though I have practiced the holy life throughout my entire life in the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, the unsurpassed field of merit, Kāśyapa, I have not attained a single virtuous quality.

"By the root of virtue of having practiced the holy life throughout my entire life, may I, in the teaching of that very one whom the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, prophesied to the brahmin youth, his preceptor, saying: 'Brahmin youth, you, in a future age when the human lifespan is one hundred years, will encounter a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha and Blessed One named Śākyamuni' — may I, having gone forth in that one's teaching and having abandoned all afflictions, directly realize the state of arhathood. And just as this preceptor was proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, as the foremost among those of household faith, so too may I be proclaimed as foremost among those of household faith by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the chief sovereign of the Śākya kings." Having thus set this aspiration, by the power of that aspiration he has now been proclaimed by the Tathāgata as foremost among those of household faith.

Monks, thus it is that the karmic maturation of utterly dark actions is utterly dark, the karmic maturation of utterly bright actions is utterly bright, and the karmic maturation of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandoning utterly dark actions and mixed actions, you should strive for utterly bright actions. Monks, you should train yourselves accordingly.

The eightfold transgression of going at an improper time is complete.

The Vinaya-vibhaṅga, the sixty-eighth bundle.

Summary verse:

With food, at dawn, just now,
needle-case and bed-leg,
spreading out, cotton quilting and wool,
great cloth, the well-gone one's Dharma robe.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder. The venerable Ānanda would go to that householder's home from time to time, and the householder had taken refuge and been established in the training precepts. On another occasion, Ānanda extensively praised to him the seven bases for accumulating merit through material things. The householder said: "Noble one, I too shall perform some of the bases for accumulating merit through material things." Ānanda said: "Excellent — do so. What will you do?" The householder replied: "I shall offer a meal to the community of monks headed by the Buddha." "Householder, generate a vast mind and offer the meal. Noble one, it is fitting that you invite the community of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal at my quarters tomorrow, in my name." The householder agreed.

Then the venerable Ānanda took leave of that householder, went to the monastery, and in that householder's name invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal at a different house. The monks then said: "Venerable Ānanda, if that householder is a person of no faith, how did you get him to participate?" Ānanda replied: "Venerable ones, is this not enough for a friend? Not only did he participate, but he has also taken refuge and been established in the training precepts." The monks said: "Well done — go and eat. By convention, whoever has invited the community of monks, it is customary for that person to arrive first. Therefore, venerable Ānanda, you should go there ahead of time." And so the venerable Ānanda went ahead to that place and said to the householder:

"Householder, I am going into the house. In the meantime, please prepare the food. And until I return, do not serve it." Having said this, he departed.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and inform the monks that since the householder does not know the custom, he will not be sending a formal invitation. Go ahead early." The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he conveyed the message to the monks. The monks made ready and came. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks and with the community of monks going before him, proceeded to that householder's dwelling, and stood waiting at the door.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go inside and say to the householder: 'A buddha and the community of monks are standing at your door — please do as is convenient.'" The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he went inside and said to the householder: "Householder, a buddha and the community of monks are standing at your door — please do as is convenient." The householder replied: "Noble one, I have not sought your comfort and convenience — rather, I have prepared seats for you alone. Please be seated." The venerable Ānanda then reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the householder has said: 'I have not sought your comfort and convenience — rather, I have prepared seats for you alone. Please be seated.'"

The Blessed One declared: "If that is what he says, then tell him: 'Since you have prepared seats for us alone and done what is convenient, we shall come in and sit — there need be no regret in this.'" And so the Blessed One and the community of monks seated themselves. As they sat there, the hour of midday drew near.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and say to the householder: 'Midday is drawing near — please serve the food. What use will this food be to you?'" The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he conveyed the message to the householder. The householder said: "Has the noble Ānanda arrived?" The venerable Ānanda replied: "Householder, he has not yet come." The householder said: "Noble one, please wait just a little while until he arrives."

The venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when I conveyed the householder's words, he asked whether noble Ānanda had come, and I said he had not. Then he said: 'Please wait just a little while until he arrives.'"

The Blessed One waited a short while and then again said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and say to the householder: 'Midday has passed — the food will spoil. What use will it be to you?'" The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having heard this from the Blessed One, he conveyed the message to the householder. The householder said: "Has the noble Ānanda arrived?" The venerable Ānanda said: "Householder, he has not yet come." The householder said: "Noble one, please wait just a little while until he arrives."

The venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when I conveyed the householder's words, he asked whether noble Ānanda had come, and I replied that he had not. He then said: 'Please wait just a little while until he arrives.'"

The Blessed One then declared:

"Ānanda, go and ask the householder: 'Will you not serve food if the friend has not arrived?'"

The venerable Ānanda, saying "As you command, Venerable One," heard this from the Blessed One and conveyed the words to the householder. The householder replied: "Noble one, he will not be fed."

The venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, he says he will not be fed."

Then at that moment the Blessed One declared these verses:

All that depends on others is suffering;
all that depends on oneself is happiness.
What is shared brings harm,
and ties are exceedingly hard to sever.

When the shadow had fallen to the edge of the sundial's measure, the friend arrived and said: "Householder, why do you sit here so improperly?" The householder replied: "Noble one, it came from your own mouth that I should wait a little while until you arrived — and now you say this?" The friend, overcome with shame, sat there saying nothing at all.

The householder then began to serve the meal. By the time the shadow had passed beyond the sundial's mark, some of the monks had received food and stopped eating, while others stopped eating without having received food at all. The Blessed One then gave thanks and departed.

The friend, his heart burning with embarrassment, remained right there on the spot.

That same day, the presiding elder of the restoration ceremony was sitting off to one side. He duly addressed the monks and said: "Is the venerable friend not present? Has anyone taken his turn?" The monks replied: "He has not come, and no one has taken his turn either."

Other monks then said: "Venerable ones, the friend roused us all in the morning for the sake of material offerings, and now he is rousing us for the sake of the Dharma as well." Monks of few wants condemned him, saying: "Why is it that monks, having been invited as guests to a house with food, wander from house to house in the morning and again in the afternoon?" They criticized him, mocked him, and spoke ill of him.

The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this incident, with this as the occasion and this as the context, convened an assembly of the monastic Saṅgha, and so forth, just as before. That the awakened Blessed Ones knowingly pose questions, and so forth, is likewise just as before.

The awakened Blessed One questioned the friend: "Friend, is it true that, having been invited as a guest to a house with food, you wander from house to house in the morning and again in the afternoon?" "Venerable One, it is true."

The awakened Blessed One then censured him, saying that conduct unbecoming an ascetic, conduct that is not appropriate, not suitable, not in conformity with good conduct — such conduct is not to be performed by one who has gone forth.

Having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits clearly, a training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya shall be established," and so forth, just as before. "My śrāvakas shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk who, having been invited as a guest to a house with food, wanders from house to house in the morning and again in the afternoon, incurs a transgression."

Thus did the awakened Blessed One establish this training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

Now, certain gravely ill monks who were bedridden were unable to remain sitting for a long time, and those monks who attended the sick neglected their duties toward the patients.

The monks who attended the sick were also neglecting the duties of the Saṅgha. The Blessed One therefore declared, "One should send word to the laypeople who are present in the house." Having declared, "The Blessed One says one should send word to the laypeople who are present in the house," a certain monk had left his almsbowl and his robe in another dwelling, and while he was away a fire broke out there. The monk set out to go back, and when he had reached the halfway point of the road, the thought arose to him, "I have not yet sent word to the laypeople who are present." So he turned back, and by the time he had sent word to the laypeople who were present, his almsbowl and his robe had burned. When he arrived at the place, the householder said, "Noble one, why have you come so late? That is why your almsbowl and robe have burned. Had you come quickly, your almsbowl and robe would not have burned." The monk was left in a state of want. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, circumstances such as these shall be excepted."

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of the wish to train, of respect for the training, and of supplying provisions for the training, addressed the monks with words accordant with this, weighty in significance, and endowed with qualities befitting the occasion. He then declared to the monks, "Monks, the former rule has been established, and this is now permitted. My śrāvakas shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Any monk who, having been invited as a guest to a house with food, wanders from house to house in the morning and again in the afternoon without sending word to the laypeople who are present — except in circumstances such as these — incurs a transgression."

Now, "any monk" means a son of the Śākyas who has gone forth, or another of that sort. "With food" means together with an invitation. "To a house" means to a house of a brahmin or a householder. "Having been invited" means for the sake of alms-rounds. "In the morning" means in the morning itself, wandering past more than two houses. "In the afternoon" means in the afternoon itself, wandering past more than three houses. "From house to house" means the houses of brahmins and householders. "Wandering" means going about. "Without sending word to the laypeople who are present" means to whatever laypeople happen to be present there. "Except in circumstances such as these" means excepting circumstances of that kind. "Incurs a transgression" means it causes burning, scorching, and falling into the bad destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts (pretas), evil states, and states of ruinous fall. Furthermore, as long as the transgression is neither confessed nor individually confessed, it obstructs wholesome qualities — and therefore it is said to incur a transgression.

As to how a transgression arises in this regard: a monk who has been invited as a guest to any dwelling with food and who in the morning wanders past more than two houses, or in the afternoon wanders past more than three houses, incurs a transgression in every such instance. If he has not been invited there, there is no transgression. There is no transgression for a first offender, for one who is deranged, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feelings.

The eighty-first offence of the class of transgressions relating to wandering through villages is complete.

Summary verse of the training rules up to the rule on closing doors:

Nanda, Ānanda, seven days and good giving, binding together, ethical conduct,
Blackman, verse, and the writing board,
ten items, the sequence of training rules,
two cities, the battle-ground,
the goddess, the hanging bowl,
blue-green, purified, the royal sovereignty, Poka,
the gift of a meal to a mother —

the lord of footwear, Śrāvastī,
the former conduct, Noruzang,
the sages and the temple,
the one who gives joy, the one who retains,
a thousand ascetics, the pastoral dwelling,
the handed-down transmission, the purified blue-green,
born among those without grief,
the great hero, the supreme hunchback,
the incomparable woman, the blacksmith,
Siṃhala and the easterner,
the sweet speaker and the burned one,
the hunchback and the one who holds what is heard,
the maidservant and the brahmin woman,
Joyful-giver who became glorious,
and those who entered through Śāriputra —
these are what is comprised in the chapter on closing doors.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, meditate with concentration in such dwelling places as these: forests, the roots of trees, empty houses, mountain ravines, mountain caves, thatched huts, open spaces without cover, charnel grounds, woodland groves, the foot of a mountain, and lodgings at the edge of a threshing floor. Monks, practise with diligence so that you will not come to regret it afterward. This is my instruction and subsequent guidance to you."

Having said this to the monks, the Blessed One continued, and the monks entered into forests, the roots of trees, empty houses, mountain ravines, mountain caves, thatched huts, open spaces without cover, charnel grounds, woodland groves, the foot of a mountain, and lodgings at the edge of a threshing floor. Some meditated on the terraces of Mount Meru (Sumeru). Some meditated on the seven golden mountains. Some meditated beside the great lake Anavatapta. Some meditated beside the gently flowing pond. And some meditated in towns and villages, hamlets, districts and their surroundings, and in various quarters of the royal palace — places suited to yogic practitioners.

The king of mountains, Mount Meru, extends eighty thousand leagues into the water and rises eighty thousand leagues above the water, making a total extent of one hundred and sixty thousand leagues. Each face of Mount Meru measures eighty thousand leagues by eighty thousand leagues, giving a total of three hundred and twenty thousand leagues on its faces. Mount Meru, made of four precious substances, is beautiful of form, pleasing to behold, and lovely. There, the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda were born, and with their bodies they coiled around it three times and took hold of it, remaining there for an eon, so that Suparṇa — Garuḍa, king of birds — was unable to lift it. These two thought to themselves, "This place of merit has come about for the two of us." But being completely enveloped by miserliness, three times each day they exhaled an inimical wind, and by this wind the deer and many birds dwelling on the terraces of Mount Meru were caused to suffer in an improper way.

Now, those monks who were meditating on the terraces of Mount Meru were also left pale and haggard by that inimical wind. They became emaciated, feeble, thin, and their bodies wasted away. When the three months of the summer rains retreat had passed, they came to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and the monks who saw them said: "Welcome, venerable ones. Welcome. From where have you come? Where did you commit to spend the rains retreat?"

Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, we have come from the terraces of Mount Meru. We committed to spend the rains retreat on the terraces of Mount Meru."

The monks said:

The monks said: "Venerable ones, why have you become pale and haggard, emaciated, feeble, thin, and wasted in body?"

Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, on the terraces of Mount Meru there were born two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda. The two of them coiled their bodies around the terraces of Mount Meru three times and settled there, remaining for an aeon, holding the earth fast — so that even Suparṇa, king of the winged ones, was unable to drive them away. The two of them thought: 'A source of merit has arisen for us.' And so, overcome entirely by miserliness, three times each day they sent forth an inimical wind, which caused the many deer and birds dwelling on the terraces of Mount Meru to suffer in an improper way. We too, by that inimical wind, became pale and haggard, emaciated, feeble, thin, and our bodies wasted away."

The monks then said: "Venerable ones, were you not able to tame those two?"

Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, we were not the ones to tame them."

"Then who is able to tame them?"

"They can be tamed by a great śrāvaka."

At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then considered: who would be capable of taming those two? He saw and knew that they could be tamed by the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and so he spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, go and attend to the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, on the terraces of Mount Meru."

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied: "Revered one, I shall do as you command," and having heard the Blessed One's words, he entered into such a meditative absorption that, just as his mind settled in equipoise, he disappeared from Śrāvastī and arrived on the terraces of Mount Meru. He remained there in that very meditative absorption.

Now at that time the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, were asleep. Mahāmaudgalyāyana began to rouse them with a snap of his fingers, but the two did not wake. He then began to strike them from above, yet still the two did not wake. He entered between them and began to thunder like a great storm cloud, yet still the two did not wake.

He then coiled the body of a great nāga around the king of mountains, Mount Meru, seven times, and sitting there, made a great pressing weight upon it. The two were awakened by the crushing heaviness of that weight, and as they woke and saw that a great nāga was pressing down upon them, they thought: "A nāga of great supernatural power has come, and we two will be displaced from this place. We must flee." Recognizing this with fright, they displayed themselves in the form of young brahmin boys and began to run away.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana withdrew the supernatural display he had performed, sat down before the two, and said: "O two lords of nāgas, where are you going?"

The two replied: "A nāga of great supernatural power has come, and we two will be displaced from this place — we are fleeing."

He said: "Come back. Let us see what that nāga looks like."

When the two returned together with him and looked, nothing was to be seen. The two then said: "Noble one, did you play a trick on us two?"

He replied: "I did. So then — what wrong have we two done?"

"You two, who are subject to aging, gave no thought to the arrival of the Buddha's messenger. Noble one, are you the Buddha's messenger?"

"I am the Buddha's messenger."

"Noble one, if you are the Buddha's messenger, please tell us what we two should do."

"Come. Go to none other than the presence of the Blessed One."

"Noble one, we will not refuse — we will do just so."

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana led the two nāga kings, Nandaka and Upanandaka, to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said this to the Blessed One: "Lord, Blessed One, the two — the nāga king Nandaka and Upanandaka — for whose sake you gave me the command, are here."

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the nāga king Nandaka and to Upanandaka: "Lords of nāgas, you two, through misdeeds committed in a former life, have been born in the wretched existence of nāgas. And you two at present are violent, your hands stained with blood, addicted to harm and extreme harm, robbing other beings of their lives, living by cutting off the lives of others. When you pass from here, what will become of your destiny? What will become of your rebirth? What will become of your future life?"

The two replied: "Blessed One, please command us as to what we two should do."

The Blessed One declared: "Lords of nāgas, come to me. Take refuge and undertake the training precepts, and grant fearlessness to the wild animals and the birds dwelling on the terraced slopes of Mount Meru."

The two said: "Lord, we two will go for refuge in the presence of the Blessed One, will take the training precepts, and will grant fearlessness to the wild animals and the birds dwelling on the terraced slopes of Mount Meru."

The two took refuge in the presence of the Blessed One and undertook the training precepts, then bowed their heads at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The monks arose with doubt, and, asking the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubt, they said: "Lord, what karma did the nāga kings Nandaka and Upanandaka perform, such that through the ripening of that karma they were born among the nāgas? And what karma did they perform such that they came to possess a dwelling built of the four precious substances, along with the food of the gods' nectar-ambrosia to eat and honey-mead to drink, and each came to have a retinue of two thousand five hundred? And what karma did they perform such that, dwelling for a vast eon as lords of the earth, they were not struck down when the king of birds, Suparṇa (Garuḍa), the fair-winged, came to seize them?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, these two performed and accumulated a karma that was found, whose condition had fully ripened, that abides close at hand like a flame, and that was certain to arise. And what these two performed and accumulated — could it be experienced by some other person separately? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, karma — virtuous and non-virtuous — that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense sources (āyatanas). As it is said:

Even were a hundred eons to pass,
karma performed is never wasted.
When the conditions and the time are met,
embodied beings will encounter their fruits.

Monks, in this very good great eon of the past, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher — the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world —

the charioteer who tames persons fit to be tamed, the unsurpassed teacher of gods and humans — appeared in the world as the buddha, the Blessed One, named Kāśyapa. He dwelled in the proximity of the forest of the deer park at the place called Ṛṣivadana, near the city of Vārāṇasī, attended by twenty thousand monks.

At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī there reigned a king named Kṛkī.
