His realm was prosperous and flourishing, the years were good and happy, filled with great numbers of people and a teeming populace. Strife and conflict, foreign enemies and internal disturbances had been thoroughly pacified. The land was free from thieves and famine. Fields of rice and rows of sugarcane abounded, and cattle and buffalo were plentiful. Thus a righteous dharma-king ruled his kingdom by the Dharma.

King Kṛkī heard that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa — endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, charioteer who tames persons fit to be tamed, the unsurpassed teacher of gods and humans — had appeared in the world, and was dwelling attended by twenty thousand monks in the forest of the deer park at Ṛṣivadana, near the city of Vārāṇasī. Upon hearing this, the king set out with his great royal retinue and his great royal power toward where the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa was to be found.

King Kṛkī then beheld the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa: his body beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being, his form gloriously arrayed with the eighty minor marks of excellence, his body ornamented with a radiance extending a fathom on every side, his light surpassing that of a thousand suns, splendid as a mountain of precious jewels moving through space.

The moment King Kṛkī saw him, profound faith arose in him toward the Blessed One Kāśyapa. He went to where the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa was, arrived, and bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, then sat to one side.

The perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, having understood the intention, the latent dispositions, the elements, and the intrinsic nature of King Kṛkī, taught the Dharma in such a way that, while the king remained seated on that very seat, the vajra of wisdom shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, and he directly realized the fruit of stream-entry — thus teaching the Dharma in a manner that brought about a genuine and thorough understanding of the Four Noble Truths.

Having seen the truth, the king gave utterance three times, with express and deliberate intention, to these words: "What the venerable Blessed One has done for me is something my father never did for me, my mother never did, no king ever did, no gods ever did, no ancestors of former times ever did, no renunciants (śramaṇas) or brahmins ever did, and no assembly of friends, companions, or kinsmen ever did: he has dried up the ocean of blood and tears; he has freed me from mountains of bones; he has closed the doors to the lower realms; he has opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; he has lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; and he has established me among gods and humans."

And the king spoke further:

By your power, O most excellent and stainless one,
the trail to the lower realms, laden with many faults, is barred,
and the path to the higher realms, rich in merit, is laid open —
thus have I attained even the trace of nirvāṇa.

Relying upon you, utterly pure one,
today I have gained the eye free from all faults and clear,
I have reached the peaceful and noble state of liberation,
and found the rejoicing of the noble ones.

I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.
Venerated by gods, demigods, and humans as I wander through existence,
freed from birth, old age, illness, and death,
one who sees the thousand existences as empty — how rare!
O Sage, today there is fruit in having seen you.

Having spoken these words, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa three times, and prostrated with his head to his two feet. Then he departed.

Now at the very moment when King Kṛkī saw the truths in the presence of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, he remained there on the spot and spoke to his ministers, townspeople, and subjects: "Listen, O ministers, townspeople, and subjects! Because I have seen the truths in the presence of the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, I am no longer able to rule the kingdom by both right and wrong means. Therefore, let the young man Sujanma be installed as the sovereign lord of the kingdom. As for me, I shall go before the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from home into homelessness with genuine faith."

Now at that time there were two of the foremost ministers, named Priya and Apriya. These two fell at the king's feet and said: "Your Majesty, please remain if only in name, and we two shall see to it that the kingdom is governed by right Dharma." The king replied: "If that is so, then let it be done." So these two were allowed to govern the kingdom by right Dharma for as long as they could. But then they began once again to administer the kingdom by both right and wrong means, whereupon the relatives of those two who had gone forth under the teaching of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa came to the two of them and said: "You venerable ones — please govern the kingdom by right Dharma. Do not administer it by both right and wrong means. Do not cause sentient beings to fall into the hells." When the two heard this from them, they again governed the kingdom by right Dharma for as long as they could, but then once more began to administer it by both right and wrong means. Those relatives came to them again and said: "You venerable ones — please govern the kingdom by right Dharma. Do not administer it by both right and wrong means. Do not cause sentient beings to fall into the hells." But the two replied: "O noble ones, we ministers were given authority to govern the kingdom in exchange for payment in accordance with agreed terms. Governing by right Dharma alone carries no extra reward, so we shall certainly remove those who are unworthy and protect those who are worthy." Those relatives then said: "In that case, have a temple built with every requisite in full, and offer it to the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa together with his Saṅgha of hearers. Give to the monks the renounced goods of the young prince's household, and give to the nuns the renounced goods of the queen's retinue. This will be for the long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness of you both." The two replied: "Noble ones, we shall do exactly that — please do not be offended." And so those two had a temple built with every requisite in full and offered it to the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa together with his Saṅgha of hearers, giving to the monks the renounced goods of the young prince's household, and giving to the nuns the renounced goods of the queen's retinue.

Monks, those two who were at that time the foremost ministers of King Kṛkī — Priya and Apriya by name — are now the nāga king Priya and

the nāga king Priya and the nāga king Apriya. The two of them caused the kingdom to be governed by both Dharma and non-Dharma — and it is because of that which was not Dharma that they were born among the nāgas. Because they caused a temple with every requisite in full to be built and offered it to the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa together with his Saṅgha of hearers, they came to have a dwelling place manifestly accomplished, made of four kinds of precious jewels, with food of divine ambrosia and drink of honey-wine, each of them attended by a retinue of two thousand five hundred. And because they gave to the monks the renounced goods of the young prince's household, and gave to the nuns the renounced goods of the queen's retinue, they remain throughout an aeon in that place, dwelling on the terraced slopes of Mount Meru, unable to be dislodged even by Suparṇa, the king of birds with wings adorned with fine feathers.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of actions that are altogether dark is altogether dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are altogether bright is altogether bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is mixed.

Monks, therefore, abandon actions that are altogether dark and those that are mixed, and strive for actions that are altogether bright. Monks, you should train yourselves accordingly.

Now, at the time when the Blessed One led the two nāga kings, Priya and Apriya, to take refuge and established them in the foundations of training, these two came on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day of the month to the terraced slopes of Mount Meru and paid reverence to the Blessed One. When they came to pay reverence to the Blessed One at night, they did so in the dress of a celestial palace; and when they came to pay reverence to the Blessed One during the day, they did so in the dress of householders.

On a certain occasion the two came before the Blessed One during the day in the dress of householders. At just that time, Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, was also going to the Jeta Grove. Now, the warrior class is by nature proud, and so when this king would go before the Blessed One, he thought to himself: "Surely when I go before the Blessed One, there will be no one who does not rise to greet me in person." He therefore sent ahead an attendant of impure rank. So Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, remained at the gate of the Jeta Grove and said to this attendant of impure rank: "Go inside and look to see who is paying reverence to the Blessed One." The attendant of impure rank replied: "As the king commands" — and, hearing this from Prasenajit the king of Kośala, he went to where the Blessed One was. He saw two householders paying reverence to the Blessed One. Having seen them, he went back to where Prasenajit the king of Kośala was, and said to him: "Sire, two householders are paying reverence to the Blessed One. They appear to be dwellers in the realm of the gods — they have not been cut down." The king thought: "These two householders dwell in my realm, so if they see me they will surely rise to greet me." And with that thought he went to where the Blessed One was.

The two nāga kings, Priya and Apriya, saw Prasenajit the king of Kośala from a great distance. Upon seeing him, the two said to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, shall we for now pay reverence to the holy Dharma, or shall we pay reverence to the king?" The Blessed One declared:

"You two lords of nāgas, pay reverence for now to the holy Dharma. All the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold the holy Dharma in reverence, and even the arhats place the Dharma above all else."

Then the Blessed One spoke these verses on the occasion:

All the buddhas who have passed away,
all the buddhas who are yet to come,
and the buddhas who dispel sorrow,
the many who abide even now —
each and every one of them
has dwelt, does dwell, and will dwell
in reverence toward the holy Dharma.
This is the very nature of buddhahood.
Therefore one who wishes well for oneself,
who aspires to true greatness,
and who would honor the teaching of the buddhas —
let that one hold the holy Dharma in reverence.

The two nāga kings did not rise to show reverence to Prasenajit, the king of Kośala. The king was furious and thought: "These two householders dwell in my realm, yet they will not rise to greet me." Consumed by anger, he nonetheless prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. The Blessed One, perceiving that the king was consumed by anger, began to speak on other matters and did not teach the Dharma. At this the king implored:

"Blessed One, please teach the Dharma.
Sugata, please teach the Dharma."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One declared these verses:

One who lacks serene delight of mind,
who is full of aversion and agitation —
such a one is incapable of knowing
all the holy Dharma of the perfectly and completely awakened one.
But one who has subdued the arising of faults,
who has set aside the mind that lacks serenity,
and who abandons this brooding resentment —
that one will come to know what is well proclaimed.

The king was greatly angered at the two of them and thought: "Because of these two, the Blessed One has even interrupted the flow of teaching the Dharma." Realizing this, he said, "Stay here," prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed.

Now, while the two nāga kings Priya and Apriya were paying reverence to the Blessed One throughout the day, their retinues — who sustained themselves on dairy provisions — built a solid wall of enclosures on both sides of the road all the way from the terraced slopes of Mount Meru to Śrāvastī, and placed it there.

Prasenajit, king of Kośala, gave orders to his ministers: "Wise ones, the moment these two householders emerge from the presence of the Blessed One, cut off their heads at the neck and throw them to the ground."

When these words were spoken, the retinues of the two nāga kings Priya and Apriya heard them. Upon hearing, they were enraged and began to hurl at Prasenajit, king of Kośala, single-pointed vajras, discuses, great arrows, and weapons with single-pointed blades, along with other such weapons.

Now, the Blessed Ones, the buddhas, possess the quality of never being forgetful. Therefore the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, extend your loving care to Prasenajit, king of Kośala, together with his retinue, and to the assembled people dwelling in Śrāvastī."

The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard the Blessed One's command, replied, "As the venerable one commands," and then entered into meditative absorption in the samādhi of loving-kindness. By virtue of his entering that absorption, all those weapons — the single-pointed vajras, the discuses, the great arrows, the weapons with single-pointed blades, and all the rest — were transformed into divine flowers: utpala, padma, kumuda, white lotus, and māndārava blossoms.

And they began to fall upon Prasenajit, king of Kośala. Yet even as they fell — filling everything with those divine flowers, the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, the white lotus, and the māndārava blossoms — they entered into the city. The king then addressed the queens' retinue, the young princes, the ministers, the civic officers, the townspeople, the country people, and the brahmins, saying, "You who are wise — from the moment of my entering the Jeta Grove until now, our home has been filled with divine flowers: utpala, padma, kumuda, white lotus, and māndārava blossoms. What is this? Whose power is it?"

Those among them who were skilled in speaking pleasingly and gently replied, "What other god could seek such a thing? What other being could possess such power? It is precisely because the king governs the realm according to the Dharma that this is the king's own power."

The king said, "You who are wise, that is true — because I now take up the Dharma in governing the realm, and it has not fallen apart, this is my power."

The queens' retinue said, "We do not go to the side of any man other than the king, and we do not stray from our lord — therefore this is our power."

The young princes said, "We revere our father and mother and hold them in great honour — therefore this is our power."

The ministers said, "We assist the king in governing the realm according to the Dharma — therefore this is our power."

The civic officers said, "We carry out the king's commands in accordance with the Dharma — therefore this is our power."

The townspeople and the country people said, "We pay tribute to the king in accordance with the Dharma — therefore this is our power."

The king reflected: "Each of these says 'it is our power,' 'it is my power' — yet none of them truly knows whose power it is. The buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, all-seeing, and has attained unexcelled mastery in knowledge and objects of knowledge. I shall go to ask the buddha, the Blessed One." Having resolved this, he filled his cupped hands with those divine flowers — the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, the white lotus, and the māndārava blossoms — and made his way to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side.

Seated to one side, Prasenajit, king of Kośala, then reported all of this at length to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Great king, it was not your power, nor the power of the queens' retinue, nor the power of the young princes, nor the power of the ministers, nor the power of the civic officers, nor the power of the townspeople, nor the power of the country people, nor the power of the brahmins. Rather, it was the power of the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Had the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana not directed his mind toward you, your queens' retinue, your princes, your ministers, your townspeople, and your country people, Śrāvastī would this very day have ceased to exist as an inhabited realm. It was through the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana's directing his mind toward you, your queens' retinue, your princes, your ministers, your townspeople, and your country people that this came to pass — therefore place your trust in him with wholehearted faith."

The king said, "Blessed One, if it is indeed the power of the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana and not of the Blessed One, nor of any other great śrāvaka, how am I to understand this?"

"Great king, it was not my power, nor the power of any other great śrāvaka —"

"This was indeed the power of the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana. If you have any doubt or misgiving about this, then take these divine flowers — the utpala, the lotus, the kumuda, the white lotus, and the māndārava — and cast them upon the ground." He cast them upon the ground, and they turned into nothing but weapons: single-pointed vajras, wheels, great arrows, single-pointed blades, and the like. Seeing this, the king was struck with terror and asked, "Blessed One, what is this?"

The Blessed One declared, "Great king, it came about because you aroused a mind of intense hatred toward the nāga king Nandaka and his companion Upanandaka."

The king said, "Venerable one, I do not even recall having seen the nāga king Nandaka and Upanandaka — how could I have aroused a mind of intense hatred toward them?"

"Great king, let me remind you."

"Venerable Blessed One, please do remind me."

"Great king, do you remember that two householders who were listening to the Dharma in your presence did not rise to greet you?"

"Blessed One, I do remember that."

"Great king, those two householders were none other than the nāga king Nandaka and Upanandaka."

The king asked, "Blessed One, were those two not disturbed by that?"

"Great king, those two themselves were not disturbed, but those who depend on them for their livelihood were disturbed."

"Blessed One, how am I to make amends to those two?"

"Great king, you must ask their forgiveness."

"Blessed One, those two dwell on the terraced slopes of Mount Meru, and I am here — how am I to ask their forgiveness?"

The Blessed One declared, "Great king, those two come here to pay homage at my feet on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day of the month. You too should come here on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth — I will point them out to you, and you may ask their forgiveness, and they will forgive you."

The king asked, "Venerable one, am I to touch their feet with my head?"

The Blessed One declared, "Great king, you are not to touch their feet with your head. When a person of noble birth bows at the feet of someone of low birth, the principal men take hold of that person's arms — so instead, extend your right arm and ask the two lords of nāgas to forgive you, saying, 'Lords of nāgas, grant your forgiveness,' and they will forgive you."

The king said, "Venerable one, I shall not fail — I will do exactly so," and having spoken, he bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One and departed.

Some time later, the nāga king Nandaka and Upanandaka came to the terraced slopes of Mount Meru, took on the appearance of householders, made their way to where the Blessed One was, bowed their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, also went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side, whereupon the Blessed One gave him a sign. Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, rose from his seat, drew his outer robe over one shoulder, extended his right arm, and said, "Lords of nāgas, grant your forgiveness." The two replied, "Great king, we forgive you." Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, together with the nāga king Nandaka and —

Having asked forgiveness of Nandaka and his companion, Prasenajit turned to face the Blessed One, joined his palms, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One, saying: "May the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, please be so gracious as to accept, for seven days at midday, my invitation to a meal in honor of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana." The Blessed One granted this to Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, by his silence. Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that permission had been granted, bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One and departed. He then issued instructions to his ministers: "Wise ones, I have invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas and monks, to midday meals for seven days in honor of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Beautify the city and make preparations for the midday meal. Kings accomplish things through words, the gods accomplish things through mind, and yogins accomplish all things through mere intention — therefore, ministers, act at once upon the royal command." Having heard this from Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, they adorned in the most beautiful manner all the roads between the Jeta Grove and Śrāvastī, and put Śrāvastī in impeccable order, free of stones, gravel, and uneven ground. They sprinkled it with sandalwood water, placed near at hand vessels filled with sweet-smelling incense, hung masses of silk garlands, raised victory banners and pennants, scattered flowers of every variety, and made it delightful in appearance — as lovely as Sudharmā, the assembly hall of the gods. They set out food that was fine in color, fragrance, and flavor, accompanied by various condiments and made splendid with many beautiful things to look upon. And with such abundance as this, each day the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas was invited to midday meals at the royal palace.

Now, one night, fire broke out among those who were on night watch, and as a result many of the excellent elephants belonging to Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, were burned.

When the seven days of midday meals had passed, Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, had a proclamation announced by drum throughout Śrāvastī: "Henceforth, no one in Śrāvastī is to light a fire at night. Whoever lights a fire shall be punished with a fine of sixty kārṣāpaṇas, or shall be subjected to hand torture until death."

At that time there lived in Śrāvastī a householder named Supriya — wealthy, of great riches and possessions, of broad and extensive property, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa (the god of wealth), rivaling Vaiśravaṇa himself in riches. He had taken a wife from among his equals in rank, and he lived together with her in sport, in joy, and in pleasure.

Then, at a later time, he went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived there, bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One thoroughly instructed, established, encouraged, and gladdened the householder Supriya with Dharma-rich discourse. In many ways he thoroughly taught, established, encouraged, and gladdened him with Dharma-rich discourse, and then fell silent.

Then the householder Supriya rose from his seat, drew his outer robe over one shoulder, turned to face the Blessed One, joined his palms, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, would you be so kind as to consent to take your meal tomorrow with the Saṅgha of monks?" The Blessed One gave his consent to the householder Supriya by remaining silent.

Then the householder Supriya, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That very night the householder Supriya made preparations for the meal: clean and excellent food was readied. Rising early the next morning, he arranged seats, set out water vessels, and invited the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, please be pleased to know that it is now the right time." Then the Blessed One, in the forenoon, dressed in his lower robe and took up his bowl and outer robe, and surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the Saṅgha of monks proceeding before him, he went to where the householder Supriya's house was and arrived there, and sat down on the seat that had been prepared, at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the householder Supriya, perceiving that the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, satisfied and nourished them with his own hands with clean and excellent food and drink. In many ways he satisfied and nourished them with his own hands with clean and excellent food and drink. Having done so, and perceiving that the Blessed One had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, he took a seat lower than the Blessed One's and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, having understood his aspiration, his latent dispositions, his constitution, and his character, taught the Dharma in such a way that, while the householder Supriya sat there together with his wife, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of wisdom, the fruit of stream-entry was directly realized, and in just that way the Four Noble Truths were individually and rightly understood.

Having seen the truth, he solemnly proclaimed three times: "What you, reverend Blessed One, have done for me — this was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by a king, nor by the gods, nor by my ancestors of old, nor by ascetics and brahmins, nor by friends, companions, and kinsmen. The ocean of blood and tears has been dried up. I have been freed from the mountains of bones. The doors to the lower realms have been closed. The doors to the higher realms and to liberation have been opened. My feet have been lifted out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and I have been placed among the gods and humans."

And he further said:

Through your power, I, who was laden with many faults,
have blocked the path to the lower realms, rich now in merit,
have opened the way to the higher realms, and have come
to attain even the path that leads to nirvāṇa.

Relying on you, supremely pure, today I have obtained
a seeing free of fault and utterly clear,
and I have reached the noble peaceful state of joy;
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Worshipped by beings — asuras, humans, and gods —
free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
rare indeed is one who sees existence as empty:
O Sage, today I behold you — and there is fruit.

When the Blessed One had taught the Dharma, he departed. On that very day on which the householder Supriya together with his wife had come to see the truth, a being entered into his wife's womb.

The householder Supriya also invited the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha of hearers to another house and offered them a meal. There the Blessed One taught the Dharma in such a way that, upon hearing it, both the householder Supriya and his wife realized the fruit of non-return and also attained supernormal powers.

On the very day that the householder Supriya and his wife realized the fruit of non-return and attained supernormal powers, his wife gave birth. The boy who was born was handsome in form, pleasing and beautiful to behold, with a complexion like shining gold, a head like a parasol, long arms, a broad brow, joined eyebrows, a high nose-bridge, and a prominent nasal septum.

His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — three sevens of days after the birth — they held a great birth-celebration and then set about giving the child his name, asking what name he should bear. The relatives said: "Since this boy was born on the very day his two parents realized the fruit of non-return and attained supernormal powers, his name shall therefore be Rdzu-'phrul-len — 'Miracle-Taker.'" And so the name Miracle-Taker was given to him.

The boy Miracle-Taker was entrusted to eight nurses: two nurses to hold him in their laps, two nurses to suckle him, two nurses to clean him, and two nurses to play with him. These eight nurses nourished him and caused him to grow — sustaining him with milk, curds, butter, clarified butter, cream of butter, and other principal provisions of the finest kind, so that he grew swiftly, like a lotus in a pond.

When he had grown up, he applied himself to letters, arithmetic, calculation, counting on the fingers, throwing, casting, and placing, and reached mastery in writing — in composing, reading, scholarly knowledge, practice, clear exposition — and became expert in these eight kinds of appraisal: appraising jewels, appraising land, appraising cloth, appraising wood, appraising elephants, appraising horses, appraising women, and appraising men.

He then went to the court of the retinue of Queen Prasenajit, the king of Kosala. The queen's retinue threw down a garland of flowers at him from the upper terrace of the palace. Now the world being what it is — divided into friends, enemies, and those who are indifferent — certain others spoke to King Prasenajit of Kosala, saying: "The young nobleman Miracle-Taker is seeking to ingratiate himself with the royal ladies' retinue." Since kings are prone to act without inquiry, the king gave orders to his ministers: "Wise ones, I am sending away the youth Miracle-Taker, the son of the householder Supriya." The ministers then bound garlands of kāravīra flowers around his neck, dressed the men who were to escort him in blue garments, and led him out through the middle of the city to the place of execution, where he was made to be killed.

The people of Śrāvastī and those who had come from various other regions said: "This sinful king acts without due investigation — he is wicked. He has killed the householder's son, the youth Miracle-Taker, who harbored no enmity, who sought no rivalry, and who had done no wrong." Likewise, the queen's retinue, the young nobles, and the ministers also said that this wicked man had killed the householder's son, the youth Miracle-Taker, who harbored no enmity, who sought no rivalry,

and who had done no wrong. "Killing Miracle-Taker was not good. It was very wrong indeed," they all said.

The householder Supriya reflected: "Everything I own and possess, which I have never fully given away to anyone, was held in reserve for the sake of the youth Miracle-Taker. But now, through the fault of past karma, the king, without due investigation, had him executed on that very fifth day. For whose benefit, then, should it now be cut off? I shall give it all away to the lowly, the unprotected, the poor, and the destitute." With this in mind, he set aside one kārṣāpaṇa as capital for trading, and gave away all other forms of wealth to the lowly, the unprotected, the poor, and the destitute. With that single kārṣāpaṇa he bought and sold goods, and gained four kārṣāpaṇas in return. With one of those he purchased perfumed plaster and anointed the Blessed One's perfume chamber. With the second he prepared food for the attendants and retinue. With the third he made an offering of Dharma instruction for monks on behalf of the Saṅgha. The fourth he set aside as trading capital.

Because the household's resources had grown thin, he gave even poor gifts and gave even the very worst of gifts, and so he came to be known by the ill name "Bad Supriya."

He went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. As he sat there to one side, the Blessed One spoke to the householder Bad Supriya in these words: "Householder, is it so that gifts are given and merit is made in your house?" "Venerable One, it is just so — gifts are given and merit is made in my dwelling, but they are poor gifts and the very worst of gifts."

The Blessed One said: "Householder, whether one gives poor gifts or good ones, both produce a karmic maturation of wealth. Yet, householder, whether one gives poor gifts or good ones, if that giving is not done with faith, not with respect, not by one's own hand, not at the right time, and not without harm to others — then when the time comes to individually experience the ripening of that karma, one's mind will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of great household wealth, will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant food, will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant clothing, will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant lodging and bedding, will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant vehicles and mounts, and will not be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects. Householder, the ripened fruit of giving in such a manner is to be understood as being of just that kind.

"Householder, whether one gives poor gifts or good ones, if that giving is done with faith, with respect, by one's own hand, at the right time, and without harm to others — then when the time comes to individually experience the ripening of that karma, one's mind will be inclined toward the enjoyment of great household wealth, will be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant food, will be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant clothing, will be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant lodging and bedding, will be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant vehicles and mounts, and will be inclined toward the enjoyment of abundant forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects. Householder, the ripened fruit of giving in such a manner is to be understood as being of just that kind."

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the sixty-ninth fascicle.

Householder, in times past there was a brahmin named Kālaprabha who was like a great śāla tree. He gave gifts to brahmins such as these: elephants adorned with gold,

adorned with gold, beautified with gold, bearing golden victory banners, and draped with golden netting — eighty-four thousand such elephants he gave as gifts to brahmins. Horses adorned with gold, beautified with gold, bearing golden victory banners, and draped with golden netting — eighty-four thousand such horses he gave as gifts to brahmins. Chariots of four kinds — made of gold, made of silver, made of lapis lazuli, and made of crystal; covered with lion skins, covered with tiger skins, covered with leopard skins, and canopied with fine woolen cloth; victorious and pleasing in appearance — eighty-four thousand such chariots he gave as gifts to brahmins. Mansions of four kinds — made of gold, made of silver, made of lapis lazuli, and made of crystal — eighty-four thousand such mansions he gave as gifts to brahmins. Thrones of four kinds — made of gold, made of silver, made of lapis lazuli, and made of crystal; upholstered with fringe; fitted with a cushion spread upon them; laid with an inner cushion of fine fabric; laid with a spotted cushion; laid with a great cushion; laid with a fine cushion; covered with a canopy of sumac cloth; furnished with a covering cloth spread over it; and set with two red backrests — eighty-four thousand such thrones he gave as gifts to brahmins. Golden vessels — eighty-four thousand he gave as gifts to brahmins. Silver vessels — eighty-four thousand he gave as gifts to brahmins. Golden vessels filled with silver dust — eighty-four thousand he gave as gifts to brahmins. Silver vessels filled with gold dust — eighty-four thousand he gave as gifts to brahmins. Pairs of cloth of four kinds — fine Kāśika cloth, fine silk cloth, fine Dukūla cloth, and fine Kautamba cloth, by the pair — eighty-four thousand such pairs he gave as gifts to brahmins. Cows with golden horns, with hooves made of silver, with matching calves, giving sweet-tasting milk, draped with cloths of crafted fine fabric — eighty-four thousand such cows he gave as gifts to brahmins. Young women wearing golden armlets and necklaces, adorned with excellent ornaments — eighty-four thousand such young women he gave as gifts to brahmins. Food and drink, provisions, things to eat, things to lick, and delicacies — need one even speak of such things? — he gave to the brahmins in just that way.

Householder, though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, one who would give a single meal to even one hundred ascetics who, among the desire-filled wandering sages (tīrthikas), were free from attachment — that giving would bear greater fruit than the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred such wandering sages free from attachment — one who would give a single meal to even one ordinary person who had come to the Jambu Grove — that giving would bear greater fruit than the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a meal to such an ordinary person who had come to the Jambu Grove — one who would give a single meal to even one person who had entered the stream (that is, one who has entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry) — that giving would bear greater fruit than the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and

though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers — one who would give a single meal to even one person who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning would bear greater fruit from that giving than from all the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning — one who would give a single meal to even one once-returner would bear greater fruit from that giving than from all the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning — one who would give a single meal to even one non-returner would bear greater fruit from that giving than from all the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners — one who would give a single meal to even one person who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship would bear greater fruit from that giving than from all the former.

Though the brahmin who was like a great śāla tree gave gifts to brahmins in such abundance and in such a manner, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred wandering sages free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship —

— and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one arhat — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred arhats — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving, which is the offering of a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred arhats, and though one offered a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and though one had a temple built in that very pleasure garden — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry,

and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred arhats, and though one offered a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and though one had a temple built in that very pleasure garden, and though one offered furnishings such as these in that very temple — thrones, chairs, cushioned seats with inner padding, bolsters, coverlets, and blankets — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred arhats, and though one offered a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and though one had a temple built in that very pleasure garden, and though one offered furnishings such as these in that very temple — thrones, chairs, cushioned seats with inner padding, bolsters, coverlets, and blankets — and though one offered in that very temple a permanent endowment of offerings appropriate to the occasion, and though one went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma, went for refuge to the Saṅgha, and took up the foundations of training — that giving surpasses all of those, and this giving yields the greater fruit.

O brahmin, even giving of that kind — giving as immense as a great sal tree, given at due seasons to brahmins — and though one gave a single meal to one hundred ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of stream-entry, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred stream-enterers, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of once-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred once-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of non-returning, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred non-returners, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred who had entered the path with the aim of directly realizing the fruit of arhatship, and though one gave a single meal to one hundred arhats, and though one offered a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and though one had a temple built in that very pleasure garden, and though one offered furnishings such as these in that very temple — thrones, chairs, seats, cushioned seats with inner padding, bolsters, coverlets, and blankets — and though one offered in that very temple a permanent endowment of offerings appropriate to the occasion, and though one went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma,

went for refuge to the Saṅgha, and undertook the bases of training — and whoever cultivates a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and living creatures — this act of giving is of greater fruit than all those acts of giving.

Householder, like a great sal tree measured by the season, one who has given such gifts to brahmins, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred non-Buddhist sages (tīrthika ṛṣis) free from attachment, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred who have entered the stream in order to directly realize the fruit of stream-entry, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred stream-enterers, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred who have entered the path in order to directly realize the fruit of once-returning, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred once-returners, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred who have entered the path in order to directly realize the fruit of non-returning, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred non-returners, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred who have entered the path in order to directly realize the fruit of arhatship, and one who has given a single meal to a hundred arhats, and one who has offered a pleasure garden to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and one who has had a temple built in that very pleasure garden, and one who has offered furnishings in that very temple — thrones, chairs, seats, cushioned seats with inner padding, bolsters, coverlets, and blankets — and one who has offered in that very temple a permanent endowment of offerings appropriate to the occasion, and one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, and undertaken the bases of training, and whoever cultivates a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and living creatures, and whoever remains in continued contemplation of all formations as impermanent, dwelling therein — seeing them as subject to decay, seeing them as free from attachment, seeing them as cessation, and seeing them as relinquishment, and remaining so — this act of giving is of greater fruit than all those acts of giving.

Householder, therefore you should train yourself in this way: to continue seeing all formations as impermanent and to dwell in that seeing — seeing them as subject to decay, seeing them free from attachment, seeing them as cessation, and seeing them as relinquishment, and remaining so. This is how you should train. Householder, you should train in just this way.

Then the householder Citta (Supriya) praised and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had declared, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

At another time, late at night in his own home, he lit a lamp and was reading the word of the Buddha. Men who lived in Rājagṛha by foraging in the streets caught sight of this through a crack in the door, and they said to him: Householder, the king has had it announced by the beat of the drum that in Śrāvastī no one may light a fire at night. Whoever does so will be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas, or will be clapped in irons and put to death — so the king has decreed. Why then have you lit a fire at night?

He replied: Friends, this is not a fire; it is a lamp.

Householder, is it not the case that this too performs the function of fire? Then either pay sixty kārṣāpaṇas, or sit in irons.

Friends, where would I get sixty kārṣāpaṇas? I will sit in irons.

Now the court of Prasenajit, king of Kosala, had three tiers. Those who were the principal men were placed on the upper tier; those of middling rank were placed in the middle tier;

Those who were of wicked character were placed at the bottom, since they were not the principal ones, and so they placed them on the upper tier.

Then, at the first watch of the night, the four great kings went to where the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked was, and upon arriving, they addressed the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked in these words: Householder, it is not fitting that you should be sitting in irons. Why then are you sitting in irons?

He replied: Friends, I am not sitting in irons of my own free will. The king's grain-pension retainers put me in irons. Why? For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not have that amount, I am therefore sitting in irons.

Householder, therefore rouse your mind and speak the words. Your house, or whatever reservoirs of water there may be, shall be filled with silver and gold. Friends, take heart — and the king, through faith in me, will act according to the power of that faith. If you wish, remain seated, and I shall teach you the Dharma.

They sat before him to hear the Dharma, and as they sat there, their bodies were like this: like four great masses of fire blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, their flames merged into one, burning and scorching. Prasenajit, king of Kosala, at the first watch of the night, while sitting in irons, saw four great masses of fire blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, their flames merged into one, burning and scorching.

Then, at the midnight watch, Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, went to where the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked was, and upon arriving, addressed the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked in these words: Householder, it is not fitting that you should be sitting in irons. Why then are you sitting in irons?

He replied: Kauśika, I am not sitting in irons of my own free will. The king's grain-pension retainers put me in irons. Why? For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not have that amount, I am therefore sitting in irons.

Householder, therefore rouse your mind and speak the words. Your house, or whatever reservoirs of water there may be, shall be filled with silver and gold. Kauśika, take heart — and the king, through faith in me, will act according to the power of that faith. If you wish, remain seated, and I shall teach you the Dharma.

He sat before him to hear the Dharma, and as he sat there, his body was like this: like a great mass of fire surpassing those previous four — blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching — a great mass of fire more exalted and more splendid, blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching. Prasenajit, king of Kosala, at the midnight watch, while sitting in irons, saw a great mass of fire surpassing those previous four — blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching — a great mass of fire more exalted and more splendid, blazing, burning fiercely, blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching.

Then, at the last watch of the night, Brahmā, lord of the Brahma world, went to where the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked was, and upon arriving, addressed the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked in these words: Householder, it is not fitting that you should be sitting in irons. Why then are you sitting in irons?

He replied: Brahmā, I am not sitting in irons of my own free will. The king's grain-pension retainers put me in irons. Why? For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not have that amount, I am therefore sitting in irons.

Householder, therefore rouse your mind and speak these words: that your house, or whatever water-sources you have, shall be filled with silver and gold. Brahmā, do this with only a small portion of your heart, and the king will be moved by faith to act under the power of that faith toward me. If you wish, remain seated, and I shall teach you the Dharma.

As he sat before Brahmā to hear the Dharma, his body was such — it was like a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching — surpassing and more magnificent than the previous four great masses of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, their flames merged into one, burning and scorching — and even surpassing and more magnificent than that great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching.

Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, in the last watch of the night, when he was inspecting the palace courtyard, saw a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching — surpassing and more magnificent than the previous four great masses of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, their flames merged into one, burning and scorching — and even more magnificent than that great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching.

Having seen this, he summoned the men on guard over the palace courtyard and said: I had a proclamation announced throughout the city that no one in Śrāvastī should light fires in the night. Why then was a great mass of fire lit right here last night in my very own courtyard?

They replied: Your majesty, a deity entered the palace courtyard in the night and lit a fire. What that deity saw there, we could not tell.

The king said to his grain-pension retainers: You wise men — is this true or false? Investigate the courtyard. They went and examined the courtyard, but not even ashes were to be found. They returned and reported to the king: Your majesty, we examined the courtyard and there was not even any ash.

The king said to the men guarding the palace courtyard: Who is the chief man here in the inner palace? Your majesty, the householder Bhadra-datta the Wicked is present. Call him. And so, in accordance with the king's command, they called him.

The king said to him: Householder, I had a proclamation announced throughout the city that no one in Śrāvastī should light fires in the night. Why did you light a fire right here in the courtyard last night?

He replied: Your majesty, if I had not even stirred for a single moment, what need is there to speak of lighting fires in the middle of the night? Householder, I myself in the first watch of the night saw four great masses of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, their flames merged into one, burning and scorching; and in the middle watch of the night a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching, surpassing and more magnificent than the previous four; and in the last watch of the night a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching, surpassing and more magnificent even than that — a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one, burning and scorching, surpassing and more magnificent still — a great mass of fire burning, blazing, and blazing all around,

its flames merged into one, burning and scorching — and yet you say to yourself: "If I had not lit even a small fire for so much as a moment, what need is there to speak of the whole night?" What does this mean? That god was astonished, and he said: "I did not light a fire in the night watch, and yet it was thus: last night, in the first watch of the night, the four great kings came to where I was and said to me, 'Householder, it is not fitting that you should be crouching there doing obeisance — why are you crouching in obeisance?' And I said to them, 'My lords, I am not crouching in obeisance of my own accord; it is those who live on the king's wages who have made me do obeisance.' They then said to me, 'Why is that?' And I said to them, 'For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not possess that amount, that is why I am crouching in obeisance.' Then they said to me, 'Householder, therefore make the resolve and speak the word, and your house or whatever bodies of water you possess shall be filled with silver and gold.' And I said to them, 'My lords, do not be faint-hearted; the king has faith in me, and through the power of that faith he will act as one who is controlled by faith. If you wish, stay, and I will teach you the Dharma.' And when they came before me to hear the Dharma, their bodies were like this — to give a simile, like four great masses of fuel burning, blazing, and blazing all around, their flames merged into one and scorching.

Then, in the middle watch of the night, Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, came to where I was and said to me, 'Householder, it is not fitting that you should be crouching there doing obeisance — why are you crouching in obeisance?' And I said to him, 'Kauśika, I am not crouching in obeisance of my own accord; it is those who live on the king's wages who have made me do obeisance.' And he said to me, 'Why is that?' And I said to him, 'For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not possess that amount, that is why I am crouching in obeisance.' Then he said to me, 'Householder, therefore make the resolve and speak the word, and your house or whatever bodies of water you possess shall be filled with silver and gold.' And I said to him, 'Kauśika, do not be faint-hearted; the king has faith in me, and through the power of that faith he will act as one who is controlled by faith. If you wish, stay, and I will teach you the Dharma.' And when he came before me to hear the Dharma, his body was like this — to give a simile, like a great mass of fuel surpassing and more magnificent than those previous four masses of fuel, burning, blazing, and blazing all around, their flames merged into one and scorching — like a great mass of fuel burning, blazing, and blazing all around, its flames merged into one and scorching.

Then, in the last watch of the night, Brahmā, lord of the Akaṇiṣṭha realm, came to where I was and said to me, 'Householder, it is not fitting that you should be crouching there doing obeisance — why are you crouching in obeisance?' And I said to him, 'Brahmā, I am not crouching in obeisance of my own accord; it is those who live on the king's wages who have made me do obeisance.' And he said to me, 'Why is that?' And I said to him, 'For sixty kārṣāpaṇas — since I do not possess that amount, that is why I am crouching in obeisance.'

Then Brahmā said to me, 'Householder, on that account rouse your mind and speak the words. I shall fill whichever houses or water-places of yours you wish with silver and gold.' And I said to him, 'Brahmā, make light of that. The king will act toward me in accordance with his faith, out of devoted trust. If you wish, stay and I shall teach you the Dharma.' And when he came before me in order to hear the Dharma, his body was like this — to give a simile, it was like a great heap of brushwood blazing, fully blazing, blazing all around, its flames merged into one and scorching, and surpassing even that a great heap of brushwood blazing, fully blazing, blazing all around, its flames merged into one and scorching, and surpassing even that a great heap of brushwood blazing, fully blazing, blazing all around, its flames merged into one and scorching.

The king said, 'Householder, if that is so, then I too shall grant you a boon — speak whatever you desire.' The householder said, 'Sire, if you have faith in me, I wish to read the words of the Buddha in the lamplight up on the roof at night.' The king said, 'Not only is this granted to you alone, but by reason of you yourself, this is also granted to all others who wish to read the words of the Buddha in the lamplight at night.'

Then the householder Nanda Bhadra, having been sent away with the king's leave, was delighted and overjoyed. He departed from the king's presence, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side.

Prasenajit, king of Kosala, also went to the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. But since the kṣatriya clan is proud by nature, he stopped at the gate of the Jeta Grove and said to a man of impure standing, 'Go inside and see who is attending upon the Blessed One.' That man of impure standing, obedient to the royal command, went and reported back to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, having seen where the Blessed One was. And there he saw that the householder Nanda Bhadra was attending upon the Blessed One. Having seen this, Prasenajit, king of Kosala, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he said to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, 'Sire, the householder Nanda Bhadra is here, attending upon the Blessed One.' The king thought, 'Since that householder lives in my domain, if he sees me, he will surely stand up in his presence.' And so the king went to where the Blessed One was.

The householder Nanda Bhadra caught sight of Prasenajit, king of Kosala, from quite a distance. Having seen him, he said to the Blessed One, 'Venerable One, tell me — should I pay homage to the holy Dharma first, or should I pay homage to the king?' The Blessed One declared, 'Householder, pay homage to the holy Dharma first. The blessed buddhas themselves revere the holy Dharma, and arhats too hold the Dharma as supreme.'

Then the Blessed One, with regard to this event, declared these verses:

All the buddhas of the past,
all the buddhas yet to come,
the buddhas who dispel sorrow,
and the many who abide now —
all of them have dwelt in reverence
for the holy Dharma, do so still,
and will continue so to dwell:
this is the very nature of a buddha.

Therefore, whoever wishes me well
and desires for me true greatness,
if they would honor the Buddha's teaching,
let them hold the holy Dharma in reverence.

Now, the wicked householder Suppabuddha had not risen to his feet in the presence of Prasenajit, king of Kosala. The king was furious and thought to himself: "This householder lives in my domain and yet he does not stand up for me." Seething with anger, he nevertheless bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One, knowing that the king was consumed with anger, began making other conversation and did not teach the Dharma. The king then made this request: "Blessed One, please teach the Dharma. Sugata, please teach the Dharma." When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One declared these verses to him:

One without genuine joy of heart,
one full of aversion and agitation —
such a one cannot come to know
the holy Dharma of the perfectly awakened.

But one who has subdued the onset of faults,
who has removed the mind devoid of joy,
and here abandons brooding resentment —
that one will come to know the well-spoken word.

The king then thought: "Because of this householder, the Blessed One has cut short even the hearing of the Dharma." An intense feeling of anger arose in him. He said, "Stay," and then bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Thereupon Prasenajit, king of Kosala, gave orders to his ministers: "Learned ones, the moment the wicked householder Suppabuddha departs from the presence of the Blessed One, you are to inform him that he is no longer to remain in my domain."

Then a certain deity who held the householder Suppabuddha in high regard sent out many creatures — tremabukas and trailatākas — and these surrounded and seized the king. Terrified, the king fled on his own to his home, where his retinue of queens, his young attendants, ministers, troops from the capital, elephants, and horses were all likewise surrounded and seized. The entire multitude of people dwelling in Śrāvastī was surrounded and seized as well.

The king was struck with fear. As quickly as he could, he mounted his elephant and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Venerable One, what has just occurred? The nāga kings Nanda and Upananda have become enraged — but who has provoked this? What has befallen the great king? Blessed One, I have been surrounded and seized by the creatures the tremabukas and trailatākas. My retinue of consorts, my young attendants, ministers, troops from the capital, elephants, and horses have all been surrounded and seized. The entire multitude of people dwelling in Śrāvastī has been surrounded and seized. Great King, it is you who have generated a mind of fierce hatred toward the householder Suppabuddha."

"Blessed One, has that householder been thrown into turmoil?"

"Great King, he is a non-returner, and so he does not produce turmoil. Rather, it is the deity who holds him in great devotion who has become enraged."

"Blessed One, what should I do about this?"

"Great King, you must go and ask his forgiveness."

"Blessed One, am I to touch my head to his feet?"

"Great King, you need not touch your head to his two feet. For when a person of high standing bows at the feet of people of low birth, it is the principal men who take him by the hand. You should simply extend your right hand and ask the householder's forgiveness, saying, 'Householder, please forgive me,' and he will forgive you."

Then Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, praised and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had declared, touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Now in Śrāvastī there were two householders named Saṃdhaka and Śīlavaṇij. Of these, Saṃdhaka was upright toward those who kept their pledges, and Śīlavaṇij was upright toward those who broke open the four great seals. Moreover, this latter man, being one possessed of shame, would walk far from the place where people defecated.

In Śrāvastī there was a band of thieves known as the Last-Month Left-Handers. Their practice was this: as soon as the invitation ceremony had concluded, they would assemble and deliberate among themselves, saying, "Wise ones, what shall we do so that we may enjoy ourselves and live comfortably for a full year without being sought out for it?" Among them, one said, "Wise ones, this householder Saṃdhaka is a keeper of pledges — let us question and examine him." Others said, "Indeed, let us do so. As for the householder Śīlavaṇij, he is upright toward those who break open the four great seals, and moreover, being possessed of shame, he walks far from the place where people defecate — so let us seize him, intimidate him, and he will open the four great seals." And so they made him their target, caught him when he had gone to the place for defecating, and accosted him, saying, "Householder, will you live or die?" He replied, "Wise ones, do as you will." They said, "Householder, if that is so, then we will bring a charge of a hundred or a thousand against the householder Saṃdhaka, and through that ruse, you shall open the four great seals." He replied, "Wise ones, shall I do so truthfully or untruthfully?" "Householder, untruthfully." He said, "Wise ones, I will not open the four great seals by means of untruth. I cannot, in order to be free from suffering for one lifetime, generate suffering for many lifetimes." They said, "Householder, if you open the four great seals, well and good. If you do not, we will cut off your head at the neck and throw it to the ground." He then spoke in verse:

If I abide in the Dharma, better to die quickly than not.
If I turn my back on the Dharma, may I not remain alive.
One who abides in the Dharma enjoys the bliss of the gods of the Thirty-Three.
One who falls from the Dharma tumbles into the fearsome lower realms, beyond bearing.

Then those Last-Month Left-Handers touched their heads to his two feet and said, "Householder, grant us fearlessness." He said, "I grant it." Those Last-Month Left-Handers touched their heads to his two feet and departed.

Now in Śrāvastī there was a younger brother of Prasenajit, king of Kosala, a prince named Kṛṣṇa, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, possessed of faith, good in character, and of virtuous mind, who had gone for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha. While he was keeping the eightfold restoration observance, a goddess of the māra class came to him and sought to invite him — in a manner not called forth by right reason — but he did not receive her. On another occasion, the evil householder Subhūtidatta, the householder Saṃdhaka,

the householder Śīlavaṇij, and Prince Kṛṣṇa all went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they touched their heads to the Blessed One's two feet and took their seats to one side.

Prasenajit, king of Kosala, also came with great royal wealth and great royal power to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the Blessed One spoke to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, in these words: "Great king, this is the evil householder Subhūtidatta."

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, rose from his seat, extended his right hand, and said: "Householder, I beg your pardon." The householder replied: "Your majesty, I grant it."

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable one, I am a king of the warrior caste, consecrated at the crown — is it not remarkable that I should seek pardon from a subject dwelling in my own realm?" The Blessed One declared: "Great king, it is indeed remarkable that a lord should seek pardon."

Then the householder Subhūtidatta addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable one, I had a single kārṣāpaṇa coin. I traded in goods and sold them, and from that I produced four kārṣāpaṇas. Of these four, with the first I anointed the Blessed One's perfumed chamber with a fragrant paste. The second I used to offer a feast for the monks on behalf of the Saṅgha. The third I used to provide livelihood for my servants. The fourth I set aside as the price of the goods. Venerable one, is it not remarkable — such generosity from one who has no wealth?" The Blessed One declared: "Householder, generosity without wealth is indeed remarkable."

Then the householder Śīlavaṇij addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable one, I was travelling abroad, and some left-handed men of the last month of autumn seized me and threatened me, saying: 'Householder, will you live or will you die?' I said to them: 'Wise ones, what do you have in mind?' They said to me: 'Householder, if that is how it is, we shall make a wager with you — a hundred or a thousand — and challenge you to a contest of arbitration. You must open the four seals.' I said to them: 'Wise ones, on what basis — truthful or untruthful?' They replied: 'Householder, on an untruthful basis.' I then said to them: 'Wise ones, I will not open the four seals on an untruthful basis. I cannot create suffering for many lifetimes in order to be free from the suffering of one lifetime.' They said to me: 'Householder, if you will open the seals just this once, that is well. But if you will not, we shall cut off your head at the neck and throw you to the ground.' I then spoke these verses:

If I remain in the Dharma, let me swiftly die — that is better.
If I turn my back on the Dharma, may I not live.
One who abides in the Dharma enjoys the happiness of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
One who falls from the Dharma plunges into a dreadful lower realm, unbearable and terrifying.

When I had spoken thus, they touched my two feet and said to me: 'Householder, grant us fearlessness.' I said to them: 'I grant it.'

"Reverend one, even when I had fallen into poverty, I did not abandon the Dharma. Is it not remarkable that when I had fallen into poverty I still practiced the Dharma?" The Blessed One declared: "Householder, it is indeed remarkable that when you had fallen into poverty you still practiced the Dharma."

Then Prince Kṛṣṇa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend one, while I was observing the restoration ceremony of the eight branches, a goddess of the māra class came and, since she was not someone born of a noble lineage, when she sought to be entertained as a guest I did not accept her. Blessed One, is it not remarkable that I, one possessed of great wealth, kept myself apart from sensual desires?" The Blessed One declared: "Young man, it is indeed remarkable that one possessed of great wealth kept himself apart from sensual desires."

Then the Blessed One spoke these verses concerning these events:

A lord who is patient and gives without possessions,
one who practices the Dharma even when fallen into poverty,
and one who keeps apart from sensual desires though possessed of great wealth —
these four things are exceedingly difficult to do.

Then the householder Duṣṭanandidatta, the householder Saṃgrāhaka, the householder Śīlavāṇijaka, and Prince Kṛṣṇa requested the Blessed One to reveal the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the Blessed One gave them ever-higher teachings in reply.
