And Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, sat there looking upon their faces. After listening for a while to the talk full of Dharma, he prostrated with his head to the two feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed. He entered the inner quarters of the queen's retinue and said to Queen Mālavikā: "Mālavikā, today the householder Duṣṭanandidatta, the householder Saṃgrāhaka, the householder Śīlavāṇijaka, and Prince Kṛṣṇa requested the Blessed One to reveal the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the Blessed One gave them ever-higher teachings in reply. I too sat there looking upon their faces, and then I rose and departed, somewhat abashed."

Queen Mālavikā said: "Your majesty, why did you yourself not make a request to the Blessed One?" He replied: "Mālavikā, I have little learning, while they have much learning — what was there for me to request?" She said: "Your majesty, why do you not yourself have the word of the Buddha recited?" He replied: "Mālavikā, I am constantly occupied with royal affairs and royal duties — how could I have it recited? But if you were to have it recited by someone, I would have it read to me from you in the evenings." She said: "Your majesty, I shall do so."

The king then said to Queen Kṣatriyāvarṣā: "From whom do you have it recited?" She replied: "Your majesty, from the noble Śāriputra." He then said to Queen Mālavikā: "From whom do you have it recited?" She replied: "Your majesty, from the noble Śārka."

Then Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, went to where the venerable Śāriputra was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head to the two feet of the venerable Śāriputra and addressed him thus: "Noble one, if the noble Kṣatriyāvarṣā wishes to have the word of the Buddha recited from the noble Śāriputra, please grant her leave to do so." He replied: "Your majesty, make the request to the Blessed One." Thereupon the venerable Śāriputra went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend one, Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, has said this: 'Please grant leave for Kṣatriyāvarṣā to recite.' What should I say to him in reply?" The Blessed One declared:

"Let Śārika's son recite." The venerable Śāriputra accepted, saying to Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, "Your majesty, leave to recite has been granted." The king prostrated with his head to Śāriputra's two feet, and then the venerable Śāradvatiputra went to where Śāradvatiputra was — arriving there, he prostrated with his head to the venerable Śāradvatiputra's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, addressed the venerable Śāradvatiputra thus: "Noble Mālavatī wishes to recite the word of the Buddha from a noble one; please grant her leave to do so." He replied: "Your majesty, make the request to the Blessed One." Thereupon the venerable Śāradvatiputra went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Śāradvatiputra addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend one, Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, has said this: 'Please grant leave for Mālavatī to recite.' What should I say to him in reply?" The Blessed One declared: "Let Śāradvatiputra recite." The venerable Śāradvatiputra accepted, saying to Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, "Your majesty, leave to recite has been granted," and the king prostrated with his head to his two feet and departed.

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga. The seventieth fascicle.

Now the venerable Śāriputra, knowing the proper times and understanding right occasion, would go at the fitting moment to engage the Kṣatriyā in her recitation of the Vinaya and would not go at an improper time. The venerable Śāradvatiputra, however, did not know the proper times and did not understand right occasion, and so he would go both at fitting times and at improper times to engage Mālavatī in recitation.

On one occasion, at some other time, some matter arose for Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, at another rocky retreat, and he rose that very night and went there. The noble Śāradvatiputra was awakened by the sounds of elephants, horses, and conches, and he thought to himself: "I shall go and give Mālavatī her recitation." He went to the gate of the royal palace, and the gatekeeper said to him: "Noble one, this is not the right time; do not enter the royal palace now — wait a while and enter afterward." At this he grew angry and said: "As long as this great fat beggar lives, I shall enter here both at proper times and at improper times. When he dies, this place will be the domain of outcastes and thieves; it will become a place of filth, a prison, and a jackal-haunt." The gatekeeper, frightened, said nothing, and the venerable Śāradvatiputra entered within.

Mālavatī was lying asleep, and he roused her with the sound of snapping his fingers. She prostrated at his feet and sat before him. Now Mālavatī was wearing robes befitting the queen's retinue, and the venerable Śāradvatiputra sat with his senses collected. Mālavatī thought: "Why does the noble Śāradvatiputra sit with his senses collected?" Then she thought again: "I am wearing robes befitting the queen's retinue — that is why the noble Śāradvatiputra sits with his senses collected." Understanding this, she went into her chamber, put on thick robes, and came back out. The venerable Śāradvatiputra then gave her the recitation, and other scriptures were also transmitted. Mālavatī said: "Noble one, has the Saṅgha been invited today, or is this an alms round?" He said: "I am going on an alms round." Mālavatī said: "Noble one, if you are going on an alms round, who is there to offer you more generous alms than I?

"I myself will offer it," she said, and filling the alms bowl with clean and choice food and drink, she presented it to him. The venerable Śāradvatiputra took it and departed. As he was leaving, he met the venerable Śāriputra, who was just entering, and Śāriputra said to him: "With such little effort as this, have you brought your defilements to exhaustion? Or is it that you have only just arrived? As for me, I have given the recitation and other scriptures have also been transmitted, and I have obtained this alms bowl filled with clean and choice food and drink." The venerable Śāriputra then said to him: "That is why you belong to the group of six." When monks of little conscience heard this, they spoke disparagingly, saying: "Why do monks, before dawn, before the break of day, pass through the firmly shut gates — or through the precincts of the firmly shut gates — of a king consecrated with the royal consecration over the heads of the warrior caste, without having first gathered jewels or those counted as jewels?" They reproached them, made accusations, and spread talk. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One convened the Saṅgha of monks in light of this occurrence, this basis for promulgation, and this occasion — and so on, as before. "The awakened Blessed Ones, though knowing, yet act as if they do not know" — and so on, also as before. The awakened Blessed One then questioned the venerable Śāradvatiputra: "Śāradvatiputra, is it true that before dawn, before the break of day, without having first gathered jewels or those counted as jewels, you passed through the firmly shut gates — or through the precincts of the firmly shut gates — of a king consecrated with the royal consecration over the heads of the warrior caste?" "Reverend One, it is true." The awakened Blessed One said: "What is unbecoming of an ascetic, what is not in accord, what is not fitting, what does not accord with proper conduct — that is not to be done by one who has gone forth. And why? Because, monks, there are these ten dangers in going to a royal palace. What are the ten? Monks, consider this: a king is sitting together with his queen, and a monk also goes to the royal palace. The queen then, upon seeing the monk, smiles. At that the king thinks: 'Might the reason the queen smiles upon seeing the monk be that the monk intends to commit some misdeed with her in private?' That is the first danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the king has gone to the queen's chambers, or a pregnant woman has entered among the queen's retinue, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, the king will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the second danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if a jewel or something reckoned as a jewel has gone missing from the royal palace, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, the king will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the third danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if a secret word has spread to the outside from the royal palace, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, the king will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the fourth danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if someone intends to kill the young princes, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?'

That is the fifth danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the young princes intend to kill the king, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the sixth danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the king demotes high ministers to a lower rank, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the seventh danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the king promotes low ministers to a higher rank, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the eighth danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the king arms his fourfold military host — the host of elephants, the host of cavalry, the host of chariots, and the host of infantry — and marches forth to the provinces and returns, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the ninth danger of going to a royal palace. Furthermore, if the king causes one who has not come to come, and causes one who has come to stay, and having proclaimed victory, pursues them afterward with great punishment, and a monk also goes to the royal palace, those who are displeased will think: 'Could it not be the monk's doing, his going to this royal palace?' That is the tenth danger of going to a royal palace.

Monks, it is thus that going to a royal palace may give rise to harm from elephants, harm from horses, harm from chariots, and harm from infantry. Monks, going to a royal palace is not fitting, not in accord with proper conduct, not in accord with the ways of an ascetic — and so he censured it.

Then the Blessed One, having censured it in many ways, declared to the monks: 'Monks, therefore, having discerned ten genuine benefits, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established' — and so forth, as before. 'My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk, before dawn has broken and before valuables or things reckoned as valuables have been collected, crosses the fixed gate or the precincts of the fixed gate of the palace of a king consecrated with the head-anointment of royal consecration, he commits a transgression.'

Thus did the Blessed One establish that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka's bamboo grove of the Cool Forest. At that time there were in Jambudvīpa two great cities: Rājagṛha and one called Campā. Whenever Rājagṛha fell into decline, Campā would flourish; and whenever Campā fell into decline, Rājagṛha would flourish.

In the great city of Śraghoṣa there reigned a king named Utrayaṇa, under whose rule the kingdom was prosperous and flourishing, the seasons were good, the land was filled with people and a great populace, conflicts and quarrels, foreign enemies and internal strife were utterly pacified, and it was free from thieves, famine, and disease. With rows of śāla trees and sugarcane, and an abundance of cattle and buffalo, it was a land of Dharma, and a righteous king caused it to be governed as a righteous kingdom. There too the trees perpetually bore flowers and fruit, and the gods sent the rains in timely and excellent succession, so that the harvests became exceedingly abundant. This king had a queen named Moonlight, beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and endowed with every wholesome quality of limb and feature, a crown prince named Tsugphudchen, and two foremost ministers named Heruka and Bhiruka.

In the city of Rājagṛha there reigned a king of the Magadha lineage named Bimbasāra, under whose rule the kingdom was likewise prosperous and flourishing, the seasons were good, the land was filled with people and a great populace, conflicts and quarrels, foreign enemies and internal strife were utterly pacified, and it was free from thieves, famine, and disease. With rows of śāla trees and sugarcane, and an abundance of cattle and buffalo, it was a land of Dharma, and a righteous king caused it to be governed as a righteous kingdom. There too the trees perpetually bore flowers and fruit, and the gods sent the rains in timely and excellent succession, so that the harvests became exceedingly abundant. This king had a queen named Elevated Body, beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and endowed with every wholesome quality of limb and feature, a crown prince named Ajātaśatru, and a foremost minister, belonging to the great officers of Magadha, named the Brahmin Varṣatūla.

Now, at a certain time, merchants from Rājagṛha took up their packs and set out to other lands, and, after passing through villages, towns, districts, and royal palaces in succession while surveying the markets, they arrived at the great city of Śraghoṣa. When king Utrayaṇa was seated in a place of business surrounded by his assembly of ministers, those merchants presented themselves and went before king Utrayaṇa. King Utrayaṇa received them with the words "Welcome!" and settled them according to their needs. King Utrayaṇa, having seen them, said to his ministers: "Wise ones, is there any other king who possesses a kingdom so prosperous and flourishing, the seasons so good, filled with such people and such a great populace, where the trees perpetually bear flowers and fruit like this, and where the gods send the rains in timely succession so that the harvests are exceedingly abundant?" Those merchants said: "Sire, in the eastern lands there is a city called Rājagṛha, in which a king named Bimbasāra makes the kingdom prosperous and flourishing, the seasons good, and the land filled with people and a great populace. There too the trees perpetually bear flowers and fruit, and the gods send the rains in timely and excellent succession, so that the harvests are exceedingly abundant." Upon hearing this, king Utrayaṇa became filled with longing, and he said: "Wise ones, what is scarce in that king's land?" The ministers replied: "Sire, you are the lord of jewels, and that king is the lord of cloth; therefore jewels are scarce there." The king said:

"Wise ones, if that is so, let the jewel-appraisers be summoned!" The king had the jewels examined and examined again, filled a chest with them, and sent them as a gift into the hands of those merchants. He also wrote a letter: "O joyful and well-suited one, you are a friend I have not met with my own eyes. If there is ever anything at all that you need in the city of Śrāvastī, send word to me and I shall accomplish everything." This he wrote and dispatched. Then those merchants took the gift, the letter, and the price of the goods, set out for Rājagṛha, and in due course arrived at Rājagṛha. There they rested from the weariness of the road, and then, taking the jewel chest and the letter, they went to king Bimbisāra, touched their heads to his two feet, presented the chest and the letter, and said: "Sire, the king of the resounding city, he who is called king Utrayaṇa, sends these gifts and this letter to Your Majesty." King Bimbisāra read the letter and said: "Wise ones, what is scarce in that king's land?" The ministers replied: "It is much like your own land, Sire." But the ministers then added: "Sire, that said, the king himself takes up arms, and he goes to battle and engages in combat together with the kings of the neighboring fortresses around him." Now king Utrayaṇa possessed a jewel armor of five parts, which at every joining of its sections was pleasant to the touch, difficult to cut, difficult to pierce, impervious to poison, and possessed of a luminous nature. King Utrayaṇa said to his ministers: "Wise ones, if that king himself takes up arms and goes to battle and is about to engage in combat together with the kings of the neighboring fortresses, then send him this jewel armor; make the envoys ready at once." They made the envoys ready. Then king Utrayaṇa had this jewel armor prepared along with a letter that said: "O joyful and well-suited one, I send you this jewel armor as a gift. It too possesses five qualities: at every joining of its sections it is pleasant to the touch, difficult to cut, difficult to pierce, impervious to poison, and possessed of a luminous nature. Therefore you yourself keep it on your person with care, and do not give it to anyone." This he wrote and dispatched. The envoys took the gift and the letter, set out for Rājagṛha, and in due course arrived at Rājagṛha.

Then, after resting from the weariness of the road, the envoys took the jewel armor and the letter and went before king Bimbisāra (Skt. Bimbasāra), prostrated at his feet, and presented the jewel armor and the letter, saying: "The divine king Utrayaṇa sends your majesty this gift and this letter."

King Bimbisāra read the letter, and when he saw the jewel armor he was filled with the greatest wonder. He said to his ministers: "Wise ones, summon the jewel appraisers." When the jewel appraisers had been summoned, the king said: "Wise ones, assess the value of these jewels." The jewel appraisers began to examine each of the jewels set in the jewel armor, but as they looked at each jewel in turn they found that none of them could be given a price. They said to the king: "Your majesty, not a single jewel in this piece is one that can be priced. By the very nature of things, the value of a jewel that cannot be priced is counted as ten million." King Bimbisāra counted the jewels, and then, dismayed at the thought of what gift he could possibly send in return, he rested his chin on his hand, sat lost in thought, and spoke to his ministers: "Wise ones, king Utrayaṇa sends me a gift such as this — what gift in return shall I send him?" Then the brahmin Varṣatula, the chief minister of Magadha, spoke: "Your majesty, in your own land too there has appeared a jewel supremely exalted above all three worlds: namely, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha. Your majesty should have a likeness of the Buddha drawn on cloth and send it as a gift in return." The king said: "If that is so, then I shall ask the Blessed One." And with that, king Bimbisāra went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head, and sat down to one side. Sitting there to one side, king Bimbisāra addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, I have a friend in the city of Śrāvastī called king Utrayaṇa whom I have never seen. He has sent me as a gift a jewel armor possessing five qualities. In return, if the Blessed One would grant it, I would have a likeness of the Blessed One drawn on cloth and send it to him as my return gift." The Blessed One declared: "Great king, I grant it — have it sent. Your intention is good. The moment king Utrayaṇa sees it, faith will arise in him and he will come to perceive the truth." King Bimbisāra bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence. He then summoned all the painters residing throughout his realm and said: "Wise ones, draw a likeness of the Blessed One on cloth." They replied: "Your majesty, we shall draw it." As they began to capture the Blessed One's features, however, they found themselves unable to do so, for the buddhas, the blessed ones, are such that one can never look at them enough, and so the painters were unable to capture the Blessed One's features. Disheartened, they went before the king and said: "Your majesty, we have been unable to make a start on capturing the Blessed One's features. If your majesty would invite the Blessed One to another palace and have him sit in measured shade, then we would be able to make a start on capturing the Blessed One's features."

King Bimbisāra invited the Blessed One to another palace, but since the buddhas, the blessed ones, are such that one can never look at them enough, whenever the painters beheld the Blessed One's form they found themselves not yet satisfied in their looking at this or that feature, and so were still unable to capture the Blessed One's likeness. At that point the Blessed One spoke: "Great king, let the painters not be disheartened at their inability to capture the Tathāgata's likeness. Have a cloth brought, and I shall cast my shadow upon it." The king had a cloth presented, and the Blessed One cast his shadow upon it. He then spoke to the painters: "Skilled ones, fill in this shadow with paints of many colors." He also spoke to the king: "Great king, once the image is made, below it write the going for refuge, the bases of training, and the twelve links of dependent origination in forward order and in reverse. Above it compose and set down these two verses:

Arise and engage the Buddha's teaching,
like a great elephant in a house of mud.
Crush the army of the lord of death.
Whoever dwells in thorough heedfulness
and practices this Dharma of taming
shall, having fully abandoned the wandering of birth,
make an end of suffering at last.

Write these words there. And send messengers to convey the image to distant lands with great honor and reverence. If anyone asks what this is, let them say: 'This is an image of the Blessed One, the buddha who is supremely exalted above all three worlds.' If anyone asks what is written below, let them say: 'This is the profession of faith, these are the bases of training, and this is the arising and ceasing of the world.' If anyone asks what is written above, let them say: 'This is something to inspire great joy.' So instruct them."

The king had everything written down and rolled up, perfumed with many fragrant substances, neatly rolled together, placed in a golden tube, that golden tube placed inside a silver tube, the silver tube inside a bronze tube, and the bronze tube wrapped in cloth scented with many fragrances. It was then loaded onto an elephant's back and sent forth from the city with great splendor of streets and roads. To King Udayana the king sent a letter bearing these words: "To you, Udayana, my dear and beloved friend, I send this gift which is supremely exalted above all three worlds. You, for three and a half leagues, shall beautify the city and the roads, and I myself, with a fourfold army, shall come to receive it. In an open and spacious region let it be received with great offerings and honor and unveiled." So he wrote and dispatched it. He also instructed the messengers: "You shall say to him thus and thus." They took the image and the letter and set out, proclaiming it aloud as they went. Traveling in stages, proclaiming as they went, they arrived at the frontier of those proclamations and sent the letter on from there to King Udayana. When King Udayana read the letter he was overcome and surrounded on all sides by anger, and he said to his ministers: "Wise ones, listen to what this letter he has sent me says. He sends me some kind of gift, and for that reason he says I am to beautify the city and the roads for three and a half leagues, and that he himself will come to receive it with a fourfold army."

"Ready the fourfold army and go now — devastate that king's realm." The ministers said: "Your Majesty, that king appears to be a great sovereign. Since sending him a vile gift to his face before your own royal presence would be unseemly, it would be wiser to investigate the matter more carefully. If it pleases Your Majesty, so much the better. If it does not, then we shall find the right moment to deal with him." They had the roads beautified for up to three and a half leagues, and the city was proclaimed throughout: stones, gravel, and rubbish were cleared away; it was sprinkled with sandalwood water; vessels filled with fragrant incense were set out; festoons of silk streamers were hung up; parasols and victory banners were raised; flowers of every variety were strewn about; and everything was made as joyful as the pleasure groves of the gods. Then the king himself, at the head of his fourfold army, received the guest and had him conducted into the city.

Thereupon many hundreds of thousands of living creatures gathered there, and many hundreds of thousands of gods gathered in the midst of the sky, and in that wide open space a great offering was made in their midst. When the image was unveiled, many merchants who had come from the interior of the country, bearing their packs, had arrived in the city just as the proclamation was being made. They saw the image of the Buddha and, all at once, every one of them raised a single cry: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha!"

King Udayana, hearing for the very first time the word "Buddha," felt every single hair on his body stand on end. Filled with wonder, he gazed steadily for a long while and then spoke: "Wise ones, who is this called 'Buddha'?"

They replied: "Your Majesty, in the interior of Jambudvīpa, near the face of the Snow Mountains, beside the river on the bank where the fortunate charioteer dwells, not far from the hermitage of the yellow-robed sages, there was born a youth of the Śākya clan. The brahmin astrologers and mark-readers prophesied: if this youth remains within the palace, he will become a wheel-turning king, victorious in all four directions — a king of Dharma, endowed with Dharma, possessed of the seven precious things. Those seven precious things will be as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious queen, the precious householder, and the precious general is the seventh. He will have brave and bold sons of excellent bodily form, a full thousand in number, who crush all enemy forces. He will govern this great earth reaching to the oceans, utterly without harming or injuring, and he will dwell having established it well in accordance with Dharma, equitable and just. But if he shaves his hair and beard, dons the ochre robes, and goes forth from home into homelessness with sincere faith, then he will become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened Buddha — renowned throughout the world with the sound of that fame." So it was prophesied. Your Majesty, this is his image.

The king was greatly delighted and said: "Wise ones, ask about this on my behalf — I wish to know: what is this writing below?" They said: "Your Majesty, this is his accepted precepts. These are the bases of the training. These are the arising and ceasing of the world." "Wise ones, ask about this also on my behalf — I wish to know: what is this writing above?"

"This god is one to be rejoiced in." King Utraya then repeatedly recited the twelve links of dependent origination in forward order and in reverse order, taking them firmly to heart. As dawn broke through the night, he set aside all purposes and all ends of action, sat down in cross-legged posture, held his body straight, settled his mindfulness in its proper orientation, and gazed upon the twelve links of dependent origination arising in forward order and ceasing in reverse order, as follows:

When this exists, this arises; because this is born, this comes to be. That is: conditioned by ignorance, formations arise; conditioned by formations, consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact; conditioned by contact, feeling; conditioned by feeling, craving; conditioned by craving, clinging; conditioned by clinging, becoming; conditioned by becoming, birth; conditioned by birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and turmoil arise. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering come to be.

When this does not exist, this does not arise; because this is not born, this does not come to be. That is: with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and turmoil all cease. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering cease.

As he gazed upon the twelve links of dependent origination in their forward and reverse order, the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a self constituted by the aggregates), accumulated since beginningless time, was shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and he directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he spoke this verse:

The Buddha who dwells in the far distance
has thoroughly purified the eye of wisdom.
To the supreme physician who possesses
such medicine as this — I bow down.

Knowing this, filled with faith, he sent a letter to King Rūpasāra with these words of heartfelt joy: "In dependence upon you, I have lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; I have been established among gods and humans; I have brought cyclic existence to an end; I have dried up the ocean of blood and tears; I have been freed from the mountains of bones; I have cut off the doors to the lower realms; I have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation. By the vajra of primordial wisdom, I have shattered the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, and have directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. I wish to see a monk, and so it would be fitting for you to send some monks." Such was the letter he wrote and sent.

King Rūpasāra read that letter, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One in prostration, and sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, King Rūpasāra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, King Udayana, having seen the truths, sent me a letter saying, 'I wish to see a monk; it would be fitting to send some monks.' What should be done in this regard?"

The Blessed One reflected: considering who among the monks might be the one to tame King Udayana along with his retinue and the multitudes dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, he perceived that they were the disciples to be tamed by the venerable Mahākātyāyana. The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Kātyāyana, go to King Udayana, his retinue, and the multitudes dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, and tend to them."

The venerable Mahākātyāyana replied, "Venerable One, I shall do as you command," and having received this instruction from the Blessed One, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One in prostration and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

That very night having passed, when morning came, the venerable Mahākātyāyana put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having made the rounds for alms through Rājagṛha and taken his meal, he returned from the after-noon alms round, prepared his lodging in the manner to which he was accustomed, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and set out with a retinue of five hundred monks for the city of Śrāvastī.

King Rūpasāra, for his part, wrote a letter to King Udayana saying: "With joy and the greatest delight, for your sake I am sending this monk who is like the Teacher himself, together with five hundred attendants. You should have the road and the city beautified over a distance of three and a half leagues, and I myself will come to receive him with a fourfold army. Have five hundred temples erected outside the city, and provide five hundred thrones, smaller thrones, fine-cushioned seats, footrests, footstools, and round cushions; arrange for five hundred alms-portions as well — and thereby you will acquire great merit." Such was the letter he wrote and sent.

King Udayana read the letter, and joy and the greatest delight arose in him. He had the road and city beautified over three and a half leagues, then went forth himself with a fourfold army and a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of people to receive them. With great honor he had them conducted into the city of Śrāvastī, had five hundred temples erected outside the city, had five hundred thrones, smaller thrones, fine-cushioned seats, footrests, footstools, and round cushions offered, arranged for five hundred alms-portions, and had spacious, well-spread seats set out in an open area.

The venerable Mahākātyāyana seated himself on a prepared seat at the head of the assembly of monks. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered there — some drawn by curiosity, others impelled by roots of virtue from former lives.

Then the venerable Mahākātyāyana, having thoroughly understood the dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and characters of that assembly, taught the Dharma in such a way that the many hundreds of thousands of living beings, upon hearing it, came to a great and profound realization. Some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some directly realized the fruit of once-returning; some directly realized the fruit of non-returning; and some went forth into renunciation and, by abandoning all afflictions, directly realized arhathood. Others aroused the mind of awakening on the path of a śrāvaka.

Some aroused the mind of awakening on the path of a pratyekabuddha, and some aroused the mind of awakening oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. The greater part of the assembly was established in devotion to the Buddha, in reliance upon the Dharma, and in refuge in the Saṅgha.

Now in the city of Śroṇā there lived two householders named Rgyal and Karrgyal. These two went to where the venerable Mahākātyāyana was staying, approached him, bowed their heads to his feet, and sat down to one side. Seated thus, the two householders Rgyal and Karrgyal said to the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Noble Mahākātyāyana, may we two receive the going-forth into renunciation and the full ordination as monks in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya? May we practice the holy life in the presence of noble Mahākātyāyana?"

The venerable Mahākātyāyana then gave them the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon them. Having bestowed instructions and guidance, and as the two applied themselves with enthusiasm, effort, and exertion, they attained progressively higher levels of mental cultivation. Knowing this very wheel of cyclic existence to be fivefold, both agitated and unagitated, and being overwhelmed by the nature of reality — that all formations are subject to decay, downfall, dispersion, and disintegration — they abandoned all afflictions. Thus, noble sons, that supreme culmination of the holy life for the sake of which men shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and, with genuine faith, go forth from home into homelessness — that very culmination they realized and accomplished in this very life through their own direct knowledge. They understood: "My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. I shall not know any further existence." They became arhats — freed from attachment, beyond the three realms, with minds equal toward a clod of earth and gold, equanimous as space and the palm of the hand. Like sandalwood laid down, their wisdom split open the shell of the egg of ignorance. They attained the higher knowledges, supernormal powers, and the individual perfect understandings. They turned their backs on existence, on gains born of desire, and on worldly honors. They came to be worshipped, revered, and openly praised by the gods together with Indra (Śakra) and their attendants.

The two performed miracles of blazing fire, brilliant radiance, falling rain, and flashing lightning, and then passed completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. Their relatives paid bodily honors to their bodies and caused two stūpas to be built — one for Rgyal and one for Karrgyal.

King Uttarayana went daily to the venerable Mahākātyāyana to hear the Dharma, and he described to the ladies of his retinue how noble Mahākātyāyana teaches the Dharma, sweet and ever sweeter, like a bee drawing out honey. They said: "Your Majesty, the arising of a buddha is indeed fruitful — as is shown by the fact that you listen to the Dharma. If that is so, why do you not also listen? Your Majesty, we are modest; how could we go there and hear the Dharma? If noble Mahākātyāyana himself were to come here and teach the Dharma, then we too would hear the Dharma." King Uttarayana said to the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Noble one, the ladies of the retinue wish to hear the Dharma." He replied:

"Great King, monks do not enter among the ladies of the royal retinue and teach the Dharma. The Blessed One has forbidden monks from entering among ladies of the retinue. Noble one, then who shall teach the Dharma to the ladies of the retinue?" "Great King, nuns shall."

King Uttarayana sent a letter to King Bimbisāra with the following message: "With mutual goodwill and affection — my ladies of the retinue wish to hear the Dharma, and for that purpose it would be fitting to send some nuns." Having read that letter, King Bimbisāra went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, King Bimbisāra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable one, King Uttarayana has sent a letter saying that his ladies of the retinue wish to hear the Dharma, and requesting that some nuns be sent for that purpose. How is this matter to be accomplished?"

The Blessed One considered the matter. Reflecting on which nun would be able to discipline the women of King Uttarayana's retinue and the women dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, he saw that nun Rimā was their disciplinarian. The Blessed One then spoke to nun Rimā: "Rimā, devote yourself to the women of King Uttarayana's retinue and to the women dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī." Nun Rimā replied: "Venerable one, I shall do as commanded." Having heard this from the Blessed One, she bowed her head at the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That same night having passed, in the early morning nun Rimā donned her lower robe, took up her begging bowl and outer robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having completed the alms round in Rājagṛha and finished the meal, she returned from the after-meal alms round, set her dwelling in order for use as needed, took up her begging bowl and outer robe, and set out with a retinue of five hundred toward the city of Śrāvastī.

King Bimbisāra also sent a letter to King Uttarayana with this message: "With mutual goodwill and affection — for your sake I am sending this great śrāvikā, praised by the Teacher, along with a retinue of five hundred. You, for your part, shall beautify the road and the city for a distance of three and a half leagues, and you yourself shall come out to receive her with the fourfold army. In the city you shall also have five hundred summer residences built, five hundred thrones, chairs, cushions with fine inner coverings, foot-rests, head-rests, and pillows provided, and five hundred alms supplies arranged. By doing this you shall gain great merit." Having sent this letter, King Uttarayana read it and felt joy and the greatest delight. He had the road and the city beautified over three and a half leagues, and himself went out to receive her with the fourfold army and a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of people; he escorted her into the city with great honor. In the city he had five hundred summer residences built, and five hundred thrones, chairs, cushions with fine inner coverings, foot-rests, head-rests, and pillows provided, and five hundred alms supplies arranged.

Day by day nun Rimā entered among the ladies of King Uttarayana's retinue and the women dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, and taught them the Dharma.

Now King Uttarayana was skilled in the lute,

Queen Moonlight was skilled in dance, and so at a certain time King Uttarayana played the lute while Queen Moonlight danced. As she danced, he perceived the signs of decay upon her, and examining her from head to foot, he reflected: "In seven days she will die." At that moment the lute slipped from his hands and fell to the ground.

Queen Moonlight said: "My lord, was my dancing not good? What was the fault?"

"Moonlight, it is not that your dancing was poor. It is that as you danced I perceived the signs of decay upon you, and on the seventh day you will die."

Queen Moonlight prostrated herself at the king's feet and said: "My lord, if that is so, and if I have served you well, and if my lord grants it, I wish to go forth into homelessness."

The king replied: "Moonlight, since the time is right, I grant it. If, having gone forth, you abandon all afflictions and directly realize arhathood, that itself will be the end of your suffering. But if you die with residual bonds remaining and are reborn among the gods, then, having become a deity, come and visit me."

She replied: "As my lord commands."

King Uttarayana entrusted Queen Moonlight to the nun Rimā and said: "Noble one, please grant Queen Moonlight the going forth and the full ordination of a fully ordained nun in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya. It is fitting, noble one, that you perform for her this going forth and full ordination."

The nun Rimā said: "I shall do so," and she gave her the going forth and conferred upon her full ordination. Then nun Rimā reflected, and she gave her the instruction: "Cultivate the perception of death."

Queen Moonlight began to cultivate the perception of death, and on the seventh day, when her time arrived, she passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.

Now it is the nature of divine sons and daughters that shortly after birth three thoughts arise: from where one has passed away, where one has been reborn, and by what karma one has been reborn. The divine daughter Moonlight reflected: "From where have I passed away?" — and she saw that she had passed away from among human beings. "Where have I been reborn?" — and she saw that she had been reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings. "By what karma have I been reborn?" — and she saw that she had been reborn through the very practice of the holy life in the teaching of the Blessed One.

Then the divine daughter Moonlight thought: "It would not befit my character to go into the presence of the Blessed One to see him and pay homage while dwelling in my former dwelling; I will go into his presence to see him and pay homage without relying on my former dwelling at all."

And so the divine daughter Moonlight, her earrings and jeweled hoops swaying, wearing a spotless garment, her body adorned with necklaces and ornaments, held a basket filled with heavenly blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses, and with a radiance of surpassing brilliance she came in the night. She went to where the Blessed One was, and when she arrived she scattered flowers over the Blessed One, bowed her head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage, and sat to one side. In this way, through the power of the divine daughter Moonlight's radiance, the entire Kalandaka grove of Veṇuvana was filled with a great light.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the intention, the latent disposition, and the faculty of the divine daughter Moonlight —

— having fully understood her intrinsic nature, the Blessed One, while the divine daughter Moonlight sat there on that very seat, shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, and taught the Dharma in such a way as to bring her to a direct realization of the Four Noble Truths, causing her to actualize the fruit of stream-entry. Upon seeing the truth, she declared three times, with deliberate and heartfelt utterance: "What the venerable Blessed One has done for me in this way — this my father did not do, nor my mother, nor any king, nor the gods, nor my forebears of former times, nor any ascetics or brahmins, nor any gathering of friends, companions, or relatives. He has drained the ocean of blood and tears, freed me from the mountains of bones, closed the doors of the lower realms, opened the doors of the higher realms and liberation, and drawn my feet out from the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, placing me among gods and humans."

Then she spoke these verses:

Through your power you have closed off the lower path
laden with many faults and filled with great harm,
and opened the way to the higher realms. Now I
have also won the path that leads beyond sorrow.

Relying on you, utterly pure, today
I have gained the unstained eye, clear and free of fault,
attained the exalted peace of the noble station,
and crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Worshipped by beings — asuras, humans, and gods —
free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
rare indeed is one who sees existence as empty:
the Sage — today there is the fruit of having seen you.

Then, bowing down with her unclasped and pendant necklace trailing as she prostrated, she paid homage at his feet, arose with joy, circumambulated him to the right, and departed into the sky in the direction of the divine world.

Thereafter, the divine daughter Moonlight was like a merchant who has found great profit, like a farmer whose harvest is abundant, like a hero victorious in battle, like a patient freed from every illness — and in the very same attire in which she had come before the Blessed One, she went back to her own abode.

She thought to herself: "I have made a promise to King Udayana, and now the time has come to fulfill it." So the divine daughter Moonlight went to where King Udayana was.

At that time King Udayana was lying alone on the uppermost floor of his fine palace. She filled the space with a great spreading light and roused him with the sound of her anklet ornaments. His eyes were heavy with sleep and his consciousness was not clear, and he said: "Who are you?"

She replied: "I am Moonlight."

The king said: "Come, let us enjoy pleasures together."

She replied: "My lord, I have died and passed away at my time, and been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings. If you wish to meet with me again, go forth into renunciation before the Blessed One. And if in this very life you fully abandon all afflictions and directly actualize the state of arhathood, that itself will be the end of your suffering. But if you die with residual formations still remaining and are reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, then there you will meet with me again."

Having said this, she vanished from that very spot.

Vinaya Analysis, the seventy-first fascicle.

King Udayana, having determined in his heart to go forth that very night, rose early the next morning and said to his ministers: "Wise ones, go and see where Queen Moonlight is."

They replied: "Your majesty, she has passed away at her time."

King Udayana reflected:

"Since the goddess has urged me, it would not accord with my nature to remain a householder, dwelling within a household, fully enjoying possessions and pleasures. Therefore I shall invest the young prince Topknot with sovereign power over the kingdom, shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with true faith go forth from home into homelessness." With this resolve, he sent for his two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, and when they had come before him, he said: "You two wise ones — just as it has been for me, so too it shall be for the young prince Topknot. You two must shield him from harm and devote yourselves unfailingly to his benefit. As for me, I am going forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya." The two of them, upon hearing this, stood with their eyes filled with tears.

The king then said to the young prince Topknot: "My son, just as you have heeded my words and taken my counsel to heart, so now you must heed the words of these two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, and take their counsel to heart. As for me, I am going forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya." He too, upon hearing this, sat with his eyes filled with tears.

Then King Udayana had the town crier make a proclamation throughout the city, and addressed the townspeople, the palace attendants, and the assemblies of people who had come from various districts: "Wise ones, hear me. I am shaving off my hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, and with true faith going forth from home into homelessness. Now that I have set one in my place to govern the kingdom, forgive me for whatever slight wrong I may have done you." This was the announcement he gave. The townspeople, the palace attendants, and the assemblies who had come from various districts all held the king dear, and upon hearing this, every one of them stood with their eyes filled with tears.

King Udayana then installed the young prince Topknot over the kingdom, asked forgiveness of those close to him, gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and the destitute, performed meritorious deeds, and, without seeking any honor, turned away from Rājagṛha and departed.

Then King Topknot, together with the queen's retinue, the young prince, the ministers, the palace attendants, and the assemblies of people who had come from various districts, followed along behind him, one after another. Escorted by many hundreds of thousands of living creatures, he came forth from the city. He paused for a while in a pleasure grove adorned with various flowering trees, possessing flowers and fruit and many streams, where swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, pheasants, cuckoos, and śaṅgaśateka birds were calling out. He gazed back at the city from a distance and then said to King Topknot: "My son, because I have installed you to govern the kingdom by the Dharma, this is why so many hundreds of thousands of living creatures have followed after me. You too must govern the kingdom by the Dharma." Then he addressed the assembled people and said: "Wise ones, I have appointed this one as your king. Now return home and fare well." And with these words he departed.

King Topknot, together with the queen's retinue, the young prince, the ministers, the palace attendants, and the assemblies of people who had come from various districts, their eyes blurred with tears, looked back again and again for a little while, then returned to the city.

Then King Udrayana made his way gradually to the city of Rājagṛha and took up residence there in a pleasure grove. He said to a certain man: "Go and report to King Bimbisāra that King Udrayana is staying in the pleasure grove." The man went and reported to King Bimbisāra: "Your Majesty, King Udrayana is staying in the pleasure grove." Upon hearing this, Bimbisāra rose at once and said to those who subsisted on his bounty: "Wise ones, that king comes with a great army — if he had not sent word beforehand, none of you would have known he was coming." One of them said: "Your Majesty, what army does he have? He has come with just a single attendant." King Bimbisāra thought to himself: "Since I performed the consecration of this king of royal lineage by anointing his crown, it would be improper for me to receive him into the city in an ordinary way. I shall have him enter with great honor." Knowing this to be fitting, he had the roads and the city adorned, and then went out to receive him with the four-limbed host of his army. A canopy was provided, and Udrayana rode upon the back of an elephant and was escorted into the city of Rājagṛha. He was bathed with water mixed with various perfumes, beautifully adorned with robes befitting a king, with incense, garlands, materials for anointing, and various unguents, and given food; and when the weariness of the journey had been soothed, Bimbisāra spoke: "With power harmoniously rejoiced in, the kingdom flourishing — leaving behind the retinue of your queens, your young prince, your ministers, the people of the palace and your court — for what purpose have you come here? Has some other king ravaged your realm? Or has the young prince, coveting the kingship, been incited by some corrupt minister and rebelled? Or has something come between you?" Udrayana replied: "It is not so, O harmonious one. I seek going forth and full ordination as a monk in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."

Upon hearing this, King Bimbisāra rejoiced and was glad. He raised his upper robe, stretched out his right hand, and three times proclaimed aloud: "O the wonder of the Buddha! O the wonder of the Dharma! O the wonder of the Saṅgha! O the wonder of this very well-proclaimed Dharma — that such a pre-eminent being as this, having abandoned a flourishing kingdom, a flourishing retinue of queens, friends and kinsmen in their great multitudes, treasuries, granaries, and vast mansions, should wish to go forth and take full ordination as a monk in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya!" Having proclaimed this three times, he took King Udrayana and went to where the Blessed One was.

At that time the Blessed One was dwelling in the presence of a great assembly of many hundreds of thousands of followers and was teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One, from a great distance, caught sight of King Bimbisāra of Magadha approaching together with King Udrayana. Having seen them, he said to the monks: "Monks, this is King Bimbisāra — he is coming to me along with a new arrival. Such a birth as this Tathāgata's birth is thus: there is nothing quite like a birth ripe for taming." Having said this, he remained in silence.

King Bimbisāra prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, King Bimbisāra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, this King Udrayana desires going forth and full ordination as a monk in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Out of compassion, may the Blessed One please grant him the going forth and confer upon him full ordination."

The Blessed One granted him the going forth with the words "Come, monk," and declared, "Come, monk — live the holy life." And at the very end of the Blessed One's utterance, he found himself with a shaven head and wearing patched robes, with a growth of hair and beard of just seven days, holding in his hand a begging bowl, attended by a water-pot carrier, abiding in the manner of a monk fully ordained for a hundred years.

Then this verse was spoken:

When the Tathāgata declared "Come,"
he was clad in body with shaven head and patched robe,
and in that instant his faculties grew perfectly still —
the Buddha's intention having covered over his bodily form.

Thereafter, the venerable Udrayana, having put on his lower robe in the early morning, took up his begging bowl and outer robe and went forth on alms-round in Rājagṛha. When the great multitude of people saw him, a sound rang out through all of Rājagṛha: "The Blessed One has granted King Udrayana the going forth and full ordination, and now he has entered Rājagṛha on alms-round." Upon hearing this, countless hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered together, and women who dwelt within their homes came and stood at windows, latticed windows, and balconies to look upon him.

The ministers spoke to King Bimbisāra (Skt. Bimbisāra, "the one who is the essence of form"): "Your Majesty, King Udrayana has entered Rājagṛha on alms-round, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of living beings."

Upon hearing this, King Bimbisāra went to where the monk Udrayana was and, having arrived, addressed the monk Udrayana in these verses:

You who once commanded a thousand cities,
with their proclamations of royal glory —
now you seek alms that are thrown away:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who used vessels of gold and silver
weighed out in hundreds of measures —
now you make do with an earthen begging bowl:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who once used clean-washed rice of śāli grain,
moistened with meat —
now you carry a bowl filled with warm scraps:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who once wore fine wool, cotton, silk,
and robes of Kauṭambaka cloth —
now you patch together rags from charnel grounds:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who slept in a multi-storied mansion
with doors firmly shut against the wind —
now you dwell at the foot of a tree:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who slept on soft couches like beds of cotton —
now you lie on a mat of grass:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

Your consorts, lovely and evenly matched,
who lay at your side with reverence and sweet words —
you have abandoned them, so many of them:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who traveled mounted on great elephants,
on palanquins, and on horses —
now you wander the earth on foot:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

You who possessed storehouses full of great wealth
and many mansions —
now you have attained to having nothing:
how can you not feel anguish at this?

Udrayana replied:

O King, one who is difficult to tame
and is sustained by the food of others —
that one is tamed by something not yet attained,
as a yoke-post tames an ox.

King Bimbisāra said:

O King, are you not at ease?
Why do you speak as though you were lowly?
I will give you half my kingdom —
enjoy your wealth as before.

O King, are you not at ease?
Why do you speak as though you were lowly?
Whatever your mind desires,
the finest of enjoyments I will give you.

Udrayana replied:

O King, whoever in this world
is free from poverty by touching the Dharma of the body —
he will certainly become a god,
or else will pass beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa.

Whatever lord of men has abandoned the Dharma
and in its place delights in what is not Dharma —
that king should be known as impoverished;
he goes from darkness into deeper darkness.

I shall instruct you in the Dharma.
O Great King, listen to me.
Having heard the Dharma, the king
will go wherever he desires.

For a body devoid of virtue,
there is one supreme virtue alone:
however one takes it up and holds it,
so accordingly will one follow after it.

These ten tens of a king
are said to be the greatness of a person.
Yet in sons, in wives, in wealth —
what pleasure is there, truly?

A son shows delight,
a wife speaks of her contentment,
a thief works to acquire wealth,
and kings are freed from their bonds.

Against the one who brings the end, neither medicines
nor wealth nor kinsmen can protect.
Neither all the spells and armies,
nor valor and austerity can protect.

Here in this world, even gods of great power
who dwell on high, long-lived —
even they, when their life is spent, must wane.
Who today escapes from death?

Viṣṇu, of great power, possessed of wealth and blazing fame,
who made a kingdom spread across the world,
and Śiva the Destroyer, ill-omened, his dreadful sound resounding —
even they could not turn death back.

O King, with vows, with austerity and practice,
with deeds, with diligence, with discipline,
with vast retinues and riches —
how can one be free from death?

Whether one is in the middle of the sky, in the midst of the ocean,
or has entered a cleft in the mountains —
there is no region anywhere, no place,
where the lord of death cannot reach.

Whether one is in the middle of the sky, in the midst of the ocean,
or has entered a cleft in the mountains —
there is no region anywhere, no place,
where karma cannot reach.

Bones the color of a white dove,
cast aside and scattered in every direction —
of whatever kind they may be,
seeing them, who could rejoice in this?

Skulls the color of a conch,
tossed aside like fallen water pots —
of whatever kind they may be,
seeing them, who could rejoice in this?

O King, what you call your own self —
that which shades you in the heat
and wraps you warmly in the cold —
even that is destroyed by death.

However much a person has eaten and worn,
or given away — that may be counted as one's own.
The rest will be abandoned and go elsewhere.

A treasure that no human thief can steal,
that is shared with no other —
is generosity, or else
good deeds: these cannot be hidden by others.

As a tiger kills a deer and drags it away,
so old age and death drag you swiftly along.
Your assembly of dear friends, ministers, and advisors
cannot remove your illness.

Of the spent goods, the remaining grain and wealth,
the gold and silver that remain —
sons, wife, and retinue together
think of these as their own share.

If a father dies and a son falls into debt,
the beloved son does not carry the fire for him.
When one has died, those who are as if dying themselves do not weep,
and do not say "my father" or "my lord."

"He was rich" — so they call him "father"
and cry with disheveled hair and tear-streaked faces.
They carry the fire before him
and say: "Alas, now he becomes a god."

Covered with cloth they carry him,
set the fire, and then burn him.
The kinsmen weep, and with a single piece of cloth
they abandon what is burned and enjoy what remains.

Each one is born in a single birth,
and likewise each one dies in a single death.
In this birth, one alone experiences suffering,
and wanders through saṃsāra without a companion.

Seeing this, those who are noble
do not live at home after going forth.
Free from all attachment,
henceforth they will not enter a womb again.

Then King Rūpasāra, answered at length and pressed repeatedly by the monk Udrayana's confident replies, fell silent and, his confidence gone, departed.

Then King Tufthead, having for a time allowed the righteous rule of the Dharma-kingdom to continue, began to have the kingdom governed by what was contrary to the Dharma.

At that point the two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, spoke: "Your Majesty, please govern the kingdom according to the Dharma, and do not govern it by what is contrary to the Dharma. And why? Because the people of your realm are like flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees. Consider this example: flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees, when they are well cared for at the proper times, produce flowers and fruits in season without interruption through unceasing effort. Just so, when the people of the realm are well cared for at the proper times, they too will offer tribute and annual revenue in season without interruption through unceasing effort."

When those two remonstrated in this way, the king, who had meanwhile begun once more to govern the kingdom contrary to the Dharma after having allowed it to be governed according to the Dharma, would not desist even when the two spoke up three times in succession, for he was moved by the impulse toward a different existence. Enraged, he spoke to the other ministers: "Gentlemen, what is the punishment for one who countermands the command of a king of royal lineage anointed with the coronation water, even three times in succession?"

Then certain corrupt ministers spoke: "Your Majesty, what wrong has been done here? The punishment for such a one is death." And they also recited these verses:

Ministers who are corrupt
and teeth grown loose and shifting,
and food that has gone bad —
it is best simply to cast them out.

A minister who is wise,
skilled in discernment and in discipline,
who holds his rank from the treasury —
the one who does not kill such a man will be killed instead.

King Tufthead then said: "Gentlemen, these two were appointed by my father, so I will not have them killed. Nevertheless, they shall not remain in my sight." He turned those two away and appointed two other corrupt men as ministers. Those two then spoke: "Your Majesty, sesame seeds that have not been beaten, not pressed, not heated, and not squeezed do not yield sesame oil. The people under human authority are the same." The king said: "What you two have done is supremely diligent." And those two set about doing harm to the people of the realm.

Then some time later a merchant, carrying his goods and crying out news through the city, arrived at Rājagṛha. The venerable Udrayana saw him, recognized him, and said:

Why do you cry out, O Tufthead —
with your retinue and assembly, are you powerful and well?
Are there no enemies encroaching upon you,
and are you administering your own kingdom according to the Dharma?

The merchant replied:

Your Majesty, just so I cry out, O Tufthead.
With your retinue and assembly, powerful one — I seek no boon.
There are no enemies encroaching upon him.
Yet he governs the kingdom always contrary to the Dharma.

Then the venerable Udrayana began to question him further: "Now, among the ministers, who is chief and who is not chief? Through whose influence does Tufthead do harm to the people of the realm?" The merchant replied: "Your Majesty, the two chief ministers Heruka and Bhiruka were turned away, and two other corrupt men were appointed ministers. It is through their influence that Tufthead does harm to the people of the realm."

Udrayana then said: "Sir, go back now and cry your news. May the assembled people who remain there breathe easy and take heart. I will return there once more —

I myself will turn Tufthead back from doing harm to the people of the realm, no matter what it takes, and I will firmly set things on a course of benefit."

The merchant changed his goods, took his trading goods, and departed. He went ahead and, passing on by stages, arrived to cry the news. There he told his kinsmen privately, saying: "Friends, I took my goods and entered Rājagṛha, and there I saw the aged king. From his own lips came the message: 'Go, sir, cry your news, and let the assembled people who remain there breathe easy and take heart. I will return there once more, and I myself will turn Tufthead back from doing harm to the people of the realm, no matter what it takes, and I will firmly set things on a course of benefit.'"

These kinsmen told others, and those others told yet more, so that the news passed from ear to ear in this way, until it reached the ears of the two corrupt ministers. The two of them thought: "If the old king comes back, he will certainly reinstate Heruka and Bhiruka as the highest ministers, and that will mean harm for the two of us. Therefore we must find some way to have him killed right there on the road."

With this in mind, the two of them went to King Tufthead and said: "Your Majesty, we have heard that the aged king will come."

Tufthead replied: "He has gone forth into renunciation. Why would he come here?"

The two said: "Your Majesty, the one to whom you granted sole sovereignty over the realm — he cannot possibly be glad to have no kingship at all. He too will seek to be granted the kingship once more."

Tufthead said: "If he were to become king, I myself would become the young prince. What objection could there be to that?"

The two replied: "Your Majesty, that would not be proper. You granted him the kingship to the prostrations of thousands of joined palms — from the young prince, the ministers, the palace retinue, and the people of the realm — and then to remain again in the position of prince, having sent away the entire surrounding domain, is simply not fitting. Consider this example: it is like a man who rides atop an elephant, then descends to ride on the back of a horse, then from the horse descends to a chariot, and from the chariot descends to go on foot alone. To grant him the kingship and then oneself to remain in the position of prince is exactly like that."

Deceived by the two of them, Tufthead said: "Well then, what is to be done in this matter? How should it be accomplished?"

The two replied: "Your Majesty, you should have him put to death. If Your Majesty does not grant that he be killed and he is not slain on the road, then the corrupt ministers will band together with him and bring about Your Majesty's own death."

When these words were spoken, Tufthead sat there for a moment overcome, saying nothing, his heart wilting as though in compassion, tears welling in his eyes, his mind struggling. Then he said: "Wise ones, how could it be fitting to put one's own father to death?"

The two replied:

"Whether it be father, brother,
or even a son born of oneself —
if he has entered the ranks of the enemy,
let him be used to increase one's store of earth.

Have you not heard that said? And again:

If one possesses a thousand sons
and all of them have boarded the same boat,
yet a single enemy has arisen among them —
for that one's sake, let him go under.

Have you not heard that said? And from another source:

For the sake of a house, give up one man;
for the sake of a village, give up a house;
for the sake of a district, give up a village;
and for the sake of oneself, give up the entire land.

Have you not heard that said? Your Majesty, there is nothing here that should give you pause. He must be killed — and so you should grant that he be put to death."

"If he is left alive and those youths, ministers, palace retainers, and people of the realm who are devoted to him become stirred to rebellion, that will cause harm to His Majesty without Gora having been killed. Since there is no wicked act one will not commit in the pursuit of desires, let it be done as I have said." And so it was agreed.

Then those two corrupt ministers, filled with delight, joy, and great exultation, said to the executioners: "Men, today you shall slay the old king, and his wealth and possessions shall be divided among you." Now all the palace retainers and people of the realm were devoted to that king, and so there was not a single one among them who was willing to kill him. When those two, up to three times over, tried to rouse them with offers of silver, gold, and the gift of villages and the like, not a single one was roused. Then those two, consumed and wrapped about with rage, gave orders to the palace guards: "Men, today put those people — together with their sons, wives, kinsmen, friends, and assembled relatives — in bonds." When the guards heard this they were afraid, and they said: "May His Majesty deign not to punish us — we are servants who obey royal command." And with that they tucked sharp swords under their arms and fled.

Now the venerable Uttarayana, the three months of the rains retreat having passed, and being possessed of a robe made according to Dharma and having received it in the proper manner, took up his alms-bowl and robe and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable sir, I wish to go and make proclamation through the city." The Blessed One declared: "Uttarayana, go. Keep in mind the work that is to be done as your own task." Then the venerable Uttarayana prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That very same night having passed, in the early morning Uttarayana put on his lower robe, took up his alms-bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having made his alms-round through Rājagṛha and completed the meal, he returned from the alms-round of the afternoon meal. He set out what was needed for making use of his lodging, took up his alms-bowl and robe, and went forth, drawn onward by the power of karma.

Karma leads beings far away;
by karma from afar are beings led.
Wherever karmic deeds come to fruition —
thither karma utterly draws one on.

Going to where the city proclamation was being made, he walked through it gradually to the end, and at a cliff-face beside the road he entered for alms. From there, having made his alms-round and moved on, he encountered those executioners, and they saw him. He too recognized them, and he agreed to spend the night with them together in a pleasure grove. Then he began to question them:

How is it in Rājagṛha? Does he of the topknot,
with his retinue and host, stand strong and free of sickness?
Does no adversary's faction stir against him,
and does he govern his kingdom with Dharma?

They replied:

Majesty, even so — he of the topknot in Rājagṛha,
with his retinue and host, stands strong and untroubled.
No adversary's faction has arisen against him,
yet the kingdom he ever governs contrary to Dharma.
You, O noble man, whatever supreme and evident thing
is in accord with your own way — that you should do.
Whatever is in accord with the way of that peaceful one —
that shall become visible and near this very day.

The venerable Utraya then said: "Wise ones, does he not take pleasure in coming here today?" They replied: "Majesty, he takes no pleasure in it." He said: "Wise ones, if that is so, let him turn back and not come."

They then spoke in verse:

O brave man, where do you go back to now?
The prince, while alive, takes no pleasure in your coming.
We are those appointed by the wicked king —
it is to put you to death, O sir, that we have come.

The venerable Utraya said: "Wise ones, are you then men who have come to kill me?" "Majesty, we are the executioners sent to put you to death."

The venerable Utraya then reflected: "The Blessed One declared to me, 'Go, Utraya, and keep in mind the task that is yours to do.' This, then, is what that means." And understanding that saṃsāra is in every respect wretched, without essence, and subject to destruction, he said to them: "Good fellows, the aim for the sake of which I went forth has not yet been attained by me. Wait just a moment while I accomplish my own purpose."

They conferred among themselves and said: "Majesty, let it be so."

Then the venerable Utraya seated himself in cross-legged posture against a tree, settled like a king of serpents coiled in sleep, and remained with peaceful composure.

Now the Blessed One had declared that there are five benefits to extensive learning: mastery of the aggregates (skandhas), mastery of the elements (dhātus), mastery of the sense bases (āyatanas), mastery of dependent origination, and the ability to teach and instruct others in its meaning without dependence on anyone else. Rousing his diligence upon this, Utraya understood directly this very fivefold wheel of saṃsāra, both its stirring and its stillness. Overwhelmed by the very nature of the dissolution of all formations — their decline, downfall, dispersion, and destruction — and having abandoned all afflictions, he realized in this very life by his own direct knowledge that supreme end of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family shave hair and beard, don the ochre robe, and go forth from home into homelessness with sincere faith, and he understood: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. The task is done. There is no further becoming beyond this." He became an arhat, free from desire for all three realms, his mind equal toward a clod of earth and gold, equal toward sky and the palm of his hand, like sandalwood placed there, his mind's eye having split open the sheath of ignorance. He attained the three knowledges (vidyās), the superknowledges (abhijñās), and the discriminating awarenesses (pratisaṃvids). He turned his back on the gains and honors and pleasures of existence and desire, and became worthy of veneration, reverence, and open praise by gods together with Indra and his company.

Then, having attained arhatship, the venerable Utraya, in the joy and bliss of the discriminating awareness of liberation, spoke these verses:

The monk Utraya, though now freed
from bonds, afflictions, and obscurations alike,
is not yet free today from the king's law.

Having said this, he addressed those executioners: "Good fellows, what I had to attain I have now attained. Now obtain what you yourselves came to obtain." They said: "Majesty, if the king of the topknot asks us what the elder king said at the time of his death, what shall we report to him?"

Say to him these words: "For the sake of a kingdom you slew your father, thereby generating abundant demerit. I shall pass into nirvāṇa; you shall go to the Avīci hell."

Say further these words: "You have committed two heinous acts without interval: the taking of your father's life, and the taking of the life of a fully ordained monk, an arhat whose defilements are exhausted. By these two acts you will be compelled to dwell for a very long time in the great hell of Avīci, the hell of ceaseless torment. Therefore, turn away from all manner of evil deeds — and by doing so, you will be purified, utterly exhausted of them, and brought to their final end."

Then the venerable Utraya thought to himself: "It would not be right for that being to be cast down into the great hell. I shall go by means of supernatural power." But when he attempted whatever means of supernatural power he could, the weight of that being's karma was such that not even the mere appearance of movement arose, let alone any supernatural power.

Then, among those executioners, one who was devoid of compassion and utterly indifferent to the world beyond drew his sword from its scabbard, cut off that head at the neck, and cast it to the ground.

Thereupon the Blessed One smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, smile, rays of light issue from their mouths — blue and yellow and red and white, and of colors like crimson, crystal, and silver. Some of these rays go downward, and some go upward. Those that go downward descend, now cool, into the hot hells — the Reviving hell, the Black Line hell, the Crushing hell, the Wailing hell, the Great Wailing hell, the Hot hell, the Intensely Hot hell, the Avīci hell, the Blistering hell, the Burst-Blister hell, the Grinding-Teeth hell, the Shrieking hell, the Groaning hell, the Cracked-Like-a-Blue-Lotus hell, the Cracked-Like-a-Lotus hell, and the Cracked-Like-a-Great-Lotus hell — and they descend warm into whichever hells are cold.
