These rays cut off the various individual torments of those beings, and those beings think among themselves: "O friends, have we died and passed on from here? Or have we been reborn elsewhere?" In order to arouse faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. Seeing that emanation, they think: "O friends, we have neither died and passed on from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere. Rather, it is by the power of this being, never seen before, that our various individual torments have been cut off." Developing sincere faith of mind toward that emanation, and having exhausted the karma that would have led them to experience the hells, they take rebirth among those gods and humans who are fit vessels for the truths, in whatever realm they are to become so.

Those rays that go upward enter among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Heaven Free from Strife, the Joyful Heaven, the Heaven of Delight in Emanations, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, the Heaven of Brahmā's Assembly, the Heaven before Brahmā, the Great Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Minor Radiance, the Heaven of Measureless Radiance, the Heaven of Streaming Radiance, the Heaven of Minor Virtue, the Heaven of Measureless Virtue, the Heaven of Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven of Great Fruit, the Heaven of Non-Great, the Heaven of Unafflicted, the Heaven of Clear Appearance, the Heaven of Great Vision, and the Heaven of Akaniṣṭha. There they proclaim the sound of the words "impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness," and the following two verses are to be composed, caused to arise, and spread:

Enter into the Buddha's teaching,
and strive to apply yourself fully.
Like a great elephant in a bog of mud,
crush the army of the lord of death.

Whoever practises this disciplining Dharma
with thorough and careful heedfulness,
having fully abandoned the wandering of birth,
will make an end of suffering at last.

This verse too was spoken.

Then those rays of light traversed the great thousandfold world system of three thousand worlds and returned, following close behind the Blessed One. If the Blessed One wished to prophesy past karma, those rays would sink into his back. If he wished to prophesy future karma, they would sink into his front. If he wished to prophesy rebirth in the hell realms, they would sink into the sole of his foot. If he wished to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they would sink into the heel of his foot. If he wished to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost, they would sink into his big toe. If he wished to prophesy rebirth as a human, they would sink into his knee. If he wished to prophesy a kingdom of a wheel-turning king endowed with the power of might, they would sink into his left palm. If he wished to prophesy a kingdom of a wheel-turning king, they would sink into his right palm. If he wished to prophesy rebirth as a god, they would sink into his navel. If he wished to prophesy the awakening of a śrāvaka, they would sink into his mouth. If he wished to prophesy the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, they would sink into the curl of hair between his brows. If he wished to prophesy the unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, they would sink into his crown protrusion.

Thereupon those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and sank into the soles of his two feet.

Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and addressed the Blessed One in verse:

The thousand rays adorned with a variety of colors
emerged from the gate of his mouth,
and with them he illuminated all directions,
like the spreading canopy of a parasol of sunlight.

And again he spoke these verses:

Free from agitation, despondency, and pride abandoned,
the buddha who is the cause supreme of all beings' wandering,
the Victor for whom there is no cause to subdue enemies,
does not show a smile with fingers white as conch shells.

Therefore, relying on your own mind and knowing the time,
O Sage, foremost of the herd, lord of ascetics and kings of the born,
to those who have heard and who are endowed with doubt,
please, with firm words of speech and with virtue that is noble,
dispel whatever uncertainty has arisen.

As a salt mountain king stands firm and unshaking,
the buddhas who are protectors do not suddenly smile.
Since you now smile after having been so steadfast,
all these assemblies of people long to hear why.

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, it is so, it is exactly so. Ānanda, the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, hear this:

The monk Uttarayana
is free from the knot of binding, from the thorn,
and likewise liberated from obscuration,
yet today he is not free from the law of the king.

Ānanda, King Kṣudrapada, who resides in the city of Rājagraha, is surrounded by evil companions, and he has had the monk Uttarayana — who had attained arhathood — deprived of life. Because he deprived his own father, an arhat, of life, he will assuredly be reborn in the great Avīci hell."

"Venerable one, has the Venerable Uttarayana indeed attained arhathood and been deprived of life?" "Ānanda, Uttarayana has attained arhathood and been deprived of life."

Upon hearing this, the Venerable Ānanda sat weeping, with tears streaming down his face.

Then those executioners took the Venerable Uttarayana's begging bowl and

robe, and staff, and went into the city proclaiming the news aloud. They went to those two corrupt ministers and said to them: "The old king has been killed." When those two heard this, joy and supreme joy arose in them, and they went to where King Cūḍapakṣa was and said: "May Your Divinity rejoice! Now the kingdom of Your Divinity is free of thorns. The enemy of Your Divinity, whoever he was, has been slain." "Who was my enemy?" "Your Divinity, it was the old king." "How is it known that he has been killed?" The two pointed to the executioners and said: "Your Divinity, these men are the executioners, and they have slain him."

When King Cūḍapakṣa saw them, he said: "Wise ones, what power did the old king have over me?" "Your Divinity, what power did he have? Only this begging bowl, robe, and staff." When King Cūḍapakṣa saw these, he fainted and fell upon the ground. Water was sprinkled over him, and when he had revived he said: "Wise ones, what did the old king say at the time of his death?" "Your Divinity, as the old king was being deprived of life, he spoke these words:

For the sake of the kingdom you slew your father,
and thereby you have gathered great demerit.
I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa,
while you will go to the Avīci hell."

And furthermore he said these words: "You have committed two heinous acts without interval — the separation of your father from life, and the separation of the monk, the arhat, the one whose defilements are exhausted, from life. Because of these, you must dwell for a long time in the great Avīci hell, the hell of unceasing torment. Therefore turn back from evil, from evil deeds! If you do so, karma will be worn away, exhausted, and brought to its complete conclusion."

Pierced and tormented by the dart of grief, he was shaken as a blue lotus is buffeted by the wind. He summoned his two chief ministers Heruka and Bhiruka and said: "Wise ones, why did you two not restrain me from acting in that way?" The two replied: "If Your Divinity did not keep us in your sight, how could we have restrained you?" He then removed those two corrupt ministers from his presence and reinstated Heruka and Bhiruka as chief ministers. The two corrupt ministers went into hiding and secretly dug two holes in the two stūpas of the Venerable Rgyal and Skar-rgyal, placed two kittens inside, and each day fed them a piece of meat, training them with these words: "By the truth and the words of truth by which you two, Rgyal and Skar-rgyal, deceived the world with trickery and caused what was given in faith to be squandered — by that truth and those words of truth, you were born in the wretched existence of a cat. By that truth and those words of truth, eat the meat, circumambulate your own stūpas, and then enter your own holes." When those two had been well trained in this manner, the two corrupt ministers went before the queen of Uttarayana and said to her: "Your Ladyship, your son has become pale and thin, feeble, emaciated, and unable to keep his body together — why do you remain indifferent?" She replied: "Since you two yourselves caused all that to happen to him, what am I now to do?" The two said: "Your Ladyship, does the rope not fall wherever the bucket falls?" She said: "Very well, I understand that much — but if I am to keep secret his killing of his father, who will keep secret the killing of the arhat?" The two replied: "Your Ladyship, the killing of the arhat we two will keep secret." She said: "If that is so, very well." She then went before her son and said: "My son, why have you become pale, wan, thin, feeble, emaciated, and unable to keep your body together?" He replied:

"Your Ladyship, why do you too speak in such a way? How could I not become pale, wan, thin, feeble, emaciated, and unable to keep my body together? For my two corrupt ministers deceived me and led me to commit two acts without interval: the separation of my father from his life, and the separation of the fully ordained monk, the arhat whose defilements are exhausted, from his life. Because of these, I shall have to dwell for a very long time in the great hell of Avīci, the hell of unrelenting torment. How could I not become pale, wan, thin, feeble, emaciated, and unable to keep my body together?"

She replied: "My son, grant me your fearlessness, and whatever is lacking I will provide."

He said: "Mother, please speak. Tell me how things stand."

"My son, he was not your father. For I, in order to wash away the stain of my monthly impurity, took pleasure together with certain other men, and you were born of that."

He thought: "In that case, it was not killing my father," and understanding this, he said: "Mother, if that is so and there was no killing of a father, then how is the killing of the arhat to be resolved?"

She replied: "My son, I will have the learned among the wise speak to this, and they will resolve it."

Having said this, she departed. She summoned those two corrupt ministers and said: "I have already cleared away the matter of his killing his father. Now you two must also clear away the killing of the arhat."

King Crest-Topknot then commanded his ministers: "Gather together all who are learned in knowledge." The ministers gathered all the learned, and those two corrupt ministers were also assembled there.

Then King Crest-Topknot said to them: "O wise ones, I have killed an arhat. How is this to be resolved?"

At that, all the men of the royal retinue began to speak in conflicting ways. Some said: "Who ever saw His Majesty himself directly kill an arhat?" Others said: "Your Majesty, arhats are like the omniscient ones — they travel through the sky." Then those two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, why should you be troubled about this?"

He replied: "And why do you two speak in the same way — what is there to grieve about? Will you two not say that it was you yourselves who caused the arhat to be killed?"

The two said: "Your Majesty, if there are no arhats, can there be any killing of arhats?"

He said: "With my very own eyes I directly witnessed those two — Jaya and Kārtikeyajaya — performing miracles of blazing, shining, sending down rain, and emitting lightning, and then passing away into the nirvāṇa-realm that is the nirvāṇa without remainder. And yet you two say: 'If there are no arhats, can there be any killing of arhats'?"

The two replied: "Your Majesty, those two deluded the world with illusion, causing the faithful to waste their acts of giving. By that fault they were born into the miserable existence of cats, and even now they dwell each at its own stūpa — this Your Majesty can see directly for himself."

The king said to his ministers: "O wise ones, if that is so, come here and let us go to see whether it is true or not. Let a proclamation be made throughout the entire city that Jaya and Kārtikeyajaya were born as cats, that they are sitting at their own stūpas, and that they have gone before the king." When this proclamation had spread everywhere, many hundreds of thousands of living beings were seized with curiosity and followed along behind the king.

Then those two flawed ministers spoke before the king and his retinue of many hundreds of thousands of beings: "Jaya and Kārtikeyajaya, listen! By the truth, and by the power of those words of truth — the truth that you two deceived the world with trickery, squandered the gifts offered in faith, and were therefore born into the miserable existence of cats, and are now dwelling each at its own stūpa — by that truth and those words of truth, let these two cats rise, let each circumambulate its own stūpa, and let each re-enter its own den." No sooner had these words been spoken than the two cats emerged each from its own den, accepted food scraps, circumambulated their respective stūpas, and re-entered their own dens. Many hundreds of thousands of living beings witnessed this.

The two flawed ministers then said: "O king, did you see that?" The king replied: "Yes, I saw it." The two ministers said: "Your Majesty, this being so, there are no arhats in the world — it is nothing but people's flattery and empty talk."

At that moment, whatever conviction the king had previously held — that arhats do indeed exist in the world — vanished entirely. Those who had previously been without faith now acquired the view that arhats do not exist. Those who had been undecided were seized with doubt. And those who had been faithful became dejected, displeased, and filled with dismay.

Then King Śikhin reflected: "If there are no arhats in the world, why should I make alms-rounds available to the venerable great Kātyāyana with his five hundred monks, and to the nun Rimā with her five hundred nuns?" And so he cut off the alms of the monks and nuns, and the monks and nuns departed the city with the sound of a proclamation going forth. The venerable great Kātyāyana and the nun Rimā, however, looking to those who were yet to be tamed, remained right there in that place.

Some time later, when King Śikhin came back out of the city with a proclamation going before him, the venerable great Kātyāyana had entered the city for alms. Seeing the king coming, Kātyāyana thought it would not be fitting for the king to catch sight of him and feel displeasure, and so he withdrew to one side and stood there. King Śikhin saw him standing to one side. The king said to his ministers: "O wise ones, why is it that the great Kātyāyana, upon seeing me, has gone to one side and is standing there?" Following behind, two of the chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, spoke: "Your Majesty, it has occurred to the venerable great Kātyāyana in his heart that, since Your Majesty has gone off to Śakra's goddess Gaśed and Gegtsen, if he were to be seen and cause displeasure, that would not be fitting. And he also thought that the dyeing work is arduous, and it would not be fitting for the Dharma robes to be soiled with dust." The king said nothing and went on his way.

When the venerable great Kātyāyana had finished his alms-round through the city and was departing, King Śikhin went inside, and Kātyāyana likewise withdrew to one side and stood there again. King Śikhin saw him standing there once more to one side. The king then said to his ministers: "O wise ones, the first time it was the reason we know — that great Kātyāyana saw me and went to one side. What then is his reason for going to one side and standing there now?" Following behind, the two flawed ministers spoke: "Your Majesty, this one has said that he should avoid any contact with the dust of this parricide here."

Now that king was altogether undiscerning, and so when he heard those words, he was seized entirely by rage. He said to his whole retinue: "O wise ones, let each and every one among you who delights in me throw a clod of earth upon this shaven-headed ascetic." And all the throng of people threw a clod each. The king had a great army, and as each one threw a clod upon the venerable great Kātyāyana, an enormous mound of earth came to rest upon him. Yet the venerable great Kātyāyana manifested himself within it, sitting in a cross-legged posture made not of leaves, and remained there. When those clods scattered away, cowherds and cattle-herders who saw it stood around mocking. Then the two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, came following behind and arrived at that place, where the two of them asked: "O wise ones, what is this?" Those people said: "That quarrelsome, patricide king has buried the noble great Kātyāyana — who was without fault, who did no harm — under earth." The two of them, with tears streaming down their faces in the semblance of weeping, began to clear away the earth together with the cowherds and cattle-herders. The venerable great Kātyāyana then rose up, and the two prostrated at his two feet and asked: "O noble one, what is this?" He said:

It is karma — what else could come to pass?

The two then said: "O noble one, the Crest-Knot, along with all the common people — what will be the karmic maturation of their having done such an act as this?" He said: "In seven days from now, the city of Śravasti will be crushed and buried under earth. How will it unfold, O noble one?" "O pair of worthy ones, first, on the first day, a great cold wind will arise and the city of Śravasti will be stripped bare of rocks, gravel, and grass. On the second day, a rain of flowers will fall. On the third day, a rain of garments will fall. On the fourth day, a rain of silver will fall. On the fifth day, a rain of gold will fall. After that, those who live in the environs around the city of Śravasti and who have acted in accordance with karma will enter the city of Śravasti, and when they have entered, on the sixth day a rain of precious jewels will fall. On the seventh day, a rain of earth will fall." The two said: "O noble one, will we two also have a share in that karma?" "O fair-faced pair, you two have no share in that karma." "O noble one, if that is so, how shall we two depart from this city?" He said: "O fair-faced pair, have a tunnel dug from your own houses to the river, moor a boat at the house, and stay there. When the rain of precious jewels falls, load the boat with jewels and flee." The two then prostrated at his feet, entered the city of Śravasti, went before the king, and said: "Has the noble great Kātyāyana been harmed at all? Or was he truly buried under earth?" He said: "O wise pair, is he alive?" "Your Majesty, he is alive." "What did he say?" "Your Majesty, he said this: 'In seven days from now, the city of Śravasti will be crushed and buried under earth.'" "How will it unfold?" The two said: "Your Majesty, he said this: first, on the first day, a great cold wind will arise and the city of Śravasti will be stripped bare of rocks, gravel, and grass.

On the second day, a rain of flowers will fall. On the third day, a rain of garments will fall. On the fourth day, a rain of silver will fall. On the fifth day, a rain of gold will fall. After that, those dwelling in the vicinity of the city of Śrāvastī who have acted in accordance with the karma for it will enter the city of Śrāvastī, and once they have entered, on the sixth day a rain of jewels will fall. On the seventh day, a rain of earth will fall.' So they reported."

The two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, what good could come from giving alms to a brahmin and then cutting him off? Since the king gave alms to one accompanied by five hundred followers and then cut him off, leaving him buried under the earth, what else could he say other than what he has said? How could he possibly speak words of better omen than these?" King Topknot thought to himself, "That may be true." And the two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, turned their faces away, wrung their hands together, and left.

Now Heruka had a boy-child named Ngosang, and Bhiruka also had a girl-child named Ngosangchen. Heruka offered the boy Ngosang to the venerable great Kātyāyana and said: "Noble one, if there are some wholesome roots in this child, please confer the going-forth upon him. If there are none, let him be your servant." Bhiruka likewise offered the girl Ngosangchen to the nun Rimā and said: "Noble one, if there are some wholesome roots in this girl, please confer the going-forth upon her. If there are none, there is in Kauśāmbī a householder friend of mine called Gangchen — please entrust her to him." She accepted the charge.

The nun Rimā then took the girl Ngosangchen, departed from the city of Śrāvastī by her supernatural powers, entrusted the girl to the householder Gangchen in Kauśāmbī, and conveyed in full the message she had been told to deliver. The venerable great Kātyāyana remained there himself.

The two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, had a tunnel dug from their house all the way to the river, moored a boat at the riverside, and waited. In due course, on that very day, a great cold wind arose and stripped the city of Śrāvastī bare of rocks, gravel, and grass.

On the second day, a rain of flowers fell, and the two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, word has it that seven heights of hailstones have fallen north of us — yet even here this rain of flowers has fallen, so before long a rain of garments will fall." On the third day, a rain of garments fell, and the two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, this rain of garments has fallen here, so before long a rain of silver will fall." On the fourth day, a rain of silver fell, and the two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, this rain of silver has fallen here, so before long a rain of gold will fall." On the fifth day, a rain of gold fell, and the two corrupt ministers said: "Your Majesty, this rain of gold has fallen here, so before long a rain of jewels will fall." After that, those dwelling in the vicinity of Śrāvastī who had acted in accordance with the karma for it entered the city of Śrāvastī, and once they had entered, on the sixth day a rain of jewels fell. The two chief ministers, Heruka and Bhiruka, had the boat loaded with those jewels and fled.

Heruka then had a city built in another direction and named it Heruka's Fort, and it came to be known by the name Heruka's Fort.

Bhiruka likewise had a city built in another direction and named it Bhiruka's Fort, and it came to be known by the name Bhiruka's Fort, Bhiruka's Fort.

On the seventh day, a rain of earth began to fall, and a high sound and a great noise arose throughout the city of Śrāvastī. The king said: "Wise ones, what is this high sound and great noise?" The ministers said: "Your Majesty, a rain of earth has fallen." The king said: "Wise ones, if that is so, search for the two chief ministers Heruka and Bhiruka — find out where they are." When they began to search, they soon perceived that the two had fled, and they reported to the king: "Your Majesty, those two have fled and are nowhere to be found."

Then King Tuft-of-Hair himself began to flee, but the non-human beings blocked the gates. The youth Ngo Sang said: "Noble one, what is this high sound and great noise that has arisen in the city?" The venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana said: "Child, reach out the bowl through the window." He put the bowl out through the window, and it filled about halfway. The venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana thought: "There is still some domain remaining." Then when the bowl was put fully outside, it filled to the brim in an instant, and the venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana thought: "Now there is no domain left — we must go."

Then the goddess who permanently dwells in Śrāvastī went to where the venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana was, approached him, prostrated at his two feet, and said: "Noble one, I too shall come and attend upon the noble one." He accepted her offer.

The venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana said to Ngo Sang: "Child, take hold of the hem of my robe and come along." The boy took hold of the hem of the robe, and Mahā-Kātyāyana led the youth Ngo Sang and traveled through the sky above by miraculous power. The goddess who permanently dwells in Śrāvastī likewise followed after him by her own miraculous power, and the city of Śrāvastī was swallowed up by the earth.

They eventually arrived at a rocky cliff called Kharāvaṇa, and there they settled on a threshing ground. The venerable Mahā-Kātyāyana placed the youth Ngo Sang on the threshing ground and went out for alms. By the power of that goddess, grain began to multiply on that threshing ground, and a certain man who was staying there saw the youth and went up to him and said: "Ho there, child! Through your power the grain has multiplied on the threshing ground." The boy replied: "It is not through my power that the grain has multiplied on the threshing ground. It is like this: the goddess who permanently dwells in Śrāvastī has come here, and she is sitting somewhere nearby — it is through her power that the grain has multiplied on the threshing ground."

That man went toward her and, touching her two feet, said: "Goddess, I am going to my village and will return before long — in the meantime please hold these keys and this crooked key, and I ask that you give them to no one other than me." She took them, and that man then went to the rocky cliff and assembled the crowd of people dwelling at the rocky cliff and said: "Wise ones, the goddess who permanently dwells in Śrāvastī has come here and is staying at the threshing ground, and through her power the grain has multiplied on the threshing ground. I have given her the keys and the crooked key, and I said to her: 'I am going to my village and will return before long — hold these keys and crooked key and give them to no one other than me.'" Therefore he earnestly petitioned the village people that if his eldest son were invested with authority, he himself would be willing to part with his life.

"In that case, the goddess will never depart from our dwelling, and you will prosper with abundant resources, and all epidemic diseases will be pacified." With that assurance, they invested his eldest son with authority, and he himself then parted from his life.

After that, they adorned the entire place with incense and flowers, and decorated it with parasols and victory banners. Then, taking offering cakes, they went to where the goddess was, fell at her two feet, and said: "Goddess, we beseech you to remain here." She replied: "I am in attendance upon the noble great Kātyāyana, and so there is no dwelling here for me." The venerable great Kātyāyana then said: "Goddess, reflect upon from whom you received the keys and the crooked key." She turned this over in her mind, and just then, seeing that the man's time had come, she addressed the assembly of people dwelling at that place: "Wise ones, I will remain here by solemn pledge — but only if you give the same care and honour to the noble one's dwelling as you give to mine." They agreed to this, and they provided for the dwelling of the venerable great Kātyāyana in just the same manner as they provided for the dwelling of the goddess. Whatever lamps had been placed at the goddess's dwelling were taken and installed at the dwelling of the venerable great Kātyāyana as well.

Now, as the goddess was carrying a lamp and going on her way, a man sitting by a wall saw her and thought to himself: "This goddess is going to meet with the noble great Kātyāyana — she is on her way to him." She perceived his thought, and in her anger she reflected: "The assembly of people dwelling at this rocky cliff are all acting with wicked minds — they are falsely slandering the noble great Kātyāyana, who is entirely without the stench of sensual desire." So she unleashed a fear-terror upon the rocky cliff, and a great many of the people died. When the bodies of the dead were brought out, they numbered in the tens of thousands upon tens of thousands. The assembly of people dwelling at that place summoned the diviners and asked: "What has caused this?" They replied: "The goddess is enraged." The people then began to beg her for pardon, and she said: "You falsely slander the noble great Kātyāyana, who is entirely without the stench of sensual desire." They said again: "Goddess, please be patient — not one among us will fail to honour him." She replied: "I will be patient, but only by solemn pledge — if you attend upon the noble great Kātyāyana in just the same way you attend upon me, then I will be patient." They said: "We will honour the goddess with even greater distinction — please be patient." She was satisfied, and they then served the venerable great Kātyāyana with the most exceptional and distinguished honour.

The venerable great Kātyāyana accepted the rains retreat there, and he brought the blue-grey boy along, and told the goddess. The goddess said: "Noble one, please give me some token of yours, and I will make offerings to it and serve it." He gave her a begging bowl, and she fashioned it into a tent-like canopy and had it made into a stūpa, and had a festival celebrated for it. It came to be known as the Festival of the Begging Bowl, and even to this day monks who venerate stūpas offer their veneration to it.

The blue-grey boy then seized hold of the hem of the venerable great Kātyāyana's robe and hung there dangling from it as he walked, and some cowherd boys and cattle-herders saw this.

They called out loudly, "Dangling, dangling!"— and so that cry became the name by which the people of that region were known, called "the Danglers."

The venerable great Kātyāyana then went to a certain rocky cliff, and there he left the blue-grey boy at the foot of a verdant tree and went out on his alms round. At that rocky cliff it happened that the king had died without an heir, and the people of the royal court— ministers and subjects— had gathered together and were speaking: "Wise ones, who should be consecrated as king?" Some said: "Whoever is renowned for great merit and power." Others said: "But how shall we know such a person?" And others said: "Let us appoint scouts to search." They appointed scouts, and those scouts began to search in every direction. They found the boy sleeping at the foot of the verdant tree, and they began to read his marks and signs. Now as much as the shadows of the other trees fell toward the east, and shifted toward the east, and had moved to the east, they saw that the shadow of that one tree had not left the boy's body. Having seen this, they began to deliberate: "Wise ones, this boy is renowned for great merit and power— let us consecrate him as king." They woke him and said: "Boy, accept the royal kingdom." The boy said: "I do not seek the royal kingdom for myself— I am in attendance upon the noble great Kātyāyana." The venerable great Kātyāyana heard this, and he thought to himself: does this boy or does he not have the karma to become king? He looked and saw that he did, and so he said: "Son, accept the royal kingdom, but conduct it thus: rule by the Dharma." The boy agreed. They consecrated him, and they installed the blue-grey boy as king there— and from that time the kingdom of the blue-grey boy came to be called by the name "the Kingdom of the Blue-Grey."

The venerable great Kātyāyana then went to the region of Bogkā. There, the mother of the venerable great Kātyāyana had been reborn in Bogkā, and when she saw the venerable great Kātyāyana she said: "Son, it has been such a long time since I have seen you! Son, it has been such a long time since I have seen you!" And from both her breasts milk began to flow in streams. The venerable great Kātyāyana addressed her gently, calling her "Mother, mother," and she gave the venerable great Kātyāyana food to eat. Then the venerable great Kātyāyana, having fully understood her mind, her latent dispositions, her constitution, and her character, taught her the Dharma that leads to the thorough individual understanding of the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones— just as though, while she remained seated on that very seat, the twenty-towering peak of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection (the view that takes the aggregates to be a self) had been shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and the fruit of stream-entry had been made directly manifest. When she had seen the truths, she said with great feeling three times over: "What the venerable one has done for me is this: my father did not do it for me, my mother did not do it for me, the king did not do it for me, the gods did not do it for me, my ancestors of former times did not do it for me, ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins did not do it for me, friends, intimates, and the circle of kinsmen did not do it for me. He has dried up the ocean of blood and tears, freed me from the mountains of bones, closed the gates to the lower realms, opened the gates to the higher realms and to liberation, lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and placed me within the company of gods and humans." And she spoke further in verse:

What a good son should do
for a mother who has borne hardship —
that you have done for me.
My mind has turned toward the higher realms.

Having drawn me forth from the lower realms,
you strove greatly to place me
in the higher realms and in liberation.
You have performed this difficult task well.

As a merchant who finds his profit,
so I have found the higher realms.
To rely closely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitras)
is indeed a good thing.

Then the venerable Mahākātyāyana, having established that young woman in the Truths, said, "Mother, look — I have come." She replied, "My son, if that is so, give me some token of yourself, so that I may make offerings to it and venerate it." He gave her his staff, and she fashioned a stūpa from it. It was installed there, and the stūpa became known by the name "The Staff Stūpa." Even to this day, monks who bow before stūpas bow before it.

The venerable Mahākātyāyana, wishing to travel to the central country, went as far as the land of Sindhu. There, a goddess who dwelt along the northern road spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana, saying, "Noble one, give me too some token of yourself, so that I may make offerings to it and venerate it." He thought, "The Blessed One has declared that one should not carry laced sandals in the central country," and so thinking he gave her those very laced sandals. She caused them to be installed as an object of veneration, and the place became known to some as "The Sanctuary of the Sandal Lord," while others knew it as "The Foundation of the Sandal."

The venerable Mahākātyāyana eventually arrived at Śrāvastī, and the monks, seeing him, said, "Welcome, venerable one! Welcome! How was your journey — pleasant?" He replied, "Friends, the journey was in part pleasant and in part painful." The monks asked, "How was it pleasant? How was it painful?" He said, "What I did for the sake of sentient beings — that was the pleasant part. As for the painful part: King Topknot and the crowds of people dwelling in the city of Resounding Sound crushing me with their feet, and the two foremost ministers Heruka and Bhiruka fleeing in great distress — that was the painful part."

Some monks of little purpose condemned him, saying, "This one is a father-killer. He struck down the venerable Utrāyaṇa, an arhat, blameless and harmless, who had realized arhatship. What happened here is but the flower of what he has done — the fruit will come later."

The monks, filled with doubt, brought their doubt before the awakened one, the Blessed One, to have it resolved. "Blessed One, what karma did Utrāyaṇa himself perform, that he was born into a wealthy household of great riches and possessions, went forth into the Blessed One's teaching, abandoned all afflictions, directly realized arhatship, and then was killed by a sword?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, Utrāyaṇa himself had accumulated a store of karma, with conditions fully transformed, abiding like a flame, certain to ripen — and the karma that Utrāyaṇa himself had done and accumulated will not be experienced separately by anyone else. Monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done and accumulated ripens within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Actions do not perish
even across a hundred aeons.
When the conditions and the time are gathered,
they ripen as fruits
for those who bear a body.

Monks, in a time long past, when no buddhas had arisen in the world, there appeared in the world certain inferior pratyekabuddhas (solitary buddhas) — compassionate toward the poor and destitute, delighting in remote and isolated dwellings, living alone like a rhinoceros, and serving as a field of merit for the world.

At a certain place there was a cliff, and a hunter sat there. Not very far from that cliff there was a small lake that had become a resort for many deer and birds. Day after day the hunter would go there, setting out snares, traps, and numerous nets in order to catch the deer and birds, to injure them, and to torment them in ways that were contrary to their nature. And those snares, traps, and nets of his did indeed prove effective.

Then on another occasion, a solitary buddha who was wandering through the region came to that cliff. Having agreed to spend the night at a divine dwelling place there, he arose early the next morning, put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and went out to collect alms at that cliff. After going on his alms round there, he thought: "This divine dwelling is busy and frequented throughout the day. Let me take my meal in the peaceful and secluded place outside the cliff." So he came out from the cliff, saying to himself, "This is peaceful, this is peaceful," and walked toward that lake. When he arrived, he placed his alms bowl and water vessel side by side at the edge, washed both feet, rinsed both hands, drew water, gathered leaves that had fallen, sat down, performed the act of eating, rinsed both hands again, washed his mouth, and set the bowl and water vessel back in their proper places. Then, having washed both feet, he leaned against a tree and sat in cross-legged posture as a king of serpents lies in repose, his body composed, his bearing entirely serene. And that very day the hunter did not catch a single one of the deer.

The next morning the hunter rose early and went toward that lake. He began to search through the snares, traps, and nets, but he did not find a single deer. He thought: "If my snares, traps, and nets are indeed effective, what is the reason that today not a single deer was caught?" So he began to walk around the shore of the lake, and he caught sight of a human footprint. He followed the tracks and came upon the solitary buddha sitting there in serene composure. The hunter thought: "These renunciants whose minds are calm take delight in places such as this. If I do not kill him, he will surely destroy my livelihood. I must kill him by any means." Thus, filled with a merciless mind and utterly indifferent to the next world, he drew a poisoned arrow, nocked it all the way to the ear of his bow, and shot it into the vital spot of that solitary buddha.

The great-souled solitary buddha thought: "This hunter, afflicted and extremely wretched as he is, will come to ruin — that would be wrong. Let me grant him a straight departure by hand." And with that, like a king of swans spreading his wings, he rose up into the sky above, and began to perform miraculous displays: blazing with fire, radiating brilliant light, raining down water, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary worldly people are quick to fix their minds on miracles. And so the hunter fell prostrate at the feet of that solitary buddha, as though a great tree had been cut down at its roots, and said: "O true field of merit, please descend! Please descend!"

"Please lead me, sunk in the swamp of affliction, up from my very roots."

Out of compassion for that hunter, the solitary buddha descended from the sky above to where he stood. Then the hunter, having cleaned the wound and carefully bound it up, spoke: "Noble one, please sit down and rest. If you would be so good as to accept treatment with a golden salve, I will provide that too." The solitary buddha thought to himself: "What there was to be obtained through this body of pus and filth — I have already obtained it. Therefore, let me now enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder." And so, right there before that very hunter, he rose up again into the midst of the sky, displayed various miraculous feats, and then passed into nirvāṇa — the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

Now the hunter was a man of wealth, and so he gathered all kinds of fragrant wood, built a pyre of the body, burned it, quenched the remains with milk, placed the bones in a golden vase, and had a bodily stūpa erected at a crossroads on the great highway. He raised canopies, victory banners, and pennants, and made offerings of perfume, garlands, incense, powders, and cymbals. Then he prostrated at the feet of the stūpa and made this aspiration prayer: "Whatever unwholesome karma I have created by harming so excellent a field of merit as this — may it not ripen upon me in accordance with that deed. And through the root of virtue that is this offering I have made, may I be born wealthy, with abundant riches and great prosperity; and may I attain such qualities as these: pleasing a Teacher far more excellent than this one, and never causing him distress."

Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, the person who was the hunter at that time and on that occasion was the monk Uttarayāṇa. Through the karmic maturation of the deed of wounding a solitary buddha with a poisoned arrow, he was tormented for an aeon in the great hell Avīci without respite; and from the remainder of that same karma, for five hundred lifetimes in that very same lake he was reborn as a wild deer, struck again and again by poisoned arrows, dying each time his appointed hour came. And even now, though he has attained arhatship, he passes into nirvāṇa pierced through by a weapon. But through the offering he made and the aspiration he set, he has now been born wealthy, with abundant riches and great prosperity; he went forth into my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhatship; and by this he pleased me — the Teacher who surpasses even ten billion solitary buddhas — and never caused me distress.

"Monks, thus the maturation of deeds that are purely dark is purely dark; the maturation of deeds that are purely bright is purely bright; and the maturation of deeds that are mixed is mixed.

"Therefore, monks, abandon deeds that are purely dark and those that are mixed, and strive after deeds that are purely bright. Monks, train yourselves accordingly."

Again, the monks fell into doubt, and asked the Blessed One — the Buddha who cuts through all doubt — their question: "Venerable one, what deed did King Topknot (Śikhin) and the crowd of citizens dwelling in the city of Resounding Noise and the Venerable Mahākātyāyana commit, so that Mahākātyāyana was overpowered by the poison of jealousy? And what did Heruka and Bhiruka, the two chief ministers, do that caused them to flee?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, those very ones found a convergence of karma, a full transformation of conditions, and remained close by, like light itself —

those deeds, being inescapably bound to arise, were performed and accumulated by those very ones themselves — and no one other than they will experience the separate ripening of karma performed and accumulated. Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the outer element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources. As it is said in verse:

Even were a hundred aeons to pass,
karma once gathered does not perish —
when conditions and the time converge,
it ripens as fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago in the past, in a certain rocky mountain valley, there lived a householder. He took a wife from his own station in life, and with her he played, rejoiced, and made merry. While they were playing, rejoicing, and making merry, a son was born to them. Again, while they were playing, rejoicing, and making merry, a daughter was born to them; and these two children they raised and nurtured until they grew up. Now, when girls the same age as that daughter would receive suitors, no suitor ever came for her. At a time when no buddhas had appeared in the world, certain pratyekabuddhas — poor and destitute, compassionate toward the wretched and lowly, delighting in forest hermitages at the world's edge, solitary as rhinoceroses, worthy objects of offering for the world — had arisen in that world. On one occasion, as a pratyekabuddha was wandering through the district, he came to that rocky mountain valley. The daughter, sweeping the house, tossed the dustcloth from atop a dust heap, and it struck the head of that pratyekabuddha as he walked on his alms round. The girl saw that it had struck him, yet not even a thought of remorse arose in her mind. Then, as fate would have it, that very same day a suitor came for her, and her brother asked her about it: "Today you received a suitor — what did you do to bring this about?" She replied: "Today I threw a dustcloth at a renunciant." He broke into a smile. The girl then spread the word to other girls, and they in turn spread it to still others, until there arose among the girls of the world this wicked and pernicious view — that whichever girl had no suitors coming for her should throw a dustcloth at a pratyekabuddha, and a suitor would come to her. Such was the nature of that sinful view that arose. Because the great accomplished ones fear being disrespected, that pratyekabuddha departed from that rocky valley. Then those girls began throwing dustcloths at seers endowed with the five higher knowledges, and when those too departed, they began throwing them at their own parents. Now, there were two virtuous householders living in that rocky valley, and these two said: "Wise ones, we must put a stop to this growth of ignoble conduct!" And the two of them restrained and put an end to it.

Monks, at that time and in that era, the girl who threw the dustcloth at the pratyekabuddha — she is none other than this very King Topknot (Śikhin). The crowd of people who were living in that rocky valley — they are these very crowds of people who dwell in the city of Resounding Noise; and through the karmic ripening of their having thrown dustcloths at the pratyekabuddha, the seers, and their parents, they were crushed to the ground. The two householders who put a stop to it — they are the two chief ministers Heruka and Bhiruka; through the ripening of that karma they were caused to flee. The girl's brother, who smiled at the news —

— he is none other than the great monk Kātyāyana himself. Through the karmic ripening of that smile he was covered with flesh. Had the great monk Kātyāyana not understood such a gathering of qualities as this, he too would have been weighed down by flesh and made to suffer in an unseemly way.

Monks, it is thus: the karmic ripening of actions that are entirely dark is entirely dark; the karmic ripening of actions that are entirely bright is entirely bright; and the karmic ripening of actions that are mixed is mixed.

Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are entirely dark and mixed, and strive instead toward actions that are entirely bright. Monks, train yourselves accordingly.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (Anāthapiṇḍada, "feeder of the destitute," the great lay patron who purchased the grove).

In the city of Kauśāmbī there lived a householder named Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin — wealthy, possessed of great riches and abundant resources. His house stood near the palace of King Śarpa, and each morning he would rise before dawn and go to inspect the full extent of his affairs. Now, because he was resonant with gold, King Śarpa knew from the resonance of that sound that the man had one hundred thousand pieces of gold stored away.

Some time later, King Śarpa was sitting in his place of counsel and said to his ministers: "Wise ones, the householder Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin rises before dawn each and every morning and goes himself to inspect his own affairs in full. It is said that he has one hundred thousand pieces of gold stored away — so why does he trouble himself with labor?" The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, how could he possibly have one hundred thousand pieces of gold stored away? If he did have one hundred thousand pieces of gold stored away, why would he trouble himself with labor?" The king said: "Wise ones, if you do not believe it, summon the householder Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin and ask him." They summoned the householder Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin, and the king asked him: "Householder, do you have one hundred thousand pieces of gold stored away?" He replied: "Your Majesty, yes. If it please you, please accept them." "Householder, I am not seeking gold for my own purposes — I merely asked whether you had it or not." He replied: "Your Majesty, it is exactly as Your Majesty already knows." The king said: "Householder, because you are resonant with gold, I knew it from the resonance of your sound."

Because the king had come to know it from his resonance, the householder Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin thenceforth came to be known as the householder Ghoṣavān — "the resonant one."

The king then said to him: "Householder, since you have become wealthy, why do you yourself take on supervision and engage in the full work of your affairs?" He replied: "Your Majesty, if I did not myself take on supervision and attend to my own affairs in full, my resources would neither grow and expand nor become abundant — and Your Majesty would not come to know me as one resonant with gold." The king asked: "Householder, why do you not travel by elephant or horse?" He replied: "Your Majesty, I am a man of the household, a commoner — it would not be fitting for someone like me to travel by elephant or horse."

The king thought to himself: "Could a person like this be put to work in the affairs of the kingdom? I know he should be made a minister, and none other." And so he said: "Householder, become a minister — I will put you to work in the affairs of the kingdom together with the others." He replied: "Your Majesty, such a command is not fitting. I am a commoner, and it is proper that I follow up on the work of my own fields and affairs — it is not fitting that I become a minister." The king understood that, pressed in this way again and again, he would surely be forced to accept sooner or later; and so, pressing him firmly, he did indeed make him accept.

Then the king made him a minister, and the householder Gāṅgeya began to carry out the affairs and duties of the king with Dharma and reason. He overshadowed all the other ministers, and they, seized with jealousy and discontentment, gathered together and said: "Wise ones, now that we have been overshadowed by the householder Gāṅgeya in this way, what is to be done about him?" Some of them said: "Why is there any need to do anything? So long as he has not yet taken firm and permanent root, we should have the king cut him down with punishment." Others said: "Not by wrongdoing — let it be done in that way." And so they all gathered and went before the king and said: "Your Majesty — who are you, Sire?" He replied: "What cause do you have for doubt? I am the king — who else would I be?" They said: "Your Majesty, Gāṅgeya is the king — you are not. If he so desires, he will have Your Majesty deposed, crown himself, and make himself the sovereign lord of the royal realm." The king said: "Wise ones, why would things become like that? He is one who places Dharma foremost — how could he act in such a way?" They replied: "We will make it plain before Your Majesty's own eyes." And so at a certain later time, when the householder Gāṅgeya was surrounded by plaintiffs and defendants seeking livelihood from the king, and had entered the royal palace — the royal palace being full to the brim with crowds of people — and after he had performed the affairs and duties of the king and came back out of the royal palace, and the royal attendants who had been standing in front also came out together with him so that the king sat without his retinue, those ministers then said to the king: "Your Majesty, do you see? What we submitted to you is precisely this: if he so desires, he will have Your Majesty deposed, crown himself, and make himself the sovereign lord of the royal realm."

The king thought to himself: "For now, this must be examined." And so he began to observe him in his coming and going. Now at a certain time a caravan leader drove a horse-train along the northern road to Kauśāmbī, and the king instructed Gāṅgeya: "Purchase horses for a hundred thousand in gold." He purchased the horses for a hundred thousand in gold. Then the king instructed Gāṅgeya: "Give half of the hundred thousand and say these words: 'I have already paid the full hundred thousand.'" He replied: "Your Majesty, that is not proper. If this were done, henceforth no one who trades in horses or any other merchant would ever come here again. Therefore, let Your Majesty give half of the hundred thousand from the royal treasury, and I will give the other half." The king said: "Householder, if you speak those same words of mine, what is wrong with that?" He replied: "Your Majesty, I would not endure bringing about suffering in many lifetimes for the sake of the suffering of a single life." Even when the king spoke to him three times, he could not be moved. Then the king said to the ministers: "Wise ones, what is the penalty for one who three times defies the command of a king consecrated with royal unction?" The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, the penalty for that is execution." He said: "Wise ones, if that is so, I hereby dismiss the householder Gāṅgeya." The ministers instructed the executioners: "Wise ones, His Majesty has commanded — execute the householder Gāṅgeya." But the king secretly instructed those same executioners: "You are not to kill the householder Gāṅgeya — you are to terrorize him in the following manner."

They placed a garland of karavīra flowers around his neck and led him through the middle of the city toward the place of execution. His kinsmen came forward and said to him: "Householder, do as the king has commanded, and do not cause yourself to be killed." He replied: "Have I broken any righteous command of the king? If the king kills someone who is innocent and has done no wrong, then let him kill — I cannot bring about suffering across many lifetimes for the sake of one life's suffering." The executioners led him to the place of execution and said: "Householder, do as the king has commanded and do not cause yourself to be killed." He replied: "Have I broken any righteous command of the king? If the king kills someone who is innocent and has done no wrong, then let him kill — I cannot bring about suffering across many lifetimes for the sake of one life's suffering." The executioners then brought him before the king and said: "Your Majesty, the householder Gāṅgeya speaks thus." The king said: "Householder, I have no desire to kill you — I wished only to test you in this way." He replied: "If it was Your Majesty's intention to test me, and you have placed me in such a situation, then had I failed the test, what would have become of me? Your Majesty, if you are pleased with me, please grant me leave to give gifts and to make merit." The king said: "Householder, if that is so, you have my leave — give gifts as generously as you please and make merit." Then the householder Gāṅgeya had a house of giving built, but appointed no steward to oversee its distribution, and announced: "Wise friends, if there should come here any ascetic (śramaṇa) or brahmin or anyone else who bears signs and marks not seen before and who is of distinguished bearing, inform me of it."

Now it came to pass that some five hundred sages were traveling through the central region, having come from the south. As they moved along the road one by one, they entered a forest path and went inside a grove, where their water ran out and, being without water, tormented by thirst, they began to wander back and forth along that forest path. As they wandered to and fro, at no great distance they saw a verdant blue-green direction where a flourishing tree stood, and some of them said: "Wise friends, in that blue-green direction there appears to be a flourishing tree — let us go there, for there is likely water. Come, let us proceed." The others said: "Good, let us do so." They set off, and when presently they saw there was no water, they began to make supplication: "Wise friends — whatever god (deva), nāga (nāga), yakṣa (yakṣa), garuḍa, gandharva, human being, or great serpent dwells in this place and in this tree — give water to us five hundred sages who are tormented by thirst."

Presently, from that very tree there emerged a figure adorned with every kind of ornament, holding a golden vessel brimming with water. The sages cupped their hands and received it and began to drink. When they tasted it, the water was possessed of eight qualities: it was cool, sweet, light, soft, clear, free of bad odor, harmless to the throat when drunk, and soothing to the stomach once drunk. When they had drunk their fill, they filled their vessels, offered words of blessing, rose up, and departed. Then a thought arose among them: "Wise friends, having witnessed such a marvel as this, we have failed to ask who you are and by what karma you came to be born here — that is a failing on our part. Let us go back and ask." So all of them gathered together, turned back, and stood before that tree and said: "O tree — whether you are a god, a nāga, a yakṣa, a garuḍa,

a gandharva, a kinnara, or a great serpent dwelling here — you who have satisfied us as we traveled the path through this desolate wilderness, afflicted, distressed, suffering, and brought to the verge of death, with water possessing the eight qualities — tell us who you are and by what karma you were born here."

Then, just as words arose from that tree, it said: "Wise friends, the people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to convince, so how should I speak when no one will believe who I am or by what karma I was born here?"

The sages said: "Friends, how could we not believe what we see directly before our eyes? Speak without hesitation."

It said: "Wise friends, if that is so, then listen. I will speak of who I am and by what karma I was born here. In the land of Kośala, in the city called Śrāvastī, there lived a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada. I dwelt at the gate of his house as a doorkeeper. Because he gave food to the destitute, beggars who came from various distant lands would arrive repeatedly and ask me which house was the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. I would extend my right hand and say to them, 'This here is the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.' I then saw how those people would depart with their hands full, their vessels full, having obtained wealth and gained what they sought. Seeing this, it produced in me the most intense joy. It is by that karma that I was born among the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings, and I dwell in this tree. That is why my right hand is exceedingly radiant, luminous, and resplendent."

They praised him with words of blessing and departed.

After some time, when they had gone to another region, their food and drink ran out. Tormented by hunger and thirst, they began to search everywhere. Then, not very far away at all, a great tree appeared with lush, gleaming green leaves. They said: "Wise friends, a great tree with lush, gleaming green leaves has appeared. In the past too it was from just such a tree that we came here drawn by the vessel of water. Perhaps a little of our need will be met." So they went there and began to make a request: "Wise friends — whatever god, nāga, yakṣa, garuḍa, gandharva, kinnara, or great serpent dwells in this land and in this tree — give food and drink to us, five hundred sages who are tormented by hunger and tormented by thirst."

Just then words arose from that tree: "Wise friends, not far from here there is a small pond, and beside it stands a tree. At the foot of that tree sits a full clay pot filled with cooked rice. Eat and drink from it and take away as much food and drink as you desire."

They went there, and they found a pond made beautiful by geese, kāraṇḍava ducks, and cranes. Beside it stood a tree, and at its foot they saw a full pot of cooked rice along with various cooked vegetables. They bathed there, ate, drank water, filled their round vessels with water, took away as much food and drink as they wished, spoke words of blessing, and departed.

Then a thought arose among them: "Wise friends, having witnessed such a marvel and yet failing to ask who you are and by what karma you were born here — that is a failing on our part. Let us go back and ask." So all of them gathered together, turned back, and stood before that tree and said:

"Whatever god, nāga, yakṣa, garuḍa, gandharva, human, or great serpent dwells in this tree — it is you who, when we were harmed, exhausted, and miserable on the road through the wilderness, on the verge of death, satisfied us with water possessed of eight qualities and with food. Tell us who you are and by what karma you were born here."

Thereupon a voice arose from that tree: "Wise friends, the people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to convince. Were I to tell you who I am and by what karma I was born here, you would not believe me. What then would be the use of speaking?"

The sages replied, "But we perceived all this with our own eyes — how could we not believe? Speak without hesitation."

It said: "Wise friends, if that is so, then listen, and I will tell you who I am and by what karma I was born here.

In the land of Kośala there was a city called Śrāvastī, and in it there lived a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who gave food to the destitute. On a rocky crag there lived a brahmin who had fallen into poverty. He thought: 'In Śrāvastī there is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, who gives food to the destitute. If I go to him, something may come of it.' So he went to him.

Now the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was wishing to offer a meal to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and had gone to the Jeta Grove for that purpose. The brahmin saw him there and said: 'Householder, invite me as a guest for food.' The householder replied: 'Brahmin, come along — let us go to the Jeta Grove, and eat there.' So the brahmin went with him.

As they were on their way, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada found a pot of yogurt on the road, and gave it to the brahmin, saying: 'Brahmin, offer this pot of yogurt to the Saṅgha.' Anāthapiṇḍada then satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent food, and the brahmin too offered that pot of yogurt to the Saṅgha.

After the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha had taken their midday meal, Anāthapiṇḍada began distributing food to the laypeople. To the other laypeople he gave excellent food, but to that brahmin he gave poor food. The brahmin said to him: 'Householder, those who have gone forth have properly undertaken the trainings — it is fitting to give excellent food to them first. But we laypeople appear not to have properly undertaken the trainings. Why then do you give excellent food to the other laypeople and poor food to me?'

Anāthapiṇḍada replied: 'Brahmin, these laypeople have also properly undertaken the trainings — they have taken the restoration ceremony with its eight limbs.'

The brahmin said: 'Householder, if I too take the restoration ceremony with its eight limbs, will you then give me excellent food as well?'

Anāthapiṇḍada said: 'I will.' So the brahmin took the restoration ceremony with its eight limbs.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada satisfied him with excellent food. After eating, the brahmin departed. Anāthapiṇḍada said: 'Brahmin, wait a moment — there will be water to drink.' He drank the water and left.

By the time the sun had set, he was not very far from Śrāvastī, at a rocky crag, where he took up lodging in a brahmin's house. That brahmin said to him: 'Brahmin, eat some food.' He replied: 'I will not eat food.' The other brahmin said:"

'Why not?' He replied: 'I have taken the restoration ceremony with its eight limbs from the ascetic Gautama.' The other brahmin said to him: 'Brahmin, if you will eat just a little, that would be fine. But if you will not eat, you may not remain in my house.' So he ate at the wrong time and the restoration ceremony was broken.

Now, the brahmin who had been staying at the rocky crag, who had taken the eight-limbed restoration ceremony and broken it — that is myself. Having taken the eight-limbed restoration ceremony and not kept it in its entirety, I could have been reborn among the gods of the Thirty-Three. But because I took the eight-limbed restoration ceremony and then ate at the wrong time, thereby breaking the restoration ceremony, I was instead reborn among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings, and I now dwell in this very tree. That is why the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings know me as the divine son Broken-Restoration, great in miraculous powers and great in might.

End of the seventy-third bundle of the Vinaya Vibhaṅga.

Those sages were utterly astonished and said: 'O wise ones, we sages have remained in ascetic conduct until this very time and do not know what the fruit of it will be. Yet this divine son, Broken-Restoration, while he was still a brahmin, took the eight-limbed restoration ceremony, and even though he broke it, he was reborn among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings. Let us too go to the place where he took the eight-limbed restoration ceremony.' Having resolved thus, they set out from Śrāvastī and eventually arrived in stages at Kauśāmbī. The people who served as attendants at the almsgiving of the householder Gāndika saw them and went to report to the householder Gāndika, saying: 'Householder, you had instructed us that if we saw anyone with signs and features not seen before we should inform you.' And so they had arrived and were standing at the gate. He said: 'Let them in.' When they were let in and the householder Gāndika saw them, he asked: 'O wise ones, where have you come from?' They said: 'Householder, from the southern road.' He said: 'O wise ones, what marvels have you seen or heard along the southern road?' They said: 'Householder, let alone the other marvels we have previously seen and heard — just listen and we shall tell you the marvels we have seen and heard most recently.' He said: 'O wise ones, speak, and I shall listen to these marvels.' They then related to the householder Gāndika in full detail everything that had happened, and when the householder Gāndika heard it he was utterly astonished. He gave them food and said: 'O wise ones, where are you going?' They said: 'Householder, we are going to Śrāvastī.' 'O wise ones, what is there?' 'Householder, there is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, upon whom the divine son Broken-Restoration relied when he took the eight-limbed restoration ceremony.' He said: 'O wise ones, if that is so, then he is a friend I have not yet met. Please spend the rains retreat here this very night, and when the rains retreat is over, I will travel together with you.' They stayed there for the rains retreat, and when the rains retreat was over, they set out for Śrāvastī. The householder Gāndika said to the lord of the eastern region, Bhadra the king of fragrant earth: 'Your Majesty, I have some small business to attend to in Śrāvastī. If Your Majesty permits, I shall go there.' The king said: 'Householder, if that is the case, go, accomplish your aim, and return quickly.'

With the king's permission, he departed together with those five hundred seers, and traveling by stages they arrived at Śrāvastī and took up residence in a pleasure grove. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the householder Gāndika had arrived and was residing in a pleasure grove. Having heard this, he thought to himself: 'It would not be in keeping with my character to have the householder Gāndika lodge here without my knowledge. I shall receive him with great honor.' And so he received him with great honor, eased the fatigue of travel, and gave him food.

Then, when the seers had arrived, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada greeted them with the customary words of welcome — "Well come!" — and said: 'Wise ones, where have you come from, and what brings you here?' They replied: 'Householder, give to us as well what you gave to the divine youth at the restoration ceremony.' He said: 'Wise ones, I do not recall. Householder, we shall remind you.' 'Wise ones, very well.' After they had reminded him, he said: 'Wise ones, shall you receive it from me, or from the Blessed One?' 'Householder, from whom did you yourself receive it?' 'Wise ones, from the Blessed One.' 'Householder, if that is so, then we too shall receive it from that very same source.' 'Wise ones, excellent — do so.' And with that he led them to where the Blessed One was.

At that time the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍada coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the monks: 'Monks, do you see the householder Anāthapiṇḍada coming from afar?' 'Venerable One, we do.' 'Monks, this householder Anāthapiṇḍada comes accompanied by a birth, and among the births of a Tathāgata, there is none other quite like the birth of one who is to be tamed in this way.'

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, together with his retinue of five hundred seers, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One in these words: 'Venerable One, these five hundred seers wish to receive from the Blessed One the restoration ceremony endowed with eight branches. For that purpose, may the Blessed One teach the Dharma in such a way that they will take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and will come to receive the status of lay practitioners.'

Then the Blessed One, having fully understood the aspirations, latent dispositions, elements, and natures of those five hundred seers, taught the Dharma in such a way that, upon hearing it, those five hundred seers directly realized the fruit of non-return by individually and correctly comprehending the Four Noble Truths.

Having seen the truths, they touched the Blessed One's two feet and implored him: 'Venerable One, we wish to go forth and receive full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, to attain the status of monks and to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One.' The Blessed One conferred the going forth upon them with the words "Come, monks," and then declared: "Come, monks — practice the holy life!" And at the very moment of the Blessed One's words, their heads became shaved, they were wearing stitched robes, there appeared on them just seven days' growth of hair and beard, their hands were holding begging bowls, and they were accompanied by carrying-vessels and water-pots —

and they abided in a manner befitting monks who had received full ordination a hundred years before.

Again it was said in verse:

When the Tathāgata spoke the words "Come, monks,"
their bodies, wearing stitched robes with shaven heads,
were in that very instant stilled in their faculties,
and by the Buddha's intention their forms were clothed.

The Blessed One then gave them instruction, and through their enthusiasm, effort, and striving, they abandoned all mental afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As arhats freed from attachment throughout the three realms, with minds equal toward clay and gold, equanimous as space and as the palm of a hand, their wisdom had split open the door-panel of the cave of existence as though it were sandalwood placed there — and they had attained knowledge, higher knowledge, and individual perfect understanding. They turned their backs on continued existence, on gain born of desire, and on honor. They became worthy of veneration, praise, and direct proclamation by the gods of the faculties and of the lesser faculties.

Then the householder Dāṅgcan went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed the householder Dāṅgcan thoroughly with a Dharma discourse befitting the occasion, leading him to take it up correctly, praising him correctly, and gladdening him completely. And what was that Dharma discourse befitting the occasion, as given formerly by the blessed buddhas — it was this: the discourse on generosity, the discourse on ethical conduct, the discourse on higher realms, the faults in savoring the objects of desire, defilement and purification, renunciation and the benefit of complete seclusion — and he taught extensively the factors concordant with the side of purification.

When the Blessed One saw that Dāṅgcan's mind was pleased, his mind at ease, his mind joyful, his mind free of obscuration, and that he was endowed with the fortune and capacity to know the teaching of supreme quality, then the blessed buddhas taught what is the teaching of supreme quality, namely: he taught extensively the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones — suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth free of any stain, when dipped in dye, takes the color excellently — so too the householder Dāṅgcan, while seated on that very seat, directly realized the Four Noble Truths: suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path.

Then the householder Dāṅgcan, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, reached the depth of the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, crossed beyond uncertainty, not relying on another in the Teacher's teaching, not led by others, having attained fearlessness with regard to phenomena — rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms, and bowed. He then addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Venerable One, I have entered the stream. Venerable One, I have entered the stream. Venerable One, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks — may I be accepted as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I take refuge with sincere and wholehearted faith."

The Blessed One then said to the householder Dāṅgcan: "Householder, what is your name?"

"Venerable One, my name is Nordaṅ. The Eastern King raised me up from the rank of Dāṅgcan, and for that reason people call me 'Householder Dāṅgcan.'"

"Blessed One, please proceed to Kauśāmbī. For as long as I live, I will serve the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks with food, alms-round provisions, lodging, medicine for illness, and all medicinal requisites."

"Householder, is there a monastery in Kauśāmbī?"

"Venerable One, there is none."

"Householder, the monks intend to travel to, journey to, and dwell wherever there is a monastery."

"Blessed One, please proceed there. I will ensure that a monastery is established in Kauśāmbī and that the monks will travel, come, and dwell there. I will see to it."

The Blessed One remained silent toward the householder Dāṅgcan, and by that silence gave his consent. The householder Dāṅgcan understood from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given. He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching his head to the ground, and withdrew from the Blessed One's presence. He completed and accomplished all the affairs and business that needed to be done in Śrāvastī, and then returned to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him in these words: "Blessed One, please grant me a companion monk, so that together with him I may build a monastery for the Blessed One."

The Blessed One considered which monk would be the one to guide the householder Dāṅgcan with his retinue and the assembled people of Kauśāmbī, and he saw that they were to be guided by the venerable Mahākudraka. The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Mahākudraka: "Kudraka, attend to the householder Dāṅgcan with his retinue and to the assembled people dwelling in Kauśāmbī." The venerable Mahākudraka accepted this charge from the Blessed One in silence.

That very night passed, and in the early morning the venerable Mahākudraka dressed, took up his bowl and robes, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having made the alms round through Śrāvastī and taken his meal, he returned from the final round of alms, put away his sitting mat as was his custom of use, took up his bowl and robes, and set out in the company of the householder Dāṅgcan. Turning in the direction of Kauśāmbī, he traveled stage by stage along the way and in due course arrived at Kauśāmbī.

Now the householder Dāṅgcan, even before entering Kauśāmbī, went from park to park, from pleasure grove to pleasure grove, from grove to grove and to outlying areas, searching for a suitable site on which to build a monastery for the Blessed One — one neither too far from nor too near to Kauśāmbī, quiet and without commotion by day, with little noise and little murmuring by night, and with few mosquitoes, insects, wind, sun, and contact with venomous snakes. Searching thus, the householder Dāṅgcan saw that his own pleasure garden, situated neither too far from nor too near to Kauśāmbī, quiet and without commotion by day, with little noise and little murmuring by night, and with few mosquitoes, insects, wind, sun, and contact with venomous snakes, was exactly such a place. Having seen this, he thought to himself: "This site is excellent — I will have a monastery built here for the Blessed One."

Then the householder Dāṅgcan and the venerable Mahākudūṣin had a monastery built in that pleasure garden for the Blessed One — a monastery furnished with lofty entrance porticos, with windows, with circular windows, and adorned with balustrades.

When the monastery had been built and was complete, the householder Dāṅgcan said to the venerable Mahākudūṣin: "Noble one, what is the measure of the resting stages that the Blessed One requires along the road as he travels?"

"Householder, it is like that of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin)."

"Noble one, and what is the measure for a wheel-turning king?"

"Householder, the resting stages of a wheel-turning king as he travels along the road are ten leagues apart."
