The householder Dāṅgcan then had resting places prepared every ten leagues, and sent a messenger into the presence of the Blessed One with this request: that the Blessed One travel to Kauśāmbī, and that he, Dāṅgcan, would attend upon the Blessed One together with the community of monks with robes, alms-food, lodging, articles for the sick, and medicinal requisites for as long as they lived.

The messenger went before the Blessed One and conveyed this request. The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'The Blessed One will travel through the countryside on an excursion. Whoever among you wishes to travel through the countryside on an excursion together with the Tathāgata, let them take up their robes.'"

The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One and accepted his command with the words "As you instruct, reverend one," announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One will travel through the countryside on an excursion. Whoever among you wishes to travel through the countryside on an excursion together with the Tathāgata, let them take up their robes."

Then the Blessed One — tamed, surrounded by a retinue that was tamed; peaceful, surrounded by a retinue that was peaceful; liberated, surrounded by a retinue that was liberated; at ease, surrounded by a retinue that was at ease; subdued, surrounded by a retinue that was subdued; arhats, surrounded by a retinue of arhats; free from attachment, surrounded by a retinue free from attachment; resplendent, surrounded by a retinue that was resplendent — set out.

He was surrounded by a herd of bulls as a supreme stallion is surrounded by his herd. He was surrounded by a company of young elephants as a great bull elephant is. He was surrounded by a company of fanged beasts as a lion is. He was surrounded by a flock of geese as the king of geese is. He was surrounded by a company of birds as the garuḍa is. He was surrounded by a company of disciples as a brahmin is. He was surrounded by a company of the sick as a skilled physician is. He was surrounded by companies of troops as a hero is. He was surrounded by those who had entered the path as a guide is. He was surrounded by a company of merchants as a caravan leader is. He was surrounded by a company of followers as a merchant chieftain is. He was surrounded by a company of ministers as a king of a fortress is. He was surrounded by a company of a thousand princes as a wheel-turning king is. He was surrounded by a company of lunar mansions as the moon is. He was surrounded by a company of a thousand rays as the sun is. He was surrounded by a company of gandharvas as Dhṛtarāṣṭra (the Guardian of the Region) is. He was surrounded by a company of kinnaras as a noble being is. He was surrounded by a company of nāgas as Virūpākṣa (the Ill-eyed, lord of nāgas) is. He was surrounded by a company of yakṣas as Vaiśravaṇa (the Wealth-giver) is. He was surrounded by a company of asuras as Vemacitrin is. He was surrounded by a company of the thirty-three gods as Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) is. He was surrounded by a company of the Brahma heaven as Brahmā is.

His sense faculties were supremely tamed; his conduct and his behavior were undisturbed.

Serene as an ocean of water, laden with moisture like a cloud, free from pride like the king of elephants, beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being, his body made resplendent by the eighty minor marks, embellished by a radiance extending a fathom around his form, possessed of a light surpassing that of a thousand suns, excellent in every way like a moving mountain of precious jewels, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three unshared foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion — he was omniscient.

He was accompanied by the great śrāvakas: Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāma, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Nandaka, and others, along with a great Saṅgha of many monks. Wandering through Kauśāmbī, he traveled on in stages and eventually arrived at Kauśāmbī. Thereafter the householder Ghoṣila offered that monastery with all its furnishings to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. And so the elders also appended to the sūtra the statement: "The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the pleasure grove of Ghoṣila." The householder Ghoṣila, having offered the monastery to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, arose with joy and supreme delight, and went home.

Then the Venerable Mahā-Kalpika went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahā-Kalpika addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Reverend One, what are the qualities such that a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance?"

The Blessed One replied: "Worthy of prompting indeed! These seven promptings are the qualities such that a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance. What are the seven?

"The first prompting by which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance: it is this prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith offers a pleasure grove to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.

"The second prompting by which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance: it is this prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith has a monastery built in that very pleasure grove.

"Yet another prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith —"

a daughter of good family with faith offers to that very monastery furnishings such as these: thrones, small seats, cushioned inner-curtained seats, pillows, mattresses, and round cushions — it is this third prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down, continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance.

"Yet another prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith offers to that very monastery offerings perpetually suited to the needs of the resident community — it is this fourth prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down, continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance.

"Yet another prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith gives gifts to those who arrive suddenly and to those setting out on a journey — it is this fifth prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down, continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance.

"Yet another prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith gives gifts to the sick and to those who care for the sick — it is this sixth prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down, continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance.

"Yet another prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — at such times as wind has arisen, or bad weather has come, or rain has fallen, or hail has fallen, whichever of these it may be, when wind arises, bad weather comes, rain falls, or hail falls — brings to the Saṅgha cooked grains, sour foods, or hot drinks, thinking: 'By this, may these noble ones not have their bodies drenched, may their Dharma robes not get soaked, and may they come to experience bodily ease and comfort' — it is this seventh prompting, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down, continually and without interruption increases merit and only merit, produces merit and only merit, and whereby a meritorious act grounded in material things bears very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great abundance.

"This prompting is such that a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith who possesses these seven bases of meritorious acts grounded in material things — the merit, or the fruit of merit, or the karmic maturation of that fruit of merit — cannot be measured by saying 'it is only this much.' Because the merit is so vast, it falls under the designation 'a great mass of merit.' This prompting is like the following example: where the five great rivers — the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarayū, the Aciravatī, and the Mahī — flow together without distinction, one could not measure the water, or bucketfuls of water, or —

hundreds of jars of water, or thousands of jars of water, or one hundred thousand jars of water — saying "there is only this much water" — one could not measure the water. In just the same way, the merit, the fruit of merit, or the karmic maturation of that fruit of merit belonging to a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith who possesses these seven bases of meritorious acts grounded in material things cannot be measured by saying "it is only this much." Because the merit is so vast, it falls under the designation "a great mass of merit."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Mahāprompting addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Reverend One, by possessing what quality would a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increase merit alone and generate merit alone: bases of meritorious acts that are not grounded in material things, of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent? Could such a prompting be given?"

The Blessed One declared: "Such a prompting may indeed be given. These seven promptings are those by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone: bases of meritorious acts that are not grounded in material things, of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent. What are the seven?

"Here, O Prompting, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith hears that a Tathāgata or a śrāvaka of a Tathāgata is residing in dependence upon some village or town, and upon hearing this, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is the first prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone: a basis of meritorious acts not grounded in material things, of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

"Furthermore, O Prompting, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith hears that a Tathāgata or a śrāvaka of a Tathāgata is traveling in that direction, coming this way, and upon hearing this, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is the second prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone: a basis of meritorious acts not grounded in material things, of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

"Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith hears that a Tathāgata or a śrāvaka of a Tathāgata has arrived there and entered the vicinity, and upon hearing this, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is a prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone:"

This is the third basis for meritorious action — not arising from material things — of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent: merit alone increasing, merit alone arising, unceasingly and without interruption.

Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith hears that a Tathāgata or a śrāvaka of a Tathāgata has arrived in that very town and come into the vicinity, and upon hearing this, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is a prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone. This is the fourth basis for meritorious action — not arising from material things — of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith goes to behold that very Tathāgata or that very śrāvaka of a Tathāgata, and goes for the sake of paying homage, and upon seeing them, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is a prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone. This is the fifth basis for meritorious action — not arising from material things — of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith listens to and hears, from the presence of that very Tathāgata or that very śrāvaka of a Tathāgata, the holy Dharma — good in the beginning, good in the middle, good at the end, of excellent meaning, of excellent words, unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, perfectly refined — as it is properly proclaimed, and upon listening and hearing, attains joy, supreme joy, vast wholesome gladness of a definitive arising. This is a prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone. This is the sixth basis for meritorious action — not arising from material things — of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith, having heard the Dharma from the presence of that very Tathāgata or that very śrāvaka of a Tathāgata, goes for refuge in the Buddha, goes for refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and takes up the foundations of training. This is a prompting by possessing which a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith — whether walking, standing, lying down, or not lying down — unceasingly and without interruption increases merit alone and generates merit alone. This is the seventh basis for meritorious action — not arising from material things — of very great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great extent.

Now, the merit, or the fruit of merit, of a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith who possesses these seven bases for meritorious action not arising from material things —

the karmic maturation of the fruit of merit cannot be measured as "this much is the fruit of merit." Because merit is so abundant, it falls into the category called "a great mass of merit."

This is a prompting. Consider, for example, the place where these five great rivers — the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarayū, the Aciravatī, and the Mahī — flow together without distinction. One could not measure the water there as "there is this much water, or this many waterpots, or a hundred waterpots, or a thousand waterpots, or a hundred thousand waterpots," because the water is so abundant that it falls into the category called "a great mass of water." In just the same way, this prompting means that the merit, the fruit of merit, or the karmic maturation of the fruit of merit of a son of good family or a daughter of good family with faith who possesses these seven bases for meritorious action not arising from material things cannot be measured as "this much." Because merit is so abundant, it falls into the category called "a great mass of merit."

The Blessed One spoke these words. Having so spoken, the Sugata, the Teacher, then further declared:

Just as rivers flowing differently,
frequented by humans and herds of game,
pour into the finest, auspicious, pure lake
with pleasant banks — that ocean, source of jewels —

so too does the stream of merit flow in every way
to a generous donor who gives robes, food, and drink,
bedding, seats, and cushions to human beings,
just as rivers and their flowing waters pour into the sea.

Having spoken thus, the venerable one rejoiced greatly at what the Blessed One had said and praised it openly. Then the householder Gāndha was one who had faith, but his retinue lacked faith, and he thought to himself: "If my retinue has no faith, how much worse will things go in my temple?" So he disguised his appearance, dressed himself in a lower garment and plain clothes, went to the temple, and bowing before the stūpa with the melody of verse began to enter the temple. Then an old man who was seated in the gatehouse bowed at his feet and said: "Noble one, whose is this temple — which ravishes the heart and eyes and has become a stairway to the heavens?" He replied: "It belongs to the householder Gāndha." "Noble one, is this a temple, or is it a place of destitution?" "Good sir, what is a temple and what is destitution?" "Noble one, a place where provisions are abundant is a temple; a place where provisions are lacking is destitution." "Good sir, this one is destitute." "How has it come to this?" "The householder himself has faith, but his retinue lacks it, and so they do not supply what is needed. Now, in this householder's home there is a daughter-in-law named Mgubyed, who has faith and good intentions, but she has no authority in that household. If she did have authority, she would supply the needs of the monks and this place would truly become a temple."

The householder Gāndha thought to himself: "Even now while I am still alive, the situation of the monks in my temple is like this — what will it be like after I die?" Realizing this, he bowed at the monk's feet, went to his own home, and said to the members of his household: "Whoever among you feels inspired to render service to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas — let that person cut a bundle of firewood." At that moment Mgubyed, taking a water pot and going out to draw water, found a strip of cloth there —

The Blessed One, wishing to benefit her, came to that place, and she began to examine the Blessed One. Through his miraculous power, the Blessed One caused her to see a strip of cloth from his robe of Dharma garments, and she thought: "If only the Blessed One would accept this piece of cloth of mine, I would offer it to him." The Blessed One, knowing her mind, declared: "Mgubyed, if you are giving it up completely, then offer it." She, with her mind filled with confident faith in the Blessed One, aroused reverence and made the offering. The Blessed One, right there before her, mended the tear in his robe with the strip of cloth, and the color became perfectly matched. Moved by faith, she touched her head to his two feet, made an aspiration: "By this root of virtue, may I not become a slave-girl; may I not be impoverished." Having said this, she filled her water pot and returned home.

When the householder Gāndha instructed the members of his household to cut firewood, Mgubyed said: "Householder, what is this?" Gāndha replied: "Mgubyed, whichever one of you feels inspired to render service to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas — let that person cut firewood, and I have abundant wealth." She immediately set down her water pot, took up the firewood, and said: "I feel inspired to render service to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas. I will render service to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas with all requisites — please set your mind at ease." And so she undertook to serve the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas with all requisites, rendering service with reverence.

The householder Gāndha, for his part, made his appearance plain, dressed in a lowered lower garment, went to the temple, and, chanting verses, made prostrations at the stūpa and began to remain in the temple. Then an elderly woman who had entered the gatehouse there prostrated at his feet and asked: "Noble one, whose is this temple that captures the heart and eye and has become a stairway to the higher realms?" He replied: "It belongs to the householder Gāndha. Noble one, is it a temple or is it impoverished?" The well-favored one replied: "What is a temple, and what is impoverished?" "Noble one, where all requisites are complete — that is a temple; where requisites are absent — that is impoverished." "Well-favored one, formerly it was impoverished, but now it has become a temple. How did this come about?" "Well-favored one, the householder Gāndha has a bondswoman named Mgubyed who possesses faith and is good and of wholesome intention. That householder appointed her to work here and instructed her to serve the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas with all requisites. Now she is rendering service to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the buddhas with all requisites, and therefore this is a temple, not an impoverished place."

The householder Gāndha, hearing this, was delighted. He went home and placed in the hands of the girl Mgubyed the keys — both the keys and the crooked keys — and said to the members of his household: "You are all to abide by whatever Mgubyed directs." He also gathered the assembly of people dwelling in Kauśāmbī and proclaimed: "Friends, know that I have released the girl Mgubyed from her condition of bondage and have made her the mistress of the household."

The monks, being uncertain, brought all their doubts before the buddha, the Blessed One, to be resolved. "Venerable One, look upon the householder Gāndha — he is being summoned by King Śarpa to account for Gāndha's affairs." The Blessed One declared:

Monks, not only now, but even in times past, this householder Gāndha was recognized by King Śarpa through Gāndha's own affairs. Listen to this.

Monks, in former times there was in the city of Vārāṇasī a king named Brahmadatta whose realm was prosperous, flourishing, and happy, with good harvests, filled with many people and a great population, where foreign enemies, internal strife, and violent conflict had been thoroughly pacified, and which was free from bandits, famine, and disease — a realm made abundant with rows of rice and sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. He was a righteous king, a dharma-king, who governed his kingdom in accordance with the Dharma.

Then at a certain time, astrologers prophesied that rain would not fall for twelve years. King Brahmadatta had this announced throughout his realm with the beat of drums, dispatching proclamations in all directions: "Let all those dwelling in my kingdom, and all those in the palace retinue, hear this. The astrologers have prophesied that rain will not fall for twelve years. Therefore, those among you who have provisions for twelve years are to remain. Those who do not have such provisions are to depart for other lands and may return after twelve years have passed."

At that time in Vārāṇasī there dwelt a householder named Dhāraṇī (Skt. dhāraṇī — here used as a proper name), wealthy, possessed of great riches, with extensive property, and with storehouses vast and spacious. He called his steward and said: "Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself and my household?" The steward replied: "Yes, my lord, you do."

Now when buddhas do not appear in the world, pratyekabuddhas — humble and poor, devoted to solitude in remote dwelling places, solitary as rhinoceroses, having become a field of merit for the world — arise in the world. At this time five hundred pratyekabuddhas, while wandering through the countryside, came to Vārāṇasī and went to the house of the householder Dhāraṇī. They arrived and said: "Householder, would you be able to provide for the needs of five hundred renunciants like ourselves for twelve years?"

He replied: "Noble ones, please ask the steward, and it shall be given." So he called the steward and said: "Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself and my household together with these five hundred renunciants?" The steward replied: "Yes, my lord, you do."

The householder Dhāraṇī then said to the five hundred pratyekabuddhas: "Noble ones, it is here — please remain and be provided for." And they stayed there.

Then another five hundred pratyekabuddhas, while wandering through the countryside, also came to Vārāṇasī and likewise went to the householder Dhāraṇī's house, where they arrived and said: "Householder, would you be able to provide for the needs of five hundred renunciants like ourselves for twelve years?"

He replied: "Noble ones, since I am already providing for you — why would I do so again? You, householder, belong to those others, and we too belong to those others. Noble ones, please ask the steward, and it shall be given." So he called the steward and said: "Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself and my household together with a thousand renunciants?" The steward replied: "Yes, my lord, you do."

The householder Dhāraṇī then said to those five hundred pratyekabuddhas as well: "Noble ones, it is here — please remain and be provided for." And they too stayed there.

The householder Dhāraṇī had a house of giving built, appointed people to serve as stewards of the giving and as summoners, and the summoner went out day by day and called at midday.

The summoner kept a dog, and each day that dog would go along with the summoner. Then one day it happened that the summoner was occupied with some business, and thinking "I will finish this task and invite them later," he went elsewhere. The dog, not finding him, went from force of old habit to where the pratyekabuddhas were, and not seeing the summoner there either, it began to bark. The elder of the pratyekabuddhas' Saṅgha said: "Venerable ones, the summoner has been detained past the hour, and this dog is summoning us — let us proceed inside." They agreed, and those noble ones came in. When the summoner arrived and the dog saw him, it began to bark again, and the summoner understood: "This one summoned them, and that is how these great ones came to arrive without missing their time." He said: "Noble ones, who summoned you?" They replied: "Good sir, this dog did." He said: "Noble ones, please forgive me. From now on, whenever I am occupied with something, this very one shall be your summoner. Please go on now."

Then the monks were told: "At that time and on that occasion, the householder Dhāraṇī was none other than myself. The steward at that time and on that occasion was the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The summoner at that time and on that occasion was the king Prasenajit of the East. The dog at that time and on that occasion was the householder Yaśasvin, and the householder Yaśasvin had in that life come to know through a bark — and so too in this life has he understood through a bark."

When the Blessed One was in Magadha, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, an artisan-king of noble form and substance, came to where the Blessed One was together with eighty thousand gods of Magadha and many hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders of Magadha, and the Blessed One established them in the truths. At that time the king had a drum-proclamation made throughout Rājagṛha and gave this command: "Let all who dwell in Rājagṛha, all people of the royal court and its environs, and all assemblies of people who have come from various lands — listen, wise ones! In my realm, let no one commit theft. Whoever commits theft in my realm I shall banish from the realm, and the property of those who have been robbed I shall give from my own treasury and storehouse."

When the Blessed One was in Kosala, King Prasenajit, tamed by the example of the young man, likewise had a drum-proclamation made throughout Śrāvastī and gave this command: "In my realm, let no one commit theft. Whoever commits theft in my realm I shall have put to death, and the property of those who have been robbed I shall give from my own treasury and storehouse."

Now the bandits who were dwelling in the land of Magadha and the bandits who were dwelling in the land of Kosala went and stationed themselves at the border between the two kingdoms. Those who came as accomplices from Magadha they would rob, and those who came as accomplices from Kosala they would rob as well. Thus it spread everywhere: the bandits stationed in Magadha and the bandits stationed in Kosala went to the borderlands and stationed themselves there, robbing all those who traveled as accomplices, so that the coming and going of such accomplices ceased entirely, and the proclamation became known in these words: "The king's taxes and the annual tribute will not be collected."

When King Rūpasāra heard this, he sent one regiment, but it was defeated and routed, and came back. In the same way, when he sent a second regiment and a third, those too were defeated and routed, and came back. Meanwhile, an accomplice traveling from the land of Magadha to Kosala, frightened of the bandits, had entered Rājagṛha seeking an escort. The ministers said to the king, "Sire, this man Sahasrathūra lives by the king's provisions — why does he not escort the accomplices?" The king said, "Let him go — release him at his own discretion." The ministers summoned the man and said to him, "Hey, you there — you live by the king's provisions, so why do you not carry out the king's command?" He replied, "Tell me what you have ordered me to do, and if I have not done it, then say such words." They said, "Escort this accomplice who is traveling to the land of Kosala." He said, "Very well, I shall do so," and taking two quivers of five hundred arrows each, he mounted a chariot and rode out ahead of the accomplice.

The bandits, seeing him coming from a great distance ahead of the accomplice, sent a messenger ordering him thus: "The bandit commander says: turn the chariot back — you will come to harm." He replied, "Give a warrior his warrior's portion." The bandit's messenger said, "Are you the only one who is brave? We are brave too — turn back." Then they began to shoot arrows at one another, and he struck the bandit's messenger in a vital spot, and the messenger turned back. In the same way, two bandits came, then four, then eight, then sixteen, then thirty-two, then sixty-four, and up to five hundred bandits came forward, and he struck each of them in a vital spot and they turned back.

Then another five hundred bandits came forward, and he said to them, "If I kill your five hundred bandits, would you not prefer to save your own lives? Turn back." The bandits said, "You have not killed even one of us, so why should we turn back? Whether you or we — we'll see." He said, "If you do not believe me, then remove the armor from those I have already struck." They began to remove it, and as each one's armor was removed, the moment the time came, those bandits said, "This man is a yakṣa," and fled. Sahasrathūra remained stationed at the borderland, and he would escort those accomplices coming from Kosala and those coming from Magadha alike. Then he thought, "Why should I go back and forth? I shall simply stay right here," and he built a house there and settled down, becoming a resting place for the accomplices of both kingdoms. Since he took up residence in the countryside, that place came to be known by the name "Countryside Dwelling."

The seventy-fourth fascicle of the Vinaya Analysis.

At Countryside Dwelling the accomplices gathered, and some of them began selling fruit, some began selling flour, some traded in cotton goods, some carried loads, some began selling pills, and liquor sellers began selling liquor as well. With all of them settled right there, a market town took shape in that place. Countryside Dwelling sent a letter to King Rūpasāra saying, "Sire, I have established a market here — it would be fitting that the king send a customs officer here." The king thought to himself:

"The very place where my three brigades were broken, thoroughly routed, and put to flight — he has established a market town there. So be it — let that place remain just as it is." With that thought, he sent a letter to Countryside Dwelling saying: "I hereby grant you that market town. Whatever customs duties and annual revenues accumulate there, do with them entirely as you please."

Having established a market town at Countryside Dwelling, the place came to be known by the very name "Countryside Dwelling."

The people of the community dwelling at Countryside Dwelling reflected among themselves: "Friends, whatever comfort and ease we enjoy here — all of it is due to the power of Countryside Dwelling. We should not let an opportunity pass to do him some benefit." Then some among them said: "Quite right — let us do exactly that. But what shall we do?" Others among them said: "Whoever among us gives a bride or takes a bride shall provide him and his retinue with food and shall also present him with a set of garments." "Quite right — let us do so." And so it was that whoever among them gave a bride or took a bride would provide Countryside Dwelling and his retinue with food and present him with a set of garments.

Now it happened that a certain poor man was about to take a bride, and he thought to himself: "Where would I find the means to provide Countryside Dwelling and his retinue with food and present him with a set of garments? What I shall do instead is this: after I have taken that bride, I will first offer her to Countryside Dwelling for his pleasure alone. After he has taken his pleasure, then I myself shall enjoy her." With that resolve, he went to Countryside Dwelling's compound, bowed his head in reverence, and said: "Village lord, I am about to take a bride, yet I have no means to offer you a meal with your retinue and present you with a set of garments. Therefore I propose this: after I have taken that bride, I will first offer her to you for your pleasure alone. After you have taken your pleasure, then I myself shall enjoy her."

Countryside Dwelling replied: "My friend, there is no need for anyone who takes or gives a bride to provide me and my retinue with food and present me with a set of garments. Go then and take your bride without any worry." "Village lord, be that as it may — nevertheless, please accept my offer with gladness." Since the domain of women is such that it seizes and occupies the senses, Countryside Dwelling accepted with willingness. The man thereupon took his bride and first offered her to Countryside Dwelling, and Countryside Dwelling indeed took his pleasure with her.

Countryside Dwelling was now overwhelmed with passionate desire in his craving for sensual objects, and he began to show affection toward that man. Another person said to him: "My friend, for what reason have you become so fond of Countryside Dwelling to such a degree?" The man recounted what had transpired, and the other, hearing this, also began to do the same. Yet another person asked him about it, and he too recounted what had happened, and that one also began to do the same. And yet another asked, was told, and likewise began to do the same. In this manner, unwholesome practices began to multiply in that place.

Countryside Dwelling had a temple built in that market town, and whenever anyone there took a bride, that man would have the girl circumambulate the temple and then send her to Countryside Dwelling's compound, and Countryside Dwelling would take his pleasure with her first.

Then at a later time, a certain young woman of great beauty was about to be given in marriage, and she thought to herself:

"It would be wrong for me to be enjoyed first by Countryside Dwelling and only afterward by my husband. I must find some means by which this Countryside Dwelling will be killed." With that thought in mind, she turned to one side — toward a spot where a great crowd of common people had gathered and were conversing — squatted down, and urinated. The crowd saw this, and they were displeased, and they said: "Shameless and immodest girl! Whose daughter is this, who squats down and urinates facing the crowd of common people?"

When she heard that, she replied: "Are you not men yourselves? Then what am I? You are not men — it is only Countryside Dwelling who is a man, for he takes all your wives and enjoys them first, and afterward you clean up his filth."

At that, they said to one another: "Wise friends, if this one is going to keep living among us, how are we to deal with him?" Some said: "What else is there to do? Kill Countryside Dwelling." Others said: "We should deliberate on how exactly to kill him." While they were thus taking counsel, it happened that another householder was about to offer a garden party, and so they said: "Wise friends, a certain prominent householder is about to offer a garden party. When he invites Countryside Dwelling there as a guest, we shall kill him." And presently that householder did indeed give his garden party, and he invited Countryside Dwelling, who gladly accepted.

King Bimbisāra had heralds make a proclamation throughout the land: "In my realm, if any monk should come to someone's home and there is food and drink in the storehouse or the house, they are to be given a meal. If there is none, whoever sees the monk shall give from their own means, and afterward I will repay them double." He also had this written down as a standing order.

In the meantime, the venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were wandering on tour through the villages of Magadha and came to Countryside Dwelling. Countryside Dwelling's headman heard that the venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana had come to Countryside Dwelling while wandering on tour through the villages of Magadha. Upon hearing this, he thought to himself: "King Bimbisāra, never satisfied with merit, gives gifts and makes merit. Why should I not also give gifts and make merit?" And so he went to where the venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were, arrived there, prostrated at their feet with his head bowed, and sat before them in order to hear the Dharma. The two of them taught him the Dharma, and then he invited them for alms and gave them food.

The householder sent for Countryside Dwelling with an urgent summons, but Countryside Dwelling, paying no heed to the message that had been given to him, simply went off to attend the garden party. The crowd of people dwelling in Countryside Dwelling, too, made a signal; armed with weapons, they rushed to the spot. When Countryside Dwelling entered the garden enclosure, on the pretext of washing his hair they poured boiling water over his head, so that his eyes streamed with tears and he could see almost nothing. Then they began hurling at him weapons such as a razor-wheel, a single-pointed vajra, great arrows, and single-pointed iron spikes, and they made ready to kill him. He cried out: "Wise friends, what wrong have I done you?" They said: "You have enjoyed our brides first, and afterward we have had them." He replied: "It is you yourselves who brought forth this impure custom. What fault is mine in it? Do not kill me — let me go!"

As they were wailing in this way and setting about killing him, he — at the very moment of losing his life, at the very moment of death, his mind cutting free — aroused the awakening mind and made an aspiration prayer: "By the root of virtue I have made in offering alms to the noble Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana, those two who are worshipped by gods and humans alike — by that merit, may I be reborn in the very place where these men will be killed." Because it is the nature of reality that a misdirected aspiration prayer made at the moment of death takes swift effect, he made that misdirected aspiration and died. When his time came, he was reborn among the vicious yakṣas.

Then, wishing to dwell there, he went before the great king Vaiśravaṇa and said: "Lord with forbearance, grant me a place to dwell." Vaiśravaṇa replied: "The wilderness is your place — go to that same wilderness." So he came to the wilderness, was driven out by human beings, and a great many people perished, dying in their thousands upon thousands.

The people dwelling in that wilderness summoned their diviners and asked: "Wise friends, what is the cause of this plague that has broken out upon us in this way?" They replied: "Wise friends, the herdsman whom you killed made a misdirected aspiration prayer and was reborn among the vicious yakṣas, and it is he who has brought about this plague." The people began to flee, loading their wagons, and he too manifested himself in a great and terrifying form and stood before the fleeing crowd of wilderness-dwellers and declared: "Where are you going? I shall eat every last one of you!" They were all struck with fear and cried: "Village lord, forgive us who have done evil!" He replied: "I shall forgive you on one condition: if you offer me one thousand people every single day, I will pardon you." They said: "Village lord, if we were to offer you a thousand people every day, before long there would be no one left in this wilderness. In consideration of the present circumstances, let us off for now — forgive us who bow down to you." He said: "Good folk, I have long desired that this wilderness would be emptied of people. Nevertheless, let five hundred be offered to me each day, and I will forgive you." They petitioned him again in the same way, and he reduced his demand, saying that between two hundred fifty and one hundred should be offered. They then said: "Village lord, even so we will be diminished — what use is a multitude? Let us offer you, each and every day, a wagon laden with provisions and drawn by six oxen, along with one person to lead it, and please forgive us." He replied: "Very well, on this condition: do not offer them weeping; they must be brought with dancing, with singing, and with the sound of musical instruments." And they agreed to this.

Then all the people dwelling in that wilderness gathered and began to deliberate: "Wise friends, the yakṣa has treated us so — how are we to manage this? Some said: "Let us take turns, one after another." Others said: "If we announce whose turn it is, disputes will arise. Rather, let us write down all the household names and put them in a jar, and whichever household name is drawn, that person must go. And they must not send a servant in their place — they themselves must go, or send a son. If one whose name is drawn is occupied and cannot be present when it comes their turn, the household tablet is placed upright before that person's house and left there."

At that time there lived in a rural settlement a certain householder who had no son. For a long while he had been praying, "Alas, may I come to have a son!" and through the power of that aspiration a being entered into his wife's womb. When the time of his wife's delivery arrived, the householder had gone out on some business. That very day the household tablet came round requiring the offering of food-portions to the yakṣa, and the people whose duty it was to make that offering placed the tablet upright against his door and left it there. At just that moment his wife gave birth, and a baby boy was born.

As soon as the householder came home, he saw the household tablet as he was about to enter, and grief and distress arose in him. He went inside and sat without saying a word. His wife said to him: "Lord's son, be glad! Your son has been born!" Yet still he sat without saying a word. His wife spoke to him thus three times, but still he sat without uttering a sound. Then his wife said again: "Lord's son, you have prayed for so long — 'Alas, may I come to have a son!' — and now one is born. Why do you sit without saying anything? Please, be most glad!"

He said: "Good woman, this one was born, and so I am as good as dead."

"Lord's son, what do you mean? Good woman — the household tablet has come for the offering of food-portions to the yakṣa."

"Lord's son, if that is so, your son will be going. But if we could just see him a little while first, then your son will still have existed for you."

"Good woman, this is a drop of our own blood — how can we send him?"

"Lord's son, has the community not established it as a rule that one must go oneself or send a son? This is your son. There is nothing else as dear to us as he is. Send this son."

He then relented and said: "If you are willing, so be it."

Thereupon the householder's wife sat up through the night without sleeping. She made offerings with butter lamps, incense, garlands, and flowers, turned her face toward the east, and began to pray:

The world's virtuous, the peaceful, the tamed,
and those of subdued power — to them this hall is never empty.
For my child's sake I bow before them:
I pray, protect my little one.

Now it is the very nature of buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that they possess not even a trace of unknowing, unseeing, ignorance, or failure to discern. Endowed with great compassion, entered into benefiting the world, they are the one protector, the solitary hero, without a second, not speaking of a second, abiding in calm abiding and insight, making the three knowledges clear, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the threefold basis of the tamed life, crossed beyond the four rivers, well established in the basis of practice through the four legs of miraculous power, long purified in the four means of gathering beings, not intimidated by the four fearlessnesses, having abandoned the five obstructing factors, fully passed beyond the five destinies of beings, endowed with the six limbs and the six perfections brought to complete fulfillment, established in the six constant abidings, enriched with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, teaching the eight limbs of the path, skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, possessed of the power of the ten powers, their renown fully spread in all ten directions — these most supremely distinguished ones, lords over a hundred hundredfolds: it is the very nature of such buddhas to survey the world with the eyes of a buddha three times by day and three times by night, and to see who has declined, who has flourished, who has been harmed, who has fallen into distress, who has fallen into misfortune, who has come to harm and distress and misfortune, who is inclining toward the lower realms —

— who is inclining toward the lower realms, who has already fallen into the lower realms — I shall raise up from the path of the lower realms and establish in the higher realms, in liberation, and in the fruit. Whoever has sunk into the mire of desire, I shall pull up by the hand. Whoever is deprived of the wealth of the noble ones, I shall establish in lordship over the wealth of the noble ones. Whatever world is adorned by the arising of a buddha, I shall cause to bear fruit. In whoever the roots of virtue have not yet been produced, I shall produce them. In whoever the roots of virtue have already been produced, I shall bring them to full maturation. And whoever has fully matured, I shall bring to complete liberation. With such knowing and seeing does a buddha engage.

Then it was spoken in verse:

One who dwells in the realm of the sea-monster may yet pass beyond their appointed time,
but the loving-kindness of a buddha toward those to be tamed
shall never pass beyond its appointed time.

Just as a mother tends to her one beloved child
with constant thought and preserves that child's life,
so too the Tathāgata tends with constant thought to those to be tamed
and preserves their lives.

The mare of compassion that dwells in the stream of omniscience
tirelessly seeks out the foal of those to be tamed.
The loving-kindness toward those exhausted by existence and the lower realms
is like a cow's love for a foal that has utterly collapsed.

The Blessed One then reflected: this youth has previously rendered great service to the past buddhas; I shall therefore benefit him, and the yakṣa (yakṣa) of the wilderness is also to be tamed. With this understanding, the Blessed One journeyed through the regions of Magadha and came to the wilderness, and consented to spend the night at the dwelling of the wilderness yakṣa.

At that time the wilderness yakṣa went to the gathering assembly of the yakṣas. The yakṣa Boṅguba saw the Blessed One spending the night at the dwelling of the wilderness yakṣa. Having seen this, he went to where the wilderness yakṣa was, and when he arrived, he said to the wilderness yakṣa: "Village chief, what a fine and excellent find you have made — the Blessed One has consented to spend the night at your dwelling. Village chief, has even a human being ever consented to spend the night at your dwelling?" The wilderness yakṣa replied: "Village chief, indeed so." "Indeed so? Then know this: he is the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha." "Village chief, is he truly the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, or is he not? This I must now find out."

Then the wilderness yakṣa, having quelled the gathering assembly of the yakṣas, went to his own dwelling. When he arrived, he said to the Blessed One: "Ascetic (śramaṇa), come out!" The Blessed One reflected: this one is held in check by another. And so he emerged. "Ascetic, go back in!" The Blessed One entered, for the sake of decisively subduing arrogance and pride. Again, a second time, the wilderness yakṣa said to the Blessed One: "Ascetic, come out!" The Blessed One reflected: this one is held in check by another. And so he emerged. "Ascetic, go back in!" The Blessed One entered, for the sake of decisively subduing arrogance and pride. A third time the wilderness yakṣa said to the Blessed One: "Ascetic, come out!" The Blessed One reflected: this one is held in check by another. And so he emerged. "Ascetic, go back in!" The Blessed One entered, for the sake of decisively subduing arrogance and pride. And yet again the wilderness yakṣa said to the Blessed One: "Ascetic, come out!"

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the wilderness yakṣa: "Village chief, you have summoned me to enter three times, and now I will not come again. Therefore, yakṣa, ask me your questions. If the one who answers satisfies your mind, well and good. But if your mind is not satisfied, then your thoughts will be scattered, your heart will burst, you will vomit hot blood from your mouth, and you will be seized by both arms and flung to the far bank beyond the river of the fortunate charioteer." The Blessed One then declared: "Village chief, I have looked throughout this world with its gods, its māras, its Brahmās, its assemblies of ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, and I do not truly see anyone who could scatter the thoughts of a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha, or cause his heart to burst, or draw hot blood from his mouth, or seize him by both arms and fling him to the far bank beyond the river of the fortunate charioteer. Therefore, village chief, ask freely whatever you wish."

Then the wilderness yakṣa at that moment offered these verses:

With what, and in what manner, and
by what does one cross over, and with what?
What here is the supreme wealth of a person?
What, well practiced, brings a life of ease?

Among flavors, which is the sweetest?
Show us how the finest life is lived.

The Blessed One replied:

Faith is the supreme wealth of a person.
Practicing Dharma well brings a life of ease.
The flavor of truth is the sweetest of flavors.
Living with wisdom — that is the finest life.

The yakṣa asked:

How does one come to have renown?
How does one come to possess prosperity?
How does one come to receive a good name?
And how does one come to find good friends?

The Blessed One replied:

Through moral discipline one gains renown.
Through generosity one comes to possess prosperity.
Through truthfulness one receives a good name.
Through compassion one comes to find good friends.

The yakṣa asked:

By how many things does a person arise in the world?
By how many does one come to gain familiarity?
By how many is one honored in the world?
By how many does one come to prevail over the world?

The Blessed One replied:

By six a person arises in the world,
by six one comes to gain familiarity,
by six one is honored in the world,
and by six one comes to prevail over the world.

The yakṣa asked:

What is this flood — tireless, without pause —
that comes and comes and cannot be crossed?
Without a fixed support, without an anchor,
what is so deep that none can plumb it?

The Blessed One replied:

One possessed of moral discipline in every way,
with even composure, and endowed with wisdom,
inwardly attentive, possessed of mindfulness —
this one crosses over what is so very hard to cross.
One free from perception bound to sense desire,
gone to the limit of all engagement with form —
such a one will not sink into that depth
which is without fixed object and without support.

The yakṣa asked:

By what does one cross over the flood?
By what does one cross the ocean?
By what does one abandon suffering?
By what is one completely purified?

The Blessed One replied:

By faith one crosses over the flood.
By heedfulness one crosses the ocean.
By diligent effort one abandons suffering.
By wisdom one is completely purified.

Ask other ascetics and brahmins, one by one,
in many different places,
whether there exists any other Dharma
apart from the giving up of truthful restraint.

The yakṣa replied:

Why should I go asking ascetics and brahmins
one by one, as if I did not know?
For you, O great hero,
have explained this Dharma excellently well.

Alas, O yakṣa Dongbu-pa,
the peerless caravan-leader, the Buddha,
has been revealed to me.
For what you have done for me, I am grateful.

From this day forth, from village to village,
from home to home, together with the fully awakened one,
I shall practice in reverence
for the excellent nature of reality in the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the yakṣa of the wilderness:

"Good-faced one, by feeding the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana you were to have been reborn among the gods of the Thirty-Three. Yet because you made a wrong aspiration, you were born instead among the fierce yakṣas. Now you are violent, your hands are stained with blood, you are attached to degradation and utter degradation, you seize the lives of others, and you live by taking the lives of others. When you die and pass from here, what will your destiny be? What will your birth be? What will your next life be?"

He replied: "Blessed One, please command me as to what I should do."

"Good-faced one, come here. Take refuge before me and receive the training precepts, and grant fearlessness to the assembly of people who dwell in the wilderness."

"Venerable one, I take refuge before the Blessed One and receive the training precepts, and from this day forward I grant fearlessness to the assembly of people who dwell in the wilderness."

And so he took refuge before the Blessed One and received the training precepts. Having received the training precepts, he spoke these verses:

Alas, the Teacher came to bind me
for my own sake, in perfect truth.
Today I have come to understand clearly
the welfare of future lives.

Then that householder loaded a cart drawn by six oxen with food, placed the boy in the cart as well, and sent it off to the yakṣa accompanied by the sounds of dance, song, and music. Some noble ones, brahmins, and householders who heard this said: "O wise ones, what is this sound of dance, song, and music?" Some replied: "Do you not know? They are carrying a drop of blood as a tribute to the yakṣa."

A great crowd of ordinary people assembled and said: "O wise ones, this drop of blood will not please the yakṣa. If it is not turned back, the yakṣa will surely be provoked and will bring harm to all of us. It must be turned back." And they began to turn it back.

But the man said: "O wise ones, the law of the assembly requires that one go oneself or send one's child. Since this is my own son, why should it be turned back? It will not be turned back; let it go forward."

They had nothing to say to this and stood in silence.

The Blessed One heard the sounds of dance, song, and music. Having heard them, he spoke to the yakṣa of the wilderness: "Village-chief, what are these sounds of dance, song, and music?"

"Venerable one, though I have turned back from those evil, unwholesome deeds, the people still cling to the old ways. I do not know how to put a stop to this."

The Blessed One said: "Village-chief, what is this? Tell me how it has come about."

When it was explained, the Blessed One said: "Village-chief, today do not accept even food, drink, or an ox."

The man thought: "So be it — I shall offer this last meal of mine as alms to the Blessed One."

The householder took the boy out of the cart and gave him to the yakṣa. The yakṣa in turn offered him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then gave him back to the father.

The father then asked: "Blessed One, by what name should this boy be called?"

The Blessed One replied in verse:

The child, passing from the hand of the yakṣa into my hand,
and from my hand into the hand of his father —
for that reason he shall be known as Passed-Through-Hands.

So the name Passed-Through-Hands was given to him.

The householder took the boy and set off for the pastoral settlement. When the crowd of people there saw him, they said: "Good people, look what has happened! He went off carrying drops of blood, yet through him the yakṣa of the pastoral settlement has been stirred up — and now he has come back without a scratch!"

He replied: "Good people, how could the yakṣa have been stirred up in anger? Out of compassion for this child, the Blessed One graciously agreed to spend the night at that place, and the Blessed One tamed him, established him in the going-for-refuge and in the bases of training, and commanded him to give fearlessness to the crowd of people dwelling in the pastoral settlement and to leave them free from harm and oppression."

They were overjoyed and said: "Since this boy was just born and the yakṣa of the pastoral settlement was tamed, let this child's name be Passed-Through-Hands of the Pastoral Settlement." And so the name Passed-Through-Hands of the Pastoral Settlement was given to him.

When he grew up he became highly learned in writing, letters, and various other arts.

Now when his beard had turned bluish-gray and his hair was ready to be trimmed back, he was visited by a multitude of supplicants: kings, wealthy men, merchant leaders, caravan leaders, Śākyas, Kaudyas, Licchavīs, and many others besides. The householder Dignified One sat there pressing his hand to his cheek, his mind sunk in thought, thinking: "So many people are coming with bluish-gray beards seeking gifts, and those to whom she does not give will become my enemies."

When Bluish-Gray Beard saw this, she said: "Father, why do you sit pressing your hand to your cheek, your mind sunk in thought?"

He said: "Daughter, kings with bluish-gray beards have arrived as supplicants, along with wealthy men, merchant leaders, caravan leaders, Śākyas, Kaudyas, Licchavīs, and many others. Those to whom you do not give will become my enemies. How could I not sit pressing my hand to my cheek, lost in thought?"

She said: "Father, if that is how it is, do not be displeased. From today, in seven days' time, I myself will seek out a dwelling place."

He said: "Daughter, do so. But first go and make a petition to the king." So she went to the eastern flank of the king of the realm of Bhadra and said: "Your Majesty, from today in seven days' time Bluish-Gray Beard will seek out her own dwelling — may the king please grant permission."

The king thought: "Apart from me, to whom else would she go seeking a dwelling place?" and gave his permission.

Having received his permission, he gave orders to his ministers: "Good people, have the city adorned, and let this proclamation be made: 'From today, in seven days' time, Bluish-Gray Beard will seek out her own dwelling — therefore let all of you assemble as your means allow.'"

The ministers cleared the city of stones, gravel, and weeds, sprinkled it with sandalwood water, set out vessels of fragrant incense and sweet perfumes, hung up streamers of silk, raised victory banners and pennants, scattered flowers of every kind, and made it as delightful as a divine pleasure grove. Then they had the following proclamation cried out: "All people dwelling in Kauśāmbī, the people of the palace and its surroundings, and the crowds of people who have come from various lands — good people, hear this! In seven days from today, Bluish-Gray Beard will seek out her own dwelling. Therefore let each of you assemble according to your means!"

Then, when many hundreds of thousands of living beings had gathered, on the seventh day Bluish-Gray Beard, adorned with all her ornaments,

she mounted a chariot, took up a garland of flowers, came forth, and began to survey the assembled crowd of common people. The king of Vatsa, Śarpa, thought to himself, "Without fail she will toss the garland of flowers onto me," and so he gathered his mind and sat attentively watchful. Bluish-Gray Beard gazed all around at the assembled crowd and then asked, "Good people, who are those riding upon the backs of elephants?" They answered her, "This one is King Rūpasāra. This one is King Prasenajit. This one is King Brahmadatta. This one is King Śarpa of Vatsa." In the same way she inquired separately about all the wealthy householders, the merchants, the caravan leaders, the Kauḍyas, the Śākyas, the Licchavīs, and many others besides. Then afterward she spoke: "Good people, the one called Lagbryud Drogné, whom the Blessed One freed from a yakṣa — let him come forward here!" The crowd replied, "He has not come. In which direction does he dwell? Is he somewhere nearby?" She turned her face toward his direction and, declaring "He is my husband," flung the garland of flowers. Thereupon the kings, the wealthy householders, the merchants, the caravan leaders, the Kauḍyas, the Śākyas, the Licchavīs, and all the many other assembled people dispersed and departed each to their own lands. The householder Gāndha, ashamed and uneasy at heart, said to Bluish-Gray Beard, "Daughter, if by your choosing him you bring harm upon me from the kings, that is not acceptable — go quickly." She replied, "Father, do not be troubled; I shall do as you say." The householder Gāndha provided her with a fine vehicle, had her adorned with various ornaments, and sent her off with an escort to the wilderness retreat.

At that very time, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones — in whom there is not even a particle of unknowing, unseeingness, ignorance, or misperception; who are endowed with great compassion; who have entered into the benefit of the world; who are the solitary protectors, the uniquely courageous, the without-second, those who speak of nothing as dual; who abide in calm abiding and special insight; who illuminate the three knowledges; who are well trained in the three trainings; who are skilled in the ground of the three bases of taming; who have crossed beyond the four rivers; who move by means of the four bases of miraculous power; who dwell well upon the ground of conduct; who from of old have perfectly purified the four means of gathering beings; who are without any trembling by virtue of the four fearlessnesses; who have abandoned the five limbs; who have genuinely transcended the five destinies; who are endowed with the six limbs; who have fully perfected the six perfections; who dwell by means of the six constant abidings; who are rich in the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening; who teach the noble eightfold path; who are skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions; who are possessed of the power of the ten powers; whose fame has perfectly spread throughout the ten directions; who are supremely exalted as rulers over a hundred times ten — the nature of such ones is to survey the world three times by day and three times by night with the eye of a buddha, beholding: who has declined, who has flourished, who has been harmed, who has become wretched, who has become unhappy, who has come to harm and wretchedness and suffering; who inclines toward the lower realms, who is falling toward the lower realms, who has fallen into the lower realms. "Those who are heading along the path to the lower realms I shall rouse and establish in higher rebirth, in liberation, and in its fruit. Those who are sinking in the swamp of desire I shall draw forth by the hand. Those who lack the wealth of noble riches I shall establish in the lordship of noble riches. The worlds adorned by the arising of buddhas I shall cause to have fruit."

"Those in whom roots of virtue have not yet arisen, I shall cause them to arise. Those in whom roots of virtue have already arisen, I shall bring them to full ripening. Those who have fully ripened, I shall bring to liberation." Such is the engagement of his knowledge and vision.

Then it was said in verse:

The venomous one who dwells in the crocodile's lair
may at times transgress the appointed hour —
but the loving-kindness of a buddha toward those he tames
shall never transgress its appointed hour.

Just as a mother, for her one beloved child,
thinks of that child always and guards its life,
so too the Tathāgata thinks always of those he tames
and guards their lives just so.

The mount of compassion residing in the stream of omniscience
grows not weary in seeking the foal of those to be tamed.
The loving-kindness toward those who have fallen in existence and the lower realms
is like the loving-kindness of a cow for the calf that has strayed far away.

The Blessed One then considered: "If the herdsman of Lagavud comes to see blue-green grass without having seen the truths, he will not become a vessel for those truths. I shall therefore go to his pasture-encampment in order to benefit him." Knowing this, as he was traveling through the countryside of Magadha, he came to the pasture-encampment and on the night road of the cattle path, in the place where the grass had been strewn, he consented to rest.

The cowherds, the herdsmen, those who cut grass, those who cut wood, those who lived by the road, and those who made their living as wayfarers — all of them saw the Blessed One resting in the night on the cattle road where the grass had been strewn. Having seen this, they went quickly, as quickly as could be, to the tent of the herdsman of Lagavud and said: "Householder! The Blessed One, by whom you were freed from the yakṣa, has come to the encampment and is resting in the night on the cattle path where the grass was strewn."

The herdsman of Lagavud then thought: "If I go tomorrow, the Blessed One may have departed to another place, and such a moment would be lost. I myself should go." Knowing this, he set out at once, going as fast as he could, and arrived just at the point when the noble gate was closing. And at that very time, Nīlapīta too arrived at the gate, but not having gotten inside, he agreed to spend the night at the gateway.

When dawn broke, the herdsman of Lagavud, moving with all possible haste, mounted his chariot and came out from the encampment. And Nīlapīta, also mounting a chariot, was entering the compound. The herdsman of Lagavud said: "Move your chariot aside!" And Nīlapīta said back: "You move your chariot aside!" But neither would move aside for the other. Then Nīlapīta looked carefully and said: "Are you the herdsman of Lagavud?" He replied: "People know me as such." The herdsman of Lagavud then said: "And are you Nīlapīta?" He replied: "People know me as such."

The herdsman of Lagavud said: "I am going before the Blessed One — move your chariot to the side. And you, go home for now." Nīlapīta replied: "Go to the holy man yourself!" and had his chariot moved to one side. The herdsman of Lagavud went toward where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and performed the appropriate courtesies of a householder in his individual way, gladdening the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, did you rest well?" — greeting him with individual courtesy.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the herdsman of Lagavud: "Lagavud, among those in the world who rest in ease, I too am sometimes one."

"Venerable One, on hard, rough ground, on a bedding of thin cloth set over cattle dung, in the winter season, in the middle of the eighth month of the cold period, when the frost rises with the moonlight not yet broken, and these ochre robes of yours are thin and torment the whole body —

"Lagavud, that is why I asked you directly. Answer as you are able to endure.

"Lagavud, consider this example. Suppose there were some householder or householder's son who was wealthy, with great possessions and extensive resources. For his sake a fine mansion was built, and within that fine mansion a multi-storied dwelling was built. Within that multi-storied dwelling was laid a couch draped with coverlets and cushions, a couch with an inner lining, a couch with a variegated spread, a couch with a great spread, a couch with a fine spread — and over these was placed a double-backed red cushion covered with a canopy of threefold cloth, together with an upper coverlet. Sesame-oil lamps burning through the night were set up, and a charming wife was placed nearby for pleasure and delight. Lagavud, what do you think? Would the sleeping arrangements of that man be comfortable or painful?"

"Venerable One, I think that man would indeed be among those in the world who rest in ease."

"Lagavud, what do you think? To a man who possesses such comfort and such pleasantness, could there arise torments born of desire, torments born of aversion, and torments born of delusion, arising and tormenting him? And being tormented by those torments, would that man sleep in suffering and not in ease?"

"The torments born of desire, torments born of aversion, and torments born of delusion — these the Tathāgata has fully known and cut off at the root, rendering them like a palm tree that has been felled: non-apparent, without a base, of a nature never to arise again. For this reason I said: among those in the world who rest in ease, I too am sometimes one."

Then at that moment the Blessed One spoke these verses:

The brahmin who has passed beyond all sorrow,
who is unstained by desire,
who is fully freed from the aggregates —
in every way that one rests in ease.

One who has cut off every craving,
who has dispelled the fever of the heart,
who has attained complete stillness and peace —
that one rests in ease of mind.

Then the Blessed One instructed, established, uplifted, and delighted the herdsman of Lagavud with a Dharma discourse befitting the occasion. And he taught at length the Dharma discourse that the blessed buddhas have from ancient times undertaken: the discourse on generosity, the discourse on moral discipline, the discourse on the higher realms, the faults and defilement of sensual pleasures, the affliction of complete defilement, the benefit of purification, and the benefit of renunciation and of thorough seclusion — expounding the teachings that accord with the side of purification.

And when the Blessed One saw that the herdsman's mind was gladdened, composed, joyful, free from obscuration, and that he was endowed with the fortune and the capacity to understand the supreme teaching that the blessed buddhas proclaim — at that moment the Blessed One taught at length the supreme teaching of the blessed buddhas, namely the four noble truths in their fullness: suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth free of all stains, when dipped in dye, takes the color evenly and well — so too the herdsman of Lagavud, seated right there, in that very sitting,

realized the cessation and the path directly.

Then the herdsman of Lagavud, having seen the Dharma, having obtained the Dharma, having understood the Dharma, having reached the depth of the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, having crossed beyond uncertainty, having no further need to rely on another in the Teacher's dispensation, being one whom no other can lead astray, having attained fearlessness with respect to all phenomena — he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May you accept me as a lay practitioner. From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, with sincere and heartfelt faith, I go for refuge."

Then the herdsman of Lagavud, having thus taken refuge before the Blessed One and having taken up the bases of training, attained the fruit of non-return. He then addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable one, today I was sought out by Śyāmāvat, and today I have directly actualized the fruit of non-return — how then shall I fulfil my obligations in this regard?"

The Blessed One declared: "Lagavud, go. Your training is this: provide Śyāmāvat, as she has agreed, with whatever food and clothing she needs. That is the way of the world."

Then the herdsman of Lagavud bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed to his own home, and said to Śyāmāvat: "Today you sought me out, and today, for my part, I went for refuge before the Blessed One, took up the bases of training, and attained the fruit of non-return. Therefore, if you wish, go to your father's household. If you do not wish to go, remain here, and I will provide you with whatever food and clothing you need."

She reflected: "If I were to leave, people would say that Lagavud found her inauspicious and did not keep her. Since this man is a son of the Buddha, I shall wait upon him and remain here." And so she stayed right there.

The herdsman of Lagavud then had a temple built, fully appointed with all necessary furnishings, and offered it to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. And so the elders composed a sūtra colophon saying: "The Blessed One resided in the pastoral lands, in the finest forest of the pasture region."

The Vinaya Vibhaṅga, the seventy-fifth bundle.

Then at another time the herdsman of Lagavud was struck by illness, suffering greatly from a severe sickness. And the herdsman of Lagavud passed away from that very illness. The moment he passed away, he was reborn among the gods of the heaven free from torment.

Then the divine son who had been the herdsman of Lagavud reflected thus: "It would not be fitting for me to go into the presence of the Blessed One to see and pay homage to him while still dwelling in my celestial abode. Rather, I shall go into his presence to see him and pay homage without relying on my celestial dwelling at all."

Then the divine son who had been the herdsman of Lagavud, just as a person endowed with strength might extend a bent arm or draw back an extended arm — so swiftly did he vanish from the heaven free from torment and

appeared in the presence of the Blessed One. And there the divine son who had been the herdsman of Lagavud let his body sink into the earth without touching the surface — just as melted butter, or oil with fine sand, or ash, when poured upon the ground, sinks in without touching the surface.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud: "Lagavud, manifest yourself now with a coarse body, arouse the perception of solidity, and call to mind the mark of sitting."

Then the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud, manifested a coarse body, aroused the perception of solidity, and calling to mind the mark of sitting, went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage. He sat to one side. And by the power of the divine son's radiant complexion, all the finest highland forests roundabout were pervaded with a vast and brilliant light.

Seated to one side, the Blessed One addressed the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud, with these words: "Divine son, whatever teachings you recited and learned when you were formerly a human being — do you still know them now?"

"Venerable one, whatever teachings I recited and learned when I was formerly a human being, I know those now all the more clearly. And whatever teachings I recited but did not manage to learn when I was formerly a human being — those too I now know. For the Dharma well taught by the Blessed One is easy to hold in mind and easy to proclaim.
