"Just as the Blessed One dwells in Jambudvīpa surrounded by the fourfold retinue — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — and those beings think: 'Whatever Dharma teachings the Blessed One may teach us, we shall listen to them and practice accordingly, for that will be for our long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness' — in just the same way, venerable one, when I dwell in the heaven free from torment, surrounded by the gods of that heaven, the gods there think: 'Whatever Dharma teachings the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud, may teach us, we shall listen to them and practice accordingly, for that will be for our long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.'"

"Lagavud, through insatiable and unabandoned pursuit of how many teachings did you, after leaving a body, take birth in the heaven free from torment?"

"Venerable one, through three teachings that I never tired of and never abandoned, I left a body and was born in the heaven free from torment. Which three? Venerable one, I was never sated with beholding the Blessed One, and never abandoned it — and through that I left a body and was born in the heaven free from torment. Venerable one, I was never sated with listening to the Dharma, and never abandoned it — and through that I left a body and was born in the heaven free from torment. Venerable one, I was never sated with attending upon the Saṅgha, and never abandoned it — and through that I left a body and was born in the heaven free from torment."

Then, in that very moment, the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud, spoke these verses:

With seeing the Blessed One,
hearing the true Dharma, and attending upon the Saṅgha —
even many times over, I never
grew sated or turned away.

Taking up the noble teachings,
devoted to taming avarice,
through insatiable pursuit of these three things,
Lagavud was born free from torment.

Then the divine son, the herdsman of Lagavud, expressed his delight and rejoicing at what the Blessed One had declared. He touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished then and there.

The monks, having arisen in doubt, asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to cut through every doubt. They said: "Venerable Blessed One, please look upon this: that the yakṣa herdsman of Lagavud, having separated from defilement, took refuge and was established in the bases of training."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, I am now one who is free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion; who is fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, from grief, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation; who is omniscient, who sees all things, who has attained mastery over all knowledge and all objects of knowledge. Is it then any great wonder that the yakṣa herdsman of Lagavud, having separated from defilement, took refuge and was established in the bases of training? In times past, even while I was not yet fully liberated from attachment, aversion, and delusion, from birth, old age, sickness, and death, from grief, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation, the yakṣa herdsman of Lagavud, having separated from defilement, took refuge and was established in the bases of training. Listen now to that.

"Monks, long ago in the city of Vārāṇasī there lived a caravan leader by the name of Great Courage — wealthy, of great riches, with extensive resources, broad and vast in what he held, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivalling Vaiśravaṇa in treasure. At a certain time he set out along a wilderness road together with five hundred merchants. That road was threatened and blocked by a hairy demon. Great Courage then began to advance toward that demon's domain. Now the hairy demon, having openly transformed himself into the appearance of a brahmin, stood in the road and said to Great Courage: 'Caravan leader, this road is threatened and blocked by a hairy demon; I myself have come only with great difficulty — go by another road.' The caravan leader replied: 'Brahmin, be not so faint of heart. What can he do to me? I shall go.' When he had spoken thus, the hairy demon became enraged and changed his form. Stretching out both hands with his matted hair spread out along the ground, making his eyes red and glaring wide with both eyes, he said: 'Caravan leader, come then and attack me — and then leave!' 

"Thereupon Great Courage the caravan leader, seeing how utterly terrifying he was, filled his bow to the ear and began to shoot arrows. But every one of them was caught in the matted hair. He shot the bow itself, and that too was caught. Likewise, spears and clubs and the like that were hurled — all of these too were caught in the matted hair. Then, without hesitation, he pressed forward with all his strength, and his whole body became entangled in the matted hair. The demon then spoke these verses:

Your two hands and two feet,
and fifth, your head as well, are caught;
your very body is caught upon my body —
what is there left that is not caught?

"The caravan leader in turn spoke these verses:

My two hands and two feet,
and fifth, my head as well, are caught;
my very body is caught upon your body —
but what is not caught is my mind.

For as long as my resolve and diligence
remain unbroken in secret,
for that long I will contend with you.
Hold firm — you will not harm me.

"The demon too spoke verses in reply:

To one of such diligence as this,
to you, O Great Courage, I bow.
With such diligence as yours,
you are able to flee from all suffering.
I know there is no other person
who is your equal, O Great Courage."

By your power the merchants
shall go forth in happiness and ease.
You who feel compassion for all beings —
to you, O caravan leader, I bow.
By your power the merchants
shall go forth in perfect peace.

And so it was that there, at that time, the caravan leader of great courage, having heard what he heard from the hairy demon, taught the Dharma in just that way — purifying the hairy demon of defilements and establishing him in the five disciplines.

Monks, the one who was at that time and on that occasion the caravan leader of great courage — that was none other than myself. And the one who was at that time and on that occasion the hairy demon was the yakṣa Drokné. At that time too I purified him of defilements from that very deed and established him in the five disciplines; and now as well I have purified him of defilements from that very deed and established him in the going for refuge and the bases of training.

Then the monks, having grown uncertain, put all their doubts to the Blessed One, the buddha. "Venerable One, what deed did Lakgyü Drokné do such that he was given at birth as a food-offering to a yakṣa, and yet the Blessed One strove to liberate him?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, Lakgyü Drokné accumulated a mass of karma, fully transformed the conditions, remained like a lamp nearby — and having performed and gathered actions that are certain without fail to arise — the karma performed and accumulated by Lakgyü Drokné, who else would experience it individually? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens solely in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Actions do not perish, even over a hundred aeons;
when the conditions and the time are met,
for beings who possess a body,
they will come forth as their fruits.

Monks, in this very great and excellent aeon of the past, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans — the Blessed One Kāśyapa — appeared in the world. He dwelt in reliance upon the Forest of the Sages and the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī. In his dispensation there was a layman.

In a certain mountain retreat there lived a king who was exceedingly fond of a particular bird. Whenever any business at the royal palace arose, he would immediately take that bird on his hand and go before the king. Then one time when some business at the royal palace arose for that layman, he went there in the same way, but the king did not accomplish his purpose. Others then said to him: "This king is fond of birds — if you need your matter accomplished, offer him a bird." He offered the king a bird, and the king, entrusting it to the many birds in the aviary, accomplished that layman's purpose.

The layman then thought: "What I did in offering the bird was wrong — I should buy it back." He paid the aviary keeper a price, freed the bird, and made an aspirational prayer.

"By this wholesome root of having freed the impoverished bird from its captivity — that it might counteract the karma of having offered the bird to the king out of desire for personal gain — may the Blessed One strive to liberate me, who am impoverished and in captivity, to freedom." Such was the aspiration he made.

Monks, the layman of that time and occasion is this one who dwells in the wilderness by way of lineage. The karma of his having offered the bird to the king out of desire for personal gain ripened as his being given as a food-offering to the yakṣas. The karma of his later arising of remorse, his freeing of the bird, and his making of an aspirational prayer ripened such that I strove to liberate him, and I freed him from the yakṣas.

The monks, having arisen in doubt, asked the Blessed One — the buddha, the Bhagavān — who cuts through all doubt, to look into how the one dwelling in the wilderness by way of lineage had been freed from the blue-green yakṣa and established in the fruit of non-return. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is not only now. In the past as well, I freed this one who had a physical body from bondage and established him in the five superknowledges. Listen to this.

"Monks, long ago in Vārāṇasī there was a king named Brahmadatta who caused his kingdom to flourish, to prosper, and to enjoy good fortune year after year. The realm was filled with many people, utterly pacified of strife, conflict, external enemies, and internal discord, and free of thieves, famine, and disease. He caused it to abound in rows of śāli rice and sugarcane, in cattle and buffalo, and as a righteous king endowed with Dharma, he caused the kingdom to be governed by Dharma.

"His court herald took a wife from among women of equal station and sported with her, delighted in her, and made merry with her. At another time, a being entered the womb of this court herald's wife with whom he sported and delighted and made merry. Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth there came a boy whose hands and feet were joined by webbing. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — three times seven days — after the birth they held a great naming celebration, and they deliberated on what name to give the boy. They thought: 'Because this boy's hands and feet are joined by webbing, the boy's name shall be Webbed-Hands-and-Feet.' And so they gave him the name Webbed-Hands-and-Feet.

"Again, at another time, a being entered the womb of this same court herald's wife with whom he sported and delighted and made merry. Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth there came a boy whose hands and feet were not joined by webbing. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day after the birth they held a great naming celebration and deliberated on what name to give the boy. They thought: 'Because this boy's hands and feet have no webbing, the boy's name shall be No-Webbed-Hands-and-Feet.' And so they gave him the name No-Webbed-Hands-and-Feet. The two were raised and reared and grew to be young men.

"When the elder son, Webbed-Hands-and-Feet, saw his father installing the court herald's duties by means of both what was Dharma and what was not Dharma, he thought: 'When I succeed my father and become the court herald, I too will be made to perform the herald's duties by both what is Dharma and what is not Dharma. If I am made to perform the herald's duties by what is Dharma and what is not Dharma and am thereby drawn toward the hell realms, that would be wrong. In every respect I shall go forth.' And so he went to his father and said: 'Father, will you permit me to go forth?' The father said:"

"Son, the herald's duties come to you ready-made — the offerings given, the fire sacrifices performed, the ascetics tormented. Why would you go forth?"

The son spoke these verses in reply:

Wearing robes of bark stripped from trees in the forest, eating fruits,
dwelling with fierce and savage beasts — that I deem the higher life.
A wise one, fearing the world to come, should not for the sake of a kingdom
perform the deeds of killing, binding, and beating — these are wrong to do.

The father, recognizing that the moment had come to yield, gave his permission. The son went among the sages, went forth, and through joy, effort, and striving he came to develop the five supernormal knowledges.

Now the second son, Without-Webbed-Hands-and-Feet, went to another region in search of a secret teaching, for the sake of a secret instruction. Along the southern road, on a certain rocky cliff, there sat a brahmin who had taken a wife of equal caste and was sporting with her, rejoicing and taking his pleasure. While he was sporting and rejoicing with her, his wife bore him a daughter. He thought: "I will not give this daughter away for the sake of caste, nor for wealth. I will give her to one who has recited the four Vedas. Whoever learns the four Vedas from me — to him I will give this daughter."

Now as the brahmin youth Without-Webbed-Hands-and-Feet was wandering about in saṃsāra, he went along the southern road and rested in a certain other direction, weary from the journey. He heard, word passing from one to another, of that brahmin, and he went to him. Speaking face to face, he said: "I wish to serve at the feet of the master. Why? For the sake of reciting the Vedas." "Son, so be it." The youth began to recite the Vedas with him, and being keen and clear in his conduct, within a short time he had fully mastered all four Vedas. Once he had mastered them, that brahmin gave the daughter to him.

When that brahmin youth lay in the upper chamber with her, it happened that the girl's fan fell below. He stretched out his arm like the trunk of an elephant and retrieved it. Seeing this, she was alarmed. Then the lamp went out, and again he stretched out his arm like the trunk of an elephant and revived it. When she saw this as well, she was greatly alarmed and would not sport, rejoice, or take her pleasure at ease with him. The girl said: "Prince, why is it that when you see me you contract your senses and will not sport at ease with me?" The youth said: "Do you see anyone sporting at ease with the lord of death?" The girl said: "Prince, do not be afraid — she has no thought of being unfaithful to her husband." The youth said: "In this matter, I must be mindful of the time."

The girl, frightened, sat while he fell asleep. The youth, without actually sleeping, lay in the manner of one asleep. When the girl perceived that he was asleep, she went in among the women of the household. The youth quietly rose and followed after her. When he saw all those household women disheveled, with hair unbound, sitting in frightful and fearsome postures, he was utterly alarmed and terrified, and he turned back. She too came after him, and he said: "My good woman, I cannot bear to stay — I will go." Seeing that he was absolutely resolved, she knew the moment had come to yield and said: "Prince, if you are truly determined to go, then go — but say nothing to anyone." Without saying a word to anyone, he went to that brahmin and said:

"Brahmin, I have come to you for guidance." The brahmin said: "My son, if that is the case, then go and bring the girl along with you." "Brahmin, it is from that very woman that I flee in fear." "My son, why do you fear her?" "Brahmin, she has no physical form." "My son, why would she be like that?" He said nothing more and went away.

The brahmin then said to the girl: "Daughter, do you not look after your own household?" Her father said to her what the youth had said. "Father," she replied, "he says that I have no physical form." "My daughter, you most certainly do have a physical form. He has slandered you with a grave falsehood and gone away." And he said nothing more and sat in silence.

Now that formless woman, tightly bound all over with a fierce binding, with her limbs and eyes contorted, went along the road and sat down before him and said: "Son of a nursing mother, she asked you to say nothing to anyone — yet you went and said it to her very own father. Now I shall utterly destroy you." And with that she began to do him harm. Terrified, he cried out with a great cry: "Homage to the noble one with webbed hands and feet! Homage to the noble one with webbed hands and feet! Homage!" he called out.

At that moment the goddess who delights in the noble one with webbed hands and feet swiftly went to him and said to the noble one with webbed hands and feet: "Noble one, your younger brother is in danger, in distress, and in pain — please have regard for him." He went there by miraculous power and said to her: "Do not harm this girl. What wrong has she done to you? If I drive her away, she will tell my father that I have no physical form — so I shall consume her. You, be gone." She replied: "This rakṣasī is a wretched creature — it is enough to let her go with a scolding." He said: "Noble one, I will release her by a vow — on the condition that she take ordination." She said: "Sister, let her go — and I will give her ordination." He released her, and she in turn ordained her. He gave her instructions, and with zeal, effort, and exertion she accomplished the five supernormal knowledges.

O monks, he who at that time and on that occasion was the elder son, the one reciting before the assembly, with webbed hands and feet — that was none other than myself. He who at that time and on that occasion was his younger brother without webbed hands and feet — that is this one here, Lagbrug Drogné. She who at that time and on that occasion was the formless woman — that is this one here, Ngobangschen. And at that time too I liberated this Lagbrug Drogné from the formless woman and established him in the five supernormal knowledges. And now likewise I have liberated this one from Ngobangschen and established him in the fruit of non-returning.

When the time came for Lagbrug Drogné, Ngobangschen had gone to Kauśāmbī, and on the very day that Ngobangschen went in search of Lagbrug Drogné among the people of Kauśāmbī, Lagbrug Drogné attained the fruit of non-returning. Saying nothing at all, that girl came back here. This news was heard and passed from one to the next, until the Eastern King of Badsā heard it. He summoned the householder Dangchen and said: "Householder, it is said that on the very day Ngobangschen went in search of Lagbrug Drogné, Lagbrug Drogné attained the fruit of non-returning and that girl came back here without a word being said. Is this true, or is it false?" He replied: "Your Majesty, it is true." "If that is so, why do you not give her to me?" "Your Majesty, I offer her." The king placed her within the retinue of his queen and also gave five hundred female attendants.

Every single day she also gave one thousand kārṣāpaṇas worth of materials for incense and garlands. She was also given a fine mansion called the Flower Porch. She had an attendant girl named Sgur Mchog, and every day that attendant would spend one thousand kārṣāpaṇas to purchase incense and garland materials. Then at some other time she began keeping company with a young incense-seller, and of the thousand kārṣāpaṇas he received each day, he would spend five hundred on flowers, incense, and garlands, while the other five hundred he spent on food and drink together with her.

Now, that young incense-seller was a man of faith. He invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to another house for the midday meal, and he said to Sgur Mchog: "I have invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to another house for the midday meal; you too should come and make preparations." That very night she readied clean and pure food and drink, rose early in the morning, spread the seats, set out water vessels, and sent the invitation. She invited the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable one, please consider lending your presence at the midday hour. Blessed One, please consider that the time has now arrived." Then the Blessed One put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and Dharma robe, and surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the Saṅgha of monks going before him, he proceeded to the place appointed by the young incense-seller and took his seat on the prepared seat at the head of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the young incense-seller, together with Sgur Mchog, perceived that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, and with their own hands they satisfied and refreshed them with clean and pure food and drink. Having in many ways satisfied and refreshed them with their own hands with clean and pure food and drink, and knowing that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks had finished the midday meal and that the bowls had been set aside, Sgur Mchog took a low seat and sat in the presence of the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, having fully known Sgur Mchog's intention, her latent tendencies, her constitution, and her character, and having heard what had occurred, taught the Dharma to her as she sat on that very seat in such a way that it would cause her to individually and correctly realize the Four Noble Truths — striking down with the vajra of gnosis the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection that she had accumulated since beginningless time, and thereby directly producing the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, she spoke thus:

"Venerable one, by relying on the Blessed One as my virtuous friend, what the Blessed One has done for me here is something that neither my father did for me, nor my mother, nor the king, nor the gods, nor my ancestors of old, nor the śramaṇas and brahmins, nor my friends and companions, nor the company of my relatives. He has dried up the ocean of blood and tears; he has liberated me from the mountains of bones; he has sealed shut the doors of the lower rebirths; he has opened the doors of the higher realms and liberation; he has lifted my foot out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; he has placed me among gods and humans; he has brought cyclic existence to its end. Having struck down with the vajra of gnosis the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I have entered the stream. Venerable one, I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. I request to be accepted as a laywoman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge with sincere and wholehearted devotion."

Then the Blessed One taught the Dharma to the two of them and departed.

Śrīgupta spoke to the young incense-seller: "Son of my lord, now please present me with goods worth a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, taking nothing that has not been given — not so much as another person's sesame husk — without the taint of theft."

The boy replied, "By all means, gladly," and gave him goods worth a thousand kārṣāpaṇas.

The boy took them and went to Śyāmāvatī's palace. She asked, "Śrīgupta, how did you come to sleep with your head turned away tonight?"

He replied, "My lady, I used to steal. But now I have understood a quality of such a kind that henceforth I will never again engage in afflictions of that sort."

She asked, "And what did you do today?" Since she was one who retained what she heard, he related the occasion to her in full.

She then said, "Śrīgupta, you must go and hear the Dharma in the Blessed One's presence, and then tell it to me. That is your task."

He replied, "My lady, it shall be done."

Thereupon Śrīgupta heard the Dharma in the Blessed One's presence and related it to her.

The Blessed One had asked Śrīgupta, "Śrīgupta, do you teach the Dharma to the queen's retinue?"

Śrīgupta answered, "Blessed One, you teach; I teach as you teach, standing before them, and they come and listen."

The Blessed One declared: "If they ask you, 'Śrīgupta, teach us the Dharma,' you should say, 'I will not teach.' And why? Because the Blessed One completed the six perfections over three immeasurable eons, through hundreds of thousands of acts of austerity, and thereby came to know unsurpassable knowledge. How then could I teach to those among you who show no reverence, who are without the proper grounds of respect, and who are seated on thrones higher than mine? That is what you should say."

Some time later, Śrīgupta heard the Dharma in the Blessed One's presence and entered among the queen's retinue. They said to him, "Śrīgupta, teach us the Dharma."

He replied, "I will not teach."

"Why not?"

"Because the Blessed One completed the six perfections over three immeasurable eons, through hundreds of thousands of acts of austerity, and thereby came to know unsurpassable knowledge. How then could I teach to those among you who show no reverence, who are without the proper grounds of respect, and who are seated on thrones higher than mine?"

When Śyāmāvatī heard this, she had a lion throne set up. Others spread woolen cushions, and still others raised and arranged them accordingly. Śrīgupta sat upon the lion throne, and taught them what he had heard. Through this, Śyāmāvatī and the other five hundred women gained a profound understanding: some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, and some the fruit of non-returning. Such was the Dharma teaching he gave.

These women then gave rise to faith born from the cause of the Dharma through Śrīgupta, and they spoke to the eastern king of Bādrā: "Lord, we wish to see the Buddha."

He replied, "So it shall be," and saying, "Let us go into the presence of the Blessed One," he went to where the Blessed One was. He arrived, bowed with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, and sat to one side.

Sitting to one side, the king of Bādrā addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, the retinue of the court wishes to see the Blessed One."

The Blessed One then declared:

"Great King, Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not enter into the inner quarters of the royal consorts."

The king went and told the women this. Then Śrīgupta spoke: "Lord, if the Blessed One will not come into the inner quarters of the consorts, then let many windows be opened in the wall of the flowering palace, and please allow us to look upon the Blessed One through the windows."

The king had five hundred windows opened in the wall of the flowering palace. When the Blessed One came in that direction, those women of the royal retinue saw the Blessed One through the windows and made offerings and showed reverence, scattering flowers, incense, garments, and garlands of blossoms.

Now, a wandering merchant named Many-Colored Tamer had a wife named Burma, and she gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful, lovely, and fair, possessed of every perfect limb and feature, whose bones were so fine and delicate that no comparison could be made. Her relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day they held a great birth celebration, and they deliberated on what name to give the girl. The relatives said: "This girl is beautiful, lovely, and fair, possessed of every perfect limb and feature, and her bones are so fine and delicate that no comparison can be made. Because she is beyond compare, let her name be Incomparable," and so they gave her the name Incomparable.

She was nursed and raised and grew to be a young woman. Her mother thought: "I will not give this daughter of mine to anyone merely on account of lineage, nor for wealth, nor for learning. I will give her only to one who equals or surpasses her in beauty."

At that time the Blessed One was traveling through the land of Kuru, and coming to Many-Colored Tamer he stayed in the town of Many-Colored Tamer in the land of Kuru. Then in the early morning the Blessed One put on his lower robe, took his alms bowl and Dharma robe, and entered Many-Colored Tamer for alms. Having completed his alms round in Many-Colored Tamer and taken his meal, he returned from the subsequent alms round, arranged his seat according to custom, and leaned against a tree, sitting cross-legged like a lion at rest.

At that time, Incomparable had gone out to gather flowers and firewood. From a great distance she saw the Blessed One — beautiful, inspiring faith, his faculties calm, his mind serene, perfectly tame in spirit, abiding in perfect peace — blazing like a golden shrine tree. Seeing him, joy and supreme delight arose in her, and she thought: "A mendicant as beautiful and inspiring as this would be worthy to be master of all of Jambudvīpa — to say nothing of being master of Incomparable, for I have found a husband." Recognizing this, she went to her home and spoke to her mother: "Good woman, know this: I have found a husband for my daughter. Adorn her and give Incomparable to him."

She asked, "To whom shall she be given?"

He replied, "To the mendicant Gautama."

She asked, "How shall we proceed?"

And just then, right there on the road, as they set out together, a thought arose in him, and he spoke these verses:

"I, a brahmin, saw that great sage
entering Many-Colored Tamer for alms —"

The ground where he had stepped turned red, and when he lifted his foot, even the low ground rose up high. The householder said to the young man: "Do not rely upon her. Go back and proceed to your own enclosure." And he too spoke a verse:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,
even then one would go on enjoying sensual pleasures."

Then they adorned Incomparable with garments and ornaments, and set out to meet the noble one. But the Blessed One had already departed from that grove to another grove. At that moment, the wandering mendicant saw a seat of grass that had been spread out for the Blessed One. Upon seeing it, he spoke to his wife: "Good woman, know this: this is the seat of grass spread out for our daughter's bridegroom." And he spoke a verse:

"The bed of one filled with attachment is disturbed.
The bed of one filled with aversion is full of doubt and restlessness.
The bed of one filled with delusion ends up at the foot of the feet.
This one is the resting place of one utterly free from attachment.
The householder said to the young man: Do not rely upon her.
Go back and proceed to your own enclosure."

And he too spoke a verse:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,
even then one would go on enjoying sensual pleasures."

Then the wandering mendicant saw the footprints of the Blessed One. Upon seeing them, he spoke to his wife: "Good woman, these are the footprints of our daughter's bridegroom." And he spoke a verse:

"The footprints of a man filled with attachment are not clear.
The footprints of one filled with aversion are sunken deep.
The footprints of one filled with delusion are scattered and disordered.
The footprints of one utterly free from attachment are like these.
The householder said to the young man: Do not rely upon her.
Go back and proceed to your own enclosure."

And he too spoke a verse:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,
even then one would go on enjoying sensual pleasures."

Then the Blessed One cleared his throat, and the wandering mendicant heard the sound of the Blessed One clearing his throat. Upon hearing it, he spoke to his wife: "Good woman, this is the sound of our daughter's bridegroom clearing his throat." And he spoke a verse:

"The voice of a man filled with attachment is rough and harsh.
The voice of a man filled with aversion is coarse.
The voice of a man filled with delusion is confused and agitated.
This drum-sound of Brahmā is a buddha.
The householder said to the young man: Do not rely upon her.
Go back and proceed to your own enclosure."

And he too spoke a verse:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,
even then one would go on enjoying sensual pleasures."

Then the Blessed One, from quite a distance, cast his gaze upon the wandering mendicant, and the wandering mendicant saw the Blessed One looking at him. Upon seeing this, he spoke to his wife: "Good woman, this is our daughter's bridegroom, looking." And he spoke a verse:

"A man filled with attachment looks with darting, flickering glances.
A man filled with aversion looks like a fierce venomous serpent.
A man filled with delusion looks as though groping in darkness.
One utterly free from attachment looks with a gaze steady as a balance-beam.
The householder said to the young man: Do not rely upon her.
Go back and proceed to your own enclosure."

And he too spoke a verse:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,

she will only go back to indulging in sensual pleasures."

The Blessed One was walking in meditation, and a wandering woman chanced to see the Blessed One as he walked. Having seen him, she said to her husband: "My good man, this is the son-in-law of a girl — he is out walking."

She spoke a verse:

"How he looks with those eyes, and how he walks with that steady, composed bearing,
how his complexion and face
appear utterly free from dust and stain —
householder, do not rely on that young man.
Go back and proceed to your own enclosure."

And he too spoke verses:

"Alas, inauspicious daughter-in-law, you are unlucky!
At an auspicious time, do not speak of inauspiciousness.
If one were to take her by means of an ascetic vow,
she will only go back to indulging in sensual pleasures.
The settled golden Otala trees too
are bewildered by desire for the sake of a son,
and by offering this in accordance with Dharma,
the sages have perpetually and continuously fathered children."

Then the wandering woman went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"My noble daughter, possessed of beautiful form,
adorned with silks, seeking her heart's desire —
I offer her to you; look upon her,
as one looks upon the autumn moon amidst the heavens —
rejoice well together with her, I pray."

The Blessed One reflected: "If I were to speak words of affection toward the Incomparable One, there would arise a situation in which the Incomparable One, tormented by attachment, would bring about her own end. Therefore I should speak words of anger toward her." Recognizing this, he declared a verse:

"Brahmin, I have defeated the daughters of Māra —
Craving, Delight, and Pleasure —
and not once, toward all those objects of desire,
have I ever generated a mind of longing.
As for this body filled with urine and excrement,
I feel no inclination even to touch it with my foot."

The mother then offered a verse:

"Do you see my daughter as deficient in beauty,
lacking in desirable qualities?
As you are strongly inclined toward pleasing forms fit for sensual enjoyment,
why do you not act toward her likewise?"

The Blessed One in turn declared verses:

"Brahmin, the deluded one who is attached to sense-objects —
it is your daughter who cultivates that state,
who has entered into attachment and anger toward objects.
A person deeply deluded like this is not free from attachment.
I am the buddha, the chief among sages, sovereign lord;
I have attained unsurpassed, peaceful awakening.
Just as a lotus is unstained by water,
I move through the world without attachment.
As a blue lotus born in mud and water
is unstained by the mud and water,
so too, brahmin, do I move through the world,
engaging with objects of desire with a mind fully liberated."

Then the Incomparable One, having been addressed by the Blessed One with the words "urine and excrement," was stripped of her satisfaction and became inwardly uncomfortable. The entire binding web of her attachment was dissolved, and aversion arose, causing her bones to become prominent and her two eyes to become sunken like those of a skull.

At that moment, an aged woman happened to be seated at the edge of the Blessed One's robe. That aged woman then addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"O All-seeing One, you have accepted a woman.
Blessed One, grant her to me, I pray.
O Hero, this one adorned with pride —
I shall pursue her in a way that is pleasing."

When she had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed that aged woman:

"You deluded creature, get away from my presence!"

Angered, she spoke a verse:

"May this begging bowl of yours and this Dharma robe of yours,
and these round lumps of food as well, all be exhausted!
May this training of yours likewise become like that of a mother —"

"— embracing one as young as a child in one's arms."

Having spoken those words, the aged woman surrendered her training, entered the state of one who has fallen away, and went to where there was a wandering woman named Madugā. Arriving there, she said to the wandering woman Madugā: "Madugā, matchless one — give her to me." Madugā, angered, replied: "Old woman, I would not even give you a glance — let alone a touch, what need is there to speak of it?" When she had spoken thus, such a state of total anguish arose in that aged woman that she vomited hot blood, and when her time came, she died and was reborn in the hells.

Here ends the seventy-sixth fascicle of the Vinayavibhaṅga.

Doubts having arisen among the monks, they asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to resolve all doubts. "Venerable Blessed One, consider the time when Madugā, the matchless one, was found and taken in."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is not only now. In the past as well, when I found her, I did not take her. Listen to this.

Monks, long ago there was a blacksmith living on a certain rocky crag. He had taken a wife of equal birth, and together with her he sported, rejoiced, and lived in delight. While he was thus sporting, rejoicing, and living in delight with her, at another time his wife conceived. Eight or nine months passed, and she gave birth — a daughter was born, beautiful of form, lovely and fair to look upon. He raised and nurtured her, and she grew up.

The blacksmith thought: 'I will not give this daughter to just anyone — not on account of family, not on account of beauty, not on account of wealth. Rather, I will give her only to one whose craft equals or surpasses my own.'

Now, as it happened, a young brahmin entered his house to beg for alms. The daughter, carrying food, came out. The young brahmin saw her and said: 'Girl, have you given to anyone, or not?' She replied: 'According to what my father says, it would be hard for him to give me to anyone at all.' 'What does your father say?' 'My father says: I will not give this daughter to just anyone — not on account of family, not on account of beauty, not on account of wealth — but only to one whose craft equals or surpasses my own.' 'And what craft does your father know?' 'He knows how to forge needles that float upon water.'

The young brahmin thought: 'Though I have no need of this matter myself, I will break her pride.' Since he was skilled, he went to the various workshops and workplaces, examined the blacksmith's tools, and forged needles of the kind that float upon water — and in addition forged one thick needle, and threaded seven fine needles through its eye, all floating together upon the water. Having forged these, he came to the blacksmith's house and called out: 'Buy needles! Buy needles!'

The daughter saw him and spoke a verse:

"Friend, have you gone mad,
or have you lost your senses?
Why have you come to sell needles
here in a blacksmith's house?"

He too spoke in verse:

"Good lady, I have not gone mad,
nor have I lost my senses.
It was to break your pride
that I applied myself to the craft.
If your father should recognize
that my craft is equal to his,
then give me yourself and wealth besides —
many other things as well."

She said: "And what craft do you know?"

He replied: "I know how to make needles that float on water like those."

He whispered to her mother: "Dear lady, there is a young craftsman here." She said: "Let him come in." When he was let in, the blacksmith's wife asked: "What craft do you know?" He told her, and she in turn whispered to her husband: "This young man, the son of a noble lord, wishes to display such-and-such a craft." The husband said: "If that is so, bring some water and let us see." She filled a vessel with water and offered it to him. He placed one needle in it, and it began to float. Likewise, when he placed the second needle, and so on up to the seventh, they too began to float. He placed the thick needle in, and it too began to float. Then he placed one needle there in a different manner, and even so it began to float. Likewise, he placed the second, and so on up to the seventh in that other manner, and even so they began to float.

The blacksmith thought to himself: "This one's craft surpasses my own; I shall give him my daughter." Knowing this, he adorned his daughter with all her ornaments, took her hand in his left hand, held a ball of lac in his right hand, sat down before that brahmin youth, and said: "Young brahmin, I give this girl to you as your wife."

The youth replied: "I have no desire for this. I did all of this only to break your pride and to demonstrate my craft to you."

"O monks, he who was the brahmin youth at that time and on that occasion — that was none other than myself. He who was the blacksmith at that time and on that occasion — that is this wanderer Māra. She who was the blacksmith's wife at that time and on that occasion — that is Burmā. And she who was the blacksmith's daughter at that time and on that occasion — that is this Upamā. And just as I found Upamā then and did not take her, so even now I have found her and have not taken her."

Again, doubts arose among the monks, and having doubts they addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha, to resolve them all: "Venerable one, look upon how this elder, on account of Upamā, comes to suffer through improper conduct."

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, it is not only now. In times past as well, on account of Upamā, he fell into suffering through improper conduct together with a queen and her retinue. Listen to this.

"O monks, long ago, in a certain royal palace like a lion's hall, there reigned a king named Siṃhakeśarī — Lion-Maned — whose realm was prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and subjects. Foreign enemies and internal strife were thoroughly pacified; the realm was free from thieves, famine, and disease; and he caused it to abound in rows of śāli rice and sugar cane, in cattle and buffalo. He was a righteous man, a righteous king, who caused his kingdom to be governed according to the Dharma.

"At that time, in that same royal palace like a lion's hall, there lived a merchant chief named Siṃha — the Lion — who was wealthy, richly endowed with possessions, of vast and extensive holdings, with wealth to rival the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, the son of the All-Hearing, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa himself in riches. He took a wife from among those of equal station, and with her he played, rejoiced, and took his pleasure. While he played with her, rejoiced with her, and took his pleasure, a being entered the womb of his wife.

"Now, there are certain women who are skilled in the ways of women and who possess five unmistakable qualities. What are these five? They know when a man has developed attachment and when he has ceased to be attached; they know the proper time and recognize the lunar signs; they know when a being has entered the womb; they know from whom a being has entered the womb; and —"

they know whether a being is male or female. If it is male, the being rests leaning to the right side of the womb; if it is female, it rests leaning to the left.

She was glad and rejoiced, and she said to her husband: "My lord's son should know that a being has entered my womb, and since it rests leaning to my right side, it will certainly be a boy." He too was glad and rejoiced, and he made this solemn declaration, saying aloud: "For long have I desired to see the face of a son — one who is born in harmony with me and not discordant with me, one who will carry on my affairs, one who will repay the care I give him, one who will enjoy his inheritance, and one who will cause my lineage to endure for a long time. And when we have died and the proper time has come, may he give gifts — whether few or many — and make merit, and may he follow us both to whatever realm we are reborn in, reciting the dedication of merit by name." When he realized a being had entered the womb, in order to bring to full maturity the one dwelling in the womb, he arranged that the upper chambers of the fine house served as her quarters: when it was cold, she was attended with things that bring warmth; when it was warm, with things that bring coolness. The physician-prescribed food was not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too hot, and not too pungent — free from the extremes of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, heat, and pungency. She was adorned with necklaces and garlands, her body bedecked with ornaments, moving about as if she were a goddess's daughter sporting in a pleasure grove. She was carried from seat to seat, from couch to couch, so that she never set foot on the bare ground, and she never heard even the slightest unpleasant sound. In this way she was attended, entirely without discomfort.

When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth, and the boy who came forth was handsome, beautiful, lovely, and radiant, with a complexion like gold, a head like a parasol, long arms, prominent collarbones at the shoulders, graceful eyebrows, and a high nose-bridge.

His relatives assembled and gathered together, and on the twenty-first day — three weeks of seven days — after the birth, a great birth-feast was held, and they proceeded to give the boy his name. His relatives said: "Because this boy is the son of the caravan leader Siṃha, let his name be Siṃhala." And so he was named Siṃhala.

The boy Siṃhala was entrusted to eight nurses: two who held him in their laps and suckled him, two who gave him milk, two who bathed and cleaned him, and two who played with him and kept him company. These eight nurses nourished him, caused him to grow, and made him flourish swiftly, like a lotus dwelling in a pond. When he had grown up, he entered upon the study of letters, arithmetic, accounting, finger-reckoning, and the arts of giving and receiving and keeping records. He became thoroughly accomplished in writing — in analysing, reading, mastering, and clearly applying it — and he became expert in the eight kinds of appraisal: the appraisal of jewels, appraisal of land, appraisal of cloth, appraisal of carriages, appraisal of elephants, appraisal of horses, appraisal of women, and appraisal of men.

His father then established three households for his wife — superior, middling, and inferior. He had her installed in three seasonal residences — one for winter, one for spring, and one for summer. He had her installed in three seasonal pleasure gardens — one for winter, one for spring, and one for summer.

In the upper mansion, in the inner quarters where no men were present, the women entertained themselves with music, made merry, and enjoyed themselves in delight.

Then, at another time, the young man spoke to his father: "Father, please grant me permission to set out upon the great ocean." His father replied: "Son, I have wealth of many kinds. Even if you were to spend jewels just as freely as one spends sesame, rice, barley, and beans and the like, still my resources would not become thin, be exhausted, or run out. Therefore, for as long as I am alive, take your pleasure, make merry, and enjoy yourself in delight, and when I am gone, then apply yourself to acquiring wealth." But the young man asked again and again: "Father, please grant me permission to set out upon the great ocean." The father, knowing that the time for his passing was surely at hand, said: "Son, let it be so. In this matter, you must endure the dangers and the terrors you will encounter."

The father then had a proclamation announced throughout the royal palace, like the roar of a lion: "Hear this, all wise merchants who dwell in the royal palace and who have come from various lands. The caravan-leader Siṅgāla is about to set out upon the great ocean. Whoever among you wishes to venture into the great ocean together with caravan-leader Siṅgāla — without makeshift rafts, without ropes, without a stitched-together vessel — let them make ready their provisions for the journey to the great ocean." Five hundred merchants made ready their provisions for the journey to the great ocean.

Then the caravan-leader Siṅgāla gazed upon his father and mother and the other dear kinsmen to whom he was bound, and, having chosen a day, a date, an auspicious moment, and a favorable conjunction — auspicious, fortunate, and propitious — he loaded the provisions for the great ocean journey onto carts, pack-loads, and burdens, and onto mules, female elephants, cattle, and many donkeys, and set out accompanied by the retinue of five hundred merchants. Traveling onward through villages, towns, hamlets, districts, and royal residences, surveying the trading centers along the way, he arrived at the shore of the great ocean. There he fitted out five hundred old vessels, took on board those five persons who make their living from the sea — the bailer, the caulker, the ship's carpenter, the chief swimmer, and the one who reads the winds — and after a triple proclamation was made, he set out upon the great ocean.

Then those merchants thought to themselves: "Wise friends, for those of us who are going into the midst of the great ocean, it is difficult to be certain of crossing safely, one and all. We who seek to acquire wealth, each from our own [store of] poverty, have taken up our swimming-boards for use in the water and entered upon the great ocean. Some of us have brought flat boards of the śālmalī tree, some have brought bundles of reeds and wool, some have brought gourd floats, and some have brought goat-skin bladders." And so those wealth-seekers, having thus each made their own reflections, took each from their own poverty's provision their swimming-boards for the water — some carrying flat boards of the śālmalī tree, some carrying bundles of reeds and wool, some carrying gourd floats, and some carrying goat-skin bladders — and entered upon the great ocean.

As they ventured into the midst of the great ocean, sea-monsters of the fish kind wrecked the ocean vessel. When the vessel was wrecked, those who had brought along swimming-boards for the water, each drawn from their own poverty's store, mounted them accordingly: some rode upon the flat boards of the śālmalī tree, some rode upon bundles of reeds and wool, some rode upon gourd floats,

and some rode upon goat-skin bladders, floating upon the water.

By the karmic maturation of their deeds, a wind arose from the north and drove them to the southern shore. On the copper-colored island there dwelt rākṣasīs known as Young Cranes, and these began to deceive the shipwrecked merchants with sweet words and joyful airs. They had two kinds of victory-banners: one suited to a place of joy, and one suited to a place of poverty. As soon as they began waving the victory-banner suited to a place of joy, they called out: "Dear brothers, the ocean vessel of the merchants of Jambudvīpa was wrecked by sea-monsters of the fish kind — come, come without delay, we are searching for you along the shore!" And so they began searching along the ocean shore.

Then the rākṣasīs saw a great mass of ordinary people swimming toward them on all manner of swimming-boards. Seeing them, they transformed themselves into the appearance of beautiful women, adorned themselves with various ornaments, draped themselves in divine garments and garlands of flowers, and began calling from the ocean shore: "Come hither, masters! Come hither, fair-faced ones! Be the husbands of those of us who have no husbands! Be the lords of those who have no lord! Be the home of those who have no home! Be the island of those who have no island! Be the protector of those who have no protector! Be the refuge of those who have no refuge! Be the ally of those who have no ally! Here are your sources of food, your sources of drink, your sources of clothing, your sources of lodging, pleasure gardens that will delight you, forests that will delight you, lotus ponds that will delight you — and here are the many precious things of Jambudvīpa: jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, the essence of stone, rubies, red gems, and right-spiraling conches. Come hither! Sport with us, rejoice with us, and make merry with us! But let none of you, even if you become very drunk, ever walk southward." This is what they said.

The Blessed One then declared: "O monks, I have not seen any other form by which the form of a woman so captivates a man, so intoxicates him, so fills him with desire, so becomes dear to him, so engenders affection, so brings on infatuation, so stupefies him, so binds him, so enthralls him, and so thoroughly engages him."

When the rākṣasīs called out to them in this way, the men crossed the great ocean and went to sport with them, to rejoice with them, and to make merry with them. Through their consorting with those rākṣasīs in sport, rejoicing, and merriment, sons and daughters were born.

Then the navigator Siṃhala thought to himself: "Why do these women guard the southern road so vigilantly?" He resolved that he would sleep together with one of these women, and when he knew she had fallen asleep and gone to bed, he very quietly and slowly slipped out of the great bed, tucked a sharp sword under his arm, and set off southward.

Then the navigator Siṃhala, having known that the woman with whom he lay had fallen asleep and gone to bed, very quietly and slowly slipped out of the great bed, tucked a sharp sword under his arm, and set off southward. There he heard the sound of a great many people wailing and lamenting: "Alas, father! Alas, mother! Alas, brothers! Alas, sisters! O you who will rejoice in Jambudvīpa in every varied way — you who will rejoice in Jambudvīpa, have you abandoned us?" Hearing this, he was seized with fear, dread, terror, and his hair stood on end.

Then the navigator Siṃhala sat for a little while without saying a word, and when he had dispelled that fear, dread, terror, and the standing of hair on end, he continued along that same southern road. There he saw a great iron city, tall and broad. Thinking there might be some window in that city, he went all the way around it, but going all the way around that city he could not find so much as an opening through which a cat might enter.

On the northern face of that city there stood great tall and broad śirīṣa trees. He climbed one of those great tall and broad śirīṣa trees and addressed that great multitude of people in these words: "O wise ones, why do you wail and lament so grievously — 'Alas, father! Alas, mother! Alas, brothers! Alas, sisters! O you who will rejoice in Jambudvīpa in every varied way — you who will rejoice in Jambudvīpa, have you abandoned us?'"

They replied: "O patient one, we are merchants of Jambudvīpa who sought wealth, fitted out a ship for the ocean, and desired to venture out onto the great ocean. We thought to ourselves: 'O wise ones, it is very difficult to cross the great ocean safely and with certainty. Therefore, we wealth-seeking merchants, each providing according to our means for the sake of the destitute, took flotation devices and set out upon the great ocean. Some among us brought planks of the śalmali tree; some brought logs of thorn-covered wood; some brought gourds; and some brought goat-hide floats.' Then we merchants, having each thus deliberated and each taken a flotation device according to his means for the sake of the destitute — some taking śalmali planks, some taking logs of thorn-covered wood, some taking gourds, and some taking goat-hide floats — entered the great ocean. While we were venturing into the great ocean, sea-monsters of the fish species smashed our ship. When our ship was smashed, we mounted the flotation devices we had each brought for the sake of the destitute — some riding on śalmali planks, some on logs of thorn-covered wood, some on gourds, and some on goat-hide floats — and drifted upon the water. By the karmic maturation of our actions, a wind arose from the north and drove us to the southern shore. Here on this copper island there dwell rākṣasīs known as 'Young Cranes,' who deceive us shipwrecked merchants with fair words and pleasing displays. They have two kinds of banners: one that corresponds to a place of joy, and one that corresponds to a place of misfortune. Just as soon as they began to wave the banner that corresponds to the place of joy, those rākṣasīs said:"

"Dear brothers, the banner corresponding to the place of joy has been waved! The ships of the merchants of Jambudvīpa have been wrecked by the sea-monsters, and those who were not lost outright have been sought — come, we are searching for them along the shore!" And with those words they began to search along the seashore. Before long, they caught sight of us — a great multitude of ordinary merchants drifting in on various floats. When they saw us, they each manifested a beautiful form, adorned themselves with varied ornaments, wrapped garlands of flower-strands about them, and draped themselves in divine garments. Then, from the shore, they began to call out: "Come hither, masters! Come hither, fair ones! Be husbands to those of us who have no husbands! Be lords to those of us who have no lords! Be a home to those of us who have no home! Be an island to those of us who have no island! Be a protector to those of us who have no protector! Be a refuge to those of us who have no refuge! Be companions-in-arms to those of us who have no companions-in-arms! Here you will find places of food and places of drink, places of clothing and places of lodging; pleasure groves that bring delight, and woodland gardens that bring delight, and lotus-ponds that bring delight; and the many precious things of Jambudvīpa — gems and pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, essences of stone, conch shells, red gems, and right-spiraling shells. Come hither! Take pleasure with us, take joy with us, make merry with us! And though any among you may become utterly intoxicated, do not go southward!" they said.

We were enticed by those rākṣasīs, crossed the great ocean to them, and took pleasure with them, took joy with them, and made merry with them. From our consorting with them as we sported and rejoiced and made merry, sons and daughters were also born. Those women sported with us and took joy with us and made merry with us — and so it continued, until the time when we heard that yet more merchants of Jambudvīpa, their ships wrecked by the sea-monsters, were coming. At the moment those women heard that a very great number of other merchants of Jambudvīpa were coming, their ships wrecked by the sea-monsters, they came in among us and ate those others; and when they devoured a man in this fashion, they left not even the remnants of hair, body-hair, nails, and teeth — none of it was left. And when they devoured those men, whatever drops of warm blood fell upon the ground, those too they licked up with their fingertips, again and again, and placed in their mouths along with the dirt. As for those who had not yet been eaten — that was ourselves. They put us in this great iron fortress, and: 'Know this, patient one — those patient women are rākṣasīs, so protect yourself!' Siṃhala then said: 'O wise ones, is there any means by which both you and I might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being?' They replied: 'Patient one, we know of no means whatsoever by which we might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being.' 'And why is that?'

'If we were to think, "Let us tunnel beneath this iron fortress and escape," it would redouble and treble underneath. If we were to think, "Let us scale over the top of this iron fortress and escape," it would redouble and treble on top. And so, patient one, that is why there is no means whatsoever by which we might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being. But for you there is a means by which you might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being.' 'O wise ones, what is that means by which we might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being?' 'Patient one, we have heard from above the sound of gods moving through the air, proclaiming this: "Ho, you foolish merchants of Jambudvīpa! On this very day, the fifteenth day of the restoration ceremony, make for the northern road! There stands the king of horses, named Cloud-Swift, who has been eating the grain of unharvested, unsown rice, and is well-fed, healthy, strong, and with his senses fully satisfied, standing with his upper body raised — who will go across? Who will go across? Who is to be carried across? Who is to travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being?" — this proclamation made three times, three times deliberately. Go to where that horse stands and say these words: "We will go across! We will go across! Take us across! Bring us to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being!" That, patient one, is the means by which you might travel to Jambudvīpa in safety and well-being.'

Then the caravan-leader Siṃhala took those words spoken by the assembled common folk firmly to heart, committed them to memory, and quietly, slowly and gently descended from that great śirīṣa tree and went back to that very same bed. Then, perceiving that the woman with whom the caravan-leader Siṃhala had been sleeping was sound asleep and settled in bed, he lay down quietly, softly and gently. Then the caravan-leader Siṃhala rose early the next morning and went to where the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa were gathered, and having gone there he addressed the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa with these words: 'O wise ones, come here. In a secluded garden grove there is a matter I must discuss with you privately and confidentially. And if any among you should become very inebriated, do not bring any boys or girls along.' Then the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa rose early the next morning and went to where the secluded garden grove was.

Then the caravan-leader Siṃhala recounted in full to the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa everything that had been said in the interval by the assembled common folk, and said: 'O wise ones, these are not women — these are rākṣasīs, so protect yourselves!'

Then the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa set out on the northern road on that very fifteenth day of the restoration ceremony. At that time the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, was there, eating the grain of unharvested, unsown rice. A merchant who was of a steady disposition saw the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, eating the grain of unharvested, unsown rice, and having seen him, said this to the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa:

'O wise ones, the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, is standing here eating the grain of unharvested, unsown rice. Go to him and say these words: "We will cross to the other shore! We will cross to the other shore! Carry us to the other shore! Bring us safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa!" — this is what you must say.'

Then the caravan-leader Siṃhala spoke these words to the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa: 'O wise ones, having understood what was said by that great assembly of common folk, it is now time for us to go to the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, and say these words: "We will cross to the other shore! We will cross to the other shore! Carry us to the other shore! Bring us safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa!" — the time for saying this has not yet passed. For I have understood what that great assembly of common folk said: when the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, has eaten the grain of unharvested, unsown rice and is comfortable, healthy, full of strength, and with his senses satisfied, he will lift his upper body and call out three times, solemnly and deliberately: "Who will cross to the other shore? Who will cross to the other shore? Who shall be carried to the other shore? Who shall be brought safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa?" — and at that very moment we must go to the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, and say: "We will cross to the other shore! We will cross to the other shore! Carry us to the other shore! Bring us safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa!" — this is what must be said.'

Then the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, having eaten the grain of unharvested, unsown rice, comfortable, healthy, full of strength, and with his senses satisfied, lifted his upper body and called out three times, solemnly and deliberately: 'Who will cross to the other shore? Who will cross to the other shore? Who shall be carried to the other shore? Who shall be brought safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa?'

Then the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa went to where the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, was standing, and having arrived, they arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in reverence toward the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, bowed, and spoke these words to the king of horses, Cloud-Swift: 'We will cross to the other shore! We will cross to the other shore! Carry us to the other shore! Bring us safely and in wellbeing to Jambudvīpa!'

Then the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, spoke to the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa: 'O wise ones, those women, having made themselves even more beautiful, even more lovely to behold, even more enchanting, and taking up boys and girls, will call out: "O lords, come here! O fair-faced ones, come here! Be the husbands of those of us who have no husbands! Be the masters of those who have no master! Be the home of those who have no home! Be the island refuge of those who have no island refuge! Be the protector of those who have no protector! Be the shelter of those who have no shelter! Be the ally of those who have no ally! These are your places of food, your places of drink, your places of clothing, your places of lodging; these are gardens that will bring you delight, groves that will bring you delight, ponds that will bring you delight —'

these many precious things of Jambudvīpa — jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, the essence of stone, conch, carnelian, and right-coiling shells — bring them here! Come and play with us, rejoice with us, and make merry with us! But if none of you will trouble yourselves on our behalf, then take your boys and girls and depart, each to his own.'

Now, those among you who think: 'These are my wife, my son, my daughter — these are my places of food, my places of drink, my places of clothing, my places of lodging, these are the gardens that bring delight, the groves that bring delight, the ponds that bring delight — these many precious things of Jambudvīpa: jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, the essence of stone, conch, carnelian, and right-coiling shells' — those men will have mounted upon my back or ridden in my wake, yet they shall fall just as ripe fruit tumbles from the tips of branches, and those women shall come again and again and devour them. When they devour a man in this way, they shall eat without leaving a single hair, a single body-hair, a single nail, or the least remnant of teeth. And when they devour a man, whatever drops of warm blood fall to the ground they shall scrape up again and again with their fingertips along with the very earth and push them into their mouths.

But those among you who do not think: 'These are my wife, my son, my daughter — these are my places of food, my places of drink, my places of clothing, my places of lodging, these are the gardens that bring delight, the groves that bring delight, the ponds that bring delight — these many precious things of Jambudvīpa: jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, the essence of stone, conch, carnelian, and right-coiling shells' — those men, even if they have grasped my very hairs, shall arrive safely and happily in Jambudvīpa.'

Having thus instructed them well, fully, and correctly, the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, waited. Then, of those very many merchants of Jambudvīpa, some mounted upon the back of Cloud-Swift, some rode in his wake, and some grasped hold of his hairs.

Then the king of horses, Cloud-Swift, gradually mustered the full force and strength of his body, and flew upward into the sky above. The rākṣasīs began to wave their banners of destitution and longing, and thought: 'From their waving of the banners of destitution and longing that accord with our nature, surely the very many merchants of Jambudvīpa will become separated from us and fall away!' And so they transformed themselves into forms yet more beautiful, yet more lovely to behold, yet more radiant, and taking boys and girls in their arms they cried out: 'O lords, come here! O fair-faced ones, come here! Be the husbands of those of us who have no husbands! Be the masters of those who have no master! Be the home of those who have no home! Be the island refuge of those who have no island refuge!

Be the protector of those who have no protector! Be the refuge of those who have no refuge! Be the ally of those who have no ally! These here shall be your sources of food, your sources of drink, your sources of clothing, your sources of lodging, your sources of delight in pleasure groves, your sources of delight in forests, your sources of delight in lotus ponds — and the many precious things of Jambudvīpa, namely: jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, essences of stone, conch shell, carnelian, and right-coiling shells — come, take them! Come, sport with us, take pleasure with us, make merry with us! But if none of you will look after us at all, then at least take these boys and girls of yours and depart!'

Now among those merchants, those who thought: 'My wife, or my son, or my daughter, or sources of food, or sources of drink, or sources of clothing, or sources of lodging, or sources of delight in pleasure groves, or sources of delight in forests, or sources of delight in lotus ponds — or the many precious things of Jambudvīpa, namely: jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, essences of stone, conch shell, carnelian, and right-coiling shells — these are truly mine' — those men, even though they had already mounted upon the trail and the path away from the rākṣasīs, fell down like ripe fruits dropping from the tips of branches, and the rākṣasī women came again and again and devoured them. When they devoured a man, they consumed without remainder even whatever hair, body hair, nails, and remnants of teeth there were. And when they devoured the men, whatever drops of warm blood fell to the ground, those too they licked up with the tips of their fingers, again and again, together with the earth itself, and put them in their mouths.

But among those merchants, those who did not think: 'My wife, or my son, or my daughter, or sources of food, or sources of drink, or sources of clothing, or sources of lodging, or sources of delight in pleasure groves, or sources of delight in forests, or sources of delight in lotus ponds — or the many precious things of Jambudvīpa, namely: jewels, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, silver, gold, essences of stone, conch shell, carnelian, and right-coiling shells — these are mine' — those men, even though the rākṣasīs had already seized hold of their body hair, arrived safely and in well-being in Jambudvīpa.

O monks, in the same way, those of you who think: 'I am the eye. It is my eye. I am the ear. I am the nose. I am the tongue. I am the body. I am the mind. It is my mind. I am form. It is my form. I am sound. I am smell. I am taste. I am touch. I am phenomena. They are my phenomena. I am the earth element. It is my earth element. I am the water element. I am the fire element. I am the wind element. I am the space element. I am the consciousness element. It is my consciousness element. I am the aggregate of form. It is my aggregate of form. I am the aggregate of feeling. I am the aggregate of perception. I am the aggregate of formations. I am the aggregate of consciousness. It is my aggregate of consciousness' — those monks are just like the merchants who were made to suffer by the rākṣasīs.

Those monks among you who do not think 'I am the eye. It is my eye. I am the ear. I am the nose. I am the tongue. I am the body. I am the mind. It is my mind. I am form. It is my form. I am sound. I am smell. I am taste. I am touch. I am phenomena. They are my phenomena. I am the earth element. It is my earth element. I am the water element. I am the fire element. I am the wind element. I am the space element. I am the consciousness element. It is my consciousness element. I am the aggregate of form. It is my aggregate of form. I am the aggregate of feeling. I am the aggregate of perception. I am the aggregate of formations. I am the aggregate of consciousness. It is my aggregate of consciousness' — those monks are like the merchants who traveled safely across to the far shore, who were childlike people without faith in the Buddha's teaching, just as those merchants were made to suffer by the rākṣasīs. Those people who possess wisdom and place their faith in the Buddha's teaching are like the merchants who traveled safely across to the far shore on account of Cloud-Force — though all those other merchants fell from the horse-king Cloud-Force and were devoured by those rākṣasīs, only the merchant Siṃhala alone went safely and in good health to Jambudvīpa.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, seventy-seventh fascicle.

The rākṣasī who had been the wife of the merchant Siṃhala was addressed by the other rākṣasīs, who said to her: "We have each eaten our own husbands, yet you have let yours go. If you bring him back here, well and good. If you do not, we shall eat you yourself." Frightened, she replied: "If you give me time and wait a short while, I will bring him back." They said: "Very well then, do as you say." She then transformed herself into a supremely terrifying form and went with great speed until she stood before the merchant Siṃhala. He drew his sword from its scabbard and threatened her, and she, frightened, fled.

Now, it happened that in time a delegation arrived from the central country, and the rākṣasī prostrated herself at the merchant's feet and said: "Master, I am the princess of the king of Tāmradvīpa, given in marriage as consort to the master Siṃhala. When the boat in which I traveled across the great ocean was broken by sea-creatures — fish and the like — they abandoned me, deeming me unlucky. I beg you, out of compassion for me, to consent to take me back." He agreed, saying he would take her back.

He went to her side, and after speaking some words of comfort, sat with her a short while and then said: "My friend, you must not abandon the princess of the king of Tāmradvīpa whom you have taken — that would be improper. Have patience with her." He replied: "My friend, she is not that king's daughter. She is a rākṣasī who has come from Tāmradvīpa." "Then how has she come to be here?" When he told him what had happened, the man sat in silence saying nothing more.

The merchant Siṃhala eventually returned to his own home. The rākṣasī, carrying a child, went to the royal palace like a lioness and took up her station at the gate of the merchant Siṃhala's house. When the gathered people saw the child and recognized it by its features, they said: "Friends, we can see that this boy is the son of the merchant Siṃhala." The rākṣasī said: "Friends, as you can see, this is indeed his son." They asked: "Rākṣasī, where have you come from? Whose are you?" She replied: "Friends, I am the princess of the king of Tāmradvīpa, given as wife to the merchant Siṃhala."

"The ship that had sailed into the great ocean was wrecked by the race of water-serpents, and he abandoned me in a place that was not my home, saying I was ill-omened. How did I come to arrive here? I humbly ask that the merchant Siṃhala show forbearance toward me and toward this small child." Those people then went and reported this to his parents. His two parents said to him: "Son, do not abandon this princess. Show forbearance toward this small child and this afflicted one." He replied: "Father, Mother, she is not a princess. She is a rākṣasī who has come from Tāmradvīpa." His parents said: "Son, all women are rākṣasīs — show her forbearance." He said: "Father, Mother, if you are pleased with her, take her into the household. As for me, I shall go elsewhere." His parents said: "Son, we have taken her in very warmly for your sake. If you do not want her, why should we not drive her away?" And so the two of them drove her away.

Then that rākṣasī went before King Siṃhaketu, and the ministers reported to the king: "Sire, a woman of such beauty, come to the bloom of youth, stands at the royal gate." The king said: "Let her be brought in and looked upon." And they brought her in. Since a woman's form is something that ravishes the senses, the king, upon seeing her, was tormented by attachment and welcomed her with every courtesy, then approached her and said: "Good woman, from where have you come here? Whose are you?" She prostrated at his two feet and said: "Sire, I am the princess of the king of Tāmradvīpa, given as companion-wife to the merchant Siṃhala. The ship that had sailed into the great ocean was wrecked by the race of water-serpents, and he abandoned me in a place that was not my home, saying I was ill-omened. How then did I come to arrive here? Sire, may I ask you to grant that the merchant Siṃhala show forbearance toward me and toward this small child." The king then soothed her and gave instructions to his ministers: "Wise ones, summon the merchant Siṃhala at once." They summoned him, and the king spoke to him: "Siṃhala, do not abandon this princess. Show forbearance toward her and toward the small child." He replied: "Sire, she is not a princess.
