She is a rākṣasī who has come from Tāmradvīpa." The king said: "Merchant, all women are rākṣasīs — show her forbearance. But if you do not want her, give her to me." He replied: "Sire, since she is a rākṣasī, I will not give her away nor take her back myself." The king then had her placed among the retinue of his consorts, and she brought the king under her power.

Some time later she put the king, together with his consorts and their retinue, to sleep, then went to Tāmradvīpa, into the midst of those rākṣasīs, and said: "Sisters, what need have you of the merchant Siṃhala? I have put King Siṃhaketu to sleep along with his consorts and their retinue — come here and eat them." Those rākṣasīs, rolling their limbs and their eyes, manifestly took on their own terrifying forms of great fearfulness, and at nightfall they pounced upon the royal palace like lionesses. They devoured King Siṃhaketu together with his retinue. When dawn broke, the gates of the royal palace were not opened. When they remained closed, many carrion birds began to circle above the royal palace. The ministers, the heads of the town guilds, the people of the districts, and the people of the countryside all gathered at the gate of the royal palace.

A sound like that of lions rang out everywhere through the royal palace, proclaiming: "The gates of the royal palace are not opened." Since they remained closed, many carrion birds were circling above the royal palace, while the ministers, the heads of the town guilds, the people of the districts, and the people of the countryside all gathered and stood assembled at the gate of the royal palace — and so the news spread abroad.

When the caravan-leader Siṃgala heard this, he very swiftly tucked a sword under his arm and went forward, declaring: "Men of wisdom, the rākṣasī has devoured the king! Think of a plan!" The ministers said: "What is to be done about this? Let someone bring a ladder so we can climb up and look." They brought one, and the caravan-leader Siṃgala, sword in hand, climbed up and threatened the rākṣasīs. Those rākṣasīs thereupon fled — some carrying human limbs, others carrying heads.

Then the caravan-leader Siṃgala opened the gates of the royal palace, and the ministers cleared out the palace. They assembled the palace attendants, the ministers, and the people of the land, and addressed them: "Men of wisdom, the king together with his queen and retinue has been devoured by the rākṣasīs, and there is no heir. Who then shall be consecrated as king?" At that, some said: "Whoever is courageous and endowed with wisdom." Others said: "Who could be more courageous and endowed with wisdom than the caravan-leader Siṃgala? Let the caravan-leader Siṃgala be consecrated as king." All agreed: "So it shall be done." And they said to the caravan-leader Siṃgala: "Caravan-leader, accept the royal kingdom!" He replied: "I live by the livelihood of a merchant — what use to me is royal sovereignty?" They said: "Caravan-leader, we cannot allow another to take charge of the kingdom; accept it!" He replied: "It must be accepted with a solemn pledge — provided that you act according to my words." They replied: "We will do so. Accept it without hesitation!" They adorned the city and with great ceremony consecrated the caravan-leader Siṃgala over the royal kingdom.

King Siṃgala then summoned masters of magical incantation (vidyā) who resided in various lands and had them extensively instructed in those incantations. Likewise he summoned masters of archery dwelling in various lands and had them extensively instructed in archery. He then issued orders to his ministers: "Men of wisdom, arm the four divisions of the military forces — we shall drive those rākṣasīs out of the Copper-Colored Island!" The ministers armed the four divisions of the military forces, and King Siṃgala loaded those four-divisioned armies — the host of elephant-riders, the host of cavalry, the host of chariot-warriors, and the host of foot-soldiers — onto boats and set sail for the Copper-Colored Island.

At length they reached the shore of the ocean. The rākṣasīs, perceiving that their banner corresponding to the place of danger was being waved, began to deliberate among themselves: "Sisters, the banner corresponding to the place of danger is being waved. Let those men of Jambudvīpa who wish to do battle come — we shall watch without flinching." Having gone to the ocean shore, they looked and saw a great many large ships arriving at the shore of the ocean. Seeing this, those rākṣasīs arrayed themselves for battle. Then the masters of incantation brought down the rākṣasīs by means of their incantations, and the masters of archery slew the greater part of them. The survivors prostrated at the feet of King Siṃgala and said: "O King (literally: deva), please have mercy!" He replied: "Mercy shall be granted by solemn pledge — provided that you leave this city of yours and go elsewhere, and cause not the slightest harm in my land, mercy is granted."

They replied: "So it shall be done. We have caused no offense." They left those cities and went and settled elsewhere. And King Siṃgala then built a city there, and because King Siṃgala dwelt in that place, the island of Siṃgala came to be known by the name "the Island of Siṃgala."

"Monks, the merchant-captain Siṃgala of that time — that was none other than myself. The King Siṃgala of the Lion's Mane of that time — that is this elder here, now present. The rākṣasī of that time — that is this woman Incomparable, and even then this Incomparable one caused wrongful suffering to this queen and her retinue, and she causes wrongful suffering to her still today."

Now, the wanderer took Incomparable away and came to Kauśāmbī, and there she was dwelling in a pleasure garden. The keeper of the pleasure garden reported to King Śarpa: "O divine one, there is a woman in the pleasure garden — beautiful of form, lovely to behold, and fair. She is truly fit for a king." When the king heard this, he went to the pleasure garden and saw her. Since the realm of women is one that steals away the senses, the moment he saw her he was seized with desire. He spoke to the wanderer woman: "Old mother, whose daughter is this?" "O divine one, she is my daughter." "To whom have you given her?" "O divine one, to no one has she been given." "Why do you not give her to me?" "O divine one, I am suppliant before you." The king took her as a bride, placed her within the queen's retinue, and gave her as well half of a magnificent mansion adorned with a garland of flowers. He gave five hundred attendants in service to her, and every single day he gave five hundred and five hundred kārṣāpaṇas' worth of perfumes and garlands. And the wanderer woman he appointed as chief minister.

Now at that time King Śarpa of Vatsa had three chief ministers: Snare-Holder, Melodious, and the old woman. Some time later, a man came before King Śarpa of Vatsa, and the king asked him: "Who are you?" The man replied: "O divine one, I am Sweet-Speaker." The king instructed his ministers: "Gentlemen of wisdom, provide Sweet-Speaker with a living." And they gave him a livelihood. Then again at another time a man came before the king, and the king asked him: "Who are you?" He replied: "O divine one, I am Harsh-Speaker." The king instructed his ministers: "Gentlemen of wisdom, provide Harsh-Speaker with a living." They replied: "O divine one, since even your majesty might well hear something unpleasant, we will not grant this one a livelihood." The king said: "Gentlemen of wisdom, give generously as befits a king's affairs." And so they gave that one a livelihood as well.

Then at another time, King Śarpa of Vatsa was sitting together with his queen Nīlajālikā and with Incomparable, and the king became intoxicated. Nīlajālikā said, "Homage to the Buddha," and Incomparable did obeisance to the king, then said: "O divine one, look — Nīlajālikā pays homage not to you the king, but to the ascetic Gautama." The king replied: "Incomparable is not at fault here. Nīlajālikā is a laywoman, so naturally she may pay homage to the ascetic Gautama." And he said nothing more.

Then Incomparable spoke to the maidservant: "My girl, whenever the king is alone together with Nīlajālikā in a private place, at that moment you are to roll down a clay bowl from the top of the stairs." The maidservant replied, "Whatever my mistress commands, so shall I do." Then at the very moment when they were seated together, she rolled a clay bowl from the top of the stairs, and at that instant Nīlajālikā said, "Homage to the Buddha" —

Incomparable said, "Homage to the king," and then declared: "Your majesty, do you see that Nīlajālikā makes no offering in the divine precinct and yet pays homage to the ascetic Gautama?" The king replied, "Incomparable, stop. Do not contrive a fault. There is no wrongdoing here — Nīlajālikā is a laywoman, so naturally she pays homage to the ascetic Gautama." And he said nothing more.

Now the king alternated: one day he would take his meals at the quarters of Nīlajālikā, and the next day at the quarters of Incomparable. Incomparable then gave instructions to her maidservant: "On whichever day it falls to Nīlajālikā to serve the king his meal, on that very day you are to bring him a bowl of rice porridge with live embers beneath it." And so, on the day the king dined at Nīlajālikā's quarters, the maidservant brought him a bowl of rice porridge with live embers beneath it. The king said, "Take it to Incomparable." When Incomparable heard this she replied, "Your majesty, it is not my turn — it is Nīlajālikā's turn." The king said, "Very well, maidservant, go and deliver it to Nīlajālikā." The maidservant brought it to Nīlajālikā and said, "For your majesty's sake, please stir it." Nīlajālikā replied, "What, is she a maidservant? She does not kill living creatures, so be off with you." The maidservant returned to the king and reported, "Your majesty, word from Nīlajālikā: 'What, is she a maidservant? She does not kill living creatures, so be off.'" When Incomparable heard this, she said to the king, "Your majesty, if she had been told to stir it for the sake of the ascetic Gautama, she would stir it along with her entire retinue." The king thought, "That may well be so," and he said to the maidservant, "Go, and have her stir it saying it is for the sake of the Blessed One." The maidservant was also instructed by Incomparable in private to tell her this and then kill her. The maidservant killed the embers, brought the bowl to Nīlajālikā, and said, "By his majesty's command: 'Stir it for the sake of the Blessed One.'" Nīlajālikā, together with her retinue, thereupon began to stir it.

The maidservant went and reported to the king, "Your majesty, Nīlajālikā is stirring it together with her retinue." Incomparable said, "Did your majesty hear that? If she will not kill living creatures for your majesty's sake and will not do it even for the Blessed One's sake — that is one thing. But if she will do it for the Blessed One's sake and not for your majesty's sake — what kind of thing is that?" The king fell into a rage, drew his bow, and shot. The arrow fell halfway along the path. He shot a second arrow, and it turned back and fell at the king's own feet. As he prepared to shoot a third arrow, Nīlajālikā said, "Your majesty, do not shoot. Do not bring about the destruction of all that you have in every direction." The king was frightened and said, "Who are you — a goddess, a nāga woman, a yakṣa woman, a gandharva woman, a garuḍa woman, a kinnara woman, or a great serpent?" She replied, "Your majesty, I am none of these — not a goddess, not a nāga woman, not a yakṣa woman, not a gandharva woman, not a kinnara woman, not a great serpent. Then who are you? Your majesty, I am a śrāvaka of the Blessed One — a never-returner. I have actualized directly in the presence of the Blessed One the fruit of never-returning. And these five hundred women have also seen the truths." The king was filled with confidence and said —

"Tell me, what noble gift shall I give you?" She replied, "If your majesty truly has confidence in me, then whenever I enter the retinue of the royal consort, let your majesty regard me with the perception of a sister." The king said, "Certainly, it shall be so, without fault."

The king then experienced play, delight, and pleasurable sport together with Apalāmā. He aroused in Śyāmāvatī faith arising from the cause of the Dharma, and whatever fresh crops, fresh fruits, and fresh delicacies of the season were obtained, these too he would first of all offer to Śyāmāvatī.

Now the nature of women's quarters is one of jealousy, and so Apalāmā thought: "This king plays, rejoices, and sports pleasurably with me, and yet whatever fresh crops, fresh fruits, and fresh delicacies of the season are obtained, he first offers them all to Śyāmāvatī. I must devise some means to bring about her death." So she set about searching for a fault in her, keeping this constantly in mind.

Then some time later, the king of a neighboring land from the eastern mountains launched a raid. The king sent one contingent against him, and it was beaten back and returned utterly routed. He sent a second and a third contingent, and these too were beaten back and returned completely crushed. The ministers then said, "Your majesty's forces are weakening while those of the mountain king are growing strong. Unless your majesty goes in person, such a situation will arise that it will be difficult for you to prevail." So the king had a proclamation announced throughout Kauśāmbī: "Let all who live by weapons in my realm, however many there be, depart to war." Having given this order, he departed.

The king said to his chamberlain, "You shall supply Śyāmāvatī with whatever she needs, and remain here in this very place." He replied, "Your majesty, that is not right — I too will go to war alongside your majesty." The king said to his musician, "You shall supply Śyāmāvatī with whatever she needs and remain here." He too replied, "Your majesty, that is not right — I too will go alongside your majesty." The king then ordered his mother, saying, "Supply Śyāmāvatī with whatever she needs, remain in this very place," and departed. But she escorted him to the door, and three times petitioned him, saying, "Your majesty, that is not right — I too shall accompany your majesty." Three times she made this appeal, but the king did not grant it, and so she accepted the charge. The mother went to Apalāmā's quarters, and Apalāmā asked her, "Whom has your father the king left here?" "He has left me here." Apalāmā thought, "Surely this friend will be able to warm up the grudge-meat for me," and so she said, "Dear mother, do you know what Śyāmāvatī has become to your father? She is his cherished daughter, his great lady." "Dear mother, do you know what quality is most harmful in the women's quarters?" "Dear daughter, I do — it is jealousy and miserliness." "Dear mother, if that is so, then stifle Śyāmāvatī." "Dear daughter, do I have two heads?" Three times the king had declared, "Supply Śyāmāvatī with what she needs," but had not mentioned Apalāmā's name at all. Apalāmā then said, "Dear mother, are you so foolish? Who is there who would look even a little to a daughter's interests for a father's sake? He loves her even without cause. Therefore, if she were killed, that would be best. And if she is not killed, she will reduce you to your former station." She was frightened and thought, "The king has come under this woman's power, and so it will indeed be as she says." So she said —

"Dear daughter, it is not possible to kill her outright like that. We must devise some sort of stratagem." She replied, "Mother, do not worry — do it just so." She then said to Śyāmāvatī, "Noble lady, please command what is to be done." Śyāmāvatī replied, "Mother, there is not the slightest thing to be done. It is simply that these girls need to go at night to read the word of the Buddha by lamplight, and for that they need grain, oil, ink, pens, and cotton." She said, "Noble lady, do not worry — I shall supply it," and had a large quantity of supplies prepared, packed them inside, and then stacked them in a heap at the gatehouse and left them there.

Śyāmāvatī said, "Mother, that is enough — let them go." Apalāmā said, "Noble lady, you may enter. But henceforth I shall not allow you to enter again and again," and having let her in, she set the last load of grain alight and allowed them to enter. The fire, blazing up, spread to the gatehouse, and the crowd of people dwelling in Kauśāmbī came running to put it out. Apalāmā drew a sword from its scabbard and cried, "Why do you want to enter among the retinue of the king's queen? Stay back!" and began to drive the crowd away. A master of mechanical arts said, "I shall use a machine to move this burning gatehouse to another place." Apalāmā drove him back in the same way.

Śyāmāvatī rose up into the sky by her supernormal power and spoke: "Sisters, we have performed and accumulated deeds — deeds that have gathered their conditions, that abide like a shadow, and that will without fail come to fruition. Whatever deeds we have performed and accumulated, who else could experience them separately on our behalf? The Blessed One himself has declared:

In the midst of the ocean of the sky,
in the clefts of the mountains though one hides —
there is no place in any direction
where one can escape from one's own deeds.

It is upon us that these deeds will fall."

Then she spoke in verse:

Through the lattice of the wall
I came to see the Blessed One,
and all the truths within the Buddha's teaching
I came to know completely.

And they, like scattered flour tossed upward, leapt up and fell into the fire. Then Śyāmāvatī and the other five hundred women perished in the flames. Uttarā escaped through the drain of the water channel.

Apalāmā discarded the corpses of those five hundred women in the charnel ground, and swept clean the inside and outside of the royal palace. Then she turned back the clouds of people — those dwelling in Kauśāmbī and those who had come from other regions.

Then a great many monks, in the early morning, having put on their lower robes and taken up their bowls and Dharma robes, went for alms in Kauśāmbī. As a great many monks were wandering through Kauśāmbī for alms, they heard that some five hundred women of the retinue of the queen of the king of the Vatsa realm — Śyāmāvatī and the rest — had perished in a fire in the eastern region. Having heard this, they continued their alms round in Kauśāmbī, finished their meal, and returning from the midday alms round, set aside their dwelling things as they were accustomed to use, washed their feet, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with their heads, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, a great many monks addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, here today, as we many monks had donned our lower robes in the early morning, taken up our bowls and Dharma robes, and entered Kauśāmbī for alms —

"Venerable One, we, a great many monks wandering on alms round in Kauśāmbī, heard that the royal consorts of the king of the eastern lands — Śreṇika — along with his retinue of ladies, headed by Lady Śyāmāvatī and some five hundred women, had been burned alive.

"Monks, whoever set fire to and burned those five hundred women — the royal consort's retinue headed by Śyāmāvatī, who had accompanied King Śreṇika to the eastern lands — that person, deluded, generated abundant demerit. Yet, monks, though that deluded person generated abundant demerit, those women did not pass away fruitlessly or untimely. Why is that? Because among that retinue of royal consorts, there were women who, having abandoned the five fetters pertaining to the lower realm, were born by spontaneous birth and would pass fully into nirvāṇa there, never returning — those of such attainment who are non-returners (anāgāmins) to this world, were present in that royal retinue. And women who, having abandoned the three fetters, and with attachment, aversion, and delusion thinned, were once-returners (sakṛdāgāmins) — those who would come once more to this world and put an end to suffering — were also present in that royal retinue. And women who, having abandoned the three fetters, were stream-enterers (srotāpannas), of the nature of not falling back into error, certainly oriented toward complete awakening, who at most after seven more existences — seven rebirths alternating among gods and humans — would put an end to suffering, were also present in that royal retinue. And women who would not transgress the trainings even to preserve their own lives were also present in that royal retinue. And women who, having passed away with minds full of faith in me, are reborn from this body in a happy realm, in the higher world among the gods — those women too were present in that royal retinue. That is why I say so.

"Monks, come now — let us go to the funeral pyre of those five hundred women headed by Śyāmāvatī."

The monks replied to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, as you command," and listened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then set out together with a great many monks and arrived at the funeral pyre of those five hundred women. Upon arriving, he declared to the monks:

"Monks, these bodies of the five hundred women — these were the ones for whom King Śreṇika felt attachment, clinging, intoxication, entanglement, infatuation, intense passion, and lingering desire. Now who would even touch these with their feet?"

He then spoke these verses:

The world is hollow, without essence, busy with distraction.
Who among the fortunate would look upon it?
The childish, bound by affliction,
utterly surrounded by darkness,
see as noble what is not noble —
yet in what they see there is nothing at all.

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: even toward a charred post one should not arouse a mind of intense aversion — how much less, then, toward a body endowed with consciousness. Monks, you should train yourselves in this way."

The people of Kauśāmbī and the members of the royal court assembled and began to deliberate: "Good people, when such harm has befallen the king, which among us should go and report it to the king?" At that, some said: "Let a bearer of unpleasant tidings be sent — let him be the one to tell it." Others said: "Do not do it carelessly." And so they summoned such a messenger and spoke:

"Report this unpleasant news to His Majesty in the proper order." The messenger replied: "When you said you would give me my livelihood in return for bearing unpleasant tidings, the time has now come — so you yourselves go and report it." They replied: "It is precisely for this purpose that we gave you your livelihood. Who else would go and report it? You must go and report it." He replied: "Then swear an oath to this: whatever I say must be done, and I will go and report it." They said: "Speak, and it shall be done." He continued: "Then I shall make the report in this manner and order. You must give me five hundred elephants, five hundred she-camels, five hundred horses, five hundred mares, five hundred young men, five hundred young women, a hundred thousand in gold, cloths, a residence in Kauśāmbī, a fine mansion with a garden gate, and as for what has happened in the meantime with the wheat: how the load of grain mixed with chaff had fire set to it in the inner storehouse; how the gatehouse caught fire; how, when the crowd of people living in Kauśāmbī rushed to extinguish the fire, Mādu drew his sword from its scabbard and drove them back; how, when the master of mechanical arts said that the burning of the gatehouse could be moved elsewhere by machinery, Mādu likewise drove them back; and how five hundred women led by Ngo-bsangs-can, leaping up flat as flour-dust, again and again, fell into the fire — all of this must be painted in pictures and presented." They said: "So be it." And so they gave him five hundred elephants, five hundred she-camels, five hundred horses, five hundred mares, five hundred young men, five hundred young women, a hundred thousand in gold, cloths, a residence in Kauśāmbī, a fine mansion with a garden gate, and then pictures were painted depicting: how the load of grain mixed with chaff had fire set to it in the inner storehouse; how the gatehouse caught fire; how, when the crowd of people living in Kauśāmbī rushed to extinguish the fire, Mādu drew his sword from its scabbard and drove them back; how, when the master of mechanical arts said that the burning of the gatehouse could be moved elsewhere by machinery, Mādu likewise drove them back; and how five hundred women led by Ngo-bsangs-can, leaping up flat as flour-dust, again and again, fell into the fire — all of this was painted and presented.

Then the bearer of unpleasant tidings sent a letter to the ministers, saying: "Such harm has befallen the king. I have reported it by this means. You must support me." Having sent that letter to them, he donned the armor of a four-divisioned army, went off to another region, and settled there. Then he sent a letter to the eastern king worded thus: "My lord, I am the king of a certain pleasant land. The Lord of Death has stolen my son, and because of that I am going to war against him. If by fighting for a time I am able to defeat him, well and good. If not, I shall offer five hundred elephants, five hundred she-camels, five hundred horses, five hundred mares, five hundred young men, five hundred young women, and a hundred thousand in gold, and in exchange retrieve my son and return." He wrote this and dispatched it.

The eastern king, the cliff-dweller, did not come with his army. He spoke to his ministers thus: "Wise ones, look at how foolish that king is. Is there anyone who is able to avenge what the Lord of Death has taken? How indeed could there be?"

He met with him and sent a letter to that effect, saying: "One of my cliff-dwellers has gone astray and not returned — please be my ally in this, and in turn I shall later be your ally." He wrote this and dispatched it.

The ministers wrote a letter to that effect and sent it. Upon reading the letter, that king came to the cliff at once, and encamped not very far away. When the cliff-dwellers heard this, they thought: "Our kings have cut us off and surrounded us from all ten directions. Now this second king has drawn near as well. The land we may recover in every respect, but our lives we cannot recover — so let us surrender." Thereupon they put sword to their own throats, came out, and prostrated at the feet of the eastern king. The eastern king made them pay a fine and a tribute.

Then the messenger of the king Duḥśrava went before the eastern king and said: "O lord, the Lord of Death has stolen my son — please, lord, be my ally! I shall go out and do battle alongside him. If by fighting for a time I am able to defeat him, well and good. If I cannot, I shall offer him five hundred elephants, five hundred she-camels, five hundred horses, five hundred mares, five hundred young men, five hundred young women, and a hundred thousand in gold, and retrieve my son." The eastern king replied: "Well indeed — you are a fool! Is there anyone at all who is able to take back what the Lord of Death has taken?" The messenger said: "Is it that your lordship cannot? Then he cannot. If that is so, look at this picture." He unrolled a picture, and the king examined it. Pierced to the quick as if struck in a vital point, the king said with anguish: "What is this — are these what they call the five hundred women, Śyāmāvatī and the rest, burned alive by fire?" The messenger then struck him with crown and headdress and spoke in verse:

I am no king, no royal power do I hold.
O lord, I live by the service of your feet.
Only to bring this sad news before you
have I come here to your feet.

The king examined it very carefully and concluded: "This is the city of Kauśāmbī. This is the royal palace. This is the gateway of the flower pavilion. This is the harem. These are the women being burned by a pyre heaped with wheat and such. And these are the five hundred women, Śyāmāvatī and the rest, leaping and leaping upward like scattered flour, and falling into the flames." Having analyzed it thus, he declared: "Your Honor, what is this — are these what they call the five hundred women, Śyāmāvatī and the rest, burned alive? O lord, I did not say that. It is thus: the lord himself said that." "Your Honor, you have only entreated me with clever means. Otherwise I would have had your head cut from your neck and thrown to the ground." So saying, the king fainted and collapsed to the ground. Then water was sprinkled on him, his breath returned, and he spoke: "Wise ones, arm the fourfold host. We march to Kauśāmbī." The ministers armed the fourfold host, the king set out for Kauśāmbī, and in due course arrived at Kauśāmbī. He then summoned all who were most knowledgeable among the people of the palace household. Next he gave orders to his chief minister Prayogadhara: "Prayogadhara, go — put the harem women in a building of lac and burn it. As for Dīpamatī, bind her to the leg of an unbroken colt and drag her." Prayogadhara put the harem women in the building of lac and burned them. Then he pondered:

As for Dīpamatī, Prayogadhara thought: "If the king, having reflected on the matter, should say, 'Bring Dīpamatī,' what will I have done? Let her wait for now." And so he placed Dīpamatī in an underground chamber and left her there.

On the seventh day the king's grief lifted, and once it had lifted he spoke: "Prayogadhara, where is Dīpamatī?" Prayogadhara replied: "Sire, I bound her to the leg of an unbroken colt and let her loose." The king said: "You have done no wrong. At that time I killed Nīlañjanā in anger, and you would have killed Dīpamatī as well — but now I shall go forth into homelessness." Prayogadhara said: "Sire, it was for that very reason that I placed Dīpamatī in an underground chamber. Let us see whether she still lives." He brought her out from the underground chamber, and in that very same moment she was found to be free of all affliction and uninjured in body.

When the king saw this he thought: "How is it that she has remained, in that very condition, free of affliction and uninjured in body — that she neither fell ill nor ate food, yet was born without losing her place and lived in pleasure together with others?" Understanding this, he said: "Dīpamatī, you have been unfaithful." She replied: "Sire, what sin have I done? I did nothing of the sort. What does this mean? Sire, do you have faith in the Blessed One?" The king said: "I have met him. At that time he was called the ascetic Gautama; now he is called the Blessed One. Yet someone like me, of such a character, would not petition the Blessed One on your behalf. I will petition the Blessed One on behalf of Nīlañjanā." And so he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet, and sat to one side.

Seated to one side, the king of Vatsa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, Nīlañjanā and the five hundred women — what had they done? The king was torn apart by the thrusting of lances, and the foremost of the chiefs fled through the drain-hole of a cistern."

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, those very women gathered a mass of karma, transformed the conditions, remained close as a flame, and performed and accumulated deeds that must inevitably arise. Those deeds which they themselves performed and accumulated — who else could experience them separately? Great King, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, it does not ripen in the element of water, it does not ripen in the element of fire, it does not ripen in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Actions are not destroyed even across a hundred aeons;
when the conditions and the moment are gathered and met,
they will assuredly become results
for those who bear a body.

Great King, long ago in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī there was a king named Brahmadatta who caused his prosperous and flourishing realm, with its good harvests, its many people of every kind, its wars and conflicts, its foreign enemies and domestic strife all thoroughly pacified, its freedom from bandits, famine, and disease, its abundance of rice, rows of sugar cane, cattle, and buffalo, to be governed and administered — and he himself, a righteous king, caused the kingdom to be governed by Dharma. At that time, when buddhas had not arisen in the world, certain lowly pratyekabuddhas — solitary buddhas who were compassionate toward the poor and destitute and who delighted in remote forest dwellings — arose in the world as single rhinoceros-like ones, fields of merit for the world. Now at a certain time, as one such pratyekabuddha was wandering and traveling through the land, he came to Vārāṇasī and took up residence in a crouching posture in a certain pleasure garden.

The five hundred ladies of the retinue of Queen Brahmadatta came to that pleasure garden. After the queen's attendants had bathed in the pleasure pool and were shivering with cold, the noble queen spoke to her maidservant: "It is extremely cold and I am shivering — go and bring fire to this resting bower." The maidservant lit a lamp and went, and upon seeing the pratyekabuddha there, she said to the noble queen: "Your Highness, there is a renunciant dwelling here." The queen replied: "Whether a renunciant is there or not, whether anyone else is there or not — go and bring fire!" When the maidservant did not convey the fire herself but fled from the place, the noble queen grew angry and sent the fire herself, and the pratyekabuddha escaped from within.

The other ladies of the queen's retinue then expressed their approval, saying: "Your Highness, it was well done that you drove him out — we all approve!" Now that great being, the pratyekabuddha, reflected: "These afflicted members of the queen's retinue have spoken with extreme contempt. If they should come to harm and ruin as a consequence, that would not be right. I shall give them a helping hand from this situation." Thinking thus, he soared up into the sky above, spreading his wings like the king of geese, and began to perform miraculous displays — blazing with fire, shining with radiance, sending down rain, and releasing lightning.

Now ordinary people quickly turn their minds to trust upon witnessing miracles. And so the ladies of the queen's retinue, as though trees cut down at the root, fell prostrate at the pratyekabuddha's feet and said: "O true field of merit, please descend! Please descend! Please draw us up by the hand from where we have sunk into the mire of afflictions!" Out of his compassionate care for those ladies of the queen's retinue, the pratyekabuddha descended from the sky above to the ground below. They made offerings to him, prostrated at his two feet, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue — by the act of making offerings in a manner discordant with the karma of the harm we have caused to such a genuine field of merit — may we attain qualities such that we please a Teacher far more supremely excellent than this pratyekabuddha, and such that we do not cause that Teacher vexation."

Now, great king, the noble queen of King Brahmadatta at that time — she is the one known in the present as Utpalavarṇā. The four hundred and ninety-nine other women who were there at that time — they are these same four hundred and ninety-nine women of the present. The maidservant who was sent at that time — she is the one known in the present as Uttarā. Because of the karmic maturation of having burned the pratyekabuddha's resting bower and having rejoiced in that act, they burned for many long years in the great hells, and even up to the present time, until they beheld the truth, they continued to be scorched by fire. As for Uttarā, because she was unable to carry through with sending the fire and fled instead, in the present she has escaped through the water-drain.

The aspiration they made after offering to the pratyekabuddha — it is that very aspiration which has now caused them to behold the truth in my presence, and by which they have pleased me, a Teacher supremely more excellent than the pratyekabuddha by a hundred thousand million times, without causing me vexation.

Great king, that being so: the karmic maturation of actions that are purely dark is itself purely dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are purely bright is itself purely bright; and the karmic maturation of actions that are mixed is itself mixed. Therefore, great king, purely dark actions and

mixed actions are to be abandoned, and one should strive toward actions that are purely bright. Great king, you should train in this way.

Then the great king of Bādas, having heard what the Blessed One declared, expressed his delight and rejoicing, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from his presence.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the seventy-eighth fascicle.

The monks, having fallen into doubt, asked the Blessed One, the awakened Bhagavān, who cuts through all doubts. They asked: Venerable one, what action did the Elder Śgur perform, that by it he became a hunchback?

The Blessed One declared: Monks, the Elder Śgur himself had gathered a collection of karma, had fully transformed the conditions, and had performed and accumulated deeds that would infallibly arise, abiding as though in a flame. It is those very karmas, performed and accumulated by him, that he — and no one else — experiences individually. Monks, karma performed and accumulated does not mature in the earth element of the outer world, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma performed and accumulated in that way matures in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Actions, though a hundred aeons pass,
do not perish but accumulate;
when the time arrives with conditions met,
they ripen as results for beings with a body.

Monks, in a time long past, there was a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and happy, with good harvests, filled with many people of all kinds. External enemies and internal strife had been fully pacified; it was free from bandits, famine, and disease; rich in crops of rice and sugarcane, with abundant herds of cattle and water buffalo. A righteous king, a Dharma-king, he governed his realm in accordance with Dharma. At a certain time, astrologers prophesied that rain would not fall for twelve years, and King Brahmadatta had it proclaimed throughout Vārāṇasī: whoever has provisions for twelve years may remain; whoever does not should go elsewhere, and may return again after twelve years have passed.

At that time there was in Vārāṇasī a householder named Dhāraṇī, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and extensive resources, with broad and wide storehouses, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa himself in his treasure. He summoned his steward and said: Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself and my retinue? The steward replied: Yes, my lord. In that time — when no buddhas had appeared in the world — there arose in the world certain pratyekabuddhas, poor and destitute, who showed compassion to the lowly and wretched, who delighted in remote and solitary dwelling places like rhinoceroses, each alone, and who had become fields of merit for the world. Now, five hundred pratyekabuddhas were wandering and traveling through the region, and when they came to Vārāṇasī they went to the home of the householder Dhāraṇī. Arriving there, they said: Householder, are you able to provide sustenance for the twelve years required by us five hundred who have gone forth? He replied: Noble ones, ask the steward; I will inquire on your behalf afterward. And the steward was summoned and asked: Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself with my retinue, and for these five hundred who have gone forth? The steward replied: Yes, my lord. The householder Dhāraṇī said to the five hundred pratyekabuddhas: Noble ones, please remain — I shall provide for you.

They remained there as well. Now, while another five hundred pratyekabuddhas were wandering and traveling through the land, they came to Vārāṇasī and went to the home of the householder Dhāraṇī. Arriving there, they said: Householder, are you able to provide sustenance for the twelve years required by us five hundred who have gone forth? He replied: Noble ones, if you were to ask the steward, why would anything fail to be accomplished? Noble ones, they are other, and we too are other — ask the steward, and I shall inquire afterward. And he summoned the steward and said: Dear steward, do I have provisions for twelve years for myself with my retinue, and for these thousand who have gone forth? The steward replied: Yes, my lord. He then said to the other five hundred who had gone forth: Noble ones, please remain — I shall provide for you. They too remained there.

He had a giving-hall built, and he appointed both an attendant in charge of the giving of food and an usher. Each day a thousand pratyekabuddhas took their meal there. Then it came about that one pratyekabuddha fell ill, and that very day he did not come. The daughter of the householder Dhāraṇī said to her father: Father, today one who has gone forth did not come. He asked: Daughter, what was he like? She bowed and replied: Father, he was like this — and described him.

O monks, she who was at that time the daughter of the householder Dhāraṇī is none other than this very Śreṣṭhā. It is through the karmic maturation of the act she committed — striking a pratyekabuddha — that she came to be hunchbacked.

Now the monks, filled with doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, to dispel all their doubt: Venerable One, what karma did Śreṣṭhā perform such that she became a holder of scripture? The Blessed One declared: O monks, Śreṣṭhā herself accumulated a mass of karma, fully turned the conditions, dwelt near like a flame, and made deeds that would inevitably arise. Of the karma thus performed and accumulated by her alone, who else could experience its separate fruits? O monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, karma — whether virtuous or non-virtuous — that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense sources (āyatanas).

Actions, though a hundred eons pass,
do not perish; they do not come to naught.
When the conditions and the time are met,
their fruits arise for those who bear a body.

O monks, the elder of the Saṅgha at that almshouse of the householder Dhāraṇī — the very almshouse for those thousand pratyekabuddhas — suffered from wind disease. When he ate his meal, his hand trembled and he caused the alms-bowl to shake. The daughter of Dhāraṇī then removed a bracelet adorned with bells from her own hand and offered it to that pratyekabuddha, saying: Noble one, please place the alms-bowl on top of this. He set the alms-bowl upon it and sat there perfectly still. She then touched his two feet and made this aspiration: Just as this alms-bowl rests without shaking, so too may the Dharma teachings that have entered into my stream remain without wavering. Through the karmic maturation of that act, she has now become a holder of scripture.

Again the monks, filled with doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, to dispel all their doubt: Venerable One, what karma did Śreṣṭhā perform such that she became a slave? The Blessed One declared: O monks, Śreṣṭhā herself accumulated a mass of karma,

having transformed the conditions, abiding near like a flame, certain to arise — karma accumulated in just this way cannot be experienced by any other person. O monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even across a hundred aeons
karma does not perish;
when the conditions and the time are met,
it ripens for embodied beings as its fruit.

O monks, in that very former life, she, intoxicated with the pride of power and authority, habitually addressed the people of her retinue with the words of a slave. Through the karmic maturation of that action she has now become a slave.

Again the monks, filled with doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, to dispel all their doubt: Venerable One, what karma did Upamā perform such that she was given a house for seven years without food, without being afflicted in mind, and without her body being harmed?

The Blessed One declared: O monks, Upamā herself accumulated a mass of karma, having transformed the conditions, abiding near like a flame, certain to arise — karma accumulated in just this way cannot be experienced by any other person. O monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in verse:

Even across a hundred aeons
karma does not perish;
when the conditions and the time are met,
it ripens for embodied beings as its fruit.

O monks, in a former time there was a rocky cliff where a daughter of the warrior class (kṣatriya) and a brahmin girl dwelt together as close friends. This was a time when no buddhas had appeared in the world, and there arose in the world certain solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas) — humble and poor, cherishing compassionate concern for all, delighting in remote and secluded dwellings, dwelling alone like a rhinoceros horn, serving as a field of merit for the world. Now it came about that one such solitary buddha agreed to spend the night in a peaceful place nearby, and the next morning, having girded his robe and taken up his alms-bowl and Dharma robe, he entered that rocky cliff on his alms round. The daughter of the warrior class, on that very day, gave him alms. In the same way, on the second day and the third day, she began to offer him alms without interruption for a full day's cycle.

On another occasion, that daughter of the warrior class was invited by the brahmin girl and went to her house. Meanwhile that same solitary buddha, going on his alms round, entered the house of the daughter of the warrior class, and finding her absent, he continued on and eventually entered the house of the brahmin girl. The daughter of the warrior class, seeing him, said to the brahmin girl: "Girl, offer alms to this noble one." But the brahmin girl replied: "So long as I have not given to the gods, to the brahmins, and to my dear and close kinsmen, how could I give to this shaven-headed ascetic?" The daughter of the warrior class then said: "Sister, if that is so, let me for now go and give him alms myself and then return." The brahmin girl said: "Very well then, if that is so, please wait —"

"I myself shall give him alms." She gave him alms, and then made a perverse aspiration, saying: "As for this gift of alms that I have made to this shaven-headed ascetic, may it bear no karmic fruit for me in this world, and may it bear no karmic fruit for me in the world beyond." Such was the aspiration she made.

Monks, the brahmin girl of that time and place is none other than Aupamānavatī here. She gave alms to the pratyekabuddha and made this perverse aspiration: "May this gift of alms that I have made to this shaven-headed ascetic bear no karmic fruit for me in this world, and may it bear no karmic fruit for me in the world beyond." Through the karmic maturation of that very action, she was locked in a cellar for seven days without food, then released, unharmed and without injury to her body.

At another time, Aupamānavatī had grown old, and at the hour of her death she made an aspiration: "By whatever root of virtue I have gained through serving the community of monks as long as I have lived, may I be reborn in the womb of the finest wife of the householder Gāndika, and may I become just like a stretch of clear water tinged with blue, and may the eastern king of the region of Batsā become my husband." She died and when her time came, she was reborn in the womb of the finest wife of the householder Gāndika. On the very day she was born, that house blazed with radiant splendor. After eight or nine months had passed, a daughter was born — beautiful to behold, lovely and fair. From the very moment of her birth, she caused her father's house to blaze even more brilliantly with radiant splendor. Her relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day after her birth they held a grand birth-celebration, at which they turned to naming her: "By what name shall this girl be called?" The relatives said: "Because on the very day this girl entered her mother's womb the house blazed with radiant splendor, and because at her birth she caused her father's house to blaze broadly with radiant splendor, therefore let her name be Śrī — the Illustrious One." And so she was named Śrī.

When she had grown old enough to speak, she would go before any monks who came to that house for alms, bow at their feet, and inquire after their health. Then, when the venerable Ānanda came there for alms, she went before him and, bowing at his two feet, said: "Venerable Ānanda, how is the Blessed One? How are the monks, the elders, and the great elders? Are they of little affliction, of little discomfort? Are they agile? Do they live with strength? Are they at ease? Are they free from fault? Do they abide in contact with happiness?" He replied: "Sister, the Blessed One, the monks, the elders, and the great elders are of little affliction, of little discomfort, agile, living with strength, at ease, free from fault, and abiding in contact with happiness." Upon hearing these words, the household members of the householder Gāndika were struck with the utmost wonder. Then the venerable Ānanda exchanged pleasantries and departed, went to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and reported: "Blessed One, a young girl, the daughter of the householder Gāndika, has been inquiring after the health of the Blessed One and the monks, the elders, and the great elders; and the household members of Gāndika, upon hearing this, were struck with the utmost wonder." The Blessed One then declared:

"Ānanda, do you not know that girl?" "Blessed One, I do not." "Ānanda, she is Mgubyed. Through the power of aspiration she was born in the womb of the chief wife of the householder Gāndika, and she is now called Śrī."

When Śrī had grown to adulthood, mendicant kings, wealthy men, merchants, caravan leaders, Kauḍyas, Śākyas, Licchavīs, and many others began to arrive seeking her hand. The householder Gāndika thought: "Many mendicants are coming for Śrī, and those to whom I do not give her will become my enemies." With this thought he rested his chin in his hand and sat lost in worry. Śrī, seeing this, said: "Father, why do you sit resting your chin in your hand, sunk in such worry?" He replied: "Daughter, mendicant kings, wealthy men, merchants, caravan leaders, Kauḍyas, Śākyas, Licchavīs, and many others are coming, and those to whom I do not give you will become my enemies — how can I not sit resting my chin in my hand, sunk in worry?" She replied: "Father, do not be troubled. I myself will find a husband." "Daughter, who is it?" "Father, it is the eastern king of Prasenajit." "Daughter, if that is so, then make careful arrangements." "Father, what kind of arrangements?" "Daughter, invite this eastern king of Prasenajit himself here. When he comes to dine, you shall sit at the base of the upper chamber and toss down a flower garland." "Father, I shall do exactly as you say."

He then invited the eastern king of Prasenajit to dine at another household, and when the king had eaten, Śrī, seated at the base of the upper chamber, tossed down a flower garland. The king began to look upward, and when he saw her he said: "Gāndika, you said that Ngorang Sanchen — the Blue Lotus — had come of age; is this not she who stands here?" "Your Majesty, this one is not the Blue Lotus." "Then who is this?" "Your Majesty, this is the younger sister of the Blue Lotus, called Śrī." "Will you give her to someone?" "Your Majesty, she has not been given to anyone." "If that is so, why will you not give her to me?" "Your Majesty, I will." The householder Gāndika gave her, and the eastern king of Prasenajit took Śrī with great splendor as his bride and installed her within the royal retinue of queens.

At another time she said to the king: "Your Majesty, I wish to see monks." The king replied: "You may wish to, but monks do not enter the royal palace." She said: "Your Majesty, if that is so, I offer myself utterly to prison. If you will not permit me to see monks, from this day forward I will take no food, I will make no obeisance, I will pay no homage." And she entered upon a fast. The king then said to the householder Gāndika: "Householder, are you not aware?" "Your Majesty, what is it?" "Śrī has entered upon a fast." "Your Majesty, why does she wish to see monks if monks do not enter the royal palace?" "Your Majesty, then how shall this be accomplished?" "Householder, for this reason let a courtyard be enclosed in your own name and invite the Saṅgha of monks there, and provide them with a meal in the gateway area between." The householder Gāndika's house was adjacent to the king's palace, and so the king had the fence opened to that courtyard and had the ground swept clean.

Then Śrī went to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, bowed her head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the Blessed One then rightly instructed, rightly established, rightly encouraged, and rightly gladdened the householder Gāndika with words of Dharma. In many ways he rightly taught, rightly established, rightly encouraged, and rightly gladdened him with words of Dharma, and then fell silent.

Then the householder Gāndika turned toward the Blessed One, pressed his palms together, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, may the Saṅgha of monks together with the Blessed One consent to receive a meal at my courtyard enclosure tomorrow." The Blessed One consented to the householder Gāndika by remaining silent.

Then the householder Gāndika, understanding that the Blessed One's silence signified consent, bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

That very night the householder Gāndika prepared clean and refined foods and drink, rose early the next morning, arranged the seats, set out the water vessels, and invited the Blessed One: "Blessed One, may it please you to know that the time has come." The Blessed One arrived, and the Saṅgha of monks including the venerable Śāriputra entered.

The Blessed One remained in the courtyard enclosure and proceeded to go on alms round. Buddhas, blessed ones, remain in courtyard enclosures and proceed to go on alms round for five reasons. What are the five? They wish to practice inner stillness; they wish to teach Dharma to the gods; they wish to visit the sick; they wish to inspect the lodgings; and they wish to establish rules of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya. In the present case, the Blessed One remained in the courtyard enclosure and proceeded to go on alms round because he wished to establish rules of training for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

As the venerable Śāriputra was entering, the king was seated there with his queen and retinue, and when he began to withdraw on that account, the king saw him and said, "Noble Śāriputra, please proceed." Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the monks, "Venerable ones, there are four kinds of words that must not be disrupted: the word of the Tathāgata, the worthy one, the perfectly awakened buddha; the word of a monk who is an arhat with defilements exhausted; the word of the head of discipline; and the word of a king of royal lineage consecrated at the crown. Therefore, venerable ones, be mindful and proceed." Having so entered, he took a seat that had been spread before the Saṅgha of monks and sat down there.

Then the queen Śrī, knowing that the Saṅgha of monks including the venerable Śāriputra was comfortably settled, satisfied and refreshed them with clean and refined foods and drink from her own hands. In many ways, serving them with clean and refined foods and drink from her own hands, and knowing that the Saṅgha of monks including the venerable Śāriputra had finished their meal and had set aside their hands from their bowls, she took a seat lower than the rest and sat down before the venerable Śāriputra in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the venerable Śāriputra rightly taught, rightly established, and rightly encouraged the queen Śrī with words of Dharma.

In many ways, making her rightly rejoice with words of Dharma, he rightly taught, rightly established, rightly exhorted, and rightly made her rejoice. Yet through all of this, she had not seen the truths. The venerable Śāriputra thought: "Does she have roots of virtue or does she not?" He saw that she did have them. "On whom do they depend?" He saw that they depended on herself. So he taught her the Dharma and analyzed it for her, and as he was doing so the time came when the sun had set, and the monks rose from their seats and departed.

The venerable Śāriputra thought: "Though the Blessed One has not yet given permission, there will surely come to be such a case as this, where such circumstances will serve as the occasion for permission being granted." With that in mind, out of regard for her training, he remained right there. Then the venerable Śāriputra, having fully understood the mind, the latent dispositions, the faculty, and the nature of queen Śrī, taught the Dharma in such a way that, upon hearing it, while queen Śrī remained seated on that very seat, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, which had been heaped up since beginningless time, were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and the fruit of stream-entry was made directly manifest.

Having seen the truths, she said: "Noble one, through relying on you, the spiritual friend who is the noble Śāriputra, the noble one has done for me what is like this: my father did not do it for me, my mother did not do it for me, the king did not do it for me, the gods did not do it for me, my ancestors of former times did not do it for me, contemplatives and brahmins did not do it for me, and friends, companions, and the assembly of relatives did not do it for me. The ocean of blood and tears has been dried up. I have been freed from the mountains of bones. The doors to the lower realms have been shut. The doors to the higher realms and to liberation have been opened. My feet have been lifted out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and I have been placed among gods and humans. Cyclic existence has been brought to its end. The twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time have been shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and the fruit of stream-entry has been attained. Venerable one, I have entered directly. Venerable one, I have entered directly. Venerable one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I be accepted as a laywoman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge from the very depths of my heart with utter sincerity."

Then the venerable Śāriputra established queen Śrī in the truths and departed. He went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, and prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, then sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Śāriputra then reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, excellent, excellent! The words of those seven are not to be violated: the word of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha; the word of a monk who is an arhat whose defilements are exhausted; the word of an elder of the Saṅgha; the word of the ceremonial supervisor; the word of an abbot; the word of a preceptor; and the word of a king of the warrior caste anointed at the crown."

Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of those who desire training, who are respectful toward training, and who are furnished with the requisites for training, addressed the monks accordingly with words of Dharma that were consonant with this, that expressed its import fully, and that were in accord with it, and then declared to the monks:

"Monks, therefore the former ruling was the established rule, and this is the allowance. My hearers are to recite the basis of training in the Vinaya in this way:

Furthermore, whatever monk, before dawn has come, before the aurora has risen, without having gathered jewels or things spoken of as jewels, crosses beyond a city gate or the guard post of a city gate — except in circumstances such as these — commits a transgression.

Now, 'whatever monk' means one who is a novice or any other such person. 'Before dawn has come' means while it has not yet become dawn. 'The aurora' refers to the three phases of the aurora: the first aurora, the middle aurora, and the last aurora. Of these, the first aurora appears bluish, the middle aurora appears yellowish, and the last aurora appears reddish — and here it is the last aurora that is intended. 'Has risen' means has appeared. As for 'jewels': jewels means gems, pearls, beryl, white crystal, coral, gold, silver, the essence of stone, red precious stones, and right-spiraling shells. As for 'things spoken of as jewels': things spoken of as jewels means all weapons used in battle and all instruments used for music. 'Without having gathered' means without having bundled them up. 'A king of the warrior caste anointed at the crown' means this: if one is anointed to kingship by a woman consecrated to royal authority, that too is a king of the warrior caste anointed at the crown; and if one anointed to royal authority is of the warrior caste, or of the brahmin caste, or of the merchant caste, or of the common caste, that too is a king of the warrior caste anointed at the crown. 'A city gate' means there are three kinds of gate: the gate of a city, the gate of a royal palace, and the gate of the queens' quarters. 'From the guard post of a gate' means from the vicinity of that gate. 'Crosses' means goes. 'Except in circumstances such as these' means that circumstances such as these are set aside. 'Commits a transgression' means it causes scorching, burning, and falling into hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, wretched states, evil destinies, and states of downfall. Moreover, as long as a transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the virtuous phenomena. Therefore it is said to 'commit a transgression.'

Now, how does one come to transgress? If a monk, perceiving it as before-dawn when it is before dawn, crosses beyond a city gate, that becomes an offense. If a monk, with doubt about it being before dawn when it is before dawn, crosses beyond a city gate, that becomes an offense. If a monk, perceiving it as before-dawn when it has in fact become dawn, crosses beyond a city gate, that becomes an offense. If a monk, with doubt about it being before dawn when it has in fact become dawn, crosses beyond a city gate, that becomes an offense. If a monk, perceiving it as dawned when it has not yet dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the royal palace, that becomes an offense. If a monk, with doubt about it being before dawn when it has not yet dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the royal palace, that becomes an offense. If a monk, perceiving it as before-dawn when it has in fact dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the royal palace, that becomes an offense. If a monk, with doubt when it has in fact dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the royal palace, that becomes an offense. If a monk, perceiving it as before-dawn when it is before dawn, crosses beyond the gate of the queens' quarters, that becomes a full transgression."

If a monk, with doubt about it being before dawn when it has not yet dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the queens' quarters, that becomes an offense. If a monk, perceiving it as before dawn when it has in fact dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the queens' quarters, that becomes a wrongdoing. If a monk, with doubt when it has in fact dawned, crosses beyond the gate of the queens' quarters, that becomes a wrongdoing.

When summoned by the king, a queen, a young prince, or ministers, and in the case of the eight obstacles — namely the king, thieves, humans, non-humans, dangerous beings, fire, water, and nāgas being nearby — there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations. This is the offense of going to the royal palace at night. The eighty-second rule is complete.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that the Prātimokṣa sūtra should be recited at the fortnightly restoration ceremony. When the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra was taking place at the fortnightly ceremony, the group of six, although making a show of respect, did not listen to the Dharma. They did not treat it as something supreme. They did not treat it as a post. They did not take it to heart. They did not make their minds one-pointed. They did not lend their ears. They did not listen to the Dharma with their whole minds engaged. And they also said to the monks: "Venerable ones, we have only just now come to know that this teaching too is included within the sūtra and gathered within the sūtra." The monks then said to them: "Have the venerable ones only just now heard the Prātimokṣa sūtra being recited? How can you say such a thing?" Those monks replied: "Venerable ones, are we to be restricted to only that much? We must also examine thoughts of sensual desire. We must also examine thoughts of ill-will and thoughts of harmfulness. Why, venerable monks, should monks of little concern fail to listen attentively when the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited at the fortnightly ceremony — not treating it as something supreme, not treating it as a post, not taking it to heart, not making their minds one-pointed, not lending their ears, not listening to the Dharma with their whole minds engaged — and also say to the monks: 'Venerable ones, we have only just now come to know that this teaching too is included within the sūtra and gathered within the sūtra'?" And saying this, they rebuked them, spoke out against them, and reproached them. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One convened the community of monks in light of what had occurred, on account of this basis, and in this context, and so forth, as before. "The Blessed Ones who are buddhas, knowing full well, act in a deliberate manner" — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One rebuked the group of six: "Monks, is it true that when the Prātimokṣa sūtra was being recited at the fortnightly ceremony, you, making a show of respect, did not listen to the Dharma, did not treat it as something supreme, did not treat it as a post, did not take it to heart, did not make your minds one-pointed, did not lend your ears, did not listen to the Dharma with your whole minds engaged, and also said to the monks: 'Venerable ones, we have only just now come to know that this teaching too is included within the sūtra and gathered within the sūtra'? Is this true, venerable ones? It is not so."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, rebuked them, saying that such conduct was not the way of a renunciant, was not fitting, was not proper, and was not in accordance with the training — it was not something that one who has gone forth should do. Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing the ten benefits, one should establish rules of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so on, as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk, when the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited, says these words — 'Venerable ones, I have only just now come to know that this teaching too is included within the sūtra and gathered within the sūtra' — and if the other monks know that that venerable one was present at two or three previous fortnightly restoration ceremonies, to say nothing of many times: since that venerable one is not absolved through his not knowing, he is indeed one who possesses a transgression. He should be made to carry out whatever transgression has arisen in accordance with the rule. Moreover, you, at the time when the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited, did not listen to the Dharma with respect, did not treat it as supreme, did not treat it as a post, did not take it to heart, did not make your mind one-pointed, did not lend your ears, did not listen to the Dharma with your whole mind engaged. Venerable one, you have not gained what is to be gained; you have gained what is not to be gained; you have found fault, not what is good. He should be made to feel remorse. To cause that venerable one to feel remorse — that is the transgression."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to the group of six or any others who are likewise. "The fortnightly recitation" refers to the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa. As for "Prātimokṣa," the Prātimokṣa consists of the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha, the two indeterminate rules, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules entailing confession, the four rules entailing individual confession, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for settling disputes. "Reciting the sūtra" means applying it fully. "At the time of recitation" means at the time of teaching it clearly. "These words" means when one says these words. "Venerable ones, I have only just now come to know that this teaching too is included within the sūtra and gathered within the sūtra" — this refers to the Dharma spoken by the Blessed One. "If the other monks also" means the monks who were present there. "That venerable one" refers to whichever monk that is. "Was present at two or three previous fortnightly restoration ceremonies" means that he is known to have heard the Prātimokṣa twice or three times. "To say nothing of many times" means, how much more so when he is known to have been present many times. "Since that venerable one is not absolved through his not knowing" means that since he is not absolved of the transgression by that means of not knowing, he is indeed one who possesses the transgression. "Whatever transgression has arisen" means the act of transgression. "He should be made to carry out in accordance with the rule" means he should be made to confess it. "Moreover, you, at the time when the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra is being recited, did not listen to the Dharma with respect, did not treat it as supreme, did not treat it as a post, did not take it to heart, did not make your mind one-pointed"

did not lend an ear, did not listen to the Dharma with the whole mind attending — in that case, you, venerable one, have not gained; you have not gained but have acquired fault; you have not gained what is good. He should be made to feel remorse, saying: "You should feel remorse." The phrase "the venerable one should feel remorse in this way" means that he should be made to feel remorse in exactly that manner.

"It causes downfall" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the hells (naraka), into the animal realm, into the wretched realm of hungry ghosts (preta), into the lower destinies, and into states of utter ruin. Furthermore, so long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs the arising of wholesome Dharma qualities — and therefore it is said to cause downfall.

As for how a downfall comes about: when a monk, at the time of the recitation of the four rules that constitute defeat, the thirteen rules requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha, the two rules of indeterminate case, the thirty rules of forfeiture-and-confession, the ninety rules of confession, the four rules of individual acknowledgment, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for the settlement of disputes, has not listened to the Dharma with reverence, has not treated it as supreme, has not treated it as a post, has not taken it to heart, has not made his mind one-pointed, has not lent an ear, has not listened to the Dharma with the whole mind attending, and moreover says: "Venerable ones, I have only now come to know that this Dharma, too, is included within the sūtra, is gathered within the sūtra" — in every such case a downfall arises.

If one has grown old having strayed from the path and simply does not know with accuracy, there is no downfall. For one who is a beginner, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is overcome by painful feelings, there is no downfall.

The offence that causes downfall by contemptuously dismissing the object that is the basis of the training — the eighty-third — is complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the seventy-ninth section.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (bhagavat), was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a carpenter who was known as a hearer of the Dharma of the naked ascetics, and he was deeply devoted to the naked ascetics. Then at another time, a monk who lived as a mendicant tamed him by teaching the Dharma, and he too took refuge in the monk and undertook the bases of training. The mendicant then extensively praised to him the seven bases of meritorious action arising from material things, and the carpenter, having become full of faith, said: "Noble one, I too will properly undertake and engage in a small portion of the seven bases of meritorious action arising from material things." The monk said: "Good sir, what will you do?" The carpenter replied: "Noble one, I will personally prepare and serve a meal to the Saṅgha of monks." The monk said: "Good, do just so."

The mendicant went to the monastery and said to the monks: "Venerable ones, this one, known as a hearer of the Dharma of the naked ascetics, has been established in refuge and in the bases of training, and he wishes to personally prepare and serve a meal to the Saṅgha of monks. Whoever among you wishes to do so may go to him."

Then a certain monk, being without needle and thread, went to the carpenter and said: "Good sir, I have no needle and thread — please provide them." The monk replied: "Noble one, what kind shall I make for you?" The carpenter said: "Whatever is best." "Noble one, what is made from ivory is best." The monk said: "Good sir, make one from ivory." So the carpenter made an ivory needle-case for him and gave it to him. That monk then showed it to the other monks, and other monks likewise had him make them, and yet others did so as well.

Yet others too had him make them, until his supply of ivory was exhausted. Then yet another monk came and said: "Good sir, my needle-case has fallen apart." "Noble one, what kind shall I make for you?" "Whatever is best." "Noble one, if one made of ivory is best, then ivory is already gone. If you wish, I can make one of bone." "Good sir, please make one without fail." So he made a bone needle-case for him and gave it to him. That monk showed it to the other monks, and other monks likewise had him make them, and yet others did so as well, and yet others too — until his supply of bone was also exhausted.

Then yet another monk came and said: "Good sir, my needle-case has fallen apart." "Noble one, what kind shall I make for you?" "Whatever is best." "Noble one, if one made of ivory is best, the ivory is gone." "Good sir, if that is so, then make one of bone." "Noble one, the bone is gone too. If you wish, I can make one of horn." "Good sir, please make one without fail." So he made a needle-case of horn for him and gave it to him. That monk showed it to the other monks, and other monks likewise had him make them, and yet others did so as well, and yet others too — until his supply of horn was also exhausted.

Now this man, working for the monks at his own expense, using his own food and his own materials, had become impoverished. The naked ascetics (tīrthikas), seizing the occasion for mockery, began to say: "At the time when we had full confidence in our teaching, all this abounded in abundance. But now, out of misplaced confidence in the śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya, people even beg for food." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks on account of this incident, this basis of legislation, and this occasion — and so forth as before. The awakened and blessed buddhas, even while knowing, ask — and so forth as before. The Blessed One then asked the monks: "Is it true, monks, that you had needle-cases made of ivory, of bone, and of horn?" "Venerable one, it is true." The Blessed One then censured those who have great desires, who know no contentment, who are difficult to support, and who are difficult to satisfy. Having done so, the Blessed One then spoke in praise of those who have few desires, who know contentment, who are easy to support, who are easy to satisfy, who are diligent, who are restrained in their requisites, who are trained, who are of good conduct, who are scrupulous, and who are energetic — and then he declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, having clearly seen ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before.

"My śrāvakas shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: Whatever monk has a needle-case made of ivory, or of bone, or of horn, he shall break it and incur a downfall."

Now, "whatever monk" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma community. "Of ivory" means ivory itself. "Of bone" means bone itself. "Of horn" means horn itself. "Needle-case" refers to two kinds: one that has a hollow tube, and one that is like a container. Both meanings are intended here. "Has made" means by oneself or through another. "He shall break it and incur a downfall" means: having broken that object, he incurs a downfall — a transgression requiring confession. "He incurs a downfall" means he falls into the hell realms, into the animal realm, and into —
