the realm of hungry ghosts, the realms of misfortune, the lower destinies, and the states of wrong rebirth — burning him, scorching him, causing him to fall. Furthermore, so long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually acknowledged, it obstructs the virtuous qualities of Dharma — and it is for this reason that it is called "a downfall." This is what was declared.

Now, as to how a downfall comes about: whenever a monk makes or causes another to make even so much as a needle-case of ivory, bone, or horn, a downfall is incurred in every case. The monk in whose presence it is offered must ask: "Did you break that object?" If it is offered and accepted without asking, it becomes a wrongdoing. That transgression, since it has not been confessed, must be confessed again. There is no transgression for one who is acting for the first time, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one afflicted by painful feeling. This completes the eighty-fourth downfall, that of making a needle-case.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, a certain monk who was traveling through the districts came to Śrāvastī, and having grown weary from the road, he rested from his fatigue and went to the Jeta Grove, where he sat in the gateway. He found a low seat, and having washed both feet before it, he sat cross-legged there. Now it happened to be the season of hot weather, when snake-venom spreads rapidly. Tormented by the heat and longing for coolness, a certain creature had coiled up and was lying right there in that spot. As the monk, exhausted from the road, began to doze, his body twitched slightly again and again, and the seat made a creaking sound. The creature whose venom spreads rapidly thought, "This one is going to harm me," and drew itself up, coiled and alert. Then, as the monk's body twitched again and the seat creaked once more, it instantly seized him. Dying right there in that very posture, when the time came, he was born among the excellent company of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

While he was there, a group of divine maidens arrived, but he drove them away with a snapping of his fingers. They went before Śakra, the lord of the gods (Indra, king of the gods), and said: "O God, this divine son, newly born and not long arisen, sits cross-legged; when we approached him, he drove us away with a snapping of his fingers." Śakra said: "Goddesses, he was formerly a monk. Hold up a mirror before him and he will recover his memory." They held a mirror before him, and seeing himself adorned with shoulder ornaments, ear-rings, earrings, garlands, and various jewels, he recovered his memory.

Then he began to desire those maidens, and they said: "Patient one, we do not attend on you in that manner. We attend on whoever pays homage to Śakra, the lord of the gods." He reflected: "I have paid homage to the Blessed One, who is free from the foul smell of desire — so how could I now pay homage to Śakra, the lord of the gods, who revels in sensual enjoyment?" Realizing this, he said: "Sisters, is there any means by which one need not pay homage to Śakra, the lord of the gods? There is, patient one — among those divine sages who dwell there practicing celibacy, whoever among them practices the celibate life does not pay homage to Śakra, the lord of the gods, for it is Śakra himself who pays homage to such a one." He then entered among those divine sages. When Śakra, the lord of the gods, heard how that one had joined the divine sages and was living the celibate life, Śakra went to him, paid homage at his feet, and departed.

Then the former monk, now a divine son, thought to himself:

"The reason I have been maintaining the celibate life is precisely in order to go before the Blessed One and pay homage to him. To go before him merely in order to see and venerate the Blessed One while maintaining the celibate life would not be in keeping with my condition. So I shall go before the Blessed One to see and pay homage to him without maintaining the celibate life any longer."

Then the former monk, now a divine son, took up spotless earrings with pendants swaying, adorned his body with necklaces and bracelets, and filled both his hands with divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white night-blooming lotuses, and white day-blooming lotuses. At the very depth of night, blazing with surpassing brilliance of color, he went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he scattered flowers over the Blessed One, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet in homage, and sat down to one side. And through the radiance of that divine son's luminous form, the entire Jeta Grove was pervaded with a great and boundless light.

Then the former monk, now a divine son, addressed the Blessed One in verse, singing:

That grove they call the Benighted —
proclaimed throughout by throngs of goddesses,
surrounded as if by flesh-devouring she-demons —
how might one pass through it without dying?

The Blessed One declared:

Along the road called Straight,
to the place called the Fearless Quarter,
a chariot named the Soundless One,
driven by the thought of Dharma —
its focus is a sense of shame,
and mindfulness its retinue.
The driver is wisdom herself,
and right view is the guide.
Whatever man or woman has
a vehicle of this kind,
if they mount such a vehicle,
they journey to the Fearless Quarter.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the intention, the latent dispositions, the constitution, and the nature of that former monk, now a divine son, taught the Dharma in such a way that — having heard it — the divine son, while sitting in that very seat, shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of views that constitute the perishable collection, and thereby directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. In precisely this way, the Blessed One caused him to thoroughly understand each of the four noble truths of the noble ones.

Having seen the truths, he solemnly proclaimed three times: "What the venerable Blessed One has done for me is something my father never did, my mother never did, no king ever did, no god ever did, no ancestor ever did, no ascetic or brahmin ever did, no group of loving friends, dear companions, or relatives ever did: he has dried up the ocean of blood and tears; he has freed me from the mountains of bones; he has sealed shut the doors to the lower realms; he has opened wide the doors to the higher realms and to liberation; he has drawn my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; and he has placed me among gods and humans."

Then he said further:

Through your power, mighty and supreme, laden with my many faults,
the trail of lower realms blocked off, richly endowed with merit,
the path to the higher realms opened wide — and I myself
have even come to reach the trail that leads beyond all sorrow.

Relying on you, most utterly pure, today
I have gained the flawless, purified eye of Dharma.
I have attained the peaceful, noble, exalted state with joy,
and have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Among all beings, worshipped by gods and humans and asuras,
free from birth and aging and sickness and death —
to see existence as empty is exceedingly rare:
O Sage, today there is the fruit of seeing you.

Then, with his ornaments arranged and his pendant necklace flowing free,
he bowed at your feet, and with joy arising,
he circumambulated the Subduer from the right,
and rose into the sky, heading toward the divine world.

Then the monk who had formerly been a god became like a merchant who has found a fine profit, like a farmer whose harvest has come in abundantly, like a hero who has triumphed completely in battle, and like a sick man who has been fully delivered from every illness. Wearing the very same robes in which he had come before the Blessed One, he returned to his own dwelling.

Now, at a certain moment, as the night was giving way to dawn, the guestmaster opened the door and, taking up a broom, began to sweep the guesthouse. He saw the monk sitting cross-legged, and said to him, "Venerable one, do wake up. Are you, too, practicing meditative concentration as before?" When the monk did not speak a word, the guestmaster took hold of him by both arms and began to shake him. And at that moment he perceived that the monk had passed away. He then began to examine what had caused the death, and presently saw beneath the bed a swift-acting venomous serpent lying there. Frightened, he went to the other monks and said, "Venerable ones, the monk who was sleeping in the guesthouse has been seized by a swift-acting venomous serpent and has passed away."

The monks carried the body to the charnel ground, performed the cremation, and then returned. Upon their return they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: every fault and harm that has arisen here has come about because a monk made his bed on a low sleeping platform and washed both feet in front of it. Having thus reflected, he declared, "Therefore, a monk shall not make his bed on a low sleeping platform, nor wash both feet in front of it." The Blessed One having spoken and declared, "A monk shall not make his bed on a low sleeping platform, nor wash both feet in front of it," it then came about that monks who possessed no sandals were being harmed. So the Blessed One declared, "Those who possess no sandals may wash both feet separately, one side and then the other, and in this they need feel no remorse."

Then the group of six monks heard that the Blessed One had prohibited a monk from sleeping on a low sleeping platform after the monk sleeping on such a platform had been seized by a swift-acting venomous serpent and had passed away. They thereupon had beds made with legs twelve cubits high and installed ridiculously tall headboards. The other monks said to them, "Venerable ones, what are you all doing?" They replied, "Who is doing anything wrong? Did you not see that the monk was seized by a swift-acting venomous serpent and passed away? Even you, the group of six, could be seized by a swift-acting venomous serpent and pass away. Do you want to divide up our funeral goods? For such a trifling matter, why do monks rebuke monks? Is that what you call giving reproofs, hurling accusations, and speaking ill?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this case, and this situation, convened the community of monks, and so forth as before. And the passage beginning "The blessed buddhas, while knowing, feign not to know" and what follows is also as before. The blessed Buddha reprimanded the group of six monks: "Is it true, monks, that when the other monks rebuked you, you spoke in such and such words?" "It is true, Blessed One." The blessed Buddha then censured them, saying that what is contrary to the conduct of an ascetic, what is not fitting, not proper, not in accord with the code — that is not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

Then, having censured them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing the ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and so forth, as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk has a throne or a stool made for the Saṅgha, he shall have it made to the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata. If he has one made that exceeds that, it entails cutting it down and a transgression" — thus did the Blessed One establish that training rule for the hearers in the Vinaya.

Now the Venerable Charka's knees were exceeding the measure, and when they came to touch the footrest, the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "In that case, a socket for the leg is permitted."

Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of those who desire training, who revere training, and who gather the requisites for training. Having addressed the monks with words consistent with that praise, more weighty than that praise, and endowed with qualities suited to it, the Blessed One then spoke to the monks: "Monks, what was established before was a rule, and this is a further allowance. My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk has a throne or a stool made for the Saṅgha, he shall have it made to the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata, except for inserting a socket for the leg. If he has one made that exceeds that, it entails cutting it down and a transgression.

"A monk" means one who belongs to this Dharma. "Of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. "A throne" means a throne proper. "A stool" likewise means a stool proper. "Has it made" means either by himself or by another. "Except for inserting a socket for the leg" means that inserting a socket for the leg is permitted. "He shall have it made to the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata" — "the Sugata" means the Teacher. The eight finger-breadths of the Sugata constitute the measure of one standard cubit. "That exceeds that" means above that measure. "It entails cutting it down and a transgression" means that after cutting the object down, it entails a transgression that must be confessed. "A transgression" means that it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad migrations — into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of misfortune. Moreover, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities — and therefore it is called "a transgression."

Now, how does a transgression come about in this case? If a monk has a throne or a stool made — exceeding the measure of eight finger-breadths of the Sugata, other than inserting a socket for the leg — to whatever degree it exceeds, a transgression is incurred in every instance. Before accepting the excess, one should ask the person who is making it: "Have you cut that part of yours down?" If one accepts it without having asked, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing. That transgression too, not having been confessed, must also be confessed. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by feeling.

This is the eighty-fifth transgression, concerning adjusting the legs of a throne. It is complete.

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Because Nandaka was a newly admitted monk, his throne had been seized by the most senior monk, and now the time for allocating lodgings had arrived as well. He thought to himself: "What method is there so that no one seizes my throne?" Then, having obtained some cotton wool for a certain purpose, an idea came to him concerning it: "I will spread cotton wool over it and leave it there." So he spread cotton wool on top of the throne and left it.

When a certain very senior monk arrived and saw it, he asked: "Venerable one, whose is this?" The novice replied: "It is my cotton wool." Then a monk who was sitting nearby said: "What the novice says is true — the cotton wool is the novice's. But the throne itself belongs to the Saṅgha." When he said this, the novice became angry and, taking the cotton wool, spread it little by little over that throne.

The monk did not inspect the matter and simply lay down there. By the time dawn came and he rose in the morning, all his robes had turned grey with the cotton wool fibers. The other monks said to him: "Did you sleep on a battlefield?" He explained how it had come about, and the monks, rebuking those few monks, said: "Why do monks spread cotton wool on the Saṅgha's thrones or small thrones and place them there?" They criticized, disparaged, and complained about it. Then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this occasion, and this circumstance, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth as before. The passage beginning "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, though knowing, feign ignorance" also proceeds as before. The awakened Blessed One then questioned the venerable Nandaka, saying: "Nandaka, is it true that you spread cotton wool on the Saṅgha's throne?" He replied: "Blessed One, I did so." The awakened Blessed One reproached him, saying that such conduct was not in keeping with the way of a renunciant, was not fitting, was not proper, and was not in accord with the rule — it was not something that one who has gone forth should do. The Blessed One censured him thoroughly.

Having censured him in many ways, the Blessed One then addressed the monks, saying: "Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits clearly and truly, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk spreads cotton wool on a throne or small throne belonging to the Saṅgha, or has it spread, incurs a transgression that must be confessed after having been gathered in summary.

Whatever monk: this refers to Nandaka, a son of the Śākyas, or anyone else who is similarly situated. Of the Saṅgha: this means the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers. Throne: a throne proper. Small throne: a small throne proper. Cotton wool: any one of the five kinds — the cotton wool of the śalmali tree, the arka, the kaśa, the buka, or the eraka. Spreads: by oneself. Has it spread: through another. Incurs a transgression that must be confessed after having been gathered in summary: having gathered that thing, it is a transgression that must be confessed — it is a downfall that must be confessed. As for the meaning of incurs a transgression: it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinations of the hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, into the lower realms, and into states of wrong falling. Furthermore, as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous dharmas — that is why it is said to incur a transgression. Now, how does such a transgression come about?"

Whatever amount — however small — a monk spreads wool shearing-by-shearing or in loose layers onto the chair or small stool of the Saṅgha, he becomes one who has committed a transgression in all cases. The person in whose presence he is placing it must ask him: "Have you gathered that article?" If he accepts and takes it without having been asked, it becomes a wrongdoing. That downfall, too, since it has not yet been confessed, must be confessed. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by painful sensations. This is the transgression-entailing offense regarding defiling with wool — the eighty-sixth, now complete.

The Blessed One (the Buddha), the awakened one, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that monks should be permitted to make seat coverings (gdingba). When monks were engaging in making seat coverings in excess of the proper measure, and when the Blessed One declared, "Monks should be permitted to make seat coverings," there were cases where, in that same context, monks were censuring other monks, hurling accusations at them, and speaking ill of them for engaging in making seat coverings in excess of the proper measure. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, with respect to this incident, this initial occasion, and this circumstance, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed Ones who are buddhas, knowing yet acting as if unaware, and so forth — this too is as before.

The Blessed One, the buddha, then questioned the monks: "Monks, when I declared 'Monks are to be permitted to make seat coverings,' is it true that you were engaging in making them in excess of the proper measure?" "Venerable One, it is so." The Blessed One, the buddha, then censured great desiring, not knowing contentment, being difficult to nourish, and being difficult to satisfy. Thereupon the Blessed One praised having few desires, knowing contentment, being easy to nourish, being easy to satisfy, being lean of body, having few possessions, being of refined qualities, being of beautiful conduct, and being aware of what is sufficient. He then addressed the monks thus:

"Monks, therefore, seeing the ten benefits precisely as they are, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth as before. "My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk is making a seat covering, let him make it within the proper measure. The proper measure for a seat covering is this: it may reach at most to the height of the Sugata, and in width to one and a half of the same measure. If one makes it exceeding that, having cut it, he commits a transgression." Thus the Blessed One established that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The venerable Charka, because his seat covering exceeded the proper measure and could not adequately serve as such, placed bundles of leaves to the side at the foot of his bed in order to protect his sleeping place. It is the very nature of reality of the Blessed Ones, the buddhas, who live and abide, who are alive and alert, to travel out of compassion for beings who are to be tamed, going at the appropriate time into the realms of hell-beings, ranging among the animals, ranging among the hungry ghosts, ranging among the gods, ranging through the provinces, ranging along the rivers, ranging through the mountains, ranging through the charnel grounds, and proceeding to temples. In this matter, it being the Blessed One's intention to proceed to a temple, the Blessed One went to the place where the temple of the venerable Charka was.

The Blessed One saw that beside the venerable Charka's sleeping mat, bundles of leaves had been placed. Having seen this, he spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, whose sleeping mat is this?"

"Venerable sir, it is the venerable Charka's."

"Then why have bundles of leaves been placed beside the mat?"

"Venerable sir, the Blessed One has permitted monks to make bed-frames; he has permitted them to be made according to the proper measure. The measure for a bed-frame is this: as high as the Sugata's height, and in width half a height plus one height-unit. If one exceeds that, the article shall be cut down and there is a transgression." Responding to this rule of training laid down in the Vinaya for the hearers, the venerable Charka's bed-frame exceeded the measure by far; being unable to lower it to the measure, he had placed bundles of leaves beside the mat in order to protect his sleeping place.

"Ānanda, for that reason, let it be lowered by a full Sugata height."

The Blessed One then gave praise for desiring the training, for revering the training, and for equipping oneself with the requisites of the training, and he addressed the monks with words in keeping with that theme, words of greater import, and words endowed with qualities appropriate thereto. He then declared to the monks:

"Monks, what was laid down before was the rule; what follows now is the permission. Let my hearers recite this rule of training in the Vinaya in this way: When a monk makes a bed-frame, he is permitted to make it to the proper measure. The measure for a bed-frame is this: as high as the Sugata's height, and in width half a height plus one height-unit. Let it be lowered by a full Sugata height. If one exceeds that, the article shall be cut down and there is a transgression."

Now, "a monk" means a person subject to these rules. "A bed-frame" means a frame elevated in tiers. "Makes" means making it oneself or having another make it. "Permitted to make it to the proper measure" means making it in accordance with whatever the proper measure for a bed-frame is.

"The measure for a bed-frame is this: as high as the Sugata's height, and in width half a height plus one height-unit." Here, "height" means in the vertical dimension. "The Sugata" means the Teacher. "His height" means three standard cubits. "Width" means the horizontal dimension. "Half a height plus one height-unit": the Sugata's half height plus one height-unit equals one standard cubit and six finger-breadths.

"Let it be lowered by a full Sugata height" means that if the measure cannot be met, it is to be lowered by a full Sugata height; and a full Sugata height is one and a half standard cubits plus one height-unit. Therefore the maximum permissible height for a bed-frame is one and a half standard cubits plus five units.

"If one exceeds that" means going above this. "The article shall be cut down and there is a transgression" means: after cutting down and removing that object, the transgression of having cut it is to be confessed. "There is a transgression" means it causes one to burn, to be cooked, and to fall into the bad destinies of hell-beings, animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong downfall. Moreover, for as long as such a transgression is neither confessed nor individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. For that reason, it is said "there is a transgression."

How does a transgression occur? Whenever a monk makes a bed-frame exceeding, by however little, the maximum measure in height of one and a half cubits plus five units, and in width of one cubit and six finger-breadths, a transgression is incurred in every case. One must ask the person in whose presence the enlargement is being made: "Has your article been cut down?" If, without having asked, one accepts and uses it, an offense is committed. That transgression too, being unconfessed, must again be confessed.

There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is mentally disturbed, for one who is distracted in mind, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This concludes the eighty-seventh offense entailing a transgression arising from a mattress cover.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "A monk may have a mattress cover made." Some monks, having had one made exceeding the measure, the Blessed One, having declared "A monk may have a mattress cover made," reproached those monks, saying: "Why, monks, do you have one made exceeding the measure?" — censuring, rebuking, and disparaging them. Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and then the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, this basis for discussion, and this occasion, convened an assembly of the community of monks — and so forth, as before. The passage beginning "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, make inquiry" — that too is as before. The Blessed One then questioned the monks: "Monks, when I declared 'A monk may have a mattress cover made,' is it true that you had one made exceeding the measure?" "It is true, Blessed One." The Blessed One then censured great desire, not knowing satisfaction, being difficult to maintain, and being difficult to fill. Thereupon the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of few desires, knowing satisfaction, being easy to maintain, being easy to fill, of being thin, of few requisites, of purified qualities, of beauty, and of knowing warmth, addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits in full, a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya is to be established" — and so forth, as before.

"My hearers are to recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk has a mattress cover made, let him have it made according to the measure. The measure of a mattress cover is this: four Sugata-cubits in length and one Sugata's width in width. If he has one made exceeding that, having cut it down, a transgression is incurred."

The phrase "a monk" refers to one who holds this Dharma. "Mattress cover" means a garment for the ill. "Has it made" means either by oneself or by another. "Let him have it made according to the measure" means in accordance with whatever the measure of a mattress cover is. "The measure of a mattress cover is this: four Sugata-cubits in length and one Sugata's width in width" — the word "length" means in the long direction. "Sugata" means the Teacher. "Four of his cubits in length" means six standard cubits. "Width" means across. "One Sugata's width in width" — the Sugata's width means three standard cubits. "If he has one made exceeding that" means more than that. "Having cut it down, a transgression is incurred" means: having cut that article down, a transgression is incurred — a transgression that must be confessed. "A transgression is incurred" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower realms, and the states of wrong descent. Moreover, for as long as that transgression has not been confessed and individually disclosed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. For that reason, it is said "a transgression is incurred." How does a transgression occur?

If a monk has even a little of a robe-covering made and has it made to exceed six sugata-spans in length and three sugata-spans in width, it constitutes a transgression in every case. One should ask the person in whose presence it is being sewn: "Has that article of yours been cut?" If it is sewn and accepted without having asked, it becomes a wrongdoing. That transgression, moreover, not being a transgression requiring confession, must still be confessed. There is no transgression for one who is a beginner, one who is insane, one who is mentally disturbed, or one who is afflicted by feeling. This is the transgression arising from a robe-covering. The eighty-eighth rule is complete.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that monks should have a rains-season outer robe made. Monks then had one made exceeding the measure by far, and some monks of little means censured, upbraided, and spoke ill of them, saying: "The Blessed One has declared that monks should have a rains-season outer robe made — why do you monks have one made that far exceeds the measure?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence and this occasion, convened an assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed Buddhas, knowing full well, inquire — and so forth, also as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned the monks: "Monks, I declared that monks should have a rains-season outer robe made — is it true that you had one made far exceeding the measure?" "Venerable one, it is so." The Blessed One, the Buddha, then rebuked having great desires, not knowing contentment, being difficult to maintain, and being difficult to satisfy. Then the Blessed One spoke in praise of having few desires, knowing contentment, being easy to maintain, being easy to satisfy, being meek, keeping few possessions, having purified qualities, being refined, and knowing warmth, and addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: If a monk has a rains-season outer robe made, let him have it made according to the proper measure. The proper measure of the rains-season outer robe is this: in length, six sugata-heights at most; in width, three and a half sugata-heights. If one has it made exceeding that, it is cut and a transgression is incurred."

"A monk" means one who belongs to this Dharma. "A rains-season outer robe" means a garment for protection from rain. "Has it made" means either by oneself or by another. "Let him have it made according to the proper measure" means according to whatever the proper measure of the rains-season outer robe is. "The proper measure of the rains-season outer robe is this: in length, six sugata-heights at most; in width, three and a half sugata-heights." Here, "at most" means at the limit. "Sugata" means the Teacher. "Six of his heights" — six of those heights amounts, in standard cubit measure, to nine cubits. "In width" means across. "Three and a half sugata-heights" — three and a half of the Sugata's heights amounts, in standard cubit measure, to three cubits and eight finger-widths. "If one has it made exceeding that" means beyond that amount.

"Having cut it, it becomes a downfall" means that having cut that article, one incurs a downfall of the kind that must be confessed. "It becomes a downfall" means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the bad destinies — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower rebirths, and the states of wrong falling. Furthermore, for as long as that downfall is neither confessed nor individually confessed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. Therefore it is said to become a downfall. As for how the downfall occurs: if a monk has a rains-season outer robe made that exceeds, in any degree whatsoever, the maximum of nine cubits in length and three cubits and eight finger-widths in width, in every case it becomes a downfall. One should ask the person before whom one is about to receive it: "Have you cut that article?" If one accepts and receives it without having asked, it becomes a wrongdoing. Since that downfall also remains unconfessed, it must again be confessed. Those who are beginners, those who are insane, those who are mentally disturbed, and those overcome by sensation incur no downfall. Thus is completed the eighty-ninth rule derived from the rains-season outer robe.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Venerable Ānanda went to the dwelling of Kalpika the carpenter and sat for a little while in conversation, then said: "Friend, are you able to sew a robe of the Sugata's robe-measure?" He replied: "Noble one, what use to you is a robe of the Sugata's robe-measure?" Then he said: "Poor man, what would I put here for you? If you want wages, sew it." Ānanda thought: "What this fellow says is not wrong — what would he put here for me? It is because I need wages that I will sew it." Realizing this, he said: "Noble one, sew it." So Ānanda gave him cloth and wages, and he sewed it. Ānanda put on a small portion of it and carried the remainder over his shoulder, and a monk who saw him and Ānanda said: "Elder, look at that patch-cloak — let it rest." Ānanda replied: "Reverend, this is not a patch-cloak." "Then what is it?" "It is a robe of the Sugata's measure." The monk said: "Elder, is it fitting for you to wear a robe of the Sugata's measure? It would be fitting if one were being pressed down under the heel of enemies." The monk said: "Does the elder then have enemies?" "From the very beginning you are the chief enemy of my enemies — therefore I cannot bear that you wear a robe of the Sugata's measure." Monks of little account then reproached, jeered at, and censured: "Why do monks wear robes of the Sugata's robe-measure?" The monks reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on account of this incident, this occasion, and this context, convened an assembly of monks, and so on, just as before. "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while knowing full well, feigned ignorance" — and so on, also just as before. The Blessed One then asked Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you had a robe of the Sugata's robe-measure made?" "Reverend one, it is not." The Blessed One then rebuked what was not in accordance with the conduct of a renunciant, not in accord with propriety, not fitting, not in conformity with the training — declaring that it was not something a person who has gone forth should do. After rebuking in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, seeing fully the ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so on, just as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: 'Furthermore, whatever monk has a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's robe — that is a transgression.'" In this way the Blessed One laid down that training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya.

Now, after the Blessed One had laid down the training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya — declaring that whatever monk has a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's robe commits a transgression — the venerable Ānanda caused others to exceed that measure. And when a number of monks began to rebuke, revile, and speak ill of those monks, saying: "Why do you have robes made exceeding what the Blessed One prescribed?" — the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, the earlier rule was the original ruling, and this is the supplementary ruling. My śrāvakas are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows: 'Furthermore, whatever monk has a robe made to the measure of the Sugata's robe, or has a robe made exceeding the Sugata's robe — that is a transgression.'

The measure of the Sugata's robe is this: ten of the Sugata's spans in length, and six of the Sugata's spans in width. That is the measure of the Sugata's robe.

Now as to the words 'whatever monk': this means Ānanda, son of the Śākyas, or anyone else of that kind.

'The Sugata' means the Teacher.

'Of the measure of his robe' means of whatever measure the Sugata's robe is.

'Robe' means any one of seven types: woollen cloth, hemp cloth, silk cloth, cotton cloth, fine linen cloth, cotton-hemp cloth, or solar cloth.

'Has made' means either by oneself or through another.

'Exceeding the Sugata's robe' means anything larger than that.

'Transgression' means it burns, scorches, and causes one to fall into the wretched states — the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the lower destinies, and the states of downfall. Moreover, so long as the transgression is not confessed and not individually confessed, it obstructs virtuous qualities. Therefore it is called a transgression.

The measure of the Sugata's robe is this: ten of the Sugata's spans in length, and six of the Sugata's spans in width. That is the measure of the Sugata's robe. As for the ten spans of the Sugata in length, that is twenty-five standard forearm-lengths. As for the six spans of the Sugata in width, that is nine standard forearm-lengths.

How does a transgression arise? Whenever a monk has a robe made that is even slightly equal to the measure of the Sugata's robe, or a robe exceeding the Sugata's robe, a transgression arises in every case. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, or one afflicted by painful sensations.

Here ends the ninetieth transgression arising from the measure of the Sugata's robe."

Here ends the collection of transgressions.

The Vinaya Analysis, the eightieth fascicle.

Summary verse:

A village, and another's house,
the trainings, and a forest retreat —
by the speech of the Buddha, speaking benefit,
it is taught that each is to be confessed separately.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Kalandaka bamboo grove at Veḷuvana. In the city of Rājagṛha there lived a certain householder who was wealthy, of great riches, of abundant possessions, whose property was extensive and vast, who was endowed with wealth rivaling that of Vaiśravaṇa, competing with Vaiśravaṇa in his riches. He took a wife from among his social equals and together with her he played and took delight and enjoyed pleasure. While he was thus playing and taking delight and enjoying pleasure, his wife at a certain other time became with child. Eight or nine months passed, and from that birth there arose a daughter who was beautiful of form, lovely to behold, fair, with eyes like blue lotuses, possessing the fragrance of blue lotuses, and with a complexion resembling the color of blue lotus petals. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — three weeks of seven days — they held a grand birth celebration for the daughter, and they proceeded to give her a name. "What shall this daughter be called?" The relatives said: "Since this daughter has eyes like the blue lotus, possesses the fragrance of the blue lotus, and has a complexion like blue lotus petals, let her name be Blue Lotus Hue." And so the name Blue Lotus Hue was given to her. She was nurtured and raised and grew to be a young woman.

Her father had no son, and he thought to himself: "I shall not give this daughter to anyone on account of lineage, nor on account of wealth, nor on account of beauty. Rather, I shall give her to whichever man agrees to dwell in my house as a resident son-in-law."

Now there was another householder in Rājagṛha who had taken a wife from among his social equals and together with her he played and took delight and enjoyed pleasure. While he was thus playing and taking delight and enjoying pleasure, his wife at a certain other time became with child. Eight or nine months passed, and from that birth a son was born. He too was given a name in keeping with his lineage, was nurtured and raised, and grew to be a young man.

Then at a certain other time that young man's parents both passed away in their time. As he wandered here and there, destitute, it happened by chance that he came to the house of that householder. The householder said to him: "Young man, whose son are you?" "I am the son of such and such a householder." "Young man, where is your father?" "He has passed away." "Young man, where is your mother?" "She too has passed away." "Young man, if that is the case, I shall give you my daughter in marriage — become my resident son-in-law, dwelling in my house." "Your lordship has done no wrong. Since I too am bereft of both parents and wander here and there in wretched desolation, may it be as you say — you have spoken no wrong; I shall do just so."

That householder gave him Blue Lotus Hue, and on an auspicious day and date, with a brief ceremony, he sent her as a bride. The young man then began to dwell in that house.

Now after some time had passed, the father of Blue Lotus Hue passed away, and her mother, dwelling as she pleased and wandering about, being attended with good food and fine clothing, began to be afflicted by the afflictions. She thought to herself: "If I were to bring another man here, my son-in-law would come to know of it. Let me instead play and take delight and enjoy pleasure together with him." And so she made her feelings known to him.

The domain of a woman captivates the senses and stirs desire, and so he had begun to look upon her with longing. Then she displayed her bodily signs to him, and he lay together with her. In time, a being had entered the womb of Blue Lotus Hue, and when the moment of giving birth drew near, she sent a servant girl to her mother, saying: "Go and summon my mother." When the girl went and found her sitting alone together with her son-in-law in a secluded place, she waited there for a short while, thinking it over. When the mother came out, the girl said: "Blue Lotus Hue is calling for you — please go." The mother went, and before long Blue Lotus Hue gave birth to a daughter. Blue Lotus Hue then said to the servant girl: "What is keeping you?" The girl replied: "May your mother and your husband be well." Blue Lotus Hue said: "What do you mean?" The girl told her what had happened, and Blue Lotus Hue said: "Girl, are you slandering my mother and my husband?" The girl replied: "My lady, if you do not believe me, I shall make it plain before your very eyes." And so she set about watching for an opportunity for the two of them, and when at last the two were sitting alone together, she went quickly and said to Blue Lotus Hue: "Come quickly — look for yourself!" Blue Lotus Hue went quickly and looked, and she saw the two of them lying together. Blue Lotus Hue thought to herself: "This wretched woman — is there no other man to be found that she takes my son-in-law to bed with her? And this wretch of a man — is there no other woman to be found that he lies with my own mother?" Recognizing what had happened, she was overcome with intolerable fury, and she hurled the infant at the son-in-law, crying: "You wretch, from this day forward enjoy yourself with her!" The child struck against the father's body, tumbled onto the threshold of the door, and its head was shattered. Blue Lotus Hue covered her head and left the house.

Before long, she encountered a merchant caravan that had suffered losses and was ruined. She fled away with them, and the caravan leader saw her and became attached to her beauty and her youthful bloom. He asked: "Young woman, whose are you?" She replied that she belonged to whoever was giving her food and clothing. The caravan leader took her as his wife, and the caravan that had been ruined and broken gradually came to ruin completely, and he settled down there with her.

After a time, the caravan leader traded in the market, took the proceeds of his trade, and returned to the countryside. The merchants there were inviting one another to feasts at each other's houses and holding celebrations. The caravan leader did not contribute anything, and the merchants said to him: "Caravan leader, you borrowed things from us and gave nothing in return." He replied: "You men have wives at home, and that is why you can hold feasts, but there is no one to tend to me, so how could I give anything?" They said: "If that is the case, why not look for a wife?" He replied: "If there is a young woman resembling my wife, I will take her as a bride." They said: "Tell us, then — what does your lady look like?" He described the beauty and youthful bloom of Blue Lotus Hue, and they said: "Caravan leader, she is a precious woman indeed. But if there is anyone else like her, we shall search for such a one." And so they began to search, and before long they came upon Blue Lotus Hue's own daughter, who so closely resembled her that they raised the matter with the girl. They urged her to go along, saying: "For whom?" "For a great caravan leader." "Friends, if we are to depend on a gift, know this — there is a fault in him: he has already taken a wife and abandoned her, and now he roams about. We will not hand her over."

"If that is the case, then let the gift be made." And so they persuaded her, and the caravan leader took her as his wife. After that, the merchants disposed of their goods, took the proceeds, and set out toward the place where they had previously suffered great loss — and in due course, as the place of ruin drew near, they came to a rocky cliff. The caravan leader left the goods and the girl there at the cliff and went on ahead with a small party toward the place of ruin. As he went, Blue Lotus Hue came and greeted him with the word "Welcome," and said: "Caravan leader, have you arrived in good health?" He replied: "Good woman, how could I be well? I have been ruined." "Though you, prince, have come alive — and that is cause for joy — the wealth too shall come again." After a little while he said: "Good woman, I am going to search for the goods that were lost." She said: "Go without delay." As soon as he had gone, one who had been his companion came along and asked Blue Lotus Hue: "Where has the caravan leader gone?" She replied: "He has gone to search for what was lost." "Where, and lost by whom?" "I do not know. He only said, 'I have suffered loss; I am going to search for what was lost.'" The companion said: "The way he arrived just now in such fine condition — never in earlier times did he arrive in such fine condition — that means he has deceived you. Say something that will match the occasion." "What else is there to say? He laid down a stone and brought a landowner's wife of this sort — you would not even be fit to wash her two feet." "Companion, is that true?" "It is true." At that he told her to remain, and sat in silence, saying nothing.

Before long the caravan leader returned, and he opened with a dismissive remark, saying: "Prince, have you searched for the lost goods?" "Good woman, I searched." "Prince, she has deceived you. No one anywhere has ruined you. She heard how you said you had laid down a stone and brought along a landowner's wife — bring her here and expel her. Whoever's property is placed in two households will become thin, wholly exhausted, and utterly depleted." "Good woman, even if that were so, have you not heard that in a house where a man has two wives there will be times of bitterness — they will not drink cold water from the same vessel — there will be quarreling, wrangling, and strife? Prince, let this be peacefully settled. It will not come to that. Bring her in and expel the other. If she is somewhat like a younger sister, I shall treat her with the perception of a younger sister. If she is somewhat like a daughter, I shall treat her with the perception of a daughter." He said: "Good woman, if that is how it is, then I shall bring her — no harm done," and so he brought her. When he saw her, desire arose in him toward her.

On another occasion, as Blue Lotus Hue was beginning to arrange the girl's hair, she noticed that there was a wound on her head. Seeing it, she asked: "What fault has this girl committed?" The girl replied: "It was no fault of mine. My grandmother told your mother's father, and he grew angry with you and threw you out, and you fell on the threshold step — that is how this wound came about." "What is your grandmother's name?" "She is called Che-ge-mo." "What is your mother's name?" "Blue Lotus Hue." She thought to herself: There I was a mother, great and small; here I am a daughter, great and small — and so I shall proceed in every way. She covered her head and left the house. Before long, going her own way, she saw that favorable conditions were gathering in Vaiśālī, and she too joined that departing company; and together with that company and those merchants she traveled in happiness and ease, and went to Vaiśālī. The organized women who were dwelling in Vaiśālī said: "These ruined merchants — let them play with us and —"

— but they shall not let them enjoy pleasures and delights." Then one of the organized women spoke up: "These merchants have brought along some sort of earth-holder — we would not even stoop to wash her two feet, so why should they enjoy playing with us and experiencing pleasures and delights?" The organized women gathered together and went before Blue Lotus Hue and said: "Earth-holder, if you are going to provide for our livelihood, why do you not join our house?" She removed the covering from her head and said: "From this day forward I shall join your house" — and so she entered among them.

Then one day when those organized women had gathered in a drinking session and were talking amongst themselves, they said: "Of all of us, which one has managed to strip which merchant of how much wealth?" One woman said: "I stripped such-and-such a merchant named Che-ge-mo of this much wealth." Others said: "We stripped merchants named Che-ge-mo of this much wealth." And yet others said: "We too stripped merchants named Che-ge-mo of this much wealth."

Now there was in Vaiśālī an unattractive young man who sold perfumes, and none of the organized women had taken him on as a client. So the organized women said: "Whichever of us is able to take on as a client a Che-ge-mo young perfume-seller — her we shall declare to possess the qualities of a true woman." Blue Lotus Hue asked: "Is he actually male, possessed of a man's faculties?" They replied: "He is male, possessed of a man's faculties." Then they said: "If you manage to take him on as a client, we shall give you the place of the youngest among us. Very well. And if you are not able to take him on, what then? She shall pay you sixty kārṣāpaṇas. Oh, come now — do it like this."

Blue Lotus Hue then engaged the services of the landlord of the young perfume-seller's premises, and he arranged for a young girl to be sent as a serving-maid, instructing her: "Girl, you shall purchase perfume each and every day from the young perfume-seller named Che-ge-mo. If he asks to whose account you carry it, say: 'A young man of good family has come, and I carry it to him.'" So the serving-maid went and bought perfume from the young perfume-seller day after day. He said to her: "Girl, to whose account do you carry the perfume each day?" She replied: "A young man of good family has come here, and I carry it to him."

Then again Blue Lotus Hue spoke to the serving-maid: "Girl, go to the young perfume-seller and buy medicines — both cooling and heating. If he asks to whose account you carry them, say: 'That young man of good family is ill here, and I carry them for his medicines.' And if he asks whose account it is to be charged to, say: 'To Blue Lotus Hue's account.'" The serving-maid took the kārṣāpaṇas, went to the young perfume-seller, and said: "Give me medicines — both cooling and heating." He asked: "For whose account?" She replied: "A young man of good family is ill here, and I carry them for his medicines." He asked: "Whose account?" She said: "Blue Lotus Hue's."

He thought to himself: This is a great lady of rank indeed — she tends to the sick with her own medicines. And feeling affection arise in him for her, he said to the girl: "Girl, go and tell Blue Lotus Hue that the young perfume-seller wishes to visit her." The girl went and told Blue Lotus Hue, and she replied: "Girl, go back and say this: 'The young man of good family has not yet recovered.'"

She went and told him this. Again and again he kept asking the girl when he might come. She would report this to Blue Lotus Hue, who thought to herself: He has grown even more attached — I must devise a clever stratagem. So she fashioned a dummy, laid it upon a bier, carried it to the charnel ground, burned it there, and then, disheveling her hair and weeping, began to walk not far from the shop of the young perfume-seller. The young perfume-seller saw her.

Now the Blessed One — the Buddha — had declared that women bind men by eight means: by dancing, by singing, by music, by laughter, by weeping, by a glance, by touch, and by provoking a wound. And so, becoming intensely attached to her, the young perfume-seller said again to the girl: "Girl, I shall come now." She reported this to Blue Lotus Hue, who said: "Girl, go back and say this: 'Young man of good family, the time has come — yet since the grief has not yet cleared, how could a meeting be possible?'"

The more Blue Lotus Hue drew back and kept him at a distance, the more the young perfume-seller burned with longing to see her. So Blue Lotus Hue sent word that, rather than coming to meet her directly, he should await her in a pleasant park. The young perfume-seller came to that park carrying abundant food, drink, fine robes, and garlands, and there the two of them ate and drank together for a while. Then, in the merriness of it all, with the force of wine his own wits left him. Blue Lotus Hue thought to herself: Now is the moment — let this be witnessed by many people. She placed a garland upon his head, rolled him in a blanket, and led him home. When the women of her company saw this they were filled with the greatest wonder and said: "How well this earth-holder has done in taking the ugly little perfume-seller under her wing!" And they installed him in the place of honor.

He played with her, rejoiced with her, and lived in pleasure with her, until in the course of time a child quickened within her.

Now in Vaiśālī there were two gate-keepers — one to the east and one to the west. These two had become friends, and one of them said: "Dear friend, is there any means by which, even when we both die and our time has come, the bond of our friendship might not be severed?" The other replied: "Dear friend — let our daughters pledge themselves to each other in a mutual pact. If I have a son and you have a daughter, give your daughter to my son; if you have a son and I have a daughter, I shall give my daughter to your son. In this way, even when we two die and our time comes, the stream of friendship will not be cut." The first said: "So be it — excellent!"

When nine months had passed, Blue Lotus Hue gave birth, and a boy was born. She thought to herself: Whichever woman has a young son — men will completely abandon her. Knowing she would be forsaken, she said to the nursemaid: "Girl, take this infant and a lamp, go out onto the main road, set the child down in one spot there, light the lamp, and stay to one side until someone takes him." The nursemaid carried him and set him down in a place not far from the eastern gate, lit the lamp, and stood to one side. The eastern gate-keeper, seeing the lamp, went over in puzzlement to investigate. When he saw the infant, he took him, went home to his wife, and said: "Dear one, here is your child." And she received him with great joy.

Then, as night turned to dawn, there was celebration. The neighbours spoke among themselves: "Good people, what has brought such joy to the house of this western gate-keeper?" Some said, "A son has been born to him." Others said, "If his wife was not with child, how could a son have come?" And others said, "Good people, there are women in whose womb a child lies without showing." The eastern gate-keeper heard this and thought: "Since a son has been born to him, if I were to have a daughter, she could become his bride." And so he sent that household gifts of clothing and ornaments.

The child was nursed and raised, and when he had grown up, he entered the assembly. Then at another time, a living creature entered the womb of a woman with the complexion of a blue lotus. Nine months passed, and when she gave birth, a daughter was born. The mother thought: "Men will completely abandon a woman who has a young daughter." Knowing she would be forsaken, she said to the nursemaid: "Girl, take this infant girl and a lamp, go out onto the main road, set the child down in one spot there, light the lamp, and stay to one side until someone takes her." The nursemaid carried her and placed her in a spot not far from the western gate, lit the lamp, and stood to one side. The western gate-keeper, seeing the lamp, went over in puzzlement to investigate. When he saw the infant girl, he took her, went to his wife, and said: "Dear one, here is your daughter." And she received her with great joy.

Then, as night turned to dawn, there was celebration. The neighbours spoke among themselves: "Good people, what has brought such joy to the house of this eastern gate-keeper?" Some said, "A daughter has been born to him." Others said, "If his wife was not with child, how could a daughter have come?" And others said, "Good people, there are women in whose womb a child lies without showing." The western gate-keeper heard this and thought: "Since a daughter has been born to him, she shall become my son's bride." And so he sent that household gifts of clothing and ornaments.

The girl was nursed and raised, and when she had grown up, she too entered the community of women. Then at another time, five hundred members of the assembly went out to the pleasure grove and began to take counsel together: "Let us likewise go to the pleasure grove and there, whatever happens, let us abduct some woman who is suitable to share among us." "So be it." "Whom shall we abduct?" "The Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one." "Good — let us establish this as a rule: any one of us who refuses to take pleasure and sport with her shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas by the assembly."

They hired the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, brought her to the pleasure grove, and all five hundred members of the assembly took turns sporting with her in pleasure. Now the son of the eastern gate-keeper was unwilling to take part in the sport, and the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one said to him: "Young master, take your pleasure and sport. Otherwise, these men will impose a fine of sixty kārṣāpaṇas upon you." Fearing the penalty, he joined in the sport, and thereby attachment to the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one arose in him. He then took her to himself alone as his wife.

The Licchavīs were furious, and they declared: "The son of the eastern gate-keeper has taken as his own wife alone a woman who was meant to be enjoyed in common by the assembly — we will go and kill him." Now the world has friends, enemies, and those who are neutral; and so someone went to the eastern gate-keeper and told him what had come to pass. The eastern gate-keeper was frightened. He went before the Licchavīs, prostrated at their feet, and said:

"Give me your son's alms." They said, "What fault is there with the master of the house?" And he explained the whole matter to them at length. Then some of them said, "O wise ones, this eastern gate-keeper has long been of benefit to us. If his son does not wish to share the woman with the assembly, then let her be given to him." Others said, "No blame — let it be so." And thus they gave the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one to him. Without any shame, the son of the eastern gate-keeper took the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned girl as his own wife, having obtained her from the assembly. Then his father went to the western gate-keeper and said, "Friend, give your girl as a bride to the boy." He replied, "Friend, your son has already taken a wife — what use is another bride?" He said, "Friend, the earlier match fell through, so give her now. And if prosperity should come to me, I will arrange a household retinue befitting the wife of my son." Because the earlier match had indeed fallen through, the western gate-keeper gave his daughter to the son of the eastern gate-keeper. And that son of the eastern gate-keeper, determining the auspicious day and date and propitious moment of conjunction, took her as his bride.

Now at that time, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was going to the home of that eastern gate-keeper, and he said to the girl: "Young woman, the senior woman of your household is your mother. The householder here is your elder brother. Do not give rise to a mind of deep hostility toward your mother. Do not let yourself be drawn toward the hell realms. Play with the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one, delight with her, and enjoy yourself in good cheer." Now from that play, delight, and merry enjoyment with the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one a child was born, and the girl began pushing that little boy outside the gate. Just then a brahmin who was passing along that road saw this and spoke a verse:

Among human beings, highest of the highest and supreme among the supreme,
a śrāvaka of the unrivalled Victor, the Protector,
lovely as a mandāra flower in full bloom —
sister, what is this boy to you?

She too spoke a verse in reply:

Brahmin, this one is my elder brother,
and this one is the son of my elder brother, and the thread that binds us.
This one's father is my own father,
having become my elder brother, he is now my husband.

When the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one heard this, she sent the girl-messenger to him and asked, "What are these two saying?" She said, "They are speaking nonsense — not good words at all. As to what is true in this: the son whom I abandoned at the eastern gate is now your householder husband. The daughter whom I abandoned at the western gate is now your sister-in-law." The Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one thought: "Before, I became the elder sister-in-law of my mother, and then I became the elder sister-in-law of the daughter. Now I have become the elder sister-in-law of the daughter, and the son has become the householder. In every direction there is nowhere to go." She wrapped her head in her shawl and left the house. As chance would have it, she saw a congenial companion on the road to Rājagṛha, and she went with him to Rājagṛha. There she sustained herself by the life of a courtesan. Then it came to pass that five hundred young men from the pleasure grove came and began to deliberate: "O wise ones, let us go likewise to the pleasure grove and do whatever comes to pass — let us abduct some courtesan." "Let it be so." "Whom shall we abduct?" "The Earth-Holder." "No harm" — and with that they hired the Earth-Holder, the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one, for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and led her to the pleasure grove. They ate and drank and played with her, delighted with her, and enjoyed themselves in good cheer. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the time had come to tame the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one, was walking and sitting beneath a tree not far at all from them.

Then one member of the pleasure party said: "This great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana — he is liberated from such bonds of affliction, whereas we are sunk in the swamp of desire." The Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one said: "I engaged the ugly little perfume-seller's boy in Vaiśālī." The one in the pleasure party asked: "What do you mean by that — do you wish to engage this one too?" She replied: "Well, is this one endowed with a man's faculties?" "He is indeed endowed with a man's faculties." She then said: "If I were to draw him in, what would you give me?" "Five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." "And if you cannot draw him in, what will befall you?" "You may take my wife for yourself alone." "Very well then — do it thus."

The Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one accepted the wager and went to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was. She arrived and began to display the wiles of a woman, the coyness of a woman, the enticements of a woman, the artful tricks of a woman. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, however, had withdrawn his senses and sat in composure. She thought to herself: "The touch of a woman's domain is a poison — if I embrace him, he will come under my power." And she began to move to embrace him.

At that, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose up into the sky above, spreading his wings like a king among swans, and spoke these verses:

A contorted machine of bones,
wound all around with sinews,
foul, rotting, and foul-smelling,
leaning on another, calling it "mine."
You, a bladder filled with filth,
hollow-eyed, bulging-socketed, exhausted,
from nine channels always and without cease
exuding impurity.
Just as I see you for what you are,
were people to see you likewise,
they would turn far away and abandon you
as one avoids an exposed place of mud in the rains.
Because childish ones, covered over
by the darkness of delusion, do not know,
they cling to you as an old ox
cleaves to a muddy wallow.

Then the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one also spoke verses in reply:

Great is the fortune — as the noble one has just declared —
a contorted machine of bones,
wound all around with sinews,
foul, smelling of bone,
leaning on another, calling it "mine" —
I, a bladder brought forth in filth,
hollow-eyed, bulging-socketed, exhausted,
from nine channels always and without cease
exuding impurity.
Just as the noble one knows me truly,
were people to seek me out,
they would turn far away and abandon me
as one avoids a rain-season quagmire.
Because childish ones, covered over
by the darkness of delusion, do not seek clearly,
they cling to me as an old ox
cleaves to a muddy wallow.

O greatly fortunate one, come down,
and please, noble one, teach me the Dharma.
In the supreme teaching of wisdom,
I shall become your hearer and disciple.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended from the midst of the sky above. Having thoroughly understood her intention, her latent tendencies (vāsanā), her constitution, and her nature, he taught her the Dharma in such a way that — while the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one remained seated right there on that very seat — the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) were shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and she directly realized the fruit of stream-entry, comprehending the Four Noble Truths individually and correctly, one by one.

Having seen the truth, she said: "Noble one, it is through relying upon you as a virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) that you have done such a thing for me as this — something not done for me even by my father, nor by my mother.

nor by any king, nor by the gods, nor by my ancestors of former times, nor by any ascetic (śramaṇa) or brahmin, nor by the assembly of friends, companions, and kinsmen. You have drained the ocean of blood and tears, you have freed me from the mountains of bones, you have closed the doors to the lower realms, you have opened the doors to the higher realms and to liberation, you have lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, and you have placed me among gods and humans. By shattering with the vajra of primordial wisdom the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection accumulated since beginningless time, I have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Noble one, I have entered upon it — I have entered upon it! Noble one, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of fully ordained monks. Please accept me as a laywoman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I go for refuge wholeheartedly and with utmost joy."

Then the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned noble daughter touched her head to the two feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if I may obtain the going forth and the full ordination as a fully ordained nun in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, I will live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

He said: "Sister, go and ask your householders."

She went to them and said: "Royal sons, do you permit me to go forth?"

They replied: "Earth-holder, why do you ask us?"

She said: "I wish to go forth; I am not asking."

They said: "If that is so, go forth."

Once they had given their permission, she went to where the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was. He took her and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, she bowed her head to the two feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, this Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one seeks the going forth and full ordination as a fully ordained nun in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."

The Blessed One declared: "It is good that she goes forth — let it be so." Having so declared, he himself began to write a letter to the Great Queen of the People.

While the Blessed One was composing the letter, King Śuddhodana arrived and inquired: "Blessed One, why has this kinswoman come here?"

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, do not say such a thing. This Dharma-sister of yours wishes the going forth and full ordination as a fully ordained nun in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."

"Blessed One, where is the letter being sent?"

"Great King, to the Great Queen of the People in Śrāvastī."

"Blessed One, I too will provide her with an escort."

"Very well, Great King."

The king appointed an escort for her. The Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one took the letter and departed for Śrāvastī. The Great Queen of the People, Gautamī, gave her the going forth and performed her full ordination, gave her instructions, and then, dwelling alone in seclusion, with heedfulness, with diligence, and with her self fully surrendered, she came to know this very saṃsāric wheel in its five divisions — moving and unmoving — and all aspects of the formations subsided, along with transgressions, dispersions,

and by the nature of reality that dissolves all things, having utterly subdued and abandoned all mental afflictions — this, daughters of noble family, is why she shaved her hair, donned the ochre robes, and with genuine faith went forth from home into homelessness: the supreme culmination of the holy life (brahmacarya). That very life she realized and accomplished in this very existence through her own direct knowledge, and she understood: "My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What was to be done has been done. I know of no further existence beyond this." And she became an arhat, free from attachment, beyond the three realms, with a mind even toward mud and gold, equal toward sky and the palm of the hand, who with wisdom had split open the shell of the eggshell of the senses, as though sandalwood had been set aside — one who had attained the threefold knowledges, the direct cognitions, and the individual perfect understandings; who had turned her back on the gains and honors of existence and desire; and who was to be venerated, revered, and openly praised by the gods with their faculties and near-faculties.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Among my female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great might, this one is supreme — namely, the nun of utmost excellence, the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one."

The monks arose in doubt and, to have all their doubts resolved, addressed the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable One, what action did the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one perform such that she came to have eyes like a blue lotus, a fragrance like a blue lotus, and a complexion like the stamens of a blue lotus? What action did she perform such that she was never in want of men, and, having gone forth in the Blessed One's teaching and abandoned all mental afflictions, she directly realized arhathood? What action did she perform such that she was declared supreme among the female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great might?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one performed and accumulated a mass of karma that, through a reversal of conditions, abides like a flame and will inevitably come to pass. And these actions performed and accumulated by the Blue-Lotus-Complexioned one — who else could experience them individually? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth; it does not ripen in the element of water; it does not ripen in the element of fire; it does not ripen in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Actions, even through a hundred aeons,
are never lost or wasted.
When the conditions and the time arrive,
they bear their fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago in the past, a householder lived by a rocky cliff. He took a wife of equal rank, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and lived in delight. Then one day he took his goods and departed for another region. His wife, corrupted and harmed by the afflictions through fine clothing and food, observed that in a nearby harmonious household men were constantly coming and going. She thought: 'This woman has accumulated merit; that is why men never leave her wanting. What means is there by which I too might be free from want of men?' While she was thinking in this way, a female śrāvaka (śrāvakā) of the naked ascetics came to her and said: 'Sister, is there any means by which whatever one wishes and whatever one undertakes may all be fulfilled?' She replied: 'Sister, there is a great adept among my own brothers who has gone forth and accomplished austerities. Offer him food and receive his aspiration; then whatever you wish and whatever you undertake shall all be fulfilled.' She said:"

'Sister, if that is the case, go and invite that great adept to her home for a meal.' So she invited him for a meal. The householder's wife prepared food and adorned her hands with utpala flowers. Now the naked ascetics eat at proper times and also at improper times, so it was some while before he arrived. In ages when no buddhas have appeared in the world, pratyekabuddhas arise — humble and poor, compassionate toward the lowly and the destitute, delighting in remote dwellings, solitary as a rhinoceros horn, and serving as a field of merit for the world. At such a time there was a pratyekabuddha wandering through the countryside, and he came to that rocky cliff. Early that morning, having tied his lower robe and taken up his almsbowl and monastic robes, he wandered for alms and entered that house. The householder's wife saw his beautiful body and his beautiful mind, and she thought: 'This is the great adept of accomplished austerities; I shall offer him food.' She satisfied him with excellent food and also made an offering to him with utpala flowers.

Now that great adept teaches Dharma through his body but does not teach Dharma with words. So the pratyekabuddha, having received the gift of food, and out of compassion for her, rose up into the sky above like a king of geese spreading his wings, and began to perform miraculous displays — blazing with fire, shining with light, releasing rain, and sending forth lightning. Ordinary people are quickly moved to faith when they behold miraculous powers, and so the householder's wife, filled with reverence and earnest devotion, prostrated at his two feet and made this aspiration: 'By this root of virtue accrued through my offering to such a true field of merit, may I never be without men in all my future births, and may I also attain qualities of such a kind that I please a Teacher far more excellent than this one, and never displease him.'

Monks, that householder's wife of that time and that age is this Utpalavarnā (she of the utpala hue) now. Because of the karmic maturation of that act — having given food to the pratyekabuddha and made offerings of utpala flowers — she now has eyes that resemble the utpala, is endowed with the fragrance of the utpala, and has a complexion like the filament of the utpala. And because of that aspiration she made — 'By this root of virtue accrued through my offering to such a true field of merit, may I never be without men in all my future births, and may I also attain qualities of such a kind that I please a Teacher far more excellent than this one, and never displease him' — she was never without men in her births, and then, having gone forth in my teaching and abandoned all afflictions, she directly actualized arhathood. And she has pleased me, the Teacher, with qualities surpassing those of a hundred thousand billion pratyekabuddhas, and has never displeased me.

She who has been declared foremost among the female śrāvakas of great miraculous powers and great might — this came about through the power of her aspiration. And where did she make that aspiration? Monks, in this very great and good aeon, in an earlier age, at a time when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher — the Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata (well-gone one), knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One — the buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, and he dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Grove of the Sages (Ṛṣipatana) near Vārāṇasī.

In the teaching of that buddha, this one went forth as a nun, and the nun who ordained her was declared by the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, to be the foremost among his female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great spiritual might. Now, although this one practiced the holy life for as long as she lived, she did not attain even a single accumulation of good qualities.
