Then, at the time of her death, she made this aspiration: "Throughout my entire life I practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha, the supreme field of merit, Kāśyapa, and yet I did not attain even a single accumulation of good qualities. By the root of virtue that I have accumulated through practicing the holy life for as long as I lived, may I, just as my preceptress was declared by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, to be the foremost among female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great spiritual might — so too may I, under the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the sovereign chief of Śākya kings, likewise be declared foremost among female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great spiritual might." She began to set this aspiration, and through the power of that aspiration she has now been declared by the Tathāgata to be foremost among his female śrāvaka disciples of great supernatural power and great spiritual might.

Now the monks, having grown uncertain, put all their questions to the awakened Blessed One: "Venerable One, what action did Utpalavaṛṇā perform that caused her to become such a seeker?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was Utpalavaṛṇā herself who performed and accumulated those karmic deeds — deeds with their conditions fully ripened, dwelling close like a flame, certain without doubt to arise. Whatever karma Utpalavaṛṇā performed and accumulated, no one else will experience its separate fruits. Monks, karma once performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, karma — whether virtuous or non-virtuous — once performed and accumulated, ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Actions do not perish even after a hundred aeons;
when the conditions and the time come together,
they will bear their fruit
for those who hold a body.

Monks, long ago in the past, in a mountain crag, this one was a woman who kept a brothel. There she gathered many who were like sons together with those who were like mothers, and many who were like brothers together with those who were like sisters. Through the karmic ripening of that deed she has now become such a seeker.

Monks, thus the ripening of exclusively dark karma is itself exclusively dark; the ripening of exclusively white karma is itself exclusively white; and the ripening of mixed karma is itself mixed.

Therefore, monks, abandon exclusively dark karma and mixed karma, and strive for exclusively white karma. Monks, you should train yourselves in this way."

The conduct of Utpalāvarṇā was this: she would go on alms rounds and offer the first and finest portion of what she had collected to the Saṅgha, then go around a second time and eat the remainder herself. Once, on a certain occasion, she went on her alms round, offered the first portion to the Saṅgha, and then went around a second time for her own sake. At that moment a monk who had newly arrived went on his alms round, and being unfamiliar with the neighborhood he found nothing at all. Utpalāvarṇā saw him and said, "Noble one, did you find nothing?" "Noble sister, I found nothing." She then offered him her own alms-food, and so his meal was provided for. Ānanda saw this and thought, "This sister has not only faith in the Saṅgha but appears to have faith in individuals as well — I should put her to the test." The following day Utpalāvarṇā went on her alms round, offered the first portion to the Saṅgha, and was completing her second round for her own sake, when Ānanda also arrived and said, "Noble sister, do you have even a little food?" She replied, "Noble one, if you are asking, what remains is like the leftovers of a divine dwelling." He said, "Noble one, if that is so, please hold out your bowl." She held out her bowl, and she offered that alms-food into his bowl. Utpalāvarṇā had thus gone without food for two days, and weakened by the exhaustion of her frail state, she fainted and fell to the ground. Those who lacked faith seized upon this opportunity, and though it was known among the wise that Utpalāvarṇā was free from attachment, they began to revile her, saying, "Look at this handsome young Śākyan — she sees him and, overcome by desire, has fallen fainting to the ground." In this context of such censure, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then convened the assembly of monks on account of this incident, this occasion, and this matter — and so forth as before. The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, though they know, act as though they do not — and so forth as before.

The Blessed One then questioned Ānanda: "Ānanda, is it true that you took food that had been set aside and prepared for a nun who is not your relative, sitting along the road on her way to the village for alms, and that you received it and ate it with your own hand?" "Blessed One, it is so." The Blessed One then censured this as unworthy of a contemplative, as improper, as unsuitable, as contrary to proper conduct — it is not to be done by one who has gone forth. Having censured it in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the śrāvakas in the Vinaya" — and so forth as before. "My śrāvakas are to recite this training rule in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever monk takes with his own hand and eats food that has been set aside and prepared for a nun who is not his relative, sitting along the road on her way to the village for alms — that monk shall go out to the outer park and confess before the monks, saying: 'Venerable ones, I have committed an offense worthy of blame, an improper act that should be individually confessed. I confess to that offense, that dharma, individually.' This is a matter for individual confession. This is an offense requiring individual confession.

'Whatever monk' means a son of the Śākyans — Ānanda or any other like him. 'A nun' means one who holds this Dharma. 'Who is not a relative' means a maternal grandmother or

a great-grandfather, and any relative within seven generations descended from one's ancestors counts as a relative; beyond that, one is not a relative.

"Sitting along the road" means having gone into the street.

Regarding "going to the village for alms," "village" means a place where there are streets, lanes, crossroads, and intersections. "Alms" means food obtained from others. "Hard food and soft food" means the five kinds of hard food and the five kinds of soft food. "With one's own hand" means hand to hand. "Having taken" means having received and brought into one's power. "If he partakes of or eats" means if it passes down the throat.

"That monk" means whichever monk it is. "Shall go out to the outer park" means shall go to the monastery outside the village. "Before the monks" means before whichever monks are gathered there. "Venerable ones, I have committed an offense worthy of blame" means something that should be condemned. "An improper act" means something contrary to proper conduct. "That should be individually confessed" means that should be disclosed. "That offense" means the offense that has arisen. "That dharma" means what is not truly the Dharma but has been spoken of using the word "dharma." "I confess" means "I disclose." "Should be individually confessed" means should be disclosed. "This is a matter for individual confession" means this is a matter to be disclosed, and therefore it is said to be a matter for individual confession.

Now, how does a transgression arise? If a monk, perceiving as a non-relative a nun who is not a relative, sitting along the road on her way to the village for alms, takes hard food or soft food with his own hand and partakes of it or eats it, this becomes a matter for individual confession. If he takes hard food or soft food with his own hand and partakes of it or eats it while entertaining doubt about whether she is a non-relative, this also becomes a matter for individual confession.

If a monk, perceiving as a non-relative a nun who is in fact a relative, sitting along the road on her way to the village for alms, takes hard food or soft food with his own hand and partakes of it or eats it, this becomes a wrongdoing. If he takes hard food or soft food with his own hand and partakes of it or eats it while entertaining doubt about whether she is a relative, this also becomes a wrongdoing.

For one who acts for the first time, for one who is insane, for one who is mentally disturbed, and for one who is overcome by pain, there is no transgression.

The first matter for individual confession regarding receiving food from a nun is hereby complete.


The Vinaya, its Analysis. The eighty-first fascicle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a severe famine had arisen, and food was difficult to obtain even for wandering mendicants in the wilderness; indeed, parents themselves found it hard to feed even their own children, let alone mendicants, so the situation was all the more dire for wandering monks. The group of six monks, in the morning, having fastened their lower garments, taking their bowls and robes, entered Śrāvastī for alms. Some obtained food and some did not; and being threatened by hunger, they went to the dwellings of the group of twelve monks. The group of twelve spread out seats, saying: "Noble ones, please be seated." When they had taken their seats, the group of twelve prostrated at their feet, sat before them, and said: "Noble ones, are you well? Sisters, how do you live here? We ourselves are threatened by hunger."

The noble ones replied: "If that is so, come tomorrow for a meal — we invite you to share our food."

The group of twelve said: "Sisters, if you give tomorrow, who will have authorized you to give?"

"Noble ones, we ourselves will provide the meal."

"Sisters, you will not be able to sustain yourselves in that way."

"In this way, wherever the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha has been invited, you should serve them there, and give repeatedly to us as well — in that way we shall be able to live." Bombhā Gāmo said: "Noble ones, is that permissible?" "Sisters, it is entirely appropriate. It is most fitting." "Who forbade it? Where was it forbidden?" They replied: "Noble ones, if it is permissible, then do so without hesitation — do it just as you have said." With that, they took their leave, saying "Very well," and departed.

Shortly thereafter, a householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another house at the hour of midday. The Saṅgha of monks went. The Blessed One, remaining in a certain place, was fulfilling his alms round. Now, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remain in a certain place and fulfil the alms round for five reasons. What are these five? They wish to store things properly indoors; they wish to teach the Dharma to gods; they wish to care for the sick; they wish to review the dwelling places; and they wish to lay down the rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya. In this instance, the Blessed One, the Buddha, remained in that place and fulfilled the alms round because he wished to lay down the rules of training for the hearers in the Vinaya.

The householder, together with his household servants, began to serve the Saṅgha of monks, and Bombhā Gāmo, the elder woman, was seated to one side. She said: "Householder, this is the noble Ānanda — gone forth from the Śākyas, master of the three scriptural collections, a Dharma teacher, one possessed of the confidence of reasoning and liberation — please serve him again. This is the noble Rāhula. This is Laghumāna. This is Kāmanda — these too have gone forth from the Śākyas, are masters of the three scriptural collections, are Dharma teachers, possessed of the confidence of reasoning and liberation — please serve them again as well. This is the noble Arcaka — gone forth as the son of a Brahmin reciter, master of the three scriptural collections, a Dharma teacher, possessed of the confidence of reasoning and liberation — please serve him again and again." The householder accordingly gave to each of them repeatedly. Likewise Bombhā Gāmo spoke to those who were doing the serving, and they too gave to each of those monks repeatedly.

As a result, some monks received a surplus of rice, some received a surplus of soup, some received a surplus of condiments, some received a surplus of food in general. Some, having received a little food, had their rice bowls filled to overflowing. Some had their rice bowls filled to overflowing without having received any at all in the ordinary way.

Then the monks who still had all their bonds present reproached the householder: "Householder, if you do not have sufficient wealth, why do you invite the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha?" He replied: "Noble ones, I had prepared an abundant meal, but since the elder Bombhā Gāmo was seated to one side among the elders, and kept directing portions to that one side again and again, what was I to do?" With that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then convened the Saṅgha of monks in response to this occurrence, this basis of address, and this occasion — and so on as before. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while knowing, act as though unaware — and so forth, as before. The Blessed One, the Buddha, questioned the group of six: "Monks, did you truly do something so unseemly?" "Venerable One, we did not." The Blessed One, the Buddha, declared that this was conduct unworthy of a renunciant, not in accord with the Dharma, not fitting —

not in accord with proper conduct, and not something to be done by one who has gone forth — and he rebuked them in this way. Then, having rebuked them at length and in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, seeing ten benefits clearly, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers" — and so forth as before. "My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

When many monks have been invited as guests to various households and are eating a meal there, and if at that time a nun is standing at the door, and someone says, 'Give her a portion of this; give her cooked rice; give her legumes; give her more of this,' then those monks must send word to that nun saying: 'Sister, please wait for just a moment until the monks have finished eating.' If even one of those monks should be unable to say this to the nun, then all those monks must go to the outer recreation ground and confess to the venerable ones there: 'A transgression has arisen for us, venerable ones, a matter unseemly, unfit for confession — this very matter has come to pass, and this dharma we confess.' This dharma, too, is to be confessed."

Now, "many monks" means more than two — more than two constitutes "many." "In various households" means in the households of brahmins and householders. "Invited as guests" means invited for the sake of a meal. "While eating a meal" refers to the five kinds of soft food and the five kinds of solid food. "If a nun" means one such as Sthūlanandā or anyone else of that kind. "To that nun" means to Sthūlanandā or to anyone else of that kind. "Those monks" means whichever monks happen to be present there. "Saying thus" means to convey the following words. "Send word saying: 'Sister, please wait for just a moment until the monks have finished eating'" — this means one should say: "Sister, please remain silent for a short while, just a moment, until the monks have finished eating." "If even one of those monks should be unable to say this to that nun" — this means if even one monk has not said this to her. "All those monks" means all those monks who are present there. "Going to the outer recreation ground" means going to the assembly hall outside the village. "A matter unseemly for us, venerable ones, a matter for which we are to be reproached" means something deserving censure. "Unfit" means contrary to proper conduct. "To be confessed" means to be acknowledged. "Has arisen" means a transgression has arisen. "This dharma" refers to that which is not genuine Dharma but is expressed by the name of a dharma. "We confess" means "we acknowledge." "Is to be confessed" means "is to be acknowledged." And "this dharma, too, is to be confessed" means this matter, too, is to be acknowledged; and for that reason it is said to be confessed.

Now, how does a transgression come about in this matter? When monks are eating in upper rooms and others are eating in middle rooms, and if at that time a nun is standing at the door, those monks must send word to her. If they eat without sending word, a transgression requiring confession arises. As for those eating in the middle rooms, they should inquire whether word has been sent to the nun. If they eat without making that inquiry, an offense of wrongdoing arises.

When monks are eating in lower rooms and others are eating in doorway rooms, and if at that time a nun is standing on watch, those monks must send word to that nun. If they eat without sending word, a transgression requiring confession arises. Those who are eating in the doorway rooms should inquire whether word has been sent to the nun. If they eat without making that inquiry, an offense of wrongdoing arises. When some monks have finished eating and are leaving while others are entering, those who are entering should inquire whether word has been sent to the nun. If they eat without making that inquiry, an offense of wrongdoing arises. If she has been invited as a guest on that occasion, or if one is being admitted to full ordination, there is no transgression. If one is being shown decorative drawings, or if someone is being led in to give what has not yet been given, there is no transgression. For one who is a first offender, or who is insane, or whose mind is disturbed, or who is afflicted by painful feelings, there is no transgression. The second rule requiring confession — namely, eating after admitting to a seat-row someone who has not come in proper sequence without turning that person away — is complete.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pool. At the time when the general Siṃha beheld the truths in the presence of the Blessed One, he took hold of one portion of his wealth and, uttering words of supreme excellence, roared with the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly: "From this day forth, the door is closed to the naked ones, to the naked women, to the female hearers of the naked ones, and to the male hearers of the naked ones. The door is open to the monk-hearers of the Blessed One, to the nuns, to the laymen, and to the laywomen." And he proclaimed that all the fields of his former activity were likewise blameworthy, and he abandoned them entirely. He was endowed with faith and had a good and virtuous intention. There was nothing he did not offer and fully give over to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to agreeable monks. And because he offered and gave everything in this way, his resources became thin and were entirely exhausted, reaching their very end.

At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were wandering on their rounds and arrived at Vaiśālī. The general Siṃha invited both of them to another household for a meal and, in order to prepare food for the two of them, went himself to the market. The naked ones saw him and, aware of this, began to mock him, saying: "Formerly, when the general Siṃha was devoted to us, everything flourished magnificently for him. Now, being devoted to the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan, he comes and goes here for nothing — he does the work of a householder himself." When this mockery was under way, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, you should give the training-vow to the general Siṃha and to others like him. It should be conferred in this way: having prepared a seat, struck the gong, and properly informed the monks using the words of inquiry, once the entire Saṅgha is seated in harmony, a single monk should perform the formal act by motion alone, saying: 'Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The general Siṃha is endowed with faith and has a good and virtuous intention. There is nothing he has not offered and fully given over to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or to agreeable monks. Because he offered and gave everything in this way, his resources became thin and were entirely exhausted, reaching their very end.'"

"If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, may the Saṅgha grant permission. The Saṅgha hereby confers the training vow upon General Siṃha." This is the motion.

To the one upon whom the Saṅgha has conferred the training vow, a monk must not go to his house, must not make use of his seats, must not eat his alms-food, and must not teach the Dharma there.

The Blessed One declared: "To the one upon whom the Saṅgha has conferred the training vow, a monk must not go to his house, must not make use of his seats, must not eat his alms-food, and must not teach the Dharma there."

After this declaration, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who had previously been invited as guests, also did not go to his house. Then General Siṃha prepared the food and went to where the venerable Śāriputra and the great Maudgalyāyana were staying, and having arrived, he bowed his head at their feet and said: "May the two noble ones please think to lend me the loan of an umbrella's shade — please be mindful that the time has now come."

The two of them replied: "Householder, the Saṅgha has conferred the training vow upon you; we will not go."

He said: "Noble ones, I invited the two of you before — please come."

The two replied: "Householder, then let us ask the Blessed One." And the two of them reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "Whoever was previously invited as a guest may eat there; one should not feel regret about this."

The two of them proceeded toward General Siṃha's house, and as they went, the noble ones and the group of six monks saw the two of them and said: "Where are you two going?" "To General Siṃha's house." "Did the Saṅgha not confer the training vow upon him? They conferred it, and yet he invited us two before. Moreover, when General Siṃha, in the presence of the Blessed One, saw the truths, he grasped one portion and, speaking words of the great bull of the herd, proclaimed with a lion's roar in the midst of the assembly: 'From this day forward, the door is closed to the naked ones, the naked women, the male hearers of the naked ones, and the female hearers of the naked ones. The door is open to the Blessed One's hearer monks, hearer nuns, male lay practitioners, and female lay practitioners.' It is because of this that he invited us before." The two said nothing and continued on their way, and those monks followed close behind the two of them, one after another.

When General Siṃha saw that a great many monks were coming, he was filled with great delight, and he had all the requisites of the household distributed among the monks. After they had eaten and were departing, his children began to serve more food, and he said: "Children, distribute all the household requisites among the monks as well — wait a little longer until the other matter is resolved."

Hearing his children begin to cry, certain monks of little purpose asked: "Why do you monks, who are under training, go uninvited to the very houses upon which the Saṅgha has placed the training vow, serve food with your own hands, take and distribute it, eat it, criticize, throw things about, and quarrel?" This matter was then reported to the Blessed One by the monks.

Thereupon the Blessed One, regarding this incident and making it the basis of instruction —

On this occasion, the phrase "the Blessed One convened the assembly of monks" and what follows proceeds as before. Likewise, the phrase "the blessed buddhas, though knowing, act as though they do not know" and what follows also proceeds as before.

The blessed Buddha then questioned the group of six monks: "Monks, is it true that you went uninvited to the very houses of those under training that have been bound by the Saṅgha's training vow, and with your own hands took the food that had been prepared, distributed it, and ate it?" They replied: "Venerable One, it is true." The blessed Buddha rebuked them, saying that such conduct was not the way of a contemplative, not in accord with propriety, not fitting, not in keeping with proper conduct — it was not something to be done by one who has gone forth.

After rebuking them in many ways, the Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, seeing fully the ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya" — and the rest proceeds as before.

"My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows: In the case of those houses of those under training that have been bound by the Saṅgha's training vow — if any monk goes uninvited to such houses of those under training that are bound by the Saṅgha's training vow, and with his own hands takes food that has been prepared, and distributes or eats it, that monk shall go to the outer assembly hall and confess before the community of monks, saying: 'Venerable ones, an occasion has arisen that is improper and blameworthy for me, and I confess it individually. That rule of conduct I individually transgressed.' Thus shall he confess individually. This too is to be individually confessed."

Now, once the Blessed One had thus established that rule of training for the hearers in the Vinaya, no monk at all went to the house of the general Siṃha. Then the wife of General Siṃha said to General Siṃha: "My lord's son should know: the Saṅgha has imposed a training vow upon us, and no monk comes at all. In effect the Saṅgha has cut off the monks' alms from our house with a wooden ladle — yet what fault could there be in our using the seats and in teaching the Dharma?" This was then reported by the monks to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, go to the house of General Siṃha; make use of the seats; teach the Dharma — but do not accept alms."

The monks then began to enter that house with empty bowls alone at first and then to leave. When the wife of General Siṃha saw this, she began to weep, saying: "Before, these noble ones would enter my house first with empty bowls and leave with bowls full and hands full — now they enter with empty bowls and leave with empty hands." This was then reported by the monks to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, you shall not enter that house first with empty bowls alone."

The monks then went on their alms round and, with their bowls full, began to enter that house. When the young children of the household asked the monks for the prepared food, and the monks did not give it to them, the Blessed One declared: "Give it to them." When the monks began to give it to them in large portions, and the boys took it and distributed it among themselves and went outside, some naked ascetics (tīrthikas) saw them and asked: "Boys, where did you get this food?"

"The noble ones gave it to us." "No harm done. Fill a bowl with a bowl — give to them, and they will give to you," the boys said. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, do not give the prepared food all in one lump, but break it into pieces before giving it."

Some time later, the wife of the general Siṃha offered the monks who had come on their round various fruits such as mangoes and breadfruit, along with roots and vegetables such as watercress. When the monks did not accept them, she said: "Noble ones, will these things fill our storehouses and granaries? Please do accept them." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, you may accept fruits such as mangoes and breadfruit, roots, and vegetables such as watercress when these come from a household."

Now at that time certain Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were gathered in conversation at the assembly hall. When they saw those monks coming out from the house of the general Siṃha, those among them who were without faith said: "Friends, ever since the general Siṃha developed devoted faith in the ascetic Gautama, his wealth has become depleted, exhausted, and utterly consumed." But those among them who had faith said: "Friends, how could it be that someone who has devoted faith in the Blessed One would have their wealth depleted, exhausted, and consumed? It is like this: the general Siṃha, having seen the truths in the presence of the Blessed One, cut off all the blameworthy edges of his field-work — and it is because of that cutting off that his wealth has become depleted, exhausted, and consumed."

The Licchavīs of Vaiśālī then deliberated among themselves and spoke to the general Siṃha's farmworkers: "Friends, why are you not attending to all the field-work for the general Siṃha? Have you not been receiving your wages?" They replied: "Friends, we have been receiving our wages. But when the general forbids us, what are we to do?" The Licchavīs said: "The assembly has authorized you. Go now and attend to all of the general's field-work." And so, at the bidding of the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, those workers set about attending to all the field-work of the general Siṃha. The gods then sent down a fine and steady rain in good season, and a great abundance of crops arose.

The general Siṃha, now prosperous in his wealth again, went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the general Siṃha addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable One, formerly my wealth became depleted, exhausted, and utterly consumed. The Saṅgha, wishing me well and seeking my benefit, granted me the training vow. Now that the assembly of Licchavīs of Vaiśālī has restored my wealth and it has grown again, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would be pleased to dissolve my training vow, that would be excellent." The Blessed One said nothing to the general Siṃha, and by that silence gave consent.

The general Siṃha, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been granted, prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with his head and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, for the general Siṃha and for anyone else who is in such a situation, the training vow is to be dissolved. It is to be dissolved in the following manner:

Having prepared the seats and struck the wooden sounding board, the monks are duly informed through the words of inquiry, and once the entire Saṅgha is seated and in harmony, the general Siṃha bows, seats himself at the end of the row of elders, slightly to one side, joins his palms, and speaks as follows:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the general Siṃha, am one possessed of faith, of good character, and of wholesome intention. There is nothing whatsoever that I have not offered or fully given to a buddha, to the Dharma, to the Saṅgha, or to those monks worthy of reverence. Having thus offered and thus fully given, my resources have been depleted, consumed, and entirely exhausted. Now the Saṅgha, wishing my good and wishing my benefit, granted me the training vow, and yet my resources have increased once more. Therefore I, the general Siṃha, who was granted the training vow and who request the dissolution of the training vow, ask that the compassionate venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, be pleased to dissolve my training vow."

This is to be recited a second time and a third time.

Then the general Siṃha is moved from within earshot to within eyeshot, and a single monk performs the motion alone:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. The general Siṃha is one possessed of faith, of good character, and of wholesome intention. He has nothing whatsoever that he has not offered or fully given to a buddha, to the Dharma, to the Saṅgha, or to those monks worthy of reverence. Having thus offered and thus fully given, his resources were depleted, consumed, and entirely exhausted. The Saṅgha, wishing his good and wishing his benefit, granted him the training vow, and yet his resources have now increased once more. The general Siṃha, having been granted the training vow, requests from the Saṅgha the dissolution of the training vow. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and it meets with approval, let the Saṅgha grant consent, and let the Saṅgha dissolve the training vow for the general Siṃha. This is the motion."

For whoever's training vow the Saṅgha thus dissolves, the monks may visit that person, make use of his seat, accept alms from him, and teach him Dharma.

As for the phrase "those in training," "those in training" refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. The phrase "whatever households" refers to the households of brahmins and householders. The phrase "of the Saṅgha" means of the Saṅgha of hearers of the Tathāgata. The phrase "who have been bound by the training vow" means through the act of the motion. The phrase "whatever monk" refers to the group of six or any others of that kind. The phrase "in such households of trainees bound by the Saṅgha's training vow" means in households such as those described. The phrase "without having been invited beforehand" means without having been asked in advance. The phrase "having gone" means after going. The phrase "with his own hands" means hand to hand. "Prepared and cooked foods" refers to the five prepared foods and the five cooked foods. The phrase "having received" means having caused it to be placed in receipt. The phrase "if he eats or consumes it" means if he swallows it down his throat. The phrase "that monk" means whichever monk it may be. The phrase "having gone to the outer pleasure garden" means having gone to the vihāra outside the town. The phrase "to the monks" refers to whatever monks are gathered there.

"Venerable ones, 'a ground for blame' means something worthy of blame. 'Improper' means not in accordance with the rule. 'To be confessed' means to be disclosed. 'Has arisen' means a transgression has arisen. 'That Dharma' refers to what is not the Dharma but was spoken of by the name 'Dharma.' 'I acknowledge it' means 'I disclose it.' 'It is to be confessed' means it is to be disclosed. 'This too is to be confessed' means this too is to be disclosed — and therefore it is said 'it is to be confessed.'

Now, how does a transgression come about in this matter? Whenever a monk, no matter how little he may be in training, goes uninvited to the homes that are bound by the training rules of the Saṅgha — homes of that kind — and takes with his own hand prepared and cooked foods and then distributes or eats them, in every such case a confession is required. Where one has been invited beforehand, there is no transgression. There is no transgression for one who is a first offender, for one who is insane, for one whose mind is disturbed, or for one who is afflicted by painful sensations.

This is the third confessable rule, concerning one who has abandoned the training and entered lay life.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, consented to observe the rains retreat at the Śākyan settlement of Śakyā, in the forest of that settlement. The Blessed One then declared to the monks that whenever, on the seventh or eighth day before the monks' invitation ceremony is to take place, they should announce to the villages within their domain: "On such-and-such a day the invitation ceremony will take place." The monks went and made the announcement accordingly.

Then the Śākyans dwelling at the Śākyan settlement, on the fifteenth day of the invitation ceremony of both communities, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and with their heads bowed to his two feet paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One properly instructed the Śākyans dwelling at the Śākyan settlement with words endowed with Dharma, properly aroused and engaged them, properly praised and encouraged them, and properly delighted them. With many categories of words endowed with Dharma he properly instructed, engaged, praised, encouraged, and delighted them, and then said nothing further.

The Śākyans dwelling at the Śākyan settlement, rejoicing and delighting in what the Blessed One had declared, then addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, would you grant that tomorrow, on this very day, you and the community of monks accept our midday meal? Tomorrow, let no monk go out for alms either. We will ourselves go to beg alms and, with the Blessed One together with the community of śrāvaka monks, will satisfy and nourish you from our own resources."

The Blessed One gave his consent to the Śākyans dwelling at the Śākyan settlement by saying nothing. The Śākyans dwelling at the Śākyan settlement, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, bowed their heads to his two feet in homage, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One. They went to the Śākyan settlement and that very night prepared and set ready pure and excellent prepared and cooked foods. Then, rising early the next morning, they loaded carts with prepared and cooked foods and said to the Śākyan women: "You all mount your carriages and go on ahead; we will follow behind." The Śākyan women, adorned with all their ornaments, mounted their carriages and set out.

Now, the environs of the Śākyan settlement were dense with forest, and along the road some brigands caught sight of them and said to one another: "Friends, look — these Śākyan women are adorned with all their ornaments. Let us go and seize and plunder them!" The commander of the brigands then said:

"Friends, what would be the point of attacking them when we are already on our way and done with the matter? The ruthless Śākyans who crush their enemies are sure to retaliate — let them go." But the others said: "Who sees the back of the moon, commander? Attack!" And so, overriding his words, they fell upon them, stripped them of all their clothes and ornaments, and departed.

The Śākyan women, seized with fear and dread, hid themselves among the thorny thickets and the trees of the forest and remained there. The carriage-drivers, also terrified, fled. The oxen, their yokes cut loose, wandered wherever they pleased. The carriages stood unhitched, separated from their yoke-poles.

The Six Group monks then began to confer with one another: "Friends, dear companions, we who are the Śākyans' close friends have been delayed here a long time — shall we just fast, or shall we go for alms?" They agreed to go for alms, and so, taking their bowls and robes, those noble ones set out, and presently along the road they saw carriages standing about with their yoke-poles detached and laden with food, and oxen that had broken free of their yokes wandering wherever they pleased. They looked at one another in astonishment and began to call out: "Friends, is anyone here?" When a sound came in response, the Six Group monks said: "Who are you?" "Noble ones, we are the Śākyan women. Come here — approach us. We have been attacked by bandits and are hiding in the thickets. Come, noble ones — remain distant for a moment, then approach: whatever of your limbs and members that we have not seen before, come so that they are concealed by leaves as you approach and serve us."

And so the Śākyan women, covered with leaves, came out and were served by them. Then the Six Group monks said: "Dear friends, dear companions, look at these Śākyan women — what do their eyes look like, their noses, their mouths, their breasts, their hands, their waists, their feet? Have a look!" When the women were pestered in this manner, they retreated from shame back into the very same thickets and forest and hid there.

Scouts then ran to report to the Śākyans: "The Śākyan women have been attacked." Thereupon the Śākyans took up bows and arrows and weapons, went straight along the road, blocked the path, and there they seized those bandits. Some among the Śākyans said: "What is there to consider? Kill them!" Others said: "Wait — bring them there and ask the Śākyan women: whoever has committed an offence against whichever woman, that one should be executed." So they dragged them before the Śākyan women and said: "Come here — tell us: of these bandits, which one committed what offence against you?" The women said: "The bandit commander here is innocent — he did no harm, for he tried to restrain the others, but they would not be stopped. Let this one go." And so they released him.

He, having been given back his very life when it was nearly cut short, prostrated at their feet and said: "Noble ladies, since you are people of faith and are going to offer the midday meal to the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha, what would be gained by killing these men? Please also release those who did commit offences." And so the Śākyans had the plundered goods returned and released them all.

Then the Śākyan men helped the Śākyan women put on their garments and ornaments, yoked the oxen back to the carriages, and mounted the carriages and proceeded into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One was seated on a prepared seat before the Saṅgha of monks, and the Śākyans, both men and women, began to serve food to the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha.

The Śākyan women did not offer food to the six groups of monks, and the Śākyan men said, "Why are you not serving food to the noble ones?" The women replied, "They have already eaten." "Where did they eat?" "Right here." "Who served them?" "We did." "How did you women serve them?" "Because of what these men did — they grabbed us, stripped us, and covered us with leaves, then emerged from the thickets and undergrowth and began to violate us — there is much that could be said about them. But enough of that. These men habitually engage in vile conduct, and so we will not give them food." The six groups of monks said nothing and remained silent.

The women then made complaint to the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "Noble ones, when the Blessed One declared that this road was dangerous and instructed us to travel with care, we said we would do so and came along" — at which point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a monk who patrols the forest shall be appointed. A monk who patrols the forest possessed of five qualities shall not be appointed even if not yet appointed, and if already appointed shall be removed. What are the five? He goes out of desire; he goes out of aversion; he goes out of delusion; he goes out of fear; and he does not know which parts of the forest have been patrolled and which have not. A monk who patrols the forest possessed of five qualities shall be appointed even if not yet appointed, and if already appointed shall not be removed. What are the five? He does not go out of desire; he does not go out of aversion; he does not go out of delusion; he does not go out of fear; and he knows which parts of the forest have been patrolled and which have not.

"He shall be appointed in the following manner. After a seat has been prepared and the gong struck, having properly informed the monks with the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is seated together in harmony, he shall first be asked if he is willing: 'You who are called such-and-such — are you willing to be the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk?' If he is willing, he should say, 'I am willing.'

"Then one monk shall make the motion and perform the formal act. 'Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The monk named such-and-such wishes to be the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk. If it is timely for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, may the Saṅgha appoint the monk named such-and-such as the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk, so that he named such-and-such shall be the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk. This is the motion.

"'The formal act is to be performed thus. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear. The monk named such-and-such wishes to be the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk. Accordingly, the Saṅgha hereby appoints the one named such-and-such as forest-patrol monk; the one named such-and-such shall be the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk. Any venerable one who consents to the appointment of the one named such-and-such as forest-patrol monk shall remain silent; any who does not consent shall speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved; the Saṅgha has appointed the monk named such-and-such as forest-patrol monk. The one named such-and-such is the Saṅgha's forest-patrol monk. Since no one has spoken, it is so taken.'

"I shall now set down the rules of conduct for the forest-patrol monk. The forest-patrol monk shall patrol the forest within a radius of half a league in all directions around the camp."

The Blessed One having thus declared that the forest-patrol monk shall patrol the forest within a radius of half a league in all directions, there were monks who became weary from the road and who found themselves alone and afraid. The Blessed One then declared:

"If he wishes, he may be given a young attendant and also a companion. If the forest is indeed frightening, he should tame a domestic animal as a signal. He should raise a blue banner. He should place leaf-fans along the path. If the forest is not frightening, he should raise a white banner."

If a forest-patrol monk does not properly take up and practice the rules of conduct prescribed for his behavior, he incurs an offence.

On a certain occasion, monks of little purpose — that is to say, certain monks — before the forest-patrol monk had gone on his rounds, took provisions and food from outside the boundary of the monastery's pleasure-garden and ate there, criticizing him, lodging complaints against him, and speaking ill of him. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this occurrence, on account of this incident, and in this connection, convened the assembly of monks — and so forth as before. The Blessed One, the buddha, though knowing, feigned not to know — and so forth as before. The Blessed One then questioned the group of six: "Monks, is it true that before the forest-patrol monk had gone on his rounds, you took provisions and food from outside the boundary of the pleasure-garden and ate there?"

"Blessed One, it is so."

The Blessed One rebuked them: "That is not the conduct of a renunciant; it is not fitting, not suitable, not in accordance with proper conduct. This is not something one who has gone forth should do." And so forth as before.

Then, having rebuked them in many ways, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore, having seen these ten benefits, I shall establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers — and so forth as before. My hearers shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya as follows:

Whatever lodgings and hermitages of the Saṅgha are known to be dangerous, known to be frightening, known to be menacing on account of various kinds of fear — and whatever monk, in such lodgings and hermitages of the Saṅgha known to be dangerous, known to be frightening, known to be menacing on account of various kinds of fear, before the forest-patrol monk has gone on his rounds, takes provisions and food from outside the boundary of the pleasure-garden and eats them — that monk shall go to the outer pleasure-garden and confess before the venerable monks, saying: 'An improper matter deserving of censure has arisen for me; I confess it individually.' This is the individual confession for this offense. This matter too is subject to individual confession.

The expression 'of the Saṅgha' means: of the Tathāgata's assembly of hearers.

The expression 'whatever lodgings and hermitages' — as for 'hermitage': six extremely fine particles make one fine particle; six fine particles make one water-particle; six water-particles make one iron-particle; six iron-particles make one rabbit's-hair particle; six rabbit's-hair particles make one sheep's-wool particle; six sheep's-wool particles make one ox-hair particle; six ox-hair particles make one sunbeam-mote particle; six sunbeam-mote particles make one louse-egg; six louse-eggs make one louse; six lice make one barleycorn; six barleycorns make one finger-breadth; twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit; one and a half cubits make one pace; four cubits make one bow-length; five hundred bow-lengths make one krośa; one krośa from a village constitutes a hermitage. Whatever temple (vihāra) exists there, that is a monastic hermitage-lodging.

"Known as a place of apprehension" means: it is known to be frightening on account of thieves and rogues. "Known as a place of fear" means: it is known to be frightening on account of lions, tigers, and leopards. "Known as a place of fear, rendered fearful by various distinct dangers" means: it has become known as a place of fear, rendered fearful by the various distinct dangers of mosquitoes, stinging insects with long mouthparts, wind, sun, and venomous snakes.

"Whatever monk" refers to the group of six or anyone else of that sort. "Monastic hermitage-lodgings of the Saṅgha that are known as places of apprehension, known as places of fear, and known as places of fear rendered fearful by various distinct dangers — in such as these" means: in those that are as described. "Not having previously reconnoitered the forest" means: not having previously reconnoitered it by wandering through the forest. "Outside the assembly hall's enclosure" means: outside the temple. "Food and drink" means: the five kinds of food and the five kinds of drink. "Having received" means: having taken them into one's power by accepting them. "When one eats or drinks" means: when one swallows them down the throat. "That monk" means: whichever monk it is. "Having gone to the outer assembly hall" means: having gone to the temple outside the village. "To the monks" means: to whichever monks were assembled there. "Venerable ones, I have incurred grounds for censure" means: grounds for being censured. "Improper" means: contrary to proper conduct. "That which is to be confessed" means: that which is to be disclosed. "A transgression has arisen" means: a downfall has arisen. "That Dharma" means: that which is not Dharma but was spoken under the name of Dharma. "I individually acknowledge" means: "I disclose it." "It is to be individually confessed" means: it is to be disclosed. "This Dharma too is to be individually confessed" means: this too is to be disclosed — and therefore it is said: it is to be individually confessed.

Now, in what way does a transgression arise? If a monk, with the perception that a forest not yet reconnoitered has not been reconnoitered, receives food and drink outside the enclosure of the assembly hall and eats or drinks them, it becomes a matter for individual confession. If, with regard to a forest not yet reconnoitered, one acts with doubt and receives food and drink outside the enclosure of the assembly hall and eats or drinks them, it becomes a matter for individual confession. If a monk, with the perception that a forest already reconnoitered has not been reconnoitered, receives food and drink outside the enclosure of the assembly hall and eats or drinks them, it becomes a wrongdoing. If, with regard to a forest already reconnoitered, one acts with doubt and receives food and drink outside the enclosure of the assembly hall and eats or drinks them, it becomes a wrongdoing. If the one who has reconnoitered the forest dies or flees, there is no transgression. For one who is a beginner, or who is mentally deranged, mentally disturbed, or afflicted by painful feelings, there is no transgression.

This concludes the fourth matter for individual confession, arising from the examination of the forest. The matters for individual confession are complete.

The Vinayavibhaṅga, the eighty-second fascicle. Summary verse:

Wearing the lower robe in a rounded fold, the Dharma robe in a rounded fold,
not covering the head, not making offerings,
not averting the eyes, not sending ahead,
receiving what is good, eating what is good, step by step,
not having grains mixed together, not slapping with the hand,
carrying the alms bowl tilted, covering the head and wearing it on one shoulder,
riding an elephant,
using a carrying pole, standing upright,
and not climbing trees —
these are the condensed summary of one hundred trainings.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling in Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, the place where sages speak. At the time when the Blessed One, finding no fault in the five and admitting them to the monkhood, established them in the state of monks, those monks, through the force of their former habits, put on their lower robes just as householders do.

When faithful brahmins and householders saw this, they said: "Noble ones, you wear the lower robe in the same manner as wealthy men, merchants, and caravan leaders do." At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "What the householders say is true. Let me consider how the śrāvakas of the perfectly enlightened buddhas of former times used to wear the lower robe." Then the gods addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable one, it is like this: it was just as the gods of the Pure Abode do." And to the Blessed One himself there arose knowledge and vision of this: it was just as the gods of the Pure Abode do. Thereupon the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Therefore, this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train in wearing the lower robe in a rounded manner." When the Blessed One had declared that one shall train in wearing the lower robe in a rounded manner, the five monks began wearing their lower robes in a rounded manner. In the same way, the group of five junior monks, the fifty who had excelled, the sixty of the Bhadra group, and moreover those monks who had gone forth through the Blessed One's transmission all began wearing their lower robes in a rounded manner.

When the group of six went forth, they began wearing their lower robes far too high, and faithful brahmins and householders saw this and criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, peacocks, crested birds, and the sons of weavers arrange their lower robes in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe so extremely high." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?" "Because at the outset you yourselves were freed from ignorance and became trained." Hearing that people had engaged in widespread criticism of them, the monks at that point reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train in not wearing the lower robe so extremely high."

When the Blessed One had declared that one shall train in not wearing the lower robe so extremely high, the group of six began wearing it so extremely low. Faithful brahmins and householders saw this and criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, women living in the region of Takkasilā and brides of good family arrange their lower robes in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe so extremely low." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?" "Because at the outset you yourselves were freed from ignorance and became trained." Hearing that people had engaged in widespread criticism of them, the monks at that point reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall wear the lower robe in a manner that is not so extremely low."

When the group of six wore the lower robe, they let the front hang down, and faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, young children, those intoxicated with alcohol, spirits, and those gorged with meat arrange their lower robes in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe like this." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?"

"Friends, for the first time you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have become trained." When the monks heard that the brahmins and householders had taken to criticizing them extensively, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that occasion. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the lower robe not as an elephant's trunk."

When the group of six wore the lower robe, they folded it up at the sides. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, dancers in the midst of a troupe arrange the lower robe in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe like this." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?" "Friends, for the first time you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have become trained." When the monks heard that they had taken to criticizing them extensively, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that occasion. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the lower robe not folded up like a palmyra leaf."

When the group of six wore the lower robe, they folded it at the side and stuck it up so that it jutted out like a spike. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, wealthy men, merchants, caravan leaders, and women arrange the lower robe in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe like this." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?" "Friends, for the first time you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have become trained." When the monks heard that they had taken to criticizing them extensively, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that occasion. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the lower robe not like a grain spike."

When the group of six wore the lower robe, they arranged it below the navel in the manner of a serpent's hood. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, those who adorn themselves arrange the lower robe in just this fashion — this is not fitting. Do not wear the lower robe like this." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a purpose for it." "Noble ones, what purpose is there?" "Friends, for the first time you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have become trained." When the monks heard that they had taken to criticizing them extensively, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that occasion. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the lower robe not in the manner of a serpent's hood."

The condensed training rule is this: one shall train to wear the lower robe evenly; not too high, not too low; not like an elephant's trunk; not folded up like a palmyra leaf; not like a grain spike; and not in the manner of a serpent's hood.

The Blessed One declared: "A monk shall train to wear the lower robe evenly; not too high, not too low;"

not like an elephant's trunk; not folded up like a palmyra leaf; not like a grain spike; and not in the manner of a serpent's hood. One shall train to wear it thus."

Having declared this, the monks did not know how to wear the upper robe, and so the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, one shall train to wear the upper robe evenly."

Having declared that one shall train to wear the upper robe evenly, the group of six then began wearing the upper robe pulled up far too high. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, ascetics and garland-sellers and fishermen's sons drape their upper garments in just such a manner — this is not fitting. Do not wear the upper robe like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the upper robe not pulled up too high."

Having declared that one shall train to wear the upper robe not pulled up too high, the group of six then began wearing it falling far too low. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, the residents of the region of Tagka and the daughters-in-law of noble families drape their upper garments in just such a manner — this is not fitting. Do not wear the upper robe like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to wear the upper robe not falling too low."

Then the group of six began going to the houses of others with their arms and legs thrust out, and faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, young boys and those drunk on beer and spirits who are possessed and intoxicated go about thrusting out their arms and legs in just such a fashion — this is not fitting. Do not walk about in that manner." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected, thinking: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore this shall be promulgated as the basis of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train to go to the houses of others in a composed and restrained manner."

Then the group of six began going to the houses of others with the upper robe bundled up and slung over the shoulder. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, those going to a wrestling arena drape their upper garments in just such a manner — this is not fitting. Do not wear the upper robe like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained."

When the monks heard that they had become the object of widespread criticism, they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and then declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others with the robe properly adjusted."

Then the group of six went to the houses of others making a loud clamor. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, children and young boys, people drunk on ale, spirits, and those who have eaten meat go about making just such a loud clamor — this is not fitting. Do not go about making such a clamor." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained."

When the monks heard that they had again become the object of widespread criticism, they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others with the voice lowered and with few words."

Then the group of six went to the houses of others with wandering, distracted eyes. They were walking alongside runaway elephants, runaway horses, runaway chariots, and runaway foot soldiers, being jostled and shoved about by these, and so were flung into filth, into muddy puddles, and into piles of sweepings. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, why do you look about like those who gaze at the stars or like those who squeeze their eyes shut? What harm is there in looking at the ground? This is not fitting. Do not go about with such distracted eyes." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained."

When the monks heard that they had again become the object of widespread criticism, they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without letting the eyes wander."

Then the group of six went to the houses of others gazing far into the distance. They lost their proper deportment, strayed from the path, and fell into various mishaps. Faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, why do you look about like those who gaze at the stars or like birds of prey scanning the ground? This is not fitting. Do not go about gazing thus." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a purpose in this." "Noble ones, what is the purpose?" "First of all, you yourselves are rid of ignorance, and you have trained."

When the monks heard that they had again become the object of widespread criticism, they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others with the gaze cast down the distance of a yoke."

The summary verse of the training rules is as follows:

One shall train to wear the robe in a rounded manner.
One shall train to wear the robe neither hitched up too high
nor trailing too low.
Composed and restrained, properly robed,
with the voice lowered, without letting the eyes wander,

The group of six would go about with their heads covered when visiting other houses, and believing brahmins and faithful householders would censure them, saying: "Noble ones, brides of good family, people with eye ailments, and those frightened by bees behave in this way — it is not fitting conduct. Do not cover your heads like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without covering the head."

The group of six would go about with their lower robes hitched up when visiting other houses, and believing brahmins and faithful householders would censure them, saying: "Noble ones, people who defecate and urinate behave in this way — it is not fitting conduct. Do not hitch up your robes like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without hitching up the robe."

The group of six would go about with their dharma robes slung over one shoulder when visiting other houses, and believing brahmins and faithful householders would censure them, saying: "Noble ones, peacocks, jesters, and acrobats' sons behave in this way — it is not fitting conduct. Do not sling your robe over one shoulder like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without slinging the robe over one shoulder."

The group of six would go about with their arms folded up over the yoke of their shoulders when visiting other houses, and believing brahmins and faithful householders would censure them, saying: "Noble ones, peacocks, jesters, and acrobats' sons behave in this way — it is not fitting conduct. Do not fold your arms up over your shoulders like that." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without folding the arms up over the shoulders."

The group of six went to the houses of others with their arms folded up behind their backs, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, servants behave this way, and it is not proper that you should do so — do not fold your arms up behind your backs like that." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Monks, therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without folding the arms up behind the back."

The summary sūtra of the training is as follows: one shall train to go to the houses of others without covering the head, without looking about from side to side, without peering around, without folding the arms across the chest, and without folding the arms up behind the back.

The group of six went leaping over shadows as they went to the houses of others, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, those who are frightened and fleeing in fear behave this way, and it is not proper that you should do so — do not leap about like that." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without leaping about."

The group of six went to the houses of others with excessively long strides, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, those who are drunk on liquor, those who are possessed by spirits, and those who have gorged themselves on meat behave this way, and it is not proper that you should do so — do not stride about in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without striding with overlong steps."

The group of six went to the houses of others walking on tiptoe, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, those with an unsteady gait, those who are lame, and young children behave this way, and it is not proper that you should do so — do not walk in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others not walking on tiptoe."

The group of six went to the houses of others walking on tiptoe, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones do not play about like children chasing fireflies, striking their heels like this — this is not proper conduct; do not walk in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others not walking on tiptoe."

The group of six went to the houses of others with both hands resting on their hips, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, wealthy persons, merchants, and ship captains walk in such a manner — this is not proper conduct; do not walk in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without resting the hands on the hips."

The summary training rule is: one shall train to go to the houses of others without jumping, without stretching out the legs, not squatting, not walking on tiptoe, and without resting the hands on the hips.

The group of six went to the houses of others swaying their bodies, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, dancing girls, elephants, and she-yaks move in such a manner — this is not proper conduct; do not walk in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without swaying the body."

The group of six went to the houses of others swinging their arms, and the faithful brahmins and householders censured them, saying: "Noble ones, peacocks, finely adorned persons, and the sons of wrestlers move in such a manner — this is not proper conduct; do not walk in such a manner." The six replied: "Friends, there is a need for it." "What need, noble ones?" "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without swinging the arms."

The group of six went to the houses of others with their heads turning from side to side, and

brahmin householders who were faithful censured them, saying: "Noble ones, great elephants and pure animals move in this manner — it is not fitting. Do not walk in such a way." The monks replied, "Worthy ones, there is reason for this." The faithful ones said, "Noble ones, what is the reason?"
