The monks answered, "First of all, you yourselves have been freed from ignorance and have trained." When the monks heard that these laypeople had entered into extensive censure, at that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and thought to himself, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without turning the head from side to side."

The group of six went to the houses of others with their shoulders jostling one another. Now, just as a person adorned with perfume and flowers walks along regarding the world as his child, so it was with them. When this happened, the group of six said: "Dear friend, look at this poor wretch walking along and regarding the world as his child — surely he must think that the group of six has never before held perfume and flowers. Come, let us make him displeased." Having agreed to do so, one after another they jostled each other shoulder to shoulder, and also jostled others shoulder to shoulder, until the man was knocked down and fell to the ground. He said, "What wrong have I done to you?" The others replied, "Poor wretch, because you walk along regarding the world as your child, as though the group of six had never before held perfume and flowers — that is why we should make you displeased." He then censured them, mocked them, and spoke harshly. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered it, thinking, "That householder censures them justifiably," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without jostling with the shoulders."

The group of six went to the houses of others with their arms linked together. Now, just as a person adorned with perfume and flowers walks along regarding the world as his child, so it was with them. The group of six said: "Dear friend, look at this poor wretch walking along and regarding the world as his child — surely he must think that the group of six has never before held perfume and flowers. Come, let us make him displeased." Having agreed to do so, one after another they linked arms and also linked arms with others, until the man was knocked down and fell to the ground. He said, "What wrong have I done to you?" They replied, "Poor wretch, because you walk along regarding the world as your child, as though the group of six had never before held perfume and flowers — that is why we should make you displeased." He then censured them, mocked them, and spoke harshly. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered it, thinking, "That householder censures them justifiably," and declared: "Therefore my hearers shall recite the following training rule of the Vinaya and train accordingly: one shall train to go to the houses of others without linking arms."

The condensed summary of the training rules is as follows: one shall train to go to the houses of others without swaying the body, without swinging the arms, without turning the head from side to side, without jostling with the shoulders, and without linking arms.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a brahmin of fastidious purity who had prepared a sleeping place in his gatehouse. There a girl was sitting holding a fan and keeping away the flies. The Venerable Ānanda entered that householder's dwelling for alms and the brahmin said to him:

"Girl, go to the brahmin's storehouse and tell Ānanda to stay in the gatehouse." She replied: "Noble one, I cannot leave, as I am here keeping away the flies." He said: "Girl, if that is so, I shall keep watch for a while — you go and tell him." When she had gone, Ānanda climbed up with his feet onto the sleeping platform and sat upon it. When the brahmin came back out, he saw Ānanda sitting upon the sleeping platform with his feet up on it. Seeing this, he said: "The standards of purity in the world are different things — why are you sitting here with your feet up?" Ānanda replied: "Brahmin, whatever use a monk makes of a sleeping place is a benefit conferred on you through seven generations of your family." When the brahmin heard this, he began to abuse him, to slander him, and to spread ill reports of him. Upon hearing this, the monks at that time reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, having reflected — thinking that the brahmin was reproaching the community — declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas shall be trained in this rule of the Vinaya: one shall train not to sit down uninvited on a seat in another's home."

Now, there was a time when the Venerable Charka had subdued a violent woman, and she prepared a sage's seat for the Venerable Charka to use, and he would use it as he went about. Then on another occasion he said to the violent woman: "Sister, watch over things — I am going for a walk." She said: "Noble one, please return quickly; do not make me weary of staying here." He said: "Sister, do not worry — it shall be so." He looked back at her and went to the Jeta Grove. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks: 'The Blessed One will go for a walk on the seventh day. Whoever among you wishes to go for a walk together with the Blessed One, let him prepare his robes.'" The Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One, respectfully complied and announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One will go for a walk on the seventh day. Whoever among you wishes to go for a walk together with the Blessed One, let him prepare his robes." The Venerable Charka thought: "Since there are eighteen benefits to a buddha's going for a walk, I shall go together with the Blessed One himself." And so he set out at once. At that time there was in the violent woman's house an infant boy who had been born not long before. She said to the girl: "Girl, lay this infant boy on the sage's seat — may he live long and may his life be protected." The girl dressed him in a white cloth and laid him down there. The Venerable Charka had entered Śrāvastī for alms and thought: "I shall go to the violent woman's house to use the seat, and then afterward collect alms and go." So he went there. Now, arhats do not engage their knowledge and vision without prior reflection, and so he sat hesitating on that very seat, uncertain. The people of the household, not thinking carefully, called out "Boy! Boy!" to the noble one. He rose up quickly, and when they saw that the moment had come, they began to weep. He said: "Sisters, why are you weeping over this? Such is the nature of reality for all conditioned formations. Nevertheless, it is in dependence on me that the Blessed One will establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas, and so I must take care of this matter." Having heard them weeping without stopping, out of the loving-kindness toward relatives that sentient beings in saṃsāra have been habituated to since beginningless time, the monks at that time reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let this be established as a rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas: one shall train not to sit upon a seat in another's home without first examining the seat."

Now, twelve years had passed since the Blessed One had gone forth, and six years since his perfect awakening, when he came to the settlement of Uruvelā. On the first day, he sat beneath a parasol on his father's side. On the second day, when he sat beneath a parasol in the retinue of his own queen, the venerable Charka stepped on the queen Yaśodharā's train, and though she was endowed with strength and did not fall, she said to the queen Sādhuvādā: "Sādhuvādā, the noble Charka has lodged a formal accusation against me before the community of monks led by the Buddha." When the queen told him what had happened and what had come of it, he replied: "Let it be made clear that from now on such conduct shall never occur again, and let it be a matter of displeasure."

Some time later, on another day, Queen Yaśodharā had a small stool wrapped in cloth and sent a maidservant with a message, saying: "Girl, go and wait for a while at the gate of the royal palace. When the noble Charka arrives, you are to say to him: 'Brahmin, brahmin.'" And if the brahmin should ask what is wanted, you are to say: 'You are being summoned to the queen's retinue.'"

The girl did so, and the venerable Charka arrived as well, and she began calling out: "Brahmin, brahmin." He asked: "Girl, what does the brahmin want?" She said: "Noble one, you are being summoned to the queen's retinue." He thought: "I should go quickly, so as to give alms without delay," and he went quickly. Queen Yaśodharā said to the girl: "Girl, she told you to call him 'brahmin,' so why did you call out 'shaven-headed ascetic' instead, and he said nothing?"

The venerable Charka replied: "If I were to say that I went forth from the home of your householder — does that make me any less a brahmin? If one is a brahmin, one recites: 'Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.' But if one has gone forth, then:

Commit no evil act whatsoever;
cultivate virtue fully and completely;
tame one's own mind thoroughly —
this is the teaching of the awakened ones.

That is what one recites."

She said: "Whether you are a brahmin or an ascetic, she made a vow that if the Blessed One came to the settlement of Uruvelā while he was still practicing austerities, she would offer such-and-such to a brahmin on his behalf."

He replied: "The Blessed One has freed many hundreds of thousands of living beings from the forms of wrong view, and yet he has not freed you from the forms of wrong view."

She said: "Noble one, the domain of women is difficult to leave — what can one do?" He replied: "Come and see. Look at what is given to the nun practitioners." He said: "Noble one, take this bowl of yogurt and this bowl of flour, stand up and drink it, and sit upon this stool. Will you give me this stool as well?" She said: "Noble one, I will not give you the stool."

He thought: "If she will not give the stool, then I shall break it," and knowing this, he sat down upon that very stool with the full weight of his body, then leaned forward, so that the bowl of yogurt and the bowl of flour were poured over her head. Her attendants then beat him with riding switches, and seizing him by his arms and legs, threw him into the bodhisattva's pleasure pond.

He rose from it and wrung out his robes. The monks, seeing this, said: "What transgression has the venerable Charka committed?" He replied: "I did something a little reckless, and this is the kind of trouble it has brought." They began to rebuke him and cried out in protest.

When the monks heard the complaints being made, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One considered the situation and thought, "They are criticizing them justifiably," and so declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train to sit upon a seat in another's home without pressing down with the full weight of one's body."

The Group of Six then sat in other people's homes with their legs crossed, and faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "The noble ones sit thus — like weavers, like traders, like fishermen's sons. This is not proper conduct; do not sit in such a manner." The Group of Six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for it." "Noble ones, what reason could there be?" "Precisely because, first and foremost, you yourselves are free from ignorance and have been trained."

When the monks heard that they had fallen into extensive criticism once again, they reported it to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One considered the situation and thought, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train to sit upon a seat in another's home without crossing one's legs."

The Group of Six then sat in other people's homes with their knees crossed, and faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "The noble ones sit thus — like weavers, like traders, like fishermen's sons. This is not proper conduct; do not sit in such a manner." The Group of Six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for it." "Noble ones, what reason could there be?" "Precisely because, first and foremost, you yourselves are free from ignorance and have been trained."

When the monks heard that they had fallen into extensive criticism once again, they reported it to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One considered the situation and thought, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train to sit upon a seat in another's home without crossing one's knees."

The Group of Six then sat in other people's homes with one cushion stacked upon another, and faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "The noble ones sit thus — like weavers, like traders, like fishermen's sons. This is not proper conduct; do not sit in such a manner." The Group of Six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for it." "Noble ones, what reason could there be?" "Precisely because, first and foremost, you yourselves are free from ignorance and have been trained."

When the monks heard that they had fallen into extensive criticism once again, they reported it to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One considered the situation and thought, "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas shall recite this rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train to sit upon a seat in another's home without stacking one cushion upon another."

The Group of Six then sat in other people's homes with their legs drawn up and tucked in. When laywomen came and paid their respects, the monks did not say a word of acknowledgment in return. The laywomen said: "Noble ones, why do you not say anything in acknowledgment?" The monks replied: "You paid respects to our feet, not to us." When the laywomen then bowed to their feet, the monks spread their buttocks wide to be measured, and said: "Ānanda, Upānanda — look at the remarkable size of these two's hindquarters!" The laywomen were mortified and stood there in silence. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to sit on a seat in another's home without drawing the legs up and tucking them in."

The group of six then sat in others' homes with their legs stretched out, and when laywomen came and paid their respects, the monks called them contemptible and slovenly. The laywomen said: "Noble ones, why do you call us contemptible and slovenly?" The monks replied: "You did not pay respects to our feet." When the laywomen then bowed to their feet, the monks spread their buttocks wide to be measured, and said: "Ānanda, Upānanda — look at the remarkable size of these two's hindquarters!" The laywomen were mortified and stood there in silence. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to sit on a seat in another's home without stretching the legs out."

The group of six then sat on seats in a sprawling, lounging manner, appearing disheveled, and faithful brahmins and householders reproached them, saying: "Noble ones, there are children and young boys here, people giddy with drink, spirits, and those reeking of meat — it is not fitting that you sit in such a manner. Please do not sit like this." The monks replied: "Good people, there is a purpose to this." The laypeople said: "Noble ones, what purpose could there be?" The monks replied: "First and foremost, it is to free yourselves from ignorance and to become trained." Hearing that they had embarked on extensive mockery, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, thinking: "What the laypeople say is true," and declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to sit on a seat in another's home without appearing disheveled and sprawling."

The condensed sūtra of the training rules: one shall train not to sit on a seat in another's home without having arranged one's robe; not to lower one's full body weight carelessly onto the seat; not to cross one's feet; not to cross one's knees; not to place one knee upon the other; not to draw the legs up and tuck them in; not to stretch the legs out; and to sit on a seat in another's home without appearing disheveled and sprawling.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the fearsome forest thicket on the hill where Śiśupāla was killed by the crocodile, the forest preserve of wild animals. Prince Udāyin invited the monastic Saṅgha of monks to his fine lotus palace, which had been painted with one hundred and one colors, and offered them a meal. Prince Udāyin was himself a man of faith, but his retinue was not, and the servants — those who served the rice and the vegetables — smashed the monks' bowls with their ladles. The group of six then devised a plan: "Let us make these people displeased," and as the rice and vegetables were being served, the group of six tipped their bowls back, so that the bowls fell to the ground. The monks then said: "Noble ones, you have made the floor of Prince Udāyin's fine lotus palace, painted with one hundred and one colors, unfit." The group of six replied: "Wretches! If you are displeased that the floor is made unfit, then what about the monks whose bowls have been broken?" Hearing this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to receive food properly."

The group of six entered Prince Udāyin's home for alms-round and —

At first, when they took as much cooked rice as would fill their bowl, the alms-givers said: "Noble ones, where shall we pour the curry?" They replied: "Right here — pour it on top." When they poured it on and it spilled over and fell to the ground, those present said: "Noble ones, you have made the floor of Prince Udāyin's fine lotus palace, painted with one hundred and one colors, unfit." The group of six replied: "Wretches! For now, you do not know where Prince Udāyin will be reborn, having become so greatly attached to this place. But as for you — having become so greatly attached to this place, you will be reborn among the drooling hungry ghosts." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to receive food without taking it to the level of the rim."

The group of six entered Prince Udāyin's home for alms-round. At first, when they took as much curry as would fill their bowl, the alms-givers said: "Noble ones, where shall we pour the cooked rice?" They replied: "Right here — pour it on top." When they poured it on and it spilled over and fell to the ground, those present said: "Noble ones, you have made the floor of Prince Udāyin's fine lotus palace, painted with one hundred and one colors, unfit." The group of six replied: "Wretches! For now, you do not know where Prince Udāyin will be reborn, having become so greatly attached to this place. But as for you — having become so greatly attached to this place, you will be reborn among the drooling hungry ghosts." When this was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to receive food without curry being in excess."

When the group of six were eating their rice, they would not take any curry and then, after a long while, would call out for it, causing the servers to be flustered. When this was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore this training rule in the Vinaya shall be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one shall train to receive food in due sequence."

At Śrāvastī there lived a householder who had invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to another house for a midday meal. Having prepared various foods for the offering, he began by serving rice. As the monks began to take large portions, he said: "Noble ones, I have prepared various foods — please do not take so much." The group of six said: "Dear friend and beloved householder, this wretch is trying to obstruct your rice too — take as much as you like." And so the monks took a great deal.

Now, when the servers who were arranging portions for the elders at the far end of the row were seen by the group of six, and they noticed an elderly monk sitting below that position, while looking toward the elders' seats at the far end, the group of six filled that monk's bowl from the ladle used for the rice. When the householder came to serve those seated at the far end, he gave a portion to the elderly monk, and it fell to the bottom of the bowl. The elderly monk then began to look at the householder's face. The householder said: "Noble one, why have you taken so much rice?" The monk replied: "Householder, I did not take it."

The householder said: "Then where did all this come from? I do not know." The group of six said: "Householder, it is well known that when we were young, a rain of coins fell for seven days. In the same way, a rain of cooked rice has fallen into this elderly monk's bowl." While the elderly monk sat there saying nothing, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "For this reason, my śrāvakas shall receive and uphold the following rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train to look into the alms bowl while accepting food."

When the group of six were on their alms round, whenever alms were not being given, they would stand holding their bowls and wait, and they would then abuse the faithful brahmins and householders, saying: "Noble ones, why do you stand there holding your bowls like beggars, with nothing put in them and nothing to eat? This is not fitting conduct — do not behave in this way." Those monks replied: "Friends, there is a need for this." The others asked: "Noble ones, what need is there?" They replied: "First, you yourselves will be freed from ignorance, and you will have trained." When the monks heard that they had engaged in such extensive abuse, they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter and concluding that the householders' complaints were justified, declared: "For this reason, my śrāvakas shall receive and uphold the following rule of training in the Vinaya: one shall train not to hold the alms bowl in front of oneself when food has not yet arrived."

In Śrāvastī, a certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks, together with the Buddha at their head, to his house at midday. That householder had an abundance of cooked rice but little curry. The group of six covered the curry with the cooked rice. When the householder saw the cooked rice, he said: "Noble ones, is there no curry?" They replied: "Householder, look here." He then gave additional curry as well. The monks went to the monastery and said: "Venerable ones, that householder prepared fine cooked rice, yet the curry was so little." The group of six replied: "As for us, we obtained plenty of curry." When the monks described to them how it had come about, the monks said: "Was it right for you to act in that way?" They replied: "It may have been right or it may not have been right, but as for us, we did act in that way." When this was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "For this reason, a monk shall train not to cover curry with cooked rice."

Again in Śrāvastī, a certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks, together with the Buddha at their head, to his house at midday. That householder had an abundance of curry but little cooked rice. The group of six covered the cooked rice with curry. When the householder saw the curry, he said: "Noble ones, is there no cooked rice?" They replied: "Householder, look here." He then gave additional cooked rice as well. The monks went to the monastery and said: "Venerable ones, that householder prepared fine curry, yet the cooked rice was so little." The group of six replied: "As for us, we obtained plenty of cooked rice." When the monks described to them how it had come about, the monks said: "Was it right for you to act in that way?" They replied: "It may have been right or it may not have been right, but as for us, we did act in that way." When this was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared:

Therefore, monks must train not to cover cooked rice with curry, nor curry with cooked rice.

At Śrāvastī, a certain monk who was going on alms round received cooked rice and curry. He then received more curry and more cooked rice, and regret arose in him, thinking: "Did I cover the curry with cooked rice, or did I not cover the cooked rice with curry?" When the monks reported this occasion to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, in this case there is no offense. Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: Out of desire, one must not cover curry with cooked rice, nor cooked rice with curry. Train accordingly."

The group of six, having placed their bowls on top of the food that had been set out and the food that was to be eaten, were criticized by faithful brahmins and householders, who said: "Noble ones, purity is surely something different. Why then do you place your bowls on top of the food that has been set out and the food to be eaten? This is not in accordance with proper conduct; please do not do so." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a reason for this." The faithful brahmins and householders asked: "Noble ones, what reason?" They replied: "Precisely so that you yourselves may first be freed from ignorance and become trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter, thought: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: Train not to hold the bowl over food that has been set out and food to be eaten."

The summary training rule is this: Train to take food properly — not going beyond the rim, not making a hole in the middle, not leveling the curry, not heaping it toward the edge, not looking into the bowl with attachment, not receiving the bowl before food that has been set out and food to be eaten has arrived, not covering curry with cooked rice out of desire, not covering cooked rice with curry, and not holding the bowl over food that has been set out and food to be eaten. Train accordingly.

This is the eighty-third section of the Vinayavibhaṅga, and the last one.

The group of six, eating food with various condiments, were criticized by faithful brahmins and householders, who said: "Noble ones, you eat along with small boys and young lads, and with women of the streets in such a manner — this is not in accordance with proper conduct; please do not do so." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a reason for this." The faithful brahmins and householders asked: "Noble ones, what reason?" They replied: "Precisely so that you yourselves may first be freed from ignorance and become trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter, thought: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: Train to eat food properly."

The group of six, when eating at the home of another, took their mouthfuls far too small, and were criticized by faithful brahmins and householders, who said: "Noble ones, you eat in such a manner — like small boys and young lads, like daughters-in-law of good families, like women of the streets — this is not in accordance with proper conduct; please do not do so." The group of six replied: "Friends, there is a reason for this." The faithful brahmins and householders asked: "Noble ones, what reason?" They replied: "Precisely so that you yourselves may first be freed from ignorance and become trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter, thought: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train to eat food in morsels that are not too small. When the group of six ate at another household, they ate in very large morsels, and the faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, greedy ones beg in this manner — this is not in accordance with proper conduct; please do not do so." They replied: "Friends, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason?" "Precisely so that you yourselves may first be freed from ignorance and become trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter, thought: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food in morsels that are not too large."

When the group of six ate at another household and ate in morsels of improper size, the faithful brahmins and householders criticized them, saying: "Noble ones, children and boys and greedy ones beg in this manner — this is not in accordance with proper conduct; please do not do so." They replied: "Friends, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason?" "Precisely so that you yourselves may first be freed from ignorance and become trained." When the monks heard that widespread criticism had arisen, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter, thought: "What the householders say is true," and declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food in properly sized morsels."

In Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another household at midday. Now, beneath the group of six there sat a senior monk who raised his face and gazed to the side of the elder. A lay attendant then filled his mouth with food and said: "Sir, eat this." When the monks heard of this, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to open the mouth before the morsel has been brought close."

When the group of six spoke with their mouths stuffed full of food, their speech became garbled. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to speak with the mouth stuffed full of food."

The summary sūtra of the trainings: One shall train to eat food well — in morsels that are not too small, in morsels that are not too large, in properly sized morsels; one shall train not to open the mouth before the morsel has been brought close; and one shall train not to speak with the mouth stuffed full of food.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A householder there invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another household at midday, and in preparation he had arranged sweet dishes as appetizers. Then the group of six called out aloud and said: "Dear friend, attendant — the appetizers are sour!" Upon hearing this, the householder was embarrassed and sat in silence. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train to eat food without making smacking sounds.

In Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another household at midday, and having no proper vessel, he cooked a pot of rice and poured it into a box. While it was still hot, the group of six called out aloud and said: "Dear friend, attendant — this rice is too cold; blow on it with your breath and eat it!" Upon hearing this, the householder was embarrassed and sat in silence. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train to eat food without making huffing sounds.

In Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to another household at midday. He cooked a pot of rice and spread it out on a tray, and when it had gone cold, the group of six called out aloud and said: "Dear friend, attendant — this rice is too cold; heat it up with your breath and eat it!" Upon hearing this, the householder was embarrassed and sat in silence. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train to eat food without blowing on it.

When the group of six were eating at another household, they stuck out their tongues to inspect the food, then licked both lips. The monks said to them: "Venerable ones, why do you stick out your tongues and look about like that?" They replied: "Venerable ones, it is not proper to swallow without having tasted the food first — so we look first." When the monks began to censure them, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train not to eat with the tongue stuck out.

The condensed sūtra of the trainings is as follows: one shall train to eat without making smacking sounds; without making slurping sounds; without making huffing sounds; without blowing on one's food; and without eating with the tongue stuck out.

When the group of six were eating at another household, they picked up the rice grain by grain and nibbled at it, and this caused faithful brahmin householders to censure them, saying: "Noble ones eat in this manner — like little children, like crows, like sparrows, like crows that peck — this is not fitting conduct; do not eat this way." The group of six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason might that be?" "First and foremost, it is to separate yourselves from ignorance and to become trained." When the monks heard that they had gone so far in inviting censure, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows:

One shall train to eat food without separating out the grains. When the group of six were eating at another household, on the occasion of their saying "Venerable ones, this curry is far too spicy" and "Far too sour," the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without finding fault with it."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they would transfer morsels from mouthful to mouthful and eat in this way. The brahmin and householder faithful censured them, saying: "Noble ones, it is not fitting conduct to beg in this manner, like little children, like boys, like hungry creatures; do not eat this way." The group of six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason might that be?" "First and foremost, it is to separate yourselves from ignorance and to become trained." When the monks heard that they had gone so far in inviting censure, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without transferring morsels from mouthful to mouthful."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they would make slurping sounds, and the brahmin and householder faithful censured them, saying: "Noble ones, it is not fitting conduct to beg in this manner, like little children, like boys, like hungry creatures; do not eat this way." The group of six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason might that be?" "First and foremost, it is to separate yourselves from ignorance and to become trained." When the monks heard that they had gone so far in inviting censure, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without making slurping sounds."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they would take a mouthful and stuff half into their mouth while letting half fall into the bowl, and the brahmin and householder faithful censured them, saying: "Noble ones, it is not fitting conduct to beg in this manner, like little children, like boys, like prostitutes; do not eat this way." The group of six replied: "Wise ones, there is a reason for this." "Noble ones, what reason might that be?" "First and foremost, it is to separate yourselves from ignorance and to become trained." When the monks heard that they had gone so far in inviting censure, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, reflecting that what the householders said was true, declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without letting morsels drop and scatter."

The condensed sūtra of the training rules is as follows: One shall train to eat food without separating out the grains, without finding fault, without transferring morsels from mouthful to mouthful, without making slurping sounds, and without letting morsels drop and scatter.

When the group of six were eating at another household, they licked their hands, and the monks said: "Venerable ones, why do you do something so unseemly?" The group of six replied: "Venerable ones, we are fond of whatever has the finest essence." On the occasion of the monks censuring them, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without licking one's hands."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they scraped their bowls clean, and the monks said:

"Venerable ones, why do you do something so unseemly?" They replied: "Venerable ones, we are fond of whatever has the finest essence." On the occasion of the monks censuring them, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without scraping one's bowl clean."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they shook their hands, and the water from their hands splashed the monks nearby. On the occasion of the monks censuring them, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without shaking one's hands."

When the group of six were eating at another household, there was a monk seated below them wearing a reddish-yellow patched robe. The group of six said: "Friend, dear friend, this poor wretch in our midst — we suspect that in the past he has never once worn a robe of this quality, which is why he is displeased with it." Then they tilted their bowls, and the water from the bowl ruined that monk's robe. On the occasion of the monks censuring them, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train to eat food without tilting one's bowl."

At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had faith in the adherents of the naked ascetics (the Nirgrantha tīrthikas). Later he came to have faith in the Blessed One, and he invited the community of monks to his home for a midday meal. He served them flour, and the group of six kneaded it together and arranged it in the shape of a stupa. They then served the hollowed-out middle portions and arranged those upright like a central pillar. They served the outer portions and arranged those on top of the pillar in the shape of an umbrella. Then they said: "Friend, dear friend, this stupa is the one that consummates evil destinies — it is a 'consummator.'" Then they broke it apart and ate it, saying: "Friend, dear friend, the stupa that consummates evil destinies — the 'consummator' — has fallen." When the householder heard this, he said: "Noble ones, I myself have been freed from that sinful view, yet you have still not been freed from aversion." Whereupon they sat in silence. On that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to eat food by breaking it into the shape of a stupa."

The summary sūtra of the training rules is: one shall train to eat food without licking one's hands; without scraping one's bowl; without shaking one's hands; without tilting one's bowl; and without breaking food into the shape of a stupa and eating it.

When the group of six were eating at another household, a monk seated near them was eating a great deal. The group of six mocked him and said: "Friend, dear friend, look at this old one — look how much he is eating!" On that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to look into the bowl of a monk seated nearby in order to find fault with how much he eats."

When the group of six were eating at another household, they took hold of a water vessel with hands raised above the food,

those who lacked faith cried out that the śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya, were unclean because they were grasping a water vessel with hands soiled by food. On that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to grasp a water vessel with hands soiled by food."

When the group of six were eating at another household, there was a monk seated below them wearing a patchwork robe of reddish-yellow. The group of six said: "Friend, dear friend, this poor fellow must be thinking to himself, 'People like us have never before in our lives worn a robe as fine as this,' and so he is displeased with it." They then splattered him with the water left over from the food, and that monk's patchwork robe was ruined by the food-water. When they then proceeded to mock him, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to splatter a monk seated nearby with water left over from food."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the forest grove of Mṛgadāva on the fearsome wooded mountain of Śiśumāragiri. The prince Prasenajit invited the community of monks to his fine lotus palace painted in one hundred and one colors, and offered them a meal. The group of six poured the rinse water from their bowls right there on the spot, and the sweepers and cleaners rebuked the noble ones, saying: "You have defiled the floor of Prince Prasenajit's fine lotus palace painted in one hundred and one colors." The group of six replied: "For now Prince Prasenajit has developed an attachment to this place, but he does not know where he will be reborn. As for you, having developed this attachment, you will be reborn among the slobbering hungry ghosts." When they proceeded to mock them in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One shall train not to pour rinse water at another household."

At Śrāvastī, a householder had monks come to his walled home and invited the community of monks for a midday meal. The monks began pouring their rinse water outside the house, and the householder said: "Noble ones, please pour it right here — my household will make use of it." On that occasion the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If a householder says 'Pour it here,' then one may pour it there. Otherwise, one shall not pour it." He then declared: "Therefore my śrāvakas shall recite this training rule for the Vinaya as follows: One shall train not to pour rinse water at another household without asking the householder present."

The summary of training rules: One shall train not to look into the bowl of a monk seated nearby in order to find fault. One shall train not to grasp a water vessel with hands soiled by food. One shall train not to splatter a monk seated nearby with water left over from food. One shall train not to pour rinse water at another household without asking the householder present.

At Śrāvastī there was a brahmin whose son had fallen ill. The son went to a physician and said: "Good sir, my son is sick — please prescribe a medicine." That physician was a person of faith, and he said: "Brahmin, wash yourself with the rinse water from the bowl of the noble ones." The man went to the Jeta Grove, and —

One of the group of six had left the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended, so the Venerable Ānanda was walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. The brahmin approached him, bowed at his feet, and said: "Noble one, my son is sick. Please grant us some bowl-rinse water of the noble ones." He replied: "Brahmin, wait here a moment; I will bring bowl water and come." He went to the monastery hall and poured into a bowl a little flour, a little cooked rice, a little broth, a little meat, and a little bone, then filled it with water and came back out, saying: "Brahmin, take this." When the brahmin saw it, he said: "Noble one, is this the kind of bowl-rinse water you have?" He answered: "Brahmin, it is exactly this kind." The brahmin then said: "Noble one, it would be better for my son to die than to be washed with such filth as this," and with that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to dispose of food remains by pouring them into the bowl." Further, if someone wishes to request bowl-rinse water, the bowl shall be washed three times, and water from the bowl over which the sacred verses have been recited shall then be given.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Some monks were placing their bowls on ground that had no underlining support, and insects nested in them and were eaten along with the food. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to place the bowl on ground that has no underlining support."

Some monks were placing their bowls on the edge of a ledge, and they slipped and broke. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to place the bowl where there is no ledge-edge."

Some monks were placing their bowls at a precipitous drop, and they slipped and broke. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to place the bowl where there is no precipitous drop."

Some monks were placing their bowls on a steep slope, and they slipped and broke. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to place the bowl where there is no steep slope."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A monk was standing and washing his bowl, and the other monks said to him: "Venerable one, do not stand to wash the bowl." He replied: "What does it matter? It might slip and break, but what else would happen?" When they tried to dissuade him he would not relent, and the bowl slipped and broke. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to wash the bowl while standing."

On an occasion when monks washed their bowls over a drain and a bowl slipped, rolled, and broke, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to wash the bowl not over a drain."

On an occasion when monks washed their bowls over a precipice and a bowl slipped, rolled, and broke, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to wash the bowl not over a precipice."

On an occasion when monks washed their bowls on a steep slope and a bowl slipped, rolled, and broke, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train to wash the bowl not on a steep slope."

On an occasion when monks held their bowls against a swift current of flowing water to scoop up water, and the bowl slipped and was carried away by the current, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to scoop up water with the bowl against a swift current of flowing water."

The summary training rule is as follows: one shall train to pour the food remnants into the bowl and not throw them away; one shall train not to set the bowl down on a surface that has no support beneath it; one shall train to set the bowl down where there is no drain, no precipice, and no steep slope; one shall train not to wash the bowl while standing; one shall train to wash the bowl where there is no drain, no precipice, and no steep slope; and one shall train not to scoop up water with the bowl against a swift current of flowing water.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks, teaching Dharma to a seated assembly while themselves standing, were rebuked by faithful brahmin and householder devotees, who said: "O noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections (pāramitās) through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you teach Dharma while standing to an assembly that is seated, showing no deference and no respect?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while standing to an assembly that is seated."

On another occasion, the group of six monks, teaching Dharma while seated to an assembly that was lying down without illness, were rebuked by faithful brahmin and householder devotees, who said: "O noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you teach Dharma while seated to those who lie down without illness, showing no deference and no respect?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while seated to an assembly that is lying down without illness."

The group of six monks, without illness, were sitting on a low seat and teaching Dharma to those sitting on a high seat, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, teach Dharma while seated on a low seat to those who are seated on a high seat?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while seated on a low seat to those who, without illness, are seated on a high seat."

The group of six monks, without illness, were walking behind those who were walking in front, and teaching Dharma, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, walk behind those who are walking in front and teach Dharma?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while walking behind those who, without illness, are walking in front."

The group of six monks, without illness, were walking along the roadside and teaching Dharma to those walking on the road, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, walk along the roadside and teach Dharma to those walking on the road?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya for my śrāvakas is to be set forth as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while walking along the roadside to those who, without illness, are walking on the road."

The summary of trainings is as follows: one shall train not to teach Dharma while standing to those who, without illness, are seated; one shall train not to teach Dharma while seated to those who, without illness, are lying down; one shall train not to teach Dharma while seated on a low seat to those who, without illness, are seated on a high seat; one shall train not to teach Dharma while walking behind those who, without illness, are walking in front; one shall train not to teach Dharma while walking along the roadside to those who, without illness, are walking on the road.

The group of six monks were teaching Dharma to those without illness whose heads were covered, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, teach Dharma to those whose heads are covered?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

Therefore this is how the training rule in the Vinaya is to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one must train not to teach Dharma to those without illness whose heads are wrapped.

The group of six monks were teaching Dharma to those without illness who had their garments pulled over their heads, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, teach Dharma to those who have their garments pulled over their heads?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: Therefore this is how the training rule in the Vinaya is to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one must train not to teach Dharma to those without illness who have their garments pulled over their heads.

The group of six monks were teaching Dharma to those without illness who had their robes draped over one shoulder, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, teach Dharma to those who have their robes draped over one shoulder?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: Therefore this is how the training rule in the Vinaya is to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one must train not to teach Dharma to those without illness who have their robes draped over one shoulder.

The group of six monks were teaching Dharma to those without illness who had their garments wrapped around their necks, and the faithful brahmins and householders rebuked them, saying: "Noble ones, the Blessed One perfected the six perfections through many hundreds and thousands of acts of austerity over three immeasurable eons and thereby attained unsurpassed wisdom — and you, showing no deference and no respect, teach Dharma to those who have their garments wrapped around their necks?" When the monks fell silent and said nothing in response, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: Therefore this is how the training rule in the Vinaya is to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas: one must train not to teach Dharma to those without illness who have their garments wrapped around their necks.

The condensed sūtra of the training rules is as follows: one must train not to teach Dharma to those without illness whose heads are covered, who have their garments pulled over their heads, who have their robes draped over one shoulder, who have their garments wrapped around their necks, or who have their garments wrapped around their shoulders.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upananda urinated and defecated while standing, and the faithful brahmins and householders criticized him, saying: "The noble ones — if the śrāvakas of the Teacher are people of moral shame, how could a śrāvaka without shame or modesty urinate and defecate while standing?" The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore shall my śrāvakas recite this rule of training in the Vinaya: One shall train not to urinate or defecate while standing when one is not ill."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upananda went to the dwelling of a laundryman and said: "Good fellow, wash this robe and give it back to me." The laundryman said: "Noble one, you used to look after us in former times; since you no longer do so these days, why should I wash your robe and give it back?" Upananda said "Wait," and went away. He thought: "I shall make that wretch unhappy." So he took a purgative medicine, and when his bowels had moved, he filled a pot with filth and poured it into the laundryman's washing place. Early the next morning the laundryman arose and began to wash the robes, and as the stench of the filth arose, he rested his hands on his hips, inwardly seething with anger. Upananda, deliberately thinking of him, went to that spot and said: "Good fellow, why are you sitting there seething inwardly?" The laundryman replied: "Noble one, someone has poured filth into this washing place so that it cannot be used; now I am at a loss as to how I shall prepare the washing water." Upananda said:

"Poor fellow, do not be so displeased." When he had begun to scold that person, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas is this: one shall train not to defecate or urinate into water when it is not frozen. The exception is when the water is completely frozen solid and there is no alternative. Just as with defecating and urinating, so too one shall train not to spit, blow mucus, vomit, or discharge phlegm into water. The same rule applies equally."

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park. The venerable Upananda went to the gardener's garden and said: "Good fellow, give me a small bunch of flowers." The gardener replied: "Noble one, in former times you used to look after us, but nowadays you do not, so why should I give you flowers?" Saying "Wait there," the gardener went off, thinking to himself, "I shall make that poor fellow displeased." He then took a purgative medicine and, when his bowels had moved, he filled a basket with filth, and taking it with a broom, he scattered filth all over the flower garden and ruined every part of it. Attracted by the stench of the filth, foxes gathered there and ruined the garden further. Then early the next morning the gardener rose to pick flowers for sale and went to the garden, where he saw that the entire garden had been strewn with filth and eaten over by foxes and was entirely unfit for market. He stood there resting his hands on his hips, seething inwardly. Upananda, deliberately thinking of him, went to that spot and said: "Good fellow, why are you sitting there seething inwardly?" The gardener replied: "Noble one, someone has scattered filth all over this garden and made it entirely unfit for market; now I do not know how I shall make my livelihood." Upananda said: "Poor fellow, do not be so displeased." When he had begun to scold that person, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, the rule of training in the Vinaya to be proclaimed for my śrāvakas is this: one shall train not to defecate or urinate on ground where there is green grass when it is not frozen. The exception is when the ground is completely covered with green growth and there is no alternative. Just as with defecating and urinating, so too one shall train not to spit, blow mucus, vomit, or discharge phlegm onto ground where there is green grass. The same rule applies equally."

The condensed sūtra of training rules is as follows: one shall train not to defecate or urinate while standing when it is not necessary; one shall train not to defecate or urinate into water, or to spit, blow mucus, vomit, or discharge phlegm into water, when it is not necessary; and one shall train not to defecate or urinate on ground where there is green grass, or to spit, blow mucus, vomit, or discharge phlegm there, when it is not necessary.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī a householder invited the Saṅgha of monks, with the Buddha at their head, to another home for a midday meal. It then fell to the venerable Upananda's turn to carry the roster-bowl for the duty-monk. He thought to himself: "What means could there be to cut short this duty-monk roster?" And he thought: "If someone were to ask me how far it is from Śrāvastī to the Jeta Grove, I shall tell him whatever I like and say to him in every way, 'Measure the ground with your steps.'" With that in mind, while the other was measuring the ground with his steps and walking very slowly, the duty-monk thought: "If he is delayed for a long time and I miss the meal it will not do — I had better look out." He climbed up into a tree and began to look, and when he saw the venerable Upananda coming very slowly and deliberately, he thought:

"From the way he is walking, I can see that he intends to cut short my meal." Realizing this, he climbed down from the tree and sat down. When the venerable Upananda arrived, the midday shadow had just passed, and Upananda said to him: "Venerable one, from the way you walked in such a fashion, it is clear that you deliberately caused me to miss my meal. How did you see me? I climbed up into a tree and looked." "Is it permitted for you to climb up into a tree?" "It may be permitted; it may not be permitted — but I did climb up." At that, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks are to train themselves not to climb trees." After the Blessed One had declared that monks are to train themselves not to climb trees, some monks who wished to do painting work did not know where to set up a plumb line, and so the Blessed One declared: "One may climb a tree to the height of a man. Therefore, monks are to train themselves not to climb a tree higher than a man's height." After the Blessed One had declared that monks are to train themselves not to climb a tree higher than a man's height, a certain monk was traveling through the wilds at night together with companions going the same way, following the path to a solitary hermitage, when a tiger appeared as a threat. His companions climbed high up into the tree and settled there. The monk climbed only to a man's height and stayed there. When the tiger arrived and drew near, his companions called out: "Venerable one, a tiger is here — quickly, climb higher!" He thought: "The Blessed One has not permitted climbing a tree higher than a man's height, so how can I climb higher?" And so he remained exactly where he was, and the tiger leaped up and killed him. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, my śrāvakas are to understand this as the rule of training in the Vinaya in this manner: except when harm arises, monks are to train themselves not to climb a tree higher than a man's height." The many rules of training are complete.

Summary verse:

Directly, by recollection, without intoxication —
and likewise by the many, and by essential nature —
like grass that is strewn,
and also by acknowledgment.

To one who is fit to be tamed directly, taming is given directly. To one who is fit to be tamed by recollection, taming is given by recollection. To one who is fit to be tamed without intoxication, taming is given without intoxication. To one to whom many procedures are fit to be given, many procedures are given. To one who is fit to be sent to seek the essential nature of the matter, seeking the essential nature of the matter is given. To one to whom the manner of strewn grass is fitting, the manner of strewn grass is given. To one who is fit to make acknowledgment, acknowledgment is to be made. When disputes have arisen, they are to be tamed, quieted, and fully pacified in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's teaching by means of these seven procedures for settling disputes. The seven procedures for settling disputes are complete.

Patience is the supreme austerity and discipline —
nirvāṇa is the highest, so the buddhas say.
One who has gone forth and harms others,
who injures others, is no true ascetic.

In this world of the wise, who sustain life,
just as the helpless and downtrodden fare —
in the presence of beings endowed with sight —
abandon all wrongdoing utterly.

Speak no slander, do no harm,
be restrained in the rules of individual liberation,
know also the measure in food,
and dwell in remote and secluded places.
Apply yourself to the higher mind —
this is the teaching of the buddhas.

Just as a bee, taking nectar from a flower,
without harming its color or its scent,
draws the fluid and flies away —
so let the Sage pass through a town.

One should examine what is fitting and unfitting for oneself — not looking to the discord of others, nor to what others have done or left undone. With care applied to the higher mind, train in the rules of restraint taught by the Capable One. The Protector who is ever mindful and fully pacified is free from sorrow.

Through generosity, merit grows abundantly. Through good restraint, enemies and the like do not arise. Endowed with virtue, one abandons wrongdoing. Through the exhaustion of afflictions, one passes beyond sorrow.

Commit no evil whatsoever,
accomplish virtue in full perfection,
tame your own mind completely —
this is the teaching of the buddhas.

Restraint of body is excellent,
restraint of speech is excellent too,
restraint of mind is excellent,
and restraint in all things is excellent.
The monk who is restrained in all things
is fully liberated from all suffering.

Guard your speech and discipline your mind thoroughly,
and commit no non-virtue with the body.
If these three pathways of action are thoroughly purified,
you will attain the path proclaimed by the sages.

The buddha endowed with perfect vision, the crown-protrusion, protector of all;
the destroyer of cyclic existence, the golden sage, the radiant preserver;
Śākyamuni, Gautama, the god of gods;
the unsurpassable guide of the untamed, the great charioteer —
the supreme protector and guardian of the world;
these seven courageous buddhas, the illustrious ones,
taught the individual liberation from bondage
in its extensive elaboration.

In this, whatever buddhas there are, and
the śrāvakas of the buddhas, are also respectful.
Since you have become endowed with this reverence,
attain the unconditioned.
Undertake it and lift it up,
enter into the teaching of the buddhas;
and like a great elephant against a house of reeds,
crush the ranks of the Lord of Death.

Whoever practices this discipline of taming with full diligence
will, having utterly abandoned the cycle of birth,
bring suffering to its final end.

Here ends the Vinaya-vibhaṅga in full.

By command of the illustrious and sovereign divine king, the most excellent lord of power, this text was translated from the noble tradition of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya holders, following the Kāśmīra sub-school, by the master Jinamitra and the great-editor translator, the monk Nāgarājadhvaja, who also revised and established it definitively. This work contains twenty-five thousand verses and has been arranged into eighty-three sections. May there be auspiciousness.

Here begins the Vinaya, volume ten.

This concludes the translation. The following are translator's notes.

The verse "the buddhas who dwell in dependence upon it / regard it with reverence and honor it as their guru" refers to the well-known teaching that even the buddhas respect and abide by the Vinaya, a common encomium found in Vinaya preambles.

The line rendered "like an eel's fin shaken by a nāga" is a somewhat obscure simile. The Tibetan reads "ཨེ་ལའི་འདབ་ཀླུ་བཞིན" — literally "like the wings/fins of an eel, a nāga." The point appears to be that improper recitation of the Buddha's words leads to an animal rebirth, the eel being a lowly aquatic creature; the precise force of the simile is uncertain and may reflect an idiom whose background is not fully clear.

The phrase translated "this is both the Teacher himself and the treatise directly" reflects the classical Tibetan Vinaya hermeneutic in which the Vinaya is not merely a secondary treatise about the Buddha's teaching but is identified with the Buddha's own voice and presence, hence deserving double reverence — as both the Buddha and the Dharma simultaneously.  The verse "Even across ten million eons..." through the blessing-verses that follow are drawn from or echo well-known canonical Pali sources (the Dhammapada and related texts), here embedded in the Tibetan Vinaya narrative; the translation preserves the enumerative, aphoristic character of the original.

The phrase rendered "the Self-Arisen One himself" refers to the Buddha as svayambhū, the self-arisen, indicating that the praise of the Vinaya cited above was spoken by the Buddha himself.

"Vaiśravaṇa" (Tibetan: rnam thos kyi bu) is the god of wealth; the text explicitly compares Supriya's wealth to his.  The list of meal-types — porridge, soup for drinking, regular turns, invited meals, eighth-day and fourteenth-day feasts, fish feasts, and small special visits — reflects a well-attested Vinaya-period catalog of monastic food-offerings; the specific items are rendered according to their standard contextual meanings rather than loan-words, as the Tibetan itself is already a translation of Indian categories.

The phrase rendered "something improper" translates "ma bya ba" literally "something not to be done / something unbecoming," left deliberately vague because the text itself is building narrative suspense; the exact nature of the incident is clearly to be disclosed afterward.  The phrase rendered "women's treasure," "women's dowry," and "substance that is women's domain" translates three distinct Tibetan terms for categories of a woman's personal property or inheritance; the exact legal nuances of these categories in the Vinaya context are not fully recoverable from the Tibetan alone, but the general sense is clear.

The expression "lunar signs are favorable" renders a phrase literally meaning "the time has arrived and she is accompanied by lunar signs," which likely refers to a woman's fertile period as determined by lunar reckoning, a detail relevant to the narrative's purpose of enticing the monk back to lay life.  The phrase rendered "a being in his last existence, one who seeks conduct, one who had grasped the essence of liberation, one oriented toward nirvāṇa" translates a cluster of epithets applied to Bhadradatta that are standard in Vinaya narrative to explain why his transgression does not constitute a full defeat: as a last-birth being already firmly set toward liberation, his lapse is treated with particular nuance in the subsequent commentary. The term translated "seed" throughout renders a Tibetan euphemism used in this Vinaya context for semen and the act of conception.  The name Sāvana is a reconstruction from the Tibetan "sa bon pa," which means "seed-person" or "he of the seed." The Sanskrit original is likely Bījavana or a similar compound; "Sāvana" is a placeholder rendering.

The phrase rendered "announced by name the offering of gifts" translates a technical expression for a formal proclamation made at occasions such as birth feasts, in which the names of donors and the amounts of their offerings are publicly declared. The syntax of the entire passage in which Śyāmā makes this announcement is notably compressed and indirect in the Tibetan.

The final sentence is incomplete in the source text as provided.  The phrase rendered "the gods of the sense faculties and those with faculties close by" translates དབང་པོ་དང་ཉེ་དབང་དང་བཅས་པའི་ལྷ་རྣམས, which likely refers to specific classes of gods associated with the faculties (Indriya-class devas); the precise referent is not entirely certain, though the general sense of divine veneration is clear.

The verse presents a minor doctrinal puzzle: the arhat says he "learned only after much procrastination" and "was greatly delayed in youth," which is a moment of self-deprecating reflection on the long path to his realization. This is consistent with the narrative context and requires no emendation.

The phrase rendered "liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom" (སེམས་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བ་དང་ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བ) corresponds to the standard Pāli pair cetovimutti and paññāvimutti, a well-attested formulation in early Buddhist literature.  The passage contains a slightly awkward internal sequence where the monks ask Śāṇavāsa whether he has any distress, he replies in what appears to be a merged construction, and then the narrative continues. The Tibetan grammar at that point is compressed; the translation follows the most natural reading of the dialogue, attributing "what is the mental distress that afflicts you?" as the monks' follow-up question implied by the structure, and his answer as the statement that follows. This is a minor structural ambiguity, not a doctrinal one.

The phrase rendered "inquire knowingly" translates a term literally meaning "to ask while knowing," a Vinaya formula describing the Buddha's rhetorical method of posing questions to which he already knows the answer, as a pedagogical and procedural device. This is standard Vinaya narrative convention.  The tenfold list of benefits for establishing Vinaya rules is a standard canonical formula appearing across Pāli and Sanskrit Vinaya recensions. The rendering follows the standard ordering preserved in this tradition.
