"Sa le sbram" may refer to a type of grain or granary wealth rather than a jewel, and "rdo'i snying po" likely means a precious stone essence or a specific gem such as crystal or rock crystal; these renderings are reasonable but not fully certain. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the Tibetan text itself is incomplete at this point.  The phrase rendered "adjudicator" translates the Tibetan term for a toll or customs official who weighs or measures goods (ཤོ་གམ་པ, literally one who deals with dice or weights used for measuring toll); it refers to a checkpoint toll-collector or customs weigher. The rendering "adjudicator" is an approximation; "toll-keeper" or "customs officer" would be equally defensible. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the provided Tibetan text, in the middle of the praise of the Blessed One.  The phrase rendered "not limited to a particular time" translates the Tibetan "dus chad pa med pa," which is the standard Tibetan equivalent of the Pāli "akālika" — meaning the Dharma bears results immediately, not only at some future time. The translation given follows the traditional commentarial interpretation.

The "three bases of merit-making" refers to the Three Jewels, which are the primary objects toward which merit-making is directed. The passage is slightly elliptical in the Tibetan but the referent is clear from context.  The phrase rendered "rubbing his two hands together" describes a gesture of bewilderment or emptiness, literally "making the two hands go around each other," indicating the monk searched his bundle and found nothing, then made an empty-handed gesture. This is a conventional narrative idiom for the moment of discovering a loss.

The customs-post episode turns on a specific Vinaya rule: a monk may not carry goods past a customs station without paying the due levy, since doing so constitutes a form of theft by means of the monastic robe as cover. The caravan leader resolves the problem by surreptitiously taking the cloth into his own declared goods, thus technically "stealing" it from the monk, so that no customs violation accrues to the monk. The ironic exchange between monk and customs officer and then monk and caravan leader illuminates this Vinaya technicality.  The phrase rendered "serious offense" for "འགལ་ཚབས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ" is a Vinaya technical term indicating an offense of wrong-doing with aggravating circumstances; it is not a pārājika but a significant disciplinary infraction. The precise Vinaya category is left deliberately broad in the translation since the text itself does not specify a class here.  The phrase rendered "goods subject to customs duty" translates the recurring Tibetan term for dutiable or taxable goods being transported, consistent with the preceding passage's context about the customs post. The expression "anoint oneself with pressed cow-dung or wash with it" refers to a hygiene or medicinal use of cattle byproduct permitted under duress; the exact practical referent is somewhat opaque in the Vinaya context but the literal rendering is retained. The final sentence is left open as the Tibetan breaks off mid-scene, clearly continuing into the next passage.  The phrase rendered "stitched just as it was" reflects the Tibetan sense that the cloth was bundled or folded but not cut and sewn into a proper robe. The word translated "bundle" is the same term used for the unstitched roll of cloth throughout.

The passage describing the north road as a place "where women behave lewdly at every turn" follows the Tibetan closely; it is likely a stock topos for an undesirable route rather than a precise geographical description.  The term translated as "gaming supervisor" renders a compound that literally reads "one who knows all regarding dice." The phrase is the beginning of what appears to be a longer explanation about the city of Śrāvastī that is cut off at the end of this passage. The term rendered "white-robed robbers" refers to lay people or civilians who operate criminal schemes under the guise of respectability, a recognized stock phrase in this narrative literature.  The phrase rendered "well-matched and splendid caravan" translates a term that literally means something like "a caravan of compatible purpose, fully excellent." This appears to refer to a caravan whose goods perfectly match the local demand, making it commercially ideal — a term from merchant vocabulary in this Vinaya narrative.

The gambler's final exchange turns on a proverbial idiom: asking whether a river flows against its course is Upananda's way of saying that food, once placed in a monk's bowl as alms, does not flow back to the giver — an implicit refusal dressed in rhetorical wit.  The phrase rendered "strike a knife with my fist and pound grass into the stone of my own loom" is an idiomatic expression of frustrated anger whose precise force is difficult to determine. The Tibetan reads literally "I shall hit a knife with my fist and poke grass into my own warping stone," which appears to be a proverbial expression for self-defeating rage or resolving to take revenge regardless of cost to oneself. The sense of frustrated indignation is clear even if the exact idiom is opaque.

The phrase "with a touch of the head" in the merchants' mocking speech refers contemptuously to a token or nominal payment, implying that Upananda accepted a pittance rather than real compensation.  The phrase rendered "show them the mark" refers to Upananda brandishing or displaying something as a demand token or sign of debt owed — the exact nature of the "mark" (Tib. mtshan ma) in this merchant-debt context is slightly elliptical in the Tibetan, but the narrative context makes clear it is a physical sign or token of the debt claim. No doctrinal uncertainty is involved; this is a Vinaya narrative passage.

The phrase rendered "slipping through the window so that the tax revenues are not collected" reflects a situation where gambling debtors are escaping without paying what is owed to the authorities, creating liability for the official dice-hall keepers.  The phrase "dice of omniscience" versus "dice of wrongdoing" is a wordplay central to this passage. The Tibetan ཀུན་ཤེས་པའི་ཤོ་གམ་ཅན and ཉེས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་ཤོ་གམ་ཅན appear to designate two different types of dice or dice-players — those who merely know the game thoroughly versus those who cheat. The rhetorical structure, with its repeated formulaic exchanges, is characteristic of Vinaya narrative and has been preserved intact. The name Arada Brahmadatta (རྒྱལ་པོ་འ་ར་ད་ཚངས་བྱིན) is a royal name appearing in Vinaya narrative literature; it has been transliterated as given.  The phrase rendered "those who practice cupping" translates a term for practitioners of a form of bloodletting or suction therapy using animal means, likely leeches or related creatures; the exact technical identity of "ཁ་ལུངས་པའི་ཡ་བ་ན་དག" is uncertain. The passage breaks off mid-explanation, as the text continues beyond what was supplied. The phrase "burned away" for "ཚིག་པ་ཡིན་ནོ" reflects the idiomatic Tibetan expression meaning that the conduct has been utterly destroyed or ruined, used here as a term of abuse.  The passage on "cupping" practitioners is a continuation of the preceding unit and presents some difficulty. The worm-creatures being "intoxicated" by drinking various liquids is a technical reference to the use of vermicular creatures in a therapeutic practice resembling wet cupping, in which the creatures are induced to draw blood; the text's framing is slightly unusual and the precise procedure is not entirely transparent from the Tibetan alone.

The phrase rendered "beeswax-leaf wrapping" translates a compound referring to leaves of the zha-nye plant used as a lid or cover for a begging bowl; identification of the exact plant is uncertain, but context clearly indicates it is a leaf-covering for a bowl.

"Mules" for rnga-mo: the term standardly denotes female mules or asses; "mules" is used for readability.  The verse summary is a mnemonic condensing a series of case-scenarios. "Undefeated, concealed by a companion" condenses two further case-types. The verse is intentionally telegraphic and its individual clauses only become fully clear in the prose that follows; this is standard for Vinaya summary verses.

The creature names in the list of many-legged creatures include two terms — rendered here as "beetles" and "crawling insects" — that correspond to partially transliterated Sanskrit or Prakrit terms in the Tibetan and whose precise zoological identity is uncertain. This is noted for scholarly completeness but does not affect the legal discussion.  The phrase rendered "Are you going to remove your sandals merely at the sound of water?" is a Tibetan idiomatic expression meaning something like "why are you hesitating over a trifle?" or "why flinch at the mere prospect?" — the idiom of removing sandals at the sound of water (i.e., preparing to ford a stream one has not yet reached) conveys premature, unnecessary caution.

The names Sudarśana and Dhanadata are reconstructed from the Tibetan Mtshen bzangs and Nor gyis byin respectively: Mtshen bzangs = "fine marks / good appearance" = Sudarśana; Nor gyis byin = "given by wealth" = Dhanadata.  The name rendered "Candragarbha" is given as Zla bas sbas in the Tibetan, which literally means "Hidden by the Moon" and corresponds more closely to Śaśigarbha or a similar Sanskrit name; the parallelism with Mi pham (Ajita) and the description of renown suggest these are stock character names. The rendering follows the literal Tibetan meaning.

The phrase "works for wages" renders gla rngans kyis las byed pa, a Vinaya technical term for a monk performing labor in exchange for material compensation — here contrasted with acting out of generosity or merit-seeking. The ruling that there is no offense when one takes an object believing it to be one's own reflects a standard Vinaya principle: criminal intention is required for a defeat-level offense involving theft.  The name rendered in the preceding passage as "Ajita" corresponds to the Tibetan "mi pham pa," literally "the Undefeated," which is a standard equivalent of Sanskrit Ajita. The passage plays on this name when Ajita declares he would not deserve to be called "Ajita" if he failed to steal the robes — a pun on the name's meaning as "unconquered" or "invincible." This wordplay is preserved in the translation by keeping the name Ajita.  The summary verse at the center of the passage is a condensed mnemonic listing the storyline topics of a cluster of Vinaya cases, in the traditional sūtra-vibhaṅga style. The name "Avasaṭha" is a proper name called out by the following nun to her companion; it appears to be an alternate name or epithet for the nun born in the east and is retained as-is since no Sanskrit normalization is certain.  The term "avasatha" appears to be a Prakrit or regional dialect term for a storehouse or storage place; the nun uses it as a technical term native to her home region, which is why the Blessed One rules she has committed no transgression — the ruling turns on the doctrine that regional or dialectal usage does not constitute a violation of the rule. The Sanskrit reconstruction would be āvasatha, meaning a lodging, storehouse, or receptacle.

The phrase rendered "a term specific to language, a term specific to region, and a term specific to locality" represents a standard Vinaya triad of contextual linguistic qualifications that determine whether a given act constitutes a formal transgression.

The office rendered "rector" for the Tibetan dge skos corresponds to the Sanskrit karma-kāraka or karmadāna, the monastic officer responsible for the proper conduct of the community's formal acts.  The phrase rendered "conquered all that is to be conquered" translates rnam par rgyal bar bya ba las rnam par rgyal ba, a standard Vinaya epithet for an arhat. The first occurrence names the category of attainment (what is to be conquered) and the second affirms its completion.

The term bskas / sbyar here rendered "sesame oil" is 'bru mar, literally "grain oil" or "seed oil," most commonly sesame in Indian context; the rendering is standard.

The phrase bgam par bya'o, rendered "I want to find out" or "I should test/find out," carries a sense of deliberate testing or exposing — the young woman suspects and wishes to ascertain whether his motives are impure. The word bkam can mean "to examine, test, expose"; this reading governs the episode's logic.  The phrase rendered "those of the last month of autumn" translates a name meaning roughly "those active in the final month of the autumnal season," apparently a specific gang of thieves identified by the time of year they were most active. The precise idiomatic force of this epithet in the original social context is uncertain, but the literal rendering is transparent enough for the listener.  The Tibetan "མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན" is a standard rendering of the Sanskrit Anāthapiṇḍada, the famous lay patron whose name means "feeder of the unprotected." The text uses it as a proper name throughout, so it is retained as Anāthapiṇḍada rather than translated.

The prince "འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ" literally means "nobly born" and here functions as the Tibetan rendering of Ajātaśatru, the crown prince later notorious as a parricide. The identification with Ajātaśatru is consistent with the narrative context of Śrāvastī and Kośala under Prasenajit.  The phrase rendered "the group of six monks" refers throughout to the notorious ṣaḍvargika monks, a stock group of ill-disciplined monks frequently appearing in Vinaya narratives. The names Nanda and Upananda are two of that group's members.

The term translated "Ārokya dwelling" appears to be a proper name for a specific residence in the monastery. The final sentence's list of procedural acts is a formulaic Vinaya inquiry about who may legitimately preside over or perform these monastic legal acts, and the translation renders the series as closely as the Tibetan syntax allows.  The phrase rendered "miscreants of the last month of autumn" translates a term for a particular class of criminals known by the season in which they were active. The epithet of King Bimbisāra rendered here as "one of handsome form, essence of the splendid" follows the Tibetan གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ, a standard Tibetan rendering of "Bimbisāra." The epithet applied to King Bimbisāra throughout this passage is "Bimbisāra of Magadha, the skilled craftsman of form" — a somewhat unusual royal designation. The phrase rendered "Seniya, son of the King of Magadha, a prince of fine appearance and handsome form" translates a Tibetan epithet that literally means "the king of Magadha of polished or refined form and excellent core" — this appears to be a proper name or compound epithet for the prince Seniya (Bimbisāra's son or a named prince). The exact identity and precise force of the Tibetan epithet "bzos byangs gzugs can snying po" (refined, well-formed, excellent one) is somewhat opaque; it may be a personal name or a descriptive epithet for the Magadhan prince. The names "lha-bong" and "tse-göd" are etymological folk-explanations embedded in the text for the Tibetan terms for "servant" and "groundskeeper" respectively. The phrase rendered "the Last Month of Autumn" for "ston zla tha chungs" refers to the final month of autumn in the Indian calendar; "gyon can" meaning "left-handed" gives the gang's name a sinister connotation, which the translation preserves. The figure "Ānanda" named in the final paragraph is identified by the Tibetan term "ཉེ་དགའ་" which is the standard Tibetan rendering of Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, though in this narrative context he appears to be serving as a temple attendant or sexton — a role consistent with Ānanda's portrayal in certain Vinaya narratives.  The phrase rendered "the wicked ones of the last autumn month" translates a Tibetan expression for a group apparently identified by the final month of autumn; the exact identity of this social group is context-dependent and may refer to seasonal laborers or a specific caste designation in the Sanskrit original, which is not preserved here.

The phrase "opening the matter of the five classes of transgressions" renders a technical Vinaya expression concerning the five categories of offences; the precise procedural sense is preserved from context.

The passage shifts between direct speech and narrative rapidly in the original; paragraph breaks have been introduced for clarity in spoken delivery without distorting the text.  The elder "Norchen" renders the Tibetan name meaning "possessor of wealth" — this is Pilindavatsa's interlocutor in the preceding narrative frame, presented here as the monk who first caused a blemish in the Saṅgha through an act of taking what was not given. The passage then transitions into a cosmogonic account that closely parallels the Aggañña Sutta of the Pāli canon, describing the dissolution and reformation of the world and the origin of craving from the tasting of earth-essence. The phrase rendered "taking what was not given" is the standard Vinaya formulation for the second pārājika offense. The term "film" renders the Tibetan word for the skin that forms on cooled liquid, here describing the primordial earth-crust.  The Tibetan term rendered "growth" for the second food that appears after the earth-essence disappears is ཞག, which in this cosmogonic context refers to a ground-growth or fungal-type substance that is the next stage of food in the world-formation narrative. Some editions gloss it as a kind of creeper or spreading growth. The translation "growth" is deliberately neutral to preserve the ambiguity.

The exclamation "Alas, the essence!" renders ཀྱེ་མའོ་བཅུད, where ཀྱེ་མའོ is a cry of lament or wistful longing and བཅུད means "essence" or "vital extract." The text itself then explains that later humans use this expression when finding delicious food, not knowing its original referent — a rare piece of folk etymology embedded in the sūtra.  The passage is part of a Buddhist cosmogonic narrative describing the gradual decline of primordial beings and the emergence of food, social distinctions, and sexual differentiation — a narrative well-known from the Pāli Aggañña Sutta and its Tibetan parallels. The phrase rendered "It is gone! It is gone!" (ཕར་སོང་ཕར་སོང་) is a lament of loss; the text explicitly explains it as an ancient idiom whose original meaning has been forgotten, just as "Alas! Alas!" (ཀྱེ་མའོ) was explained above. The sāli rice description — springing back when pressed — is a standard formulaic passage in this literature indicating miraculous, self-regenerating grain.  The phrase rendered "victorious sovereigns" translates rgyal ba dbang po, literally "victor-lords." In context this appears to be a reference to righteous kings, with the Victor-epithet here applied to royal sovereignty rather than to buddhas. The sentence is somewhat abrupt in the original and may be a gloss or interpolation within the cosmogonic narrative; its precise doctrinal import is uncertain.

The repeated exclamation "Vile creature! Doing what should not be done" renders sems can ngan pa grong pa bya ba ma yin pa byed pa, a formulaic cry of social censure. The term grong pa here may indicate "village-dweller" or may carry a sense of "civilized being," so the cry could also be read as "Wicked creature, doing what a village-dweller should not do." The rendering adopted preserves the sense of social impropriety without over-specifying.  The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text and the translation reflects this; the sentence about the sāli rice regrowing is clearly the beginning of a clause that continues in the following passage. The description of the grain as "four-fingered in size" renders སོར་བཞི་པ, literally "four finger-breadths," a standard ancient Indian grain measurement. The repeated lament is placed in direct speech as the grammar indicates the entire retrospective account is voiced by the assembled sentient beings. The phrase ས་ཞག (earth-film or earth-crust) follows the standard sequence in this cosmogonic narrative: earth-essence, then earth-film, then sprout-thickets.  The passage contains a recurring exclamatory particle rendered "Hey, creature!" which is a colloquial address used throughout this cosmogonic narrative in the Aggañña Sutta context. The phrase translated "the boundary of property" renders a technical term indicating the first establishment of fixed ownership and territorial demarcation, which in the Pāli parallel (Aggañña Sutta, DN 27) marks the origin of the institution of kingship. The phrase rendered as "honored by the many, honored by the many" reflects the etymological wordplay in the Pāli and Sanskrit traditions on the name Mahāsammata or its Tibetan equivalent, where the repeated formula explains the origin of the title through the act of being chosen and honored by the community. The phrase rendered as "one with a mouth" translates a term that literally means "having a beak or snout" and likely refers to a particular case or character in the Vinaya narrative to follow; the exact referent becomes clear only in context. The final lines of Rubbing's speech present a lament in a rhetorical, almost rhythmic style. The phrase rendered as "as close as the width of a silk cloth" and "as close as the thickness of a veil" translates two similes used to express how near and certain higher rebirth and liberation are for a person of good conduct — the Tibetan uses "dar gyis chod pa tsam" (cut off only by a silk cloth) and "yol bas bsgriba pa tsam" (obscured only by a curtain or veil). The passage "the good years are only as much as a silk curtain drawn across them, and liberation is only as much as a veil drawn over it" is a highly compressed, gnomic utterance by Śirikā justifying her desire for death. The imagery suggests that both favorable rebirth and liberation are fleeting or obscured, and life itself is therefore not worth continuing — this reflects a distorted view used to rationalize suicide, not a doctrinal statement endorsed by the text.  The passage shifts between two distinct Vinaya episodes, each following the same formulaic narrative structure. The name "གདོལ་པ" rendered here as "butcher" refers in the Vinaya context to one who slaughters animals — specifically a killer or slaughterman — and the simile is of aggressive, ruthless intent. "དུས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ" literally means "he became endowed with the dharma of time," a standard Vinaya idiom meaning he died; rendered accordingly as "he met with what is the nature of time."  The passage uses the third-person feminine pronoun strategy common in classical Tibetan narrative, where the wife speaks of herself in the third person as a rhetorical device of indirection and complaint. This is preserved in translation by shifting between first and third person as the Tibetan does, though it may sound unusual; it is an intentional stylistic feature of the original, not an error.  The phrase rendered "a deer is not cured by a deer" is a proverbial expression whose precise import is somewhat opaque; it appears to mean that one should not return to the same familiar haunt that caused one's trouble, advising the newly ordained monk to avoid his former household domain. The interpretation given here follows the contextual logic of the surrounding instruction.  The term rendered throughout as "child in the womb" (mngal na gnas pa) literally means "one dwelling in the womb," a standard Vinaya expression for a foetus. The phrase translated as "a wife's final break of estrangement" (bud med kyi khon tha chad) is somewhat compressed; it refers to a wife's definitive rupture or final declaration of grievance, used here as the kinsman's rationalisation that such an extreme estrangement will compel his elder brother to return. The repeated passage is a verbatim refrain in the Tibetan and has been translated consistently throughout.  The name rendered "Doṇakṛta" here corresponds to སྡེ་པ་དོན་ལེགས་པར་གྲུབ, a Tibetan calque meaning "the householder whose aim is well accomplished," i.e., Doṇakṛta or a similar Sanskrit name. The narrative refers to the elder as "Sena" (rendered in the preceding passage as the elder brother figure, Tibetan ཉེ་སྡེ), and to the young monk as "Kinsman" (Tibetan ཉེ་སྡེ for the younger figure). The phrase ཀཱར་ཥཱ་པ་ཎ་དག refers to kārṣāpaṇas, the standard coin of the period; rendered as "coins" for natural TTS flow.  The phrase rendered "like the appearance of a white mushroom" translates a simile for something of unknown origin — a fungus that simply appears without visible cause. The point is that Sena is a stranger with no traceable connections, making the crime seem safe.

"Neyade" renders the Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit name Neyade (Tibetan: ཉེ་སྡེ). In some canonical versions this figure is identified as a monk and arhat; the passage confirms he is an arhat by the remark about arhats not employing knowledge and vision without deliberate reflection.

The passage about the snake dying and being reborn repeatedly in successive locations is a karmic illustration: each rebirth in an ever-finer form and ever-closer proximity is the consequence of the dying Sena's wrong aspiration directed against the monk.  The passage contains a classical Buddhist catechism of no-self, running through the twelve sense bases (the six internal sense faculties and six external objects), the six elements (earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness), and the five aggregates, each stated in two forms: "X is the self" and "X belongs to the self." The Tibetan precisely mirrors the standard Pāli/Sanskrit formula found in Abhidharma-adjacent sūtra literature. The final verse set is incomplete in the submitted passage; the last verse breaks off mid-stanza and is rendered accordingly without fabrication of the missing lines.  The verses identifying specific nāgas and beings by name present difficulties. Names such as Āṅkura, Lābu, Gautama (here a nāga name, not the Buddha), and epithets like "the swiftest" and "son born with a crest" appear to be names or epithets of specific snake or nāga beings in a traditional snake-protection list. Their exact identities are not always recoverable from the Tibetan alone, and the Sanskrit Vorlage would clarify them further. The rendering follows the literal Tibetan as faithfully as possible.

The phrase rendered "sentient beings that dwell in the throat" is unusual and may refer to serpents or creatures that inhabit hollow spaces or dens; the Tibetan literally says beings dwelling in the gullet or throat region, which may point to a specific class of creatures in the original context of the snake-protection charm.

The mantra syllables are transliterated as they appear and are not translated, as is standard for dhāraṇī material.  The phrase rendered "solitary buddhas of inferior rank" translates a compound distinguishing lesser pratyekabuddhas from the highest type; the qualifier "inferior" or "of lower standing" reflects the Tibetan modifier meaning something like "lesser" or "mediocre" in the hierarchy of pratyekabuddhas.

The phrase "like a serpent king coiled at rest" translates a Tibetan expression for the posture of a great nāga lying in repose, used as a simile for a dignified seated meditation posture.  The phrase rendered "a bodily reliquary stupa" translates the Tibetan term for a stupa built to house the physical remains of a holy being. The phrase "field of merit" renders the Tibetan "yon gnas yang dag par gyur pa," literally "one who has become a true basis for offerings," a standard epithet for a being whose spiritual attainment makes offerings to them especially meritorious. The closing identification of the hunter as "this very intimate disciple" refers to a specific member of the Buddha's assembly whose identity would have been made clear in the surrounding narrative context.  The phrase rendered "my lord's son" in the wife's speech is a respectful form of address directed toward the merchant himself, using an oblique honorific construction common in classical Tibetan narrative prose. The wife is deflecting blame by framing her mistreatment as discipline befitting the heir of the household.  The list of precious substances near the end presents some interpretive challenges. The rendering follows the most standard identifications: "gold" for sa le sbram (though this term can vary by context), "the essence of the earth" for rdo'i snying po (lit. "essence of stone," sometimes rendered as coral-essence or mineral essence), and "burnished metal" for spug. The "swastika" renders g.yas su 'khyil pa, literally "that which spirals to the right," a classical auspicious symbol in Buddhist iconography.  The phrase rendered "invited for midday" translates an idiom about the midday meal offering; the word for "midday" here is literally "umbrella-shadow time," a classical Indic expression for noon. This is transparent enough not to warrant glossing in the body text but is noted here for completeness.  The two similes "as close as a silk curtain" and "as near as a veil that merely covers it" render idioms describing the proximity of fortunate rebirth and liberation respectively. The Tibetan phrases use dar (silk cloth) and yol ba (a screen or curtain) as metaphors of something just barely separating the practitioner from the goal. The precise nuance is that only the thinnest barrier remains — the images are vivid but somewhat idiomatic, and different commentators read them slightly differently.

The name Skyong-ma is a Tibetan servant-name left in transliteration here since it functions as a proper name throughout the narrative; it means roughly "the guardian" or "the caretaker."

The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source, as the instruction sequence is interrupted — this is not a translation omission but reflects the text as given.  The phrase rendered "the higher realms will be fully covered with silk; liberation will be fully covered with a curtain" is highly idiomatic and its exact sense is obscure. The Tibetan literally reads that the higher realms are "cut off as if by silk" and liberation is "covered as if by a curtain," suggesting these goods are near yet veiled or just out of reach. The wife's speech appears to be a garbled or deliberately cryptic paraphrase of the monk's Dharma teaching, filtered through her grief and incomprehension, which is part of the narrative's irony.

The final sentence, "This, moreover, occurred before the time: the Blessed Buddha does not, in the Vinaya, lay down a rule of training for the hearers," is a standard Vinaya formula indicating that this incident is a precedent case preceding the formal promulgation of a rule, and the rule itself will follow in the next passage.  The river name སྤོང་བྱེད is the standard Tibetan rendering of the Varaṇā river (Skt. Varaṇā), distinct from Vārāṇasī; in some Vinaya recensions this passage is set at the Vaggumudā or a similar stream, but the Tibetan here reads Varaṇā and is rendered accordingly.

Migalandika (Tibetan: རི་དགས་ཟློག་དགེ་སྦྱོང་སྦེད) is a well-known figure from the Pārājika section of the Vinaya in connection with the rule on killing; the name is kept as a proper name throughout.

The phrase rendered "breathing out where they have not yet breathed out" is the literal Tibetan idiom for bringing relief or ease to those not yet at ease, a conventional expression in Vinaya narrative for conferring benefit; it does not refer to a physiological act.  The phrase rendered "without breaking its flow" for the river translates a somewhat unusual descriptive. It may indicate the god came to the very bank or crossed without disturbing the current — the sense is that the god appeared at the riverside. This is a minor ambiguity and does not affect the narrative meaning.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, cutting off as Migalandika moves from dwelling to dwelling; the translation preserves this open ending consistent with the passage being a continuous excerpt.  The epithet Migalandika appears in the preceding passage and is carried forward here consistently. The phrase rendered "breathe out" follows the Vinaya's idiomatic usage for relief from the burden of existence, preserved from the preceding context. The fourfold classification of monks at the close is a standard Vinaya analytical category; the fourth type, "the monk by reason of having subdued the afflictions," refers to the arhat who is genuinely a monk by virtue of having destroyed the mental afflictions.  The term rendered as "water-blade" for ཆུ་གྲི is uncertain. It may refer to a razor or a specific blade used with water; some Vinaya parallels suggest a razor. The translation preserves the literal reading.

The phrase rendered "one who has obtained, within the mother's womb, these six faculties" describes the defining criteria for "human being" in the Vinaya analysis: possession of the six sense faculties from conception is the standard Vinaya criterion for human status, relevant to determining the gravity of killing.

The phrase "fourfold formal procedure with a motion" renders the technical Vinaya term for the standard ordination act: a motion followed by three proclamations, which is the normative form of full ordination.  The phrase rendered "as close as the span of a silk cloth" and "obscured only by a veil" are Tibetan idiomatic expressions indicating, respectively, how near a heavenly rebirth is and how close liberation is — meaning they are virtually within reach. The imagery is of a thin silk cloth barely separating one from a high realm, and a fine veil barely concealing liberation. These are stock rhetorical flourishes used in this Vinaya passage to entice the listener with proximity to good rebirths and liberation.  The phrase rendered "extending a helping hand" translates a compound meaning literally something like "casting out the arm" or "extending the arm in giving," which is an idiomatic expression for the practice of generosity in action. The rendering follows the contextual sense within the list of virtuous qualities being praised. The list of the sick person's missing requisites — bowl, robe, net, cup, belt — follows standard Vinaya enumeration of a monastic's allowable possessions; "net" here likely refers to a straining cloth used to filter water, a standard item in monastic equipment.  The technical list at the close of the passage describing what constitutes full ordination reflects the standard Vinaya legal formulary for defining the validity of the ordination act. The terms "initial examination" and "thorough examination" render a pair of procedural steps in the ordination ceremony; the Tibetan here uses terms equivalent to the Sanskrit vicāra and paricāra or similar procedural vocabulary, and the precise Sanskrit equivalents vary by recension.

The phrase rendered "a confused tangle of thoughts and hasty conclusions" translates two terms denoting mental agitation or vacillation and impulsive, unreflective speech; the exact nuance is somewhat difficult to render, but the sense is clearly one of foolish, unexamined utterance, which is the doctrinal point.  The catalogue of weapons toward the end of the passage contains several technical terms for bladed or projectile instruments. The identifications of some items such as the saw-tooth type, the karavīra-leaf-shaped blade, and the bird's-beak blade are reconstructed from context and parallel Vinaya literature; their precise shapes cannot be determined with certainty from the text alone.

The term "ma ning" rendered throughout as "person of indeterminate sex" refers to a pandaka or person of a third gender category recognized in Vinaya literature; this rendering follows standard scholarly convention.  The term rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates ma ning, a Vinaya category for individuals who are neither fully male nor female; the Sanskrit equivalent is paṇḍaka in some contexts, though ma ning more precisely renders napuṃsaka or a related term. The precise referent varies across Vinaya traditions.

The phrase "inserts a stake up to its cross-piece" renders the Tibetan for driving a restraining peg or stake into the ground to fix the binding — a detail of the method of earth-binding being described. The exact implement is somewhat uncertain, but the sense is that the person is staked to the ground and left exposed.  The term rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates the Tibetan term for a third-gender category recognized in Vinaya literature, referring to those who are neither male nor female in the conventional sense, sometimes rendered "hermaphrodite" or "neuter person" in older translations. The rendering here follows standard modern Vinaya scholarship.

The phrase "ransom-seekers" renders a term for those who hold persons for ransom or extort release payments; the precise Vinaya sense is of persons who detain and demand payment for release. Some editions read this differently; the meaning is in any case a category of criminal or dangerous agent through whose action the death might be brought about.

The passage ends mid-enumeration, continuing into the next section.  The passage describes an elaborate ritual for animating a zombie-like corpse (ro langs, Skt. vetāla) as a murder weapon, a topic treated in the Vinaya as a case study for the pārājika rule on killing. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the passage's end; it is part of a longer list of protective countermeasures that would prevent the zombie from killing its intended victim.

The phrase rendered "a scattering of mustard seed set out" translates mchig mchig gu dang bcas pa bzhag pa; the term mchig mchig gu most likely refers to mustard seeds or similar small grains used as a protective scatter, though the exact identification is mildly uncertain. The rendering "black wood" for nags kyi phreng ba (literally "forest-garland" or "garland of wood from the forest") may refer to a specific protective material; some commentators understand it as a garland made from the wood of a specific tree associated with cemetery rituals.

The verse summary at the center names the sub-cases of the killing pārājika covered in the surrounding prose sections: the zombie (ro langs), the half-zombie (ro langs phyed), pressing the side or flanks (dku mnyad pa), cutting off life, a precipice, water, fire, an emissary, and cold and heat.  The list of "great sūtras" presents notable difficulties. The Tibetan titles given are formulaic names appearing in Vinaya literature for specific protective sūtras. "The Lesser Emptiness" and "the Greater Emptiness" correspond to the shorter and longer Śūnyatā-sūtras. "The Fifty-Three" refers to a sūtra known by its enumeration. "The Net of Illusion" is likely the Māyājāla. "Reception by the Embodied Essence" renders a title whose Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain. "The All-Pervading" and "the Non-Pervading" are standard paired titles in this context. The identifications of the remaining titles are conventional within the Vinaya commentarial tradition, but their precise Sanskrit equivalents are not always recoverable with certainty.

The term rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates the Tibetan for a person who is neither clearly male nor female, corresponding to the Sanskrit category of a paṇḍaka or a related category in Vinaya classification; in context here it covers the full range of persons other than men and women.  The passage on the "seven lines" drawn on the ground and the mantra recitation are part of a series of ritual-homicide scenarios involving sympathetic magic: mixing grains, transforming liquid to blood, sewing a patch, drawing lines. These are standard Vinaya casuistry enumerating progressively more indirect means of killing, and the legal outcomes follow the same two-tier pattern throughout: grave offence if the intended victim survives, defeat if death results.

The term rendered "met their end" for དུས་བྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ (literally "came to make the time / met their time") is a Tibetan idiom for dying; the rendering captures the sense without disrupting the legal formula.  The passage describing cold-weather exposure is syntactically dense. The phrase rendered as "the eighth-day intervals of those months when piercing winds arise that let no light through" refers to specific calendrical cold periods in the Indian reckoning, identified by the arising of sharp, light-obscuring winds. The translation follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan enumeration of conditions.

The term rendered "bundle of grass" (སོག་མ) can also refer to a handful or sheaf of dry grass or straw used as a crude instrument of torment in freezing conditions — the doctrinal point being that even so minor an act of aggravation, combined with lethal intent and exposure, triggers the full rule.  The term kārṣāpaṇa (rendered phonetically from the Tibetan transliteration) is a standard Indian copper or silver coin unit; no gloss is strictly required but context makes it clear it is currency.

The phrase rendered "person of indeterminate sex" translates the Tibetan term for a third-sex or intersex individual (Skt. paṇḍaka or napuṃsaka), consistent with Vinaya usage.

The summary verse is a mnemonic verse (uddāna) cataloguing the preceding case-types; some category names are terse technical labels whose full referents are spelled out in the surrounding Vinaya prose.  The term rendered "empty alms-bowl day" translates a phrase meaning literally "making the alms-bowl empty," which functions here as a technical term for a special day of work offered by monks in lieu of receiving alms — essentially a day when the monks labor for a lay donor and forgo alms-rounds. The precise nature of this institution is somewhat obscure; the translation follows the contextual sense throughout this passage.

The word rendered "pot-scraping tools" or "pot-scraper" refers to a scraping or scouring implement used in cleaning vessels; the exact implement is uncertain, but the narrative context makes the sense clear.  The Tibetan "གཏུམ་མོ" in this narrative context means a fierce or wild woman, not the tantric practice of inner heat; the rendering "wild woman" reflects the narrative sense. The name "འཆར་ཀ" is rendered as Śārika, a well-known monk disciple, though the spelling is an unusual Tibetan transcription. The phrase "གཞི་མ་ཟིན་པ་ལ་མཁར་ལེན་གྱི་སྟོངས་མོ་བྱའོ" is somewhat compressed and could mean either carrying the empty frame or scaffolding before the ground is prepared; the translation follows the most contextually plausible reading.  The list of eighteen benefits of travelling as a buddha appears to contain only fifteen items as enumerated in the text. The final term rendered "crocodiles" is a tentative identification of a water-creature; the Tibetan term could refer to a type of aquatic animal more broadly. The closing passage shifts abruptly to a new narrative setting, which is a standard transitional formula in Vinaya literature indicating the opening of a new episode; the two figures mentioned as "a pair joined in close mutual affection" appear to be introduced but not yet named in the extant passage.  The Tibetan "དུས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་ནས" is a standard Vinaya euphemism for death, literally "came to have the quality belonging to his time," meaning he died. This has been rendered accordingly.

The king of Magadha named "བཟོ་སྦྱངས་གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ" literally means something like "Essence of Well-Trained Form," a Tibetan rendering of Bimbisāra. The identification with Bimbisāra is the standard traditional reading and has been used in the translation.

The name Āryajanman renders the Tibetan honorific epithet meaning "noble-born one" and is used here as a proper name or title for the military officer throughout.  The repeated phrase rendered "died at the right time" translates the idiom of "falling to their time" — that is, dying at the moment determined by their karma. The satirical logic of Skyongma's reasoning is that by dying in this way the robbers would be reborn as infants and thus drink their mothers' milk, which she has apparently taken as a positive rebirth. The nuns' exclamation at the end is a formulaic rebuke, calling her one whose karmic share has run out — meaning a person of thoroughly exhausted merit who will fill her belly at the expense of others' misfortune. The name Skyongma is retained as a proper name; its literal meaning is "Protectress," which is ironic in context.  The phrase rendered "born near Sārpaskṛta" reflects the Tibetan "sar pa skyes," a place name that is uncertain in its Sanskrit reconstruction; some witnesses read Sārpaskhṛta or similar. The rendering "died at the right time" throughout follows the Vinaya idiom for natural or timely death, not violent killing. The term rendered "disciplinarian" translates dge skos, the monk charged with ringing the gong and managing communal duties. The phrase "making noise" for ṭron byas renders a Vinaya term for a collective tumult or commotion, here suggesting boisterous group behavior. The tickling episode and its fatal outcome are standard Vinaya narrative elements establishing the involuntary nature of the resulting death, which is the doctrinal point of the passage.  The compound rendered as "a defeat downfall" translates ཕམ་པར་གྱུར་པའི་ལྟུང་བ, which literally means "a downfall that has become a defeat" — that is, a pārājika, the most serious class of Vinaya transgression entailing expulsion from the Saṅgha. The contextual implication is that the monk who died was their companion bound by the same brahmacarya community, and his loss is described in terms of a Vinaya defeat because the tickling incident led to his death and thus to the irrecoverable dissolution of their group's integrity. The doctrinal and Vinaya framing here is slightly compressed and ambiguous in the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "acts without interval" refers to the ānantarya-karman (Skt. ānantarya), the five heinous acts that lead without interval to hell rebirth, of which killing one's father is one. The passage turns on the ruling that no intention to kill was present, hence no actual downfall.

The six teachers named here, with Pūraṇa at their head, are the six heterodox teachers (tīrthika teachers) frequently mentioned in Buddhist canonical literature as contemporaries of the Buddha residing at Vaiśālī; the Tibetan reads "Pūraṇa and so forth, the six teachers," taking Pūraṇa (rdzogs byed, "Pūraṇa Kāśyapa") as the first of the standard list. The list of hell realms names the standard eight hot hells and eight cold hells of Abhidharma cosmology. The cold hells are named after the sounds of suffering and the physical effects of extreme cold — including the utpala and lotus "split" hells — all standard Abhidharma enumerations. The Tibetan term rendered "sea-monster" throughout is chu srin, the makara (a mythological aquatic creature); "fish-species of the sea-monster" renders chu srin nya'i rigs, indicating a class of beings associated with that creature. The list of divine heavens follows the standard Abhidharma cosmology of the desire realm and form realm. The sequence moves through the six desire-realm god realms and then through the form-realm Brahmā heavens, concluding with Akaniṣṭha at the summit of the form realm.

The phrase rendered "king of power" for the first wheel-turning king and simply "wheel-turning king" for the second reflects a distinction in the Tibetan between a chakravartin of great power and a standard chakravartin, though the precise doctrinal distinction between the two categories here may vary by commentarial tradition.

The brahmin student lineage names — Kutsā, Bātsā, Śāṇḍilya, Bhāradvāja — are standard Vedic gotra names. The fifth and fifth-adjacent lineages likely refer to other well-known brahminical gotras. The phrase rendered "struck with earthen pots shattered over their heads" follows the Tibetan literally: opponents are defeated by having ash-filled or dust-filled pots broken over them, a classical Indian debating-contest humiliation ritual. The image of the catapult fulcrum and the crow is a simile for keeping a great distance from a powerful adversary. The proper name "Śerśkya Śiwa" renders the Tibetan "སེར་སྐྱ་ཞི་བ," a compound meaning roughly "Yellow-robe Tranquil." The phrase translated as "consistent with what belongs to others that is contrary to their part" renders the technical Vinaya formula for a false accusation of defeat, in which the accuser frames someone as belonging to the category of those who have incurred a pārājika defeat, when in fact they belong to the opposite category, that of nirvāṇa. This is a standard Vinaya technical expression and the rendering, though necessarily awkward, follows the traditional commentarial interpretation: "what belongs to others" refers to nirvāṇa as the proper domain of an arhat, while the four defeat offenses are "contrary to that part."

The distinction between the two grades of offense is technically significant. When the diversion is to any other party — another individual or the Saṅgha — it yields only a "wrong act" (Skt. duṣkṛta) in both the attempt and the receipt, a lesser grade of offense. Cūḍapanthaka (འཆར་ཀ) is a tentative identification. The opening passage about going to the "one who can thread a needle" is an idiomatic expression in this Vinaya context referring to a monk with practical skill suitable for overseeing construction work; the literal phrasing has been preserved.  The phrase rendered "what began as first will become last for me" reflects the idiom that the wooden vessel analogy suggests: just as food cooked in a wooden pot destroys the vessel, accepting the superior offering would mean discarding what was received first in the alms-round, violating the training rule about not seeking superior food after already receiving alms. The simile is compressed in the Tibetan and the doctrinal point concerns the precept against seeking to exchange inferior alms already received for superior fare.  The epithet "Dundubhissara" is a monk's name consistent with the broader narrative context; the Tibetan renders it phonetically. The "black-bowled ones" refers to a group of wayward monks identifiable in the Vinaya context by their distinctive black bowls, associated with the Group of Six monks who cause disruptions. The "seven bases of merit-making arising from material things" is a standard Vinaya list of meritorious material endowments to the Saṅgha. "Mahāmaudgalyāyana" renders the Tibetan "skul byed chen po," literally "the great instigator," which is a known Tibetan epithet for Mahāmaudgalyāyana; "Ghositārāma" renders "gdangs can gyi kun dga' ra ba," a name of a monastery associated with Vaiśālī, here treated as a proper name in the narrative.  The phrase rendered as "not to accumulate virtue and to confess wrongdoing" is a formulaic Vinaya expression; the more precise sense is that the Buddha had taught the monks not to store up merit through inaction while transgressions remain unconfessed, but the Tibetan here reads idiomatically as a paired injunction and is rendered accordingly.

The instruction about spending the first watch in the temple makes best sense in context as the Buddha deploying the spiritual power of monks in meditative absorption to structurally stabilize the badly built temple overnight, a standard Vinaya narrative device.  The phrase rendered "as flat as if a she-fox had been rolling in it" translates a Tibetan idiom for utter ruination or flattening to the ground. The elder among the Group of Six who speaks this line bears a grudge and is taunting the brahmin rather than consoling him, which explains the cruel phrasing.

The expression "worldly intention" versus "supramundane intention" reflects a doctrinal distinction in the text between the Buddha deliberately lowering his awareness to an accessible level so that even animals can read his mind, versus operating at the level of transcendent gnosis, which exceeds the cognitive reach of even pratyekabuddhas.  The passage "སྒོའི་སྦུབས་དང་། གཏན་པ་དང་སྣང་བའི་གནས་ཇི་ཙམ་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ས་བརྟག་པ་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ་ཕ་གུའི་རིམ་པ་འཇིམ་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་གཉིས་སམ། གསུམ་བརྩིག་པར་བྱའོ" is the Vinaya regulation on building height and is technically dense. The rendered passage reflects the standard commentarial interpretation: the monk must survey the site with awareness of the space needed for the door-frame, foundations, and window-openings, and then build only two or three courses of brickwork including plaster. This corresponds to the pārājika-adjacent rule in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya regarding large buildings, parallel to the Pāli Saṅghādisesa rule on construction. The precise architectural terminology is slightly uncertain but the doctrinal point — the numerical limit on construction — is clear.  The summary verses at the end are mnemonic indexes listing the titles or key terms of the preceding rule-sections and sūtras; they are not meant to be read as continuous prose. The rendering follows the standard Vinaya convention of keeping such colophon-like verses as verse. The phrase rendered "the old myna bird" translates a Tibetan term for a bird of the starling or myna family; the identification is not perfectly certain but is the most consistent rendering given the context of the bird fable. The phrase "presiding officer of the assembly" renders a term literally meaning "one appointed to the head of the hand," a Vinaya idiom for a designated leader or chair of a monastic assembly.  The list of nuns' names in the opening passage presents several difficulties. The Tibetan renders Indian names phonetically and some are partially obscured. Kulamātā, Nandā, Madavā, Paṭhācārā, Sukhā, Candā, and Utpalavaṇṇā are recognizable from parallel Pāli and Sanskrit Vinaya sources. "Droganāsa" (འབྲོག་གནས) is uncertain; the Tibetan may be a phonetic rendering of an Indian name not clearly recoverable here. "Gautamī Śyāmā" renders གཽ་ཏ་མཱི་སྐེམ་མོ, where སྐེམ་མོ likely means "thin" or "dark," possibly corresponding to Kṛṣṇā or Śyāmā. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, and the translation preserves that open ending.  The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the supplied Tibetan. The translation follows the text precisely to its end without completion.

The phrase rendered "settle into inner stillness" translates ནང་དུ་ཡང་དག་འཇོག, literally "to place correctly inward," a standard idiom for post-meal meditative rest or composed sitting in solitude.

"The cool of the morning" renders ཕྱེ་མ་རེད, which more precisely denotes the early cool period before full day; some editions read this as a specific time marker but the general sense is clear.  The phrase rendered "this is my self" (bdag gi bdag) is a doubled genitive construction literally meaning "self of my self," reflecting the Pāli attā in its role as both possessive and substantive. The three-part formula "this is mine / this I am / this is my self" corresponds exactly to the Pāli etaṃ mama / eso'ham asmi / eso me attā, a standard formula for the three modes of self-grasping in Nikāya literature.  The passage repeats a structural error in the third "Excellent" section, where Ānanda's summary says "these six groups of contact are to be seen as without self" when the context has just shifted to feeling and then craving. The Tibetan itself carries this apparent inconsistency, likely a scribal repetition of the contact formula; it has been rendered faithfully as it stands rather than corrected. The term སྲེད་པ is rendered throughout as "craving," corresponding to Sanskrit tṛṣṇā, the eighth link of dependent origination.  The passage uses a stock formula for the arising and passing of phenomena — "when those phenomena arise, such phenomena come to arise; when they cease, such phenomena come to cease, subside, cool, and pass away" — which is a variant of the standard dependent origination arising-and-cessation formula adapted here to describe impermanence rather than causal sequence. The rendering follows the Tibetan closely rather than importing the canonical Pali wording.  The "six outer sense sources" refers to the six external sense objects or, more precisely, the six outer āyatanas — the visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental objects that serve as the outer bases of sensory experience. The distinction between "outer" and "inner" sense sources is standard Abhidharma usage.

The simile of the butcher and the cow's hide is a well-known canonical image, paralleled in Pāli sources. The point of the image is that just as the cow's flesh has been wholly severed from the hide even though it is wrapped back in it, so too the mind of one who has seen through impermanence is inwardly severed from clinging even while remaining within a body — the passage breaks off here and continues in the next section.  The term rendered "Progenitrix" for སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ is literally "great mistress of beings" or "great mother of beings," a standard Pali epithet for Mahāpajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's maternal aunt and the first ordained nun. "Great Progenitrix" conveys her role as mother-figure and founder of the nuns' order without being overly literal. The preceding section's phrase "Venerable Ānanda" refers to the monk Ānanda, whose name appeared in the passage given as context.  The phrase rendered "conditioning factors by which they would come again to this world" translates kun du sbyor ba, which corresponds to Sanskrit saṃyojana, the "fetters" or "bonds" that bind beings to further rebirth. The doctrinal point is that Ānanda's teaching has reduced their fetters to the point where, had they died then, none of the remaining fetters capable of producing rebirth in this world would have persisted — hence the prophecy of non-return. The moon simile on the fourteenth day is a classical image for near-but-not-quite-complete attainment.  The phrase rendered "great Progenitress Gautamī" translates skye dgu'i bdag mo chen mo Gautamī, literally "great sovereign lady of beings, Gautamī." This refers to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, and the first woman to receive full ordination. The epithet skye dgu'i bdag mo ("sovereign of beings") is a honorific specific to her in this tradition.

The simile of the full-moon night is textually unusual: the Tibetan says "the fifteenth day of the waxing moon" as the occasion when people do not distinguish whether the moon is still waxing or already full, because it has clearly reached its culmination (mthar thug pa). The doctrinal point being made is that the nuns' attainment is equally complete and unambiguous. The connection to Ānanda's possible death and the phrase "culmination of suffering" (sdug bsngal gyi mthar gyur pa) is somewhat elliptical; the sense appears to be that if Ānanda were to die now it would represent the acme of tragedy — but the simile reframes it as a completion, not a loss.

The "group of six monks" (dge slong drug sde) is a standard Vinaya expression referring to a well-known group of disreputable monks who frequently serve as the occasion for the Buddha establishing new rules. Their behavior here — described as overly familiar, playful, noisy, and physically inappropriate with the nuns — is the narrative prompt for a new Vinaya ruling.  The phrase rendered "sent the remaining monks off on errands" translates "lhag ma rnams brel bar byas," literally "made the remainder busy/occupied." This is a standard canonical evasion tactic: dispersing the quorum so that a proper formal act cannot be performed. The rendering captures the procedural intent.

The passage moves from narrative into verbatim Vinaya procedural language for a formal Saṅgha act (karmavācanā), with its standard motion-and-proclamation structure. The translation preserves the formulaic repetition characteristic of Vinaya legal texts, as this repetition is doctrinally and legally significant, not stylistic redundancy.

The closing series of four "impossibility" statements has a strong parallel in Pāli canonical literature (cf. Dhammapada verses on self-discipline as prerequisite for teaching others); the passage appears to be setting up a verse or further declaration that follows in the next section.  The phrase rendered "language of the city" reflects an unusual qualification for an instructor of nuns. The text glosses "city" as the palace and its surroundings, which likely refers to formal or refined court speech as opposed to rustic dialect. This is a technical Vinaya qualification whose precise import is debated in the commentarial tradition.

The closing scene shifts abruptly into a new narrative episode (a brahmin story), which is the standard Vinaya storytelling mechanism for introducing the next rule. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation ends there accordingly.  The phrase rendered "Dharma-endowed heartfelt wishes" for the Blessed One's blessing differs slightly from the earlier occurrences where the tīrthikas and monks simply say "heartfelt wishes of both parents." The Tibetan adds "chos dang ldan pa'i" — "endowed with Dharma" — to the Blessed One's version alone, a meaningful distinction preserved in the translation. The name Mahāpanthaka (Tibetan: lam chen pa) is a well-known figure in the Buddhist tradition, and the etymology given here, "great road," matches the standard Sanskrit derivation from mahā (great) and pantha (road/path).  The passage contains two Sanskrit syllabic pairs — "sid / dhāṃ" and "oṃ / bhū" — that appear to be fragments of Vedic or brahminic recitation used to illustrate Cūḷapanthaka's inability to retain even the simplest formulas. The Tibetan transliterates these syllables directly; I have retained them as they appear. The second pair "oṃ bhū" is recognizable as the opening of the Gāyatrī mantra (oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ), lending doctrinal plausibility to the sequence.

The girl's laziness causes her to sit on a side path rather than at the great crossroads as instructed, which is the textual mechanism by which the second child receives the name Cūḷapanthaka (Little Road / Side Path) in contrast to Mahāpanthaka (Great Road), established in the preceding passage.  The passage contains the phrase rendered "whatever is born a brahmin is by that very birth a god" — this reflects a standard brahminical self-conception preserved in Buddhist narrative literature, presenting the brahmin's internal reasoning rather than the author's endorsement.

The term translated "secret brahmin recitations" renders a compound meaning the esoteric or confidential syllables/formulas of brahmin learning; the Vedic context makes "secret brahmin recitations" the most natural rendering.  The phrase "the fivefold wheel of cyclic existence, moving and unmoving" is a somewhat unusual formulation. The "five" likely refers to the five aggregates or the five-spoked wheel of existence; the "moving and unmoving" aspects may refer to conditioned and unconditioned, or to animated and inert aspects of saṃsāric existence. The exact doctrinal referent is not entirely transparent from the text alone.

The final lines of the passage break off mid-sentence; the translation renders up to the point where the text ends, as supplied.  The name "Mahāpatha" (Tibetan lam chen pa, literally "great path") functions both as a proper name and as a significant epithet throughout this passage, paired with "lesser path" (lam chung ba) for the unnamed traveler. These are kept as rendered proper names consistent with the preceding translation.

The verse translated as four lines preserves the structure of the original gāthā. The line "do not approach whatever suffering brings harm" renders gnad ldan sdu bsngal (literally "suffering that has a vital point" or "injurious suffering"), which the commentarial tradition glosses as harmful or injurious pain — rendered here in a way that flows naturally for a listener.  The phrase rendered "utterly wretched — the most wretched of the wretched, the most petty of the petty" translates a sequence of superlative diminutives that is idiomatic in Vinaya narrative, indicating someone of zero standing in terms of learning and attainment. The Tibetan "bul ba / mchog tu bul ba / chung ba mchog tu chung ba" is a rhetorical intensification; the rendering preserves the contemptuous register without overly literalizing the gradations.

The verse at the close is Mahāpanthaka's reassurance to Panthaka: being criticized by the wise is more valuable than being flattered by fools — an implicit endorsement of the expulsion as a form of compassionate pedagogy. The passage breaks off mid-declaration, so the Blessed One's further words are not yet given.  The passage ends mid-sentence with "With joy, with effort, and with" — this reflects the raw cut of the supplied Tibetan, which breaks off at that point. The translation has been carried to the exact end of the source text.

The two-word formula "Dispel the dust! Remove the stain!" renders "rajas" and "mala" respectively, a famous pair from the Vinaya account of Panthaka (also found in Pāli as "rajoharaṇaṃ" and "malaharaṇaṃ"). The doctrinal point is that the Blessed One chose these words deliberately to trigger Panthaka's meditation on the inner meaning.  The passage contains a series of named individuals — Lāmpa (lesser and greater), Lāmachenpa, and Tsojezhönnu — that appear to be Tibetan phonetic renderings of Indian names. "Lāmpa" likely renders a Sanskrit name such as Nanda or similar (the "lesser Nanda" ordination narrative is well attested), but without the Sanskrit source confirmed, the Tibetan phonetics have been preserved consistently as proper names. The phrase "lesser Lāmpa" and "greater Lāmpa" reflect the Tibetan lam pa chung ba and lam chen pa, which in context function as personal names or epithets distinguishing two individuals, not as adjectives meaning "lesser path."

The five-part wheel of saṃsāra (saṃsāra's wheel in its five parts, moving and unmoving) is an unusual formulation; the text reads as a technical reference that would require fuller commentary context to resolve with certainty.  The phrase rendered "that despised woman's territory" translates a somewhat elliptical Tibetan expression involving a woman of low standing whose territory or domain Lāmpa failed to master even a single verse about in three months. The exact referent is slightly obscure in context; it appears to be a derogatory comparison the nuns use to diminish Lāmpa's learning. The remark about "the ninety-six wonders" likely refers to the ninety-six non-Buddhist teachers or their followers, a standard enumeration in Buddhist literature, though the syntax of that sentence is terse and the connection to "overpowering a woman's domain" is not entirely clear. The phrase "child of the womb-eater" is a Tibetan idiom of abuse or displeasure, rendered literally here. The passage ends mid-sentence in the supplied text, as it breaks off at the crossroads and junctions.  The phrase rendered "wandering monk who follows behind" translates a figure who appears to be a male wandering ascetic acting as a secondary or attendant figure to the nuns' teacher; the Tibetan suggests a contemptuous contrast between a full established teacher and a mere attendant-follower ascetic. The crowd's disparagement — that Lampā could barely master one verse in three months — is a narrative device underscoring the miracle that follows, a standard hagiographic pattern in Vinaya-related narratives of the great śrāvikās.  The phrase rendered "inspired with confident faith" translates a term meaning to cause persons to become faithfully devoted or to instill conviction — here used in a slightly ironic or cautious framing by the monks, who hedge by saying "if she has not failed to do so." The passage has a mild rhetorical texture that the translation attempts to preserve.

The reference to the wheel of Dharma turned "in twelve aspects" alludes to the three turnings of each of the Four Noble Truths — recognition, duty, and accomplishment — yielding twelve aspects total. This is the standard first turning at Vārāṇasī.  The phrase "མཚམས་ཀྱི་ཕྱི་རོལ་དུ་བསྐོས་ཤིང་མཚམས་ཀྱི་ནང་དུ་མ་བསྐོས་" refers to the Vinaya technical distinction of appointment valid within the sīmā (boundary) versus outside it. The sīmā is the formally delimited boundary within which monastic acts such as the poṣadha and formal appointments are canonically valid. The translation renders this as "within the boundary" and "outside the boundary" accordingly.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text provided; the translation likewise ends at that point without completing the clause.  The term rendered "like a senior elder acting as a deputy" translates a compound meaning a monk of standing sufficient to serve as a substitute or representative for an elder of seniority, a specific procedural qualification in the Vinaya for the appointment of a preceptor-instructor for nuns. The "eight rules entailing defeat" are the eight pārājika offenses of the nuns' code, and the "eight weighty rules" are the eight gurudharmas incumbent upon nuns. The phrase rendered "expelled by a nun through physical contact" refers to a nun having formally censured or rejected the monk on grounds of an improper physical touch, a procedural disqualification that can be remedied if the transgression is properly confessed and reversed before the Saṅgha.  The venerable Lampā referred to here is a monk who appears in the surrounding narrative context as the figure whom the twelve groups of nuns attempted to harm but inadvertently benefited. The passage moves between Vinaya rule-formulation and a Jātaka-style tale of past-life precedent, which is a standard feature of Vinaya narrative.

The term translated as "coarse grain husks" renders a phrase indicating rough, inferior rice or husks given as food, contrasted with the fine śāli variety; "dishwater" renders a phrase for thin, valueless liquid, contrasted with rich broth. The two-compartment pot trick is the daughters-in-law's scheme to make it appear before the sons that good food miraculously degrades when offered to the brahmin, thus discrediting his complaint.  The phrase rendered "coarse grain husks" and "boiled dregs" translates terms that contrast sharply with the fine śāli rice and whey broth given to the husbands — the comic and moral point being that the brahmin, supposedly of great accumulated merit, receives the inferior portion while the sons get the best. The verse plays on the same theme: even a two-chambered pot, which in other households would simply mean two portions, here still yields only one mouth's worth for the unfortunate father.

The snake-charmer episode turns on the folk-medical idea that the venom of an angry snake concentrates at its head and tail, making the middle of the body safe to consume and indeed medicinally beneficial — here restoring the brahmin's sight.  The name Lampa renders the Tibetan ལམ་པ, which appears to be a proper name; it has been retained as established in the preceding translation. The term kārṣāpaṇa (Skt. kārṣāpaṇa) is a standard ancient Indian monetary unit, retained as a recognizable technical term rather than rendered loosely as "coins." The phrase དབང་ཕྱུག་གི་བདག་པོ་ཆེན་པོ, literally "the great lord of the master of power," is rendered "the great lord of mastery," understood here as a Buddhicized allusion to a high attainment (possibly an ironic or honorific reference recontextualizing the deity Maheśvara); this is a genuine point of interpretive difficulty. The sentence structure in several passages follows the Tibetan closely where narrative logic requires it, and minor ellipsis in the Tibetan has been filled only where required for readable English prose.  The name "Byi-dbyi-pa" rendered literally as "Rat Boy the Jeweller" reflects the Tibetan formation: byi ba (rat) plus dbyi pa (jewel-trader), combined as a nickname epitomizing the whole story of his rise from a dead rat to a successful jeweller. The Tibetan keeps this as a proper epithet; in a Sanskrit context this might correspond to something like Mūṣikā-maṇivaṇik. The translation retains the Tibetan-derived name alongside the gloss for narrative fidelity.  The list of precious substances includes a number of terms that the Tibetan renders in slightly loose equivalents of Sanskrit gemological vocabulary. The rendering "mother-of-pearl" for sa le sbram and "carnelian" for dmar po follow standard identifications in the tradition but the precise stones intended are not entirely certain. The phrase "right-whorled shells" for g.yas su 'khyil pa refers to the auspicious dextral conch shell, a well-known Buddhist symbol. The five-man ship's crew with their specific roles is a formulaic list that recurs in several Pali and Sanskrit narrative parallels.  The term "kumbbhīra" (rendered from ཆུ་སྲིན་ཀུམ་བྷི་ར) is a Tibetan transcription of Sanskrit kumbhīra, a crocodilian sea-monster. The phrase "fish-swallowing great fish, the danger of fish-swallowing-fish-swallowing great fish" renders a triple escalating construction in the Tibetan that describes ever-larger predatory fish devouring one another; the translation preserves this escalating structure. The phrase "dark-clad and white-clad pirates" renders སྔོན་པོ and དཀར་པོ (literally "blue/dark" and "white") as a conventional description of different categories of pirates or bandits. The siren-like she-demons called "Young Cranes" (སྲིན་མོ་ཁྲུང་ཁྲུང་གཞོན་ནུ་མ) are a standard motif in this sūtra genre, likely corresponding to the Pāli rakkhasī / Sanskrit rākṣasī episode in merchant-voyage narratives.  The four-line verse is incomplete in the source passage as given — the text breaks off after the second line. Only two lines are translated; the remainder presumably continues in the next passage.

The phrase rendered "brought low, supremely low, and utterly supremely diminished" (བུལ་བ། མཆོག་ཏུ་བུལ་བ། ཆུང་བ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཆུང་བར་གྱུར) is a stock Vinaya formula for a monk reduced in status or subjected to a formal act of discipline; the exact Vinaya procedure referenced may require context from the preceding fascicles to identify precisely.

The name Lampā (ལམ་པ) is kept consistent as in the prior translation convention established by context.  The term rendered "blind pigs" translates a compound meaning pigs that are blind, which is contextually significant as it explains their particular vulnerability and helplessness when tied and boated. The word "mongpo" in Tibetan here means blind.

The phrase "given to, supremely given to, lowly and supremely lowly" reflects the Tibetan bul ba, mchog tu bul ba, chung ba, mchog tu chung ba, a formulaic descending gradation indicating extreme baseness and insignificance in karmic result. No cleaner English idiom precisely captures the fourfold formula, so it is rendered as literally as readability allows.

Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta is a famous physician of the Buddha's time; his name is kept in Sanskrit as it is a proper name, and "Kumārabhṛta" means "nourished as a youth" or "raised as a child," which the Tibetan tsho byed gzhon nus gsos kyis renders literally.  The name "Lamba" appears as a monk who is conspicuously excluded from the invitation both when Jīvaka addresses the Blessed One and when Ānanda relays the invitation. The Tibetan gives "བཙུན་པ་ལམ་པ" throughout, which is the Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit proper name, almost certainly "Lamba" or a similar form. The exact identity and the reason for his exclusion are not stated in this passage; the matter presumably continues in the following section.  The term bhṛṅgāra (rendered directly from the Tibetan transliteration བྷྲྀང་ག་ར) denotes a golden water-vessel or pitcher used for ritual purposes; it is distinct from the ordinary water-pitcher (ཆབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན) mentioned in the same sentence. The passage is somewhat compressed here, and the syntax suggests that Ānanda is told to set down the pitcher because Jīvaka already holds the golden bhṛṅgāra vessel ready, and the Blessed One is waiting for the full assembly before the water-offering ceremony begins.  The verse presents a minor structural complexity: the first three lines establish three similes of constant positive qualities, the fourth and fifth lines introduce a contrasting simile of constant fault in ordinary people, and the final two lines return to praise of noble ones and arhats. The rendering preserves this chiastic movement.

The place name rendered "Ultimately Worshipped" translates the Tibetan literally; it may be a proper place name whose Sanskrit original is unknown.  The passage contains a standard narrative formula describing an ideal Buddhist king's realm, with the phrase "kings of the lands under the sun" rendering a conventional expression for subordinate rulers. The phrase rendered "horse-master" for རྟ་ཅང་ཤེས translates literally as "one who knows horses," meaning an expert judge or inspector of horses, which in context appears to function as a royal official responsible for assessing the quality of horses across the kingdom. The final sentence draws on the Jātaka literary convention that in the earliest age of the world, animals possessed human speech; this is flagged here as the foal is about to become the story's speaking protagonist.  The phrase rendered "a hundred thousand in gold" (གསེར་འབུམ) literally means "a hundred thousand of gold," a standard large sum in classical Indian narrative. The unit is left implicit in the Tibetan, as is normal.

The verse passage contains an ambiguous moment where the horse speaks of "self-healed, re-grown roots" (རང་སོས་གཏུབས་པའི་རྩ་དག) as a reference to the meager food he subsisted on while with the potter — the exact botanical referent is unclear but the sense is roots or plant stems that have grown back after being cut, i.e., scavenged forage. This reading is adopted as the most contextually coherent.

The phrase གདུགས་སྲོག་ཤིང་བརྒྱ་པ is literally "a parasol with a life-pole of a hundred" — understood as a ceremonial parasol with a hundred ribs or spokes, a standard royal insignia in Indo-Tibetan narrative. The passage about the six groups defeating sixty naked ascetics is deliberately ironic and self-aggrandizing on the part of the six groups, contrasted unfavorably with Śāriputra's genuine victory; the monks of few desires rebuke the six groups for boasting about physical combat or coercive means rather than true Dharma teaching.

The closing narrative frame shifts scene abruptly from the regulatory episode back to an earlier story thread involving a householder and a cliff-side shop; this is characteristic of Vinaya narrative compilation, where multiple story strands are interwoven. The four fruits enumerated follow the standard śrāvaka path: stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. The verses at the end present a genuine interpretive challenge: "One who dwells first on a mountain is like refined gold being polished; but when one begins plotting harm to people, that mountain becomes just what it is." The metaphor may carry the sense that what begins as something refined and promising becomes harsh and unforgiving once ill-intent enters. The Tibetan is terse and the verse logic is compressed. The verse list of ill omens appears to be a quoted proverb or popular gāthā: chewing lac-tree wood, sleeping turned to the back at evening, heavy sleep, drinking whey or curds, and marrying a right-side daughter are enumerated as things that destroy even a person's tranquility. The definitions of the large and small bowls are technical and the Tibetan is compressed.
