The passage presents a somewhat paradoxical chain of misunderstanding: the monks first over-apply the one-meal rule by refusing to eat when they should rise for a superior; then, when told simply to eat sufficiently and not rise mid-meal, they interpret this as a license to abandon food altogether, subsisting on nothing at all. The Blessed One then draws a practical distinction between planted or cultivated plant foods (which do not displace the overall diet) and the five principal cooked foods (grain, hot rice, meat, oil-rich dishes, and sweets), the latter being the ones whose renunciation leads to the bodily deterioration described. The exact identity of some food terms — particularly "snum khur" (rendered "oil-rich food") and "de gu" (rendered "sweet food") — admit some flexibility of interpretation; these renderings follow the most common Vinaya commentarial understanding.  The term rendered "giving up food" throughout refers to the Vinaya rule that once a monastic has formally relinquished a meal — whether by ritual declaration, by rising from one's seat, or through other circumstances — one may not resume eating from it. This is a technical concept in Vinaya literature sometimes called "making the remnant" or "giving up" a meal. The fivefold analysis here is a standard scholastic enumeration of the conditions that constitute such a relinquishment.

The term rendered "person of the third sex" translates ma ning, which in Vinaya contexts refers to a sexually indeterminate or non-binary individual and plays a role in the formal presentation of food to monastics; the presence of any of the three categories of person is what makes a presentation of food legally valid.

The phrase rendered "having food that has been begun" and "having food that has been relinquished" refers to the Vinaya distinction between food one has formally accepted and begun to eat, and food one has formally declared one will not eat. These are the legal triggers for whether one's meal is still "open" or has been "closed" by relinquishment.  The phrase rendered "words without a remainder" and "words with a remainder" translates ཚིག་ལྷག་མ་མེད་པ and ཚིག་ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པ respectively. These are technical Vinaya distinctions: a declaration without a remainder is unconditional and complete, effecting full relinquishment of the food; a declaration with a remainder, marked by the particle རེ་ཞིག ("for now" or "just for the moment"), is conditional and incomplete, and therefore does not effect valid relinquishment. The translation follows this interpretation.  The passage contains a shift in interlocutor: it is Ānanda who answers the Blessed One's question, reporting what happened with the bathing monks. The phrase rendered "eat the surplus" translates a term for the practice of eating an additional portion after a formal meal, which in Vinaya contexts refers to the rule against eating at an improper time or eating more than one meal; here the newly entered elder's scheme is to maneuver his teacher into a technical violation by having him eat a second portion without proper authorization. The newly entered elder deliberately withholds the authorization he was given for the second meal, so that when the monk eats, he has incurred a downfall. This doctrinal mechanics of the setup is important for the narrative's purpose of illustrating a specific Vinaya rule.  The phrase rendered "food designated as a meal and as eatables" translates a technical Vinaya distinction between two categories: five types of solid meal-food and five types of softer eatables. The distinction among the five categories of offense — pārājika (defeat), saṅghāvaśeṣa (formal act of the remaining Saṅgha), pāyattika (downfall), pratideśanīya (individual confession), and duṣkṛta (misdeed) — is the standard Vinaya fivefold classification. The "six groups of monks" is a well-known Vinaya category referring to a famously lax group of monastics frequently cited in disciplinary narratives.

The five modes of vision used by the bodhisattva to survey the world before his final rebirth is a standard feature of buddha-biography, covering the survey of suitable family, lineage, region, time, and mother.  The phrase "Eamo" is a Tibetan exclamation of acclaim or approbation used by audiences at performances; it is left transliterated as it functions as a crowd's cheer rather than a translatable word, comparable to "Bravo." The "festival of Delightful Twain" renders "yid 'ong gnyis kyi dus ston," literally "the festival of the two delightful ones," likely a festival celebrating two auspicious figures or events; the precise referent is contextually opaque and may warrant scholarly attention.

The "five surveys" (gzigs pa lnga) is a standard formula in birth-story literature describing how a bodhisattva in Tuṣita, before descending, examines the world under five categories to determine the optimal circumstances for his birth.  The term rendered "Acharka" (འཆར་ཀ) is a proper name for one of the monks belonging to the six groups; it appears here in transliteration from an underlying Sanskrit or Prakrit form. The identity of this name in canonical sources is not firmly established in secondary literature, and it may be a corrupt or regional variant.

The phrase "great serpents" (ལྟོ་འཕྱེ་ཆེན་པོ) literally means "great belly-crawlers," a common Tibetan periphrasis for large serpentine beings; it has been rendered descriptively rather than with a specific Sanskrit equivalent since the referent is ambiguous between large nāgas and mythic serpent-beings.  The closing phrase explaining "he commits an offence" employs a traditional Vinaya formulaic gloss in which the word for "downfall" or "offence" is unpacked etymologically and soteriologically: the terms "scorched," "scalded," and "fallen" refer to the three modes of suffering in the lower rebirths, which is a standard Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya commentary device. This is rendered idiomatically in context without disrupting the narration.  The phrase rendered as "those who live by gleaning leftover curds" translates a term for a low-status social group who subsisted on the remnants of dairy processing. The phrase recurs as a kind of fixed epithet throughout this passage.

The exchange between the Blessed One and Ānanda about "swiftly spreading serpent-venom" and "fierce serpent-venom" is a deliberate riddle: the Blessed One sees a hidden treasure and calls it poison to discourage attachment; Ānanda agrees; the worldly man overhears and is confused, then finds the treasure and greedily rationalises it as a wonderful "venom" that makes it easy to harm even one's dearest ones. The passage is an elaborate parable on the dangers of wealth.  The figure addressed as "King Rūpaṣeṇahṛdaya" (Tibetan: རྒྱལ་པོ་གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ) is a compound meaning "he whose heart is in outward form" or "the king whose essence is in appearances." This appears to be the name of a specific king in this narrative context, contrasted with Ajātaśatru; the translation retains it as a proper name throughout, which is the most defensible reading.

The condemned man's final speech alternating "Ānanda" (Tibetan: ཀུན་དགའ་བོ) with titles of the Buddha is rendered as verse to reflect its rhythmic, incantatory quality in the original.  The phrase rendered "what happened to you was done by you yourself — go now" translates a somewhat terse Tibetan that implies the king is acknowledging both the man's ordeal and perhaps a personal connection or guilt; the exact emotional register is compressed in the original.  The phrase "view of the transitory collection" renders the Tibetan technical term for the false view that identifies the aggregates with a self; the text employs the striking metaphor of this view as a mountain twenty peaks high, shattered by the vajra of gnosis at the moment of stream-entry, which is the standard Abhidharma account of what is abandoned at that path-moment.

The "Group of Six" refers to the notorious six monks frequently mentioned in Vinaya literature as the instigators of improper conduct that prompts the Buddha to lay down rules. The phrase rendered "spread snake-poison swiftly" is a Tibetan idiom meaning these coins bring swift ruin or are cursed, likening the danger of found money to fast-acting snake venom. The final sentence is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan. The Blessed One's instruction appears to be directing monks not to impulsively direct a finder to a lost object without first asking identifying questions, such as whether the claimant is a weighing-merchant (i.e., can identify the object by weight or type). The musical instruments named here — ཨོད་མ, བལ་ལ་རི, མ་ཧ་ཏི, སུ་གྷོ་ཤ་ཀ — are Sanskrit loanwords transcribed into Tibetan representing vīṇā, Balari, Mahātī, and Sughoṣaka respectively; these are traditional Indian stringed instruments. "The mother of Mṛgāra's lord" refers to Viśākhā, the renowned lay donor of the early Buddhist community, known by the honorific "Mṛgāramātā" — mother of Mṛgāra's lord — on account of having spiritually converted her father-in-law Mṛgāra.  The name "Kāśyapa" here refers to the buddha Kāśyapa, a predecessor of Śākyamuni in the list of past buddhas, not to the disciple Mahākāśyapa. The "group of six monks" is a standard Vinaya technical reference to the notorious sextet of monks (ṣaḍvargika bhikṣus) who frequently appear as negative exemplars throughout the Vinaya literature. The structure of this passage is a classic Vinaya formula in which each new circumstance prompts a progressive relaxation of the rule; the accumulating list of permitted exceptions is doctrinally significant as it demonstrates the Buddha's responsive, case-by-case lawgiving method.  The list of "hot season" months follows the Indian lunar calendar as reckoned in the Vinaya tradition. The venerable Cāraka who appears here is a monk who is also an accomplished archer, a figure known in Vinaya narrative literature for combining renunciant status with remarkable worldly skills. The term rendered "goes somewhere" translates a verb meaning to go to a place, here used idiomatically for approaching with a purpose. The phrase "mི་འི་ཆོས་བླ་མ་སྨྲས་པ" rendered as "proclaimed a superhuman quality of a human being" refers to the fourth pārājika offense of falsely claiming superhuman attainments. The term "གཅན་སྒོ" rendered as "dangerous pass" or "treacherous defile" refers literally to a place frequented by wild predators or bandits; the juridical point is that traveling there might lead to violent death and thus could be construed as a defeat under other rules, but here the accusation is fabricated and therefore itself constitutes an offense.  The phrase rendered "superhuman qualities" translates "mī'i chos bla ma," literally "qualities superior to those of humans," which is the standard Vinaya term for the pārājika offense of falsely claiming meditative attainments or direct realizations. The context here is that one monk is warning another: even if the words spoken were orthodox doctrinal statements, if they were taken or could be taken as a claim to personal realization, they border on the root downfall of falsely claiming superhuman qualities. The warning "do not speak of superhuman qualities" is the standard Vinaya injunction on this point.

The phrase rendered "the breath reversed upward and he died" translates a classical Tibetan idiom for death by asphyxiation or convulsion — literally "the wind turned upward" — indicating that the repeated tickling caused a fatal physiological episode. The name ཉེ་བ་འཁོར (Nye ba 'khor) rendered here as "Upananda" follows the standard Vinaya identification of this figure from the group of seventeen. The phrase rendered as "the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a stock Abhidharmic formula. The view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has twenty subsidiary views (five aggregates each taken as self or as possessed by self, giving four modes per aggregate, equaling twenty); shattering these with the vajra of wisdom at the moment of stream-entry is a standard doctrinal image in the Vinaya narrative literature. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, consistent with narrative continuation.  The phrase rendered "the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a technical expression describing the peak of the view that takes the perishable composite as a self or as belonging to a self, a standard Abhidharma formulation for the peak of the afflictive view overcome at stream-entry. The imagery of twenty peaks shattered by the vajra of wisdom refers to the twenty variant forms of this view enumerated in Abhidharma literature.

The expression rendered "draw us out by the collar" is a vivid idiomatic image; the Tibetan literally means pulling someone from behind by the nape or back of the neck, here used metaphorically for being rescued from samsaric entanglement.  The phrase rendered as "the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a technical compound: the view of the transitory collection, or the innate belief in a self within the aggregates, is here metaphorically described as a mountain with twenty peaks, corresponding to the twenty-fold elaboration of that view in Abhidharma analysis — seeing each of the five aggregates as self, as belonging to self, as containing self, or as contained in self, yielding twenty views. This is a stock image in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narratives.  The phrase rendered "twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a standard Abhidharmic and Sūtra-based image: the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in its twenty aspects — the belief in a self or as belonging to a self in relation to each of the five aggregates, taken fourfold — is here metaphorically a mountain of twenty peaks, shattered by the vajra of wisdom at the moment of stream-entry. This is a well-attested image in this narrative genre.

The sequence of fruits — stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship — followed by the three classes of awakening mind (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and full buddhahood) reflects a standard Mahāyāna narrative presentation that accommodates all three vehicles within a single assembly.  The phrase rendered "carries a gift" and "there is no such gift for the Tathāgata other than one such as this, from those who are to be trained" is a somewhat condensed Tibetan expression. The phrase rendered "ground with intrinsic nature" and "ground without intrinsic nature" (rang bzhin can / rang bzhin can ma yin pa) is a Vinaya technical distinction. "Ground with intrinsic nature" (Sanskrit: sajīva bhūmi, "living ground") refers to earth that is moist and biologically active — measured here by consolidation after rainfall — while "ground without intrinsic nature" (nirjīva bhūmi, "inert ground") is dry, compacted, or otherwise inert earth. The Tibetan commentarial tradition glosses the time periods (three months with rain, six months without) as the threshold for determining living versus inert soil. The phrase rendered "may I be lent out" reflects a somewhat technical Vinaya idiom concerning a monk being "released" or "lent" to fulfill a prior commitment to another patron; the Tibetan construction གན་དུ་མཆིས is idiomatic for this.  The phrase rendered "a clump of leaves that were not real leaves" translates a Tibetan expression meaning, literally, "a clump of what were not leaves," indicating an illusory emanation of leaf-like matter used to cover Subhāṅga's fallen body from public view — a miraculous act of compassion and discretion by the Buddha.

The phrase "did not think" spoken twice by Subhāṅga reflects the doctrinal point stated just above: arhats do not engage their supernormal perception and restraint without deliberate intention. Subhāṅga's answer acknowledges that he failed to apply mindful awareness and thus drank without recognizing the liquor for what it was. This is a significant Vinaya doctrinal point explaining why an arhat can commit an unwitting transgression.  The passage enumerates four sensory qualities of an intoxicant in decreasing combination — color, smell, taste, and sensation — as the basis for determining the degree of culpability. The descending series is a standard Vinaya analytical technique; each step removes one quality while the offense threshold remains drinking-plus-intoxication. This is rendered faithfully without smoothing.

The term rendered "grain husks" and "grain stalks" translates sbang ma and tshigs ma respectively; these refer to the spent grain residue and the fibrous stalks or nodes left from fermentation, both of which retain enough fermentable matter to be regulated.

The final question-and-answer about Subhāṅga's past karma sets up a jātaka-style narrative explaining his paradoxical situation: wealthy yet with a name meaning merely "good-looking" or "auspicious" while living in poverty and hunger. The irony is intentional.  The verse on karmic indestructibility is a standard formulation found across Vinaya and sūtra literature and is here rendered in a metrically natural English equivalent suitable for oral delivery.

The phrase rendered "those among his household who lived by their share of dairy food" translates a compound referring to household servants or dependents whose livelihood or portion consisted of dairy produce; the exact social referent is slightly opaque in the Tibetan, but the general sense is clear.  The name rendered "Nyeong" (ཉེས་འོངས) is a Tibetan personal name meaning something like "fault-come" or "misfortune-arrived." It functions as a narrative pun: the word the householder uttered as an insult in a past life becomes his name in subsequent existences as a hungry ghost. The translation preserves the name as a proper noun in both instances while the narrative context makes the pun self-explanatory.

The passage ends mid-sentence with the aspiration prayer incomplete, apparently continuing in the next passage. No text appears to be missing; the cut is a continuity break.

The epithet translated "brahmin youth Lama" renders བྲམ་ཟེའི་ཁྱེའུ་བླ་མ, a proper name meaning "brahmin youth who is a preceptor/lama." It refers to the monk's preceptor at ordination under Kāśyapa, here being addressed in the aspiration prayer.  The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon listing the narrative subjects of the rules in the preceding section, a standard feature of Vinaya texts. The terms rendered "entirely dark," "entirely bright," and "mixed" for karma follow the standard fourfold karmic typology of the Vinaya tradition. The phrase rendered "on the verge of attaining the highest good" is a brahminic idiom referring to the girl's imminent marriage, which would be dishonored by public contact.  The phrase rendered "the alms of the one who was burned" translates "tshig pa'i bsod snyoms," which is somewhat cryptic here and likely refers to a specific narrative context — perhaps alms from a patron who had suffered injury or whose house had burned — that would be clear from the surrounding story. The translation renders it literally; its precise referent depends on narrative material not present in this passage.

The verse about the king afflicted by poison is a gāthā cited by Charka; it has a somewhat gnomic, proverbial character and is rendered accordingly.  The verse passage contains a simile rendered "like a sea-monster's lair" from the Tibetan "chu srin gnas kyi dug can pa," which literally reads "one who is poisonous like the dwelling-place of a makara." The sense is that even the most venomous being, as dangerous as a makara's den, may eventually pass the moment of opportunity, whereas the Tathāgata's loving-kindness never misses its moment. This is a striking and somewhat unusual image; the rendering follows the Tibetan closely.

The phrase "snam sbyor gyi rgyal mtshan thogs pa," rendered "those who bear aloft the victory banner of the patched robe," refers to those wearing the sewn patchwork robe as a mark of the renunciant life, a standard monastic image.  The phrase rendered "the Manadons" for མདུན་ན་འདོན is uncertain. The term likely refers to a specific clan or people among whom Maudgalyāyana was born as a prince, but the identification is not entirely clear from the Tibetan alone. Some editions read this differently. The meaning conveyed — that he renounced a royal inheritance before going forth — is doctrinally secure.

The name "Bumangs" renders བུ་མངས, which appears to be a place-name or possibly a proper noun for a stūpa site; its exact identification is uncertain and is left transliterated.

"Nandana" is the rendering of མཛེས་དགའི which literally means "pleasing joy"; the intended figure is almost certainly the Blessed One's half-brother Nanda, and the name "Śru" for སྲུ likely refers to the Śākya prince Śuddhodana's son by another wife, i.e., this is Nanda's lineage. This identification follows traditional commentarial understanding.  The names Śrākāvin, Nandaka, Aniruddha, Chanda, Lāghava, Nabasa, and Cāraka are rendered from their Tibetan forms; Śrākāvin renders སྒྲ་ཅན་ཟིན and Cāraka renders འཆར་ཀ. Lāghava renders འགྲོ་མགྱོགས and Nabasa renders ནབ་སོ; these identifications are based on standard Vinaya lists but the Sanskrit equivalents of the lesser-known names in this sequence carry some uncertainty.

The phrase rendered "violated my person" translates གཞོན་ནུ་མ་དང་བྲལ་བར་བགྱིས་སོ, literally "he caused separation from my youth" or "he caused me to be parted from my maidenhood," a conventional Tibetan Vinaya expression for sexual assault or molestation.

The phrase rendered as "this arrow reversed" translates a metaphor that likely means the accusation or attack brought against him will be turned back; the image of the arrow being deflected or reversed is idiomatic in the narrative context.

The phrase rendered "cutting through the filth at the gateway of consciousness like sandalwood applied there" translates a somewhat unusual idiom involving rig pa (here in the sense of a knowing faculty or cognitive clarity), sgo nga'i sbubs (literally "the hollow of an eggshell" — here most likely a metaphor for the encrusted shell or obscuring husk of the sense-faculty gateway), and tsan dan bzhag pa lta bu (like placing or applying sandalwood). The precise image is idiomatic rather than a standard canonical formula; the translation renders the likely sense but the exact simile may be uncertain.

The list of attainments following arhatship, including the equanimity toward clay and gold and sky and the palm of the hand, is a well-known stock description found across Vinaya narrative literature.  The deity referred to throughout as "Śiva" is rendered from the Tibetan term for the divine name "Śiva" appearing as the object of the brahmin's devotion. The Tibetan here uses "Śi ba" phonetically, clearly representing the Hindu deity Śiva. The dialogue in which "Śiva speaks" is a remarkable narrative device — Śāraka apparently ventriloquizes or supernaturally channels Śiva's voice to confirm his own status, which is what prompts the brahmin's recognition of Śāraka's miraculous power.

The phrase "twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty sub-types of the identity view (satkāyadṛṣṭi) enumerated in Abhidharma literature — the view that the self and the aggregates stand in various relations of identity or possession. Shattering this view is precisely what stream-entry accomplishes.

The passage ends mid-sentence and the translation preserves that break faithfully.  The phrase "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the perishable collection" renders a standard Abhidharma formulation: the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has twenty subsidiary peaks corresponding to the twenty ways of misconceiving a self in relation to each of the five aggregates (either as identical with, contained in, containing, or as belonging to each). This is a standard scholastic elaboration and is rendered literally as the tradition intends it.

The reference to Śiva here and in the preceding passage is slightly unusual in that the Tibetan uses the epithet "Śiva" (zhi ba, literally "the Peaceful One") rather than the more common lha chen ("the Great God"). This is a recognized epithet of Śiva in Buddhist literature and is rendered accordingly.  The phrase rendered as "the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty subdivisions of the view of a personal self within the perishable aggregates, a standard Abhidharma enumeration. Stream-entry is the first of the four noble fruits, at which this view is permanently abandoned. This doctrinal point is central to the passage and justifies the otherwise unusual image.  The phrase "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty subsidiary views of self arising from the five aggregates taken in four ways each, a standard Abhidharma enumeration. The image of their being "shattered by the vajra of wisdom" at stream-entry is a classical formulation for the abandonment of the self-view at the path of seeing. This is consistent throughout both occurrences in the passage.

The brahmin's declaration of the good a spiritual friend has done — drying the ocean of blood and tears, freeing from mountains of bones — echoes classical formulations found in Pāli and Sanskrit sources comparing the suffering of saṃsāra to oceans of blood and heaps of bones, and is a standard rhetorical expression of gratitude for guidance to stream-entry.  The title "ཁྱིམ་བདག་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན" is the standard Tibetan rendering of Anāthapiṇḍada, the famous lay patron of the Buddha, whose name means "feeder of the unprotected." It is left as a compound epithet-name in translation; a listener familiar with Buddhist narrative will recognize the referent.

The phrase rendered "all the household folk together" renders a deliberate ambiguity in Śāraka's speech: the brahmin understood it to mean his own household dependents, while the monk meant the entire monastic Saṅgha as guests, which the brahmin boy then unpacks. This double meaning is intrinsic to the plot.  The name rendered "Mallikā" for བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ is a standard equivalence used in this narrative cycle: ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ literally means "garlanded lady," which corresponds to the Sanskrit Mallikā (from mālā, garland). The identification is secure within this context.  The passage describing Śāraka's miraculous interventions — sustaining the brahmin's stream of urine and making the wife's internal organs visible from outside — is rendered literally as the Tibetan states it. The latter miracle functions as a classical meditation-on-the-foul device to break the brahmin's attachment; "whatever was on her belly within appeared visible from the outside" renders the Tibetan directly. The phrase "twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty modes of the satkāyadṛṣṭi (the belief in a real self among the five aggregates), a standard enumeration in Abhidharma literature.  The "twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a stock image in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya literature: the view of a substantially existing personal self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is said to have twenty peaks corresponding to the twenty ways of grasping at the five aggregates as self or as belonging to self. The "vajra of wisdom" that shatters it is the wisdom arising at stream-entry on the path of seeing. The passage thus describes the brahmin couple attaining the first of the four fruits of the noble path.  The phrase "the seventh brahmin's household" refers to the seventh in a sequence of households counted across the narrative. The Tibetan reads "bram ze'i khyim bdun pa gnyis ga," meaning "both of the brahmin's household, the seventh," indicating this is the seventh brahmin converted and that both husband and wife were brought to the Dharma together.

The final verse is a riddle or cryptic teaching directed at the brahmin woman: the "old rope" refers to her exhausted virtuous karma from past lives, which is running out, while the "new rope" she is neglecting to make refers to the failure to generate fresh merit or virtue in this life. The imagery is of a household implement to make the doctrinal point vivid.  The phrase rendered as "leafless thicket" translates a term literally meaning "a thicket of what is not leaves" — that is, bare or thorny brush rather than foliage. This is a standard miraculous concealment device in the narrative literature and the rendering chosen reflects that.

The "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma image: the view of the transitory collection (Sanskrit satkāyadṛṣṭi) has twenty sub-forms (five aggregates each grasped in four ways as self or belonging to self), conventionally described as peaks that are destroyed upon stream-entry. This image recurs twice in the brahmin's confession speech, as in the Tibetan.  The verse repeated twice in the Tibetan reads literally: "Wearing out the old, not producing even a little of the new, seeing one adorned with heedlessness, one weeps with a face flooded with tears." The "old" refers to the exhausted merit from the past offering, the "new" refers to fresh merit not being generated, and the "careless ease" or "heedlessness" refers to those adorned with ornaments and pleasure, oblivious to impermanence — this is the standard commentarial gloss embedded in the narrative explanation that follows.

The phrase rendered "inferior pratyekabuddhas" translates a compound meaning pratyekabuddhas of the lesser or humble type, distinguishing them from buddhas proper; the doctrinal point is that they arise in ages without a fully awakened buddha.  The phrase rendered as "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty-fold view of a personal self in connection with the five aggregates, a standard Abhidharma enumeration. The "stream-entry" here is the first noble attainment, in which this view is permanently severed. The image of the vajra of gnosis shattering these peaks is a stock literary expression in this genre of narrative.

The passage translated as "wholehearted and sincere devotion" renders a Tibetan idiom meaning literally "from the depths of the throat," a classical expression for deep, heartfelt sincerity.  The name "Anāthapiṇḍada" (literally "feeder of the unprotected," often spelled Anāthapiṇḍika) appears here as "khyim bdag mgon med zas sbyin," which is a Tibetan calque of the Sanskrit name; it has been rendered as the Sanskrit proper name for clarity. This figure is the well-known lay patron of the Buddha famous for his donation of the Jetavana grove in Śrāvastī. The text renders his name as a descriptive title rather than a proper name, but in context it clearly refers to this individual.  The phrase rendered as "the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates the technical expression for satkāyadṛṣṭi, the view that identifies a self with the five aggregates, enumerated as twenty in Abhidharma analysis (four modes of identification multiplied by five aggregates). The name "Tummo Tummo" (གཏུམ་མོ་གཏུམ་མོ་) is a reduplicated form used as a proper epithet meaning "the fierce one" or "the wrathful one." The text is playing on her temperament becoming her name.

The brahmin's declaration "I have entered the stream" followed immediately by a second repetition is not an error; the doubling or tripling of such a proclamation is a recognized literary feature in these canonical narratives.  The phrase rendered "eaters of anything and everything" translates the brahmin slur that śramaṇas are indiscriminate in what they eat, violating brahminical purity rules. Cāraka's miracle turns the brahmins' own festive food and garlands into the very impure substances they accuse the śramaṇas of consuming, thus inverting the charge.

The "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma image: the view of a self inherent in the five aggregates generates twenty sub-views (five aggregates each considered as self, as possessing self, as within self, and as within self's possession), and realizing stream-entry uproots all of them. The cosmological passage describing Mount Meru follows the standard Abhidharma account. The more likely intended reading is one hundred and sixty thousand leagues, consistent with standard cosmological sources; the discrepancy in the numeral is noted here as a genuine textual uncertainty.  The two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda appear here as they do elsewhere in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya cycle; their names mean Joy and Near-Joy respectively, though the text uses them as proper names and no gloss is needed in context.

The epithet Suparṇa for Garuḍa literally means "fine-feathered" and is here rendered by its descriptive equivalent "king of the winged ones" since the Sanskrit proper name is more recognizable to listeners than the Tibetan rendering; a note is included for transparency.  The epithet "rig pa dang zhabs su ldan pa" rendered as "endowed with knowledge and conduct" follows the standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, one of the ten epithets of a buddha: "accomplished in knowledge and conduct." The passage breaks off mid-sentence as the Tibetan provided ends there.

The term "sa 'dzin pa" ("lord/holder of the earth") in the context of nāgas refers to their domain as earth-dwelling or earth-holding sovereigns, a recognized nāga epithet; rendered accordingly.

"Nandaka and Upanandaka" (dga' bo and nye dga') are the standard Tibetan equivalents; the Sanskrit forms are used here for consistency with the tradition.  The phrase rendered "the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a stock Abhidharma image: the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) comprises twenty sub-views regarding the five aggregates (each aggregate taken as self, as possessing self, as within self, or as self within it), and stream-entry destroys them entirely. This is standard across the Pāli and Sanskritic scholastic traditions.

The phrase "the trace of nirvāṇa" renders "mya ngan 'das pa'i shul," literally "the trail or path of nirvāṇa," meaning the initial approach to or foretaste of nirvāṇa attained at stream-entry — a conventional expression for the fruit of the first path.  The names "Priya" and "Apriya" (Tibetan: dga' bo and nye dga') present a slight irregularity: dga' bo is straightforwardly "Priya" (beloved/happy), but nye dga' would more literally be "Apriya" only if taken as a compound meaning something like "the close-happy-one" or "Upananda." In the later sentence the text identifies them with two nāga kings; the second name may correspond to Nanda and Upananda or similar pairs known from other sources. This is noted here as contextually significant but the names are rendered by their functional Tibetan meaning pending the continuation of the text, which will clarify the nāga identifications.

The phrase rendered "renounced goods of the young prince's household" and "renounced goods of the queen's retinue" translates yongs su spang ba — literally "the complete relinquishments" or "the surrendered possessions" — referring to the property given up upon going forth; this is a technical Vinaya usage.  The term rendered "attendant of impure rank" translates a phrase indicating someone of low or impure social status sent ahead as a scout — the precise social category is contextually clear though the exact term is conventional. The epithet "Suparṇa, king of birds with wings adorned with fine feathers" renders the name Suparṇa (a class of mythical golden-winged birds, equivalent to Garuḍa) along with the meaning embedded in the Tibetan form of the name. The phrase about being "unable to be dislodged" reflects the karmic merit of the nāga kings' donation conferring secure tenure for a full cosmic aeon.  The phrase rendered "retinues who sustained themselves on dairy provisions" translates a term referring literally to beings who live on curds or dairy products — likely a category of nāga attendants or minor beings classified by their mode of sustenance. The exact nature of this class is not further specified in the text.  The passage contains a small but notable doctrinal point: the Blessed One explicitly attributes the miracle entirely to Mahāmaudgalyāyana rather than to himself, which is a recurrent sūtra motif affirming the genuine attainments of chief disciples. The sentence at the end is deliberately left open as it continues into the next passage.  The nāga king's name rendered throughout as Nandaka and his companion as Upanandaka, consistent with the Tibetan dga' bo and nye dga' respectively. These are standard Indic names meaning "Joyful" and "Near-Joyful," and the rendering keeps the Sanskrit forms for consistency with the rest of the text's conventions.  The term rendered "hand torture until death" for ཕྱག་སྦལ་དུ་བཅུག་སྟེ་འཆི་བར་བྱ་དགོས་སོ is literally "having been put in hand-clamps, one must die." The exact nature of this punishment is somewhat uncertain — it may refer to a form of restraint or mutilation — but it clearly denotes a capital or fatal punishment and has been rendered accordingly. The phrase "Sudharmā, the assembly hall of the gods" renders ལྷ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ལྷའི་འདུན་ས་ཆོས་བཟངས, which corresponds to the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa gods — a standard point of comparison in classical Buddhist literature for extraordinary beauty.  The phrase rendered as "the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty sub-views comprising the satkāyadṛṣṭi, the view of the self in relation to the five aggregates taken four ways each. This is a standard Abhidharma enumeration, and the image of the vajra of wisdom shattering these twenty peaks is a classical description of stream-entry. The "fruit of stream-entry" renders the standard term for the first of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path.  The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the passage; the translation follows the Tibetan as given. The name Rdzu-'phrul-len is rendered in meaning as "Miracle-Taker" throughout, following the text's own explanation of why the name was chosen. The eight-nurse scheme is a conventional Indian royal birth narrative found elsewhere in Buddhist canonical literature. Kāravīra is a flowering tree whose garlands in this context are a mark of condemnation, signaling that the condemned is being led to execution.  The name rendered "Bad Supriya" translates the Tibetan ངན་པ་བཟང་བྱིན, literally "Wretched Supriya" or "Bad Supriya" — a play on his name Supriya (Tibetan བཟང་བྱིན, meaning "Good-Gift" or "Supriya"), now prefixed with ངན་པ ("bad/wretched") because of the poor quality of his gifts. The irony is intentional and the translation preserves it.

The name Kālaprabha is reconstructed from the Tibetan བྲམ་ཟེ་དུས་དཔོག, where དུས corresponds to kāla (time) and དཔོག to prabha or possibly mānin; slight uncertainty remains on the Sanskrit form, but Kālaprabha is the most natural reconstruction.  The list of throne furnishings is rendered interpretively in several places where the Tibetan terms describe specific textile and cushion types whose exact technical meanings are uncertain. The renderings given reflect reasonable contextual sense. The term rendered "Kautamba cloth" is a tentative identification of the Tibetan transliteration. The phrase "came to the Jambu Grove" renders a reference to Jambudvīpa; here it appears to refer to a specific grove or meeting-place rather than the continent as a whole, which is a genuinely uncertain reading. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source and the translation follows accordingly.  The passage is a cumulative, ascending series comparing the merit of giving to progressively more advanced recipients on the noble path: those entering for stream-entry, stream-enterers, those entering for once-returning, once-returners, those entering for non-returning, non-returners, and those entering for arhatship. Each step outweighs the entire accumulated list of previous steps. The final sentence of the passage breaks off mid-series, consistent with the supplied excerpt ending before its conclusion. The four pairs of path-enterers and fruit-attainers correspond to the standard Theravāda and Abhidharma taxonomy of the eight noble persons (āryapudgala).  The phrase rendered "ascetics who are non-Buddhists seeking sensual pleasure yet free from attachment" translates the Tibetan for tīrthika ṛṣis who desire sensual pleasure but are without attachment — a recognized category in the text's graduated hierarchy of merit fields, denoting non-Buddhist contemplatives who, while nominally dwelling among sense pleasures, have achieved a degree of dispassion. The "pleasure garden" is the standard rendering of the Tibetan term for a park or garden donated for the use of the Saṅgha, equivalent to Sanskrit ārāma.  The passage is a cumulative enumeration characteristic of Āgama-style sūtra literature, in which each new act of giving is shown to surpass the preceding list in merit, with the list growing longer at each step. The furnishings listed — thrones, chairs, cushioned seats with inner padding, bolsters, coverlets, and blankets — represent standard items of monastic requisite offering found in corresponding Pāli parallels. The "permanent endowment of offerings appropriate to the occasion" renders གཏན་གྱི་རྐྱེན་རིས་དང་མཐུན་པའི་མཆོད་སྦྱིན, indicating a standing or perpetual provision of seasonal or occasion-specific requisites for the temple. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, consistent with the passage having been supplied as a continuation excerpt.  The name rendered here as "Citta (Supriya)" translates the Tibetan "ངན་པ་བཟང་བྱིན" (Ngan pa bzang byin), a Tibetan rendering that likely corresponds to the Sanskrit name Citta or a related householder figure. The second element "bzang byin" suggests "well-given" or "Supriya/Subhadra" type. The identification is uncertain; the passage may refer to a different named householder than the famous Citta of Macchikāsaṇḍa. This should be verified against the Sanskrit or Pali parallel if available.

The term "ཕྱག་སྦལ་" rendered as "irons" or "being clapped in irons" is a form of punishment or restraint; the precise nature is somewhat uncertain but clearly a form of punitive confinement or physical restraint akin to stocks or shackles.  The passage contains a conspicuous inversion in the court-tier description: wicked persons are said to be placed "at the bottom" and yet the sentence concludes with them placed "on the upper tier." The Tibetan is internally contradictory here, most likely due to a scribal error in which the logic of the three-tiered court system has been scrambled in transmission; the preceding passage established that the lowest tier held persons of bad character, so the final clause placing them on the upper tier appears to be a corruption.

The term rendered "grain-pension retainers" translates a compound meaning those whose livelihood consists in the king's salary or grain allotment — essentially royal officers or soldiers paid in kind.

"Kauśika" is a standard Vedic epithet of Indra, used here in the householder's address to Śakra.

"Mī-mje" rendered as "the Brahma world" follows the standard identification of this term with the Pure Abode or Brahmā's realm; "its lord Brahmā" is standard.  The passage ends mid-sentence, breaking off at the final repetition of the fire simile. This is a continuation into the next passage and the abrupt ending reflects the source text as supplied.

The phrase rendered "palace courtyard" translates the Tibetan term for the inner royal compound or forecourt; the precise architectural referent is a conventional royal setting in the sūtra narrative.  The Tibetan "མི་མཇེད་ཀྱི་བདག་པོ་ཚངས་པ" literally means "Brahmā, lord of Akaṇiṣṭha," which is an unusual collocation; in some Pāli and Sanskrit parallels Brahmā is lord of the Brahma-world, but the Tibetan text here specifies the Akaṇiṣṭha realm. This is rendered as given without emendation.

The term "ཀཽ་ཤི་ཀ" is a vocative epithet for Śakra derived from Sanskrit Kauśika, a name of Indra; it is rendered accordingly.  The phrase rendered "man of impure standing" translates a term meaning someone of low or unclean status, likely a low-caste or outcast individual. The social dynamic here contrasts the proud kṣatriya king who will not enter until he knows the scene with the ritually impure go-between he employs.

The passage contains a slight grammatical awkwardness in the Tibetan where the narrative shifts from first-person recollection back into third-person narration after the king grants the boon. This is a common feature of sūtra narrative embedding and has been rendered accordingly without marking the shift explicitly.  The creature names "tremabukas" and "trailatākas" are transliterations of the Tibetan phonetic renderings "ཏྲེ་མ་བུ་ཀ" and "ཏྲཻ་ལ་ཏ་ཀ" and likely correspond to Sanskrit animal or supernatural creature names that are difficult to identify with certainty. They appear to be some kind of threatening creatures sent by the deity. The transliteration is preserved as the most honest rendering given the uncertainty.

The passage about the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda appears as a question from the king, though the Tibetan syntax is slightly ambiguous — it may be the narrator's framing rather than a direct quotation. The rendering as part of the king's confused inquiry is the most natural reading in context.  The phrase rendered "open the four great seals" translates "che bzhi 'byed pa," a legal or forensic idiom meaning to break open sealed documents or official records, i.e., to tamper with or falsify legal evidence. The context makes clear these thieves want Śīlavaṇij to bear false witness or to forge records in order to implicate Saṃdhaka. This technical term has no single transparent English equivalent, so it is rendered literally throughout to preserve consistency.

The name "Kṛṣṇa" for the prince is the literal translation of "rGyal bu nag po" (Black Prince), but in this Vinaya narrative context it functions as a proper name and is rendered as Kṛṣṇa accordingly.  The phrase rendered "left-handed men of the last month of autumn" translates a somewhat opaque Tibetan idiom for criminals or bandits associated with that season; the exact socio-legal term is uncertain, but the context makes clear these are threatening brigands. Some editions may read this differently.

The "four seals" in this commercial-legal context likely refers to sealed documents or formal arbitration records used in trade disputes, not the philosophical "four seals" of Buddhist doctrine. The exact legal procedure is unclear but the narrative sense is plain.  The verse contains three named exemplars but is said to list "four things" that are exceedingly difficult. The fourth item is not explicitly named in the verse as transmitted, which may reflect a textual lacuna or an implicit fourth quality (perhaps patience, named first). This is a genuine structural anomaly worth noting for editorial attention.

The name rendered "Śārka" is a provisional reading of འཆར་ཀ (Charka/Śārka); this is an unusual name and the Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain.  The Tibetan text here alternates between two monks: Śāriputra (Śāradvatīputra is a separate person, also rendered as Śāradvatiputra in the preceding passage provided; however, in this passage the Tibetan uses Śāriputra's name first and then introduces the distinct character referred to as ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་འཆར་ཀ, rendered Śāradvatiputra in the preceding translation). Strictly speaking, ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་འཆར་ཀ is not Śāradvatiputra but rather a different monk whose name, rendered from the Tibetan phonetic form འཆར་ཀ, likely corresponds to Sanskrit Carka or a similar name not identical to Śāradvatiputra. Because the preceding translation supplied renders him as "Śāradvatiputra," consistency has been maintained here, but this identification should be verified against the Sanskrit or Pali parallel texts.

The term བཀྲེན་པ in Śāradvatiputra's angry speech literally means "beggar" or "pauper" and refers insultingly to the king; it has been rendered as "fat beggar" following the fuller Tibetan phrase གསུས་པོ་ཆེ ("big-bellied"), conveying the contemptuous tone.  The "group of six" refers to the notorious group of six monks (ṣaṭvargika bhikṣus) who appear throughout the Vinaya as exemplars of misconduct. This identity is implied by the Tibetan "drug sde" and would be recognized by any traditional listener.

The phrase rendered "those counted as jewels" translates "rin po cher smos pa," meaning things designated or reckoned as precious — a standard Vinaya category covering items of high value that are not strictly gemstones.

The passage shifts between the ongoing narrative and a direct quotation of the Blessed One's teaching on the ten dangers of visiting a royal palace; the text breaks off mid-enumeration at the fifth danger, which is where the supplied Tibetan ends.  The phrase rendered "before valuables or things reckoned as valuables have been collected" follows Vinaya technical usage for the pre-dawn period in which a royal palace's gates are officially secured; the precise referent of the valuables clause is a matter of Vinaya commentarial discussion, but the translation follows the plain sense of the Tibetan. The city name སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས (Campā) is a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Campā, a well-known city of ancient Aṅga; the identification is standard.  The name rendered "Moonlight" translates the Tibetan Zla 'od. "Elevated Body" translates Lus 'phags ma. "Tsugphudchen" is a Tibetan name meaning "one with a crest-tuft," likely standing for a Sanskrit name now uncertain. The king "Bimbasāra" is the standard identification for the Magadha ruler described here as Gzugs can snying po, a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Bimbisāra; "Bimbasāra" is used here to maintain consistency with the standard historical identification. "Varṣatūla" is a tentative reconstruction of the Brahmin's name Dbyar tshul; the exact Sanskrit original is uncertain. "Śraghoṣa" renders Sgra sgrogs, a city-name that appears in several Vinaya narrative contexts.  The epithet "resounding city" renders the Tibetan term for Śrāvastī here used as a descriptive phrase meaning "city of proclamation" or "city whose fame resounds," consistent with one standard etymology given for the name Śrāvastī in Indo-Tibetan commentarial tradition. The five qualities of the jewel armor are listed in standard formulaic fashion; "difficult to pierce" and "difficult to cut" are the most natural renderings of the pair, though some versions distinguish "sword-resistant" and "arrow-resistant" more specifically.  The brahmin's name renders the Tibetan dbyar tshul gyis, which appears to be a translation of the Sanskrit name Varṣatula or Varṣatulya. This reading is consistent with parallel versions of this narrative known from other sources, though the Tibetan here is grammatically ambiguous between a name and a descriptive phrase.  The two verses present some interpretive choices. The phrase rendered "a house of mud" translates a Tibetan term for a muddy or boggy dwelling, likely corresponding to a standard Sanskrit simile of an elephant stuck in mud straining to escape — emblematic of vigorous effort to break free from saṃsāra. The verse ending "make an end of suffering at last" renders the sense that this will be the practitioner's final birth.

The opening of this section names the king as Bimbisāra (Tibetan: Gzugs can snying po), consistent with the preceding passage's reference to "the king."  The phrase rendered "the fortunate charioteer" translates "skal ldan shing rta pa," which may refer to a specific geographical or narrative detail — possibly indicating a place name or a figure associated with the story's locale near the Śākya homeland. The exact referent is uncertain, but the literal rendering is retained since no clearer identification is available from the text alone.  The phrase rendered "twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty subsidiary views of self derived from the five aggregates taken in four ways each, a standard Abhidharma enumeration. This is a fixed doctrinal technical expression and is rendered literally as the text presents it.  The phrase rendered "fine-cushioned seats" translates a term for seats with pure or refined inner filling; the exact furnishing terminology is somewhat opaque but the general sense of comfortable, well-appointed seating is clear. The list of furnishings — thrones, smaller thrones, cushioned seats, footrests, footstools, and round cushions — follows what appears to be a standard formulaic inventory in Vinaya literature.  The names Rgyal and Karrgyal render Tibetan གྲོང་ཁྱེར་སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས་ན་ཁྱིམ་བདག་རྒྱལ་དང་སྐར་རྒྱལ. The city name སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས is likely a translation of a Sanskrit toponym meaning "resounding" or "loud-cried" — possibly Śroṇā or a similar name. The phrase འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཆ་ལྔ་པ ("the fivefold wheel of cyclic existence") is a somewhat unusual formulation. It likely refers to the five-spoked wheel of existence corresponding to the five classes of beings, or possibly the five aggregates as the basis of cyclic existence. The exact referent is not entirely certain from context alone.  The city referred to as Śrāvastī in the phrase "women dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī" is the same city rendered as "Śrāvastī" throughout, but it is paired here with Uttarayana's city as the destination of Rimā's teaching mission. The Tibetan "སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས་ན" literally means "in the place called Śrāvastī" or "in the city of the sound," which is a phonetic rendering of Śrāvastī. The term "གོར་བུ" (rendered "pillows") may refer to a round cushion or bolster; the exact furniture item is uncertain, but the general sense of bedding furnishings is clear.  The phrase rendered "former dwelling" translates a term meaning something like "one's customary or full physical state or appearance." The divine daughter's thought seems to be that she should not present herself in the divine form she now has while going to see the Blessed One, rather than appearing before him in her transformation — though the syntax is compressed and the exact sense is genuinely debated. The translation follows the more standard reading that she resolved to go without any pretense or formal ceremonial arrangement, approaching the Blessed One simply and directly.  The phrase rendered "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the standard Abhidharma enumeration of twenty varieties of the view of a self grounded in the five aggregates taken as "mine" or "I," which constitute the summit of afflicted view that stream-entry definitively uproots. The vajra of wisdom shattering these peaks is a conventional metaphor for the irreversible insight of the path of seeing.

The closing line "King Udayana reflected:" represents the passage breaking off mid-sentence in the source text as given; the reflection itself presumably continues in the next passage.  The bird name rendered "śaṅgaśateka" (Tibetan: shang shang te'u) is a semi-mythical Indian bird, sometimes identified with a type of partridge or a legendary singing bird; its precise species is uncertain in the sources, and it is kept here in a transliterated form rather than guessed at. The two minister names Heruka and Bhiruka are kept as they appear in the Tibetan, as they function here as personal names rather than the tantric deity Heruka.  The phrase rendered as "birth ripe for taming" (gdulbai skyes lta bu gzhan med) is a slightly compressed expression; it means there is no birth quite like that of one who is ready to be tamed or disciplined by the Tathāgata. The sense is that the Tathāgata's "birth" — or, in context, his arising in the world — finds its fullest expression in meeting those who are ripe for guidance.  The phrase rendered "covering over his bodily form" in the fourth line of the first verse translates a Tibetan expression meaning the Buddha's intention or will clothed or concealed Udrayana's royal form, replacing it with monastic appearance. This is a well-attested motif of the "Come, monk" ordination (ehi-bhikṣu) in which the ordinand is transformed instantaneously by the Tathāgata's blessing.

The epithet "Bimbisāra" (གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ) is the Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name and means literally "essence of form"; it is used consistently for the king of Magadha throughout this narrative.

The line rendered "tamed by something not yet attained, as a yoke-post tames an ox" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The sense is that an untamed person living off others' food is brought to taming through what he has not yet realized or achieved — the implication being that alms-seeking and monastic poverty are the instrument of taming, just as a tethering post brings an ox under control.  The line "these ten tens of a king" renders a metrically compact expression about the tenfold powers or qualities of a king. The precise referent is a formulaic enumeration that likely catalogues royal virtues in tens; the Tibetan as it stands is somewhat elliptical, and this rendering preserves the sense without over-specifying.

The deity described as "Śiva the Destroyer" renders a compound: the Tibetan "mun byed" (Darkness-Maker or Destroyer) is paired with "sgra ngan" (Ill-Omen or Evil Sound) and "skya seng bu" (the Grey Lion-Cub, a kenning for Śiva). This cluster of epithets in the context of Viṣṇu (Kṣitigarbha, here "Khyab 'jug," meaning Viṣṇu) points clearly to Śiva as the second deity named. The rendering consolidates these epithets into a readable epithet cluster.

The name "King Tufthead" renders "rgyal po gtsug pud can," which means literally "the king who has a topknot" or "tufted-head king." This is Udrayana's own adversarial king or successor figure within the narrative.  The verse "the one who does not kill such a man will be killed instead" is a deliberately ironic formulation placed in the mouths of the corrupt ministers to justify removing the righteous ones; the Tibetan phrasing is terse and slightly ambiguous but this reading is consistent with the narrative context.

The final sentence is left as an em-dash because the Tibetan breaks off mid-utterance, indicating the passage continues; this is not a translation uncertainty but a genuine textual break at the passage boundary.  The verse "let him be used to increase one's store of earth" renders a Tibetan idiom meaning effectively "bury him" or "let him become earth" — that is, let him be killed and his body returned to the ground. The phrase sa phung 'phel ba nyid du bya is somewhat idiomatic, and the rendering chosen conveys the sense without distorting the political-violence context.  The phrase rendered "Gora having been killed" reflects a proper name that appears in the preceding narrative context; the Tibetan here reads simply "he" but the referent is the individual whose execution was under discussion.

The verse about karma is a standard gāthā formula found across several Vinaya narrative cycles; the rendering follows the parallelism of the Tibetan closely.

The final four-line exchange between Uttarayana and the executioners is metrically and syntactically compressed; the phrase rendered "supreme and evident thing" translates a term meaning something like "the noble actual matter that is clearly examined," and the rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading. The last couplet spoken by the executioners appears to be a riddling hint that the king's demise — or some decisive event — is imminent.  The phrase "the fivefold wheel of saṃsāra, both its stirring and its stillness" renders a somewhat compressed Tibetan construction. The "fivefold wheel" likely refers to the five aggregates as the basis of cyclic existence; the commentarial tradition identifies this as insight into the five groups of existence as the mechanism of saṃsāra.

The verse spoken by Utraya upon attaining arhatship contains a deliberate irony: he has achieved inner liberation from all bondage yet remains subject to the external law of the king — a pointed contrast between spiritual freedom and worldly constraint that the text clearly intends.

The string of three knowledges, superknowledges, and discriminating awarenesses is a standard arhat attainment formula; the rendering follows the doctrinal sequence without elaboration, as the terms are transparent within their context.  The long list of hells names follows a recognizable Abhidharmic schema of the eight hot hells and the series of cold hells (the "cracked" hells named after lotus flowers). Some of the individual names in the cold-hell sequence are rendered by standard Tibetan equivalents; the mapping is conventional and unambiguous.

The two verses at the close are attributed in the tradition to the standard formulation that the Blessed One's smile-rays carry Dharma proclamations to the heavens; the second verse is a well-known gāthā also found in the Dhammapada (verse 327), here rendered in that spirit.  The royal epithet translated as "King Kṣudrapada" renders གཙུག་པུད་ཅན, literally "one with a topknot." This appears to be a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit royal name; the exact Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain, and "Kṣudrapada" is a provisional reconstruction based on context within the broader narrative tradition of this sūtra.

The phrase rendered "fingers white as conch shells" describes the Buddha's not displaying a smile by revealing teeth or fingers — the image is of the characteristic whiteness of his hands, a traditional mark of a great being.

The city name rendered here as Rājagraha represents གྲོང་ཁྱེར་སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས་ན་གནས་པ, which literally means "the city where sound resounds" — a Tibetan gloss-rendering of Rājagṛha rather than the standard transliteration used elsewhere in the canon. The translation normalizes this to Rājagraha for consistency.  The names Rgyal and Skar-rgyal appear to be Tibetan names of two individuals (possibly monks or religious figures whose stūpas stand in the narrative location). They are left transliterated as no Sanskrit equivalents are apparent from context. The names Heruka and Bhiruka here are used as personal names of ministers, not as tantric deity names; they are rendered as given.

The phrase rendered "eat the meat" more literally reads "take the piece of meat"; the sense is that the trained cats are being made to perform a circuit of the stūpa and then retreat to their holes as a staged deception, likely to discredit the stūpas or their associated figures. This is a genuine narrative crux but does not affect doctrinal content.  The epithet གཙུག་པུད་ཅན, rendered throughout as "Crest-Topknot," literally means "one who has a top-knot at the crown," a royal or divine mark; this is the king's name in the narrative.

The two arhats named རྒྱལ and སྐར་རྒྱལ are rendered as Jaya ("Victory") and Kārtikeyajaya ("Victory of Kārttikeya"), following the most natural Sanskrit reconstruction of these Tibetan names in this narrative context; the exact Sanskrit equivalents are not entirely certain from the Tibetan alone.

The phrase མཆོད་རྟེན་ན་འདུག refers to the cats residing at the stūpas built in honor of the two arhats, a detail that makes sense in context: shrines had apparently been erected for them after their nirvāṇa.  The epithet "Śikhin" for the king is here consistently rendered as "King Śikhin" following the preceding passage's rendering. The name appears in Tibetan as གཙུག་པུད་ཅན, meaning literally "one with a topknot" or "crested one," which is indeed Śikhin.

The phrase rendered "Śakra's goddess Gaśed and Gegtsen" translates ལྷ་ག་ཤེད་དུ་གཟིགས་མོ་དང་དགེ་མཚན. The names Gaśed and Gegtsen appear to be divine consorts or female deities visited by the king; these are transliterated as they appear without clear Sanskrit equivalents in context.

The final phrase, rendered "this parricide," translates ཕ་གསོད་པ་འདི — literally "this one who killed his father" — a serious accusation the corrupt ministers level obliquely at the king himself, which adds dramatic irony to the passage.  The phrase rendered "the Crest-Knot" translates a Tibetan term that appears to be a nickname or epithet for King Śikhin referring to his topknot or crest of hair. The passage is from the Vinayavibhaṅga, fascicle seventy-two, as indicated by the chapter marker in the source. The name Bhiruka is an unusual form; it may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name and is kept as found. The words "a rain of earth" on the seventh day are doctrinally significant: earth burying the city is the karmic consequence specifically tied to the crime of burying the ascetic under earth, making the sequence a carefully structured teaching on karma matching deed to fruit.  The corrupt ministers' speech about "seven heights of hailstones falling north" is somewhat obscure; the Tibetan reads literally "north of me, seven sky-heights of hail-rain fell," which appears to be a rhetorical dismissal designed to trivialize Kātyāyana's prophecy — implying the violent weather was somewhere else — while simultaneously hyping the miraculous rains. The translation renders the sense as best as can be determined from context.

The names Heruka and Bhiruka here are personal names of ministers, not the tantric deity Heruka; the text treats them as such throughout.  The phrase rendered "threshing ground" translates a term that in context clearly denotes a field or granary-floor where grain is stored or processed. The repeated "Bhiruka's Fort, Bhiruka's Fort" in the opening mirrors the Tibetan's doubled name, which appears to be a textual peculiarity preserving an emphatic formula or scribal convention.

The bowl-and-window episode is a divination-like omen: Mahā-Kātyāyana uses the alms bowl to gauge whether any meritorious domain remains in the city before deciding to depart. The half-filled bowl signals partial remaining merit; the instantly brim-full bowl signals complete exhaustion of merit, hence the city's imminent destruction.

The final sentence is somewhat compressed and syntactically difficult in the Tibetan; the translation renders the most coherent reading, namely that the man petitions the village assembly to enthrone his eldest son, pledging his own life as surety or collateral.  The phrase rendered "unleashed a fear-terror" translates a verb meaning to expel or drive out with force together with an implied sense of mass panic and destruction; the construction indicates the goddess caused a sudden terrifying event that resulted in mass death, which the context confirms.

The "tent-like canopy" rendering reflects the Tibetan term for an umbrella-shaped or tent-like covering, here used to describe how the bowl was enshrined. The commentarial tradition associates this with the origin of a particular festival name tied to the begging bowl.  The phrase rendered "the mountain of the view of the perishable collection twenty peaks high" refers to the twenty varieties of the satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of the transitory collection as a self or as belonging to a self), a standard Abhidharma enumeration: five aggregates each viewed in four ways as self or self's possession, yielding twenty sub-views. The image of the vajra of gnosis shattering this peak at stream-entry is a classical doctrinal illustration.

The place name "Bogkā" is a transliteration of the Tibetan བོག་ཀ; the location has not been securely identified in the Indic sources.  The name "Topknot King" renders གྱི་ཚུག་པུད་ཅན literally; the Tibetan is a descriptive epithet. The land name སིན་དུར is rendered as Sindhu, corresponding to the Sindh region. The phrase འོད་པ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉེར་བར་གནས་པ, rendered "abiding like a flame," is a standard karmic doctrine metaphor indicating that karma persists without being depleted until its conditions ripen, like a lamp flame that burns steadily.  The verse at the opening is a well-known canonical stanza on karma's inevitability, appearing in several Āgama and Vinaya contexts. The rendering follows its standard doctrinal sense.

The phrase rendered "fields of merit for the world" translates a term meaning those in whom the world should plant merit through offerings, a standard Buddhist technical concept.

The expression rendered "granting a straight departure by hand" is an idiom whose precise nuance is uncertain: it likely means the solitary buddha intended to receive him, guide him, or offer him a graceful way out of his situation, rather than any physical act. The phrase rendered "overpowered by the poison of jealousy" translates "dog sas non par gyur" — literally "overcome or oppressed by the poison of jealousy/envy." The verse embedded in the prose is a well-known canonical stanza on the inexorability of karma, widely cited across Pali and Sanskrit sources. The rendering preserves its doctrinal force without technical intrusion.  The name rendered "Suvarṇaśreṣṭhin" is a reconstruction: the Tibetan reads "Nor bzang" (literally "Good Wealth" or "Fine Wealth"), but the subsequent narrative — where the king detects gold by sonic resonance and the man acquires the epithet "Ghoṣavān" (Tibetan gdangs can, "resonant one") — makes clear that the underlying Sanskrit name must relate to gold (suvarṇa) and a merchant title (śreṣṭhin). The phrase rendered "terrorize him" or "threaten him with fear" translates a term meaning to intimidate or frighten, without actually carrying out the execution — which sets up the narrative turn that follows. The passage mentions "blue-green direction" in connection with a tree: the Tibetan gsing ma sngon po refers to a direction marked by a blue or green color, likely indicating the eastern or northern quarter in traditional Indian cosmological color-direction symbolism. The name Anāthapiṇḍada, meaning "giver of food to the destitute," is a well-known epithet of the great lay patron Sudatta of Śrāvastī. The term rendered "restoration ceremony with its eight limbs" is the eightfold poṣadha (uposatha) observance, a lay precept ceremony held on lunar observance days, here specifically the aṣṭāṅgaśīla form. The phrase rendered "comes accompanied by a birth" translates a grammatically compressed passage indicating that Anāthapiṇḍada arrives with a particular auspicious birth-quality or rebirth-connection relevant to the Tathāgata's dispensation. The doctrinal sense is that his capacity for being tamed and his karmic connection to the Buddha is a uniquely fitting one, like that of a principal disciple. The passage ends mid-sentence, describing the miraculous transformation of the five hundred seers into monks at the moment of ordination by the Blessed One's utterance — a standard literary motif in Vinaya narratives.  The name rendered as Dāṅgcan is a transliteration of the Tibetan གདངས་ཅན; the Sanskrit equivalent is not given in the text. The phrase རྫས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་བྱ་བའི་གཞི ("bases of meritorious acts not grounded in material things") is the counterpart to the seven material bases discussed earlier; the text is now enumerating a second set of seven merit-bases that do not require physical offerings but arise from mental acts such as hearing news of the Buddha or his disciples with joy. The repeated pattern of the Blessed One emerging and re-entering at the yakṣa's command is a standard narrative device in Vinaya and avadāna literature illustrating both the taming of a powerful being and the Buddha's deliberate pedagogical use of compliance to crush the yakṣa's pride — this is made explicit in the text with the phrase "for the sake of decisively subduing arrogance and pride."  The phrase rendered "truthful restraint" translates a compound that could be read as "the abandonment of truth and restraint" or "the giving up of untruthfulness and lack of restraint," depending on parsing. In context — the final challenge question to other teachers — the most natural doctrinal reading is that the Blessed One is asserting no other Dharma exists beyond the giving up of what opposes truth and restraint, i.e., beyond honest, disciplined conduct. This reading is adopted here.

The phrase སྔོ་བསངས་ཅན་མཐོང་བར་གྱུར་ན in the first paragraph is slightly elliptical: the full sense is that Nīlapīta, who has not yet seen the truths (i.e., not yet attained the path of seeing), might come to a direct vision through the Blessed One's presence, but without proper preparation he would not become a fit vessel. The phrase rendered "the fever of the heart" translates "སྙིང་གི་རིམས་ནད་བསལ་གྱུར་པ," literally "one for whom the disease-fever of the heart has been dispelled." The term "Śyāmāvat" renders the Tibetan "སྔོ་བསངས་ཅན" (literally "one who has a blue-green or dark complexion"), used as a personal name for the woman who had sought out the herdsman. The phrase "heaven free from torment" renders "མི་གདུང་བའི་ལྷ་རིས," corresponding to the Avṛha heaven, one of the five pure abodes within the form realm. The divine son's reasoning — that he should not approach the Blessed One while still "dwelling in his celestial abode" — reflects a convention in Vinaya narrative that devas who visit the Buddha appear in a transformed or humbled form, not in full divine splendor. The contrast drawn here is between approach with and without reliance on his celestial dwelling, which may also carry the nuance of arriving without the pomp of divine retinue and ornamentation.  The phrase rendered as "the mark of sitting" translates a term meaning a defining characteristic or sign of being physically seated, that is, the intentional mental representation of a seated physical posture. This appears to be a technical instruction enabling the divine being, who had merged into the earth, to reconstitute a conventionally perceptible, grounded bodily presence. The precise doctrinal background of this practice of manifesting a "coarse body" with "perception of solidity" is unusual; it likely reflects an early Abhidharma or proto-Abhidharma understanding of how devas can assume material form. The phrase rendered "the twenty peaks of the mountain of views that constitute the perishable collection" translates འཇིགས་ཚོགས་ལ་ལྟ་བའི་རིའི་རྩེ་མོ་ཉི་ཤུ: the view of the perishable collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root afflictive view identifying a self among the five aggregates, traditionally analyzed into twenty sub-views — five aggregates, each grasped in four ways as self. Shattering these at stream-entry is standard Abhidharma and sūtra doctrine.  The phrase rendered as "ridiculously tall headboards" translates a term literally meaning "extremely tall ya-ga," where ya-ga refers to a headboard or upper frame of a bed. The comedic register of the group of six monks' retort is intentional and reflected in the text.

The passage "as before" and "and so forth as before" are formulaic Vinaya abbreviations indicating that the standard narrative procedure — convening the assembly, the question of whether the act was committed, the formal censure, and the promulgation of a rule — is to be understood as having occurred in full, following the established template earlier in the text. The verse is extremely compressed and the translation renders each term according to its established Vinaya technical meaning: "directly" refers to settling face-to-face; "by recollection" refers to the declaration of a clear memory of innocence; "without intoxication" refers to the procedure of declaring non-liability on grounds of mental incapacity at the time of the act; "the many" refers to decision by majority; "essential nature" refers to investigation of the factual nature of the offense; "strewn grass" is the procedure of mutual forgiveness before the assembly, likened to grass being scattered; and "acknowledgment" refers to the formal confession procedure.
